Ulaanbaatar to introduce BYD’s Sky Shuttle electric transit system

Ulaanbaatar to introduce BYD’s Sky Shuttle electric transit system
A Memorandum of Understanding has been signed with "BYD Company Limited" to introduce the "Sky Shuttle" electric transit system to Ulaanbaatar’s public transportation network, MONTSAME reports.
Under the preliminary agreement, the project's feasibility study will be finalized by December, with construction work set to begin in March 2027.
Purevdagva Byaruuzana, Governor of the Capital City and Mayor of Ulaanbaatar, stated, "We are firmly committed to initiating BYD Group's 'Sky Shuttle' project as a top priority in 2027. Pursuant to the Governor's decree, a working group covering three main operational directions with BYD Group has been established, led by my senior advisor, Batbayasgalan J. The engineering and design work will be completed by December 5 this year. We aim to start construction in March 2027 and conduct trial operations of the battery-powered public transit system by November of the same year. The project will be implemented either through a competitive selection process or via a public-private partnership (PPP) model."
The "Sky Shuttle," a novel public transit solution, operates on electric batteries along dedicated elevated tracks.
Officials highlighted that this system will enable reliable public transit operations unimpeded by road traffic congestion. "BYD Company Limited" is a global leader in electric vehicles, battery technology, and renewable energy, having sold over 17 million electric vehicles worldwide.
In June 2026, BYD initiated a project to construct 20,000 ultra-fast charging stations capable of fully charging electric vehicles in nine minutes across China, with 7,000 stations completed to date. The "Sky Shuttle" system, powered by BYD's proprietary Blade Battery technology, is currently operational across 10 cities in China as well as in São Paulo, Brazil.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh would pay a state visit to Germany from October 19 to 22 at the invitation of German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier.

Italy probes Israel’s Katz over abuse, sexual assault of flotilla activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:48:54 UTC
07:48:54 KST

Italy probes Israel’s Katz over abuse, sexual assault of flotilla activists
Rome prosecutors also name 12 senior military, police and prison officials over alleged abuse of detained activists.
Italian prosecutors have placed Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and 12 senior military, police and prison officials under investigation over the treatment of activists detained on Gaza-bound solidarity boats, widening a probe that had centred on far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The Rome prosecutors’ office said on Friday that the case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of activist boats heading towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026.
It opened the investigation after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions last year and this year.
Those named as suspects include Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir.
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission in 2025 reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism. Those on the second mission in 2026 reported harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark and the use of tasers and rubber bullets, the statement said.
The activists reported at least 15 cases of sexual assault, including rape.
Luca Poggi, an Italian economist who was detained, told Reuters news agency in May: “We were stripped, thrown to the ground, kicked.”
Ben-Gvir dismissed news of the investigation in June, saying he would “continue to stand proudly alongside” Israeli soldiers.
Flotilla organisers say they aim to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza by delivering humanitarian aid.
What prompted the case
The first Global Sumud Flotilla set sail from Barcelona in September 2025 with 42 boats and 462 activists. Israeli forces intercepted it in international waters in early October that year, with hundreds detained and later deported.
The second mission left Barcelona in April 2026. Israeli forces began intercepting its vessels near the southern Greek island of Crete on April 30, and by May 19 had detained about 430 people on some 50 ships in international waters, with the final interceptions taking place off Cyprus.
Ben-Gvir later posted a video showing him taunting activists who were cable-tied and kneeling at a makeshift prison at the port of Ashdod while Israel’s national anthem played.
Prosecutors said they sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility, but did not say whether Israel had responded.
They also held talks at Eurojust, the EU’s judicial cooperation agency, as other similar investigations are under way in other European countries.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
If the investigation finds the charges warranted, prosecutors could formally request a trial.

Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:47:04 UTC
07:47:04 KST

Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Ukraine could reduce mobilization exemptions for employees of companies deemed critical to the country, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky has said, arguing that employers are exploiting the current system.
The country declared mobilization shortly after the escalation of the conflict with Russia in February 2022, barring most military-age men from leaving the country.
However, approximately 1.4 million Ukrainians currently hold employment-based exemptions from military service, according to Economy Minister Aleksandr Kravchenko.
Speaking during a Q&A session in the Ukrainian parliament on Friday, Koretsky said the government is considering stripping critical-sector employers of the right to exempt 100% of their staff. He cited cases in which companies had significantly expanded their workforces, with all employees automatically shielded from conscription.
“Unfortunately, there are many abuses, and additional exemptions continue to be granted every month,” Koretsky said.
“If you have a 100% exemption, it means you can expand your workforce indefinitely and exempt people from mobilization, regardless of whether they actually work as repair technicians, energy workers or in other roles. Unfortunately, this practice has already become widespread,” he added.
Koretsky said some companies had received blanket exemptions despite not meeting the criteria for being classified as critical. As an example, he cited an unnamed contractor for Ukrenergo, the national power grid operator. “When we looked into the details, it turned out that only 20 out of 100 employees were actually working for Ukrenergo. Yet all 100 were exempted,” Koretsky said.
The prime minister called for audits to determine how many employees at a given company perform tasks essential to its operations and the country’s needs. He added that stricter criteria could be applied to businesses as a whole, with only those supporting Ukraine’s defense capabilities and other essential state functions qualifying as critical.
Earlier this week, opposition MP Yaroslav Zhelezhnyak published what he claimed was a draft of the proposed changes, reducing exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Multiple lawmakers and businesses have warned that such measures would exacerbate existing staffing shortages in critical industries.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian outlet Strana UA reported on Thursday, citing sources, that relations between Koretsky and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had deteriorated. The outlet claimed that Zelensky could dismiss Koretsky in the spring of 2027 and blame him for government failures during the winter months.
Koretsky, who was appointed prime minister in a government reshuffle in July, has been linked by local media to disgraced businessman and former close Zelensky associate Timur Mindich, who fled to Israel amid an investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme involving state nuclear power operator Energoatom.
According to Strana UA, Koretsky has defied Zelensky’s expectations by developing political ambitions, disregarding some of his requests and communicating directly with European partners without Zelensky’s involvement.
Amid mounting battlefield losses and desertions, Ukraine’s conscription drive has been marred by incidents of draft officers forcibly detaining military-age men on the streets, sparking spontaneous protests, clashes and outrage on social media.
While Kiev does not regularly publish figures on its battlefield losses, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed last month that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month. Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that Ukrainian casualties reached 500,000 in 2025 alone.

Sky closed over Moscow multiple nights in row as Ukraine resumes refinery strikes

Sky closed over Moscow multiple nights in row as Ukraine resumes refinery strikes
Flights over the city of Moscow were restricted for the sixth night in a row on Oct. 16-17, according to flight-tracking data and updates from Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya).
The latest restrictions coincide with President Volodymyr Zelensky's announcement on Oct. 15 that Ukraine would no longer hold back from attacking Russian oil refineries. That same night, flights were grounded in both Moscow and St. Petersburg.
Rosaviatsiya announced late in the evening of Oct. 16 that three of Moscow's four major airports — Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovksy — were suspending operations due to security risks.
"Temporary restrictions have been introduced on the arrival and departure of aircraft," the agency said. "These restrictions are necessary to ensure flight safety."
Earlier in the day, Russia's Transportation Ministry said that civil aviation operations in Moscow Oblast had been placed under "special monitoring" by the ministry and Rosaviatsiya. The previous evening, Rosaviatsiya announced that flights were grounded at all four of Moscow's airports as well as at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg.
While the agency did not at first announce restrictions at Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport the night of Oct. 16-17, independent flight-tracking data indicated that the facility was also experiencing disruptions and delays.
According to aviation monitor Flightradar24, Sheremetyevo Airport is currently the fifth-most disrupted airport in the world and is experiencing "major problems."
Rosaviatsiya then announced temporary restrictions at Sheremetyevo Airport at around 2 a.m. local time.
Meanwhile, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that nearly 30 drones bound for the capital have been intercepted as of 1:30 a.m. local time on Oct. 17.
The latest closure marks the sixth consecutive night that restrictions have been imposed on air travel over Moscow, leading to long passenger queues and hundreds of flight delays. Russia's Transportation Ministry said it was deploying additional staff to the capital's airports in response to the situation.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Ukraine fired nearly 500 drones at the region overnight on Oct. 13-15, all of which he said were intercepted by Russian air defense units. The following night, he claimed nearly 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Moscow.
Ukraine had refrained from strikes on Russia's refineries for three days to accommodate demands from U.S. President Donald Trump, who unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow.
Trump has claimed that Ukraine's refinery strikes are driving up oil and diesel prices worldwide, despite evidence that the U.S. war in Iran is in fact the primary culprit.
While Zelensky attempted to accommodate Trump — who threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine and struck a deal with Russian President Donald Trump to buy diesel from Moscow — Russia hammered Ukrainian cities and energy infastructure in large-scale attacks.
On Oct. 15, Zelensky said Ukraine's refinery attack pause was over.
"We're done," he said.

Fighting restricts access to maternal health services in Yemen's Taiz: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:43:06 CST
07:43:06 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Escalating hostilities in Yemen have cut access to Taiz City, preventing women and girls from receiving essential maternal care, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Friday.
More than 147,000 women and girls of childbearing age in Taiz have been cut off from life-saving care. Only five of the city's 27 emergency maternal and newborn care hospitals are partially functioning, said OCHA, citing the UN Population Fund.
More than 13,000 pregnant women in the city cannot access maternal health services, including 1,500 due to give birth in the next two weeks, with at least 500 of them expected to require emergency obstetric care.
Nearly three-quarters of services that protect women and girls from violence across Taiz governorate have been suspended, including safe spaces and shelters. Dignity kits cannot reach Taiz City, leaving displaced women and girls even more vulnerable to exploitation and violence, OCHA said.
The office reiterated its call on all parties to protect civilians and to allow "safe, rapid and unimpeded" humanitarian access to reach people in need. ■

China willing to deepen cooperation with Croatia: Chinese FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:42:54 CST
07:42:54 KST

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, holds talks with Croatian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Gordan Grlic Radman in Zagreb, Croatia, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
ZAGREB, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- China is willing to work with Croatia to achieve greater outcomes in bilateral cooperation, said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi when holding talks with Croatian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Gordan Grlic Radman here on Friday.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that Croatia, an important stop on the ancient Silk Road, has once fostered mutual learning between Eastern and Western civilizations. This marks the first visit to Croatia by a Chinese foreign minister in 33 years, and serves as a reciprocal visit following Radman's trip to China last year.
The China-Croatia relations have developed in a mature and steady manner over the years, setting an example for the relations between countries of different sizes, Wang said.
The success of bilateral relations rests on equality, mutual respect and trust, win-win cooperation and friendly exchanges between the two peoples, Wang said, adding that these ties inject more certainty and stability into a complex and volatile international landscape.
China is willing to work with Croatia to take next year's 35th anniversary of establishing diplomatic relations as an opportunity to draw on experience and chart a course for stronger ties over the next 35 years, Wang said, calling on the two sides to work together for following high-level exchanges and bring bilateral ties to a new high.
Wang stressed that China respects Croatia's sovereignty and territorial integrity and supports its constructive role in international and regional affairs. China also appreciates Croatia's longstanding commitment to the one-China policy, which has strengthened the political foundation of bilateral relations and opened up broad prospects for cooperation, he added.
Wang said China is ready to work with Croatia to leverage "three major engines" to drive further progress in bilateral cooperation. First, at the bilateral level, the two sides should focus on infrastructure and renewable energy as key areas, while expanding cooperation into new sectors such as nuclear energy, ports, telecommunications, and artificial intelligence. Second, at the regional level, China-Croatia cooperation can be advanced through the broader framework of China-EU (the European Union) cooperation, as the Peljesac Bridge serves as an example of successful trilateral cooperation between China, the EU, and Croatia. Third, at the sub-regional level, the two sides should promote cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs). Croatia has been a builder, contributor, and beneficiary of this cooperation mechanism. China stands ready to work with CEECs to plan the next phase of engagement and deliver more tangible results.
Emphasizing that China and the EU share extensive common interests, Wang said that both sides advocate multilateralism, uphold the central and leading role of the United Nations and are committed to resolving international and regional disputes through political dialogues. China and Europe also share common ground on global issues such as climate change, he added.
Recent progress at the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism has shown that bilateral differences can be resolved through dialogues on an equal footing, he said.
China is willing to deepen its comprehensive strategic partnership with the EU and hopes that Croatia, as an EU member, will play a constructive role in advancing China-EU relations, Wang said.
Radman said that Croatia attaches great importance to its relations with China and respects China's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Croatia has consistently adhered to the one-China policy and will continue to uphold it firmly, neither participating in nor supporting any "Taiwan independence" activities, he added.
Croatia is willing to take the 35th anniversary of establishing diplomatic relations as an opportunity to elevate bilateral ties, and will work to expand cooperation with China in areas such as transportation and logistics, renewable energy and automobile manufacturing, Radman said.
He added that China has played an important role in maintaining world peace and stability. As key partners, the EU and China share responsibility to jointly safeguard international order and promote global security and development.
Croatia values the cooperation framework between CEECs and China, Radman said. He thanked China for organizing activities under the framework and expressed hope that further cooperation would yield more results and bring greater benefits to the peoples of both sides.
During their talks, Radman also shared his views on the situation in the Western Balkans. Wang said that Croatia is an important country in the region, adding that China does not interfere in the internal affairs of Balkan countries and respects the choices made by their peoples.
China is willing to be a friend and partner of these countries and hopes they will foster harmonious relations and work together to build a shared future, Wang said. ■

World Insights: EU summit ends with mounting bills, unresolved divisions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:42:43 CST
07:42:43 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The two-day European Union (EU) summit concluded in Brussels on Friday without a breakthrough on the bloc's long-term budget, as rising security commitments and soaring energy costs exposed a growing gap between Europe's ambitions and its ability to deliver.
Behind the summit's limited progress lay three pressing challenges: a budget difficult to agree upon, a growing security bill complicated by tensions with Washington, and an energy crisis testing Europe's economic resilience.
TOUGH BUDGET NEGOTIATIONS
The European Commission has proposed a nearly 2-trillion-euro (2.24 trillion U.S. dollars) budget for 2028-2034, seeking to increase investment in competitiveness, defense and technology.
The Irish presidency's latest compromise would reduce the Commission's proposal by around 141 billion euros (158 billion dollars), yet the revised plan has drawn resistance from opposing camps.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that the compromise would cut budgetary flexibility by half, leaving 99.5 percent of funds predetermined.
"This proposal puts us in a straitjacket," she said.
According to Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, six fiscally conservative countries led by Germany favor a smaller budget, while 17 "Friends of Cohesion," including Italy and Spain, seek to protect agricultural subsidies and regional development funds.
Brussels-based think tank Bruegel argued that both camps supported greater investment in common European priorities but placed national interests first.
It said that the Irish plan as the "worst possible compromise," warning that it could leave emerging priorities, including competitiveness and defense, severely underfunded while protecting traditional spending.
Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, has likewise argued that Europe's expanding investment needs cannot realistically be financed through national budgets alone, calling for innovative financing arrangements, including new common borrowing.
The disagreements leave European Council President Antonio Costa facing a difficult task as he seeks a budget agreement by year-end.
GROWING SECURITY BILLS
Europe's fiscal pressures are compounded by a growing security bill and differences with Washington over Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said at the summit that the war would cost Ukraine 155 billion euros (173 billion dollars) in 2027 and requested at least another 70 billion euros (78 billion dollars) in assistance.
The EU has already agreed on a 90-billion-euro (100 billion dollars) loan covering 2026-2027. However, Ukraine's additional financing needs remained under assessment, with European leaders seeking further input from the Commission and international financial institutions.
In its final conclusions, the European Council explicitly expressed regret over the U.S. decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel, a move also criticized by Zelensky.
Meanwhile, recent restrictions on the U.S.-controlled Starshield satellite communications service disrupted Ukrainian military operations, exposing another vulnerability in Europe's security capabilities.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can't replace this capability," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.
Analysts noted that this episode highlights Europe's reliance on critical U.S. military technologies even as transatlantic differences over Ukraine become more pronounced.
For Europe, the dilemma is increasingly apparent: greater security responsibilities require additional resources, while some of the capabilities underpinning those commitments remain beyond its immediate control.
SOARING ENERGY COSTS
Energy has become another source of financial strain. According to von der Leyen, the Middle East conflict has added 106 billion euros (119 billion dollars) to the EU's fossil fuel import bill, highlighting Europe's vulnerability to external energy shocks.
The International Energy Agency is accelerating the release of emergency oil stocks, including diesel, with plans to bring another 100 million barrels to the market over four months, while Brussels is pursuing temporary support for energy-intensive industries and measures to improve refining capacity.
Yet the summit exposed divisions over how far climate policies should be adjusted to ease immediate costs.
Italy, Greece and the four Visegrad countries pushed to postpone the EU's second emissions trading system, ETS2, until 2030, arguing that carbon pricing would impose further burdens on households and businesses.
However, Nordic countries resisted, concerned that weakening the system would undermine investment certainty and longer-term climate objectives.
The summit ended without an agreement on further postponement. Leaders instead requested an updated assessment of ETS2's design, impact and safeguards.
Researchers at the European Council on Foreign Relations argued that Europe's green transition was facing growing political resistance shaped by economic insecurity, competing national interests and the distribution of costs.
The dispute reflects a difficult choice: easing today's energy pressures could weaken incentives for long-term investment, while maintaining ambitious climate policies risks adding to the burden on businesses and households.
For European leaders, agreeing on common goals remains easier than deciding who should bear the costs of achieving them. ■

Missiles strike Yemen's Aden, explosions rock city
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:42:30 CST
07:42:30 KST

ADEN, Yemen, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Three ballistic missiles struck the southern Yemeni port city of Aden on Friday night, triggering powerful explosions across the city, a local security official and residents told Xinhua.
Aden's security administration said in a statement posted on social media platform X that two missiles launched by the Houthi group landed inside the grounds of Aden International Airport, with preliminary information indicating no casualties.
The statement said the missile strikes posed a serious threat to civilian facilities and air traffic, particularly with international flights operating and passengers present in departure and arrival halls.
Shortly after the attack, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV cited a military leader within the group as saying that the group had targeted "the headquarters of Saudi forces and weapons depots" at Badr military camp near Aden International Airport.
A local security official earlier told Xinhua that two missiles had landed near Aden International Airport, while a third struck a military base near the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces in Al Buraiqa district in western Aden.
Three powerful explosions rocked the city during the attack, a Xinhua reporter on the ground and local residents said. Ambulances were seen heading toward the affected areas.
Friday's attack came a day after missiles struck the Al-Ma'ashiq Presidential Palace compound in Aden, the temporary seat of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, killing five people and wounding 16 others, according to the government.
A local security official told Xinhua Thursday that five missiles hit the palace compound, while another targeted the headquarters of the Saudi-led coalition forces. The Houthi group later claimed responsibility for the attack, saying it had targeted a "Saudi military operations headquarters" inside the presidential palace compound.
The repeated attacks come amid an escalating exchange of strikes between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with the group launching missiles and drones deep into the kingdom and targeting Yemeni government forces backed by the coalition.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, forcing the government out of the capital. ■

07:42:13 KST

RIGA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Latvia's Central Election Commission on Friday officially confirmed the results of the 15th parliamentary election and the list of 100 newly elected lawmakers, the Latvian news agency LETA reported.
The United List, a political alliance that includes incumbent Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, emerged as the largest force in parliament with 41 seats, falling short of an outright majority.
The United List was followed by Latvia First with 17 and the Sovereign Power/Alliance of Young Latvians with 15. The National Alliance and the Progressives each won 10 seats, while New Unity took seven.
Voter turnout stood at 51.79 percent, with approximately 807,000 people casting their ballots.
With no party or alliance securing a parliamentary majority, the formation of the next government will depend on coalition negotiations, in which the United List is expected to play a pivotal role.
Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics announced on Oct. 6 that he supported Kulbergs in leading talks on forming the next government.
Latvia held its parliamentary election on Oct. 3, with 1,428 candidates from 14 parties and political alliances competing for 100 parliamentary seats. Under the country's proportional representation system, parties and alliances must win at least 5 percent of the vote to enter parliament.
The newly elected parliament is scheduled to convene for its first sitting on Nov. 3, when it will begin its term. ■

Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:30:00 UTC
07:30:00 KST

Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
October 17, 2026
Brazil has recorded the lowest level of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in nearly 40 years.
According to data released by the Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday, between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometers (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared, the lowest level witnessed since records began in 1988.
The numbers showed a nearly 42% decrease from last year's figure of 5,731 square kilometers.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and one of its most biodiverse ecosystems, most of which lies in Brazil.
It also extends into parts of Peru, Colombia and other South American countries. Deforestation and the illegal exploitation of resources have been pushing it closer to a climate tipping point.
Drop hailed as 'historic achievement'
"It's an absolutely stratospheric drop...it's like a dream," said Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco at a press conference in the capital, Brasilia.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a post on X.
"The figures released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
"They put Brazil at the forefront of the forest protection agenda and show the world that, with political will, it is possible to stop the chainsaws and curb greenhouse gas emissions," Astrini said on his organization's website.
Observatorio do Clima said the figures were the result of a "sustained commitment" to protecting the environment by the government, which introduced greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.
The news comes ahead of the October 25 runoff election between Lula and conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro with the two running neck and neck according to polls.

Saudi Civil Defense authorities earlier issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.
Fighting between the Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.
The Yemen conflict has become another front in the wider regional war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and forced the internationally recognised government south.
A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited, targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure. In recent days, the group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of Yemen, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.

Teacher tackled and fought Oregon school shooter
BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 - A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police said on Friday.
A day into their investigation of the latest U.S. school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail Elementary School where three school children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, but told a press conference she threw her cell phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said.
As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.
Officials said the parent had followed the shooter into the school, upon witnessing him firing a shotgun from just outside campus. By the time police arrived within three minutes of receiving their first call, the shooter was dead, police said.
In the meantime the 16-year-old assailant, who had shot through locked glass doors to enter campus, had killed four people and wounded two others.
Krantz, speaking to the heroism shown by the teacher who threw herself onto the suspect and the parent who shot him, said, "I don't think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage. When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that."
He said that the bystander's actions "undoubtedly saved people," and "the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism."
Krantz identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, who was armed with 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him.
The parent who killed the shooter was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, his mother told the New York Times. She identified him as the father of two girls who attend the school, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.
"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said. "Kaylub's family, including his two daughters who attend the school, respectfully asks for privacy during this difficult time, and will not be participating in interviews at this time."
Residents of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles just outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.
"Thank God for that father. He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today. We wish him well, and thank God for him," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears.
Brooke Olsen, the mother of a kindergartener who was safely reunited with her family after the shooting, also expressed gratitude for the man who stopped the shooter.
"This is an extremely painful day of grief for everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families, and we have to think about what's next for safety measures."
Such school shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debates over gun laws in a country where a right to "keep and bear Arms" is protected under the Constitution's Second Amendment.
Some of the deadliest school attacks in the US include those at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018 and Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022. REUTERS

Türkiye’s export value per kilogram surges as high-tech sectors boost revenue: Trade minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:17:46 UTC
07:17:46 KST

Ugur Aslanhan and Emir Yildirim
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
Türkiye’s average export unit value rose to $1.73 per kilogram as of September, the Turkish trade minister said during the second day of the Türkiye Innovation Week (TIW) in Istanbul.
The 13th edition of one of Türkiye’s most comprehensive innovation gatherings began Thursday and continued on Friday, organized by the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TIM) under the theme “Humanity 6.0.” Anadolu is its global communications partner.
Trade Minister Omer Bolat said Türkiye’s average export unit value, excluding high-tonnage, low-value items like cement and marble, hit $2.11 per kilogram.
“This rate in the defense industry reached $61.5 per kilogram, or 39 times the average, while the rate in the pharmaceutical sector hit $25, the ship and yacht sector $14, and in the auto sector $9 per kilogram,” he said. “Turkish ready-to-wear exports reached a per-kilogram value ranging from $80-100 -- all these figures show how innovation and value-added contributions rose among exports.”
Bolat stated that Türkiye entered a new era that is focused on research and development (R&D), innovation, branding, design and added value.
“This year’s event is centered on our goal for humans to leverage technology and work within a productive system, as here we have gathered to seek answers to how humans will take advantage of artificial intelligence (AI) systems and how wealth generated by AI gains will be shared more fairly,” he said, noting that AI is projected to drive global trade by 40% by 2040 with its massive economic potential.
“The share of medium-high and high-tech exports among total exports was 30.4% in 2002, making up $10 billion, but this figure reached $112 billion by the end of 2025, grabbing a share of 43.7% among total exports. We aim to boost our exports in labor-intensive products where our country has a competitive edge, while increasing exports of other products with high added value,” he said.
Bolat noted that the year-end target for goods and services exports was set at $410 billion, and that, as of September, the figure had already reached $409 billion on an annual basis.
He stated that Türkiye significantly increased its research and development (R&D) spending, patent applications and academic capacity, such as the growth in technoparks, qualified production zones, and industrial and design centers, in the last 23 years, all of which contributed to Türkiye’s rising high-quality exports.
The minister emphasized that Türkiye maintained economic stability despite regional conflicts, rising trade protectionism, surging commodity prices, and a domestic counterterrorism campaign, ensuring continued growth for 16 years, with national income reaching $1.7 trillion and $18,300 per capita.
He noted that Turkish exports rose 5.2% year-on-year in September, reaching $283.7 billion, exceeding the year-end target.
“We allocated a $30 billion fund to investments to develop the country’s technology and value-added production through tax incentives, grants, and low-cost financing,” he said, referring to the HIT-30 (High-Technology Investment Program) and the investment- and commitment-based advance credit scheme.

M9.9 quake warning issued by mistake in Japan, disrupting trains

FIFA orders partial stadium closure for Spain over anti-Muslim chants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:15:21 UTC
07:15:21 KST

Dilara Hamit
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
FIFA has ordered Spain to partially close its stadium for its next home friendly after supporters directed anti-Muslim chants during a match against Egypt, the football governing body said.
FIFA said in its decision that at least 15% of the available seats must remain closed, primarily in the stands behind the goals.
The world football governing body also fined the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) $20,000.
Subject to FIFA's approval, the federation may allocate the affected seats to community or special-interest groups, including families, students and anti-discrimination organizations.
Any proposed plan must include visible anti-discrimination measures and be submitted to FIFA at least 15 days before the match.
The sanction stems from Spain's goalless friendly against Egypt on March 31 at the RCDE Stadium in Barcelona.
During the first half and shortly after the second half began, a group of Spanish supporters resorted to discriminatory chants targeting Muslims.
An anti-discrimination warning appeared on the stadium screen, while an announcement urged supporters to stop the chants.
The warning was repeated early in the second half, prompting whistles from some sections of the crowd.
FIFA subsequently opened disciplinary proceedings over what it described as Islamophobic and xenophobic conduct.
The RFEF argued that the chant did not constitute discrimination and that the word "Muslim" was not inherently insulting.
FIFA's Disciplinary Committee rejected the argument, finding that words not offensive in isolation could become discriminatory when used to ridicule or demean a religious identity.
The committee said the federation could not "persuasively maintain both that the chant was entirely harmless and that it warranted activation of anti-discrimination measures."
FIFA acknowledged that Spanish officials had introduced preventive measures, cooperated with match authorities, publicly condemned the incident and sought to identify those involved.
Following the match, the RFEF denounced the chants.
Spain coach Luis de la Fuente described the incident as "intolerable," saying violent individuals were using football as a platform.
Spanish winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, also condemned the chants, saying that using religion as a taunt was disrespectful and racist.
The Egyptian Football Association called the chants a "repugnant act of racism," stressing that the conduct of a small group would not damage relations between the two national federations.
The sanction applies only to Spain's next home friendly, not a competitive fixture.
Its implementation could be delayed depending on Spain's Nations League and Euro 2028 qualifying schedule.

Colombia deepens ties with Israel, considers Holocaust alliance membership after embassy opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:35 UTC
07:12:35 KST

As Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar affixed a mezuzah to the entrance of Colombia’s new embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday, the two countries were exploring another step in their rapidly improving relationship. Colombia is considering applying to join the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA), Israeli Ambassador to Colombia Vivian Aisen revealed to The Media Line.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Aisen said Sa’ar and Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar discussed the possibility during Bula’s visit to Jerusalem. Colombia adopted the IHRA working definition of antisemitism in June 2022, but it is not currently a member or observer country. No formal application has been announced.
The alliance promotes Holocaust education, remembrance, and research. Countries seeking full membership must first obtain observer status and then proceed through an intermediate liaison stage.
Colombia inaugurated its Jerusalem embassy on October 14, becoming the 10th country with an embassy in the city, according to Israel’s Foreign Ministry, and the fourth Latin American country to do so, following Guatemala, Honduras, and Paraguay.
The opening was the most visible part of a broader diplomatic reversal under Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose government has restored full relations with Israel, lifted reciprocal visa requirements, removed restrictions on coal exports, and renewed implementation of the countries’ free trade agreement.
At a Foreign Ministry reception later Wednesday, attended by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Bula announced that Colombia had formally requested to withdraw from the Hague Group, a coalition established to coordinate diplomatic and legal measures against Israel over the war in Gaza. He also announced plans for a national initiative to combat antisemitism.
Colombia's Jerusalem embassy signals diplomatic reversal
The embassy opening fulfilled a promise made before de la Espriella’s election. Sa’ar said the two met in Buenos Aires in November 2025, when the future president pledged to relocate Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem if elected.
“He made a promise, and he kept it,” Sa’ar said. “Just two months after he took office, we inaugurated the Embassy of Colombia in Jerusalem.”
The embassy occupies a stone building dating to 1920. The inauguration brought together Bula, Sa’ar, Colombian Ambassador to Israel Tania Gilinski Bacal, Aisen, and Jerusalem Mayor Moshe Lion.
Palestinian officials criticized the decision. Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al Sheikh condemned the move, saying it disregarded international law and Jerusalem’s disputed status. Jordan’s Foreign Ministry also objected, describing the embassy opening as a violation of international law and relevant resolutions.
Israel considers all of Jerusalem its capital, while the Palestinians seek East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state. Most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv or nearby, arguing that Jerusalem’s final status should be determined through Israeli-Palestinian negotiations.
For Aisen, who arrived in Bogotá eight weeks ago, the initial assignment was to rebuild diplomatic ties after former Colombian President Gustavo Petro severed relations with Israel in May 2024 over the war in Gaza.
“We did not come with the intention of returning to what we were,” Aisen said. “We came to strengthen our relations and go much further.”
The countries have since restored their diplomatic representation, appointed ambassadors, and resumed practical cooperation. Reciprocal visa requirements ended on September 1, while Colombia lifted Petro’s prohibition on coal exports to Israel.
Israel and Colombia restore trade and security cooperation
The free trade agreement required a more technical process. On October 13, the governments completed an exchange of diplomatic notes restoring the agreement, which originally took effect in August 2020.
Israel’s Foreign Ministry described the move as reversing Petro’s termination of the agreement. Aisen explained that the previous Colombian government had attempted to cancel the treaty but had not completed the country’s domestic procedure for withdrawing from an international agreement. The new government therefore needed to reactivate the existing accord rather than negotiate a replacement.
The renewed economic relationship builds on decades of commercial and security cooperation. Colombia has long used Israeli military equipment, and the governments are discussing expanded ties in cybersecurity, technology, agriculture, and other fields.
In a recorded message to Wednesday’s reception, de la Espriella described Israel as a friend and strategic partner. He identified security, intelligence, counterterrorism, organized crime, agriculture, science, innovation, and trade as priorities.
Colombia distances itself from international action against Israel
Colombia’s diplomatic realignment also extends to international institutions.
On September 18, Bogotá notified the International Court of Justice that it was withdrawing its declaration of intervention in South Africa’s case accusing Israel of violating the Genocide Convention during the Gaza war.
The court confirmed the withdrawal four days later. Colombia had intervened in April 2024 to submit its interpretation of the convention. Its withdrawal does not end South Africa’s case against Israel, which rejects the genocide allegations.
The court decision is separate from Colombia’s request to leave the Hague Group, which Bula announced at Wednesday’s reception.
“We reject that approach,” Bula said of the coalition.
He presented the request as another step toward restoring a relationship that began when Colombia recognized Israel in 1949 and established diplomatic ties in 1957.
Antisemitism concerns emerge amid renewed Israel ties
Bula said Colombia’s Foreign Ministry would work with other government ministries and the Confederation of Jewish Communities of Colombia to develop a national initiative against antisemitism.
The effort would also draw on advice from the US State Department’s Office of the Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism, he said, while seeking Israeli participation.
During Wednesday’s reception, Bula criticized the previous administration for what he described as its failure to condemn terrorism clearly and accused it of contributing to “what may be the most virulent wave of antisemitism in Colombia’s recent history.”
“The government of President de la Espriella, this Foreign Ministry and this foreign minister will not remain silent,” Bula said. “We will not let this scourge go unchecked and unchallenged across the country.”
Aisen said attitudes toward Israel became increasingly polarized after the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza. She said some anti-Israel rhetoric had drawn on longstanding antisemitic conspiracy theories.
“If you open my Twitter account, you will see comments that go back to medieval antisemitism,” she said.
One example she cited concerned Israel’s humanitarian response to Colombia’s devastating earthquake in August. Israel deployed approximately 80 rescue and medical personnel and sent additional medical equipment following the disaster.
Aisen said online allegations had circulated claiming that Israeli rescue personnel had come to Colombia to take children. She described the claims as an example of antisemitic conspiracy theories directed against Israel.
Her particular concern is that hostility toward the Israeli government can extend to Colombia’s Jewish population, with Jews held responsible for Israeli policies or actions.
“The Colombian Jewish community became guilty for everything that the State of Israel does,” she said. “That antisemitism has to be confronted.”
Yet Aisen said her personal experience in Colombia had been markedly different from the hostility she encountered online.
“I feel extremely welcome by everyone I meet, not only people in the government but also members of the general public,” she said. “They thank me for Israel being back in Colombia. They feel that Israel can contribute a great deal to the country and that those two lost years were regrettable.”
Marcos Peckel, executive director of the Confederation of Jewish Communities of Colombia and commissioner to combat antisemitism at the Latin American Jewish Congress, attended both the embassy inauguration and Wednesday evening’s reception.
“For those of us who know the history of what this means, it gave us goosebumps,” Peckel told The Media Line. “It shows that President Abelardo de la Espriella is completely determined to take the relationship between Israel and Colombia to its highest level.”
Peckel, who has served on the World Jewish Congress Executive Committee since 2013, said Colombia’s population, regional influence, and history of commercial and security cooperation with Israel give the embassy decision considerable diplomatic weight.
Peckel's concern is whether the renewed relationship can survive future changes of government.
Thousands of demonstrators took to the streets in Colombian cities on October 14 to protest de la Espriella’s domestic policies, with some also opposing his renewed partnership with Israel and closer ties to the United States.
Aisen acknowledged that Israel has become part of Colombia’s domestic political divide. The Jerusalem embassy, one of de la Espriella’s most visible foreign policy decisions, could become a target for his opponents, she said.
“As an Israeli, it hurts me to see that Israel became an issue that divides the public,” she said. “It should not be that way.”
Peckel believes cooperation in agriculture, water management, scientific research, trade, and other practical fields could make bilateral relations more resistant to political shifts. He wants partnerships with institutions and influential sectors of Colombian society that can endure beyond the current administration.
“These changes have to outlast governments,” Peckel said. “The challenge in Latin America is to create very strong roots with the people and with important sectors such as agriculture and water, so that if another government comes, it cannot simply undo what is being built.”

'Sad we are fighting in public': Ex-Shin Bet deputy director demands full October 7 inquiry

Former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) deputy director Israel Hasson called for an investigation into the failures surrounding the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, following statements by the then-Prime Minister's military secretary, Maj.-Gen. Avi Gil and then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar that contradict Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's accounts of events before and after the attack.
Speaking on 103FM, Hasson addressed the conflicting accounts and questioned how Israel had reached a point where senior security officials and political leaders were publicly disputing responsibility rather than conducting a comprehensive examination of the failures.
"I sat through the Shin Bet's investigation for four and a half hours," Hasson said. "An investigation is measured by whether there are questions that were not asked."
"I told them, 'I salute you. I don't have a single additional question that you haven't asked yourselves, but I'm leaving here without an answer.'"
Hasson pointed to the scale of the October 7 attack and the absence of specific intelligence warning beforehand.
"Three thousand people participated in this attack, and we had no concrete warning," he said.
Former Shin Bet deputy chief explains intelligence available to Netanyahu's military secretary
Hasson emphasized that the prime minister's military secretary has access to a broader intelligence picture than any single intelligence agency possesses at a given moment.
"Avi Gil has the complete intelligence picture, which is not available at every moment within the Shin Bet," he explained.
"There are 15 officers in the military secretariat. All of Israel's intelligence information is available to them. His picture is much more comprehensive and complete."
According to Hasson, the military secretariat is responsible for consolidating intelligence assessments from different agencies and presenting them to the prime minister in an organized manner.
"To avoid a situation where, in quotation marks, everyone is confusing the prime minister, the information goes through a channel that can say: 'This is what the Shin Bet says, this is what Military Intelligence says, this is what the Mossad says, and what another hundred bodies are saying.'"
Hasson says inquiry must establish responsibility for October 7 failures
Hasson expressed frustration over the public disputes surrounding the events of October 7, arguing that a formal investigation is needed to determine where the failures occurred.
"It is so sad that we have reached this point," he said. "It is so sad that we are fighting in public instead of going and investigating this matter."
He said a commission of inquiry might not necessarily uncover information unfamiliar to experienced security officials, but would provide the public with a clearer understanding of the failures and their causes.
"A commission of inquiry probably won't discover something I don't already know," Hasson said.
"But it will show the public where the problem was and what caused it. Conclusions will have to be drawn and corrections made to prevent something like this from happening again."
Hasson cites Agranat Commission on political and military responsibility
Hasson acknowledged that not all intelligence sources can be disclosed to the public, but questioned whether withholding certain information would undermine the ability to establish responsibility.
"It is perfectly legitimate that you and I are not given access to all our intelligence sources," he said. "The question is whether that currently affects the conclusions."
He referred to the Agranat Commission, which investigated the failures surrounding the 1973 Yom Kippur War, and its findings regarding intelligence assessments and political responsibility.
"The Agranat Commission said that when there is intent and capability, you do not wait for a warning," Hasson said.
"They established that. They also established that if the military echelon says one thing, it does not absolve the political echelon of responsibility."
Hasson argued that security decision-makers should prioritize precautionary action rather than wait for definitive intelligence before responding to a potential threat.
"It is better to call off a state of heightened readiness than to start looking for a reason to act," he said.
He also referred to previous recommendations to target Hamas leaders in the years leading up to October 7.
"I know how many times in the five years before 2023 there were demands to strike Hamas leaders," Hasson said.
"There were demands to neutralize them. They said the money was going toward armament. They said everything they said."
Former Shin Bet deputy chief addresses Ronen Bar's lawsuit against Netanyahu
Hasson also addressed the lawsuit filed by former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar against Netanyahu, describing the dispute as extending beyond the former agency director personally.
"In my view, this is not Ronen Bar filing a lawsuit against the prime minister. This is the Shin Bet filing a lawsuit against the prime minister," Hasson said.
He sharply criticized Netanyahu's allegations against Bar, calling the extremely serious.
"He attacked him at a level that amounted to betrayal," Hasson said.

Did Netanyahu’s phone call with Sharaa change Israeli-Syrian relations? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:18 UTC
07:12:18 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that he spoke by telephone with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa during deadly clashes in southern Syria in July 2025, claiming the conversation helped stop the killings. Damascus has not confirmed the call, which Netanyahu disclosed less than two weeks before Israel’s parliamentary elections.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
Netanyahu made the announcement on October 15 at a Likud campaign gathering with members of Israel’s Druze community in Yarka, a northern Israeli town. He described the conversation as brief and tense but did not explain how it was arranged or provide further details.
The Israeli prime minister also discussed Israeli military operations during the violence in Syria’s predominantly Druze Sweida Governorate, including airstrikes against the Syrian Defense Ministry building and a target within the presidential palace compound in Damascus.
Violence erupted in July 2025 following clashes between Druze and Bedouin groups, with Syrian government forces and tribal fighters subsequently becoming involved. Israel carried out strikes against Syrian military positions, saying it was acting to protect the Druze community.
In its first response to Netanyahu’s announcement, the Syrian government neither confirmed nor denied the conversation. An unnamed official source quoted by the state-run Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) rejected attempts to involve Syria’s Druze community in Israeli election campaigning, describing it as an integral part of the country’s national fabric.
The source accused Israel of interfering in the July 2025 violence and arming an unauthorized armed group to destabilize Sweida. The allegation has not been independently verified.
According to the Syrian government, Israeli airstrikes during the clashes prevented Syrian forces from intervening to restore order. Damascus maintained that US mediation, rather than Netanyahu’s reported conversation with Sharaa, had brought those strikes to an end.
Syria also reaffirmed its cooperation with the United States and Jordan on a roadmap intended to restore stability in Sweida and called for international pressure on Israel to comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
The Media Line sought comment from Ahmad Mowaffaq Zaidan, media affairs adviser to Sharaa, and Mohammad al-Jafal, adviser for Afro-Asian affairs at Syria’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates. Neither had responded by publication time.
Israel, Syria continuing to pursue security negotiations
The disclosure comes as Israel and Syria pursue US-mediated security negotiations despite continuing disagreements over Israeli military deployments and Syrian sovereignty.
Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in 1967 and expanded its military presence in southern Syrian territory following the fall of Bashar Assad’s government in December 2024. Damascus demands that Israeli forces withdraw from areas entered after Assad’s removal and that both countries return to the arrangements established under the 1974 agreement.
Israeli authorities maintain that their military operations and deployments are necessary to protect the country's northern border.
Although Israel and Syria have no formal diplomatic relations, contacts between senior officials have become an important part of efforts to prevent further confrontation.
In August, Reuters reported, citing informed sources, that Mossad chief Roman Gofman spoke with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on August 14 about Turkey’s military presence in Syria.
Jordan subsequently hosted US-mediated talks between senior Syrian and Israeli delegations on August 23, according to SANA. Those discussions addressed Israeli military operations, measures to reduce tensions, and the possibility of reaching a security agreement.
Netanyahu’s disclosure suggests that contact may also have occurred directly between the countries’ leaders, although Damascus has yet to acknowledge such an exchange.
Netanyahu-Sharaa call could signal willingness to reduce tensions
Syrian political analyst Firas Allawi told The Media Line that the reported conversation could signal a willingness to communicate despite the deep disagreements between Damascus and Israel. He cautioned against interpreting it as evidence of an approaching peace agreement.
“Any political contact between the two sides could represent an initial step toward reducing tensions, but it does not necessarily mean that a peace agreement is close,” Allawi said.
“The issue depends on the willingness of both sides to address outstanding matters, foremost among them Syrian sovereignty and the Israeli military presence. The timing of Netanyahu’s announcement also calls for an examination of his domestic political calculations, without overlooking the possibility that these contacts are part of broader efforts to reshape the regional landscape.”
Allawi’s comments come as Netanyahu campaigns ahead of Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections. The prime minister made his announcement before Druze voters while describing his government’s efforts to protect members of their community in Syria.
The timing raises questions about the political purpose of the disclosure, although the contacts reported between Israeli and Syrian officials in recent months suggest that discussions have continued beyond the immediate circumstances of the 2025 clashes.
For retired Syrian military pilot and analyst Khaled Mansour, the value of direct political communication depends on whether it can lead to practical arrangements that reduce the risk of further fighting.
“Moving from military confrontation to political understandings requires tangible measures on the ground, including ending escalation, limiting military operations, and establishing clear security arrangements that prevent renewed clashes,” Mansour told The Media Line. “The success of any negotiation process will also remain tied to addressing the Israeli military presence inside Syrian territory and providing mutual security guarantees that do not undermine Syrian sovereignty.”
The dispute over the buffer zone established under the 1974 agreement remains a central obstacle. Syria seeks the withdrawal of Israeli forces from territory entered after December 2024, while Israel insists on security arrangements intended to prevent hostile forces from operating near its border.
Mansour said sustained negotiations would require more than occasional direct contacts between senior leaders.
“Political contacts may help prevent military miscalculations and establish channels for containing crises, but building lasting peace requires enforceable understandings and clear mechanisms for monitoring compliance, not merely contacts or political statements.”
Despite continued US diplomatic involvement, Israel and Syria have yet to reach a comprehensive agreement governing military deployments and security arrangements along their shared frontier.
Beyond those disagreements, the possibility of direct communication between Netanyahu and Sharaa has raised hopes among some Syrians that dialogue could eventually help end decades of conflict.
Bakhour Shmantoub, head of Syria’s small Jewish community, told The Media Line that he hoped contacts between the governments could develop into a broader peace process.
“Yes, it could open the door to peace. The region is tired of wars, and peace is necessary,” Shmantoub said.

Israel risks winning the war while losing the world - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:12:06 UTC
07:12:06 KST

The decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay – who chaired a UN commission that concluded Israel was committing genocide in Gaza – should be a wake-up call. Whether intended or not, the award signals how receptive the world has become to that accusation. Israel’s strategic environment is changing dramatically, and our future is at stake.
Israelis are divided into two camps. One believes the country is doing well. After recovering from the October 7 massacre, Israel’s security position is stable – even stronger than before, as the Yellow Lines in Gaza and southern Lebanon attest. The economy is thriving despite three years of war – witness the strong shekel. And despite our bitter divisions, civil society remains vibrant, enterprising, and marked by solidarity – witness Israel’s high ranking in the World Happiness Report.
The other camp sees a country in crisis. The war drags on, with no diplomatic settlement in sight to ensure lasting stability. The flawed strategic assumptions that preceded October 7 remain unexamined, as no official commission of inquiry has been established to date. This leaves us vulnerable to another disaster. The ultra-Orthodox community shirks its share of the national burden, threatening our economic and security future. Trust in state institutions is eroding, and social tensions are mounting – to the point that some fear civil war.
Yet both camps must confront a danger that transcends their differences: Israel stands on the brink of severe international isolation. That could trap us all in a harsh new reality with potentially grave consequences. This strategic warning demands a fundamental change of course at home, across political lines.
Israel is on the brink of international isolation
Europe, Israel’s largest trading partner, is moving toward sanctions that could seriously damage our economy. Britain and 11 other countries, including Canada, have announced or are considering restrictions on trade in settlement goods. But Israel’s economy does not stop at the Green Line. Almost every major Israeli company could find itself exposed to looming sanctions.
That could trigger a chain reaction. Businesses worldwide might avoid trading with Israel for fear of being branded sanctions violators. Even friends of Israel could pull back – not out of hostility but out of commercial caution. A creeping de facto boycott could transform BDS – boycott, divestment, and sanctions – from a radical fringe cause into a sweeping movement that reshapes life in Israel. We could become a pariah state alongside Russia, North Korea, and Iran.
The United States is Israel’s principal security and diplomatic anchor. Relations with American administrations have sometimes been tense, but broad bipartisan public support held firm. Today, the reverse is true – and this is the heart of the strategic warning.
Cooperation with the current administration is impressive. But it offers tactical reassurance while obscuring a troubling strategic shift: American sympathy for Israel is eroding. The decline extends beyond Democrats, reaching younger Republicans and even young Evangelical Christians.
Anti-Israel attitudes once associated with the radical Left and the fascist Right have gained a foothold in the mainstream. For the first time in decades, Americans are no more likely to sympathize with Israelis than with Palestinians. They are David; we are Goliath.
Israel is on a slippery slope toward a dangerous defeat – economic and diplomatic, and perhaps even in the security arena when a new US administration takes office in just over two years. No one can know how likely each part of this scenario is to materialize.
Shifts in public opinion, national interests, and governments abroad could still work in our favor. But we cannot cling to the complacent belief that “everything will be okay,” or to the illusion that an isolated, self-sufficient “Sparta” could survive. A sudden diplomatic collapse – a “6:29 a.m.” moment echoing the shock of October 7 – is a real possibility.
The forces driving these developments are complex, and not all are within Israel’s control. Still, coalition and opposition alike have a duty to weigh every action, every statement, and every failure to act in light of the long-term implications for Israel’s diplomatic standing, national security, and economy.
This is not a call for Israel to sacrifice its vital interests to appease world opinion. But there is ample room for constructive action. We can take steps most Israelis support – such as stamping out Jewish terrorism – and refrain from rhetoric most Israelis reject, including calls to flatten Gaza or force its residents to emigrate. Israelis in both camps share an overriding interest in preventing this strategic warning from becoming a tragic reality.
The writer is president of the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) and professor emeritus of law at Bar-Ilan University.

Weight loss medications alter how the brain and kidneys manage body fluids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:00:15 UTC
07:00:15 KST

Medications like liraglutide help treat diabetes and obesity, but they also influence how the body handles water and sodium. A new study shows that these drugs directly lower levels of a key water-conserving hormone, altering chemical signals sent from the brain to the kidneys. The findings were published in Science Advances.
Drugs known as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists mimic a natural digestive hormone. These medications make people feel full and prompt insulin release to manage blood sugar. Doctors notice that patients taking these drugs often lose water and sodium in their urine. Common side effects include nausea and diarrhea, which can lead to dehydration.
Patients are often advised to drink plenty of fluids to counter this water loss. Until now, researchers have not fully understood how these medications communicate with the biological systems governing basic fluid balance.
The primary way the human body regulates water involves a hormone called arginine vasopressin. Produced by specialized neurons in the brain, this hormone travels to the pituitary gland for storage. When the body needs to conserve water, the pituitary releases the hormone into the bloodstream.
The hormone then travels to the kidneys, prompting them to absorb water back into the blood rather than excreting it as urine. Michael P. Greenwood, a researcher at the University of Bristol, along with a team of colleagues, wanted to know if liraglutide disrupts this chain of events.
The researchers first conducted a small study involving sixteen healthy human adults. They took blood and urine samples from the volunteers before and after administering a single dose of liraglutide. The participants also consumed a slightly salty drink to prompt mild changes in their hydration levels.
After analyzing the samples, the researchers found that liraglutide acutely reduced the amount of arginine vasopressin in the blood. They also saw drops in a secondary marker molecule called copeptin, which the body releases alongside the primary water-conserving hormone. The drug also led to lower plasma potassium levels and higher amounts of sodium in the volunteers’ urine.
Because humans take these medications for extended periods, the researchers turned to an animal model to observe longer physiological changes. They injected male and female rats with either liraglutide or a saline placebo over the course of fourteen days. They then tracked the animals’ daily food and water consumption.
During the first few hours, the drug predictably reduced both food and water intake. Over the full fourteen days, the rats receiving the medication started consuming more water relative to their food intake compared to the control group. The medication essentially scrambled their normal daily drinking patterns, indicating a disturbance in their overall fluid regulation.
The team then examined the specific tissues involved in producing and storing the water-conserving hormone in these animals. They looked at the hypothalamus, the brain region that manufactures the hormone. They found no changes in the activity of the genes responsible for the hormone’s initial production.
However, when they looked at the pituitary gland where the hormone is stored, they found a decrease in the actual amount of the stored hormone. In female rats, they also observed lower levels of the marker molecule copeptin circulating in the blood after fourteen days. The drug appeared to be halting the release of the hormone from its storage site.
To understand why the pituitary gland was holding onto less hormone, the researchers analyzed the entire landscape of proteins within the tissue. They extracted tissue from the rat pituitary glands at four hours and fourteen days after drug administration. Using advanced protein-scanning techniques, they mapped both the abundance of different proteins and the chemical tags attached to them.
Cells often modify their proteins by attaching phosphate groups to them after they are built. These chemical tags act like molecular on-off switches, changing how a protein behaves or interacts with other molecules. By scanning for these tags, the researchers could see exactly which cellular machines were activated or deactivated by the drug.
The protein landscapes looked vastly different depending on the duration of the treatment and the sex of the animal. At the four-hour mark, both male and female rats showed broad changes in protein tagging. After fourteen days, female rats exhibited a massive shift in protein abundance and tagging, while male rats showed fewer alterations.
Many of the modified proteins belonged to a category of molecules that control how cells package and release hormones. Specifically, the researchers noticed heavy modifications to proteins guiding the microscopic storage bubbles that hold arginine vasopressin. Two proteins known to manage these storage bubbles acquired distinct chemical tags in the female rats following the fourteen-day treatment.
To test if these specific protein modifications directly alter hormone release, the researchers engineered a laboratory cell culture. They grew cells in a dish and introduced synthetic genes to mimic the exact protein modifications they had observed in the rat pituitary glands. They then measured how well these engineered cells could release a glowing marker molecule designed to imitate arginine vasopressin.
Altering these specific release-guiding proteins directly inhibited the cells’ ability to secrete the glowing marker. Mutating the proteins to block the chemical tags prevented the cells from holding back the secretion. This confirmed that the drug changes how the pituitary gland physically manages its hormone reserves at a microscopic level.
Finally, the researchers looked at the end of the line in the signaling pathway, which is the kidney. They examined kidney tissue from the treated rats to see how the organs were responding to the altered hormone levels. Under normal conditions, arginine vasopressin tells the kidneys to deploy tiny water channels called aquaporins to reabsorb fluid.
The team found that the genes responsible for building these water channels were less active in the treated rats. They also observed changes to the chemical tags on the aquaporin proteins themselves. These specific changes mark the channels for destruction rather than deployment. The drug was actively dampening the kidney’s ability to retain water.
The study outlines how these diabetes medications alter fluid dynamics, but it has some limitations. The human portion of the research was a small study involving only healthy individuals taking a single dose of the drug. The human trial did not have enough participants to measure potential differences between men and women.
In the animal studies, the researchers did not directly measure the volume of urine the rats produced. Future research will need to examine how these hormonal shifts affect patients taking the drug over months or years. Understanding these mechanisms could eventually help doctors assess kidney and cardiovascular risks for patients with fluid retention issues.
The study, “A clinical and experimental investigation of liraglutide effects on the brain-kidney axis,” was authored by Michael P. Greenwood, Mohammed I. Alotaibi, Soledad Bárez-López, Nathan W. P. Cantley, Sharon Merritt, Danijela Tatovic, and David Murphy.
