Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week
Zelensky’s diesel-fueled burnout
This week did not start well for Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, who was apparently blindsided by US President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel supplies after talks with the Kremlin. The deal won’t alleviate the global diesel shortage, but it’s already cooling speculative markets and easing pressure on Trump ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
For Zelensky, it’s a “diplomatic nightmare,” as Russian analyst Sergey Poletaev wrote for RT. Trump rubbed salt in the wound on Saturday when he openly suggested that Ukrainians “get a new leader who can make a deal” and halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump went on to claim, “wants to make a deal more than Zelensky.”
Backed into a corner, Zelensky began throwing haymakers. Accusing the American president of empathizing with dictators, Zelensky demanded air defense missiles from the US before vowing to continue his drone campaign against Russia’s refineries – with or without American support.
The US apparently sent a warning signal to Zelensky by throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to SpaceX’s high-speed Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services, which are vital tools in guiding attack drones used against Russia, and in detecting incoming retaliatory strikes. Neither Trump nor SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would take responsibility for the communications drop-off, but even if they had, their message would likely have fallen of deaf ears.
Zelensky escalates the energy war
The Ukrainian leader followed through on his promise to keep hitting Russian refineries, despite Trump’s announcement of an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kiev (which neither side confirmed). Ukrainian forces attacked facilities in Russia’s Saratov and Ryazan regions on Wednesday, before firing a barrage of four long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing kamikaze drones at the Ryazan refinery again on Thursday.
Debris from an intercepted UAV triggered an intense fire at the facility, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.
Retaliation was swift, from both Moscow and Washington. Russian forces used missiles and drones to strike six power plants in Kiev, Kharkov, and the surrounding regions, as well as military logistics hubs and data centers. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, confirming reports that Zelensky launched the refinery strikes knowing Ukraine lacked adequate air defense supplies to repel the retaliation.
Trump went on to savage Zelensky in a Newsmax interview on Thursday. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country,” he said, before accusing the Ukrainian leader of selling missiles given to him by the US “on the open market.”
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump concluded.
Nord Stream trial begins
As Ukraine doubles down on its infrastructure war, the costliest infrastructure attack in history is finally being litigated in a German courtroom. Sergey Kuznetsov, a Ukrainian military officer, went on trial in Hamburg this week, accused of leading the team that sabotaged the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in September 2022, an act that German prosecutors consider a “war crime.”
Kuznetsov is staying silent, refusing to admit or deny a role in the bombing. The evidence against him is circumstantial, and his lawyers are confident that without a confession, he “cannot be convicted.”
As RT has explored in depth, the prosecution’s version of events is riddled with plot holes and inconsistencies. However, to pick apart the alternative story – that the pipelines were destroyed in a CIA operation – would call the relationship between Washington and Berlin, the foundation of the postwar liberal order, into question.
While a guilty verdict against Kuznetsov would directly implicate the Ukrainian military in a war crime against its largest foreign donor, the trial, at least at this stage, appears set up to avoid this outcome.
Russiagate resurrected
Speaking of reopening old wounds, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham dug up the bloated corpse of ‘Russiagate’ this week to bolster his efforts to undo the 2016 Brexit referendum and rejoin the EU. Burnham claimed that he had “clear” evidence that Russia interfered in the vote, in which Britons voted by 51.89% to 48.11% to leave the union.
Just as the original ‘Russiagate’ claims against Trump fell apart under questioning, Burnham’s allegation crumbled once subjected to some basic scrutiny. The British PM was unable to back up his accusation when grilled in Parliament, and his foreign secretary, Stephen Doughty, humiliated himself on national television when he attempted to evade questioning on the claim.
The final nail in the coffin came when Burnham’s own domestic intelligence chief cautioned against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
However, Burnham couldn’t be faulted for his timing and opportunism. As he spoke of Russian bots and influence campaigns in Parliament on Monday, Zelensky, his Polish and Baltic backers, and his army of internet supporters claimed that a Ukrainian strike on a Yandex data center in Russia the previous day had wiped thousands of “Russian bots” from social media.
As it turned out, none of this was true. The strike interrupted the activity of Yandex’ web crawler bots, which archive websites for search users, but with the help of an AI-created graph and some creative interpretation of the word “bot,” the hoax made it all the way to the Warsaw Security Forum.
French riots spread
French students took part in a fifth wave of demonstrations this week, which they say are aimed at securing more school funding and better learning conditions. Every wave of protests thus far has descended into rioting and vandalism, and this week’s marches were no different, with participants torching cars and battering police officers with cobblestones and fireworks in Paris.
RT’s Nadege Abderazzak watched heavily armored police baton-charge crowds of rioters in the French capital on Wednesday, noting that officers now outnumber protesters two-to-one at some rallies.
With French President Emmanuel Macron determined to increase military spending and continue arming Ukraine, France’s financial situation is in dire straits, and right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is on track to win the country’s next presidential election.
Meanwhile, Albanian students have taken a page out of their French counterparts’ book. After large protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha over corruption allegations, a crowd of students breached the fence of the Education Ministry in Tirana on Wednesday and torched the building.
Rama’s response has also drawn from the Western playbook, with the Albanian PM accusing protesters of waging “hybrid war” against the country.
What we’re watching
Zelensky may be in Trump’s bad books, but he can still count on the support of Macron, Burnham, and the rest of his European backers, whom he met in Brussels on Thursday and Friday. In his address to the European Council on Friday, the Ukrainian leader asked for another “70 billion euros” for ammunition, missiles, and air defense. Should Ukraine “fall,” Zelensky warned, another 20 million Ukrainian migrants will flood into the EU.
We’ll be keeping an eye on what kind of promises the cash-strapped Europeans make after this blatant shakedown.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will fly to Tehran on Monday for talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. The two diplomats are expected to focus on de-escalating the simmering US/Iran conflict in the Middle East, and any progress on this front will likely be reflected in global energy markets.
Lavrov will also meet Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic on Friday, ahead of critical parliamentary elections on October 25. Amid student protests, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic called the election early and stepped down to run as prime minister, a high-stakes move that turned the vote into a referendum on his nine years in power. With pro-Western students and right-wing ‘patriotic’ forces squeezing Vucic from either side, we’ll be keeping an eye out for polls, protests, and interference from the usual suspects.
For more on all of these stories, stick with RT.

Israeli settlers beat up and rob WaPo journalist in West Bank (VIDEOS)
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine has been badly beaten by Israeli settlers and stripped of her equipment while covering attacks on Palestinians harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank.
The assault occurred on Friday near the village of Abu Falah, the latest in an ongoing string of attacks staged by organized settler groups. Masked settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinian villages, hurling stones and setting orchards on fire in an apparent effort to disrupt the autumn harvest. The Israeli military, which is usually present, has taken little to no action against the settlers.
Levine, a veteran photographer who has covered conflicts across the Middle East and elsewhere for decades, was caught in a settler charge on the Palestinians. The mob threw the journalist, who was wearing a blue protective vest clearly marked ‘PRESS,’ to the ground, repeatedly kicking her while stealing her cameras and phone.
“They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times,” Levine told reporters after the incident.
Footage from the scene shows the immediate aftermath, with Levine seen prone on the ground after the settlers were repelled by the villagers. The journalist was badly shaken but apparently spared more serious injuries thanks to her protective vest and helmet.
Severe settler + soldier attack on olive harvesters in Abu Falah. American WaPo journalist Heidi Levine badly wounded. Machine gunfire—at least one Palestinian shot. Tear gas. Soldiers assaulting journalists. pic.twitter.com/He61cNYk0c
— jasper nathaniel (@infinite_jaz) October 16, 2026
The photographer was evacuated by Palestinian paramedics and treated at a hospital in Ramallah for her injuries. Later on, another group of journalists was reportedly pelted with stones by settlers at the site. Oren Ziv, a journalist who also witnessed the attack, reported that at least one Palestinian was wounded by gunfire. It was not immediately clear whether Israeli settlers or the military fired the shots, but the IDF reportedly did nothing to stop the violence.
The Washington Post strongly condemned the attack and called for a full investigation. “While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities,” Matt Murray, executive editor of the Post, said in a statement.
Ten days earlier, veteran Palestinian photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, who has been working with AFP, suffered a similar assault during a settler raid on Palestinian olive farmers. The journalist, marked as press, was attacked by armed Israeli settlers, who beat him with rifle butts and robbed him of his equipment. The violence was reportedly witnessed by an IDF unit that did not intervene.
Journalists documenting settler violence have increasingly become victims of it. The Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least 16 incidents involving 35 Palestinian, Israeli, and international journalists in the first eight months of 2026 alone, with the figures already surpassing those recorded in 2025.

Meta employees say Lula’s accounts restricted in Brazil election: Report
The messages, reported by a Brazilian daily, say the platform recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and his WhatsApp channel.
Employees at Meta have acknowledged in internal communications that the Instagram accounts of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were negatively affected by restrictions during the country’s election, media reports say.
The messages, reported on Friday by Brazilian daily Folha de S Paulo, also acknowledged the platform recommended the profile of Lula challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as well as his WhatsApp channel. Folha, the Sao Paulo-based paper, cited messages it had reviewed.
Meta told the Reuters news agency that the technical issues cited in the report were already public and the conversations it referenced related solely to the severity of the issues, not political interference.
“Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it added in a statement.
Lula, the left-wing incumbent, will face right-wing challenger Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff on October 25, following a stronger-than-expected performance by the senator in the first-round vote earlier this month.
Friday’s report came on the heels of a Brazilian court ruling on Thursday that ordered Meta to immediately adopt measures to provide equal treatment of the two candidates ahead of the runoff.
The ruling by a judge in Brazil’s top electoral court was made shortly after Lula filed a complaint that accused the tech giant – which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp – of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election.
Justice Marco Aurelio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies.
Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,700) per day if it fails to comply.
According to Lula’s party, some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach. Options for reactions, sharing, audio or accelerated speed were also missing.

Sean “Diddy” Combs, who was convicted of prostitution-related crimes, has been moved to a federal prison in Pennsylvania after reports that the disgraced music producer was living the high life and was injured in a fight at his New Jersey lockup, according to reports.
The US Bureau of Prisons (BOP) is transferring Combs, 56, from FCI Fort Dix to FCI Allenwood Low, a low-security facility south of Williamsport and about 155 miles (250km) west of New York City, a person familiar with the matter said to the Associated Press. The person was not authorized to speak publicly and did so on condition of anonymity.
Agence France-Press later reported being told by a BOP spokesperson that Combs had been moved from Fort Dix to Allenwood Low.
Combs’s spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer, said “decisions about inmate placement are made by the BOP, and we are not in a position to speak to the circumstances surrounding this transfer”.
“Sean remains focused on moving forward, and we hope that his time at the new facility will be productive and without unnecessary disruption,” Engelmayer said.
Combs was given a four-year-and-two-month sentence for his 2 July 2025 conviction on prostitution-related charges for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called “freak-offs”. It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment’s most influential figures.
In September, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy cognac; having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages; and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend’s nude selfies.
TMZ on Wednesday then reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the BOP refuted TMZ’s report, telling the AP: “The story you are referring to is false and did not happen.”
In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison’s special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to 2 March 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter who spoke to the AP.
The second US circuit court of appeals in April heard arguments in Combs’s effort to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

In Brazil, deforestation in the Amazon has fallen to its lowest level ever recorded, earning praise for the president
Kyiv • UNN
Over the year, deforestation in the Amazon fell to 3,335 km² — the lowest level since 1988. At the same time, the number of fires in the state of Amazonas increased by 253%.
Brazil recorded a record reduction in deforestation in the Amazon rainforest. Over the past year, the area of destroyed forest decreased by 41.8%, reaching its lowest level since satellite monitoring began in 1988. Bloomberg reported this, citing Brazil's Ministry of the Environment, writes UNN.
Details
According to official data, 3,335 square kilometers of forest were cleared in the Amazon over the 12 months through July 2026. This was the result of the strengthened environmental policy of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who returned to power in 2023.
His administration revived the operations of the Amazon Fund, stepped up the fight against illegal mining and land clearing, and expanded protected areas. In 2023, deforestation fell by more than 20%, and in 2024 by a further 31%.
Record reduction in deforestation accompanied by large-scale fires
Our goal remains to achieve zero deforestation by 2030
At the same time, the situation with forest fires remains difficult. In the state of Amazonas, the number of fires increased by 253% compared with last year. Climate change, the El Niño phenomenon and human activity are cited among the causes.
Environment Minister João Paulo Capobianco said that the authorities were investigating a possible link between deliberate arson and the presidential elections. Special rescue units were deployed to fight the fires.
The new environmental figures were released ahead of the second round of the presidential election, in which Lula is set to face Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Under the latter's rule, deforestation in the Amazon reached a 15-year high.

KFC in the United States will replace Pepsi with Coca-Cola. PepsiCo could lose approximately $500 million in annual sales and some restaurant partnerships.
The American fast-food restaurant chain KFC has decided to stop serving Pepsi beverages and switch to Coca-Cola products at its U.S. locations. Analysts forecast that, due to the loss of its long-standing partner, PepsiCo could miss out on approximately $500 million in annual sales. Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to estimates by Bank of America analysts, ending its cooperation with KFC could lead to an approximately 3% decline in sales of Pepsi beverage concentrates in North America. At the same time, Coca-Cola could increase the corresponding figure by 2.5% thanks to the new partnership.
KFC's decision has created an additional challenge for PepsiCo, which is already facing weak demand and rising costs in the North American market. The company's return to profitability is progressing more slowly than expected, forcing it to step up cost-cutting measures.
Why the loss of KFC could become a problem for PepsiCo
Jefferies analysts believe that the main threat to PepsiCo lies not so much in the financial losses as in the weakening of the brand's position and the possible review of other long-standing contracts with restaurant chains.
The fact that a longtime Pepsi customer is switching to a competitor raises the question of whether other partners that previously seemed out of reach could now also change suppliers
Richard Exon, founder of the independent creative agency Joint, also believes that investors view KFC's decision primarily as a signal of changing competitive positions in the market, rather than as a critical financial loss for PepsiCo.
Thus, KFC's switch to Coca-Cola could have broader implications for the U.S. soft-drinks market, as it draws attention to the stability of PepsiCo's other partnerships with major restaurant chains.

Ukraine has accumulated record-high gas reserves in six years ahead of winter — Naftogaz
Kyiv • UNN
Gas reserves in underground storage facilities have reached 16 billion cubic meters — the highest level since 2020. Naftogaz has additionally contracted more than 1 billion cubic meters.
Ukraine has accumulated 16 billion cubic meters of gas in underground storage facilities ahead of the heating season. This is the highest level since 2020, despite intensified Russian attacks on energy infrastructure. Acting Chairman of Naftogaz Serhiy Fedorenko said this in an interview with Reuters, reports UNN.
Details
According to him, during 2026, Russia attacked the company's facilities more than 400 times—twice as often as last year. Oil and gas production, processing, and transportation facilities, as well as thermal power plants in frontline regions, came under attack.
This year, most of our facilities have been hit
Will Ukraine have enough gas for the winter?
The current reserves exceed the minimum volume of 13.2 billion cubic meters that the government has deemed necessary to get through the winter. For comparison, Ukraine began the previous heating season with reserves of less than 14 billion cubic meters.
At the same time, gas consumption in the country is declining. According to Fedorenko's forecast, it will amount to about 20 billion cubic meters in 2026, compared with 21 billion last year. One of the reasons was the shutdown of some industrial enterprises due to Russian shelling.
To provide additional security for the heating season, Naftogaz has already contracted imports of more than 1 billion cubic meters of gas, 25% of which will be liquefied natural gas. The supplies are scheduled for the period from December to March.
Ukraine has also offered the European Union the use of its underground gas storage facilities, whose total capacity is about 30 billion cubic meters. A third of this capacity is ready to be allocated to European partners.
Despite the record reserves, Naftogaz is cautiously assessing the prospects of getting through the winter because of the constant threat of new Russian strikes and possible damage to energy infrastructure.

Details are beginning to emerge about Kaylub Giamanco, the man who brought the deadly shooting at elementary school in Bend, Oregon on Thursday, to an end by fatally shooting the 16-year-old suspect in the midst of a violent rampage.

Giamanco was driving by the school when he heard gunfire and saw the gunman entering the school. “He’s an absolute HERO. However, we are not speaking to media at this time. He’s not ready, nor is the family.”
Though she did not name him, Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, praised the man who followed the shooter into the school during a news conference on Thursday.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life,” she said, “your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well.”
Authorities are still investigating what led to the deadly attack, and have not released a motive. The suspect was using a pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, according to reporting from the Associated Press.
“This is going to be a long investigation,” Bend’s police chief, Mike Krantz, said, adding that the police would maintain a large presence at the school for the next few days.

====================================================================================================

A decade after Theranos imploded, here’s what scientists want you to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:35:32 UTC
05:35:32 KST

Around a decade ago Theranos, one of the buzziest science start-ups ever, imploded. Swamped by allegations of fraud, the actions of the company and its enigmatic CEO, Elizabeth Holmes, shone a harsh light on problems with scientific start-ups. Now scientists say these issues have only gotten worse.
In a new documentary titled You Can See Everything, filmmaker Nathan Fielder follows Holmes in the lead-up to starting a prison sentence in May 2023, after she was found guilty of fraud.
The film retraces the saga of Theranos, which claimed to have a machine that could perform hundreds of clinical tests using a single drop of blood. After years of fundraising, high-publicity support and partnerships with pharmacies to make the tests accessible, scientists and journalists revealed in 2015 that Theranos’s claims were false: there was no scientific evidence that its product worked.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Theranos is, in many ways, a cautionary tale and a relic of 2010s Silicon Valley. But for scientists, Theranos’s problems are anything but history.
Canaries in the Coal Mine
John Ioannidis is a professor at Stanford University’s medical school and was among the first to question Theranos’s bona fides in a 2015 article. Eleven years later Ioannidis says he worries the problems of transparency and a lack of strong evidence in science and technology start-ups are, if anything, worse today.
“I feel kind of uneasy about this being presented as a sensationalist, movie-quality story [about] a single bad apple because I see very similar phenotypes to Theranos,” Ioannidis says.
Ioannidis argues that, in some ways, claims of scientific progress are a public relations game. As private companies have become increasingly powerful agents in driving research forward, the trend has shifted fields away from more traditional, publicly funded research and academia.
“Holmes is in jail, but the recipe of her success has been even more widely adopted,” he says.
Ian Papautsky, a microfluidics researcher at the University of Illinois Chicago, says that Theranos’s public downfall and time in the spotlight create a strong case for validating scientific findings. But he, too, worries that, as start-ups and private companies increasingly drive discovery, opportunities for secrecy or fraud may grow.
“Many of the start-ups are not transparent in their technology development,” he says. “On the one hand, you would argue that they have to be, because they’re trying to compete with everyone else. But that also makes it a lot easier to hide the mismanagement and all these other various issues.”
Holmes’s husband, Billy Evans, who also appears in the documentary, is himself quietly building a new blood testing company. The start-up, called Haemanthus, plans to use artificial intelligence tools to run diagnostic tests. Holmes is listed as a scientific adviser to the company, and Evans has raised millions of dollars in funding, according to NPR.
“The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again,” Evans tells Fielder in the movie.
A Lasting Effect
Theranos has made it harder for academics who study blood testing or microfluidics to get funding, says Umut Gurkan, a biotechnology researcher at Case Western Reserve University. He creates blood testing products for conditions such as sickle cell anemia. Gurkan remembers going to Silicon Valley in 2015 to seek funding and being told, “We don’t invest in diagnostics anymore.”
Even as diagnostic technology has advanced, it remains difficult to bring it into markets, he says.
“Trust in science is fragile, and ‘a drop of blood’ now sounds like a scam,” Gurkan says. “Honest companies trying to save lives pay that tax. And at the end of the day, patients and real people pay the price with lack of working diagnostics and technologies that deserve to be in the market.”
As for Theranos’s claims: even after more than 10 years of advancement in clinical testing and microfluidics, its premise remains impossible, the researchers consulted for this article say—at least at the scale that Holmes promised. A drop of blood doesn’t hold nearly enough biological information to conduct the hundreds of tests that Theranos claimed.
Theranos’s mission was noble, Papautsky says, but the science did not and does not hold up.
“Doing multiplex testing on a small volume of blood is a good concept—it would be an important advancement in technology,” he says. “But having experts with the right knowledge and good management is very important, and it’s becoming more and more important these days. Expertise is not necessarily being valued as it used to be.”

Hurricane Isaias knocks out Gulf Coast power, NASA images show
Isaias became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season on October 8 and made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9 as a Category 2 storm, with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles (170 kilometers) per hour, NASA’s Earth Observatory reported.
Isaias brought heavy rain, flash flooding and damaging winds to parts of the southeastern United States, including Alabama and the Florida Panhandle. Fallen trees and power lines left many residents without electricity.
Using data from the NOAA-20 satellite’s VIIRS instrument, NASA’s Black Marble HD product captured changes in nighttime lighting before and after the storm. Images from October 11 showed sharp declines in nighttime lighting around parts of Pensacola and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin, suggesting widespread power disruptions.
A comparison of images from October 11 and 12 showed nighttime lights beginning to return in some areas. By October 14, lighting patterns appeared similar to pre-storm conditions.
Ranjay Shrestha of NASA’s Black Marble science team said the high-resolution imagery helps identify where outages persist and recovery is progressing, supporting emergency responders in prioritizing resources. However, satellite observations complement ground-based outage reports rather than replace them.
NASA’s Disasters Program is also supporting the Alabama Red Cross and the Alabama Emergency Management Agency in their response to Hurricane Isaias, in coordination with FEMA and the USGS Coastal Storms Team.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that NASA scientists had developed a more precise method to track Earth’s shifting center of mass, revealing how seasonal changes in water, ice and air subtly alter the planet’s balance.

Elka Rоuskov is the newest among “Bulgarian Woman of the Year” laureates
Lyutvie Gencheva named “Audience Favourite Bulgarian Woman”
Friday 16 October 2026 22:26
Friday, 16 October 2026, 22:26
Elka Rouskov with the Bulgarian Woman of the Year award
PHOTO BTA
Font size
For the 15th time, the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad has presented its “Bulgarian Woman of the Year” award to one of the many Bulgarian women who devote their energy, knowledge, emotion and a significant part of their personal time to causes aimed at preserving and strengthening the ties between Bulgarian communities around the world and their homeland. This year, 29 Bulgarian women from 11 countries were nominated.
At a special ceremony in the Maxima Hall of the University of National and World Economy in Sofia, the jury presented the St Zlata Meglenska Award to Elka Rouskov from the United States. She received a bronze statuette and an icon of the saint, the heavenly patroness of Bulgarians abroad.
“I am absolutely delighted to be the newest little bird in the flock of women honoured with this prestigious award,” Ms Rouskov said, dedicating the distinction to Bulgarian schools, folk organisations, libraries, community centres and cultural clubs in the United States and Canada.
“For me, ‘Bulgarian Woman of the Year’ means connection, communication, a bridge and a bond with Bulgaria, as well as great responsibility and love. I cannot sum up this moment or my work for my country in a single word, but it is about connection, a bridge and love for Bulgaria,” she said emotionally in an interview with Radio Bulgaria immediately after the award ceremony.
With Elka Rouskov’s support, a number of ongoing cultural programmes and groups have flourished. They include the Bulgarian Voices women’s choir in Seattle, the Seattle Cheta folk ensemble, the Medena Pitka children’s folk group and the Glagolnitsa literary circle. Through their work, Bulgarian culture is not merely a memory of the past, but a living experience passed down from one generation to the next.
The concerts, theatre performances and cultural events she organises in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Phoenix, San Diego, Las Vegas and Seattle build bridges between Bulgarians in different parts of America and showcase the richness of the Bulgarian spirit to a wider audience.
Elka Rouskov also makes a point of engaging young people. At her initiative, the Little Bulgarian School in Chicago organises the Bulgarian poetry recitation competition How Beautiful You Are, My Homeland.
Elka Rouskov with Zivka Bubalova-Petrova, Director of the Little Bulgarian School in Chicago
PHOTO Joan Kolev
“What matters to me is that we continue our work in support of Bulgarian organisations abroad,” Elka Ruskova said. “They need this support enormously because they are involved in educating Bulgarian children abroad every day. I can say this because I have witnessed their work for years. I believe that, particularly in the United States, we should strive to work together with Bulgarian organisations, community centres, libraries, folk ensembles, festivals and schools. This will be my next mission to bring people together, and I am glad and hopeful that I will have the strength and support to pursue it, as I have had until now.”
Ms Ruskova added that she would be happy to support initiatives that could unite members of the newly established Club of Bulgarian Woman of the Year - St Zlata of Meglen laureates around shared causes.
Plaques recognising contributions to the promotion of the Bulgarian language, folklore, culture and spirituality abroad were presented to Elisaveta Yordanova, founder and choreographer of the Gorana ensemble in New York; Teodora Mileva, representing the management of the Sts Cyril and Methodius Bulgarian Cultural and Educational Organisation in Vienna; Elka Rouskov, one of the co-founders of the Bulgarian Cultural Centre in Seattle; and Yana Belichka, head and choreographer of the Zornitsa ensemble in Montreal.
PHOTO Joan Kolev
To mark the 15th presentation of the Bulgarian Woman of the Year - St Zlata Meglenska 2025 award, special lifetime achievement distinctions for promoting Bulgarian culture and spirituality around the world were presented to Diana Glasnova of Zagreb, Croatia, editor-in-chief of the Rodna Rech magazine, and Violeta Zhelyazkova of Boston, United States, who helped establish a Bulgarian cultural centre in the city 25 years ago.
Special recognition was also given posthumously to Kamelia Ilieva, editor-in-chief of the Bulgarian magazine Roden Glas, published in the Czech Republic. Her husband, Sasho Iliev, accepted the plaque on her behalf.
Once again, the “Audience Favourite Bulgarian Woman” award was also presented. This year’s recipient was Lyutvie Gencheva of Freiburg, Germany, founder and driving force behind the folk dance ensemble Mladost na Megdana (“Youth on the Village Square").
The Executive Director of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Raina Mandzhukova, presents Lyutvie Gencheva with the "Favorite Bulgarian of the Audience" award
PHOTO BTA
The ensemble brings together Bulgarian school pupils and young people aged 15 to 25 from Germany, France, the Netherlands, Spain, England and Sweden. It came into being spontaneously at the end of the tenth edition of the Na Megdana na Drugata Bulgaria (“On the Village Square of the Other Bulgaria”) festival, held in Lyon in 2025. Today, its members have already performed at an impressive number of events in Bulgaria and across Europe.
“We hardly dared to dream that it would develop this way,” Ms Gencheva admits, listing some of the dance troupe’s upcoming appearances: in London on 24 October, in Arbanasi on 30 October, and in Sofia on 31 October, when it will perform at the National Palace of Culture alongside the Trakia ensemble. 
On 7 November, the group will take part in a concert marking the tenth anniversary of the Association of Bulgarian Folk Ensembles Abroad.
Lyutvie Gencheva with the "Audience's Favorite Bulgarian" award
PHOTO Joan Kolev
“The award means a great deal to me because the Audience Favourite is a woman people have voted for, and people vote only when they know someone and are familiar with what she does. I am grateful to everyone who voted for me, especially as there were 29 Bulgarian women nominated this year.
“Metaphorically speaking, each one of them is a storm wherever she lives, striving in her own way and drawing on her own strengths to preserve the Bulgarian community or guide it in a particular direction. I would very much like these women to have the opportunity to unite around common goals in the future, so that they can move things forward together and 29 storms can become a hurricane.”
Anita Ekenova, Lyutvie Gencheva, Radoslava Nedyalkova
PHOTO Joan Kolev
The Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad established the Bulgarian Woman of the Year - St Zlata of Meglen award in 2009. According to tradition, Zlata was a young Bulgarian woman who, during Ottoman rule, refused to renounce her Christian faith despite the cruelty inflicted upon her. She died a martyr and is now revered as the patron saint of Bulgarians living abroad.

US deficit hits $2T in a year, highest level since 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:31:15 UTC
05:31:15 KST

The US budget deficit has grown to almost $2 trillion over the past year, reaching its highest level since 2021.
The expansion comes amid growing worries about the massive $40.3 trillion US debt load, rising inflation, and climbing borrowing costs.
Refunds of the Trump administration's tariffs, after they were overturned, have further widened the budget gap.
The federal deficit, which occurs when government spending exceeds its revenues, rose to $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, the Treasury Department said.
This marked a 12-percent increase from the prior year, when the shortfall came in at $1.78 trillion.
A key driver of expenditures was the rising interest paid on public debt, which jumped $144 billion to a record $1.36 trillion.
Interest costs on around $32 trillion in publicly held US debt have been ballooning in recent years, and climbing bond yields have sparked further concerns.
Treasury bond yields, which influence interest rates for mortgages and auto loans, have jumped this year, with steeper borrowing costs adding to pressures that US voters face ahead of November's midterm elections.
Treasury data released Friday showed $145 billion in customs refunds over the year, primarily from tariffs, erasing significant gains from Trump's duties.
Overall, government revenues climbed by three percent to $5.40 trillion in the latest fiscal year, which ended September 30.
But spending was much higher, rising by six percent to $7.40 trillion.
War risks
The Trump administration has pledged to cut deficits and government spending since it returned to the White House last year.
Besides slashing the federal workforce and foreign aid, the Republican-controlled Congress pushed through cuts to the Medicaid health insurance scheme and moved to shrink the federal food assistance program too.
But they also extended expiring tax cuts and provided fresh funding for administration’s migrant deportation drive.
The latest data released on Friday showed that higher tax collections from individuals and customs revenues were offset by more refunds and lower corporate tax collections.
Among other sectors, spending on defence military programs increased by $48 billion, or six percent, over the year to $917 billion.
Taken together, a Treasury official estimates the US deficit-to-GDP ratio is around 6.2 percent, up from 5.8 percent last year.
This stands in contrast to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's previously stated goal of bringing the deficit down to three percent of GDP, alongside other targets like spurring economic growth of three percent.
The latest budget figures come less than three weeks before US midterm elections, where US President Trump's Republican party is fighting to retain control of Congress.
Ahead of the crucial vote, both Republicans and Democrats have raised ideas that could widen the budget shortfall further.
Democrats say they are looking to reverse Medicaid cuts and revive health care tax breaks.

Sanchez rejects criticism of Spain's migration policy: 'Words do not match reality'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:30:13 UTC
05:30:13 KST

Spain's prime minister defended the country's record on tackling irregular migration amid criticism of its mass regularisation plan, while Ursula von der Leyen called for full implementation of the EU migration and asylum pact.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Friday rejected criticism from several European leaders over Spain's migration policy and defended his government's approach to tackling irregular immigration and managing migration flows.
"If you look at the facts, at the figures - which is kind of always what happens with the far right - it's like night and day," he said in Brussels, where he is attending the European Council summit. "What is being said has nothing to do with reality (...) one thing is the blah, blah, blah and another is reality."
Sanchez was responding to comments by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, who have questioned the Spanish government's migration policies, particularly its extraordinary regularisation plan for migrants.
Sanchez drew a distinction between his disagreements with the Danish prime minister and the Czech leader's criticism, which he likened to far-right rhetoric.
"With the Danish prime minister we have disagreements, but indeed, it has nothing to do with what the prime minister of the Czech Republic said, which, by the way, sounds very much like what the far-right Vox says in Spain," he said.
Babis had accused some European leaders of being willing to "replace the population" to stay in power and warned that his country could tighten border controls to prevent migrants from arriving from other EU countries.
Stocker, meanwhile, described Spain's regularisation plan as a "bad signal", arguing that it could have consequences for the EU as a whole. Frederiksen has called on the European Commission to examine the implications of Spain's measures.
Sanchez points to Spain's record
In response to the criticism, Sanchez argued that Spain is making progress in controlling irregular arrivals and cooperating with countries of origin and transit.
"The migration and asylum pact that we secured under the Spanish presidency is working," he said, adding that Spain is "a model pupil" in the fight against irregular immigration.
The prime minister cited interceptions in the Atlantic, returns and refusals of entry at airports as examples of Spain's migration policy. He also rejected claims that Spain is part of routes used for secondary movements of migrants within the European Union.
"The reality, the data show that Spain is pursuing a very responsible policy in the fight against irregular migration, in managing regular migration flows and in cooperation with transit and origin countries," he said.
Sanchez also stressed the importance of maintaining a progressive government in Spain, arguing that "because Europe indeed needs a contrast of opinions and political positions", and urged his European partners to continue implementing the migration and asylum pact.
Von der Leyen calls for stronger external borders
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed the need to move forward with implementing the EU migration and asylum pact and strengthening cooperation between member states. She noted that irregular crossings of the EU's borders have fallen by more than 56% over the past two years.
Von der Leyen outlined three priorities for EU migration policy: fully implementing the migration and asylum pact, strengthening the management and protection of external borders, and improving preparedness for potential border crises.
She also announced that the Commission will propose strengthening Frontex, the EU's border agency, to expand its capacity to support member states when needed. She stressed that responsibility and solidarity must go hand in hand, while acknowledging that more work remains to be done.
"To succeed, it is necessary to continue acting together," von der Leyen said, as European leaders remained divided over how to manage migration and tackle irregular arrivals.
Some countries push for changes to summit conclusions
Denmark, Poland and Italy pushed for changes to the summit conclusions, including an indirect reference to Spain's plan to regularise the status of 600,000 undocumented migrants. Spain and France opposed the proposed changes.
A revised draft seen by Euronews urged member states to avoid "measures that may create incentives for illegal migration". However, the broader wording was ultimately rejected in favour of a shorter, less forceful version.
The draft also called on the European Commission to strengthen coordination between national migration policies that could affect other member states. The proposal, jointly backed by the three countries, was seen as an implicit criticism of Spain's left-wing government.
Macron backs Spain
French President Emmanuel Macron said after the summit that "ideological divisions" between EU member states over migration were making them "ineffective", while expressing support for Spain over the Ceuta crisis.
"We have had a bad debate," Macron said. "My assessment is that when we politicise this debate at the table, we create divisions. And when we are divided and fall back on national solutions, we become ineffective," he added.
Macron described the Ceuta crisis as a "humanitarian tragedy" and noted that France had not signed the letter sent to Brussels by 22 EU countries.
"Spain was the target of a hybrid attack," he said, adding: "There was no need to wait until today to know who attacked Spain just after what happened in Ceuta."

The Trap Was Only 100 Meters Wide. Russian Troops Kept Walking Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:29:46 UTC
05:29:46 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
The Trap Was Only 100 Meters Wide. Russian Troops Kept Walking Into Ukraine’s Kill Zone
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps has detailed unusually heavy Russian losses during Operation Vivaldi, which its commanders attribute to the tactical isolation of the combat zone, according to the video released on October 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In the footage, Kucher, a battalion commander in the 3rd Army Corps, claimed his unit killed more than 250 Russian troops at one location. Another commander, Zhora, explained how Ukrainian forces used the terrain to their advantage against Russian troops.
“This site is interesting because it has a small open area, about 100 meters,” Zhora stated. He noted that Russian troops did not understand Ukrainian maneuvers for a long time and kept sending reinforcements to the same spot. “He had no other option than to constantly send infantry exactly where we needed them,” he explained.
Kucher described a pattern in which Russian commanders, seeing no progress, kept ordering fresh waves forward. He recalled that a Russian soldier would emerge to film the area with his phone, and Ukrainian troops deliberately left him alone.
“The guy comes out, shoots everything on camera, we don’t touch him on purpose, he turns back, the crowd runs for 15 minutes. The crowd dies,” Kucher said of the sequence, according to the footage.
An hour later, he added, the same routine repeated, with the following wave running for 20 minutes before being destroyed. Kucher described the scene as “quite humiliating.” He also stated that Ukrainian forces knowingly avoided striking a nearby checkpoint or capture point in a small forest area, so that Russian commanders would keep feeding troops into the kill zone.
Kucher said the dead came from across Russian ranks. They included:
- artillerymen;
- assault groups;
- pilots who were rotating in or out of the area;
- about a dozen and a half special forces troops from one of the regiments.
The commanders presented isolation as the decisive factor. “We completely hid his infantry maneuvers at the tactical level, which led to additional losses and the inability to build normal defense around the green valley,” Kucher declared. “In terms of enemy losses, this is the biggest result, in fact.”
Zhora outlined the operation’s objective. “The ultimate goal was to take control of all logistical routes, cut off the forces of the enemy, which hold the defense, from possible replenishment, rotation, and some infantry maneuvers,” he wrote. He added that the aim was also to create an encirclement zone.
Zhora concluded that cooperation among all branches of the 3rd Army Corps was highly effective during the operation. In his words, it allowed the corps to work efficiently and “save a large number of our infantrymen’s lives.”
The losses come as Operation Vivaldi continues to push Russian forces back in the Donetsk region. By September 20, the 3rd Army Corps had taken full control of Drobysheve and liberated Shandryholove and Derylove, bringing the territory returned across the operation's first two seasons to 125 square kilometers.
Another 800 Russian troops were killed in that phase, pushing total losses across both seasons above 3,000 personnel. The first season alone cleared 75 square kilometers of the northern Donetsk region and retook Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, and Yarova.

The storm was located southwest of Acapulco, in the southern state of Guerrero, according to Mexico’s National Meteorological Service (SMN).

Authorities urged residents in coastal communities and areas prone to flooding and landslides to follow official weather bulletins and civil protection recommendations.
Trudy’s development comes during the eastern Pacific hurricane season, when tropical systems can bring heavy rainfall and damaging winds to Mexico’s Pacific coastline.
The SMN and the NHC continue to monitor the storm and issue updates on its intensity, movement and potential effects.

Daisy Edgar-Jones Is the Austen Heroine We Need in a Charming Sense and Sensibility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:27:24 UTC
05:27:24 KST

When news got around that a new movie version of Sense and Sensibility was in the works, cries of dismay rang forth from Bath to Brooklyn. How could anyone dare try to top Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation, penned by—and starring, alongside Kate Winslet— Emma Thompson? But the idea that fine adaptations of great books need to be stopping points, rather than springboards, is alarming by itself. Why is a new adaptation of any Jane Austen novel such a bad thing? There are always new movie audiences, eager for their own fresh take. And just as important, why shouldn’t another generation of actors have a crack at these roles? Our ability to stream anything we want, whenever we want, hasn’t necessarily made us more adventurous; sometimes it’s just a way of clinging to familiar favorites at the expense of welcoming anything new. Austen herself, with her aversion to sentimentality, would have disapproved.
Then what would she make of Georgia Oakley’s amiable, if occasionally a little sluggish, reading of her debut novel, published anonymously in 1811? It’s hard to say for sure, but there’s nothing that’s offensive about this new Sense and Sensibility, and plenty that’s lovely. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles play Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, sisters in a close-knit family whose temperamental differences temporarily drive them apart. As the film opens, Elinor and Marianne, along with their mother (Caitríona Balfe) and younger sister Margaret (Bodhi Rae Breathnach), are just learning that they’ll soon have to vacate the airy, comfortable house they’ve called home for years. The girls’ father has just died; his property will not go to his daughters, but to his son from a previous marriage, John (Tom Brooke), who nevertheless hopes to do right by making sure his father's second family well provided for. But his disagreeable wife Fanny (Stacy Martin), feels differently, and to maintain their pride, the Dashwood women choose to move into far more modest quarters, in an arrangement brokered by a family friend, Mrs. Jennings (a blissfully dithery Fiona Shaw).
Mrs. Jennings is also an unrepentant meddler, and she believes she can easily marry off the two eldest Dashwood girls. Ever-sensible Elinor, who never asks for much, has already met, and fallen for, Edward Ferrars (George MacKay), Fanny’s brother, as kind and modest as Fanny is arrogant. And Marianne, a dreamer who lives for music and books, has her sights set on flirty, fun Mr. Willoughby (Frank Dillane): He loves to laugh and sing and dance, and Marianne is sure he’s perfect for her, though another potential suitor, the stalwart and rather dull Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum), is also circling. If you’ve never read Austen’s lively and perceptive novel—or seen either Lee’s 1995 version or the 2008 BBC miniseries adaptation—you’re left to guess which men the sisters will end up with, which is just one of the story’s delights.
But as always with Austen, there’s more to love than romance: The economics of “making a good match” are always, by necessity, lurking somewhere in these characters’ minds. In the case of the sisters Marianne and Elinor—one too dreamy, the other perhaps not dreamy enough—the differences in what they look for in a partner are almost enough to pull them apart. Oakley, who previously directed the 2022 drama Blue Jean, has a deft touch with the material and a deep respect for the English countryside setting. There are drowsy closeups of wildflowers, and shots of placidly grazing deer; a country dance feels lively and lived-in, contrasted with a later ball, set in London, where the steps are more formal and regimented—Oakley leaves no doubt as to which is more fun. Shot by Arnaud Potier, the film has a handsome, genteel look. And if at times the movie comes off as a bit decorous and stiff, the actors, particularly Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles, do their best to keep the proceedings whirring. Creed-Miles shows that there’s a slightly self-centered quality to Marianne’s romantic preoccupations—she takes pride in wearing her heart on her sleeve, though in some sense it’s also a means of getting her way. And yet as Creed-Miles plays her, it’s impossible to dislike her. When Marianne become truly hurt, we hurt for her, thanks to the bruised anguish in Creed-Miles’ eyes.
And Edgar-Jones plays Elinor, the practical sister, with just the right amount of subdued fire. Elinor is the one who always matches her expectations with reality, and as much as she loves Edward Ferrars, she doesn’t put up much of a fight when she learns she might have to give him up. Edgar-Jones gives us clues to Elinor’s submerged longing, but only in flashes. And in a pivotal scene, where Marianne accuses Elinor, angrily, of “always being right,” we can see how wounded she is, even as she recognizes that Marianne is onto something: Elinor would rather be correct than look foolish. Edgar-Jones plays Elinor as reserved without making her recessive; we can see the ways in which she wants to want more. In an age of lowered expectations—for movies, for romance, for just about everything—maybe she’s the Austen heroine we need, ready to break out of the box she’s drawn around herself. Austen knew what she was talking about, and time hasn’t eroded her wisdom.

Trump's team is in chaos as midterms enter final stretch

Trump’s team is in chaos as midterms enter final stretch
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Trump’s press secretary, Katie Zacharia, resigned Friday, her fifth day on the job.
- Public anxiety over corruption in government under the Trump administration has surpassed the economy as the top concern of voters, according a Fox News poll.
WASHINGTON — President Trump bypassed his White House chief of staff last week in selecting Katie Zacharia as his press secretary and chief messenger, triggering days of scathing headlines about her credentials and abilities before her ignominious resignation on Friday.
Susie Wiles, that senior-most aide ostensibly in charge of the president’s team, is facing his scrutiny over a different set of problems: widespread public anxiety over corruption in government under the Trump administration. The issue has surpassed the economy as the top concern of voters entering next month’s election, according a Fox News poll released this week.
Marco Rubio, the president’s secretary of State and national security advisor, has been silent on Trump’s decision to cut a deal with Moscow on diesel sales that could fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine. The president’s poll numbers have been below water across the board, but especially so on foreign policy, where over two-thirds of Americans disapprove of his job performance and support Kyiv’s fight for freedom.
And on Thursday, the president was forced to reverse a course set out by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon to live-stream the execution of a convicted mass shooter by firing squad.
Kimberly Guilfoyle has resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece amid allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure.
In the final stretch of the 2026 midterms, nearly two weeks out from election day, a White House that has enjoyed relative stability over the past two years has returned to the state of disarray that characterized much of Trump’s early political career, anticipating sweeping losses to Democrats in the House and Senate.
Staff upheaval is expected as officials brace for a blame game over Republican performance, with some distancing themselves from what they see as a fading political movement.
Polls suggest that Republicans are likely to lose control of the House, setting up two years of relentless congressional probes through the twilight of the Trump era, and that Democrats could even flip the Senate, winning in ruby red states from Ohio to Alaska.
It is historically a time for closing arguments, when politicians deliver their final pitches to voters in neat, disciplined packages.
Yet Trump’s campaign blitz across the country in recent weeks has generated a muddled message, dismissing the importance of the election itself at the risk of depressing Republican votes, overshadowing local candidates seeking distance from his record and touting an economy unrecognizable to most Americans.
The president’s selection of Zacharia, who lasted just five days on the job, raised fresh questions about his message discipline in the final stretch.
And infighting within the White House has reinforced a narrative among political pundits that Democratic gains are a fait accompli, despite Zacharia, in her first and only press briefing, foretelling of Republican energy and excitement “never seen before in the history of midterms thanks to President Trump.”
Election officials across the country fear that, anticipating inevitable losses, Trump may be laying the ground to challenge the authenticity of the election results themselves.
“You know, this is the only guy that — it’s ‘promises made, promises kept,’ but he did more things than he promised,” Trump said Thursday, referring to himself in the third person. “I think we did. We did much more than we promised.”
The extent of the coming West Wing shakeup could be extensive, reaching into a Cabinet that has had far less turnover than Trump experienced in his first term.
Zacharia is the second senior official forced out by Trump in just three days, after Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of one of Trump’s sons who served as U.S. ambassador to Greece, was revealed by the Wall Street Journal to have asked a Trump donor to pay off her $100,000 credit card bill.
Now, the president has begun asking political allies and donors about Wiles’ job performance, according to a recent Politico report, and several top administration officials are vying for her role, anticipating her resignation after the elections next month.
Trump’s got a diesel problem and not even Russia can save him. Could California be the answer?
The conclusion of the midterms will also kick off the start of the 2028 presidential election season, when Republican hopefuls — including many from Trump’s Cabinet — are expected to launch exploratory committees.
“We have to get through the midterms first,” Trump said at the end of August, asked about Hegseth reportedly considering a run. “I bet there’s a lot of people considering it that you don’t know about. You have a lot of people.”
The party of incumbent presidents regularly loses seats in midterm elections, and it is common for presidents to shake up their staffs halfway through a term.
But the last time a term-limited Republican president faced voters in midterm elections, in 2006, Democrats swept into power in both houses of Congress — and President George W. Bush’s political capital never recovered.
That year, 37% of voters said they approved of Bush’s job performance. Polls published this month by AP and Reuters have found Trump already below that threshold.
In the GOP presidential primaries that followed, candidates jockeying to replace Bush distanced themselves from his legacy. He ultimately left office with an approval rating of 25%.

Morocco's King Mohammed VI appoints new government
Morocco's King Mohammed VI formally appointed on Friday the members of his country's new government, led for the first time in its history by a woman prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri.
Her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) came out on top in September elections, and has entered into a coalition with the right-wing Istiqlal party and two smaller left-wing parties. Together they hold 210 of the parliament's 395 seats.
Thirteen out of 31 ministers from the previous government were retained in the incoming cabinet, including Nasser Bourita as Minister of Foreign Affairs and Abdelouafi Laftit as Minister of the Interior.
PAM newcomer Fouzi Lekjaa -- a budget minister in the outgoing government better known as the head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation -- has been promoted to economy minister.
The new government also includes seven women, counting the prime minister, as did the previous one.
Following her royal audience on Friday, Mansouri touted an "ambitious government programme that can meet citizens' expectations".
September's vote, which saw the lowest turnout in nearly 20 years, was marked by concerns about the cost of living, employment and inequality.
The incoming government will have to address those concerns while also preparing for the 2030 World Cup, which will be co-hosted with Spain and Portugal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has no interest in peace negotiations in any form, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, warning European and NATO countries that Moscow’s ambitions extend well beyond Ukraine’s borders.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels Friday, Oct. 16, Zelensky dismissed the Kremlin’s portrayal of its strikes on Ukraine as merely retaliatory, describing it as a “parody” of a genuine willingness to see the war end.

“Putin wants to destroy us. He does not respect us, our sovereignty or our territorial integrity. He truly believes that we are not a country, not a nation,” Zelensky said.
“Do you really believe that the eastern part of our country is enough for him [Putin]? Then why, when the full-scale invasion began, did he go for Kyiv? Is that Donbas? No, it is the capital. Without the capital, there is no state,” he continued.
The war could spill beyond Ukraine’s borders
In recent months, Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign – from espionage, cyber attacks and drone incursions – has increased to the point that several EU members are saying that the continent is already at war with the Kremlin.
Russian diplomats have made serious threats to the Baltic states in particular, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed that European preparations for a possible war with Russia could provoke one.
2 Killed, 6 Injured in Russian Strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Region
“This position could turn out to be a self-fulfilling prophecy,” Lavrov said during the 81st United General Nations Assembly (UNGA) in New York late September, where 51 countries have separately signed a joint letter urging Moscow to agree to an immediate ceasefire.
So, it does not come as a surprise that Zelensky also questioned where Russia would stop should it achieve the military objective it set in Ukraine.
He pointed to the growing number of Russian drones crossing into European and NATO airspace, accusing European governments of avoiding responding forcefully to individual incursions out of fear of escalation.
In his view, the countries will practically be forced to take the threat seriously once Russia begins using ballistic and cruise missiles, alongside drones to violate NATO’s airspace, as it already does in Ukraine.
His warning came a day after Romania said Russian drones had entered its airspace three times in less than 24 hours, as attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea killed eight people.
Diesel deal could open the door to wider sanctions relief
Zelensky criticized US President Donald Trump’s diesel agreement on Oct. 9 with Moscow that allowed imports of Russian diesel to enter the global markets. Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
He warned that the deal could set a precedent for further concessions, predicting that gas deals would follow, gradually extending sanctions relief to Russia’s banking system, chemical industry and sanctioned individuals.
Ukraine had no choice but to oppose such steps diplomatically, since no one else would defend Kyiv’s interests, Zelensky said.
Trump’s move came while Ukraine’s negotiating delegation was holding talks with Trump’s administration in Miami, hoping to reach a breakthrough and end Russia’s aggression.
Only three weeks earlier, on Sept. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law. His latest decisions appeared to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s military-industrial complex, as well as networks close to Putin himself.
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators signed a joint letter on Oct. 13, urging Trump to rescind his diesel agreement with Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.
Starlink speed still not fully restored, Zelensky said
Addressing recent restrictions on Ukraine’s Starlink terminals, Zelensky said the service had not been switched off but slowed, preventing Ukrainian forces from shooting down a number of Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones that target civilians.
He rejected claims that Ukraine uses Starlink for attacks inside Russia. Instead, he said, the system supports interceptor drones, mid-range strikes on Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory, and drone deliveries of food and water to soldiers who spend weeks or months on the front line. All three were disrupted while the restrictions were in place.
According to Zelensky, speeds are now recovering but have not returned to previous levels.
The restrictions took effect overnight on Oct. 13-14 after the US aerospace giant’s CEO Elon Musk tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (roughly 100 miles per hour) without prior warning.
Musk claimed that speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals are set by the US military, including Trump himself, not the company.
Washington has not taken responsibility for the restrictions.

Meet the Task Force Trying to Turn Golden Dome Into Reality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:10:24 UTC
05:10:24 KST

A Golden Dome task force established under U.S. Northern Command earlier this year has a broad remit, which includes fielding the capability to defend the U.S. against missile and drone attacks, its leaders said this week. Some of the primary focuses right now are ensuring Golden Dome can defend itself against cyber threats and that it will work in the real world.
NORTHCOM established the group, dubbed Joint Task Force-Gold, in January. It is led by the head of the Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command, Lt. Gen. John Rafferty, with Army Col. Kevin Stonerook as his deputy.
Speaking with reporters Oct. 14 at the annual Association of the U.S. Army conference in Washington D.C., Stonerook said the task force has about 100 personnel based at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The team works closely with SMDC to integrate and coordinate Golden Dome capabilities across the air and missile defense enterprise.
Practically, that includes a range of responsibilities, including leading site surveys for future Golden Dome locations—the first confirmed hub is in Fort Story, Va.—and providing expert operators to inform the architecture. Stonerook said that lately one of the group’s major focuses has been on building a team to develop a defensive cyber capability for Golden Dome, or GDA.
“We are helping put together the team of teams, all the different stakeholders—be that vendors and other government agencies—to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA,” he said. “That’s one of the main things that we’re really focused on.”
The Pentagon envisions Golden Dome as a sweeping network of sensors, satellites, and interceptors designed to protect the United States from an array of air and missile threats—from drones to ballistic missiles to hypersonic weapons. The architecture will depend on a command-and-control network to connect and orchestrate its many parts. Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein has described the C2 system as the program’s “glue layer.”
The Army’s Space and Missile Defense Command plays a key role in the Golden Dome plan. The command already has an important role in operating the limited anti-missile defense for the U.S. homeland that was first fielded more than 20 years ago. It is responsible for approximately 40 Ground-Based Midcourse Defense interceptors that protect America from ballistic missile attacks as well as the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System surrounding Washington.
“We have the most experienced air defense force we’ve ever had,” Rafferty said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s a mission that we do already with the ground-based interceptors in Alaska and under SMDC, and in the defense of the National Capital Region and other key locations in the homeland. We’re going to scale that. We have people who do that 24/7, 365, and have, for many years: an incredible base to build on.”
The Army is also responsible for missile defense across the globe. Iran’s attacks on U.S. forces in the Middle East have taxed and tested the Army’s THAAD and Patriot ballistic missile defense batteries. The U.S. has sent Army air defenders and air defense systems from Europe and Asia to the Middle East and has expended hundreds of Patriot and THAAD interceptors to combat Iranian ballistic missiles, which have become increasingly more advanced. The Army, in turn, has tried to learn from the flurry of attacks.
Golden Dome will use some existing technology, but its overall goal of creating a comprehensive missile defense shield will require cutting-edge and novel tech too. Joint Task Force-Gold is seeking to bring real-world experience into the picture.
“They’re in a sprint to deliver materiel,” Rafferty said. “We better be ready to train it, to man it, to have the right organization, the sustainment for it.”
Rafferty compared bringing those issues to ones he faced earlier in his career leading the Army’s Long Range Precision Fires Cross-Functional Team, the Army’s effort to modernize surface-to-surface weapons. He wanted to deliver equipment “as quickly as we could.” But personnel needed to learn how to use it. “The rest of everybody was sprinting to, ‘Hey, how are we going to fight with this thing?’”
Likewise, JTF-Gold is to attempt to ease the transition of Golden Dome from concept to reality. By working with the Pentagon’s Golden Dome office—officially titled the Direct Reporting Program Manager—to develop capability, Rafferty says JTF-Gold’s goal is to examine how the system will work on a practical basis.
In support of the Pentagon’s push to field an initial Golden Dome capability by 2028, JTF-Gold has also hosted a series of planning sprints, bringing together all of the companies and agencies working on the program “to really focus on operationalizing GDA,” Stonerook said. The task force held the first of these events in February in Colorado Springs, Colo., and drew more than 300 people. The next one is scheduled for late October.
The task force has also been involved in the large-scale test events run by the Golden Dome program office. Over the past year, the program has conducted at least two tests, which officials say were successful, though they haven’t discussed the objectives or outcome in detail.
Rafferty said the tests helped JTF-Gold better understand what it might take to one day operate the capability.
“Some of the testing events that the DPRM’s office has run have been really instructive about the types of soldiers that we need to man this,” Rafferty said. JTF-Gold is “bringing those issues to light and then creating opportunities for learning about the systems as they’re coming out, so the teams can lean forward on what the training package is or what kind of individuals we need.”
“We have the most experienced, combat-proven air defense force in the world ready to come and help man an expanded Gordon Dome from America,” Rafferty said.

'Finish what we started': After student protests, France braces for return of the Yellow Vests
