'Finish what we started': After student protests, France braces for return of the Yellow Vests
An online movement against rising fuel prices has gained momentum ahead of planned nationwide demonstrations on October 17 with former Yellow Vest figures set to join the protests in support of high-school students. Some are drawing parallels between the latest action and the 2018 cost-of-living protests that rattled President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office.
Issued on:
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
After weeks of student protests, is France about to witness a resurgence of the Yellow Vest movement?
Protests, roundabout blockades and gatherings in front of gas stations and oil depots are among the actions planned for Saturday’s nationwide demonstrations.
A map published on Thursday on the website 17octobregiletjaune.net listed more than 1,000 events plannd around the country to denounce rising fuel prices and support high-school students who have been protesting for nearly a month to demand better classroom conditions.
Read more'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing
The initiative began with a viral TikTok video posted by a young man frustrated by rising prices at the pump. It was later backed by left-wing politicians including Communist Party leader Fabien Roussel and Green leader Marine Tondelier.
Saturday's planned demonstrations were not initially linked to the original Yellow Vest movement, which began in 2018 with widespread protests over rising fuel prices before growing into a broader revolt against economic inequality that drew tens of thousands onto the streets. The movement takes its name from the fluorescent yellow high-visibility vests that French law requires drivers to carry in their vehicles and which protesters wore during demonstrations.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Some of the Yellow Vests' former leading figures were initially wary of the latest protest action, including Maxime 'Fly Rider' Nicolle, who recently announced that he would travel to Paris to demonstrate after changing his mind about participating.
"No Yellow Vest was behind the (October 17 protests). Now, as soon as people talk about fuel and discontent, they are immediately labelled 'Yellow Vests'. It's almost become a brand," said Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent figure in the Yellow Vest movement who lost an eye after being struck by a rubber-ball grenade during a protest in 2019.
During the 2018-2019 protests, nearly two-dozen people suffered the loss of an eye, mainly after being hit by rubber bullets fired by police. In total, 2,500 protesters and 1,800 police officers were injured over the course of a year. France's crowd-control tactics drew widespread criticism, including from the United Nations, and have come under renewed scrutiny amid the high-school student protests.
“We didn't coordinate beforehand with other prominent figures to call for protests but we all had the same reaction when we saw the police violence against high-school students,” François Boulo, another prominent Yellow Vest figure, told AFP.
'More serious than back then'
Rodrigues sees Saturday's demonstration as a continuation of the high-school student protests, saying students have faced police “repression” similar to that experienced by the Yellow Vests.
Read moreSevere injuries at French student protests draw scrutiny to police tactics
Police meanwhile have opened internal investigations into 36 claims of officer violence against protesters, including four children who were allegedly "mutilated" by explosive weapons and six who suffered "significant injuries." Other complaints included physical blows, insults, and alleged sexual assault.
Rodrigues said the protests reflected shared concerns over the future of workers, families and pensioners facing rising consumer and fuel prices. “But we are also talking about the future of our high-school students and young people as a whole, with dilapidated schools, staff shortages and overcrowded classrooms," he said.
"We are all connected by this common thread. Ultimately, the Yellow Vests' demands have become more pressing because the situation is even more serious than it was back then," he added.
A different landscape from 2018
Activist Sophie Tissier also sees parallels between the 2018.protests and Saturday's mobilisation. She was the first to officially register Yellow Vest demonstrations with the Paris police prefecture during the 2018 movement – a strategy that was intended to bring the protests into the mainstream, but that drew criticism from within the group.
For Saturday, she said she had registered a demonstration on the Champs-Élysées, as she did at the height of the Yellow Vest protests.
Read moreA year of insurgency: How Yellow Vests left ‘indelible mark’ on French politics
“This movement is entirely legitimate. French people are exhausted,” Tissier said. “They've had enough of the dismantling of public services. The standard of living has dropped dramatically with the rise in energy and fuel prices. And then there's a deep disgust with a political class riddled with scandals.”
Tissier said that the root of the problem is "a dysfunctional political system".
"There is no separation of powers. We claim to live in a healthy democracy and republic. In reality, we don't at all,” she said, recalling the Yellow Vests' demand for greater participatory democracy through a citizens' initiative referendum, known in France as the RIC.
But original Yellow Vests also acknowledge differences between the current protests and the movement that emerged in 2018.
“The Yellow Vests were never co-opted by a political party because most of the time, as soon as (politicians) showed up, they were immediately kicked out,” Rodrigues said. “Today, the high-school students are quite closely guided by certain political parties. So, the framework is a little more institutional compared with the spontaneous demonstrations we were used to organising.”
Read moreFrench student protesters are being 'exploited' by political forces, Macron says
Uncertainty over turnout
Environmental groups and a farmer's union have also called on people to join the protests on Saturday.
However, the hard-left CGT (General Confederation of Labour) union has taken a more cautious approach, saying it would take part "wherever the conditions are met" while keeping its focus on November 5, when France's main trade unions have called for strikes.
Tissier said she did not yet see a genuine convergence between the different protest movements and the high-school students. After attending Tuesday's demonstration, she said there was no “real cohesion”, criticising what she described as attempts by the radical left, “from the Communist Party to France Unbowed”, to co-opt the movement.
With October 17 approaching, it remains unclear whether the enthusiasm on social media will translate into significant turnout, particularly as France's autumn school holidays begin.
Priscilla Ludosky, whose 2018 petition calling for lower fuel prices at the pump gathered more than 1 million signatures and helped spark the Yelloow Vest protests, is sceptical.
“People often say our movement was spontaneous. Not at all. It may have seemed disorganized …but we had been building momentum around the issue for more than six months with my petition, then connecting people across France. When we sent the media a map showing 700 gatherings announced on Facebook, it became tangible,” she said.
“Here, no one is putting themselves forward behind these calls. We don't know who to follow or how large October 17 will be,” Ludosky told Reporterre.
A source close to the interior minister said around 250 protest actions could take place nationwide on Saturday.
Rodrigues is also cautious about the prospects of a movement on the scale of the one that emerged in November 2018. However, he still hopes to see a resurgence of the Yellow Vests.
“As Yellow Vests, we still carry the frustration of not having finished the fight. Perhaps we were waiting for a new wave of popular mobilisation that we could join, so that we could finish what we started.”

AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push

AOC transfers $1m to Michigan candidate El-Sayed in progressive push
Progressive stalwart, who is seen as potential 2028 candidate, says she wants to combat ‘smears’ against El-Sayed.
United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1m to support Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in a major progressive push for the upstart politician.
Ocasio-Cortez, who has become a progressive stalwart since her surprise 2018 congressional victory, confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and a speech in Michigan. The transfer was first reported by the New York Times.
The lawmaker pointed to political attacks against El-Sayed, a large portion of which have focused on his Muslim faith, his Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine.
“I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement, in reference to the November 3 congressional midterm election. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.”
Speaking at an event in the Detroit area, Ocasio added that she transferred the money from her own campaign to show “the cavalry is coming”.
“And the only reason I’m doing that is because I see the energy of each and every one of you stepping up to make an effort,” she said.
The move comes as Ocasio-Cortez has been campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan, joining him on a bus tour of the conservative-leaning Upper Peninsula area before hosting three events on Friday in the state’s largest city, Detroit.
El Sayed’s populist progressive message has gained traction with voters in the state, where he currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of high-quality polls.
The support from Ocasio Cortez, who is weighing a potential 2028 presidential candidacy, also underscores a wider effort by progressives to court disaffected Trump voters. The pair highlighted economic issues while on the trail in the midwestern state.
Trump’s approval ratings are at a career low ahead of the midterm vote. A slate of recent polls has shown widespread public disapproval of Trump’s handling of the US economy and the knock-on effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Recent polls have also shown an appetite for a more comprehensive change in US government, signalling a potential opening for candidates running outside of the establishment of both major parties.
An AP-NORC poll released this week found that 80 percent of respondents said they supported either a “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in how the country is run.
Speaking alongside Ocasio-Cortez on Friday, progressive House Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which raises and allocates funds for Senate candidates, to make “an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates” like El-Sayed, Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon and Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom.
El-Sayed, who received an early endorsement from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, has also recently been embraced by a handful of more centrist Democrats, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Sanders donated $250,000 to El-Sayed’s campaign, CNN reports.
Big spending
The new financial support from Ocasio-Cortez, which was given to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, arrived as the Michigan Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the state’s history, topping $268m as of October 15, according to the Detroit Free Press.
El-Sayed, meanwhile, outpaced Rogers in fundraising from July 1 to September 30, bringing in $30.6m compared to Rogers’ $9.6m. Still, Rogers’ campaign had more cash on hand as of September 30, with $6.5m compared to El-Sayed’s $3.8 million.
Michigan is among the key Senate races that could determine control of the chamber for the final two years of US President Donald Trump’s term.
Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member body.

Jillaroos lived up to their end of the bargain, but fans need to follow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:06:12 UTC
05:06:12 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Jillaroos lived up to their end of the bargain in Rugby League World Cup opener. Now fans need to follow
Seeing the Jillaroos in action is a rare privilege — a collection of the best women's rugby league players in the world, in the sport's global showpiece, on home soil.
The three-time defending champions opened their World Cup at Western Sydney Stadium with a flexing 40-0 win over Samoa, in a campaign that should engage and excite Australians and the vast diaspora of the other competing nations.
While that was the case for the earlier men's game between Samoa and France, with 13,174 fans, mostly representing western Sydney's large Samoan community, they left in large numbers at the end of that game.
And there were very few supporters — Samoan or Australian — left by the end of the women's clash, in a disappointing sight for an event of this stature.
This is not a new dilemma for women's sport. When and where to play, whether to have double headers, how best to engage existing fan bases and draw in new ones?
Women's State of Origin has been a good example of elevating the women's game in its own way, standing separately to the men's series, often in smaller venues, but packing them with passionate fans who are there only to watch the women. And drawing big numbers on TV too.
The World Cup presents a different challenge, with Australia currently in a league of its own on the field and another trophy considered by many as a fait accompli.
But the world is starting to catch up, and as the tournament progresses over the next month, it would be a shame for the event to go under the radar.
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner summed it up simply afterwards.
"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, and particularly this Rugby League World Cup. We've got a lot of talented women across all of the teams," she said.
"Stay and support that and the growth. Something really cool is happening in this generation of sport with our ladies, and you're going to miss it.
"There's history making moments over this World Cup, no doubt, and want to see our fans, particularly in the green and gold, to be a part of that. But also just in general, come and have a look."
Samoa coach Frank Pritchard suggested the late 8pm kick off didn't help, and the women were keen to play before the men.
"Our fans and our supporters will always stick through it and and stay there," he said.
"I've seen a lot of blue jerseys out there. We had plenty of support, that's for sure."
Jillaroos captain Isabelle Kelly was less concerned with the crowd, than with ensuring the Jillaroos achieve what they set out to at this tournament. And all signs point to a four-peat.
Jillaroos just warming up
It was a straightforward win for the Australians, who were not at their ruthless, rampaging best, but instead showed they are warming to the task, and will likely ignite as the tournament progresses.
Five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher had an impressive first outing in the green and gold. She was player of the match on debut, continuing the form that saw her guide the Sydney Roosters to the NRLW Premiership.
"Her kicking game was amazing. And she took her opportunities when she had them as well," Skinner said.
"So couldn't get better than that in a World Cup debut for the Jillaroos, become part of a legacy piece, and you get player of the match. So really proud of her."
Olivia Kernick made crucial gains through the middle, Tamika Upton pulled the strings in bursts without being at her fully devastating best, and Jaime Chapman, Julia Robinson, and Jess Sergis surged as needed, with all seven tries scored by different players.
There were scrappy moments though, times where Samoa's defence jolted, and the visitors found ways to cut through the Australians when going direct.
Freedom Crichton Ropati's bone cruncher on Tiana Penitani Gray in the dying minutes was a highlight, epitomising Fetu Samoa's dedication to valiantly protecting their line, even with the result long gone.
Leading 28-0 at half time, the Jillaroos were restricted to just two tries after the break.
Overall, it was an effort that was enough for the Jillaroos to be content, without being complacent, and for Samoa to find light at the end of the tunnel, rather than wallowing in darkness.
"We spoke about pride in the jersey and what it takes to be here, sea of blue, effort on effort, and definitely showed that in the second half," Pritchard said.
"That second half proved to us that competing and staying in the fight is more than just a footy game."
Starting to see it
Athletes often speak of the honour of representing their country and their family on the world stage.
But for many of the Pasifika nations competing at this tournament, filled with players from the diaspora in Australia and New Zealand, it hits a little different.
As with the men, tears streamed down the faces of the Fetu Samoa players during the national anthem.
And they continued afterwards, not of disappointment, but of deep understanding of what it means to be here.
"What our ladies are doing for our young girls at home with sport in general, especially rugby league, is massive," Pritchard said.
"It's something that our girls can gravitate towards."
It was an especially meaningful game for Evania Isa'ako, who has previously represented Australia.
"For me, it was not just coming and playing and putting on this jersey; it was being able to learn [about the culture]," she said.
"So off the field, culturally, everything that we've done. All the work that Frank's put in behind the scenes… outsourced people to come in and teach us, that's the really important stuff behind the scenes that people don't see."
They might not see it yet, but come the end of the tournament, maybe there'll be more eyes watching.

Katie Zacharia Was Linked to an AI Rare-Earths Startup. It’s Even Weirder Than It Sounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:05:08 UTC
05:05:08 KST

Before being fired five days into her stint as White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia spent much of the day attempting to explain her past.
Throughout her brief tenure, Zacharia’s resume was the source of much intrigue. Foremost was the fact that despite claiming to be an attorney for much of her career, she never actually passed the California bar, as she was eventually forced to admit. Another element of her professional history, WIRED reported, was a role as an affiliate marketer for Beachbody, a fitness MLM.
WIRED has now uncovered new details of her relationship to an AI-powered rare earths mining operation called NRED Intelligent Mining, which counts former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem as a strategic advisor.
On June 24, NRED—then known as NovaRed Mining, a small copper-and-gold exploration company in Vancouver, Canada—issued a release to share that Zacharia, who had left a role as a DHS spokesperson two months before, was joining the advisory board alongside Noem.
In her new role, according to the release, Zacharia would provide “strategic guidance” to NovaRed’s board of directors as it advanced exploration projects as well as “emerging artificial intelligence initiatives.”
It does not appear, though, that she ever worked there. When asked on Friday whether she was still on the board, she said, “That was fake,” and referred WIRED to Sam Amsterdam, a “strategic marketing and media engagement professional” whose clients have included the government of Kazakhstan and political parties in Georgia, Nigeria, and Zimbabwe.
“That release was not approved by Ms. Zacharia and was issued without her consent,” says Amsterdam, whose brother is listed as a member of NRED management on the company’s website and said he was speaking as a friend and colleague of Zacharia, not a representative. “I know all that to be factual.” He quickly added that while there had been discussions of her joining the company, she hadn’t actually done so.
Valentin Saitarli, who was NRED’s chief technology officer and says he is onboarding as CEO, confirmed that there were discussions about a role, but said that it “never materialized,” adding, “It was a bit like signing up for a gym but never actually going for a workout.” Describing NRED, Saitarli says, ”We go full robots and AI.”
Despite Amsterdam’s understanding that it had been withdrawn, the press release claiming Zacharia was joining the company remained on NRED’s website as of Friday. An archived version of their website showed Zacharia listed as management as of at least July.
When WIRED asked Saitarli about this, he said that the site was being updated.
Zacharia, whose NovaRed role was announced eight days after Noem’s appointment was announced, worked under Noem as DHS’s deputy assistant press secretary for public affairs for about a month, and was reported to have close ties with de facto DHS chief of staff Corey Lewandowski. (She denied any such ties to The Daily Mail.)
The announcement that Noem was joining the advisory board of a Canadian mining company triggered an outcry among Canadians, who pointed to past statements she made referring to Canada as the “51st state.” At that time The Globe and Mail described NovaRed as “a copper and gold exploration company that generates no revenue.” The paper noted that in January, NoraRed was holding only $65,689 in cash, which the company said “wouldn’t be enough to cover all of its expected expenses for the next 12 months.”
But around the spring, something changed. NovaRed began stacking its advisory board not with geologists and technical consultants—which would be typical for a junior mining company—but with heavy hitters with ties to the defense sector, MAGA, and other international entities.
Earlier this month, NRED announced that it was pivoting away from its flagship Wilmac Copper-Gold Project, and putting all its resources into developing and commercializing “MetalCore,” its “ AI-assisted mineral exploration platform.”
“I want to build a new generation of robotics and mining,” Saitarli tells WIRED. “Do we want to get stuck in the Stone Age or horses age? No, we want to live on Mars, spend time in hotels in space, have a wedding party on the moon…We will bring robotics and AI to global mining and beyond our planet, hopefully.”
Phil Ehr, a retired US Navy commander who is running for Congress as a Democrat in Florida, was brought into NovaRed earlier this year. “I know nothing about mining. I know nothing about commodities,” Ehr tells WIRED in a phone call. “But I do know that we need more copper. I do know that we need more critical minerals.” He had only been at the company for a couple of months when, he said, he was blindsided by NovaRed’s announcement that Kristi Noem and “another DHS spokesperson”—whom he recalls being Zacharia—had also been brought onto the advisory board.
“To the best of my knowledge, [Zacharia] came at the same time as Kristi Noem did without any consultation to me and was just like, boom, there,” recalls Ehr.
Noem, who did not immediately reply to requests for comment, was fresh off overseeing the disastrous ICE occupation in Minneapolis, and Ehr didn’t want to be associated with her. “So I asked the company, “Why is Kristi Noem here? I just can't work with her because she is so controversial. We are on different sides of what's right and wrong in, in the federal government,” says Ehr.
He thought it was odd that NovaRed seemed to be stacking its ranks with people who, like him, didn’t know very much about the mining industry. He expected some geologists in the mix, or technical consultants. Instead, some of the other people hired included Gregory Fedun, who previously “served as a key advisor to the United Arab Emirates’ Al Mualla Royal Family on a range of international projects,” and media executive Lee Caplin, coproducer of HBO’s True Detective series. Ehr resigned from the advisory board not long after Noem joined.
While she was attempting to clarify the nature of her relationship to NRED, Zacharia was also tending to other matters. On Thursday evening, while she still held her position as White House press secretary, Zacharia reached out to a WIRED reporter to suggest they contact fitness influencer named Jenelle Summers for “clarity” on Beachbody, the MLM she was previously affiliated with and which Summer brought her into.
Summers said she didn’t recall much about Zacharia—whom, she said, she met online—other than that “she was always kind to me and someone that was into fitness and believed in the products and programs.”
“To my recollections,” she added, “she didn't do much with it.” Summers rejected the idea that she had been involved in a “pyramid scheme,” which is how Zacharia had characterized the company to WIRED. ”That's kind of old school thinking,” Summers said. “It was a network marketing business model.”
“I don't have any comment on that other than to say she's always been kind to me,” she said when asked what she made of Zacharia’s rise to prominence.
Zacharia did not respond to requests for comment on her firing. When asked if he had comment on her having been let go, Amsterdam told a WIRED reporter, “Well, that’s news to me!”

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia will continue launching strikes against Ukrainian defense enterprises and logistics centers, Russian President Vladimir Putin said while visiting an auxiliary command post of the Joint Force.
He stressed that the establishment of a buffer zone will not be open to discussion with Kiev and thanked Russian troops fighting to liberate Dobropolye and Alexeyevo-Drushkovka in the Donetsk People’s Republic (DPR).

Successes

The liberation of Dobropolye "opens a direct route toward the DPR’s borders."

BRUSSELS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Union (EU) leaders concluded a two-day summit in Brussels on Friday with differences remaining over the bloc's next long-term budget, while outlining measures to ease soaring energy costs.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that the latest negotiating framework for the 2028-2034 EU budget would cut spending flexibility by 50 percent compared with the current budget, leaving 99.5 percent of funds predetermined.
"This proposal puts us in a straitjacket," she said at a press conference, stressing the need for greater flexibility to respond to future crises.
European Council President Antonio Costa said leaders aimed to conclude budget negotiations by year-end, pledging to accelerate work on new EU revenue sources while keeping national contributions reasonable.
On energy, von der Leyen said the EU planned to extend its temporary state aid framework, postpone certain obligations under the Methane Regulation by one year and launch a strategic dialogue on European refining capacity.
The Commission also planned to strengthen joint energy purchasing by aggregating demand and engaging a market operator to buy energy supplies.
Von der Leyen stressed the importance of reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels through nuclear power, renewables and improved electricity grids.
"Last year, we installed 80 gigawatts of renewable capacity, but six times more capacity is still waiting to be connected," she said.
On Ukraine, Costa said EU leaders had asked the Commission to propose ways to address Kyiv's additional financing needs for 2027, following President Volodymyr Zelensky's request for another 70 billion euros (78 billion U.S. dollars). ■

Sleep loss reduces muscle endurance by rewiring brain networks, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:00:11 UTC
05:00:11 KST

A new small study reveals that getting less than four hours of sleep reduces physical endurance by altering how different networks in the brain communicate. Rather than muscles tiring out faster, sleep-deprived brains struggle to maintain the neural signals required to sustain a physical effort. These findings were published in the International Journal of Psychophysiology.
Physical fatigue is often viewed as a straightforward matter of muscles running out of energy and accumulating metabolic waste. Yet the brain plays a primary role in determining how long a person can sustain a physical effort. This concept is known as central fatigue. When the brain senses a lack of resources, it can prematurely reduce the electrical signals sent down the spinal cord to the muscles.
This protective mechanism causes a person to feel exhausted even if their muscle tissues are still physically capable of continuing the activity. To understand how central fatigue develops, researchers look at the brain as a collection of distinct networks rather than isolated regions. For instance, the default mode network is highly active during mind-wandering, introspection, and rest. The central executive network handles focused cognitive tasks and goal-directed attention.
The sensorimotor network manages the planning and execution of physical movements. Finally, the salience network acts as a neural switchboard, helping the brain identify important sensory information and shift attention between the inward-focused default mode and the outward-focused central executive networks. Puyan Chi and Chengcheng Zhu led a research team to investigate how a severe lack of sleep affects physical endurance and the coordination of these large-scale brain networks.
The researchers focused on a specific type of physical effort known as an isometric contraction. This occurs when a muscle generates force but does not change in length, such as when holding a heavy box directly in front of you. The team wanted to observe how acute sleep restriction changes the frequency of brain waves as participants perform an exhausting isometric task.
The researchers recruited 35 healthy male college students who regularly engaged in strength training. For the experiment, each participant completed two different sleep conditions separated by at least three days to prevent lingering fatigue. In the normal sleep condition, participants slept for more than seven hours while wearing a sleep monitor. In the restricted sleep condition, participants stayed awake until three in the morning and were woken up at seven in the morning, ensuring they slept for less than four hours.
Following each sleep condition, the participants arrived at the laboratory for testing. The researchers first recorded their brain activity while they rested quietly using an electroencephalogram. This non-invasive device measures electrical activity through dozens of sensors placed across the scalp. The researchers used software to clean the data, filtering out the electrical noise caused by blinking and minor head movements.
The participants then performed a physical task. They sat against a wall with their right arm bent at a ninety-degree angle. The researchers applied a load to their wrist equal to thirty percent of their maximum bicep strength using an elastic band. This required the participants to maintain a steady isometric contraction of their bicep muscle at a moderate intensity.
The participants held this position until they were completely exhausted, reporting a high degree of perceived exertion and eventually failing to keep their arm bent. During the physical task, the researchers continuously recorded both the participants’ brain waves and the electrical activity of their bicep muscles. The muscle activity was tracked using an electromyogram, which detects the firing rate of muscle fibers.
The researchers broke the brain wave data down into different frequency bands, such as slower theta waves and faster beta and gamma waves. By tracking these frequencies, they analyzed the strength of the neural connections between the default mode, central executive, sensorimotor, and salience networks. The sleep-restricted participants exhausted their muscles much faster than they did after a normal night of sleep. The data from the muscle sensors showed that the bicep muscles tired in a very similar manner under both sleep conditions.
The electromyogram readings revealed no statistically significant differences in the rate of peripheral muscle fatigue. Because the physiological rate of muscle exhaustion did not change, the researchers concluded that the early termination of the task stemmed from the brain prematurely halting the effort. The brain wave analysis revealed notable changes in how the participants’ neural networks communicated. While resting after restricted sleep, the participants exhibited heightened connectivity across several brain networks in the theta, beta, and gamma frequency bands.
The central executive network in particular formed stronger connections with the other regions. The researchers interpreted this as a compensatory state. The sleep-deprived brain was working harder and consuming more energy just to maintain a basic level of wakeful alertness. Once the physical task began, this neural pattern shifted.
The sleep-restricted brains showed weakened connectivity across the theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands compared to the well-rested brains. The connections between the sensorimotor network and the default mode and salience networks broke down. This breakdown made it difficult for the brain to integrate sensory feedback from the straining arm with the motor commands needed to keep the bicep contracted.
Under normal sleep conditions, the researchers observed a negative correlation between physical endurance and the connection between the sensorimotor network and the default mode network. A weaker connection meant better physical performance. This indicates that a well-rested brain efficiently suppresses the daydreaming default mode network, directing all available energy toward maintaining the physical task.
After sleep restriction, this relationship completely reversed. Higher connectivity between the sensorimotor and default mode networks correlated with the duration the participants could hold the bicep contraction. The researchers suspect that the sleep-deprived brains lost their ability to exert top-down control. Instead of suppressing the default mode network, the struggling brain attempted to recruit it to help maintain the muscle contraction, revealing a state of profound neural inefficiency.
The study relied on a small sample of young, healthy men, meaning the results might not apply to women, older adults, or clinical populations. The research only evaluated a single instance of severe sleep loss rather than chronic sleep deprivation, which might alter the brain differently over time. The experiment also tested only one type of stationary muscle contraction at a single intensity level.
Dynamic exercises like running or weightlifting could place entirely different demands on the central nervous system. Future investigations will need to track subjective factors like motivation and mood, which might influence physical performance alongside the observed neural changes. The study, “Changes in athletes’ brain network connections during isometric muscle contractions after sleep restriction,” was authored by Chengcheng Zhu, Ting Peng, Jing Song, Aiping Chi, Xin Wei, and Puyan Chi.

U.S. Representative Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced a bill on Oct. 16 that would block the Trump administration's plan to import Russian diesel.
The move comes a week after U.S. President Donald Trump shocked both Ukraine and the United States by announcing a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy millions of tons of diesel from Moscow — a deal Trump claimed would lower gas prices for Americans.
Meeks' new legislation, titled the Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, bans the U.S International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russian energy products and mandates the White House impose sanctions on Russian fuel. It also nullifies the general licenses issued by the Treasury Department and prohibits any future licenses.
"This deal won't lower costs for the American people, who are already paying for
Trump's failed war of choice in Iran," Meeks said. 
"It will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity. At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with
Ukraine." 
Meeks called on all his fellow congressmembers to support the legislation. The bill thus far has 17 co-sponsors in the House — all Democrats, with the exception of Republican Rep. Don Bacon.
Trump's diesel deal drew vocal bipartisan outrage from lawmakers after it was announced on Oct. 9. Members of Congress from both sides of the aisle argued the move would undermine recently enacted sanctions against Russia, potentially provide Moscow with billions of dollars to grow its war chest, and contradict U.S. efforts to pressure Putin into peace talks.
Republicans currently control both chambers of the U.S. Congress — but that could change with the upcoming midterm elections in November. Trump's approval rating has dipped drastically, with even conservative voters dissatisfied with his handling of key issues such as inflation, the economy, tariffs, and foreign policy.
Trump has chosen to blame Ukraine for the skyrocketing gasoline and diesel costs in the U.S., saying Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil refineries have caused the price hike. The claim is heavily disputed by experts, who point to the U.S. war in Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Chief of General Staff of Poland Inspects Turkish SRBM TAYFUN System Amid Search for Long-Range Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:57:38 UTC
04:57:38 KST

During a visit to Turkey, General Wiesław Kukula, Chief of the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces, visited facilities of the ROKETSAN Group, where he familiarized himself with the Turkish TAYFUN SRBM.
This was reported by the press service of the Polish Armed Forces.
In addition, Polish military officials were shown the TRG/TRLG families of guided rockets, which align with Poland’s concept for developing the capability to deliver high-precision strikes deep into enemy territory.
Poland also expressed interest in multi-layered air defense technologies, particularly the ALKA system, which combines laser weapons with electronic warfare capabilities, as well as the PUSU anti-drone solutions and the SUNGUR man-portable air defense system (MANPADS).
“The visit was part of an effort to familiarize ourselves with modern technologies and areas of development in operational capabilities that are important for the transformation of the Polish Armed Forces and the strengthening of the country’s defense potential,” the ministry emphasized.
Poland aims to develop the capability to deliver high-precision strikes at ranges of over 1,000 kilometers. The country is considering strike drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles as potential weapons.
According to Brigadier General Grzegorz Potuszki, head of the Planning and Programming Directorate for the Development of the Polish Armed Forces, the Polish Army is currently capable of striking ground targets at a range of approximately 300 kilometers using American ATACMS missiles and South Korean CTM-290 missiles. However, the experience of the Russia-Ukraine war has demonstrated the need to use high-precision weapons at significantly greater ranges.
ROKETSAN is actively developing the TAYFUN family of ballistic missiles. The first tests of the missile took place in October 2022—the missile struck a target 561 km away after a 458-second flight.
Subsequent tests took place in June 2023 from the Rize-Artvin airfield in the northeast of the country. The tests confirmed the missile’s combat capabilities and marked another step toward the mass production of the new weapon.
In July 2025, ROKETSAN unveiled the TAYFUN Block-4 short-range ballistic missile for the first time. According to unofficial reports, its range is approximately 1,000 km.
According to the company, the TAYFUN Block-4 is an improved version of the previous model and features an increased range and higher speed, allowing it to effectively penetrate missile defense systems.
The missile weighs about 7.3 metric tons, is approximately 10 meters long, and has a diameter of 610 mm. According to the company, this is the first Turkish ballistic missile capable of striking targets at a range of several hundred kilometers at a speed exceeding Mach 5.

A 19-year-old Norwegian man has been sentenced to 20 years’ detention for conspiring to murder an unidentified target in the UK on behalf of an organized crime group linked to Iran.
Johannes Natland was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organized crime group described as backed by the Iranian regime, to carry out a killing in England, according to the BBC on Friday.
Natland was unanimously found guilty of conspiracy to murder during a retrial and sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on Friday. He had previously admitted possessing firearms and ammunition.
He was arrested at the Briar Court Hotel in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, in March 2025, with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition hidden under his bed. He arrived at Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on March 17, 2025, shortly after his 18th birthday.
Using videos sent through the messaging app Signal, he traveled to Huddersfield, where firearms, a stolen car and cash had been concealed.

Deforestation in Brazil Amazon hits nearly four-decade low

Deforestation in Brazil Amazon hits nearly four-decade low
BRASILIA - Deforestation of the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level in nearly 40 years, according to figures released on Oct 16, in welcome news for leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva days before a presidential runoff.
Between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 sq km of forest were cleared, a decline of nearly 42% over the previous year and the lowest level since records began in 1988, official statistics showed.
“It’s an absolutely stratospheric drop...it’s like a dream,” Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco told a press conference in the capital Brasilia.
The data was also hailed by Lula, whom polls show running neck-and-neck with conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of the Oct 25 runoff.
Lula, a veteran left-wing leader, returned to office promising to end unlawful forest clearance by ranchers and illegal miners, which had soared under his far-right predecessor Jair Bolsonaro, the father of Flavio.
“Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030,” he reiterated on Oct 16 on X, after the deforestation data was released.
Brazil is home to approximately 60% of the world’s largest rainforest, which plays a crucial role in absorbing greenhouse gases responsible for global warming.
The official deforestation rate is measured using the “Prodes” satellite system, operated by the National Institute for Space Research.
Deforestation has been steadily decreasing in the Amazon since 2022, with a cumulative drop of 71.2% over the four years since Lula was elected.
The figures, which have been attributed to greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging, mark a dramatic about-turn since Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, from 2019 to 2022.
The Amazon lost around 11,600 sq km of forest under his watch – almost 60% more than in the previous four years, official figures show.
Flavio Bolsonaro has praised his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for coup plotting, for having opposed what he calls a “radical environmental agenda.”
At the same time he has proposed treating the environment as a “strategic asset” and pledged to end “illegal deforestation” by 2029.
Political will
There was also good news from the vast Cerrado savanna south of the Amazon, where deforestation fell to its lowest levels since records there began in 2001.
From August 2025 to July 2026, 5,517 sq km of native vegetation were destroyed, representing a reduction of almost 24 percent in a year.
Marcio Astrini, executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, a network of over 100 civil society groups, praised the figures as a “historic victory.”
“This demonstrates that Brazil plays a leading role in protecting forests and that, with political will, it is possible to curb chainsaws and greenhouse gas emissions,” he said in a statement. AFP

What's next?
ABC Sport will live-blog the second Test in Gqeberha, starting on Sunday night.
South Africa have vowed to do better at wearing Australia's bowlers down in the second Test, desperate to rebound after the batters' meek surrender in Durban.
The Proteas are set to welcome back pace ace Kagiso Rabada for Sunday's second Test in Gqeberha, after he terrorised Australia on the last tour in 2018.
But the hosts have pointed to their batting as the biggest bridge that must be mended between the two sides after the series-opening 214-run defeat.
Aiden Markram was the only Protea to pass 50 in the Test, with seven others scoring between 30 and 49 across both innings.
That prompted coach Shukri Conrad to claim he was "pulling the very last strands out of his hair" as he axed both Tristan Stubbs and Kyle Verreynne.
South Africa number three David Bedingham spoke of the relentless nature of Australia's attack on Friday, with Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon offering little reprieve.

"It's just about trying to take them to 80 overs, 100 overs, 120 overs," Bedingham said.
"And then, I know they're machines, but everyone gets tired eventually. Well, hopefully…
"When Kesh (Maharaj) and Simon (Harmer) were batting around the 68th over in the first innings, I'm not saying they were tiring, but the ball was a lot softer.
"It looked a lot easier. So if we could have maybe been four, five down there, then maybe the game would have a different angle."
Meanwhile, Rabada looks almost certain to play, as the Proteas fight to avoid their first home series defeat since England toured in 2019-20.
Rabada's record of 58 wickets at 21.39 is the second best of any quick against Australia this century, behind only Jasprit Bumrah.
He was the Proteas' arch-villain in the 2018 series, colliding with Steve Smith after taking his wicket in Gbqerha (then Port Elizabeth) and only avoiding a ban on appeal.
Rabada has steamed in at South Africa training this week, showing no signs of the hamstring tear that sidelined him for through the ODIs and first Test.
"He's massive for us," Bedingham said.

"Even if you look back last year in the World Test Championship final, he took nine wickets against Australia.
"Against any team he plays against, he's ready. Hopefully, come this next Test, he takes nine or 10 wickets; that would be quite nice."
Batters Marques Ackerman and Matthew Breetzke are expected to come in at St George's Park, with Ryan Rickelton to take gloves from Verreynne.

F-22 Pilot Directs CCA in Flight as ‘Airborne QB’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:48:36 UTC
04:48:36 KST

A U.S. Air Force F-22 pilot controlled a YFQ-44A Fury Collaborative Combat Aircraft this month while both aircraft were in flight, according to an Oct. 16 release, another milestone in the service’s ambitious CCA efforts.
The human F-22 pilot acted as an “airborne quarterback” for the YFQ-44 drone by sending it high-level tactical directives, according to the Air Force statement. The YFQ-44’s on-board autonomy software then interpreted and carried out those orders in real time to carry out “dynamic flight maneuvers and simulated combat tasks,” the statement reads.
Anduril Industries, the manufacturer of the Fury, said in follow-up statements that the flight took place out of Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., during the week of Oct. 5.
Mark Shushnar, Anduril’s vice president of autonomous airpower, said the Fury and F-22 both took off at Edwards, and then joined up midair. The Raptor pilot then sent an updated mission plan to the Fury CCA using a tactical data link, “commanding Fury through operationally relevant maneuvers from the cockpit of the crewed quarterback” fighter.
For this demonstration, the F-22 was controlling a single YFQ-44A. But the Air Force’s plan is to eventually have each fighter pilot capable of controlling multiple CCAs as a formation—extending the service’s combat mass and reach.
In a statement, Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach said the demo “shows the power of crewed-uncrewed teaming and the advantage it provides our warfighters” and pledged to build on it quickly.
“We must test often, learn fast, and give commanders what they need, when they need it,” he said.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink also touted the need to move quickly in touting the flight.
“This achievement demonstrates what is possible when we are aligned with industry on a shared imperative: delivering capability to the warfighter at unprecedented speed,” Meink said in a statement. “We are driving urgency into every part of acquisition from rapid integration and flight learning to disciplined assessment, so we can turn promising technology into combat capability at the pace the threat demands.”
The mission lasted multiple hours and was a success, Shushnar said, and shows how quickly progress is being made to creating an operational CCA program.
“The U.S. Air Force’s CCA program is the fastest moving, most mature CCA program anywhere in the world, and will be the first to field operational aircraft,” Shushnar said. “Getting there demands that Anduril and the U.S. Air Force work together to prove out the capability, define the operational procedures, and build trust between operators and their semi-autonomous wingmen.”
The Air Force said data from the test will help with future software integration, developmental testing, and future CCA concepts.
The test included personnel from the Air Force’s 412th Test Wing at Edwards, the 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., the 309th Software Engineering Group at Hill Air Force Base, Utah, the CCA Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev., the F-22 System Program Office, and the CCA Software Autonomy and Teaming Branch.
The Air Force has previously conducted flight tests with a “surrogate” drone meant to represent a CCA—General Atomics’ MQ-20 Avenger. In February, an F-22 in the air controlled an MQ-20 Avenger, and in May, an F-35 that remained on the ground also controlled an Avenger that was in the air.
The Air Force wants to have 500 CCAs in the field by 2032, and eventually a fleet of 1,000 or more to carry out a variety of missions that could include air-to-air strikes, air-to-ground strikes, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, or electronic warfare. This first iteration—which includes General Atomics’ FQ-42 and Anduril’s FQ-44—is focused on the air-to-air mission. The Air Force wants them to cost at most $20 million apiece for the air vehicle, excluding the cost of sensors, weapons or other equipment CCAs might carry on board.
While the focus of the CCA program has been on manned-unmanned teaming with pilots in the air, the Air Force has also been working on a capability for Airmen to command the CCAs using stations on the ground.

Israeli settlers attack US photographer covering West Bank

Israeli settlers attack US photographer covering West Bank violence
Israeli settlers on Friday attacked an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post while she was covering violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.
Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack, with photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.
The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, days ahead of elections in which he is seeking settlers' support, insisted the circumstances behind the incident were unclear, in contrast with the full-throated condemnation offered by his chief rival.
The attack comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the West Bank olive harvest, Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.
Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that "more than 50" masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya in the central West Bank.
"All of a sudden they jumped me and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on and I... kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face," she said.
"They just kept kicking me and kicking me," she added.
After receiving initial care in Ramallah, Levine was transferred to Israel's Beilinson Hospital in Petah Tikva, where doctors found she had suffered four broken vertebrae and would need surgery.
The Washington Post said Levine had been wearing a flak jacket clearly marked "Press".
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, said in a statement.
'No mercy'
Netanyahu's office said Levine had been "allegedly assaulted", adding that the circumstances were "unclear and are under investigation".
"Those responsible will be held accountable," it said in an X post, giving a version of events in which "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths", with both sides throwing objects at the other.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main rival in the upcoming polls, blamed Friday's "unacceptable" attack on a "handful of rioters" whose actions, he said, "stain an entire nation".
A US State Department official said it condemned "criminal violence by any party in the West Bank" and called for "legal accountability for those responsible".
The official added the department had "reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance".
AFP news agency reported that a journalist working for the agency reported witnessing Palestinian medics tending to someone in the area and Israeli soldiers pushing away journalists trying to approach.
The Israeli military said troops and border police forces were deployed to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation".
"A female journalist had been injured during the confrontation," it said, adding the circumstances would be examined.
"Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts," the military said.
The Israeli police said it had opened an investigation into incidents in Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya.
"We were on our land, picking olives, and suddenly the settlers came down on us and started hitting us, throwing stones," said Mukhlis Zuhdi, a farmer from Abu Falah.
"There was even a foreign journalist whom they beat. These people have no mercy or compassion in their hearts," he told AFP.
'Brazen violence'
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said the settlers stole Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.
Reporters Without Borders said it strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault".
"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
Excluding east Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.

Top global climate science body meet ends without deal on review timeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:45:37 UTC
04:45:37 KST

Top global climate science body meet ends without deal on review timeline
A meeting of the members of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was suspended without an agreement on a timeline to publish its next review of the latest science on the warming planet, the IPCC said on Oct 16.
The impasse over the timeline, which has lasted nearly three years, could leave countries to decide the next phase of climate action without consensus on critical issues, including the extent to which some global warming might be reversible.
The meeting was suspended after it ran over its planned duration on the last day and many delegations from least-developed countries and small island states had to leave, the IPCC said in a statement.
Agreeing publication dates for its next review of the latest science was the main agenda of the IPCC meeting of 195 member states in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa this week.
Governments are set to assess progress toward goals set in the 2015 Paris agreement at the UN climate talks in November 2028, in a so-called “Global Stocktake”.
The discussions on the review timeline and the IPCC budget “remain open,” and the panel’s deliberations will resume at the earliest opportunity, the IPCC said, without providing details.
The possibility that the IPCC’s reports might not be ready in time for the 2028 climate talks has alarmed a coalition of 30 countries, including European, Latin American and small-island states pushing for immediate action.
However, countries including India, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, Russia and China are pressing for more time to prepare the IPCC’s next reports to ensure scientists from less-resourced countries can make meaningful contributions.
“We were here to work, but found every proposal dismissed – on inclusivity, on the relevance of the science for our national planning, on the necessity of evidence to inform the next Global Stocktake,” said Tina Stege, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands.
“Progress was blocked, down to the end – a shameful play for time when there is no time to waste.”
The IPCC’s reviews carry weight as they are written by hundreds of international experts and approved by every member state, and are used by governments to plan responses to climate change and cited in international court rulings.
The UN Environment Programme has said repeatedly that global efforts to limit warming are falling short and that deeper emissions cuts are needed to avoid climate-related disasters. REUTERS

Ukraine Seeks to Scale Up Civilian Protection With Finland’s Support
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on October 16 to address the urgent need for expanded protective infrastructure across Ukrainian cities.
Discussions focused on safeguarding civil energy grids and municipal facilities against ongoing Russian aerial strikes, according to President Zelenskyy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The discussions focused on speeding up joint defense efforts and deploying additional interceptor assets to protect critical infrastructure.
During the discussion, both leaders prioritized the progress of the Shelter Coalition, a collaborative effort created alongside Helsinki to ensure accessible and secure protective facilities in every local municipality.
President Zelenskyy emphasized the imperative to accelerate civil defense preparations and noted that additional defense decisions and support measures from Finland are anticipated later this month.
"Together with Finland, we established the Shelter Coalition, and now this work needs to be accelerated. Proper shelters must be available in every Ukrainian city and community," President Zelenskyy stated.
"We constantly need weapons to shoot down missiles and drones, to protect human lives and critical infrastructure facilities. There will be new decisions in support of Ukraine this month. Finland always helps us, and we deeply appreciate this," he added.
At the same time, Ukraine is set to receive an additional 15,000 long-range artillery shells from Denmark as part of a new military aid package, with a portion of the ammunition already delivered, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense.
In October 2025, Finland confirmed that its network of more than 50,500 bomb shelters was fully operational and capable of accommodating 4.8 million people, according to government assessments.
The nation's civil defense inventory showed that nearly 91% of the shelters were built to withstand conventional attacks, while 83% included air filtration systems designed to protect against nuclear, biological, or chemical threats.

Russian forces liberate key Ukrainian stronghold in Donbass – MOD
Russian forces have liberated the key Ukrainian stronghold of Dobropolye in Donbass, Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov has reported to President Vladimir Putin.
During a meeting on Friday, Gerasimov said assault units from several brigades had taken part in the operation and were searching basements for any remaining Ukrainian troops.
Putin praised the “coordinated and highly professional” actions of the Russian assault units, noting that Ukrainian forces had turned Dobropolye into a “robust stronghold.”
In late September, the Russian Defense Ministry announced that its forces had encircled Dobropolye.
The town’s capture marks another step in Russia’s advance toward the Slavyansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration, a cluster of cities in northwestern DPR that forms Ukraine’s last major fortified stronghold in the region.

Russia’s Ryazan oil refinery shuts down key processing unit after drone attack – Reuters
Reuters reported this, citing two industry sources, according to Ukrinform.
According to the sources, the drone attack forced the shutdown of CDU-6, one of the refinery’s main processing units. It was also taken offline last month following an attack. Several pipelines at the facility were damaged in the latest strike as well.
The sources told the agency that the refinery has three other primary crude distillation units – CDU -1, CDU -3 and CDU -4. They remain operational and may partially offset the shutdown of CDU -6.
The Ryazan refinery, which supplies fuel to Moscow, has been attacked repeatedly this year.
The facility has an annual processing capacity of 17 million metric tons per year (about 340,000 barrels per day). It can produce 3.4 million tons of gasoline and 3.8 million tons of diesel fuel annually.
As reported by Ukrinform, the Ryazan oil refinery caught fire overnight on October 15 following a drone attack.

GTA developer denies firing staff over union activity
A senior executive at Rockstar Games, the developer behind the Grand Theft Auto video game, denied monitoring employees' union membership as an employment tribunal examined the dismissal of 34 workers, Anadolu Agency reports.
Robert Spampinato, the company's vice president of human resources, told the tribunal in Glasgow, Scotland, that allegations he had instructed managers to "keep tabs" on union membership were "categorically not true."
Twenty-three former employees, most previously based at Rockstar North in Edinburgh, are challenging their October 2025 dismissals with support from the Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB).
The union alleges the workers were targeted for trade union activities, while Rockstar maintains they were dismissed for sharing confidential company information on a Discord server.
The tribunal heard that an anonymous employee had passed information about union meetings and recruitment activities to Human Resources managers.
Spampinato acknowledged that the information helped management follow workplace grievances but denied any attempt to suppress union activity.
Asked why the dismissals occurred in October 2025 despite some information being available earlier, he said Rockstar was in "crisis mode" because of delays to Grand Theft Auto 6.
"We were in a moment when we knew we were running late on the development," he said.
The game is scheduled for release on Nov. 19 after two delays.
The tribunal proceedings are continuing.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Rockstar Games’ upcoming PS5 lineup includes the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, scheduled for release on November 19, 2026, while updated versions of Red Dead Redemption 2 and Grand Theft Auto IV were reportedly in development.

The eighth local ceasefire mediated by the IAEA has begun near the ZNPP. It will allow the damaged 330 kV substation to be repaired.
On Thursday, October 15, a new local ceasefire near the ZNPP took effect, allowing repairs to be carried out on equipment at a distribution substation. This was stated in an IAEA statement, reports UNN.
A new local ceasefire came into effect this morning, reached through the mediation of the IAEA Director General, and aimed at preventing a nuclear accident in Ukraine amid the military conflict. Restrictions on Starlink: Consequences for Ukrainian Drones and the Search for Alternatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:42:06 UTC
04:42:06 KST

On the night of October 14, SpaceX, at the request of the White House, unilaterally and without warning imposed restrictions on Starlink accounts with special Starshield military accounts for Ukraine.
Starshield is a secure version of the Starlink satellite communications system, developed for the needs of government, military, and intelligence agencies and managed by the U.S. Department of Defense.
It first became known in December 2024 that the Armed Forces of Ukraine had gained access to the secure U.S. military satellite communications network Starshield. According to sources cited by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu, the current contract for the service is valid through April 2027 and is funded by Germany.
Communications began to drop out at varying speeds, ranging from 72 to 161 km/h, on various unmanned platforms and across different units. On October 15, the speed threshold for SpaceX’s military communications system was raised to 160 km/h, but as of October 16, its operation had still not been fully restored.
Kirill Lyukov, head of the unmanned technologies department at the Serhiy Prytula Charitable Foundation, told Militarnyi that communication issues with Starlink terminals have been reported since the night of October 14 across the entire combat zone, in the temporarily occupied territories, and in Ukraine’s rear regions. At least three units reported regular loss of connection at speeds of 75 km/h.
According to him, afterStarlink was blocked for Russians in the temporarily occupied territories, additional restrictions were imposed, causing the terminals to lose connection at speeds averaging over 70 km/h. To identify military users, special accounts are used for which this restriction has been lifted. This allows the Ukrainian Defense Forces to operate at higher speeds both in the temporarily occupied territories and in areas under Ukraine’s control.
Lyukov speculates that the restrictions on Starlink may be linked to political pressure from the U.S. presidential administration on Ukraine regarding the demand not to strike Russian oil refineries. At the same time, he emphasized that Starshield’s operations do not affect such strikes, since these facilities are located on Russian territory, where Starlink has been and remains unavailable to the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
He also does not rule out the possibility that a software glitch was the cause. According to him, as of the evening of October 14, Starlink terminals with Starshield accounts had begun to resume normal operations.
As the 1st Unmanned Systems Battalion High-Altitude Predators of the 59th Separate Unmanned Systems Assault Brigade named after Yakov Handzyuk told Militarnyi, the situation caused by the Starlink restrictions is complex but under control.
“We all knew that sooner or later this day would come. There are systems that don’t require Starlink,” the military personnel noted.
According to the military, the unit is switching to radio communications and drones capable of flying in autonomous mode. The restrictions on Starlink did not affect the operation of reconnaissance UAVs, UGVs, and bomber drones, but they did complicate the use of strike drones.
“A Starlink-equipped strike drone: at 80 kilometers [per hour]—that’s it, the connection drops out. There’s nothing you can do about it. Plus, there’s the problem that during a catapult launch and so on, there’s immediate high acceleration. And, basically, the drone is uncontrollable—it’s carried along, and [it] crashes,” a unit representative explained.
At the same time, reconnaissance drones can continue operating with Starlink at speeds of up to 80 km/h. After launch and reaching a circular trajectory, they establish satellite communication and carry out their missions.
According to other reports, the operation of high-speed interceptor drones and even certain models of bomber drones has also been affected.
According to military officials interviewed by Militarnyi, the reduction in strike drone activity will allow the enemy to step up its logistics. The situation is further complicated by bad weather and thick autumn fog.
At the same time, there are solutions that could operate using alternative communication systems. In particular, the military has submitted requests to procure strike drones that use radio communication and an automatic guidance system.
“Solutions, in principle, exist. The main thing is for the command to respond now and procure the equipment we need to somehow bridge the entire gap. Let’s hope that this [Starlink] will eventually be restored,” the military emphasized.
In response to a request from Militarnyi, Deviro noted that the company was one of the few that, even in the early stages of Starlink’s mass deployment, emphasized the temporary nature of this window of opportunity.
“Of course, we ensured that Starlink could be used in our products, but developing our own communication solutions—particularly Mesh technology—remained one of our priorities,” Deviro explained.
The company believes that technological independence and the ability to adapt to changes on the battlefield are more valuable than reliance on a single solution, even a highly effective one.
Deviro attributes the popularity of Starlink for middle-strike systems primarily to its ease of use and speed of integration. By the time the technology was actively being implemented, the terminals had already become widely adopted within the military, and personnel had practical experience working with them.
Cost was also a key factor: under certain conditions, Starlink provided a high-quality communication channel at a relatively low price compared to certain specialized radio systems. Furthermore, satellite communications long reduced dependence on the limitations of traditional radio channels in the face of electronic warfare (EW) operations. The combination of these advantages made Starlink attractive for both reconnaissance and strike drone systems.
According to Deviro’s assessment, there is currently virtually no direct alternative to Starlink that would provide a similar combination of accessibility, cost, ease of use, and infrastructure. At the same time, other technological solutions do exist: large-scale work is underway to test, refine, and integrate both new and existing communication technologies.
The company explains that due to the dynamic nature of modern warfare, a technological advantage today does not guarantee it will be maintained tomorrow. Component manufacturers, unmanned system developers, the military, and the country’s military-political leadership are becoming increasingly aware of this.
Deviro specifically emphasized the need to avoid dependence on a single technology, regardless of its current effectiveness. To achieve this, manufacturers must constantly collaborate with the military, seek new solutions, test them in practice, and adapt their approaches as quickly as the war demands.
Andriy Rymaruk, Deputy Director of Ukrspecsystems, noted in a comment to Militarnyi that the company has focused, continues to focus, and will continue to focus primarily on the development and production of systems with radio modems. According to him, these systems operate independently of external technical, diplomatic, or political factors.
Rymaruk explained that by using radio communication as the system’s primary channel, the company’s systems continue to conduct reconnaissance and strike targets at depths exceeding 200 km. In particular, he described the recent destruction of an “expensive and rare radar system” at a depth of 226 km by a unit of the 429th Separate Achilles Unmanned Systems Brigade.
⚡️Уразили РЛС «Небо-У» у ростовській області

In addition, the use of radio communications allows Ukrspecsystems’ drones to operate over Russian territory, where Starlink does not function, as well as to strike and disable ballistic missile launchers.
Andriy Shevchenko, Managing Director of Helsing in Ukraine, told Militarnyi that the restrictions on Starlink have demonstrated the critical importance of autonomy for modern defense systems. According to him, military technologies must remain effective regardless of decisions made by external suppliers.
It is precisely based on this principle that Helsing developed the HX-2. As Shevchenko explained, the drone does not depend on Starlink and uses radio communication that operates effectively under enemy electronic warfare (EW) conditions. It also features visual navigation without GNSS and automatic target acquisition. At Helsing, autonomy is viewed as the foundation of the product’s operation, enabling the military to continue carrying out missions even when conventional communication and navigation systems are unavailable.
