Elon Musk approached US President Donald Trump with a proposal to limit the speed of Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine, disrupting Kyiv’s ability to counter Russian drone attacks, The Telegraph reported on 16 October, citing four sources familiar with the discussions.
The restrictions had immediate consequences for Ukraine’s defenses, forcing some drone missions against Russian positions to be called off and threatening the ability to intercept Russian jet-powered drones as they targeted Ukrainian cities at the time.
According to The Telegraph, Trump agreed with Musk’s suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to impose restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s satellite network used by Ukrainian forces.
The report contradicts Musk’s public claim that the US military and ultimately Trump were responsible for deciding any limits on the system. However, Trump denied that either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access, while an anonymous US official told AFP that the president had not requested the reduction in service.
The reported restrictions come amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The episode has raised concerns about Ukraine’s dependence on privately controlled communications infrastructure and the risk that changes to US support could weaken its battlefield capabilities.
Starshield restrictions hampered Ukraine’s drone defenses
Starshield is the military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet network. It allows Ukrainian drone operators to maintain communications with aircraft moving at high speeds, supporting both defensive interception missions and strikes against Russian targets.
The speed limit imposed on Ukrainian drones using Starshield was around 160 kph, making it difficult for them to intercept Russian jet-powered drones and missiles traveling at roughly twice that speed.
According to The Telegraph, a senior source said Musk had become concerned about potential backlash from European consumers following the restrictions. A high-ranking European official and two Ukrainian sources reportedly corroborated the account that Musk and Trump were both involved in the decision.
The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions. The report’s account also remains disputed: Trump said on 16 October that he did not believe either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access, while an anonymous US official cited by AFP said the president had not requested the reduction.
“Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
Ukraine says Starshield capabilities are being restored
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system had disrupted several military operations, including efforts to intercept Russian jet-powered Geran drones attacking Ukrainian cities.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not use Starlink to support attacks inside Russia, but relied on the system to intercept drones targeting civilians, conduct mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory, and deliver food and water to frontline troops using drones.
“When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept a certain number of jet-powered ‘shaheds,’ [Gerans - ed.]” Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that Ukrainian forces had lost the ability to carry out some operations while the restrictions were in place.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was in contact with partners and had received signals from the White House that the capabilities would be restored. However, he stressed that speeds had not yet returned to their previous levels, although restoration was underway.
Europe warns against dependence on Musk’s network
The latest episode has renewed European concerns about relying on Musk and SpaceX for critical communications infrastructure. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned Musk on social media that European customers were watching his actions, The Telegraph reported.
The European Union is developing its own satellite communications system, IRIS², intended to provide an alternative to Starlink, according to The Telegraph. The system is planned to become operational by 2030, leaving Ukraine and European governments dependent on existing providers in the meantime.
The report adds to concerns that decisions made in Washington or by private technology providers could directly affect Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.

Egypt tightens Suez Canal transit rules for aging ships, affecting Russia’s “shadow fleet”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:04:59 UTC
04:04:59 KST

The Suez Canal Authority has introduced mandatory technical inspections and testing for ships that are 25 years old or older, according to a report by industry publication Splash247. The rules, which are already in effect, could complicate Russian oil shipments to Asia, as a significant share of Russia’s “shadow fleet” is made up of aging tankers.
Under the new requirements, ships older than 25 years must undergo a comprehensive technical inspection and testing before receiving permission to transit the canal. Ships making another transit within six months will not need a new inspection provided that no defects or other technical problems have been identified in the meantime.
The rules apply to all types of vessels regardless of flag, cargo, or sanctions status. The canal authority has not yet specified how much the inspections will cost or how long the process will take.
Russian oil tankers continue using the Suez Canal
After Western sanctions were imposed following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian oil companies redirected a large share of exports from European ports to Asia, particularly to India and China. The Suez Canal, which connects the Mediterranean and Red seas, became one of the main routes.
According to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, in the first half of 2025 Russia was the largest source of oil and condensate transported through the Suez Canal and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Russian oil shipments along the route continued even after attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels prompted many international carriers to avoid the Red Sea. The EIA estimated that the volume of Russian oil moving through the Suez Canal and Bab el-Mandeb in 2024 and the first half of 2025 remained roughly at 2023 levels.
Sanctioned tankers have already been involved in incidents in the Suez Canal. In October 2025, the tanker Komander — which was carrying Russian oil — lost power and ran aground, temporarily disrupting vessel traffic. Notably, the ship was built in 2004, meaning that even under the new rules it would not be affected by the 25-year age threshold.
Most “shadow fleet” tankers are over 15 years old
Russia’s “shadow fleet” consists largely of aging vessels acquired to bypass Western sanctions on the transport of Russian oil. transport oil. These tankers frequently change owners, names, and flags, and their technical condition and insurance coverage have raised concerns among maritime regulators.
The Insider counted at least 39 vessels in Russia’s “shadow fleet” that are more than 25 years old. Another 130 tankers older than 25 years sail under the Russian flag.
According to an April 2026 estimate by the KSE Institute, 92% of shadow-fleet tankers carrying Russian oil were more than 15 years old. S&P Global analysts had earlier estimated the average age of vessels in the global shadow fleet at about 20 years, with roughly 60% older than 20.
The new Suez Canal requirements, however, apply only to vessels that are at least 25 years old, and there is no precise public data on what share of Russian shadow-fleet tankers using the route has reached that age.
The additional inspections could increase the cost of transporting Russian oil and cause delays in canal transit. Ships with technical problems are likely to be particularly vulnerable because they may need repairs before receiving clearance to pass through.
The rules come as the global merchant fleet continues to age. According to Clarksons Research data cited by Splash247, the combined gross tonnage of ships 25 years and older has exceeded 150 million gross tons, up 75% over the past five years. Tonnage for ships older than 30 years has reached a record 68 million gross tons.

Li Huifang, the person in charge of the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji District, and Zhu Jinglin, the executive principal, instructed and organized the addition of toxic materials to food served to children and staff, to make it appear more colorful and attractive for marketing.
According to a verdict issued by the Intermediate People's Court of Lanzhou City in Gansu, Li was sentenced to life imprisonment, deprived of political rights for life, and had 500,000 yuan (about 74,000 U.S. dollars) in personal property confiscated. Zhu received 15 years in prison and a fine of 300,000 yuan. Four kitchen workers were sentenced to between six and eight years in prison, each with fines, for carrying out the instructions.
According to a provincial investigation report released in July 2025, these pastries had been served to children and staff on a monthly basis since May 2024. Of 251 children tested, 247 had abnormal blood lead levels. All 247 children with abnormal blood lead levels received hospitalization or home-based nutritional intervention. By July 20, 2025, most of the affected children had completed their first treatment course and had been discharged from hospitals.
Clinical evaluation by experts demonstrated an average decrease of 40.21 percent in blood lead levels following treatment, achieving the projected therapeutic targets.
According to the July investigation report, provincial disciplinary authorities have investigated 10 local officials, including the provincial health commission director and Tianshui city leaders. The Gansu provincial government has pledged full support for the children's medical care. ■

ROME, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) won the 2026 Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Achievement Award on Friday for developing the CropWatch, a global cloud-based crop monitoring service platform.
The award was presented at the closing ceremony of the World Food Forum, hosted by FAO in Rome, Italy.
Developed by a team led by Wu Bingfang, a researcher at AIRCAS, the platform has helped more than 40 countries and regions monitor crop conditions and supports food security policymaking based on scientific data, according to the research team.
In announcing the award, FAO recognized the platform for transforming complex crop monitoring into an accessible, open cloud service and making it widely available around the world.
According to the research team, the platform has been integrated into FAO's Hand-in-Hand Geospatial Platform and the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) Knowledge Hub. It serves as an important channel and an independent source of timely crop monitoring information for users worldwide.
The team also regularly publishes the CropWatch Bulletin based on the platform, providing the public with a reliable source of agricultural monitoring information. The bulletin has served users in 173 countries and regions to date, said the team.
Speaking to Xinhua after receiving the award, Wu said the recognition affirmed the team's more than three decades of dedication.
"This is not the end, but a milestone on a new journey ahead," he said.
Wu said the team would continue to enhance the platform's innovative capabilities, ease of use and capacity to serve international users, while deepening cooperation with FAO and other international organizations. The team aims to help more countries strengthen their independent crop monitoring capabilities and contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly the goal of "zero hunger."
The FAO Achievement Award recognizes individuals or institutions for outstanding achievements in areas including fisheries, forestry, climate, land and water, and animal and plant health, particularly in sustainable agriculture and rural development and food security. ■

====================================================================================================

News analysis: Experts urge action on root causes of Red Sea humanitarian crisis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:03:22 CST
04:03:22 KST

by Xinhua writers Habtamu Worku, Liu Fangqiang
ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Following yet another deadly shipwreck off the coast of Djibouti, international experts emphasized that the escalating humanitarian crisis along the Red Sea migration corridor demands targeted preventive measures beyond reactive emergency responses.
The eastern migration corridor continues to claim hundreds of lives each year, with more than 900 migrants dead or missing along the route in 2025 alone. However, the number of people who undertake the journey is increasing, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
ESCALATING HUMANITARIAN CRISIS
In one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded on the route in recent times, at least 139 migrants died last week, while 84 remain missing after their boat, carrying 305 people toward war-torn Yemen, capsized off the Djibouti coast. Only 82 people survived. Another shipwreck in March this year left nine people dead and 45 missing.
Frantz Celestin, IOM regional director for East, Horn, and Southern Africa, expressed deep sorrow over the catastrophe.
"Given the number of days that have passed since the tragic event, we do not expect to see anyone alive, but we might still see (bodies) coming to the shore," Celestin told Xinhua recently.
"What is happening is very heartbreaking. It is difficult to hear, when we have a conversation with those who are affected, what they went through, and how some of them are even suffering survivor's guilt," he noted.
"Parents have been contacting us, sending photos with their name and saying, have you seen my kid? Or, do the ones who were buried look like this person? Something like this is very difficult to hear from a parent," he added.
The IOM classifies the Red Sea route, also known as the Eastern Migration Route connecting the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, as one of "the busiest and most dangerous migration corridors" worldwide.
Each year, tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel through Djibouti and cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen, hoping to reach Gulf countries in search of safety, stability and employment.
Agnes Igoye, a migration expert with the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, an East African bloc, told Xinhua that the route is a key pathway for irregular migrants from Horn of Africa countries as they attempt to cross "harsh overland treks through deserts and risky sea voyages" in hopes of reaching Yemen, often seen as a gateway to Gulf countries.
Noting that the promise of work in Middle Eastern and Gulf countries continues to draw young people despite the grave risks, she said limited safe and regular migration pathways, coupled with economic hardships, leave many with few alternatives.
Highlighting an annual average increase of about 20 percent in movements along the route over the past four years, Celestin warned that this trajectory will continue unless root causes are addressed.
"If things do not change in their home countries, or their home communities, we can expect people to move," he said. "The only way to reduce the number of people on the move is to change the conditions that are forcing them to move."
BEYOND EMERGENCY RESPONSE
Experts urged to address underlying structural factors behind rising fatalities along the maritime corridor, including limited economic opportunities, socioeconomic inequalities and climate vulnerability.
According to Celestin, over 500,000 movements were recorded along the eastern route last year alone, while more than 130,000 migrants have landed in the war-torn Yemen so far this year. The number has already marked an increase of about 20 percent, compared to last year's total of 110,144, and more than doubled the 60,897 recorded in 2024.
"That is a lot of people moving. We need to find a way to reduce the likelihood of that many people moving, and the solution for people to move the regular pathways in a safe and regular manner," Celestin said.
Highlighting the search for safety, stability, and better socioeconomic opportunities as primary push factors, he argued that unproductive agricultural lands caused by climate change, insecurity and conflict, as well as limited employment and economic opportunities are forcing vulnerable populations to seek better conditions abroad.
Experts emphasize that addressing these deep-seated root causes requires comprehensive strategies focused on expanding domestic youth employment, enhancing vocational skills training, and building economic resilience across vulnerable communities in the Horn of Africa.
Sustainable solutions require interconnected initiatives, said Igoye. These include improving border governance, fostering cross-border collaboration, increasing protection services, investing in return and reintegration programs, and working with destination countries to establish safe, legal migration options and regulated employment opportunities.
Celestin called for robust structural reforms, international solidarity, and expanded regular migration pathways to curb dangerous irregular migration.
"We at IOM want to make migration a choice instead of a necessity, and this is what we are working on closely with governments and local communities -- to address the needs of those who tend to move," he added. ■

NAIROBI, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Kenya's Ministry of Health on Friday confirmed the country's third case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease.
The patient, a 65-year-old woman, is a primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases. She had been in quarantine since Oct. 6 and had developed a fever, sore throat and malaise, the ministry said.
She later tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute laboratory.
"Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease," the ministry said.
The second patient remained in stable condition and was responding well to supportive care, the ministry added.
Reassuring the public, officials emphasized that the overall risk of Ebola transmission remained low, as there was currently no evidence of community transmission.
"Of the 130 contacts listed, 127 (97.7 percent) have been traced and are in quarantine. This is above the global benchmark of 85 percent required to break the chain of transmission," the ministry said, adding that health authorities are continuing efforts to trace and quarantine the three remaining contacts.
The ministry said additional cases among quarantined individuals remained possible until their monitoring period ended, but assured the public that any new cases would be swiftly detected and treated.
Kenya confirmed on Oct. 6 its first case of Ebola linked to the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, involving an individual who boarded a commercial flight to Nairobi on Oct. 3. A family member then took him to hospital, where medical staff immediately placed him in isolation.
Despite receiving supportive care, the patient died on Oct. 5 and was buried the following day in accordance with the country's safe and dignified burial protocols for viral hemorrhagic fevers. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- China has approved four-year pilot programs for comprehensive hydrogen energy applications in five city clusters, according to a government circular made public Friday.
The programs will cover the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and three cross-regional groups linking northeast China, including eastern Inner Mongolia, with the Yangtze River Delta, Xinjiang with the Chengdu-Chongqing twin-city economic circle, and the Yellow River bend with the Central Plains.
The circular, jointly released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Finance and the National Development and Reform Commission, calls on participating cities to accelerate the implementation of four lists of priority tasks covering hydrogen technology and equipment development, industrial hydrogen projects, fuel cell vehicle promotion, and hydrogen refueling station construction.
Cities are also urged to strengthen industrial and supply chains, promote smooth domestic circulation and avoid local protectionism. The circular also calls for better planning of major projects, stronger safety management, and timely assessment of the pilot programs' economic, social and environmental benefits.
The three departments will assess the pilot programs, with the results serving as the basis for allocating central government reward funds. The funds must be disbursed promptly and used only to support hydrogen energy applications, helping lower hydrogen-use costs and pass the savings on to end users, according to the circular.
The initiative comes as China seeks to expand the use of cleaner energy in industry and transport. Hydrogen produced using renewable electricity can help reduce carbon emissions, although high costs and challenges in storage and transportation remain obstacles to wider adoption.
China is already the world's largest producer and consumer of hydrogen, with output exceeding 39 million tonnes in 2025, according to official data.
Under a policy issued in March, China aims to have 100,000 fuel cell vehicles nationwide by 2030, while each city cluster can receive up to 1.6 billion yuan (about 238 million U.S. dollars) in central government reward funds over the four-year pilot period. ■

YEREVAN, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for faster and stronger global action to protect biodiversity, warning that efforts to halt nature loss remain far behind international targets.
Speaking at a leaders' summit in Yerevan, Armenia's capital, Guterres urged countries to show "more action, more speed, and more will" ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), scheduled for Oct. 19-30.
"Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability," he said, urging countries to assess their progress in protecting nature.
More than 1 million species face extinction, threatened by climate change, invasive species, overexploitation of natural resources and pollution, he warned.
Guterres said the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, had laid out a path to "make peace with nature," but progress remained uneven and far too slow.
Nearly 90 percent of parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity have set national biodiversity targets, while more than half have developed implementation plans. Since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square km of land and 6 million square km of ocean have come under formal protection, he said.
However, even if current national commitments are fulfilled, only 26 percent of land and 12 percent of marine areas would be protected by 2030, falling short of the global target of 30 percent for both.
Funding also remains a major obstacle. Citing a report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, Guterres said biodiversity financing stood at less than half the annual target of 200 billion U.S. dollars set under the framework.
"Biodiversity is not a separate challenge," he said, stressing its links to climate change, conflict, food insecurity and disease.
Guterres urged governments, financial institutions and businesses to accelerate implementation of the framework, calling for sustainable agriculture, circular economies, stronger environmental monitoring and stricter enforcement of existing laws. ■

Belgium To Transfer Ten F-16s to Ukraine by the End of Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:02:29 UTC
04:02:29 KST

Belgium plans to transfer ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever made this announcement after meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels, according to a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent.
“We will transfer ten this year. We have a slight delay, but it’s not our fault—it’s due to a delay in the delivery of the F-35s. We must be able to fulfill our NATO commitments, so we need the aircraft. The F-35s are now starting to arrive, and this allows us to transfer the F-16s to Ukraine,” de Wever said.
He emphasized that Ukraine urgently needs the fighter jets, particularly to combat Russian jet drones.
“The jet-powered drones that Russia now possesses have given it an advantage in the drone war. And the F-16, with its 20-millimeter cannon, is one of the few types of weaponry that can be widely used to defend against them,” explained the Belgian prime minister.
According to him, Ukraine also needs air cover to protect grain exports through the Black Sea, as well as its energy infrastructure and bridges.
De Wever said he discussed with Zelensky the possibility of accelerating deliveries, as well as the transfer of 20-millimeter ammunition manufactured by the Belgian company FN Herstal.
“We can help him. We have that capability. In particular, we can help with 20-millimeter ammunition,” he noted.
In June, Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken announced that by the end of 2026, the country would transfer seven F-16s to Ukraine, three of which are intended for combat missions and four for spare parts.
De Wever did not specify how many of the now-promised ten aircraft would be designated for combat use and how many for spare parts.
In May 2024, Belgium committed to supplying Ukraine with a total of 30 F-16 fighter jets by 2028. The overall plan calls for the transfer of 53 Belgian F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2029.
Initially, it was planned that Ukraine would receive the first Belgian fighter jets as early as 2024. However, the delivery was postponed due to delays in the arrival of American F-35s, which are set to replace the F-16s in the Belgian Air Force.
In early October, it was reported that Belgium’s transfer of three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine would take place immediately after the signing of an agreement with France on the transfer of technology to a third party.

Greece’s violation narrative defends an airspace boundary that does not exist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:59:01 UTC
03:59:01 KST

Above the Aegean lies an imaginary boundary that Athens has imposed for years, treating a line drawn for civil aviation as a unilateral declaration of sovereignty.
On that basis, the Greek General Staff regularly issues “violations and infringements” bulletins, systematically labelling Turkish aircraft activities that comply with international law as “airspace violations”.
Greek media carry the same framing in the same language, and a 10-nautical-mile airspace claim, resting on no international treaty, is planted in the public mind day after day.
This pattern produced its most recent example a few days ago.
On October 5, 2026, two Turkish F-16s came into close contact with Greek fighter jets off Meis.
Greek authorities announced a tally of seven aircraft for that day (two armed F-16s, one maritime patrol aircraft and four unmanned aerial vehicles) and released the figures as “seven FIR infringements and nine violations of national airspace”.
Those figures were released on the eve of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Athens on 6 October, and a fresh “15 violations” bulletin was announced on the day of the visit.
Yet flight information region (FIR) responsibility and sovereignty over national airspace belong to different categories. Turkish aircraft fly within the Athens FIR while remaining in international airspace, and Athens counts that airspace as its own on a legally invalid basis.
Greece thereby merges two separate categories under a single heading of sovereignty violation in its political discourse, keeping its maximalist claim alive.
This is precisely where the real issue surfaces: a flight information region, which carries a technical aviation responsibility, is being turned into a state boundary in political discourse and into propaganda against Türkiye.
Limits drawn by international law
Sovereignty over national airspace finds its legal basis in the 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation.
Article 1 affirms that every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory, and Article 2 defines “territory” as the land areas and the adjacent territorial waters under that state’s sovereignty. The extent of airspace is therefore tied to the extent of territorial waters.
That principle of sovereignty offers no basis for attributing sovereignty to FIRs responsible for providing air traffic services in international airspace.
An official working paper (A35-WP/109) submitted by the United States to the 35th Session of the Assembly of ICAO (International Civil Aviation Organization) states that FIR arrangements bear no direct relation to sovereignty, that delegating air traffic service responsibility to another state does not derogate from national sovereignty, and that the authority of the state providing that service is limited to technical and operational considerations.
The paper grounds these findings in ICAO Annex 11, which governs air traffic services.
Air traffic service responsibility in those parts of the Athens FIR that cover international airspace therefore confers no right on Greece to establish sovereignty over those areas or to require prior flight plans from state aircraft.
This is the legal distinction on which Türkiye’s objection rests: air traffic service responsibility is not equated with sovereign authority, and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs records plainly state that “there is no such concept” as a “FIR violation”.
Türkiye’s refusal to meet the flight plan request also rests on the Convention itself. Article 3 states that the Convention applies to civil aircraft and not to state aircraft, so no flight-plan obligation arises for military aircraft.
That same article establishes the authorisation requirement for flights over another state's territory, and the band between 6 and 10 nautical miles falls outside the definition of territory in Article 2.
As for the provision Greek military authorities invoke, it obliges states, when issuing regulations for their own state aircraft, to have due regard for the safety of civil aircraft navigation.
It gives no state the authority to request another's flight plans.
Athens’ own official statements carry the argument to a more striking point. Greece’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs states plainly on its “Athens FIR” page that the FIR arrangement does not concern sovereignty; it concerns only jurisdiction.
Even so, statements Greek military authorities publish under the heading of FIR violation systematically blur the distinction between air traffic service responsibility and sovereignty over national airspace.
On its own page of terms, the General Staff defines national airspace as 10 nautical miles based on a 1931 decree and states that entry into the Athens FIR without a flight plan counts as an infringement.
Two institutions of the same state tell two different versions of the law on the same question. Through military bulletins, a responsibility officially acknowledged to bear no relation to sovereignty is converted into a stream of data that feeds a claim of sovereignty.
This claim traces back to a decree that entered into force in 1931.
Its title in the United Nations repository of national legislation on the law of the sea reveals the nature of the instrument, which defines the extent of territorial waters for the purposes of aviation and the control thereof and fixes the territorial waters referred to in Civil Aviation Act No. 5017 at 10 nautical miles from the coast.
Greece’s actual territorial waters at that date measured 3 nautical miles.
When Athens extended them to 6 nautical miles in 1936, it retained the 10-mile figure devised for aviation purposes, creating a 4-mile gap between sovereignty at sea and airspace, one that has lasted to this day.
One territorial sea for aviation, another for seafaring…
The Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs recounts how the claim was promulgated on its own website. According to the ministry, the 10-mile limit was entered into aeronautical information publications and maps; the ministry submitted the maps to ICAO in 1955, and the minutes of the 1958 regional meeting referred to them.
Every document offered as the basis of a sovereignty boundary consists of domestic legislation and technical aviation records, and none of them carries the character of a treaty that establishes a boundary.
Türkiye rejects this claim.
Its Ministry of Foreign Affairs records that the band between 6 and 10 nautical miles forms part of international airspace, describes the Greek thesis as arbitrary, and defines it as an attempt to reduce the international airspace of the Aegean by 50 percent.
Indeed, a claim to airspace wider than the territorial waters beneath it finds no basis in the Convention or in general practice.
One of Athens’ closest allies has confirmed this maximalist claim's legal weakness through its official position.
A report prepared under the Eastern Mediterranean Security and Energy Partnership Act of 2019 stated that Washington officially recognises airspace of up to 6 nautical miles in the Aegean and does not share the Greek government’s view.
The report also noted that Congress could not be provided with the list of Turkish violations it requested because the boundaries are disputed.
Airspace coinciding with territorial waters is settled international practice, and Greece’s thesis falls outside it.
A claim resting on a domestic decree and unrecognised internationally amounts to nothing more than a unilateral, maximalist political choice.
Narrative of victimhood
When Athens presents its legal disputes with Türkiye to international opinion, it positions itself as the party whose sovereignty and security are under threat, and it has turned this into something close to a policy.
By framing the Aegean disagreements as a challenge to Greece’s rights, this approach equates Türkiye’s legal objections with threats and places Athens’ theses at the centre of the debate.
Official statements from the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs regarding disputes in Turkish-Greek relations provide clear examples of this approach.
On issues such as Aegean airspace, the demilitarised status of the islands, maritime jurisdiction, and FIR responsibility, Athens presents its own theses as legal facts while characterising Türkiye’s objections as a challenge to Greek sovereignty.
This narrative merges disputes with different legal bases and different historical trajectories into a single discourse of “Turkish pressure”.
This pushes Greece’s own maximalist choices into the background and automatically recasts Türkiye’s objections, grounded in international law, as problematic conduct.
Carrying this discourse to the European Union level is also politically striking. The European Commission’s November 4, 2025 Türkiye report offers a current example of bilateral disputes entering the language of an institutional text.
That report records that Türkiye has conducted no unauthorised flights over Greek islands since 2023. Its overall narrative, however, treats the Aegean disputes through Greece’s claims and lends Athens’ theses an institutional weight they have not earned.
Greece continues to broaden its political support for its theses by bringing bilateral disputes onto the EU agenda. Using EU membership for that purpose does nothing to turn Athens’ claims into theses that international law accepts.
Athens’ avoidance of judicial settlement on this question marks the weakest point in the narrative. Greece’s January 14, 2015 declaration recognising the International Court of Justice's compulsory jurisdiction excludes from the Court’s jurisdiction disputes concerning state boundaries or sovereignty over its territory, and, in framing that exception, expressly lists disputes over the breadth and limits of its territorial sea and airspace.
A party that claims its sovereignty has been violated has, by its own hand, closed off the compulsory judicial route that would determine where that sovereignty's boundary runs.
Confidence in a legal position does not require shielding it from review.
Resolving the Aegean disputes requires a consistent assessment based on the relevant international instruments and the parties' legal grounds.
Athens needs to stop manufacturing tension over imaginary boundaries; otherwise, no genuine ground for dialogue in the Aegean can be established, even in the long term.

German expert: Trump ready to make any deal with Putin for his own gain
Stefan Meister, Head of the Center for Order and Governance in Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“…Trump has no problem with Putin whatsoever. He can make any deal with him. Ukraine is relatively irrelevant to him. I’ll say that quite frankly,” the political scientist said.
Commenting on the latest agreements between the U.S. President and Putin on supplies of Russian diesel fuel and the easing of related sanctions, Meister said he believed the decisions were driven primarily by Trump’s domestic political interests ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
“I think everything with Trump is short-term. Very little is thought through for the long term or has a strategic basis. So, I assume that he is primarily thinking about the midterm elections to Congress. He wants to quickly bring down the prices of diesel fuel and gasoline, and for that reason he is moving closer to Russia,” the expert said.
In his view, this behavior points to a fundamental shift in the nature of U.S. foreign policy under the current administration, which is increasingly focused on economic gain and deal-making rather than values-based principles.
“There is no carefully thought-out strategy behind this, but this interest-driven policy, focused on economic gain and deal-making, means that Trump is ready to do business with virtually any autocrat, including Putin. If he sees a benefit for himself, he is ready to make any deal. This is a fundamental change in U.S. policy,” Meister said.
The political scientist emphasized that such a policy by Washington does not contribute to ending Russian aggression, while Putin does not regard Trump’s calls for a ceasefire as sufficient incentive to change his own plans.
According to the German expert, the U.S. President has no influence whatsoever over the Kremlin leader.
“Trump has no influence over Putin whatsoever. I even think that Trump’s chaotic policy and his attempts to move closer to Russia primarily provoke contempt in Putin. For Putin, this is a sign of weakness,” he said.
In Meister’s assessment, without real consequences for Moscow, Washington’s diplomatic initiatives are unlikely to change the Russian leadership’s calculations or stop further attacks against Ukraine.
As reported, U.S. President Donald Trump criticized Ukraine’s decision to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries in an interview with Newsmax, saying that they allegedly contribute to keeping global energy prices high. He also said that Ukraine should elect a different president to negotiate with Moscow.

Whalefall Is the Most Disgusting Tearjerker You'll See This Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:58:25 UTC
03:58:25 KST

Warning: This post contains spoilers for Whalefall, now in theaters.
It's been a big few months for Austin Abrams moaning and groaning his way through some of the worst situations imaginable. First, as medical courier Bryan Hodukavich in Resident Evil, he was forced to contend with an onslaught of mutant zombie monsters. Now, as Jay Gardiner in Whalefall, he spends the majority of the film's 106-minute runtime getting repeatedly maimed inside the belly of an 80-foot-long sperm whale that weighs 60 tons.
Directed by Brian Duffield (No One Will Save You, Spontaneous) and co-written with Daniel Kraus (the author of the best-selling 2023 novel on which the movie is based), Whalefall follows Jay as he plunges into the treacherous depths off Northern California's Monastery Beach to retrieve the unrecovered remains of his late father Mitt (Josh Brolin), a legendary local diver who became severely ill from advanced, terminal Mesothelioma. The movie's opening scene shows Mitt leaving sealed letters for his wife and three children in a cooler on his boat before taking his own life by strapping diving weights to himself and jumping into the ocean. A year later, Jay still hasn't opened his letter when he is swallowed by a massive whale who's on the hunt for a giant squid in those same waters.
With just about an hour of oxygen left in his diving tank, Jay must endure a series of increasingly agonizing ordeals as he searches for a way to escape his terrifying predicament. There's a nasty encounter with the giant squid's razor-sharp beak, exposure to corrosive stomach acid, and the ever-present threat of being crushed by the whale's constricting organs or suffocating on the toxic, unbreathable methane gas inside its body. Amid the visceral horror of Jay's ingestion, we learn more about his complicated relationship with Mitt, a harsh and often emotionally abusive man, through a series of flashbacks.
Eventually, the whale breaches the surface and Jay nearly manages to break free by climbing out of its open mouth. But he ends up tumbling back inside the whale as it dives deep down into the ocean, causing Jay's eardrums to explode and him to start to hallucinate from lack of oxygen and panic. It's then that Jay, believing he is likely going to die, begins hearing his late father's voice speaking to him through the whale. As the whale is attacked by orcas, saved by its own pod, and returns to the surface, Jay is forced to process his trauma, confront the guilt and grief he feels over not visiting his dad before he died, and come to the realization that the only way he's going to survive is by applying the tough-love diving lessons Mitt drilled into him as a child to his current situation.
"The whole story is based on his relationship with his father, and not being able to take in what his father is trying to impart because of his father's personality and the way that he does it," Brolin told the Direct of Whalefall's overarching message. "And I think what the whale represents a symbol of how to get out of our own way in order to inhale those gems that you need, because I think the father really wants him to become self-sustaining, and he does it in a way that's almost paranoid. So the son can't hear it, and then when the son needs it, you see that he heard it. He just didn't hear it in the way that [his father] wanted him to, and I don't blame him, by the way."
In the end, Jay is able to escape the whale, who has already succumbed to its orca injuries, by managing to blow it up from the inside. The whole thing is overly sappy and obviously a bit preposterous, but if you're able overlook the absurdity of the premise and some particularly cheesy lines of dialogue, then you may be left feeling some type of way about the meaning of unconditional love. As the whale version of Mitt somberly reminds Jay, "The whale is forever."

Clashes erupted between protesters and police during Argentina’s fifth Federal University March on Thursday, as thousands gathered outside Congress in Buenos Aires to demand that President Javier Milei’s government implement the University Funding Law.
At least 10 people were injured and 31 detained, including two minors, local media outlet La Nacion reported Friday.

The organizers demanded that the government implement legislation guaranteeing funding for public universities, including provisions on staff salaries and student scholarships.
The central rally ended earlier than scheduled at around 4.40 pm local time (1940GMT) due to heavy rain and clashes in the surrounding area, La Nacion reported.
Organizers condemned the police response and reiterated their demand that the government comply with the funding law.
Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva defended the police operation in a post on US social media company X, saying the right to demonstrate did not justify violence.
She warned that those who attacked security personnel or damaged public property would face justice.
Authorities estimated damage to public infrastructure around Congress at 90 million Argentine pesos ($59,376), according to La Nacion.
The protest took place amid a prolonged dispute between Milei’s government and public universities over funding.
University representatives have warned that budget constraints are eroding staff purchasing power and undermining student support.
The government has pursued austerity measures to reduce public spending, prompting repeated demonstrations by university staff and students demanding greater resources for public higher education.

Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:57:40 UTC
03:57:40 KST

Kenya records third Ebola case, linked to first patient who died
Nairobi says 65-year-old female patient in quarantine with Bundibugyo strain; no signs of community transmission.
Kenya has recorded its third case of the Bundibugyo virus disease – a strain of Ebola that has killed thousands of people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) – 10 days after reporting its first case and death in Nairobi.
The latest confirmed case – a 65-year-old woman – was a “primary contact and a close relative of the first and second cases”, Kenya’s Health Ministry said in a statement on Friday, adding that the patient has been in quarantine since October 6.
After developing symptoms, she was isolated and then tested positive for the virus, it added in a statement.
“Once she developed fever, sore throat and malaise, she was isolated and specimen collected for testing. She tested positive for Ebola,” the Health Ministry said. “She was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care improving her chances of recovery.”
Kenya’s cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, which is the second-largest on record globally  with more than 9,000 cases and over 4,300 deaths since it was officially detected in May.
Kenya’s first case emerged last week after a Kenyan man, who had been ill in the DRC about a month before travelling by road to Uganda, flew to Nairobi on October 3, where a relative drove him to the hospital. He died on October 5.
In its statement on X, the Health Ministry moved to reassure the public that there was no community spread of the disease and that the risk to the Kenyan public remained low.
Out of 130 contacts listed, 127 had been traced and were in quarantine, it said.
Efforts to control the spread of the Ebola outbreak have been complicated because the Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine. Research is under way to develop one or more vaccines that work against the strain and some of these vaccines are already in the early phases of testing in humans.
Transparency demands over Ebola response funds
The new case in Kenya was reported as Africa’s top public health body and Congolese health authorities called for greater transparency in how Ebola response funds are used.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said financial information provided by aid organisations indicated that more than $700m of donor money was unaccounted for.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa CDC, told the Reuters news agency that international donors disbursed about $962m to organisations implementing Ebola response activities in DRC, rather than to the government.
Kaseya said those organisations reported receiving $228m, of which $127m had been spent and roughly $100m remained available.
But he said it was too early to speak of embezzlement.
In a post on X, Congolese Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba warned aid groups were required to provide details on funding sources to his ministry or risk being barred from working in DRC and blacklisted across Africa.
Meanwhile, on the ground in the DRC, Ebola cases have been detected in a new province bordering the Central African Republic, two health officials told Reuters on Thursday.
The two cases were confirmed in North Ubangi, the eighth Congolese province affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak, the officials said. Congolese authorities have not yet officially announced the outbreak has spread to North Ubangi.

From Terah to today: The many roads that lead Jews home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:53 UTC
03:56:53 KST

For thousands of years, Jews lived in exile, far from the land of our ancestors. Scattered across the world, we dreamed of returning to the country we had once inhabited. Wherever Jewish history carried us, our hearts remained attached to the same place.
We lived in countless countries, spoke different languages, and belonged to different cultures. Through centuries of wandering, one truth remained unchanged. There is only one Jewish homeland.
The first Zionist
Though there is only one Jewish homeland, there are many roads that lead home. This was always true. Terah, the father of Abraham, was raised in a world of idolatry. Yet he felt an inner tug to leave Mesopotamia, modern-day Iraq, and journey toward the Land of Israel. He received no Divine command. He did not believe in the one God, yet something stirred within him, drawing him toward a distant land.
Ironically, he was the first Zionist, the first person described by the Torah as setting out for the Land of Israel from his homeland. His motives are unknown. He gathered his son Abraham and other family members and traveled toward Canaan. Along the way, Terah settled in Haran, where he eventually died.
His son Abraham later heard the voice of God commanding him to continue the journey his father had begun. Abraham traveled to the Land of Israel with a religious mission: to spread belief in the one God. Yet his pagan father had begun the journey.
Evidently, God implanted within the Jewish soul an instinctive attachment to its homeland. He gave us the ability to respond to the pull of land, peoplehood, and historical destiny even without religious commitment or prophetic revelation. At history’s dawn, this attachment could awaken even in a heart that had not yet awakened to faith.
The age of “isms”
This ancient echo reemerged millennia later. The 19th century witnessed a dramatic weakening of organized religion. The Enlightenment and the Age of Reason promised to lift humanity out of the ignorance and suffering of the medieval world. Science, discovery, and individualism propelled humanity toward an era of progress.
Organized religion, and Christianity in particular, was increasingly blamed for centuries of human suffering. Its unholy alliance with monarchy and political power had contributed to bloodshed and feudalism. Religion’s walls were crumbling.
Into this widening void emerged new ideologies. Society abhors a vacuum, and ideologies rushed to replace religion. Socialism, utilitarianism, communism, and other movements competed for the hearts and minds of Europeans.
It was the great age of “isms,” as new systems of thought offered competing visions of human identity, social order, and historical progress.
Yet perhaps the most powerful “ism” of all was nationalism. Increasingly, people defined themselves primarily by their nation rather than their religion. “John” was no longer primarily a Protestant who happened to live in England, but a proud Englishman who happened to be Protestant.
“Gustave” was no longer primarily a Catholic who happened to live in France, but a proud Frenchman who happened to be Catholic. National identity swept across a continent long shaped by religion and religious rivalries.
A Jewish awakening
Unfortunately, Judaism did not fare much better than other religions. With Emancipation, for the first time in our long exile, we were invited to become full-fledged members of an enlightened European society.
Many combined these newfound freedoms with traditional Jewish observance, but others abandoned their Jewish roots entirely.
Many Jews look back with reverence upon the great age of the yeshivot, when brilliant young men devoted years, sometimes decades, to intensive Torah study. This remarkable era helped lay the foundations for the phenomenal growth of Torah study in the modern world.
Yet there was another side to this history. Far more Jews were drawn into the universities and intellectual circles of Europe than into its great yeshivot. For many, the door swung in only one direction: away from Jewish religious life.
Millions of Jews faced the threat of losing their Jewish identity and disappearing into the surrounding culture. Traditional religious appeals no longer spoke to them. If Jewish identity depended exclusively upon religious commitment, an enormous portion of the Jewish people was in danger of being lost to history.
As Jewish identity weakened across Europe, God awakened that ancient echo. In the age of nationalism, Jewish nationalism emerged, offering Jews a way to identify with their land, their people, and their history. It captured the hearts of Jews, including many who had drifted away from religious observance.
Secular Zionism was a Divine impulse, awakening an ancient attachment to our land and people that had lain dormant for centuries. As religious commitment weakened, God stirred a different form of Jewish consciousness. Millions of Jews today express their deepest connection to their people through their commitment to our national project of return and to the modern State of Israel.
Oct. 7 demonstrated how deeply the State of Israel stands at the center of contemporary Jewish identity and how much more vulnerable Jewish life would be without it.
This became even more evident in the subsequent eruption of anti-Zionism and its frequent convergence with antisemitism, which further underscored Israel’s centrality to Jewish identity and the Jewish future. Israel has become a powerful anchor of Jewish belonging, even for Jews whose connection to religious observance is limited.
Thousands of years ago, Terah felt the pull of our land without profound religious conviction. Thousands of years later, countless Jews, far less detached from God than Terah had been, followed a similar path. They felt drawn to the same land, the same people, and the same historical destiny.
Across the centuries, Jews have found their way home through countless different journeys, shaped by different convictions, circumstances, dreams, and personal attachments. There is one home, but there are many roads which lead home.
Another road home
The roads leading to our homeland are as varied as the Jewish people themselves. Some are paved with religious conviction, others with national identity and historical consciousness.
Many Jews harbor a lifelong dream of aliyah and eventually fulfill that dream by building their lives and families in Israel. Still other roads emerge unexpectedly, shaped by circumstances, personal attachments, and the bonds of family.
My mother, of blessed memory, passed away this past Sukkot. She took a different road to our one homeland. We were raised in a Zionist home, though not an especially ideological one, and Zionism was not a central part of our upbringing.
Our family grew up in Brooklyn during the 1970s, when it was a thriving center of Modern Orthodox Jewish life, with flourishing synagogues, schools, and communities.
Moving to Israel was never part of her plan. However, her children developed a deep attachment to Israel, and all eventually moved here and built their families.
Wanting to be close to her children, grandchildren, and eventually great-grandchildren, my mother and father moved to Israel at an advanced age.
Their aliyah was not the fulfillment of a lifelong dream. It was not driven primarily by ideology or Zionist conviction. It was driven by a deep love of family.
Yet leaving behind a familiar world and beginning a new life so late in life required enormous courage and determination. I will always be grateful to my Mommy for making that sacrifice and giving us those precious years together. My mother made that journey, and now she is buried just a few minutes from our home in Gush Etzion.
There are many roads that lead home. Some are paved with ideology, conviction, and Zionist dreams. Others are paved with something simpler and more personal: the love of family.
May God bless her soul, and may her love and devotion continue to inspire our family for generations.
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, at mtaraginbooks.com

Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:50 UTC
03:56:50 KST

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.
But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.
The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.
This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.
Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.
The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%).
However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.
Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.
These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.
The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.
The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.
The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soya monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.
It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.
The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country.
Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.
The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.
Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.
Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible.
“However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”

Thai authorities inspect Chabad House in Chiang Mai, find no violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:46 UTC
03:56:46 KST

Thai law enforcement authorities conducted a multi-agency inspection of the Chabad House on Chang Khlan Road in Chiang Mai on Wednesday, led by Deputy Provincial Governor Boonlue Thammatharanurak, finding no legal violations or irregularities at the Jewish community center.
At a press conference after the inspection, the deputy governor said Thai law does not clearly regulate premises that also serve as Jewish places of worship. He noted that gatherings primarily take place on Fridays and Saturdays, attracting approximately 100 to 200 participants, mostly Israelis attending communal meals, and recommended that the center maintain a "low-key" approach to its activities.
The inspection involved representatives from the provincial administration, military, immigration police, provincial cultural authorities, Chiang Mai Municipality, and the Internal Security Operations Command (ISOC). Authorities reported finding no violations, with the deputy governor describing the visit as a "routine inspection" that had not been prompted by any complaint.
Officials examined the legality of the property's lease and operating licenses. According to local media reports, Chabad rents restaurant premises from a local resident under a lease valid until 2028 and holds a food service license covering up to 200 square meters, as well as an alcohol license issued by the Excise Department.
Chiang Mai Chabad inspection follows raids on Jewish institutions in Bangkok
The Chiang Mai inspection differed significantly from the raids carried out in Bangkok on October 8, when Thailand's Department of Special Investigation (DSI) conducted searches under judicial warrants, with the involvement of the justice minister and several government agencies.
The Bangkok operation involved police, tax authorities, immigration officials, the Lands Department, and the Anti-Money Laundering Office, among other agencies.
During searches at the Chabad Foundation, the Jewish Association of Thailand, and related offices, investigators seized documents, identified foreign workers from Myanmar and Laos without valid work permits, and found dozens of companies registered at the same address.
The operation formed part of an investigation into suspected nominee ownership arrangements, property holdings, and financial activities involving Israeli-linked businesses.
Unlike the Bangkok raids, the Chiang Mai inspection was presented by authorities as a routine enforcement visit, with no reports of search warrants or seized materials.
The Chabad House in Chiang Mai has operated since 2004 and has undergone inspections over the years. However, a coordinated inspection involving so many enforcement agencies had never previously taken place at the center in more than two decades of operation.
Thailand expands investigations into Israeli-linked businesses and Chabad centers
The inspection comes amid a broader wave of enforcement operations involving Chabad institutions across Thailand, including Phuket, Bangkok, and other locations.
The operations, expanded partly under instructions from Thailand's deputy interior minister, are linked to investigations into business and property networks associated with Israeli nationals.
Authorities have raised concerns regarding foreign ownership, financing arrangements, and commercial practices, against a backdrop of public tensions involving Israeli tourists.
Israeli Ambassador to Thailand Dr. Alona Fisher-Kamm visited the provincial government building and met with the deputy governor approximately one month ago. She also visited the Chiang Mai Chabad House separately during the same period.
Thai authorities said they would continue monitoring the premises but emphasized that there were currently "no irregularities."
Journalists were not permitted to enter the building during the inspection. According to reporters at the scene, Chabad security personnel prevented them from entering.
Chiang Mai Chabad rabbi says center operates in full compliance with Thai law
Rabbi Yossi Pikel and his wife, Chani, have served as Chabad emissaries in Chiang Mai, northern Thailand, for 17 years.
The couple welcomes Jewish visitors and travelers to the city, providing assistance, guidance, and support throughout their stay.
The Chabad House offers prayer services, Shabbat and holiday meals, and classes on Hasidic teachings and the weekly Torah portion.
The center also operates a synagogue, a kosher meat restaurant offering packaged food for travelers, a women's mikveh (ritual bath), a travelers' shop, and additional services.
Speaking to Walla, Rabbi Pikel said the inspection had been coordinated in advance. He explained that inspections take place periodically but acknowledged that a joint visit involving so many agencies was unusual.
"I'm glad they came to inspect, and I'm glad they saw that everything was in order," Pikel said. "We operate by the book and try to do everything properly."
The rabbi also emphasized his efforts to build positive relations with the local Thai community, noting that the restaurant is open to Thai residents as well as Jewish and Israeli visitors.
He said that all visitors are welcome, subject to the center's security screening procedures.
"The place is open to everyone," Pikel said.

Israeli media's polling obscures the majority opposed to Netanyahu - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:16 UTC
03:56:16 KST

Israel’s media is reporting astonishing news this week: in the polls, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc has overtaken that of Gadi Eisenkot.
After all the failures, disasters, scandals, and debacles of recent years, could Netanyahu really be heading for another victory? According to the reports, apparently so. In reality, not so much. We are seeing a misreading of the polls.
According to recent surveys, Netanyahu’s bloc has about 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Eisenkot’s bloc stands at 51 or 52 – but only because of artificial exclusions.
When all the parties opposed to Netanyahu’s continued rule, meaning the right-wing and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) bloc, are counted together, the total reaches about 67 seats. That is a solid parliamentary majority, six seats above the threshold required, and virtually unprecedented in Israel’s modern political era.
For at least the past half-century, since the end of Mapai’s one-party dominance era, a prime minister whose opponents held 67 seats two weeks before an election would have been described as heading toward defeat.
Instead, the public is being told that Netanyahu is leading.
How does this happen? Quite simply, the political blocs are being counted in a way that serves Netanyahu.
Parties opposed to him are excluded from the change bloc because they are not considered natural coalition partners, prefer a national unity government, or because they have ideological disagreements with other opposition parties.
The result is the false appearance of a close race, or even a right-wing advantage, when the numbers themselves tell a very different story.
Herein lies the fundamental mistake: a solid political bloc and a governing coalition are not the same thing. Elections first determine the balance of power in the Knesset. Only afterward do negotiations over forming a government begin.
A party can oppose Netanyahu without committing to join an Eisenkot government, and it can support a government from outside the coalition without becoming part of it. A recommendation to the president is another matter entirely.
The conflation of these concepts has become a powerful political tool in Netanyahu’s hands.
Three factors illustrate just how misleading the conventional arithmetic has become: the Reservists party, the Arab parties, and Ofer Winter’s party.
Start with the Reservists party. This new outfit, which receives four seats in some polls, is excluded from the change bloc because its leaders favor a national unity government. Fine.
But a preference regarding the composition of a government is hardly equivalent to supporting Netanyahu’s continued rule.
The Reservists’ positions on the judicial overhaul, equality in military service, the political system, and even the Palestinian issue are considerably closer to those of the camp seeking to replace Netanyahu than to his alliance with Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the haredi parties.
Even if they are unwilling to commit in advance to an Eisenkot-led coalition, there is no political logic in portraying them as an entirely neutral force.
At the very least, they should be regarded as potential members of the change bloc, even if they would be reluctant partners who set conditions. Their preference for unity does nothing to change the fact that the current government is a long way from the political vision they present.
Arab parties and Ofer Winter
The second distortion is much larger and more consequential: the Arab parties.
This may be Netanyahu’s most impressive political achievement.
For years, he has managed to persuade large sections of the public, including his political opponents, that the votes of Israel’s Arab citizens somehow count for less when determining who has won an election.
The Right is allowed to count all its natural allies, while the Center-Left is expected to behave as though a substantial portion of its potential majority simply does not exist.
There are, of course, profound ideological differences between the Arab parties and the Zionist parties of the Center and Left. Israel’s Jewish character creates discomfort, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and national security present genuine difficulties.
It is also clear that Eisenkot, Avigdor Liberman, and Naftali Bennett are reluctant to form a government dependent on Arab parties, or even to be seen as willing to do so.
But this is where the confusion Netanyahu has so successfully cultivated begins: whether a particular party will join a coalition is a different question from whether its seats can prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
Israeli history has already provided examples. In 1992, Labor and Meretz won 56 seats, while the five seats held by Hadash and the Arab Democratic Party gave Yitzhak Rabin’s camp a parliamentary majority of 61. Nobody doubted Rabin had won.
Rabin formed a government with Shas, but after its departure he relied on outside support from the Arab parties.
In 2021, Yair Lapid succeeded in assembling the coalition that removed Netanyahu from power, with the four seats of the Islamist Ra’am party forming an essential part of its majority: 61, to which Bennett, much like Shas in Rabin’s day, simply added his seats.
Netanyahu, by contrast, is never required to explain why the haredi parties, which oppose drafting their young men into the military and demand budgets and privileges that provoke widespread public resentment, are legitimate partners in his bloc. Their seats are counted automatically.
But when it comes to Arab parties, ideological disagreements suddenly become grounds for excluding them from the calculation. Suddenly, unlike in years past, they have disappeared from the opposition bloc in the media’s pie charts.
Netanyahu has managed to turn this double standard into a political convention.
The third factor, and perhaps the most intriguing of all, is a new party led by firebrand Brig.-Gen. (res.) Ofer Winter.
Winter has declared that he will recommend to the president that Netanyahu be tasked with forming the next government, so it is natural to count him initially with the Right.
Although Winter is an unmistakably right-wing figure, he also supports drafting haredi men into the military, a position that puts him on a collision course with Netanyahu’s haredi partners.
How can he sit in a government dependent on parties that oppose one of the central reforms he wants to advance?
Suppose Winter recommends Netanyahu, as promised. Even with Winter, however, Netanyahu reaches only 53 seats, according to the numbers under discussion. He is eight short.
A presidential recommendation cannot manufacture parliamentary seats that do not exist, and if Netanyahu cannot recruit additional partners, he cannot form a government.
At that point, another possibility could open up for Winter: joining a government of change focused on rebuilding the country.
There is no guarantee he would choose that path. But there is also no reason to assume that a declaration of loyalty to Netanyahu during an election campaign necessarily determines his behavior under every possible post-election scenario.
Urgent national tasks
The next government of change would face an enormous agenda, much of which would not require agreement on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
It would need to repair Israel’s foreign relations, address the military draft crisis and relations with the haredim, restore basic standards of good governance, combat rampant crime, and establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures of October 7.
These are urgent national tasks on which broad agreement could emerge, even among people with radically different views about the future of the territories.
Winter would not be a natural partner for a major diplomatic initiative with the Palestinians. But such an initiative is unlikely to get underway in the first year or two of the next government anyway.
During that period, simply preventing further damage would be an important achievement: curbing Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, halting the establishment of illegal outposts, and avoiding measures that would deepen Israel’s international isolation.
Agreement with Winter on some of these issues would be difficult, but there is no reason to assume in advance that every compromise is impossible.
Eisenkot, Bennett, and Lapid are projecting growing confidence that they can form a government based on a Jewish parliamentary majority, without relying on the Arab parties. Clearly, that confidence rests on precisely the scenarios described above.
And with the addition of outside support from the Arab factions, something they have already promised free of charge, such a government could conceivably enjoy an enormous parliamentary majority.
The coming election could therefore very well bring Netanyahu’s rule to an end.
That possibility may be considerably closer than the public realizes, simply because the media continues to present the political landscape according to rules that Netanyahu himself has managed to establish.
Caution is necessary, of course, because polls are not votes cast at the ballot box. But it is equally important to read the polls correctly. That matters if the change bloc is to find the fighting spirit needed to bring masses of voters to the polls.
And there is room for hope. As Theodor Herzl famously put it, “If you will it, it is no dream.”
Especially when the alternative is failure and Netanyahu somehow remaining in power, which would be a catastrophe threatening the very future of the state.
The writer is a former Cairo-based Middle East editor and London-based Europe/Africa editor of the Associated Press. He served as chairman of the Foreign Press Association in Jerusalem and authored two books about Israel.

FAA bars unauthorized drones along US-Mexico border, citing security concerns
