FAA bars unauthorized drones along US-Mexico border, citing security concerns
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 - The Federal Aviation Administration said on Friday it is barring unauthorized drones along the US border with Mexico as the government steps up efforts to address concerns about illegal cross-border drug shipments.
The temporary flight restriction bars any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet (122 m) above ground level and extends one nautical mile north of the US-Mexico border. In April, the FAA and Pentagon signed an agreement allowing the government's use of a high-energy laser counter-drone system along the southern US border with Mexico to address drone threats.
The Pentagon has said there are more than 1,000 drone incursions along the US-Mexico border each month. US security officials have increasingly expressed alarm about the use of drones by Mexican cartels to drop drug packages or surveil trafficking routes.
"By restricting unauthorized drone activity, we are giving commanders greater awareness, greater decision space, and more options to defend the homeland," said Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, adding that the military "will shoot down any cartel drone that threatens America’s sovereignty.”
In February, the FAA said it would halt all flights for 10 days at the El Paso, Texas, airport because of the use of the Pentagon laser system by Customs and Border Protection without completion of an FAA safety review. CBP is part of the Homeland Security Department.
The FAA lifted the El Paso shutdown order after about eight hours following the White House's intervention.
The US military days later shot down a CBP drone with the laser-based system, leading the FAA to expand an area in which flights were barred around Fort Hancock, Texas.
DHS vowed closer communication with other agencies after the incident.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday that the restrictions "will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border."
Earlier this year, media reports said drones were seen over Fort McNair in Washington where Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Hegseth live.
In May, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told Reuters the counter-drone system is used only along southern border and is not used at Fort McNair, which is close to Reagan Washington National Airport. REUTERS

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia exiting role
October 16, 2026
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is on the way out from her position, The New York Times and other US news outlets reported on Friday.
Zacharia's departure leaves Trump without a key spokesperson with a little over two weeks before November's midterm elections.
Zacharia's week on the job
Zacharia started her new role just five days ago, taking over for Karoline Leavitt. She had a nervy first White House briefing with journalists on Tuesday, fielding just three questions and leaving the podium after fewer than 14 minutes.
The White House website said later that day that "Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary."
Earlier on Friday, President Donald Trump suggested that Zacharia might be leaving. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters.
He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"
Controversy over Zacharia's legal background
Last Friday, Trump announced Zacharia's appointment as the new press secretary. However, she became embroiled in controversy when it was revealed that her earlier claims of being a lawyer were false.
Until last week, Zacharia was a commentator for conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax. She also advised Trump Media and Technology, the company behind Trump's Truth Social platform.
Zacharia has also long described herself as a lawyer, but her credentials remain unverified. While she graduated from law school, neither she nor the White House has provided evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.
According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia was an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. She was also a general counsel at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell, from 2024 to 2025. Grenell served as acting director of national intelligence in 2020.
Zacharia earned her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. While nearly all licensed US lawyers first obtain a law degree, law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.

Russia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test
Unknown

Russia's war reaches Bulgaria's shores, putting Radev's Moscow-friendly stance to the test
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Oct. 6, 2026. (Nikolay Doychinov / AFP via Getty Images)
The balancing act of Bulgaria's Moscow-friendly leader stands on shaky ground.
Since taking office in May, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has taken a harsh line on Ukraine while adopting steps his critics say are accommodating to Moscow.
Radev's course has now come under scrutiny as Bulgaria, a southeastern NATO member state, feels first-hand the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Four merchant vessels were hit by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast in October. Two of the vessels sank and several sailors are reported dead or missing.
Under fire from opposition, Radev, a former military officer and Bulgaria's ex-president, only cautiously hints at Moscow's complicity — stopping short of a direct accusation.
"Radev’s balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him."
With Russian drone incursions and Moscow-backed hybrid operations on NATO territory growing ever more brazen and frequent, Bulgaria has no guarantee that the strikes in its waters will come to an end.
Radev's room to maneuver between Bulgaria's NATO membership and a thaw in ties with Moscow is shrinking, observers say.
"I have argued for some time that Radev's balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him," Dimitar Keranov, an analyst at the German Marshall Fund's European Resilience program, told the Kyiv Independent.
"It now has."
Russia's war reaches Bulgarian waters
Two Turkish-managed ships were hit by naval and aerial drones about 70 nautical miles (130 kilometers) east of the Bulgarian town of Byala on Oct. 6, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The Alfa Watan, flying a Togo flag, sank, with 10 crew members — including nine Syrian nationals — presumed dead.
Two more vessels were hit by drones near the Bulgarian Black Sea coast on Oct. 13, including the Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, hit east of Byala. Its crew, including seven Ukrainians, was rescued.
The second ship, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, was hit by drones east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets and sank, with 11 sailors reported missing.
The attacks came amid escalating hostilities in the Black Sea, with Moscow attempting to impose a blockade on Ukrainian trade by attacking ports and merchant ships.
Several commercial ships were also hit in and around Romanian waters over the past weeks.
While Ukraine has blamed Russia, Radev was initially hesitant to name the origin of the drones, saying only "they were clearly either Russian or Ukrainian."
Both Russian and Ukrainian drone incursions have been recorded along NATO's eastern flank over the past months, with the latter being a result of Russian jamming diverting Ukrainian unmanned vehicles.
But Radev's hesitation has provided an opening to the country's opposition.
On Oct. 6, lawmakers from the GERB–SDS, a center-right opposition coalition, blasted Radev for failing to properly identify the culprit.
The coalition's junior partner, the SDS (Union of Democratic Forces), even called the attack "an act of aggression by the Russian Federation in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone."
Finally, after the second attack, Radev acknowledged that Russia was the one to benefit from the attacks, and Sofia summoned the Russian envoy.
Nevertheless, Radev has not formally accused Moscow, citing a lack of decisive evidence.
Keranov summarizes this position as a "convenient deflection."
"Formal attribution takes time, but once a government concludes that the logic points to Moscow, it does not need a final forensic report to act on that assessment."
But Ruslan Stefanov, a program director and chief economist at the Center for the Study of Democracy, a Sofia-based European public policy institute, says waiting for proof is reasonable.
On the other hand, "continued failure to identify Russia as the main driver of instability and unsafe navigation in the Black Sea does not reflect operational reality and is widely seen as part of a broader pattern of unnecessary and harmful caution toward Moscow," he said.
"Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO’s southern flank."
The maritime attacks are not the only security-related incidents hitting Bulgaria in recent weeks and months.
Earlier in October, two masked men were said to have set fire to 11 out of 17 Starlink antennas at a facility near Sofia.
Ivaylo Mirchev, one of the leaders of the opposition Democratic Bulgaria (DB), hinted at connections to "Russian-style sabotage."
Yet Radev has remained tight-lipped about who was behind the arson, even though Poland blamed Moscow for a similar attack against a Starlink station on Polish territory in September.
Ukraine widely uses Starlink network services, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for both civilian purposes and to support military operations.
And in August and September, explosions hit two arms facilities of the EMCO company, which supplies weapons to Ukraine.
The company called the September incident sabotage, while the Bulgarian Interior Ministry did not rule out either foreign interference or company neglect.
NATO's 'weak link'
As Bulgaria's president, Radev was ranked among the most Ukraine-skeptical voices in the EU — often compared to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Since assuming the premier office, he has pulled Bulgaria out of the U.K.- and French-led Coalition of the Willing and halted arms supplies to Ukraine from Bulgarian army stocks.
He has also lambasted Western military aid for Kyiv, claiming it prolongs the war, and instead urged a diplomatic resolution.
At the EU level, Radev's government has blocked the inclusion of Moscow Patriarch Kirill in the 21st sanctions package and pushed to water down the EU's language on Ukraine's accession.
In light of these steps, drone strikes off the Bulgarian coast put Radev in an "uncomfortable position," Stefanov said.
"He built his campaign on the claim that there can be no military victory over Russia and that Bulgaria's interest lies in de-escalation," the expert noted.
"Those choices now raise the obvious question of why Bulgaria has not been spared."
Keranov believes that "Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO's southern flank."
Most NATO members along the alliance's frontier — from Romania to the Baltics — have already toughened their response to Russian provocations, with allied jets repeatedly downing invading drones.
Their leadership is also less reluctant to openly blame Moscow for the incursions.
While Radev's hesitation has provided ammunition to his domestic opponents, the prime minister's political position remains strong, Keranov said, adding that his popularity at home is not the real question.
"It is whether Bulgaria acts like a strong NATO member or keeps signaling indecision."

Russia’s Chief of General Staff Valery Gerasimov reported to Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin that Russian forces are now specifically targeting strategic bridges, railway infrastructure, and data centers across Ukraine.
Gerasimov made the remarks on Friday, Oct. 16, during a briefing to Putin at a command post of Russia’s Joint Group of Forces, Interfax-Russia reported citing the Kremlin. He confirmed that massive attacks have been launched on the country’s energy infrastructure as well.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“According to the General Staff’s plan, strikes are being carried out on bridges of strategic importance, railway transport facilities, and data centers used to support the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine,” Gerasimov said.
Putin ordered commanders to keep up the military campaign, with a particular focus on sustaining large-scale strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial complex, according to TASS.
Strikes on Kyiv bridges
Gerasimov’s statement amounts to an official acknowledgment of a campaign Russia has been conducting for a few weeks.
Between Sept. 23-25, Russian forces carried out a series of attacks on Ukrainian data centers, including those operated by DATAGROUP, MiroHost, and UTELS. Other communications infrastructure has been hit as well, leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukraine’s citizens without internet access.
President Volodymyr Zelensky convened a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief on Sept. 26, ordering Ukrainian authorities to take additional measures to protect the country’s telecommunications infrastructure.
2 Killed, 6 Injured in Russian Strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Region
Since Oct. 1, Russian drones have repeatedly hit Kyiv’s South (Pivdennyi) Bridge and later the North Bridge, forcing closures that paralyzed traffic across the capital.
A new bridge in Zaporizhzhia was also targeted.
According to Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) Major Artem Bilyk, Russia is using a “small cuts” approach, with repeated strikes that force bridges to close for inspections and repairs rather than destroy them outright.
Moscow has also been known to carry out “double-tap” strikes – launching a second attack on the same location while rescuers are responding to the scene.
Around the same time, Zelensky said that Putin had ordered his military commanders to abandon previous constraints on aerial attacks and intensify strikes on civilian sites.
Russia intensifies strikes after Trump’s self-proclaimed ceasefire
The remarks come amid mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington, which appear to be helping Russia’s war effort.
On Oct. 9, US President Donald Trump announced an abrupt diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets. Another 500,000 tons would follow in November and 1 million tons after that.
The move came while Ukraine’s negotiating delegation was in Miami, hoping to reach a breakthrough with senior US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and it was condemned by senators of both parties, the EU and Ukraine.
Trump then announced a self-proclaimed energy ceasefire on Truth Social on Oct. 11 without either side formally agreeing to it, and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Oct. 14 that Russia could not be accused of breaking a truce that was never defined.
Although Ukraine abided by it for several days, Russia amplified its attacks on the country’s power plants and left more than 600,000 people without electricity.
Ukraine’s defenses have also come under strain after restrictions on Starlink terminals disrupted its drone operations overnight on Oct. 13-14, including interceptors used against Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds.
Neither SpaceX CEO Elon Musk nor Trump has claimed formal responsibility for the restrictions. Musk, however, said speed limits on Ukraine’s military Starshield terminals are set by the US military, including Trump himself, not by SpaceX.
Around the same time, US officials threatened Kyiv that intelligence sharing could be cut off if it kept striking Russian energy targets.
Trump has since insisted that cooperation continues.
NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, confirmed that there had been no sign that the sharing had stopped, although Ukraine received no early warning from its Western partners about the incoming Russian ballistic missiles for two nights in a row at the beginning of the week.

Kindergarten head gets life sentence for poisoning 247 children in NW China
A court in northwest China’s Gansu Province has sentenced six people for producing and selling toxic food that poisoned 247 preschool children at a kindergarten in Tianshui City, with the facility's person in charge receiving a life sentence, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Xinhua.
According to a verdict issued by the Intermediate People's Court of Lanzhou City on Friday, Li Huifang, head of the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Tianshui's Maiji District, was sentenced to life imprisonment, stripped of political rights for life and had 500,000 yuan ($74,000) in personal assets confiscated. Executive principal Zhu Jinglin was sentenced to 15 years in prison and fined 300,000 yuan.
The court found that Li and Zhu instructed staff to add toxic substances to food served to children and employees to make the products appear more colorful and attractive. Four kitchen workers who carried out the orders received prison terms ranging from six to eight years and were also fined.
A provincial investigation report released in July 2025 found that contaminated pastries had been served to children and staff monthly since May 2024. Tests showed that 247 of 251 children examined had abnormal blood lead levels.
All affected children received hospital treatment or nutritional interventions at home. By July 20, 2025, most had completed their first round of treatment and had been discharged from hospital. Medical experts reported an average 40.21% reduction in blood lead levels, meeting projected treatment targets.
The investigation also led to disciplinary probes involving 10 local officials, including the provincial health commission director and senior leaders in Tianshui. The Gansu provincial government has pledged continued support for the children's medical care and recovery.

Lukashenko Orders “People’s Militia” Units in Every Belarusian Village Council

Lukashenko Orders “People’s Militia” Units in Every Belarusian Village Council
Belarusian leader Alexander Lukashenko has ordered the creation of “people’s militia” units in every village council across the country, expanding a defense structure introduced after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported on October 16.
Lukashenko announced the move while observing training by one such unit in Belarus’s Verkhnedvinsk district, according to the report.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Moscow has sought to draw Belarus more directly into Russia’s war against Ukraine. It was previously reported by The Wall Street Journal that the Kremlin threatened to reduce financial support for Minsk if Lukashenko resisted deeper involvement.
“We need to expand. We need to create more such basic units somewhere. They must be connected to each other,” Lukashenko stated.
The Moscow Times reported that Lukashenko described the militia as the first level of Belarus’s defense system. Territorial defense forces responsible for protecting infrastructure would form the next layer, followed by the regular army.
“When creating this structure, I meant that every village council should have a people’s militia unit. This is the core,” Lukashenko said. “In the event of hostilities, this core can expand.”
He added that weapons had already been prepared for the units.
“You will have an assault rifle, grenades, a machine gun,” Lukashenko stated.
Lukashenko had previously instructed the Belarusian Society of Hunters and Fishermen to recruit people with experience handling weapons into the militia, The Moscow Times noted.
Belarus began creating the “people’s militia” after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Defense Minister Viktor Khrenin previously linked the decision to the “military-political situation” and presented the force as a deterrent against a potential attack.
Since the beginning of 2026, Belarusian authorities have intensified military and security exercises, The Moscow Times reported. The drills have included mobilization scenarios, responses to missile strikes involving mass casualties, and wartime civil-defense measures.
Exercises involving both territorial defense forces and the “people’s militia” were also held in the Vitebsk region over the summer.
The militia expansion comes amid broader signs of Belarusian military preparations near NATO borders. A recent report found that Belarus is modernizing railways, communications networks, and defense production with Russian support, with some facilities expected to reach full capacity by spring or mid-2027.

Two women have filed a federal lawsuit accusing former US Representative Matt Gaetz, President Donald Trump’s first pick for attorney general, of participating in a sex trafficking ring while serving in Congress. Gaetz has faced similar allegations for years, and has denied any wrongdoing.
The lawsuit, filed in Florida on Thursday, alleges that Gaetz and several other men, including former Seminole County Tax Collector Joel Greenberg and former Florida legislator Christopher Dorworth, sexually exploited the plaintiffs between 2017 and 2019.
The women, identified as Jane Doe 1 and Jane Doe 2, are seeking unspecified damages under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act.
According to the complaint, Greenberg recruited financially vulnerable young women through the dating website SeekingArrangement.com and introduced them to Gaetz.
The lawsuit alleges that Gaetz had sex with Jane Doe 1 and a 17-year-old girl at a July 2017 party where narcotics were distributed. He allegedly paid the minor $400 in cash and transferred $500 to Jane Doe 1 three days later.
Gaetz and Greenberg subsequently made at least 19 payments to Jane Doe 1, ranging from $150 to $1,000, the complaint claims. Jane Doe 2 alleged that she first had sex with Gaetz in exchange for money in October 2017.
The plaintiffs also accused the defendants of providing drugs and financing trips to Miami, Las Vegas, the Bahamas and other destinations in exchange for sex.
The men allegedly used “their public office, power, and wealth to prey on the economic vulnerability of Plaintiffs,” the lawsuit states. Both women were in their early twenties when they met Gaetz.
Greenberg pleaded guilty to federal charges, including sex trafficking of a minor, in 2021 and was sentenced to 11 years in prison.
Responding on X on Thursday, Gaetz appeared to mock the lawsuit, posting a photo of three women in swimsuits overlooking the ocean in the Bahamas.
“Jane Doe Strikes Again!” he wrote, sarcastically questioning why nobody had responded to the women’s supposed cries for help on Instagram. He later told reporters he looked forward to disproving the allegations.

03:39:16 KST

Khalid Mejdoub
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Morocco announced a new cabinet on Friday, ushering in a historic era with the country’s first female prime minister leading a four-party coalition.
According to state-run Maghreb Arabe Presse (MAP), King Mohammed VI received members of the new cabinet, led by Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, and presided over their appointment ceremony at the Royal Palace in the capital Rabat.
El Mansouri is the first Moroccan woman to hold the country’s top government post.
She will lead a new government formed by a four-party coalition comprising her Authenticity and Modernity Party, the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
The new government includes seven women, including El Mansouri, compared with six in the previous government led by Aziz Akhannouch.
The new government comprises 32 members, including ministers and ministers-delegate, according to official figures.
Abdelouafi Laftit kept his post as interior minister, alongside Nasser Bourita as foreign minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi as justice minister and Ahmed Toufiq as minister of Islamic affairs and endowments.
The new cabinet also established a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence, Digital Transformation and Administrative Reform, headed by Ahmed Rahhou.
On Monday, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, Istiqlal Party, Socialist Union of Popular Forces and Party of Progress and Socialism announced in a joint statement that they had formed the governing majority following the conclusion of the second round of consultations on forming a government, which began on Sept. 30.
On Sept. 29, King Mohammed VI tasked El Mansouri with forming a government after her party, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, came first in the Sept. 23 elections with 97 seats.

Macron says France accelerating missile deliveries to Ukraine, offering satellite data support
French President Emmanuel Macron said this at a press conference following a meeting of the European Council in Brussels, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
“We will not leave Ukraine and Ukrainians without support, because this is a war of resistance to Russian aggression. At a time when there are uncertainties and some are wavering, the role of Europeans is to firmly uphold their position. This is about Europe’s security and protecting international principles,” Macron stressed.
According to him, Europe continues to provide budget support to Ukraine. In particular, the European Commission has announced a new tranche of funding.
The French President also said that France was accelerating the implementation of agreements reached with Ukraine in July.
“We have accelerated the delivery of new missiles, as well as all the work we are doing in the areas of drones and missile defense. Additional meetings will be held in the coming days to accelerate the licensing process, that is, granting permission for certain types of our weapons to be produced more quickly by third parties directly on Ukrainian territory,” he said.
Macron added that France also intends to develop joint defense projects with Ukraine.
“In addition, we are actively working to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to withstand aggression through satellite imagery and early warning systems, which are critically important. And Europe has solutions in this area,” the French President emphasized.
As reported, following a meeting with European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that key topics included energy support, strengthening air defense and opening negotiating clusters.

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. As a result of 12 massive Russian strikes this fall, 30 Ukrainian defense industry companies and logistics centers have been hit, thereby significantly reducing Kiev’s ability to produce long-range weapons, including cruise and ballistic missiles, Russian Armed Forces’ General Staff Chief Army General Valery Gerasimov told President Vladimir Putin.

US imposes temporary drone flight restrictions along southern border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:35:11 UTC
03:35:11 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The US Departments of Transportation, Defense and Homeland Security on Friday announced a coordinated initiative to strengthen airspace security along the US-Mexico border, imposing temporary flight restrictions on unauthorized drone operations.
The temporary flight restriction (TFR), which takes effect Friday, will bar any unauthorized drone activity up to 400 feet (122 meters) above ground level and extend one nautical mile (1.9 kilometers) north of the US-Mexico border.
According to the statement, the new measure is intended to reduce risks to border security operations, protect federal personnel and facilities, and counter what the administration describes as threats posed by drug cartels and other illicit activities.
US Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said the measure builds on President Donald Trump’s efforts to strengthen border security and address drone-related threats.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the restrictions would provide military commanders with greater awareness of potential threats and more options for responding to drone activity.
“The United States government will maintain 100% operational control of our border: land, air, and sea,” Hegseth said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the initiative would build on the administration’s border security efforts and help protect federal personnel while countering drone threats.
“This action will help counter cartel drone threats, protect our personnel, and strengthen security in the airspace above the border,” Mullin said.

'US tilting toward Russia: Europeans are standing more and more solidly with Zelensky'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:33:13 UTC
03:33:13 KST

'US tilting toward Russia: Europeans are standing more and more solidly with Zelensky'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
As transatlantic relations confront renewed geopolitical uncertainty, former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves delivers a pointed assessment of Washington's shifting approach to Russia's war on Ukraine and the profound implications for European security. At the heart of his analysis lies a fundamental question: can Europe develop the political unity, strategic independence and military capabilities necessary to defend its interests in an increasingly unpredictable international order? Ilves response: "If there's any time for Europe to begin to act as Europe and not as being strictly self-interested, then this is the time for it."
Ilves argues that the Trump administration's apparent rapprochement with Moscow is shaped partly by domestic electoral calculations, while Ukraine finds itself navigating an increasingly precarious diplomatic and military landscape. Yet he challenges the assumption that Washington retains overwhelming leverage over Kyiv, pointing to Europe's growing financial commitment to Ukrainian defence and the potential domestic political costs of withdrawing American intelligence support.
Beyond the immediate confrontation, Ilves identifies a more consequential challenge: the emergence of a fragmented European political landscape in which nationalist movements, competing security priorities and divergent attitudes towards Russia threaten the continent's capacity for collective action. His central contention is that European strategic autonomy is no longer an abstract institutional ambition but an urgent geopolitical necessity.
Can the European Union transcend national self-interest and emerge as a coherent strategic actor, or will they remain vulnerable to the decisions of external powers and the divisions within its own borders? "If we don’t take that issue seriously," Ilves warns, "I fear we will have far more vociferous tendencies within the European Union between those that take the security side of this seriously and those countries or leaders that will block progress simply for their domestic audiences."

Trump’s new press secretary looks close to exit after just one week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:31:42 UTC
03:31:42 KST

Katie Zacharia fired after less than week as Trump’s new press secretary
WASHINGTON - White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was pushed out on Oct 16 after less than a week in the high-profile job, following a series of blunders that added to distractions for her embattled boss President Donald Trump.
“Can confirm,” a White House official told AFP, after Fox News reported that Zacharia, 41, was “transitioning out.”
The writing was on the wall earlier when Trump made clear he was ready to see his newly minted spokeswoman go amid criticism that she had pretended to be a lawyer and over her one, much-mocked press briefing.
“I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?,’” Trump told reporters. “I said, ‘Katie, you don’t have to do this’... I said to her, ‘Honestly if I were you I’d reconsider.’”
Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.
Zacharia had gotten off to a rocky start with her first press room briefing on Oct 13.
It lasted less than 15 minutes, starting with a remarkably slow reading out of what she said were Trump’s many accomplishments – then taking just three questions from journalists.
She then plunged into controversy when it emerged that her previous claims to be a lawyer were not true.
The kerfuffle is a distraction for 80-year-old Trump as he flies around the country trying to boost Republican candidates ahead of the Nov 3 congressional midterm elections, with polls predicting a drubbing.
The Republican leader himself also faces ever-lower polls as Americans sour over the war against Iran, inflation and perceptions of corruption.
‘Not a real lawyer’
Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
While she does have a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged on Oct 15 she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practicing law in the United States.
She embarked on a series of damage-control interviews on Trump-friendly outlets, but they did no good.
In one of them, Fox News’ Sean Hannity, a close Trump ally, appeared dismissive of Zacharia.
He asked the press secretary if she ever retook the bar exam. She replied: “I did not.”
“It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” she said.
In another interview on Oct 15 with pro-Trump outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam but was “distracted and overwhelmed” by plans to move to China with her husband.
Zacharia said that “many people in the field” had assured her that she could “label myself a lawyer,” given her law degree.
China’s toilets
Fox and Friends, which often conducts friendly interviews with Trump administration officials, was unusually direct on Oct 16 when a host asked Zacharia if she still had the confidence of the president.
“I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me,” she said, sidestepping the question.
Zacharia further stirred controversy on Oct 15 when she disparaged China, whose leader Xi Jinping was recently Trump’s guest in a pomp-filled Washington visit.
The press secretary recalled the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the United States.
“I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,’” she told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in an interview.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded on Oct 16 that Zacharia should “visit China more often.” AFP

Romanian president calls for greater NATO oversight in the Black Sea in Euronews interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:30:38 UTC
03:30:38 KST

In an interview with Euronews, Romanian President Nicușor Dan warns that Black Sea security is under growing pressure as drone attacks hit commercial vessels off Romania and Bulgaria.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has said the Black Sea would only become safe after Russia’s war in Ukraine ends, as he called for greater NATO oversight in the region following drone strikes on commercial vessels in an interview with Euronews.
“I’m very optimistic that we’ll have the support and the capabilities in order to be better protected, because it’s an important economic question for Ukraine and for the whole region,” he said on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels held Friday.
The Romanian leader said frequent drone incursions into his country’s territory had begun roughly a year and a half ago, and that Bucharest had been “not prepared”. The country now faces a similar lack of preparedness to its east, Dan said.
“At the Black Sea, we are in the same situation,” he said, adding: “We have to protect the water under our territory.”
He also expressed confidence in continued support from US President Donald Trump, both for security in the Black Sea and for Romania’s position within the NATO military alliance.
“On defence, I think it’s a mutual benefit between us because we have an excellent position to project force towards other parts of the world,” Dan said.
The confidence comes amid bellicose statements from US President Donald Trump regarding Ukrainian and European security, such as troop cuts and a force posture review.
The president was in the Belgian capital for a quarterly summit attended by EU heads of state to discuss support for Ukraine, the bloc’s long-term budget and its growing trade deficit with China.
However, the increasingly hostile security situation in the Black Sea pushed the Romanian leader and his Bulgarian counterpart, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, to bring security threats higher up the agenda.
Dan told reporters after the summit that France had pledged “necessary equipment” and to “better understand our specific requirements in the Black Sea”.
“There are always new challenges, but fortunately, Romania has allies,” he said.
The escalating situation also prompted a meeting between the two leaders and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte to discuss stronger support. Bulgaria requested combat aircraft and anti-drone systems during the talks.
Rutte said afterwards that NATO would continue to strengthen its posture along the eastern flank, including by expanding its counter-drone capabilities.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” he said in a statement on the social media platform X.
Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian ports along the Black Sea and the Danube River, leaving the war-torn country dependent on alternative routes to sell its grain to African and Middle Eastern markets.
However, this has exposed Europe’s shipping lanes to attacks.
Drones have damaged commercial vessels in the Black Sea off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania for three consecutive days leading up to the meeting in Brussels, as well as during the previous week. At least one vessel sank after being attacked by drones last week, killing two seafarers.
Neither Sofia nor Bucharest has definitively blamed Russia for the attacks. However, Radev told reporters earlier in the week that “logic” would suggest the Kremlin stood to benefit from the deadly incursions.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it,” he said.
Investigations into all the incidents are ongoing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at a press conference after meeting European leaders on Thursday that “you do not need a ground war for an invasion to occur”.
He added that Russia was testing Europe’s response to the attacks, referring to incidents in the Black Sea as well as an explosive-laden drone found at an airport in Leipzig.
“Violating another country's airspace is already an incursion,” Zelenskyy said.
“We have seen drones cross airspace and borders in Romania, Poland and Germany. A corresponding drone was found in Germany, by the way. Moldova and Bulgaria have also been affected. A great deal is happening today.”
Zelenskyy and other senior Ukrainian officials have publicly blamed Russia for some of these incidents, most notably a deadly drone attack that struck a vessel carrying Ukrainian grain off the Bulgarian coast.

reclaiming swiss auto waste, it all remains turns decommissioned cars into building resources

reclaiming swiss auto waste, it all remains turns decommissioned cars into building resources
it all remains, an installation by giona bierens de haan, addresses automotive waste in switzerland by reinterpreting decommissioned vehicles as structural building blocks and local resources for a post-fossil-fuel architecture.
prefer designboom on google
SWISS AUTOMOTIVE EXPORTS HIGHLIGHT UNTAPPER MATERIAL RESOURCES
It all remains, an art and architectural installation by Giona Bierens de Haan, addresses the future of automotive resources and material reuse in Switzerland. With nearly 5 million registered vehicles circulating domestically, averaging 0.5 cars per inhabitant, and 200,000 removed from service annually, two-thirds of decommissioned automobiles are exported to countries with less stringent environmental regulations.
CONVERTING OBSOLETE VEHICLES INTO STRUCTURAL BUILDING BLOCKS
The project by designer Giona Bierens de Haan responds to this reliance on foreign markets for domestic waste management by proposing local material revalorization. Anticipating a post-fossil-fuel transition where automobiles become obsolete, the conceptual installation redefines decommissioned cars not as waste, but as structural resources and foundational building blocks for future architectural construction.

Tatarstan interested in IT professionals, medical personnel, welders from India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:29:29 UTC
03:29:29 KST

KAZAN, October 16. /TASS/. Tatarstan is interested in English-speaking engineering and technical professionals, IT specialists, medical personnel, and highly skilled welders from India, the republic’s Labor, Employment, and Social Protection Minister Elmira Zaripova stated.
“Today, our needs align in terms of qualifications. India is not only a source of labor, but also of English-speaking engineering, technical, and IT professionals, medical personnel, and highly skilled welders. I would like to point out that welders from India are familiar with Russian federal standards, particularly those on manual submerged-arc welding. In other words, they are familiar with our standards, and this also brings us closer together,” she noted during “The Labor Market: Challenges and Prospects” session held within the framework of the second Russian-Indian Business Forum "TIME: Tatarstan Initiative Mutual Efficiency."
According to Zaripova, unemployment in Tatarstan is practically nonexistent. There are nearly 3,000 unemployed citizens, accounting for less than 0.2% of the economically active population. At the same time, there are 14-25 job openings for every unemployed person.
The regional minister also noted that Tatarstan received a quota in 2026 to recruit more than 3,000 Indian citizens and that more than 600 work permits were issued to Indian citizens in the republic in 2025. Currently, more than 1,000 Indian citizens are officially employed in the region. The average age of an Indian worker is 29, an age at which people focus on long-term career prospects. In addition, nearly 1,300 Indian students are enrolled in Tatarstan universities, primarily in medical and technical programs.
“The key to future progress lies in harmonizing standards for the recognition of professional qualifications. Without this, workers trained in their home countries will not be hired here, especially in fields such as welding, engineering, medicine, and IT. This is a priority that is now being addressed at the federal level as well,” Zaripova concluded.
The second Russian-Indian Business Forum "TIME: Tatarstan Initiative Mutual Efficiency" is taking place on October 14–17 at the Center for Unique Craftsmanship in Kazan. TASS is the forum’s general information partner.

White House Press Secretary Zacharia exits role after short tenure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:29:00 UTC
03:29:00 KST

White House press secretary Katie Zacharia exiting role
October 16, 2026
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is on the way out from her position, The New York Times and other US news outlets reported on Friday.
Zacharia's departure leaves Trump without a key spokesperson with a little over two weeks before November's midterm elections.
Zacharia's week on the job
Zacharia started her new role just five days ago, taking over for Karoline Leavitt. She had a nervy first White House briefing with journalists on Tuesday, fielding just three questions and leaving the podium after fewer than 14 minutes.
The White House website said later that day that "Katie Zacharia delivered a commanding inaugural press briefing as the 37th White House Press Secretary."
Earlier on Friday, President Donald Trump suggested that Zacharia might be leaving. "I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters.
He added: "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'"
Controversy over Zacharia's legal background
Last Friday, Trump announced Zacharia's appointment as the new press secretary. However, she became embroiled in controversy when it was revealed that her earlier claims of being a lawyer were false.
Until last week, Zacharia was a commentator for conservative outlets Fox News and Newsmax. She also advised Trump Media and Technology, the company behind Trump's Truth Social platform.
Zacharia has also long described herself as a lawyer, but her credentials remain unverified. While she graduated from law school, neither she nor the White House has provided evidence that she passed the bar exam in any state or in China, where she worked for a large law firm years ago.
According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia was an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from 2011 to 2013. She was also a general counsel at Fix California, an advocacy group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell, from 2024 to 2025. Grenell served as acting director of national intelligence in 2020.
Zacharia earned her law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011. While nearly all licensed US lawyers first obtain a law degree, law school graduates cannot legally practice law in the US without first being admitted to a state bar.

Ukraine war latest: Drone attack sparks fire at industrial facility in Russia's Surgut district

Ukraine war latest: Drone attack sparks fire at industrial facility in Russia's Surgut district
Key developments on Oct. 16:
- Drone attack sparks fire at industrial facility in Russia's Surgut district, governor says
- Pope Leo urges Putin to allow humanitarian aid, evacuations from Russian-occupied Oleshky
- Ukrainian military strikes million-dollar Russian radar in Krasnodar Krai, General Staff claim
- Zelensky's ask: 300 Patriot missiles, 70 billion euros, and Russian assets
- Emergency blackouts in Kyiv, as Klitschko announces start of heating season
A fire broke out at an industrial facility in Russia's Khanty-Mansi Autonomous District following a drone attack, regional governor Ruslan Kukharuk said on Oct. 16, while Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko said the facility was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant.
"As a result of a drone attack on an industrial facility in the Surgut district, a fire broke out. Emergency services are working at the scene," Kukharuk said.
He added that specialists were assessing the scale and nature of the damage. Kukharuk did not identify the facility or say who was responsible for the attack.
"The Defense Forces struck the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant," Serhii Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist and volunteer who previously served as an adviser to then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, said. The facility is located more than 2,400 kilometers (1,490 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
In videos shared by Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova, a large fire and thick dark smoke can be seen on the territory of an industrial facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify that the facility reportedly hit was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant. Ukrainian officials have not publicly claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Surgut plant processes gas condensate and produces petroleum products, including motor and aviation fuel. Its designed processing capacity reaches 12 million metric tons of raw materials per year, Sternenko said.
The reported strike comes amid a dispute between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil and energy infrastructure.
U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising global fuel prices, a claim disputed by energy experts. His administration also threatened to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support unless Kyiv stopped targeting Russian energy facilities, according to Ukrainian and European officials.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets despite sanctions imposed following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia subsequently eased restrictions on diesel exports.
Two days later, Trump announced what he described as an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian officials said Kyiv had not been informed of the agreement in advance.
Ukraine initially halted strikes on Russian refineries following the announcement, while Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. On Oct. 15, Zelensky said that Kyiv had lifted the pause due to Moscow's continued attacks.
"The block is out. We're done," Zelensky said.

Pope Leo urges Putin to allow humanitarian aid, evacuations from Russian-occupied Oleshky
Pope Leo expressed concern over the worsening humanitarian crisis in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson Oblast during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, the Vatican said.
The pope called for a local ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe evacuation of civilians from the front-line city, where around 2,000 residents remain trapped amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Despite Russia's failure to cooperate with evacuation efforts, Putin blamed Ukraine for the crisis in Oleshky.
"Putin provided the pope with detailed explanations of the Kyiv regime's responsibility for the humanitarian situation in Oleshky," Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Oleshky is an occupied front-line city on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, where civilians live amid a Russian military presence and attacks from both Ukrainian and Russian forces.
The humanitarian situation has worsened since the summer, as evacuation efforts have come to a halt. Continued attacks have made it increasingly difficult to deliver essential food and medicine.
Ukraine had prepared an evacuation mission, with the International Committee of the Red Cross ready to participate and Ukrainian forces preparing to observe a ceasefire, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. Russia, however, had not confirmed its willingness to proceed, he said.
The call came as Leo remains hospitalized in Rome after undergoing surgery for lung cancer on Oct. 13. It was his second known phone conversation with Putin since becoming pope in 2025.

Ukrainian military strikes million-dollar Russian radar in Krasnodar Krai, General Staff claim
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian Nebo-U radar near the settlement of Magri, in Krasnodar Krai, on the night of Oct. 16, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
"The Nebo-U is a long-range, three-coordinate radar designed to detect and track aerial assets, including aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles," the General Staff said in a statement.
"Striking such systems reduces the enemy's ability to monitor airspace and detect aerial assets in time. The estimated cost of the radar station is about US $100 million," they said.
The General Staff did not give details about what Ukrainian munition was used to carry out the strike.
A day prior, an overnight attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh region carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system hit six Su-34M bomber jets, destroying four and damaging two, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15.
On Aug. 23, Ukrainian drones struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said then.
Krasnodar Krai, a strategic region along Russia's Black Sea coast, has increasingly come under Ukrainian drone attacks as Kyiv extends the range of its strikes deep into Russian territory.

BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky used his appearance at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels to list the main things Kyiv needs to survive the winter and beyond, but those asks won't come cheap.
"I am grateful for your support for Ukraine," Zelensky told EU leaders.
"Without a determined European Union capable of making strong decisions Putin would have gone much further by now," Zelensky said.
But with Russia ramping up its use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones to pummel Kyiv, and the U.S. taking steps to undermine Russia sanctions and Ukrainian security, Zelensky also came to the bloc with new requests for help.
"We need a winter package... 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The U.S.-made Patriot are considered the only technology currently capable of consistently taking down Russian ballistic missiles, and several European countries still hold stocks of them, such as Spain and Greece.
But for Spain, European diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that there is a real fear that Madrid will not receive any more Patriot missiles in the future because of U.S. President Donald Trump's personal dislike for Spain's center-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
Greece on the other hand has a visceral fear that depleting its own supplies of Patriots might be perceived as a sign of weakness by neighboring Turkey, which Athens fears Ankara would act upon by annexing Greek islands near the Turkish coast.
Likewise, Ukraine's demand to "deal with the frozen assets," unsettles several countries around the table.
Using the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of Russian assets immobilized within the EU to support Ukraine came up in late 2025, but consensus on the idea was out of reach.
"We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war," Zelensky said.
Aside from the fears of holders of those assets, principally Belgium, about Russian retaliation for such a move, several European countries also fear that entering into such appropriations could fracture the global financial system, as countries move their wealth only into jurisdictions deemed friendly to them.
For Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, touching those assets remains very much a no-go.
"My personal view is that if you have immobilized assets, like in every war, even the Second World War, they were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there's always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever told journalists at a press conference during the night of Oct. 15.
"Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier? ... Yes, there are ... Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," De Wever said.
And the risk of Russia's assets being returned, despite some wishful thinking from the U.S. that Europe would hand them over, is nonexistent. The EU bound itself in December 2025, so that any vote to unfreeze the Russian immobilized assets must be unanimous.
"Nobody could ever dream of operationalizing those immobilized assets without unanimity here around the table," De Wever said.
On top of requesting the Russian assets, Zelensky also asked the EU to fill Kyiv's budget hole for 2027.
"The war will cost 155 billion euros ($174.5 billion) next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion) more from you," Zelensky said.
"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he added.
But the request for 70 billion euros comes only six months after the bloc approved a 90 billion euro loan to help Ukraine until the end of 2027. The idea was always that third countries would step in to help bridge the remaining gap, but so far only Norway has done so.
And the government has been notoriously unclear at communicating its financial needs, as noted earlier that day by Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
However, Zelensky's estimate of a 70 billion euro shortfall does match the estimated shortfall figure that a senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's financial situation shared with the Kyiv Independent.
On all three requests, even if they land on sympathetic ears, a decision would still not be expected the same day.
And because there is nonetheless a European consensus to support Ukraine, the demands are very likely to dominate discussions in Brussels over the next weeks.

Police reviewing social media post by writer Sarah Helm, wife of Burnham’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell.
British police are reviewing a social media post by the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell in which she appears to endorse Palestine Action, a group proscribed in the country as a “terrorist” organisation.
“God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action,” Sarah Helm, a writer who is married to Powell – Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s national security adviser – wrote on X on Thursday.
She was responding to a post defending Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in the United Kingdom over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
A Metropolitan Police spokesperson on Friday said Helm’s post is “being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.
A government spokesperson cited by the Reuters news agency said the views expressed in Helm’s post “are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity”.
‘Absurdly authoritarian ban’
UK-based activist group Defend Our Juries defended Helm for defying what it called an “absurdly authoritarian ban on Palestine Action”.
“We know of 36 people who have been arrested and had their homes raided for similarly expressing support for Palestine Action on social media,” said a spokesperson for the group.
“We hope Sarah will not face the same treatment for standing up for free speech and Palestinian lives.”
The UK government outlawed Palestine Action in July 2025, after activists from the group broke into a Royal Air Force base and sprayed red paint on two aircraft to protest against UK military support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Being a member or a supporter is punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
Since the ban went into effect, police have arrested more than 3,500 people in the UK for alleged support of the group, many of them for holding up placards, according to rights group Amnesty International.
Palestine Action has contested its proscription, but the Court of Appeal upheld it in June.
The UK’s new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband last month said the government was “looking at” the Palestine Action ban, adding that he did not believe mass arrests resulting from its proscription were “anyone’s intent”.

Chicago-Area Cops Helped HSI Spy on Minnesota Anti-ICE Activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:21:54 UTC
03:21:54 KST

Chicago-area law enforcement officers took part in an undercover probe by Immigration and Customs Enforcement into Minneapolis mutual aid networks last spring as part of the feds’ conspiracy investigation into 15 Twin Cities activists facing federal felony charges for resisting Operation Metro Surge, according to newly released documents reviewed by WIRED.
An April report by ICE’s investigations wing, Homeland Security Investigations, titled “Antifa Roadshow,” details in-person and electronic surveillance by a joint task force of an April 2 talk. The task force was made up of 14 law enforcement officers—six local cops and eight HSI Chicago agents. The talk included self-described anarchists in Minnesota who spoke about their organizing experiences during the three-month immigration surge, which resulted in the killings of two US citizens.
The document, released by the 15 Minnesota activists’ defense team as part of the ongoing federal case against them, exposes close cooperation between local police, sheriffs, and HSI agents on a prosecution that critics say crosses the line into political repression. The Chicago HSI task force, which included officers from Chicago, Aurora, Downer’s Grove, Cook County, and Kane County, used two undercover agents, unspecified electronic surveillance, audio recordings, license-plate-reader data, and surveillance cameras from Chicago’s sprawling CCTV network to identify the April 2 event’s attendees and build connections to other anti-ICE protests in Illinois and other states.
Records produced by the Kane County Sheriff’s office show the unit in question is the Chicago-area Homeland Security Investigations Task Force. Local cops who join the unit are accepted on either a full- or part-time basis for two years, with the sign-off of their superiors.
Since Operation Midway Blitz in Illinois last autumn, residents in Chicago and surrounding communities have pressed elected officials for answers about cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. While Illinois state law prevents local law enforcement from participating in immigration enforcement operations, criminal investigations by HSI appear to fall outside those restrictions because they pertain to ICE’s other law enforcement functions.
Chicago police have substantial approval requirements for surveilling and infiltrating protests or public gatherings, per a 2017 departmental order. It is unclear how these regulations apply to Chicago Police Department agents participating in joint task forces with federal agencies.
In response to questions from WIRED, the CPD claims that no First Amendment notifications to CPD’s chain of command or the department’s general counsel were made for the April 2 investigation, and says its work with HSI is permitted under Illinois law because it pertained to criminal enforcement, not immigration. A source with knowledge of the matter stated that CPD believed the early April surveillance operation was in service of a federal racketeering investigation. The only financial element mentioned in the report is a GoFundMe account to support the Crimethinc speaking tour. There is no mention of funds solicited or received at the April 2 event.
The Chicago Mayor’s Office did not provide comment ahead of publication. In response to queries from WIRED, ICE would neither confirm nor deny details of past or present investigations and said individual agents are not authorized to speak to the media.
HSI is also emerging as the point agency for Trump’s war on internal dissent and opposition politicians: Its agents, not the FBI, conducted the Minnesota 15 investigation and served a search warrant earlier this month on congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.
The targeted April 2 event was held at Co-Prosperity, a Leftist gallery in the Southside Chicago neighborhood of Bridgeport. Several speakers from the Twin Cities area attended the event to share information about resisting federal immigration surges. This was part of a national tour last spring that was organized by the longtime anarchist collective Crimethinc, whose meetings have been infiltrated by federal informants repeatedly over the decades and contributed to the convictions of Eric McDavid, as well as 2008 Republican National Convention protester Matthew DePalma.
Per the four-page HSI report, a plainclothes cop from suburban Aurora was dropped off at the Co-Prosperity event by Officer Mike Xu from the wealthy village of Downers Grove; HSI undercover agent #9147 walked in five minutes later, once the undercover cop from Aurora confirmed no security checks were done at the door.
The undercover HSI agent transmitted a live recording of the event to the rest of the surveillance team for an hour, until transmission was lost. The recordings of the incident were uploaded and shared with HSI agent Kenneth Popovits, a financial crimes investigations supervisor who was working on a temporary assignment in Minneapolis.
Remarks by defendant Callum Robinet from the April 2 talk in Bridgeport about building rapid-response networks are included in the federal conspiracy indictment brought against the Minnesota 15, implicating the Chicagoland law enforcement that participated in surveillance in the controversial prosecution.
The Aurora Police Department, Downer’s Grove Police Department, and Kane County Sheriff did not respond to requests for comment.
The HSI Chicago surveillance team logged 219 vehicles parked in the vicinity of Co-Prosperity. Several subjects already under investigation, including some of the speakers on the tour, were identified by ICE. Ryan Wasson, a Kane County Sheriff’s deputy, spotted a hooded, masked man outside the venue removing an object from his trunk. Running the license plate, Wasson identified the man as the subject of an October 4 arrest during Operation Midway Blitz whose prosecution had been declined by assistant US attorney Christopher Veatch.
Outside the venue, agents Joel Sullivan and Michael Finerty spotted an unnamed subject already under investigation for running “an anti-ICE Signal chat and group called ‘ICE Cream Patrol’” and noted an orange Hyundai had been documented near two March 2026 protests outside the ICE detention center in Broadview, Illinois. The surveillance lasted for roughly two hours until 8:30 pm local time on April 2.
Nick Nunez, a veteran Chicago Police detective detailed to the joint task force, filed a request to obtain surveillance footage from a CPD camera outside the venue; the request would take a week to complete, and it is unclear whether he received footage. All information obtained during the April investigation in Chicago was shared with HSI St. Paul/Minnesota, according to the agency’s report.
Ed Yohnka, a spokesman for the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois, calls the surveillance of the Bridgeport gathering “very troubling,” adding that local law enforcement should make a full accounting of their role in the incident and participation in joint task forces with federal agencies.
“No one should be subjected to surveillance and infiltration by law enforcement simply for engaging in constitutionally protected activity, including the ability to gather together and express dissatisfaction with public policy,” Yohnka says. “It is also a moment for local law enforcement to reexamine their participation in task forces with the Trump administration, especially any group focused on combatting ‘terrorism.’”
The April 2 meeting in Bridgeport is not the only out-of-state gathering spied upon by HSI during the Minnesota 15 investigation. Reports obtained by defense attorneys through discovery show that events on the same Crimethinc tour in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Seattle, Washington, were monitored in person by local HSI agents, who reported the speech’s contents back to their colleagues in Minneapolis.

How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:21:43 UTC
03:21:43 KST

How Iran messaging highlights cost of war ahead of US midterm elections
Through statements in English, Iranian officials are emphasising gas prices and issues with the US economy.
In messages that appear to be directed at the American public, Iran has been highlighting the cost of the war that the United States and Israel launched against the country ahead of the United States midterm elections.
Iranian officials have published articles in state-affiliated outlets stressing the disastrous impact of the war on oil prices and the US economy, while Iran’s chief negotiator and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has actively targeted US officials about rising costs and military spending.
Sina Toossi, a senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, said Tehran is looking to increase the political cost of the war for Trump by trying to talk directly to the American public.
“It’s not necessarily that they’re trying to get Democrats in power or manipulate US politics in a certain direction, other than just overall increasing the costs on this issue of the Iran war, and just playing that game of information warfare and getting out their own narrative and propaganda as well,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.
Trump’s Republican Party is looking to retain control of the Senate and House of Representatives in next month’s midterm vote. But the Democratic Party, which largely opposes the war with Iran, is mounting a strong challenge across the congressional electoral map, including in areas that have been conservative strongholds for decades, such as Texas.
On Wednesday, Ghalibaf shared a news story on inflation rising to 3.7 percent last month along with a collage of negative headlines on the US economy.
The social media post also featured a comic strip from the Road Runner cartoon showing Wile E Coyote building a catapult that misfires and launches a boulder at him.
“Let’s ‘play the percentages’. Not in odds, but in the % increases,” Ghalibaf wrote in a message to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has been leading the sanctions campaign against Iran.
Bessent said last month that he represents “the house”, likening the economy to a casino while addressing the national debt and bond market.
Ghalibaf’s remark referred to the increase in inflation, underscoring that the cost of living keeps rising due to the war despite Bessent’s assertions.
Days earlier, he shared an image of a ghost shaped like a bell curve, with diesel prices rising and housing affordability and consumer confidence falling.
Since the start of the war on February 28, Iran has disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, sending energy prices soaring. In the US, the price of diesel is at an all-time record of $6.33 per gallon (3.8 litres), according to the American Automobile Association, and gas is $4.33, up from less than $3 before the war.
Iran has intensified its attacks on vessels around the strait in recent days after Trump and his aides repeatedly stressed that the waterway is under US control.
The uptick in energy prices has fuelled overall inflation in the economy, leading the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates last month at a time when Trump has been calling for them to be cut to stimulate economic activity.
In a letter to the American public on September 29, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) accused Trump of lying about the cost of the war and the state of the US economy, dismissing the president’s claims that oil prices would soon nosedive.
“Countries around the world have lost their faith in the US economy. Demand for American bonds has plummeted. In fact, countries are starting to offload their US bonds. Soon, the dam will break, and the economy will implode, causing, unfortunately, great pain for Americans for many many years,” the IRGC said.
“Americans need to wake up. They need to wrest control back from corrupt politicians. Now is the time, as the American political system is at its weakest.”
The US midterm elections are seen as a turning point in the conflict – not because of their potential outcome, but because of what Trump might do after the vote.
Trump has suggested that he would either strike a deal with Iran or return to a full-scale war after the November 3 legislative elections. He has also dismissed the idea that the vote will have any impact on his Iran policy.
“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don’t realise is that I’m not running,” Trump said at the United Nations General Assembly last month.
“I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election. When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
If the Democrats gain control of Congress, they can push for measures to curb Trump’s ability to continue the war, including through withholding funding for the military campaign.
But Toossi said there is a debate within Iran on the potential impact of a Democratic victory in November.
While some point to foreign policy hawks among the Democrats to argue that little would change, others say a midterm defeat would make him politically vulnerable and likely constrain his war powers.
“I don’t think they’re hedging their bets either way, and I don’t think it necessarily affects their overall strategy of increasing the costs [of war] regardless of whatever happens in November,” Toossi told Al Jazeera.

A “well-known individual” is trying to secure a permanent injunction against the Guardian and ITN to prevent them from publishing details of serious allegations made against him.
At a high court hearing on Friday, the claimant’s legal team said there was a serious risk that he could harm himself should the allegations be made public.
They have told the court publishing the claims would breach articles two and three of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), the former of which relates to the right to life.
A trial is due to take place later this month to examine whether an injunction preventing reporting of the allegations should be made.
An earlier ruling by the judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said the case included two media organisations that had “conducted a journalistic investigation into allegations concerning the claimant’s conduct towards a number of individuals”.
“The proposed publications concern serious allegations about the claimant’s conduct over a period of years,” it stated.
“The matters alleged are said to have arisen in a variety of professional and personal contexts.”
The judge explained that the claimant had given a broad denial of the allegations which the defendants propose to publish.
In a submission to the court, the claimant’s legal team, led by Sara Mansoori KC, said he was “a well-known individual who suffers from very serious mental health problems”.
The submission stated he had attempted to take his own life on two occasions and remained seriously ill.
ITN and the Guardian are opposing the injunction sought. In their own written submission to the court, their legal team set out their position on the questions that fall to be decided at trial.
In a skeleton argument, they said the relevant duties under the ECHR were not triggered and should not prevent publication, and in any event, mitigations could be put in place to protect the claimant.
Nicklin said on Friday that it was important to have the proceedings as open as possible, adding: “This case is going to be controversial either way it is decided.”

Musk asked Trump to restrict Ukraine's Starlink service, Telegraph reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:19:45 UTC
03:19:45 KST

'They were both in on it' — Musk suggested Trump restrict Ukraine's Starlink service, Telegraph reports
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of restricting Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces, the Telegraph reported on Oct. 16, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
The news comes after SpaceX abruptly implemented a speed cap on Ukraine's vital Starshield service on Oct. 14, with no warning to Kyiv in advance. The sudden restriction disrupted multiple battlefield operations, including mid-range drone strikes and air defense.
Conflicting reports about the reason for the cutoff — and who was responsible — have left Ukraine with questions even after Starlink service stabilized on the front lines.
But the Telegraph on Oct. 16 reported that it was Musk who proposed the speed cap to Trump — and Trump "agreed," one source said.
The claim contradicts Musk's own comments on the matter. Following the Oct. 14 disruption, Musk wrote on his social media platform X that any Starlink restrictions applicable to the military were the ultimate decision of the White House.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government," he said. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president)."
Musk neglected to mention his own role in the change.
A senior source told the Telegraph that after the chaos and violence that followed the restriction, Musk was concerned about negative consumer reactions in Europe.
"He tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the U.S. administration that did it," the source reportedly said. "The reality is that they were both in it."
This account was confirmed by two Ukrainian sources and a high-ranking European official, according to the Telegraph.
Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations, including its "middle strike" campaign against Russian forces and logistics in occupied Ukrainian territory and interceptor drones used against Russian long-range attack drones.
The impact of the Starlink restriction in Ukraine was immediate, and carried high stakes for both soldiers and civilians. President Volodymyr Zelensky highlighted the deadly consequences in comments to reporters on the sidelines of an EU leaders' summit in Brussels Oct. 16.
"We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that strike our civilians and kill our families," Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, interceptor drones relying on Starlink operate at high speeds, but the restrictions had reduced connectivity for some Ukrainian systems to around 70 kilometers per hour (43 mph).
"When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept some of the jet-powered Shaheds. We were unable to use a tool to protect civilians," he said.
The restrictions also affected deliveries of food and water to troops operating in areas under constant Russian drone surveillance, the president said. Zelensky stressed that Ukrainian forces do not use Starlink for deep strikes inside Russia.
The Starlink incident came amid heightened tensions between Kyiv and the White House, with Trump demanding that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia.
The White House threatened to halt intelligence sharing if Ukraine refused to comply — even as Russia continued to pound Ukraine's energy grid night after night and attack civilians with ballistic missiles.
But Trump has also dodged responsibility for the decision to restrict Starlink.
Reuters reported on Oct. 15 that the order to restrict Starshield came from within the White House, citing two U.S. officials and a Western official. The officials did not identify who issued the order, while a senior U.S. official denied that Trump personally requested the restriction.
In remarks at the White House on Oct. 16, Trump said he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for the slowdown.
The Pentagon has given no public explanation regarding the restriction.
The future of Ukraine's Starlink service also remains murky. Zelensky said on Oct. 16 that Starlink is not yet operating at its former speed, but that speed is in the process of being restored.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15 that connectivity had "been restored and remains operational," but military personnel in Ukraine's drone sector have continued to report uneven performance.
