Carney Warns U.S. Is Trying to ‘Break’ Canada as Trump Revives ‘51st State’ Threat

2026-10-16
18:19:39 UTC
03:19:39 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday warned that the United States is trying to sow discord as he urged Albertans not to vote for a separation referendum.
“The stakes are high. This referendum, it comes at the worst possible time. The world has become more dangerous and divided,” Carney said at a rally in Calgary ahead of Monday’s vote, which will see residents decide whether the oil-rich province should hold a referendum on independence. “There are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they can own us.”
While Carney didn’t explicitly name the U.S., the remarks echoed his previous warnings of the dangers of American dominance. Carney's statement came a day after U.S. President Donald Trump revisited his ambitions to annex Canada, telling the crowd at a rally in Arizona that the country will “end up being the 51st state, because it's the only way it works.” Trump again accused Canada of treating the U.S. “very badly” and vowed he won’t allow it to happen anymore as “it’s a whole different ballgame now [that] Trump is in town.”
The U.S. and Canada remain in a contentious trade standoff after negotiations collapsed in August. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last month, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. Carney has encouraged Canadians to band together and take back their economic power by choosing Canadian products over those made in the U.S. The trade tussle comes after months of Trump repeatedly threatening Canada’s sovereignty—a move that has stoked tensions between the U.S. Administration and Canadian officials.
In light of Trump’s most recent remarks about possible annexation, Canada’s former deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland said it would be dangerous to deepen or maintain close economic ties with a neighbor that “openly says they want to take you over.”
Carney admitted in an interview with the New York Times last month that he had studied the risk of a U.S. invasion, given Trump’s charged rhetoric. “I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” he said. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to [prepare].”
Amid the U.S.-Canada tensions, Carney is desperately trying to promote his “Canada Strong” strategy—one that he hopes will very much include Alberta. Polling conducted by 338Canada suggests that as of Oct. 11, 75% of Albertans would vote to remain part of Canada. But Carney’s resolve is being tested on more than one front, after the separatist Parti Québécois won Quebec's provincial election earlier this month. Incoming Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already stated his intention to hold a referendum on Quebec independence. While he has vowed not to initiate a vote so long as Trump is in office, the looming presence of a separatist movement undoubtedly complicates matters for Carney at a time when he is striving to show that Canada is strong enough to prosper without relying on the American market.
With the U.S. and Canada locked in a trade stalemate, and with annexation threats once again dominating the conversation, here’s a look at the reality Carney is facing as he deals with both domestic and international pressures.
Trump's remarks complicate Carney’s unity efforts
Trump’s accusations that Canada has taken advantage of the U.S. on matters of trade and security date back to before Carney became Prime Minister in March 2025, meaning the friction we’re currently seeing goes deeper than a simple clash between Trump and Carney. Trump would often refer to Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau as the "governor" of the "great state of Canada."
In terms of any physical threat facing Canada, Patrick Leblond, a professor of public and international affairs at the University of Ottawa, says that Carney “put it best when he talked about tail risk” in his interview with the Times. “It’s the financial term for something that has potentially high impact, but low probability,” Leblond explains.
Trump’s economic actions and threats have proven to be far more damaging than his annexation remarks, experts note.
“He has weaponized market access to the U.S.,” says Leblond. “What we can expect is more economic pressure from the White House in the coming months. Trump and his acolytes certainly [appear to] see Canada as a small, weak country that the United States should try to squeeze further.”
The U.S. is Canada’s largest trading partner, with almost $2.6 billion worth of goods and services passing across the border daily in 2024. According to the Office for the U.S. Trade Representative, trade between the two was down 4.6% from 2024 to 2025, but still saw $872.3 billion worth of goods and services cross the border.
Still, there are concerns that any suggestion of annexation, however unlikely it may be, could damage Carney’s high-stakes domestic campaign to unite the country.
On the home front, the success of a separatist party in Quebec is another threat to the unity that Carney is striving for. However, despite the Parti Québécois' victory (they fell five seats short of securing a majority government), the desire for separatism among Quebec residents remains low—with only 31% in favor of sovereignty for the province, according to data from 338 Canada released on Oct. 11.
“If Quebec is on a path to separation or not, it would never be because they were looking for further alignment with the United States,” argues Lori Turnbull, a professor in political science at Dalhousie University. “Quebec has a variety of cultural protections in the Canadian federation. They would have none of that in the United States.”
The more immediate risk for Carney lies in Alberta, with residents preparing to vote on whether the province should hold a referendum on independence.
Carney, who was raised in Edmonton, Alberta, on Thursday framed the referendum as an opportunity for voters to “stand up for Alberta, the heart of Canada” and “recognize that we're all responsible for each other.”
How Trump’s threats could also help Carney
The pressure and rhetoric from the U.S. could actually work in Carney’s favor, experts tell TIME.
“The effect of Trump's comments has been unifying,” says Turnbull. Despite discussions of independence in Alberta and Quebec, she says “there isn't widespread panic that the country is coming apart.”
In fact, research conducted by the Environics Institute for Survey Research in 2025 found that “in almost every province, the proportion of residents who are very attached to Canada is greater than the proportion who are very attached to their province.”
Between Trudeau’s resignation on Jan. 6, 2025, and a federal election in Canada months later on April 28, Carney’s Liberal Party went from 20% to 42.8% in the polls, according to CBC, with Carney’s message of defiance in the face of Trump proving to be a rallying point.
This falls in line with depleting favorable views of the U.S. among Canadians. In July, 44% of Canadians had a favorable opinion of China compared to 33% of Canadians who held the same view of the U.S., according to a Pew Research Center survey. “When China is more popular than the U.S. in a country like Canada, you have to ask yourself: ‘What's going on?’” says Leblond.
Continued annexation threats could bring Canadians even closer together. “Already, trust is very low, and [more threats] would confirm even more that the United States is [perhaps] not a trustworthy partner at this time,” Leblond argues.
Since the U.S.-Canada trade war reignited in August, Carney has seen his domestic approval rating bounce back up. On Oct. 15, it stood at 62% according to Poliwave, compared to 56% in mid-July. Carney’s resistance against American economic pressures could help his cause, particularly in possible separatist provinces.
“In August, when Carney walked out of the negotiations with the U.S., the highest levels of support for him were found in Quebec,” says Leblond. Indeed, Carney’s approval rating in Quebec grew from 76% to 80% between Aug. 17, and Sep. 7, the highest in any province, according to Liaison Strategies.
Turnbull says the support behind Carney’s decision to walk away from negotiations prompted a strong sense of “patriotism and loyalty.”
That attitude among Canadians has been reflected in the burgeoning “Buy Canadian” movement, in which consumers across the country have joined a boycott of U.S. products in an effort to feed back into the Canadian economy.
Carney strengthens international alliances to end reliance on American market
In September, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to work toward becoming the bloc’s first “associate member,” in what she described as an “urgent” reimagining of partnerships.
While addressing the European Parliament as a guest of honor in Strasbourg, France, Carney insisted “Europe and Canada are stronger together” and said “Canada and the European Union can anchor our ground to hold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive.”
Trump called the unique membership proposal “laughable” and has threatened economic punishments if the E.U. moves forward with von der Leyen’s plan.
Carney’s shift towards other partnerships “doesn't mean that Canada is not going to do business with the U.S., but it's no longer a preferred partner,” says Leblond, noting that Carney wants to build relations with partners that “share the same values in terms of rules-based trade and investment.”
In January, after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Carney announced a new strategic partnership with China, focused on “energy, agri-food, and trade.” Carney agreed to cut his country’s 100% tariff on Chinese electric cars in return for lower tariffs on Canadian farm products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
These stronger international ties that diversify trade and security away from the U.S. are proving popular on the homefront, according to data.
According to Abacus Data, a survey conducted in September found that 49% of Canadians would support Canada joining the E.U. An Ipsos poll conducted in January, in light of Carney’s visit to China, found that 54% of Canadians also said they support stronger trade ties with China.

Belgium plans to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of 2026, Prime Minister Bart De Wever announced on 16 October, raising the expected number from three amid delays in transferring the aircraft.
The expanded commitment comes as Ukraine faces sustained Russian drone and missile attacks and needs additional combat aircraft to strengthen its air defenses.
De Wever made the announcement at a press conference in Brussels alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Anadolu Agency reported. He said Belgium’s deliveries had fallen behind schedule because its new US-made F-35 fighter jets arrived later than expected.
Belgium also discussed supplying more ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16s.
F-16 deliveries delayed by F-35 schedule
“We will deliver 10 this year,” De Wever said, explaining that delays in receiving Belgium’s F-35s had held up the transfer of its F-16s. The new aircraft are now beginning to arrive, allowing Belgium to move forward with deliveries to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy confirmed that Kyiv expects additional F-16s from Belgium by the end of the year and thanked Brussels for the agreement.
The announcement marks an increase from Belgium’s previously reported plan to send three F-16s to Ukraine by the end of 2026. The new figure would more than triple the number expected under that earlier commitment.
F-16s to help counter Russian jet-powered drones
De Wever said Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets and described the F-16 as one of the few weapons capable of effectively countering Russian jet-powered drones.
The aircraft can also intercept cruise missiles and other aerial targets, while carrying out electronic warfare and combat missions. Ukraine received its first F-16s in 2024 after allies agreed to supply the aircraft and train Ukrainian pilots.
Belgium rushes three F-16s to Ukraine as Russia expands its drone and missile assault
Belgium discusses ammunition and financial support
Zelenskyy and De Wever also discussed supplying additional ammunition for Ukraine’s F-16s, including 20 mm rounds produced by Belgian defense company FN Herstal.
The leaders also reportedly discussed Ukraine’s financial needs, though neither provided details on potential next steps. Belgium remains at the center of discussions over frozen Russian assets, as Brussels hosts Euroclear, which holds a large share of the immobilized funds.

Russia plans winter strikes to cut off electricity, heat, and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa to force Ukraine’s surrender, NYT reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:16:05 UTC
03:16:05 KST

Russia plans winter strikes to cut off electricity, heat, and water in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa to force Ukraine’s surrender, NYT reports
Russia expects to force Ukraine to capitulate this coming winter by disabling its energy system, particularly by leaving Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa without electricity, heat, or water, The New York Times reported. The newspaper reviewed a Russian government plan that Ukraine intercepted and showed to its European allies in September.
According to the plan, Russia would need about 70 ballistic missiles, 720 long-range drones, and 150 guided aerial bombs to cut off water, electricity, and heat to Ukraine’s three largest cities. Russian military planners believe a month of strikes at that intensity would destroy Ukraine’s energy system.
With the war now in its fifth year, previous attacks have left Ukrainian power plants unable to operate at full capacity, and each new strike quickly knocks them offline, the newspaper reported. Before the war, for example, the three combined heat and power plants supplying Kyiv had a total generating capacity of about 1.3 gigawatts. That has now fallen to about 500 megawatts.
If Russia’s plan succeeds, Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa could lose 90% of their power generating capacity and see heat supplies cut by 90%, disrupting water and sewage systems, according to the newspaper.
Russia’s confidence that the plan can work stems largely from Ukraine’s shortage of air defenses, particularly Patriot interceptor missiles, without which Ukrainian forces are virtually unable to defend against ballistic missiles.
Analysts agree that Moscow now has a better chance of succeeding in its air campaign than at any other point in the war. Ukraine’s missile defenses have been depleted by cuts in American aid, Russia’s missile and drone arsenal has grown more powerful and effective, and years of strikes have left Ukraine’s energy infrastructure far more vulnerable.
This makes Moscow extremely unlikely to agree to any version of the energy ceasefire Kyiv has repeatedly proposed. “The only card they have to pressure the Ukrainians are these air attacks. They don’t have anything else,” Harry Nedelcu, a director at the consulting firm Rasmussen Global, told The New York Times.
But history shows that such bombing campaigns, which devastate economies and civilian life, usually fail to force an enemy to surrender, the newspaper reported. The United States failed to achieve its aims this way in Vietnam, during the Persian Gulf War in the early 1990s, and in the current war against Iran.
“Punishing the adversaries’ civilian population and trying to break its will has a very poor historical track record for coercing it to concede defeat,” Seth Jones, a military expert at the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies, told the newspaper.

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Czechia recorded 26 cyber incidents in September, the third-highest monthly total in the past year, the National Cyber and Information Security Agency (NUKIB) said Friday, according to Radio Prague International.
Only January, with 32 incidents, and August, with 28, recorded higher figures.
The agency reported an average of around 17 incidents per month last year.
Of the 26 incidents recorded in September, only one was classified as significant. The others were considered less serious, while none was rated as highly significant, the agency said.
The incidents targeted user accounts, websites, email servers and cloud servers.
In several cases, attackers gained unauthorized access to internal networks through virtual private networks (VPNs).
The agency also reported security breaches and incidents involving malicious software.

No 10 leaves option open to impose Chinese EV tariffs if UK joins EU scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:09:34 UTC
03:09:34 KST

No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme.
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”.
 
“We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

EU Commission chief urges to change energy consumption as fossil fuel imports cost bloc extra $119B

03:08:08 KST

Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Friday reiterated calls for Europe to change the way it consumes energy, warning that the bloc's dependence on imported fossil fuels has increased costs by €106 billion ($119 billion) without delivering any additional energy.
Speaking at a press conference after an EU leaders' summit in Brussels, von der Leyen said Europe's reliance on imported oil and gas continues to expose its economy to geopolitical developments beyond its control.
She said gas prices surged by around 140% since late February, while diesel prices doubled, highlighting the economic consequences of the ongoing energy crisis.
"We must also change the way we consume energy," von der Leyen said, calling for the replacement of foreign fossil fuels with electricity produced in Europe.
She stressed that Europe must remain committed to its energy transition, focusing on affordable, clean and domestically produced energy sources, including nuclear power and renewables.
European Council President Antonio Costa also highlighted the impact of high and volatile energy prices on households and businesses, describing energy costs as a crucial component of Europe's competitiveness.
He said the bloc was paying the price of its dependence on fossil fuels and the absence of a fully integrated single energy market.
Costa also announced that he would convene another informal meeting of EU leaders in Alden Biesen, Belgium, in February 2027 to assess progress on defense and competitiveness following previous discussions. 
Short-term measures
Von der Leyen outlined several short-term measures agreed upon to mitigate the impact of rising energy prices.
Those include the release of 100 million barrels of oil and diesel over the next four months, managed by the International Energy Agency, extending the scope and duration of a temporary state aid framework introduced in February, and postponing implementation of the methane regulation by one year.
The EU will also launch a strategic dialogue on European refineries, with the aim of strengthening refining capacity within the bloc and helping bring prices down.
Von der Leyen also addressed concerns over the EU's trade relationship with China, calling for a substantial and rapid rebalancing of economic ties.
She said the bloc's trade deficit with China reached €1 billion per day in 2025, and warned that the imbalance was expected to worsen in 2026. 
Ukraine, migration
Costa said the bloc's commitment to Ukraine remained strong, and that the EU had identified the means to cover the country's financial needs for this year and called on the European Commission to propose measures addressing additional financing needs for 2027.
Von der Leyen added that Ukraine faced a financing gap of €70 billion in 2027, calling on international partners to increase their contributions.
On migration, Costa said irregular border crossings into the EU had fallen to their lowest level since 2021, but acknowledged that the bloc's migration and asylum system still needed improvements.

Ukraine Intl Trade Commission rescinds anti-dumping tariffs on Chinese steel fasteners
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
21:05:06 EEST
03:05:06 KST

The Interdepartmental Commission on International Trade (ICIT) has decided to revoke definitive anti-dumping measures on imports into Ukraine of steel fasteners originating in the People's Republic of China.
The ICIT adopted the relevant decision No. AD-609/2026/441-01 on October 12.
According to the document, pursuant to Ukraine's Law "On the Protection of the National Producer from Dumped Imports," at the request of PJSC Druzhkivka Metal Products Plant (DMPP), the ICIT, by its decision No. AD-587/2025/441-01 of September 26, 2025, initiated a review of anti-dumping measures on imports into Ukraine of steel fasteners originating in the PRC due to the expiration of the period of their application. The review was assigned to Ukraine's Ministry of Economy and Environment.
The review covered imports into Ukraine of products described as follows: articles of iron or steel, threaded, namely screws, bolts and nuts, specifically: hex socket head bolts (screws) with a diameter of 6 mm to 20 mm, inclusive (excluding Confirmat screws, whose technical specifications and appearance are set out in the annex to ICIT decision No. AD-465/2020/4411-03 of September 21, 2020, as amended), classified under code ex7318 15 68 90 in accordance with the Ukrainian Classification of Goods for Foreign Economic Activity (UCGFEA); hexagon head bolts with a diameter of 6 mm to 30 mm, inclusive, classified under code ex7318 15 82 90 in accordance with the UCGFEA; hexagon head bolts or hexagon head bolts with a flange, with a diameter of 6 mm to 30 mm, inclusive, classified under code ex7318 15 88 90 in accordance with the UCGFEA; square head or eye bolts (screws) with a diameter of 6 mm to 20 mm, inclusive, classified under code ex7318 15 95 90 in accordance with the UCGFEA; and hexagon nuts or hexagon nuts with a flange, with diameters of 6 mm to 12 mm, inclusive, and 14 mm to 36 mm, inclusive, classified under codes ex7318 16 92 90 and ex7318 16 99 90 in accordance with the UCGFEA.
The designation "ex" next to a classification code means that the anti-dumping duty applies exclusively to goods whose description is specified in the decision.
The investigation period ran from January 1, 2022, through June 30, 2025, and the review period covered July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.
In accordance with the law, the Commission reviewed the materials submitted by the Ministry of Economy and the report on the results of the review. Following its examination, the Commission established that the applicant qualified as a national producer within the meaning of Paragraph 16 of Article 1 of the law; the product manufactured by the national producer was like the product under review; and imports into Ukraine of goods originating in the PRC were made at dumped prices during 2022–2024.
During the investigation period, the national producer suffered material injury, as evidenced by the deterioration of a number of socioeconomic indicators. In particular, production volumes and capacity utilization fell by 33.17%; the financial result from sales of the product on the domestic Ukrainian market declined by 95.48%; the profitability of sales on the domestic Ukrainian market deteriorated by 113.78%; average employment fell by 43.56%, while the number of employees directly involved in production decreased by 40.19%; investment ceased; and the cash balance in hryvnias declined by 58.83%, or by 67.89% in U.S. dollar terms.
The position of exporters and economic conditions in the PRC are such that the possibility of new forms of dumping cannot be ruled out, which would cause injury to the national producer. Specifically, during 2022–2024, the volume of available production capacity in the PRC significantly exceeded consumption of the like product in Ukraine.
Extending the anti-dumping measures on imports into Ukraine of steel fasteners originating in the PRC was found to be inconsistent with Ukraine's national interests, in particular because the national producer had already suspended production activities for an extended period, and its main production facilities were located in territory where hostilities were taking place or had taken place; the national producer had not confirmed its ability to manufacture certain types of steel fasteners under current conditions; and the anti-dumping duty covered a range of other products not manufactured by the national producer.
The main facts and findings resulting from the review were submitted to all interested parties. The comments provided by interested parties did not contain sufficient evidence that could have affected the conclusions reached by the Ministry of Economy in the course of the review.
"Taking the above into account and guided by the provisions of Articles 18 and 19 of the law, the Commission adopted decision No. AD-609/2026/441-01 of October 12, 2026, 'On the Revocation of Definitive Anti-Dumping Measures on Imports into Ukraine of Steel Fasteners Originating in the People's Republic of China,' under which it decided to conclude the review and revoke the anti-dumping measures introduced by Commission decision No. AD-465/2020/4411-03 of September 21, 2020, 'On the Application of Definitive Anti-Dumping Measures on Imports into Ukraine of Steel Fasteners Originating in the People's Republic of China' (as amended), and Commission decision No. AD-591/2026/441-01 of January 26, 2026, 'On the Application to Imports into Ukraine of Steel Fasteners Originating in Malaysia of Definitive Anti-Dumping Measures Introduced by the Decision of the Interdepartmental Commission on International Trade No. AD-465/2020/4411-03 of September 21, 2020, "On the Application of Definitive Anti-Dumping Measures on Imports into Ukraine of Steel Fasteners Originating in the People's Republic of China (as amended),"'" the ICIT decision said.
The Commission's decision No. AD-609/2026/441-01 of October 12, 2026, entered into force on the date this notice was published, namely October 13 of this year.
PJSC Druzhkivka Metal Products Plant specializes in the manufacture of metal hardware, including bolts, nuts and rivets for general engineering, rail fastenings for railway track superstructures, and high-strength fasteners for building and bridge structures. In May 2022, the company issued an order suspending employment contracts due to Russia's military aggression and the impossibility of conducting production and business operations. The company subsequently changed its registered legal address from Druzhkivka, Donetsk region, to Dnipro, Dnipropetrovsk region.
According to data from the National Depository of Ukraine (NDU) for the fourth quarter of 2025, individual shareholder Oleksiy Spiridonov owned 14.9949% of the company's shares; Olena Mishchenko-Solona, a resident of Spain, held 13.0304%; Iryna Mischenko held 24.5167%; Serhiy Popkov held 5.8611%; Anton Malikov held 9.75%; Olena Malikova held 8.25%; and Valeriy and Dmytro Malikov each held 9.774%.

Control of Congress: How past midterms shine a light on Republican challenge in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:04:39 UTC
03:04:39 KST

The US midterm elections, scheduled for November 3, will determine control of Congress and shape the last two years of President Donald Trump’s final term.
All 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, the lower chamber of Congress, will be up for grabs in the midterms – the informal term for the nationwide polls held in the middle of every four-year presidential term.
Elections will also be held for 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress, on the same day.
Currently, the Republican Party has a slim majority in both chambers.
Without a majority in Congress, the incumbent president finds it difficult to pass legislation or make key appointments.
But historical patterns show that the party of the sitting president usually loses House seats in midterms. That has been the case in roughly 20 of the last 22 midterm cycles.
Experts say the trend is likely to continue, even though rising polarisation in US society, along with other factors, complicates any major shift in voting patterns.
“During the past 10 years with Trump dominating the political scene, many of the old rules and historical traditions have been defied,” John Zogby, a public opinion pollster and co-founder of the Arab American Institute, tells TRT World.
Since 1982, every first-term president – with the sole exception of George W Bush in 2002 – has lost seats in the first congressional election after his ascendancy, he notes.
Presidents Ronald Reagan, Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Trump himself in 2018 “lost a huge number of seats” in the midterms.
“As things stand right now, all of the ingredients appear to be in place for the opposition Democratic Party to continue this legacy,” Zogby says.
Trump’s approval ratings are at a low point. They are particularly low on affordability, the economy, and the war in Iran, which are issues that “matter most to American voters”.
Barely a fortnight before the election, “the president’s party appears to be in trouble,” he says.
According to David Schultz, a professor of political science at Hamline University and editor of Presidential Swing States: Why Only Ten Matter, the historical pattern of the president's party losing House seats in midterms should be treated only as a “strong tendency”, and not a law.
The exceptions of 1998 when backlash to Clinton’s impeachment helped Democrats – and 2002 when the September 11 attacks created support for George W Bush – show that “unusual external events” can override the ordinary midterm referendum dynamic.
“As of (now), the major polling averages put Trump’s approval between about 36 and 38 percent,” Schultz tells TRT World.
He points out that the share of swing voters in the electorate has shrunk from 10-15 percent in earlier decades to closer to 0-5 percent.
Meanwhile, the number of truly competitive House seats has fallen from around 120 to about 30.
With fewer voters available to switch sides, outcomes depend more heavily on who turns out on the day of election.
“Detachment from Trump is not the same as attachment to Democrats,” Schultz says.
He expects Republicans to lose House seats, but the size of their seat losses is “far less certain” at this point.
Trump’s name on the ballot?
Presidential approval among voters in midterms ranks among the strongest single predictors of the outcome, experts say.
Zogby points to past cycles in which weak presidential approval, paired with economic stress or unpopular policies, produced large losses: Reagan amid a recession in 1982, Clinton in 1994, and Obama after the Affordable Care Act in 2010.
Trump has reinforced the personal nature of the contest, telling supporters to “vote like his name is on the ballot”, Zogby notes.
Schultz cautions that the relationship between the presidential approval and midterm outcomes is not automatic.
Presidential approval works better when paired with economic perceptions, he says.
Both signals are negative for Republicans this year: voters are sour on the economy and the country’s direction, he adds.
A survey by Quinnipiac University, a non-partisan polling service, has shown only about 32 percent approving of Trump’s handling of the economy against 65 percent disapproving.
But Schultz notes many reasons why poll numbers may overstate Democratic gains.
Roughly 79 percent of Republicans still approve of Trump, according to Quinnipiac polling.
Disapproval does not automatically translate into a vote for the other party, he insists, adding that independent voters now make up a smaller, more disengaged share of the electorate than in earlier eras.
Issues that matter
Zogby describes the top concerns among the electorate as having “melded into one super issue”, as affordability, the war in the Middle East, and inflation.
This goes against Republicans because they currently hold power at House, Senate, and presidential levels.
Even on issues long favourable to Republicans – such as immigration and crime – the Republican Party’s ratings have slipped, he says.
For Schultz, core concerns among the US electorate are grocery and gas prices, housing, and the cost of health care.
Other than immigration and tariffs – which have contributed to the overall affordability problem – another important issue for the electorate is the war against Iran.
The so-called war of choice – now in its eighth month – remains unpopular among voters. Polls show only 29 percent approving of Trump’s handling and 65 percent disapproving.
What distinguishes 2026 from past midterms is that a “small set of issues is nearly inseparable from President Trump himself”, Schultz notes.
“The election, therefore, functions as a referendum on a person more than a contest between issue platforms,” he says.
“Because Democrats have not offered a clear alternative economic message, affordability may produce disengagement as often as it produces Democratic votes,” he adds.
The wild cards
Several conditions can possibly allow Republicans to limit losses or retain at least one chamber of Congress, experts say.
Zogby identifies Democratic vulnerabilities as a major wild card.
“Voter trust for the Democrats is at the lowest point ever,” he says.
Overall, the Democratic Party has a 26 percent positive rating, which includes about 65 percent of Democratic voters – down from 85 percent who trusted their own party in November 2024, Zogby says.
“Democrats also lack an agenda going forward. Those that do have an agenda for action are the progressive wing, and even moderate Democrats are attacking them for being too radical,” he says.
This leaves open the possibility of “last-minute revulsion” by late-deciding voters, he says.
Trump himself remains a wild card who has “rewritten the rule book many times”, he adds.
Schultz outlines a number of factors that can possibly affect the midterm outcomes.
One, partisan loyalty can outlast disappointment with the president, he says.
Many unhappy Republicans will still support their candidate for Congress when they think the alternative offers no clear programme.
Two, the “Democratic brand” imposes a ceiling: only about 21 percent of voters approve of Democrats in Congress, but more than three-fourths of Democratic voters describe their vote primarily as “opposition to Trump”, he says.
Three, a change in the news, such as a durable settlement of the Iran war, falling gas prices, or easing inflation, can improve Trump’s standing by a few points in key places, Schultz says.
Schultz also points to the structure of the Senate. It favours Republicans, while Democrats must defend all their seats and gain a net four, several of them in states Trump carried comfortably.
Finally, polling and turnout error can be consequential if low-propensity voters who dislike Trump decide to stay home on the day of the election.
“Taken together, my judgement is that Republicans are far better positioned to hold the Senate than the House,” he says, adding that maintaining the majority in the House would require a combination of strong Democratic abstention and durable Republican loyalty – something the current polling does not show.

Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:03:43 UTC
03:03:43 KST

Saudi Arabia’s biggest problem may be its enemy’s smallest weapons
The Houthis continue to strike Saudi Arabia despite Riyadh’s threats of a forceful response and promises to enlist outside partners to defend the kingdom.
By targeting airports and oil infrastructure, Ansar Allah is seeking to raise the cost of Saudi involvement in Yemen’s conflict and force the kingdom’s leadership to reconsider the terms of a settlement.
The latest wave of Houthi attacks has targeted facilities of particular importance to Saudi Arabia. On the evening of October 13, a strike hit Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, home to the company’s key management operations. The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire, though miraculously no one was killed.
Ansar Allah also claimed strikes on an oil refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport. The choice of targets suggests the Houthis want to put virtually all of the kingdom’s oil revenue at risk and disrupt its international air connections.
These targets also suggest that the movement is trying to influence Saudi leaders’ decisions directly. Oil infrastructure generates government revenue, airports connect the country to the outside world, and confidence in the kingdom depends on the security of both. Even limited damage can therefore produce an impact far greater than the cost of the weapons used.
What is driving the conflict?
The Houthis have their own history of confrontation with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in northern Yemen, fought a series of wars against the central government between 2004 and 2010, and seized the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Its rise was rooted in Yemen’s political system, local conflicts, and the collapse of state institutions. Iranian support strengthened an already established force with its own social base and political objectives.
The Saudi intervention in 2015 cemented Riyadh’s position as the movement’s principal foreign adversary. For the kingdom, the aim was to prevent a hostile force from consolidating power along its southern border and to support Yemen’s internationally recognized government. For the Houthi leadership, the war became both a threat to its survival and a rallying cause. Invoking foreign aggression allowed the movement to portray its struggle for domestic supremacy as a defense of national sovereignty.
That logic remains relevant to the current escalation. Saudi support for an offensive by Yemeni government forces threatens the Houthis’ territorial gains and bargaining position. Striking deep inside the kingdom allows them to raise the price of that support. Their apparent calculation is to make continued Saudi involvement in the war carry a recurring cost on Saudi soil.
The movement’s demands are concrete: an end to strikes, limits on assistance to its Yemeni adversaries, the lifting of transportation and trade restrictions, and agreements on revenues and payments. These issues were under discussion long before the latest escalation. The framework for a roadmap presented by the UN in December 2023 included a nationwide ceasefire, payment of public-sector salaries, the resumption of oil exports, and an easing of restrictions on Sanaa airport and the port of Hodeidah.
By increasing Riyadh’s costs, Ansar Allah hopes to extract concessions and retain control of the territory it has seized. A ceasefire on those terms, however, would consolidate the movement’s position without resolving how power should be shared in Yemen.
Attacks on Saudi Arabia also serve Ansar Allah’s domestic political interests. The movement uses its ability to strike deep inside the kingdom to bolster its standing among supporters. Confrontation with Riyadh also allows the Houthis to cast themselves as Yemen’s defenders against foreign intervention and use that claim to justify their bid for power.
Iranian military and technological assistance has undoubtedly expanded Houthi capabilities considerably. But the relationship with Tehran does not erase Ansar Allah’s own interests in Yemen’s power struggle or its confrontation with Saudi Arabia. Reducing the movement’s actions to the execution of Iranian orders fails to explain either the conflict’s local roots or the Houthi leadership’s objectives.
A more accurate description would be a partnership with unequal resources in which the Yemeni side retains substantial autonomy. Weakening Saudi Arabia may serve both partners’ interests, but their preferred terms for ending the war may differ. Ansar Allah must consider conditions on Yemen’s battlefields and the survival of its own rule. Agreements between Iran and outside powers therefore do not guarantee an automatic halt to Houthi operations.
The economics of war
The development of domestic missile production and an expanding network for procuring components make it harder for Riyadh to bring Houthi attacks to an end. If the movement can replenish its arsenal from several sources, restricting Iranian supplies will have only a partial effect. An agreement with Tehran alone would therefore be insufficient to secure Saudi facilities. Much will depend on whether the Houthis themselves believe continued strikes serve their interests.
Nor do the Houthis need to match Saudi Arabia in the quantity or quality of their weapons. They can choose their targets and pause between attacks, while the kingdom must continuously defend airports, oil facilities, and cities across a vast territory. Even a single hit can disrupt a facility’s operations, trigger flight cancellations, or bring business activity to a halt. Purchases of American air defense systems reduce that threat but do not eliminate it. Riyadh’s problem is that military superiority has yet to deprive its adversary of the ability to inflict economically painful blows. That is precisely the capability the Houthis are trying to turn into negotiating leverage.
Saudi military spending exceeds $82 billion per year, yet the kingdom still struggles to protect its infrastructure from Houthi attacks. This exposes the gap between the cost of the weapons it has purchased and their effectiveness in this particular war. Advanced fighter jets and missile defense systems give Riyadh a considerable advantage, but detecting small drones and low-flying cruise missiles requires extensive radar coverage and rapid information sharing between units. Without those capabilities, expensive equipment cannot reliably detect and engage targets in time.
In a prolonged confrontation, the disparity in weapons costs also becomes significant. According to cited estimates, a Patriot interceptor costs more than $3 million, while some Houthi drones cost just $15,000–25,000. Defenders have to use such interceptors against cheap aircraft to protect far more valuable assets. But sustained defensive operations deplete stocks that cannot be replenished quickly, particularly amid strong global demand for air defense systems. This gives the Houthis an opportunity to wear down the kingdom’s defenses even when most of the aircraft they launch fail to reach their targets.
Technical difficulties are compounded by the structure of the Saudi armed forces. The separation of the regular military and the National Guard has historically served, in part, to protect the monarchy against a coup. But separate chains of command and highly centralized decision-making can hinder coordination and limit commanders’ initiative. Another weapons purchase, then, will not solve the problem on its own. Even additional detection and interception systems will deliver limited results if information arrives late and coordinating a response takes too long.
The Houthis can reasonably expect these shortcomings to take time to address, leaving them able to continue inflicting painful blows in the meantime. Domestic production and broader supply networks help sustain that campaign. The movement does not need to destroy major industrial facilities or shut down air travel altogether; a recurring threat is enough to make airlines reconsider routes, investors postpone decisions, and Saudi leaders spend more on protecting infrastructure.
Will help come from abroad?
Statements by Türkiye and Pakistan expressing their readiness to defend Saudi Arabia do not yet provide grounds to expect either country to enter the war fully, much less fight the Houthis inside Yemen. At an October 5 meeting, the parties to the Mecca Agreement announced that they would provide forces and equipment for the kingdom’s defense. The political weight of those promises, however, will depend on whether the allies can actually reduce the number of attacks and the damage they cause. As long as the strikes continue, Houthi leaders may view such declarations as rhetoric unlikely to be followed by a dangerous expansion of the war.
Ankara’s position reinforces that calculation. Turkish Foreign Affairs Minister Hakan Fidan outlined possible assistance with air defense, electronic warfare, and technical support, while explicitly ruling out Turkish troops taking part in offensive operations on foreign soil. Türkiye has thus set clear limits on its role from the outset.
Pakistan also has reasons to avoid direct intervention. Joining the war in Yemen would mean additional military spending and the risk of worsening relations with neighboring Iran. It would therefore be premature to expect Islamabad to take on the task of defeating the Houthis on Riyadh’s behalf. Its commitments to the kingdom leave room for a role limited to defending specific facilities and providing military assistance.
A similar distinction applies to the American position. Intelligence sharing and targeting assistance support Saudi operations, but they do not mean Washington is willing to stop the attacks at any cost. The Houthis appear to be counting on precisely these limits to outside involvement. Their bet is that the kingdom’s allies will help it defend itself but will be reluctant to become embroiled in a prolonged war to achieve Saudi objectives in Yemen.
Until that support produces a substantial reduction in attacks, threats to bring in allies may carry little weight with Ansar Allah.
***
The Houthis are seeking to demonstrate that continued Saudi intervention will bring losses that neither a vast defense budget nor foreign partners can prevent. If that pressure prompts Riyadh to scale back assistance to their adversaries or accept settlement terms favorable to them, the movement will have an opportunity to translate its battlefield gains into lasting political advantages.
Such an outcome would also benefit Iran by weakening Saudi Arabia’s position. Its most immediate consequence, however, would be to strengthen Ansar Allah itself in the struggle for power in Yemen.

North Kazakhstan receives first shipment of pedigree livestock from Australia
North Kazakhstan region has received its first shipment of pedigree cattle from Australia, with 305 Aberdeen Angus animals arriving via a special cargo flight through Astana International Airport, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The imports are being carried out under Kazakhstan's 2026-2030 Comprehensive Livestock Development Plan, which aims to strengthen the national breeding base, improve herd genetics, boost domestic breeding capacity, and increase output of competitive livestock products.
The plan envisions the purchase of 50,000 head of breeding livestock, including 40,000 head of cattle and 10,000 head of small ruminants. Kazakhstan has already imported approximately 9,500 head of cattle.
Those participating in the herd renewal program are Shal Akyn AGRO-2020 LLP and Asyl Farms LLP. According to Gabiden Balginbekov, director of Asyl Farms, the company selected the Aberdeen Angus breed because of its strong fattening performance and high-quality meat.
"The import of Australian livestock will allow us to establish our own highly productive herd and further develop pedigree breeding directly in the North Kazakhstan Region," he said.
The region has compiled a portfolio of 23 projects for the purchase of pedigree livestock with a total value of 15 billion tenge.
Since the beginning of the year, the region has imported more than 3,000 head of breeding livestock from Germany and Denmark. By the end of the year, another 10 cargo flights carrying pedigree livestock from Australia are expected to arrive. The total number of imported animals in the region is projected to reach around 11,000 head of cattle and more than 1,500 head of small ruminants.
At the same time, the North Kazakhstan region is expanding infrastructure required for the livestock industry development. The region currently operates 118 dairy farms, including 50 modern facilities. 57 veterinary stations are under construction, with total funding of 1.5 billion tenge.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries, with shipments worth 1.6 billion US dollars.

Psilocybin therapy has mostly reached the well-off. A small Oregon study tested a cheaper group model for low-income patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:58 UTC
03:00:58 KST

Group psilocybin therapy appears feasible and well tolerated among low-income adults with depression, according to a small study conducted within Oregon’s state-regulated psilocybin program. Participants’ depression scores dropped substantially after two group dosing sessions, though the study had no comparison group, so the role of psilocybin itself remains uncertain. The findings were published in the Journal of Psychedelic Studies.
Psilocybin is the primary psychoactive compound found in certain species of fungi, often known as “magic mushrooms.” Under supervision, it is consumed to induce an altered state of consciousness that can help people process difficult emotions. Major depressive disorder is a common mental health condition characterized by persistent feelings of sadness, fatigue, and a loss of interest in daily activities.
Interest in psilocybin as a depression treatment has grown rapidly. For example, a 2020 randomized clinical trial found that psilocybin, paired with psychotherapy, produced rapid and substantial reductions in depression. But the people taking part in this research have tended to be better off than average: a 2025 systematic review found that only about 1 in 8 psychedelic trials reported participants’ income, and in U.S. trials, participants were far more educated and wealthier than the general population.
“Much of the research up to this point has unintentionally skewed toward higher income earners and I felt that something ought to be done about that,” lead author Matthew Hicks, an adjunct faculty member and affiliate research investigator at the National University of Natural Medicine and the Helfgott Research Institute, told PsyPost.
In 2020, Oregon voters passed Measure 109, creating a legal, state-regulated framework for adults to access supervised psilocybin services. The program has served over 15,000 people as of mid-2025. But a single session can cost around $2,000, making the program inaccessible to most low-income people.
Health economists and clinicians have been exploring ways to reduce these costs. A 2023 study calculated that treating patients in small groups rather than one-on-one cuts therapist costs by roughly a third. This economic rationale aligns with a study covered by PsyPost in 2022, which estimated that MDMA-assisted therapy for severe PTSD could save about $133 million in health care costs per 1,000 patients over 30 years compared with standard care.
“My motivation for doing the study is to start a longer series of studies aimed at demonstrating the potential cost-effectiveness of psychedelic therapies, especially in groups, so that they might one day be covered by insurance,” Hicks explained.
To test whether a more affordable group model could work in a real-world setting, Hicks and his colleagues designed a trial specifically for low-income patients. The authors noted that this represents the first clinical trial conducted within a state-regulated psychedelic program, as well as the first psychedelic study focused specifically on a low-income population.
The researchers designed a feasibility study, a small preliminary trial meant to test whether a treatment approach can be carried out in practice, focusing on recruitment, retention, safety, and acceptability. The study had no control group, and neither participants nor researchers were blinded; changes in depression were examined only as exploratory outcomes.
The team recruited adults living in Oregon whose income fell at or below 200 percent of the Federal Poverty Line. Participants had to have a formal diagnosis of major depressive disorder, maintain stable housing, and be actively engaged in regular psychotherapy outside of the study.
Out of 26 eligible volunteers, 20 began the treatment process, and 19 completed the full study. The participants were divided into small cohorts of up to six people. To minimize travel barriers, the researchers conducted two 90-minute preparation sessions online, followed by two in-person psilocybin administration sessions scheduled one week apart. Among those who enrolled, participants averaged 43 years old, 12 were women, and 17 identified as white.
During the dosing sessions, participants gathered in a single room on floor mats and drank a tea made from homogenized whole psilocybin mushrooms of the B+ strain. Within the allowed range, participants chose their own dose with guidance from the facilitators. Those taking SSRI or SNRI antidepressants, which can dull psilocybin’s effects, could take up to 50 milligrams of psilocybin, the maximum permitted under Oregon rules, while all others could take up to 35 milligrams. During the first session, a common approach was to start with about 18 to 20 milligrams and take an optional booster about an hour later.
Two facilitators oversaw the room, playing ambient music and offering individual support in a separate space if needed. Two days after each administration session, the cohort met online for a 90-minute integration session to share and process their experiences.
The study met its feasibility goals: 19 of 20 participants completed it, and attendance at study sessions was 98 percent. Several participants said the online preparation and integration sessions made it possible for them to take part, including some from rural areas, and volunteers received $200 for completing the follow-up interview. No severe adverse events were reported, and participants rated their satisfaction at an average of 4.8 out of 5, with no one rating it below 4.
The most common side effects were temporary nausea, headaches, and passing unease. One participant had nausea and vomiting for about two days after eating the blended mushroom rather than straining it from the tea, and another reported worsening depression that they later attributed to difficult life circumstances.
Depression scores, which the researchers treated as an exploratory outcome, dropped substantially. On the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale, where higher numbers indicate worse depression, participants’ average score fell from 22.21 at baseline to 8.79 two days after the second dosing session. At the three-month follow-up, the average had risen somewhat to 11.89 but remained roughly half of its starting level.
Participants also reported broad improvements across various quality-of-life measures. The largest improvements were in depression, fatigue, and the ability to take part in social roles and activities, and most of these gains held at three months, though they were somewhat smaller.
“One of the takeaways here is that low-income earners can benefit from these therapies if they are able to access them,” Hicks said. “Given the huge financial burden of depression and other mental health issues on our healthcare system and economy generally, my hope is that we can reduce all that suffering while also saving money in the long run.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that group-format psilocybin therapy produced sustained reductions in depression severity. However, that earlier trial examined depression in people with cancer using a different depression scale, whereas the new study focused on low-income adults assessed via the Hamilton Depression scale.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study involved only 20 participants and did not include a control group, so there is no way to compare these outcomes with those of people who received a placebo or standard care. Because everyone also continued their regular psychotherapy and took part in group preparation and integration sessions, and because neither participants nor researchers were blinded, it is not possible to say how much of the improvement stemmed from psilocybin itself.
Participants’ expectations were high, averaging 7 to 8 on 9-point scales, and those who said they would more confidently recommend the treatment to friends tended to show larger improvements. The two facilitators who guided the sessions were also two of the study’s authors, and the follow-up lasted only three months. The research team also noted that their sample lacked racial and ethnic diversity, with most participants identifying as white.
“The scope of my feasibility study was simply to demonstrate that it can be done with this population with these methods,” Hicks noted. “I hope it will provide sufficient justification to fund larger and more rigorous studies that can offer more definitive claims to persuade healthcare payers (like Medicaid and private insurance companies) to cover these services thus providing greater access.”
Future research with larger, more diverse groups and rigorous comparison conditions will be needed to confirm these early results. Such trials could help assess if group psilocybin therapy is a cost-effective alternative to standard mental healthcare.
The study, “Low-income group psilocybin assisted therapy for depression: An Oregon feasibility study,” was authored by Matthew Hicks, Olivia Hicks, Ryan Bradley, and Heather Zwickey.

If the economic narrative doesn’t improve, things could get ugly for Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
If polls are right, voters are in a mood to send Labor into the wilderness
Labor's sprawling backbench has been a sight to behold ever since the 2025 electoral bushfire that consumed the Coalition, leaving behind a lot of empty stumps and toasted tussocks.
The view from the press gallery seats drives this home. Below the viewer sprawls the government's 94-seat majority. It dominates the green benches of the lower house, spilling across the chamber's centre line deep into what is normally opposition upholstery.
It's the literal embodiment of political weight. All those bums on seats.
But for the first time in this parliament's life — and we're pretty much at the half-way mark — those rows upon rows of Labor MPs this week looked more like one of those forests where too much fuel has accumulated.
A lot of wood ready to ignite.
Anecdotes galore of rattled and angry Labor MPs
If polls are right then voters are increasingly in a mood to light the match of a political conflagration. Many of those backbenchers would become oncers.
That was the underlying vibe this week in private conversations in the corridors of parliament, where there were stories and anecdotes galore of unhappy, rattled and angry Labor MPs venting their frustrations.
Some of this might be overblown, but the fact it's out there is new.
Discipline and internal unity have been a mark of the Albanese government, now in its fifth year. Yet for the first time in years, there are plenty of rumblings.
Some backbenchers have been eager to unload their feelings on journalists and several newspapers reported growing agitation across Labor ranks.
Even ministers are at it.
The whole nervous scene was bad enough for the prime minister to resurrect his old line to colleagues — he used it in the lead-up to the 2022 and 2025 elections — that despite how tough it feels now, they'll all be "kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter" come election time.
As the grizzling and fretting continued, the prime minister jumped on ABC Afternoon Briefing on Tuesday to put on a brave face.
"We need to be focused not just on — with due respect here on ABC 24 — on the 24-hour media cycle. We need to make sure as well that we're focused on where we are a year ahead, five years ahead, 10 years ahead," he told Patricia Karvelas.
"What I'm saying is that I'm not spooked by that … we act as an orderly government."
But gnawing at the government's storyline of competence is the ongoing effort to sort out the budget, which is now five months old.
Defeat in the jaws of victory
Legislation has been brought in to address a series of unintended consequences from the introduction of a 30 per cent tax on trusts.
The government says that was always the plan to bring on these changes later this year, given they're not slated to take effect until future years. But the whole thing is another reminder of how much unfinished and unanticipated business sits in the government's in-tray.
Then, at a dinner hosted by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry on Tuesday night, the prime minister appeared to take all the credit for pushing the Australian Tax Office to delay its ban on credit card payments, even though the treasurer had indicated he was already moving to address that issue when it blew up late last week.
Amid talk of the prime minister throwing the treasurer under the bus, Anthony Albanese told parliament that "the whole premise of it is completely wrong".
"The treasurer and I had a discussion last week," he said. "We convened the expenditure review committee, and we unanimously, right across the leadership of the government, agreed that the decision by the ATO to have a limited period of pause on the ban that had been imposed needed to be extended so that there would be proper consultation with small business."
It's a solid explanation. And it would have normally sufficed. But with the government struggling to keep command of the political narrative, the negative headlines reinforced the sense that it keeps finding defeat in the jaws of victory.
The credit card surcharge issue was supposed to be a positive thing. Instead, it turned into a headache that reinforced a notion that Labor doesn't understand business or the economy.
Then, on Wednesday, the Senate pulled the rug out from under one of the government's bigger budget savings — the plan to wind back a rebate to over-65s for health insurance, a $3 billion measure that Health Minister Mark Butler said would be redeployed for aged care services.
Crossbench, Greens and Coalition senators joined forces to scupper the measure, which the government promptly reintroduced.
Loading
The Senate's growing hostility
There are different ways to read this clash.
The government says it shows the Coalition is not serious about finding savings, despite its rhetoric on the need for budget repair.
The Coalition reckons older Australians, pensioners in particular, shouldn't be made to pay for the broken budget.
Interestingly, Barnaby Joyce told this column on Friday that "Labor has a point" on the rebate issue.
"If that's not where you want the savings, then where do you want to find savings?" he said.
"You've got to move away from just talking about being financially prudent and put meat on the bones."
Either way, the Senate's growing hostility to the government's agenda is worth watching closely.
The Greens under new leader David Shoebridge have come out swinging, eager to throw sand in the government's wheels.
And some of that new mood of disruption is because all the big players are starting to focus on the next election. While not due until May 2028, its influence on political behaviour has already begun. Not least as the prime minister can always call an election early, perhaps for a year from now.
The Greens have already shown they're starting to rethink their approach. And the Liberals will have to make a threshold decision in coming months on whether they stick with Angus Taylor to lead them to the next election.
If they think he can't deliver, they'll need to give whoever they opt for time to prepare. For now he looks as safe as you'd expect of any major party leader struggling to reach a primary north of 20 per cent to be. Which will make the lead-up to Christmas a nervous time for him.
Labor will also eventually need to make strategic decisions in coming months, particularly about when and how to renew the frontbench, many of whose members have been in their portfolios since 2019.
If the economic and budget narrative doesn't improve, things could get ugly.
"Usually they're brilliant at discipline," Joyce told this column of Labor. "But we've had different views coming forward. When you see a little bit in public you know there's a lot going on behind closed doors."
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Could a whale really swallow a human? A marine scientist says yes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Just when you think it's safe to go back in the water, along comes Whalefall.
Based on Daniel Kraus's 2023 novel, the thriller follows Jay Gardiner (Austin Abrams), a young scuba diver who attempts to shake off the grief of his father's recent passing with a dive.
But his swim turns dangerous when Jay's diving gear becomes tangled with a giant squid that has been marked as lunch by a hungry sperm whale, and Jay is swallowed with his mollusc companion.
Stuck in the belly of a whale, Jay must figure out a way to escape in 60 minutes before the oxygen in his scuba tank runs out.
When the trailer for Brian Duffield's Whalefall film adaptation hit the internet this year, fans were thrilled to see Kraus's story of grief and acceptance hit cinema screens.
But a question remained: Could a human actually be swallowed by a whale and survive?
Dr Vanessa Pirotta, a lecturer and whale scientist in the Marine Predator Research Group at Macquarie University, has written books on the gigantic creatures and addressed the National Press Club in 2025 on the importance of ocean research to our wider environment.
She's currently conducting Australian-led research as a part of the Sydney Offshore Megafauna Surveys to find out how many gentle giants we have in our waters.
We're talking about Whalefall. But before we dive into it, I must ask: what is your favourite whale fact?
Oh, God, where do I start? I think the one I love is that whales have belly buttons because they're mammals. They live birth.
Wow, how big is a whale belly button?
I've done many whale necropsies where I've measured a whale but I never thought to measure the actual width of the belly button. I would say, focusing on an adult whale, maybe it's like the size of a clenched fist.
One of my favourite things and most interesting things to do as a whale scientist is understanding, working with pathologists and vets, to understand why the animals died. It sounds completely morbid, but the only opportunity for me really to see and learn about whale anatomy is by investigating dead whales and it's really the most interesting thing in my life that I do.
I've got to ask you the question on everybody's mind. Could a human be eaten and swallowed by a whale?
This is the billion-dollar question. So, when we're talking about Whalefall, the movie, it's a sperm whale.They're a toothed whale, as opposed to the humpback whale or toothless whales. They have baleen plates, which are hair-like strands hanging from the roof of their mouth.
They're designed not to bite down on food but to engulf lots of tiny, tiny food and water and then get rid of the water out the side of their mouth.
So, what I'm trying to say is, the biology of the whale that we're dealing with in this movie, you could potentially as a human go down the throat but whether you make it alive or not, I don't think anyone knows that.
Full disclosure: I have not yet done a sperm whale necropsy, but a human could easily fit inside their mouth and potentially be sucked into their throat.
Incredible. In the movie, Austin Abram's character is accidentally swallowed while tangled up with a giant squid, which the whale is hunting. Could this situation ever happen in real life?
This is where the movie is doing my head in. That feeding behaviour would usually happen kilometres, at least a kilometre or so, underneath the ocean, so there's huge pressure. The animal is equipped for pressure. So technically, if a sperm whale was feeding at that shallow a depth, then potentially you could. The sperm whale wouldn't use its teeth to crunch you up and bite you and chew you like what we would be doing.
They would simply use the teeth to grab onto you, like it's doing with the squid. The teeth are there to be like a fork. So, I would say that that's why it's doing my head in because, A, it's not usual to see a sperm whale feeding at this depth and, B, how has it miraculously followed a giant squid all the way to the surface? The squid would have been gone by that stage.
Humans are not part of a whale's diet, I must point out. So, these animals are not targeting humans. A human would be dead and implode by the time they get down to that depth.
Abrams is also covered in the plastic and metal of his scuba gear. Would a whale not realise that was not viable sustenance?
If that did all happen at the subsurface, my assumption would be that the whale would probably bite onto the tank attached to him and instantly know that something's not right.
There have been other divers that have been kayaking or swimming next to humpback whales or other baleen whales with no teeth, and these animals have had these people at least touch their mouths but realise very soon after that something wasn't right and then they usually open their mouth and eject whatever it is.
Those whales with the kayakers, those kayakers are simply basically hanging out where their dinner plate is and then the whales don't give a hoot about them. So, by no means is the whale targeting the humans.
There's never been a swallowing of a human, to my understanding.
Whales just want to eat. They don't want to hurt humans. They're not aggressive animals, are they?
Not necessarily, but nor is a shark. This is the thing. Whales just want to eat their food. That's what sharks just want to do, too. That's why there's so much anthropomorphising in these movies. But as a scientist, I welcome these movies. They're getting a whole generation of people to think about and educate them about these whales and the environment that we know so little about.
If this is showing us a fantastical version of what a whale's stomach would look like, what does a whale's digestive system look like? Do whales have the same kind of digestive acids that we do?
I've looked in many whale digestive systems and I can tell you they're slimy and they're not pretty and they stink. I don't think there'd be much air in there, although the dude is on scuba.
Yeah, he's got 60 minutes of oxygen in his tank.
They would have acids in their stomach. Sperm whales are famous for ambergris. Yeah. Whale vomit. So there probably is a whole heap of squid beaks in that stomach that are undigested because they can't digest them.
So, if hypothetically a human does make it to the stomach but things go wrong, could a whale potentially fully digest and expel a human?
OK, I've been asked lots of questions in my lifetime. But this one …
So, given the fact that this guy is inside a whale with a scuba tank, I would say the scuba tank would probably cause this whale to die. But if this dude was sucked in the whale without a scuba tank and just as a human, then there is potential for this guy to be broken down and passed out.
So, I would say the impeding factor here is the tank. But even before a tank could even get into a stomach of a whale, a whale is not dumb and would probably be like, 'What the hell is this? I'm used to eating things that are squishy, soft'.
Whalefall isn't just the name of the movie, it's a real scientific term — can you explain it to us?
See, this is again another star, in my opinion, for this movie because now I get to tell you what it is.
Whalefall is essentially when a whale dies, it will float to the surface and for a period of time sharks or other animals will break it down. Then the animal will fall to the bottom of the ocean, moving a whole heap of nutrients and carbon with it. So, even in death, whales will transfer carbon from our atmosphere down to the deepest part of the oceans and lock it away.
We've got to thank whales for so much. Whales are environmentally and economically important alive and even more so environmentally important in death.
Is there a reason we're behind in knowing about whales or is there a reason we don't know more than we should?
Yes, because so much of the world is focused on what's above and not below and deep-sea research and research on whales is very expensive.
So, when it comes to learning about our deep blue, we know so little. In fact, we know more about space than we do about whales in terms of their environment, rather. Someone will eat me alive for saying that. So if anything, a nice silver lining is the fact that people learn about whalefalls and the role of whales and their ecosystem.
What do you think people should know about whales that is largely unknown at this moment?
They're so environmentally, economically important, and their whale poo drives the movement of iron — it's called the iron pump — around the ocean. So, we have whales to thank for the functioning, healthy ecosystems that we enjoy.
But also, we can do our role for whales, and especially humpback whales, making sure that we don't remove krill from the ocean because we need to keep their food there. If you're a little kid, I always say don't release your balloons at birthday parties. If you're an adult, don't buy krill oil tablets.
Our actions for these animals can be simple, but we need to have them front of mind, not out of sight. What is it? Out of sight, out of mind? In this case, it takes a very popular movie so that we can connect and learn so much, and that's what I absolutely love about Hollywood in this case.
This interview is lightly edited for clarity and brevity. Whalefall is in Australian cinemas now.
