TEHRAN- A Persian translation of Italian writer Donato Carrisi’s debut novel “The Whisperer” has recently been published by Vazn-e Donya Publications in Tehran.
The book has been translated into Persian by Azam Rasouli.
“The Whisperer” is a psychological crime thriller that combines a disturbing series of disappearances with an increasingly complex investigation into the nature of evil. Originally published in Italian as “Il suggeritore” in 2009, the book became an international bestseller and was translated into numerous languages.
The book begins with the discovery of six severed arms buried in a forest clearing, setting off a chilling investigation. Arranged in a mysterious circle, five of the arms are believed to belong to young girls who have disappeared. The sixth victim remains unidentified, and investigators have no bodies to establish whether the missing children are alive or dead.
The case brings together Mila Vasquez, a police investigator with a particular talent for locating missing children, and Dr. Goran Gavila, a distinguished criminologist who leads the investigative team. Although their personalities and approaches differ, they must work together to uncover the truth behind the gruesome discovery.
The investigators initially believe they have identified the perpetrator, whom they associate with the name “Albert.” However, the apparent solution quickly begins to unravel. Evidence connects the suspect to the first disappearance but fails to establish his involvement in the subsequent cases. Clues surrounding another missing girl point in a different direction, raising the possibility that the team has misunderstood the crimes or that someone is deliberately manipulating the investigation.
As the case develops, the detectives confront a succession of disturbing discoveries and apparent contradictions. The possibility of a copycat killer further complicates their efforts, while the investigation exposes weaknesses within the team and places increasing pressure on its members. Vasquez and Gavila must reconsider their assumptions repeatedly as they attempt to understand the logic behind the crimes.
The search becomes more than a conventional hunt for a serial killer. It turns into a psychological contest in which the investigators must determine who is controlling the flow of evidence and why the truth remains so difficult to grasp. Their professional partnership is tested as the danger intensifies, and their personal vulnerabilities become increasingly relevant to the case.
The novel builds toward a series of revelations that challenge the investigators’ understanding of the crimes. Carrisi uses misdirection and shifting perspectives to keep readers uncertain about the identity, motives and methods of the person behind the disappearances.
The book received significant recognition in Italy, winning the 2009 Premio Bancarella. It also earned international recognition and was translated into multiple languages, establishing Carrisi as a prominent writer of crime fiction.
“The Whisperer” is the first novel featuring Mila Vasquez, a character who returns in later books, including “The Lost Girls of Rome” and “The Game of the Whisperer”. Its success helped establish a series that explores disappearances, criminal psychology and the darker aspects of human behavior.
Critics have praised the novel’s intricate plotting, unsettling atmosphere and repeated reversals of expectation, although some have found its elaborate twists excessive. Rather than relying solely on the mystery of identifying a killer, Carrisi builds suspense around the possibility that the investigation itself is being manipulated. The result is a dark, layered thriller that examines the difficulty of distinguishing evidence from deception and understanding the motives behind apparently incomprehensible crimes.
Born in Martina Franca, southern Italy, in 1973, Donato Carrisi studied law before specializing in criminology and behavioral sciences. He worked as a television screenwriter before making his literary debut with “The Whisperer”. His academic background informs the novel’s detailed treatment of criminal investigation and psychological behavior.

Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:04:41 UTC
02:04:41 KST

Beijing’s mediating power in international crises
TEHRAN – In the new international order, the concept of “power” is no longer defined solely by the number of nuclear warheads, overseas military bases, or classical security alliances; rather, the new geometry of global power is shaped by the capacity of supply chains, currency exchanges, infrastructure investments, and economic interdependence.
Within this novel framework, China has managed to elevate its position from a mere trading power in the late twentieth century to a “structural actor in international crisis management”—an actor whose primary tools for intervening in crises are not missiles and sanctions, but economic integration and financial leverage.
The defining distinction of China’s approach to international crises is rooted in the theory of “developmental peace” as opposed to Western “liberal peace.” Beijing believes that the primary root of many geopolitical conflicts and security instabilities in the Middle East, Africa, and Central Asia lies not in a vacuum of Western democracy, but in poverty, a deficit of infrastructural development, and a lack of connection to global markets. Therefore, Beijing utilizes initiatives such as the Belt and Road and strategic energy partnerships as efficient tools to contain security shocks. When countries share tangible, mutual economic interests in the continuity of joint projects, the cost of escalating tensions and war increases dramatically for them.
A concrete and successful example of this strategy can be seen in Beijing’s historic mediation between Tehran and Riyadh. Leveraging its immense weight as the largest buyer of Persian Gulf energy and the primary trading partner of both countries, China provided an economic-strategic platform for a political agreement without the need for ideological alignments. This model demonstrated that Beijing’s crisis management levers are built on a commitment to mutual interests and non-interference in internal affairs—a factor that has made Beijing’s model attractive and acceptable among the countries of the Global South.
Furthermore, in complex crises such as the war in Ukraine or tensions surrounding maritime security, China has managed—by relying on its position as a core commodity buyer—to prevent devastating fractures in the global energy and food markets. China’s policy is to maintain a balance between trade with Russia while simultaneously safeguarding Western markets; a strategy that prevents the deepening of acute international deadlocks and the uncontrolled spread of crises into the global economy.
Ultimately, Beijing has demonstrated that economic power is not merely a source of wealth, but a decisive lever for containing shocks and moderating geopolitical behavior. Although China’s cautious policy and avoidance of direct security guarantees may appear to limit its role in certain acute crises, an undeniable reality remains: in the current post-hegemonic world, no major international crisis can be managed, sustainably resolved, or contained without considering Beijing’s capacities, considerations, and economic levers.
Mahdi Zolfaghari is an Associate Professor at the Department of Asian Studies in Allameh Tabataba’i University

Syria rejects Israeli 'politicisation' of Suweida's Druze community

In a statement on Thursday evening carried by Syria’s state-run news agency, a government source said the Druze community in Suweida "has been and will remain an integral part of the national fabric of the Syrian Arab Republic," rejecting what it described as attempts to draw the community into Israeli political campaigning.
The statement came after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that he had spoken by phone with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa during the violence in Suweida in July 2025.
Addressing an election campaign gathering of Druze citizens in the northern Israeli town of Yarka, Netanyahu described the call as "short and very sharp" and claimed he had helped stop a massacre.
"We took down the Ministry of Defense [headquarters] in Damascus, just like that, it’s gone. We struck inside the [Presidential] Palace compound, and I made a phone call to Sharaa. It was a very brief, very sharp conversation, and the massacre stopped," Netanyahu said.
Damascus has neither confirmed nor denied that the call took place.
The Syrian government source said Israel had played a "major and deliberate role" in undermining civil peace in Suweida in July 2025, accusing it of arming an outlawed militia to foment unrest and create a pretext for drawing Syria into a wider war. The source also said the government had thwarted those efforts and was monitoring what it described as continued Israeli attempts to destabilise the province.
The source said US mediation had led to a halt in Israeli airstrikes in July 2025, which it claimed had prevented the Syrian government from intervening to end the clashes between Druze and Bedouin groups.
It also said Damascus was continuing to work with the United States and Jordan to implement a joint roadmap for Suweida, aimed at reintegrating the province under a national framework that safeguards residents’ rights and promotes security and stability.
In September 2025, Syria, Jordan and the United States announced the roadmap, which included commitments to rebuild trust, promote community reconciliation, investigate violations and hold those responsible to account, as well as facilitate humanitarian aid and restore essential services. It remains unclear how far these commitments have been implemented.
A ceasefire has been in place in Suweida since July 2025, following deadly clashes that began between Bedouin tribes and Druze groups before escalating with the intervention of government forces and tribal fighters who arrived in the province to support the Bedouin side.
The fighting involved grave human rights abuses against Druze civilians, including summary executions, according to reports documenting the violence.
A Syrian investigative committee said in March that 1,760 people from all sides had been killed and 2,188 injured. Other monitoring groups have reported higher death tolls.
Suweida remains largely outside central government control. Some factions aligned with Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri have called for Israeli protection or closer ties with Israel, while other Druze religious figures, activists and armed groups have rejected Israeli intervention and called for the province to remain part of a unified Syria.
Israel currently occupies parts of southwestern Syria, which Israeli forces stormed in December 2024 following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s regime. Damascus has repeatedly called on Israel to withdraw from these territories and return to the 1974 disengagement agreement.
The Israeli-occupied Syrian Golan Heights are also home to a Druze community. Israel has occupied the territory since 1967 and later annexed it, a move recognised by the United States and Colombia but rejected by most of the international community.
Syria is emerging from a brutal 14-year civil war, and the new government has struggled to reassert central authority across the country amid continuing security, social and economic challenges.

Caught in an imbroglio, Trump resorts to more blatant lies and misleading claims

The strategic waterway normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil supply, making any disruption to maritime traffic there a serious threat to global energy security.
Although fuel prices are influenced by several factors, including supply and demand, sanctions, and geopolitical tensions, the impact of the war on Iran cannot simply be ignored. Russia’s oil and gas sector has also faced extensive Western sanctions since Moscow launched war on Ukraine in February 2022. Blaming Kyiv for rising fuel prices while overlooking the consequences of the war on Iran is therefore a misleading way to explain the pressures facing American consumers.

Even when oil, gas, and mineral deposits are present, turning them into commercially viable projects can take years and requires substantial investment and infrastructure. Presenting such developments as imminent achievements risks creating expectations that the available evidence does not support.
Trump’s misleading statements are unlikely to convince all American voters that his war on Iran has nothing to do with their economic difficulties. As households struggle with rising fuel costs, many will want concrete answers about the causes of these increases and the administration’s plans to address them. Blaming foreign leaders and promoting unfulfilled promises will not necessarily shield the president from public criticism.

As the election approaches, the president has a strong political incentive to divert attention from the war’s costs and portray his administration as being in control. Yet repeated assertions that conflict with the available evidence could further undermine his credibility.
As the war’s objectives become increasingly difficult to achieve, some media outlets and analysts have also raised concerns about the possibility of further escalation, including the specter of nuclear war. In an interview with Newsmax broadcast on Thursday evening, Trump sought to dismiss the need for nuclear weapons, saying, “I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to.”
All these developments suggest that Trump is caught in an increasingly difficult situation. The war has imposed economic and geopolitical costs on the United States, challenged its military reputation, and created serious political risks for his administration. If these problems persist through the November midterm elections, Republicans could lose control of Congress, weakening Trump’s ability to advance his domestic agenda.
The consequences could extend well beyond the current election cycle. Preparations are also going ahead for his planned trip to South America in November, The Holy See added.
Leo’s cancer diagnosis for a pope known to be energetic and who was elected only in May 2025 caused shock and raised questions about the future shape of his papacy.

Israeli firm weaponized online ads to hack targets, spy on hundreds of millions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:03:50 UTC
02:03:50 KST

Israeli firm weaponized online ads to hack targets, spy on hundreds of millions
TEHRAN — An Israeli advertising company turned the banner ad into a hacking tool, and for at least two years the companies running the world’s ad platforms failed to stop it.
Two investigations published October 15, by Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto and the New York security firm Confiant, describe how Discover-Tech, founded in 2020, let surveillance vendors identify internet users and infect chosen ones without a single click.
The company’s platform, Controlium, profiled users in bulk and stripped away their anonymity. Citizen Lab calls the technique AdFection. A person opens a website or app, and dozens of firms bid in milliseconds for the ad slot. If Discover-Tech wins, it learns who is looking. If that person is on a client’s list, spyware can follow within seconds.
The ads sold phones, earbuds, games and telecom plans. Nothing about them looked wrong. They only had to load.
Citizen Lab examined roughly four billion ad records and found Discover-Tech material on more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps.
Confiant counted at least 10 million ads a day. Through cookie matching, its cofounder Jerome Dangu said, the firm could track people beyond its own ads. “Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech,” he said.
Al Jazeera in the crosshairs
The best-documented victims worked for Al Jazeera. Between 2024 and 2025, 45 Windows computers at the Qatari broadcaster were infected with spyware from Candiru, the Israeli vendor the U.S. Commerce Department blacklisted in 2021 over its use against officials, journalists, activists and academics.
Al Jazeera’s own technicians had spotted strange activity and brought in Citizen Lab, which confirmed the attack from the network’s logs.
The implant can read files, emails and messages, log keystrokes, take screenshots and switch on microphones and cameras. It is understood to have cost several million dollars.
Al Jazeera called it an assault on press freedom and demanded accountability. It has been here before. In 2020, Citizen Lab found that 36 phones belonging to the network’s journalists and executives had been hacked with Pegasus, made by another Israeli firm, NSO Group.
A whole population under watch
Dangu said the Palestinian territories were especially saturated. Almost any site there carried a Discover-Tech ad, he said, giving the firm “a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country.”
Israel already controls movement, borders and much of daily life in the occupied territories. This added a layer inside the browser.
The same ads appeared in networks tied to the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the United Nations, NATO, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments, along with chipmakers such as Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron.
They also reached the International Criminal Court, which issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant in 2024.
Platforms act late
Google says it removed Discover-Tech “for systematically violating our policies.” Europe’s Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) suspended the firm last week after an audit, and Comcast’s Beeswax dropped it.
Yandex did not comment. Discover-Tech and Candiru’s owners did not answer Reuters. Confiant noted that ads it tied to Candiru were a tiny fraction of the volume.
Citizen Lab’s Wolfie Christl called it disastrous that major vendors missed the operation for years, and urged U.S. and European regulators to investigate.
Candiru has been on a U.S. blacklist for five years. The pipeline that carried its code ran through American-owned platforms until outside researchers forced the issue.

The UK’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, is under pressure to distance himself from a comment made by his wife, the award-winning writer Sarah Helm, in support of Palestine Action.

Under terror laws, this could constitute a criminal offence, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years in prison. The ban has so far resulted in more than 3,700 arrests for backing the group, with more than 2,250 people formally charged as terrorists.
In response to comments by the broadcaster Adam Boulton that Rooney’s support for Palestine was “anti-Jewish”, Helm wrote: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action. Sounds like Adam would have all our books swept off the shelves in a jiffy.”

Helm’s works include a book about the women imprisoned by the Nazis at the Ravensbrück concentration camp, and Loyalty, a play about the Iraq war, inspired by her husband’s decade as the chief of staff to the then prime minister, Tony Blair.
The author, who is writing a book about Gaza, married Powell in 2007. He was appointed in 2024 as a national security adviser under Keir Starmer.
According to government guidance, being married to a suspected or convicted terrorist would normally result in the revocation of security clearance. Under the vetting framework for a job as national security adviser, being married to someone tied to a proscribed terrorist organisation is viewed as creating an automatic, unmitigated national security risk.
Responding to questions about Powell’s position after his wife’s comments, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

But her defiance further exposes the absurdity of a ban that cannot be enforced against everyone who challenges it. However, the Campaign Against Antisemitism called for Helm to “face the full force of the law”.

“But this raises extremely serious questions for Jonathan Powell and the government. A Met Police spokesperson said: “We have been made aware of an X post on Thursday, 15 October referencing Palestine Action. It is in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required.
Hundreds of writers have signed an open letter in support of Rooney, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, warning that “a country that bans its writers for speaking out is not a free country”.
The letter has been signed by 419 novelists, poets, editors and illustrators including Ali Smith, Kamila Shamsie, Robert Macfarlane, Daisy Johnson, Eliza Clark, Jeanette Winterson, Alice Oseman, Derek Landy, Louise O’Neill, AM Dassu and Nikesh Shukla.
The letter states: “As authors, illustrators, poets, and editors, we stand with Sally Rooney and Faber Books, and condemn a government whose actions, and inactions, have led to her books being pulled from sale in the UK.
“Writers already face book bans worldwide and at home. It is unconscionable that a government can now effectively ban a single author for protesting that government’s own conflation of protest with terrorism. What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all.”
Rooney said she had made the decision to withdraw from the UK market with her publisher, Faber, after learning that passing earnings on to her for the sale of her books in the UK could constitute a serious criminal offence. In a letter shared with the Guardian, Rooney said she was “wholly prepared to accept the consequences”. Faber will continue to sell Rooney’s books in other countries.

U.S. embargo, sanctions on Cuba impacting power supplies, access to medicine
Havana, Cuba – Cubans are experiencing power blackouts and facing obstacles accessing medicine amid a strict U.S. embargo and sanctions that seek to put pressure on Cuba's Communist government.
The Trump administration has made it clear it wants to remove Cuba's regime. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the economic campaign is engineered to make the government feel like there are no escape valves, which is how people in Cuba describe feeling.
A strict U.S. embargo on oil imports has left the country's electrical grid in a state of near-collapse. Most places in Cuba, including Havana, receive only a few hours of electricity a day. Very often it's less than that.
The energy crisis coupled with crumbling infrastructure have sent prices of basic goods skyrocketing.
CBS News saw parents lining up for care at a children's hospital. But doctors in Cuba's once-renowned public health system say they can no longer source critical, lifesaving drugs for pediatric patients.
Some have turned to free, community-run pharmacies. Retiree Sara Emilia Marquez showed CBS News medicine that was donated after her monthly prescription started coming just once every three months, if at all. Others have taken to buying from black-market street vendors.
The Trump administration has amped up its pressure campaign on Cuba in recent months, including by imposing new sanctions against Cuba's state-run bank on Thursday, claiming it has ties to Iran. Cuba's foreign minister insists the bank is "absolutely legitimate," and calls the move collective punishment.
For the roughly two-thirds of Cubans employed by state entities, the sanctions are just the latest obstacle to securing money. Pensioners can wait for hours to collect their government wages, with some saying they go hungry.
At a bread line in one of Havana's more upscale neighborhoods, a woman was picking up several loaves for herself and friends. Bread prices here have risen tenfold just this year. And with a government salary of less than $20 per month, she said she tries to stretch each baguette she buys for at least two days.
Cuba has enacted a raft of economic reforms aimed at opening up the private sector, but Cuba's leaders have said not to expect political reform. While they have shown willingness to negotiate with the U.S. government, talks currently appear to be at a standstill.

This year’s flu season is starting early. Does that mean it will be more severe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:03:13 UTC
02:03:13 KST

The beginning of fall and back-to-school time means cold virus season has arrived. Usually, colds hit as lesser-evil infections before influenza season takes over. But already, the flu is popping up early in pockets of the U.S. Here’s why that might be and everything else you need to know as we head into the dreaded annual flu season.
According to the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention’s latest FluView report, released on October 9, flu activity has been climbing since early September. Flu season in the U.S. generally begins gaining momentum in the fall, with activity peaking between December and February. But surveillance indicators show that certain strains of influenza are rising fast. The CDC’s latest data show a nationwide percent positivity rate for influenza—the percentage of all positive influenza tests—of 3.6 percent. That’s a sixfold increase compared with this time in 2025, when the rate was 0.6 percent.
Parts of the U.S. are showing much higher positive rates. The CDC splits the country up into regions, and Region 9, which includes Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada, had 9.5 percent positivity, according to the latest data. Experts say that is exceptionally high for this time of year.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“It’s not unheard of to see things rising at this stage,” says Andrew Pekosz, an immunologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “But it’s also something that we probably shouldn’t be seeing until maybe November or December at the earliest.”
Flu can be caused by different types of influenza, including influenza A (and its subtypes) and influenza B. Usually, flu season brings a mix of types. Right now, in the areas of the country with the highest positivity rates, H1N1, a subtype of influenza A, is dominant. According to the CDC, the most recent weekly testing data showed that 98.4 percent of the positive tests indicated H1N1 and that 1.6 percent revealed H3N2, another influenza A subtype.
Still, experts say it’s too early to predict whether these spikes could signal a particularly severe winter flu season.
Will this year’s flu vaccines work well?
One of the best ways to protect yourself from the flu is to get a flu vaccine. Every year experts reformulate these vaccines depending on what strains of the virus are circulating or predicted to circulate during the coming winter season.
Whichever subtype dominates matters because it can help predict which groups will experience the greatest disease burden. It can also determine how well existing immunity will protect people, as well as how the year’s flu vaccines will perform.
H1N1 and H3N2 are both influenza A subtypes, but they are evolutionarily distinct and can affect people differently. H3N2-dominant seasons have historically been associated with particularly severe illness among older adults. H1N1, on the other hand, has had a greater effect on younger populations—but both can cause serious disease at any age.
“The version [of H1N1] that’s circulating seems to be a little bit different from the vaccine strain that we have and from H1N1 strains that have circulated before. It’s what we call an antigenic drift,” Pekosz says. That could be why the virus is emerging so early, he adds. If it can evade prior immunity, the pathogen will be easier to transmit.
But it’s still too early to know how that might influence the effectiveness of the current flu vaccines.
When is the best time to get vaccinated?
Trish Perl, a professor of internal medicine and a specialist in infectious disease at UT Southwestern Medical Center, says that right now is the best time to get a flu shot.
“Immunity from the flu vaccine is strongest for about four to six months, and we usually expect flu to peak in December or January,” Pekosz says. “So a September or October vaccination will get you through the worst part of the flu season.”
Perl agrees—she says that she often tells her people to, at the very least, get a flu vaccine before Thanksgiving. Because after that, she says, people have unlimited excuses for why they can’t find the time.
And with certain areas already seeing spikes, getting the shot earlier than usual may be best, Pekosz adds.
“The best time to get vaccinated is before you see influenza in your area,” he says.
What about the newly approved mRNA vaccine for flu?
On August 5, 2026, the Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna’s mFLUSIVA, the first mRNA seasonal influenza vaccine, for adults aged 50 and older. In a phase 3 clinical trial, the vaccine was found to be 26.6 percent more effective at preventing the flu than a standard flu shot.
FDA approval and inclusion in federal vaccination recommendations—informed by guidance by the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP)—are separate regulatory steps, however. The disruption to ACIP under the Trump administration has made incorporating newly approved vaccines into guidance more complicated.
Moderna had said the vaccine would be available at select retailers during the 2026–2027 flu season. But so far, access appears to be limited.
Experts, including Pekosz and Perl, say that if people who qualify for the new mRNA vaccine have access to it, they should consider it. “The data would suggest that if you can get the mRNA vaccine, you probably will get a stronger response to most of the components in the vaccine than if you get the standard one. But again, the standard one is pretty good as well,” Pekosz says.
He and Perl are optimistic about the potential of mRNA technology to improve flu vaccines in the future. Because mRNA vaccines can be developed and manufactured more quickly than traditional shots, scientists could wait until later in the year before selecting which influenza strains to target. That added time could help us better predict which strains will circulate during flu season—ultimately meaning more effective vaccines.
The best thing anyone can do right now is to get their flu shot as soon as possible. And if you do end up getting sick, Perl says not to forget about antivirals, such as Tamiflu, which can be very effective and, in many cases, could reduce the amount of time you are infectious.

The end of Saudi Arabia’s Yemen 'containment strategy'

The end of Saudi Arabia’s Yemen 'containment strategy'
Saudi Arabia’s bid to “contain” the Ansarallah in Yemen while doubling down on economic growth at home is collapsing, posing one of the most serious tests for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since he rose to power, according to analysts and diplomats.
A decade ago, the crown prince led the kingdom into a war aimed at ousting the Ansarallah from power. The conflict turned into a quagmire for Saudi Arabia, sapping its resources and sparking widespread backlash due to its devastating bombing campaign. In the end, Saudi Arabia cut its losses and maintained an uneasy truce with the Ansarallah since 2022.
“This is the collapse of Saudi Arabia’s containment strategy,” Rob Geist Pinfold, an international security expert at King's College London, told Middle East Eye.
“The way Saudi Arabia approached the Houthis (Ansarallah) in the last few years was not dissimilar to how Israel treated Hamas in Gaza before 7 October [2023]. The Saudis felt they had the Houthis where they needed them. They weren’t at the stage to reach a political solution, but they felt they had disincentivized them from escalating again.”
The conflict erupted again after Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport in July to prevent a plane carrying Ansarallah officials from landing.
The Ansarallah declared a blockade against Saudi shipping as a result, and launched a lightning offensive down the Red Sea coast last month, which the kingdom and its Yemeni allies have struggled to counter.
Unlike the last time a full-scale war raged in Yemen, Saudi Arabia now has more to lose from a widening of the conflict, and the Ansarallah have become more sophisticated adversaries, experts say.
Saudi Arabia faced Ansarallah missile and drone attacks during the last round of fighting, but they were nowhere near as precise as this time.
In the last week alone, the Ansarallah struck Riyadh’s international airport three days in a row. A strike on Oct. 10 killed at least 13 people and injured 300. The group’s targeting capabilities were underscored again on Oct. 13 when they hit the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state oil giant, Aramco, in the eastern city of Dhahran.
The strikes have caused some to question the capabilities of Saudi Arabia’s military.
The kingdom is a major buyer of American weaponry, including Patriot and THAAD air defense systems. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the kingdom spends 6.5 percent of its GDP on military gear, one of the highest ratios in the world.
“It’s quite striking, literally, that the Houthis can hit, at will, these incredibly important facilities in Saudi Arabia and the Saudis can’t defend them,” Gregory Gause, an expert on the Persian Gulf at the Middle East Institute, told MEE.
“They clearly have much better missiles and targeting technology than they did before,” he said.
A Western defense official in Riyadh told MEE that Saudi Arabia is absorbing the vast majority of missiles and drones fired at it, saying the number is likely in the low 90 percent range. But the Ansarallah are more skilled at penetrating the kingdom’s air defenses.
“The Houthis are a lot more effective than Iran was back in February. They learned from earlier this year,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “It is a combination of innovation, rapid speed and the latest intelligence,” the official said.

The illusion of victory over Iran

Be more elephant but be less cat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:01:32 UTC
02:01:32 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at animal role models.
On Oct 20th, I’m hosting our first Mini Philosophy Salon for members. In the salons, I’ll introduce a topic and invite people to share their thoughts. The first topic is “Being authentic.”
If you’d like to register, upgrade to become a member.
This might be my most controversial opening.
You might have noticed how I tend to stay clear of all the culture-war, shouty stuff in this newsletter. I talk about the philosophy of religion and political theory, of course, because they’re key parts of the discipline. But as a general rule, I try to avoid the especially inflammatory things. This isn’t because I don’t have opinions or thoughts about them, but it’s just that I think some conversations are better had in person.
Until today. Because today, I’m going to put my cards on the table and say something controversial: I dislike cats.
Not only do I think dogs are superior to cats in almost every category, but I think cats, in themselves, embody certain vices I dislike in human beings. That’s why, in my Big Think column this week, I take issue with philosopher John Gray’s argument that we should all be more like cats.
I think cats are cold, vain, and aloof. They will love-bomb their human when it’s clear they need food, or warmth, or have gone too far.
What with the Gray column and a recent visit to the zoo, I’m a little animal-minded right now. And this focus has got me thinking about just how often we turn to the natural world to understand our own nature. We easily fall into this habit of seeing animals as embodying certain virtues and vices. Like some Stone Age cave dweller, drawing bears on the wall, we extrapolate from animals.
And so, this week, I want to look at the moral archetypes of animals.
Go well,
Jonny
Be like the crane
In the early weeks of September, I was at Cotswold Wildlife Park with my dad. The kids were off meddling somewhere, and we were sitting on the bench overlooking the prairie dogs.
“What animal are you?” I said to my dad.
“Huh?”
“What animal are you most like?”
“Well, a donkey, of course,” he said, and we chortled. It’s funnier when you’re in your late 70s.
“Yes, very good, Pops,” with a roll of the eyes. And then he sat thinking for a while.
The big conversations worth having
W. Kamau Bell invites those he admires—like Michael Lewis, Robert Reich, Anna Sale, and others—to connect, share how we can make the world a better place, and find reassurance in these hectic times.
“I think a crow,” he said. “I like puzzles and stuff, but I also like to be alone in my nest. Also, I like to think I’m some kind of evil omen to curse you.”
It’s a nice answer. I’m sure you’ve had a similar conversation because humans often look to the animal kingdom for examples. It’s why all those “What animal are you?” quizzes or “What’s your spirit animal?” questions are so popular. We want to embody what the animal represents.
This is an ancient tradition. Culturally, shamans, totems, and prehistoric religious rites almost always feature animals prominently. Egyptian falcon-heads, Indian monkey gods, and a Greek Minotaur roaring around a labyrinth. In a bygone world, we simply lived among animals much more.
Philosophers, too, have long leaned into animal metaphor — “Be more like the lion: brave, proud, and strong!” For a long time, before science took all the fun away with “empirical proof,” philosophers even built a kind of biological metaphysics around animals. In the 17th century, it was common to say that humans were a microcosm of passions, virtues, and vices, whereas animals contained only one or a few. Meanwhile, “theriophilia” is the belief that animals are morally superior to humans. To be a good human is to be more animal.
So, let’s look at what history’s theriophilists had to say about five animals.
The ant
In the book of Proverbs, we get this line: “Go to the ant, thou sluggard… Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer.” And Plutarch observed that ants nip seeds so they can’t sprout while stored inside the nest. The ant embodies diligence and prudence. They work hard for the greater good. They toil through the summer to give themselves fodder for the winter.
To be more ant-like, we should plan better. Put money away into your retirement account. Nurture your friendships. Invest in your skills and talents. Do Pilates. Tomorrow will come in a blink.
Fact check: Mostly true; ants do just do their thing without a “ruler.” The beauty of DNA. But when it comes to seed nipping, it’s only harvester species that do that.
The elephant
The elephant is probably philosophers’ most cherished animal. The ancient Greek and Roman world became borderline obsessed with them, first through dubious secondhand accounts from distant empire-building armies like Alexander’s, and then when the Romans faced Hannibal and his elephants firsthand. Pliny calls elephants wise because it was thought they could follow orders, practice things they got wrong, and bury their fallen tusks so as not to attract hunting humans.
So to be more elephant, we should reflect more. Take stock of when things went wrong, why they went wrong, and work out how to prevent it in the future. Practice. Get better.
Fact check: All pretty much true, but we’ve not replicated Pliny’s observation of hidden tusks.
The dog
A classic. Dogs and wolves are the archetypal pack animals. Both Pliny and Cassius Dio retell the story of Titius Sabinus’s dog, who stayed by his executed master and then swam into the Tiber trying to keep Titius’s body afloat. More recently, you’ve probably heard the story of Hachikō, the Japanese Akita dog who waited for his owner at Shibuya Station for nearly 10 years after the owner’s death. Heartbreaking, yes, but also deeply admirable.
To be more dog means putting aside all the many temptations of life to stay true to your people. Stand up for a friend in a meeting. Go see your sibling when they need you. Never sell your mother.
Fact check: Hachikō existed, and this makes Titius’s dog more likely. Dogs are famously loyal and protective — there are countless data points to prove it.
The crane
Pliny again, but it was repeated often enough to become an ancient legend. The story goes that night sentry cranes will clutch a stone, so a drowsy guard drops it and is found out. The crane has developed a tool to keep itself alert, like a dozing grandfather holding some keys.
Be more crane by “self-binding” yourself. When you want to do a task, make failure unthinkable. Make yourself accountable, put something valuable up for forfeit, deny yourself something you love if you get it wrong. Find a “rock” to hold that will let others know you’ve fallen asleep.
Fact check: Most dubious of them all. Even Aristotle, before Pliny, called out this folk legend as nonsense. Cranes — like a lot of birds — will eat rocks to mash up their food as part of digestion. But what is true is that cranes will often simply share and rotate their watch duty as any human guard might do.
The cat
The anti-archetype. Thomson (yes, me) observed that cats are cold, vain, and aloof. He thinks they use affection as a weapon to get what they want. So, “to be more cat” means to schmooze your boss the week before your review, eat the last chocolate in the box, and trash the house and expect others to tidy it up for you.
Fact check: Thomson’s theories are almost entirely based on a childhood experience with an especially grouchy, scratchy, aggressive cat called Mabel, who he likely rubbed the wrong way. His anecdotal prejudice is not corroborated by millions of powerful, wealthy cat-lovers who have the means to sue Mini Philosophy for libel.
So, what is your spirit animal? What virtue or passion do you want to embody more from the natural world?
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

Iran, 19 countries condemn Colombia’s embassy opening in occupied Al-Quds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:58:36 UTC
01:58:36 KST

Iran, 19 countries condemn Colombia’s embassy opening in occupied Al-Quds
TEHRAN — Iran and 19 other countries have condemned Colombia’s decision to open an embassy in occupied al-Quds, warning that the move violates international law, undermines the internationally recognized status of the Palestinian city and runs counter to efforts to establish an independent Palestinian state.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry issued a strong condemnation on Thursday evening, describing the decision as contrary to the Charter of the United Nations and fundamental principles of international law. A joint statement by the foreign ministers of Turkey and 18 other countries followed on Friday, calling on Bogotá to reverse the move and uphold its international obligations.
The dispute has renewed attention to the international legal status of al-Quds, the consequences of relocating diplomatic missions to the occupied city, and the long-standing international consensus against unilateral measures intended to alter its status.
In its statement, Iran’s Foreign Ministry stressed that al-Quds is an inseparable part of Palestinian territory and that states are obligated under international law to refrain from actions that could be interpreted as recognizing Israel’s occupation.
The ministry said Colombia’s decision contradicted the country’s international obligations concerning the Palestinian people’s right to self-determination and risked legitimizing the occupation of Palestinian land. It also argued that the move conflicted with the historical struggles for independence and justice in Colombia and across Latin America.
Iran called on the Colombian government to accept responsibility for the consequences of its 'unlawful and unjustifiable' decision.
Joint condemnation by 19 countries
The joint statement, issued by Turkey’s Foreign Ministry on Friday, was endorsed by the foreign ministers of Turkey, Algeria, Djibouti, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Malaysia, Oman, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.
The ministers expressed their unequivocal rejection of Colombia’s embassy opening, saying the decision violated relevant UN Security Council resolutions and weakened international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.
They reaffirmed that measures intended to change the legal or historical status of occupied al-Quds, or to recognize the city as Israel’s capital, are null and void and have no legal effect.
The statement cited UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980. These resolutions rejected Israel’s attempts to alter the character and status of the city and called on states with diplomatic missions there to withdraw them.
The ministers emphasized that al-Quds is part of the Palestinian territory occupied in 1967 and urged Colombia to reconsider and reverse its decision, respect international law and avoid actions that prejudice the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
Iran’s condemnation came alongside separate objections from Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Algeria. The Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) had also previously denounced the planned embassy opening, describing it as an unlawful step and a departure from Colombia’s longstanding support for Palestinian rights.
From the 1980s diplomatic withdrawals to the US embassy move
The controversy over diplomatic missions in al-Quds has deep roots in international diplomacy. Israel declared the city its capital after occupying East al-Quds in 1967 and later took steps to consolidate its control over the city. These measures have not gained broad international recognition.
In 1980, Israel adopted a law declaring a 'united Jerusalem' its capital. The UN Security Council rejected this move through Resolution 478, determining that measures seeking to alter the city’s character and status had no legal validity and calling on states that had established diplomatic missions in Jerusalem to withdraw them.
Following the resolution, countries that had maintained embassies in Al-Quds moved their missions to Tel Aviv. For decades, the overwhelming international practice was to keep embassies outside the city, reflecting the position that its final status should be determined through negotiations rather than unilateral action.
A major departure from that practice came under US President Donald Trump. On December 6, 2017, Trump announced that the United States recognized Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. The US Embassy was subsequently relocated from Tel Aviv to Quds on May 14, 2018, during his first presidential term.
The decision marked a significant shift in longstanding US policy and drew widespread criticism from Palestinians and many governments, which warned that recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital without a negotiated settlement prejudged one of the most sensitive issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
The United States became the first country to move its embassy to Quds in the modern wave of diplomatic relocations following the 2017 announcement. Guatemala followed in May 2018, while Paraguay briefly moved its embassy to the city that year before reversing the decision later in 2018. Honduras moved its embassy in 2021. A small number of other countries have also taken steps to recognize Quds as Israel’s capital or relocate their diplomatic missions there, although most governments have continued to keep their embassies elsewhere.

It added that participants had erected structures and laid basic infrastructure near the border fence, in an area opposite Gaza City, in preparation for moving the outpost into the Strip.
Nahala called on the Israeli government to immediately approve the transfer of the outpost to the buffer zone occupied by the Israeli military in northern Gaza, urging it not to yield to external pressure. The movement claimed that “Gaza is an inseparable part of the Land of Israel” and argued that taking control of territory and establishing settlements were the means to impose defeat on the Palestinians.
It also called for the re-establishment of settlements in Gaza, the repeal of the Disengagement Law and the encouragement of Palestinian emigration to be included among the core principles of the next Israeli government.
The movement said that Israel’s Communications Minister Shlomo Karhi, a member of Likud, had participated in the settlement activity overnight. In a video recording, he was seen saying: “One more step forward; we are getting closer and closer to the desired goal,” referring to the re-establishment of Israeli settlements inside the Gaza Strip.
Meanwhile, the Hebrew-language news website Walla reported that Israeli police had dispersed settlers who attempted to establish the outpost in Simhoni Forest, located between the Israeli settlements of Nahal Oz and Kfar Aza and the border fence with Gaza. It added that the military had closed roads leading to the area and declared it a closed military zone, fearing that settlers might bypass the barriers, reach the border fence or cross into the Strip.
The website quoted Israeli military sources as saying that around 50 settlers had actually been present at the site, contradicting Nahala’s announcement that more than 700 people had participated in the operation. It explained that the settlers had erected structures in the area between Israeli communities and the border fence but had not entered the Gaza Strip during this attempt.
For its part, the Hebrew-language newspaper Israel Hayom reported that Nahala had established the outpost as a first step towards moving settlers into the Strip. It noted that the organisers were demanding that the government adopt a decision permitting the establishment of settlement communities in Gaza. The Israeli government has not announced its approval of the outpost’s establishment or its transfer into the Strip.
This latest attempt is part of a series of initiatives led by the Nahala movement, whose prominent leaders include settler activist Daniella Weiss, to re-establish settlements in the Gaza Strip since the war began in 2023.
In January 2024, the movement organised a conference in Jerusalem in cooperation with other settlement groups, under the title “Victory Conference”. The event called for the re-establishment of settlements in Gaza and the northern West Bank and was attended by Israeli political figures, including 10 ministers from Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and members of the governing coalition in the Knesset. Among them were National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

Iran raps UK for reversing roles of aggressor and victim
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei has condemned Britain’s accusations against Iran, accusing London of reversing the roles of aggressor and victim despite two rounds of unlawful aggression against the Islamic Republic in just nine months, including while Tehran was pursuing negotiations.
In a message posted on his X account on Thursday, Baqaei attributed the turmoil engulfing the region to unlawful interventions, including those supported or facilitated by Britain.
“The chaos engulfing our region is the consequence of unlawful interventions, including those backed or contributed to by the UK,” he wrote.
Baqaei criticized British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband for portraying Iran as the aggressor after two rounds of unlawful attacks against the country within nine months, even as Iran was engaged in diplomatic efforts to resolve disputes.
“For the UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to portray Iran as the ‘aggressor’ after two rounds of unlawful aggression against it in just nine months, even as it pursued negotiations, is a grotesque reversal of victim and aggressor,” Baqaei wrote, describing the remarks as another low point in Britain’s long record of hostile campaigns against Iran.
Drawing a historical parallel, the spokesman said the British position was as absurd as depicting Nazi Germany as a defender of peace while portraying Britain and its allies in World War II as the aggressors.
Baqaei’s remarks came after UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on October 13 that he had spoken with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, offered condolences over the death of a US citizen in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia, and discussed what he described as ending Iran’s aggression, including in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran maintains that such accusations disregard the circumstances surrounding the US-Israeli war of aggression against the country and overlook the wider consequences of foreign military intervention in West Asia.
Tehran has repeatedly emphasized that diplomacy must be pursued based on respect for national sovereignty and international law, arguing that efforts to assign responsibility for regional instability must take account of the actions that have fueled the conflict rather than isolate Iran’s response from the events that preceded it.

Police seek answers after children killed in Oregon school shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:55:39 UTC
01:55:39 KST

‘Great hero’ praised for saving lives in Oregon school shooting
WASHINGTON - The “hero” who shot dead a teenage gunman after he had already killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school was named on Oct 16, as the US entered a familiar – and likely fruitless – debate about gun control in the wake of the latest tragedy.
Kaylub Giamanco raced into Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, after the shooter, identified by local media as 16-year-old John J. Griffin II, blasted his way through locked doors and opened fire on youngsters.
Kyle Giamanco said 36-year-old Kaylub, who has two children at the school, was driving home for his lunch break on Oct 15 when he heard gunshots and saw Griffin going into the special education room of the school.
Kaylub Giamanco has a permit to carry a concealed weapon, his brother told NBC, adding that he was having difficulty processing events at the moment and feels guilty that he did not save more people.
A woman identified as his mother told the local Fox affiliate she was “very proud” and that her son was “an absolute hero” before she read a prepared statement.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support,” she said.
US President Donald Trump hailed Giamanco as a “great hero.”
“As bad as it was, we had a great hero that went in and did the business,” Trump told journalists. “It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it.”
The small city of Bend, in the US north-west, was struggling to come to terms on Oct 16 with a tragedy that took the lives of children aged five, eight and 11, as well as a teacher, the latest victims of America’s epidemic of gun violence that all-too-frequently afflicts the nation’s schools.
Streets were quiet in an area known for its natural beauty, with hiking trails and ski pistes nearby that attract tens of thousands of visitors every year.
Kristen Vanetsky, 52, told AFP she was in shock over the shooting at her grandson’s school.
“My grandson should be in his classroom, with all of his friends,” she said.
“Everybody should be in there learning, having fun, looking forward to their weekend, and it’s just vacant,” she said. “There’s nothing. Even the birds are not here.”
Gun violence
Even as the city tried to process the tragic events, the familiar contours of an argument that plays out after every school shooting in the US began to harden.
The politically powerful National Rifle Association (NRA) praised the then-unidentified bystander who stepped in to prevent even greater loss of life.
“Yesterday’s terrible act of violence in Oregon serves as another reminder of the importance of a law-abiding armed citizenry,” the NRA said in a post on X.
The man’s actions “exemplify the heroism of everyday citizens who are prepared and ready to respond when innocent lives are on the line,” it added.
The NRA has invested millions of dollars campaigning for gun rights and supporting politicians who block the limits on ownership that the vast majority of Americans support.
The organisation’s opponents again lamented the ready availability of weaponry in a country where rates of gun-related death rates are among the highest in the developed world.
“America’s gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough,” gun-control group GIFFORDS said on X.
More than 360 mass shootings have been recorded across the United States in 2026, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines them as incidents in which at least four people are shot, excluding the gunman.
Long gun
Griffin’s neighbours told AFP they had seen his mother taken away from the house she shared with the suspect the afternoon of Oct 15 in a police patrol car.
That woman, Shauntai May Nickerson, was seen on Oct 16 smoking a cigarette on the porch outside of her apartment and crying.
“If I could have prevented this, I would have,” a tearful Nickerson said, according to The New York Times. AFP

The Leader's message commemorating National Nurse’s Day
Unknown

2026-10-16

The Leader's message commemorating National Nurse’s Day
TEHRAN- The Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, has issued a message commemorating the birth anniversary of Lady Zeinab (pbuh) and National Nurse’s Day. In his message, he spoke of the presence of the women and daughters, who were like Lady Zeinab in Islamic Iran during the nation’s unprecedented Bi’tha (rising up), as being extraordinary.
Pointing to the role of nurses who revive people, bring hope, and their important influence on the physical and spiritual health and security of society, he directed officials in the health sector to pay special attention to those in the nursing profession.
The full text of the Leader’s message is as follows:
In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful
The fifth of Jumada al-Awwal each year serves as a reminder of the blessed birth of a woman who was raised in the light of the love, nurturing, and close company of the Five Pure Souls (pbut) who are considered to be the most exalted of divine creation. For over 50 years, the upbringing and growth of Zeinab al-Kubra (pbuh) in this luminous school of thought gave rise to such a multifaceted display of honor and excellence in this shining star of the ages that she has continuously been praised, admired, and spoken proudly of by those closest to God. The peak of this brilliance emerged in the epic of Ashura: on one hand, manifesting an endless abundance of patient compassion, benevolence, and solicitude for the oppressed on the plain of Karbala, while being one of the most revered symbols of steadfastness and courage.
From the beginning, the history of the Islamic Movement and Revolution has been replete with scenes showing the presence of Iranian women and girls inspired by Zeinab. This presence took on remarkable dimensions, both qualitatively and quantitatively, during the nation’s unparalleled Bi’tha (rising up) that took place in the Third Sacred Defense. Today, Islamic Iran’s women inspired by Zeinab are at the forefront in elucidation in action and resistance with their presence in various arenas, particularly in city and village squares, behind the front lines of the military war. This is to such an extent that the tyrants of our time – who are perpetually seeking the suffering, pain, and suppression of this nation – are incapable of confronting this vast army.
The people of this land, devoted as they are to the Pure Progeny of the Prophet (pbut), have rightly designated the birth anniversary of Lady Zeinab al-Kubra as a day to honor nurses in view of her kindness, her empathizing with those in pain, and her selfless devotion to them. Indeed, many of these moral virtues and human values may be clearly seen in the hardworking, admirable members of the nursing profession.
The work of nurses, like that of certain other groups – including doctors, teachers and educators, religious scholars, and relief workers – revives and inspires hope. It’s for this reason that a nurse is sometimes thought of as an “angel of mercy,” because in the face of the irritability and distress of those who are suffering and in pain, nurses help bring patients comfort and hope, speed their recovery and healing, and thereby prepare the conditions for divine mercy to descend.
However, the role of nurses in treating patients, unlike that of physicians, requires a continuous, attentive, patient presence. The impact of their presence extends far beyond physical healing. It acts as a balm for psychological and spiritual wounds, frequently preventing feelings of despair from taking over. In this way, that which is beyond the reach of medicine alone is achieved due to their compassionate devotion.
In this era, the evil network of Global Arrogance spares no effort to inflict various forms of oppression and crimes on free, resilient nations – especially the Iranian nation – and seeks, among other things, to bring suffering on the great Iranian nation by creating various restrictions in healthcare and medicine. Attending to the needs of nurses, strengthening the nursing community, and maintaining and enhancing nurses’ knowledge, skills, capabilities, morale, motivation, and dignity – particularly those who have devoted themselves to working in non-private institutions – have an important impact on the physical and psychological health and security of society. Thus, it’s expected that our officials in the health sector treat these vital matters as a top priority in continuing their conscientious efforts.
I extend my congratulations on these two occasions (Lady Zeinab's birth anniversary and National Nurse's Day) to our dear nation, to the conscientious and determined women of our Islamic homeland, and especially to our sisters and brothers in the nursing profession.
In closing, I pray for God’s mercy for the guiltless, self-sacrificing martyrs from the nursing community, particularly the nurses who were martyred during the Second and Third Imposed Wars, and also in the sedition of Dey 1404 (Jan. 2026). I am hopeful that with the prayers of our Master [Imam Mahdi], may God hasten his noble reappearance, Almighty God will grant the Iranian nation increasing honor and power, and He’ll bestow upon them all that’s befitting for those who follow Zeinab’s (pbuh) school of thought.

====================================================================================================

The Guardian view on the banks: too big to fail cannot mean too big to tax | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:52:37 UTC
01:52:37 KST

John Healey is planning to tax British banks, the Guardian revealed, in the forthcoming budget. It’s about time for the chancellor to act. Banks have been raking it in. The campaign group Positive Money reported this summer that Britain’s four biggest banks made £29bn in the first half of this year, up a fifth on 2025. These windfalls owe more to higher interest rates than better products or services. Households and businesses pay more to borrow. Meanwhile, the Bank of England pays the banks tens of billions in interest on their reserves, with the Treasury footing the bill.
The chancellor is said to favour restoring the bank surcharge from 3% to 8%, which could raise around £2bn a year. This would recover a very modest share of the sector’s bonanza. Louis XIV’s finance minister, Jean-Baptiste Colbert, said that “the art of taxation consists in so plucking the goose as to obtain the largest possible amount of feathers with the smallest possible amount of hissing”. Britain’s banks have plenty of feathers. That hasn’t stopped them hissing. The banks say that they already face higher taxes than other companies, that they won’t be able to lend as much, and that their profits won’t last.
But banks aren’t taxed on their windfall gains, and what levies they face are less than those paid by oil and gas companies. The Bank of England said banks spent £7.7bn on dividends and buying back shares in the first quarter of 2026 without affecting lending. Higher taxes might mean trimming shareholder payouts. There’s nothing to suggest productive lending must take the hit. Over the past five years Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and NatWest – which control the majority of UK personal and business accounts – made profits of £200bn. Positive Money says that households lost out on £44bn in deposit interest in 2025. Some of this paid for banking services. But that does not explain why the sum is five times the equivalent average figure for 2009-21.
The chancellor could be more radical. The precedent here is not a socialist one. Margaret Thatcher taxed banks’ windfalls in 1981. A comparable 2.5% levy on today’s interest-free deposits would, a paper by the New Economics Foundation and Positive Money suggests, raise more than £11bn. In August, Positive Money suggested looking at Spain’s success in levying a windfall tax on banks’ net income above €800m. It says that such a windfall tax – levied at the same rate as that paid by fossil fuel companies on a comparable tax base – would bring in £19bn from the UK arms of the big four banks. That would pay for a universal and comprehensive adult social care system.
Banks need to be both public utilities and good corporate citizens. Yet the sector is paying the highest bankers’ bonuses since the 2008 global financial crisis. “Most financial sector activity,” concluded a paper published in The Manchester School journal this month, “is simply negative for overall economic performance.” Politicians should stop mistaking finance lobbyists’ demands for a growth strategy. Their job is to curb a finance sector so large that it risks crises and weaker growth. Taxpayers rescued the banks after they helped crash the economy 18 years ago. Public protection carries public obligations. As Sir Philip Augar, the author and former banker, told the BBC: “Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”

AI has enhanced Iran’s intelligence and targeting capabilities: Taeb
TEHRAN— Hossein Taeb, head of Iran’s Basij Organization, says the use of artificial intelligence in defense and intelligence operations has improved the accuracy of target identification and precision strikes, highlighting the technology’s growing role in Iran’s military capabilities.
Speaking on Thursday at the first Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity Conference in the southeastern city of Kerman, Taeb said AI had strengthened intelligence gathering and target assessment, adding that its applications had extended to the naval and aerospace divisions of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) and other branches of the armed forces.
Taeb also discussed 'the objectives of the US-Israeli war against Iran,' arguing that attacks on military commanders, scientists and air-defense systems were intended to weaken the country’s defenses and undermine the scientific foundations of its development.
Protecting Iran’s scientific capabilities
Referring to the 12-day war, Taeb said the simultaneous targeting of military commanders and scientists was part of a strategy to weaken Iran’s security infrastructure and damage the scientific capabilities underpinning its technological progress.
He said the campaign against Iranian scientists had failed to eliminate the country’s nuclear expertise. According to Taeb, the scope of attacks expanded during the 40-day war, extending to other scientific fields and claiming the lives of researchers.
Taeb argued that the objective of such attacks went beyond military damage, encompassing efforts to undermine public security and weaken the country’s capacity for scientific and technological advancement.
"Targeting one scientist would not halt the country’s progress, as more specialists would emerge to continue the work," he said.
AI and the changing landscape of military operations
Taeb described investment in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity as a strategic decision for Iran’s future, calling for these priorities to be translated into practical action by government institutions, policymakers and leading experts.
He said AI had already produced tangible results in the defense sector by improving intelligence assessment and the accuracy of target identification.
He further said AI-assisted systems had improved the detection of military vessels operating near the Strait of Hormuz and helped increase missile accuracy. Taeb argued that these capabilities had affected US military calculations and contributed to the relocation of American naval vessels farther from the area.
His remarks underscore the growing importance of AI-enabled intelligence, surveillance and targeting systems in contemporary military operations. Such technologies can help process large volumes of information, identify patterns and support faster operational decisions, although their effectiveness depends on data quality, system reliability and human oversight.
Taeb highlights disparity in military spending
Taeb also contrasted Iran’s defense resources with the much larger military budgets of the United States and Israel. He cited figures for US military spending and additional wartime funding requests, and said Israel had received $22 billion in additional US assistance for the conflict.
Despite Iran’s limited defense resources in foreign-currency terms, Taeb said the country had been able to withstand the military campaign. He argued that a comparable emphasis on scientific capability, technological innovation and strategic planning was necessary to sustain progress in the fields of AI and cybersecurity.
He called for artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to move beyond isolated technological initiatives and become part of a coordinated national strategy involving public institutions and the country’s scientific community.
The conference’s focus on young technology specialists, Taeb said, reflected Iran’s intention to expand its pool of skilled researchers and developers. In his view, strengthening domestic expertise in emerging technologies is essential not only to defense preparedness but also to the country’s broader scientific and technological development.

Global timekeeping rules change: leap second scrapped from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:49:56 UTC
01:49:56 KST

Global timekeepers have voted to end the practice of adding extra seconds to UTC, citing risks to computer systems and the prospect of the first-ever negative leap second.
The world’s official time standard will stop adding leap seconds from 20 May 2027. The General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) decided to end the practice on Thursday 15 October 2026.
The resolution was adopted at the conference’s 28th meeting in Versailles, where delegates discussed the future of world time.
Until now, leap seconds have been added from time to time to keep atomic time in line with the Earth’s rotation. But from 20 May 2027, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) will run continuously, with no interruptions.
Why the leap second is being scrapped
The old rules were meant to keep two different ways of measuring time in step. UTC is based on extremely precise atomic clocks. Astronomical time depends on the Earth’s rotation, and that rotation speed varies slightly.
To keep the gap between the two time scales small, 27 leap seconds have been added since 1972. The most recent was at the end of 2016. As a result, one minute could exceptionally last 61 seconds.
These corrections are barely noticeable for people, but they can cause technical problems. Computer systems, telecoms networks, satellite navigation and power infrastructure all depend on precise, reliable time synchronisation. Past leap seconds have already disrupted computer systems and online services.
Earth’s rotation makes new rules necessary
One reason for the decision is the way the Earth’s rotation is evolving. A negative leap second raised new risks.
Over very long periods, tidal forces slow the planet down, but in recent years it has at times been spinning slightly faster.
That raised the possibility that, for the first time, a so-called negative leap second might be needed, with a second removed rather than added. Because this has never been done, it is uncertain how reliably technical systems would cope.
The international expert community therefore chose to end the existing rules ahead of schedule. Under the new regime, the gap between UTC and astronomical time will be allowed to grow, potentially reaching 3,600 seconds, or one hour.
Experts believe, however, that it will still be some time before such a gap would actually require any correction, so the measure is essentially precautionary.
The CGPM: little known, but many member states
The CGPM brings together representatives of member states and of associated states and economic areas and usually meets every four years.
According to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), it currently has 69 member states and 34 associated states and economies.
In Europe, they include Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Poland and Ukraine.
The Americas are represented by the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico and Peru, Asia by China, Japan, India, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand, and Africa by South Africa, Egypt, Morocco, Tunisia and Kenya. Australia and New Zealand are also represented.
What does this mean for the UK?
For everyday life in the United Kingdom, the decision will not bring any immediate change.
Scrapping the leap second is a technical adjustment to the international time reference and must not be confused with the familiar switch between summer time and winter time.
According to the GOV.UK Clock Change Guide, the clocks go back one hour on Sunday, 25, October, 2026, at 2:00 AM.
As such, the local clock time in the UK will still follow Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), which is UTC+0 in winter, and British Summer Time (BST), which is UTC+1 in summer. Seasonal time changes will be unaffected.
A step towards more stable world time
The impact will be felt more strongly in specialist fields that need exceptionally precise alignment with the Earth’s rotation. These include astronomy, geodesy (the science of measuring and mapping the Earth and determining its shape, size and gravitational field) and certain satellite-based applications.
For these disciplines, accurate knowledge of the Earth’s rotation will remain crucial. Because leap seconds will no longer tie world time to that rotation, they will have to account separately for the growing gap between clock time and astronomical time when necessary.
In principle, the aim of the new rules is to make international timekeeping simpler and more reliable in the long term. In particular, digital systems will no longer have to cope with extra seconds being inserted at irregular intervals.
