‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:49:46 UTC
01:49:46 KST

‘Mother of all bombs’ will not rescue Trump from Iran war quagmire
TEHRAN — The possible use of America’s largest non-nuclear bomb against Iran may offer President Donald Trump a dramatic display of military power, but it is unlikely to resolve the strategic predicament facing Washington, analysts have warned, arguing that a spectacular explosion cannot substitute for a viable path out of a protracted war.
CNN reported on October 14 that the US military had developed strike plans that could include the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, commonly known as the “mother of all bombs,” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if Trump orders a resumption of combat operations. The report cited multiple US officials familiar with the planning.
The prospect of deploying the weapon has raised questions about whether Washington is seeking a decisive military outcome or a dramatic action that could allow the president to declare victory without achieving his stated strategic objectives.
 
Even within US military planning circles, doubts have emerged over the weapon’s effectiveness in changing the course of the war, CNN reported. Reuters subsequently reported the story, noting that it had not independently verified CNN’s account.
A dramatic explosion, but what strategic result?
Dani Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official, told the BBC that even using the “mother of all bombs” would not force Iran to surrender.
“Even the use of the [mother of all bombs] will not force Iran to surrender; although such an attack could have psychological effects and give Trump an opportunity to claim an imaginary victory,” he said, according to the quotation provided in the BBC-attributed report.
The assessment points to a fundamental distinction between the destructive power of a weapon and its ability to achieve political objectives. A strike can cause extensive damage without compelling an adversary to accept the attacker’s demands or bringing a conflict to a favourable conclusion.
Sina Azodi, director of the Middle East Studies Program at George Washington University, similarly questioned the strategic logic behind the reported option.
“Trump has a strange fascination with the symbolic use of American military power and wants to advertise it on his personal social media account through a grand spectacle and a massive explosion,” Azodi said, according to the quotation provided.
He also highlighted the weapon’s limitations against deeply buried targets, noting that it detonates in the air and has limited capacity to penetrate far underground.
The distinction matters because the MOAB was designed primarily to produce devastating blast effects over a broad surface area. It is not the same as a specialised penetrator designed to attack deeply buried, hardened facilities.
In an October 15 Al Jazeera explainer, military analyst Elijah Magnier said that using the MOAB would not guarantee the destruction of Iran’s deeply buried nuclear installations and could amount to little more than “political theatre.”
A weapon cannot resolve a strategic deadlock
The reported plans have emerged as the Trump administration faces pressure to demonstrate progress in a war that has failed to produce a clear political resolution.
In a CNN broadcast on October 15, senior national security reporter Zachary Cohen said Trump and his advisers had spent months discussing options that could be presented to the American public as a “definitive end” to the war.
Cohen said the military had been tasked with developing fresh strike options amid the absence of a diplomatic resolution and growing unpopularity of the conflict.
He also reported that the administration’s stated strategic goals remained unfulfilled.
That assessment raises a central question: what would a MOAB strike actually accomplish that previous attacks and existing military pressure have not?
The bomb’s destructive capacity is not in dispute. The uncertainty concerns whether its use would change Iran’s calculations, compel Tehran to capitulate or create conditions for a durable settlement.
A dramatic strike might generate powerful images and headlines. But if it does not achieve its declared objectives, it could instead expose the gap between the administration’s military capabilities and its ability to translate them into a political outcome.
The limits of spectacle
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. Its deployment would represent a major escalation, but its size alone does not make it an appropriate weapon for every target.
CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Colonel Cedric Leighton explained in a broadcast on October 15 that the MOAB is designed to inflict damage over a large surface area, whereas Iran’s hardened and deeply buried nuclear facilities present a different targeting challenge.
He contrasted the MOAB with the Massive Ordnance Penetrator, a different weapon specifically designed to attack hardened underground targets.
Leighton also questioned the suitability of the aircraft required to deliver the MOAB for the Iranian operational environment.
The technical limitations reinforce the broader strategic problem. A weapon capable of producing an enormous explosion is not necessarily capable of destroying every intended target, still less of compelling a country to surrender.
A face-saving exit is not the same as victory
The most consequential possibility raised by the reporting is that the proposed strike could be intended partly to shape the political narrative of the war.
CNN’s reporting suggested that the administration was examining military options that could enable Trump to present the conflict as decisively concluded. Such a scenario would make the distinction between a battlefield achievement and a politically useful declaration of victory particularly important.
Citrinowicz’s assessment, as quoted by the BBC, captures that concern: the attack might provide an opportunity to claim victory without necessarily producing the underlying result.
This is the danger of treating military spectacle as a substitute for strategy. An attack can be visually overwhelming and still leave the fundamental dispute unresolved.
For Washington, the question is not simply whether the United States can deploy a powerful bomb. It is whether doing so would bring the war closer to an outcome that can be sustained politically and strategically.
 
The quagmire remains
The possibility of using the MOAB does not, by itself, demonstrate that Trump has authorised such an attack. The reports describe contingency planning, not a confirmed decision to deploy the weapon.
Reuters said it could not independently verify CNN’s initial report. CBS News separately reported on October 15 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans for possible use of the weapon if ordered by the president.
If the bomb fails to achieve its intended military objectives, the administration could find itself confronting the same fundamental problem after an even more dramatic attack. If it is used primarily to create the appearance of a decisive outcome, the gap between the declaration of victory and the realities on the ground could become harder to conceal.
The “mother of all bombs” may offer Trump a spectacle of overwhelming force. But an explosion, however large, cannot by itself deliver a political settlement, compel an adversary’s surrender or guarantee a way out of war.
The real test is not the size of the blast. It is whether the strategy behind it can produce an outcome that military power alone has so far failed to secure.

Brazil’s Lula says he now backs lowering age of criminal responsibility to 16
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:47:35 UTC
01:47:35 KST

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility for “heinous” crimes from 18 to 16, reversing a longstanding policy in what is widely seen as a desperate electoral gambit.
The U-turn, which Lula announced during a Thursday night interview with TV Globo, comes with the presidential runoff in just over a week. The incumbent faces an uphill battle to overturn the first-round victory of his opponent, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who remains slightly ahead at the polls.
Both the senator and his father, the former president, Jair Bolsonaro, have long supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility – they want it reduced to 14 rather than 16 – but Lula and his party have always opposed the change.
After repeated opinion polls, the latest of them this week, showed that 80% of the population supports lowering the age, Lula said: “My view, as a Brazilian citizen, is that for any and every heinous crime, I am in favour of lowering the age.”
He answered “yes” when the reporter asked whether he meant lowering it to 16.
The list of crimes classified as “heinous” under Brazilian law is extensive, ranging from murder and rape to the falsification of medicines and drug trafficking – the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving prison sentences in Brazil were incarcerated.
Human rights organisations and security experts have long criticised proposals to lower the age of criminal responsibility, arguing that they do little to tackle violence while increasing recruitment into organised crime in Brazil’s overcrowded prisons.
On Thursday, before Lula’s interview, the proposal had been discussed in the senate. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation, had criticised it for “not addressing the causes of violence”, adding that placing young people “prematurely in the prison system tends to deepen cycles of violence and exclusion, undermining their rehabilitation”.
The columnist Josias de Souza wrote in his UOL column that, by reversing his longstanding position, Lula “decided to change himself. It was no ordinary transformation. On public security, Lula turned himself inside out. He began defending what he had always rejected.”
The incumbent has doubled down in recent days in an effort to overturn Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead by appealing to independents and undecided voters. He has secured congressional approval for a shorter working week – a proposal on which Bolsonaro himself U-turned and decided to support at the last minute, when it appeared ready to pass – and debt relief for microentrepreneurs, as well as promising free public transport on weekends.

Barack Obama pays tribute to Manchester cotton workers and cites them as an inspiration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:47:32 UTC
01:47:32 KST

Barack Obama cited the “wonderful” story of how Manchester cotton workers stood in solidarity with enslaved African Americans as an inspiration for our times in a live appearance in the city.
Tens of thousands of people packed Co-op Live in the city on Thursday for An Evening With Barack Obama, where the former US president was interviewed by the writer and broadcaster Afua Hirsch.
Obama closed the 90-minute event, punctuated by cheers, whoops, laughter and applause from the audience, by discussing the work of the Obama Presidential Center, a museum, library and education project in Chicago, and that of his foundation – committed to challenging economic inequality, the climate crisis, education and health, with programmes for women and girls, global emerging leaders, and journalists in oppressive regimes.
He spoke of the hope he took from the younger people he worked with, and from the Lancashire cotton famine, in which workers from Manchester and surrounding towns supported Abraham Lincoln’s blockade of cotton from enslaving Confederate states.
Obama said the centre was about reminding people what was possible. “I was reminded being here at Manchester of just this wonderful story of the cotton workers here at Manchester. During the American civil war in 1862 at a time when their livelihoods depended on cotton and the union had set up a barricade and prevented cotton from leaving the South as part of the civil war effort.
“And yeah, the business people and manufacturers, and I think even the Guardian editorialised ‘don’t mess with that, you know, this is our lifeblood’ and over at the Free Trade Hall, a bunch of British working workers who are hungry and not sure whether they’re gonna be able to hold things together, sit there and they meet, and they collectively say, we are going to stand with those who are fighting for freedom, even if it’s going to cost us.
“And so you hear a story like that. And they write a letter to Lincoln and he writes back. And commends them for a historic expression of Christian humility and charity, and grace. And so you then say to yourself, if they could do it, why can’t we?
“There was no guarantee that they were gonna benefit in any way from it, but somehow, their life was better for that. Even in the midst of hardship. And I think if we could tell each other those stories, and pass those to our children and are our grandchildren. We’ll get through these times too.”
The Guardian’s Cotton Capital series launched in 2023 to explore its founders’ links to the cotton trade and transatlantic enslavement, including how the newspaper covered the subject at the time.
Hirsch spoke of the huge impact Obama’s 2008 A More Perfect Union speech had had, including for her as a “a black British person of mixed heritage”.
Asked to share the ways his identity is reflected in his politics and leadership, Obama said it did so in ways “particular to the United States”, and ways that were “more universal”.
He added: “Race is this faultline of so much of American history … our union made a series of compromises, including, essentially, tacitly ratifying slavery, and a civil war was fought and enormous struggle to secure a more inclusive notion who we the people are.
“And for whatever variety of reasons, I became, I think, a symbol of that journey that our country took. Not to get to a post-racial America, that was never possible, but I do think it marks the point in time in which the idea that ‘we the people’ means all people and not just some, seemed to have been validated for at least a moment.
“It marked a promise, and I was mindful of that. It did not erase the institutional, structural legacies of slavery and Jim Crow. But it did signify that the country changed, that the change was possible. Namely, through efforts of sacrifice of countless people, many of them nameless.”
Obama described democracy as a “journey”, that required “continual replenishment” to avoid falling back into “old ways”, amid great economic, social and technological disruptions, saying “we tend to forget how recently democracy has taken hold and how fragile it is … For most of human history for millennia, societies were organised around caste and hierarchy, violence and force.”
The statesman said it was a “good thing” for the prime minister and former Greater Manchester mayor, Andy Burnham, to “have [the Ukrainian president] Zelenskyy here and remind people what’s at stake”.

Egypt discovers parts of giant pharaoh statues (PHOTOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:45:52 UTC
01:45:52 KST

Egypt discovers parts of giant pharaoh statues (PHOTOS)
Egyptian archaeologists have uncovered the remains of two royal statues, at least one depicting Pharaoh Ramses II, during excavations in the Nile Delta, the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced on Wednesday.
The discovery was made in the village of Behbeit el-Hagar in Gharbia Governorate after a local resident, Khaled el-Shahat Khalil, found an inscribed stone block on his property and alerted the authorities. Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy later visited the site and rewarded the man and his wife with a pilgrimage to Mecca for reporting the find.
According to Hisham el-Leithy, secretary-general of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, the first find is a 1.6-meter-high head of Ramses II wearing the double crown symbolizing the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt. Part of the statue’s back pillar was also recovered, bearing an inscription of one of the pharaoh’s royal titles. Archaeologists estimate that the complete monument, including its base, may have stood around 8.5 meters tall.
The second discovery includes a 2.4-meter section of another royal statue, also believed to depict Ramses II. The figure is missing its legs and base, but its head remains well preserved, with facial features resembling those of the first statue. Excavators also uncovered a 1.3-meter block of pink granite bearing hieroglyphic inscriptions with two of the pharaoh’s titles, including “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” and “Son of Ra.”
The ministry said archaeologists are continuing to study the artifacts, and their exact age has yet to be determined. However, the discovery sets clear links to Ramses II, who ruled Egypt from 1279 to 1213 BC. It’s not the first finding of the kind. In February 2024, archaeologists uncovered the upper section of a statue of the pharaoh in Minya Governorate, nearly a century after its lower half was discovered in 1930. The restored statue, standing about 6.7 meters tall, was re-erected in 2026.
Other recent finds in Egypt include three New Kingdom tombs uncovered at Saqqara in July and a Roman-era tomb discovered in the Dakhla Oasis in September, containing pottery, funerary inscriptions and a coin depicting Emperor Constantine.

Yorkshire ambulance service NHS trust has launched an investigation into two members of staff at the trust, which responded to emergency calls on Saturday when William Chapman climbed into the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.
There may have been “two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information without a legitimate reason”, the ambulance service said after being contacted by HSJ, the trade publication for NHS policy.
Chapman, 23, was mauled to death by the 200kg male Siberian tiger named Altai at the zoo after climbing into its enclosure.
The park reopened on Friday after being closed since the attack.
An inquest opening on Thursday heard how Chapman had schizophrenia and had experienced bouts of psychosis but was “highly functioning and independent with no care requirements”.
His family, who did not attend the hearing at Doncaster coroner’s court, expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services before his death.
Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS foundation trust has launched an investigation into its contact with him.
The inquest heard Chapman was a self-employed online trader who was living in Doncaster at the time of his death. An initial postmortem found that he died from multiple traumatic injuries.
The coroner’s officer Caitlin Brookes said: “He was approached by the tiger and the ensuing physical contact between the tiger and Mr Chapman led to him sustaining multiple traumatic injuries which rapidly led to his death.”
Park staff secured the tiger and Yorkshire ambulance service paramedics attended and confirmed Chapman’s death at the scene. The senior coroner Nicola Mundy said her office was awaiting a more substantial report on the extent of Chapman’s injuries ahead of a full inquest on 18 March.
The potential breach of Chapman’s medical records happened after the attack and has been reported to the Information Commissioner’s Office.
The trust said it had “identified an information governance concern in relation to this tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park and William’s family has been informed of our ongoing investigation into this. We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so.”
It said: “We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits.”
Ahead of reopening on Friday, Yorkshire Wildlife Park said safety was the “highest priority”, and it thanked members of the public who had sent “messages of support and love for our team at this time”.
Wildlife and zoo experts have told the Guardian it is unlikely the wildlife park could have done anything to prevent the death.

FIFA fines Spain over anti-Muslim chants at Egypt game
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:45:30 UTC
01:45:30 KST

Breadcrumb
FIFA fines Spain over anti-Muslim chants at Egypt game
FIFA has fined world champions Spain $20,000 over Islamophobic chants by supporters during a friendly against Egypt earlier this year.
The chants were heard during Spain's 0-0 draw with Egypt at Espanyol's RCDE Stadium in Barcelona on 31 March.
Sections of the crowd chanted "Whoever doesn't jump is Muslim", while Egypt's national anthem was also jeered before kick-off.
Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants after the match as disrespectful and intolerable.
"Using a religion as a taunt on the field makes you look ignorant and racist," he said.
FIFA said its appeals committee had upheld the sanction following an earlier ruling by its disciplinary committee.
The Spanish Football Federation has been ordered to pay a $20,000 fine and must also close at least 15% of the seating at Spain's next home friendly.
FIFA said the affected seats could instead be allocated to groups including families, students and anti-discrimination organisations.
The governing body's disciplinary judges said "harsh sanctions were necessary", while acknowledging that it was the Spanish federation's first offence and that officials had acted quickly after the chants began.
Stadium announcements were made during the match calling on supporters to stop discriminatory behaviour.
The Spanish federation also condemned the chants and co-operated with authorities seeking to identify those responsible.
Spanish police opened an investigation the following day into what they described as "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chanting.
The incident came amid wider debate over racism and discrimination in football. FIFA's current anti-racism framework includes a crossed-arm gesture allowing players and officials to report racist abuse during matches.
FIFA rejected the Spanish federation's argument that the word "Muslim" was not inherently insulting, ruling that otherwise neutral language can become discriminatory when used as a taunt or marker of inferiority.
The federation said on Friday that it considered the punishment disproportionately severe and would appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
FIFA has also imposed sanctions elsewhere this year for breaches of anti-discrimination rules, including a fine against the Israeli Football Association over its handling of racist behaviour by Beitar Jerusalem supporters.
The March incident came before Spain went on to win the 2026 World Cup, defeating Argentina in the final in July.
The Egypt match had already drawn wider attention to anti-Muslim sentiment in European football, an issue TNA has examined in the context of the growing far-right backlash against Muslim players and supporters.

Trump move to restart direct US flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:45:26 UTC
01:45:26 KST

Trump move to restart direct US flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
Oct 16 - The United Nations aviation agency has found Lebanon's main airport lacks valid certification, according to a report summary seen by Reuters, in a setback to US President Donald Trump's move to revive direct US-Beirut flights.
Trump made the announcement in July and signed an order last month for the US government to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight 847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.
While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Trump's order "a significant first step toward restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States."
However, the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Beirut-Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system.
The findings, which two senior industry officials familiar with the matter expect to delay the resumption of service, complicate efforts to follow up on an order Trump signed after meeting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun. Washington has backed Aoun as it pushes for Iran-backed Hezbollah to be disarmed.
The agency sent its internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), to Lebanon in September.
AIRPORT LACKS EMERGENCY PLAN: ICAO
Beirut airport's firefighting resources are equipped for single-aisle planes, but not twin-aisle jetliners used for long-haul flights, according to a summary of ICAO's report. The airport also lacks an emergency plan, and its conditional certification has expired, the report said.
"This is a serious and time-critical matter that must be addressed immediately to preserve the airport's operational status," the summary said.
The report also found the Lebanese regulator LCAA lacks qualified inspectors to oversee air traffic control licensing, and has no fully established, operational and independent aircraft accident investigation authority with clearly defined roles.
Such concerns were flagged during a two-day workshop last month where officials from ICAO, Lebanon's government, the FAA and others discussed efforts to revive direct air service, according to the industry officials and an agenda of the meeting seen by Reuters.
Lebanon's Minister of Public Works and Transport Fayez Rasamny said Lebanon was taking steps to address the concerns, with efforts to certify the airport starting on Saturday. The LCAA expects to issue conditional certification in the coming days.
"Most of the issues highlighted in the report had already been identified by the LCAA, and corrective action had already been initiated," Rasamny said in a statement, adding that progress had been delayed by war. Israeli forces remain in southern Lebanon and have continued strikes despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed in June between Israel and Lebanon. Hezbollah, which was not party to the deal, has rejected it.
The FAA declined to comment. ICAO said it cannot comment on matters concerning specific countries, but said it conducts targeted analyses for member states.
The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Lebanon given safety concerns. It said the FAA advises caution for flights operating in Lebanese airspace due to heightened military activity in or around Syria, including the risks of errant long-range surface-to-air missiles originating from Syrian territory.
MIDDLE EAST UNREST DISRUPTS AIR TRAVEL
Foreign airlines have avoided large swathes of Middle East airspace because of missile and drone threats since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February triggered regional hostilities, with an airport in Saudi Arabia the latest site to come under attack.
Lebanon and its national carrier have been praised domestically for maintaining air navigation services and flights, helping to prop up an economy that depends on tourism and remittances.
Three US airline officials told Reuters on the condition of anonymity they do not think any American carriers would resume flights to Lebanon in the near term, citing security concerns.
While there are no direct flights between Beirut and the United States, such service exists between Lebanon and some large European cities.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency said it was aware of the ICAO report and added that EU airlines must conduct their own assessment of an airport's safety and operational readiness before launching services. REUTERS

Six-figure payout for senior civil servant sacked over Peter Mandelson vetting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:44:34 UTC
01:44:34 KST

Olly Robbins, the former head of the Foreign Office sacked by Keir Starmer over his role in vetting Peter Mandelson, has received a six-figure payout from the government over his dismissal.
Robbins had applied to the high court for a judicial review of the prime minister’s decision to remove him as the top civil servant at the Foreign Office after he was dismissed in April.
He was removed from his post by Starmer after the Guardian’s disclosure that he had overturned a recommendation from UK Security Vetting (UKSV) to deny clearance for Mandelson.
In a statement on Friday, Robbins said he was “grateful for all the support and good wishes from former colleagues, friends and strangers, which have helped me and my family during this difficult time”.
He added: “I want to thank the FDA [union] for their assistance in reaching this settlement and I am looking forward to moving on to the next chapter of my life.”
Dave Penman, general secretary of the FDA, which represents senior civil servants, said: “This settlement may bring an end to the judicial review proceedings, but this whole unprecedented affair has damaged the bond of trust between civil servants and ministers, which is essential to the effective running of government.
“The scapegoating of Sir Oliver, to mask the misjudgment of the previous prime minister, marked one of the lowest points in the recent history of civil service-ministerial relations – which is quite the feat.
“We urge the government to clarify quickly the issues raised by this affair over ministerial involvement in the vetting process.”
The government will ultimately have to publish how much it has given Robbins in a settlement, which is believed to be six figures but not as much as the record £860,000 given to former cabinet secretary Chris Wormald after he was forced out by Starmer after just a year in post.
At the time of his dismissal, Downing Street said Robbins had lost the confidence of Starmer and Yvette Cooper, then foreign secretary, due to his handling of the vetting of Mandelson, who was sacked over the extent of his links to the convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
The Guardian later revealed that Mandelson’s associations with senior figures in China, Russia and Israel had been among the concerns raised by UKSV when it concluded he should be denied clearance. His relationship with Epstein was not among the reasons.
Robbins’ legal submission had made the case that Starmer had no statutory authority to dismiss him as the head of the diplomatic service, and that there had been “no fair procedure” and “no process at all” in the dismissal. It also said Robbins had been given “irrational” reasons for being fired.
There had been strong support for Robbins within Whitehall, with senior civil servants said to believe he had in effect been sacked for doing what No 10 wanted by swiftly passing Mandelson through vetting, and that the focus should instead have been on the prime minister’s initial decision.
The Commons foreign affairs select committee has previously said that Robbins believed he was “delivering the outcome that was wanted” and concluded that his dismissal “seems to have been taken without full due process and the establishment of the facts”.
Questions remain about the defence Robbins mounted, both of his own actions and the system through which the national security establishment vets people, and the lack of mitigation put in place to get around the security concerns.
The Foreign Office refused to hand over a summary of Mandelson’s security vetting to the official tasked with compiling documents detailing his appointment as ambassador to the US, in response to a Commons motion forcing the release of documents linked to the process.

US defense firm planning local drone production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:43:17 UTC
01:43:17 KST

Kratos Defense is seeking US government authorization for Taiwan to produce the jointly developed Mighty Hornet IV one-way strike drones, Kratos representative Steve Fendley said.
Fendley, president of Kratos’ uncrewed systems division, was speaking after taking part in the uncrewed aerial vehicle’s (UAV) flight certification tests held recently in a facility in southern Taiwan.
Kratos has received inquiries about the Mighty Hornet IV from dozens of countries, including seven that have allotted budgets or requested estimates on pricing for the system, Fendley said.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Designed around the affordable mass concept, the Mighty Hornet IV is a jet-engined loitering munition that possesses 90 percent of a crewed fighter jet’s strike capabilities for US$500,000 per unit, he said.
The Mighty Hornet IV can reach a top speed of 0.7 to 0.85 Mach (864kph to 1,049kph), significantly faster than conventional propeller-driven designs, he said.
The jet-powered drone can engage targets maneuvering at high speeds and create a dilemma for the opposing force of expending expensive interceptor munitions or allowing its assets to be destroyed, Fendley said.
The drone uses an airframe based on Kratos Defense’s Firejet, and the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) designed its sensors, navigation system, electronic warfare suite and high-explosive warhead, he said.
It is an integrated system designed for Taiwan’s operational environment, Fendley said.
Under the Kratos-NCSIST partnership, the transfer of Mighty Hornet IV technology would begin with Kratos producing airframes and Taiwan outfitting them with mission-critical components and the payload, he said.
In the next phase, Kratos would supply NCSIST with kits to assemble, incrementally increasing Taiwan’s manufacturing, quality control and system integration capabilities, he said.
The end goal is for Kratos to secure technology transfer licenses from the US Department of State to establish full assembly lines in Taiwan, Fendley said.
Taiwan could expect Mighty Hornet IV orders from the US government, should NCSIST successfully develop domestic mass-production capabilities, he said.
Another Kratos Defense and NCSIST project is aimed at developing a variant of the former’s XQ-58 Valkyrie, a stealth autonomously piloted collaborative combat aircraft, Fendley said.
This type of platform is designed to add its sensors, electronic warfare suites and strike capabilities to support crewed aircraft in missions, he said.
The XQ-58A utilizes an open architecture and an internal weapons bay, enabling modularity in its sub-systems, he said.
The drone can use its onboard artificial intelligence (AI) to operate singly or in swarms, he said.
The US Marine Corps has selected the XQ-58 for its collaborative combat aircraft program, and Kratos is bidding for the German air force’s “loyal wingman” contract, Fendley said.

The Asian Cup soccer tournament is on track to take place in Saudi Arabia early next year, local organizers said yesterday, but golf’s Asian Tour has postponed the Saudi International indefinitely in the aftermath of a deadly attack on Riyadh.
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed responsibility for the strike on Riyadh’s international airport, which killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300.
Australia also withdrew its team from the urban cycling World Championships yesterday, citing safety concerns over travelling to Riyadh, where the event is scheduled to take place early next month.
Photo: AP
The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has already been moved from this month to December, while FIFA on Thursday postponed the FIFAe Finals video game competition in the Saudi capital until an unspecified future date.
In that environment, serious questions were being asked over whether the 24-team Asian Cup could still go ahead in Saudi Arabia from Jan. 7 to Feb. 5 next year.
Asian soccer chief Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said earlier this week that a postponement of the continental championships until 2028 was possible if necessary, but the local organizing committee said yesterday they were sticking to the original schedule.
“Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services,” it said in a statement.
The US$5 million Saudi International, which is sponsored by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), is the flagship event on the Asian Tour and had been scheduled to take place at Riyadh Golf Club from Nov. 18 to 21.
“The decision to postpone was taken following an assessment of the organizational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is delivered to a standard befitting its international stature,” an Asian Tour statement said.
AusCycling said its decision to withdraw the Australian team from the urban World Championships was made “with the safety and wellbeing of our athletes and staff our highest priority.”
The Australian government is advising travelers to “reconsider” trips to Saudi Arabia in general and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport in particular “due to recent security incidents.”
The Saudi government has invested heavily in sport through the PIF in the past few years and the Asian Cup was pitched as an early rehearsal for hosting the soccer World Cup in 2034.
According to a report on US news Web site Semafor earlier this week, PIF is preparing to tell FIFA that it would be scaling back stadium plans for the 2034 tournament as part of a broader review of domestic spending.

Economic growth to be highest in 39 years: CIER
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:43:08 UTC
01:43:08 KST

Taiwan’s economy is projected to grow at its fastest pace in 39 years this year, supported by robust domestic demand and exports, the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (CIER, 中華經濟研究院) said yesterday.
The think tank raised its growth forecast to 12.16 percent for this year, up 1.81 percentage points from its forecast of 10.35 percent in July.
“This is a very strong year, with both domestic and external demand performing very well,” CIER president Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明) told reporters before the presentation, citing the Chinese-language Liberty Times (sister company of the Taipei Times).
Photo: Liao Chia-ning, Taipei Times
Domestic demand is expected to contribute 55 percent to the overall projected annual growth, while net overseas demand would account for the remaining 45 percent, the institute said in its presentation.
Much of the economic momentum continues to be driven by vigorous demand for artificial intelligence (AI)-related products, which has supported robust export growth and stronger investment and consumer spending, it said.
CIER raised its economic growth forecast largely due to better-than-expected increase in domestic demand rather than exports.
In terms of domestic demand, global cloud service providers are continuing to expand capital expenditures, leading local manufacturers to increase capacity, Lien said.
That rise in capacity, combined with increased investment in automation by non-tech industries, led the institute to project that private investment would grow 10.77 percent this year, he said.
Private consumption is forecast to expand 4.94 percent, the think tank said.
The institute estimated third-quarter growth of 12.73 percent, followed by 8.2 percent in the fourth quarter as a higher base of comparison weighs on the year-on-year figure.
The fourth-quarter forecast was raised from July’s estimate of 6.04 percent. Taiwan recorded growth of 15.43 percent and 12.93 percent in the first and second quarters respectively, government data cited by the think tank showed.
CIER cited monetary policy changes in major economies, financial market movements, domestic investment, geopolitical risks and cross-strait relations as potential drags on Taiwan’s high-growth environment.
Inflation is forecast to rise 2.06 percent this year, slightly above its July estimate of 2.02 percent. Fourth-quarter inflation is expected to expand 2.42 percent from a year earlier.
For next year, the institute raised its growth forecast to 5.97 percent from 3.71 percent in July, buoyed by continued expansion at a more moderate pace.

Global Tek forecasts double-digit growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

Precision metal component maker Global Tek Fabrication Co Ltd (時碩工業) yesterday said it expects revenue this year to grow by at least a double-digit percentage from last year’s NT$4.97 billion (US$153.47 million), driven by volume shipments of key components for artificial intelligence (AI) liquid cooling systems.
Global Tek said it began ramping up production of key components last quarter from its factory in Wuxi, China.
The growth would also be fueled by rising demand for key components used in industrial applications and aerospace devices, the company said.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
The momentum is expected to extend into next year, as the company has secured orders from several major cloud service providers in the US and Japan for liquid-cooling components, Global Tek president Donald Huang (黃亞興) said at an earnings conference in Taipei.
The products include microchannel cold plate components, universal quick-disconnect fittings, manifolds, valve bodies and other fluid-control components, Huang said.
The company is on track to boost AI-related and other emerging businesses to account for 20 percent of revenue in the first half of next year, from 6.2 percent in the first nine months of the year from thermal management systems for AI data centers, driven by new overseas orders for liquid-cooling systems, Huang said.
Global Tek mainly manufactures precision metal components for automotive, industrial and aerospace applications. Industrial applications components were the largest share of revenue during the first nine months of this year, accounting for 35 percent, company data showed. During the period, revenue expanded 23.41 percent annually to NT$4.64 billion.
Revenue is expected to remain robust this quarter, supported by steady demand from established automotive and industrial control businesses as well as growth in aerospace, AI, semiconductor equipment and humanoid robot applications, Huang said.
Shipments of precision components for a Chinese humanoid robot maker entered small-volume production this quarter and are expected to provide additional growth momentum next year, he said.
In Thailand, the company plans to inaugurate a new factory on Tuesday next week in Chonburi Province, where it also operates two other factories. The new factory is to enter volume production next year. In total, the company has invested NT$1 billion in the Thailand site, it said.
The Thailand factories produce components used in semiconductor equipment and robot-related applications, with aerospace aluminum alloy casting and stainless-steel precision casting to be added, Huang said.
The first phase of the aerospace aluminum alloy casting production line is expected to involve about NT$150 million in equipment investment, with mass production of the casting line scheduled to begin by the end of 2028, he said.
Global Tek would continue to expand capacity in its Wuxi, Suzhou and Xian factories, given the Chinese sites’ manufacturing advantages in terms of scale and costs, Huang said.

Meeting demand for kindergartens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

The Ministry of Education described its progress in efforts to expand publicly funded kindergarten and childcare capacities. Since 2017, the government has subsidized the establishment of more than 4,100 additional classrooms at kindergartens nationwide, bringing the total to about 270,000 places.
This year, the ministry is allocating more than NT$500 million (US$15.46 million) to fund further expansions.
Recent policy efforts have focused on two-year-olds: Local governments have received targeted assistance to establish dedicated classes based on the number of children they have aged two to five, the number of publicly funded places available and enrollment numbers in each administrative area. In some areas with plenty of affordable places for three-to-five-year-olds, classrooms have been converted to cater to two-year-olds.
After a decade of capacity expansion, the challenge is to match supply to demand within local communities and ensure that services are accessible.
Although the total number of places nationwide is substantial, parents are most concerned about whether they can find a suitable location near their home or work. New urban redevelopments, technology park precincts and other areas with population inflows might still have waiting lists, but townships experiencing population decline might struggle to attract enough enrollments.
The ministry’s adjustments to class cohort numbers based on supply and demand could also be extended to the level of local communities. Local governments could publish annual figures on the population of children aged two to five, publicly funded places, waiting-list numbers and average commuting distances, alongside three-year demand forecasts. Areas experiencing rapid residential growth should set aside space, while elementary schools with declining enrollments could consider converting unused classrooms into kindergarten facilities, allowing resources to be adjusted in line with demographic changes.
When children move from infant daycare centers or home-based childcare into kindergartens, families often have to navigate changes in schedules, entry dates and care arrangements. The ministry’s priority of establishing dedicated kindergarten bands for two-year-olds at elementary schools that already have infant daycare centers should help facilitate the transition. It could share data with the Ministry of Health and Welfare so that families can understand the availability of nearby services when their children are about one year old. They could also explore establishing a single information portal that integrates details on places for children up to age six, fees, enrollment periods and waiting lists, reducing the burden on parents of comparing information across multiple platforms.
Families also need childcare that accommodates their work hours. For working parents who do not clock off until 5pm or 6pm, the reliability of after-hours kindergarten care, programs during winter and summer holidays, and the availability of extended care services directly affects how useful care providers are. Shift workers face particular difficulties.
The central government could assess working patterns in areas with concentrated industrial activity and encourage local governments to extend care hours in response to demand.
Additional staffing and funding should be provided to kindergartens offering longer service hours, while taking into account the working hours and workloads of early childhood educators. Adequate staffing would allow shifts to be arranged without compromising service quality. Whether the policies genuinely support families often comes down to the difference made by just one or two hours at the beginning or end of the day.
The expansion of publicly funded kindergartens has passed its large-scale growth phase. Going forward, the government should establish a comprehensive annual performance report that tracks not only the number of new classes and available places, but also waiting-list rates, supply and demand for dedicated classes for two-year-olds, commuting distances, uptake of extended care, staff turnover and parental satisfaction.
Taiwan’s declining birthrate might be reducing the total number of young children, but demand continues to change with population movements, family structures and working patterns. The 4,100 new classes and 270,000 extra places provide an important foundation.
However, families’ actual needs can only be met when services are located where they are needed, transitions between childcare and kindergarten are seamless, and service hours fit the realities of family life.
Arthur Chen is a manager in the electronics industry.

Taiwan to donate rice to 17 nations:agriculture ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

Taiwan is to donate more than 20,000 tonnes of locally grown rice to 17 countries that require food assistance this year, the Ministry of Agriculture’s Agriculture and Food Agency said on World Food Day yesterday.
Taiwan began providing international food assistance in 2002 through the Food Humanitarian Aid Program, with the program entering its 25th year this year.
Food aid from the program is offered free of charge without affecting domestic food security or international trade, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Agriculture and Food Agency
This year, the agency would grant up to 24,876 tonnes of government-stored white rice, which would be shipped to 17 countries in Africa, Latin America and Asia that urgently need food assistance, it said.
The shipping and unloading of the rice would be handled by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in collaboration with non-governmental organizations, including the Buddhist Compassion Relief Tzu Chi Foundation, World Vision Taiwan and Good Neighbors Taiwan, the Agriculture and Food Agency said.
The NGOs would help extend the food aid to people of disadvantaged backgrounds in remote areas around the world, it said.
Each bag of rice would be printed with the national flag of Taiwan and the words “Love From Taiwan,” which is expected to warm the hearts of people around the world with food and hope amid volatile global situations, it said.
To ensure food safety for aid recipients — including elderly people living alone, refugees and orphans — the rice was subjected to food safety testing in Taiwan, with the stipulation that it meets CNS Grade 2 quality standards and has passed food safety testing, the agency said.
The agency used 10kg or 30kg drop-resistant packaging to ensure the rice grains would remain intact after long-distance transportation, it said, adding that loading for shipment had begun.
“Taiwan can help” is never just a slogan, but a regular practice that makes Taiwanese proud, the agency said.
Taiwan would continue to work with the international community to help globally based on the spirit of humanitarian care and mutual assistance, it said.

South Africa looks for European cup win after losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

The European Champions Cup has proved a surprising struggle for South African clubs whose entry into the rugby competition four years ago was expected to intensify the battle for silverware, but whose results have been underwhelming.
Since the 2022 season, none of the South African representatives have made it beyond the quarter-finals and in the past two years have not even got past the last 16. South African teams have lost more Champions Cup games than they have won over the past four campaigns.
This season’s edition kicked off yesterday and three South African representatives — the Bulls, Stormers and Lions — faced intense scrutiny over how they would approach the competition.
Photo: AP
The Johannesburg-based Lions are taking part for the first time while the Bulls and Stormers have competed in all four previous editions involving South African clubs, but have only one quarter-final appearance each.
“We need a South African team to make a semi-final or even a final this season,” Stormers coach John Dobson said this week.
“From our side we want the participation in the Champions Cup to continue and we want to respect the competition, and the best way to make that point is to do well in it,” he added.
The poor performance of the South African teams has had much to do with trying to manage players’ workload.
They have often sent fringe squads to away matches and spared marquee players the arduous travel to have them fresher and in better shape for home games, where they have a better chance at victory and collecting bonus points.
It has drawn a lot of criticism, including from former England flyhalf Stuart Barnes, who wrote in The Times that South African sides fielding second-string teams away in the Champions Cup “damages the competition.”
Also hampering selection is the need to manage the playing time of international players, in agreement with the South African Rugby Union, so that they are fresh to play for the Springboks. It would be a top priority over the next 12 months leading up to the Rugby World Cup in Australia in October next year.
There is also a perception that the South Africans prioritize the United Rugby Championship, where they have been much more successful.
This year’s Champions Cup starts earlier than usual and there is a lengthy break after this weekend’s opening round of pool matches before the next round in December. That offers a less intense initial schedule for the South Africans and would encourage them to select stronger sides.
The Bulls and Stormers kick off at home this weekend while the Lions face a baptism of fire against former winners La Rochelle in France today.
“It’s our first game in the Champions Cup, so we’d like to start that strong,” said Lions coach Ivan van Rooyen, whose side departed for France on Monday to have more time to acclimatize and will then stay overseas for back-to-back URC matches in Scotland.

Official urges air travelers to manage time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:57 UTC
01:42:57 KST

People departing on trips should manage their time wisely, consumer protection officials said, citing an incident in which a family of four missed check-in for a flight by one minute.
The family from Yilan County planned to fly to Fukuoka, Japan, on an AirAsia flight at noon on July 9, but were unable to check in, prompting a consumer dispute.
No agreement was reached after the airline said that it had followed standard operating procedures.
Photo: Taipei Times
The man said that the family had to check in at the airport after a glitch on a third-party ticket purchasing platform prevented him from completing online check-in for his children.
Upon arriving at Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport, he said he informed ground staff of their destination and was directed to line up, only to realize that they were standing in line for an Okinawa-bound flight instead of Fukuoka.
When he raised the issue with staff, they told him that the Fukuoka check-in counter had closed and refused to check them in, advising him to arrange alternative transportation, he said.
Calling the refusal a severe violation of his family’s travel rights, the man filed for consumer dispute mediation, demanding a full refund, compensation for consequential financial losses and punitive damages.
AirAsia in a written response said that the Fukuoka flight was scheduled to depart at 12pm, with check-in counters closing at 11am.
According to surveillance footage, the man arrived at counter No. 3 at 11:01am and raised the online check-in issue at 11:02am without specifying his destination, the company said.
Ground staff mistakenly assumed that the family was traveling to Okinawa and guided them to wait in that line, it said.
The man did not mention going to Fukuoka until 11:09am, by which time the counter was closed, it added.
The company expressed regret over the inconvenience and the additional ticket costs incurred, saying that it could not fulfill requests for financial compensation based on its investigation.
The man said he would proceed with a lawsuit to seek maximum punitive damages under the Consumer Protection Act (消費者保護法).
Citing “quite a few” complaints recently regarding missed flights due to timing issues, Yilan County Consumer Protection Officer Wang Ya-lin (王雅琳) last week urged travelers to manage their time wisely.
Given frequent congestion in Yilan on weekends and holidays, travelers should factor in potential delays and head to the airport early to avoid ruining their trips, Wang said.

Why Europe just cannot quit the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:56 UTC
01:42:56 KST

Last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, standing in front of the Parthenon, declared that US President Donald Trump’s administration sought to partner with Europe in defending the “distinct character” of Western civilization. It was meant to exhort, perhaps.
To Europe, it sounded like a threat. The US, said Rubio, had chosen “the unapologetic pursuit of national power.” The implication was that European nations had not and thus resigned themselves “to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.” Yet few on the continent would think that a partnership with the US, defined by the kind of the obedience Rubio and Trump expect, would be much better than servitude.
Trump’s White House has not concealed its desire to control Europe’s choices. The national security strategy it released at the end of last year identified “cultivating resistance to Europe’s current trajectory within European nations” as a priority.
The administration has also shown that, if it decides to push these countries in a direction other than the one their citizens might choose for themselves, it has the levers to do so.
Trump pulled one of them earlier this month, when he threatened to withhold fossil-fuel exports unless Europe released some of its strategic diesel reserves. On this occasion, Trump’s concern was that high prices at the pump might cost him the midterms. However, when such threats prove effective, they tend to be used again and again.
Europe’s leaders have, since Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, tried to break free of Russian gas. They must confront the fact that this effort has just increased their dependence on a Washington that talks about intervention in their politics with the same hunger as the Kremlin.
In the past few years, Europe’s leaders have spoken often about their search for strategic autonomy. However, in every field that matters to European independence — defense, tech, energy — the continent has become more reliant on the US over the past decade, not less.
Consider Europe’s much-discussed rearmament. Perhaps, a decade from now, its military-industrial complex might be revived. What we know for sure is that the value of proposed sales of US equipment to European NATO members, as recorded under official programs, was only 28 percent of those countries’ spending on military equipment between 2019 and 2021; between 2022 and 2024, that proportion rose to more than half.
European militaries are particularly dependent on the US for strategic enablers — the systems, such as those for transport, command and control and communication, that are essential for modern war-fighting. Public recognition that this could not be allowed to continue came last month, when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her annual policy address to announce a proposal for a new “European instrument for strategic enablers.”
Then there is tech, where the continent is often called a laggard. Mario Draghi’s 2024 report on European competitiveness pointed out that, if you exclude the technology sector, EU productivity growth over the past 20 years was the same as that of the US. Over the same period, American tech has become more essential for European growth, security and survival — 41 percent of EU enterprises are, according to official statistics, “highly dependent” on cloud services, 70 percent of which are controlled by US companies.
That has left Europe’s politics increasingly fevered and open to manipulation. Leaders talk often about Russian infiltration into the continent’s information economy, but Elon Musk and other US tech billionaires are allowed to shape it far more openly. A British prime minister might complain that Moscow tried to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum; yet in the years since, it is a US vice president who has intervened in support of pro-Russian right-wingers in Hungary and Romania and openly backed the AfD in Germany.
This week, the EU announced an agreement with Beijing that it hoped would give its car industry some breathing space. It is just the latest example of the massive time and effort the bloc has devoted to planning countermeasures against China and Russia. Perhaps some of that energy should go to figuring out what to do about the US. Europe does not need the US to tell it how to defend its civilization. It needs to find a way to ensure Washington does not get to decide what that civilization should be.
Mihir Sharma is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist. A senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, he is author of Restart: The Last Chance for the Indian Economy. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.
Taiwan might just give up. That’s the argument Simon Shuster made in The Atlantic’s October issue. The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal

In attempting to stir up fear with talk of community centers, drugs and needles, Chiang’s comment section exploded. Rather embarrassingly, many commenters made a point

Democratic leaders must tolerate criticism, even on ceremonial occasions, but Han misused his position and a national celebration to insinuate that Taiwan’s elected president was steering the country toward dictatorship and cast himself as a statesman offering reconciliation. Media personality and politician Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康) yesterday shot back at critics who called for his expulsion from the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) for interviewing Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate.
“Will a couple of my interviews cost the KMT the election? Am I really that important?” he asked in response to requests for comment.
Jaw’s remarks came hours after local news media reported that KMT Central Standing Committee member Chiang Yung-hsiung (江永雄) has initiated a petition to remove him over disapproval that Jaw’s two interviews with Shen over the past week.
Photo courtesy of the Shen campaign office via CNA
Shen, a DPP lawmaker, is challenging incumbent Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT in next month’s Taipei mayoral election.
Jaw, former chairman of the Broadcasting Corp of China, served as a KMT lawmaker and as environmental minister from the late 1980s to the early 1990s.
He has remained a prominent voice in Taiwan’s media and politics, and he ran unsuccessfully on the KMT ticket for vice president in 2024.
The KMT does not appear to be performing well in most polls and its supporters appear to be outnumbered in Taipei and New Taipei City, although many might be keeping silent in fear of judgement, Jaw said yesterday.
“The KMT also has many stupid, out-of-touch supporters who think that they alone are always right and that the people are wrong, that anyone who disagrees with them is by default on the wrong side,” he said. “These guys are incapable of listening, just as the KMT most needs to learn the humility and patience needed to be receptive of the voice of the people.”
Jaw reiterated that he did not care in the slightest if he was expelled from the party, but said the issue needed to be made clear.
The media should provide a fair platform to all sides and not treat the platform as the exclusive domain of their own party or faction, he said.
Chiang is scheduled to appear on his program next week, Jaw said, adding that each guest’s performance speaks for itself and listeners can make their own judgements.
Separately, when asked by reporters for comment, Chiang said he wished Jaw the best upon hearing the news about the petition.
Asked whether he would urge KMT supporters to refrain from attacking each other, Chiang said he hoped people would approach the issue rationally and focus on the facts.

Haas choose Camara, dash hopes of Doohan return
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

Brazilian Rafael Camara is to race for Haas next season on a multi-year deal, with the US-owned Formula One team saying on Thursday he was clearly the quickest in a shoot-out test for the seat.
The 21-year-old Ferrari Academy driver leads the Formula Two standings with two rounds remaining, after winning the F3 title last year.
He would be the second Brazilian on the starting grid, with Gabriel Bortoleto already racing for Audi, and plans to take the number 50 since his compatriot races with the 5 that would have been his first choice as a driver born on May 5, 2005.
Photo: AP
Camara replaces Frenchman Esteban Ocon, whose departure was announced last month, at the Ferrari-powered team. Britain’s Oliver Bearman, who also came through the Ferrari Academy, is yet to be confirmed but sure to stay as the more experienced team leader.
The signing dashed the immediate hopes of Australian Jack Doohan, the reserve who had been hoping for a return to a full-time race seat after a split from Renault-owned Alpine last year.
“He [Camara] was the quickest, very simple answer. He was impressive,” Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu told reporters on a video call when asked what had decided the choice.
Komatsu said Doohan’s future with the team was “still up in the air,” but the door remained open for him to continue in his current role.
“We’ve been talking with him and his manager to see if we can do something together beyond this year,” he added.
Camara, a former teammate of Mercedes’ 20-year-old Formula One championship leader Kimi Antonelli in the FRECA European junior series, showed his pace when he drove last year’s Haas in a Testing of Previous Cars outing in Portugal at the Algarve Circuit in August.
“He showed... that he could handle himself very well with not a huge amount of time to learn the car, he showed us more than just raw speed,” Komatsu said. “Rafa managed to create an environment to get the best out of himself, it was very impressive and certainly the laps he completed were special,” he added.
The Recife-born Brazilian, who leads Red Bull-backed Bulgarian Nikola Tsolov by seven points in the F2 standings, said his first reaction when Komatsu called to say he had the job was to reply: “are you sure?”
“I’m extremely happy, especially for my parents,” he said. “It was a lot of sacrifice on their side. We are not even from the motorsports world, we didn’t really know exactly what was the way to go and to be here.”
“We moved from Recife to Sao Paulo and then eventually they were always travelling with me. So their life, the normal life that they had, they couldn’t be doing any more,” he added.
Camara revealed that his grandmother had raced with a DKW Vemag in the 1960s, but said that was not the reason he had started.
Instead the adventure began when the son of a work colleague of his father began karting and his brother then also got the chance, but proved reluctant and eventually stopped.
“I was always the one that was following and wanting to go but I was still too young, I was five,” said Camara, who has the late triple champion Ayrton Senna as his racing hero. “When I was six I kept asking my dad... and it became something a bit more serious now.”
Haas are seventh of 11 teams ahead of next week’s US Grand Prix in Austin, Texas. Bearman has scored 23 of their 30 points.

Indonesia stocks sink on MSCI downgrade warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

Indonesian stocks yesterday suffered their worst rout in nearly three decades after MSCI Inc warned the country’s emerging-market status was in jeopardy, raising the prospect of its removal from global indices and stoking fears of foreign capital flight.
The benchmark Jakarta Composite Index tumbled nearly 12 percent, its biggest one-day decline since January 1998, in a selloff that triggered a 30-minute trading halt. Yesterday’s sell-off added to an already punishing year for local equities, cementing their position as the world’s worst-performing market. The rupiah also neared a record low while bonds declined.
The index provider is launching a consultation and weighing what is effectively a double downgrade for Indonesian equities, bypassing frontier status and relegating the Southeast Asian nation to standalone-market status because of the severity of its investability problems, it said in a statement.
Photo: EPA
It expects to go ahead with its final decision in June unless there is clear evidence of material improvements in market governance.
At the heart of MSCI’s concerns are opaque shareholding structures, suspected coordinated trading and weak enforcement, it said.
While Jakarta has announced reforms, including greater ownership disclosures and higher minimum free-float requirements, the index compiler said that institutional investors want to see consistent implementation and evidence of material impact.
“It’s a massive hit to credibility,” said Felix Darmawan, an analyst at PT BCA Sekuritas. “MSCI is basically calling out the Financial Services Authority on opaque structures and lack of real enforcement. June 2027 gives the securities regulator some time to clean house, but the damage to foreign confidence starts right now.”
If downgraded, Indonesia would fall into the same country classification as Palestine or Lebanon. The review brings renewed scrutiny to governance under Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, who has been working to restore confidence and lure investors back to the region’s biggest economy after a bruising year.
His government is already contending with criticism over funding for its ambitious lunch program, concerns about central bank independence and unease over growing state control over key industries.
Mirae Asset Sekuritas Indonesia estimates that a reclassification to standalone could trigger about US$3 billion in passive outflows based on Indonesia’s remaining weight of about 0.4 percent in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index. Citigroup Inc puts that figure at mid-single-digit billions.
In response, the Indonesia Stock Exchange said it plans to seek clarification from MSCI on the rationale behind the reclassification plan, pointing to what it called “significant progress and reform measures.”
Meanwhile, the financial services regulator said it is reviewing the assessment and is committed to strengthening law enforcement in the market.

A new UK app called Birdex is changing how people explore nature by turning birdwatching into a game. To encourage people to step outside, the app allows users to collect digital cards of birds whenever they spot one. Users also earn points for each sighting, with rarer species offering higher rewards.
However, the app has faced criticism for its AI-generated bird illustrations. Critics argue that these images lack accuracy and may fail to educate users properly. In response, the developers explained that limited funding led them to use AI tools, but they plan to hire human artists in the future. Viola Ross-Smith of the British Trust for Ornithology also questions whether this app puts vulnerable birds at risk by driving people to seek out rare species.
新推出的一款名為 Birdex 的英國應用程式將賞鳥變成一種遊戲，因而正改變人們探索大自然的方式。為了鼓勵大眾走出戶外，這款應用程式讓使用者每看到一隻小鳥就可以蒐集鳥兒的數位圖卡。使用者每次觀測到鳥兒還能獲得點數，較稀有的物種點數較高。
Photo: Ivy English 照片: 常春藤解析英語
不過這款應用程式因人工智慧生成的鳥類插圖而遭受非議。批評者認為這些影像缺乏準確性，可能無法正確傳遞知識給使用者。開發者對此做出回應，他們解釋因資金有限才使用人工智慧工具，但他們計劃未來聘請人類藝術家。英國鳥類信託組織的薇奧拉．羅斯-史密斯也提出疑問：這款應用程式會不會因促使民眾找尋稀有物種而讓易危鳥類陷入險境呢？
What Did You Learn?
1. Why do some people doubt Birdex can help users learn about birds correctly?
參考答案:
1. Its AI-generated illustrations / images lack accuracy.
Words in Use
1. species n. 物種（單複數同形）
The government works hard to protect endangered plant species in this region. 政府致力於保護該地區瀕臨消失的植物物種。
2. reward n. 獎勵
Players receive rewards after completing missions. 玩家完成任務後會獲得獎勵。
3. criticism n. 批評 critic n. 批評者
The actor faced strong public criticism for his rude behavior. 該演員因不禮貌的行為面臨社會大眾猛烈的批評。
The controversial policy has many critics. 這項有爭議的政策受到許多人批評。
4. illustration n. 插畫，圖案
The textbook includes a clear illustration of the human brain. 這本教科書包含了一張清楚呈現人類大腦的插圖。
5. accuracy n. 準∕正確性
The researchers checked the data again to ensure the accuracy of the results. 研究人員再次檢查數據以確保結果的正確性。
Practical Phrases
1. in response 作為回應∕應對
The number of sea turtles dropped sharply. In response, conservation teams stepped in. 海龜數量大幅下降。保育團隊相應做出行動、介入其中。
2. put... at risk 使……陷入險境
Driving too fast in stormy weather can put your life at risk. 在暴風雨的天氣中車速過快會讓生命置於危險之中。
3. seek out... / seek... out 尋找∕找出…… (動詞 seek 的三態為：seek, sought, sought。)
We sought out shelter during the storm. 暴風雨期間，我們找地方躲雨。

Have you ever bought a product simply because everyone around you seemed to own one? Or have you ever supported an idea after seeing many classmates agree with it? If so, you have experienced the bandwagon effect, a psychological phenomenon in which people adopt certain behaviors, attitudes, or beliefs because others are doing the same. The term originates from 19th-century American politics. Campaign managers would hire a bandwagon, a decorated wagon carrying musicians, to parade through towns, attracting crowds and signaling popular support. Legislature passes NHI senior subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:53 UTC
01:42:53 KST

The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan yesterday passed a legal amendment requiring the central government to fully subsidize National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for certain senior citizens.
The amendment to Article 22 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), proposed by lawmakers from the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP), passed by a vote of 60 to 39.
Under the amendment, the central government must cover the full NHI premiums of seniors whose total consolidated income in the most recent year, as assessed by tax authorities, falls below the tax filing threshold or is subject to an income tax rate of less than 20 percent.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
According to the Ministry of Finance’s progressive income tax brackets for this year, net consolidated income of NT$1.38 million (US$42,674) or less is taxed at a rate below 20 percent. This means people aged 65 or older with annual net income within that threshold would qualify for the subsidy.
The TPP caucus said the policy fulfills a campaign pledge made by its founding chairman, Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), during his 2024 presidential campaign to provide comprehensive NHI premium subsidies for people aged 65 or older.
The party added that Ko introduced subsidies for the NHI premiums of older people when he was Taipei mayor, covering residents aged 65 or older as well as indigenous residents aged 55 or older. Several other local governments later adopted similar policies, but some financially strained cities and counties with large elderly populations were unable to afford them.
However, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) expressed concern about the amendment, saying it departed from the NHI system’s principle of contributions based on ability to pay and could undermine its long-term sustainability.
“An election is temporary, but the NHI system is something people rely on and needs to be stable and sustainable,” he said.
Shih warned that breaking the principle could lead to further measures that disrupt the system’s operations.
The change could create intergenerational unfairness and lead to increases in premiums, limit growth in the overall NHI budget and exacerbate the difficulties faced by medical institutions, or require the government to allocate more tax revenue to health insurance at the expense of other welfare programs, he said.
Taiwan has become a super-aged society, with people aged 65 or older accounting for one-fifth of the population.
Shih said this group already accounts for more than 42 percent of NHI spending, while annual funding for long-term care has risen from less than NT$5 billion in 2015 to more than NT$110 billion this year.
He cautioned that the financial burden would grow as Taiwan’s population ages, saying the eventual fiscal impact could exceed initial estimates and threaten the sustainability of the health insurance system.
The TPP caucus estimated that the amendment would add nearly NT$39 billion in annual government spending, based on a monthly subsidy of NT$826 per senior.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus secretary-general Fan Yun (范雲) said that determining who should bear the cost and where the funding should come from is a serious issue.
Bypassing committee reviews to send a bill straight to a second reading is the worst possible approach, DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said, adding that bills involving major expenditures should clearly explain how costs would be allocated between the central and local governments, or whether the central government would cover the entire cost.
Additional reporting by Lin Hsin-han
