Europe’s big election season could change everything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decisionmaking has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under US President Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This might be about to change.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez rolled the dice last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s Party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonized by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is ahead in the polls at the moment.
In addition to Spain, France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe.
Illustration: Kevin Sheu
Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Center-right and far-right groups are able to form a majority in the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. While this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump.
This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party was punished at the polls and the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is being reversed, after Viktor Orban was ousted in a landslide election. In Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing center-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats, scraped a victory. So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend — Alternative fur Deutschland’s victory in eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe — it does not hold everywhere, at all times.
If the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirm Giorgia Meloni as Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically.
If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. However, they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defense and technology.
And it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanizing and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by US MAGA supporters and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outside Italy is that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sanchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jaroslaw Kaczynski and Alberto Nunez Feijoo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project — a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in the past few years — but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months.
The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK might have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade, publicly recognize that Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has done.
It has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism — just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now could be the time for the UK to remind its European neighbors what it means to be out there, all alone.

A total of 10 candidates running for city and county council seats in next month’s local elections have been ruled ineligible, including New Party candidate You Zhi-bin (游智彬), the Central Election Commission (CEC) said yesterday.
Of the 10 disqualified council candidates, five were running for special municipality council seats and five for county or city council seats, the CEC said in a news release.
You, who is running for a Taipei City Council seat, was born in China’s Fujian Province.
Photo: Taipei Times
The CEC said he was originally a resident of China and submitted proof that he had relinquished his Chinese household registration in April 2025.
Under the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例) and relevant election laws, people in You’s circumstances must have been registered as residents in Taiwan for at least 10 years after submitting proof that they had relinquished their mainland household registration.
You had not met this requirement, the CEC said.
In addition, four disqualified city council candidates were ruled ineligible because of criminal convictions, or sentences that had not been fully served, the commission said.
They were Lin Cheng-feng (林正峰) of New Taipei City, convicted of money laundering; Cheng Po-chi (鄭伯其) of Taichung, convicted of fraud; Tsao Wei-kuo (曹暐國) of Tainan, convicted under the law governing firearms and ammunition; and Hsiao Hsiang-han (蕭湘瀚) of Taoyuan, whose sentence for offenses including obstruction of official duties remained uncompleted.
The five disqualified county and city council candidates were Chung Jen-ming (鍾任明) of Yunlin County, Ho Po- lun (何博倫) of Chiayi County, Chou Chun-yu (周駿宥) of Hualien County, Shih Yung-cheng (石永城) of Kinmen County and Chang Fang-li (張芳麗) of Keelung.
The CEC said candidate numbers will be drawn at local election commission offices on Oct. 23. Candidates’ financial disclosure information will also be published online for one year from the date the candidate lists are finalized.
The 2026 local elections, slated for Nov. 28, are also known as the “9-in-1” elections because voters in Taiwan’s 22 cities and counties will cast ballots for candidates vying for nine different local government posts, including city mayors, county magistrates, and city and county councilors.

No trade in obedience to Beijing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

When Beijing announced new restrictions on a company it identifies with Shen Tu-cheng (沈土城), the father of Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), it portrayed them as an exposure of hypocrisy.
Puma Shen, the Democratic Progressive Party’s Taipei mayoral candidate, opposes China while working with relatives to profit from Chinese businesses, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said.
The announcement raised the more consequential question of whether trading with Chinese companies obliges someone to accept Beijing’s politics and does that obligation extend to the trader’s children?
On Oct. 14, the office announced restrictions on VWAY, alleging that Shen Tu-cheng had used it to circumvent restrictions imposed last year on another company, Sicuens International Co. It prohibited VWAY from transacting or cooperating with Chinese organizations, businesses and individuals.
The allegations require evidence. Yet the political justification was explicit: Beijing would not permit businesses associated with people it calls “Taiwan independence diehards” to profit from China.
Puma Shen’s Taipei campaign acknowledges that his father’s Latin American trading business purchases products from Chinese suppliers, alongside suppliers elsewhere. Whether transactions occurred as Beijing alleges remains a separate question, but the acknowledged trading relationship does not itself establish political misconduct.
A purchase is simply an exchange. A supplier delivers goods for payment, while a trader buys those goods expecting a margin on resale. Because both parties are pursuing their own commercial interests, neither is bestowing a favor that entitles them to political loyalty.
Yet Beijing’s accusation treats commercial opportunity as a benefit bringing by the Chinese state, carrying an obligation of gratitude and obedience. Under that logic, criticizing the government becomes an act of ingratitude.
Consider where that reasoning leads. A Taiwanese businessperson who buys Chinese machinery would be expected to refrain from challenging Beijing. If that person’s son enters politics, he too must consider whether his views will endanger the family’s access to suppliers, effectively turning a routine commercial tie into a leash on public expression.
Governments impose sanctions, of course. Financial relationships can also warrant scrutiny, particularly when public officials have interests they should disclose. Neither point should be dismissed.
However, genuine scrutiny requires specific questions. Does an official own the company? Have they concealed financial benefits? Have they sought preferential treatment or used public office to advance a private interest? Have they condemned conduct in others while exempting themselves from the same standard?
Those are questions about accountability and a father’s purchases from Chinese suppliers do not answer them.
Nor is opposing Beijing’s coercion equivalent to opposing every commercial exchange with China. A person can buy Chinese products, respect Chinese people and still reject the Chinese Communist Party’s demands, because economic contact does not erase political differences.
Indeed, the restrictions expose precisely the danger that critics of dependence on China have long warned about: An ordinary business relationship can easily be turned into leverage over someone’s political choices.
The family dimension makes that leverage especially troubling. Pressure need not fall directly on a critic to affect them; punishing a parent’s business creates costs that travel through personal relationships, signaling to others that their public positions might bring consequences for relatives who bear no responsibility for them.
Beijing might hope the hypocrisy accusation damages Puma Shen. It might also want to demonstrate that restrictions cannot be escaped by changing companies.
However, the announcement can be read another way: Puma Shen’s opposition has persisted despite the potential cost to his family.
While that does not prove his integrity, it certainly undermines the claim that commercial ties dictate political allegiance.
Taiwanese officials should face scrutiny for their conduct, disclosures and decisions. Allegations should be tested against evidence, without granting anyone immunity merely because Beijing is the accuser.
The same standard requires rejecting conclusions that the evidence does not establish. Trade is not proof of allegiance, just as family association is not proof of misconduct.
Beijing can restrict access to its market. What it cannot reasonably claim is that a commercial transaction purchases the buyer’s political conscience — or that of the buyer’s son.
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong now living in Taiwan.

Warsh optimistic about US resilience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh voiced optimism yesterday about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been “hanging in there” amid continued energy shocks and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation.
He said the US and many other economies were benefiting from an “investment surge” driven by artificial intelligence (AI) but broadening to other sectors, creating a near-term demand shock that was putting upward pressure on inflation.
“I came out of meetings here yesterday and today and it’s hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices,” Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
Photo: EPA
With inflation a “common challenge,” Warsh said global central banks undertook “a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world, and that means there’s no free riders.”
In the US “we made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” he said in a reference to the Fed’s interest-rate hike last month.
However, in keeping with his style since taking the reins as Fed chief in May, he gave no preview about whether he feels more interest-rate hikes would be needed, or when.
“I don’t prejudge meetings,” Warsh added in the discussion with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva. “I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”
Financial markets have taken those remarks on board and are betting the Fed would wait until December to raise rates.
That remained true even after reports this week showed two different measures of inflation running higher than expected and heading in the wrong direction from the Fed’s 2 percent goal.
Warsh was optimistic about the impact of AI on economic growth and productivity in the medium-term, even as he said it would be a “very bumpy” path toward what he expected would be faster productivity growth in the “real economy” that would bolster wealth.
“It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s going to hit the supply side of the economy,” he said. “We don’t know in the next 12 or 18 months its effect on employment, but if you believe like I believe, which is it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive, that it’s going to make it so that we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing.”
A task force convened to advise the Fed on the impact of AI on productivity and jobs would hold a “field hearing” in San Francisco on Nov. 16, he said, in what would be a first public peek at the group’s work.
Warsh said that central bankers meeting in Bangkok had a common vision to safeguard price stability and were taking action to back that view, which was giving “confidence to businesses and households that’s so important for growth to continue.”
“I believe optimistically — you might think naively — at least in the United States, we’re going to come out of this stronger with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth,” Warsh said.

Infantino offers apology, but ‘no answers’ for FFE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:43 UTC
01:42:43 KST

FIFA president Gianni Infantino gave “no satisfactory answers” when grilled on Thursday during a meeting to discuss his attempts to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, senior members of soccer’s global governing body said, but he did offer an apology for the failed project.
“We asked a great many critical questions, but there were no satisfactory answers from my point of view,” said Bernd Neuendorf, the head of the German Football Association, who is also a member of the FIFA Council.
Neuendorf was speaking after the Council met behind closed doors at the body’s Zurich headquarters, where Infantino’s FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was one of the main topics on the agenda.
Photo: AFP
Infantino has been under severe pressure since his announcement in late July that he wanted to open FIFA’s premium competitions such as the World Cup to private investors. That plan was ultimately abandoned in the face of widespread criticism, with a rebellion led by European governing body UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF, which runs the sport in North and Central America and the Caribbean.
“I apologized for the mistakes that we made in relation to the communication and consultation process related to the FIFA Forward Enterprise project,” Infantino said in a video published by FIFA.
“But what is important to remember is that it was a proposal, so in no way a done deal, just a proposal, that actually intended to enable FIFA to invest more in our member associations.”
However, the FIFA chief reaffirmed that the FFE initiative “has been permanently withdrawn and will not reappear in any form.”
Infantino has headed FIFA since 2016 and is running for re-election in March, despite calls for him to stand down in the wake of the FFE plan.
So far, no heavyweight candidate has put themselves forward to run against him.
Debbie Hewitt, the chair of the English Football Association who is also a FIFA vice-president, told reporters that Infantino is “not fit to be FIFA president” unless he releases all documents pertaining to the failed sell-off plan and answers key questions. Hewitt and Neuendorf are among the 36 members of the FIFA Council, along with Infantino.
“We were asked to submit our questions” in relation to the plan which was not put to the FIFA Council before the July announcement, Hewitt said.
Many leading European national associations have withdrawn their support for Infantino in the upcoming election because of the uproar caused by FFE and other controversies, including his relationship with US President Donald Trump.
Chief among those were Infantino’s decision to create a FIFA Peace Prize and award it to Trump in December last year’s World Cup draw, and the decision to suspend a ban for US striker Folarin Balogun following a red card during the World Cup after Trump intervened directly by phoning Infantino.
“I speak for myself as a Council member — from my position nothing has shifted,” Hewitt added. “I have no new information that makes me feel any differently to how I felt when I went in, other than we do have a president of FIFA who is apologetic about what has happened, and secondly a promise again that we will get the information that we have requested.”
FIFA confirmed its intention to set up a US$6.35 billion development fund for the next four years, a plan which is expected to be finalized by the Council at its next meeting in December.
To finance the fund, which would allow money to be distributed to FIFA’s 211 federations as well as to the regional confederations, it would draw in part on its financial reserves after this year’s commercially successful World Cup. The plan would allow for the payment of US$25 million to all 211 member federations. Infantino may hope the latest plan reinforces his position ahead of the election.
The deadline for submitting candidacies is Nov.18.

EDITORIAL: Pregnancy and migrant care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:43 UTC
01:42:43 KST

The Ministry of Labor on Tuesday rejected claims that employers must financially support a migrant domestic worker’s entire family if she becomes pregnant.
The statement came as a result of a complaint by a family who, shortly after hiring a migrant domestic helper, discovered that she was pregnant. TVBS reported that the family had applied to hire the woman from Indonesia in April, but discovered that she was pregnant less than a month after she had begun working. The family accused the employment agency of withholding information.
However, given current laws, it is unlikely that the agency was aware of the woman’s pregnancy. The Regulations Governing the Management of the Health Examination of Employed Foreigners (受聘僱外國人健康檢查管理辦法) do not require that medical reports submitted in workers’ home countries to apply for a Taiwan visa include a pregnancy test.
In 2007, pregnancy tests were removed from mandatory health checks conducted within three days of a worker’s arrival in Taiwan, a measure intended to align local regulations with international human rights standards, gender equality and non-discrimination principles.
Moreover, the Gender Equality in Employment Act (性別平等工作法) prohibits employers from using pregnancy as a reason to terminate an employee’s contract.
From a legal perspective, pregnancy alone should not jeopardize a migrant domestic worker’s employment. However, the TVBS report highlights a long-standing conflict between migrant domestic workers, their employers and the regulations governing their employment.
A decade ago, an Indonesian caregiver who was reportedly unaware of her pregnancy gave birth in her employer’s home, prompting calls to reinstate mandatory pregnancy tests for migrant workers prior to employment. However, as the government said, that would be discriminatory. As more than 95 percent of migrant domestic workers in Taiwan are women, such a policy could reinforce the inequalities that employment protections are intended to prevent.
Families that employ caregivers might be concerned about the practical and financial implications of their employee becoming pregnant. Many are ordinary families struggling to provide round-the-clock care for elderly relatives while balancing work, childcare and other responsibilities. Employers have complained that hiring a migrant caregiver can cost up to NT$40,000 (US$1,237) per month and that they have few alternatives if a worker cannot perform their duties.
The government must recognize these pressures and ensure that its long-term care system can respond to them.
However, the difficulties are largely questions of policy, not reasons to question workers’ basic rights. A caregiver might be able to perform many of her duties while pregnant, depending on her health and the demands of the job.
For the employer, the immediate concern is how to maintain care for a dependent family member.
However, for a pregnant worker, the consequences can extend far beyond a temporary interruption to employment. She might face an extended period without income while preparing for childbirth and childcare, as well as the risk of discrimination or pressure to leave her job.
Those difficulties might be compounded by living in a foreign country without family, friends or sufficient language skills to seek support. The burdens are not equivalent, particularly when migrant workers have considerably fewer financial and legal protections.
The government’s Long-Term Care 3.0 program provides up to 52 days per year of respite and short-term care services for families requiring temporary assistance. The labor ministry said that NT$2 billion was allocated for such services.
The measures are a step in the right direction, but the government must ensure that families can access support when a caregiver becomes pregnant or otherwise needs time away from work. At the same time, it must consider what support is available to the workers themselves.
Taiwan is expanding access to migrant domestic workers in response to its aging population and growing demand for the industry. In a field dominated by women, it is only natural that the issue of pregnancy would arise — but it should never be grounds for refusing to hire or terminating a worker.
The government must find ways to help families arrange alternative care while ensuring that pregnant workers have adequate financial and employment protections. Neither the workers nor employers should have to bear the burden alone.

Scientists under pressure to delay key report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:42 UTC
01:42:42 KST

Scientists are coming under pressure from some petrostates and major developing countries to delay publication of a key global report on the climate, despite pleas from vulnerable countries worried that postponement could spell disaster for them.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-convened body of the world’s leading climate scientists, is meeting this week in Addis Ababa to discuss its seventh assessment report, a comprehensive survey of all that is known about the climate crisis.
The report, known as AR7, was scheduled to appear in 2028 in time for deliberations at the 33rd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP33).
COP33 is scheduled to critique governments’ actions to cut greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris agreement’s target of limiting temperatures to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels.
However, a group of countries, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia and including India and China, is pressing for publication of the report to be pushed back to 2029.
They say this is in order to allow developing countries to have more input into the scientific findings. Climate science has been dominated for three decades by countries and blocs including the EU, the UK and the US, though under US President Donald Trump’s administration it has been severely curtailed.
Many poor and vulnerable countries — which are among those contributing least scientifically — strongly oppose any such delay. Ministers from 34 members of the High Ambition Coalition, made up of some of the poorest countries and those most at risk from climate breakdown, as well as the EU and the Least Developed Countries grouping, called on Friday for publication of AR7 to be expedited.
Jess Gasper, a minister for the Marshall Islands, said: “We cannot allow political interests to determine which science the world is willing to hear.”
Jiwoh Emmanuel Abdulai, the minister of environment for Sierra Leone, said: “The Paris agreement can only deliver on its promise if the best available science continues to guide climate change negotiations.”
Global temperatures have already exceeded the threshold of 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, though the IPCC has claimed there is still a way to restore them. If national emissions targets are met, global temperatures would exceed 1.8°C. That is a very big “if,” as most countries do not have fully articulated plans for meeting the targets, meaning far higher temperatures are likely.
The global stocktake at COP33 in 2028 is meant to provide a check on whether governments need to ramp up their efforts, and is crucial to the Paris agreement “ratchet” which demands stronger action.
AR7 is the latest in a series of comprehensive reports on climate science dating back to 1988 that have grown increasingly stark in their warnings of the impacts of pouring carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. The last such assessment, published in three parts in 2021 and 2022, found that unless emissions were swiftly reduced the world would face unstoppable impacts that would swiftly become catastrophic and in some cases irreversible.
AR7 is expected to strike an even more urgent note, as greenhouse gases in the interim have continued to rise, and the impacts such as rising temperatures, heatwaves, floods and droughts are increasingly apparent. This year has seen temperature records tumble and drought grip swathes of Europe and the US, while the El Nino weather system, supercharged by the climate crisis, is forecast to bring extreme weather and rising food prices.
The IPCC is supposed to carry on its work free from government interference. However, key documents known as the “summary for policymakers,” published alongside the thousands of pages of the official reports, are subject to approval from all governments that wish to play a role.
The Guardian has uncovered evidence of interference in the IPCC’s assessments by representatives of oil interests under control of Saudi Arabia’s monarchy.
Despite these flaws, the IPCC is the most authoritative global body on climate science, and many experts say delaying its input to the COP33 talks would weaken the global response to the climate crisis at a time when adverse geopolitics already threaten progress on emissions. The US is leading attacks on climate action, but far-right populist politicians across Europe also want to water down the EU’s regulations, and in Latin America a tide of rightwing populism, particularly in Brazil, Colombia and Argentina, threatens the same.
Within this context, waiting for developing countries to be able to contribute more science makes little sense, according to Claudio Angelo of the Observatorio do Clima in Brazil.
“It’s extremely concerning the way the structural issue of equity is being weaponized by some big developing countries,” he said. “It’s true that integrated assessment [climate science] models are mostly built by global north countries and therefore biased. [But] that’s not a problem that can be fixed just by giving the IPCC an extra few months to work. We can’t afford to leave Addis without a decision [to press ahead with the 2028 timetable].”
Angelo asked why countries such as India and Saudi Arabia were claiming to be standing up for developing countries by backing a delay: “They have the money and the technology to send rockets to the moon — why couldn’t they bother to build their own models to be reviewed by the IPCC?”
The row has exposed splits within the environmental NGO movement. Some civil society groups are sympathetic to calls for more science from developing countries, and some are considering backing the call for a delay.
The IPCC declined to comment. The Guardian has approached Saudi Arabia, Russia, China and India for comment.

The US is unreliable, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) leadership is aligned with the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), and Taiwan does not have the military capability to defend itself in a prolonged war without help. What hope does Taiwan have? Quite a bit more, in fact, than Shuster lets on. Shuster points to genuine problems. The first Donald Trump administration had a mostly positive record on Taiwan policy. It regularized the arms sales process, enhanced the military-to-military relationship, and treated Taiwan more like a normal

China proposes AI export curbs to manage security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:39 UTC
01:42:39 KST

China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to keep closer control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector.
The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds.
Chinese AI startups have this summer made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models such as Moonshot (月之暗面) AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s (深度求索) latest editions offer better pricing, and Chinese companies also favor the approach of sharing the weights — used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer — of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them. They are also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI Co (北京智譜華章科技) making their wares available on US cloud service providers such as Amazon Web Services.
Photo: Reuters
The proposed export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of AI technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defense industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities.
“The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models containing at least 2 trillion parameters — such as Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding Ltd’s (阿里巴巴) Qwen3.8-Max — or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety. The curb would cover model weights, checkpoints, source code and architecture.
The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licensing regime and potential US sanctions.
AI models trained on China’s “core data,” as defined by relevant legislation such as the Data Security Law, would be banned from export, the proposal said. The Data Security Law describes state core data as “data concerning national security, the lifeline of the national economy, key public livelihoods and major public interests.”
Open-source technology and research already in the public domain would not be covered, and the government would provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies. Beijing said the measures were not aimed at any particular country, region or entity.
China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. The measure took effect yesterday and applies to transactions already underway but not completed, including intellectual-property transfers, overseas licensing and changes that place Chinese technology owners under foreign control.

Newly identified green star leaves astronomers amazed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:36 UTC
01:42:36 KST

Astronomers for the first time have identified a green star, documenting a dense stellar remnant called a white dwarf that became a ghostly shade of chartreuse after ingesting rocky debris from planets that had once orbited it.
A star’s color is typically governed by its temperature, with cooler stars appearing orange, the sun and stars similar to it appearing white, and the hottest ones appearing a pale blue.
However, the formula is different for a white dwarf, which is the leftover core of a low to medium-mass star that burned through its nuclear fuel and blew off its outer layers. Most white dwarfs have colors similar to other stars, and their average color is white, but changes in their chemistry over time can turn some of them into rarer colors.
Photo: Reuters
The newly identified green one, named WD J1330+6435, is a white dwarf in the Milky Way galaxy that is about 280 light-years from Earth in the constellation Draco.
“We first became interested in this white dwarf because bits of planetary material have fallen onto its surface, enriching its outer layers in elements including calcium, lithium and, in particular, sodium,” said astrophysicist Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick in England, lead author of the study published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.
In normal stars, sodium absorbs a very specific wavelength of orange — the same orange that gives sodium street lamps their characteristic color.
“In this particular white dwarf, however, the density is so high that the sodium atoms are constantly being bombarded by surrounding helium atoms, which alters the sodium atomic energy levels,” Hollands said.
“The end result is that the sodium atoms no longer absorb one very narrow wavelength of orange — they absorb the yellows, oranges and some of the red wavelengths. And what you’re left with is a star that has a beautiful chartreuse green glow, something that wouldn’t be possible for sun-like stars,” Hollands said.
The discovery was part of a project assessing the color of white dwarfs as human eyes would see them. A white dwarf typically has half the mass of the sun compacted into the size of Earth.
“Because white dwarfs are super-dense stars — they are roughly the size of the Earth, but contain about 165,000 times its mass — even a small amount of sodium blocks out a large amount of the orange light coming out of the star,” University of Warwick astrophysicist and study coauthor Boris Gansicke said.
“In the end, it’s all very similar to the mixing of colors in the palette of a painter. They start with a few basic colors, then mix them together to form any color they need for their painting. Take away some of the color going into the mix, and the output will change,” Gansicke said.
‘SALMON PINK’
The researchers studied 151 white dwarfs within about 65 light-years of Earth, with white the average color.
One showed perhaps the reddest hue of any known star, a salmon pink. Named WD J1011+2845, it is 48 light-years from Earth in the constellation Leo Minor. This time, it was not sodium that was changing the palette, but carbon.
“Rather than something hitting the star, in this case the carbon comes out from its deep interior,” Gansicke said.
Data used by the researchers included light spectrum observations from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey using a telescope in New Mexico, as well as white dwarf spectrum models they developed.
They found that white dwarf colors divide into distinct groups based on atmospheric composition. Carbon-rich white dwarfs usually were pink or purple. Those enriched with debris from shattered remnants of planetary systems leaned toward yellow. Lower-temperature white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres tended toward a cyan or pale blue hue.
In all, they spanned almost every color of the spectrum.
While WD J1330+6435 was the first documented example of a green star in the real world, green stars have existed in science fiction, including in the recent comic book movie Supergirl.
“It does show that the universe is sometimes just as weird as anything science fiction can conjure up,” Hollands said.

Avoid Chinese SYS events: MAC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:36 UTC
01:42:36 KST

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) has recommended that Taiwanese avoid events in China next month for the anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen (孫逸仙), lauded by Taipei and Beijing for bringing an end to the last imperial dynasty, and a major historical fault line.
China announced last year that it would honor the 160th birthday of Sun on Nov. 12. Sun died in 1925 after helping to lead the 1911 revolution that ended centuries of rule by emperors and empresses.
Sun founded the Republic of China (ROC), which fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s (毛澤東) Chinese communists, and which remains Taiwan’s formal name. In a statement on Thursday, the MAC said people should not travel to China for anniversary events and “echo the Chinese communists’ narratives.”
Photo: Reuters
China’s interpretation of Sun “does not stay faithful to historical fact... It uses these commemorations to promote a narrative of ‘opposing Taiwan independence and promoting unification,’” the council said.
Beijing says Sun is a national hero and patriot, as well as the forerunner of China’s 1949 revolution. China has not announced what events it has planned for the anniversary.
In 2016, Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) said Sun opposed attempts to “split the country,” adding that the “complete reunification of the motherland” was a sacred duty for all Chinese.
In Taiwan, Sun is officially called the “father of the ROC” and his portrait hangs in the Presidential Office, although his political philosophy the “Three Principles of the People” is no longer a required school text for children.
While President William Lai (賴清德) and the ruling Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, they have been striking a tougher tone with Beijing on the role of the ROC.
Taiwan’s government has demonstrated irritation with Beijing’s attempts to claim credit for the Allied victory in World War II, saying it was the ROC government that fought with the Allies against Japan, as the People’s Republic of China did not exist then.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to a request for comment.

====================================================================================================

The not-so-secret vulnerability in Ukraine’s drone arsenal? Chinese technology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

Since Russia invaded more than four years ago, Ukraine has become a global leader in military drone innovation, enabling its forces to grind a much larger enemy to a stalemate.
But this technological force multiplier has come with an unsettling vulnerability: Ukrainian drone makers are highly dependent on electronics made by China, a key Russian ally.
Ukraine’s greatest fear is that the Chinese government could severely restrict its access to these critical parts. It also worries that Russian defense companies that need these same supplies could be given preferential treatment by Chinese factories.
Photo: AP
Over the past two years, Ukraine has sought to break its dependence on China by expanding domestic manufacturing and importing more supplies from Taiwan, Europe and the US. That has minimized its need for Chinese-made electric motors, flight controllers and other parts.
Yet Ukraine cannot entirely break free from China, whose lower costs and vastly greater production capacity cannot be matched by allied suppliers.
“If China stops their production to us ... we are blinded,” said Andrii Taganskyi, an executive at Odd Systems, a Ukrainian weapons manufacturer that develops cameras for drones. “This is the scariest part.”
China has tightened controls on exports of drones and related equipment for several years, citing concerns about prolonging the war in Ukraine. While the restrictions have not stopped the flow of Chinese components to Ukraine, they have caused delays and driven up costs, pushing Ukrainian companies toward intermediaries in third countries.
“China has leverage,” said Robert Tallost, a researcher at the think tank RUSI. “They could direct more material to Russia while restricting supplies to the West.”
China’s Foreign Ministry said Beijing takes a “prudent and responsible” approach to military exports. It said it opposes the use of civilian drones for military purposes, and urged all sides to find a political settlement of the war.
SWITCHING WOULD BE EXPENSIVE
Ukraine has earned worldwide recognition for its cutting-edge drone industry, designing and assembling systems that have changed modern warfare. Yet many of the materials and components that go into Ukrainian drones cannot be localized anytime soon.
Magnets, motors, chips, thermal sensors, battery cells and more still largely come from China, a dozen Ukrainian manufacturers said.
Switching entirely to Western alternatives could raise costs by as much as 60 percent and cut production by a similar amount, said Oleksandr Yakovenko of TAF Industries, a major Ukrainian defense company. That is not a viable tradeoff, Yakovenko and other executives said.
Still, Ukrainian drone makers have begun to wean themselves off of China.
Three years ago, the Ukrainian drone maker Vyriy relied upon China for nearly 90 percent of the components in its attack drones. “Today, about 70 percent to 80 percent of our components are made in Ukraine,” said Vyriy’s founder, Oleksii Babenko.
This increasing self-reliance has an extra benefit in the midst of a grueling war. Drones and drone components made domestically can be redesigned in a matter of days to meet urgent demands on the battlefield, whereas it can take months for such changes to filter through foreign supply chains, said Artur Savchii, an analyst at the Kyiv-based think tank Serpens Center for International Security.
At the beginning of 2024, nearly 90 percent of Ukraine’s imported drone parts came directly from China. In the first eight months of this year, it was just 28 percent, according to Ukraine Customs data.
But the drop may not be as dramatic as it seems. Many components recorded as coming from Poland and the Czech Republic, for example, very likely were manufactured in China and routed through those countries.
CHINA HARD TO REPLACE
Ukraine can assemble batteries but must import the cells inside them. Motors require imported magnets and copper. And while Ukraine can manufacture some electronics, Chinese companies can produce them at far greater scale and roughly half the cost.
Thermal cameras show just how difficult it is for Ukraine to break its dependence.
Ukrainian companies design the cameras themselves but still rely on imported sensors, which detect infrared radiation, and lenses that cannot be made domestically, manufacturers said. One of the key raw materials is germanium, an element that China has in abundance, making Chinese lenses far cheaper than European alternatives.
Although the US and Europe also make sensors, most of them are used domestically.
Ukraine could build thermal cameras entirely from European components, Taganskyi said, but capacity and cost are barriers: Europe produces about 600,000 thermal sensors a year, versus Ukraine’s estimated need for 4 million, he said.
For now, some Chinese components remain essential.
“Without this 5 percent, there is no camera,” Taganskyi said.
COMPETING WITH RUSSIA FOR COMPONENTS
To be sure, Russia is even more dependent on China than Ukraine, experts say – in part because of Western sanctions that restrict its access to other markets. The difference is that Moscow doesn’t face the risk of its allies in Beijing tipping the scales in favor of Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed Russia’s advantage vis-a-vis its relationship with China during a recent interview.
“They are slightly on Russia’s side. And by ‘slightly,’ I mean not direct weapons supplies, but a greater openness to them, a greater willingness to help them rather than us – and for a country as large as China, ‘slightly’ means a lot,” Zelenskyy said.
Competing with Russia for the attention of the same Chinese factories carries another risk for Ukraine: revealing its needs to the enemy.
The risk is clear to Babenko. A Russian drone recovered by the Ukrainian army on the front line was equipped with highly sophisticated antennas useful for long-range reconnaissance and guidance, and Babenko’s company traced the technology to a Chinese supplier. When the Ukrainians reached out to buy several hundred, the supplier initially refused, then agreed on the condition that they keep the deal private because the technology had been developed for Russia, Babenko said.
The episode underscored why domestic production is a matter of strategic security, Babenko said.
“We should be ready for that situation when China will fully choose the Russian position,” he said.
GETTING AROUND RESTRICTIONS
China has tightened export controls on drones and related components several times since 2023. The restrictions have made it impossible for Ukrainian companies to purchase some long-range civilian drones, motors, cameras and infrared imaging equipment directly from Chinese companies.
The restrictions, which were tightened this summer, have forced Ukrainian defense companies to adapt by using intermediaries in third countries to keep Chinese-made drones and parts moving. Many said they suffered disruptions and higher costs.
“We just need to have partner companies which purchase it in other countries, then a third, then to Ukraine,” said one Ukrainian drone executive. “It’s like a special operation.”
Another executive said companies also get around export controls by altering product descriptions on government paperwork. “Sometimes you have to be creative,” he said. Both executives spoke anonymously to avoid revealing their tactics.
For now, Chinese factories’ willingness to do business with Ukrainian buyers, and the ease of routing goods through third countries, makes the trade difficult to shut down, said Joseph Webster, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.
“This dependence is not going to go away in a war where both sides are burning through equipment at a horrifying scale,” said Samuel Bendett, an analyst of military robotics. “Where domestic industry cannot keep up, China can.”

Artificial intelligence cracks centuries-old ciphers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:34 UTC
01:42:34 KST

Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the wartime missive written in code, creating a puzzle that went unsolved for more than 200 years — until artificial intelligence (AI) cracked it in a matter of hours.
AI is helping non-specialists unlock the secrets of historical sources, a trend described as a “turning point” in a field previously the preserve of academics and dedicated hobbyists.
One new sleuth is Carter Church, a 27-year-old AI engineer who decrypted a 19th-century letter to one of Napoleon’s generals.
Photo: AFP
Without digital tools, the task could have taken weeks, but the latest model from OpenAI broke the cipher in six hours.
“What AI mostly brings is persistence,” Church said, adding that he felt “an unbelievable sense of satisfaction and excitement when I saw the result.”
The message from 1809 — detailing French and allied troops’ positions in two dozen lines of symbols, numbers and letters — had lain ignored in an online academic archive.
Because traditional, low-tech methods to crack ciphers are effective, but time and labor-intensive, historians “have more important problems to solve, so many ciphers like this often sit unattended,” Church said.
To find the solution, Church, who works at US cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, needed to learn “very little” about code-breaking techniques or the historical period.
He spent some evenings going over it, then consulted Japanese patent engineer Satoshi Tomokiyo, who maintains an online list of unsolved ciphers, to verify it.
“2026 will be remembered as a turning point for codebreaking of historical ciphers,” Tomokiyo wrote on his Web site Cryptiana, a go-to resource for the small, but enthusiastic global community of amateur cryptographers.
Researchers were already developing AI models to break ciphers, but the public release of state-of-the-art generalist tools has unleashed dozens of new solutions.
Although Church used OpenAI’s most powerful model, GPT-6 Astra, other people have used top offerings from US lab Anthropic instead.
Tomokiyo said that since the middle of last month, most of the ciphers on his list have been cracked using AI.
“There remain some tough problems,” which could stay an enigma for years to come, because there is less relevant data available to help AI figure them out, he said.
“I’m excited long-time problems are now solved, but on the other hand, I have mixed feelings, because AI seems to have solved these difficult problems so easily,” he said.
With technology draining the satisfaction of being first to crack a cipher, a fellow code-breaker told Tomokiyo: “I feel useless.”
AI is surpassing human abilities in pursuits from mathematics to computer programming, while threatening to alter or even eradicate many jobs. The technology is transforming the work of historians not only by decoding documents, but also by analyzing millions of medieval manuscripts or helping read ancient scrolls.
Too fragile to be unrolled without risking destruction, the Herculaneum Papyri — hundreds of papyrus scrolls carbonized in the eruption of Vesuvius in 79AD — are now being X-rayed and analyzed by AI to reveal the hidden writing inside.
Researchers in Italy announced in June the first complete virtual unrolling of a scroll, which turned out to be a treatise on ethics.
AI is also being used to build a huge, searchable collection of previously inaccessible sources on Jewish history and culture by transcribing 10 million pages of Hebrew manuscripts.
“It’s gigantic. No human being could process such a quantity” of data, said project leader Daniel Stoekl Ben Ezra, of the Ecole Pratique des Hautes Etudes in Paris.
Researchers hope the databases created using the digitized text — which he likens to a kind of “huge Facebook of the past” — could help bring to light links between people, places and ideas.
And at the French capital’s Notre Dame Cathedral, an AI system has been trained to transcribe 14,600 Latin pages from the church’s medieval archives — a task not dissimilar to code-breaking.
“These are minutes drawn up by notaries who abbreviate their decisions. The script is highly administrative, very pragmatic ... with rather technical vocabulary,” said historian Julie Claustre, who leads the e-NDP project.
With character recognition rates ranging between 88 and 94 percent, the project has revealed information about the cathedral’s daily life, its building work, its staff and the care of abandoned children.
Doing the same by hand would take “several decades,” but “it’s not just a time-saver,” Claustre said.
Automation enables “inquiries that were not previously possible; it transforms the conditions of research,” she said.

Sunak drew from a metaphor by former Singaporean prime minister Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀): A big fish will eat a smaller fish, and the smaller fish will eat the shrimp. Maritime issues need framework for a crisis: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:31 UTC
01:42:31 KST

Experts at the International Conference on Sea Lane Security on Wednesday called for early preventive measures, including the establishment of international maritime cooperation mechanisms, to safeguard shipping routes through the Taiwan Strait against Chinese maritime coercion.
China’s maritime quarantine operations would more likely come in the form of “law enforcement,” “maritime governance,” or “rights protection” instead of a formal quarantine, Institute for National Defense and Security Research associate research fellow Lee Jyun-yi (李俊毅) said at conference hosted by the Ocean Affairs Council.
While most studies assumed that the China Coast Guard (CCG) would be deployed in the vicinity of Taiwan, the institute’s research showed that a quarantine could enforce an outright termination of maritime traffic to and from Taiwan, he said.
Photo: Coast Guard Administration via AFP
“Taiwan might find it difficult to do anything if the CCG operates in waters well beyond Taiwan’s jurisdiction,” Lee said.
Lee considered maritime quarantine a political and military attack involving the CCG — a paramilitary force — that China would use to test Taiwan’s sovereignty and jurisdiction or disrupt energy and food imports.
He called for preventing such efforts from snowballing into a crisis in which Taiwan might be forced into negotiations on terms favorable to China.
Taiwan should improve communication with the shipping and commerce industries to sustain their confidence in sailing through the Strait, Lee said.
British Royal Navy retired vice admiral Duncan Potts said the international maritime community requires confidence to trade.
“We want the global trading community to continue coming to Taiwan,” he said, adding the global trading community is not an entity that can be summoned or a partnership that can be formed without regional countries.
Potts called for building maritime security architecture and partnership before a crisis breaks.
“Understand the triggers and what time you would have to deal with things,” he said, adding that early preparations like preplanning or tabletop exercises would make it easier to respond to emergencies.
Chisako Masuo, associate professor of Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Social and Cultural Studies, presented a photo of a transcontinental cargo train with more than 50 containers running from Europe to China.
China not only continued to build such railways heading to Europe, but also has many gas or oil pipelines linking to Russia, Pakistan and Myanmar, she said.
“If quarantine happens on the maritime side, our economic life would be stopped,” Masuo said of not only Taiwan, but of Japan and South Korea as well.
However, China can survive with the help of its continental neighbors thanks to the economic corridors it has built, she said.
Most discussion about Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) maritime strategies focused on military and overlooked his attempt at hybridizing civil and military deployments, Masuo said, adding that Xi sought to dominate the economic side of maritime governance as well.
She called for surveillance of the Chinese maritime safety agency’s activities, which has the authority to initiate maritime quarantine.
Masuo cited the Chinese National Cultural Heritage Administration’s participation in a maritime law enforcement meeting in March, saying that China might be building a new mechanism for “underwater law enforcement.”
Korean Institute for Asian Strategy Studies president Lee Changhyung said a maritime quarantine is different from a military blockade, and such a crisis could embroil all of northeast Asia instead of Taiwan alone.
Maritime quarantine would be more difficult to define than military blockade, as the CCG and Chinese maritime authorities or militia could stand in for the Chinese military in disrupting shipping operations, he said.
Navigational warnings, exercise zones or shipping inspections could be applied to pressure global businesses into rerouting their ships around the Strait, Lee said.
That would increase the costs of transportation and insurance, he said, adding stability in the Strait is an issue of economic security for South Korea.
“China also benefits from safe and open sea routes in East Asia,” Lee said. “Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are not only in the interest of Taiwan, South Korea, Japan or the US, but also in China’s interest.”

Photo: Taipei Times

People who suspect they are being surveilled or who are subjected to violence or intimidation are urged to preserve evidence and immediately report the incidents to police, while putting their personal safety first, it said.
The bureau is expanding its intelligence gathering and multi-agency cooperation to combat the threat of transnational repression, it said.

Where there’s friction, there’s fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

A leading voice in Europe’s contemporary dance scene, the Greek minimalist choreographer Christos Papadopoulos makes his Taiwanese debut this month, as ARTQUAKE Festival opens with his latest group piece, My Fierce Ignorant Step.
For Papadopoulos, the road to international recognition and to the playbill of Taipei’s National Theater has never been the result of a series of carefully calculated moves.
Early in his career, he recalls feeling that he was “no one and had nothing great to say.” That changed when his first works, Elvedon (2015) and OPUS (2016), attracted attention through the European dance platform Aerowaves.
Photo courtesy of Pinelopi Gerasimou for Onassis Stegi
“Presenting my work with Aerowaves helped me to achieve what would normally take me five or 10 years,” Papadopoulos says about the connections he established with European theaters and festivals through this platform.
Since that breakthrough, Papadopoulos has created works for leading institutions, including Nederlands Dans Theater and the Ballet de l’Opera national de Lyon. He last year became the first recipient of the inaugural Rose International Dance Prize.
For the choreographer, however, what constitutes success is less a question of awards and international tours, and more of the hard work that happens inside the rehearsal studio alongside his dancers and artistic collaborators.
“Every work of mine, it’s in the same pot with all the rest,” he says.
Each creation brings new discoveries and understandings that feed into the next, accumulating into a continuous artistic evolution rather than a sequence of isolated achievements.
That way, Papadopoulos lives by the advice given to him by his colleague choreographer and friend Dimitris Papaioannou, to not panic over international recognition, but to just “ignore it, go into the studio, make good work, and all the rest will follow.”
“Winning the Rose Prize offered some financial breathing room,” Papadopoulos says. He re-invested the prize money directly into his team and his next work, My Fierce Ignorant Step, now bringing 10 dancers to Taiwan.
My Fierce Ignorant Step emerged from a personal reckoning. After roughly a decade of relentless work, Papadopoulos realized that he had neglected his health, friendships and need for time away.
He worried that continuing at the same pace would make him resent his profession, while political victories of the far-right, wars and corruption left him feeling increasingly hopeless.
To find a way forward, he looked back to adolescence, when he possessed a fierce belief that he could help make the world better simply by fighting for it.
The work became an attempt to recover that conviction. Rather than offering uncomplicated optimism, he wanted to explore whether reconnecting with others could restore a sense of agency.
“If we find each other again,” he says, “we might also re-find our connection with action and activism.”
That idea was embodied through a demanding choreographic process, in which Papadopoulos experienced almost constant failure in the first month and a half, trying to grasp that feeling of youthful euphoria.
Eventually, he found something essential in the complex movement sequences that demanded almost inhuman powers of memorization. As the dancers struggled to memorize and execute the material, they began helping one another.
For Papadopoulos, these moments revealed the work’s central idea: difficulty could make people withdraw, but it can also encourage them to reach out for one another.
The choreography itself resists predictable patterns. Its irregular rhythm become a small rebellion against uniformity, opening space for friction and the unexpected.
Making this piece also changed Papadopoulos’ personal working methods. He reduced his working week from six days to five, and split the creative process into two blocks separated by two months of rest and reflection.
“If it wasn’t so rewarding, it would be impossible to keep creating and performing at this pace,” he says, aware of both the privilege and joy of pursuing his artistic vision and the personal sacrifices it demands.
For audiences encountering his work for the first time, Papadopoulos offers a simple suggestion: “Resist the urge to decode everything, just sit back, relax and enjoy.”
He sees no problem in allowing the mind to wander. In fact, he encourages audiences to embrace absent-mindedness, which should be seen as a sign of feeling safe enough to follow your own thoughts.
With My Fierce Ignorant Step, Papadopoulos invites us to rediscover the passion and defiance of youth, and reminds us that hope itself can be an act of resistance, that the courage to imagine a different world is neither naive nor lost.

Tesla unveils a new rocket-powered Roadster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:27 UTC
01:42:27 KST

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.
The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the maneuver.
Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he has explored by discussing their overlap.
Photo: Tesla, via Reuters
The reveal gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors.
“It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers,” Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster said on social media platform X.
“The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can’t wait to bring [Tesla] and [SpaceX] together,” Munster said.
Musk has played down the car’s importance to Tesla’s finances, describing it in 2023 as a “small potato situation” that would not “move the needle in a major way financially.”
However, the car still carries symbolic weight.
“Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker’s best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla’s new halo car,” Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said last month.
“That was the most insane product demo I’ve ever seen,” Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. “I just saw this in person, and I’m still asking how this wasn’t AI.”
Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday’s event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of US$200,000 for the vehicle.
Tesla’s reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday’s event showed a “Performance” version of the vehicle requiring a US$50,000 deposit and a “Thrust” version with “acceleration thrusters” requiring a US$250,000 deposit. A “Rocket” variant, which Tesla says is “invite only,” is described as a single-seat model with a “full flight system.”
The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 97kph in less than one second and can hit a top speed of more than 230mph (370kph), Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said.
“Definitely much faster than that,” an excited Musk said. “I think you’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound.”
The Roadster can also travel more than 480km on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020.

2026 Elections: Man loses NT$1.04m in fraud scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:25 UTC
01:42:25 KST

The Criminal Investigation Bureau has warned the public about a new type of election-related scam after an auto repair shop owner lost NT$1.04 million (US$32,160) to a fake investment scheme involving “election campaign advertisements.”
The bureau said the fraud group exploited voters’ enthusiasm for political candidates by claiming that although the statutory limit for political donations to a single candidate is NT$100,000 per year, individuals can offer additional support by buying shares in the candidate’s political advertisements and receive a share of the profits if the candidate gets elected.
Scammers said that investors could later join stock trading online chat groups personally managed by political figures, promising them guaranteed profits with zero risk of loss, the bureau said.
Photo courtesy of the Criminal Investigation Bureau
According to the bureau, an auto repair shop owner surnamed Wang (王), driven by strong support for a particular candidate, paid NT$1.04 million to the fake advertisement investment fund in August through bank transfers and promissory notes.
The fraud outfit later enticed Wang with a new lure — investing in stocks managed by the politician, promising a 12 percent return on principal within three months — to urge him to double down on “investments,” the bureau said.
Drawn to the idea, Wang even mortgaged his vehicle for a NT$900,000 loan through a pawnshop introduced by the fraud group and was ready to “invest” more, it said.
The bureau said that a friend warned the victim, and he realized that something was wrong and pressed the scammers for details, only to be blocked and deleted immediately from the chat group, confirming that he had fallen victim to a scam.
As election campaigning heats up, people should express their support to candidates through legal channels of donation and request receipts, the bureau said.
Any scheme that promises substantial returns or guaranteed profits from investing in a candidate’s political ads or buying shares in a candidate is definitely a scam tactic used by fraud groups, it added.
Candidates’ advertisement and campaign funds are not open for public investment, so if people are contacted by individuals claiming to be campaign headquarters’ staff inviting them to “invest” and request wire transfers or promissory notes, it is most likely a scam, it said.
They should first call the bureau’s 165 Anti-Fraud Hotline or verify the claim using the online 165 Anti-Fraud Dashboard smart customer service, it said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia on Thursday acknowledged that she had failed the bar exam, as her credentials face scrutiny.
Zacharia has described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.
However, the legal credentials of the press secretary, who US President Donald Trump appointed last week, were called into question after she gave an inconclusive answer about where she had passed the bar exam.
In a Fox News interview on Thursday, host Sean Hannity asked Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in 2011: “You took the bar exam, but you didn’t pass the bar exam, correct?”
“Yes,” she responded.
In a separate interview with right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec on the conservative media outlet Real America’s Voice on Thursday, Zacharia said she had registered to take the bar exam, but was “distracted and overwhelmed” by plans to move to China with her husband.
“The results are somewhat inconsequential because I knew I wouldn’t need the bar in China,” she said.
Foreign nationals cannot sit China’s bar exam, although they can undertake certain legal work at Chinese law firms.
Hannity later asked Zacharia if she had ever taken the bar exam a second time, to which she said: “I did not.”
“I had four kids in six years,” she said. “It was never my intent to go into the practice of law.”
Zacharia said on Real America’s Voice that “many people in the field” had assured her that she could “label myself a lawyer,” given her law degree and experience in business law gained in China, where she worked at a Beijing law firm.
She added that she could “provide legal analysis, not legal advice.”
“I was very careful how I executed this,” she said.
The Campaign for Accountability, a political ethics organization, on Wednesday called for the California Bar Association to launch an investigation.
“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” the organization said in a press release.
During the interview with Posobiec, she also said that China lacked “proper toilets.”
She said that the perception in 2016 was that China would soon overtake the US.
“We were all being told Hillary [Rodham Clinton] was going to win [the US presidential election]. The golden days or the glory days of America were over. That China was on the horizon,” she said.
“I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking: ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,’” she added.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday suggested she might want to make another trip to the country.
“We welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity,” spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) told reporters, fighting back a smile.

01:42:23 KST

The US and Myanmar’s military-backed government held talks in Tokyo last week, people familiar with the matter said, their second meeting in a month as Washington steps up re-engagement with the generals it shunned after their 2021 coup.
Earlier talks in Myanmar’s capital, Naypyidaw, in the middle of last month focused on securing the release of a US businessman and shutting down scam centers that target Americans, but could pave the way for broader discussions, including on Myanmar’s rare earth mineral deposits, Reuters previously reported.
It was not immediately clear exactly what the two sides discussed at last week’s talks, disclosed to Reuters by three people with knowledge of the engagement. The people, including one US official, all requested anonymity because of the sensitivity of the meeting.
Photo: AFP
US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance again led the Tokyo talks, which involved more than a dozen US officials, one of the people said. Reuters could not establish who represented Myanmar.
The US Department of State did not respond to a request for comment on the latest talks, but says it engages with all groups in Myanmar on issues affecting US interests. A spokesperson for the junta did not respond to a request for comment.
Asked about its role in hosting the talks, the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in an e-mailed statement it had been “communicating as necessary” with both sides, but declined to comment on specific diplomatic exchanges.
Last month’s meeting in Naypyidaw between Vance and Myanmar’s coup leader-turned-president, Min Aung Hlaing, provided an opening for broader discussions, people familiar with those talks previously said. The quick return to the negotiating table in Tokyo suggests both sides are keen to keep the dialogue going.
A major focus of the US push is securing Myanmar’s help in shutting down scam hubs that run romance and other frauds and have swindled Americans out of billions of dollars, the people said.
Researchers say many scam operations are based in areas controlled by army-backed militia, with some proceeds flowing to the military, raising doubts about whether the Burmese leaders are serious about enforcement. The junta has said it is participating in a multinational effort to curb scam centers.
US officials have also discussed access to Myanmar’s large deposits of heavy rare earths, which are used in products ranging from electric vehicles to wind turbines. US officials acknowledge significant obstacles: The deposits are largely located in territory controlled by ethnic armed groups fighting the military, while China, the main buyer of Myanmar rare earths, could balk at any US role.
The US last week lifted sanctions on the daughter of a Burmese businessman accused of supporting the country’s military, saying the move was part of a new approach to the country.
“This approach highlights the importance of pursuing dialogue with all groups involved in Burma’s civil war and commits to re-examining the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country,” the State Department said of the sanctions move.
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses.
It is unclear whether Japan has any stake in the US-Myanmar talks beyond playing host, including for earlier talks in the Japanese capital in June, but there are signs that Tokyo is also moving to re-engage with Myanmar.
Japan’s acting envoy to Myanmar met with the foreign minister of the junta earlier this month in their first known public engagement. Tokyo does not formally recognize the administration.
That meeting followed a visit last month by Japanese ruling party lawmaker Hiromichi Watanabe to Naypyidaw, which he said was aimed at restarting bilateral cooperation and resuming development aid to Myanmar, the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar newspaper said.
The Japanese foreign ministry said the acting envoy raised issues such as protection for Japanese nationals and support for Japanese companies, while Watanabe’s trip was in his capacity as an individual member of parliament and “does not in any way prejudge” the position of the government.
Watanabe said his trip was aimed at preparing the environment to normalize relations, though he acknowledged that barriers remained.
