On Tuesday last week, Lin Chien-cheng (林健正), a retired National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University professor, wrote on Facebook comparing the “Han wave” (韓流) that led to now-Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu’s (韓國瑜) surprise 2018 Kaohsiung mayoral victory to the “Ocean wave” (洋流) of support for Legislator Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign as the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate.
Lin said not to underestimate the power of momentum.
The 1998 Taipei mayoral election involving two men who went on to be president seemed to show that it is electoral forces beneath the surface of the waves that matter most.
A poll released on Sept. 22 by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association put support for Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) at 41.7 percent as he seeks a second term and Shen at 40.5 percent, a difference of just 1.2 percentage points. However, neither a single poll nor enthusiastic crowds at campaign events necessarily predict the election’s outcome.
The “Ocean wave” — which Shen’s campaign team refers to as the “Taipei Current” in English — has generated several notable moments. When Shen’s campaign headquarters opened on Oct. 4, television host and writer Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) was photographed at the event. Amid backlash, including from China, Tsai said he attended to “see what it was like.”
On the same day, a vendor in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area began selling cakes using molds that made them in the Chinese characters for: “Your mayor, Puma Shen.” The vendor said that a friend received a call from the stall’s landlord asking that sales of the Shen-themed cakes stop. It was unclear whether anyone else prompted the landlord’s request.
The developments reflect a level of electoral momentum, but they still cannot predict the election’s outcome.
The 1998 Taipei mayoral election offers an instructive perspective. Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) won the mayoralty in 1994 with 43.67 percent of the vote and was seeking re-election. Despite his vote share rising to 45.91 percent four years later, he nevertheless lost to Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), who secured 51.13 percent.
National Chengchi University conducted studies that indicated that public satisfaction with Chen’s administration was typically above 70 percent during his tenure, yet he still fell short.
Polling and research suggest that, at the time, party identification, views on unification versus independence and identification as being Chinese or Taiwanese were all associated with split-ticket voting, a reminder that a candidate winning public approval and voters ultimately casting their ballots for them are two different things.
That is not to say 1998 is destined to repeat itself next month. Nearly three decades have passed, Taipei’s population, generations and political identities have changed, and the conclusions drawn from in 1998 cannot necessarily be applied to the present. The focus should be on how voters assess the candidates and whether Shen’s and Chiang’s ability to govern can translate into tangible improvements in housing, transportation, long-term care, accessibility, education and public infrastructure.
In 2018, Han’s mass rallies translated into victory, but not when he ran in the 2020 presidential election. Meanwhile, Taipei’s 1998 mayoral race showed that an administration’s high approval ratings do not guarantee re-election. What needs watching is not just how high a wave rises, but what electoral structures lie below.
Hopefully, Taipei residents see through the noise and carefully consider each candidate’s abilities, policies and performance. They should each use their own judgement to choose the person best equipped to govern.
Hsiao Hsi-huei is a freelancer.

The National Immigration Agency (NIA) yesterday said it has revoked a Chinese exchange student’s entry permit and deported him over a gesture it said targeted President William Lai (賴清德).
Lai on Monday delivered a speech at the closing ceremony of the Taiwan Bridge Program at National Taiwan University (NTU).
A Chinese exchange student surnamed Wang (王) on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, posted footage of Lai speaking at the event, along with remarks widely seen as threatening, including: “Is this the only chance you’ll ever get?” and “Take down little Lai Ching-te.”
Photo courtesy of the NIA
The post also included slogans such as: “Unification across the Taiwan Strait is a historical inevitability” and “Oppose separatist acts promoting Taiwan independence.”
The post sparked an outcry online, with many calling on the Ministry of the Interior to deport Wang. As the controversy grew, Wang,
on an exchange program at NTU, issued an apology, saying he had no intention of physically harming anyone.
Photo: Screengrab from Threads
The agency said it had completed its investigation in accordance with the law and consulted the Ministry of Education, the Mainland Affairs Council and other government bodies.
It concluded that Wang’s conduct violated the principle of mutual respect and dignity and had caused social unrest in Taiwan.
Wang was deported at 3pm yesterday, and barred from entry for five years, it said.
Under the Regulations Governing the Entry of People from Mainland China into the Taiwan Area (大陸地區人民進入台灣地區許可辦法), Chinese nationals who engage in conduct that violates the principle of mutual respect and dignity while visiting Taiwan with official approval may have their permits revoked.
In Wang’s case, the agency said it revoked his entry permit and deported him.
Wang is also barred from applying to visit Taiwan for five years, and any subsequent applications will be subject to strict scrutiny, it said.
Taiwan is a democratic, free, open and diverse society that respects differing opinions and normal exchanges, the agency said.
However, Chinese nationals visiting Taiwan must abide by Taiwanese laws and regulations to ensure orderly cross-strait exchanges, it said.
The agency said it would continue to strengthen interagency cooperation and its handling of legal and regulatory violations to safeguard national security, social stability and order in cross-strait exchanges.
In response to the case, NTU said yesterday it had accompanied the student when he was questioned by authorities and providing him with assistance.
NTU said it respected the government's enforcement of relevant rules and remained committed to freedom of expression and an open, diverse and respectful campus.
It hoped that the incident would help students better understand that exercising free speech should also involve respecting others, NTU said.

Appliance repair focus of ministry voucher program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:22 UTC
01:42:22 KST

The Ministry of Environment is planning to provide vouchers to encourage home appliance repair.
Most people replace small appliances — such as fans, rice cookers or blenders — when they stop working, as the cost at an official authorized repair service can approach the cost of a replacement. That has an environmental effect, including additional load on incinerators.
With the Resource Circulation Promotion Act (資源循環推動法) passing its third reading in the legislature in June, product lifecycle management — including design, manufacturing, consumption, recycling and reuse — has been written into law.
Photo: Huang Yi-ching, Taipei Times
The ministry since 2024 has encouraged local communities and civic groups to set up stations to repair and maintain appliances.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭?明) on Sunday said more than 800 repair sites have been catalogued nationwide.
The goal is to set up 1,000 such sites, making appliance repair and maintenance so accessible that it becomes part of people’s daily life, Peng said.
The ministry would soon launch a voucher mechanism to incentivize more people to use the services, he said.
The vouchers would be worth at least NT$100 each and be distributed on a registration basis in limited quantities, he said.
Chen Yen-nan (陳彥男), head of the Resource Circulation Administration’s Sustainable Consumption and Recycling Division, said that small appliances are most often dumped when they stop working, as the cost of repair can often make buying new more attractive.
However, the service life of small appliances can easily be extended by maintenance, Chen said.
Maintenance requires labor and knowledge to prevent risks such as electrical fires, he said, adding that training programs are available at local environmental protection bureaus or community colleges.
For appliances such as vacuum cleaners, including robot vacuums — which people often complain break shortly after their warranty expires — the “rent, don’t buy” approach might be appropriate, Chen said.
Many vendors have launched appliance renting services, he said, adding that the public should adopt the services to promote sustainable use of larger appliances.
Small Appliance Repair Workshop, a mobile repair and maintenance service group founded in 2016, has nearly 30 employees and volunteers who provide such services.
Tsai Yah-hsuan (蔡亞軒), a senior campaigner at the Circular Taiwan Network, does repairs and maintenance at the workshop.
The workshop was formed following the example of “repair cafes” in other countries, Tsai said.
Many staff at the workshop do not have backgrounds in electrical engineering, Tsai said.
They join the workshop out of interest and to learn repair knowledge through hands-on experience with experts, he said.
Half of the workshop’s staff are women, Tsai said.
The workshop last year published a report on small appliance repairs, he said.
Coffee machines and vacuum cleaners are the small appliances most repaired in Western countries, but in Taiwan it is mostly electric fans and rice cookers, he said.
More than 70 percent of the appliances brought to the workshop are fixed, he said, adding that the rate shows how effective the work is.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr and his government yesterday protested remarks by a Chinese envoy, calling them “a thinly veiled threat of the use of force” in the latest flare-up in the two Asian countries’ longstanding territorial dispute in the South China Sea.
On the sidelines of a Manila forum on Thursday, Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan (井泉) was asked by reporters to comment on Philippine Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro Jr’s remarks pointing to China as a “troublemaker” in the region.
Jing said that characterization was “nonsense” and added that the Philippines should feel fortunate to have China as a neighbor.
Photo: Malacanang Presidential Communications Office via AP
“If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not choose force and we love peace,” Jing said. “In this region, we enjoy peace. Look at other regions: Ukraine, Gaza and even Venezuela.”
When asked to comment on the Chinese ambassador’s statement, Marcos said it sounded “very much to me like a threat and it is not a very diplomatic statement to be made.”
He added that he would like to understand what Jing exactly meant.
China and the Philippines have long clashed over territorial disputes in the South China Sea. Tense confrontations at sea and heated verbal exchanges have escalated between Manila and Beijing in the past few years.
China claims virtually the entire waterway, a key global trade route, as its sovereign territory. Taiwan, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei all have separate claims to the waters.
The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said in a separate statement that it was “regrettable” that Jing “had a poor choice of words that would seem to convey a thinly veiled threat of the use of force, which is hardly helpful in the context of the complicated bilateral ties between the two nations.
“It is hoped that all diplomats accredited to the Philippines take greater care in the language used in public statements so as not to further erode mutual trust and confidence, nor derail the advancement of dialogue and constructive engagement,” it said.
The Chinese embassy suggested that the Philippine foreign affairs department has taken Jing’s statement out of context and employed “selective quotation and overinterpretation” of Jing’s remarks.
“China-Philippines relations are currently at an extremely sensitive stage,” the embassy said. “We urge the DFA to play a more responsible role in preventing such actions, thereby ensuring that China-Philippines relations are not pushed into a dangerous and uncertain situation.”
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning (毛寧) said Beijing’s position on the bilateral relationship “is clear,” adding that “we hope the Philippine side can understand it comprehensively and accurately.”
Teodoro, one of the harshest critics in Asia of China’s increasingly assertive actions, told Philippine radio station DZMM that Jing was clearly threatening the Philippines.

Taiwan should not rule out any energy source or abandon environmental sustainability in favor of ideology and short-term benefits, President William Lai (賴清德) said in an interview, calling for a “professional assessment” of whether nuclear power should be reintroduced into Taiwan’s energy mix.
In an online interview with influencer Yu Ting-hao (游庭皓) that aired yesterday, Lai reiterated his position on nuclear power.
SHIFT
Photo courtesy of Presidential Office
Lai’s remarks marked a shift from the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP’s) longstanding opposition to nuclear power.
As premier from 2017 to 2019, Lai pushed for more gas-fired power capacity while sticking to the DPP’s nuclear free homeland ideology and rejected the idea of extending the service life of its nuclear power plants.
Taiwan phased out nuclear energy in May last year, fulfilling the nuclear free homeland pledge.
That occurred as Taiwan continued to rely on fossil fuels for more than 80 percent of its electricity mix, and questions remained over the electricity supply given the country’s development of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
In the interview with Yu, Lai said the Legislative Yuan has passed bills providing a legal basis for reintroducing nuclear power, and state-run Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) has been making preparations accordingly.
The government would begin work to resume nuclear power generation if nuclear safety and nuclear waste disposal issues can be resolved through a professional assessment in a way that wins public support, Lai said.
AI INDUSTRY
Meanwhile, asked how the government would balance efforts to develop the AI industry against the regulation of AI applications, Lai said it would promote the industry’s responsible development.
He cited the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act (人工智慧基本法), which took effect in January, saying it requires the government to uphold human autonomy, privacy, information security, fairness, non-discrimination, transparency and accountability while developing the AI industry.
To prevent AI from exacerbating the uneven distribution of wealth and resources between the high-tech and non-tech sectors, Lai said the government would provide NT$100 billion (US$3 billion) over eight years to help micro, small and medium-sized enterprises transform their businesses.

‘Kinmen’ approved as name for 1km asteroid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:42:18 UTC
01:42:18 KST

The International Astronomical Union has approved the name “Kinmen” — referring to Kinmen National Park — for asteroid 755922, which was discovered by National Central University’s (NCU) Lulin Observatory, the university said yesterday.
The asteroid was discovered by Lulin Observatory director Lin Hung-chin (林宏欽) and Ye Quanzhi (葉泉志), an associate research scientist in the University of Maryland College Park’s Department of Astronomy.
Measuring about 1km in diameter, the asteroid orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter. Its closest approach to the sun is about 269 million kilometers and is about 438 million kilometers away at its farthest, completing an orbit in about three years and seven months, Lin said.
Photo courtesy fo the NCU via CNA
The name was chosen because the national park is an important stopover for migratory birds in East Asia and a habitat for the endangered Eurasian otter, he said.
The name also reflects the county’s military history, traditional settlements and natural environment, where history, culture and conservation coexist, he said.
NCU president Hsiau Shu-san (蕭述三) said the name links Kinmen National Park’s historical and natural heritage on Earth with space exploration.
Hopefully, the name would inspire young people in Kinmen County to take a greater interest in science when looking up at the night sky, Hsiao said.
Lulin Observatory has discovered more than 800 asteroids since launching the Lulin Sky Survey in 2006, NCU said.
By naming asteroids after places and cultural landmarks, the observatory has introduced Taiwan’s landscapes, heritage and scientific achievements to the world, it said.
The naming of the Kinmen asteroid extends the county’s presence from the map to the solar system, it said.

Ghada Karmi: Zionism is racism motion is a ‘beacon of light’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:40:54 UTC
01:40:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Ghada Karmi: Zionism is racism motion is a ‘beacon of light’
Palestinian academic Ghada Karmi has called the Green Party’s Zionism is Racism motion "a beacon of light" in a press conference hosted by Greens for Palestine on Friday.
The motion was passed on 4 October with 1,022 votes in favour and 813 against.
Born in 1939, Karmi, who came to London in 1949 after her family was forcibly expelled from Palestine in the Nakba (Arabic for catastrophe), said the motion is “the best thing that’s happened to me, personally, since 1948.”
The motion has been met with backlash both from political opponents and from within the party.
Green MP Adrian Ramsay said he was "deeply upset" after the motion passed.
Lawyer Adam Wagner, who has previously represented the Campaign Against Antisemitism, said the motion may violate the Equality Act of 2010 because it "will discriminate against and harass people who hold Zionist beliefs and Jewish people more generally."
Green Party leader Zack Polanski, who is Jewish, said in a statement, “antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct.”
"No-one will be made unwelcome because of their background, their faith, or where they worship."
Karmi, who thanked both Polanski and Lubna Speitan, who proposed the motion, responded to the criticism, saying, “I don’t know what the fuss is about; of course it’s racist.”
"The essence of this is really nothing to do with being Palestinian. It's to do with being non-Jewish," she said.
"We're the wrong ethnicity, and that's why we're being prosecuted. If that's not racist, I don't know what is," she continued.
The motion states that Israel is an "apartheid," "ethnonationalist" state, and calls for the establishment of a single Palestinian state "with equal rights for all."
An amendment which would have removed the call for a single Palestinian state was voted down, as was one which would have prevented people from being disciplined by the party for membership of Jewish institutions with a Zionist stance, including synagogues.
Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham responded by ruling out a future coalition with the Green Party as long as the motion stands.
In September, Labour’s Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced limited sanctions against Israeli settlements in the West Bank, but the Labour government has continued to arrest protesters supporting the proscribed group Palestine Action.
Speitan, who proposed the motion, said at the press conference that she hopes other organisations, including trade unions and political parties, will adopt the stance that Zionism is racism.

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:39:31 UTC
01:39:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, news agency Reuters reported- citing four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
Reuters reports, citing a US military official, that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade.
Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:38:25 UTC
01:38:25 KST

Iran reaffirms Strait of Hormuz closure, says passage must be coordinated
TEHRAN — Iranian military officials have reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to uncoordinated maritime traffic, linking any easing of restrictions to 'respect for Iran’s rights' and warning that continued US military presence in the region will deepen insecurity.
Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deputy coordinator of the Iranian Army, said on Thursday that any vessel seeking to transit the strategic waterway must coordinate its passage with the Iranian authorities who are in charge. His remarks came as Army Chief Commander Major General Amir Hatami and Army Spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia issued separate statements emphasizing Iran’s military readiness and its determination to maintain control over the security environment around the strait.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a ceremony honoring Army nurses, Sayyari argued that the impact of restrictions on maritime traffic was evident in international fuel markets.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed. If it were open and oil were passing through it, gasoline prices in the United States would not have risen,” he said.
Sayyari outlined the deployment of Iran’s armed forces around the waterway, saying the naval forces of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) maintained a firm presence to the west of the strait, while the Iranian Army operated to its east and extended its presence northward into the Sea of Oman.
He stressed that any passage through the waterway must be coordinated, warning that vessels attempting to transit without such coordination could face consequences.
Hatami links reopening to respect for Iran’s rights
Army Chief Commander Major General Amir Hatami has also made clear that, in Iran’s view, the future of the strait is directly linked to the treatment of the country and its rights.
Speaking at Imam Ali Officers’ University in Tehran on Thursday, Hatami said the Strait of Hormuz had been closed following the outbreak of the war and would remain closed until Iran’s rights were respected.
He attributed the conflict to a ‘fundamental miscalculation by Iran’s adversaries,’ who had underestimated the country’s military capabilities and assumed that it was in a weakened position.
According to Hatami, the Iranian Army and the IRGC responded from the earliest hours of the conflict with extensive strikes against hostile targets. He argued that the adversaries had failed to achieve their military and strategic objectives.
Rejecting US assertions that Iran’s military capabilities had been weakened, the Army chief pointed to continued missile and drone operations and the functioning of the country’s air-defense systems as evidence of its sustained operational capacity.
Hatami also said Iran had taken firm action against vessels that violated its regulations, leaving maritime traffic through the strait severely restricted.
He added that Iran’s armed forces had used the pause in hostilities to repair damage and strengthen their readiness. Iranian ground, naval, air-defense and missile units, he said, remained equipped and prepared to defend the country’s territorial integrity.
Hatami further warned that any attack on Iran’s infrastructure would prompt a response inflicting substantially greater damage on the infrastructure and interests of its adversaries, including Israel and those cooperating with it.
Army says US military presence fuels regional insecurity
In separate remarks on Friday, Army spokesman Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia said Iran was developing new operational plans that would force hostile US naval vessels to withdraw even farther from the country’s coastline.
Akraminia said Iran’s air-defense capabilities had advanced beyond their prewar and wartime levels, adding that Iranian air-defense units had intercepted several US drones in the country’s airspace in recent weeks. He also said US military vessels had been pushed to distances exceeding 500 kilometers from the coasts of the Persian Gulf.
The spokesman described the US military presence as a central source of insecurity in the region and called on regional countries and the international community to recognize ‘Washington’s role in fueling instability.’
“If America leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, and collective security will be established with the participation of the region’s countries, and the global economy will improve. If it doesn’t leave, we’ll expel it,” Akraminia said.
He added that Iranian forces had rehearsed advanced, coordinated and innovative military operations, while nationwide air-defense coverage had been significantly strengthened.
A strategic waterway with global economic consequences
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world’s most strategically important energy corridors, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Arabian Sea. A substantial share of global oil shipments and significant volumes of liquefied natural gas pass through the waterway, making disruptions a concern for energy-importing countries, shipping operators and financial markets.
Restrictions on traffic through the strait can raise shipping and insurance costs, disrupt energy supplies and add volatility to oil and fuel prices. The effects depend on the scale and duration of the disruption, the availability of alternative supplies and routes, and market expectations about the conflict.
Iran’s latest statements place the waterway at the center of its broader security position: Tehran says passage must be coordinated, its armed forces remain prepared, and any change in the current situation depends on respect for Iran’s rights and the future of foreign military deployments in the region.
The statements also underscore the competing approaches to security in the Persian Gulf. While Washington has emphasized maritime security and freedom of navigation, Iranian officials argue that lasting stability requires regional cooperation and an end to ‘destabilizing foreign military intervention.’
With energy markets and international shipping exposed to developments around the strait, any sustained change in maritime traffic is likely to have consequences well beyond West Asia. For Iran, however, the issue is not solely one of commercial passage: its military leadership has framed the waterway as a strategic lever tied to national security, sovereignty and the outcome of the wider confrontation.

NPC "Ukrenergo" has completed the restructuring of its sustainability-linked Eurobonds. Approximately $135 million in savings will be directed toward the recovery of the energy sector. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal reported this, according to UNN.
Details
NPC "Ukrenergo" has successfully completed the restructuring of sustainability-linked Eurobonds issued in 2021. The main result is approximately $135 million in savings, which will be directed toward restoring power grids damaged by Russian attacks and strengthening the resilience of Ukraine's energy system
As a result of the restructuring, the total amount of the claim under the Eurobonds was reduced to $494.75 million at 8.6% per annum, with final maturity in 2041. New unsecured bonds worth $395 million were also issued at 8.5% per annum, maturing in 2031. The transaction was supported by holders of 97.49% of the Eurobonds.
According to him, the restructuring will allow more financial resources to be directed toward restoring the damaged grid and will minimize the burden on the electricity transmission service tariff.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police and prison officials have been placed under investigation in Italy over the treatment of Gaza flotilla activists, Italian prosecutors have said.
The Rome prosecutors’ office said on Friday that the probe, previously focused on far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage during Israeli interceptions of Gaza-bound boats in 2025 and 2026.
Investigators opened the case following complaints from 50 Italian citizens detained by Israeli authorities during two Global Sumud Flotilla missions, in September–October 2025 and April–May 2026.
Besides Katz and Ben-Gvir, prosecutors named 12 senior Israeli military, police and prison officials as suspects, including military chief Eyal Zamir.
Death threats, beatings
The investigation into Ben-Gvir followed international condemnation of footage he released in May showing detained flotilla activists kneeling with their hands bound.
In one clip, officers forced an activist to the ground after she chanted “Free, free Palestine”.
Italy’s government condemned the treatment as “unacceptable” and summoned the Israeli ambassador. Rome subsequently called for the European Union to discuss sanctions against Ben-Gvir.
Activists detained during the first mission reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism, prosecutors said.
Those involved in the second mission said they faced even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark and the use of tasers and rubber bullets.
Investigators said they had identified individuals within the military and police chains of command involved in the operations.
Prosecutors sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
They also held talks at the European Union’s judicial cooperation agency, Eurojust, as similar investigations into the two missions were under way in other European countries, which they did not identify.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation does not imply guilt or automatically lead to a trial. Prosecutors could formally request a trial if they determine that charges are warranted.
Flotilla organisers say the missions aimed to break Israel’s blockade of Gaza and deliver humanitarian aid.

Latest poll shows Bolsonaro maintaining edge over Lula in Brazil run-off
Experts still consider race a toss up despite slate of polls showing right-wing senator leading left-wing president.
Another poll has shown leftist Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva trailing behind right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in the October 25 run-off election.
The survey, released by CNT/MDA on Friday, showed Bolsonaro taking 46.8 percent of the vote, compared with 45.9 percent for Lula.
The latest projection comes a day after a Quaest poll found Bolsonaro carrying 46 percent of the vote, compared with Lula’s 44 percent. A separate Datafolha poll found Bolsonaro taking 47 percent of the vote against Lula’s 45, down from 49 percent a week earlier.
All three polls currently fall within a 2 percent margin of error, meaning the race is still considered by many experts to be a toss-up. Still, they underscore an uncomfortable political climate for Lula, who had a month ago been projected to easily sail to victory at the ballot box.
That was before Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, took the most votes out of any candidate in the first round of voting on October 4.
Bolsonaro won 56,104,503 votes compared with Lula’s 53,879,538.
The senator has hewed closely to the political persona of his father, who has been barred from running for re-election until 2030 after an electoral court ruled he abused his authority to cast doubt on the 2022 presidential election.
The elder Bolsonaro has remained under house arrest while serving a 27-year sentence connected to efforts to overturn the 2022 vote, which he lost to Lula.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 42, has pledged a crackdown on crime and drug trafficking and to cleave taxes used to pay for government programmes. A win would make him the latest conservative leader closely aligned with US President Donald Trump to take power in the region.
Lula, meanwhile, has been holding regular rallies hoping to energise his supporters. The 80-year-old politician is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term after a political career spanning nearly five decades.
On Wednesday, the country’s Congress approved an amendment to give workers two paid days off a week, as opposed to one.
The move gives Lula a major victory on one of his top social reform promises just days before the vote.
The election comes at a pivotal time for Latin America’s largest economy. Brazilians are grappling with concerns over crime and the cost of living, while the country faces an increasingly tense relationship with the United States. The vote is also being closely watched across a region that has shifted sharply to the right in a series of recent elections.

UK police review Palestine Action post by wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell

British police said Friday they were assessing a social media post by Sarah Helm, the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, after she appeared to express support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned under Britain's terrorism laws.
Helm, a journalist and author, made the comment on X in response to a post about Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who announced this week that her books would no longer be sold in Britain because she intends to use royalties from her work to support Palestine Action.
"God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action," Helm wrote.
A spokesperson for London's Metropolitan Police said the post was "being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required." Police did not say whether a formal investigation had been opened. 
Palestine Action was designated a terrorist organization by the British government in 2025, making expressions of support for the group a potential criminal offense under UK law. The designation has been challenged by the organization and criticized by civil liberties groups, which argue that it restricts freedom of expression and peaceful protest.
Asked about Helm's comments, a government spokesperson distanced the administration from her remarks. "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity," the spokesperson said.
Palestine Action has carried out protests targeting companies connected to Israel's defense industry, including acts of vandalism. The group disputes the government's characterization of its activities as terrorism. Four of its members were jailed in June over a 2024 raid on a factory operated by Israeli defense company Elbit Systems that caused more than 1 million pounds in damage.
According to Amnesty International, more than 3,500 people have been arrested in Britain on suspicion of supporting Palestine Action since the ban took effect. Many were detained after displaying placards expressing support for the organization.
The group challenged its designation in court, but Britain's Court of Appeal ruled in June that the ban was lawful. The legal dispute is continuing, with the Supreme Court expected to examine the case. 
The controversy surrounding Helm comes as Rooney's decision has drawn renewed attention to the consequences of Britain's terrorism legislation for writers and activists. Rooney and her publisher, Faber & Faber, agreed to withdraw her books from the British market over concerns that payments connected to her work could violate the law because of her financial support for Palestine Action.

British students, like their French peers, have been known to challenge authority | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:32:58 UTC
01:32:58 KST

Reading Kitty Sayers’ interesting article, I was reminded of the rich, and perhaps too easily forgotten, history of direct action by British schoolchildren (Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why, 10 October). Far from being historically meek or unquestioningly compliant, they have demonstrated a remarkable capacity for challenging authority.
At Marlborough college, troops were once summoned to dislodge rebellious pupils occupying an island in the school grounds. In the late 1700s, Winchester college experienced several rebellions.
Nor was such defiance confined to the more privileged. In 1889, strikes by schoolchildren in the Scottish lowlands spread across Tyneside, London, Bristol and Cardiff. In 1911, a strike beginning at Bigyn school in Llanelli developed into a remarkable wave of protest, reaching some 60 towns across England and Wales.
Schoolchildren and their families also played their part in the extraordinary 1914 Burston school strike, which endured for 25 years and became the longest‑running strike in British history.
Those of us of a certain generation may also recall the National Union of School Students in the 1970s, whose challenges to established educational authority infuriated traditionalists such as the headmaster Rhodes Boyson, who later became a Conservative minister.
The history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction. It also has a rich tradition of collective action and resistance to perceived injustice. Schoolchildren challenging the established order is hardly a peculiarly French phenomenon. There is a substantial, if sometimes overlooked, British history of such action too.
 
Pete Crockett
 
Royal Wootton Bassett, Wiltshire
Kitty Sayers is illuminating on French attitudes to protest, but she misses the mark when describing English attitudes. She says that Britons are subjects rather than citizens; that word deserves more analysis.
In This Land is Our Land, Marion Shoard argues that England is in effect a colonised country, but conquered so long ago that we no longer notice how much it shapes us. Within a generation of 1066, the English landowning class had been almost entirely replaced, and many free peasants were pressed into serfdom. Shoard argues that when, centuries later, the English poor did protest, “as a defeated class, they looked only to improve the terms of their subjection, and … they failed even in that.”
France, by contrast, eventually overturned its feudal order. Edward Carpenter wrote (in Towards Industrial Freedom) that victory at Waterloo had been a misfortune for England, denying us the upheaval that swept such structures away elsewhere. Perhaps that is why a French teenager reaches for the barricade and an English one reaches for a petition.
The British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition is rightly presented as a marvel. As we queue to admire it, we should ask whether we still see the conquest it depicts, and its long shadow over our country, with necessary clarity.
 
Simon Dawson
 
Winterbourne Gunner, Wiltshire
Kitty Sayers identifies the differences between the French and British education systems as a major contributory factor in why French students protest and British students don’t. Another may be in how protests are framed by the mass media in the UK.
Often, the default position is what is known as the “protest paradigm”, which leads journalists to emphasise the methods used by protesters over the message; and in which even legitimate protests then receive delegitimising coverage.
Changing the optics could bring more people out on to the streets, particularly if they feel they have a legitimate reason for doing so, and the media have a major role to play in creating and maintaining that environment for legitimate protest.
 
Kevin Donnelly
 
Sanremo, Italy

LUANDA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Angolan President Joao Lourenco has reviewed the government's achievements since 2017 and outlined economic and social challenges ahead of the 2027 general elections.
He delivered his State of the Nation address on Thursday at the opening of the National Assembly's fifth legislative session, the final parliamentary year before the 2027 general elections.
According to figures presented by the president, Angola's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 3 percent in 2025 and 5.3 percent in the first quarter of 2026. Inflation declined from 27.5 percent in 2024 to 10.8 percent in June 2026, while unemployment fell to 21.3 percent.
Public debt dropped from 115.9 percent of GDP in 2020 to 51.2 percent in 2026, he said, adding that non-oil exports increased by 66 percent and food imports declined by approximately 595 million U.S. dollars between 2022 and 2025.
The president stressed the importance of boosting domestic production, attracting private investment and creating jobs to support economic diversification.
In the social sector, he highlighted improvements in education and healthcare, including the construction of 736 healthcare facilities since 2017 and the expansion of school infrastructure.
On infrastructure and energy, Lourenco said Angola rehabilitated and paved about 3,500 km of roads over the past nine years, while installed electricity generation capacity rose from 4,659 megawatts in 2017 to 6,322 megawatts in 2026.
Regarding anti-corruption efforts, he said assets valued at approximately 13 billion dollars had been seized and confiscated in Angola and abroad between 2022 and 2026.
Acknowledging difficulties across various sectors, Lourenco identified hard work, increased production, responsibility and patriotism as key factors in achieving sustainable development. ■

Netflix has classified the show as Kuwaiti and Middle Eastern horror, describing it as ominous, psychological and suspenseful.
The series arrives as part of the streaming platform's Halloween 2026 slate, alongside titles including Below, Haunted Hotel and Balaraw: Blood Island.
Its release also marks a relatively unusual addition to Arab television, where horror has traditionally been produced less frequently than drama, comedy and romance.
Netflix has increasingly invested in Gulf productions, including the Kuwaiti romantic comedy Honeymoonish, released in 2024.
Arab filmmakers have nevertheless returned to supernatural stories periodically over the decades.
Egyptian films such as Al-Ins wal-Jinn and Al-Ta'weeza became prominent early examples of the genre, while Tunisia's Dachra, released in 2018, brought North African folk horror to a wider audience.
Netflix itself has previously experimented with Arabic-language supernatural drama.
Its 2019 Jordanian series Jinn followed teenagers confronting supernatural forces in Petra and became controversial in Jordan over its portrayal of sex, drinking and drug use.
The series was Netflix's first Arabic-language original from the Middle East, with the platform saying at the time that it planned to continue investing in Arabic-language productions.
Netflix has since expanded its regional catalogue considerably, with global titles such as Stranger Things also attracting large audiences across the Middle East.
The company's Gulf output has meanwhile included a growing number of Kuwaiti series and films, with Kuwaiti drama already forming part of Netflix's Arabic catalogue before its more recent push into locally produced originals.
Obsess now brings that approach to horror, combining a recognisably Gulf setting with psychological and supernatural themes.

Commission and Ukraine launch joint task force over EU accession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:30:51 UTC
01:30:51 KST

The Commission and Ukraine launched a joint task force meeting twice a week to speed up accession reforms on the rule of law and anti-corruption, after Hungary lifted its veto and two more negotiating clusters were opened.
The European Commission announced on Friday a joint task force with Ukraine to speed up accession work, after Hungary lifted its veto on opening further negotiating clusters.
EU and Ukrainian officials will sit on the task force, which is meant to help Kyiv complete its accession homework. Earlier this week, member states agreed to open two more clusters. The remaining two are now expected by the end of the year.
“Ukraine is among the countries making most progress towards EU membership. Following the opening of two more negotiating clusters this week, I discussed the next steps with PM Serhii Koretskyi. We agreed to launch a joint Task Force,” Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said on X.
The task force will focus on the so-called interim benchmarks, the mid-process targets a candidate must meet before it can start closing negotiating chapters.
It will work through a list of outstanding requirements under the benchmarks on the fundamentals of accession, namely the rule of law and anti-corruption reforms.
“This is an important step to have a joint task force that will be meeting in fact twice a week over the next several months to really try to accelerate the work,” Katarína Mathernová, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, told Euronews.
Hungary’s veto was lifted only after Kyiv agreed on an education law for the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia. The Ukrainian parliament passed the law with a broad majority, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy swiftly signed it.
The vote raises hopes that Ukraine’s political elite will keep up the broad consensus needed to adopt the reforms required for EU membership.
"The task force follows the model used for Montenegro and Moldova," a Commission official told Euronews, adding that it gives Ukraine’s accession process new momentum.
Kyiv is also due to receive a roadmap breaking up the main steps, and an indicative timeline to complete the accession process as part of a broader enlargement package expected at the beginning of November.
“This step shows our commitment to supporting Ukraine’s path to EU membership. Our success will require unity and commitment from all involved Ukrainian partners,” Kos said.
Sasha Vakulina contributed to the reporting.

21 things we learned at the EU leaders’ summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:30:49 UTC
01:30:49 KST

This was supposed to be an EU summit about the EU’s long-term budget. But things are never easy for EU leaders, and world events have a nasty habit of making their way onto the itinerary.
That meant this European Council had a lot more on the agenda than the last handful of summits, at least: Energy, migration, enlargement, Ukraine, and more besides were covered — and very little, if anything, was decided.
Have FOMO because you weren’t there? Don’t worry, we’ve got you covered. Here’s POLITICO’s rapid roundup of what we learned at the European Council.
Advertisement
1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate
The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff.
Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries.
The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night.
2) Budget negotiations are a marathon…
Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough.
Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.”
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee.
Advertisement
3) … and a sprint
European Council President António Costa is still aiming to get a budget deal before the end of the year, according to two EU officials. He announced that leaders will hold a special summit at the end of November to try and make progress (and there’s a December summit too). But that timing leaves them up against the clock to reach a deal by year’s end.
See you all back here on Nov. 26!
4) EU leaders may need to bring extra luggage next time
If leaders do hope to agree on the EU’s long-term budget this year, they should prepare for long negotiations in November and December.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested the pre-Christmas summit could last longer than the scheduled two days. “For the December summit, we should pack a few more shirts than usual,” he said. Gulp!
5) Your next holiday to Cyprus might be a little easier
Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides told reporters he hopes EU leaders will discuss his country’s bid to join the Schengen travel zone at the December summit.
“All technical preparations have already been completed, and we hope that the matter will be discussed by the relevant council in December so that the final political decisions can be made,” he said.
Advertisement
6) Rose-colored glasses have come off when it comes to Costa
European Council President António Costa drew the ire of some leaders over his handling of negotiations to curb high energy prices, which had become a “mess,” three EU diplomats told POLITICO, with another two diplomats saying that leaders were fuming at Costa for allowing talks to go off the rails.
7) Drink (a little) less beer to help Ukraine
Ahead of the summit, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters that supporting Ukraine costs each European the equivalent of one beer a year.
“That one beer is just a cost [for EU citizens]. There, it’s a cost of life. We drink less, their lives are saved,” he said. “Simple as that.”
He didn’t say whether he meant a beer bought in Stockholm or Prague. As anyone in Belgium knows, not all beers are created equal — or cost the same.
8) The EU Parliament wants you to know it matters too
The European Parliament’s two lead negotiators on the EU budget made the rounds of the press room to make sure journalists heard their views. Siegfried Mureșan (of the European People’s Party) and Carla Tavares (Socialists and Democrats) both stressed that the Parliament’s position is important.
Meanwhile, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola joined leaders for the first part of the summit. Metsola said she had made it clear to them that “the Parliament is not a rubber-stamp and never will be.”
Advertisement
9) Talking China (without mentioning China)
Leaders discussed trade imbalances (read: China) over lunch on Thursday and welcomed the deal the European Commission struck with China last week to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles. Czech PM Andrej Babiš even went so far as to call the deal “fantastic.”
POLITICO scooped that the European Commission is expected to work on trade measures tackling imports of chemicals and industrial machinery in an effort to protect European industry from unfair Chinese competition.
10) New bromance brewing
Hungarian PM Peter Magyar posted a late-night selfie with Dutch PM Rob Jetten on social media after day one of the summit. The two were all smiles and “tired, but not sad”, as Magyar put it in his tweet.
In reaction to the tweet, Jetten told reporters, “We are more or less of the same generation and a tad more direct and pragmatic than some colleagues in the European Council, so there’s a click.”
We started at 7:30 this morning in Brussels. The second shift begins after 10 PM, with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten @MinPres. Tired, but not sad. pic.twitter.com/dmtSMbqG4m
António Costa announced that another competitiveness summit at Alden Biesen castle in the Belgian countryside will take place in February 2027, three EU diplomats told POLITICO.
Leaders already visited the castle earlier this year, and they clearly loved the Belgian countryside so much they want to return (or Costa is forcing them to go).
Advertisement
12) Still reeling from Ceuta
Ahead of Friday’s talks, 16 EU leaders met to discuss migration over breakfast (before discussing migration over lunch with everyone else).
According to one EU diplomat, leaders broadly agreed that the EU should be able to suspend asylum applications when faced with a sudden influx of migrants that may have been engineered on purpose. But would that mean the EU will implement pushbacks (which are banned under EU law)?
13) Denmark, Italy and Poland want to be tougher on migration
The three leaders joined forces to argue that migration is a concern for many EU citizens and is contributing to rising crime rates. That caused a delay to an already shockingly long summit.
14) There were some agreements
Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Spain’s Pedro Sánchez found some time on the sidelines of the summit to chat about Rome’s restrictions on Spanish nationals sparked by the Ceuta crisis.
Plus, France and Germany said they had struck a deal to favor European-made cars under the Industrial Accelerator Act in exchange for weakening a 2035 vehicle emissions target, ending months of wrangling between the bloc’s two biggest economies.
15) EU leaders get the good stuff to eat
Thursday’s lunch menu featured a “full-flavored vegetable jus.” Not a little flavor, not a medium amount of flavor, but the full flavor. Then on Friday there was a “rich jus”. There was also a Champagne sauce. Only the best for our leaders!
Advertisement
16) The same can’t be said for reporters
Some POLITICO journalists lamented the lack of vegetarian options at the Council canteen. Pray for us.
17) No harsh words from EU to Zelenskyy
At a press conference on Friday afternoon, Volodymyr Zelenskyy was asked whether EU leaders had expressed annoyance at his recent tone toward U.S. President Donald Trump. The question followed reports that some capitals were frustrated with him and worried he was further riling the White House.
But it was all love from Zelenskyy, who said there had been no harsh words during his time in the summit room. “I heard from my European colleagues support and only support, and I’m grateful for this,” he said.
18) No hugs for Fico
As Zelenskyy entered the European Council building, he was seen hugging and kissing fellow leaders — with one exception: Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico received no hug. That may well have been because Slovakia is preparing to revive a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow.
19) 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war
Zelenskyy issued a stark warning to Europe: if Russia wins the war, as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe. Over 4 million Ukrainians already live in EU countries under temporary protection status, according to Eurostat.
20) EU leaders have forgotten about Britain … or have they?
There was plenty of talk across the Channel this week about the U.K. potentially rejoining the bloc, but the subject did not come up at the summit, even with an EU-U.K. summit due next month. EU leaders have more pressing issues on their minds.
Advertisement
Still, some had things to say about the U.K.’s relationship with the EU. Foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said “all our friends are welcome to join,” naming Britain alongside Canada, Norway and Iceland as partners seeking closer ties.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs suggested the U.K. “should come back to the family,” although he also said that Russia “had its hands on Brexit.”
21) At POLITICO, we save the best for last
Covering European Councils often involves a lot of waiting around, but during this summit conditions were a little tougher because of a phantom farter among reporters waiting for Zelenskyy’s press conference. POLITICO went viral in Brussels’ diplomatic and journalistic circles for reporting the hard facts on our live blog.
While this summit’s agenda was packed, in the end not many concrete decisions were taken. Some might say the summit was a load of hot air.

British police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser’s wife
LONDON - British police said on Oct 16 they were assessing a social media post after the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell appeared to express support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organisation.
Journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to Powell, responded on X to a post about the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.
Helm said in the post: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”

Palestine Action was proscribed under terrorism laws in 2025, so expressing support for the group constitutes a criminal offence.
Asked for comment, a government spokeswoman said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”
Palestine Action has carried out protests including vandalism in support of Palestinian causes, and denies that this amounts to terrorism. Four members of the group were jailed in June over a 2024 raid on a factory operated by Israeli defence firm Elbit which caused more than £1 million (S$1.7 million) of damage.
Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested in Britain for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned last year, many of them for holding up placards.
Palestine Action challenged the government's decision to ban the group, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that the proscription was lawful. REUTERS

Here’s Exactly How Tesla Made Its New 230-Mph Car ‘Fly’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:30:12 UTC
01:30:12 KST

Last night, with considerable showmanship, Tesla CEO Elon Musk proudly unveiled the Roadster 2 just nine years after first announcing the car, and made it “fly.” While undeniably impressive, you could also describe the spectacle as Tesla making its long-delayed luxury car “do a big hop” and then, as Buzz Lightyear would say, “fall with style.”
During the reveal in McGregor, Texas, at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility, the two-seater Roadster 2 launched itself over the automaker’s entire lineup, shot from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second, and then drove upside down off a high ramp to then flip over midair and land back down on the ground, cushioning its rapid descent using onboard thrusters.
All this was pure gold for social clips (though at the time of publication, Tesla’s stock price was down after the event), but how did Tesla make its new EV prototype perform these tricks? Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy went into detail with auto lifestyle and insurance brand Hagerty before yesterday’s event, explaining how the Roadster 2 works.
Franz von Holzhausen, Tesla’s chief designer since 2008, designed the angular exterior. He also helmed the aesthetic of the Cybertruck, Models S, X, 3, and Y, as well as the Semi. Blacked-out windows obscured any view inside the EV, which carried no human driver anyway because, as Musk said, Tesla wanted “to make sure we don’t kill anyone” during the gravity-defying demonstration.
Powertrain and Battery
The Roadster 2 will be rear-wheel-drive only, a departure from Tesla’s track record of all-wheel-drive EVs. Two motors will deliver over a megawatt of power (1,341 horsepower) and over 1,400 newton-meters (Nm) of torque, meaning this car will have more torque and power than a three-motor Plaid. But all of that power goes through just the rear wheels.
The car will be light, at “just under 1,700 kilos” (under 2 tons), according to Moravy, not significantly heavier than the original 1,300-kg (1.4-ton) Roadster, despite a larger size.
Tesla claims a range of over 300 miles for the Roadster and hopes to mitigate this distinctly average range by also giving the EV the fastest-charging battery the automaker has ever produced, supposedly capable of zipping from 15 to 80 percent in 10 minutes.
Sucking Fans
At a 2013 auction, Elon Musk bought the iconic "Wet Nellie" Lotus Esprit S1 submarine car from the 1977 James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me for just shy of $1 million. Musk is so taken with his Bond memorabilia that it apparently inspired one of the Roadster 2's key abilities.
That submarine Bond car has four propellers at its rear, so Tesla decided to ape this with four 20-kilowatt fans on the Roadster 2. Moravy says these fans break the laws of tire physics and dramatically increase the EV's traction by becoming what Tesla calls the car’s “sucker system.” Four independent replaceable skirts drop down on the sides of the car, allowing the Roadster 2 to stick (or suck) to the road at lower speeds where its aerodynamic wings aren't yet contributing to downforce. Moravy claims the system can produce over 2 g's in a corner when accelerating, even below 50 mph.
This type of aerodynamic manipulation also appears on the McMurtry Spéirling Pure, which uses two high-speed electric fans spinning at up to 23,000 revolutions per minute to actively suck air from underneath the chassis, generating up to 2,000 kg (around 4,400 pounds) of downforce.
This extreme suction lets the Roadster 2 drive up the vertical ramp at the Texas demonstration and hold onto the surface even when upside down.
Rocket-Powered Thrust
So how does the Roadster 2 hover, correct itself, and dampen its fall? That's thanks to what Tesla calls the car’s “SpaceX system,” referring to Musk’s aerospace company, which helped with this part of the car’s development.
Originally, the Roadster was meant to have a 2+2 cabin. Now it’s a two-seater because behind the seats sits a 200-liter carbon-overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) that holds up to 10,000 PSI to supply the car’s cold gas thrusters, which use expansion of pressurized nitrogen gas to generate thrust, a tech predominantly used for spacecraft stabilization. Cold gas thrusters are the simplest manifestation of a rocket engine.
This combination of suction system and thrusters helps the car hit 0 to 60 mph in supposedly under a second. In this launch mode, Moravy says the rear thrusters produce more than 80 kilonewtons of thrust, which, staggeringly, matches the Dassault Falcon 10X jet. Tesla has seemingly cracked the sub-second race, while the aforementioned McMurtry Spéirling Pure can only manage this feat in a bowel-clenching 1.3 seconds. During this astonishing acceleration, the driver will endure up to 5 g's.
The Roadster 2's Performance model will feature the sucker system and no thrusters, so 0 to 60 will take a touch longer at 1.6 seconds and a top speed of 210 mph. The Thrust model gets the whole package and a top speed of 230 mph.
Moravy says the “flight system,” as he calls it in Hagerty’s walk-through, requires yet another 400-liter cold gas COPV, occupying the space where the passenger seat is, making the car a single-seater and bringing total thrust fuel up to 600 liters. This “flight system” also requires six extra thrusters: one in each corner, plus two at the front to yaw.
Bursting the Balloon
Unlike in space, where cold gas thrusters provide consistent levels of thrust until the last drop of fuel is used, on Earth the “flight system” will lose thrust as the compressed gas depletes. Moravy likens it to blowing up a balloon then letting the air out: “When I open the end of a balloon, all the gas comes out, and at a certain point, it starts tapering off. That same thing will happen here.”
Apparently, refilling the 600-liter nitrogen tanks takes Tesla six to seven hours, but the company is supposedly working on a system to dramatically reduce this to 30 minutes.
The current Roadster 2 prototypes are being used for further development, and production won’t begin until 2028—but remember that Musk previously said Roadster deliveries would begin in 2020, so take this with a very large pinch of salt. That's without talking about how the Federal Aviation Administration will react to this "flying" car.
Still, for the Tesla faithful, a reservation page is already live where a $5,000 reservation fee secures the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with a whopping $245,000 due within 10 days.

All six of Smart Holding's business segments in Ukraine have suffered losses of one kind or another as a result of the war, with gas production hit particularly hard, the group's CEO Ivan Herasymovych said.
"The group currently has more than 55 companies in Ukraine, structured into six business segments, and each of them is suffering losses and being affected by Russian attacks. First and foremost, this is gas production. We have been subjected to targeted missile strikes: four missiles were launched at our assets in Kharkiv region, followed by 32 Shahed drones. "There is no insurance. We are surviving on our own resources," he said.
At the same time, the CEO once again called for gas production to be unblocked at the group's assets in Poltava region, noting that its losses from military risks were smaller than the losses to the state budget in the form of taxes resulting from the production shutdown under the sanctions regime.
"As a result of our downtime in Kharkiv and now in Poltava, the state budget has lost UAH 3.1 billion. Do something to unblock production in Poltava," Herasymovych urged.

Smart Energy, part of the Smart Holding investment group, develops projects for the exploration and commercial development of hydrocarbon deposits. It was among Ukraine's five largest private gas producers, extracting a combined total of more than 1 million cubic meters of gas per day before the start of Russia's full-scale military aggression.
Before the war, hydrocarbon reserves at Smart Energy's gas-producing assets were estimated under the C1+C2 categories at 22.633 billion cubic meters of gas and 3.722 million tonnes of condensate.

US pressures Lebanon to scrap Israel boycott laws
Unknown

Breadcrumb
US pressures Lebanon to scrap Israel boycott laws
The United States is stepping up pressure on Lebanon to repeal or amend laws criminalising contact with Israel, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio raising the issue directly with President Joseph Aoun.
Rubio discussed Lebanon's 1955 Boycott of Israel law during a phone call with Aoun on Thursday, according to a statement from the US embassy in Beirut.
He described the legislation as "impractical" and said it was being used in politically motivated prosecutions that obstructed efforts towards peace.
Rubio also urged Lebanon and Israel to establish direct military-to-military communication to reduce the risk of clashes and help implement a US-backed framework agreement between the two countries.
The renewed pressure follows controversy over a legal complaint against Lebanon's ambassador to Washington, Nada Hamadeh Moawad.
The complaint was filed after Lebanese and Israeli media reported that Moawad had contacted Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter following an attack in the occupied West Bank in which his son was injured.
Moawad did not publicly confirm or deny the reports.
The complaint was referred to Lebanon's military judiciary, prompting a strong response from Washington.
The State Department said it was "shameful" for a military court to consider a complaint against an ambassador "simply for implementing her legitimate government's policy and participating in US-led negotiations".
Judge Claude Ghanem, the government commissioner at the Military Court, closed the case on Wednesday after finding insufficient evidence that Moawad had violated Lebanon's boycott legislation.
President Aoun also defended the ambassador, saying the alleged contact had not taken place.
"If the aim of those doing this is to target the path we have taken to end the state of war and save Lebanon, then they are committing a crime against the country," he said.
The case has nevertheless brought Lebanon's anti-normalisation legislation back to the centre of political debate.
The 1955 Boycott of Israel law prohibits Lebanese individuals and companies from entering into agreements or transactions with Israeli entities or people based in Israel.
Lebanon's Penal Code also criminalises certain forms of contact with an enemy state, with some offences classified as treason.
Although Lebanon and Israel remain formally in a state of hostility, they began direct US-mediated negotiations in April and signed a framework agreement in Washington on 26 June.
US officials now argue that Lebanon's existing laws are incompatible with that diplomatic process.
Sources told The New Arab that US Ambassador to Beirut Michel Issa has been pressing Lebanese political figures, particularly MPs opposed to Hezbollah, to support changes to the legislation.
Washington reportedly sees repeal or amendment of the laws as part of a broader package of demands on Beirut.
These include accelerating efforts to disarm Hezbollah, reforming the Military Court and implementing financial, monetary and political reforms.
US officials have also expressed frustration at what they see as slow implementation by the Lebanese government.
The pressure comes as Lebanon and Israel prepare for another round of US-sponsored negotiations, expected to take place in Florida later this month.
The legal debate has grown as direct contact between Lebanese and Israeli officials becomes increasingly routine under US mediation.
Some Lebanese legal experts argue that the existing framework has effectively become harder to enforce as official negotiations expand.
Lebanese media outlets have also increasingly interviewed Israeli officials and journalists, while contacts once considered politically or legally taboo have become more common.
Washington's latest intervention is likely to intensify a wider domestic debate over whether Lebanon can continue formal negotiations with Israel while retaining legislation that criminalises many forms of contact with it.

Ukrainians warned of the risk of new power outages amid Russia's massive attacks on the energy sector
Kyiv • UNN
Russian drones damaged energy facilities supplying the Rivne region, causing widespread power outages. Repairs are ongoing in Lutsk, and new restrictions are possible.
Russian forces attacked the main power grid of NPC "Ukrenergo" with drones, damaging facilities that supply electricity to Rivne region. The strikes caused widespread power outages in Rivne and nearby areas. In Lutsk, energy workers continue restoring the power grids after the overnight attacks. "Ukrenergo" reported this and warned Ukrainians about the risk of new outages, reports UNN.
Details
According to the company, the energy infrastructure responsible for supplying electricity to Rivne region suffered serious damage as a result of the Russian drone attack. As a result, widespread power outages were recorded in Rivne and the surrounding areas. Energy workers are currently trying to restore electricity to consumers as quickly as possible using backup power supply schemes. This will make it possible to partially restore electricity supplies even before repairs to the damaged equipment are completed. At the same time, specialists will be able to begin full-scale emergency restoration work only when the security situation allows it.
However, the company is not yet specifying the exact timeframe for restoring electricity supplies.
The aftermath of the overnight attacks continues to be dealt with in Lutsk
At the same time, energy workers are working to restore electricity supplies in Volyn region. In particular, repair work is continuing in Lutsk following Russian drone attacks during the night of October 16. According to "Ukrenergo", the grids supplying the city with electricity suffered serious damage. Specialists continue to eliminate the consequences of the strikes in order to restore the stable operation of the power grids.
At the same time, the exact number of consumers left without electricity in the affected regions is not currently being specified.
Ukrainians warned about the risk of new outages
Against the backdrop of the damage to the energy infrastructure, "Ukrenergo" urged citizens who have electricity to conserve it as much as possible.
It is especially important to reduce consumption during the evening hours, when the load on the power system traditionally increases. The company explained that economical use of electricity will help energy workers eliminate the consequences of Russian attacks more quickly and avoid additional restrictions. In particular, Ukrainians should, whenever possible, avoid switching on several powerful electrical appliances at the same time and postpone the use of energy-intensive equipment until another time.
"Ukrenergo" emphasizes that reducing the load on the power grids is particularly important now, as the power system is operating with damaged infrastructure following the Russian strikes.
If consumption remains high, forced restrictions on electricity supplies may become necessary during the evening peak.
We remind you
As a result of another Russian air attack by the Russian army on Ukraine on October 16, civilian infrastructure was damaged in Vinnytsia; four people were reported injured, two of whom were hospitalized. In Rivne and nearby settlements, meanwhile, disruptions to electricity supplies occurred.
