Did Egypt's Sisi hint at stepping down in 2030?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:22:37 UTC
01:22:37 KST

Breadcrumb
Did Egypt's Sisi hint at stepping down in 2030?
A series of statements by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has raised questions over whether the former military general will step down when his current term ends in 2030.
Speaking at the 44th Armed Forces Educational Symposium on Wednesday, Sisi reaffirmed that Egypt's constitution would remain protected and unchanged, remarks that were welcomed by supporters but also drew scepticism.
The president said the constitution would remain untouched, and warned against attempts to incite unrest in Egypt.
“There is a constitution for this state, there is a constitution that we approved for this state, no one will touch it … no one will touch it," Sisi reiterated.
The remarks have sparked debate in Egypt, with some interpreting them as a sign that he does not plan to pursue constitutional changes that would allow him to remain in power for longer.
Here, The New Arab takes a closer look at what the constitution states and what his comments could be hinting at.
What does the constitution say?
Egypt's 2014 constitution, prior to being amended in 2019, stipulated in Article 140 that the country's president is elected to serve a four-year term, with the possibility of re-election only once.
In 2019, an amendment that maintained the two-term limit but extended each term to six years forwarded by a pro-government bloc, was approved by parliament.
The amendment was later approved in a public referendum which saw 88.8 percent of voters vote in favour and 11.1 percent against, with a turnout of 44 percent.
Rights groups and monitors warned at the time that the moves would entrench repression in Egypt, with reports of intimidation of referendum voters and journalists, arrests of opponents of the amendments, and vote buying by state-aligned entities.
Why is Sisi making these statements now?
Sisi's latest statements come amid calls from supporters for him to extend his rule over the country, including the launch of an online petition calling for the president to stay in his post until 2050.
This, however, has prompted widespread backlash, as many have decried it as undemocratic and have cited Sisi's crackdown on dissent.
Saeed Sadek, a professor of political sociology, told The New Arab that the president's statements appear to be aimed at closing the door to speculation about his political future.
The comments also come at a time when Egypt is facing several challenges, particularly from upheaval in the region and a sustained domestic economic crisis.
Sadek added, however, that the statement raises the political cost of any attempt to amend the constitution in the near future, though it does not completely shut the door to changes.
The constitution, he highlighted, contains mechanisms for amendments which can be activated with the necessary political will and backing of parliament.
Sadek notes that Sisi had made similar statements prior to the 2019 amendments.
What has been the response?
While Sisi did not explicitly say he would step down or rule out standing for re-election in 2030, his words have sparked some optimism for many.
Hamdeen Sabahi, Karama Party founder and former presidential candidate who stood against Sisi in 2014, described the president's comments as the "best of words", and expressed his hope that they would be followed up by the "best of actions".
In statements to the press, Sabahi expressed hope that Sisi would hand over power in 2030, paving the way for a new era in Egypt.
Amr Hashem Rabie, an expert at the Al-Ahram Center for Political and Strategic Studies, also told The New Arab that Sisi's statements indicate that Egypt is heading towards the election of a new president in 2030, unless unforeseen circumstances alter this course.
He added that some political parties, such as Nation's Future Party, Homeland Protectors, and the National Front Party, might push for street rallies to demand the president's continued rule, in addition to the role of some media figures who might promote the idea that there is no viable alternative to the president.
Sisi's remarks were also welcomed by Justice Party leader Abdel Moneim Imam, who similarly expressed hope for a peaceful transfer of power.
Egypt's Civil Democratic Movement was among those who welcomed the remarks, though cautioned that the constitution should not be subject to amendment according to circumstances or individuals.
Many Arabic-language reports from outside of Egypt have further expressed skepticism about the president's remarks, given that he holds such a tight grip on the state's institutions.
Sisi took power after removing Egypt's first democratically elected president, Mohamad Morsi, in 2013, and has led a crackdown on dissent within Egypt. By 2030, the former military general would have served as Egypt's president for 16 years.

The leader of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) youth movement, Abhijeet Dipke, was detained by police on Friday as authorities cracked down on fresh anti-government protests in the Indian capital.
Dipke was detained before a planned Friday evening demonstration he had called in central Delhi, urging supporters of the movement to come out and hold up the Indian flag.
The Cockroach movement initially emerged back in May as online satire, but has since grown into one of the most substantial challenges to the powerful Modi government over its 12-year rule.
Alongside student groups and opposition parties, its supporters have in the past month been out on the streets across India’s biggest cities calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of India’s electoral rolls that allegedly favours the ruling Narendra Modi government with the deletion of 130m names. The election commission and Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) deny the claims.
The authorities, particularly in Delhi, have met the recent protests with a draconian crackdown, including bans on public gatherings, the deployment of tens of thousands of police, and detentions of thousands last weekend.
Friday’s protest was called by Dipke after the arrest and jailing of two of his fellow CJP leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka. They were sentenced to five days in jail this week for jumping police barricades and holding a brief protest – including waving the Indian flag – at a site recently restricted by police for demonstrations in Delhi.
At a press conference on Thursday, Dipke condemned the “repressive” attempts to silence the CJP movement and called on supporters to come out and show Narendra Modi “that we are not afraid”. He added: “If waving the Indian national flag lands you in jail, we are ready.”
Delhi police had once again taken extreme measures to try to prevent Friday’s demonstration, due to be held at a park in a busy commercial centre in the heart of Delhi, from going ahead. Police were deployed en masse to the area and a police notice was sent to Dipke instructing him to call off the protest. The Delhi local authority also shut down the park where the protest was due to take place.
When Dipke refused to call it off, police detained him en route, just as people began to assemble for the protest. In videos captured of his arrest, the CJP leader was seen holding an Indian flag aloft and saying: “I have not broken any law right now … how can you detain me?” as he was led away by dozens of police officers.
In a post after his detention, the CJP posted on social media: “This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag.”
Neha Bora, a student leader who has become a figurehead of the protests, was also detained on Friday as she began a march in the centre of the capital.
Despite Dipke’s detention, about 2,000 protesters still gathered and unfurled flags at the protest around Delhi’s Connaught Place. Among them was 23-year-old Sanna, who said the brutal police crackdown on peaceful protests over recent weeks demonstrated that India was “on a pathway to dictatorship under the Modi government”.
“We are only out here to peacefully hold up the Indian flag and they treat us as if we are criminals, not citizens exercising our democratic rights,” she said. “Gyanesh Kumar must resign, and no matter what the police do, detaining us or crushing our skulls, we still won’t stop protesting until he is gone.”
Smaller protests also took place in Mumbai, Bengaluru and Patna on Friday.
The BJP has claimed that the Cockroach movement and the political opposition alliance have been holding protests to cause “anarchy” in the country. “Their sole intention is to stage a coup in the country,” said the BJP’s national spokesperson, Sambit Patra.
The authorities have also gone to unusual lengths to punish figures who have been seen at the recent protests calling for Kumar’s resignation.
In Mumbai, the Bollywood actor Imran Khan was given a notice to leave the country after he was detained by police while attending a demonstration last weekend. Khan, who holds a US passport, was told to leave the country by the end of the month, an order he is now challenging in the courts.

Thank Gen Z for the ‘Girls’ Revival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:21:38 UTC
01:21:38 KST

It’s official: Lena Dunham’s millennial magnum opus Girls is coming back, and it’s in large part thanks to Gen Z giving the show its long overdue redemption arc.
Using their native tongue: the internet, Gen Z proselytized the show through memes, clips, and podcasts, and now, as if by collective manifestation, it’s being rebooted for five episodes, which HBO announced Wednesday.
When Girls first aired in 2012, it was cataclysmic. Rave reviews were usurped by the relentless onslaught of sexism and misogyny, which commented on Dunham’s body, the kind of sex depicted onscreen, and the nepo baby allegations against the show’s stars—as well as the series’ lack of diversity. There was endless backlash and backlash to the backlash; it became everyone’s favorite show to both fairly criticize and willfully misunderstand, and creator Dunham was the one stuck grasping onto the lightning rod of so much ire, as she began to stand for everything wrong with millennial white women.
But then something happened. A decade after it aired, everyone started rewatching Girls. It’s not just that people were talking about it online; the series’ viewership doubled between November 2022 and January 2023, compared with the previous three months, The New York Times reported. On Tiktok and Instagram, memes and supercuts started unfurling: Marnie poised with a microphone in the infamous teal dress; Hannah snapping “I am busy, trying to become who I am,” or Shoshanna saying, “Obvi we’re the ladies!” It finally clicked for viewers, spawning a cultural and critical resurgence. While the reviews aged like milk, the show had aged like wine.
It was a phenomenon largely fueled by Gen Z viewers who had missed the show the first time around. (As well as prominent millennial Girls “truthers” like Hunter Harris, Peyton Dix, and Evan Ross Katz.) Among these Gen Z viewers were Amelia Ritthaler and Evan Lazarus, Brooklyn comedians who launched the Girls Rewatch podcast in 2023.
“I think the rest of society caught up to (Dunham),” says Ritthaler, 28. “Everybody was kind of under the impression that they weren’t allowed to be publicly saying that they loved the show and thought it was great. But me and Evan were like, this show is amazing. Why is everybody mad at her?”
Gen Z especially was able to identify with a style that so many millennials had failed to grasp. “So much of what we were raised on was this post-ironic, emotionally removed, ‘world is burning, but let’s dance through it’ kind of social media,’” she says. “I feel like when it was coming out, millennials were just kind of in their earnest era. The millennial optimism of it all. I feel like Gen Z never got that, so we were always watching it from this satirical lens that Lena wrote it in.”
Ritthaler and Lazarus posted Girls memes on TikTok and Instagram, amassing a following that allowed them to have guests like Dunham, as well as cast members Allison Williams (Marnie), Andrew Rannells (Elijah), and Zosia Mamet (Shoshanna) on the show. “I think this was like 70% cuz of you guys,” Jemima Kirke (Jessa) commented on the podcast’s Instagram account the day the revival was announced. “I feel like I loved my favorite show back to my life,” Lazarus said in a teary-eyed video.
The show’s redemption arc coincided with Dunham’s memoir Famesick, published in April, further fueling the Girls nostalgia. “I feel like reading Famesick felt like getting a director’s cut of girls,” says Dix, who hosts the podcast Lemme Say This with Hunter Harris.
The book was an instant New York Times bestseller with a buzzy tour. More importantly, there was a public reckoning around the way culture mistreated Dunham. It felt like a bow tied neatly around the physical and mental toll making Girls. She had moved to London, gotten sober, written extensively about chronic illness, worked on shows like Industry and Too Much. Last month, she announced she’d welcomed a baby via surrogacy.
There were never explicit fan calls for a reboot, particularly after the universally-panned Sex and the City reboot And Just Like That… But the swell in the show’s popularity undoubtedly caught the attention of HBO execs, thanks to the tenacious Gen Zers who spread the good word online. In a Substack post published Wednesday, Dunham credited the fans for helping her be ready to return to the series. “Maybe there was once a part of me that wanted to outrun Hannah and her ladies,” she writes. “Seeing the love you’ve so generously shared for it helped to turn me around.”
“The fans are just tender queers and sensitive girls who journal and heart their eyes,” says Dix. “The people she’s reaching and nurturing aren’t critics anymore, it feels like, or people who want to make weird comments about her body. It’s just young people, she wants to help inform or entertain.”
Part of the reason for the revival is, of course, that everything has come back: Gossip Girl, Pretty Little Liars, iCarly, and countless others have also seen reboots and sequels in recent years. “It’s nostalgia-core for sure,” Ritthaler says. “But it sucks that we don't have any new IP that has topped it. I walk around Brooklyn every day, thinking ‘how did we make Girls in 2012 and then everything went back to being worse?’”
But Gen Z is also ripe for a millennial optimism they never got to experience. Nostalgia for the mid-2010s has been cropping up online, with people posting photos of themselves in 2016, longing for fixed gear bikes, sepia toned photos, and stomp-clap music.
“I think there’s an energy, particularly in New York right now, that really embodies millennial optimism, and I think that Girls is absolutely a part of that cultural conversation,” says Dix. “It falls neatly into this new world we’re building that is kind of based on ‘Obama first-term joy.’ It’s nice to feel joy again when it’s really difficult to find it.”

Andy Lord appointed Interim Chair of NAD Group Advisory Board
The Board provides independent support and challenge, helping to ensure the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.
Andy Lord has been appointed Interim Chair of the National Armaments Director (NAD) Group Advisory Board.
Andy is currently Commissioner of Transport for London, responsible for the delivery of safe and reliable transport services across the capital.
He joined TfL in 2019 as Managing Director of London Underground, subsequently becoming Chief Operating Officer before his appointment as Commissioner. Throughout his career, he has held several senior engineering, operational and customer-service roles.
Andy also served as a Non-Executive Director and Board member for Defence Equipment & Support from 2018 until March this year.
Andy has been appointed by Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, until April 30, 2027.
The appointment comes as the NAD Group continues to establish a simpler, more integrated governance model designed to support effective decision-making, clearer accountability and stronger management of performance and risk across the Group.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce said of the appointment:
  I am delighted to welcome Andy as Interim Chair of the NAD Group Advisory Board. Andy brings extensive experience both within our organisation, having served as a DE&S Board member and trusted critical friend for eight years, and in leading large, complex organisations.
His insight, challenge and independent perspective will be invaluable as we continue to build the NAD Group into an integrated, mission-focused organisation.
The new Advisory Board’s role is to provide independent support and challenge to the NAD and senior leadership, helping to ensure that the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.
On taking up the role, Andy said:
  I am delighted to be appointed the Interim Advisory Board Chair. I have seen first-hand the expertise and commitment that exists across the organisations that now make up the NAD Group, and the vital contribution they make to Defence.
The opportunity now is to build on those strengths, bringing together expertise from across the Group to deliver even greater impact. I look forward to supporting the leadership team as it continues to drive integration, transformation and operational excellence in support of its mission.
The Board provides a strategic, Group-wide perspective, testing whether the organisation is moving in the right direction and identifying where further support, challenge or intervention may be valuable.
These contributions support the NAD Group’s ambition to create a high-support, high-challenge environment, in which leaders are empowered to deliver while remaining accountable for results.
Alongside Andy, the NAD Group’s Non-Executive Members (NEMs) are Robert MacLeod, Tony Meggs, Tracy Sheedy, Carolyn Battersby, Claire Hawkings and Sarah Albon (Safety & Security Committee only).
NEMs are not part of the NAD Group’s executive management structure. Their value comes from their independence and the breadth of experience they bring.
The Board will be supported by three specialist committees covering nominations and remuneration; audit and risk assurance; and safety and security.

This is directly linked to the humanistic culture that needs to be instilled in young people. It involves the holistic development of a person through education, work, culture, science, moral responsibility and openness to the world. Our goal is to prepare not only a person who has mastered a profession, but an individual capable of consciously fulfilling their potential in that profession, creating value and contributing to the development of society,” Maria Furman, Director of the Business Education Center at the Institute of Psychology and Entrepreneurship, emphasized at a roundtable discussion at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Friday.
Iryna Khomenko, Head of the International Development and Partnerships Department at the Institute of Psychology and Entrepreneurship (IPP), in turn, emphasized the importance of a humanistic and ontopsychological approach to education and personal development.
“The transfer of knowledge is a fundamental, but not the only, task of education. Secondary and higher education institutions work with individuals during the period when their identities are being formed, when their perceptions of themselves, their own capabilities, and their professional and life orientations are taking shape. And responsibility for this process extends far beyond the development of professional competencies,” she added.
Tetiana Harets, Director of the Professional College of Management and Psychology, linked teenagers' communication difficulties to the war and distance learning. The college currently operates the Start Week and Team Challenge programs, project-based learning using EduScrum and Agile approaches, the IPP COIN motivation system, while students create a mini-company in the OpenSpace business laboratory.
“A traditional report card simply shows the grades a student receives in an academic subject. It says nothing about whether the student has learned to coordinate people's actions, make decisions, respond to feedback or take responsibility for a shared result. That is precisely why we created an individual student portfolio – a chronological account of a person's development, rather than just a folder of certificates,” Harets explained.
Oleksandr Strukov, Head of Sales at the DMNTR media holding company, noted that companies can teach technical skills but expect candidates to have communication skills and a willingness to develop.
“If we talk about what exactly businesses want from candidates, it is now far from being only about technical aspects. It is about leadership potential, personal resource potential and soft skills. I am convinced that no business can function without communication,” the employer emphasized.
Entrepreneur Yurii Skilskyi, a partner of the BOARD community in Kolomyia, identified initiative, learning, stress resilience and responsibility as key factors in the development of modern education and called for stronger business mentorship.
“I suggest that business representatives visit young people more often and share their experience. Visits to companies can be organized so that they can see everything with their own eyes. For us as entrepreneurs, it is important to support young people and unlock their potential,” Skilskyi emphasized.
In turn, Olha Bondarenko, HR Director of a technology holding company, highlighted the desire for development, independent thinking, responsibility and the ability to create value. She added that in the defense technology industry, the security of the country may depend on an employee's decisions.
“Responsibility is formed primarily through practical experience, through the opportunity to make a choice, through the need to make a decision, through awareness of its consequences and, of course, through mistakes. But here I want to draw a clear line: the right to make a mistake is not the right to be irresponsible. A mistake becomes experience when you are able to acknowledge it, analyze it and change your subsequent actions,” the specialist emphasized.
Tetiana Spivakovska, Candidate of Economic Sciences, Associate Professor at IPP and Deputy Director of the Sofia Academy in Dubai, reported that, thanks to the recognition of learning outcomes obtained abroad, the academy had managed to integrate more than 30 pupils into the Ukrainian education system within a year.
“For Ukrainian higher education institutions, this means a fundamental change in the competitive environment. They are now competing for young people in the global educational space. It is necessary to create unique educational offerings, ensure high-quality teaching, develop international partnerships and modern infrastructure,” Spivakovska said.
Nataliia Shumska, Head of the 3S AGENCY recruitment agency, warned against replacing independent thinking with the search for ready-made answers. According to her, the IPP publishing project translated and published five books by Antonio Meneghetti in Ukrainian over the course of a year.
“Today, students can obtain a significant portion of information independently. Artificial intelligence can explain a complex topic, prepare notes, write an essay – these are enormous opportunities. But if thoughts, arguments or conclusions are increasingly formulated for a person, do they not risk gradually losing the habit of doing this independently?” Shumska added.
IPP students Anna Sytnyk and Nataliia Kozlovska spoke about practical work and mentorship. Kozlovska, who also mentors first-year college students, emphasized the significance of ontopsychological pedagogy in working with young people.
“It seems to me that the task of education is not simply to give a person knowledge, but also to help them better understand themselves. Especially at a young age, we do not always fully understand what we want, what our strengths are and where we can realize our potential. That is why it is important for education to provide not only theoretical knowledge, but also opportunities to try ourselves in different fields, work on practical tasks, make decisions and see the results of our work,” the student noted.
IPP graduate Serhii Andriichenko, Head of Development and Innovation at 3S AGENCY, highlighted the Work and Study program, which combines education with employment, and emphasized the value of the educational community.
“The institute develops a new generation of leaders, but a leader cannot be developed through lectures alone. A leader is shaped by the environment. This includes the Work and Study program, a theoretical foundation, face-to-face meetings with entrepreneurs, elective classes, professional events, activities and the student community,” he emphasized.
In conclusion, Maria Furman announced the IPE Leader 2027 international platform, featuring a year-long program of more than 20 events for young people, educators and businesses.
“This is an international platform that brings together education, business, science, leadership and humanistic culture. We invite young people, as well as representatives of business, culture and science, to join this platform. It is a large year-long program that will include intellectual activities and lectures by scientists, speakers and teachers from the business sector,” Furman said.
According to her, a hackathon for young people aged 15 and over is scheduled for October 23–24, while the Ukrainian Leadership Forum will begin in November. Its participants will propose social projects for schools and communities, form teams and present their results in May 2027. The IPE Leader 2027 Awards, covering ten categories for young people, scientists, philanthropists and businesses, have also been announced for May.
The platform is scheduled to open on October 23. The organizers invite attendees, speakers, companies and non-governmental organizations willing to support youth initiatives.

EU–Turkey summit in October aims to restart Cyprus talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:21:32 UTC
01:21:32 KST

President Christodoulides said the high-level meeting would focus on resuming negotiations over Cyprus and advancing EU-Turkey relations.
A high-level meeting between the European Union and Turkey is expected to take place in October, focusing on efforts to restart talks on the Cyprus issue and the future of EU-Turkey relations, Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides said on Friday.
Speaking to journalists, he said he had been informed of the planned meeting following recent discussions in New York with UN Secretary-General António Guterres, as well as talks between Guterres and EU leaders. The meeting, being organised at the request of the UN Secretary-General, aims to explore ways to create the conditions needed to resume negotiations on the Cyprus issue.
“I am pleased, I repeat, because from the briefing I had yesterday from the heads of the institutions, such a meeting will be held in October, following a request by the UN Secretary-General himself, so that we can see how conditions are created for the resumption of negotiations,” the President said.
Christodoulides stressed that progress in EU-Turkey relations depends on the resumption of negotiations on Cyprus under the agreed framework.
“Any progress in EU-Turkey relations depends on the resumption of talks on the basis of the agreed framework,” he said.
He also mentioned the expected visit to Cyprus by the UN Secretary-General’s personal envoy in late October, saying these developments could help create conditions for progress.
"Our clear political will is a given and I repeat that the EU can play a leading role," he said.
Christodoulides recalled that his administration had prioritised greater EU involvement in efforts to restart negotiations from the outset. He also welcomed the appointment of a senior European Commission official, saying it reflected the EU's approach to the Cyprus issue.
EU contacts with Turkey over UN Climate Conference COP31
Asked whether the European Council's conclusions would refer to the UN Climate Conference COP31, Christodoulides said the issue had been discussed on Thursday and that he had briefed his European counterparts on the latest developments.
He said that following a statement by the Turkish Cypriot leader, the EU had contacted the Turkish government on behalf of its 27 member states and received written responses.
"If these replies are implemented in practice, then we will be satisfied," he said, adding that Cyprus was prepared for any eventuality.
Migration: "No clashes between member states"
Referring to discussions on migration, Christodoulides warned that disagreements between EU member states could send the wrong message to citizens.
"A clash is certainly not the most appropriate or the best message we can send to European citizens, especially on an issue we know concerns all member states," he said.
Despite the challenges, he pointed to progress in managing migration across the EU, citing a 90% drop in arrivals in Cyprus and a 180% increase in returns compared with 2022.
He said talks should focus on identifying gaps and considering further measures, including a possible EU mechanism to respond to the use of migrants as a tool of political pressure.
Energy costs and ETS2 dominate EU talks
Nikos Christodoulides described Thursday’s discussions on energy costs and rising prices as extensive, noting that some member states initially reluctant to support proposals from Mediterranean and Central European countries, as well as the Balkan B4 group, had now recognised the need to adopt them.
On the EU’s second Emissions Trading System (ETS2), Christodoulides welcomed the wording agreed in the European Council’s conclusions.
"As it stands at the moment, as agreed last night, the wording satisfies us," he said.
He added that the European Commission appeared to recognise the need to further delay the system’s implementation, warning that it could place an additional burden on households and businesses already struggling with high energy costs. He also stressed that it remained unclear when the energy crisis would end.
Hard-fought negotiations on the EU budget
Commenting on the negotiations over the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the President described the position of the Irish Presidency as difficult, noting that the Cypriot Presidency had previously managed to secure agreement on key aspects of the budget.
He said the matter now lies in the hands of the President of the European Council and expressed the view that discussions will focus on more concrete proposals for new EU own resources.
According to him, the objective is to avoid any further reduction of the EU budget or, if this proves unavoidable, to keep it to an absolute minimum.
Asked about the reaction of some member states to the proposals for new own resources, Christodoulides said that certain countries had expressed reservations due to national priorities, but noted that some ideas had been received positively by member states.
Tough negotiations over EU budget
Commenting on negotiations over the EU’s Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), Christodoulides said the Irish Presidency faced a difficult task, noting that the Cypriot Presidency had previously secured agreement on key budget issues.
He said the matter was now in the hands of the European Council President, adding that discussions were expected to focus on more concrete proposals for new sources of EU revenue.
The aim, he said, was to avoid further cuts to the EU budget or keep them to a minimum if unavoidable.
Asked about member states’ reactions to proposals for new EU revenue sources, Christodoulides said some countries had raised concerns over national priorities, while others had responded positively to certain proposals.

12 Symptoms ENT Doctors Say Never to Ignore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:19:39 UTC
01:19:39 KST

You might see an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) doctor for recurring sinus infections. Someone else might see one for a thyroid tumor, a voice that won’t return after a cold, or trouble breathing during sleep. They’re all within an ENT’s purview.
These doctors, formally called otolaryngologists, treat conditions involving the ears, nose, throat, and much of the head and neck. That includes problems affecting your hearing, swallowing, breathing, and voice—and some that require urgent care. “A lot of people will think, ‘Oh yeah, there’s no emergencies at ENT,’ and there absolutely are,” says Dr. Ryan Salvador, an ENT surgeon at Sinus & Snoring Specialists in Austin.
We asked three otolaryngologists what they wish patients wouldn’t ignore.
Sudden hearing loss in one ear
You answer your phone and realize you can barely hear your friend’s voice out of your left ear. Switch to your right side, and everything sounds normal. It’s tempting to assume the muffled ear needs to pop, Salvador says. But an abrupt change in hearing can be a medical emergency.
One possibility is sudden sensorineural hearing loss, which affects the inner ear. Salvador knows how easily it can be mistaken for something else: His father went to urgent care and was told he had fluid behind his eardrum. By the time he saw an ENT, about eight weeks had passed. “He’s completely deaf in that ear now,” Salvador says.
An ENT can examine the ear and arrange a hearing test to find out what’s causing the loss. If it is sudden sensorineural hearing loss, steroids may help—but, as Salvador puts it, “the earlier the better.” Seek medical care immediately if you suddenly lose hearing, even if your ear just feels full or you’ve recently had a cold.
A neck lump that doesn’t hurt
You might discover it while shaving, when your razor passes over a spot that suddenly isn’t smooth. Or perhaps you notice an unfamiliar bump in the mirror. Because it doesn’t hurt, you decide it can’t be that serious.
Dr. Arnbjorn Toset, the director of head and neck surgery at Good Samaritan University Hospital and Catholic Health in New York, hears that reasoning from patients: “Doctor, it’s not hurting me. I don’t have any symptoms.” But pain isn’t a reliable way to judge a neck lump. It might be an enlarged lymph node, a thyroid nodule, or a growth in a salivary gland. But some lumps are cancerous.
Dr. Shaun Desai, chair of otolaryngology at New York Medical College and Westchester Medical Center in New York, recalls a medical student who assumed his lump was related to a cold. “For eight months he sat on this lump in his neck,” Desai says. It turned out to be a salivary gland tumor. If a new lump has no clear explanation or is still there after two weeks, make an appointment.
A sore throat that keeps getting worse
A sore throat is hardly unusual. One that progresses from “this hurts” to “I can barely swallow” is another matter. Salvador pays particular attention when the pain keeps worsening and you’re also having trouble opening your mouth or your voice sounds muffled. “You talk like you’ve got a hot potato in your mouth,” he says.
Those changes can signal an abscess—a pocket of pus that forms around a tonsil. “These can be life threatening,” Salvador says. If swelling makes it difficult to breathe, seek emergency care. Worsening throat pain with trouble swallowing, opening your mouth, or speaking normally also warrants prompt evaluation.
Your partner says you stop breathing at night
Your partner hears you snoring. Then, suddenly, nothing. After a pause, you gasp and start breathing again. By morning, you may have no idea it happened.
The snoring may be what your partner complains about. Desai wants to know about the silence. “The bigger worry is, does your partner kind of stop breathing for a couple of seconds?” he says. Repeated pauses can be a sign of obstructive sleep apnea, in which the airway narrows or closes during sleep. You might wake up exhausted despite spending the whole night in bed. Untreated sleep apnea can also contribute to high blood pressure; Desai worries about people who become so sleepy during the day that they struggle to stay awake while driving.
Tell your doctor about the pauses, gasping, and any daytime sleepiness. A sleep study can show whether apnea is the cause. As Desai puts it, “Apnea is the bigger question, and that can be dangerous if not treated.”
Swelling around an eye during a sinus infection
Sinus pressure can make the area around your eyes ache. What Salvador doesn’t want you to chalk up to ordinary sinus misery is new swelling around an eye—especially if the area is red or your vision changes.
“The only thing that separates the sinus cavity from the eye is a very thin plate of bone,” he says. Rarely, an infection spreads into the tissues around the eye. Salvador has treated patients whose infections formed pockets of pus that had to be drained to protect their vision.
Get urgent medical attention for a newly swollen eye during a sinus infection. If you develop double vision or have trouble moving the eye, seek emergency care. Don’t wait for those symptoms to appear: Double vision is “a pretty late sign,” Salvador says.
Swelling under your jaw when you eat
Halfway through a meal, you notice a tender bump beneath your jaw. It settles down later—then returns the next time you eat.
Toset says that pattern can point to a blocked salivary gland. Eating triggers saliva production, but a stone can keep the saliva from draining, causing the gland to swell. It may also become painful or red.
If it keeps happening, have it examined. Toset says the cause is often benign, but an exam and sometimes imaging can distinguish a stone from another problem with the gland. If the swelling keeps returning, have the gland checked—even if it goes down between meals
A voice that won’t come back
You talked all weekend. You recently had a cold. Of course your voice sounds rough—or maybe it’s become oddly breathy, and you can’t project the way you used to. These are reasonable explanations for a temporary change, Desai says. They become less reassuring when your voice doesn’t recover.
Salvador remembers a teacher who was struggling to speak loudly enough for her class. “I can’t project,” she told him. When he examined her, he discovered that one of her vocal cords wasn’t moving properly because of a thyroid tumor. Persistent hoarseness can have other explanations, including irritation or a benign growth, but an ENT needs to look to find out.
If hoarseness lasts four weeks, see an ENT—sooner if you smoke or have other concerning symptoms. The doctor may pass a small camera through your nose to look at your vocal cords. If that sounds daunting, Desai says the office exam “just takes a minute or two.”
Dentures that suddenly don’t fit comfortably
Your dentures fit fine last month. Now they rub the same spot every time you put them in, or they don’t sit quite right. You might need an adjustment—or someone to look at what’s going on underneath.
Toset says new discomfort may draw your attention to “a little ulcer on the gum line.” Rubbing can cause a sore, but a growth in the mouth can also change how dentures fit. That’s one possible sign of oral cancer, though there are other explanations.
Ask your dentist to examine the tissue beneath the denture, especially if a sore hasn’t healed after two weeks. They can check what’s changed before adjusting the fit.
A nosebleed that won’t stop
Most nosebleeds start near the front of the nose and stop with pressure. A bleed that starts farther back can be harder to control. The blood vessels there can “pump and pump and pump,” Salvador says, and blood may run down the back of your throat. Doctors call this a posterior nosebleed.
If your nose starts bleeding, lean forward and pinch its soft part with steady pressure for 15 minutes. If the bleeding is heavy or won’t stop, or you feel weak or lightheaded, seek emergency care.
A nosebleed that does stop can still be worth investigating if it keeps coming back. Salvador remembers a man in his 30s who had consistent nosebleeds for about six months before an examination revealed a tumor inside his nose. That’s an uncommon cause, but a good reason to tell your doctor about repeated bleeding—especially if it keeps happening on the same side.
Ear pain when nothing seems wrong
Your ear hurts, so you probably have an ear infection, right? Not necessarily. Sometimes an examination turns up nothing wrong with the ear itself. Nerves in the head and neck carry a signal from somewhere else, and sometimes, “your brain is tricking you” about where it started, Toset says.
The source might be your jaw joint, which sits just in front of your ear. Less commonly, it could be a problem in your throat or at the base of your tongue. If the pain persists despite a normal ear exam, ask your doctor what else should be checked—especially if it hurts to swallow or you’ve noticed a lump in your neck.
One nostril that stays blocked
Colds and allergies can make your whole nose miserable. A blockage that sticks around on just one side gets Desai’s attention. “When you can’t breathe out of one nostril, it’s always a little more concerning,” he says.
The explanation might be a deviated septum, but a growth inside the nose or sinuses can also block one side. Desai worries about the delay when people tell themselves, “Oh, it’s a cold,” or “I just have a bloody nose.” If the blockage outlasts what seems like an ordinary cold—especially if that side also bleeds repeatedly—have it examined.
A sore on your tongue that won’t heal
Most small mouth sores clear up within a week or two. Toset is more concerned about one that stays put, grows, or becomes increasingly painful—particularly on the side of the tongue.
He remembers seeing a young woman in the emergency room on a Friday night. She had developed swelling in her neck, and the doctors who called Toset thought it might be an abscess. During his examination, he noticed a sore on the side of her tongue. She’d seen dentists and other specialists, and earlier biopsies had come back benign, but the sore had persisted for about six months.
“I had a biopsy. Biopsy was negative, so I left it alone,” Toset recalls her telling him. He examined the sore and grew concerned. “I had to break it to her,” he says: “I think you have tongue cancer.” Another biopsy confirmed it; the swelling in her neck was where the cancer had spread.
A reassuring biopsy shouldn’t be the end of the conversation if the sore is still there. Any mouth sore that hasn’t healed after two weeks should be evaluated, according to the American Academy of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery.
“I’d rather see someone early on in the process where I can pick up on something that is possibly benign or an early type of cancer,” Toset says, than see them after a delay that makes treatment more difficult.

Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed appoints interim Tigray government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:19:00 UTC
01:19:00 KST

Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed appoints interim Tigray government
October 16, 2026
Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday announced an interim government in the northern Tigray region.
The move follows an outbreak of fighting in recent weeks involving a rebel alliance and the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF).
"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle of conflict," Abiy said in a statement posted on X.
What the PM's office has said
Ahmed's office said on social media that "repeated efforts" to resolve the conflict in the region have ultimately failed.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) leadership "did not desire peace," it said, and instead initiated the latest "devastating war."
The prime minister's office said that in order to secure peace, an interim administration was being appointed in the region and would administer Tigray for the next 6 months.
Ahmed's office listed 10 primary tasks, among them, "free and fair elections" within a 6-month period.
Returning displaced communities, the restoring of government services and protection of basic infrastructure were also among the tasks listed.
What was the TPLF's reaction
The TPLF has not yet responded to the announcement. However, TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa told the AFP news agency that the region "cannot be ruled by puppets of the genocidal regime" in Addis Ababa.
Earlier, the TPLF denounced Tigrayans who collaborate with the federal government as "traitors" in a Facebook post. The statement said these individuals would face "accountability and public judgment."
Recent return to hostilities
In September, the TPLF and six other armed groups launched an offensive against Abiy's administration.
Federal forces have managed to push the rebel alliance back, resulting in the loss of strongholds, including the regional capital Mekelle.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, while Asmara denies the allegation and says Addis Ababa is using the conflict as a means of justifying military action with the aim of seizing control of the Red Sea Port of Assab.
More than 600,000 people were killed in a civil war from 2020 to 2022, and the region is still battling with large numbers of internally displaced people.

Drones Reach Russia’s Siberian Energy Heartland, Spark Fire 3,000 Kilometers From Ukraine

Drones Reach Russia’s Siberian Energy Heartland, Spark Fire 3,000 Kilometers From Ukraine
Drones attacked an industrial facility in Russia’s Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug on October 16, triggering a fire roughly 3,000 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
Ukrinform reported the attack, citing Radio Liberty and Russian regional authorities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Khanty-Mansi Governor Ruslan Kukharuk confirmed that drones struck an industrial facility in the Surgut district, causing a fire. He added that specialists were assessing the extent and nature of the damage but did not identify the affected enterprise.
The Ukrainian OSINT monitoring channel Supernova+ claimed the target was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant named after Viktor Chernomyrdin, who served as Russia’s prime minister from 1992 to 1998 and previously headed the Soviet gas industry. The facility's identification has not been independently confirmed.
The plant, operated by Gazprom Pererabotka, is Russia's largest facility for processing oil and gas condensate mixtures. It is located near Surgut in Western Siberia, approximately 3,000 kilometers from Ukraine.
The Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug is one of Russia's major oil and natural gas production centers, making its industrial infrastructure significant to the country's energy sector.
The attack followed a series of drone alerts across Russia's remote Siberian energy-producing regions. Earlier on October 16, authorities declared drone threats in the Khanty-Mansi and neighboring Yamalo-Nenets autonomous districts, as well as the Tyumen, Chelyabinsk, and Sverdlovsk regions.

01:17:42 KST

Temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures were imposed at 27 Russian airports, Deutsche Welle reported on 16 October, citing its own calculations based on reports from Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines on 1 September that “Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe.” Overnight, most of the airspace over European Russia was closed.
By morning, more than 200 flights had been canceled or delayed at Moscow airports, Deutsche Welle reported, citing figures compiled by a Russian Telegram channel.
The list included airports in the capital. All four Moscow airports temporarily suspended arrivals and departures, the Russian outlet Astra reported on 16 October. Russian authorities said they had shot down dozens of drones, while flights were delayed and diverted to alternate airfields, according to the report.
Massive drone attack on Russia: 644 UAVs in one night, 94 shot down near Moscow
The temporary airport shutdowns were likely a consequence of a massive drone attack on Russia. From 8:00 p.m. on 15 October to 8:00 a.m. on 16 October, Russian air defenses allegedly intercepted and destroyed 644 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles across 26 Russian regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black Sea, according to Russia’s Defense Ministry.
According to the list of regions published by the Russian Defense Ministry, the drone attacks covered a vast area of Russia, from regions bordering Ukraine to the Moscow region, the Volga region, the country’s northwest and southern regions, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black Sea.
Russian air defenses shot down a total of 94 drones approaching Moscow over the evening of 15 October and overnight, according to calculations by the Russian outlet RBC Radio, citing statements by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
In the Kaluga region, air defenses destroyed 27 drones over the evening and night, the regional governor reported. At 9:27 a.m., he updated the figures, saying another 48 UAVs had been shot down overnight, bringing the total to 75. According to preliminary information, there were no casualties or infrastructure damage.
In the Tula region, air defenses allegedly destroyed a total of 32 Ukrainian drones. There were no casualties, according to regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev in his Telegram channel.
In the Vladimir region in western Russia, authorities repelled drone attacks overnight. In the city of Vladimir, a drone attempted to attack a heating infrastructure facility, but the attack was stopped, Vladimir Region Governor Alexander Avdeyev reported. Minor damage was reported, but there was no information about casualties.
Ukraine has not yet commented on its involvement in the attacks.
The practical consequences of canceled Russian flights
Passengers on flight SU6312 from Kaliningrad to Moscow were unable to land in Moscow because of airspace closure, so the aircraft was diverted to Nizhny Novgorod, Terravia reported. After landing, passengers remained on board for about two hours before being allowed to disembark at 3:30 a.m. Instead of continuing their journey to Moscow by air, they were supposed to be transported by bus, with the trip expected to take about seven hours, the outlet reported.
Passengers were not provided with food or drinks, and one woman could not find a seat on the bus, so she purchased a ticket for an early-morning train herself.
Since the beginning of the year, all four Moscow airports have been completely shut down simultaneously at least 19 times, the Russian outlet Agentstvo reported. During the first 14 days of October, the restrictions lasted 101 hours and 38 minutes, compared with 46 hours and 33 minutes in September, according to the report.

Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:17:34 UTC
01:17:34 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Starlink Speeds Rise Again in Ukraine—but Key Frontline Missions Are Still Disrupted, Zelenskyy Says
Starlink connectivity has improved in Ukraine following reported signals from the White House to restore higher operating speeds, but the system remains restricted, and Ukrainian forces still cannot carry out some frontline missions as before, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s partners said there had been signals from the White House regarding the restoration of Starlink’s higher-speed capabilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Have they returned to the previous speed? No. But has the speed increased? Yes,” Zelenskyy said.
The restrictions have become a significant battlefield issue because Ukraine uses high-speed Starlink connectivity on rapidly moving unmanned systems. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukrainian forces do not currently use Starlink for deep strikes inside Russia.
“No, we do not use Starlink for attacks or retaliatory strikes on the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to open up such a capability for us. If we had it, we obviously would not be asking,” he said.
Zelenskyy described the sudden restrictions as an unpleasant and dangerous “surprise,” particularly because Starlink is used in operations intended to intercept Russia’s new jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered ‘Shaheds’ that fly in and strike our civilians, killing our families. We use special interceptors—drones that move at high speed and use Starlink,” Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that the service was not completely switched off. Instead, its effective speed limit was sharply reduced, which prevented some Ukrainian interceptor drones from keeping their satellite connection while pursuing fast-moving Russian targets.
“And when the speed was reduced, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of these ‘Shaheds.’ That is very painful and unpleasant. In other words, we were unable to provide protection for the population. The ‘Shaheds’ were flying at more than 400 kilometers per hour, while our speed was reduced to 78 km/h,” he said.
That means Russian jet-powered drones were traveling at more than 249 mph, while Ukrainian Starlink-equipped systems reportedly faced connectivity restrictions at around 48 mph.
The restrictions have also affected Ukrainian middle-strike operations against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory. Zelenskyy said Starlink connectivity had previously supported those missions, but the new limits made some of them impossible.
“And we can no longer do this,” he said.
Beyond combat missions, Zelenskyy emphasized that the restrictions have also complicated battlefield logistics. Ukrainian units use drones connected through Starlink to deliver food and water to troops holding isolated or difficult positions.
“Many people are within reach of enemy drones; we use UAVs to deliver water and food to people who have been holding positions for a long time. We use drones and Starlink. So this affected our ability to protect the population,” Zelenskyy said.
Previously, Germany called for speed restrictions affecting Starlink service in Ukraine to be lifted, stressing that Berlin itself finances part of the satellite communications equipment used by the country.

IN BRIEF: Key statements by Deputy PM Novak at Russian Energy Week plenary session
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:16:46 UTC
01:16:46 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The Russia-US diesel deal is beneficial to all parties, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told a plenary session of Russian Energy Week.
He stressed that EU criticism of the agreement goes against the interests of European consumers.
Novak stressed that Russia has been and remains a reliable energy supplier to global markets, including the West.
TASS has summarized the key takeaways from the deputy prime minister's speech.
Russia-US diesel deal
"I view this deal as a pragmatic solution that is advantageous for all market participants."
"As for criticism from our European partners, we have grown accustomed to their political decisions and statements running counter to the pragmatic demands of the market and consumers. It is European consumers who suffer first and foremost."
"The market is currently experiencing a significant shortage - we estimate it at about 25% of global trade. This is primarily due to supply disruptions from the Persian Gulf to external markets. Furthermore, Russia banned exports in July to supply its domestic market."
"On a per-barrel basis, the current diesel price is roughly $200 per barrel against a crude oil price of $120. Crack spreads for diesel relative to crude oil have widened."
Russia’s reliability and Europe’s costs
"The key factor for reliability today is physical access throughout the entire supply chain - from production and processing to delivery. In this regard, Russia has always been a reliable supplier of energy resources - both to Western Europe, where long-term infrastructure projects for oil and gas have been built since the 1960s, and to global markets today."
Europe's costs have risen since it began shifting away from affordable and stable Russian supplies: "Many industrial operations have relocated to other countries; there are bankruptcies and business closures. Yet, today, politics takes precedence over rational decisions that would benefit consumers. In my view, everything they do regarding energy policy is to the detriment of their own economies and consumers."
Russia is prepared to boost energy supplies to Europe, including under existing long-term contracts: "We are ready to provide larger supply volumes [to Europe]. It was not us who rejected affordable and stable energy supplies from Russia; Europe made that decision for political reasons."
"We remain committed to fulfilling our contracts, including long-term agreements - some of which, for gas, run until 2035-2040. A refusal to take supplies under these contracts is a unilateral decision that has no basis in the existing legal and regulatory framework."
Russia has supplied energy resources to Europe worth $320 billion since 2022, including $21.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026.
Situation in global energy markets
Energy consumers are seeking alternatives to hydrocarbons as global demand declines: "Today, consumers are exploring options for accelerated energy substitution, reducing energy expenditures, and improving energy efficiency," Novak stated.
"We are witnessing a decline in global demand for energy resources this year, which also impacts consumer costs. Amid this structural transformation - and particularly the fallout from geopolitical events in the Strait of Hormuz - we are seeing a sharp price shock. This affects not only insurance and freight but also the overall cost of oil and petroleum products, which have nearly doubled since the beginning of the year."
Russia is "ready to balance energy markets and maintain our role in ensuring energy security based on long-term partnerships."
Russia advocates for closer international cooperation in the energy sector: "It is clear that the shock we experienced this year - as well as other shocks over the past 15 years - has prompted countries to take more unilateral approaches to safeguarding their own energy security," the deputy prime minister noted. "In my view, this is a misguided trend, because global energy security can only be ensured through cooperation and joint action.

====================================================================================================

Extreme heatwaves in Europe not changing Britons’ holiday plans, say travel bosses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:16:25 UTC
01:16:25 KST

After a year marked by extreme heat and war sending fuel prices skywards, British travel executives hoped for solace in Madeira’s benign subtropical climate, separated by hundreds of miles of blue sea from the overtourism protests and six-hour EU-entry queues seen on the Portuguese mainland.
As bosses admitted, holidays will be ever less affordable, AI is coming for their jobs, and the visitable world is shrinking – not least those parts where tourists remain welcome.
Some of the bigger anxieties in spring, such as widespread border chaos and planes running out of fuel, have not come to pass; others now appear chronic issues. New supplies of jet fuel, a major concern after the US first attacked Iran in February, have been established – but the cost is staying far higher for longer than most expected.
“Fuel is a huge part of any holiday and people are going to have to reckon with the cost,” said Neil Swanson, Tui UK & Ireland managing director, among the attendees at the Abta convention.
Tui and airlines such as easyJet and Ryanair escaped the worst immediate impact by having secured much of their 2026 fuel supply at a fixed price. But the latter airlines are now slashing capacity for winter.
“It’s not great for consumers, who are going to have to pay a lot more for their holidays. But airlines are going to be less and less hedged and prices are going to go up,” Swanson added.
The oil price impact goes beyond jet fuel, said Mark Tanzer, the chief executive of Abta: “The bigger worry is the squeeze on household incomes that’s going to come through their domestic costs. It will be a much tighter market.”
Perhaps surprisingly, numbers have held up – but customers have been leaving it ever later to book, he said, whether in search of a deal or because of uncertainty from disruption, war or weather.
Despite the intense heat, mass travel firms are clear that the template has not changed: most customers still want a hot holiday, in summer, on the beach.
Garry Wilson, the chief executive of easyJet Holidays, said: “Will there be long-term effects on demand? Perhaps. But in the short-term, no, we don’t see it.”
Growing “shoulder season” travel outside the school holidays for those who can, including city breaks, are driven by price more than climate, several people suggest. And talk of “coolcations” or people turning towards northern climes cuts little ice here. “We’re not seeing any of that,” said Swanson. “Nothing’s changed, the destinations are the same.”
When Tunisia was forecast a 10-day stretch of 45C temperatures this summer, Tui offered customers the chance to switch their holiday elsewhere. Swanson said: “We didn’t get the interest and take-up. People were expecting it to be hot and were happy to go there, and we’re not seeing any change in demand. Brits like a warm holiday – if it’s got a pool and air-conditioning, that works for them.”
Neither does Wilson see many heading north. Citing easyJet destinations such as Tromsø in Norway or Malmö in Sweden, he said: “They’re all very nice to launch, but we send more customers to Majorca in a week than those in a year.”
Outbound holidays prospered in the heatwave, he suggested. “People thought: ‘You know what, we maybe don’t need to go away.’ But it became apparent that the UK doesn’t have the infrastructure to cope … people actually were going abroad to escape the heat in the UK.”
For now, the big firms see little change in destinations, Swanson said, but added: “We’ll keep it under review. Who knows where the temperature’s going to go in the next few years?”
More people could get priced out. At last year’s convention, the Spanish tourist board started pushing its cooler northern destinations; but, said Tanzer, “I’m not sure the north has 100m beds” to accommodate the visitors who predominantly go to Spain’s south, east and islands.
He added: “Certain types of holiday could become more expensive just because there’s limited availability. If the snow is higher up the mountain, there’s going to be fewer skiing holidays and the price is going to go up – there’s little room at the top.”
Tui has not been immune. Its river cruises in Europe were marooned when the Danube’s water levels dipped last month to the point where some passengers spent most of their return Austro-Hungarian cruise on a boat-replacement bus.
Katy Berzins, the head of river cruises at Tui, said: “Every year has highs and lows and it’s part of river cruising, rivers are changeable.” But 2026, she said, was “unprecedented”.
The division is expanding nonetheless. Two new ships are joining its fleet – initially destined for the Seine and the Douro – that are built with lower draught levels (the vessel’s vertical depth below the surface), meaning they are able to keep sailing in shallower rivers.
Others are seeing faster change. James Thornton, the chief executive of Intrepid Travel, said the firm no longer sold active travel group tours in southern Europe in the summer; few had wanted to trek or cycle in that level of heat.
Last year, Thornton said, there were 185 different extreme weather-related incidents that affected Intrepid holidaymakers around the world. “When we first started, there would be a handful.”
Intrepid has long wrestled with its own impact on climate: for years, before offsetting fell into disrepute, it paid millions to offset its emissions. That did not cover the biggest factor, the flights taken by its customers to reach Intrepid tours – not entirely dissimilar from how an airport might declare itself net zero. Instead now the firm has a decarbonisation fund for local projects: “Ultimately you can’t have sustainable travel, you can only limit the impact,” Thornton said.
Having grown from backpacking to a A$1bn annual business, its own footprint is becoming significant. This year the firm is launching Timor-Leste, or East Timor. Thornton said: “Some customers have done 30 to 40 trips, so they’re often looking for places that they haven’t been able to travel to.”
Asked about overtourism, Thornton said: “We’re definitely worried about it.” Intrepid tries to advertise the less visited destinations, he added. “We call it the not-hot list – drawing out the places where the infrastructure is available and the locals are willing to welcome travellers.”
Rising tourist taxes around the world underline that many places feel they have more than enough visitors. For Wilson, it is “grossly unfair”; destinations such as Mallorca, he said, “built enormous economic positions on the back of mass tourism, and then pull up the bridge and put on an extra tax. All that does is go back to the days of travel being only for the rich.”
How many of the UK outbound travel industry remain in sufficient paid work to afford it may also be in question.
Shaun Morton, the chief executive of On the Beach, laid off 20% of the Manchester-based online agency’s staff this summer to “automate and streamline” processes. He told delegates: “You’ve got the technology, people, processes and you hold them all dear … We just started to ask not how do we get 10% more out of that, but how do we get 10 times that, you know?”
He added that “very bright people with a sharp head with technology” probably would keep their jobs longest, but acknowledged: “They’re worried, because they can see a little bit further ahead than everyone else.”
- The Guardian’s travel to the convention in Madeira was provided by Abta

Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:16:22 UTC
01:16:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Trump backs Israel unity plan keeping Netanyahu PM for two years after election: Report
The Trump administration is backing efforts to form a broad Israeli unity government after this month's election that could keep Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister for up to two years before handing power to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, according to an Israeli media report.
The proposal would exclude far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and bring together Netanyahu's Likud party with Eisenkot's Yashar party, Israel Hayom reported on Friday.
The newspaper cited unnamed US and foreign political officials familiar with the discussions. Neither Washington nor the Israeli parties involved have publicly confirmed an agreed plan.
Israel is due to hold a Knesset election on 27 October.
Polls have suggested neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the fragmented opposition is guaranteed a stable governing majority, raising the possibility of prolonged coalition negotiations.
According to Israel Hayom, the US and regional governments believe a broad coalition would be better placed to make major decisions on ending regional conflicts and advancing President Donald Trump's wider Middle East agenda.
One unnamed foreign official quoted in the report said a fragile minority government would be unable to make the "major and decisive political decisions" the region required.
The proposed arrangement would allow Netanyahu to remain prime minister for up to two years before Eisenkot succeeded him, according to the report.
During that period, the government would be expected to work towards ending wars on multiple fronts and reaching political agreements with regional states, particularly Saudi Arabia.
The Trump administration has been pushing Riyadh to join the Abraham Accords and normalise relations with Israel.
Washington has linked that effort to other parts of the US-Saudi relationship, including F-35 fighter jets and a civilian nuclear programme.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said, however, that normalisation with Israel would require meaningful progress towards Palestinian statehood.
The issue has also become entangled with Washington's proposed nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia, which Trump has said would depend on Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords.
According to Israel Hayom, Saudi Arabia is also seeking a different political configuration in Israel before moving forward.
US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has recently met several senior Israeli politicians, including Eisenkot, the report said.
The contacts were said to have been handled carefully because of concerns over perceptions of US interference in the election.
But Israeli politicians were reportedly told that Washington and other governments would welcome a broad and stable coalition without far-right parties.
Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has emerged as one of Netanyahu's principal challengers in the election and leads the centrist Yashar party.
The proposed government would also seek to address domestic issues that have deeply divided Israeli politics.
These include demands for an official inquiry into the failures surrounding the 7 October 2023 attacks, disputes over the judiciary and the continuing row over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has denied reports that he is directly involved in efforts to engineer a unity government.
He has nevertheless said he wants to avoid repeated elections and see a stable government formed after the vote.
The reported US effort comes as Israel's election remains highly fragmented, with Palestinian parties potentially playing a decisive role if neither major bloc secures a governing majority.

Putin says Russia is building non-negotiable ‘security zone’ in Ukraine along border
MOSCOW - Russia is establishing a “security zone” inside Ukraine along their border, which will be non-negotiable in any future talks with Kyiv, President Vladimir Putin said on Oct 16.
Putin, wearing military uniform and speaking during a visit to a command post, said the operation was in response to Ukraine’s 2024-25 incursion into Russia’s western Kursk region.
“The Russian armed forces were tasked not only with expelling the enemy from our land but also with establishing a security zone in the adjacent territory. This task is being carried out successfully,” he said in televised comments.
“Our goal is to ensure the absolute security of Russia’s border regions for the future, and we do not plan to make this a subject for potential peace negotiations with Ukraine.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the planned security zone spanned 660km, of which 70% was currently under Russia’s control.
He did not say how deep it would reach inside Ukraine.
Putin has spoken before about the need for such a zone but has not previously spelt out the planned extent of it or said it would be off-limits for talks.
It requires Russia to carve out land in the Sumy and Kharkiv regions, which are not among those it has claimed as its own territory since launching the war in Ukraine in 2022.
Putin, who rarely dons military uniform, struck a hawkish and confident tone in his comments to senior officers.
He was speaking at a critical point in diplomacy over the war, one week after a deal to sell Russian diesel to the US that has won favour with President Donald Trump and prompted a new souring of the relationship between Trump and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky.
Putin said Russian forces had yet to capture just over 10% of the territory of Ukraine’s Donetsk region, a key objective, and 16.5% of the Zaporizhzhia region.
He praised the effectiveness of Russian strikes against Ukrainian military, industrial and logistics targets, while adding there was still room for improvement in Russia’s own air defences.
Ukrainian drones have attacked several Russian data centres and a big oil refinery in the past nine days, while Russia has continued to pound Ukrainian cities, power plants and ports, among other targets.
Earlier, Putin’s investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russia and the US were discussing a range of new joint projects including nuclear-powered data centres in the wake of last week’s agreement on diesel. REUTERS

It comes amid escalating occupier violence against Palestinians and their property, particularly farmers during the olive harvest season.
Lior claimed that Palestinians do not own their land, arguing that they had not purchased it from the “people of Israel” or from any Jewish person and describing the land as “stolen property.”

READ: Bishop calls for international action after settlers attack West Bank centre for disabled children
Lior claimed Palestinians had already received sufficient compensation for planting the trees by consuming their fruit over previous years, and said both the land and harvest should return to what he called their “rightful owners.”

The ruling comes as attacks on Palestinian farmers during the West Bank olive harvest season have intensified, including assaults, preventing farmers from reaching their land, damaging trees and stealing crops.
Such attacks recur during the olive harvest, which peaks in October each year, while this month has seen an increase in attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property.
Palestinian, Israeli and international rights organizations have accused Israeli authorities of failing to stop occupier violence or hold perpetrators accountable despite attacks targeting Palestinians, their homes, farmland, vehicles and other property.
