Division in Lebanon over Hezbollah’s confiscated explosives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:09:43 UTC
01:09:43 KST

Division in Lebanon over Hezbollah’s confiscated explosives
Hezbollah said the explosives were to be used against Israel, though political figures and some analysts fear assassinations.
Beirut, Lebanon – On October 5, a minivan was stopped at a checkpoint in Dahr el-Baydar between the Bekaa Valley and Mount Lebanon region.
Lebanese security forces discovered the car was carrying hundreds of kilos of explosive materials, including TNT and C-4, according to Lebanese officials.
On Thursday, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah released a statement saying that the explosives belonged to Hezbollah which had demanded their return, along with the release of the two people detained in the vehicle.
“From the moment the vehicle was detained, the relevant bodies within [Hezbollah] immediately contacted the security and judicial agencies and informed them that the vehicle and its cargo belonged to the resistance,” Fadlallah said in his statement. “They demanded the immediate release of those detained and the return of the vehicle and everything inside it, as these are capabilities used by the resistance to confront the Israeli occupation of our land in the south [of Lebanon].”
Fadlallah indicated that the explosives were for use against Israel, which continues to occupy large parts of southern Lebanon, and not internally against the Lebanese government or other factions, as some political figures and analysts had suggested.
“We therefore warn the [Lebanese] authorities of the consequences of continuing to escalate their measures,” he said. “[Hezbollah] will defend its people’s rights and the capabilities it uses to confront the Israeli enemy and it will not tolerate any targeting by any party implementing American demands against our resistance.”
But many of Hezbollah’s political opponents, who blame the Iranian-backed group for targeting political opponents in assassinations in the past, fear that smuggled explosives will be turned against Hezbollah’s detractors.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam pointed out that C-4 explosives had been used in previous assassinations, although investigators have not established that the seized shipment was intended for such an attack.
Hezbollah has never admitted carrying out assassinations, despite repeated accusations against it, including the killing of former Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005.
Regional implications
On March 2, when Hezbollah responded to ongoing Israeli attacks for the first time in over a year in retaliation for the killing of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Salam and his government banned the group’s military activities. Salam’s coalition government includes two Hezbollah ministers who opposed the decision and the group has repeatedly defied the government’s declaration by continuing to fight Israel.
Fighting has largely subsided since June, when Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-administered trilateral framework agreement. Under the deal, pilot zones would be established as part of a phased process in which Israel would eventually withdraw its troops and the Lebanese Army would enter to disarm Hezbollah. However, the programme has had complications from the start as Israel never had a presence in some of the areas included in the pilot zones, according to locals, and Israeli demolitions continue in the areas under its occupation.
In recent weeks, Lebanese security forces have uncovered a number of operations aimed at smuggling explosives.
Lebanese officials have condemned the smuggling operations and Salam has vowed to investigate the incidents, particularly the Dahr el-Baydar incident.
“We will not be lenient in following up and expanding the investigation in order to identify all those involved in this criminal operation and those behind them,” Salam wrote on social media. “We will deal with weapons outside the legal framework with the required firmness.”
But the issue also points to growing disagreements between Lebanon’s government and Hezbollah’s leadership over the role of armed resistance.
Explosive concerns
Since the end of Lebanon’s civil war in 1990, Hezbollah has been the principal Lebanese force to keep its weapons. This was ostensibly part of a national security formula of “the army, the people and the resistance” aimed at opposing Israeli occupation – which continued until 2000 before resuming in 2024 – and aggression, while the country was also under Syrian hegemony.
That changed last year when President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Salam came to power. The Hezbollah allied al-Assad regime in Damascus had just fallen, cutting off a powerful land route of weapons and financing from Tehran. The regional power dynamic appeared to be shifting towards a decrease in Iranian power and more influence from the United States and Israel, leading Lebanon’s leaders to announce that all non-state weapons would come under control of the state.
Despite Hezbollah’s opposition to the new leaders’ decrees, the Lebanese Army went about disarming Hezbollah sites in southern Lebanon. Some Hezbollah opponents have declared the group weak and defeated, though analysts say the group still retains some fighting power and that Lebanon’s regional alliances could largely be determined by regional events.
Still, the group’s domestic influence has been challenged at times by the new Lebanese leadership, including in the Dahr el-Baydar incident.
Marcel Baloukji, a former brigadier general who oversaw the Lebanese Army’s border committee with Syria, told Al Jazeera that the recent busts, and particularly the Dahr el-Baydar incident, were connected to the security situation in the wider region, particularly concerning the US-Israeli war on Iran and the recent intensification of violence between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
He suggested that Hezbollah could be looking to follow the lead of other pro-Iranian actors in the region and intensify attacks against adversaries. But he also added that Hezbollah may need explosives for drones to attack Israeli forces occupying southern Lebanon.
Government difficulties
Despite the promises by Lebanese officials to investigate, analysts said concerns remain about how effective the investigations might be.
Issam Kayssi, a Beirut-based analyst at the Carnegie Middle East Center, raised questions over Salam’s relationship with the Lebanese security apparatus. Lebanon has multiple security agencies, some of which have competing loyalties to different political figures or parties.
“We are more than a year on from the Raouche incident,” he said, referring to a Hezbollah event held on Beirut’s seafront in 2025 to commemorate the assassination of the group’s late leaders Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine. Hezbollah projected the likeness of the two slain leaders on Pigeon Rock in Beirut’s Raouche seafront district, despite the projections being prohibited by authorities, prompting Salam to call for the arrest of those responsible. Security agents on site failed to act to prevent the projections and observers fear that elements of the security agencies may not be fully cooperative with Salam in the explosives investigations he ordered.
Baloukji described Salam’s relationship with the security agencies as “somewhat strained.” He added that it could be the latest file in a series of difficulties facing the Lebanese government, as Israel’s occupation and ongoing demolition of southern infrastructure continue.
“Our situation remains in a state of prolonged limbo, with no solutions in sight,” Baloukji said. “The framework agreement is stalled and there is no resolution to de-escalate the situation in the south.”

Pope asks Putin for truce for city of Oleshky

Unknown Publisher

Pope Leo XIV on Friday asked Russian President Vladimir Putin for a truce for the city of Oleshky in the Ukrainian region of Kherson given the dire humanitarian situation there, in a phone call between the Kremlin and his room at Rome's Gemelli Hospital where he is recovering from lung-cancer surgery. 
"During the conversation, the Holy Father expressed deep concern regarding the serious humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and requested a truce to allow for the delivery of food and medical aid, as well as the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population. 
Finally, the Holy Father reiterated the Holy See's commitment to fostering dialogue and peace," the Vatican Press Office reported.
Putin provided Leo with "a full explanation regarding the responsibility of the Kyiv regime for the difficult humanitarian situation" that has emerged in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky—a situation previously raised by the Pontiff, the Kremlin said, as cited by the Interfax news agency. 
The Russian leader further pledged support for "the Vatican's intention to help create conditions to ensure the safety of the city's population and organize the delivery of essential supplies." Putin and the Pope subsequently "agreed to coordinate their efforts in this regard."
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said it was the Pope who took the initiative with Putin.
"It was the Holy Father who took the initiative" to call Putin, "to plead the cause of this besieged city, where about 2,000 civilians are trapped and in need of exit routes—humanitarian corridors," said Parolin. 
"I believe the Pope requested a truce to allow for both the arrival of humanitarian aid—above all, food—and the evacuation of those who need to leave the city.
"I hope," he added, "that, faced with a request from the Holy Father, President Putin will—so to speak—agree to implement what has been asked of him."

Netanyahu, opposition blocs tied as 55% back unity government if election inconclusive: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:03:38 UTC
01:03:38 KST

An Israeli opinion poll published on Friday showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition tied, with neither reaching the majority needed to form a government, while 55% of respondents favored a unity government if the upcoming election produces no decisive result, Anadolu reports.
The Maariv poll, published 11 days before the Oct. 27 general election, showed that if voting were held today, both Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition would win 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset.
Arab lawmakers, meanwhile, were projected to win 14 seats, while the Reservists Party would secure four, without indicating which bloc it would support.
A government requires the backing of at least 61 lawmakers. Otherwise, Israel could face another election.
Both Netanyahu’s camp and the main Jewish opposition parties reject relying on Arab parties to form a government.
According to the poll, Netanyahu’s bloc would be divided among Likud with 18 seats, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power eight, the religious United Torah Judaism party eight, Shas seven, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism six and Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael four.
The Jewish opposition would include Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21 seats, Naftali Bennett’s Together 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats nine and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu eight.
READ: Israel elections: Palestinian state caught between Netanyahu’s incitement, Eisenkot’s rejection
Among Arab parties, the Joint List led by Yousef Jabareen was projected to win eight seats, while Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List, or Ra’am, would receive six.
The Reservists Party, headed by Yoaz Hendel, is projected to win four seats, with the poll not determining which camp it would support.
On the preferred candidate for prime minister, Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief of staff, remained ahead of Netanyahu with 48% support compared with 41% for the incumbent.
Israelis do not directly elect their prime minister. The post goes to the politician able to form a coalition backed by at least 61 lawmakers.
If the political deadlock continues, Israel could face another election unless a unity government is formed.
The poll found that 55% of Israelis prefer a national unity government over another election if the Oct. 27 vote fails to produce a clear outcome.
Another 27% said they favor holding a new election, while 18% were undecided.
The results showed differences between the two camps.
Among opposition voters, 54% said they support a unity government provided it is headed by a leader from their bloc.
Among coalition voters, 36% backed a unity government led by Netanyahu, while 32% preferred another election if no clear result emerged.
Maariv said the poll was conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute among a random sample of 700 Israelis, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points.

EU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:02:13 UTC
01:02:13 KST

EU rallies in support of Ukraine amid Trump standoff
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy asks EU leaders for extra $79bn to help fight Russia next year.
European Union leaders have urged continued support for Ukraine amid a deepening rift between Washington and Kyiv that has raised fears the country could be left more exposed to Russian attacks heading into the winter.
Top EU officials stressed the need to keep arming Ukraine and sanctioning Russia on Friday, the second and final day of an EU summit in Brussels attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
“This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine,” said European Council President Antonio Costa, standing beside the Ukrainian leader. “This is no time to relieve Russia’s sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure.”
The EU is hosting Zelenskyy at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, four-and-a-half years after neighbouring Russia invaded it.
Russian missiles and drones have rained down on Ukrainian cities daily, and Kyiv’s souring relationship with the United States has sparked fears that Washington could pull back crucial intelligence sharing and weapons support.
Arriving at the summit, Zelenskyy thanked EU leaders for their support and pointedly referred to them as “real leaders”.
That remark appeared to be a dig at US President Donald Trump, who last weekend blindsided the Ukrainian president by announcing that Kyiv and Moscow had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.
Zelenskyy abandoned that deal on Thursday, saying Russia had failed to live up to it, a move Trump called “a disgrace”.
Trump has also angered Ukraine by suspending sanctions on Russian oil products and striking a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to supply large quantities of diesel to global markets.
“This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets,” Zelenskyy said on the sidelines of the summit. “But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
He also accused the Russian leader of having no real interest in peace talks.
“Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form,” Zelenskyy said. “He’s playing with words … Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war.”
Zelenskyy asks EU for $79bn
Bracing for expected winter-time attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy asked EU leaders for an additional 70bn euros ($79 billion) in funding next year to keep up the fight against Russia.
“The war will cost 155 billion euros [$174bn] next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros more from you – for defence, for weapons and for our resilience,” the Ukrainian president said.
“This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back.”
Al Jazeera’s Rosie Birchard, reporting from the summit in Brussels, said Zelenskyy made an “emotional plea” for European support, with air defence systems at the top of his “wish list”.
Zelenskyy appealed to European countries to dig into their own stocks to help cover Ukraine’s needs in the colder winter months, said Birchard. “But of course, that would mean some European countries potentially compromising their own national security.”
‘We stand by your side’
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told the Reuters news agency that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen pledged continued EU support for Ukraine through the winter.
“Russia is trying everything to destroy the energy and water infrastructure. But we stand by your side. We will support you as we did in the other winters,” she said.
Austria, however, urged caution in the debate over new, far-reaching financial commitments to Ukraine.
“There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming from,” said Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
Al Jazeera’s Birchard said the general European solidarity for Zelenskyy was a stark difference from recent messages coming from Washington. “He is once again, at least, among friends,” she said.
However, Birchard added that some European officials were said to be appealing to Zelenskyy behind closed doors to “kind of dial down” his public criticism of Trump, which they fear could put Europeans in a tough position.
“Of course, they [European officials] want to show that they are close to Ukraine, that they are supporting Zelenskyy, but they also don’t want to antagonise the US,” she said.
Friday’s summit came as Russian strikes killed three people in Kharkiv and left hundreds of thousands of people without power in Ukraine.
The Kremlin last week said Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks after hitting Moscow with drones during last month’s election.

Outlook for Ukraine's energy this winter has worsened after latest Russian strikes

Outlook for Ukraine's energy this winter has worsened after latest Russian strikes
Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator, Ukrenergo, has said its forecasts for winter have been worsened by recent Russian strikes on thermal power plants (TPPs) that were supposed to be operating in winter, but the company does not assess the situation as critical.
Source: Interfax-Ukraine, citing Ukrenergo CEO Vitalii Zaichenko in a comment for Enerhoreforma
Details: Speaking on the sidelines of the Energy of Business Forum 2026 in Kyiv, Zaichenko said: "The situation is already worse at the moment because there have been hits on TPPs that were supposed to be ready for winter. Yes, it's slightly worse than forecast, but not critical."
Zaichenko urged the public and businesses to get their own energy sources ready in case of grid disruptions. He also advised businesses to optimise electricity consumption so that they operate more efficiently when restrictions are in place.
At the same event, the Ukrenergo CEO said Russia's 14 October attack was one of the most massive attacks against the company's facilities since the full-scale war began. Electrical substations were the main targets, and Ukrenergo's top priority is to get them quickly back up and running.
Background: On the morning of 16 October, new power outages were recorded in Kyiv and eight regions following a Russian attack. In some regions, hourly power cuts of up to two queues are planned until the end of the day.

From hospital, Pope Leo pushes Putin for ceasefire in contested Ukraine city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:01:00 UTC
01:01:00 KST

From hospital, Pope Leo pushes Putin for ceasefire in contested Ukraine city
VATICAN CITY - Pope Leo XIV spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone on Oct 16, calling for a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine, as he recovers in hospital from a lung cancer operation.
The Vatican said that Pope Leo “expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population”.
The surprise notice from the Vatican Oct 16 evening suggested that the recovering pope is still hard at work, despite having undergone an operation on Oct 13 to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung.
Residents of Oleshky in southern Ukraine are facing a worsening humanitarian crisis with shortages of food and medication as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk denounced on Oct 16 a “desperate” situation in the city, calling on Russia to enable civilians to evacuate.
In a note, the Kremlin said the two had talked and “a detailed explanation was provided regarding the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation” in Oleshky.
The Kremlin said Putin also wished the pope a speedy recovery and stressed the “importance of Russian-Vatican cooperation in promoting unifying spiritual and moral values.”
Makeshift altar
Earlier on Oct 16, Pope Leo celebrated mass on the top floor of Rome’s Gemelli hospital, as seen in the first images of him released by the Vatican since the procedure.
The images showed the 71-year-old Chicago-born pope in front of a makeshift altar in a room on the 10th floor, dressed in a green vestment.
He appeared relaxed and in good form in the two photos released, standing with his private secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard Rimaycuna, at his side.
“He celebrated with the medical and nursing staff of Gemelli, some people who were present there, who were clearly off duty at that moment,” the Vatican press office said, adding that members of the police also joined.
“He thanked all the staff, doctors, nurses, orderlies, for their service and their closeness to people, for their care of people’s fragility, and in particular, evidently, for the care, attention, and treatment given to him in these days,” the press office said.
The pope is expected to lead the traditional Angelus prayer on Oct 18, but a Vatican source would not say whether it would be from the hospital, or from the Vatican.
The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited by the pope every Sunday from the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter’s Square, to crowds of faithful gathered below.
Ongoing tests
Doctors have said that the pope’s recovery after surgery is progressing normally, but ongoing tests will determine the future course of his treatment.
His doctors said on Oct 15 that a chest X-ray indicated “good recovery of the operated lung”.
On Oct 16, they said tests had shown “a steady improvement in his general condition”.
The pope was now carrying out “his normal daily activities completely independently”, they said.
Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.
‘Better days will come’
The press office has not given an update to the possible timing of the pope’s discharge from hospital, repeating a doctor’s original statement that his recovery would take about a week.
Were Leo to recite the Angelus from the window of the Gemelli hospital, it would not be a first for a pope.
On Feb 6, 2005, 84-year-old John Paul II appeared at the hospital window while recovering from flu-related respiratory issues, as an aide beside him read out the Angelus prayer.
Pope Francis on July 11, 2021, then 84, also gave the prayer from the hospital window after surgery on his colon, telling the assembled crowd: “I am glad to be able to keep the Sunday Angelus appointment, even here.”
Also on Oct 16, the Vatican released a selection of letters and drawings sent by children at the hospital, including a picture of a tree “For Pope Leo”, complete with grass, sun and clouds, and a letter from an 18-year-old girl who wrote to Leo: “Better days will come for the both of us.”
A seven-year-old boy named Angelo wrote that he, too, had been on the 10th floor of the Gemelli hospital for the past 36 days for a head operation.
“My mother and I pray for you every night,” he wrote. “I hope you get well soon.” AFP

Hiring bias against transgender women depends on both identity and appearance, field experiment suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:00:55 UTC
01:00:55 KST

A recent field experiment provides evidence that transgender women face steep penalties in the labor market when applying for jobs, particularly when they do not look like a typical cisgender woman. The research indicates that disclosing a transgender identity and possessing physical features typically associated with males both independently reduce a person’s chances of receiving a positive response from employers, and the combination of the two results in a compounded penalty. The findings were posted as a working paper on SSRN and have not yet been peer reviewed.
Transgender women are individuals who were assigned male at birth but identify as women. They often face elevated barriers in the workforce, experiencing lower employment rates and higher rates of poverty compared with cisgender people. A study covered by PsyPost in 2026 suggests that transgender individuals experience higher rates of daily mistreatment and violence than cisgender sexual minorities. A central concept in understanding these experiences is “passing,” which refers to whether a transgender person is perceived by others as cisgender, meaning someone whose gender identity aligns with the sex they were assigned at birth.
Previous economic studies have documented hiring bias against transgender individuals, but they have generally focused on identity alone. Researchers typically sent resumes that indirectly disclosed a transgender identity without showing the applicant’s face, leaving it uncertain whether employers were reacting to the identity itself or to an assumption about what the applicant might look like.
Both labels and looks can shape how transgender people are perceived. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2018 found that potential dating partners labeled as transgender or nonbinary were rated as less attractive than those labeled cisgender, regardless of what they actually looked like. Appearance may matter as well: the paper notes that in a large U.S. survey, about 43 percent of trans women who had socially transitioned reported passing, compared with 71 percent of trans men.
The new study, conducted by Taryn Eames, a doctoral candidate in economics at the University of Toronto, sought to untangle these factors. “People with marginalized identities can face pressure to conceal their identity or conform to dominant-group social expectations, sometimes at considerable personal or financial cost,” Eames told PsyPost. “I want to understand whether discrimination reflects someone’s identity, whether they fit those expectations, or how the two interact.” She focused specifically on trans women, whose labor market disadvantages “are well documented but whose causes remain poorly understood.”
To investigate this question, Eames conducted a correspondence study in Germany, a method in which researchers send matched fictitious applications to real employers and track who gets a response. German job applications standardly include a professional headshot and reference letters from past employers, making it possible to realistically test both appearance and identity signals. The study submitted 10,022 fictitious applications in pairs to real job postings across 27 German cities and nine occupations.
The experiment independently varied two signals, starting with the applicant’s headshot. Eames used artificial intelligence to generate 30 matched pairs of “twin” headshots. The passing version depicted a woman who looked typically cisgender, while the non-passing version kept the exact same hair, makeup, clothing, jewelry, and background but altered the facial structure to include more male-coded features. No employer ever received both versions of the same face.
“This study varies physical facial features while keeping gender presentation fixed, including hairstyle, makeup, clothing, and jewelry,” Eames noted. “These features reflect genetics, pubertal development, and access to gender-affirming care—factors often beyond an individual’s control. They are not styling choices an applicant can simply change when applying for a job.”
Second, the experiment varied whether the applicant disclosed a transgender identity. In Germany, a legal name change can leave older professional documents under a previous name. Some fictitious applicants included a years-old employer reference letter under a male name, along with a note explaining that they now use a female first name, giving employers a realistic administrative reason to learn about the transition.
Control applicants all had passing headshots. Some disclosed no name change, while others disclosed a female-to-female change, such as going from Theodora to Thea. These two control groups received positive responses at nearly identical rates, suggesting that employers were reacting to the transgender identity signaled by a male-to-female change rather than to name changes in general.
The results indicated a penalty for both a transgender identity and a non-passing appearance. Among control applicants, 47.6 percent received a positive response from employers, such as an interview request. Applicants who disclosed a transgender identity but had a passing headshot received positive responses at a rate that was 4.1 percentage points lower, a 9 percent reduction compared to controls, while those with a non-passing headshot but no disclosure saw a 4.6 percentage point drop, or a 10 percent reduction.
The penalty was largest when applicants combined both signals. Applicants who both disclosed a name change and had a non-passing appearance received positive responses at a rate 15.2 percentage points lower than controls, representing a 32 percent reduction. This combined penalty was 6.5 percentage points larger than the sum of the two individual penalties, indicating that identity and appearance compound one another.
“To illustrate, suppose an otherwise comparable, presumably cisgender woman submits 100 applications,” Eames explained. “An applicant with either signal alone would need approximately 110–111 applications to receive the same expected number of positive employer responses. With both signals, she would need about 147 applications.”
“I was surprised by how strongly the two signals compounded each other,” she told PsyPost. “Employers may already infer that an applicant is transgender from masculinized facial features, so the two signals may partly convey the same identity information.”
“I therefore expected the combined penalty to be smaller than the sum of the individual penalties—instead, it was substantially larger,” she continued. “One possibility is that masculinized facial features make a disclosed transgender identity more salient. Another is that employers hold different beliefs or attitudes toward transgender women depending on their appearance.”
The strength of the non-passing appearance also influenced outcomes. Moderately non-passing headshots without disclosure produced a small penalty of about 4 percent that was not statistically significant. Strongly non-passing headshots without disclosure led to a 15 percent drop in callbacks, while pairing a strongly non-passing headshot with identity disclosure resulted in a 36 percent penalty.
The context of the job posting shaped employer behavior as well. Postings listing a male contact person showed higher appearance penalties, whereas postings listing a female contact person showed little penalty for non-passing appearance unless it was paired with a transgender identity disclosure. In exploratory analyses, the penalty for non-passing applicants was larger for jobs involving more customer interaction, and discrimination overall was smaller in tight labor markets, consistent with the idea that heightened competition for workers constrains employers from acting on biased preferences.
To explore the perceptions behind these hiring patterns, Eames conducted a follow-up survey experiment with 1,400 members of the general public from Germany and the United States. Participants evaluated brief professional profiles depicting the same conditions used in the field experiment. They rated the applicants on eight subjective traits, including competence, attractiveness, and emotional stability, alongside their willingness to offer an interview.
Respondents rated non-passing applicants about 1.4 points less attractive on a 7-point scale, regardless of whether a transgender identity was disclosed. Anticipated coworker and customer comfort was lower in every condition: about 0.3 points lower when applicants disclosed a name change but passed, about 0.5 points lower when they did not pass and made no disclosure, and up to about 1 point lower when both signals were present.
Respondents also rated all three groups of transgender applicants as less emotionally stable, with the largest drop when both signals were present. Disclosing a name change led respondents to expect that an applicant would be more likely to raise concerns about workplace comments or behavior she viewed as insensitive or exclusionary, and this expectation was more than twice as strong when disclosure was paired with a non-passing appearance.
Respondents were less willing to interview applicants with either signal, but unlike in the field experiment, the two signals did not compound. Eames suggests that survey respondents may tone down especially large rating differences that could appear overtly discriminatory, particularly when the study’s purpose becomes more obvious.
The survey also provided evidence of different types of bias among different groups of people. Older respondents tended to penalize the transgender identity disclosure more heavily, while socially conservative respondents tended to penalize the non-passing appearance more heavily.
“The main takeaway is that transgender identity and masculinized facial features each carry a hiring penalty, but the combined penalty is greater than the sum of the two separate penalties,” Eames said. “In other words, employers penalize the same facial features more heavily when an applicant is known to be transgender. More broadly, these findings suggest that deviating from dominant-group expectations can be especially costly when someone is known to belong to a marginalized group.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. Because the working paper was posted on a preprint server, it has not yet been peer reviewed. The compounding effect was also somewhat sensitive to analytic choices: while statistically significant in the author’s preferred analysis, it was smaller and less consistently significant in alternative analyses that did not adjust for baseline response rates across experimental groups. In addition, the experiment covered lower- to middle-skill jobs that do not require a university degree, measuring initial employer responses rather than final job offers.
Another consideration is that the field experiment relied on static headshots to manipulate appearance. In real life, whether a transgender woman passes depends on a wider array of traits, such as voice, height, and body proportions, meaning the study may underestimate overall in-person penalties. The direct penalty associated with non-passing headshots might also partially reflect broader biases against perceived unattractiveness, which often intertwines with traditional gender norms. And the survey respondents were members of the general public evaluating brief profiles, not hiring managers making real decisions.
Facial feminization surgery, which reshapes facial bones and soft tissue to create more typically female features, is one form of gender-affirming care that can affect whether a trans woman passes. “Understanding these sources of discrimination also yields policy implications: barriers to gender-affirming care—particularly a lack of insurance coverage for facial feminization surgery—may have consequences in terms of exposure to discrimination,” Eames said.
However, she emphasized that addressing bias should not rely on changing individuals. “These findings should not be taken to mean that the onus is on transgender women to change their appearance to avoid discrimination,” Eames added. “The goal should be to reduce discrimination while ensuring access to gender-affirming care for those who want it.”
The study, “The Cost of Being Seen: Identity, Non-Passing Appearance, and Hiring Discrimination Against Transgender Women,” was authored by Taryn Eames.

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back on front line where Starlink plays a key role
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:00:30 BST
01:00:30 KST

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
- Published
A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker.
Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back.
This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months.
The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control.
While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September – and suffered few casualties in return.
The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front".
Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day.
He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed.
This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower.
Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield.
Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability.
Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine.
Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy.
Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground.
The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion.
An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times."
He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target.
Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous".
"The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive."
Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation.
In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation.
"As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed."
"I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy".
That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present.
"The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained.
"This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvres… each of these actions is a building block towards victory."
All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low.
This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin.
Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause.
But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war.
The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front.
I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end."
Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko

Iran&#8217;s navy reports oil tanker fire in Gulf of Oman

15:57:54 UTC
00:57:54 KST

Iran’s navy said Friday that an oil tanker caught fire in the Gulf of Oman while attempting to cross a restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking systems switched off, according to a statement carried by state broadcaster IRIB, Anadolu reports.
The navy’s public relations office said monitoring teams detected the burning tanker during surveillance operations in the eastern part of the strategic waterway.
The vessel had disabled its tracking systems and was attempting to navigate a “prohibited area” in the Gulf of Oman, the statement said.
The navy warned that unauthorized movements through restricted maritime routes and areas pose security risks to other vessels.
The statement did not identify the tanker, its flag or operator, or specify what caused the fire. No information was provided on possible casualties or the condition of the crew.
The incident comes amid a series of maritime security incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has imposed restrictions on commercial shipping.
READ: Iran’s IRGC Navy threatens to sink US warships approaching Strait of Hormuz
On Tuesday, the Iranian Navy reported that another tanker caught fire after sustaining damage while attempting to cross a restricted area east of the strait with its tracking systems switched off.
On Wednesday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank after striking a naval mine while attempting to navigate an unauthorized route south of the strait.
The IRGC Navy warned local vessels and fishermen to exercise caution over containers floating on the water’s surface following the sinking.
The latest incidents come amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial passage for global oil and gas shipments.
Maritime traffic through the waterway has been severely disrupted since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

Democratic candidates have outraised Republican rivals by huge margins in key US congressional races, new campaign finance filings show, even as tech billionaire Elon Musk pumped record sums into efforts to keep the GOP in power.
The figures emerged after candidates and political groups submitted their third-quarter fundraising reports to the Federal Election Commission (FEC) by Thursday's deadline, the last quarterly disclosure before the November 3 midterm elections.
In six states viewed as pivotal to Senate control, Texas, Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Michigan and Iowa, Democrats collected between three and six times as much as their Republican opponents in the July-September quarter, according to an analysis of the figures by Punchbowl News.
The reports revealed a striking contrast between Democrats' strong fundraising at the candidate level and Republicans' advantage in money flowing through wealthy donors and outside political groups.
In Texas, Democrat James Talarico raised a record $64 million, compared with $10.2 million for Republican Ken Paxton's campaign.
In Ohio, former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown raised $23.1 million against $4.8 million for Republican incumbent Jon Husted. And in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson collected $20.4 million compared with $5.2 million for Republican Senator Susan Collins.
Democrats also outpaced Republicans in crucial House races, with at least 47 Republican incumbents outraised by Democratic or independent challengers, compared with only about six Democratic incumbents outraised by Republicans.
At least 27 Democratic candidates in competitive House districts raised more than $2 million each, against just four Republicans.
Massive advertising campaign
Yet Republicans have an enormous financial counterweight in Musk, the world's richest person, whose third-quarter donations of at least $276 million were confirmed in filings, making him the election cycle's largest known political donor.
Of that, $158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate fundraising group, which is spending the entire sum on bankrolling a massive advertising campaign in Texas supporting Paxton.
Another $20 million went to an organisation backing Republican House candidates.
Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief, has contributed some $366 million during this election cycle, according to US media analyses.
Outside groups can spend enormous amounts independently of campaigns, but candidates get cheaper advertising rates, meaning their dollars can stretch further in the final weeks before the November 3 vote.
Republicans retain sizeable cash reserves in several districts, and fundraising alone cannot determine electoral outcomes.
But the figures underscore the financial resources available to Democrats as they seek to overturn Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress.

15:57:07 UTC
00:57:07 KST

Ukraine’s government, led by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, has approved an experimental project in which drones will be used to transport medical supplies, blood samples and donor organs between hospitals.
The Heart Institute of Ukraine’s Health Ministry will serve as the first site of the pilot. The facility already operates three specialized drones capable of flying up to 700 kilometers (435 miles) and landing at hospital sites.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Based on the project, “Ukraine plans to create a Ukrainian traffic-management system for civilian drones (UTM) and establish rules for their safe use,” Koretskyi said in a statement on Friday, Oct. 16.
Faster deliveries amid the war
Each flight will need to be cleared with the military, under a defined approval procedure.
The drones will have a special status and be identifiable in the air, while separate rules will govern their operation during air-raid alerts, including the option to land at an alternative site.
Amid the war and poor road conditions, such a project could significantly improve outcomes. This is particularly important for blood and organ donations, where the speed of the delivery is crucial.
“Drones will be able to deliver medicines, medical devices, blood samples for testing and donor organs between hospitals more quickly,” Koretskyi said.
The need for alternative ways to deliver medical supplies is strongest in remote and Russian-occupied areas, such as the Kherson region, where civilians have no such option.

US agrees one-year deal to fund maternal and newborn health donations in poorest countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:55:27 UTC
00:55:27 KST

US strikes one-year deal to fund maternal and newborn health donations in poorest countries
NAIROBI/LONDON/NYANGEZI, Democratic Republic of Congo, Oct 16 - The US government has struck a deal to continue supplying some of the world's poorest nations with free life-saving medication and equipment for mothers, infants and young children, after months of uncertainty and challenges with supply.
The UN children's agency UNICEF will now procure these items, a State department spokesperson told Reuters by email, without giving details of the arrangement. UNICEF said the agreement is worth $25 million and will last for one year.
That sum represents only a small part of the aid affected by the Trump administration's cuts and dismantling of the US Agency for International Development (USAID).
But it means that some of the world's most vulnerable nations will not face another abrupt disruption to supplies they relied on while they work on new health aid deals with the US. Nine former US aid officials, NGOs and government officials told Reuters that this had been a real concern because the deal the now-defunct USAID had with its contractor was due to run out last month.
SHORTAGES
The agreement covers the procurement and delivery of maternal and child health supplies, as well as some nutrition supplies, to at least 15 countries previously covered, including Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti and Mali, UNICEF said.
It follows almost 18 months of disruption after Washington's move to freeze and then scale back many US aid programmes as part of its "America First Global Health Strategy".
In countries such as Congo, shortages due to the disruption have already been showing up on the ground.
At the Nyangezi General Hospital in eastern Congo, health workers said they had run out of supplies of life-saving medications including oxytocin to prevent and treat post-partum haemorrhage and amoxicillin, an antibiotic for paediatric use and during childbirth.
"It was a donation we received (previously) from USAID, and at the moment, there is none," midwife Alice Bulambo told Reuters.
The main government-run warehouse in the area has faced stockouts for over a year, said Olivier Kabarati Amani, chief medical officer for Nyangezi health zone.
As a result, facilities are forced to buy medicines at market prices. Over the last six months, "the cost of care has doubled, if not tripled," Amani said, at a time when the healthcare system in eastern Congo is already struggling with Ebola.
The US State Department said it "has prioritized ensuring all life-saving commodities have continued to be made reliably available."
TRANSITION
Maternal and newborn health items amounted to less than 1% of the more than $5 billion spent by the USAID Global Health Supply Chain program between 2016 and 2023, according to the most recently available annual report. The spending was channelled through private contractor Chemonics.
Reuters first reported on plans to close this programme, which also managed the donation and delivery of supplies to tackle malaria and HIV, in April, with aid officials warning that the September 30 shutdown could cause shortages.
The plans to close the Chemonics supply chain are part of the broader US global health strategy, which aims to move countries towards self-reliance alongside scaled-back US support and reduced reliance on contractors.
The US has instead signed more than 30 bilateral deals on health aid with recipient countries, including Congo, which require co-financing from the countries and are worth billions of dollars in total.
But the details of the deals are still being worked out and it had been unclear what would fill the gap in the ordering procedure in the meantime.
While many nations were already moving towards taking over their maternal and child health needs, lead times for orders can be a year or more, five former USAID officials said.
The Congolese government aims to take over by next year, but has struggled with the recent uncertainty, said Polydor Kabila, coordinator of the universal healthcare programme in the president’s office.
Alongside the UNICEF deal, the US authorities have extended the deadline for Chemonics deliveries of some key malaria and HIV items, the State Department spokesperson told Reuters. The US has also signed a deal with the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria to allow countries to order new US-funded HIV and malaria supplies through the Fund's order platform.
In a statement, UNICEF said it would work with the US to "keep health and nutrition supplies moving so more children receive life-saving care," adding that no orders have yet been placed but are expected shortly. REUTERS

Developers of Ai-Petri electronic warfare system move away from hardware in favour of AI – media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:49:19 EEST
00:49:19 KST

The developers of the Ukrainian Ai-Petri data transmission and electronic warfare (DTW) system are focusing on implementing artificial intelligence and software to automate the management of the network of counter-UAV systems, since, in the face of massive attacks, a human is unable to quickly coordinate the operation of numerous disparate systems without the use of appropriate intelligent software, according to an article published on the Militarnyi specialized portal.
"The system does not replace the weapons themselves, but rather manages their network – it distributes targets among available assets, assigns frequency channels for electronic warfare operations so as not to jam its own interceptor, and redistributes resources in real time depending on which targets have been shot down and which have just appeared. The key point: situational awareness systems, which simply display the battlefield situation on a screen for the commander, are not the same as combat management systems, which directly make decisions and issue commands to assets. There are quite a few of the former being developed in Ukraine, but far fewer of the latter, and it is precisely these, according to the developer, that are critically lacking," the article reads.
A corresponding system is already operating in experimental mode in Kyiv, Odesa, and Zaporizhia, and is now being launched in Dnipro, but its coverage remains limited. "This is a fundamentally different approach to countering drones. Instead of buying as many individual units as possible, we're building a network where each unit becomes an operational component of a unified system. Part of this architecture has already been implemented in Ai-Petri. The hardware creates a physical effect, while the software determines when, where, against which targets, and in coordination with which other assets this effect should be applied," according to the article.
The article notes that to completely neutralize a single "Kometa" navigation system – which the Shahed UAVs operate – several "Ai-Petri" complexes, arranged in a specific configuration, are required.
As previously reported, MP and leader of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko has invested over UAH 200 million since the autumn of 2023 in the production of "Ai-Petri SV" systems, which have successfully passed testing and are in use by the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Each system includes the counter-surveillance device itself, a pickup truck, a charging station, a generator, and the necessary electronics. In March 2025, Poroshenko announced a contract with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, and on June 29 of that same year, he announced the start of cooperation with the command of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' Ground Forces regarding the supply of these systems to the military. On September 9, 2026, the Ai-Petri counter-surveillance system was unveiled for the first time at the MSPO 2026 security and defense technology exhibition, held in Kielce, Poland.

Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:47:37 UTC
00:47:37 KST

At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza’s Health Ministry said Friday, Anadolu reports.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on Oct. 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5% of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza.
More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
OPINION: The ceasefire that keeps killing children: Gaza one year on
Malnutrition reaches ‘catastrophic levels’
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

Traders are betting overwhelmingly that the Federal Reserve won't raise interest rates when it meets later this month. But that judgment rests in part on assumptions about how the Fed communicates that may no longer hold under its new chairman. Kevin Warsh has left room to maneuver toward a hike, should he choose to use it.
To be clear, Warsh said outright at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok Friday morning that he wasn't signaling a decision one way or the other. His remarks nonetheless reinforced a judgment in the markets that the Fed would pause its rate increases, with the futures market assigning a 15% probability to an October hike as of Friday morning. That judgment follows remarks by other Fed speakers, including the chair's traditional top lieutenants, who indicated they were comfortable holding.
There are good reasons for investors to expect the Fed to wait. But there is also a case in the inflation data that Warsh could invoke to push the Federal Open Market Committee toward an increase on Oct. 28. Investors are overlooking that case based on longstanding past experience with the Fed.
But the chairman has repeatedly rejected the convention of telling markets what he plans to do before the committee meets. That raises the possibility that investors are dangerously complacent about the probability of a rate hike in October.
That complacency rests on a few bases. One is that the chairman's top lieutenants speak for him, or at least wouldn't contradict him in public. That was true in the past, but may not be so anymore.
In recent weeks, both Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams gave remarks that indicated they see little urgency in raising interest rates. The markets quickly repriced in favor of a hold in October.
Warsh, Jefferson and Williams make up an informal decision-making team atop the Fed known as the troika. Warsh could arguably coordinate with the troika even if he doesn't believe in communicating his own views. But outsiders can't be certain that traditional conventions surrounding the public statements of the New York Fed president and the Fed vice chair have survived the leadership transition.
Another assumption is that Warsh broadly accepts the FOMC's view of the economy. "The world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said in Bangkok of the economy since September.
That can be read as saying that relatively hot inflation readings from the consumer and producer price indexes in recent days don't disconfirm the view expressed in the Fed's most recent Summary of Economic Projections released at the conclusion of the September meeting. At the time, the median Fed official believed there would be one more rate hike in 2026 — which left room to pause in October and raise again in December.
But Warsh went out of his way at the September press conference to disclaim the SEP. "Those aren't my forecasts," he told a reporter.
Warsh set out his own idiosyncratic reading of the economy in detail at a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of August. It described the economy as growing strongly, with inflation a greater worry than the jobs market. Warsh's strongly hawkish views then set up the FOMC to unanimously raise interest rates in September. That hawkish position relied heavily on what he sees as loose credit conditions.
The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index has risen about 0.05 points since Jackson Hole but remains negative, indicating financial conditions have tightened but remain loose overall.
Does Warsh believe the market has done his work for him? Is having "removed a dose of accommodation," as he put it Thursday, enough? We can infer these answers, but we won't really know them until the FOMC press conference.
Then there is the inflation data. The consumer price index rose 3.7% for the year through September, while the producer price index gained 6.3%. The new data implies that the next reading of the Fed's preferred inflation reading, core personal consumption expenditures, will come in at 3.1% year over year. Headline PCE, which will be affected by energy prices, would be higher.
Warsh has gone out of his way to say that figures at that level are a problem. After economists questioned whether Warsh might tolerate inflation above 2%, he was unequivocal in Jackson Hole: "There should be no misunderstanding," Warsh said. The Fed's 2% PCE goal "is a firm, fixed target."
Warsh is visibly learning on the job. He may well be coming to understand that the Fed chairman can't operate alone and must rely on the staff and the rest of the FOMC to help him do his job. Likewise, he may discover that markets don't issue a clear signal independently of the Fed.
Raising rates while the markets strongly expect otherwise is a recipe for volatility. That factor has prompted interventions by officials like Jefferson and Williams in the past. A surprise decision after they were seen to guide the market could dent their credibility and make the Fed's decisions even harder to predict.
But how Warsh will settle these matters isn't clear yet. Warsh could go into the October meeting primed to muscle up wavering committee members based on booming demand for AI spending and warm readings in the inflation data. Or he could sit back and tack toward the middle of the committee once he assesses its views.
Warsh still has the potential to surprise us, and it's risky to assume otherwise.

UK clears way for German media group Axel Springer’s planned purchase of Telegraph Media Group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:45:47 UTC
00:45:47 KST

Aysu Biçer
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The UK government has cleared the way for Axel Springer’s planned purchase of Telegraph Media Group after deciding not to refer the deal for a more detailed competition investigation.
Culture Minister Lisa Nandy said Friday that she would not refer the proposed acquisition to a Phase 2 investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), the UK’s competition regulator.
“I will not be referring this matter to a more in-depth ‘Phase 2’ investigation by the Competition and Markets Authority,” Nandy said in a written statement.
She also said the Public Interest Intervention Notice (PIIN), issued in January 2024, and the related public interest merger reference order had ceased to be in force following her decision.
The decision reduces regulatory uncertainty surrounding one of the UK media industry’s high-profile ownership transactions and allows Axel Springer to proceed with its planned purchase without a more detailed competition investigation at this stage.
Axel Springer is one of Europe’s largest media groups. It owns major German newspapers, including Bild and Die Welt, as well as international digital outlets Politico and Business Insider.
The acquisition would bring one of Britain’s most prominent newspaper groups under the ownership of the Berlin-based company, marking a significant change in the UK media landscape.
The Telegraph Group was placed under receivership in 2023 after its former owners, the Barclay family, accumulated substantial debts to banks. Since then, the newspaper’s future has remained highly uncertain.
Before Axel Springer entered the picture, the UAE-backed RedBird IMI consortium had sought to acquire the newspaper.
However, the prospect of a long-established conservative British newspaper coming under the control of Gulf capital — and, indirectly, a foreign state — triggered a major political controversy in the UK.
The British government subsequently introduced legislation banning foreign state ownership of newspapers, prompting RedBird IMI to step back and transfer its acquisition rights to Axel Springer.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the U.S., saying "Starlink was switched off" in the middle of the night, preventing Ukrainian drones from intercepting Russian attacks, and ultimately contributing to civilian deaths.

prefer designboom on google
SAINT OF ATHENS TRANSLATES BRAND DUALITY INTO flagship BOUTIQUE
Designed by Saint of Athens, the Peace + Chaos flagship boutique in Thessaloniki, Greece, serves as a physical manifestation of the fashion brand’s dual identity. The interior scheme builds on a spatial dialogue between monochromatic minimalism and high-energy visual elements, reflecting the ongoing tension between discipline and creative disruption inherent to fashion design.
CONTRASTING EXPERIENTIAL ZONES PAIR neutrality WITH VISUAL CHAOS
The retail interior by creative agency Saint of Athens and designer Manos Kypritidis is structured into two contrasting experiential environments. The ‘peace’ zones employ soft neutral palettes, natural materials, clean linear geometry, negative space, and diffused lighting to establish an atmosphere of clarity representing the origins of creation. In contrast, the ‘chaos’ zones draw inspiration from backstage environments and the intensity of the fashion cycle, utilizing high-contrast color palettes, layered textures, unexpected material juxtapositions, fragmented geometries, and dynamic lighting design.
SPATIAL METAPHORS BRIDGING MINIMALISM AND EXPRESSIVE DESIGN
Rather than offering a purely complementary backdrop, the interior design acts as a spatial metaphor for the brand’s creative process. By positioning quiet, minimalist areas alongside expressive, high-contrast settings, the layout brings both sides of the brand’s identity together within a unified retail environment.

SpaceX AI policy leader grilled by NYC Council on Grok safety, sexualized images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:44:51 UTC
00:44:51 KST

SpaceX artificial intelligence policy leader Gabriela Castillo Madrid faced a tough line of questioning from NYC Council Speaker Julie Menin and other members on Friday as part of a council investigation into AI safety.
When Castillo Madrid claimed that the company had appropriate "safeguards" in place around its AI products, Menin immediately confronted her.
"I'm going to completely push back on that," Menin said. "I mean, just this morning — myself and my team — we put our own names, my own name, into Grok, and there's absolutely a sexualized image of myself. So then, how is it that within a second, I could find a sexualized image of myself using Grok?"
Castillo Madrid responded that the company has "strict controls" and would have the safety team look into that specific instance.
NYC Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, who leads the council's tech committee, told Castillo Madrid that "it is disgusting" that Grok enables users to easily "sexualize" images of real women without their consent.
"I just don't understand how you can say that there are these safe models," Menin said. "It's just unacceptable."
Castillo Madrid appeared in front of the council's tech committee by video.
Elon Musk's aerospace, defense tech and AI company originally evaded requests and a subpoena from the city council to appear alongside leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta on Oct. 5. SpaceX agreed to testify earlier this week after the council threatened to have its subpoena enforced by a judge.
The council opened its probe following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, and is aiming to use testimony and information unearthed through the investigation to guide new regulations.
Before Castillo Madrid took a role in government affairs at SpaceX earlier this year, she worked at X, Musk's social media company that's now owned by SpaceX, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to that, she spent almost three years at the U.S. Department of Commerce.
De La Rosa asked Castillo Madrid how many whistleblowers the company has fired, to which Castillo Madrid said she was "not aware" of any.
"I just want to interject for a minute because Devin Kim, one of your former employees, was reportedly fired after he sounded the alarm about serious safety concerns," Menin said.
"I'm not aware with that specific case," Castillo Madrid responded, adding that the company has a culture where "everybody has a an ability to say something when they see something."
Kim is now President of the nonprofit Center for AI Safety, a think tank focused on AI risks and safety.
Kim began his testimony before the council by outlining his experience as one of the first employees at xAI, saying that he "built the systems that researchers use to train and evaluate Grok." Kim said that he started raising concerns in January 2025 and those worries were shut down by his manager.
"My supervisor responded that AI safety was useless, and that AI would kill us and all anyways," he said.
Kim appeared by video, along with his attorney, following Castillo Madrid's questioning.
Regarding Grok-generated images, Kim said under prior standards at the company, "tasteful nudity was acceptable and is the goal."
"During my time there, there were only three employees working on AI safety, many of whom left after I resigned," Kim said. "And I think in large part due to the frustration with how safety was being handled."
The council also pressed Castillo Madrid about other areas of misuse with Grok and the types of safeguards that were in place.
Councilmember Mercedes Narcisse asked why the company promoted the idea of users uploading X-rays to Grok, asking if that was safe and if HIPPA protections applied.
SpaceX's Castillo Madrid said Grok is "not meant to be a clinician, a doctor," adding, "in terms of privacy, users decide whether their Grok conversations are used to train our models or not."
Narcisse said it was dangerous to tell people "openly on X, to put their MRI, X-rays," into Grok and expect "a definite answer" on health matters. The council member then upbraided the SpaceX representative for the vagueness of some of her replies.
"You're supposed to give us answers. You're not," she said.
In merging SpaceX with xAI in February, Musk combined his AI and social networking business with his rocket launch company, which also owns the Starlink satellite internet service. The merger put SpaceX in control of AI model Grok, which is used by some federal agencies, including the Pentagon.
SpaceX went public in June and is now valued at about $2 trillion. In August, SpaceX completed a $60 billion acquisition of AI coding startup Cursor.
In skipping the earlier NYC Council hearing, SpaceX avoided direct questioning from a member of the U.K. Parliament, Jess Asato, who testified about experiencing AI-enabled online harassment.
Asato is suing xAI in the U.K. after Grok users created and distributed sexualized images of her online without her consent. She's seeking damages, alleging misuse of her private information and breaches of European data protection rules.
According to the BBC, Asato criticized SpaceX for its "arrogance" in not appearing last week.
SpaceX didn't respond to a request for comment ahead of the meeting.
