In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:44:22 UTC
00:44:22 KST

In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
With Ireland’s lucrative tech sector hit by waves of layoffs linked to AI, the country’s nascent tech union has seen a spike in sign-ups from workers worried about their future.
DUBLIN — The Irish capital, which doubles as Europe's de facto tech capital, hosted two very different AI summits in the past week.
Most eyes were on the International AI Summit, the signature tech event of Ireland's six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, where top brass from the world's biggest tech firms discussed ways to harness artificial intelligence and minimize safety risks.
But the weekend before, a very different conversation was taking place at the Workers' AI Counter Summit, as Ireland's tech workers demanded a say in how the burgeoning technology reshapes the workplace and society.
Advertisement
Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.
There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.
“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”
The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.
Rise in layoffs
Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.
In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO. He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.
Advertisement
“The tech industry was founded on the idea that it would never have a union, because they're making people rich, and treat them really well,” Bohan said. “But post-Covid, workforce adjustments happened again and again, with layoffs and declining conditions in the sector. We started to see more people wanting to get organized around redundancies.”
The spike in sign-ups coincides with a wave of layoffs in Ireland’s tech bubble (and the tech sector globally), as companies corrected pandemic-era overhiring, and diverted investment to AI.
Ireland hosts the EU headquarters of most of the world’s largest tech companies, and more than 170,000 people are employed in the tech sector, according to the country's statistics institute.
Social media giant Meta has roughly halved its workforce in Ireland since the pandemic, axing well over 1,000 roles to offset AI investment and boost efficiency. Separately, Meta subcontractor Covalen also announced massive layoffs earlier this year, cutting more than 700 people.
Video-sharing platform TikTok announced this year it would shed around 300 Irish jobs, mostly from its trust and safety team, shifting the work to other countries, outsourced vendors or automated AI solutions.
A report by the IMF earlier this year warned that Ireland’s labor market is “relatively more exposed” to AI than many advanced economies, partly due to its concentration of tech workers.
Advertisement
The AI race is also creating new jobs on the Irish market – as AI firms like Anthropic and OpenAI are setting up Irish bases and trying to lure Big Tech workers with even bigger salaries.
Amid the uncertainty and volatility of the AI boom, tech workers are turning to unions for the first time as a safety net. One tech worker who used to work in trust and safety at a big tech firm told POLITICO that there used to be a feeling that as a “pampered” tech worker you “can't ask for your rights, because you already have it so much better."
But as layoffs continue and teams get leaner, workers in fields like trust and safety “now have to deal with these issues with fewer and fewer resources”, and face a “constant threat of being chopped,” the worker said.
That’s causing an “undoing of a certain perspective that we have of ourselves as tech sector workers,” they said, “because of undeniable experiences that now put us in situations where we clearly see our rights being violated, even if we may have it so much or somewhat better than most people."
A different tech worker who currently works for Covalen told POLITICO that there is a sense that “if they believe they can replace you with AI, they will do that.”
“All these Big Tech firms only care about profit, and what I have realized is the Irish government protects that Big Tech capital [rather than workers]," the Covalen worker said. "But the question is, what’s the government going to do when the tech bros change their mind and move elsewhere?”
Advertisement
Workers at the center
The speaker list at this week’s AI summit was a flex of the country’s strength as a tech hub, as top names from the world’s biggest companies like Google and Microsoft took to the stage.
Fionnuala Ní Bhrógáin, head of organizing and campaigning at Ireland’s Communications Workers’ Union (DATA’s parent union), was the only union voice on the line-up.
"The fact that 36 executives and industry bosses featured on the program, compared with just one trade union speaker — invited at the last minute after attention was drawn to the absence of workers’ voices — says a lot about the value the Irish government places on AI’s impact on workers," she told POLITICO.
"The reality is that a meaningful conversation about AI’s future can only happen through genuine engagement with workers and collective bargaining," Ní Bhrógáin added. "Without that voice, we risk deepening mistrust and resistance rather than creating the conditions for workers to shape these changes collectively."
DATA organized its counter-AI summit the previous weekend, to put “workers at the center of the debate about power, AI, technology and the future of work.”
The event cut through the “hype and futurism of politicians and industry figures to focus on the real present harms faced by ordinary workers and communities,” DATA's Bohan said.
The union is pushing for stronger legal protections for tech workers caught up in AI-driven layoffs in Ireland, including making it mandatory for employers to recognize unions during collective bargaining. It is also calling for a ban on cooling-off clauses that prevent laid-off workers from moving between Big Tech subcontractors.
Advertisement
A spokesperson for Ireland’s department for enterprise told POLITICO in a written statement that the government is “committed to strengthening collective bargaining and industrial relations” and has published an action plan to do so between now and 2030.
They said that employers already have to comply with obligations under Irish employment law, including consultation and notification procedures for collective redundancies, and workers who feel those rules have been broken can complain to the Workplace Relations Commission.
Firefighting to future-proofing
Naoise Ó Cearúil, a center-right Fianna Fáil lawmaker who chairs the AI committee, pointed out that while there have been high-profile job cuts in Ireland’s tech sector, “the actual net is that there has been an increase [in jobs], particularly over the past year and even five years.”
According to Ireland’s central statistics office, total employment in tech and related sectors surpassed 177,000 in the second quarter of this year, up from around 144,000 at the same time in 2021.
Ó Cearúil pointed out that many job losses were in trust and safety jobs like content moderation that are “very difficult mentally,” and now tech firms are able to “utilize AI and software to be able to do a lot of detection, rather than using humans.”
Advertisement
He has called for a national program to be established, to support workers whose jobs are at risk due to AI and automation.
A spokesperson for Ireland’s department of enterprise acknowledged that the country’s tech sector has “experienced significant adjustment in recent years,” but said the changes were generally part of wider global restructuring “rather than reflecting any Ireland-specific weakness.”
They said the Irish government is currently focused on “ensuring workers and businesses are equipped to adapt to technological change through investment in education, training, lifelong learning and digital skills."

It called for intensified efforts to tackle key technological challenges, promote algorithmic innovation, advance the coordinated development of computing capacity and electricity supply, and increase the supply of high-quality data.
The meeting also stressed the need to promote AI applications in the real economy by better aligning supply and demand, encouraging joint research and development, advancing pilot testing and validation, and cultivating application scenarios to translate AI technologies into real productive forces.
It called for coordinating development and security, adopting differentiated measures tailored to different industries, and strengthening risk assessment to ensure AI safety.
The meeting discussed and approved in principle the draft revision to the Teachers Law and decided to submit it to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for deliberation.
It called for stronger safeguards for teachers' pay and benefits, reduced non-teaching workloads, improved public services for teachers, and better protection of their professional dignity and legitimate rights and interests.
The meeting urged efforts to build a high-caliber, professional teaching workforce, improve the teacher education system, enhance teachers' ability to teach and nurture students, strengthen professional ethics and conduct, and foster an atmosphere of respecting teachers and valuing education throughout society.
The meeting also discussed and approved in principle the draft amendment to the Pricing Law and decided to submit it to the national legislature's standing committee for deliberation. It called for curbing disorderly low-price competition in accordance with the law and regulating price competition in the platform economy to foster a fair and orderly market environment.
The meeting decided to amend certain provisions of 14 administrative regulations and repeal four others. ■

Scottish government set to drop opposition to new oil and gas fields
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:40:52 UTC
00:40:52 KST

The North Sea oil rigs Noble Endeavor, center, and Well-Safe Defender, right, on the north-east coast of Scotland, pictured on April 24, 2026. | Andy Buchanan/AFP via Getty Images
ABERDEEN — The SNP-led Scottish government is set to drop its long-standing opposition to new oil and gas exploration in the North Sea.
Two senior members of the Scottish government — granted anonymity to discuss a strategy not yet ready for publication — told POLITICO the government will revise its energy plans to take a more pro-oil and gas exploration position.
Tests on compatibility with the government’s climate targets will remain, but Scotland will no longer begin from a position of opposition to new oil and gas projects. The move marks a major change in the Scottish government's energy policy.
Advertisement
The Scottish government — led by the SNP since 2007 — released a draft energy strategy in 2023 which set out its “presumption against” new oil and gas fields in the North Sea.
That draft strategy is “out of date,” one senior Scottish government official said. They said a new strategy, expected by the summer, will not contain this wording. A second person with knowledge of the policy said the new strategy will “reflect the world as it is.”
The shift in policy comes with the U.K. government widely expected to give the go-ahead to the Jackdaw gas field next week.
While the Scottish government has little power over the granting of new licenses for projects such as Jackdaw or the Rosebank oil field — where a decision is expected to come separately and at a later date — it has an important symbolic role, and can apply pressure to the U.K. government to approve licenses.
SNP politicians at the party’s conference in Aberdeen privately admitted the stance on Jackdaw has hurt the party electorally.
The party passed a resolution at its conference Friday which stated that the “utilisation of domestic production” of oil and gas is “clearly preferable to importation”. This was seen as a further softening of the position of the SNP — which governed in a quasi-coalition with the anti-exploration Scottish Greens until as recently as 2004.
Advertisement
This resolution, which changes the party’s official policy, will be used as the government writes its new energy strategy, the two people quoted above said.
In the summer, the SNP lost a key parliamentary by-election in Aberdeen to the pro-drilling Conservative Party, where their North Sea messaging was a key focus. “It was bruising ,” the official quoted above said. “But we’d been shifting our position for a while.”
Speaking in the debate at the party's conference Friday, the defeated SNP candidate in that by-election said the victorious Conservatives had hung the words ‘presumption against’ around “our necks lie an albatross.”
”We need to put to bed any suggestion that our party, or our government, supports a ‘presumption against’,” Richard Thomson said.

Saab Unveils First GlobalEye AWACS Aircraft for Swedish Air Force
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:40:46 UTC
00:40:46 KST

The Swedish company Saab has unveiled the first GlobalEye long-range airborne early warning and control (AWACS) aircraft built for the Swedish Air Force.
The company announced this on its website.
This marks the start of the testing and verification phase for the technical systems. The aircraft will make its first flight in the near future, after which the process of its final handover to the customer will begin.
Currently, the Swedish Air Force is awaiting delivery of a total of three such platforms. The Swedish government signed a contract to purchase the first two AEW&C aircraft in 2022, and the agreement also included an option for additional aircraft, which the country exercised in 2024 by ordering a third unit.
The new aircraft are intended to completely replace the Swedish Air Force’s obsolete Saab 340 AEW&C early warning and control systems, which have been in service for several decades. These aircraft were acquired, among others, by Ukraine.
Development of the GlobalEye system began in the 2010s based on the Bombardier Global 6000 aircraft.
The main component of the aircraft’s reconnaissance equipment is the Erieye ER (Extended Range) active phased array radar, which operates in the S-band. The system’s antenna is housed in a distinctive longitudinal pod above the fuselage.
By utilizing gallium nitride (GaN) technology, the developers were able to increase the target detection range by 70% compared to previous versions of the Erieye system. The radar is capable of detecting airborne objects with a small radar cross-section—including cruise missiles and aircraft—at distances exceeding 550 kilometers.
In addition to the main radar, the aircraft is equipped with a Leonardo Seaspray multi-mode under-fuselage radar for maritime and ground surveillance, an optoelectronic and infrared station, as well as electronic intelligence and self-defense systems.
The aircraft cockpit and operator workstations are integrated into a shared network that allows real-time situational data to be transmitted to ground control centers, ships, and other combat aircraft.
The Bombardier Global 6000 platform provides an endurance of over 11 hours without refueling, and its operational flight altitude reaches 10,000–11,000 meters.
In addition to Sweden, the United Arab Emirates is a major operator and customer of GlobalEye systems on the international market.

Starlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:39:41 UTC
00:39:41 KST

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service has not yet been fully restored, as media reports suggested the order to throttle the service had come from within the White House.
Zelenskyy met European leaders on Friday in Brussels, where he asked the EU for another €70bn (£60bn) next year to fund Ukraine’s defence against Russia.
The meeting offered an important opportunity for Zelenskyy and Europe to align their strategies, as Zelenskyy once again found himself embroiled in a major quarrel with the US president, Donald Trump.
Hours earlier, Trump had called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries “a disgrace” and criticised Zelenskyy, after a purported “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine failed to take hold.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher,” Trump told the Newsmax television channel. “Well, I think that’s a disgrace.”
Energy analysts told the BBC that the US-Israeli war on Iran was having the biggest impact on diesel export volumes, although the Ukraine war was also significant.
Trump’s administration is suspected of withholding intelligence from Ukraine on incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes, and of throttling Starshield, the military version of the Starlink satellite internet network, to prevent it from being used on drones flying faster than 100mph. Neither has officially been confirmed.
Speaking after meeting EU leaders on Friday, Zelenskyy said that Starshield had not yet returned to normal.
“Our defence ministry is in touch and my partners, they told me that there were signals from the White House that they would return these capabilities,” Zelenskyy said. “Have they returned to the previous speed limits? No. But is it coming back now? Yes.”
Reuters on Friday reported that the order to throttle Starshield had come from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. They did not identify the White House official who had made the decision, but said the Pentagon had been informed that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military had to be slowed.
Zelenskyy called it a “very dangerous and unpleasant surprise” that speeds had been reduced on Starlink, which Ukraine uses to support its most effective air defence systems against Russian jet-powered drones.
Starlink is produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, but controlled by the US government.
When Zelenskyy arrived for talks with EU leaders, he was applauded by the heads of state and government of the bloc’s 27 countries. Zelenskyy later said he had heard “only support”, when asked about reports that European leaders had asked him to dial down his criticism of Trump.
According to a transcript of his remarks, he told EU leaders that the war would cost €155bn in 2027. “And we need at least €70bn more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience,” he said. “This is a realistic amount.”
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, agreed with Zelenskyy that “it is clear that we have a gap of €70bn that has to be covered” for 2027, although she expected Ukraine’s other partners – which she did not name – to cover part of the sum.
The EU is currently giving Ukraine regular payments from a €90bn funding plan agreed last December that was intended to cover two-thirds of Kyiv’s civilian and military needs for 2026-27. The remaining third was to be filled by other “international partners”, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan.
The realisation that Kyiv again risks a financial crunch has put Russia’s €210bn assets frozen inside the EU back on the table. The EU takes the profits from those assets to support Ukraine, but last year decided against using the funds themselves, instead opting for an EU-backed €90bn loan.
Belgium, which hosts the vast majority of the Russian funds, remains strongly opposed to using the frozen assets, fearing it will be left to carry the financial burden if the plan goes wrong. But Zelenskyy said there could be an alternative.
“We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war,” he said.
The European Commission, a strong backer of last year’s rejected frozen assets plan, has been reluctant to propose new variants – such as an EU-controlled custodian – because it fears running into same opposition from Belgium and other sceptical member states.
Before the summit, Belgium’s prime minister, Bart De Wever, said Zelenskyy would “probably look everybody straight in the eye and say: thank you for the €90bn, but that money is going to run out because a war is a very costly thing”.
Von der Leyen said the EU had supported Trump’s energy ceasefire “but we have seen that Russia did not respect it, not a single minute” and instead had escalated its attacks. She said the EU intended to increase pressure on Russia, promising a 22nd round of sanctions and adding: “We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war.”

====================================================================================================

Russian Firms Stand to Gain Most From Trump’s Diesel Deal, Analysts Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:39:12 UTC
00:39:12 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow could do more for Russian oil companies than for the American consumers he wants to help, analysts say.
While Russian firms stand to benefit from looser export restrictions, the promised shipments may do little to bring down U.S. fuel prices.
The agreement has drawn scathing criticism from Ukraine and its European allies, as well as scrutiny from lawmakers at home. But does it make economic sense?
What does Trump want?
Trump announced that Russia would “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons thereafter.
The deal comes as U.S. diesel prices have risen to $6.179 per gallon, up nearly 70% year-on-year, amid the turmoil that has gripped the global oil market since the start of the Iran war in late February.
Reduced refinery output has sharply cut global diesel exports, which totaled about 172.2 million metric tons in the first nine months of 2026, down 10% from the same period last year.
Higher prices are hurting Americans, including the truckers and farmers who are part of Trump’s traditional support base. With just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections, 73% said they disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, according to poll aggregator Silver Bulletin.
Additional Russian supplies are not intended to directly ease a U.S. diesel shortage because the country already produces roughly a quarter more diesel than it consumes. But U.S. fuel prices are shaped by global markets. The more other countries are willing to pay for diesel, the more domestic consumers must pay in turn.
More Russian diesel on the global market could therefore help lower American prices by narrowing the gap between supply and demand, regardless of whether it is shipped directly to the U.S.
Encouraging Russia and Middle Eastern producers to increase fuel supplies is the most straightforward way for Washington to bring prices down.
That’s because U.S. refineries are already operating at close to full capacity, while restricting exports to force domestic fuel prices lower could create other problems, including storage constraints.
Can Russia help?
Like the U.S., Russia is a net exporter of diesel, meaning it produces more than it consumes and sells the surplus abroad.
That has not changed despite Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian refineries in recent months. While the attacks have caused sporadic gasoline shortages, Russia’s pre-war diesel output was more than double domestic demand, compared with a surplus of just 15-20% for gasoline.
Russia has therefore continued to export diesel, though in smaller volumes. Shipments totaled about 427,000 metric tons in September, compared with roughly 3 million metric tons a month before Ukraine intensified its strikes, Reuters reported.
These figures only cover shipments to the limited number of countries, mostly in Central Asia, exempted from restrictions Russia imposed in July to keep its domestic market supplied.
Other estimates are higher. Kpler put September shipments at 584,000 metric tons.
Energy analyst and former Gazprom Neft executive Sergei Vakulenko, citing shipping data, said Russia exported at least 1.6 million metric tons of diesel by sea between July and September, despite a broad export ban that exempted supplies to Mongolia and Central Asia.
Vakulenko, now based in Germany with the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said Russian authorities had made little effort to stop these “grey” shipments because the country lacked the storage capacity to hold the surplus.
This means that Russia could supply the 500,000 metric tons Trump requested for November without causing domestic shortages simply by legalizing existing grey exports, he said.
Moscow partially lifted its diesel export ban from Oct. 10 following the agreement with Trump.
Supplying 1 million metric tons of diesel a month during the winter is also realistic, especially as domestic demand falls after the autumn harvest season, Vakulenko added.
U.S.-based energy analyst Tatiana Mitrova also said the volumes Trump requested from Russia “would have gone to the global market anyway without any additional effort.”
So what’s the catch?
The volumes Trump announced may be realistic, but they could be too small to bring prices down significantly.
For example, 500,000 metric tons of Russian diesel equals roughly 4% of monthly U.S. consumption or 0.4% of monthly global consumption. It would cover about 13% of the estimated monthly global diesel shortfall of 4 million metric tons.
Russian supplies could have a greater impact if exports returned to levels seen before Ukraine intensified its attacks. But Kyiv has yet to agree to halt its strikes, and Moscow would need to repair its damaged refineries and restore lost capacity.
“The volumes under discussion are too small, all else being equal, to noticeably affect global prices, especially before the midterm elections,” Vakulenko said.
Without an effective energy truce, the diesel deal will largely amount to “appearances rather than a real increase in Russian diesel supplies to the global market,” he said.
The deal could provide “temporary relief to a global market facing a significant diesel deficit,” but Russia’s constrained refinery capacity limits how much additional supply it can deliver, analytics firm Kpler said in a note.
Shipping Russian oil products through the Baltic and Black seas poses another challenge, as Ukrainian drone attacks also disrupt those routes, Kpler added.
Moscow-based analyst Kirill Rodionov said Russian companies stand to reap the most benefits from the deal, as it would allow them to officially export more diesel at higher prices.
Those exports would do little to lower U.S. fuel prices, but would allow the Trump administration to claim at least a partial foreign policy success, he said.

00:37:50 KST

Gains in tackling malnutrition in Gaza remain fragile and could be undermined by disruptions to supplies entering the strip, the UN children's agency UNICEF said on Friday, urging that all crossings remain open.
Israel said on Wednesday commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza because of what it described as a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas.
That has cut off a vital source of food and other goods in Gaza, where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.
Gazans left highly vulnerable despite ceasefire agreement
Although the ceasefire has improved aid access and reduced large-scale fighting, humanitarian agencies say ongoing Israeli strikes, continued displacement and widespread destruction have left civilians highly vulnerable.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.
“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved," he said.
"We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require."
A new UNICEF report published on Friday found that while the ceasefire since October has allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said progress in pushing back the threat of famine, confirmed by a global food security monitor in August last year, had been achieved through a scaled-up food and nutrition response, the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies, and the ceasefire.
However, those gains remain fragile, it said.
“Acute malnutrition rates have fallen, but only one in three children under the age of two is currently achieving minimum dietary diversity,” the report stated. A survey conducted by UNICEF in June also found a significant prevalence of chronic malnutrition, affecting one in eight children under five.
UNICEF also called for improvements in living conditions in the largely devastated enclave, where some 800,000 children are still displaced and most live in tents or unsafe buildings as winter approaches, saying better shelter and basic services are essential to support a lasting recovery.

The Khan Yunis strikes killed Basel Nabil Abd al-Rahman Kashta and Ahmad Raja al-Shaer, with the statement describing them as having posed an immediate threat to IDF soldiers operating in the area of the Yellow Line, as well as Israeli civilians.

Gaza malnutrition and starvation at ‘catastrophic’ levels: Health Ministry

Gaza malnutrition and starvation at ‘catastrophic’ levels: Health Ministry
About 67 percent of Gaza’s population is projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached “catastrophic” levels, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, despite a United States-brokered “ceasefire” that aims in part to allow more food and medical supplies to enter the Strip as Palestinians face famine.
At least 466 Palestinians have died of malnutrition and starvation since 2024, with children accounting for one-third of the deaths, the Gaza Health Ministry said on Friday, in a statement released for World Food Day.
Elderly Palestinians accounted for the largest share of malnutrition-related deaths in the Strip, with 189 deaths, representing 40.5 percent of the total. The ministry said 11 percent of older people went without a meal for an entire day and 48 percent reduced portions so their families could eat.
The ministry estimated that 74,200 children would require treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Malnutrition was also driving up rates of anaemia among pregnant women to 61 percent in 2026, up from 41 percent before the war began in October 2023. Nearly 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded in the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded in the preceding six months.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians – 67 percent of Gaza’s population – are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026 as winter months approach, the ministry warned.
Gains in tackling hunger crisis at risk
The United Nations children’s agency, UNICEF, said that gains in tackling Gaza’s hunger crisis were fragile. It warned that the situation could worsen due to disruption of supplies entering Strip, and urged that crossings remain open.
A UNICEF report published on Friday found that while the so-called “ceasefire” between Israel and Hamas last October had allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said scaled-up food and nutrition response and the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies helped to avert a prolonged famine after it was declared in August 2025.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.
“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved,” he said. “We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require.”
Israel said on Wednesday that no commercial goods had entered the Strip in days, blaming the supply shortages on a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas. The Palestinian group dismissed Israel’s claims as “baseless” while Gaza’s Government Media Office condemned Israel’s “blatant disinformation campaign and false statement”.
Israel’s move to halt supplies has cut off a vital source of food and other goods in a territory where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.
Even before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, an Israeli land, sea and air blockade restricted the flow of food, clean water, fuel and medical supplies from entering the Strip.
Gaza’s Health Ministry has called for international action to ensure unrestricted entry of food and medicine into the Strip. It also called for support to revive local food production.

Ukraine, Turkey discuss securing Black Sea shipping as $10 billion in exports at risk
Ukraine has asked Turkey to help restore safe and stable Black Sea shipping, warning that restrictions on port operations caused by Russian attacks put around 32 million tons of agricultural products worth approximately $10 billion at risk, Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry said.
Russia’s attacks on commercial vessels and Ukrainian port operations have disrupted the country’s Black Sea shipping routes, threatening agricultural exports that are a major source of revenue for Ukraine’s economy.
With alternative routes unable to handle the full volume of maritime shipments, prolonged disruption could reduce farmers’ incomes, constrain investment in the next planting season and deepen the economic impact of the war.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi raised the issue during a meeting with Turkish Ambassador to Ukraine Fatma Ceren Yazgan earlier this week. He said alternative export routes via the Danube, railways and roads cannot fully replace maritime shipments.
"Without the restoration of stable shipping through the Black Sea, production will begin to decline in the long term," Vysotskyi said, adding that farmers need greater certainty ahead of the spring sowing season.
He warned that lower export revenues could leave farmers with fewer resources to purchase seeds, fertilizers and crop protection products, potentially leading to reduced planting areas and affecting rural communities.
Yazgan said Turkey was ready to help find practical solutions and raise the issue with international partners. The two sides also discussed cooperation on irrigation projects and the potential involvement of Turkish businesses.
Separately, Turkey has been discussing a temporary, partial ceasefire with Ukraine and Russia to protect merchant vessels carrying civilian cargo, according to Turkey’s permanent representative to NATO, Basat Ozturk. Ankara hopes to draw on its experience with the Black Sea Grain Initiative to develop a new maritime security mechanism.
Restoring reliable Black Sea shipping is critical to Ukraine’s agricultural export revenues and future production. The economic impact of any truce would depend on effective protection for commercial vessels and sustained access to Ukrainian ports.

The vote that could redraw Canada: Everything you need to know about Alberta's referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:33:58 UTC
00:33:58 KST

Alberta is holding a nonbinding referendum on Monday to ask residents if they want to remain part of Canada, marking the first time the oil-rich province has ever put the question of separation to the public.
Polls have consistently shown most Albertans — about 70% — want to stay in Canada, with roughly a quarter of residents supporting an independent Alberta.
What’s on ballot for Albertans?
The ballot has 10 questions, each with its own colour-coded option.
The last ballot question voters see is question 10: whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or start the legal process required to hold a binding referendum on separation.
A simple majority in favour of separation could trigger that process.
There are nine other nonbinding questions about immigration, access to provincial services — including education, social care and healthcare — and voter identification requirements.
Why is Alberta putting its future to a vote?
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said in May it was “time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on,” when she announced the government would add a question on separation.
Smith’s decision followed months of campaigning by a small but vocal group of separatists, who argue Alberta’s energy wealth subsidises poorer parts of the country and that Ottawa's bureaucracy has stifled the province’s economy.
Some members of the group had backed Smith's candidacy for premier. Smith says she voted to keep Alberta in Canada in advance polling, according to a video she posted on social media on Wednesday.
Has Canada faced break-up vote before?
Yes, but not in Alberta. The majority-French-speaking province of Quebec has held two referendums, in 1980 and 1995.
Quebecers voted to remain in Canada both times, but by the slimmest of margins in 1995.
The separatist Parti Quebecois (PQ) won a provincial election earlier this month and has pledged to hold a third referendum, but only after US President Donald Trump has left office and if the party holds a majority.
The PQ won a minority government on October 5, meaning it will rely on smaller parties to pass legislation.
Canada is a federation of 10 provinces and three territories.
While Ottawa handles matters of national interest, such as defence, trade and foreign policy, the provinces and territories hold significant power over medical care, education and land rights.
When will the verdict be in?
Polls are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. on Monday (0200 GMT on Tuesday).
Elections Alberta says it will count ballots by hand and count the separation question first.
Elections Alberta will publish results on its website as they arrive, and unofficial results are expected within 48 hours after voting ends.
What comes next if Alberta votes to leave?
Smith has said she will respect the result and quickly begin the process to hold a legally binding referendum. But separation would not happen imminently.
After the 1995 Quebec referendum, Canada's Parliament passed the Clarity Act in 2000, which says talks about secession can be triggered only if a clear majority of the public supports it, without specifying the necessary threshold.
The act also states provinces and territories have no unilateral right to leave Canada and that a constitutional amendment negotiated by provincial, territorial and federal governments is required.
First Nations groups have objected to an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Canada predate Alberta's entry into Confederation.
In May, an Alberta court judge ruled the province’s chief electoral officer was wrong to allow separatists to collect signatures requesting a referendum, because the process should have prompted a consultation with Indigenous peoples whose rights might be violated by separation.
Alberta has appealed the decision.
Where does Carney stand on referendum?
Mark Carney, Canada’s Prime Minister, was largely raised in Alberta and has previously said “the best place for Alberta is in Canada” and that the country cannot succeed if it's divided.
He released a video on Canadian Thanksgiving, October 12, saying national unity is critical as Canada fights threats from abroad, including a trade war with the US.
Carney has campaigned to keep Alberta in Canada.
Would Quebec referendum pass based on current polls?
Current opinion polls indicate that a Quebec sovereignty referendum may fail, with support for independence stuck in the 25–35% range and opposition often reaching 60–70% among decided voters.
Aggregators such as 338Canada show roughly 70% No versus 30% Yes once undecided respondents are excluded, while individual surveys from Léger, Pallas Data and others consistently place the No side well ahead.
Even among francophones, Yes support is not high enough to carry a province-wide majority.
While campaign events, question wording or external shocks could still move the numbers, nothing in the present data suggests a competitive race.
A Yes victory would require a dramatic and sustained shift that current polling does not forecast.

There is nothing apolitical about the scientists behind Russian weapons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:33:50 UTC
00:33:50 KST

There is nothing apolitical about the scientists behind Russian weapons
Two men attempt to escape from the National Academy of Sciences building after it was hit by a Russian drone and caught fire in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Tetiana Hryn'ova
Physicist at the French National Center for Scientific Research
A lunchtime drone attack on the head office of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv's downtown on Sept. 28, 2026, might have come as a shock to scientists based outside the country.
Unfortunately, for Ukrainian scientists, those who can be seen climbing down the ladders from the burning building, such attacks are part of the daily routine.
As documented in the UNESCO report from 2024, over 30% of Ukraine's research infrastructure has been damaged by the Russian attacks, and its institutions were forced to move, some multiple times, to safer areas which remain under Ukrainian control.
Occupied Ukrainian scientific institutions undamaged by the war, such as Crimean Astrophysical Observatory, the Marine Hydrophysical Institute, the Institute of Biology of the Southern Seas, the Nikitsky Botanical Garden, Askania Nova Biosphere Reserve, V. I. Vernadsky Taurida National University, and universities in Donetsk, Luhansk, Kerch, and Mariupol, not only saw their facilities appropriated by the Russian scientific community but also had their institutional identities usurped.
Some Ukrainian scientific facilities, such as the RT-70 radio telescope in Yevpatoria in occupied Crimea, have even been repurposed for military use.
While the Russian scientific community benefits greatly from the seizure and repurposing of Ukrainian research facilities, Russian scientists are simultaneously portrayed as victims of the war because of the sanctions and supposed international isolation brought by it.
The physical expropriation extends to a broader ideological appropriation of Ukrainian scientific heritage.
Portraying Nobel laureate Elie Metchnikoff, a pioneer of cellular immunity born near Kharkiv, George Gamow, a pioneer of Big Bang theory born in Odesa, or Serhii Koroliov, a chief designer of the Soviet space program born in Zhytomyr and the driving force behind the launch of the world's first artificial satellite Sputnik 1 in 1957, as Russian scientists symbolically incorporates their Ukrainian birthplaces into an imagined Russian scientific and cultural geography, only reinforcing claims to Ukrainian territory and legitimizing the seizure of its scientific infrastructure and resources.
By appropriating Ukrainian scientific achievements, Russia enhances the prestige of its own scientific establishment — a legacy apparently too valuable to tarnish with sanctions — while marginalizing Ukraine's contribution to global scientific progress.
The victim narrative also obscures the important role played by the Russian scientific establishment in supporting the ongoing war effort, not only through direct involvement in weapons research and development but also through knowledge and technology transfer and personnel training.
These activities are facilitated by the longstanding and close collaboration between the Russian scientific community and its military-industrial complex.
A prominent example of such cooperation is the Dubna military-industrial hub, infamously known for the Kh-101 and S8000 Banderol missile production and the development of glide bombs, which are eventually used by Russian soldiers to terrorize Ukrainian civilians.
Dubna also hosts the Space Communications Center, which supports intelligence collection and the coordination of Russian occupation forces operating in Ukraine.
For decades, international sources such as Encyclopedia Britannica have presented Dubna as a ‘science city’ centered on the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR). Such descriptions omitted the existence in Dubna of the missile design bureau Raduga and its production plant, both of which, alongside JINR, are "city-forming enterprises of Dubna."
Collaboration between JINR and Raduga was crucial for the establishment of the university in Dubna in 1994, the Dubna Special Economic Zone in 2005, and the construction of numerous housing complexes for their employees.
University students, taught by JINR scientists, are subsequently recruited by enterprises in Dubna, many of which are subject to international sanctions. JINR scientists themselves either founded or work in some of these companies.
In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, scientists from Dubna continue to be prominently represented in global organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, UNESCO in Paris, the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP) in Trieste and Geneva, and the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva, to name a few.
Participation in these organizations reinforces the visibility of JINR and lends credibility to its self-presentation as an "apolitical" institution.
In 2016, the IAEA funded a JINR project with the Institute of Biology of the Southern Seas in occupied Sevastopol, facilitating the integration of Crimea into the Russian scientific sphere.
The Global Conference of the International Decade of Sciences for Sustainable Development, organized by UNESCO in July 2026 in Paris, France, included a session dedicated to JINR.
That same month, JINR was featured at the IUPAP-organized International Conference on High Energy Physics 2026 in Natal, Brazil. Over 240 JINR scientists currently have in-person access to the CERN site, which allows them and their families to live in Switzerland and France and to freely travel within the Schengen area.
On Aug. 8, 2025, Ukraine imposed sanctions on JINR, making it the only country to have done so.
This oversight perpetuates a self-reinforcing cycle in which participation in international scientific activities allows Russian researchers to maintain access to global research networks, which can be used both to legitimize Russia's occupation of Ukrainian territories and to acquire knowledge and technologies that strengthen the Russian military-industrial complex and increase its capacity to attack Ukrainian civil and scientific infrastructure.
The examples discussed here represent only a fraction of a broader, systematic pattern that challenges the portrayal of Russian science as an apolitical enterprise and Russian scientists primarily as victims of sanctions and international isolation.
Therefore, it is time to finally put under scrutiny how scientific cooperation, institutional prestige, and continued participation in international scientific organizations can coexist with, and potentially facilitate, military production and the legitimization of occupation, while scientists in Ukraine face the physical destruction of their institutions.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Target pensions or welfare, not banks, IMF tells John Healey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:33:29 UTC
00:33:29 KST

The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.
Helge Berger, deputy director of the IMF’s European department, was asked about bank taxes after the Guardian revealed Healey plans to tap the sector for additional revenue.
Berger replied that given the UK’s current high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.
He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.
He added: “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”
As examples, he highlighted the pensions triple lock – which Labour has already said it will reform – and “better targeting [of] social benefits”, adding: “I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”
Berger was speaking in Bangkok, where the IMF has held its annual meetings this week.
City lobbyists have been out in full force, warning the government that higher taxes could force banks to throttle lending, hitting the economy and even forcing some lenders to move jobs and operations abroad.
In a letter sent to Healey and copied to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, on 12 October, days before news of the planned tax hike broke, the chief executive of UK Finance, David Postings, shared research commissioned by the lobby group.
It suggested that reversing Tory cuts to the bank surcharge – taking it back to 8% from 3% – would leave annual UK GDP £1.2bn lower in real terms by 2029-30 than it would have otherwise been.
He said it would also see banks issue fewer business loans and mortgages, with lending likely to be £10.4bn lower in 2029-2030 than if the surcharge was held at 3%.
“The UK’s banking sector already makes a vital contribution to the wider economy,” Postings’ letter said. “To sustain this vital contribution, the budget should avoid any increases in bank-specific taxes, as this would risk constraining the sector’s ability to lend and invest.”
However, TUC analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the Treasury has already lost out on £6bn over the three years since the surcharge cut came into force in 2023.
At the same time, banks have been reporting strong profits, largely off the back of high interest rates, with bosses subsequently increasing banker bonus pots and handing billions of pounds to shareholders.
Collectively, the UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays and Lloyds – reported £29.2bn in profits over the first six months of the year, with almost half, £13.7bn, pledged to investors through dividends and share buybacks. Over the past five years, those banks have raked in £200bn in pre-tax profits.
Author and former banker Philip Augar said the banks were “enjoying boom conditions”, partly due to good management but partly due to economic conditions “not of their own making”. He said there was room for a “moderate increase in taxation” that would raise about £2bn to £3bn a year.
“The prime minister has said that the burden of taxation has to fall on those with the broader shoulders, and at the moment, it’s hard to think of a sector where the shoulders are much broader than the banking sector,” Augar told the BBC’s Today programme on Friday.
While banks could not expect interest rates benefits to continue forever, Augar said that banks – including those that were bailed out in the 2008 financial crisis – could not have it both ways.
“Banking is cyclical, it’s true. But when it hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out,” Augar said. “When it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment. Banks can’t be too big to fail and too big to tax.”
Some banks have threatened to pull investment, and potentially jobs, from the UK if it hikes taxes, with lobby groups noting smaller overall tax charges in rival financial centres like Frankfurt, Dublin and Amsterdam.
Jamie Dimon, who heads up the largest bank in the US, JP Morgan, said in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile towards banks.
But Augar said the government needed to see past the bluster. “There seems to have been a coordinated campaign by the big international banks who have businesses in Britain – JP Morgan, Citigroup, Santander, HSBC and others.
“But they always say this, [and] they rarely move. I think that if the chancellor judges this right, with a moderate increase in taxation or some other form of getting money from the banks, then the business will remain in the UK.”

“We Are Not the Number One Priority”: Zelenskyy Says Ukraine Faces Severe Patriot Missile Shortage
Ukraine is facing a severe shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 interceptor missiles for its US-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said during a briefing in Brussels on October 16.
According to Zelenskyy, most available supplies of these missiles have been directed to the Middle East for an extended period.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“There is currently a severe shortage. Most PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles have been going to the Middle East for quite some time. This is no secret,” Zelenskyy said.
“We are not the number one priority when it comes to the allocation of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles. Nevertheless, we are grateful for the number of missiles we can receive through PURL,” he added.
Despite the limited availability, Ukraine continues to receive some Patriot interceptors from the United States through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative. The program allows European partners to finance the purchase of US-made military equipment for Ukraine.
“We receive PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles from the United States through the PURL program. Europe pays for them, meaning these are not free missiles or gifts,” Zelenskyy explained.
The Ukrainian president expressed gratitude to NATO, European countries financing the purchases, the White House administration, and the United States for their continued involvement in supplying air defense equipment.
With interceptor missiles remaining in short supply, Kyiv is also working with international partners to secure additional deliveries in smaller quantities.
“We are working with Europe and other countries around the world, gathering 2, 5, or 10 missiles at a time. However many we can agree on, however many of the necessary missiles we can obtain, that is how many we deliver to Ukraine to protect people,” Zelenskyy said.
The president emphasized that strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses remains particularly urgent as Russian attacks continue to threaten critical infrastructure across the country.
“Today, we are protecting infrastructure, primarily the energy sector. You are well aware of all these challenges,” Zelenskyy stated.
His remarks follow reports of an even more critical situation involving Ukraine’s Patriot missile stockpiles, with a source familiar with the matter telling CNN on October 15 that the country had completely exhausted its available interceptors.
According to the report, the shortage has significantly undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, raising concerns about the country’s vulnerability to further attacks.
The source told CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”

Ukraine expects to receive additional F-16 fighter jets from Belgium by the end of 2026, with the aircraft already proving effective against Russia’s jet-powered Shahed drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated during a briefing after talks with European leaders, Babel reported on October 16.
Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine had discussed further F-16 deliveries with the Belgian side and expected additional aircraft before the end of the year.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Today we use them to shoot down jet-powered Shaheds, and they are showing good results,” Zelenskyy stated, according to Babel.
The briefing also covered Ukraine’s wider air-defense needs. Zelenskyy acknowledged a major shortage of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles for Patriot systems, adding that much of the US supply was currently being redirected to the Middle East.
Ukraine continues receiving Patriot missiles not only from the US but also from European countries and other partners, Babel wrote.
Zelenskyy also addressed restrictions affecting Starlink. He emphasized that Ukraine was not looking to replace the service, but was working with several countries, including France, to create additional communications options.
“We are not talking about replacing Starlink. We are working with some countries, including France, to have additional capabilities,” Zelenskyy stated.
He also noted that Ukraine does not use Starlink for long-range strikes inside Russia, although Kyiv had previously asked both SpaceX and the White House to enable that capability.
According to Babel, Starlink was used in operations to intercept jet-powered Shaheds. Zelenskyy stated that after speed restrictions were introduced, Ukraine temporarily lost the ability to use the system effectively for those interceptions, and the limits have still not been fully lifted for the Defense Forces.
The Ukrainian president also addressed frozen Russian assets, emphasizing that Kyiv wants access to the funds before Moscow can regain control over them.
“We know clearly that they very much want them back. This is one of Russia’s goals. Ukraine wants to receive this money before Russia is able to do so,” Zelenskyy stated.
On intelligence sharing, Zelenskyy noted that Ukraine receives data from dozens of countries, while the US continues providing information on ballistic missile launches.
“There are many challenges with ballistic missiles. We are working on every possible option so that Ukraine can be as independent as possible,” he added.
At the same EU summit, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that Brussels was preparing a 22nd sanctions package against Russia and would not lift existing restrictions until Moscow ends the war. She also accused Russia of violating the energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump “not a single minute” after it was announced.

Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:31:40 UTC
00:31:40 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Develops Full-Body Protective Armor That NATO Armies Do Not Currently Field
Ukraine is introducing a new layer of body protection for frontline troops, centrally procuring 4,700 fragmentation-resistant suits for the first time, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense on October 15.
The roughly two-kilogram protective system consists of a specialized jacket, trousers, and pteruges designed to shield the pelvis and upper thighs.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The pteruges include an adjustable belt and seven sections containing soft ballistic inserts: two frontal, four lateral, and one rear.
Unlike rigid armor plates, the soft ballistic packages are designed to conform to the soldier’s body while providing protection against fragments and bullets. The sections can be repositioned for fit, while the rear section includes additional padding for troops operating while seated. The suit can also be worn with a standard body armor vest, extending protection to areas that are normally left exposed.
“Our task at the Ministry of Defense is to listen to the needs of the troops and supply exactly what our warriors really need,” Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik stated. The design underwent military testing among personnel whose combat duties require high mobility before the final model was approved.
The armor is intended primarily for assault troops, medics, and other personnel operating near the line of contact, where artillery shells and drones create persistent fragmentation threats. The Ministry noted that comparable protective suits are not currently fielded by NATO countries and that a prototype of the Ukrainian design was provided to Western partners for evaluation.
Ukraine's pace of battlefield adaptation has drawn growing attention from its Western partners. Earlier in October, former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll called it “humiliating” to watch Ukraine field better weapons despite a far smaller budget.
He argued that the US procurement system was too slow to keep pace. In May 2025, Driscoll created the 600-soldier Unmanned Assault Battalion, an experimental drones-first unit in Italy that worked alongside Ukrainian advisers.

Of course Trump is helping Russia in Ukraine – he’s a master of the art of betrayal | Jonathan Freedland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:30:10 UTC
00:30:10 KST

Donald Trump must find it oddly frustrating. He keeps showing the world exactly who he is, and yet the world keeps refusing to believe it. As clearly as he can, he is announcing that he is not the leader of the free world, that he is not even a reliable member of the democratic west, that he is in fact an ally of its enemies – but the west, including Britain, either doesn’t fully get the message or can’t quite bring itself to draw the obvious conclusion.
Trump had another go this week, finding multiple ways to declare that in the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is no mediator or peace broker but a partner of Vladimir Putin. In fairness to him, the US president had loudly issued that declaration within weeks of his return to the White House when, in February 2025, he delivered an on-camera dressing down of Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, seeking to humiliate the Ukrainian leader by telling him “you don’t have the cards”, even as JD Vance demanded their visitor show gratitude. That should have made Trump’s position sufficiently plain, but in the past few days he has all but put it up in lights.
Earlier this week Ukrainian forces found that an essential piece of kit – a version of Elon Musk’s Starlink system used by Kyiv to guide its drones – was no longer working at speeds greater than 100mph. That meant not only a sudden shrinking of Ukraine’s ability to strike behind the frontlines, but also the hobbling of an air defence system vital in protecting the capital from Russian jet-propelled drones. This was no technical hitch. Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is owned and controlled by the US government – and, as Reuters reported, the order to limit its use in Ukraine came from the White House. Put simply, Trump actively intervened in the war to weaken Ukraine’s ability to defend itself. “The decision will bring a lot of human losses,” Zelenskyy told Piers Morgan. “Of course, people will die.”
Trump’s move was hardly a bolt from the blue. This same week, Ukraine endured at least two nights of Russian bombardment without the usual advance warnings from the US of when or where Moscow was about to strike. Trump denied that he had broken off long-established intelligence sharing with Kyiv, but that’s exactly what it looked like.
All this followed the US president’s decision to break the international sanctions regime on Moscow, by agreeing to buy $4bn worth of Russian diesel oil. That volume will barely make a splash in the US market, where high diesel prices are imperilling the Republicans’ midterm chances in several rural states that rely on the stuff, but it will come as a welcome cash infusion for Putin’s war machine. Just as Russia’s military position was looking precarious, Donald Trump has come riding to the rescue. Throw in the US invitation to Putin to attend December’s G20 meeting at one of Trump’s golf clubs in Florida, and you have a US president who might as well be skywriting his support for Russia and his betrayal of Ukraine.
In Trump’s first term, much energy was spent trying to work out what dark secret lay behind this apparent affinity with Moscow. I tend to the view advanced by my expert colleague Luke Harding, who, when asked if Trump is a tool of the Russian intelligence services, answers with a question of his own: if Trump were a Russian asset, in what way would he behave any differently from the way he behaves now?
Whatever the motive, or whether, as Harding suggests, it’s some combination of greed, ideology, dictator envy and kompromat, the facts are unarguable. The most powerful member of the western alliance is, at best, an unreliable partner and, at worst, in league with the alliance’s chief enemy. Why this matters should not need spelling out, least of all in the week when the head of MI5 described Russia as “aggressor number one”. For years now, the Kremlin has demonstrated its willingness to attack Nato member states, usually in the form of hybrid or “grey zone” operations that are not overt acts of war but come instead with a patina of deniability. One study found that there have been than no fewer than “151 confirmed Russian-directed industrial sabotage incidents in Europe between February 2022 and February 2026”, while last weekend brought credible reports of a Russian intention to assassinate executives of key European defence firms.
What should the US’s erstwhile allies do about this new reality? The first task is to keep supporting Ukraine, all the more energetically given that Washington has, in effect, switched sides. The second is to avoid an error that is looming. The midterm elections, which are little more than a fortnight away, are expected to deliver big gains for the Democrats and a big blow to Trump. If Democrats retake one or both houses of Congress, plenty of European leaders will be tempted to exhale deeply, conclude that the orange storm has passed and that normal transatlantic service is about to resume. That would be a grave mistake.
For one thing, while the US president has been unbound by congressional restraint for most of the past two years, it’s not certain that a constrained Trump will be a tamed Trump. On the contrary, one Washington hand warns that he could become a “cornered animal”, even more extreme in the area where a president is freest to act, namely foreign affairs. Of course, Trump will be gone eventually, but there too lies the danger of false comfort. “This shift is permanent,” one former UK cabinet minister tells me. If nothing else, Trump has proved that Trump and Trumpism can happen: now we know that the western alliance is neither guaranteed nor unshakeable, but vulnerable to a change in the US political weather.
All of this means we are living in a newly dangerous world. Witness the richly reported new book War is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman, which lays bare quite how seriously leading policymakers rate the risk of a third world war. It’s an age in which we can no longer rely on others to defend us. The chilling lesson of the Starlink episode for those who depend on US hardware or software is that the US always retains an off switch. In other words, Britain and the rest of Europe have to be able to defend ourselves, with our own armies and our own arms.
The best time for governments to have made this case was the night of that shocking Oval Office scene with Zelenskyy last year. But the second-best time is now. When John Healey delivers his first budget on 28 October, this is the argument he needs to set out. As a former defence secretary, he is especially well placed to do it. The Labour manifesto of 2024 was written before Trump was re-elected, before anyone knew that in the great clash of our time the US was about to align itself with authoritarianism against democracy. Things have changed and that document can no longer be treated as holy writ. We will have to spend whatever it takes to protect ourselves in a changed and perilous world. Trump is telling us that in a crude, loud voice. We must listen.
- Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Attacks on Ukraine’s power plants show Russia has given up on military victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:28:10 UTC
00:28:10 KST

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.
Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.
The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”
The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants. But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.
This year, however, Russia appears to be putting those plans into practice. On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital. Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.
Ukraine’s energy minister first briefed European allies last month about the plan, a copy of which was first reported on by the New York Times. Russia has stepped up its attacks on the Ukrainian power grid precisely as Washington and Kyiv are embroiled in a major political quarrel. The Guardian is withholding some specifics of the military assessment at the request of Ukraine’s energy ministry, which said it could aid in further strikes against the country.
“There are two large documents, written very coldly and very clearly, with tables showing the number of weapons needed for each facility to destroy it,” Ukrainian energy minister Denys Shmyhal said last month. “The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones. We understand how they are going to act.”
The leaked documents identify bottlenecks and prescribe the number of ballistic and hypersonic cruise missiles and jet-powered drones needed to knock out power plants and substations with brutal efficiency. If that was done, it could destroy more than 90% of the power that Kyiv is budgeted for each winter, the document predicts, plunging the city into the dark and cold. A worst-case scenario could lead to blackouts lasting up to 20 hours a day until damaged equipment is repaired, according to expert projections.
The strikes on Ukraine’s energy system have become the country’s new frontlines – and the country is badly outgunned, as its stocks of US-provided PAC-3 missiles have dwindled. Zelenskyy this week castigated city authorities for poor planning for the winter and for failing to protect the city’s energy infrastructure. Protests over heat and electricity blackouts are also planned for Saturday, highlighting how the difficult conditions in winter could provoke a political crisis for the wartime government.
Economic Pravda, a leading Ukrainian news site that covers business, reported on Thursday that the three major power plants in Kyiv no longer have the ability to generate electricity, leaving the city more reliant on electricity brought from elsewhere in the country (the government generally does not confirm specific damage to critical infrastructure). The outlets’ experts predicted that, given a moderate winter and quick repairs of damaged substations, Kyiv residents could face up to eight hours of blackouts a day. Its worst case scenario of frigid temperatures and frequent attacks would leave Kyiv in the dark for up to 20 hours a day.
This is no accident for the Kremlin, which has increasingly turned to punishing Ukraine’s population in major cities as the frontlines of the conflict have frozen. “Last year, we were really on the brink,” said Volodymyr Fesenko, a Ukrainian political analyst. “But the risk this year will be even worse, so the plan [to attack Ukrainian infrastructure] does seem realistic. There’s a very high chance that Russia tries to break us this winter.” If the Kremlin believed in the chance of a clean military victory before now, he added, it may now believe that not to be possible, and focus on destroying Ukraine’s remaining infrastructure rather than trying to capture it.
The secret plan, which officials here say was intercepted by Ukrainian intelligence and then briefed to senior European diplomats by Shmyhal last month, sets itself several goals: to destroy electricity generation, heating, water and sewage systems in such a way as to to make life in Ukrainian cities unliveable. Destroying electrical generation alone, it says, would lead to a “significant decrease in the quality of life of the population.”
To do so, it specifies the number of weapons that should be allocated – Geran 4/5 jet-powered drones and hypersonic or cruise missiles – in order to destroy key infrastructure such as thermal power plants, substations, water pumping stations and more.
Considering strikes against the basis of Ukraine’s water, sewage and heating systems, the document says it would create a “large-scale municipal infrastructure crisis.”
When contacted by the Guardian, the Ukrainian Energy Ministry said that the document contained information that could aid in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. It did not reply to questions on how the current Russian bombing strategy matched with the proposals made in the document, or which Russian agency had developed the plans.

Uzbekistan's 2 ancient canals added to World Heritage Irrigation Structures List
Uzbekistan’s Dargom and Shohrud canals were recognized as World Heritage Irrigation Structures in 2026 and added to the International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage (ICID) register, UzA reports.
The award ceremony took place on October 14 during an international congress in Marseille, France. Officials received certificates and commemorative plaques recognizing the canals.
The Dargom Canal, which supplies water to the Samarkand oasis, is believed to have been built between the 5th and 4th centuries BC. Nearly 102 kilometers long, the canal still irrigates almost 178,000 hectares of land today.
The Shohrud Canal is believed to have been dug in the 3rd-4th centuries AD. For centuries, it has played a key role in the development of Bukhara and the surrounding oasis.
Uzbekistan’s Dustlik and Eski Tuyatortar canals were also added to the World Heritage Irrigation Structures list in 2025.
