Zelenskyy urges EU not to ease sanctions against Russia during leaders' meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:26:19 UTC
00:26:19 KST

Burç Eruygur
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday urged the EU not to ease sanctions against Russia, stressing the need for a “strong” 22nd sanctions package from the 27-member union.
Speaking on the second day of an EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy accused his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin of seeking to “drag out” the Ukraine war into next year, saying Europe must be ready for this.
“I urge you not to ease sanctions against Russia or anyone linked to it. Putin uses every trick he can find to get money for making more weapons,” Zelenskyy said, noting Ukraine has warned that sanctions relief will result in others taking advantage.
The Ukrainian leader argued that the diesel deal between the US and Russia will never be enough to offset the impact of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz on global markets, but will rather “put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war.”
He stressed the need for a strong 22nd EU sanctions package, particularly calling for sanctions against all involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles, advanced communications systems and drones.
Zelenskyy said the financial cost of the ongoing conflict for Ukraine will be €155 billion next year and it needs at least €70 billion more for spending, including in terms of defense purchases.
He stressed the need to deal with Russian frozen assets, as well as called on European leaders to use every opportunity to strengthen air defense, emphasizing the need for a winter package consisting of 300 Patriot interceptors against Russian ballistic missiles.
“We are grateful that the EU is moving toward us. Four EU accession clusters have already been opened this year. And we need to open the remaining two by the end of the year. We are ready,” Zelenskyy said, calling on the union to keep Ukraine and Moldova's membership processes tied together.
Defining unity in Europe as a target for Russia, Zelenskyy said that in spite of disagreements and their differences, all of them seek a security system in Europe that “really works and can deal with today’s threats.”
“So, as we work now to finally stop Putin, to stop his war, we are doing this not just for Ukraine alone. We are working for security guarantees for all of Europe. For guarantees that this war will not be passed down to our children,” he said.
He expressed gratitude to those supporting Ukraine and those trying to keep Europe and the US together. “Putin will listen to America if America really turns up the heat on him and makes one thing clear -- either he chooses peace, or he gets no more money for his war,” he said.
Zelenskyy arrived in Brussels on Thursday to attend the European Council summit and hold a number of talks on the sidelines of the event.
Zelenskyy met with the presidents of the European Council and European Commission, as well as held talks with the Hungarian, Finnish and Swedish prime ministers on Friday.
On Thursday, he met his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Belgian King Philippe, and the prime ministers of Belgium, Denmark, and Poland.

Elon Musk Is Almost Single-Handedly Funding the Republican Midterms Push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:25:18 UTC
00:25:18 KST

Elon Musk has quietly financed a major canvassing operation to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections that rivals his effort in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal filings posted Thursday night. To monitor the trillionaire’s overall influence on November’s elections, WIRED created a live-updating tracker that pulls federal filings daily.
The Musk-aligned America PAC has spent $76.7 million in the third quarter of 2026, $35.8 million of which has been spent on a field operation to drive turnout among President Donald Trump's core base across all seven Senate battleground states and a number of House races, the filings show.
That compares with the roughly $45 million America PAC had spent on putting together a field operation at the same point in the 2024 cycle, when the super PAC effectively ran the vast majority of canvassing for Trump's presidential campaign.
In short, Musk has assembled a presidential-level field operation this midterm cycle, underscoring the extent to which he has taken over the get-out-the-vote effort for the party and created something of a shadow Republican National Committee. With three weeks until Election Day, the total contributions are only set to rise even higher.
Canvassing has been America PAC’s largest expense, ahead of the $23.7 million it spent on a combination of digital ads mostly attacking Democrats, campaign literature, and phone bank efforts.
But in an effort to save Republicans' Senate majority, Musk also gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting the GOP's candidates in that chamber. The same amount appears to have been funneled into Texas PAC, which was registered with the FEC in August 2026 and is backing embattled Republican candidate and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.
Musk has been particularly focused on the Senate race in Texas this midterm cycle, where he has extensive personal and business interests. Musk lives near Austin and his businesses SpaceX and Tesla are based in the state. Musk accounted for nearly 60 percent of the $273 million that the Senate Leadership Fund raised for Texas PAC.
The stunning war chest that Musk has unleashed into all seven battleground Senate races and, to a lesser degree, a number of competitive House races, makes him the largest known donor in the midterms among both Republicans and Democrats.
Since its inception, America PAC has relied primarily on outside firms to conduct paid canvassing, in which people are hired to knock on the doors of likely Trump or Republican voters to remind them to register to vote and vote early.
The super PAC has used mostly the same contractors as in the 2024 cycle, the filings show. The biggest canvassing contract went to Blitz Canvassing, a subsidiary of the political affairs firm GP3 Partners, which helped stand up America PAC.
The other vendors listed in America PAC’s filings were the firms Patriot Grassroots LLC, The Synapse Group, In Field Strategies, Echo Canyon Group, Threshold Strategies, and GEG Strategies LLC. All but the last two also worked for America PAC in 2024.
Going into the final stretch of campaigning, America PAC has more than $12 million remaining, though Musk, the richest man in the world, may contribute more to his PAC as required.
America PAC has spent in 40 races in 17 states since July. The Texas Senate race drew the largest share, in which Musk’s team has spent $15.3 million attacking Democrat James Talarico and $3.5 million supporting Paxton.
The super PAC has also spent about $5.3 million attacking Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race against Republican Jon Husted and $3.5 million attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, according to the WIRED tracker.

German chancellor says EU leaders remain divided on next budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:24:52 UTC
00:24:52 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Friday that European Union leaders remain deeply divided over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, with a smaller group that includes Germany pushing for significant cuts to the European Commission’s proposals.
Speaking on the second day of an EU leaders’ meeting in Brussels, Merz said the 27 member states hold very different positions on the spending plan that would run from 2028 onward. He expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached by the end of the year but cautioned that success was far from certain.
“There are very different positions among the individual member states,” Merz said. “A smaller group -- which includes Germany -- believes that we must significantly reduce the European budget compared to the proposals put forward by the European Commission.”
A larger group of countries, by contrast, wants the budget expanded, he added.
From Germany’s perspective, the Commission’s figures must be brought down further, Merz stressed. All member states face fiscal tightening efforts at home, he noted, and a sharp rise in EU spending is not realistic.
“It is simply not tenable for the European budget to increase by around 50%, that is not financially feasible. And given the national contributions involved, it is something no one can afford,” he warned.
Leaders will need to discuss the issues in detail, Merz said. An additional European Council meeting is likely in November, followed by multi-day talks in December.
“I remain hopeful that we will succeed in getting the European budget for the years from 2028 onwards on track through a unanimous Council decision,” Merz said. “Whether we will succeed, I cannot say at all today; there are still too many conflicting views,” he added.

Decree-Law on Energy Bills: Italy and European Commission reach understanding to protect households and businesses
16 Ottobre 2026
The Italian Government and the European Commission have reached a common understanding on the measures set out in the ‘DL Bollette’ (‘Decree-Law on Energy Bills’, decree-law no. 21/2026), in full respect of the Middle East State Aid Framework (METSAF) and sectorial legislation.

Earth Observation Lab launches in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:24:41 KST

Earth Observation Lab launches in Switzerland
Researchers at the Swiss federal insitute of technology ETH Zurich will be able to monitor changes on Earth from a newly opened Swiss Geolab.
The facility will analyses data on landslides and crops from its home in canton Lucerne.
The establishment of the centre of excellence is being co-funded by canton Lucerne and a foundation set up by the late watch magnate Jörg G. Bucherer. By the end of 2027, the core team is expected to comprise around ten people.
ETH aims to use the facility to help tackle environmental challenges. While science cannot reverse events such as landslides, it can help ensure that disasters are detected at an early stage and their consequences better managed, according to said ETH president Joël Mesot.
The new ETH institution utilises data collected by satellites, drones or sensors in the ground and in water.

Russian arbitration courts have been forced to postpone hearings and freeze legal filings following widespread system failures caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on Yandex data centers, exiled outlet Vyorstka reported Friday.
The technical disruptions reportedly began on Oct. 8 after a Ukrainian drone attack damaged the first of three Yandex data centers in Russia.
According to Vyorstka, the outages disabled online video hearings, froze official audio recordings and prevented judges from opening or downloading case files submitted by the parties.
Judges were reportedly forced to put cases on hold, declare trial breaks or leave bankruptcy filings frozen.
Court rulings directly cited server failures at Yandex Cloud as the reason for legal proceedings.
“Difficulties operating the ‘Electronic Justice’ software package are observed on Oct. 14 due to a massive failure in the Yandex Cloud main data center,” states one judicial order by a regional court shared by the outlet.
Similar outages were recorded across at least nine Russian regions, Vyorstka reported.
PravoTech, the software provider behind Russia’s arbitration court databases, acknowledged the service degradation in an Oct. 8 post.
On Monday, it said basic search features had been restored, but warned that services were still slow due to the cloud provider’s ongoing issues.
The court system failure reflects a wider wave of digital disruptions across Russia following Ukrainian drone attacks on three of Yandex’s six data centers. Search navigation, online banking, food delivery and major retail chains using Yandex Cloud services were still affected.
Key Yandex services did not appear to be fully restored as of Friday evening, as the Kremlin sought to play down the attacks’ effects.

Yemeni army says it captured Houthi drone operations team in Taiz

Lina Altawell
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The Yemeni army said Friday that it captured a team affiliated with the Houthi group that specialized in operating and controlling drones in the southwestern province of Taiz.
The 35th Armored Brigade, part of the Yemeni army, said in a statement on US social media platform Facebook that its forces captured a Houthi team “working to control the group’s drones” on the Al-Aqrud-Kahlan front southeast of Taiz.
The brigade said the operation was part of field efforts by government forces to counter Houthi activities and strengthen combat readiness on the front lines.
The statement did not disclose how many people were captured or provide details about the circumstances of the operation.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the army’s announcement.
The development comes amid escalating clashes between government forces and the Houthis in Taiz during October.
The province has seen intensified fighting, alongside worsening humanitarian conditions and the displacement of thousands of residents due to clashes and restrictions on supply routes.
On Oct. 11, the Yemeni army said it had retaken control of two hills in the Al-Aqrud area south of Taiz during operations against the Houthis.
The army also said on Oct. 6 that 100 Houthi fighters had been killed and five drones shot down during military operations on several fronts in the province, including Al-Aqrud.
Since Oct. 5, government forces have been carrying out the military operation “Dawn of Yemen,” which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to restore state institutions from the Houthis and retake the capital Sanaa.
The developments are part of a military escalation that began in July, the broadest since a period of relative calm linked to a truce that began in April 2022.
Yemen has been at war since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, before a Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015 in support of the Yemeni government.

Russell Brand transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag a woman into a men’s toilets for a sexual encounter before she “wrenched” herself free, a court has heard.
The 51-year-old comedian is accused of indecently assaulting the woman, who told Southwark crown court: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.”
The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, said she did not report the incident then because she was “scared” as Brand was famous “and a big asset” to the TV channel.
Brand is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a dark pinstripe suit, the TV personality sat bolt upright in the dock on Friday as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen.
She said she was working at MTV in 2001 when she met Brand and they had “banter” about an I Am Spartacus T-shirt he was wearing. She later offered to show him the way to the toilets, where he allegedly assaulted her.
The woman said she felt “bewildered and confused”, telling the court: “This person went from someone jovial and friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet.”
Detailing the alleged assault, she added: “His demeanour changed. He grabbed my forearm and he was leaning into the door. It was quite forceful, the grip. It took me unawares, I wasn’t expecting that.”
In response to questions from the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, the woman said Brand began pleading with her to come into the toilets as she tried to get away.
“I said to him: ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go.’ Then he started to plead, almost ‘go on, go on, come in’,” she told the court.
She said he had a “wild” look in his eyes and she had to use her strength to escape his “hard” grip in an interaction that lasted about 20 seconds.
The woman said she told two colleagues what had happened but she did not make a police complaint until she saw a 2023 documentary that accused Brand of sexual misconduct.
“It brought everything back,” she said. “I thought I’d managed to get away. It could’ve been very different … I thought it was the right thing to come forward.”
In cross-examination, the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested the woman had reassessed her memory of the incident after the documentary, but she said it had not changed her mind.
“I don’t think it’s quite as straightforward as that,” she said. “It would have been my word against his, I had a job to consider, I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me. I managed to get myself out of the situation.”
She rejected the barrister’s suggestion that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter. She said: “You don’t drag someone by the arm, not in my world anyway. You don’t grip someone to drag them in, that’s not consensual.”
She said he had been “grabbing and pulling” her, telling the court: “That’s not inviting someone in. That’s forcing someone to do something against their will.”
Winter suggested it was “a short-lived, very, very minor incident” and that after the woman declined, Brand “left it there”. The woman responded: “The intent was there. It could have been very different.”
Earlier, the court heard evidence from witnesses relating to the first complainant, who gave evidence on Thursday. She alleges Brand raped her after a fringe cabaret show at the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth.
Andrew Dobson, a former flatmate of Brand’s who composed the music for the show, described his impressions of the comedian, saying he was “a very vibrant character, very egotistical … lively, sort of quite demanding and persuading”.
Dobson told the court: “I think sex was a huge preoccupation for him. I do recall clearly nights where the pursuit of ultimately getting somebody into bed would have been a preoccupation.”
He said there was a “hurried and rushed” tone at their shared guesthouse in Bournemouth on the morning after their final show. “I recall Russell coming in and there suddenly being an urgency to leave,” he said.
John Rogers, who wrote the show, described Brand’s reaction to an “encounter” the actor had had with a woman during the week of the conference, saying it was “a bit odd” and he appeared “flustered”.
The court also heard statements from two women whom the first complainant had told about the alleged rape after the 2023 documentary.
The trial continues.

They cited UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980, which reject attempts to change Jerusalem’s character or status and call on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions from the city.

The ministers called on the Colombian government to reconsider and reverse its decision, uphold its obligations under international law, and refrain from measures that prejudice the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
They also reiterated their support for the Palestinian people’s right to an independent and sovereign state, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

The investigation, by journalist Giulia Sorrentino, draws on intelligence reports, judicial records, and historical documents describing networks extending from Lebanon and Syria to Sicily and Rome. The material also includes an intelligence warning about a possible terrorist attack against the US Embassy in Rome.
Drug trafficking and Palestinian terrorism
One of the central documents, dated November 9, 1983, contains information gathered by Italy’s Carabinieri, the country's military police force, concerning international drug trafficking and Palestinian terrorist operations.
According to the intelligence report, members of Sicilian Mafia networks associated with the Greco and Gambino families were operating in Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, then under strong Syrian influence. The area reportedly contained narcotics-processing facilities near Baalbek.
The source alleged that six AK-47 assault rifles had reached Mafia associates and been used in attacks in Sicily. It also described a shipment of approximately 900 kilograms of morphine base reportedly sent from Lebanon toward the Sicilian city of Catania in October 1983.
The same intelligence material warned that Palestinian terrorist organizations might attack Western targets if the multinational military force stationed in Lebanon intervened against Palestinian positions. The source specifically reported knowledge of a planned attack against the American Embassy in Rome.
Sorrentino's investigation also revisits the July 29, 1983, assassination of Rocco Chinnici, an Italian magistrate who played a leading role in the campaign against organized crime.
Chinnici and three other people were killed when a car bomb containing approximately 75 kilograms of explosives detonated in Palermo. The attack's use of a remotely detonated explosive device resembled techniques employed by terrorist organizations during Lebanon's civil war.
Judicial records describe how Bou Chebel Ghassan, a Lebanese police informant, had provided information about contacts with Mafia figures and efforts to obtain weapons and morphine. Days before Chinnici's assassination, Ghassan reportedly described methods of killing investigators remotely, comparing them to those used by Palestinian terrorists in Lebanon.
No record that Palestinian operatives participated in assassinating Chinnici
Although the testimony raised questions about possible foreign connections, Italian judicial proceedings established Cosa Nostra's responsibility for Chinnici's murder. The records do not demonstrate that Palestinian operatives planned or participated in the assassination.
The investigation also revisits allegations published by Corriere della Sera on June 22, 1993. In a report from Beirut, correspondent Antonio Ferrari quoted Zeid Wehbe, a Palestine Liberation Organization representative, alleging that operatives associated with Abu Nidal had infiltrated Mafia networks.
According to those allegations, Abu Nidal's organization supplied expertise in explosives and sophisticated killing devices in exchange for assistance with criminal operations.
Abu Nidal, whose real name was Sabri al-Banna, led a Palestinian terrorist faction that broke with Yasser Arafat's PLO. His organization was responsible for attacks against Israeli, Jewish, Western, and Palestinian targets.
An Italian military intelligence report dated January 13, 1986, also described connections between Abu Nidal and circles associated with the family of Syrian President Hafez Assad. The document, identified through research by Italian historian Giordana Terracina, referred to the international terrorist known as Carlos the Jackal.
The assessment followed the December 27, 1985, coordinated attacks against airports in Rome and Vienna by Abu Nidal's Palestinian terrorist organization. The assaults killed 16 civilians and injured approximately 120 others.
Sorrentino also cites an October 1990 memorandum attributed to Italian General Demetrio Cogliandro. The document raised allegations concerning Arab banks operating in Italy, financial transactions involving Middle Eastern governments, and funds allegedly reaching Italian organized crime groups for narcotics purchases.
The intelligence records became accessible through a broader Italian government initiative launched in 2014 to declassify historical documentation relating to terrorism and political violence.
The newly published investigation does not establish that Abu Nidal's organization maintained a formal operational alliance with Cosa Nostra or participated in Mafia assassinations. The allegations in the intelligence reports have not all been independently corroborated.
However, the documents demonstrate that Italian intelligence agencies were examining possible connections between Palestinian terrorism, organized crime, and Middle Eastern trafficking networks years before allegations of an Abu Nidal–Mafia partnership became public in 1993.

The Bedouin shepherd who claimed he was a kidnapped Jewish child
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Had this been a TV drama, someone would probably have asked the writers to tone it down. In 1956, a little boy disappeared from Tirosh, a farming community between Beit Shemesh and Kiryat Malachi. His mother had left him playing in the yard with a neighbor while she went to the clinic. When she returned, he was gone.
The boy was Yitzhak Gabay, 2. His brother David was 7 and his sister Aliza was 4. “We were going for tetanus shots,” David, now 78, recalled this week. “Mom told the neighbor, ‘I’m taking David and Aliza to get vaccinated. Keep an eye on Yitzhak.’ We were gone seven minutes. When we came back, Yitzhak wasn’t there. We asked the neighbor where he was. She said, ‘I gave him a tomato, and he headed back toward the house.’”
Relatives, neighbors and police searched for the child, but found no trace of him. “There were dozens of police officers and even a tracking dog, which died after a snake bit it,” David said. His parents spent years looking. “There wasn’t a rabbi, a sorcerer or a medium we didn’t go to.”
Of all those visits, David remembers one in particular, to the rabbi known as the Baba Sali. “We went to him right after the kidnapping,” he said. “He told us exactly when we would find Yitzhak. How many years, how many months, how many days. Even how many hours.” David remains convinced that the prediction came true.
Their mother, Zohara, had been pregnant 16 times; only David, Aliza and Yitzhak had survived. Nine years after her youngest son vanished, she died at 32. The family says she died of a broken heart. Her husband, Yisrael, stayed in Tirosh while David and Aliza married and moved to Tel Aviv. As the years passed, the family kept hoping someone would come forward with information, or recognize the boy and bring him home.
About two decades after the disappearance, an argument broke out in a Bedouin family. A young shepherd named Abdullah was quarreling with a relative when the relative snapped: “Who asked you? You’re not even Bedouin. Your mother is Jewish.” Abdullah could not forget it. He began to wonder whether the people who had raised him were his parents, and whether they had kept something from him.
He later said he began dreaming of an elderly Jewish man who told him he was Jewish. Eventually, Abdullah left his family and went to the home of Rabbi Yitzhak David Grossman in Migdal HaEmek, in northern Israel. He told Grossman he believed he was Jewish and had grown up with a family that was not his own. He wanted the rabbi’s help finding out who he was.
Word spread, and the story appeared in Yedioth Ahronoth. Families with missing children began arriving at Grossman’s door. Among those who heard about the shepherd was Yisrael Gabay. Twenty-one years had passed since his son’s disappearance.
David was then serving as an army personnel officer in Sharm el-Sheikh. “One day I got a call from the police: ‘Where are you? Get on the first flight. We need you back in Israel,’” he recalled. “As soon as I landed, Dad said, ‘We need to go to Migdal HaEmek.’” His father told him about the newspaper report and the shepherd who claimed his mother was Jewish.
“Thousands came to the rabbi, all saying he was their son,” David said. “The line stretched from Tel Aviv to Petah Tikva. Everyone had identifying marks. We arrived on Thursday, almost at the end, and we had the clearest signs. My brother had had treatments on his back as a child, and they’d left scars.” Abdullah had scars on his back, too.
Grossman had invited Yisrael to come with two friends from Tirosh. The family stayed through the Sabbath, and on Saturday night the rabbi arranged an informal identification lineup. David remembers a larger group taking part. “They brought in six or 10 men who looked more or less like Dad, but this young man went straight to him. He didn’t even look at the others. And I said, ‘That’s my brother.’ He was huge, like Dad.”
For Yisrael and Abdullah, that settled it. Abdullah began calling himself Yitzhak and moved into Yisrael’s home in Tirosh. He was also known as Abdullah-Yitzhak or Ovadia Ben Yisrael. “I remember we had a party, and Bedouin families came carrying weapons,” David said. “Then he stayed with us in Tirosh, where my father lived.”
Newspaper reports from 1977, however, said a police investigation had found no family connection. They cited a new blood test that had ruled out a biological relationship between Abdullah and the Gabays. Nearly half a century later, relatives interviewed this week dispute those reports. The story is still vividly remembered by the family and by Grossman’s assistant, who first brought it to public attention.
Abdullah tried to adjust to Jewish life with the Gabays, and they tried to help him settle in. But living together was difficult. “Abdullah was bored at Yisrael’s,” said Bracha, David’s wife. “He spoke only Arabic, and the father spoke only Hebrew. There was nothing for them to do at home in Tirosh. Back in his village, there were horses and sheep.”
David said Abdullah’s Bedouin family never explained how he had come to live with them, and the Gabays never asked. “My father died knowing he had found his son, and that this was the right child,” he said. Abdullah began spending time with the people he now regarded as his brother and sister. After a serious argument with David, he moved in with Aliza, who was raising five children.
Aliza has since died, but her son, Shimon Ben Khalifa, remembers Abdullah-Yitzhak well. To him, he was simply his uncle. “I was a baby when they found him, so I grew up with the whole story,” he said. “My mother was sure he was her brother. Nobody ever thought otherwise.”
Asked about the blood-test reports, Ben Khalifa said: “I never heard of a test like that. On the contrary, I think they did another test that showed he was my mother’s brother. There was also an older aunt, his mother’s sister, who always said that was the child. That was Yitzhak.”
Life in Tel Aviv did not suit Abdullah. By then, he had married a woman from the village where he had grown up. Relatives say she was a teacher and had even considered converting to Judaism for him. The couple tried living in Tirosh, but they were far from the families who had raised them. They eventually returned to Zarzir, where Abdullah did well raising calves and tending olive groves.
He stayed in touch with Aliza’s family. “We visited his home several times,” Ben Khalifa said. “His son was at my house two months ago. My younger brother got married two years ago, and he was at the wedding.”
“To this day, I’m sure he’s my brother,” David said. “He named his eldest daughter after our mother. Once he told me he lived between two worlds, Jewish and Bedouin.” Yisrael died 12 years ago, still carrying a childhood photograph of Yitzhak in his wallet. “Until the day he died,” David said, “he believed he had found his child.”

What to Know About the Blood Clot Sidelining Jalen Hurts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:16:25 UTC
00:16:25 KST

For an NFL quarterback, a sore calf might seem like an unsurprising consequence of getting hit by a cleat. In Jalen Hurts’ case, an ultrasound revealed something else: a superficial blood clot.
The Philadelphia Eagles quarterback was struck in the calf during an Oct. 4 game and sought treatment four days later, according to a statement from the team. An ultrasound in London revealed the clot, but doctors cleared him to play in the team’s game there the next day.
Then, a follow-up ultrasound Wednesday night revealed “movement in the small blood clot.” The Eagles announced Thursday that Hurts would miss Sunday’s game against the Carolina Panthers while the team determines his treatment.
What makes a clot superficial—and when does it become dangerous? We asked doctors to explain.
What’s the difference between a superficial clot and deep vein thrombosis?
To understand blood clots, picture a road map. Your deep veins run within the muscles of your arms and legs, carrying most of the blood returning from your limbs to your heart. Superficial veins sit closer to the surface, just underneath the skin and in the tissue beneath it. Connecting veins bridge the two systems.
“You have a really well interconnected network of veins,” says Dr. William Shutze, a vascular surgeon at Texas Vascular Associates in Dallas and vice president of the Society for Vascular Surgery (who was not involved in Hurts’ care). Think of it as “a very well developed road and highway system,” with multiple routes to get where you need to go.
When a clot blocks one route, blood can take a detour through other veins.
A superficial clot forms in one of the veins near the skin. The area can become red, warm, and tender. “It’s usually very uncomfortable,” Shutze says. Some develop in varicose veins; others form where a needle or IV has irritated a vein.
You can sometimes feel the affected vein beneath your fingers. “It’s like a pencil underneath the skin, or a knot,” says Dr. Stephan Moll, a hematologist and professor of medicine at the University of North Carolina who runs an Athletes and Blood Clots Clinic (who was not involved in Hurts’ care).
Deep vein thrombosis involves a clot farther inside the body. Its symptoms can be more widespread—the whole calf or ankle might become swollen and painful, Moll says. You can’t feel the deep vein itself.
Many superficial clots stay put and get better without blood thinners. But sometimes, a clot grows into one of the deeper veins. A piece can then break off and travel to the lungs, causing a potentially life-threatening complication called a pulmonary embolism.
Doctors use ultrasound to assess the clot and check for deep-vein involvement, Shutze says. They’re particularly concerned about superficial clots longer than 5 centimeters or within 3 centimeters of where a superficial vein joins a deep one.
The Eagles haven’t specified those details. And “movement” isn’t precise enough to establish what happened. “That’s not a term we use in clinical practice,” Moll says. It could describe a clot growing or extending; it doesn’t, by itself, establish that a piece broke loose or reached the lungs.
How do these clots happen—and how are they treated?
Being in excellent shape doesn’t make someone immune to a blood clot. An injury can damage a vein, while prolonged inactivity slows blood flow. Surgery, certain inherited clotting disorders, cancer, and pregnancy can also increase risk, says Dr. Alina Mitina, an emergency medicine physician at Hackensack University Medical Center in New Jersey (who was not involved in Hurts’ care).
Veins near the skin have less cushioning when someone takes a hit. “The deeper veins are protected,” Shutze says, although a severe impact can injure those, too.
A clot can form within hours of an injury or develop over several days, he adds. If your leg already hurts from getting hit, you might not realize there’s another reason it’s sore.
Travel can add another risk: Sitting through a long flight or car ride means the legs aren’t moving as much, slowing blood flow.
Some superficial clots can be managed with warm compresses, anti-inflammatory medication, elevation, and monitoring. Others need blood thinners to help keep the clot from growing—even if it hasn’t reached a deep vein.
If blood thinners are needed, treatment is usually temporary, Moll says, often lasting several weeks.
That doesn’t necessarily mean spending recovery on the couch. “We like them to be active because we want to keep the blood flowing,” Shutze says.
Getting up for a walk, of course, is different from getting tackled. Shutze worries about athletes taking another hit where they already have a clot. Blood thinners add another concern: An injury that causes bleeding can become much more dangerous when blood doesn’t clot as readily.
In football, “you have constant significant contact,” Moll says, which raises the risk of serious bleeding, including inside the head or muscles.
What symptoms shouldn’t you ignore?
Athletes are used to being sore. “They often minimize clinical symptoms, completely understandably, because they don’t want to be taken off the roster,” Moll says.
Pay attention when discomfort feels different, persists, or worsens. Pain, swelling, discoloration, and warmth can signal a clot. Mitina says patients sometimes describe tightness in the leg; redness around a superficial clot can resemble an infection.
If you think you might have a superficial clot, “don’t ignore it,” Shutze says. Have a doctor check it out rather than assuming it’s a bruise or muscle strain.
Unexplained shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing up blood, or fainting require emergency care because they can signal a pulmonary embolism. Moll also flags an unexplained cough and fast heart rate as possible warning signs.
And getting checked once doesn’t mean you should brush off symptoms that persist or worsen. “If something feels weird or symptoms aren’t getting better, always return to the ER,” Mitina says. “You know your body best.”

Ousted US general warned before Iran war of missile defense shortages lasting until 2030: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:15:38 UTC
00:15:38 KST

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defense stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported Thursday.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began, according to US officials familiar with his assessment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was underway.
The general’s assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
The officials reportedly attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel, and limited defense industry production capacity.
The war with Iran has further strained supplies, according to the report. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with approximately 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 during the conflict.
READ: US considering using ‘mother of all bombs’ against Iran: Report
The country’s prewar THAAD inventory stood at around 355 interceptors, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that these systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defense — missile defense — that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would demand substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles remains a lengthy process, the report said. The CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take over four years to fulfill, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of 3 1/2 years.
The Pentagon rejected claims of a shortage. Chief spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: “Claims of U.S. munitions shortages are false.”
He added that Washington retains “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing.”

St. Petersburg authorities have banned foreign citizens with work patents from employment in retail, healthcare, beauty salons and fitness centers, local media reported Thursday.
Governor Alexander Beglov’s decree expands on existing restrictions, which last year banned migrant patent holders — a temporary low-skilled work visa — from driving taxis and delivering food.
Employers have been given until Dec. 15 to bring their staffing into compliance.
The decision aims to combat “shadow employment” and reduce economic reliance on low-skilled foreign labor, according to local outlet Fontanka.
According to St. Petersburg authorities, it will also facilitate “a transparent, regulated labor market where jobs are generated for Russian citizens, including young people and students.”
The restrictions do not apply to highly qualified specialists, foreigners with work permits or citizens of Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan or Kyrgyzstan.
Citizens of other visa-free countries eligible to obtain a work patent in Russia include Azerbaijan, Moldova, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
Dozens of other Russian regions, as well as occupied Ukrainian territories, have introduced similar targeted bans on foreign labor.
The measures were accompanied by a broader federal push to restrict foreign labor following the March 2024 Crocus City Hall terrorist attack, after which Russian lawmakers passed dozens of migration restrictions primarily impacting Central Asian workers.

Manufacturing output rebounded 0.3% last month following a revised 0.2% decline in August, the Federal Reserve said on Oct 16. The rise was in line with economists’ expectations. Factory production was previously estimated to have dropped 0.3% in August. Output advanced 1.1% on a year-on-year basis in September. It grew at a 0.7% annualised rate in the third quarter after accelerating at a 5.6% pace in the second quarter.
Manufacturing accounts for about 9.4% of the economy. While an artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out and businesses rebuilding inventories to meet robust domestic demand are supporting factory activity, higher energy prices, a trade war with Canada and rising borrowing costs pose downside risks to production.
Diesel prices have surged to a record high as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, and economists say the economy could soon feel the effects through higher prices for goods, including at the supermarket, which could weigh on demand.
Durable goods manufacturing production edged up 0.1%, lifted by gains in the output of primary metals, machinery, and electrical equipment, appliances and components. Production of motor vehicles and parts fell 3%. Durable goods manufacturing output increased at a 3.8% rate in the third quarter, partly boosted by a 28.4% surge in the production of semiconductors and related electronic components related to the AI spending boom.
Non-durable manufacturing production rose 0.4% over the month amid gains in printing and chemicals output. Non-durable manufacturing output, however, fell 1.6% last quarter.
Mining production rose 0.2% last month and grew at a 5% rate in the July-September quarter. Utilities jumped 3.5% amid demand for air-conditioning. Utilities output increased at a 14.8% pace in the third quarter.
Overall industrial production rose 0.7% last month after gaining 0.1% in August. Industrial output increased 2.2% year-on-year in September. It advanced at a 2.8% pace in the third quarter after growing at a 4.8% rate in the second quarter.
Capacity utilisation for the industrial sector, a measure of how fully firms are using their resources, rose to 76.9% last month from 76.4% in August. But it is 2.5 percentage points below its 1972-2025 average. The operating rate for the manufacturing sector edged up to 75.9% from 75.8% in August. However, it is 2.3 percentage points below its long-run average. REUTERS

Poland Looks to Replace Its Orlik Training Aircraft: Super Tucano and PC-21 Under Consideration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:09:00 UTC
00:09:00 KST

Poland has begun the search for a successor to the PZL-130 Orlik training aircraft, which no longer fully meet pilot training requirements.
This was stated by Major General Ireneusz Nowak, the operational commander of the Polish Armed Forces, in an interview with Defence24.
The existing aircraft have certain limitations that make it difficult to use them for training pilots to fly modern combat aircraft.
Specifically, this concerns the training of pilots for fifth-generation aircraft, as well as F-16 fighters following modernization under the Mid-Life Update (MLU) program.
As part of their search for possible solutions, the Polish military conducted demonstration flights this year and evaluated the A-29 Super Tucano turboprop aircraft from the Brazilian company Embraer and the PC-21 from the Swiss company Pilatus.
Despite being upgraded to the PZL-130 Orlik TC-II Advanced standard, these aircraft, according to the Polish military command, do not fully meet the pilot training requirements for modern combat platforms.
In particular, their capabilities may be sufficient for training pilots to fly the F-16 Block 52+ fighters currently in service with Poland, as well as, possibly, the FA-50 light combat aircraft.
Major General Novak reported that after reviewing the A-29 Super Tucano and the PC-21, the military has already drawn certain conclusions.
At the same time, he did not disclose details of the aircraft evaluation and did not specify which option might be selected.
The next step will involve taking measures to include the new training aircraft in the Plan for Technical Modernization of the Armed Forces of Poland.
This will allow the process to move from analyzing possible options to planning the corresponding re-equipment of the training aviation fleet.
Poland currently operates 28 PZL-130 Orlik aircraft in the TC II Advanced configuration. They are used by the 4th Aviation School Wing, specifically at the 42nd Training Air Base in Radom.
These aircraft play a vital role in the training system for Polish military pilots.
After completing their training at the academy and flying ultralight aircraft, young pilots transition to the Orlik, where they continue to master the next stage of flight training.
After that, the pilots move on to advanced training on the M-346 Bielik jet trainer aircraft.
It is precisely this sequence of stages that allows pilots to be gradually prepared to fly more complex combat aircraft.
At the same time, the Polish command has not yet disclosed the final choice of a new aircraft or the timeline for its potential introduction.

Zelensky calls on EU to keep Moldova's membership bid shackled to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:06:38 UTC
00:06:38 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky called on the EU to keep the membership processes of Ukraine and Moldova tied together on Oct. 15, risking holding back Moldova for years as Kyiv struggles to pass reforms.
Ukraine and Moldova are two of the EU's frontrunner countries for future membership in the bloc, and earlier that week, they took another step forward in their integration process.
The two countries have had their EU bids tied together thus far, an informal political decision made by EU leaders that was expected to end once both countries have opened all six enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms to fully align with the bloc.
"When Ukraine and Moldova are moving so closely together — that's great — when we are doing so much to support Moldova and create the conditions it needs, it would be simply wrong to split us apart on our way into the EU. I hope not. Morally wrong," Zelensky told EU leaders.
Zelensky's argument for keeping Moldova bound together with Ukraine on the membership process rests on Kyiv "protecting Moldova from Russia's attempts to cause trouble through Transnistria," a Russian-occupied territory of Moldova that borders Ukraine.
"This takes serious work from our security services and intelligence. We even have to pull some of our military forces away from other tasks," Zelensky said.
There has been no public reaction from Moldova to the idea of keeping the bids tied together, but the most senior EU officials working on the bloc's enlargement have told the Kyiv Independent that Moldova is surging ahead with integration, far ahead of Ukraine.
"Moldova is adopting EU laws faster than any country since Hungary in 2002, and the body of laws to adopt is far bigger now," one senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent earlier.
In comments to Moldovan media, French President Emmanuel Macron also backed the idea that the pace of accession should match the pace of reforms.
"Our goal is to move forward according to the approach we have established, based on each country's own merits," Macron told the regional outlet TVR Moldova.
"No one can ignore all the progress made by the Republic of Moldova."
EU leaders overnight adopted conclusions on enlargement that appeared to move toward separating the Moldovan and Ukrainian accession bids.
"The European Council recalls that the accession process is merit-based and that each candidate country advances in its accession negotiations on the basis of its individual progress," read the conclusions.
In any case, for now, the next step for both countries is to unlock the remaining two enlargement clusters, which are expected to happen before the end of the year.

Pope Leo recovering from surgery, will deliver Sunday prayer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Pope Leo recovering from surgery, will deliver Sunday prayer
October 16, 2026
The Vatican on Friday announced that Pope Leo XIV is swiftly recovering from lung surgery and will make his first public appearance on Sunday, when he will deliver the traditional noontime Angelus Prayer.
Vatican representatives did not specify whether he would deliver the prayer at St. Peter's Square or from the hospital.
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said Friday that a recitation from the hospital was a possibility but would depend on Leo's post-operation recovery.
Leo, who is 71, shocked the world and its 1.4 billion Catholics last Sunday by announcing that he would be undergoing surgery within days. Two day's later, on October 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after the pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
Doctors are awaiting the results of Leo's biopsy, which will tell them about the make-up of the tumor and give insight into whether his cancer has spread, allowing them to determine whether he may need to undergo further treatment, such as radiation or chemotherapy.
On Friday, the Vatican said Leo was going about normal activities on his own and released photos of the pontiff saying Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He was seen wearing vestments and standing next to his personal secretary, Edgard Rimaycuna, a Peruvian priest.
"His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Dr. Luigi Carbone, Leo's personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital.
The doctors said blood tests and chest x-rays had confirmed Leo's steady improvement.
"At the moment, we have not received any communication from the doctors regarding his discharge, other than what we were told from the beginning about a one-week timeframe," a Vatican spokesman said.
"The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted," said Cardinal Parolin, who added, "We can't make any predictions."
One of the first questions raised by Leo's hospitalization and surgery was whether he would be able to go through with a planned papal trip to South America in just a few weeks' time.
Though this remains an open question, the Vatican on Friday said planning was "going forward" regardless, releasing the names of those journalists accredited to travel with Leo to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17.

Is Israel fighting the wrong war? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:02:18 UTC
00:02:18 KST

What if Israel is winning the military battles but losing the war that ultimately determines its survival?
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has demonstrated extraordinary military capabilities. Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran have suffered significant blows.
Yet the fundamental question remains: Has military superiority brought Israel closer to enduring security? This may be one of the most important questions for Israelis in the upcoming elections.
Or, perhaps the question should be: Are we fighting the wrong war? It is fascinating that this question is not a significant part of the political debates leading up to the decision regarding who will lead the country.
The early Zionist movement understood something that modern Israel may have forgotten.
Nation-building was a generational undertaking. Theodor Herzl, Chaim Weizmann, and David Ben-Gurion invested decades in diplomacy, institution-building, immigration, and international legitimacy.
They understood that establishing a Jewish state required more than winning individual confrontations.
Today, Israel often approaches existential threats through military operations measured in days, weeks, or months.
Our ideological adversaries are operating on an entirely different clock.
Consider the historical memory of the Crusades. European armies conquered Jerusalem, but ultimately lost their foothold in the region.
The lesson for movements committed to a generational struggle is straightforward: survive today, regroup tomorrow, and eventually your enemy will lose his will to fight and leave.
Iran’s revolutionary leadership has demonstrated comparable strategic patience, investing decades in regional proxies, ideological networks, and the pursuit of influence.
Israel cannot assume that its adversaries define victory, defeat, or acceptable sacrifice as we do.
That brings us to the first strategic trap: deterrence.
Traditional deterrence assumes that sufficiently painful consequences will discourage aggression.
But what happens when an adversary embraces martyrdom, accepts devastating casualties, or considers organizational survival itself a victory?
Yahya Sinwar understood that October 7 would provoke an overwhelming Israeli response. Yet the resulting devastation did not necessarily negate the broader political and ideological objectives of his attack.
Israel must then employ increasingly substantial military force to defeat an adversary willing to absorb extraordinary losses.
Now introduce the second trap.
When terrorist organizations embed military operations within civilian environments, Israel faces difficult operational choices. Protecting civilians, as international law requires, by definition extends military campaigns.
Civilian casualties and destruction, whatever the military circumstances, produce images that travel around the world within seconds.
A Hamas command center may be the military objective. A destroyed building becomes the television image.
CNN, Al Jazeera, TikTok, Telegram, and countless smartphones transmit those images into millions of homes.
Military time and political time are no longer synchronized.
The longer Israel fights, the more international pressure can accumulate. The more force required, the greater the potential reputational consequences. And the more international legitimacy erodes, the less strategic freedom Israel retains.
Israel can win the battlefield while losing the conditions necessary to achieve and sustain victory.
But there is another battlefield, one extending thousands of miles beyond Israel’s borders.
The Jewish Diaspora
Jewish communities in New York, London, Paris, and elsewhere are increasingly drawn into conflicts they neither initiated nor controlled.
As the war continues, images of Palestinian suffering circulate globally, accompanied by accusations against Israel that can spill over into hostility toward Jews generally.
And what is their response?
Too often, they follow Israel’s traditional hasbara (public diplomacy) playbook.
More facts. More explanations. More historical context. More attempts to correct the latest accusation.
Necessary? Absolutely.
Sufficient? Clearly not.
Because while we are explaining yesterday’s military operation, our opponents are organizing tomorrow’s political campaign.
An October 10 Fox News investigation by Asra Nomani exposed the organizational machinery behind a coordinated international anti-Israel mobilization starting this past October 8 to the 15.
The investigation identified 179 participating organizations and 322 scheduled events across three days. Organizers had prepared graphics in seven languages, common slogans, media guidance, and political demands.
The campaign extended beyond street demonstrations into universities, workplaces, corporations, and government institutions, calling for sanctions and arms embargoes.
This was not simply spontaneous outrage. It was evidence of a prepared, interoperable international network capable of transforming individual demonstrations into coordinated political pressure, just as it did on October 8, before Israel even responded to the attacks of October 7.
Our enemies have spent years building what we now know is an extremely effective ecosystem.
Not every participant shares the same ideology. But organizations with different political identities can cooperate around common objectives without surrendering their independence.
That is the power of an ecosystem. And it exposes another weakness in our approach.
We are fighting not merely an information war, but a competition for meaning.
Psychiatrist and Holocaust survivor Dr. Viktor Frankl described the existential vacuum: the emptiness people feel when they struggle to find meaning and purpose.
He suggested that our modern society, with all its technological advances, was driving this feeling of emptiness among millions.
Ideological movements can fill that vacuum by offering something more compelling than information: identity, belonging, community, moral purpose, and agency.
Their message effectively becomes: Here is who you are. Here is what is wrong. Here is who is responsible. Here are your people. And here is what you can do.
This is why a “Free Palestine” chant at a huge Ed Sheeran concert so quickly engaged tens of thousands both at the concert and via their social media platforms.
Traditional hasbara too often responds: Here are the facts you should know.
You cannot defeat a meaning system merely by correcting its facts. This is where Israel’s strategic doctrine requires fundamental reconsideration.
Military superiority remains indispensable. But Israel and global Jewry also need a permanent, decentralized, interoperable global ecosystem supporting Jewish safety, Israel’s legitimacy, and long-term societal resilience.
Further strengthened by those who realize that the anti-Israel ecosystem is focusing on Israel first, with the West next in line.
Not another government-controlled public relations campaign.
Not another emergency fundraising appeal following an antisemitic incident.
And certainly not an organization demanding that everyone agree with their view of the world.
Instead, an international network of independent Jewish and non-Jewish institutions, educators, influencers, researchers, philanthropists, cultural leaders, public-private initiatives, and civil society organizations connected by a shared agreement on fundamental principles.
The Jewish people’s historical continuity matters. Jewish safety matters. Israel’s legitimate existence matters. Human dignity and coexistence matter.
Participants can disagree on politics while sharing those foundations.
Such an ecosystem must operate continuously, building relationships, credibility, community, and meaningful participation before the next crisis erupts.
It must strengthen the Diaspora rather than leave Jewish communities perpetually defending military decisions made thousands of miles away.
And it must become an additional dimension of deterrence.
An adversary contemplating aggression should encounter not merely a formidable Israeli military, but a society and international network capable of enduring political pressure, resisting isolation, and sustaining legitimate security interests.
The Zionist movement understood the importance of building the future before the decisive moment arrived.
We must rediscover that strategic patience.
Israel cannot fight a generational ideological conflict exclusively through military campaigns measured in months.
Our military protects our ability to survive in the short term. Our ecosystem must help protect our ability to endure for the long term.
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

Some 80 settlers, some of them carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill above a terraced olive grove where villagers from Abu Falah had gathered to pick ripe fruit, a cherished annual tradition in Palestinian life, Reuters witnesses said.

The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians. UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
The Abu Falah attack followed a similar attack on Friday morning in the area of Turmus Ayya village, where settlers burned three cars after attacking a group of farmers harvesting olives. The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack in Turmus Ayya, said the settlers "snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him."

It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force.
Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications.

"The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said.
"It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said.
The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said.
An ex-CIA official, who asked not to be named because they were discussing information that is not public, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."
Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding."
The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said.
The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race.
"We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

UK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:00:04 UTC
00:00:04 KST

A police force alleged to have promoted and protected male officers despite knowing they were accused of domestic abuse has formally apologised and paid compensation to nine women, the Guardian has learned.
The women allege they were subjected to a range of abuse including rape, assault, threats, harassment and coercive control while in relationships with male officers from Devon and Cornwall police.
Some of the officers served in positions protecting women from male violence, with one appointed after allegations were made, and another kept in the sensitive position after the force received accusations.
The women allege that the force in south-west England “covered up” the serious crimes, which it denies. The force has vowed to improve how it protects women from police-perpetrated domestic abuse.
Some women suffered for about 15 years, with their tormentors allegedly weaponising the force’s “reputation” for protecting male police abusers to break their victim’s will to seek justice.
The nine women, some of whom served in Devon and Cornwall police, say their claims were mocked or disbelieved and investigations were bungled. Three of the women were arrested after accusations from their alleged abusers. One, a teacher, was cautioned, which was eventually erased from her criminal record.
One senior source who served in the leadership of the force told the Guardian: “At best it was bad investigations, at worst it was collusion with the attackers.”
The women say at least four of the officers who abused them are still serving. The force refused to answer that question. Four of the women served in the force but have now left.
One of the male officers is accused of abusing and threatening his partner, who was then a serving police officer. The woman said: “I had my baby … in my arms. My other child was screaming as he rained punches on any area of my body he could get at. He cornered me in a room and repeatedly kicked me as he stood over me. I was terrified and was begging him to stop.”
It is alleged the male officer was promoted twice after the force received the allegations, and was appointed to a leadership position in the force’s effort to tackle violence against women and girls.
Starting in 2004, the woman complained to police for more than 14 years, and she says nothing was done.
Devon and Cornwall police has agreed to pay compensation to all nine women who sued, and the chief constable, James Vaughan, has personally apologised for the failings, the force said.
Police settled the women’s claim without admitting liability after a two-year legal battle.
Another of the accused male officers was known by colleagues as “Teflon” because nothing stuck to him despite repeated allegations, and known also as “rapey”, and was allegedly promoted.
His former partner Sarah* told the Guardian the officer pursued a prolonged, deliberate and sustained campaign of abusive, controlling and coercive behaviour over 15 years. It included physical abuse, financial abuse, intimidation, manipulation of childcare arrangements and repeated harassment, intended to undermine, distress and exert control.
Another woman, June*, a teacher, said of the officer with whom she had children: “Threats he’d made against me had been routinely dismissed, belittled and ignored. [He said] ‘you’ll lose your house, your job and the kids. Don’t make me angry, I’m about to load a gun.’
“I will never under any circumstances cooperate with the police again. I have lost all faith in their willingness … to protect women from police-perpetrated domestic violence. He knows he has the full protection of the police.”
Another, Freya*, said: “Absolutely it was a cover-up. The police harboured him until his retirement. I got called a liar by officers online.”
Other male and female officers tried to help the women but still the force failed to act, according to the combined testimony from the women.
The scandal comes after repeated promises by policing nationally to prosecute male officers who abuse women. Some of the women who received compensation and an apology say the reality was, and still is, different.
Paula Kressinger, who served in the force for 30 years and has waived her anonymity, criticised the force’s refusal to admit liability. She said: “The police are always trying to cover up their mistakes … trying to protect their reputation. However, I believe we would have more respect and trust in them if they were to … take responsibility for their failings. I know they continue to fail victims of crime.”
Sasha* said: “The police did cover up. Devon and Cornwall promoted my ex-partner … while the abuse continued. This gave a ticket to my abuser to continue his abuse post-separation.”
The inaction by the force spurred on abusers, Sasha said. “During the course of the investigation my ex-partner said everyone in the police laughed at me, and the behaviour by the investigating officers made this seem to be a true statement. The continued disrespect and disregard by Devon and Cornwall police collectively became death by a thousand cuts.
“I cannot express enough how much myself and my children have suffered over a period of 15 years, and to then be totally let down by the police …”
The Devon and Cornwall force was placed into special measures a fortnight ago because of overall poor performance. The force declined to answer a series of questions from the Guardian.
Asked what exactly the apology was for, the force replied that the chief constable met with the women in March 2026 and “apologised for the conduct of Devon and Cornwall police in its investigations of their reports of police-perpetrated domestic abuse”.
Asked whether the nine women were regarded by the force as victims of a crime, it said: “In general terms, any allegations of criminal conduct or misconduct are considered through the appropriate investigative and legal processes. These are recorded and assessed and, where appropriate, subject to criminal and/or misconduct investigation.”
The force also said: “No evidence has been identified to suggest that this was, in whole or in part, the result of a cover-up or misogyny.”
It said none of the accused male officers were any longer in positions to do with protecting women from male violence.
The legal case was brought by the Centre for Women’s Justice, a small charity.
Debaleena Dasgupta, a solicitor for the women, praised their determination and courage and said: “Litigation should never have been necessary. Each of these nine women repeatedly tried to have their reports properly investigated but instead faced errors, indifference and incompetence at every turn. Some even faced contempt.
“The similarities in the failures … indicate a broken system. And none of the safeguards one might expect to pick this up did. There have been endless reviews, inquiries and recommendations, and yet litigation remained my clients’ only option.”
The force said: “Our processes have changed. All police-perpetrated domestic abuse will now be investigated by the force’s professional standards department. We are currently in the process of creating a bespoke advocate role for victims of police-perpetrated domestic abuse and similar offences to ensure their voices are heard and that they are provided with a gold-standard service.”
* Names have been changed.

Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.
Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors, mentors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books —Silent Spring, The Jungle, Unsafe at Any Speed—that awaken the public to impending crises.
Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives.
STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift?
SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality.
You write that social media set us up for this.
Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person.
Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person?
Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame.
You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.”
When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI.
Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide.
An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact.
Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them.
If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly.
Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots.
The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection.
Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped?
I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.
