Horned dinosaurs’ weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Horned dinosaurs’ weapons evolved to handle the forces of combat
3-D skulls reveal biomechanics of ceratopsians’ headgear, giving new insight into combat methods
Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.
New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.
Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.
Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.
Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.
The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.
Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.
Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”
Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”
The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

Poll: right-wing People’s Party, and polarisation, growing ahead of 2027 elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Poll: right-wing People’s Party, and polarisation, growing ahead of 2027 elections
A year ahead of Swiss federal elections, pole parties from the right and left are gaining ground while centre-right parties lose out, a new poll finds.
The Sotomo institute’s election barometer, carried out on behalf of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (Swissinfo’s parent company), took the pulse of voters’ opinions and priorities just over a year ahead of parliamentary elections set for October 24, 2027.
The big takeaway: polarisation is growing as centre-right parties lose ground. If elections were held today, the right-wing Swiss People’s Party would be the big winner with 29.9% of the vote – a score that would surpass its own record of 29.4% set in 2015.
And in terms of progression since the last elections in October 2023, the People’s Party has also recorded the biggest jump, strengthening its electoral share by two percentage points.
The left-wing Social Democrats and Greens also currently look to be making slight gains which would boost the left’s combined strength by 1.5 percentage points in total. The increase is mainly down to the Social Democrats, currently backed by 19.3% of voters (up one percentage point since 2023); this would be the party’s best result since 2007, Sotomo notes.
Struggles for centre-right
The Centre Party, which stands at 12.6% of voting intentions, and the Radical-Liberal Party, at 13.3%, continue to shed electoral support. The two parties currently look set to lose 1.5 and one percentage point respectively compared to 2023.
Compared to a similar poll in 2025, the Radical-Liberal Party has in fact managed to gain a place and move slightly ahead of the Centre. However, its 13.3% score would still be its worst result in its entire history of House of Representatives elections, Sotomo notes.
And taken together, the Radical-Liberals and the Centre – the two traditionally dominant conservative parties – currently come to a total of 26%, an electoral share which is four percentage points lower than that of the Swiss People’s Party alone.
Climate change back on the agenda
The survey also indicates that the shake-up of support for political parties only partially reflects the population’s major concerns.
Migration, a traditional policy priority of the Swiss People’s Party, is notably moving down the list of the population’s concerns. The two political challenges currently considered most urgent by voters surveyed are the cost of health insurance premiums (39%) and climate change (36%).
The latter, “which seemed to have gone out of fashion in recent years”, has risen sharply following the heatwave-hit summer of 2026, according to Sotomo director Michael Hermann. The proportion who see it as a major challenge has jumped nine percentage points in a year.
At the same time, climate concerns have not yet translated into electoral support; while the Green Party has progressed only marginally, the centrist Liberal Greens have even dropped.
While not predicting another “green wave” like in 2019, Sotomo nevertheless notes that the current trend for the two ecological parties is “more positive than it seems at first glance” – mainly because both have “at least managed, thanks to environmental ‘branding’, to pull themselves out of the dip they were in”, the research institute writes.
Almost two-thirds (65%) of respondents in the poll think measures taken by politicians to mitigate the consequences of climate change are not sufficient. However, support for additional measures, as well as the perception of the urgency of the situation, varies greatly depending on affiliation – nearly 90% of Green voters consider climate action a priority, compared to just 5% of People’s Party voters. Concern about rising health insurance premiums, on the other hand, cuts across party lines.
Immigration and crime still big issues for the right
Behind the two prominent themes of climate and health insurance, four other issues are all cited by around a quarter of respondents: asylum policy, relations with the European Union (EU), immigration, and housing.
Concern about housing has notably progressed in recent years – from 13% in 2023 to 23% today – as has concern about crime, which has jumped from 10% to 19%. This latter is particularly mentioned by right-wing voters.
On the other hand, immigration has largely declined as a priority, after having been cited as a major challenge by 35% of respondents in 2023. But it is still the top issue for People’s Party voters.
‘Too friendly’ towards the US and Israel?
Given the importance of foreign policy issues during the current legislative term, the poll also asked about citizens’ perceptions of how the Swiss government is faring on the international stage.
Here, the population is most critical of Bern’s attitude to the US, with over 80% believing the Federal Council is too friendly with Washington – a perception which is quite uniform across party affiliations.
Similarly, nearly three-quarters of survey respondents consider the official Swiss attitude towards Israel to be too cordial. This opinion is also seen across most party bases, although less clearly for People’s Party and Radical-Liberal Party supporters.
Russia and the EU are the source of much bigger differences and ideological splits. Overall, just over half of all respondents consider Bern’s attitude towards Moscow to be too friendly: but for People’s Party voters it is less than 30%, for left-leaning voters over 70%. Meanwhile nearly 90% of People’s Party supporters consider the government to be too friendly towards the EU, compared to just 10% of Social Democrat and Green voters.
Survey respondents were also asked about their perception of the degree of influence and popularity of each member of the seven-headed federal government. Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter (Radical-Liberal Party) is still clearly on top for influence (63%), ahead of Environment Minister Albert Rösti (People’s Party), at 53%, and his party colleague, Economics Minister Guy Parmelin, at 42% – up from just 17% a year ago.
Parmelin, who currently holds the rotating Swiss presidency, and who is stepping down from the government at the end of this year, also now tops the popularity rankings (more than 60% of respondents like him) ahead of Defence Minister Martin Pfister (50%) and Keller-Sutter (46%).
The barometer – methodology
Data collection for the SBC election barometer was carried out online from September 10-23, 2026. Poll respondents were recruited partly via SBC web portals and partly via Sotomo’s online panel. Responses from 25,092 voters were used, and statistical weighting was used to make the sample conform to sociodemographic characteristics like place of residence, age, gender, education and political characteristics.
The poll’s margin of error is +/- 1.2 percentage points for an observed percentage of 50% with a 95% confidence interval.

Zelensky's ask: 300 Patriot missiles, 70 billion euros, and Russian assets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:59:31 UTC
23:59:31 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky used his appearance at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels to list the main things Kyiv needs to survive the winter and beyond, but those asks won't come cheap.
"I am grateful for your support for Ukraine," Zelensky told EU leaders.
"Without a determined European Union capable of making strong decisions Putin would have gone much further by now," Zelensky said.
But with Russia ramping up its use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones to pummel Kyiv, and the U.S. taking steps to undermine Russia sanctions and Ukrainian security, Zelensky also came to the bloc with new requests for help.
read also
"We need a winter package... 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The U.S.-made Patriot are considered the only technology currently capable of consistently taking down Russian ballistic missiles, and several European countries still hold stocks of them, such as Spain and Greece.
But for Spain, European diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that there is a real fear that Madrid will not receive any more Patriot missiles in the future because of U.S. President Donald Trump's personal dislike for Spain's center-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
Greece on the other hand has a visceral fear that depleting its own supplies of Patriots might be perceived as a sign of weakness by neighboring Turkey, which Athens fears Ankara would act upon by annexing Greek islands near the Turkish coast.
Likewise, Ukraine's demand to "deal with the frozen assets," unsettles several countries around the table.
Using the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of Russian assets immobilized within the EU to support Ukraine came up in late 2025, but consensus on the idea was out of reach.
"We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war," Zelensky said.
Aside from the fears of holders of those assets, principally Belgium, about Russian retaliation for such a move, several European countries also fear that entering into such appropriations could fracture the global financial system, as countries move their wealth only into jurisdictions deemed friendly to them.
For Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, touching those assets remains very much a no-go.
"My personal view is that if you have immobilized assets, like in every war, even the Second World War, they were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there's always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever told journalists at a press conference during the night of Oct. 15.
"Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier? ... Yes, there are ... Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," De Wever said.
And the risk of Russia's assets being returned, despite some wishful thinking from the U.S. that Europe would hand them over, is nonexistent. The EU bound itself in December 2025, so that any vote to unfreeze the Russian immobilized assets must be unanimous.
"Nobody could ever dream of operationalizing those immobilized assets without unanimity here around the table," De Wever said.
On top of requesting the Russian assets, Zelensky also asked the EU to fill Kyiv's budget hole for 2027.
"The war will cost 155 billion euros ($174.5 billion) next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion) more from you," Zelensky said.
"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he added.
But the request for 70 billion euros comes only six months after the bloc approved a 90 billion euro loan to help Ukraine until the end of 2027. The idea was always that third countries would step in to help bridge the remaining gap, but so far only Norway has done so.
And the government has been notoriously unclear at communicating its financial needs, as noted earlier that day by Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
However, Zelensky's estimate of a 70 billion euro shortfall does match the estimated shortfall figure that a senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's financial situation shared with the Kyiv Independent.
On all three requests, even if they land on sympathetic ears, a decision would still not be expected the same day.
And because there is nonetheless a European consensus to support Ukraine, the demands are very likely to dominate discussions in Brussels over the next weeks.

Qatar announces project to develop Lebanon's electricity sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:59:16 UTC
23:59:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatar to finance, implement and operate electricity project in Lebanon
Qatar on Friday announced plans to invest in Lebanon’s electricity sector and help address the country’s chronic power crisis, including through the development of a solar power plant.
During his visit to Lebanon, where he met with President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said the two sides held "lengthy discussions" on an energy project that Doha had been discussing with Beirut for years.
"Now, thank God, we see this project getting closer to becoming a reality," he said.
Speaking at a joint press conference with Salam at the Grand Serail, Al Thani said the two countries had agreed to establish a comprehensive framework for cooperation in the energy sector and provide integrated solutions through a major investment project that would benefit Lebanon’s economy.
Salam said Lebanon and Qatar were close to reaching an agreement on a joint project to rehabilitate, develop and modernise the country’s electricity generation infrastructure.
He said the comprehensive project would cover various sources of energy production and the infrastructure required to support them, with the aim of providing a more reliable electricity supply at a lower cost.
Salam said the project would follow a build-operate-transfer (BOT) model, under which Qatari entities would finance, build and operate the infrastructure before transferring it to the Lebanese state. He stressed that Lebanon’s treasury would bear no upfront investment costs.
He said he hoped to present the project to the Lebanese cabinet soon, adding that it should be prepared with support from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and adhere to the highest standards of transparency, governance and financial viability.
Salam said the aim was not to add another promise to the many previously made about the electricity sector, but to establish a sustainable solution by increasing generation, lowering costs, diversifying energy sources and improving management.
Al Thani also said QatarEnergy had agreed with TotalEnergies to jointly develop a solar power plant in Lebanon. He described this as an initial project, saying the two countries were now working towards a broader framework for energy cooperation.
He said Qatar hoped to see an agreement take shape soon, allowing Qatari institutions to work alongside their Lebanese counterparts.
Salam said his government did not want to add "another promise to the many that the Lebanese have heard" about the electricity sector, but instead hoped to establish the foundations for a practical and sustainable solution based on increasing generation, lowering costs, diversifying energy sources and improving management.
"Reliable electricity at an affordable cost is essential to reviving the economy, encouraging investment, restarting productive businesses and easing the burden on citizens," he said.
Lebanon’s Energy Minister Joe Saddi recently announced that he would no longer take part in cabinet sessions, citing what he called a lack of seriousness in dealing with the crisis and saying he refused to be held responsible for the lack of progress in the sector.
Saddi and fellow ministers from the Lebanese Forces party walked out of a cabinet session on Thursday over the issue.
Years of blackouts
Lebanon has suffered a decades-long electricity crisis which saw the emergence of an unofficial and largely unregulated network of private generators across the country. These generators typically run on fuel oil, contributing significantly to poor air quality in cities, while charging consumers high prices.
The energy sector virtually collapsed following Lebanon’s 2019 financial collapse, with the national grid barely keeping the lights on for two hours a day. Before this, Beirut, where many of Lebanon’s government institutions are located, had up to 20 hours of electricity a day, with rotating blackouts in the rest of the country.
Much of Lebanon has gradually moved to renewable energy alternatives, relying on solar panels to manage their electricity needs, although this option remains somewhat limited in larger cities like Beirut due to restricted rooftop space in residential buildings.
There has been an outcry among generator subscribers this year, with bills reaching hundreds of US dollars a month in some areas. Operators, many of whom control supply in particular neighbourhoods and are linked to sectarian political parties, have attributed rising costs to higher global fuel prices as a result of the Middle East war.
Lebanon’s electricity sector is estimated to have cost the country more than $40 billion since the end of its 1975-1990 civil war, largely because of heavy subsidies and the cost of importing fuel for ageing power stations. These costs account for a substantial share of the treasury’s losses.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:56:29 UTC
23:56:29 KST

Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) has received a dossier concerning alleged corruption at the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC), following an administrative investigation by the EU’s anti-fraud agency OLAF.
OLAF transmitted its findings to the EPPO after investigating allegations that a senior EESC official manipulated public procurement contracts, news portal Rapporteur reported Friday.
The EESC confirmed that OLAF had referred the case to the EPPO.
“The EESC was informed by OLAF today that this case has been referred to the EPPO. Under these circumstances, the EESC cannot comment further,” an EESC spokesperson told the outlet.
The allegations, which emerged in March, concern Isabel Le Galo Flores, the EESC’s secretary-general, who has been accused of running the EU advisory body as her own private business and steering contracts toward personal associates.
She has declined to comment on the allegations.
The EPPO told Anadolu that it does not generally comment on ongoing investigations or publicly confirm the cases it is handling.
“As a general rule, the EPPO does not comment on ongoing investigations, nor do we publicly confirm which cases we are working on, in order not to endanger the possible ongoing procedures and their outcome,” the prosecutor’s office said.
Earlier this month, members of the European Parliament’s Budgetary Control Committee questioned the EESC over the allegations during an annual scrutiny process.
The committee has also faced criticism over its role and continued existence.
On Wednesday, French politician Marine Le Pen described the EESC and its sister body, the Committee of the Regions, as “completely pointless.”
The EESC is an EU advisory body established under the Treaty of Rome, representing employers, workers and other civil society groups in the bloc’s policymaking process.

Slovakia to Increase Defense Budget and Troop Strength
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:51:27 UTC
23:51:27 KST

The Slovak Parliament has approved the government’s draft state budget for 2027, which calls for an increase in defense spending to €3 billion.
This was reported by Future Army, citing the country’s Defense Ministry.
The planned defense budget amounts to 2.20% of the country’s GDP, which is fully in line with Slovakia’s NATO commitments. Compared to 2026, when spending stood at 2% of GDP, funding for the defense sector has increased by €132 million.
The majority of the budget—61%—will be allocated to operating expenses, including €593 million earmarked for salaries. Under this plan, the defense ministry’s staff is set to increase by 1,815 personnel, 1,300 of whom will be professional military personnel.
Capital expenditures will account for 39% and will be used to fund contracts already signed, including the procurement of air defense systems, CV90 combat vehicles, and the development of military medical infrastructure. Capital expenditures also include the initial payments for the purchase of four additional F-16 fighter jets, in addition to the 14 previously ordered aircraft, for which the main payments are spread out through 2030.
In addition, the procurement of small arms, cargo trucks, CV90 vehicles, and anti-drone systems is planned to be financed through a loan of up to €2.3 billion approved by the EU Council under the SAFE security instrument.
At the same time, the Ministry of Defence of the Slovak Republic is preparing a new application for an additional loan of up to €3 billion under the SAFE 2 program, which it plans to submit in October or November.

Andrew Wasike 
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government announced on Friday the appointment of a new interim administration for the northern Tigray region, giving it six months to restore stability, rebuild public institutions and organize elections following renewed fighting.  
"The people of Tigray must emerge from the agony of conflict to reclaim their distant peace, reaffirm their right to self-administration, and be able to heal the developmental setbacks they have suffered over the many past years," the prime minister's office said in a statement.  
The government said the House of Federation approved the suspension of Tigray's previous interim administration, paving the way for a new federally supervised leadership structure.
The new administration will be headed by Asefa Abrahaga Hagos as chief administrator, with Tewodros Aregeay W/Selassie overseeing economic recovery and reconstruction.
Brig. Gen. Gebretensae Whatna Haylu was appointed to oversee security and peace, while Redai Halefom W/Selassie will handle political affairs and mass mobilization. Shishay Amare was named mayor of Mekelle, Tigray's regional capital.
According to the statement, the administration's responsibilities include restoring essential public services, repairing war-damaged infrastructure, facilitating the return of displaced residents and preparing the region for elections.
The government said the interim authorities must establish conditions for a "free and fair election" within six months, with the aim of returning Tigray to an elected regional government.
The administration will also coordinate with federal security institutions and regional forces to restore security, encourage armed fighters to return to civilian life and support reconstruction.
Addis Ababa said the new leadership would operate under federal guidance and oversight until an elected government takes office.
The decision follows renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal troops and forces linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which has threatened the fragile peace established under the November 2022 Pretoria agreement.
Government troops and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters have recently expanded their control across the region, including Mekelle and several strategic towns near the Eritrean border.
The conflict has also heightened tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of supporting armed opposition groups, allegations Eritrea denies.
On Wednesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged de-escalation in a telephone conversation with Abiy, warning against cross-border incursions and calling for respect for neighboring countries' sovereignty.
Tigray remains deeply affected by the 2020-2022 war, which caused widespread destruction, mass displacement and a humanitarian crisis.

UK risks losing key role in European space industry over satellite contract, says Airbus boss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:47:16 UTC
23:47:16 KST

The boss of Airbus has told Andy Burnham that choosing its US rival Lockheed Martin to manufacture military satellites could cost the UK a key role in the European space industry, intensifying a last-minute lobbying effort for the £2.4bn contract.
It is understood that Guillaume Faury, the chief executive of France-headquartered Airbus, has written to the prime minister suggesting that the choice of provider of the Skynet system could have effects for decades to come on the UK’s strength in military satellites in Europe, in an effort to tip the contract away from its US rival.
Yet politicians in north-east England have lobbied in favour of the Lockheed Martin bid, which would include a new factory in Durham.
The military satellites under the Skynet 6 contract will carry the British armed forces’ most sensitive communications up to 2042, replacing the Skynet 5 system operated by Airbus.
The delayed decision on which company will manufacture the UK’s sovereign satellites comes at a sensitive moment, after Ukraine complained that its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network was restricted, apparently at the behest of the US government.
Several sources said they believed no final decision on the contract had been made. However, some said they believed that Lockheed Martin’s bid was preferred by the Ministry of Defence. The final decision will rest with Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey.
It is thought that Faury’s letter warned of longer-term consequences for the UK’s role in the European space sector if Airbus were to lose out. Senior industry figures have previously claimed that Airbus’s UK satellite operations would not be viable without the next Skynet contract, meaning the company might close its sites at Stevenage and Portsmouth, which employ 3,000 people, including 600 working on Skynet.
The manufacturers Airbus, Thales and Leonardo are working on a long-awaited merger between their space subsidiaries, known as Project Bromo, in an effort to build a single European champion with the scale to rival the leading US companies.
Faury is understood to have warned that if its British operation were no longer viable it could mean the UK missing out on the chance to be the European hub for military satellite communications once the merger was complete.
Lockheed Martin is one of the US’s largest defence “prime” contractors, but it says its UK subsidiary will have full control over the satellites eventually built in the UK. People close to Lockheed Martin have strongly denied that the US government would have control over the satellites.
A Lockheed Martin spokesperson said the company was “unable to comment on the ongoing procurement process”, but added: “Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the north-east of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability. It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities and the potential for exports. It will have a UK design authority and a UK chief engineer.”
Luke Akehurst, the Labour MP for North Durham, said Lockheed’s bid would mean a “state-of-the-art new manufacturing facility” in the region. “This represents a massive investment in the reindustrialisation of the north-east of England, building on our region’s proud heritage of advanced manufacturing.”
The personal intervention from Faury, one of the most powerful executives in Europe, is a sign of the importance of the contract to Airbus, which is headquartered in Toulouse.
A decision had been expected in the summer but it has been delayed in part by the arrival of Burnham in office.
Unite, one of the Labour party’s biggest union backers, had warned against “handing the British space industry over to the Americans” at a time when there are increased questions over whether the UK can rely on the US government.
Burnham will also have to consider the two bids on their financial terms and the capabilities the two companies can offer.
A government document for a related system said satellites had to deal with the “proliferation of counterspace capabilities to disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space-based enablers”. It highlighted radio jamming, hacking and direct physical attacks on the satellites as possible concerns.
The first Skynet satellite was launched in 1969, well before the use of the name for a hostile artificial intelligence in the 1984 film The Terminator.
Kim McGuinness, the mayor for north-east England, said: “Bringing satellite manufacturing to the north-east is a huge opportunity to build on what we have already achieved, including the close ties we have forged between our world-class universities and industry. If secured, this investment would be a gamechanger for the space and security sector, bringing £100m of investment and creating 500 high-skilled jobs as well as a much greater impact through the supply chain.”
An MoD spokesperson said: “This is an ongoing procurement process, and no final decisions have been made. Both of the UK-based bidders are subject to full evaluation of their proposals and must offer satellites that are assembled, integrated and tested in the UK.”
Airbus declined to comment.

Italy investigates Israeli ministers, IDF chief over alleged abuse of Gaza flotilla activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:46:54 UTC
23:46:54 KST

Italian prosecutors announced Friday that an investigation into allegations of torture, kidnapping and mistreatment of Italian activists aboard Gaza-bound flotillas includes Defense Minister Israel Katz, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir. The investigation, which also involves senior Israeli military, police and prison officials, follows complaints filed by 50 Italian citizens detained during Global Sumud Flotilla missions in October 2025 and May 2026. Ben-Gvir's inclusion in the investigation was first reported in June.
According to Italian news agency ANSA, the allegations include torture, kidnapping, boarding vessels in violation of international law, robbery, poor detention conditions, degrading treatment and violations of fundamental rights, including access to legal representation. Rome prosecutors said activists detained during the October 2025 flotilla reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism. Participants in the second mission, intercepted in May, described even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark and the use of stun guns and rubber bullets.
Investigators said they had identified senior officials within the Israeli military and police chains of command involved in the operations. In addition to Katz, Ben-Gvir and Zamir, those named include former Navy commander Vice Adm. David Saar Salama and his successor, Vice Adm. Eyal Harel; senior naval officer Tal Politis; Shayetet 13 naval commando commander Col. Eldad Borochovich; and Ashdod naval base commander Col. Eitan Paz. The investigation also names Israel Police Commissioner Daniel Levy, Israel Prison Service Commissioner Kobi Yaakobi, Ketziot Prison commander Menachem Bibas, Assaf Zagori, commander of the prison service's Nahshon escort and intervention unit, and Border Police commander Yitzhak Brik.
Ben-Gvir's conduct toward detained flotilla activists had previously sparked outrage in Italy, prompting Rome to summon Israel's ambassador in protest. In footage the minister himself released from the port of Ashdod, he was seen confronting and mocking detained activists, including Italian nationals, as they knelt handcuffed and blindfolded with their faces toward the ground. Italian President Sergio Mattarella condemned the incident, saying Ben-Gvir had reached a "new low."
Katz has not publicly commented on the Italian investigation, and Reuters reported that he did not respond to a request for comment. Zamir has also yet to respond. Ben-Gvir previously rejected reports in June that he was under investigation in Rome, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters."
According to Reuters, prosecutors in Rome sent Israel a request for legal assistance in June, a month after the controversy over the treatment of detained activists. The request sought information needed to reconstruct the events and establish the individual responsibility of those involved. Prosecutors did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
Italian prosecutors also held discussions with Eurojust, the European Union agency responsible for judicial cooperation in criminal matters, because similar investigations into the two flotilla incidents are underway in other European countries. The prosecutors did not identify those countries.
Under Italian law, prosecutors in Rome can pursue criminal charges for offenses committed outside Italy against Italian citizens. However, being named in an investigation does not establish guilt or automatically lead to prosecution. If investigators determine that sufficient grounds exist to bring charges, prosecutors can submit a formal request to put the Israeli officials on trial.

He noted that since Europe began moving away from affordable and stable supplies from Russia, its costs have risen. "Many manufacturing operations have relocated to other countries. There are bankruptcies and business closures," the deputy prime minister emphasized. "Yet, politics currently prevails over rational solutions that would benefit consumers. In my view, everything they do regarding energy policy comes at the expense of their own economies and their own consumers."
Novak pointed out that since 2022, Russia has supplied energy resources to Europe worth $320 billion, including $21.3 billion in the first nine months of 2026.
"It was not Russia that walked away from cheap and stable energy supplies. Rather, it was Europe that made that decision for political reasons," Novak concluded. "We remain prepared to continue fulfilling our contracts - including long-term agreements, some of which run until 2035-2040. The refusal to accept supplies under these contracts is a unilateral decision that has no basis in the existing legal and regulatory framework."

China mulls banning, restricting export of some AI, biomedicine, photovoltaic technologies
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:45:44 CST
23:45:44 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese authorities on Friday began soliciting public opinion on a revision to the catalog of technologies that are subject to export bans or restrictions, with plans to add some technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), biomedicine and photovoltaics to the list.
The adjustment, initiated by the Ministry of Commerce and the Ministry of Science and Technology, covers 40 technologies across the three sectors, according to a notice released by the commerce ministry.
Pre-export registration management will be implemented for these technologies in parallel, the commerce ministry said.
The proposed adjustment includes 23 technologies related to large models, intelligent agents, computing power clusters, and information processing in the AI sector, five technologies related to cell and gene therapy, small nucleic acid drugs, and pathogenic microorganisms in the biomedical sector, and 12 technologies related to polysilicon, wafer and cell manufacturing in the photovoltaic sector.
In a separate statement, the commerce ministry said adjustments to the catalog have been routine since 2001, and the latest proposed revision does not target any specific country, region or entity.
The ministry noted that major economies have implemented varied export controls amid the expanding application of AI, biomedicine and photovoltaic-related technologies in sensitive fields in recent years.
China exercises necessary management in accordance with the law to prevent the risk of losing control over technologies and their improper proliferation, while safeguarding normal international technological exchanges and cooperation, it said.
Regarding the AI sector, the ministry said the move aims to ensure AI technologies are safe and controllable, noting the risk of misuse, including the employment of AI-driven malicious code generation and mutation technologies to attack sensitive systems such as information infrastructure and bypass national security defense systems.
However, the authorities have also specified multiple export scenarios to which facilitation measures can apply, reflecting a tiered and categorized management approach that enhances policy transparency and predictability.
For instance, AI technologies that have already entered the public domain through open source and published academic papers will be exempt from the export control measures. In the biomedical sector, automatic licensing will apply to outbound licensing models that do not involve a transfer of ownership.
The soliciting of public opinion lasts from Oct. 16 to Nov. 15, 2026, and the specific content of the adjustment can be found on the commerce ministry's official website. ■

Gas injection into Europe’s UGS facilities decreasing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:45:40 UTC
23:45:40 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. The rate of gas injection into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities in Europe continues to fall rapidly as temperatures in the region drop and prices rise, according to TASS calculations based on Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE) data.
To date, Europe has managed to fill its UGS facilities to 74% of the volumes required for the upcoming winter.
As of October 14, Europe’s UGS facilities were 74.1% full (14.85 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 83% in the previous year, which is still the lowest level recorded for this date since tracking began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold around 81 bln cubic meters of gas, which is 10.6 bln cubic meters lower than last year’s levels and the lowest volume since 2013.
The European Commission requests EU members to make sure their UGS facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 of each year. Moreover, 10% flexibility is allowed in the event of difficult UGS filling conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage facilities by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter period must reach at least 68 bcm to meet the filling standard.

16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Friday that the Starlink system had not been completely switched off in Ukraine, but speed restrictions affected the country's ability to use it for certain military and humanitarian purposes.
Speaking at a briefing on the sidelines of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, Zelesnkyy said the Defense Ministry remained in contact with partners and that he received indications from the White House that services would be fully restored.
He claimed Ukraine was not using Starlink to conduct deep-strikes against targets inside Russia, but relied on the system to operate interceptor drones against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

Starlink-enabled drones, he said, were used to deliver food and water to Ukrainian personnel in positions exposed to enemy drone attacks.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine receives information from the US specifically about Russian ballistic missile launches, while dozens of countries also share intelligence with Kyiv.
He said Ukraine receives PAC-2 and PAC-3 air defense missiles from the US through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, with European countries financing the deliveries.
“So it's no gift. It's not for free,” he said, acknowledging that Ukraine is not currently a priority destination for the missiles, as many are being sent to the Middle East.
The Ukrainian leader criticized the recent US-Russia diesel deal and the prospect of lifting sanctions, saying Kyiv had not been informed in advance.
Ukraine, he said, proposed an energy ceasefire and offered the US to provide Kyiv with anti-ballistic missiles to protect energy infrastructure for the duration of the arrangement. “Don't give too many. Give us for the period you'll need for the duration of the diesel deal. I have not received that,” he said.
Responding to Donald Trump’s remark that he was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy said negotiating with the US president was easier than dealing with the Russian leader.
He said ending the war remained his priority but accused Putin of showing no genuine desire for negotiations. He warned that concessions on sanctions could eventually lead to broader agreements with Moscow, including in the energy, chemical industry and banking sectors.
“In my view, we cannot perceive diesel deals, these arrangements. We cannot accept them because then there will be gas agreements. I'm sure of that,” he said.
Zelenskyy also rejected the notion that the war was solely about control of the Donbas region, saying Ukraine’s national existence was at stake. “The issue is not withdrawing from Donbas. It's the issue of our country's existence,” he said, arguing that Moscow’s objectives of the war extend beyond eastern Ukraine.
He said European countries understood the risks posed by Russia, and urged partners to continue supporting Kyiv.

Uzbekistan signs $4.7bn energy deals and outlines plans for two more nuclear power plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:43:49 UTC
23:43:49 KST

Foreign firms including ACWA Power, EDF and Toyota Tsusho are involved in projects covering 3,000 MW of generating capacity and 400 MW of storage. Tashkent is also preparing 128 oil and gas exploration blocks for investors and pursuing a future electricity connection to Europe.
Uzbekistan has signed six energy agreements worth $4.7bn (€4.19bn) and announced plans for two more nuclear power plants, as President Shavkat Mirziyoyev seeks to attract foreign investment and meet rising demand from industry and data centres.
The agreements, signed during talks in Tashkent on Friday, cover 3,000 megawatts (MW) of new generating capacity and 400 MW of energy storage, according to the presidency.
Companies named in a project list obtained by Euronews include Saudi Arabia's ACWA Power and Saudi Tabreed, the UAE's AMEA Power, Japan's Toyota Tsusho and Sojitz, France's EDF, Qatar's Nebras Power, StorEn and CRE International.
A new approach to energy investment
Uzbekistan has attracted $35bn (€31.2bn) in energy investment over the past decade, according to President Mirziyoyev.
But he acknowledged that allowing developers to choose plant locations had concentrated generation in some areas and increased transmission costs elsewhere.
“We need an integrated energy system, not isolated power plants,” he said.
Future projects will undergo competitive tenders with grid connections and electricity purchase terms disclosed in advance. Six solar and wind projects totalling 2,200 MW will be tendered separately from the newly signed agreements.
The country's first National Energy Master Plan, covering the period to 2050, is due by July 2027, with a map of grid connection opportunities expected in March.
By 2030, the government aims to add 22 GW of generating capacity, build 5,000 kilometres of power lines and 16 substations, and expand storage capacity to 4.5 GW.
Annual electricity output is targeted to exceed 129bn kWh, with renewables, including hydropower, expected to account for 54% of generation, up from 31% today, according to the presidency.
The government has also proposed 12 manufacturing projects worth $850m (€758m), aimed at increasing domestic production of energy equipment.
Najy Benhassine, the World Bank's division director for Central Asia, said fast growth would require more generation and better networks. “All of this will need energy, will need more generation, but will also need the transmission infrastructure and efficient distribution to power the future growth of the country,” he told Euronews.
Neil McKain, the International Finance Corporation's country manager for Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, identified a further weakness. “In the energy sector, I think it's energy efficiency. This is still a highly energy-intensive economy,” he told Euronews.
McKain said competitive tenders and higher electricity tariffs had also made projects more attractive to investors. He cited a 1.6 GW gas-fired plant in Syrdarya, financed with international partners and expected to start operating this year.
Nuclear expansion
President Mirziyoyev said Uzbekistan planned to build a second and a third nuclear power plant, with talks involving potential investors in the second project scheduled for Saturday.
“We have started the first nuclear power plant, and we have plans for the second and third as well,” he said.
Construction of the first plant, developed with Russia's Rosatom in Jizzakh, began in June.
Its two large and two smaller reactors would provide 2,110 MW. The project is estimated to cost up to $9.5bn (€8.48bn), with initial technical commissioning scheduled for 2029 and completion planned for 2034–2035.
Partners, costs and timetables for the additional plants have not been announced.
Oil and gas investment
Britain's BP and Azerbaijan's SOCAR are involved in exploration across six blocks in the Ustyurt region. Uzbekistan has prepared another 128 blocks for foreign investors.
Preliminary government estimates suggest these additional blocks could contain 5.8 trillion cubic metres of natural gas and 560mn tonnes of liquid hydrocarbons.
The government also wants to expand domestic processing through a methanol-to-olefins project in Bukhara, in south-western Uzbekistan, which would turn methanol into chemicals used to make plastics. It also plans to upgrade two oil refineries and introduce private participation in liquefied petroleum gas distribution.
Energy links to Europe
President Mirziyoyev said plans to export renewable electricity towards Europe through Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan were advancing.
The proposed Caspian Green Energy Corridor, backed by the Asian Development Bank and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, envisages a connection across the Caspian Sea and onward links through the South Caucasus and Black Sea.
The corridor remains at the feasibility stage.
International investors call for further reforms
President Mirziyoyev acknowledged persistent barriers to investment. “We have serious problems, shortcomings, bureaucracy and corruption,” he said.
A new Energy Investors' Council, chaired by Saida Mirziyoyeva, head of the Presidential Administration, will seek to address obstacles including land allocation and grid connections.
At the meeting, Mohammad Abunayyan, founder and chairman of Saudi Arabia's ACWA Power, called for reforms to Uzbekistan's financial and capital markets.
“We need reform in the financial sector. We need reform in capital market,” he told the president. He also urged stronger requirements for employing Uzbek workers and using local suppliers in future projects.
Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi, chief executive officer of UAE-based Masdar, said his company had invested more than $2bn (€1.78bn) since 2019, developed over 2 GW of renewables and committed to another 2 GW.
“In return, we require predictability, certainty and stability in policy, regulation and the agreements underpinning our investments,” he said.

Russia Eyes AI-Powered VPN Crackdown With 95% Blocking Accuracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:42:55 UTC
23:42:55 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Eyes AI-Powered VPN Crackdown With 95% Blocking Accuracy
Russian authorities considered using AI to identify and block VPN services with up to 95% effectiveness, according to Kommersant on October 16.
The proposal appeared in a draft national plan for introducing artificial intelligence technologies through 2030. It envisioned AI analyzing the characteristics of 70% of VPN services targeted for blocking.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s Digital Development Ministry stated that the measure is absent from the plan’s current version.
Russia currently uses what Kommersant described as “intelligent algorithms” to analyze internet traffic, but these systems are not considered AI. The ministry also plans to increase the capacity of its traffic-filtering infrastructure 2.5-fold to 954 terabits per second by 2030.
“AI automates and accelerates the analysis of connection patterns,” a source in the Russian networking industry told Kommersant. The technology could analyze packet size and timing, session duration, traffic ratios, hosting providers, and neighboring IP addresses to indirectly identify VPN infrastructure.
Industry sources cautioned that introducing AI could also increase false positives, resulting in legitimate traffic being blocked. One source estimated that the current error rate is already 5% to 6%, while another warned that early-stage AI systems could produce significant numbers of incorrect blocks.
The proposed AI layer would operate alongside Russia’s existing technical systems for countering threats, or TSPU, which are installed on telecom operators’ networks. A source noted that AI-based VPN detection would also require large-scale telemetry storage, computing clusters for model training, and infrastructure to distribute updated models to filtering nodes.
The push to detect VPN traffic is part of a broader effort by Moscow to tighten state control over mobile communications.
A day earlier, a draft Digital Development Ministry order surfaced requiring smartphones on Russia's future 5G networks to support Kuznyechik, an FSB-developed encryption algorithm, starting March 1, 2032.
Because the algorithm falls outside international 3GPP standards and must be built into modem chipsets, compliance could force Apple, Samsung, and Chinese manufacturers to produce Russia-specific hardware.

Russian Attacks Leave 2,433 Ukrainian Civilians Dead or Injured in September—85% More Than a Year Ago, UN Says
At least 328 civilians were killed and another 2,105 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine in September 2026, bringing the total number of civilian casualties to 85% above the level recorded during the same month last year, according to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.
In its latest report, published on October 16, the UN mission documented civilian deaths and injuries across 22 Ukrainian regions and the capital, Kyiv, with particularly high casualty figures recorded in Kyiv, Kherson, Kharkiv, Sumy, and Zaporizhzhia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian capital experienced an unprecedented frequency of civilian casualties, with deaths or injuries recorded on 22 of the 30 days in September. According to the mission, this was more frequent than in any previous month since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
The UN emphasized that the intensified attacks in September continued a broader trend observed throughout 2026, with civilian casualty figures significantly exceeding those documented in previous years.
The situation remained critical into October, with UN monitors reporting that the first two weeks of the month were among the deadliest periods for civilians in recent years.
“The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest for civilians in recent years,” said Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. “In just a few days, attacks by Russian armed forces resulted in mass-casualty incidents in Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kramatorsk, and Kyiv.”
The mission also documented civilian casualties in Ukrainian territories temporarily occupied by Russia. Its verified September figures included 18 civilians killed and 44 injured in those areas.
However, UN officials cautioned that the actual number of casualties in Russian-occupied territories was likely considerably higher, as limited access and a lack of independent information sources continued to complicate the verification of incidents.
The increase in civilian casualties during September and October coincided with renewed systematic Russian attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
According to UN experts, Russian forces resumed widespread strikes on energy facilities across the country, triggering emergency electricity outages and further disrupting civilian life.
The intensified strikes also come amid reports of critical shortages in Ukraine’s air defense capabilities, potentially leaving the country increasingly vulnerable to further Russian ballistic missile attacks.
A source familiar with the situation told CNN on October 15 that Ukraine had exhausted its supply of interceptor missiles for US-manufactured Patriot air defense systems.
The reported shortage has reportedly undermined Ukraine’s ability to intercept incoming ballistic missiles, with the source telling CNN that “almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the (interceptor) missiles.”

====================================================================================================

German colonialism: Why hasn't there been a reckoning?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

German colonialism on agenda in Bundestag debate on Namibia genocide
October 16, 2026
Gaob Daniel Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp.
In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany.
Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority, Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua. Speaking before the Bundestag debate, the chief said: "We call upon the Bundestag to recognize unequivocally the genocides committed against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples."
Many people wonder why the German parliament hasn't already done this — and why the government has not yet issued an official apology. There is a draft joint declaration with Namibia in which the German government acknowledges that "from today's perspective, [it] would be called genocide." But there is no German-Namibian reconciliation agreement.
The evidence is overwhelming: From 1904 to 1908, the German Empire waged a war of extermination against the Indigenous people of southwestern Africa, including the Ovaherero (also known as the Herero), the Nama, the Damara and the San. At least 100,000 people were killed, and just as many displaced. Many were subjected to forced labor and forced prostitution. The land seizures and expropriation carried out at the time continue to affect their descendants today.
Jürgen Zimmerer, a professor of history at the University of Hamburg whose research focuses on Africa, told DW that the Bundestag and government lack the will to confront this era in German history. "There are Bundestag resolutions on the Armenian genocide, one on the Holodomor [in Ukraine], and one on the genocide against the Yazidis [by the "Islamic State" in Iraq]. But there is no recognition of the genocide against the Herero and Nama by the German Bundestag." If there were any political will to do so, Zimmerer said, it could happen very quickly.
Reconstruction or reparations?
The socialist Left Party initiated the Bundestag debate by drafting a resolution calling for full recognition and compensation in collaboration with representatives of the descendants. The goal: "restorative justice." Paramount Chief Katjiua has rejected the existing agreement between the Namibian and German governments. "Development aid cannot substitute for comprehensive reparations," he said.
Since 2021, the governments have been negotiating a joint declaration that pledges €1.1 billion ($1.24 billion) in reconstruction aid to Namibia over 30 years. Once the agreement is signed, Germany's president is set to issue a formal apology.
But the Foreign Ministry warned: "Legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the recognition of genocide. With these negotiations — which are unique worldwide — Namibia and Germany have broken new ground and are pioneers in confronting their colonial past."
Political scientist Andreas Mehler, the director of the Anton Bergstraesser Institute at the University of Freiburg, said the government's plan sounded like "checkbook diplomacy."
Zimmerer also said there was a financial calculation: "If we were to recognize an obligation to provide reparations to the families of those killed — given the millions of victims of World War II, the victims of the Germans — it would ruin us."
Promise in the government's coalition agreement
Four lines in the 144 pages of the coalition agreement of the current German government — between the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — summarize the extent of the government's commitment to reconciliation with Namibia.
"We will intensify our efforts to come to terms with colonialism," the text reads. "This includes transnational research into artifacts and the restitution of cultural property in dialogue with the countries of origin. Particular attention will be paid to establishing a dignified memorial site and the repatriation of human remains."
Compared with the efforts to address colonialism led by the SPD-led government from 2021 to 2025, "the issue has lost visibility," said Alexander Stroh-Steckelberg, a professor of political scientist at the University of Bayreuth who specializes in Africa.
Zimmerer has an even more critical take: "I wouldn't even call it a stalemate anymore. I believe this government is rolling back the progress that has been made in terms of raising awareness of colonial injustices."
Restitution of culture goods and human remains
Much remains to be done, as far the descendants of the Ovaherero are concerned: The remains of tens of thousands of people are believed to still be in Germany. Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick and other descendants of the victims have been fighting to heal these wounds for generations.
In March, Germany established a coordination council, headed by the Foreign Ministry, which stated that the government did not wish to "dictate to the countries and societies of origin which cultural artifacts and human remains they should reclaim, what priorities they should set or how restitutions should be handled."
Serap Güler, a state minister in the Foreign Ministry and the chair of the coordination council, defends the government's actions so far. Recounting her own official trips — she has already been to Togo, and next week she plans to travel to Rwanda and Burundi — she said: "Everywhere I go, I receive recognition for our sincere and trusting approach to the past — as well as for our determined commitment to a future of freedom, security and prosperity."
A dignified place of remembrance?
Zimmerer said Germany "has earned a reputation as a country that takes a critical view of its own history and learns from its mistakes" — which gives it "enormous cultural capital" on the world stage. But he is concerned that this capital is currently being squandered.
The government's memorial policy does not appear to address colonialism. Zimmerer even detects an attempt to "marginalize German colonial crimes" in the recent proposal by Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer to create a dignified memorial site in Bremen. He notes that victim groups have not been included in Weimer's proposal and said the colonial capitals of the German Empire — Berlin and Hamburg — must also become sites of remembrance.
Ninety-five percent of the colonial troops set sail from Hamburg's Baakenhafen, including Commander Lothar von Trotha, who issued the orders to exterminate the Ovaherero and Nama. According to Zimmerer, the fact that a new opera house — rather than a memorial site — is being built at Baakenhafen constitutes a staggering case of "art-washing of history." Mehler also hopes that a productive debate on memorial sites will still take place and that, overall, "many more places will come to terms with colonial history."
Meanwhile, Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick continues to call for a collective effort to come to terms with the past: "Let us give opportunity to the affected communities that are being represented by us to have a seat on the table to discuss with them the rest of the way."
This article was originally written in German.

Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass as recovery from cancer surgery progresses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:41:47 UTC
23:41:47 KST

Vatican Media has released the first images of Pope Leo XIV since his hospitalisation, showing him celebrating Mass at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital as he recovers from lung cancer surgery.
Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital at noon on Friday after medical tests confirmed that his condition continues to improve following lung cancer surgery, according to the Vatican.
“His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own,” said a medical update signed by Leo’s personal physician Dr. Luigi Carbone and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The service was attended by off-duty medical and nursing staff, as well as members of the Vatican City State’s Gendarmerie Corps. During his homily, the Pope thanked hospital workers for their daily care of patients and, in particular, for the care they have provided him.
Pope's appeal to governments: Food as an 'obligation of justice'
In a message to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) marking World Food Day on Friday, Pope Leo XIV warned against using food as a weapon of war and urged governments to redirect military spending towards sustainable agriculture.
He said hunger was largely caused by a lack of political will and collective solidarity, stressing the importance of guaranteeing universal access to safe and sufficient food.
“It is an obligation of justice that binds both individual states and the international community,” the pope said.
What comes next for Pope Leo XIV?
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said it was too early to predict when the pope would resume his duties, suggesting his pontificate may need to be adjusted depending on his recovery and medical advice.
“We can’t make any type of predictions,” Parolin said Thursday. as reported by LaPresse and ANSA news agencies.
“The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted.”
The Vatican is moving ahead with preparations for Pope Leo XIV’s planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from 6 to 17 November, despite uncertainty over his recovery.

Russia, US eye new joint projects as diesel deal faces sanctions hurdles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:41:00 UTC
23:41:00 KST

Russia and the United States are preparing to unveil new economic initiatives, including potential nuclear-powered data centers, as Washington seeks to overcome sanctions-related obstacles to a recently announced Russian diesel deal, a senior Kremlin envoy said Friday.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's special envoy for investment and economic cooperation, said Moscow and Washington were exploring several areas of collaboration that could move forward even before the war in Ukraine ends.
Speaking at the Russian Energy Week conference in Moscow, Dmitriev said discussions included joint data center projects that could use electricity generated by Russian nuclear power plants.
He said additional initiatives would be announced soon, describing the diesel agreement reached between U.S. President Donald Trump and Putin as a potential model for broader economic cooperation.
The developments come as the two countries navigate a complex sanctions landscape that threatens to complicate efforts to expand commercial ties.
Dmitriev said the U.S. Treasury Department had approached the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), which he heads, for assistance in resolving payment difficulties linked to the diesel agreement.
According to Dmitriev, Washington asked the fund to facilitate transactions and address technical obstacles that could hinder implementation.
The RDIF would work to ensure payments were processed efficiently and reached their intended recipients, he said.
The agreement, announced by Trump last week, would allow Russian diesel to reach U.S. and international markets in an effort to lower fuel prices ahead of November's U.S. midterm elections.
Lower energy costs have become a key political priority for Trump, but the arrangement has drawn sharp criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and raised questions about the future of U.S. sanctions targeting Russian oil.
Implementing the deal would require Washington to ease certain restrictions, including measures imposed by the Trump administration itself.
Dmitriev acknowledged that overlapping sanctions had created considerable uncertainty over how the agreement could proceed.
"There are so many layers of sanctions piled on top of one another that everyone has become confused," he said, adding that U.S. officials were examining ways to remove the relevant restrictions.
He said discussions were already underway on possible sanctions relief, suggesting that Washington was actively seeking a workable solution.
However, Dmitriev warned that a separate U.S. sanctions and tariff measure, known as the Graham Act, could effectively shut down broader investment cooperation between the two countries.
The legislation, introduced by the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham, is intended to intensify economic pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Dmitriev argued that the measure would undermine potential Russian-American business ventures and limit both countries' ability to cooperate in stabilizing global energy markets.
He maintained that economic engagement could proceed alongside diplomatic efforts to end the conflict, with the diesel agreement potentially opening the door to additional projects.
The discussions underscore Moscow's push to revive commercial ties with Washington despite continuing tensions over Ukraine and extensive sanctions imposed on Russia.
While Dmitriev expressed optimism about further agreements, the proposed initiatives remain subject to significant legal and political hurdles as Washington weighs economic cooperation against its existing sanctions framework.

Why Ethiopia and Eritrea&#8217;s march to war demands global attention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:39:18 UTC
23:39:18 KST

The distant thunder of drones over Adigrat is not merely another African conflict. It is the sound of a continent’s most fragile peace shattering—and with it, the already slender prospects for stability across the Red Sea corridor that carries twelve per cent of global trade. Barely eight years after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and President Isaias Afwerki embraced in Asmara, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate’s handshake now lies in ruins.
Eritrean troops have crossed into northern Tigray, advancing up to sixty kilometres into Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia has responded with multiple drone strikes targeting those forces, destroying lorries and ammunition, witnesses say, amid reports of civilian deaths. Both nations have severed diplomatic ties.
Ethiopia calls it an “all-out invasion.” Eritrea calls it an “unprovoked war of aggression.” The truth matters less than the trajectory: two of Africa’s most battle-hardened armies are edging toward a conflagration neither can afford, yet both seem convinced they cannot avoid.
The roots of this rupture are not mysterious. They are anchored in geography so cruel it functions as destiny. Ethiopia, home to 130 million people, is the world’s most populous landlocked nation. It depends on Djibouti for over 95 per cent of its maritime trade, paying between $1.5 and $2 billion annually in port fees—a haemorrhage equivalent to the cost of building a Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam every three years.
A nation that once commanded the Red Sea through the ancient port of Adulis now watches its commerce squeezed through a single corridor. This is not merely an economic inconvenience. It is a structural wound that successive Ethiopian leaders have described in existential terms.
Abiy’s response has been to demand sovereign maritime access—specifically, to the Eritrean port of Assab, barely sixty kilometres from the Ethiopian border. Eritrea, which won independence in 1993 after a thirty-year liberation struggle, views this as nothing less than a threat to its territorial integrity and the very meaning of its statehood. Asmara’s information minister has accused Ethiopia of openly working to bring about regime change by sheltering and supporting armed opposition groups. The result is a security dilemma of terrifying symmetry: each side’s defensive measures confirm the other’s worst fears.
Into this vacuum have stepped external powers with interests that have little to do with Ethiopian or Eritrean welfare. Israel has publicly endorsed Ethiopia’s Red Sea ambitions, with its ambassador describing support for the effort as “clear Israeli policy.”
The strategic logic is cold: a strong, allied Ethiopia provides a non-Arab anchor in a region where Israel seeks to counter Iranian and Houthi influence, and where its recognition of Somaliland has already signalled a willingness to redraw regional alignments. The United Arab Emirates, Ethiopia’s largest investor and a quiet supplier of military technology, forms the other pillar of this de facto axis.
The United States, by contrast, has intervened with uncharacteristic directness. On 14 October, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Abiy that “the region cannot tolerate more conflict,” demanding respect for sovereignty and an immediate halt to cross-border incursions. Washington has even lifted certain sanctions on Eritrea—a pragmatic pivot driven not by any moral reassessment but by the urgent need to secure Red Sea shipping lanes against Houthi attacks. This is containment dressed as diplomacy, and it carries an uncomfortable implication: accountability for Eritrea’s role in the Tigray war has been quietly subordinated to maritime security.
The regional picture is equally troubling. Egypt and Sudan have aligned themselves with Eritrea, driven by their own existential anxieties over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Cairo views the dam as a threat to its 97 per cent dependence on the Nile. Addis Ababa views it as a sovereign right.
The result is a “river-versus-sea” confrontation in which the Nile and the Red Sea have become inseparable theatres of competition. Ethiopia’s army chief has openly accused Egypt and Sudan of backing the very rebels now fighting federal forces.
The human cost of this geopolitical chess game is already being paid. The 2020–2022 Tigray war killed an estimated 600,000 people. A renewed interstate conflict—this time involving heavy drone strikes, conventional armies, and the potential spillover onto Eritrea’s Red Sea coast—would create a humanitarian catastrophe of a different magnitude entirely. Millions of Ethiopians already face severe food insecurity.
The fragile Pretoria Agreement that ended the Tigray war has dissolved into renewed fighting across Amhara and Afar, with former allies now united in an armed alliance against the federal government. Ethiopia cannot fight a civil war and an interstate war simultaneously without fracturing.
Yet the most disturbing truth is that neither Washington’s pressure nor the African Union’s exhortations have altered the trajectory. The AU, headquartered in Addis Ababa, is structurally compromised—it cannot credibly mediate a conflict involving its host nation.
The Gulf states possess the financial leverage to broker a settlement, but the UAE’s deep ties to Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia’s alignment with Egypt make a unified mediation unlikely. The window for diplomacy is closing, and it is closing fast.
What is required is not another communiqué. It is a recognition that Ethiopia’s landlocked status is not a moral failing to be corrected by force, but a structural reality that demands a structural solution. The path forward lies in negotiated maritime access frameworks, joint port management arrangements, and regional economic integration that makes war materially irrational.
Ethiopia’s accession to the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System in October 2026 offered a glimpse of what patient, institutional cooperation could achieve. That glimpse is now being extinguished by the roar of drones.
The international community must act with a clarity that matches the urgency. The United States, the Gulf states, and the African Union must coordinate a single, unambiguous message: there is no military solution. But pressure alone is insufficient. The world’s strategic powers must offer Ethiopia a credible economic alternative—guaranteed, legally binding access to Red Sea ports under international law, backed by investment and infrastructure. Eritrea, for its part, must be assured that its sovereignty is not a bargaining chip.
The Horn of Africa has burned before. The world watched then, and the world did too little. It must not watch again. The drones over Adigrat are not a warning. They are a countdown.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Vladimir Putin is prepared to drag out his war, and we must be ready for this, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, urging European leaders not to ease sanctions against Russia.
