Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:38:51 UTC
23:38:51 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.
The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.
Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn
— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026
Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.
However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.
“Currently, this behavior is not criminalised, creating a loophole for those who exploit such situations and, under the pretext of helping migrants, aid them in their illegal stay, thus serving as a springboard for further illegal migration,” wrote deputy interior minister Czesław Mroczek, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily.
That immediately prompted concern that the law could be used against volunteers and residents of border areas who provide aid – such as food, water, medical treatment, clothing or shelter – to migrants who have crossed illegally from Belarus.
Since 2021, tens of thousands of people, mainly from Asia and Africa, have tried to cross that border with the encouragement and support of the Belarusian authorities. They have sometimes used violence against Polish border officers.
Poland and the EU accuse Belarus of “weaponising” migration as part of the “hybrid warfare” being waged by Russia and its allies against European countries. They have implemented tough border protection measures to prevent crossings and facilitate “pushbacks” of those who cross.
However, many human rights and aid organisations argue that the migrants – over 100 of whom have died around the border since 2021 – are often victims of this process and need humanitarian support.
Two dead bodies found in the river on Poland's border with Belarus likely belong to migrants from a group seen being pushed into the water by Belarusian officers as part of efforts to encourage irregular crossings into the EU, says a Polish minister https://t.co/xsnPd6FeO3
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2025
In response to the interior ministry’s proposal, 61 organisations, including Amnesty International, the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights and the Auschwitz-Birkenau Foundation, signed a joint statement condemning the plans, which they said “violate international standards binding Poland”.
The organisations warned that the proposed wording could expose medical staff treating migrants, lawyers providing legal assistance, facilities working with children, and organisations supporting victims of human trafficking to criminal liability.
“This measure is not aimed at smugglers, but rather at activists or residents of border areas who provide humanitarian aid to foreign nationals who have crossed the border illegally and are present in Poland,” attorney Radosław Baszuk told the Rzeczpospolita daily
Baszuk previously represented five Polish activists who were prosecuted for providing food, clothing and shelter to a group of Middle Eastern migrants who had entered Poland from Belarus in 2022.
A group of five activists have been found not guilty of enabling the illegal presence in Poland of Middle Eastern migrants whom they provided aid to after they had irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.
Prosecutors had been seeking prison sentences https://t.co/RpfhVWL4hY
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 8, 2025
They were acquitted last year, with the ruling made final in March this year after an appeal. But Baszuk told Rzeczpospolita that, under the interior ministry’s proposed amendment to the relevant law, his clients could been convicted.
On Wednesday, Poland’s commissioner for human rights, Sylwia Gregorczyk-Abram, also wrote to the justice ministry to “express concern” that the proposed changes “could lead to criminal liability for charitable or humanitarian activities undertaken towards individuals whose residence status has not yet been regulated”.
Even a member of the government, the minister for family, labour and social policy, Agnieszka Dziemianowicz-Bąk, expressed her “firm opposition” to the plans on social media. She is from The Left (Lewica), one of the junior partners in Poland’s ruling coalition.

In response to the growing criticism, the interior ministry announced on Friday that it was withdrawing the proposal, saying it decided to do so “to eliminate any doubts and prevent the misinterpretation of regulations”.
“From the beginning, the ministry’s sole objective has been to tighten the system and target the organisers of this practice [of migrant smuggling],” said the ministry, quoted by Rzeczpospolita.
“Legal provisions must effectively protect the state’s borders against organised crime, while simultaneously fully safeguarding humanitarian values and life-saving activities.”
The number of attempted illegal crossings by migrants from Belarus to Poland fell from 15,500 in the first half of 2025 to 235 this year – a drop of over 98%
Poland also now claims a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally https://t.co/RFZkd7CeIk
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 20, 2026
Both the former Polish government and the current one, which took power in December 2023, have regularly faced criticism from human rights groups over their response to the migration crisis on the Belarus border.
Earlier this year, the previous human rights commissioner, Marcin Wiącek, expressed concern over a ban on asylum claims introduced by the government in March 2025. He noted that the measures had been described as a temporary solution, but have remained in place ever since.
The government, however, argues that its measures have been effective in preventing the illegal trafficking of migrants. Its data show that attempted border crossings from Belarus fell from around 15,500 in the first half of last year to less than 250 in the same period this year – a drop of over 98%.
It also now claims to have a 100% success rate in apprehending migrants who manage to cross illegally.

Bulgaria ranks third in the EU for annual inflation in September
Friday 16 October 2026 16:43
Friday, 16 October 2026, 16:43
PHOTO ec.europa.eu/eurostat
Font size
Annual inflation in Bulgaria accelerated to 5.6% in September, up from 5% in August. A year earlier, it stood at 4%, according to Eurostat data.
This was the third-highest rate in the European Union, after Romania at 6.5% and Lithuania at 6.1%, and the second-highest in the euro area. Across the EU, annual inflation reached 3.8%, up from 3.2% in August and 2.6% in September 2025.
Since the beginning of this year, Bulgaria’s inflation rate has fluctuated at relatively high levels, reaching 6% in April and 6.3% in May before falling to 5.2% in June and 4.4% in July. Inflation picked up again in August and September.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices remained unchanged.

Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
- Published
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
- Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next 
  - Published2 days ago
Also on Friday, the Pope phoned Russian President Vladimir Putin from hospital to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where access to food and water has been cut off for thousands.
"The fact that he accepted the call and spoke with the Pope may, I hope, be a sign that the Pope's request will indeed be carried out," said Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state.
Without mentioning a ceasefire, the Kremlin said: "The Vatican's intention to help create the conditions necessary to ensure the safety of the town's population and to organise vital supplies has been supported".
"It has been agreed to cooperate on this matter," it added.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, made a similar plea to address what he described as a "desperate" situation in Oleshky.
The Pope's doctors said on Friday tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his surgery.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.
Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.
Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

Families wait for answers after Nigerian military plane crash
Unknown

Families wait for answers after Nigerian military plane crash
LAGOS, Oct 16 - More than a week after a Nigerian Air Force plane crash killed all 25 people on board, families say they are still waiting for answers as military teams search for wreckage and human remains in swampy terrain.
President Bola Tinubu has ordered an investigation into the October 5 crash, but relatives say they have received little information about what caused it, whether remains have been identified or how recovery efforts are progressing.
The Nigerian Air Force (NAF) said the aircraft was on a routine mission from Benin City to Lagos when it crashed in a remote area of southwest Nigeria after losing radar contact. It has not disclosed the cause. The flight was carrying 19 military personnel and six civilians.
For London-based software developer Victor Anii, the uncertainty has compounded the grief of losing his older sister, Esther Anii, a sergeant in the Nigerian Air Force.
When he woke on October 5, he found a message from Esther asking him to send money for a bus journey from Benin City to Lagos. She told him the group had flown from Abuja but stopped in Benin City because of a fault with the aircraft. Tired of waiting, she was considering continuing the journey by road.
Hours later, news broke that an NAF aircraft flying between the two cities had crashed.
"We didn't know what was going on. We just knew we couldn't reach her, and her husband couldn't reach some of his friends on the flight," he said.
It was not until the following day, when the Air Force published a list of those on board, that the family learned Esther had been among those killed.
WAITING FOR ANSWERS
Frustrated by what he saw as poor communication from the authorities, Anii posted a video online criticising the Air Force's handling of families after the crash.
Two days later, he said, an NAF commander visited his parents' home in Abuja carrying two envelopes. One contained a condolence letter. The family did not open the second because they suspected it contained cash.
"Whatever that is in it is not enough to take away the pain of my family," he said.
Asked about support for relatives and efforts to identify remains, NAF spokesperson Ehimen Ejodame referred Reuters to Air Force statements saying it had pledged support to families and intensified search and recovery operations. He did not address the allegation that money was offered.
Damilola Folorunsho, whose 36-year-old brother Sunday was among the six civilians on board, said no one had contacted her family.
"My mum has been living with me since the incident," she said. The family, who live about 200 km (125 miles) from the Igbokoda swamp crash site, do not know whether his remains have been recovered or how far the investigation has progressed.
NAF did not respond to questions about whether it is standard practice for military aircraft to carry civilians.
The crash is the latest in a series of Nigerian military aviation accidents that have raised questions about safety and accountability. A review of publicly reported incidents shows at least nine NAF aircraft accidents had killed more than 30 people in the five years before the latest crash.
For Anii, accountability matters more than compensation.
"The most important thing now is to know what happened and ensure it never happens again." REUTERS

Worsening water crisis sparks protests in Mexico's Guadalajara
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Worsening water crisis sparks protests in Mexico's Guadalajara
GUADALAJARA/MEXICO CITY, Oct 16 - Residents in Guadalajara, one of Mexico's biggest cities, are demanding answers over a worsening water-quality crisis that has left many households reporting foul-smelling, sediment-filled tap water and sparked police clashes as protesters urge government action.
A major protest last weekend put the issue in the national spotlight after police deployed water cannons and tear gas, dozens of people were injured, and officials said nearly 40 people were arrested. The incident prompted President Claudia Sheinbaum to rebuke the police for their tough response and pledge to review two water infrastructure projects for the area.
Still, further demonstrations are planned in the coming days as frustration builds, with videos circulating on social media of people collecting buckets and jars of murky brown or black water flowing from their taps.
The crisis has intensified scrutiny of water management across a metropolitan area of more than five million people that is also Mexico's largest industrial and manufacturing center, located in the western state of Jalisco. The problems echo broader concerns across Mexico, where many major cities struggle with water quality and reliability amid aging infrastructure, pollution and mounting pressure on limited resources.
A June citizen-monitoring study by the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) analyzed 184 household water samples from 90 neighborhoods and found that more than 93% contained no detectable residual chlorine, meaning much of the system lacked the disinfectant normally used to protect water from bacterial contamination.
The study also reported elevated levels of lead, mercury, nitrates and E. coli, a bacterial indicator of fecal contamination, in some samples.
Following the findings, IMDEC called for a public-health alert, independent testing by accredited laboratories and investigations into the sources of contamination.
A spokesman for Jalisco's government did not respond to a request for comment.
At a rally on Thursday evening, Aleida Morales, 54, said that for at least 15 years, the water arriving at her home has often been cloudy and brown. The situation has helped drive residents into the streets, she said, because many feel economic development in Guadalajara, which was one of Mexico's host cities for the World Cup this year, has come at the expense of environmental protection.
Guadalajara sits within the larger Lerma-Santiago watershed, one of Mexico's most polluted river systems and a region long burdened by wastewater, industrial pollution and rapid urban growth.
“There must be other, environmentally sustainable ways to create jobs," Morales said. "The current approach is poisoning us."
Thirty years ago, her grandparents described some of the region's local rivers and waterfalls as a "paradise."
"Today, they are the source of toxic contamination," she added.
LONG-STANDING ENVIRONMENTAL CHALLENGES
Federal authorities have acknowledged broader environmental challenges affecting the region.
In July, Sheinbaum and Secretary of Environment Alicia Barcena launched a 20 billion-peso ($1.09 billion) restoration program for the Lerma-Santiago basin and two other heavily polluted river systems, saying authorities had identified hundreds of priority pollution sources.
Allan Tejeda, an environmental engineering expert at the University of Guadalajara, said the crisis reflects years of accumulated pressures rather than a single contamination event.
He pointed to a combination of untreated or poorly treated wastewater, direct or undocumented discharges, rapid urban growth and chronic underinvestment in water infrastructure and treatment systems.
Existing treatment facilities face growing pressure from contaminants entering the system and are increasingly inadequate for the scale of the challenge confronting the region, he said.
"These issues have never received the attention they require," Tejeda said.
The National Assembly for Water, Life, and Territory, a Mexican rights coalition, expressed solidarity with protesters in Jalisco and called for "a real, comprehensive and verifiable solution" to Guadalajara's water crisis.
"Water is not a concession granted by governments nor a privilege reserved for those who can afford to pay for it," the group said. "It is indispensable for life, health, food, work and the survival of our communities." REUTERS

Ukraine’s plan to tighten military exemptions draws fire from lawmakers, businesses

Ukraine’s plan to tighten military exemptions draws fire from lawmakers, businesses
Ukraine's government is facing mounting criticism over proposed changes to military exemption rules, with lawmakers and businesses warning that the measures could deprive critical industries of workers needed to sustain wartime operations.
The Cabinet of Ministers approved changes to the military exemption system on Oct. 13, though the final rules have yet to be adopted and published. The proposed changes reportedly include lowering exemption quotas for defense-industrial and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
On Oct. 16, 63 lawmakers registered a draft resolution calling on the government to reverse its changes, consult with businesses, and reconsider a proposed "coordination center" overseeing the exemption system.
The dispute highlights a difficult balance for Ukraine as it tries to mobilize more troops while keeping critical industries staffed during the war. Businesses fear the revised rules could deprive them of workers essential to production, energy infrastructure, and defense manufacturing, at a time when companies are already facing labor shortages and disruptions caused by the war.
During a question-and-answer session in Parliament on Oct. 16, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi defended the need to reform the system but sought to reassure critical businesses that they should not expect sweeping changes.
"The regulation is still being worked on. It will be finalized, adopted and published. There is no betrayal there," Koretskyi said.
He said genuinely critical companies, particularly those in the defense and energy sectors, had no reason to worry.
"I can say with confidence that there will be no radical changes for these people and these industries," Koretskyi said.
At the same time, Koretskyi acknowledged that the current system has been abused. He said some companies with a 100% exemption quota exploit the system by employing people who do not perform critical functions.
During his comments in parliament, Koretskyi cited an energy company's contractor with 100 employees, only 20 of whom worked directly for the company, while all 100 received military exemptions. He also said abuses continued on a large scale, prompting the government to consider changes to the system.
"The mobilization and exemption system needs to be improved — that is an indisputable fact," Koretskyi said, adding that the General Staff needs additional soldiers to fight Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, now in its fifth year.
But he said it was too early to criticize the final rules because the government had not yet completed and published the revised regulation.
In their resolution, the lawmakers also questioned a proposed "coordination center," calling for business representatives to be included if the government decides to establish it.
Ukrspecsystems, a Ukrainian defense company that develops unmanned aircraft systems for the Defense Forces, warned that the proposed cut from 100% to 85% would hit the industry’s output.
"For production, the consequences would be immediate: delays in defense orders and an outflow of candidates who will avoid working in the defense industry because of unpredictable rules," the company said in a post on Facebook on Oct. 16.
"We expect this provision to be dropped for defense industry enterprises and the reservation rules to remain stable for the long term."

Palestinians in Gaza dread another winter with nowhere safe to shelter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:34:18 UTC
23:34:18 KST

More than 44,000 people still live in buildings marked for demolition across the territory, unable to leave because no alternative shelter exists. Euronews spoke to families in Al-Mughraqa as tarpaulin prices double and Israel blocks timber and shelter kits from entering Gaza.
When it rains, Abdullah Siyam moves his family’s bedding to the one corner of his house in Al-Mughraqa, in central Gaza, where water does not seep through the roof.
Bombardment that struck neighbouring homes left cracks in the ceiling, and the family has no alternative. “We move our mattresses there and sleep. That is the solution,” he told Euronews.
More than 4,000 damaged buildings in Gaza need to be fully or partially demolished, including more than 2,300 still inhabited by nearly 44,000 people, according to preliminary estimates cited in this month's report by the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
As the fourth winter since the war began approaches, families across the Palestinian territory are bracing for the rainy season in cracked houses and worn-out tents.
Siyam is not alone in Al-Mughraqa. His neighbour Mariam Abu Hazein spends rainy days pushing water out of her home before her blankets soak through.
She borrowed three from her daughter after her own became waterlogged, then returned them when they dried.
Water falls in the rooms and the bathroom. She has placed containers on the floor to collect it and uses a floor wiper to push it outside. “It is as if we were in the street,” she said.
Mohammed Bardawil, from the same area, said he feared facing the upcoming winter with worn-out tarpaulins, which he could not afford to replace.
“Honestly, we really do not want winter to come,” he told Euronews, saying that wind and rain create hardship “whether we are in houses or in tents.”
At the Deir al-Balah market, tarpaulin prices rose from 120 to 180 shekels (€35 to €53), with larger sizes at around 230 shekels (€68). A dome tent went up from 1,300 shekels (€384) to 1,700 shekels (€502).
Ahmed al-Siqali, displaced from Khan Younis, told Euronews by phone that equipping and reinforcing his tent cost him around 1,200 shekels (€355), covering timber for beams and two tarpaulins, a sum he raised with his brother’s help from outside the strip.
According to a June assessment cited by the Norwegian Refugee Council, 71% of families surveyed in damaged buildings said they could not afford repair materials.
The 2023-2025 Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, which resulted in the deaths of more than 70,000 Palestinians — mostly women and children — has left large parts of the Palestinian territory in ruins.
It also triggered one of the worst humanitarian crises in the region’s recent history, with aid agencies warning of famine conditions and a near-total collapse of the strip's health infrastructure.
Everything could collapse
The danger in some structures goes beyond leaks. On 16 September, the Al-Saada residential building in Gaza City collapsed, killing 21 Palestinians including 12 children and five women.
Gaza civil defence said residents received prior warnings but stayed because no alternative shelter was available, and that structural damage from the last war caused the collapse.
Civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal warned on 17 September that damaged towers collapsing in crowded areas could threaten both residents and people in surrounding tents.
He said the service received around 150 distress calls from people in dangerous buildings within 24 hours.
Gaza’s Government Media Office announced on 20 September a plan to evacuate and demolish around 255 buildings at risk of collapse and provide temporary shelter for affected families, noting shortages of heavy machinery, funding and safe land, and saying some families had not left despite warnings.
UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov called for the urgent delivery of rescue equipment, machinery, fuel, tents and tarpaulins to the most vulnerable groups within four weeks after the Al-Saada collapse.
Not letting aid in
The response faces a supply blockage. The Norwegian Refugee Council said Israeli authorities approved 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits in August, then blocked their entry on 26 August and 2 September and later rejected a renewed UN coordination request.
Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) told international media in September it would not allow heavy equipment or reconstruction materials to enter before Hamas was disarmed, accusing it of exploiting aid, a charge the group denies.
As of 18 September, the UN Shelter Cluster had received 26% of its required funding, amounting to $193.7 million.
A UN report in late September counted around 17,000 tents, tarpaulins and shelter kits across organisations’ stocks and ongoing purchases, expected to support around 50,000 families — supplies at various stages of readiness rather than items waiting at crossings.
On the ground, preparations include cleaning drains, raising shelters off the ground, repairing sewage networks and identifying sites for voluntary relocation.
A survey of more than 400 displacement sites found 217 at medium to high flood risk, hosting around 235,000 people. Making those sites safe requires clearing explosive hazards, levelling land and providing water, drainage and road access.
Siyam believes rain in Gaza is a blessing, but he does not wish for it given the state of his house. “Who would wish to drown?” he asked.

How to Dress a Tech Oligarch: Costume Designer Discusses the Evolution of Zuckerberg’s Style
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:32:25 EEST
23:32:25 KST

How to Dress a Tech Oligarch: Costume Designer Discusses the Evolution of Zuckerberg’s Style
Kyiv • UNN
Sorkin’s film shows Zuckerberg’s transition from hoodies to expensive, understated clothing. After 2024, his style turned into loud luxury.
From T-shirts and hoodies to Alexander McQueen suits featuring images of dragonflies. Costume designer Susan Lyall revealed the evolution of tech oligarch Mark Zuckerberg’s style, and also explained how fashion helps him create the necessary images and promote his own products, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Aaron Sorkin’s first film about Facebook — "The Social Network" (2010) — helped cement the image of Mark Zuckerberg in the early 2000s: a rebel against corporate norms in crumpled hoodies and T-shirts.
The next film, "The Social Reckoning," covers the period from 2019 to 2021. According to costume designer Susan Lyall, this is already the "post-hoodie" era — a time when Zuckerberg stopped demonstratively disregarding formal dress codes. At the same time, it is a period when he becomes as robot-like as possible. Zuckerberg’s restrained wardrobe — suits or identical long-sleeved shirts — emphasizes his icy calm, despite the rage boiling deep inside.
The costumes were created on the basis of extensive research conducted by Lyall herself and actor Jeremy Strong, who, she says, "cares very deeply about costumes." Since they had already worked together on Sorkin’s films "Molly’s Game" and "The Trial of the Chicago 7," they were constantly communicating by message during preparations.
"He writes to me before I even have time to write to him. This is our third film together, so I’m used to it. He’s very proactive — that’s why he’s one of my favorite actors. He knew exactly where and what (Zuckerberg) wore. He needed specific Nike sneakers — footwear was very important to him — as well as a specific T-shirt or sweater from Brunello Cucinelli, and so on," she says.
Strong is known for his devoted use of the Stanislavski system (the "method" acting system), and it seems that the "method" extends to his choice of clothing as well. "It’s essentially the first step in creating a character. Just like the haircut," Lyall notes.
Their discussions were very detailed. "You know, it’s even a little geeky — sitting around and talking about the color of shoelaces. Not many people would want to talk about that. I always joke with him: if acting doesn’t work out, you can come work in my department!" she says. Lyall found those Nike sneakers — specifically, the 2018 Nike Flyknit Trainer model in the "black anthracite" colorway — on the Grailed platform. As for the sweaters, Strong, she says, figured out how to contact the Italian luxury brand Brunello Cucinelli — whose clothes cost astronomical sums — in order to purchase specific models. "Because we don’t need new items. We need things from five or six years ago, and they really helped us get them. And it was all thanks to him. He was truly proactive."
Lyall devoted considerable time to thinking about how tech oligarchs dress. This applies not only to Zuckerberg, but also to Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and others — they partly inspired her work on another recent project: Jesse Armstrong’s film "Mountainhead" (2025), which tells the story of four scheming plutocrats.
They also often wore clothing by Brunello Cucinelli. The brand sells cashmere cardigans for $16,500 and ribbed sweaters for $4,600. Interestingly, a quote from Immanuel Kant is currently prominently displayed on the homepage of its website: "Beauty is a symbol of moral goodness."
In Lyall’s view, Brunello Cucinelli is a kind of "safety net" for people like Mark Zuckerberg. If they are unsure about their clothing choice, the high price helps them feel a little better. You know, if this little sweater costs $2,000, it must be good. It’s like a "security blanket" or simply confirmation of one’s success: if you’re wearing something that signals good taste, then everything is fine. I think [tech billionaires] have found a new way to show off
The Zuckerberg of the time of "The Social Reckoning" has already moved away from his former anti-fashion stance. In 2014, he said that he was "not a cool person" and wore gray T-shirts only because he wanted to make "as few decisions as possible… I feel like I'm not doing my job if I'm expending energy on things that are frivolous or frivolous."
According to Lyall, during the period depicted in the film, "Zuckerberg, to me, was trying to seem like an everyman, but at the same time he was beginning to understand how obsessed Silicon Valley is with questions of taste and the cost of things." He also became more fit. In Lyall's view, he was probably thinking: "My athletic build looks great in this fitted but expensive sweater." There is also an undertone of "those who know, know." At the same time, he looks like a "nouveau riche" person, but without excessive ostentation. He is not lacking in taste.
Since then, Zuckerberg's appearance has evolved into outright flaunting.
Regarding tech billionaires in general, Lyall notes: "I think something has changed. They have found a new way to show off. And it's no longer 'quiet luxury.' This is loud luxury."
As for Zuckerberg himself—whose transformation, which took place around 2024, was accompanied by conspicuous gold chains, Loewe shorts, and Alexander McQueen suits featuring dragonflies—it looks like an extraordinarily well-thought-out strategic move.
Zuckerberg's interest in fashion allows him to create an image distinct from the one we are used to: a man sitting, sweaty, in a suit before Congress. It also diverts attention from the actual state of his products and activities, offering instead an easy and harmless topic of conversation.
Zuckerberg even resorted to a classic writer's device—giving his jewelry a backstory. In 2024, when he began wearing a large gold pendant over a T-shirt, he said it had nothing to do with wanting to imitate hip-hop stars (although the internet, quite predictably, reached precisely that conclusion).
When he was finally asked about the pendant in an interview ("Oh, this?" he replied, trying to look casual), he explained that a Jewish prayer was engraved on the piece. He sings it to his children every night before bed—and the gesture reminds the public of his humanity, his faith, and how important it is to him to be there for his children.
This year, when Meta enlisted fashion stars such as Kylie Jenner to promote its "smart" glasses, Zuckerberg himself began paying even more attention to fashion: he attended Prada shows and the Met Gala.
Last month, he gave The New York Times an interview devoted exclusively to clothing. Zuckerberg claims that he buys almost his entire wardrobe himself on Instagram—which, given his enormous workload, requires considerable time and a multitude of decisions.
The brands he mentioned are mostly contemporary labels not associated with oligarch style. In particular, he named Mike Amiri, whose T-shirts cost around $400. Zuckerberg has even commissioned exclusive items from him—for example, a T-shirt reading "Building is my love language," which he wore when presenting Muse at a Facebook conference. And when he buys something cheaper online—say, for $200 rather than $2,000—he may even reply in the comments if someone praises the item, drawing attention to it: "It's from @johnelliottco—I’ve really been liking their stuff lately."
Likewise, the new personal AI assistant Muse was designed to be as charming as possible—after all, such a cute, fluffy creature resembling a Labubu toy surely cannot trigger an apocalypse! It seems that Zuckerberg's ongoing transformation is intended to make him more approachable and—ideally—more human.
However, in the world of fashion, it is not as simple as checking the box saying "I’m not a robot." For example, explaining his interest in style to The New York Times, he said: "I believe the company embodies my values," — and added that he wanted "to consciously approach how I program it."
This wording suggests that beneath the new bright clothing, the same "mechanism in cashmere" — the image portrayed in Sorkin’s film — may perhaps never have been properly switched off.

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Heart of the Beast,” “City of God” and “Fantastic Mr. Fox”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:32:15 UTC
23:32:15 KST

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Heart of the Beast,” “City of God” and “Fantastic Mr. Fox”
The weekend is approaching, bringing three stories about survival in worlds where danger can emerge from nature, violence or one’s own choices. In this edition of CineCrossroads, a soldier and his dog fight their way through the Alaskan wilderness, a young photographer searches for an escape from the violence surrounding him, and a clever fox risks everything by returning to his criminal ways. Qazinform News Agency correspondent wishes you an enjoyable viewing.
Movie of the Week: Heart of the Beast (2026)
In the wilderness, survival depends on trust between a man and his most loyal companion.
Directed by David Ayer, Heart of the Beast stars Brad Pitt as James Belmont, a Special Forces officer who survives a devastating plane crash alongside his combat dog, Odin. Stranded deep in the Alaskan wilderness, the pair must confront extreme weather, dangerous terrain and the physical limits of their endurance.
Belmont’s military experience gives him the skills needed to stay alive, but the isolation forces him to rely equally on Odin. Their relationship forms the emotional center of the film, transforming a traditional survival thriller into a story about loyalty, trauma and the bond between humans and animals.
Released in cinemas on September 25, Heart of the Beast reunites Pitt with Ayer after their collaboration on the 2014 war drama Fury. It is a fitting choice for viewers seeking action, striking natural landscapes and an emotional story about companionship under the most difficult circumstances.
Classic Pick: City of God (2002)
In a neighborhood ruled by violence, a camera offers one young man a different path.
Directed by Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund, City of God follows several interconnected lives in a housing project outside Rio de Janeiro. At the center of the story is Rocket, a quiet boy who dreams of becoming a photographer rather than joining the criminal world surrounding him.
As rival gangs compete for control, Rocket documents a community shaped by poverty, ambition and fear. His photographs gradually become both a record of the violence and a possible route out of it.
Driven by energetic editing, vivid performances and an unforgettable visual style, City of God presents violence without turning it into simple entertainment. More than two decades after its release, it remains a powerful examination of how opportunity, environment and personal choices can determine the course of a life.
Family Pick: Fantastic Mr. Fox (2009)
Some animals are simply not made for an ordinary life.
Directed by Wes Anderson and based on Roald Dahl’s beloved book, Fantastic Mr. Fox follows a former thief who has promised his wife that he will leave his dangerous habits behind. Years later, frustrated by domestic routine, Mr. Fox secretly begins stealing from three wealthy and ruthless farmers.
His actions place his family and the entire local animal community in danger. To protect them, he must use the same intelligence and daring that created the crisis in the first place.
Featuring stop-motion animation and the voices of George Clooney, Meryl Streep and Jason Schwartzman, Fantastic Mr. Fox combines dry humor, family adventure and carefully crafted visuals. Beneath its playful surface is a thoughtful story about identity, responsibility and learning to protect the people who depend on us.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Thursday urged Israel to halt "forced establishment" of settlements in the occupied West Bank and called for the full reopening of access to the Gaza Strip.
Beijing maintains that the Palestinian question is the “biggest historical injustice of this century” and that the two-state solution is the correct path to resolving it, Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog during a meeting in Baku, Azerbaijan, on the sidelines of the seventh CICA summit.
He described the current regional situation as tense and added that peace and tranquility remained far from being achieved.
The Chinese foreign minister said the urgent priority was to fully reopen access to Gaza to prevent its two million residents from facing a further humanitarian catastrophe, while calling on Israel to halt and reverse settlement expansion in the West Bank.
Wang also said Beijing was willing to work with Israel to advance bilateral cooperation and strengthen public support for ties, noting that 2027 will mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations and the 10th anniversary of the establishment of their innovative comprehensive partnership.
Wang said the Palestinian issue was at the root of the Middle East conflict, adding that both Israelis and Palestinians had the right to live in peace and establish independent states.
He said China believed that sustained commitment to peace and adherence to “the correct direction” of the two-state solution would eventually bring the peace people had long awaited.
In a separate meeting with Palestinian Foreign Minister Varsen Aghabekian Shahin on Thursday, Wang said China “firmly” supports the Palestinian people’s “just cause of restoring their legitimate national rights.”
Unless the Palestinian issue is “resolved fairly, lasting peace and stability cannot be achieved in the Middle East,” he said.
“The Palestinian question should not be marginalized, and the world must not forget the two million Palestinian people in Gaza struggling on the brink of death. Justice may be delayed but never absent,” Wang said.
He added that China would “continue to stand on the side of international justice and remain on the side of the oppressed nations, and continue to speak up for the just cause of Palestine on multilateral platforms.”
Since October 2023, Israel’s military offensive in Gaza, backed by the US, has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 others, according to the ministry. The offensive has also destroyed 90% of Gaza’s infrastructure.
Attacks by Israeli forces and occupiers against Palestinians and their property across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, have also intensified since then.

Latvia calls on the EU to block the transit of Russian grain through Baltic ports in order to open the Black Sea
Kyiv • UNN
Latvia’s prime minister proposes banning the transit of Russian grain through the Baltic states to force Moscow to open the Black Sea. This would support Ukraine’s exports.
Europe should block the transit of Russian grain through Baltic Sea ports, as this could force Moscow to seek ways to restore commercial shipping in the Black Sea. Bloomberg reports this, citing a statement by Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, Russia and Ukraine have attacked each other’s ports, terminals, and shipping infrastructure in the Black Sea, resulting in a sharp decline in exports of key commodities, including grain. Moscow redirected some grain cargoes by rail to ports in Latvia and Lithuania, prompting criticism in the Baltic countries, which are members of the European Union and NATO.
"Appropriate pressure must be applied so that Russia understands that it itself must reopen the Black Sea," Kulbergs said.
He added that Ukraine should be able to sell its grain in order to partially cover the funding shortfall it will face this winter.
Kulbergs noted that unilateral actions by the Baltic countries increase the risk of lawsuits and supported calls by Estonia and Lithuania to introduce a ban at the EU level.
"This is in all our interests," he said. "Right now, we are talking about the money and support Ukraine needs this winter."
In brief
Lithuania is calling on the European Union to ban the transit of Russian grain through European infrastructure and impose sanctions on Russian agricultural oligarchs who support the war against Ukraine. At the same time, Vilnius is strengthening controls over the origin of grain to prevent the transit of products stolen in Ukraine.

In Yemen's besieged Taiz, families take shelter as Houthis close in

In Yemen's besieged Taiz, families take shelter as Houthis close in
TAIZ, Yemen, Oct 16 - Ali Hassan and his family took shelter under a stairwell at a school in Taiz as Iran-allied Houthi forces closed in around them, tightening a siege of Yemen's third-largest city.
The 42-year-old said the latest fighting between the group and Saudi-backed government forces had forced him to flee several times. The wider conflict has also left its mark on his body: a shot from a Houthi sniper paralysed his hand in 2021, he said.
"I only have my left hand," he told Reuters. A month ago, he added, another sniper shot his sister in the spine while she was herding sheep, leaving her completely disabled. Reuters could not verify his accounts.
THEATRE IN WIDER REGIONAL WAR
The city is fast becoming the most important front in Yemen's reignited civil war — itself a new theatre in the wider regional conflict that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Houthi forces have encircled the city by cutting the main road south to Aden, forcing people from their homes and deepening a humanitarian crisis.
A Houthi victory in Taiz would mark one of the biggest turning points in a war that resumed this summer after a four-year truce. The group denies being armed by Iran and says it is fighting a corrupt system in Yemen.
Hassan said residents were facing Houthi fire and shortages of food and water as the group pushed for more territory. Last month, the Houthis tightened their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb shipping lane in a lightning advance.
On Thursday, the group fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden, killing five people, the government said.
The Saudi-led coalition has also listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in recent weeks.
The Aden strike and the Houthis' determination to take Taiz suggest the conflict could drag on, prolonging suffering in a city of almost 600,000.
FOCAL POINT OF FIGHTING
Taiz has been on the frontline between the Houthis and the government since the war's first days.
It is now the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen.
Resident Wathiq Mahyoub said prices were rising, fuel was running short and garbage was piling up on the streets.
"The siege is suffocating. It's strangling the citizens," Mahyoub told Reuters. "The Houthis refused to open the crossing for us, even to dump the rubbish."
War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south to Aden. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.
Last week, government forces launched a campaign to recapture areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping artery.
Aid agencies have warned of rapidly worsening conditions in Yemen.
HUMANITARIAN CRISIS
"There are no camps equipped to receive these families. We find some of these families living in large unfinished buildings," said Ahmed al-Jalal, director of the Executive Unit for the Management of Displaced Persons' Camps, Al-Muzaffar district, in Taiz governorate.
"Some are in shops, some in buildings unfit for living, with no essentials for living," he added.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, Zoe Brennan, spokesperson for the UN migration agency, said 233,077 people have been displaced so far in the latest conflict, 121,530 of them in Taiz.
World Health Organization spokesperson Tarik Jašarević said 12 hospitals had about four days of fuel while there was a shortage of oxygen and medicines.
"Taiz is being cut off, and its hospitals are running out of supplies as fighting has reached urban districts where the main referral hospitals stand," he said. "Unfortunately, the road closures are blocking the resupply." REUTERS

South African coalition government faces fresh rift

South African coalition government faces fresh rift
South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) has called for the Democratic Alliance’s place in the coalition government to be reviewed after its governing partner opposed its court bid to reinstate barred election candidates.
Mbalula has urged ANC leaders and other Government of National Unity (GNU) partners to reconsider the DA’s place in government, opening a new front in a partnership repeatedly tested by political and policy disagreements. The GNU is made up of 10 political parties.
The latest dispute centres on the ANC’s legal challenge over the exclusion of its candidates from six municipalities ahead of the November 4, 2026, local government election. The party approached the Constitutional Court after its failure to finalise candidate submissions before the deadline left candidates off the ballot.
The DA opposed the ANC’s challenge, putting the coalition partners on opposing sides of a legal battle with potentially significant electoral consequences. The apex heard the case on October 12 and reserved judgment. The outcome could determine whether the affected ANC candidates will be allowed to contest the elections.
Mbalula’s call for a review comes amid mounting disagreements between the ANC and DA over policy, budgets and decision-making since the GNU was formed in 2024. The parties have clashed over the National Health Insurance Act, the Basic Education Laws Amendment Act, land expropriation and proposed value-added tax increases. They have also traded accusations over consultation and the handling of major government decisions.
The DA has repeatedly criticised what it sees as unilateral action by the ANC, while the governing party has continued to advance policies that the DA opposes.
These disputes have tested a coalition formed after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in the 2024 national elections. Mbalula’s demand puts the DA’s role in the coalition under renewed political scrutiny.

Since March 2, Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed 4,389 people and injured 12,424 others, according to official figures released Monday by the Lebanese government.
The attacks have continued despite a US-sponsored “Framework Agreement” signed by Beirut and Tel Aviv on June 26, which calls for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army.
Despite the agreement, Israel continues attacks in southern Lebanon and remains in control of Lebanese areas, some occupied for decades and others seized during recent wars and military operations.

In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:28:53 UTC
23:28:53 KST

In space, no one hears Zelensky scream: No euros can buy Kiev options in orbit
No matter how European leaders pledge to support Ukraine come hell or high water and let the taxpayers foot the bill, the cold hard fact is that there are things no euros can buy, such as US intelligence and satellite communications.
Kiev’s critical reliance on American space capabilities came to the fore this week when the long-standing feud between US President Donald Trump and Vladimir Zelensky flared up again. Trump, who had struck a diesel supply deal with Russia, called Zelensky a hindrance to peace who should be replaced. Zelensky called Trump a weakling who had betrayed Ukraine, if not in those exact terms.
According to lamentations from Kiev corroborated by media reporting, the White House put a chokehold on the Zelensky government by suspending early warning about incoming Russian ballistic missiles and temporarily suspending access to Starlink satellite internet for fast-moving objects – such as drones used in Kiev’s “middle strike” operations inside what Washington recognizes as part of Ukraine.
It’s not like Kiev was not warned. During a meeting in Miami last week, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly told the Ukrainians the diesel deal announcement was coming and that Kiev should not have ignored Trump’s multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accounts shared with Axios and Reuters suggest the Americans were polite enough not to say “what a nice deal to get intelligence and internet you have; it would be a shame if something happened to it.” But they mentioned “all that the US has done for Ukraine.” The Ukrainians did take it as a threat.
Here are the alternatives Kiev would have, should Trump push the issue further.
No match for US intelligence
Intelligence that European NATO members can provide is a far cry from what the US has been delivering for years. Already, early warning about Russian ballistic missile launches has stopped coming, just as Zelensky is complaining.
The US operates the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS), whose backbone is six geosynchronous orbit satellites equipped with thermal sensors that detect launch signatures, complemented by two active and two reserve payloads in a highly elliptical orbit.
SBIRS helps identify and estimate the trajectory of a weapon, but has limited ability to track missiles after the intensive boost phase. But knowing one is incoming helps ground and airborne radar systems that guide interceptor missiles.
Other NATO members rely on SBIRS intelligence and never thought they would need their own alternative.
Satellites operated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) and the Air Force’s electronic reconnaissance aircraft, such as the RC-135U Combat Sent, also collect intelligence about Russian air defense systems. It’s unclear how much data it shares with Kiev, but the media has said the US helps plan Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia to minimize Moscow’s ability to intercept.
European NATO members do have some similar capabilities, including France’s three CERES electronic-intelligence satellites, the UK’s three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, and Germany’s SARah radar-reconnaissance space program, but there is only so much they can do to measure up to the world’s largest military spender.
OneWeb not to rule them all
On the connectivity side, Starlink and its military twin Starshield remain the most capable today. It has over 11,000 satellites in low Earth (LEO) orbit that can use lasers to route traffic between each other, boosting their bandwidth.
The Starlink Mini terminal weighs just 1.1 kg and has an integrated antenna, making it usable even on even smaller military drones. Even larger variants are compact, which makes them harder to spot, and they typically consume under 100 watts of power – both valuable features in frontline applications.
The most direct non-US alternative is Eutelsat OneWeb, which already complements Starlink access in Ukraine. It only has 600+ satellites in its constellation, but nevertheless offers a high-speed connection.
However, OneWeb’s orbital component “remains rooted in an outdated architecture and technology conceived a decade ago, without any evolution of its underlying design,” Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant, told Reuters.
OneWeb ground hardware is likewise no match for Starlink in price, size, or appetite for energy. The relatively small Hughes HL1100W terminal weighs over 10 kg and consumes around 130 watts, though there are efforts to produce smaller and less power-hungry equipment.
Kymeta Corporation announced a OneWeb terminal in March whose 100-watt consumption it said was optimized for mobile platforms. Its “compact and lightweight design” means it weighs less than 11 kg, and the producer itself is Redmond, Washington.
Dark horses in orbit
In September, EU co-founder Luxembourg announced the successful launch of the final three of a planned 13 satellites of its O3b mPOWER communication system. The low number is misleading, since the constellation is being positioned in medium Earth orbit and requires fewer satellites for coverage.
The trade off is latency, which is higher by an order of magnitude compared to LEO-based systems, but Luxembourg’s system is still good enough for some military applications and is used by NATO.
O3b mPOWER’s potential for Ukraine’s war effort is limited due to its coverage, which is between 50° north latitude and 50° south latitude. Luxembourg is right on the northern border of the band, but a large part of Ukraine, including Kiev, is outside of it. As they say, geography is destiny.
GOVSATCOM, the EU’s program to band together communication satellites owned by several member states, is somewhat of a dark horse, but public data suggests its capabilities are too limited to replace Starlink.
Amazon Leo is currently in limited preview, but it’s hard to expect an American company and a major Pentagon contractor to publicly defy Trump at Brussels’ call. Russia’s in-development Rassvet system is obviously not an option.
The EU’s proposed IRIS² system is years away from being operational, as is Canada’s Telesat Lightspeed.
In short, should Ukraine lose Starlink, in the short term Europe cannot replace it, as EU’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.

Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:27:00 UTC
23:27:00 KST

Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women
October 16, 2026
The life of Maryam Yarmohammadi came to a violent end in the early hours of October 5, when the 28-year-old mother of two was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her genitalia were mutilated. She died shortly afterward in hospital. Both her husband and brother were arrested.
Media reported that about 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests. They reportedly believed that death had been the "least severe punishment" Maryam Yarmohammadi deserved.
What the young woman's relatives considered her guilty of has not been publicly reported. Yet both the circumstances of the case and the extreme violence involved follow a familiar pattern seen in so-called honor killings.
In such cases, the underlying belief is often that a man must erase a perceived "dishonor" brought upon the family by a sister, daughter or wife. Failure to do so may expose him to rejection, humiliation or social exclusion within his community.
No opportunity to defend themselves
What constitutes "honor" or "proper conduct" is often defined by family expectations or social and cultural norms. In some traditionally conservative regions, even laughing loudly or engaging in a friendly conversation with an unrelated man may be viewed as a violation of these norms.
Women accused of such transgressions are frequently denied any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves against the allegations.
For years, women's rights activists in Iran have sought to establish nationwide support networks offering counseling and protection to women at risk. One such initiative is the Campaign to End Honor Killings.
Rezvan Moghaddam, a spokesperson for the campaign, told DW that there appeared to be no activist or local group in the region capable of supporting Maryam Yarmohammadi.
Through civil society networks, the campaign has in some cases succeeded in relocating threatened women to safe locations and securing shelter for them.
Moghaddam said that Maryam Yarmohammadi's death should not be interpreted as criticism of women's rights activists in those regions: "I myself come from Khuzestan in southern Iran and am fully aware of the restrictions that exist there."
Failure of the justice system
Based on interpretations of Shariah, or Islamic law, Iran's laws do not treat women as equal citizens in many areas of life. Their ability to make decisions about education, employment or travel may depend on the consent of their fathers or, later, their husbands.
Even after a woman's death, male relatives can, under certain legal provisions, influence the course of criminal proceedings.
Iranian criminal law applies the principle of retribution in certain offenses, including murder. In homicide cases, the victim's relatives may choose either to demand retribution, which can result in the death penalty, or to pardon the perpetrator.
These provisions raise particular concerns in cases of honor killings. When an alleged perpetrator is also among the relatives empowered to influence decisions on punishment or forgiveness, a serious conflict of interest emerges.
Such situations expose the protection gaps critics say exist within Iran's justice system regarding violence against women.
According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, honor killings — defined as the murder of a woman by male relatives such as her father, brother or uncle for allegedly violating social norms of modesty and family honor — accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provinces in western and southern Iran.
In March 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran reported that at least 179 women were murdered by men within their family circles in 2024. These cases were recorded as femicides.
Socially legitimized violence
It was the brutality of Maryam Yarmohammadi's murder that shocked Iranians. The murder triggered a wave of grief and outrage on social media. Many women reacted strongly to what they saw as a femicide driven by hatred in the name of "honor" and "shame."
At the same time, numerous comments focused on victim-blaming, or holding Maryam Yarmohammadi responsible for her own death. Others described the killing as the "punishment of an unfaithful woman" or attempted to justify it by "understanding the men's anger."
Men have been socialized to believe they are responsible for controlling women and monitoring their behavior and decisions, the psychoanalyst Saba Alaleh said. Male identity, she said, is tied to a woman's "obedience."
Violence becomes normalized when beliefs, social approval and silence reinforce one another within this structure, Alaleh said.
"When cultural, social, political, economic, legal and educational factors are closely intertwined, they acquire enormous power," she said. "Under such conditions, women are also highly economically dependent and lack sufficient social support. Preventive mechanisms are absent, as well. All of this increases the risk of violence."
Struggle for self-determination
Atefeh Rangriz, a sociologist and women's rights activist, told DW: "Femicides have always existed, and their political manifestations can be traced throughout history, from forced unveiling [under Reza Shah Pahlavi in the 1930s] to the slogan 'Either the headscarf or blows to the head' in the Islamic Republic."
Rangriz said women understood the path toward liberation and, despite tremendous obstacles, had achieved significant progress over the past decades.
Women in Iran have been driving since 1940. They have been allowed to vote and run for political office since 1963. Women account for half of all university graduates in the country. The number of women filing for divorce or mutually ending unhappy marriages has also continued to rise.
The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which emerged from the nationwide protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody in 2022, has further transformed public perceptions of women in Iran.
"Women have learned to focus on the present rather than postponing justice to the future. They demand it now," Rangriz said. "They want to exercise autonomy over their own bodies, live as they choose, and free themselves from the structures of domination, oppression and exploitation. It is a kind of radical revolution."
Many Iranian women no longer wear the mandatory hijab in public, openly defying the Islamic Republic's dress regulations.
Yet it remains unknown what the young mother Maryam Yarmohammadi wanted, or how she wished to live. She was brutally killed.
This article was originally written in German.

President Volodymyr Zelensky and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar agreed to normalize relations in Brussels on Friday, Oct. 16, ending months of tensions that have stalled Ukraine’s EU bid, bolstering Kyiv’s goal of opening all remaining accession clusters by year-end.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry described the meeting as historic, saying it marked an important step toward restoring ties between Kyiv and Budapest after years of friction over the rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today, we have truly opened a new chapter. This is a reset across all tracks: political, economic, humanitarian and others,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
The leaders met on the sidelines of the European Council summit after a breakthrough over minority education rights helped unblock part of Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations.
Trade, borders and business ties
According to the ministry, bilateral cooperation will focus on trade and economic ties, border infrastructure, business contacts and people-to-people engagement.
After the leaders’ talks, Sybiha met his Hungarian counterpart, Anita Orbán, to coordinate the implementation of the agreements.
“This is how quiet and effective diplomacy works – in the interest of the nation, not headlines,” Sybiha said.
Magyar, for his part, expressed solidarity with Ukraine against Russia’s aggression and offered diplomatic support for efforts to secure a ceasefire and lasting peace, Reuters reported, citing his Facebook statement after the meeting.
‘Not Trump’s Decision’: Lukashenko Says Ukrainians Must Choose Their President
The reset comes ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries and the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution against Soviet rule.
Minority education law helps unblock EU talks
Ukraine’s parliament adopted the education amendments on Oct. 12, and Zelensky signed them into law that day. The legislation expands education rights for national minorities whose languages are official EU languages and introduces a special status for qualifying minority-language schools.
The rights of Ukraine’s ethnic Hungarian community, concentrated in the southwestern Zakarpattia region, have long been a source of tension with Budapest. Both Magyar’s government and its predecessor, led by Viktor Orbán, linked progress in Ukraine’s accession negotiations to minority-rights concerns.
After the law’s adoption, Hungary dropped its objections to opening Cluster 2, covering the internal market, and Cluster 3, covering competitiveness and inclusive growth. Negotiations on both opened on Oct. 13, bringing the total opened to four of the six clusters.
So far, Ukraine and Moldova opened Cluster 1 – Fundamentals on June 15, and Cluster 6 – External Relations on July 14. Ukraine aims to open Cluster 4, on the green agenda and sustainable connectivity, and Cluster 5, on resources, agriculture and cohesion – before the end of 2026.
Magyar described the law and the start of its implementation as a step toward restoring mutual trust. He said discussions would continue at ministerial level.
The move comes just a day after the EU officials removed ‘urgency’ language from their draft summit conclusions on opening Ukraine’s and Moldova’s remaining negotiating clusters on Oct. 15, softening the timeline on the accession.
The updated draft keeps the expectation that the clusters will be opened under the merit-based approach but no longer includes any reference to timing.
Further meetings under consideration
Further talks could take place in Berehove, a center of Ukraine’s Hungarian community, Magyar said, according to Euronews.
Zelensky has also received an invitation to Budapest for the Oct. 23 commemoration of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, deputy presidential chief of staff Ihor Zhovkva told Euronews. He said the president was considering attending; a visit has not been confirmed.
The Brussels summit comes as Zelensky seeks European support amid continuing Russian attacks and tensions with Washington over restrictions on military satellite communications and US policy toward Russian energy exports.

On Oct. 15, Sweden extradited to the U.S. Russian national Alexander Suvorov, who is accused of setting up supplies of American microelectronic components to Russia in circumvention of sanctions. As the U.S. Department of Justice reports, Suvorov, 52, has been charged on three counts: smuggling, money laundering, and violation of the Export Control Reform Act (ECRA). He is expected to appear in court in Albany, New York, as early as Oct. 16.
According to the case materials, from March 2022 to April 2023, Suvorov ran an illicit procurement network that purchased dual-use electronic components from American companies while concealing the end buyer; the components were then delivered to Russia via Hong Kong. The Justice Department notes that some of the components which were illegally purchased and exported to Russia by Suvorov and his accomplices can be used in military communication systems and radar systems.
“My office, working together with the FBI and the Department of Commerce, will continue to aggressively prosecute these types of cases and hold offenders accountable to the fullest extent of the law. This historic extradition shows that we will fly over 3,800 miles to locate and bring to justice those who threaten national security,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York John A. Sarcone III.
The Insider established that GS Group Limited, a company registered in Hong Kong, is owned by Alexander Leonidovich Suvorov, born Aug. 15, 1974. According to a flight database, he regularly flew to Hong Kong.
It was also found that Suvorov was connected to at least 10 different companies in Russia. One of them, Forpost Trading, previously served a number of Russian defense industry enterprises (NPP Pulsar, SKB Radel). Although Suvorov is no longer the owner of the company, The Insider established he still regularly speaks by phone with its current director. The firm’s highest revenue — more than 1.2 billion rubles ($14.3 million) — came in 2023. By 2025, however, its revenue barely exceeded 200 million rubles ($2.3 million). The company’s website states that it “supplies products of global component manufacturers and works with global wholesale suppliers on the world market.”

A $330 million expansion to its Rocket Park campus in Cape Canaveral, expected to be complete in the summer of 2027, will enable it to produce up to 150 upper stages of its New Glenn rocket annually, Blue Origin said in a blog post.
"These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently," Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the post. That's spurred a flurry of investment, with $92.5 billion invested in the commercial space sector in the first three quarters of 2026, according to a report this week by venture capital firm Space Capital.
Blue Origin, SpaceX and other rocket providers are seeing increasing demand from companies and governments trying to deploy satellites into orbit. Both Blue Origin and SpaceX have their own satellite internet services, and they're launch partners for Amazon, which is in the process of standing up its full Leo low Earth orbit satellite constellation.
SpaceX's Starlink currently dominates the market with more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.

====================================================================================================

Russian court jails businessmen who sold Chinese-made AK-12 parts to Kalashnikov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:23:40 UTC
23:23:40 KST

A court in Khimki in the Moscow Region sentenced five people to terms ranging from 7.5 years suspended to nine years in prison in a case involving the theft of 37.7 million rubles ($451,000) from the Kalashnikov Concern. Investigators said contractors bought substandard parts for AK-12 rifles in China, passed them off as Russian-made, and imported them disguised as ordinary nuts. The Insider calculated that the contract with Kalashnikov was nearly 50 times larger than the supplier’s annual revenue. In 2023, the company reported revenue of just 2.23 million rubles ($27,000) and an average headcount of zero employees.
Alexei Morokhov, technical director of contractor Intertekhnika and CEO of the company Ivanovskie Kovshi, was sentenced to nine years in a maximum-security penal colony. Former Intertekhnika director Yuri Chernyshev received eight years, while Alexei Rubtsov and Olga Firsova were sentenced to 7.5 years each. Another Intertekhnika co-founder, Alexei Ledenev, received a suspended sentence of 7.5-year. Ledenev is known for winning the Russian version of “Dancing with the Stars” in 2010, when he performed with singer Anastasia Stotskaya.
The trial was held behind closed doors.
Chinese parts passed off as Russian-made
The case began in 2023, when the Kalashnikov Concern modernized its 5.45 mm AK-12 assault rifle. To implement the design changes, the company needed semi-finished components for two parts whose production could be outsourced.
That summer, Ivanovskie Kovshi owner Alexei Morokhov offered to fulfill the order. In August, the contractor delivered a test batch that passed quality control. Investigators said Kalashnikov was not told that the parts had been manufactured in China using Russian drawings.
In October 2023, the concern signed a contract with Intertekhnika LLC for 80,000 semi-finished parts worth nearly 110 million rubles ($1.3 million). The contractor agreed to manufacture them in Russia without using counterfeit or falsified products. Investigators found, however, that the company had no production facilities, equipment, or qualified employees.
Instead of manufacturing the parts itself, the defendants arranged purchases from two Chinese companies, Jiangsu Origin Machinery Co., Ltd. and Taizhou Hongze Trading Co., Ltd. The contracts were signed in the name of Ivanovskie Kovshi, and the products were listed in documents as screw nuts.
Some of the Chinese-made parts passed factory inspection. Kalashnikov accepted 2,775 pieces from one batch while rejecting another 819. A second batch yielded 14,414 accepted parts. Investigators nevertheless concluded that the products did not meet mandatory contract requirements and should not have been paid for.
The damage to Kalashnikov was estimated at 37.8 million rubles ($452,000). That figure included money transferred to the contractor and the value of six metric tons of raw material that had supposedly been provided for manufacturing the parts.
A contract 50 times larger than the supplier’s annual revenue
The Insider compared the Kalashnikov contract with Intertekhnika’s financial statements and found that the supplier’s 2023 revenue was only 2.23 million rubles ($27,000). That was 79.6% lower than a year earlier, when the company reported 10.92 million rubles ($130,000) in revenue. Intertekhnika posted a loss of 4.71 million rubles ($56,000) for 2023.
The nearly 110 million-ruble ($1.3 million) Kalashnikov contract was 49 times larger than the contractor’s entire annual revenue. According to data from Russia’s Federal Tax Service, Intertekhnika’s average number of employees in 2023 was zero, and its primary business activity was listed as manufacturing equipment for mining and construction.
Corporate records show another notable detail: when Intertekhnika signed the contract to supply AK-12 parts, half of its charter capital was owned by Maya Silkina, who later became a member of the Ivanovo regional government and head of the regional tourism department. She left the company’s ownership structure only on Jan. 25, 2024, shortly before taking up her government post. Her stake went to her husband, Alexei Morokhov, who has now been sentenced to nine years in prison. Local outlet IvanovoLive had previously reported that the contractor was tied to the official’s family.
In November 2024, Kalashnikov Concern sought to recover 30.06 million rubles ($366,000) from Intertekhnika. It later filed an additional claim for 5.35 million rubles ($64,000). The two claims totaled about 35.4 million rubles ($423,000).
Another Morokhov company, Ivanovskie Kovshi, had already been declared bankrupt by the time the verdict was issued. According to auction materials in case No. A17-10765/2024, the Ivanovo Region Arbitration Court opened bankruptcy liquidation proceedings against the company in November 2025. Its assets were put up for sale in 2026.
Former Kalashnikov procurement director tried separately
A separate criminal case against former Kalashnikov procurement and logistics director Ksenia Grashchenkova is being heard in Izhevsk. She signed the Intertekhnika contract on Kalashnikov’s behalf in October 2023. Investigators accuse her of abuse of authority in carrying out a state defense order, resulting in serious consequences. The case opened Oct. 9, 2026, in Izhevsk’s Leninsky District Court.
Morokhov’s defense had previously denied any intent to deceive the concern. In November 2024, his lawyer, Mikhail Kobets, told IvanovoNews that the customer knew the parts were being made abroad and that the deliveries were carried out under an international outsourcing agreement. The lawyer also said some of the products had passed quality control and that later complaints arose only after management changed at the plant.
The Insider has repeatedly reported that Russia’s defense industry continues to use foreign-made products despite international sanctions. German Gühring tools, for example, continued to be supplied to Russian defense companies, including to the Kalashnikov Concern. Using open-source data, The Insider found 280 contracts for such tools from 2015 to 2023 worth more than 1 billion rubles in total ($11.9 million).
In another investigation, The Insider and IrpiMedia reported on Italian weapons reaching Russia despite sanctions, finding that components made by Benelli, part of the Beretta group, were used in Kalashnikov Concern’s MP-156 semiautomatic hunting carbine.
