Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:23:00 UTC
23:23:00 KST

Can Albania's student protests bring political change?
October 16, 2026
The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.
She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.
"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."
University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.
Escalation after months of protests
Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution." The protests began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.
The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.
Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.
A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.
The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down. They say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.
"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.
Rama breaks his silence
During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.
Then, at 8:03 a.m. local time on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.
"These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.
Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.
The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.
The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the EU. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.
Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.
"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.
"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," Xhemollari told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama's administration alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.
"We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
What could come after the protests?
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.
Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

The ruling was issued by Rabbi Dov Lior, one of the most prominent religious authorities among Israeli occupiers in the West Bank, and was published by Israeli Channel 13.

Lior claimed Palestinians had already received sufficient compensation for planting the trees by consuming their fruit over previous years, and said both the land and harvest should return to what he called their “rightful owners.”
His ruling was not limited to land near illegal settlements, however, and also permitted occupiers to take olive crops from Palestinian areas farther away.
The ruling comes as attacks on Palestinian farmers during the West Bank olive harvest season have intensified, including assaults, preventing farmers from reaching their land, damaging trees and stealing crops.
Such attacks recur during the olive harvest, which peaks in October each year, while this month has seen an increase in attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property.
Palestinian, Israeli and international rights organizations have accused Israeli authorities of failing to stop occupier violence or hold perpetrators accountable despite attacks targeting Palestinians, their homes, farmland, vehicles and other property.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian land are considered illegal under international law, while Palestinians maintain their rights to their land and reject attempts to seize it.

22 House lawmakers press Trump to implement Russia sanctions law. Diesel deal draws bipartisan backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:21:37 UTC
23:21:37 KST

A bipartisan group of 22 House lawmakers is urging President Donald Trump to fully implement the new Russia sanctions law and revoke a license allowing certain Russian diesel transactions. In a letter sent on 15 October, they copied Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and requested details on planned sanctions, tariffs and waivers.
Their request comes as the law’s first requirements fall due on 18 October, while lawmakers from both parties challengethe administration’s decision to allow certain Russian diesel transactions. Some restrictions take effect automatically, while others require presidential action. The law does not specify a penalty for the president missing the deadline.
What the Russia sanctions law requires
Congress passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by votes of 86–11 in the Senate and 262–159 in the House. Trump signed it on 18 September. Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina, died in July.
Restrictions taking effect automatically on 18 October include a ban on US banks and broker-dealers processing transfers to or from the Russian government, a ban on new US investment in Russia, a ban on new US investment in Russia’s energy sector, and a ban on US energy exports to Russia.
Other measures require presidential action by the same date. The law directs Trump to review and sanction Russian officials, oligarchs and shadow-fleet vessels, sanction the Bank of Russia, specified Russian banks and state-owned companies, and impose tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods. Tariffs of up to 100% can apply to goods from countries among the five largest importers of Russian oil or gas, or among the top five countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion.
Trump may waive sanctions, restrictions and tariffs under the law if he first certifies in writing to Congress that a waiver is in the US national interest and submits a report explaining its basis.
The diesel license at the center of the dispute
House members also urged Trump to revoke General License 135, which the Treasury Department issued on 9 October and that is valid until 7 April 2027. It permits certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including imports into the United States. Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets and predicted prices would fall sharply, according to a 9 October Truth Social post.
On 13 October, a bipartisan group of 12 senators also urged Trump to rescind the deal and revoke the license. Seven senators said the deal conflicted with a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports.
The Graham Act says nothing in its provisions affects the Treasury secretary’s existing authority to issue general licenses. That provision does not resolve whether the diesel license complies with the separate 2022 law.
A White House official told Newsweek the administration would comply with the Graham Act. Bessent said the administration would use “all the legal authorities we have” and called the deal “good for the American people,” Fox News reported on 11 October.
How the sanctions could be lifted
Separately, the law sets a process for terminating sanctions, restrictions or duties against Russia. Trump must report to Congress that Russia has signed a peace agreement accepted by Ukraine’s government and ceased military hostilities against Ukraine, as well as activities to overthrow, dismantle or subvert its government. Congress has 30 days to block termination through a joint resolution of disapproval, or 60 days for reports submitted between 10 July and 7 September.

====================================================================================================

13 Habits Food-Waste Experts Practice in Their Own Kitchens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:21:12 UTC
23:21:12 KST

At the grocery store, you’re a person who roasts squash. You make salads. You have exciting plans for fresh herbs. A week later, you’re a person throwing away unused squash, salad, and wilted herbs.
Even food-waste experts know the gap between the meals we imagine and the food we actually eat. Shelie Miller, who studies sustainability at the University of Michigan, understands how an acorn squash can end up in your cart without a plan. “It’s fall. I’m feeling the fall vibes,” she says, describing the temptation. That’s why she and her husband try to stick to a shared grocery list—and know what they’ll do with what they buy.
We asked experts what else they do to keep good intentions out of the trash.
Make a kitchen-sink potato
Once a week, Miller bakes a potato and gives the odds and ends in her refrigerator somewhere to go. Leftover fajita vegetables? On the potato. Little extras from other meals? Those go on, too.
“I always call it a garbage potato, or maybe it’s better to call it a kitchen-sink potato,” she says. The toppings change often enough to keep things interesting: “My husband always plays a guessing game of what my potato is going to be this week.”
The potato solves a familiar problem: You have some food left, but not quite enough to call it lunch. Miller combines those small portions on something she already wants to eat. “It’s such a great blank canvas,” she says.
Stir-fries can serve a similar purpose. But Miller knows where her loyalties lie: “My go-to is a potato.”
Give broccoli stems a chance
Jonathan Deutsch has watched fellow cooks buy cases of broccoli, cut off the florets, and throw away the stems. He considers this a terrible loss. The tender interior of a broccoli stem, he says, is “one of the most delicious vegetables.”
Deutsch, a professor in the department of food and hospitality management and founding director of the Drexel Food Lab, cooks both parts at home. The night before we spoke, he made broccoli salad with tahini and chili crisp. The stem was woody on the outside, so he peeled it, cut up the tender interior, and then air-fried it along with the florets.
Trim the woody bottom and peel away the tough exterior as needed. Deutsch wants people to recognize the good food underneath.
“The same care and love that went into the florets,” he says, “went three inches lower into the stem.”
Give your ingredients a second assignment
A recipe that calls for half a cabbage leaves you with another decision: What happens to the other half?
Miller and her husband try to answer that before they start cooking. Cabbage rolls might take care of some; soup or a roasted side dish can use the rest. The same thinking applies to the tomato paste left in a can or the extra chicken breast in a package. “Getting comfortable with all the different ways you can prepare different ingredients really helps extend the menu,” she says.
Deutsch starts by checking what’s already in his kitchen. When his now-adult daughters were teenagers, they would announce there was nothing to eat. He could usually find the makings of a meal: a can of tuna, a can of beans, or chicken in the freezer. Only after taking stock would he figure out what he needed to buy.
“Instead of generating more waste that you have to deal with, you’re taking surplus food,” he says, “and you’re making it into new things that you want to eat.”
Put your apples in the fridge
Brian Roe is willing to commit to a Costco-size bag of apples. He just doesn’t leave it on the counter.
“I’m an apple kind of person,” says Roe, a professor of agricultural, environmental, and development economics at Ohio State University who leads its Food Waste Collaborative.
He keeps the apples in the refrigerator, where he says he rarely loses one to spoilage. On the counter, he’s more likely to throw a couple away before finishing the bag.
Shop in your freezer first
Miller knows what can happen to food you freeze with the best intentions: “It just goes into the abyss of a freezer.”
Eventually, you clean it out and find “freezer-burned chicken breasts and chili from three years ago,” she says. “What happened?”
She and her husband now make a point of shopping in their freezer before deciding what to buy or cook. Sometimes, that means discovering they already have lunches covered for the week. Other times, it means remembering the portions of tomato paste they froze after a recipe called for only a spoonful.
There are only two of them at home, so a big batch can mean eating the same dinner several nights running. “By the fourth day, the last thing you want is more gumbo,” she says.
Their approach: “We’ll eat a day or two of leftovers. We’ll freeze the rest.” Then, when they need lunches another week, they can pull out a meal they haven’t just eaten three days running.
File your soup
Miller’s husband has figured out how to fit more leftovers in their freezer: He freezes soups and other liquids flat in zip-top bags on a sheet pan. “It ends up like these little folders of soup,” she says.
Once frozen, the thin packages stack neatly, taking up less space than bulky containers. Use bags intended for freezing, leave room for liquid to expand, and follow safe cooling, storage, and reheating practices.
Keep a stock bag
Deutsch keeps a bag in his freezer for the parts of dinner that don’t make it onto the plate: onion trimmings, mushroom bits, and herb stems. When he’s ready to make stock, he has a head start.
“Stock is like magic,” he says. When people wonder why their soup doesn’t taste as good as their favorite restaurant’s, he points to what might be missing: stock, along with generous seasoning. He also uses it in place of water when cooking rice, polenta, or vegetables to give them extra flavor.
He’s selective about what goes into the stock. Add beet scraps, and “you’re gonna have a pink or brownish stock,” he says. Add broccoli trimmings, and “it’s gonna have a little bit of a cabbagey broccoli smell.” That could be delicious in broccoli mac and cheese, but it’s probably not the flavor you want in butternut squash soup. “You have to be a little strategic about what goes in there,” he says.
Make leftovers worth looking forward to
Roe’s air fryer helps him get another meal out of restaurant leftovers. Recently, he used it to reheat half a tuna steak and vegetables his wife had brought home. “That makes things kind of tasty and crispy again,” he says.
He thinks about the next meal while putting food away, taking an extra minute to make leftovers easy to reheat. The goal is “storing your leftovers in a way that helps you want to use them the next time,” he says.
Sometimes, that means turning last night’s teriyaki chicken into today’s salad. His adult son has found another opening for leftovers: breakfast. “They’re the freshest they’ll ever be because it’s the first meal after,” Roe says.
Ask for ideas before buying more groceries
Ground turkey, two green peppers, and feta: Is that dinner? Deutsch suggests asking a chatbot before adding anything else to your grocery list.
He’s experimented with AI to find ways to use ingredients on hand, and recommends giving it more than a list of what’s in the fridge. Tell it how much time you have, what equipment you’re using, and how comfortable you are in the kitchen.
“Make me an easy recipe with these ingredients,” he suggests instructing your AI platform of choice. You can ask for something that takes less than 30 minutes, too—so you don’t discover halfway through the instructions that dinner needs to marinate overnight. “You could really customize it,” he says.
Buy portions that match your appetite
Throwing away part of a chicken breast means wasting more than dinner. It also wastes the resources used to raise and feed the chicken. Animal products generally have a larger environmental footprint than plant foods, Miller explains, which makes keeping meat, eggs, and dairy from going uneaten especially consequential.
Her rule: “Respect the protein.”
Miller and her husband still eat meat, but they’ve started serving smaller portions. “Meat is an accent to the meal,” she says. They’re trying to avoid a familiar outcome: “We both have two huge chicken breasts and waste a quarter of them.”
Plan for your guests—not an army
Roe describes himself as an evangelist for buying less food—a habit that’s followed him home, “maybe not to the happiness of everybody in my household,” he says.
When they’re having people over, Roe tries to calculate what guests will actually eat, while his spouse comes from a tradition of making sure there’s enough to “feed the army.”
At Thanksgiving, Roe uses the Guest-imator, an online tool from Save the Food that estimates how much to prepare for a gathering. “A lot of it is just buying less or really thinking about what’s being purchased and why,” he says.
Don’t make plastic-free the only goal
Miller studies the environmental impact of plastic packaging. She also has a freezer full of soup in zip-top bags. “Very honestly, we go through a lot of single-use plastic,” she says.
Her research helps explain that choice. A 2022 analysis she co-authored found that plastic packaging accounted for less than 10% of the total environmental footprint of 23 out of 30 foods across most measures examined. And in a 2019 study comparing meal kits with grocery-store meals, the greenhouse-gas savings from reduced food waste outweighed the extra packaging emissions.
Miller uses reusable containers for lunches and tries to minimize disposable items. But she considers what the packaging helps her accomplish. “A good zip-top bag is really hard to compete with for certain applications,” she says.
For her, the environmental cost of throwing away food matters more than the bag used to save it. “When you look at the environmental impacts of food waste versus a single-use plastic bag, the food waste is the much more important thing,” she says.
“My big philosophy is not to sweat the small stuff,” she says.
Compost what you can’t use—but try to eat it first
Miller collects food scraps in a metal pail with a liner. “It’s nothing fancy,” she says. But she doesn’t consider composting a substitute for eating the food she buys.
“A lot of folks think, well, hey, I’m composting, so it’s OK to waste food,” she says. Composting can’t recover all the resources used to produce food that never gets eaten, so she focuses first on using what’s in her kitchen—whether it becomes lunch, soup, or next week’s potato.
When food does go uneaten, “throw it in the compost rather than the trash if you have that option available,” she says.

France's Macron warns EU leaders they need budget deal before year-end, say diplomats

France's Macron warns EU leaders they need budget deal before year-end, say diplomats
BRUSSELS, Oct 16 - French President Emmanuel Macron has warned EU leaders they should agree the bloc's next long-term budget before the end of the year because elections in several countries, including France, will make a deal harder to secure, two diplomats said.
EU leaders met in Brussels on Thursday night to discuss the bloc's next seven-year budget, which requires unanimous approval and routinely triggers some of the EU's most contentious negotiations between net contributors and net recipients. The 2028-2034 spending plan is no exception, with a special summit scheduled for late November in an effort to reach agreement.
"It's true. If you don't do it now, it will be even more difficult in 2027 and we won't be ready in 2028," a diplomat from a northern European country familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
An eastern European diplomat, confirming the French warning, said the end of December was not a hard deadline, but negotiations should not drag much beyond the first few months of 2027.
The urgency reflects a crowded election calendar across Europe next year, including a presidential election in France in April and May that could propel far-right leader Marine Le Pen to power. She has pledged to cut France's contribution to the EU budget and has urged EU leaders not to strike a deal before the French vote.
Asked about Le Pen's criticism, French officials noted that France was far from the only country heading to the polls next year. Poland, Slovakia, Italy, Greece and Finland are also due to hold elections. REUTERS

Qatar announces ‘massive’ solar plant project in Lebanon

Qatar announces ‘massive’ solar plant project in Lebanon
Sheikh Mohammed also discussed Israeli ‘violations’ in Lebanese territory with Prime Minister Nawaf Salam.
Qatar’s prime minister has announced plans to set up what he described as a “massive” solar plant in Lebanon to help ease its energy crisis.
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani made the announcement during his visit to Beirut on Friday, after meeting his Lebanese counterpart, Nawaf Salam.
“We have agreed to establish a comprehensive framework for cooperation in the energy sector and to present viable solutions,” Sheikh Mohammed said.
QatarEnergy has reached an agreement with French company TotalEnergies to jointly develop a solar power plant in Lebanon as an initial project.
The aim is to develop a major investment project “that would benefit the Lebanese economy, as well as the Qatari companies and entities participating in it”, he added.
Prime Minister Salam said he would put the plans for Lebanon’s electricity sector to the Lebanese Cabinet soon.
“The Qatari side will fund, implement and activate the project without any cost on the Lebanese state,” Lebanon’s leader said, adding that such a move is important because of the country’s financial crisis.
Lebanon’s state electricity company is one of the biggest sources of debt, haemorrhaging about $40bn over past decades with a bloated workforce and outdated infrastructure. The company provides only a few hours of electricity a day and the state, until a year ago, took advances from the Central Bank when diesel fuel ran out.
Sheikh Mohammed said Doha stands in “solidarity with the Lebanese people” and the entire region “in this dire hour”. Lebanon has been struggling with multiple energy crises in recent years and the situation has been compounded by the country’s financial collapse and Israel’s ongoing assault.
Earlier in the day, the Qatari PM also met Lebanon’s president and parliament speaker.
Among the topics discussed was the situation in southern Lebanon, where Israel continues its assault, capturing dozens of towns and villages.
Sheikh Mohammed said “Israeli violations within the Lebanese territories” were a large part of his talks.
He said that Israel should withdraw from Lebanon and cease its attacks, adding that Qatar is working in coordination with the United States to help lay the groundwork for future reconstruction in southern Lebanon to allow displaced people to return to their homes.
Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have continued despite a ceasefire agreed in June. Under the agreement brokered by the US, the Lebanese government is to disarm Iran-backed Hezbollah. In return, Israeli forces will gradually withdraw from southern areas that they occupy. However, Hezbollah is not part of the agreement and has refused to disarm until Israel withdraws from the country.
Lebanese authorities say Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people in the country since March. About 1.2 million people were also displaced in Lebanon at the height of the war.
Although most have returned home since the June ceasefire, more than 300,000 people remain displaced, according to the International Organization for Migration.
Lebanon’s PM Salam thanked Qatar for its “continuous” support during some of Lebanon’s “darkest hours”.

SIR protests: Opposition has found common ground. But can it stay united?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:19:22 UTC
23:19:22 KST

Members of INDIA bloc at high-tea hosted at Rahul Gandhi's residence in Delhi (File photo)
NEW DELHI: "All protests are one," Congress leader Rahul Gandhi declared on Wednesday as opposition parties rallied behind two Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders sent to judicial custody following demonstrations against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke welcomed Rahul's support, thanking the Congress leader for standing with the arrested protesters.Just days ago, that was hardly how things looked on Delhi's streets, where Congress and CJP appeared to be competing for space and prominence while leading separate campaigns against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The Congress-led INDIA bloc was organising its own demonstrations, while CJP, which had mobilised thousands of protesters in July, prepared separately for Jantar Mantar 2.0 on October 10.AAP, TMC and the Left were willing to join CJP's agitation, but Congress kept its distance. Their objective was the same, but they were fighting for it separately. Many wondered why.On October 10, the Delhi police enforced an unprecedented clampdown in the national capital to prevent mobilisation for CJP’s Jantar Mantar 2.0. Thousands of protesters were dragged on the streets and detained.
Delhi Police detained more than 3,000 people attempting to reach Jantar Mantar for the protest.
Such was the intensity of police action that the CJP stir could not even take off.
The top CJP leaders were arrested from a plane on landing in Delhi, drawing flak from some quarters for their easy “surrender.” Several political parties stood with the cockroaches, but the Congress stayed away.The trigger for greater unity came after CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were arrested on October 14 following their attempt to protest at Jantar Mantar by waving the Tricolour. Rahul Gandhi came out in open support for first time, and CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke thanked him.
What Rahul Gandhi said after CJP leaders were arrested.
The dynamics now seem to be changing, with Congress and CJP more willing to support each other, if not formally join forces. But why? Have both sides realised the limitations of organising separate protests for the same cause? Let's decode this shift.
From NEET protests to Jantar Mantar 2.0
In June, when CJP protested against the NEET paper leak and demanded the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Congress stayed away. Rahul was leading his own programme, Chhatron Ki Goonj, on similar issues.AAP, the Left and social activists joined CJP at Jantar Mantar. The movement gained momentum with Sonam Wangchuk and AISA leader Neha Bora sitting on an indefinite fast. But Congress continued to stay away.On July 20, Delhi Police launched a major operation against students and young protesters who had reached the capital on CJP's call. The next day, Rahul joined the agitation and staged a sit-in outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence, shifting Congress's focus from its own campaign.
Police personnel restrain Congress leader Rahul Gandhi during a protest near PMO
However, with the government entering negotiations with CJP and later accepting its demands, including Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation, Congress was left on the sidelines.The anti-paper leak protests were perhaps a wake-up call for political parties, especially Congress, as large numbers of young people mobilised behind CJP. Prime Minister Modi subsequently turned to Instagram to reach out to Gen Z, while other parties were left to rethink their youth outreach.
The SIR and 'vote chori' campaign
Congress had been at the forefront of the 'vote chori' campaign, with Rahul holding press conferences highlighting alleged discrepancies in electoral rolls. The party also led a yatra in Bihar ahead assembly elections in the state.The momentum gradually faded, before an Indian Express report on differences within the Election Commission over SIR returned the issue to centre stage. CJP took up the issue, organising a Mumbai rally and setting an October 10 deadline for Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, failing which it called for Jantar Mantar 2.0.Congress and the INDIA bloc also stepped up their campaign, announcing a six-point action plan that included an October 6 street protest. With CJP's mobilisation approaching, INDIA bloc leaders returned to the streets for four consecutive days until October 9, perhaps keen not to be left on the sidelines again. But on October 10, the D-day of CJP mobilisation, Rahul was in Chennai and the Congress stayed away.Another change had taken place between July and October. Civil society groups and activists associated with CJP's earlier movement were now actively participating in the INDIA bloc's SIR campaign.The most prominent was Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students' Association (AISA). During the October 12 march towards the Supreme Court, Rahul walked with his hands on the shoulders of Bora and Priyanka Gandhi, with senior opposition leaders following behind.
Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, along with student leader Neha Bora, during INDIA bloc's anti-CEC protests.
The moment appeared to signal Congress's willingness to bring prominent youth protest faces into its campaign. Political analyst Uday Chandra explained the significance of this shift."Congress under RG recognises that youth-led protests have mobilised ordinary people beyond the reach of traditional party organisations. Neha Bora is an interesting bridge between these worlds, though she leads AISA, a Left student organisation, not CJP," Chandra said.He also pointed to a shift in student politics. "What I find most interesting is that AISA and NSUI are fighting together today. This wasn't the case in the past," he said.
AISA president Neha Bora calls for a united fight against the BJP
As CJP leaders' arrests drew support across party lines, this cooperation was no longer limited to student organisations.
Opposition closes ranks
The support for CJP has not come from Congress alone.TMC leader Mamata Banerjee condemned the arrests as an attempt to intimidate young protesters. Party MP Abhishek Banerjee accused the BJP of arresting people for waving the national flag, calling it "BJP's new Pakistanified Bharat". Mahua Moitra also expressed solidarity.AAP chief Arvind Kejriwal questioned whether waving the Tricolour could be a crime. DMK president MK Stalin offered legal assistance to the two CJP leaders, while NCP(SP)'s Supriya Sule and Shiv Sena (UBT)'s Aaditya Thackeray condemned the arrests.The Left maintained its support. Former Kerala chief minister Pinarayi Vijayan criticised the arrests. CPI general secretary D Raja called the police action undemocratic and said his party's student and youth organisations would intensify their campaign for the right to protest at Jantar Mantar.
From Mamata to Kejriwal, opposition leaders back arrested CJP leaders
The growing opposition presence was visible beyond Delhi. On Thursday, Vijay's Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), which had stayed away from earlier anti-CEC demonstrations, joined a Congress-led INDIA bloc protest in Chennai. TVK had joined the alliance on October 3; leaders from VCK, MDMK and other partners also participated.More protests may follow. NCP(SP) spokesperson Anish Gawande said Rahul had asked INDIA bloc leaders to be prepared for further demonstrations at 24 hours' notice.These parties have their own priorities and have not always followed the same protest programme. Yet, from Delhi to Chennai, more opposition leaders are speaking out on the same issue. CJP and the INDIA bloc, however, have not announced any joint protest programme.
The counter
The BJP has rejected the opposition's allegations, accusing rivals of using street demonstrations to question democratic institutions after electoral defeats.On October 10, BJP MP Ravi Shankar Prasad said: "We are not opposed to protests, but you have weaponised street protests because of your electoral defeats."BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra also questioned whether events at Jantar Mantar represented the larger picture of India. The Election Commission has denied allegations of political bias in electoral-roll revision.
Together, but still separate?
For CJP, opposition support presents an opportunity and a challenge. The group has built its identity as an independent youth-led movement, but the detention of its leaders and criticism of its leadership raise questions about sustaining the agitation without established parties.Uday Chandra cautioned against reading too much into the cooperation."There is certainly a convergence of interests at this moment, but we should not mistake that for anything akin to a formal alliance. The police crackdown and detention of protesters have created a common cause for the CJP and the INDIA bloc," Chandra said.He noted that CJP's independence has been central to its youth appeal and that its leaders have criticised the opposition in the past.Political commentator Sugata Srinivasaraju questioned whether CJP had established a support base strong enough to sustain a larger movement. He warned that becoming an extension of Congress could cost it its independent identity. Nor was it clear whether CJP would lead any joint campaign or give way to a larger party.For Congress, CJP's ability to mobilise young people is attractive. But could closer cooperation undermine the independence that made those movements appealing in the first place?Chandra warned: "The autonomy of these youth movements is precisely what makes them politically significant. If parties or their student unions undermine that autonomy, the movement may splinter amidst loud bickering, and can even fizzle out following discord."CJP founder Dipke has maintained that the group will remain an independent pressure group, despite sharing the opposition's demand for Kumar's removal.
Dipke reiterated that CJP will always remain a pressure group.
Has the opposition finally found its feet?
The INDIA bloc has struggled to present a united front since its inception. Disagreements over leadership, seat-sharing and political priorities have divided parties, and Congress has faced criticism over its lack of efforts to keep the coalition together.The protests against the CEC have offered a different picture: common ground emerging from demonstrations rather than electoral negotiations. Differences remain, however. AAP and DMK, once part of the INDIA bloc, are still not ready to join hands with Congress.But does a greater presence on the streets mean the opposition has finally found its feet?Sugata Srinivasaraju disagreed that the opposition had been missing in action. Parties, he argued, had always been active, even if street demonstrations had recently become more frequent."More frequent protests do not necessarily mean a more effective opposition. Without planning, structure and a clear strategy, such demonstrations can become counterproductive, with little lasting political impact," he said.He also questioned what the prominence of youth leaders from outside Congress said about its leadership.
"It also reflects the opposition's inability to lead itself and absence of strong, charismatic leaders of its own. By bringing in faces from youth-led movements, it is, in a way, acknowledging that leadership gap. But there is a risk that leaders like Neha Bora could lose their independent identity within a larger political organisation, much like what happened with Kanhaiya Kumar," he said.The coming together of opposition parties has changed the picture on the streets, but questions remain over whether they can sustain protests, develop new leaders and turn a common cause into a coordinated campaign.For years, the question has been: Where is the opposition? With parties now finding common ground after months of differences, could that question finally have an answer?

Osaka: The Castle Lights Up to Celebrate 160 Years of Italy-Japan Relations
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:19:11 CEST
23:19:11 KST

Osaka Castle has been transformed into a vast canvas of light and sound thanks to the debut of “SINFONIA,” a projection-mapping show designed to celebrate the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan and, at the same time, the 45th anniversary of the sister-city relationship between Osaka and Milan. The event will run through October 25, with evening projections, for which organizers estimate an attendance of over 100,000 spectators. The lighting ceremony was attended by the Italian Ambassador to Japan, Mario Vattani; the Mayor of Osaka, Hideyuki Yokoyama; the Managing Director of Bulgari Japan, Denis Coan; and actor Ren Meguro, the brand’s ambassador. The approximately six-minute multimedia presentation traces four centuries of cultural dialogue between the two countries, with the narrative beginning with the Tenshō Mission’s first papal audience in Rome in 1585, then moving on to the establishment of official relations in 1866, and culminates in the legacy of the Italian Pavilion at Expo 2025. “This impressive multimedia project celebrates 160 years of deep friendship, blending artistic sensibilities, history, and architectural beauty in the heart of Osaka,” stated Ambassador Vattani. “Through the synergy of lights, music, and design, we tell a story of cooperation that began in the 16th century, continued through the great success of the 2025 World’s Fair, and is projected powerfully toward the future, thanks also to the determination of the leaders of both nations to strengthen and further solidify the Special Strategic Partnership between Italy and Japan.” As for the collaboration with Bulgari, according to Vattani, it demonstrates how Italian fine craftsmanship and design can respectfully integrate with Japanese traditions, giving shape to a shared narrative of their respective identities. The initiative is sponsored by the Italian Embassy, the Asahi Shimbun newspaper, Bulgari, and Dentsu, under the patronage of the City of Osaka and in collaboration with the Consulate General of Italy in Osaka.

Russian wrestler strikes gold at world championships in US
Russian wrestler Alina Shevchenko has struck gold at the Under-23 World Wrestling Championships in Las Vegas, defeating a Belarusian rival in the women’s 68kg final.
Her triumph comes as European countries continue to shut top Russian athletes out of major international competitions despite clearance from sporting authorities.
Shevchenko defeated Belarusian wrestler Kseniya Tsiarenia in the women’s 68kg final on Friday. Japan’s Rai Hoshino and Italy’s Laura Godino took bronze. The championships, which began on October 12, run until Sunday.
The victory follows a decision in May by United World Wrestling (UWW) to lift all restrictions on Russian and Belarusian wrestlers, allowing them to compete internationally across all age categories under their national flags and anthems.
The move marked a major reversal of restrictions imposed after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, when Russian and Belarusian athletes were barred from numerous international events or forced to compete under neutral status.
Russian competitors continue to face obstacles elsewhere, particularly in Europe, where several countries have denied entry to athletes despite their clearance by international sporting bodies.
Most recently, the Netherlands refused visas to three leading Russian gymnasts – Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova – for the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam, scheduled for October 17-25. The tournament is part of the qualification process for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
“There are clear attempts by certain countries to influence the outcome of competitions by deliberately excluding the strongest,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Thursday.
The Russian Gymnastics Federation condemned the Dutch decision as “direct discrimination,” saying the visa refusals violated the principle of equal conditions for Olympic qualification. Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev announced plans to seek the removal of Rotterdam’s Olympic qualifying status.
The Dutch refusal is the latest in a string of incidents. Croatia attempted to block nine Russian gymnasts from this summer’s European Championships, Russian junior canoe slalom teams missed the World Championships in Poland, and Russian archers were unable to compete at a World Cup event in Spain because of visa problems.
The restrictions persist despite World Gymnastics restoring Russian participation under national flags and anthems in May and the International Olympic Committee provisionally reinstating the Russian Olympic Committee in July.
Several European governments oppose the return, with Brussels reportedly considering visa restrictions and funding cuts for sporting bodies that readmit Russian athletes. Moscow has challenged continuing bans at the Court of Arbitration for Sport, including World Athletics’ refusal to readmit Russian competitors until the Ukraine conflict is settled.
Despite years of restrictions, Russian athletes have continued to claim international titles. Russian competitors won eight gold medals at the 2026 Winter Paralympics, while junior figure skaters swept all four disciplines at a Grand Prix event in China in August after a four-year absence. Moscow has argued that excluding some of the world’s strongest athletes undermines international sport and the credibility of its competitions.

Bulgaria Posts Eurozone’s Second-Highest Inflation at 5.6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Bulgaria Posts Eurozone’s Second-Highest Inflation at 5.6%
Bulgaria recorded the second-highest annual inflation rate in the eurozone in September, at 5.6%, while inflation across both the eurozone and the European Union climbed to 3.8%, according to Eurostat data.
Bulgaria’s Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) increased by 5.6% year over year, compared with 5.0% in August. Only Lithuania, at 6.1%, had a higher rate among eurozone members. Across the EU, Romania registered the highest annual inflation at 6.5%, placing Bulgaria third among the bloc’s 27 member states.
The National Statistical Institute (NSI) reported Bulgaria’s annual inflation at 5.7%, a slightly different figure resulting from the use of a different index.
Bulgaria’s annual inflation stood at 4% in September 2025. During 2026, it reached 6% in April and 6.3% in May, before easing to 5.2% in June and 4.4% in July. The rate then rose again in August and September.
In the eurozone, annual inflation increased to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August and 2.2% in September 2025. The EU’s rate followed the same monthly trend, rising to 3.8% from 3.2%, compared with 2.6% a year earlier. Bulgaria’s rate was 1.8 percentage points above the average for both areas.
Monthly consumer prices rose by 0.6% in the eurozone and across the EU in September, while prices in Bulgaria were unchanged from August.
Sweden recorded the EU’s lowest annual inflation rate at 1%, followed by Hungary and Denmark, both at 2.1%. Compared with August, annual inflation declined in one EU member state, remained stable in three and increased in 23.
Among the EU’s largest economies, September inflation reached 3.3% in Germany, 3.4% in France, 4.2% in Italy and 5% in Spain. Greece recorded a rate of 5.1%.
Higher energy costs were the main driver of eurozone inflation, contributing 1.71 percentage points to the annual rate. Services accounted for another 1.52 percentage points, while non-energy industrial goods contributed 0.29 percentage points and food, alcohol and tobacco added 0.25 percentage points.
Energy prices in the eurozone rose by 18.9% year over year in September, accelerating from a 14.3% increase in August. Services inflation also picked up, reaching 3.2% after 3% the previous month.
Annual price growth for food, alcohol and tobacco accelerated to 1.3% from 1.1% in August. Prices for unprocessed food increased by 4%, while processed food, alcohol and tobacco rose by 0.4%. Non-energy industrial goods became 1.1% more expensive year over year, down from 1.2% growth in August.
Core inflation in the eurozone, excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, reached 2.5% in September, compared with 2.4% in August. On a monthly basis, core inflation increased by 0.2%.

Thousands of pumpkins have transformed the grounds of Groot-Bijgaarden Castle near Brussels into a colourful autumn wonderland for the annual Pumpkimania festival. This year's theme, “The Magic of the Forest”, features towering sculptures of foxes, owls and deer covered in pumpkins of every shape and size, sourced from Belgium, Germany and Portugal.
The star attraction is a giant pumpkin weighing 772 kilograms, grown for the castle's traditional weigh-off on 26 September. Visitors can also watch giant pumpkins being turned into makeshift kayaks for rides across the castle lake.
Organisers expect around 50,000 visitors before the festival closes on 1 November. Families can take part in pumpkin-carving workshops at weekends, while the Halloween programme will see the castle open daily until 7pm from 24 October. The festivities will end with a giant pumpkin-smashing event.
Despite a difficult growing season following a hot summer, the displays have filled the estate with thousands of pumpkins. Located in Dilbeek, about 10 kilometres from central Brussels, the festival costs €16 for adults and €9 for children aged 5 to 14, with free entry for younger children.

Italy names senior Israelis, Katz in probe over Gaza flotilla activists
ROME, Oct 16 - Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz and senior military, police and prison officials have been placed under investigation in Italy over the treatment of Gaza flotilla activists, Italian prosecutors said on Friday.
The move expands an investigation that was previously focused on Israel's far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir.
The case concerns suspected torture, kidnapping, personal injury, robbery and damage when Israeli forces intercepted small fleets of boats headed towards Gaza in 2025 and 2026, the Rome prosecutors' office said in a statement.
Investigators opened the probe after complaints from 50 Italian citizens who were detained by Israeli authorities following two Global Sumud Flotilla missions in September to October 2025 and April to May 2026.
Katz did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ben-Gvir in June dismissed news that he was under investigation, saying he would "continue to stand proudly alongside our fighters".
DEATH THREATS AND BEATINGS ALLEGED
Prosecutors said activists detained after the first mission had reported beatings, injuries, death threats, insults and accusations of terrorism.
Activists involved in the second mission reported even harsher treatment, including beatings in the dark, the use of tasers and rubber bullets, the statement said.
Investigators had identified various individuals forming the military and police chains of command involved in the operations, prosecutors said.
Besides Katz and Ben-Gvir, prosecutors named 12 senior Israeli military, police and prison officials as suspects, including military chief Eyal Zamir.
Zamir also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Prosecutors said they had sent Israel a request for judicial assistance in June, seeking information needed to reconstruct events and establish individual responsibility. They did not say whether Israeli authorities had responded.
The prosecutors said they had also held talks at the European Union's judicial cooperation agency Eurojust because similar investigations into the two flotilla missions were under way in other unnamed European countries.
Under Italian law, crimes committed abroad against Italian citizens can be prosecuted in Rome.
Being placed under investigation in Italy does not imply guilt and does not automatically lead to a trial. However, if the probe determines that charges are warranted, prosecutors could lodge a formal request for trial.
Flotilla organisers say they aimed to break Israel's blockade of Gaza by delivering humanitarian assistance. Israel says its naval blockade on Gaza is lawful. REUTERS

The report comes as US President Donald Trump has ramped pressure on Zelensky to end the strikes, which he blames for surging global energy prices. In his interview with Newsmax on Thursday, Trump called Ukraine’s actions “a disgrace.”
In an article published the same day, the WSJ said that Republican Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer brought the deal to the Ukrainian leader during their visit to Kiev last Friday. The outlet claimed that it was told by unnamed sources that Zelensky had agreed to the proposal.
The extended Starlink coverage should help Ukraine target missile launchers inside Russia, according to the report.
Kiev, which is experiencing an acute shortage of US-supplied Patriot air defense missiles, has been struggling to contain Russia’s large-scale missile and drone strikes against military-related infrastructure across Ukraine. Moscow says the raids are being carried out in response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks on civilian targets in Russia, including energy facilities.
The Ukrainians, who have relied heavily on Starlink during the conflict with Russia for battlefield communications and controlling drones, have been “terrified” by the slowdown of satellite internet provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company this week, the WSJ said.
On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials and frontline commanders complained that Starlink terminals had suddenly stopped working when UAVs flew faster than 100 mph, disrupting some combat missions. According to Reuters, the order to slow down the service came directly from the White House. Zelensky said on Friday that Starlink’s speed has increased over the last couple of days, but the restrictions haven’t been fully lifted yet.
Earlier this week, Zelensky confirmed reports that the US had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kiev if it kept ignoring Trump’s demands to cease energy strikes inside Russia. Officials in Kiev also complained about receiving no advance warning from the Americans before Russian missile strikes.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that Russia was unaware of the Starlink slowdown for the Ukrainians, noting that “overall, of course, it would be better if such amazing technology… was not used for military purposes at all.”
Last month, Peskov warned that allowing Starlink to be used to facilitate strikes deep into Russian territory would be “a very harmful, potentially dangerous and misconceived step.”
The American authorities apparently don’t require consent from Musk to expand the coverage of Starlink’s military component, known as Starshield, for Ukraine. The SpaceX CEO said earlier this week that its systems “are owned and controlled” by the US government, with the Pentagon and the US president deciding on the limits on their speed or usage.
On Sunday, Musk backed Trump’s suggestion that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” In a comment to a White House video with the US president’s criticism of the Ukrainian leader, the entrepreneur said that “Zelensky has gone too far.”
Zelensky reportedly wanted to personally discuss the expansion of Starlink coverage with Musk during his US visit to Washington in July, but the SpaceX CEO turned down the meeting.

How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:12:13 UTC
23:12:13 KST

How Israeli firm’s ‘zero-click’ malware attack poses global security risk
A new ‘zero-click’ hack uses ads to target victims without any action needed on their part.
Just visiting a page or refreshing an app can be enough to fall victim to a malware attack in which your personal data is stolen from a laptop or phone, researchers have found. You are not even required to “click” on anything.
An Israeli spyware firm has been found to be behind the first-known instance of “zero-click” targeted advertising in which fraudsters or spies can steal private data and send it to external servers, with Al Jazeera journalists among the victims.
In June 2025, 45 devices used by Al Jazeera staff – including several who reported on sensitive subjects – were targeted with spyware which installed itself without the need to open or download any files.
An investigation by the Canada-based academic research unit Citizen Lab, prompted by Al Jazeera’s initial internal probe into the issue, discovered that the Israeli company Candiru was behind the attacks.
Analysts say the findings are “incredibly concerning”, as they confirm the existence of a new global security threat. “We knew we were headed in this direction and now it is out in the public,” Remesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies at the University of California in Los Angeles, US, told Al Jazeera.
“This is the next level, because people are being microtargeted,” he said. “This is the point we’ve come to when it comes to surveillance.”
How ‘zero-click’ malware works
Al Jazeera’s in-house technology team first discovered unusual patterns on devices used by some journalists in 2024. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera in 2025 provided a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Malicious advertisements were bought by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company presenting itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but which actually operates as a facilitator for mercenary spyware partners.
Its advertisement network identified Al Jazeera staff, then quietly redirected them to an infected server belonging to Candiru. The spyware firm was blacklisted by the US government in 2021, when Citizen Lab found it was responsible for the illegal hacking and surveillance of at least 100 activists, journalists and political activists across 10 countries.
Al Jazeera Media Network has condemned the targeting of its staff members’ devices and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
Cybersecurity analyst and author Eddy Willems said the advertisements used automatically infect devices the moment they pop up on the screen, but there is an important technical nuance. “Executing code inside the browser does not automatically give an attacker full control over the computer,” Willems told Al Jazeera.
“To escape the browser’s isolated environment – the ‘sandbox’ – the attacker may need a second vulnerability,” Willems said, adding that an advanced spyware operation can combine several vulnerabilities.
“The attacker attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to bypass security boundaries. This is precisely what makes this type of attack so dangerous,” the analyst said.
Once the device is infected, the malicious software is designed to collect a wide range of sensitive data, including files, documents, and browser data such as cookies, bookmarks, and saved credentials.
It can also capture keystrokes, take screenshots, record microphone and webcam input, and extract emails and messages from popular communication platforms. To avoid triggering security mechanisms, the spyware often uses encrypted communication channels and breaks up stolen data into smaller chunks sent over time.
Advertising: A new global security threat?
Analysts say Citizen Lab’s findings point to the escalation of an existing threat, which expands the scale and reach of traditional cyberattacks and makes them much harder to detect.
While “zero-click” attacks are not completely new, the findings outline a new technique through which online advertisements are used as a route to infection.
Stephen O’Shaughnessy, a lecturer in cybersecurity at the TU Dublin Blanchardstown campus in Ireland, explained that when a user opens a website or app, an automated auction sells the advertisement space in a fraction of a second. That auction shares data about the victim, including the device ID, IP address, rough location and the app or site they are on.
“Discover-Tech posed as an ordinary advertiser, used that data to find their target and win the auction for that person’s screen,” O’Shaughnessy told Al Jazeera. “Anyone with a phone or browser that shows ads can be reached, without the attacker needing their phone number or email.”
“Because no message or link is involved, there is almost nothing for the victim to notice,” he added.
Discover-Tech appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served advertisements via major networks such as Google, Yandex and Beeswax.
In its report, Citizen Lab said this illustrates the structural flaws in the online advertising system, which essentially failed to detect or prevent the abuse.
Discover-Tech advertisements have popped up on devices used by personnel in national-security-sensitive networks around the world, including those of various ministries of defence, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organisations and media outlets, Citizen Lab found.
The research unit said these advertisements have also appeared on networks used by the United Nations, NATO, the European Parliament, the European Commission and the Council of the European Union’s General Secretariat.
‘Almost nobody was watching’
Government networks have also been targeted in at least 24 countries, including the United States, Italy, Denmark, Norway, Australia, Russia, Mexico and Israel itself. Networks of media organisations have also been targeted, mainly in Australia, Denmark and Sweden, according to Citizen Lab.
In a separate report, New York-based advertising security firm Confiant said its own investigations had found that some of Discover-Tech’s advertisements also appeared in critical networks used by the Pentagon, the United Nations International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court.
O’Shaughnessy said infection has not been confirmed there – only profiling of users. “But that alone is concerning, he said. “The ad system was built to send code from strangers to billions of screens with pinpoint targeting. Almost nobody was watching it from a security angle.”
The analyst said the risk remains low for most people as these attacks are expensive and aimed at specific targets. “For individuals at high risk, like journalists and officials, the best first defence is to install an ad blocker, switch off their advertising ID through their phone’s privacy settings, keep everything updated, and turn on Lockdown Mode or Android’s Advanced Protection,” he said.
Precautions also need to be taken within the industry and at government level. “To combat this, the ad industry needs to properly vet who’s buying ads,” O’Shaughnessy said, while “regulators need to stop personal data being sprayed out to thousands of unknown bidders in every auction.”

Netanyahu, opposition blocs tied as 55% back unity government if election inconclusive: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:12:02 UTC
23:12:02 KST

Abdul Raouf Arnaout, Mohammad Sio
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
An Israeli opinion poll published on Friday showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition tied, with neither reaching the majority needed to form a government, while 55% of respondents favored a unity government if the upcoming election produces no decisive result.
The Maariv poll, published 11 days before the Oct. 27 general election, showed that if voting were held today, both Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition would win 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset.
Arab lawmakers, meanwhile, were projected to win 14 seats, while the Reservists Party would secure four, without indicating which bloc it would support.
A government requires the backing of at least 61 lawmakers. Otherwise, Israel could face another election.
Both Netanyahu’s camp and the main Jewish opposition parties reject relying on Arab parties to form a government.
According to the poll, Netanyahu’s bloc would be divided among Likud with 18 seats, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power eight, the religious United Torah Judaism party eight, Shas seven, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism six and Ofer Winter’s Amcha Yisrael four.
The Jewish opposition would include Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21 seats, Naftali Bennett’s Together 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats nine and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu eight.
Among Arab parties, the Joint List led by Yousef Jabareen was projected to win eight seats, while Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List, or Ra’am, would receive six.
The Reservists Party, headed by Yoaz Hendel, is projected to win four seats, with the poll not determining which camp it would support.
On the preferred candidate for prime minister, Eisenkot, a former Israeli army chief of staff, remained ahead of Netanyahu with 48% support compared with 41% for the incumbent.
Israelis do not directly elect their prime minister. The post goes to the politician able to form a coalition backed by at least 61 lawmakers.
If the political deadlock continues, Israel could face another election unless a unity government is formed.
The poll found that 55% of Israelis prefer a national unity government over another election if the Oct. 27 vote fails to produce a clear outcome.
Another 27% said they favor holding a new election, while 18% were undecided.
The results showed differences between the two camps.
Among opposition voters, 54% said they support a unity government provided it is headed by a leader from their bloc.
Among coalition voters, 36% backed a unity government led by Netanyahu, while 32% preferred another election if no clear result emerged.
Maariv said the poll was conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute among a random sample of 700 Israelis, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points.

Experts proposed strengthening early warning and fisheries advisories using satellite technologies (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: As climate change alters ocean temperature, marine habitats and distribution of fish stocks, scientists from govt institutions, including Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), have called for using satellite-based decision support systems and a framework for sustainable fisheries management in the country where the livelihood of about 30 million fisherfolk is linked to fisheries and allied activities.They, while participating in the 47th Asian Conference on Remote Sensing this week, proposed strengthening early warning and fisheries advisories using satellite technologies, underlining that timely information on ocean conditions, potential fishing zones and weather-related risks could help fishers make better-informed decisions.With the climate change leading to marine heatwaves and shifts in the distribution of marine species, affecting fish availability, fishing operations and the livelihoods of communities dependent on marine resources, Shubhadeep Ghosh, ICAR’s assistant director general, said, “These challenges underscore the need for science-based monitoring systems and adaptive fisheries management.”Marine experts, including scientists from ICAR-Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute (CMFRI) and Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), during the conference explored the potential of remote sensing to help address these challenges by integrating satellite-derived information on sea surface temperature, ocean colour and other oceanographic conditions with fisheries data, field observations and scientific assessments.
They said such integration can strengthen understanding of changing marine environments and support more informed fisheries planning, and pitched for improved communication and last-mile delivery of advisories to translate scientific information into practical benefits.ICAR-CMFRI in its handbook on “application of GIS as a decision support tool in marine fisheries” noted that Remote Sensing (RS) is the first satellite-based technology which overhauled marine fisheries prediction, based on ocean temperature, ocean colour and chlorophyll content.It said, “Satellite based technologies, which are capable of handling spatial data, revolutionized natural resource management over a period of time".
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:06:59 UTC
23:06:59 KST

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.
Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in West Bank towns on Friday. Palestinian authorities said they recorded attacks in eight villages, and injuries among at least 20 people.
It was the latest series of attacks in a deadly campaign of Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in recent months, violence which has drawn accusations of “ethnic cleansing”, including from the British government.
In the town of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, at least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.
The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”
Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.
“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.
The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that the facts surrounding the attack on Levine were “unclear”, suggesting the attack was the fault of “200 Arabs and far-left activists” who confronted Israeli youths. The office added that it condemned “violence against anyone”.
There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but there has been a rise in violence this year as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.
At least four Palestinians had been killed and more than 100 others injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.
Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.
The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without the approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.
The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited, for the purpose of preventing settler violence, from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026.
The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.
Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers razed trees.
Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well-documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.
Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop it.
Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.
Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.
Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.
Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

Starlink disruptions are being felt on the front lines of Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:05:44 UTC
23:05:44 KST

Starlink disruptions are being felt on the front lines of Ukraine
DONETSK REGION, Ukraine, Oct 16 - For one artillery unit fighting in eastern Ukraine, the US decision this week to reduce services provided by satellite company Starlink to the military had an immediate impact.
Communications with headquarters were interrupted and internet speeds dropped, posing risks in a war where drones present a constant danger and up-to-date information on targets and threats can make the difference between life and death.
"Immediately after the announcement that the connection with Starlink was deteriorating, it really did have a negative impact," said Ukrlan, a 28-year-old serving with an artillery unit of the Special Rifle Police Battalion.
He asked to be identified only by his callsign, in keeping with Ukrainian military practice.
"We felt it straight away," he told Reuters from his bunker near the front line in the fiercely contested region of Donbas.
"The internet speed at our position had deteriorated significantly and communication with our headquarters and our command had deteriorated significantly."
According to officials, the White House issued an order to limit SpaceX's Starshield satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations.
A US official has denied that President Donald Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Ukraine and its Western partners decried the slowdown as aiding Russia in the war, which began nearly five years ago with Moscow's full-scale invasion. The US says it wants to end the war and is working towards doing so.
While much of the focus has been on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink service, Ukrlan's comments point to broader disruptions affecting internet connectivity and speeds.
ROAR OF THE GUN
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy told leaders in Brussels on Friday that Starlink services had improved but had not yet been fully restored, which he said put civilian lives at risk.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can't replace this capability," said the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
Ukrlan's unit had been firing a howitzer at Russian targets from a heavily camouflaged position dug deep into the ground. Soldiers hurriedly prepared shells in a dark, timber-framed bunker by the light of head torches, covering their ears each time the gun roared and filled the space with smoke.
Ukrainian soldiers have said slower Starlink speeds have impaired the military's ability to detect and intercept incoming missiles and drones.
The US move to temporarily restrict the system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
He has blamed those strikes for soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party's prospects in the November midterm elections, although experts say that the spike is mainly the result of the US war with Iran.
For Ukrainians, the consequences of his approach are clear.
"At first he insisted very strongly that he would help us bring it to an end in a very short space of time," Ukrlan said, referring to Trump's promise to end the Ukraine war soon after his return to office.
"But we haven't seen any sign of that at all. And things are just getting worse every day, every week." REUTERS

On Thursday, he resumed "a little bit of work activity," including reading documents, and co-celebrated Mass, Vatican officials said. He also met with Archbishop Paolo Rudelli, undersecretary of state.
Doctors said Friday that tests confirmed "steady improvement" in his recovery.
"His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Leo's personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and the head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
The Vatican said Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone on Friday, during which he "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky" in Ukraine. Leo also called for a ceasefire to allow for food and medical assistance to be distributed in the region, as well as the safe evacuation of civilians.
"The Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See's commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," the Vatican said.
The pope also held separate meetings with Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, the dean of the College of Cardinals, and Cardinal Baldassare Reina, the vicar general of the Diocese of Rome.
The Vatican said Leo will make his first public appearance on Sunday to deliver the traditional noontime prayer. Past popes who have been hospitalized have recited the Angelus from the balcony on the 10th floor of Gemelli Hospital.
Trip to South America appears still on
Leo is scheduled to travel to South America next month. His ability to make the trip has been in question since his diagnosis, and the Vatican can change plans at any time.
However, on Friday, the Vatican published the names of journalists accredited to fly on the pope's plane with him during his Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
Posting the media list signaled that, at least organizationally, the trip was going ahead.
Cancer patients send well-wishing notes to Leo
The Vatican also released photos of some get-well notes that had been sent to Leo from patients at Gemelli's pediatric oncology ward.
One, from 7-year-old Angelo, told Leo that he had been on the 10th floor for 36 days. "My mother and I pray for you every night. Get well soon," he wrote, with little hearts at the bottom.
Giorgia, a university-aged student, wrote to Leo in his native English, saying she had long loved learning and practicing the language.
"When I heard on the news about you and your situation, I felt it a thousand times harder, because in some ways we're going through the same thing, and it made me feel closer to you," she wrote. "I pray to God that we both heal and I ask you to pray for me, too."
