Could Tesla’s flying car send sales and shares soaring?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:04:48 UTC
23:04:48 KST

Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster on Thursday in Texas, with one of the three new versions performing a jaw-dropping kickflip and demonstrating flying capabilities. However, analysts contacted by Euronews Business do not expect the model to generate significant revenue.
Elon Musk, Tesla’s CEO and co-founder of SpaceX, recreated a “Knight Rider” moment, showing off his companies’ engineering capabilities with a supercar equipped with cold-gas thrusters developed using SpaceX technology.
Tesla's share price increased on Friday, largely due to the hype, but while the demonstration impressed, analysts see limited commercial value in the new model.
Mamta Valechha, consumer discretionary analyst at Quilter Cheviot, described it as a “headline-grabbing engineering moment” designed “to generate excitement around the brand”.
Rico Luman, senior sector economist, transport and logistics, at ING, called the presentation “a publicity stunt which emphasises Tesla’s image as an innovative company, which offers brand value”, adding that cars are still about emotion and lifestyle, so the demonstration makes an impression.
Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, called the demonstration on X “an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers”.
Valechha noted that even Elon Musk had previously played down the Roadster’s likely financial impact. “The commercial value is likely to be strengthening Tesla's innovation narrative rather than generating meaningful profits.”
Musk said production is expected to start in 2028. Tesla has opened reservations, although the flying Rocket version is available by invitation only. The company has not announced final selling prices.
The Roadster was unveiled in 2017, and a year later Musk suggested that thrusters might allow it to fly. This was followed by repeated delays, as the production was originally promised for 2020. "Credibility and execution risks remain high,” summarised Valechha.
Could flying cars reach a wider market?
The flying features of the Roadster are not approved for public road use, adding another hurdle to any ambitions of a wider roll out of the technology, on top of the high production costs.
Luman said the flying car has been designed as a niche sports vehicle, but “larger scale flying car activity won’t be realistic in the foreseeable future as the same airspace rules apply as for aircraft and certification as aircraft by EASA (in Europe) is then required”.
Whether the Roadster falls within aviation regulations depends on its design, capabilities and intended operation, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) told Euronews Business.
The agency said it does not comment on “specific certification applications or activities involving individual manufacturers”.
However, “any vehicle intended to operate as an aircraft would need to meet the applicable aviation safety requirements”, the agency said. These could include pilot qualifications for the driver.
Luman added that, on top of the complex rules that apply, airspace is already rather full, particularly with increasing drone activity.
“Large numbers of uncontrolled flying cars won’t likely be allowed by authorities for safety reasons.”
Valechha also sees limits to how widely the technology could be used.
“Some technologies could filter into other vehicles over time, but flying or thruster-assisted features are unlikely to be economically viable for higher-volume cars in the foreseeable future due to cost, complexity and regulatory hurdles.”
Luman agreed, adding that some space technology could be useful in high-end cars.
“Flying cars in general may be a cheaper alternative for private jets, but not in this concept”.
Pressure to turn technology into profits
Like many big tech companies, Tesla is growing, but faces pressure to turn expensive technology projects into stronger profits.
The company is investing heavily in new technology, while profit growth is failing to keep pace with sales.
Second-quarter revenue rose 26% year on year to $28.24bn (€25.20bn), but net profit attributable to shareholders fell about 5% to $1.11bn (€990m).
First-half capital spending more than doubled to $8.28bn (€7.39bn). Tesla expects capital spending above $25bn (€22.31bn) in 2026, driven by AI and manufacturing investments.
Investors have been pricing the company's value gradually lower than at the beginning of the year, when Tesla shares traded at $438, whereas on Thursday they cost more than $362, amounting to a 14.6% fall in 2026 so far.
Other analysts also mentioned that Tesla valuation is largely based on its self-driving ambitions, the Optimus model, and SpaceX merger hopes.
Merging SpaceX and Tesla?
The technology in Tesla's Roadster, borrowed from SpaceX, fuelled expectations that the two companies are going to be merged in the future.
Barclays analyst Dan Levy has suggested an announcement could come before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting, according to Barron’s. However, a deal remains speculative, with no certainty about whether or when it would happen.
For now, the Roadster’s clearest appeal may be to wealthy enthusiasts.
“This new futuristic model is great for fans and lovers of gadgets who have the ability to spend the money on it. And I’m sure there are quite some around,” added Luman.

Saudi Arabia: Houthi attacks threaten Riyadh's regional leadership
October 16, 2026
As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen continues to escalate, Saudi Arabia's most important national priorities are increasingly at risk. On Tuesday, the Houthis hit the headquarters of Aramco, the Saudi state-owned oil company in Dhahran. On Wednesday, the Houthis vowed to continue attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, and on Thursday a cruise missile was intercepted over the Medina region. While it remains unclear who launched it, the mere attempt raises questions about Saudi Arabia's role as guardian of Islam's holiest places, the Saudi cities of Mecca and Medina.
Following last weekend's Houthi attacks that killed more than a dozen people and injured more than 300 at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, tourists and potential investors are keenly aware of the growing uncertainty over travel and security in the kingdom.
Several airlines suspended flights to Riyadh and the airport was expected to remain closed through at least October 17, according to media reports published earlier this week. Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, an economic summit that usually draws foreign leaders and key players in business to the country, plans to offer remote participation instead of hosting attendees on site.
"The hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi government challenge Riyadh's image of stability and security amid the wider US-Iran war," said Timothy E. Kaldas, deputy director of the Washington-based think tank Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy.
"The attacks on Saudi Arabia also threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify the economy," Kaldas told DW, noting that these ambitions depend on potential tourists viewing the kingdom as a safe destination.
Since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, Tehran, and later the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, have been targeting Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States. Saudi Arabia also supports the Yemeni government in its fight against the Houthis with airstrikes in Houthi-held areas of Yemen.
Houthi attacks are a blow to Saudi Arabia's ambitions
A decade ago, Saudi Arabia launched Vision 2030, a sweeping economic and social reform plan, to reduce the kingdom's reliance on oil and transform its economy and society.
"Saudi Arabia is pursuing a highly nationalist 'Saudi-First' policy, aimed at propelling the nation to the global forefront as an aviation power, a hub for artificial intelligence and a major tourism destination," Simon Wolfgang Fuchs, a professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told DW.
Fuchs views the Houthi attacks as a significant blow to these ambitions and the financial resources available to pursue them.
Pauline Raabe, a senior analyst at the Berlin-based Middle East Minds think tank, points out that Saudi Arabia urgently needs to find a solution that shields its population from the conflict while limiting the economic damage and reputational costs.
"It is a race against time," she told DW, even though the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is no new occurence. Saudi Arabia supported the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022.
"The conflict has been flaring up again with renewed intensity due to the general situation in the Gulf and is as such actually a tightening of the status quo," Raabe said.
However, she views Saudi Arabia's loss of authority as a threat on the horizon. "In the short term, Saudi Arabia is a belligerent [player] in a region ravaged by conflict," she said.
Symbolic support from partners like Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt
Fuchs agrees.
"Riyadh remains a key player through its investments, its position as the world's largest oil exporter and its role as custodian of Islam's holy sites in Mecca and Medina," he said, adding that "by virtue of this role, Saudi Arabia can count on allies and call for the formation of alliances."
In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. While the latter two have since offered intelligence and defense support for Saudi Arabia, they also made clear that they will not put boots on the ground in Yemen. France and the United Kingdom also offered limited defense support for Riyadh. Egypt, the most populous Arab country with a Sunni majority like Saudi Arabia, voiced verbal support.
"Riyadh is prioritizing the symbolic value of these countries, projecting an image of strong ties with regional powers," Kaldas said.
However, much attention has focused on Saudi Arabia's failure to secure defense support from the United States, he added. While Saudi Arabia's closest ally — the US signaled willingness to support Riyadh with intelligence sharing and targeting assistance against the Houthis — Washington has so far stopped short of committing US forces to direct strikes. For Saudi Arabia, the understanding is therefore that the US prioritzes avoiding opening another front in the regional conflict against Iran.

Many people judge candidates and policies by a single deciding feature, new research suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:00:55 UTC
23:00:55 KST

When people make complex political decisions, they tend to rely on simple mental shortcuts rather than exhaustively weighing every piece of information, according to a study published in PNAS. The research indicates that people frequently switch between different decision strategies depending on the issue at hand and the complexity of the choice environment. These findings suggest that standard survey methods in political science, which often assume people act as fully thorough evaluators, may obscure how individuals actually reach conclusions.
Social scientists frequently rely on choice-based conjoint experiments to measure public opinion on complex topics. In this type of survey, participants view side-by-side profiles of two options, such as hypothetical political candidates or policy proposals, with features that vary randomly, such as age, profession, or cost. Participants are then asked to pick the option they prefer, allowing researchers to infer how much specific features sway voter preferences on average across the entire population.
A key open question is whether people answering these multi-feature surveys actually weigh every detail, as many standard analysis methods implicitly assume, or rely on simplifying mental shortcuts known as heuristics. Some evidence points toward shortcuts. A 2020 eye-tracking study found that when survey tables included more features and options, people looked at a smaller fraction of the information on screen. In the consumer realm, a 2009 study found that although standard models assume people balance every feature against the others, a sizable minority of participants were better described by rules that rank features and decide based on the most important one.
Similar rankings appear in politics: a 2024 study of candidate choice found that voters tend to focus on party affiliation first, weighing traits like gender or race mainly when two candidates share the same party. Separately, research covered by PsyPost in 2026 found that voters often use left and right political labels as shortcuts to guess where candidates stand.
To understand the cognitive rules guiding these choices, study authors Nidhi V. Banavar, a postdoctoral scholar in the Travers Department of Political Science at the University of California, Berkeley, and Kirk Bansak, also of the University of California, Berkeley, created a mathematical framework to classify individual decision strategies. Their model analyzes a person’s survey selections to infer what attributes matter to them, which values they favor, and which cognitive rule best accounts for their behavior.
“We were interested in the question of how people go about making political choices,” Banavar told PsyPost. “When we estimate complex constructs like political attitudes, a lot of analysis methods implicitly assume that people weigh everything in front of them. We wanted to test whether that was true, and if not, to find how they were deciding instead.”
“This connects to a broader issue, which is that most political attitude research is done at the aggregate level,” Banavar explained. “The aggregate is perfect for giving us the high level snapshot and, for better or for worse, collapses a lot of the variation we see in people: both in terms of their actual preferences and in terms of how they make choices based on those preferences. We were interested in uncollapsing the aggregate and so built a model and designed experiments to do so.”
The model examines four distinct decision strategies that differ in cognitive demand. The most thorough strategy, known as Weighted Additive, involves a rational calculation where an individual weighs every single attribute and sums them up to pick the highest-scoring option. A simpler shortcut strategy, known as Tally, involves counting how many preferred traits each option possesses and choosing the profile with the higher count, without worrying about which traits matter more.
The simplest shortcut rule, called Take The Best, directs a person to choose based solely on whichever single feature matters most to them; they only examine a second feature if the options are tied on their favorite trait. The fourth classification, Contaminant, captures random guessing equivalent to a coin flip.
The scientists evaluated this model across two experiments involving 3,762 American adults recruited through Prolific, with quotas matching national demographics for age, sex, and political affiliation. Participants completed 90 choices divided into three blocks of 30 decisions across three common political topics: selecting between two hypothetical immigrants seeking admission to the United States, choosing between two Senate primary candidates, and choosing between two national climate policy packages. Each option varied across six attributes that each had two possible values.
In the first experiment, which included 1,964 participants, the researchers altered the complexity of the profiles by testing whether allowing ties changed how people decided. Half of the participants saw profiles where traits were never identical between the two options, while the other half saw profiles that contained one to three matching features, such as both candidates being in their 50s. This design was intended to test whether forcing people to look beyond their top attribute would push them toward more thorough evaluation strategies.
The results showed that the simplest shortcut rule, Take The Best, was the most common strategy across all three political domains. In the condition without ties, about 54% of participants were classified as using this single-attribute rule, while roughly 30% were classified as using the rational Weighted Additive strategy, and about 14% used the Tally strategy. When ties were introduced, forcing people to scan deeper into the profiles, use of the Take The Best rule dropped to roughly 45%, while rational strategy use increased to about 40%. Across both conditions, shortcut strategies accounted for the majority of participant behavior.
The authors also discovered that an individual’s strategy was not fixed. Depending on the condition, 67% to 76% of participants were classified as using different strategies for different issues, with about 10% using a completely different strategy across all three domains. The presentation order of the topics was randomized, and participants did not display signs of survey fatigue or increased guessing in later rounds. Instead, people appeared to adapt their decision rules to the specific context of each topic.
“On one hand, the big takeaway is the prevalence of heuristic use and how the majority of individuals use informational shortcuts,” Banavar noted. “This is an important finding – people are not exhaustively weighting and evaluating all the information presented to them.”
“However, I think a bigger takeaway is that people tend to use different strategies depending on the political domain,” Banavar added. “How someone processes information is not a trait: just because I may choose a candidate based on one factor doesn’t mean that I’ll choose a climate policy based on one factor. This means we shouldn’t put people into buckets based on how they make political choices.”
In the second experiment, which included 1,798 participants, the researchers tested another common variation in survey design: asking participants to rate each profile individually on a 1-to-7 scale in addition to making their comparative choice. Among those asked to give ratings, fewer participants were classified as using Take The Best in all three policy domains, though it remained the most common strategy. That group also had more people classified as using the more thorough strategies, along with a small increase in people classified as random guessers, which the authors suggest may reflect some respondents losing interest. The authors caution that these shifts were not consistently statistically reliable across domains.
To check whether these classifications reflected something about how people were actually thinking, rather than just statistical patterns in their choices, the researchers analyzed response times. Participants classified as using the rational Weighted Additive strategy took the longest to answer, followed by those classified as using Tally, while those classified as using Take The Best responded much faster.
When ties were present, only the Take The Best group answered more slowly; response times for the other groups were essentially unchanged. Because this shortcut requires checking additional traits only when top traits tie, the authors interpret this selective slowdown as evidence that the classifications capture real differences in mental processing, though they stop short of claiming the model directly observes thought.
“While we note that our findings were obtained (necessarily) in the context of a limited set of experiments, we do believe their theoretical and practical value has generalizability,” Banavar pointed out. “For instance, while the precise pervasiveness of heuristic usage is certainly context dependent, we still found that the simplest heuristic strategy was our most commonly classified strategy across all of our experiments, regardless of complexity manipulations. Our finding that strategy classifications are not fixed for individual people was also robust, and we have no reason to believe there would be within-person strategy variation only for our experiments and not for others.”
The researchers also investigated whether demographic characteristics predicted which strategy a person chose. Across variables such as race, gender, education, and political affiliation, associations were generally weak, and most were not statistically distinguishable from chance after adjusting for multiple tests. Older participants showed a slight tendency toward Take The Best, but the effect was small and held up after statistical correction in only 2 of 12 tests. Participants who rated a topic as less complex, or who said they knew less about it, also showed slight tendencies toward the shortcut, but these patterns appeared in only some analyses and largely did not survive correction.
“I was surprised by how difficult it was to relate strategy classification to respondent characteristics,” Banavar observed. “There’s a lot of evidence in cognitive science research showing that this is a difficult problem. There is also, however, substantial work in political science that would generate some predictions about relating strategy classification and respondent characteristics.”
“In the end we found very little, even though we considered demographics and various other measures of how meaningful a given political topic was to each person,” she said. “I think there’s a lot more to explore on this front.”
When the authors broke aggregate preferences down into individual weightings, they found that population-level averages concealed large differences. For every feature, many participants appeared to give it little or no weight, and for several of the most heavily weighted features, the pattern split into two sharp groups: people who effectively ignored the feature and a distinct group who weighted it very heavily. For example, conjoint studies commonly find that female candidates are slightly preferred over male candidates on average; the new results suggest this average blends people who prefer women, people who prefer men, and many who put little weight on gender at all.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study used simplified experimental profiles where each feature only had two possible choices, such as a candidate being either in their 50s or 70s. In real-world political decisions, options often have many more layers and continuous values, which might prompt respondents to rely even more heavily on mental shortcuts than observed here.
There are also important nuances in how mental shortcuts should be understood, especially regarding whether they reflect poorly on respondents. “First, the fact that we classify the majority of individuals as using heuristics or not using the rational strategy does not mean that they are lazy,” Banavar stressed. “We have finite resources and it is a good thing to selectively deploy them.”
The classification approach has its own limits. Because strategies were inferred from choices, someone who weighs every feature but cares overwhelmingly about one would make the same choices as a Take The Best user, and the model would classify them the same way; the response time data suggest such mix-ups were not widespread. Simulations also showed that the model tends to classify random guessers as Tally users, so guessing may be somewhat more common, and Tally somewhat less common, than the estimates suggest.
“Secondly, while we have built a cognitive model, the model doesn’t actually tell us what’s happening inside someone’s head,” Banavar stated. “It’s a model that classifies, based on the choices that people make, what decision strategies best describe their choices. It is a technical clarification but an important one.”
Future research could expand on this framework by testing features with more than two values, exploring why people pick the strategies they do, and modeling response times alongside choices.
The study, “Classifying strategy use in multiattribute subjective choice: Application to conjoint experiments in political science,” was authored by Nidhi V. Banavar and Kirk Bansak.

Baird Architects releases first furniture collection as "natural extension" of studio
US architecture studio Baird Architects has released its inaugural furniture collection, with seating, tables, and shelving, designed by in-house architects and collaborators and made in Portugal.
The twelve-piece BA Objeto collection was led by Baird Architects founder Matthew Baird, who designed several pieces and also commissioned studio employees and collaborators.
Each piece is credited to its designer, and the designers will receive a portion of the profits, according to Baird.
The works include a solid walnut "surf" table by Baird, a swooping aluminium coffee table by Ines Gulbenkian and a dark brown cork bench by Gina Jiang.
The pieces are primarily produced in Lisbon, Portugal, where Baird Architects has established a new studio to support its furniture making.
Baird said a "considered approach to materiality, a crisp aesthetic, and a desire to push the boundaries of furniture design" draws the collection together.
The move points to an expansion of the studio's work beyond one-off furniture creation and illustrates a different business model for architecture studios.
"Furniture feels like a natural extension of our architectural practice because it allows us to explore our interests in materiality, form, and craftsmanship at a more intimate scale," Baird told Dezeen.
"We also wanted to create something that celebrates the individual designers within our studio, giving them the freedom to develop pieces of their own while contributing to a collective endeavour."
Other pieces in the collection include a mirror by Portuguese designer Teresa Mascarenhas and a plywood and leather chair by designer Katy Cheng.
Baird said the collection is an extension of the furniture the studio has created for private clients over the years, and that the team is already "looking ahead" to a second collection.
From design fairs to heritage brands, designers and architects are currently attempting to restructure business models in the design world, primarily to receive more profit and credit for their work.
Recently, Dezeen spoke with design companies OMHU and Rarify about their unique business models and outlooks that aspire to change the industry.
Baird Architects previously designed a shingled house in Maine.
The photography is courtesy of Baird Architects.

Since my daughter moved out of home, my household has shrunk. A yearly tradition brings us together | Nova Weetman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:00:12 UTC
23:00:12 KST

It’s citrus season, and the trees of my streets are heavy with the bright balls of fruit. My son sometimes picks me a lemon or two on his way home from school, and I help myself to the basket of limes that hang from the fence of a nearby house. The potted plant on my balcony fruited early this season, and for weeks I watched as the hundreds of small green cumquats slowly ripened. I finally picked them when they were fattened with juice and seeds and colour, the cat squatting on the ground to watch. When I dropped a cumquat she sniffed at the skin and turned away, as if sensing the sharpness of its flesh.
Since my daughter moved out several years ago, my household has shrunk. It is now only my son and me. And the cat. A scratchy, sullen creature who delights in ignoring us both unless we are sitting in the seat she believes is hers. My son has begun cooking for himself, and so I find my services in the kitchen required less often. Except for the yearly making of cumquat jam.
The jam is a tradition I inherited from my mum. Along with her recipes for plum pudding, broad bean falafels and tomato relish. When I was a kid, Mum would scavenge each year in her friends’ gardens for cumquats and then spend close to two days chopping, deseeding, soaking, boiling and jarring the fruit to fill our cupboards with the stained glass orange jam. Years later, when I had children, Mum introduced them to the tart taste, and they were hooked too. When she died, 15 years ago, winter came and went without our usual jars to see us through. We tried eating jam made from other fruits. Seville orange, apricot, rich plum, but there were no memories to the taste, and the jars would sit unfinished in the fridge for months.
Witnessing my grief at losing my mum, some friends bought me a baby cumquat tree in a large yellow ceramic pot that proved itself hardy enough to survive my limited gardening skills. The first year that it flowered with delicate white buds, we watched, delighting in the growth of the cumquats, waiting until they were large enough to pick. My kids helped strip the tree of fruit. It was nothing like the haul Mum used to make jam with, but it filled a bowl. I hacked up the cumquats, not neatly like Mum did, but fast and furious, not bothering to remove the pips because I’d read somewhere they would float up during boiling and you could scoop them from the top with the scum. Impatiently, I didn’t follow the ratio of sugar or simmer for the correct amount of time, and that first batch was overcooked. The jam was too dark in colour, and the texture was all wrong, but we ate it anyway, the taste taking me immediately back to my childhood home, where I’d perch up at the bench each morning before school and work my way through rye toast smeared with jam.
The following year, I channelled Mum’s patience and made two large jars of jam. They were the perfect amber-colour, rich and bright, with chunks of rind and the occasional pip. It wasn’t enough to squirrel away in the cupboard like a true survivalist, but it saw us through a month or two of breakfasts. This year, I managed six jars, enough to spare for giving one to a friend, and another to my daughter when she came for dinner one night. She took half our loaf of fresh sourdough bread with her too so she could replicate the favourite breakfast of her childhood.
My son and I are now down to our last jar of jam, and we have started rationing it without discussion, eating it on toast weekly instead of daily, to make it last as long as we can. I do sometimes buy cumquat jam if I see it at a market, but it never quite tastes the same. There is something treasured in waiting each year for the tree to grow the fruit to make the jam. It is ritual that connects us to the jam that Mum once made.
My cumquat tree still lives in the same yellow pot. It has moved house twice with us, requiring four people to lift it on to a trolley, and it now grows in the strip of sun on our apartment balcony. It is not much to look at it until the flowers come and the fruit arrives, but then it brings with it all the promise of the taste of my childhood.

Türkiye raises defense equipment procurement by 229% in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:58:29 UTC
22:58:29 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye increased allocations for weapons, ammunition and other defense equipment purchases by 229% in its 2027 budget, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said Friday.
Speaking at a ceremony marking the finalization of the central government budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz outlined spending priorities spanning defense, education, health and infrastructure.
“Allocations for purchases of weapons, ammunition, weapons systems and other defense equipment, which constitute a significant portion of defense spending in the National Defense Ministry's budget, have been increased by 229%,” he said.
Including other defense expenditures, the proposed budget earmarks 2.206 trillion Turkish liras ($44.5 billion) for defense and a separate $25.2 billion for internal security.
The 229% increase applies specifically to the procurement allocations identified by Yilmaz, rather than total defense spending.
Yilmaz said Türkiye had reduced its defense industry's dependence on foreign suppliers, describing developments over the past quarter-century as a revolution.
Current global conditions demonstrated the importance of the country's earlier decision to strengthen its domestic defense industry, he added.
Beyond defense, the government proposes allocating $57.5 billion to investment, equivalent to 10.4% of the 2027 budget.
Yilmaz said investment would continue across irrigation, railways, maritime transport, oil and natural gas exploration, and mining.
Education, including higher education, would receive $75.6 billion, retaining the largest share of central government spending at 13.7%.
The proposal also provides $17.5 billion to address earthquake damage and strengthen resilience against disasters.
Yilmaz said the budget proposal had been submitted to parliament within the constitutional deadline. He will provide further details during a presentation to parliament's Planning and Budget Committee next week.

The Committee’s work is coordinated by a Secretary of State or Undersecretary of State.

Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:43 UTC
22:56:43 KST

Can Russia help ease tensions between Pakistan and Afghanistan?
Russia has close ties with the Taliban and is courting Islamabad, but analysts say its leverage remains uncertain.
Islamabad, Pakistan – Sitting with his elbows on his knees, Russia’s Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev leaned towards Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, for talks in Rawalpindi on October 14.
While Kolokoltsev was in Pakistan, Sergey Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), flew into Kabul to meet the Taliban’s intelligence chief, Abdul Haq Wasiq.
Officially, Russia, Pakistan and Afghanistan have issued little beyond standard statements about the meetings. But the signs are clear: Pakistan and Afghanistan have spent the past year exchanging fire and public threats. Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire in Doha last October and China hosted talks in Urumqi in April, but attacks inside Pakistan continued. Islamabad again struck Afghan territory in June, September and this month.
Russia now appears to be stepping in as a mediator.
Moscow’s special representative for Afghanistan, Zamir Kabulov, told Russia’s TASS news agency earlier this month that his country was ready to play peace broker between Kabul and Islamabad if both sides requested it.
Pakistan’s ambassador to Russia, Faisal Niaz Tirmizi, said in March that Islamabad had approached Moscow. The Taliban, though, have not publicly requested Russian mediation, raising questions about how much and in what capacity Moscow can push Pakistan and Afghanistan to talks when other mediators have struggled.
A complicated history adds to the challenge Russia faces.
A diplomatic opening
Pakistan’s military media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said the Rawalpindi meeting discussed issues of “mutual interest and the regional security environment, with particular emphasis on strengthening bilateral security cooperation.”
The statement did not mention Afghanistan and neither Russian officials nor the Taliban have disclosed what the intelligence chiefs discussed. Moscow has, however, voiced concern about the fighting.
“We are seriously concerned about the ongoing military confrontation between Pakistan and Afghanistan, which affects civilians, including children,” the Russian embassy in Kabul posted on X earlier this month.
The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) said Pakistani strikes between September 30 and October 1 killed at least 10 civilians, mostly children.
In decades past, the idea of Russia mediating between Pakistan and the Taliban might have been unthinkable. Throughout the Cold War and even after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russia was – and remains in many ways – one of the closest strategic and military partners of India, the neighbour Pakistan has fought multiple wars against. While in Afghanistan, Russia backed the Northern Alliance against the Taliban throughout the 1990s.
But in recent years, Russia has significantly strengthened relations with both Pakistan and the Taliban. Then Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan was in Moscow when Russian forces invaded Ukraine in 2022. Last year, Russia became the first country in the world to officially recognise the Taliban government in Afghanistan.
Those shifts have been driven by Russia’s desire to broaden its options in South Asia, at a time when India has embraced the United States and to counter the rise of the Afghan branch of ISIL, also known as the Islamic State in Khorasan Province or ISKP. While the Taliban are concerned with ruling Afghanistan, ISKP has broader territorial ambitions and carried out an attack in Moscow in 2024 that killed nearly 150 people. The Taliban and the ISKP are sworn enemies.
Fighting between Pakistan and the Taliban created regional instability and Moscow was worried that could make it easier for armed groups to spill into Central Asia, said Taimur Khan, a research associate at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad (ISSI).
“Mediation also helps Moscow preserve its regional influence and avoid a vacuum that could invite renewed extra-regional involvement,” he told Al Jazeera.
Why mediation stalled
Qatar and Turkiye brokered a ceasefire between Pakistan and the Taliban in Doha last October, but talks in Istanbul collapsed the following month and skirmishes resumed. Islamabad also launched air raids inside Afghanistan. China hosted talks in Urumqi in April.
In mid-September, Turkiye’s intelligence chief, Ibrahim Kalin, met Taliban officials in Kabul and Kandahar before travelling to Islamabad.
An attack in Kohat followed on September 18, with Pakistan striking Afghanistan on September 24 and October 1.
“Other actors have so far achieved more tangible mediation results in this conflict,” Eldaniz Gusseinov, a Central Asia analyst and head of research at the geopolitical foresight agency, Nightingale Int, told Al Jazeera.
Russia’s own effort stalled at a Moscow meeting on October 5.
Kabulov told TASS that the Afghan delegation objected to Afghanistan being mentioned too often in connection with “terrorism”.
“For Pakistan, this is a substantive security issue, not merely a matter of wording,” Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesperson, Sajjad Haider Khan, said on October 9 at a weekly media briefing.
Kabul-based security analyst Tameem Bahiss said the objection reflected Kabul’s longstanding position.
“Accepting language that repeatedly associates Afghanistan with terrorism could be seen as an acknowledgement of the very allegations Kabul has consistently denied,” he told Al Jazeera.
The TTP problem
At the Moscow meeting, Pakistan’s special representative for Afghanistan, Mohammad Sadiq, said “terrorism” remained at the core of Afghanistan’s problems.
Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said the two countries’ problems could be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, according to Afghan media.
Pakistan says the Pakistani Taliban and other armed groups shelter in Afghanistan.
Kabul rejects the allegation, saying it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries and that Pakistan’s security problems are largely internal, Bahiss said.
Moscow’s public warnings have focused on the ISKP.
“There is no visible public pressure from Russia on the Taliban over Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), and Moscow is unlikely to exert such pressure,” Gusseinov said. TTP is the official name of the Pakistani Taliban, which is behind dozens of the deadliest attacks Pakistan has suffered in recent years.
He argued that pressing the Taliban hard on Pakistan’s behalf would undermine Moscow’s standing as a neutral mediator and its partnership with the Taliban against ISKP.
“Russia’s primary concern is ISKP and it appears satisfied with the Taliban’s efforts to counter the group,” Abdul Sayed, a Sweden-based analyst specialising in armed groups and security dynamics in Afghanistan and Pakistan, told Al Jazeera.
What Moscow brings
Still, Russia has something earlier mediators did not. In July 2025, it became the only country to recognise the Taliban government.
Taimur Khan said that could give Moscow another source of influence.
“The Taliban authorities’ interest in preserving that recognition and expanding cooperation with Moscow could give Russia additional influence in seeking action against the TTP and other terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan,” he said.
In May, the two sides signed an unpublished military-technical agreement covering, according to Kabulov, the repair and maintenance of equipment the Taliban already hold, mostly Soviet and Russian-made.
Three days after the signing, the Taliban’s Defence Minister, Mohammad Yaqoob, said Pakistan would soon no longer dare to launch strikes.
On June 9 and 10, Pakistani aircraft struck Kunar, Khost and Paktika provinces, killing 13 civilians, according to the Afghan government.
“Russia has greater access to the Taliban than any other major power, but its actual leverage is considerably more limited than is often assumed,” analyst Gusseinov said.
Sayed said senior Taliban leaders continued visiting Russia and India as fighting escalated, seemingly signalling they could offset Pakistan’s military superiority through new alignments.
“While the military and political significance of these ties remains unclear, the Taliban present such diplomatic developments to the Afghan public, particularly their supporters, as political achievements that reinforce their image of strength,” he said.
Why the SCO matters
Pakistan chairs the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) for 2026-27 and will host the 10-member bloc’s summit in Islamabad next year.
The Taliban were not invited to this year’s summit in Bishkek, where members called for an inclusive government in Kabul.
On July 16, then-Foreign Office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said Afghanistan first needed diplomatic relations with member states, when asked whether Pakistan was blocking its inclusion in the SCO.
In September, Tirmizi, the Pakistani envoy in Moscow, said he did not see full SCO membership for Afghanistan as an option under the current Taliban government.
“The chairmanship strengthens Moscow’s reasons to invest in its relationship with Pakistan and manage differences over Afghanistan constructively,” Taimur Khan said.
The Foreign Office did not answer Al Jazeera’s questions about whether the Taliban would be invited next year.
“I cannot recall an instance where Kabul has explicitly requested Moscow to mediate between the two countries,” Bahiss said. “Nevertheless, Kabul’s repeated calls for diplomacy and its relatively close relations with Russia suggest that it would likely welcome Russian mediation if Moscow offered to play such a role.”

Britain Is Taking Too Long to Blame Russia for Sabotage, Labour MP Warns
Unknown

- Category
- World
Britain Is Taking Too Long to Blame Russia for Sabotage, Labour MP Warns
Britain is taking too long to publicly attribute sabotage and arson to Russia, leaving businesses supporting Ukraine without timely warnings that they may themselves become targets, Labour MP Graeme Downie told UK Defence Journal on October 16.
Downie, author of The Putin Tax report, contrasted Britain with countries such as Estonia, which recently blamed Russia within days of an arson attack on a drone manufacturer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We’ve seen other NATO countries like Estonia blaming Russia and attributing blame within days without the need to publish all of the raw intelligence,” he said.
Downie argued that Britain effectively applies a criminal standard—“beyond reasonable doubt”—when deciding whether to attribute hostile-state activity, when a lower civil standard could allow the government to act faster.
“Rather than apply the criminal bar of beyond reasonable doubt, you probably apply a civil legal bar of overwhelming evidence, and on the balance of probabilities,” he said, adding that the current approach “delays it.”
That delay can have practical consequences for British companies supplying Ukraine. Downie said firms should not necessarily be afraid, but they need to understand that they could be targeted and receive better guidance on protecting themselves.
“I think it’s not they should be worried, but they should be aware,” he said. Publicly identifying attacks more quickly, he argued, would signal to companies supporting Ukraine “that they need to get protection.”
He also warned that Britain’s subsea energy and communications infrastructure faces a serious threat from hostile activity.
“The threat to subsea infrastructure is entirely real,” Downie said, warning that even short disruptions to internet cables or energy networks could inflict major economic damage.
His comments follow the March 2024 arson attack on a warehouse in Leyton linked to aid for Ukraine. Men were later convicted over the fire, which prosecutors said had been organized on behalf of Russia’s Wagner Group.
Earlier, reports emerged that British warships and helicopters spent significantly more time tracking Russian naval activity in July as Moscow maintained an elevated presence around UK waters and across the North Atlantic.
Royal Navy patrol ships and aircraft devoted 21 days to monitoring Russian vessels during the month, up 25% from July 2025, according to figures released by the British Navy.

Ukraine Tests First Aerial Drone Designed to Evacuate Wounded Soldiers From the Front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:55:41 UTC
22:55:41 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Tests First Aerial Drone Designed to Evacuate Wounded Soldiers From the Front
Ukraine has begun front-line testing of StarGate, its first aerial drone designed to evacuate wounded soldiers from areas too dangerous for conventional vehicles or evacuation teams, the Associated Press (AP) reported on Octobe 16.
Ukraine is increasingly using unmanned ground vehicles to evacuate wounded troops from areas where Russian FPV drones make conventional rescue missions too dangerous. In April, the First Separate Medical Battalion completed six casualty evacuations with ground robots in a single day under constant drone threat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
AP received exclusive access to a field demonstration of the system before StarGate was handed to a Ukrainian combat brigade for testing under front-line conditions.
“The idea came directly from the front line, from the trenches,” a SkyFall spokesperson told AP.
The drone was developed over the past year by Ukrainian defense technology company SkyFall after a request from the commander of the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, known as Code 9.2.
In some sectors, the battlefield “kill zone” under constant drone and artillery threat extends 10 to 15 kilometers or farther, AP reported. StarGate has a one-way range of 15 kilometers and is designed to reach wounded troops inside those areas without exposing an evacuation crew.
“Covering 10 kilometers in minutes would be a drastic change on the front line,” KVN, a commander with Code 9.2, told AP.
StarGate can carry up to 150 kilograms, enough for a wounded soldier wearing body armor and combat equipment. Its evacuation compartment is built around a medical-grade stretcher.
According to AP, the drone cruises at 65 kilometers per hour and can reach 105 kilometers per hour. SkyFall states that it can be prepared for flight in about 10 minutes.
The system uses Starlink and SkyFall’s proprietary L-Link communications system, alongside AI-assisted navigation designed for environments where GPS is unavailable, spoofed, or jammed.
During the demonstration observed by AP, FPV drones simulated attacks on StarGate while electronic jamming was active. The evacuation drone deployed a net against one approaching FPV, knocking it off course.
SkyFall also states that StarGate can return toward a safe area if communications are completely lost. The drone is equipped with thermal cameras for night operations and is designed to fly in rain and snow.
The company has demonstrated that the aircraft can continue flying after losing one of its arms, although AP noted that SkyFall has not released data showing how reliably it can survive damage under combat conditions.
Each system is expected to cost at least $50,000, depending on its configuration. SkyFall aims to produce up to 1,000 StarGate drones per month by the end of 2026.
“It’s a completely new method of evacuation,” KVN told AP. “It’s difficult to talk in depth about the pros and cons right now. We need to work with it more.”
Unmanned systems already play an expanding role in Ukrainian casualty evacuation, particularly where ground vehicles face mines, craters, destroyed roads, rivers, and drone attacks. AP reported that ground robots can take two to three hours to reach some positions, while StarGate is designed to cover comparable distances in minutes.
The StarGate tests build on Ukraine’s growing use of unmanned systems for casualty evacuation. In June, the Third Army Corps reported that its ground robots had evacuated more than 600 wounded soldiers during their first year of operations, while completing more than 18,000 missions overall.

Bulgaria Asks NATO for Aircraft, Air Defenses and Counter-Drone Systems as Black Sea Attacks Intensify
Bulgaria has requested additional aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment, and air patrols from NATO as attacks on vessels in the Black Sea intensify, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said, according to Novinite on October 16.
Speaking to journalists, Stoyanov warned that the security situation in the Black Sea was deteriorating, with attacks becoming increasingly frequent. He pointed to recent strikes in Romanian territorial waters as evidence of the growing threats facing countries in the region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We have requested aviation, surface-to-air missile systems, counter-drone systems, and air patrols—essentially, the entire spectrum of available assets,” Stoyanov said, adding that the deployment of additional allied resources would also help demonstrate a stronger NATO presence in the region.
However, the minister acknowledged that it remained unclear which capabilities Bulgaria would ultimately receive. He noted that Romania and the Baltic states were facing similar security challenges, while European partners were paying increasing attention to threats in the Black Sea.
“I hope for a swift response and a strengthening of our capabilities,” Stoyanov said.
To improve regional coordination, Bulgaria is also seeking closer cooperation with neighboring NATO members. According to the minister, a meeting involving the defense ministers of Bulgaria, Türkiye, and Romania, alongside the chiefs of defense of all three countries, is expected to take place soon.
The discussions are intended to support the development of a coordinated response to emerging threats and strengthen cooperation among the three Black Sea NATO members.
Despite the requested assistance, Stoyanov cautioned that deploying additional allied forces and equipment would not eliminate all security risks in the region.
“100% security is impossible,” the defense minister said, emphasizing that the objective was to minimize potential threats rather than guarantee complete protection.
Meanwhile, Bulgaria continues to rely on its existing military resources to monitor its maritime territory and respond to potential threats.
According to Stoyanov, the country currently operates two reconnaissance systems dedicated to maritime surveillance, with a third expected to become operational by the end of the year.
The minister said the additional system would introduce technology that had not previously been deployed elsewhere.
The calls for additional security measures follow a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, including an incident near Bulgaria’s coast on October 13.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported that two commercial vessels had been struck by drones overnight, leaving one ship sunk and forcing the evacuation of the entire crew of another after three drones hit its deck and hull.
One of the vessels was the Chelsea 3, a Ukrainian-owned cargo ship sailing under the Maltese flag, which came under attack approximately 18 nautical miles east of the Bulgarian coastal town of Byala.

Estonian flags to fly on Finno-Ugric Day  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:54:16 UTC
22:54:16 KST

TALLINN – On Saturday, October 17, Estonia will celebrate Finno-Ugric Day, an occasion to honor the common origins, linguistic and cultural kinship, and cooperation of the Finno-Ugric peoples.
Finno-Ugric Day is a national flag day, requiring all state and local government agencies and public legal entities to fly the Estonian flag.
Finno-Ugric Day is celebrated in Estonia on the third Saturday of October. The aim of the day is to raise awareness of Estonians' connection to the Finno-Ugric family of peoples, to introduce the languages and cultures of these kindred nations, and to highlight the importance of their preservation and legacy.
Estonians' closest linguistic relatives are the Finns and Livonians, while more distant kindred peoples include the Hungarians, Sami, Karelians, Vepsians, Maris, Udmurts, Komis, Erzyas, and Mokshas, among others. The languages and cultures of many smaller Finno-Ugric peoples require special attention and preservation today.
Flying the Estonian flag expresses respect for our linguistic and cultural roots and solidarity with our kindred peoples. In addition to state and local government institutions, all households, businesses, and organizations are encouraged to fly the Estonian flag on Finno-Ugric Day.
Flags are to be hoisted at sunrise, or by 8 a.m. at the latest, and lowered at sunset.

Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray

Ethiopia announces instalment of interim government in Tigray
After military pushed back TPLF uprising, PM Abiy Ahmed promises free elections within six months.
Ethiopia has announced that an interim government will take control of the state of Tigray, after its armed forces retook control of the northern region.
The installation of the six-month administration was announced in a statement by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday. He pledged that free elections would then be held in the state.
The move comes after the Ethiopian military pushed back an uprising launched last month by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Tigray’s main political party had launched the insurrection after announcing in April that it was retaking control of the region, effectively ending a peace deal with Ethiopia’s federal government.
The government promised that the interim government would create “a stable political situation” in Tigray so that free elections could be held. It has appointed five officials to run the state, including the mayor of the capital, Mekelle.
The officials will carry out “directives and instructions” delivered directly from the federal government.
The TPLF has yet to respond to the announcement. The rebel group launched an ambitious offensive in September in alliance with several other armed groups aimed at toppling the Abiy government. The Ethiopian government has accused the breakaway state of Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, accusations that Eritrea has denied.
After some early gains in the Afar region, its fighters were defeated and lost Tigray’s major cities. They surrendered in Mekelle in early October. Eritrean troops who had entered Tigray withdrew after heavy drone strikes from the Ethiopian armed forces.
The TPLF governed Ethiopia for nearly 30 years until 2018, when Abiy’s party came to power. Tigray, in response, boycotted national elections and rejected the central government, creating a severe rift.
The region remains scarred by the 2020-2022 war between federal forces, backed at that time by Eritrea, and the TPLF, which resulted in the killing of almost 600,000 people.
A peace deal ended the fighting, but key promises were not kept, including the return of displaced people and the disarmament of the TPLF.
Since the recent escalation, Ethiopia and Eritrea have accused each other of inciting war, raising fears of a wider conflict.
On Wednesday, the United States urged both sides to “de-escalate” during a phone call between Abiy and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Bedroom window requirement upheld by justice chancellor
Estonia's justice chancellor has found that requiring bedrooms to have openable windows and natural light is constitutional, even in homes with mechanical ventilation.
Then-justice chancellor Ülle Madise, now Estonia's president, issued the opinion after attorney Carry Plaks challenged a regulation requiring every living room, bedroom, workroom and kitchen to have at least one openable window and natural light.
Plaks argued the rule excessively restricted property rights and imposed unnecessary architectural and financial burdens, preventing windowless interior spaces even in buildings with mechanical ventilation from being used as bedrooms.
In her response, Madise said the requirement serves a clear and important purpose: ensuring a safe and healthy living environment suitable for round-the-clock use.
"People's health can change, and someone who is ill may have to spend much of the day in their bedroom or remain in bed for an extended period," she explained, noting that natural light and the ability to open a window to air out the room are especially important in such cases.
An openable window also serves as a backup if the mechanical ventilation system fails.
Costs do not make the rule unconstitutional
Plaks also noted that the regulation, issued by the economy and infrastructure minister, sets no minimum window size. Madise stressed, however, that the requirement is not a formality: it calls for sufficient natural light, ruling out token solutions that fall short of accepted building practices, such as attic-style spaces.
She acknowledged that windows can affect a building's layout, construction costs and how a property can be used. But such costs do not by themselves make a requirement unconstitutional.
"All building requirements — whether for fire safety, accessibility, ventilation or energy efficiency — can increase construction costs or limit how space is used," the justice chancellor said.
She said the Ministry of Climate, as the policymaker which oversees the sector, could assess whether advances in construction technology and modern housing practices might eventually allow windowless living spaces.
--
Editor: Mari Peegel, Aili Vahtla

News Analysis: AI offers new route to cancer vaccines, but hurdles remain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
21:52:48 CST
22:52:48 KST

LONDON, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- British researchers are bringing artificial intelligence (AI), automated laboratories and supercomputing together to accelerate the development of personalized cancer vaccines. The effort aims to test whether a more connected research process can shorten the journey from identifying a tumor target to treating a patient.
The University of Oxford announced early this month that the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA) was providing an additional eight million pounds (about 10.6 million U.S. dollars) for the university's UK Cancer Vaccine AI Scientist and Supercomputing Project. The project combines AI tools for selecting vaccine targets with automated laboratory experiments and data analysis, under the guidance of oncologists.
"AI gives us an extraordinary opportunity to find vaccine targets faster and learn from every experiment," said Dr Lennard Lee at Oxford's Center for Immuno-Oncology.
Personalized cancer vaccines aim to direct a patient's immune system against their tumor. A central challenge is identifying tumor fragments that will trigger an effective immune response.
In a January article published in the European Medical Journal (EMJ), researchers including Lee argued that existing computational tools often address separate steps in this process. Current tools can help predict whether a tumor protein fragment will bind to a human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecule, which helps display it to immune cells. But even strong binding does not necessarily trigger an immune response.
The researchers proposed that AI models trained on genetic information, protein data, tissue images and immune responses could help connect these biological processes and improve the selection of vaccine targets. This remains a research strategy whose benefits require testing, according to the article.
According to Oxford, early laboratory tests during its cancer vaccine project's initial nine-month phase suggested that vaccine targets selected by AI could trigger measurable immune responses. But these findings do not establish that the approach improves survival or controls cancer in patients.
In the next phase, the team plans to develop automated systems to manufacture personalized mRNA cancer vaccines close to patients. A planned Phase I trial will assess the vaccines' safety and feasibility and whether they trigger the intended immune response.
Brian Wang, an ARIA program director, said cancer vaccine discovery was slowed by the separation of ideas, experiments and analysis across different teams. Oxford's project connects AI-generated targets, automated testing and clinical guidance in a single research loop, he added.
DATA AND TRUST CHALLENGES
Progress also depends on access to reliable biological and clinical data that researchers can use to train and test AI models.
A policy report published in June by the Cancer Research UK identifies fragmented datasets and inconsistent interpretations of governance requirements across institutions as obstacles to AI research. Inconsistent interpretations of patient consent, ethics requirements and data-sharing rules can make it harder to combine data across institutions, slowing research. The report calls for clearer governance and data that meet shared standards.
Shivani Sinha, a policy adviser in science and research policy at Cancer Research UK, described the practical consequences in an article: researchers can spend months seeking permission across institutions, only to discover that the data they obtain lack essential information.
"It inherits the gaps in the data and infrastructure around it," Sinha wrote of AI, warning that reuse across projects can reproduce those weaknesses at scale. She argued that datasets must represent the population more adequately and that their limitations must be made clear.
Trust also has a scientific dimension. Researchers need to establish when an AI prediction deserves further investigation and when its apparent precision exceeds the underlying evidence.
In their EMJ article, Lee and colleagues cautioned that AI foundation models can be difficult to interpret and may miss biological interactions important to cancer. They emphasized validation and benchmarking across diverse immune-system profiles, including populations underrepresented in existing datasets.
According to Cancer Research UK's report, scientists need the judgment to assess AI's limitations and recognize when its use is appropriate. Training should develop that critical capacity alongside technical skills.
Public confidence presents a related challenge. The report links trust to accountable governance and meaningful patient involvement in decisions about data access and research oversight. Concerns about privacy, security and unauthorized use of information could undermine the willingness to share data on which these projects depend.
For vaccine development, these challenges are closely connected: incomplete data can weaken predictions, while poorly explained or governed research can make the data needed to improve them harder to obtain.
EXPANDING COMPUTE, ADAPTING OVERSIGHT
Britain is investing public resources to give researchers greater access to the computing capacity needed for this work.
In January, Britain's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology announced an investment of 36 million pounds (about 47.7 million U.S. dollars) to increase the supercomputing capacity available at the University of Cambridge through the national AI Research Resource program to six times its existing level.
The announcement said the national program provides free computing access to eligible researchers and start-ups. Cambridge's DAWN supercomputer had already supported more than 350 projects across different fields, including work on AI tools that could accelerate personalized cancer vaccine development.
Access arrangements remain important. Sinha argued that national capacity figures mean little if researchers cannot secure time on the machines. She also called for bringing analysis to securely held data, reducing the need to move sensitive information between systems.
Regulators face a parallel challenge as AI potentially increases the pace and volume of new treatments.
Lawrence Tallon, chief executive officer of Britain's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), told the House of Lords Science and Technology Committee in June that the agency needed greater capacity, specialist expertise and technological investment to handle a growing pipeline.
Discussing AI tools used for medical purposes, Tallon called for closer monitoring after such products reach the market. He explained that an AI system's performance can change as the system learns and evolves. Tallon also described "predetermined change control plans," which set limits in advance on how much an approved software product can change before further regulatory review is required.
The MHRA was also exploring AI to assist its own review of clinical trial applications, while retaining human responsibility, according to Tallon.
"I emphasize that, for the foreseeable future, it will always be a human making the final decision. But AI can speed up our assessment and speed up product development," Tallon said. ■

Somalia sets 2027 dates for parliamentary, presidential polls
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
21:52:43 CST
22:52:43 KST

MOGADISHU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Somalia's electoral body on Thursday released an official timetable for the upcoming national elections, scheduling parliamentary polls for April 15 and the presidential election for May 15, 2027.
The National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission said the schedule covers elections for both houses of parliament and the presidency, in line with the country's constitution and national electoral law.
The commission also released a schedule of preparatory milestones leading up to the vote, beginning with a 21-day review of regulations governing political parties and candidate registration on Nov. 1.
The electoral body noted that this initial phase will include extensive public consultations before candidate submissions and campaign periods begin.
Under the schedule, political parties and relevant stakeholders are required to submit their parliamentary candidate lists by Nov. 22, four months ahead of the vote.
Presidential candidate registration is set for Jan. 21, 2027, fulfilling Article 34(1) of the National Electoral Law, which mandates a 60-day window prior to the vote.
Meanwhile, parliamentary campaigns will kick off on Feb. 27, 2027, while the presidential campaign period is slated to begin on March 15, 2027, exactly 30 days ahead of the election.
While the federal government welcomed the announcement as a vital step toward strengthening democratic governance, former President Mohamed Abdullahi Farmaajo rejected the timetable, warning that proceeding without political consensus could trigger renewed conflict.
Farmaajo criticized the electoral body as "one-sided," alleging that President Mohamud is forging ahead with the electoral schedule without the endorsement of opposition leaders or federal member states.
A statement from the Office of the Prime Minister said that the government views the timetable as a crucial step toward executing the electoral process and strengthening the nation's democratic institutions.
The prime minister noted that for the past 18 months, the administration has provided avenues for consultation to help all Somali parties agree on key national decisions, most notably the election framework.
"The government affirms that these consultations and negotiations will continue, and will strive to be fruitful and lead to a broad consensus," it said on Thursday evening.
"The government calls on all political parties to participate in the consultations in good faith and with national responsibility, and to work together for peaceful elections that strengthen the confidence of the people and the future of Somali governance," it added.
Somalia last held direct, one-person, one-vote universal suffrage elections in March 1969, shortly before the government was overthrown in a bloodless military coup later that year. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: Chinese hybrid rice takes root in Madagascar, boosts harvests, livelihoods
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
21:52:19 CST
22:52:19 KST

ANTANANARIVO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- As the rainy season approaches, farmer Jean Jacques Landry is busy plowing his hybrid rice paddy near Lake Alaotra, about 300 km from Antananarivo, Madagascar's capital, in preparation for the new planting season.
Landry is among a growing number of Malagasy farmers benefiting from years of China-Madagascar cooperation in hybrid rice cultivation. Since a China-aided hybrid rice demonstration center project was launched in 2007, Chinese agricultural experts have introduced high-yielding rice varieties and cultivation techniques adapted to local conditions.
To date, Chinese hybrid rice has been planted on a cumulative area of 90,000 hectares in Madagascar, with an average yield of about 7.5 tonnes per hectare, two to three times that of traditional local varieties. Madagascar now has the largest area under hybrid rice cultivation in Africa.
BETTER SEEDS, BIGGER HARVESTS
Rice cultivation has a long history in Madagascar, yet domestic production has struggled to meet the country's staple food needs due to constraints including seed quality, farming techniques, and infrastructure.
Nineteen years ago, Chinese agricultural expert Hu Yuefang and other technicians arrived in Madagascar with hybrid rice seeds and cultivation techniques under the demonstration center project, aiming to help the technology take root on the island.
Given Madagascar's diverse climatic and environmental conditions, ranging from tropical rainforests and semi-arid regions to swamps and volcanic ash soils, finding suitable hybrid rice varieties was no easy task.
"For hybrid rice to take root here, we first had to find the right seeds," Hu said.
Carrying dozens of carefully selected rice seed samples, Hu and his team conducted a series of planting trials across the island's major rice-growing regions.
Years of painstaking work paid off when the team successfully developed five rice varieties suited to local conditions. The varieties combine high yields with resistance to drought, flooding, and lodging.
According to Hu, the rice varieties yielded two to three times as much as traditional local varieties. Impressed by their high productivity, villagers fondly nicknamed Chinese hybrid rice "Tsarabe," meaning "excellent" in Malagasy.
KNOWLEDGE SHARING BOOSTS PRODUCTION
"We must not only provide good seeds, but also teach farmers how to grow good rice," Hu said.
From sowing and raising seedlings to managing pests and diseases, he demonstrated each step of the cultivation process himself. To communicate more effectively with local farmers, he spent three years learning Malagasy.
Alongside field demonstrations, Chinese experts have also held monthly classroom training sessions at a local agricultural training center.
Over the years, Chinese agricultural experts have conducted hundreds of training sessions on hybrid rice cultivation in Madagascar, directly training more than 2,000 people and passing on techniques to tens of thousands of local farmers through indirect training and knowledge sharing.
In Mahitsy, about 35 km from Antananarivo, farmer Solomampionona Nantenaina Razafimalala has been growing hybrid rice since 2020. After switching to hybrid varieties and applying an appropriate amount of fertilizer, Razafimalala's rice yields can reach 10 tonnes per hectare.
Today, his family has enough rice to meet its needs throughout the year and earns additional income by selling surplus harvests, allowing it to gradually invest in more agricultural inputs.
Fellow farmer Mbolatiana Anjarasoa Rasolonomenjanahary has had a similar experience. A paddy that once yielded only about five bags of unhusked rice now produces 12 bags with hybrid varieties.
"Our lives have truly changed. We have gained valuable farming experience and become more independent, able to manage production on our own," she said.
According to Zhang Lijun, executive director of the Africa sub-center of the China National Hybrid Rice Research and Development Center, the project has benefited more than 5,000 farming households in Madagascar. The net income from cultivating traditional local rice varieties is approximately 2,000 yuan (about 300 U.S. dollars) per hectare, compared with more than 6,900 yuan per hectare for hybrid rice.
He added that if Madagascar devoted 150,000 hectares of its existing rice-growing land to hybrid rice cultivation, the country could achieve food self-sufficiency.
DEEPENING AGRICULTURAL COOPERATION
In December 2024, the Hunan Hybrid Rice Research Center and the University of Antananarivo jointly established the China-Madagascar Belt and Road Joint Hybrid Rice Laboratory.
Through collaborative breeding of new rice varieties, personnel exchanges and training, as well as technology demonstrations and promotion, the two sides aim to strengthen Madagascar's domestic capacity for hybrid rice research and development.
Tiana Randriamihanta, Malagasy research project leader at the joint laboratory, said the facility would compare Chinese and Malagasy rice cultivation techniques to improve rice varieties and promote the local application of hybrid rice technology.
The laboratory currently has seven researchers and will focus on advancing hybrid rice research and education, boosting yields and training more technical professionals to support the development of Madagascar's hybrid rice industry.
Madagascar has also established an integrated hybrid rice industry chain encompassing breeding, seed production, cultivation, processing and sales, making it the first African country to commercialize hybrid rice. ■
