Romania finally holds Russia responsible for the drone attacks on ships off its coast, and wants a joint NATO command for the Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:51:30 UTC
22:51:30 KST

Romania has proposed a joint NATO military command for the Black Sea, as drones hit four merchant ships in 24 hours, three of them off its coast, and its foreign minister said Russia "bears full responsibility." NATO ambassadors will discuss the attacks next week.
Russia’s strikes on merchant ships in the Black Sea have escalated this autumn and reached NATO shores. Drones have attacked at least eight merchant vessels near Romania and Bulgaria since 5 October, two of them inside Romania’s territorial waters. Until now, neither country had named the attacker, and Bulgaria still says it cannot prove who it was. Romania’s patience appears to have run out, and next week’s NATO meeting will show whether the alliance is ready to go further as Russia’s war spills beyond Ukraine’s borders.
Acting Defense Minister Radu Miruță wrote on Facebook on 14 October that "the Black Sea needs a joint military command of the NATO riparian states." "The Black Sea incidents, involving drones, sunk ships, and naval mines, oblige us to act, not wait," he wrote, after a call with his Bulgarian counterpart. Leadership and location would rotate among the member states. Romania is ready to host the command on its coast from 2028 and would accept a start on Türkiye's coast until then, he said. He proposed that Romania and Bulgaria send NATO a joint letter backing the idea.
The next day, Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu wrote on X that four commercial ships had been attacked over the previous day, including in Romania's territorial waters and exclusive economic zone, and that eight people had died. "Russia is turning the Black Sea into a dangerous area for civilian ships," she wrote. "Killing sailors from commercial ships, both in this region and anywhere in the world, is a crime. Russia bears full responsibility for these developments."
Earlier that day, as two tankers burned off Romania's coast, Bucharest had said it was still checking whether drones were involved.
Two tankers burn off Romania’s Sulina as Bulgaria says it lacks proof Russia is behind the Black Sea ship attacks
Țoiu said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte had agreed to convene the allies within days, after he met Romanian President Nicușor Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Brussels. NATO ambassadors will meet next week, France 24 reported. No date has been announced.
An escalating drone strike campaign
Drones have been hitting merchant ships for weeks on the route from Ukraine's Danube and Odesa ports to the Bosporus. Besides the latest strikes off Romania, Reuters counts at least five cargo ships hit near Romania and Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors dead or missing, most of them outside any NATO member's territorial waters. This week the strikes reached Romania's own waters.
- The Comoros-flagged tanker Yara J was hit inside Romanian territorial waters late on 14 October, off Sulina, the port at the mouth of the Danube. Its crew was unharmed, and it was towed to the Romanian port of Constanța.
- Early on 15 October drones struck the San Marino-flagged chemical tanker Wine Trader about a mile outside Romanian waters, also southeast of Sulina. Five of its 12 crew were rescued. Seven were still missing on 16 October, when rescuers returned to search the ship.
- Two more ships were also targeted, Reuters reported: the Marshall Islands-flagged Sea Destiny, inside Romanian waters according to NATO, and the Tanzania-flagged Dania J, moored at the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail.
Țoiu did not say which ships her eight dead were from, and Reuters still lists the Wine Trader's seven as missing. A NATO military source told Reuters the drones that hit both tankers came from Russia.
Romania's president says too early to say
Romania's president has not gone as far as his foreign minister. Dan told reporters in Brussels it was "obvious" that the attacks were Russian attempts to destabilize Romania and Bulgaria and reduce support for Ukraine. But he also said it was too early to say definitively that Russia had launched the drones, according to Politico.
Bulgaria, Romania's partner on the command proposal, says it suspects Russia but cannot prove it. Two ships were hit off its coast on 13 October, and one, the HS Dignity, sank. The other, the Chelsea 3, is Ukrainian-owned.
Radev told parliament on 14 October that the attacks worked in Russia's favor and that "logic leads there." "The problem is that we cannot prove it," he told MPs. Sofia summoned the Russian ambassador. Radev also said EU leaders would discuss a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea.
Bucharest has blamed Russia for drones before, though over its airspace, not its shipping. On 27 July it expelled a Russian diplomat after prosecutors confirmed that fragments of drones downed on Romanian territory were Russian. Russia, Romania's Foreign Ministry said then, "bears exclusive responsibility."
Ukraine ships most of its farm exports across the Black Sea. Euromaidan Press's David Axe has written on how the fight over shipping there has escalated.

Holding elections in Ukraine

On October 15, the client handed the money to employees of the exchange office, who were acting on the lawyer’s instructions and, according to the investigation, were unaware of his alleged criminal intentions. Immediately afterward, the lawyer was detained.
He was notified of suspicion of a completed attempt to take possession of another person’s property through deception on an especially large scale (Part 2 of Article 15, Part 5 of Article 190 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The issue of selecting a preventive measure is being decided.

UK threatens African state with blanket visa ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:48:43 UTC

UK threatens African state with blanket visa ban
Britain has threatened to ban all Eritrean nationals from obtaining visas over their government’s alleged refusal to take back rejected asylum seekers and convicted criminals, prompting the East African country to accuse London of political manipulation.
The Home Office said on Thursday that Eritrea had “abruptly” withdrawn returns cooperation earlier this year and refused to engage constructively despite months of private talks.
The department removed fast-track visa processing for Eritrean officials and VIPs and required its diplomats to obtain permission to travel more than 60 km (37 miles) outside of London. It said the measures were intended to increase “pressure on countries refusing to take back illegal immigrants.” The travel curbs mirror Eritrea’s longstanding restrictions requiring British diplomats to obtain permission to travel outside the capital, Asmara, the Home Office said in a statement.
“My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK,” Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood warned.
Eritrea’s embassy dismissed the measures as a “perfunctory political gimmick,” saying Asmara had repeatedly rejected forced returns and sought dialogue that London refused. It accused Britain of offering “blanket asylum to anyone who claims to be Eritrean in a bid to undermine” the Eritrean government.
The embassy said Asmara suspended escorted returns after British authorities allegedly passed off forced repatriations as voluntary and failed to disclose that some deportees were still serving prison sentences. It said no Eritrean official had received a UK visa since 2023.
The dispute reflects Britain’s drive to curb irregular migration. Eritreans accounted for 18% of approximately 33,000 small-boat arrivals across the English Channel in the year to June 2026, the largest nationality group, according to Home Office figures.
Around 84% of Eritrean asylum claims received positive initial decisions, according to Home Office figures, while UN reporting has documented indefinite national service, arbitrary detention and risks facing people forcibly returned. Britain has used similar pressure against Angola, Namibia and DR Congo to secure greater cooperation on migrant returns.
The British government’s migration policies have also triggered a separate dispute with Rwanda after then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer abandoned a previous Conservative government’s asylum relocation scheme in July 2024. The plan would have sent some asylum seekers who arrived in Britain irregularly to Rwanda for their claims to be processed, with successful applicants settling there.
The policy cost £700 million (about $930 million) and sent only four volunteers to Rwanda, according to British ministers. Kigali pursued arbitration over unpaid commitments, but a tribunal rejected its claims, including two £50 million payments, in a ruling announced in June.

US senators called for an investigation into Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. senators called for an investigation into Starlink restrictions on October 12–14.
A group of senators from both parties in the U.S. Senate has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into reports of disruptions to SpaceX’s Starlink internet network in Ukraine. UNN writes about this, citing the BBC.
Details
In the letter sent on Thursday, October 15, to the inspector general of the U.S. Department of Defense, the senators stated that they had "serious concerns" about reports of speed restrictions between October 12 and 14.
The White House and the Pentagon did not respond to suggestions that the United States may have been involved in the alleged slowdown.
The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen, a Democratic member of the U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, calls on the inspector general to determine whether the restrictions were caused by the U.S. Department of Defense or its contractors.
It states that "the restrictions reportedly impaired Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure."
Starlink, owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, restricted speeds to 160 km/h on Tuesday evening, meaning that any weapon traveling faster than that speed lost its connection to the network, the outlet notes.
The senators also stated that they were "deeply concerned" by reports of outages or "disruptions" affecting intelligence-sharing capabilities and threat warnings relied upon by personnel conducting activities in Ukraine.
"We are particularly concerned about incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement said.
"Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require an immediate investigation," the senators added.
Signatories to the letter included Republican senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, and John Cornyn, as well as Democratic senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal, and Christopher Coons.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk suggested that the U.S. government may be behind the restrictions. On Wednesday, Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any speed or usage restrictions are determined by the U.S. military and, ultimately, [the U.S. president]."
Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas. Starshield, which relies on the Starlink network, is intended for government and military use. Both are owned by Musk’s SpaceX.

====================================================================================================

'Wake-up call for retailers': How cyberattacks threaten supermarket food supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:46:04 UTC
22:46:04 KST

Empty supermarket shelves usually suggest a shopping frenzy, panic buying ahead of a disaster or a disruption to deliveries. A cyberattack on refrigeration systems is a far less obvious explanation.
Yet that is what happened in France, where refrigerated shelves were left empty after hackers targeted systems used by several major supermarket chains.
During the attack, hackers remotely manipulated the systems, using their defrost function to raise temperatures to around 50C (122F), threatening fresh and frozen food stocks.
Systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss, as well as those from US company Copeland and Italian company Dixell, were targeted.
Affected stores disconnected their equipment from the network, while the incident raised concerns over potential food losses and disruption to supermarket operations.
French Economy Minister Roland Lescure told parliament Tuesday that around 700 food distribution centers had been affected, while initial estimates put the number of targeted stores at around 500.
As France assessed the consequences of the attack, a separate incident was reported in the Netherlands.
Albert Heijn, the country's largest supermarket chain, announced Monday that operations at several distribution centers had come to a standstill after systems were shut down "preventively" following an attempted cyberattack.
While no link has been established between the two incidents, both highlight how cyberattacks can disrupt the infrastructure that supermarkets rely on to keep food fresh and supplies moving.
Dominique Schelcher, head of French supermarket group Cooperative U, described the refrigeration attack as “unprecedented, extremely serious and unacceptable.”
Targeting equipment essential to preserving fresh products constituted “an attack on the French food supply chain,” he wrote on US social media platform X.
The incident has drawn attention from cybersecurity specialists because of its direct impact on physical operations.
"This is one of the first large-scale cyber-attack affecting directly the daily life of French people," Kevin Tellier, a cybersecurity engineer at French cybersecurity firm Synacktiv, told Anadolu.
Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at cybersecurity company Sophos, said the French and Dutch incidents illustrated "two different but equally important" risks facing retailers.
The French attacks showed "how a cyber intrusion can have direct physical consequences, disrupting refrigeration and destroying stock," he said.
The Dutch incident, meanwhile, demonstrated "how a cybersecurity event can disrupt digital services and business operations."
"Together, they reinforce that cyber risk in retail is now a business continuity issue, not just an IT issue," Pilling said.
Tellier said the French incident demonstrated how a cyberattack could disrupt everyday life, even without particularly sophisticated methods.
“A 15-year-old kid could have done this as it was not very sophisticated,” he said.
He also warned that artificial intelligence could increase attackers' capabilities, including those with limited experience.
“I don't really believe in rogue AI scenarios ... but rather in attackers using AI to augment their potential,” he noted.
Pilling said the French incident was not an outlier, although attacks with direct physical consequences were not the dominant form of cyber impact observed across Europe.
“Across Europe we're seeing increased legislative and regulatory attention to operational technology and other connected systems that were never originally designed to face today's threat landscape,” he said.
"Governments understand that this is a significant resilience issue both now and into the future," he added.
What made the French incident unusual was the visibility of its real-world consequences, Pilling said.
“Attacks that deliberately cross that cyber-physical threshold are relatively rare," he said.
Asked whether the incidents pointed to a deliberate strategy of targeting food security, Pilling said it was too early to draw such a conclusion.
“We do not yet know who was responsible or what their motive was,” he said.
Food supply chains and retail operations contribute to civilian resilience, meaning disruptions can have consequences beyond the companies directly affected, he added.
One reason such attacks can have consequences beyond the digital world is their potential to compromise operational technology (OT), the hardware and software used to monitor and control physical processes, including refrigeration and industrial machinery.
"From my technical perspective, OT is often forgotten and has been largely underestimated during the last decades," Tellier said.
OT systems are designed to operate continuously, meaning updates and security measures are often seen as potential sources of disruption, he explained. The diversity of such equipment can also make security audits and improvements difficult.
Tellier said the attack did not surprise his company, which had previously reported vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss refrigeration systems and other brands.
“I remember well my colleagues logged on the control panel three years ago while they reported the vulnerability to Danfoss,” he added.
According to Tellier, Danfoss cooperated with Synacktiv and deployed a patch after three months. However, he said it remained unclear why the same vulnerability appeared again in 2025 and could have been exploited in France again this year.
Tellier said Danfoss had described the affected models as obsolete and no longer eligible for security updates, although some were still functioning properly.
Updating OT equipment can also be time-consuming, he said, because some systems require technicians to connect a USB stick to each device to install updates manually.
Tellier also pointed to management interfaces accessible through the internet, saying their exposure could have been identified through a security audit.
“Individual Supermarkets were not aware until today that they could lose money on a cyberattack,” he added.
"Centralized management is useful to cut costs, it was implemented for this purpose. However, centralizing means introducing single points of failure that must be audited regularly," Tellier said.
Pilling said modern supermarkets rely on equipment vendors, maintenance providers, remote management platforms and connected equipment.
“Those dependencies improve efficiency, but they can also create shared points of failure if security isn't managed consistently across the ecosystem,” he said.
Centralized management software allows organizations to manage thousands of devices, but can also amplify the impact of an attack if a central platform is compromised, Pilling explained.
“The same technology that improves operational efficiency can rapidly magnify the impact of a security incident,” he said.
Food distribution systems could also be targeted to cause disruption without directly attacking traditional critical infrastructure, such as power or water networks, he added.
“A relatively small technical compromise can translate into spoiled stock, supply-chain disruption and public concern,” Pilling said.
The incident also demonstrated the potential consequences of attacks on widely deployed platforms and shared services, he said.
“The more interconnected these systems become, the greater the potential impact when something goes wrong,” he said.
Preventing similar attacks will require supermarkets to look beyond software updates and strengthen the security of the systems that keep their operations running, according to Pilling.
“This is a resilience issue as much as a patching issue,” Pilling said.
He recommended that retailers identify their refrigeration systems, check whether they remain supported by manufacturers and secure their remote-access interfaces.
“Where remote access is operationally necessary, it should be limited to trusted management networks or secured remote-access services, with strong authentication and appropriate network segmentation,” he said.
Pilling also recommended updating supported equipment, isolating obsolete controllers and monitoring systems for unexpected changes.
"Regardless of who is ultimately responsible, the French refrigeration attack should be a wake-up call for retailers and operators of connected infrastructure," he said.
Systems supporting food supplies, safety and day-to-day services are now part of the "cyber battlefield" and need to be secured accordingly, he added.

US ambassador to the NL gave $1m to Trump ballroom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:42:04 UTC
22:42:04 KST

US ambassador to the NL gave $1m to Trump ballroom
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The US ambassador to the Netherlands, Joe Popolo, donated $1 million towards president Donald Trump’s new White House ballroom, according to a leaked list of project donors.
The Washington Post, which obtained the list, said the gift was made late last year, around two months after the businessman was appointed ambassador. Popolo declined to comment further to the paper.
The list runs to the end of September and records 67 donations of $10,000 or more, with a total of $333 million pledged. Tech, AI and arms manufacturers made up a large share of the donors. Some, who asked to stay anonymous, accounted for $77 million.
According to the paper, about half of the money came from companies or individuals with business before the federal government. Democratic politicians had previously asked for the donor list without success.
The fund managing the money agreed with the government not to reveal the identities of its backers, which US non-profits are generally not required to do.
Trump said last year the ballroom would be paid for entirely by himself and a few friends, but the list shows no contribution from the president. The Washington Post reported earlier this year that half the construction costs, now estimated at $600 million, are being met from public funds.
The White House snubbed the criticism, saying the same critics would complain if taxpayers were paying for the renovations.
The ballroom, which the president says will hold nearly 1,000 guests, is being built on the site of the White House east wing, which Trump had demolished last year. The plans include a military bunker underneath.

Türkiye expects 4.2% economic growth in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:41:42 UTC
22:41:42 KST

Türkiye expects 4.2% economic growth in 2027
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye's trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7% in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2%, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yilmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5% by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation, and innovation, he said.
Employment is expected to increase by 657,000 people next year, with labor force participation reaching 53.4% and unemployment declining to 8%, from a projected 8.1% in 2026.
Yilmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30% in September, was expected to reach 28.4% by the end of this year before declining to 21% by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2% of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6% in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security, and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
Goods exports this January-September rose 5.2% year-on-year to $211 billion, bringing the rolling annual total to a record $283.7 billion, Yilmaz said.
The share of medium-high- and high-technology products in exports reached 44%, compared with around 28% in the early 2000s, he added.
Earlier, it was reported that Türkiye introduced new regulations prohibiting social media platforms from providing services to children under the age of 15.

PM-SETU clears Rs 1,195 crore for five ITI clusters in 3 states, J&amp;K
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:40:38 UTC
22:40:38 KST

NEW DELHI: The Centre has approved investments worth Rs 1,194.92 crore to upgrade five clusters of Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) across Maharashtra, Odisha and Jammu & Kashmir, taking the cumulative investment cleared under the PM-SETU scheme to Rs 3,687 crore.The five projects will be implemented in partnership with Tata Steel Foundation, BVG India, Belrise Industries, Eagle Infra India and Inderdeep Infra India. The investments are aimed at modernising ITI infrastructure, introducing industry-aligned courses, upgrading trainer capabilities and strengthening links between technical training and employment.The approvals were given at the sixth meeting of the National Steering Committee of the Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM-SETU), chaired by skill development secretary Debashree Mukherjee on Friday.The Pune cluster in Maharashtra has been allocated Rs 241 crore, while the Kataka cluster in Odisha will receive Rs 240.50 crore. The Jammu cluster has been approved Rs 240 crore, followed by the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar cluster at Rs 238.01 crore and the Srinagar cluster at Rs 235.41 crore.Each cluster will have a hub ITI and four spoke institutes, with the hub expected to anchor training and other capacity-building efforts across the cluster.
Mukherjee said the approvals would help strengthen ITIs, improve training and increase industry participation. She also urged the clusters to work towards ISO certification and include at least one WorldSkills-aligned trade or competency area in their approved implementation plans.She said progress in Jammu & Kashmir was encouraging and reflected a commitment to strengthening skilling and expanding opportunities for young people in the region.Under the approved plans, state governments, industry partners and participating ITIs will work together to upgrade facilities, introduce new-age training programmes and improve the relevance of courses to employers’ requirements.
The steering committee also reviewed progress under the scheme’s Training of Trainers component. As of October 2026, 3,744 trainers had been trained through National Skill Training Institutes (NSTIs), according to the ministry.PM-SETU seeks to transform ITIs into industry-aligned institutions through modern infrastructure, updated curricula and greater private-sector participation. The latest approvals extend the scheme’s investment footprint across western, eastern and northern India.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar discussed a number of important bilateral issues at a meeting in Brussels, including Ukraine's accession to the European Union, trade and agricultural products. They also "agreed to resume joint work and exchange visits."
"I met with Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar. We spoke one-on-one about key issues on our bilateral agenda and Ukraine's progress toward EU accession," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram on Friday.

"We discussed the diplomatic situation and efforts to end Russia's war. I am grateful for his solidarity with Ukraine and our people, and for his readiness to work together for peace. We also discussed opportunities for cooperation between Ukraine and Hungary, trade, and issues related to agricultural products," the president said.
"Ukraine always stands for good-neighborly relations and mutual strengthening. We agreed to resume joint work at various levels and to exchange visits. Our teams will work out the dates," Zelenskyy wrote.
As reported, following his meeting with Zelenskyy, Magyar said Hungary was ready to provide diplomatic assistance to secure a ceasefire as soon as possible and establish lasting peace in Ukraine.
"I assured the president of Ukraine of my full solidarity in the face of Russia's inhumane aggression against his country, which has been going on for almost five years. I told him that Hungary is ready to help by all possible diplomatic means to achieve a ceasefire as soon as possible and establish lasting peace," Magyar wrote on Facebook on Friday.
He also said that following the meeting, the parties had agreed to continue consultations at the ministerial level, with particular attention to the situation of national minorities in both countries. Magyar welcomed the political agreement between Hungary and Ukraine on strengthening the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia and described the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of a law on the educational rights of national minorities, along with the start of its implementation, as a first step toward restoring mutual trust.
Magyar also thanked the Ukrainian parliament for its September resolution on crimes committed against Hungarians in Transcarpathia in 1944-1946, particularly forced labor and mass deportation.
"We agreed that it is in both countries' interests to put political and economic relations on a new footing," he said.

Croatia initiates changes to EU conclusions on Montenegro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:39:54 UTC
22:39:54 KST

İlayda Çakırtekin
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The European Council’s conclusions on Montenegro were amended following an intervention by Croatia, with references to deadlines for the provisional closure of negotiating chapters removed, Croatian public broadcaster HRT reported Friday.
The earlier draft called for an agreement on the provisional closure of all negotiating chapters by the end of 2026, provided Montenegro implemented the necessary reforms, and for work on its accession treaty to be completed as soon as possible.
The revised conclusions welcome ongoing work on drafting an accession treaty with Montenegro and take note of the Irish Council presidency’s intention to work toward the provisional closure of negotiating chapters, provided Montenegro implements the appropriate reforms.
Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic said after the first day of the European Council meeting in Brussels that Croatia remained a supporter of EU enlargement but stressed that candidate countries must meet the required criteria.
“We amended the conclusions at our initiative, sending a realistic message to our colleagues in Montenegro that they should get down to talks with Croatia,” he said.
Plenkovic said Zagreb had raised outstanding issues with Montenegro related to Chapter 23, covering the judiciary and fundamental rights, and Chapter 31, covering foreign, security and defense policy.
Croatia has presented eight demands to Montenegro, six concerning Chapter 23 and two related to Chapter 31.

Norwegian teenager sentenced to 20 years in prison over UK murder plot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:38:32 UTC
22:38:32 KST

UK Counter Terrorism Policing said Natland had been operating under orders from someone in the Foxtrot Network, an international criminal gang based in Sweden.
A Norwegian teenager has been sentenced to 20 years in prison after being found guilty of travelling to the UK to carry out an assassination.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, is said to have agreed to undertake a contract killing in exchange for €25,000.
He was arrested at a hotel in northern England in March 2025 after having arrived at Manchester airport two days earlier, with officers discovering a bag containing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver, and 19 bullets under his bed.
Analysis of his phone and communications showed he had been instructed on how to collect the weapons and that he had received social media messages when he was in Norway asking him to carry out a shooting in the UK, the Metropolitan Police said. He had been controlled by someone called "Agent 47" - an apparent reference to the Hitman video game series.
It is not known who the intended target was.
Natland claimed that he had not intended to follow through with the shooting.
"You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself," Justice Bobbie Cheema-Grubb said at the sentencing hearing at Woolwich Crown Court, per the Associated Press. "Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to."
UK Counter Terrorism Policing said Natland had been operating under orders from someone in the Foxtrot Network, an international criminal gang based in Sweden that authorities say is involved arms trafficking and that has been linked to shootings and contract killings in Northern Europe.
The US State Department says the Iranian regime has leveraged the Foxtrot Network to carry out attacks on Israeli and Jewish targets in Europe. Both the US and UK have sanctioned the group and its leader, Rawa Majid.
Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "Natland was arrested just hours before he was due to carry out an assassination here in the UK."
"The intended target of this specific assassination has never been identified, and we found no evidence of any direct link to Iran in this case. However, as recent events have shown, CTP will seek to proactively disrupt any attempts by hostile states to carry out criminal acts in the UK," she added.

Israeli diplomats and embassy staff vote in record numbers as election turnout abroad hits 86.7%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:38:13 UTC
22:38:13 KST

Voter turnout among Israeli diplomats, government personnel stationed overseas and eligible family members reached 86.7%, according to figures released Friday after voting concluded at 99 Israeli diplomatic missions worldwide ahead of the October 27 general election. 
Of 4,863 eligible voters, 4,218 cast ballots, compared with turnout of 69.6% in the November 2022 election, an increase of 17.1 percentage points.
Voting began Thursday under a longstanding arrangement allowing Israeli diplomatic and government personnel serving abroad, along with eligible family members, to vote before polling stations open in Israel. Unlike diplomats and other authorized personnel, ordinary Israeli citizens living or traveling abroad cannot vote overseas. The Foreign Ministry and Central Elections Committee operated 101 polling stations at 99 missions, serving embassy and consulate employees, government representatives, attachés and their eligible relatives.
Because of time zone differences, voting began at Israel's embassy in Wellington, New Zealand, at 11 p.m. Israel time on October 14, followed by the embassy in Suva, Fiji, Israel's newest diplomatic mission, at 12:01 a.m. Voting then moved westward across the globe over approximately 30 hours, with the final polling stations closing at Israeli missions in Los Angeles and San Francisco at 6 a.m. Friday. The largest polling station was at Israel's consulate in New York, where more than 700 people were eligible to vote.

Lavrov says ISIS seeks to destabilize Kabul, expand 'terrorist activity' into Central Asia, Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:38:03 UTC
22:38:03 KST

Kanyshai Butun
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Friday that a branch of ISIS (Daesh) terror group seeks to undermine the Taliban government in Kabul and use Afghanistan as a base to expand "terrorist activity" into Central Asia and Russia.
Speaking at a joint conference of the Collective Security Treaty Organisation, the Commonwealth of Independent States, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization on security in Central Asia and Afghanistan in Moscow, Lavrov said "terrorist and extremist groups" maintain a significant presence in Afghanistan’s border areas near Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, including training camps and strongholds.
He alleged that militants were attempting to enter Central Asian countries, sometimes posing as refugees or tourists, and warned of attempts to smuggle weapons and drugs from Afghanistan through the region into Russia.
Lavrov called for Russia and its Central Asian partners to strengthen their coordinated response to security threats, including through regional organizations and cooperation with Afghanistan’s Taliban authorities.
He said Moscow considered engagement with the Taliban government necessary, and that Russia supported efforts to integrate Afghanistan into regional economic processes and provide economic and humanitarian assistance.
“We proceed from the premise that the government—the Taliban movement—is a reality that must be reckoned with,” he said. “An increasing number of countries around the world are already demonstrating this understanding.”
He criticized NATO’s expanding security role, saying the alliance intended to impose its will far beyond its area of responsibility.
“NATO is not about Eurasia,” Lavrov said, arguing that the continent needed a security framework developed by its own countries.
He said Eurasia needed a self-developed security framework, reiterating Russia’s support for a Greater Eurasian Partnership and a new continental security architecture involving countries and regional organizations across Eurasia.

Qatar pledges a lifeline for Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:37:29 UTC

Breadcrumb
Qatar pledges a lifeline for Lebanon's economy and reconstruction in the south
Qatar will help Lebanon revive its struggling economy, including supporting the future reconstruction of the country’s south, the Qatari prime minister said Friday.
Qatar will continue to support the Lebanese army "as a national institution that safeguards the country's security, unity and stability," Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said after meeting in Beirut with his Lebanese counterpart Nawaf Salam.
For years, Qatar has been a friendly country to Lebanon and a mediator for domestic and international political crises in the region. Qatar has also given tens of millions of dollars to the Lebanese army since Lebanon’s economic meltdown began in 2019.
The Qatari official said that QatarEnergy has reached an agreement with French company TotalEnergies to jointly develop a solar power plant in Lebanon as an initial project. He said that the aim is to develop a major investment project "that would benefit the Lebanese economy, as well as the Qatari companies and entities participating in it."
Salam said that he will put the plans for Lebanon’s electricity sector to the Lebanese Cabinet soon.
"The Qatari side will fund, implement and activate the project without any cost on the Lebanese state," Salam said, adding that such a move is important because of Lebanon's financial crisis.
Lebanon's state electricity company is one of the country's biggest sources of debt, hemorrhaging about $40 billion over the past decades with a bloated workforce and outdated infrastructure. The company provides only a few hours of electricity each day, and the state, until a year ago, had taken advances from the Central Bank when diesel fuel ran out.
Earlier in the day, Qatar's prime minister met with Lebanon’s president and parliamentary speaker and discussed with them the situation in southern Lebanon, where Israel captured dozens of villages and towns earlier this year during the latest Israel-Hezbollah war. Over the past several months, Israel has carried out large-scale demolitions in villages that its troops occupy.
The latest Israel-Hezbollah war began in early March, with Israel killing more than 4,300 people and occupied large parts of southern Lebanon.
The Qatari official said that Israel should withdraw from Lebanon and cease its attacks in the country. He said that Qatar is working in coordination with the United States to help lay the groundwork for future reconstruction in southern Lebanon, in a manner that would allow displaced people to return to their homes.
About 1.2 million people were displaced in Lebanon at the height of the war. Most have returned home since a June ceasefire, but more than 300,000 remain displaced, according to the International Organisation for Migration.

Israeli-enforced starvation persists in Gaza despite ceasefire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:36:54 UTC
22:36:54 KST

At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza's health ministry has said, as the UN confirms acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on October 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5 percent of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza. More than 1.4 million Palestinians are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
Meanwhile, a new UNICEF report has confirmed that while the ceasefire since October has allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said progress in pushing back the threat of famine, confirmed by a global food security monitor in August last year, had been achieved through a scaled-up food and nutrition response, the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies, and the ceasefire.
However, those gains remain fragile, it said.
“Acute malnutrition rates have fallen, but only one in three children under the age of two is currently achieving minimum dietary diversity,” the report stated.
“We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require,” UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires told reporters in Geneva.
Starvation as a weapon
Israel has used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinians and rights organisations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34 percent of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
Malnutrition reaches 'catastrophic levels'
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67 percent of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18 percent of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2 percent of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anaemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41 percent before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

Swiss canton using drones for speed checks
The Swiss canton of St Gallen has unveiled new drones for speed enforcement on the mountain pass road to Hulftegg, between Toggenburg and the Tösstal valley in Zurich.
Since the start of the year, the St Gallen cantonal police have been making targeted use of drones in road traffic. The drone operations are intended to improve road safety and tackle traffic offences. Operations have focused on sections of road where there are indications of speeding offences.
Speed is determined using a distance-time calculation based on aerial video footage. This year, the cantonal police carried out six drone checks, which detected two speeding offences.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded on Friday to comments made by former US president Barack Obama, in which he accused Israel of taking "land off people" and being "excessive," referring to Israel's treatment of the Palestinian people throughout the country's history.

"The Jewish people are not foreign occupiers in the land of our forefathers," Netanyahu said in a video posted to X/Twitter. "Our history is not a colonial enterprise. Our land is not stolen land. This is our homeland."
Netanyahu called Obama's Belfast comments a "regrettable statement," emphasizing the connection between the Jewish people and the Land of Israel, noting its biblical name, "Judea."
"That's where Jews come from," he said. "And we've been attached to it for thousands of years."
The prime minister differentiated Israel from European nations with colonial pasts, saying that the Jews in Israel are not "the Dutch in Indonesia... the Belgians in the Congo, we're Jews in Judea."
Obstacle to peace lies with Israel's, America's enemies, Netanyahu says
Regarding the path to a peace agreement, Netanyahu said that the obstacle to peace is not Israel, but rather the enemies in the region shared by Israel and the United States.
Specifically, Netanyahu noted the enemies' "refusal to recognize the Jewish people's right to a state of our own, in any boundary."
He cited chants of "Death to Israel" and "Death to America," which are common in states like Iran, a shared enemy of the US and Israel.
"We are the 'Little Satan,' you are the 'Great Satan,'" he said, referencing how such states often refer to Israel and the US, respectively, saying that both countries are "defending our common civilization."
"A peace built on illusions will crash against the rocks of Middle Eastern reality," said Netanyahu. "Israel will not gamble with its survival to accommodate those who refuse to accept the facts of history, to accept our right to exist, or who wish to appease terror.
"We certainly do not; we never will," he concluded.
Obama: Palestinians 'understandably' want their 'land back'
Obama's comments on Tuesday, made in a conversation with journalist Susan McKay, referred to the Palestinians' reaction to the Jewish people's exerting cultural and military control over the State of Israel by explaining that "those people understandably said, 'This is injustice, and I want my land back.'"
"The fact is that the Jewish people, for millennia, were oppressed, discriminated against, killed," said Obama at the time. "Europe was responsible for much of it. They understandably sought a refuge."
"If the attitude of Israel is, now that we are the strongest, the most technologically advanced in the region, then our security will depend on us simply doing whatever we need and taking whatever we want, and not making any concessions to anyone," he added. "That may work short-term... but you have ceded moral ground if that is the position you take."
Obama did introduce nuance into the conversation, according to The Irish Times, saying that the millions of Jews and Palestinians in the region "aren't going anywhere."
"The citizenry of Israel has to rethink, to reimagine, how your children and grandchildren are going to live in this region," he said. "Are you just going to be behind walls and wipe out everybody around you, or are you going to find some just way of defending yourself while still acting in an ethical, moral way?"
Obama added that the Palestinians must come to understand that they will not "outkill" or "outweaponize the Israelis."
"We have to look to other examples of how change comes about," he said, pointing toward "nonviolent strategies." "That's going to take some time."

EU decision could drive more Sika deer to Zurich
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:31:31 UTC
22:31:31 KST

EU decision could drive more Sika deer to Zurich
The spotted Sika deer from Japan could soon be migrating to the Swiss canton of Zurich in greater numbers. This is due to a European Union directive for member states to cull the animals.
In Germany and Austria, the EU decision announced in the summer of 2025 caused quite a stir. The media were already referring to an “extermination and culling plan”. The EU had classified the spotted sika deer as an “invasive alien species”.
Private ownership of these deer will therefore only be permitted until August 2027. Furthermore, wild populations are to be “intensively hunted”. In this way, the EU aims to prevent damage to native forests and to stop the Asian deer from interbreeding with native red deer.
More
How Switzerland is battling invasive species
Around 40 Swiss Sika deer
The decision from Brussels could have implications for the canton of Zurich. “We will notice the increasing hunting pressure in Baden-Württemberg,” says Reto Muggler, co-head of the cantonal Fisheries and Hunting Administration. This means that more sika deer could migrate into the area.
This Asian deer species already lives in the canton of Zurich, albeit only in a small area of just over 2,300 hectares. The animals can be observed north of the Rhine in the Rafzerfeld in the canton of Zurich and in the canton of Schaffhausen. This population numbers just over 40 animals.
Unlike in the EU, where culling plans are a recent development, sika deer have, however, been hunted in the canton of Zurich for years. Last year, 19 animals were shot to prevent the population from spreading. “If more sika deer were to enter the canton of Zurich, they would continue to be hunted as part of normal management,” said Muggler.
The canton does not currently fear any significant geographical spread. According to Muggler, the sika deer remains within its territory. As such, it has not yet swum across the Rhine.
Nor does Zurich regard the possibility of Sika deer interbreeding with red deer as a threat. This is because the species live far apart and are unlikely to cross paths.
Gift from Japanese Emperor
The Zurich sika deer population descends from a population in the Black Forest that has lived there since 1939. The spotted deer actually originate from South-East Asia and the Far East. They arrived in Europe – more specifically, in France – in 1890 as a gift from the Japanese Emperor. There, they managed to escape from the grounds of Rambouillet Castle near Paris.
Around 1900, sika deer were brought to Germany because it was fashionable to ‘enrich’ the native wildlife with non-native species. Many sika deer lived in parks, where – as had happened in France – they once again managed to escape. There are now five populations in Germany.
Sika deer are related to red deer but are significantly smaller. From May to September, they have a summer coat with white patches.

How US bullied Vilnius into dropping support for conference critical of Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

The US pressured Lithuanian, Canadian and EU diplomats to withdraw their support for the Disinfo 2026 conference in Vilnius, which criticised Donald Trump and America’s interference in other countries’ politics. The pressure was first felt by the conference's speakers and organisers.
“A few days before the conference, a number of colleagues started receiving emails from Michael Shellenberger who runs a Substact where he goes after democracy defenders,” Adam Fivenson, one of the speakers and an associate at the Center for Security, Innovation and New Technology at American University in Washington, told LRT.lt.
According to Fivenson, many saw this as an intimidation attempt, as Shellenberger is considered close to the US State Department and to senior figures in the Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement.
Immediately before the conference, “we started hearing that sponsors had been approached”, Fivenson said, adding that first it was the European Union’s External Action Service, the de facto foreign ministry of the bloc, then Canada and Lithuania.
“We had no intention of deepening the rift between Lithuania and the US. And we view it as tremendously unfortunate that the US chose to try to use our event and our panel as a wedge to undermine Lithuanian security,” Fivenson said.
Lithuania's Foreign Ministry did not confirm whether pressure from Washington had prompted its decision to withdraw as a conference sponsor.
In responses provided to the media, the ministry stressed it had no role in coordinating the contents of the conference and that some parts of the programme were inconsistent with the government's position and Lithuania's interests.
“Our [US] government is still quite diverse in perspectives and in many ways in terms of departments, officials, voices. I fully understand that Lithuania may still have great working relationships with some folks, while the State Department is trying to throw a wrench in things because of our panel.
“That's what gives me some confidence that there are many people on both sides that understand the stakes of the moment and wouldn't play politics with Lithuanian safety and security,” Fivenson said.
The sensitivity of the US State Department to the disinformation topic was “really strange”, Fivenson said.
“It is hard to understand why they decided to put all our security relationships at risk over a single discussion at a researchers' conference,” he added.

====================================================================================================

Businesses warn of airlines halting operations and defense contracts being disrupted
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:29:45 EEST
22:29:45 KST

Businesses warn of airlines halting operations and defense contracts being disrupted
Kyiv • UNN
Industry associations are calling for a review of the new rules for reserving employees. They predict a loss of specialists, a halt to production, and contracts being disrupted.
Industry associations continue to call on the Government to review its decision to change the reservation rules, which has sparked serious debate. The government initiative could lead to the loss of critically important specialists, the suspension of operations at individual enterprises, and the disruption of contracts. Representatives of the Ukrainian Air Transport Association (UATA) and the Federation of Employers of Ukraine warn of this, UNN writes.
UATA warns of the threat of Ukrainian airlines being forced to suspend operations
The Ukrainian Air Transport Association has appealed to Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi over the risks that changes to the procedure for reserving military-liable employees pose to the aviation industry.
In its appeal of October 15, which is at UNN's disposal, UATA emphasizes that the current reservation limit of 50% of military-liable employees already significantly restricts the activities of airlines. The introduction of additional limits, which could result in individual specialists losing their reservations, threatens not only the operation of enterprises but also the state's economic and strategic interests.
The Association explains that aviation-industry employees are not interchangeable. Pilots, engineers, and technical specialists must have the appropriate training, valid certificates, authorizations, and experience working with specific types of aircraft, and training such personnel requires years and significant financial investment.
The loss of even one certified specialist makes it impossible to form a crew, carry out mandatory maintenance, or operate flights. At the same time, it is impossible to compensate for the staff shortage by increasing the workload of other employees without violating aviation-safety requirements.
In addition, UATA reminds that civil and military aviation are interconnected, as they share the same engineering, maintenance, and technological competencies. Therefore, preserving the staffing potential of civilian enterprises is also important for meeting the state's defense needs and fulfilling government orders.
The Association emphasizes that it supports combating abuses in the reservation process, but calls on the Government not to equate fictitious employment with preserving the actual production capabilities of critically important enterprises.
According to the association, the unpredictability of the reservation rules increases the risk of personnel outflow and the transfer of Ukrainian aviation specialists to foreign employers. This primarily concerns specialists who are already working abroad, where Ukrainian airlines continue to transport passengers and cargo.
In this case, Ukraine risks losing not only individual employees, but also established professional teams, experienced instructors, and staffing potential, without which the rapid restoration of air links will be significantly more difficult. Therefore, according to UATA, the possibility of restoring civil flights in Ukraine after the airspace is opened depends on the issue of reserving aviation-industry employees.
New restrictions will exacerbate the aviation industry's existing problems
The new reservation rules could become another blow to an industry that is already operating under extremely difficult economic conditions. As noted in UATA's appeal, airlines have already faced an additional monthly financial burden following the Government's change to the procedure for financing nationwide expenditures on aviation activities.
In addition, since 2024, the State Tax Service and the Bureau of Economic Security have changed their approaches to interpreting the taxation of lease payments that Ukrainian airlines make to non-residents for the use of aircraft. This has intensified pressure on the aviation business.
Against the backdrop of these problems, according to UATA, additional reservation restrictions could lead to the cessation of operations by a number of Ukrainian airlines.
At the same time, the Association reminds that even with the airspace closed to the civil aviation sector, it continues to generate revenue for the state budget. In 2022–2025, Ukrainian aviation enterprises paid almost UAH 27 billion in taxes and fees. Companies continue to carry out international transportation and specialized aviation operations abroad, ensuring the export of services and foreign-currency revenues for the budget.
The association also draws particular attention to the participation of Ukrainian air carriers in international humanitarian missions, including UN operations, cargo transportation, and aerial firefighting. The loss of qualified personnel could jeopardize the fulfillment of these international contracts. As a result, Ukrainian companies could be replaced by foreign competitors, while returning to international markets would require considerable time and resources.
The Federation of Employers warns of the risk of defense contracts being disrupted
The Federation of Employers of Ukraine also issued similar warnings regarding the government initiative. In an appeal to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which is in the possession of UNN, the FEU called for preventing the reduction of reservation quotas for employees of critically important enterprises in the defense-industrial complex from 100% to 85%.
The appeal was supported by leading associations of defense-industrial enterprises, which, according to the document's authors, represent more than 97% of the sector's enterprises.
Representatives of the defense industry emphasize that the proposed quotas will have far more serious consequences than a reduction in the number of employees. The point is that defense production depends on the coordinated work of highly qualified specialists who cannot be quickly replaced. This concerns not only designers, technologists, engineers, machine-tool operators, and welders, but also employees responsible for procurement, logistics, financing, and the fulfillment of international contracts.
The loss of even one such specialist could halt the technological process, disrupt industrial cooperation, or jeopardize the fulfillment of the state defense order.
The Federation of Employers points out that some enterprises have increased their defense-product output four- to eightfold, and in some cases by more than 16 times. According to them, the growth in production significantly outpaces the increase in staff numbers. For example, there were cases when output increased 16-fold while the number of employees grew only 2.4 times. This indicates the high dependence of defense production on established teams, accumulated expertise, and well-established technological processes.
Therefore, an administrative 15% reduction in reservation opportunities could lead not to a comparable decrease in production volumes, but to a halt in production.
Such decisions could be particularly dangerous when defense-industrial enterprises operate in several shifts, compensate for forced downtime caused by air-raid alerts, and must fulfill state contracts within specified deadlines.
The Federation of Employers also emphasizes that the potential mobilization effect of restricting the reservation of defense-industry employees may prove disproportionate to the losses to the state's defense capability. After all, defense-industry employees account for less than 10% of the total number of conscription-eligible persons with reserved status in Ukraine.
At the same time, the removal of reserved status does not mean an automatic increase in the ranks of the Defense Forces, whereas a reduction in the production of weapons and ammunition will directly affect the provision of military personnel, the Federation emphasizes.
Representatives of the defense industry cite the possible loss of trust among international partners as an additional risk. According to the Ministry of Defense, in 2025, foreign financing of Ukraine's defense industry amounted to $6.1 billion, and the threat of contracts being disrupted—or their actual disruption—due to internal administrative decisions could negatively affect the further attraction of investment funds.
The Coordination Center could create additional risks for businesses
Business representatives are particularly concerned about the initiative to establish a Coordination Center for organizing the reservation of conscripts. Its recommendations will determine whether an enterprise receives critical status and the limits on reserving employees. In the view of business representatives, this creates additional bureaucracy and entails corruption risks.
The UATA points to insufficient clarity regarding the criteria the Center will use for evaluation, the timeframes for reviewing applications, and appeal procedures. Businesses are particularly concerned about the possibility of reviewing an enterprise’s already-granted critical status without a defined list of grounds.
Such uncertainty could lead to the rules being applied inconsistently and create additional administrative obstacles for enterprises.
In view of this, the UATA proposes establishing a special mechanism for reserving conscript employees in the air transport sector that would take into account the specifics of its operations, flight safety requirements, and the need to retain qualified personnel. The Association stated that it was ready to participate in refining the relevant provisions of the Cabinet of Ministers’ resolution.
Parliament is preparing to repeal the Government’s decision.
The Government resolution changing the reservation rules has provoked a significant public response and a wave of criticism from the business community, industry associations, think tanks, and parliamentarians. Following this, at the initiative of Member of Parliament Yaroslav Zhelezniak and 62 other parliamentarians, draft resolution 16160 was registered in the Verkhovna Rada, entitled "On reviewing the decision of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine of October 13, 2026, regarding the limitation of opportunities to reserve employees of critically important enterprises." The MPs called on the Prime Minister to suspend the resolution and hold additional consultations.
However, in response, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi stated during Question Time with the Government that the resolution was still being revised.
"This resolution is currently being processed; it will certainly be revised, adopted, and published. There is no betrayal here. All the details will be provided precisely when they are published and all the relevant decisions are adopted. Therefore, the skepticism currently being discussed in society has no basis. There are no official decisions, so there is nothing to criticize at this point," he said.
Although the Prime Minister attempted to assure the public that critical enterprises in the defense and energy sectors had "nothing to worry about," he overlooked the fate of private enterprises in related sectors, which are no less important for ensuring the state’s resilience.
In the end, MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported that the Government had nevertheless removed from the agenda of Friday’s Cabinet of Ministers meeting the issue concerning the resolution on reservations and had agreed to hold additional consultations with business. The question of whether government officials will take into account the concerns expressed by entrepreneurs, industry associations, and analysts remains unanswered.

‘They kept kicking me’: Washington Post photojournalist beaten in West Bank settler attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:28:29 UTC
22:28:29 KST

American photojournalist Heidi Levine, who works for The Washington Post, was injured Friday in an attack by masked Israeli settlers on Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to witnesses and Palestinian reports. The assault near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, was one of several violent incidents reported during the annual olive harvest, with Israeli authorities opening an investigation into the clashes.
Witnesses said approximately 80 settlers, many wearing masks and some carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill overlooking terraced olive groves where Palestinian villagers had gathered to harvest olives. Some settlers allegedly set olive trees on fire and used slings to hurl stones at the harvesters, who retreated downhill before throwing stones back. "The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes," Palestinian farmer Moutaz Abdelhadi told Reuters.
Levine, a Jerusalem-based photographer who has covered conflicts across the Middle East for decades, was among those injured. Footage from the scene showed masked individuals beating her with sticks as she lay on the ground. Other journalists and Palestinians subsequently approached her, and she could be heard saying, "I'm not okay. They took all my stuff." Her camera equipment was reportedly stolen and her vehicle damaged.
Speaking from a hospital in Ramallah, where she was reported to be in stable condition, Levine described the attack. "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me," she said. Levine said her Palestinian colleagues eventually intervened, ending the assault. She was initially taken to a clinic in Abu Falah before being transferred to the hospital. Palestinian reports said a second person was also injured in the attack.
Witnesses said Israeli military vehicles arrived during the confrontation but that the violence continued, with soldiers firing tear gas toward Palestinians. The IDF said troops and Border Police officers had been dispatched following reports of a violent confrontation and used riot control measures to disperse those involved. At another nearby location, soldiers fired warning shots into the air before shooting at a Palestinian suspect who allegedly ran toward them carrying a sharp object and posed a threat. The military said all circumstances surrounding the incident would be examined.
The Binyamin Regional Council disputed the Palestinian account, describing the incident as a "planned provocation" organized by the Palestinian Authority. It claimed that hundreds of "terrorists and anarchists" had confronted Israelis, throwing stones and firing fireworks directly at them while journalists filmed the violence. The council also alleged that Palestinian Authority vehicles were present in the area and that left-wing activists had planned confrontations during the olive harvest to promote allegations of settler violence. These claims were not independently verified.
Israeli police said they had opened an investigation into violence in Abu Falah and nearby Turmus Ayya, including suspected stone-throwing and vehicle arson. Investigators and forensic teams were sent to collect evidence and witness statements under military escort. "The Israel Police and the IDF view any manifestation of violence gravely, particularly when it involves journalists carrying out their work," police said, pledging to bring those responsible to justice.
In Turmus Ayya, Palestinian reports said settlers set fire to olive trees and several vehicles, including one belonging to the Palestinian Civil Defense. The organization said one of its members was attacked while trying to extinguish a burning vehicle. Additional violence was reported near Burqa and Birzeit, where Palestinians said olive harvesters had been assaulted. The Palestinian Red Crescent reported treating four injured people near Burqa, while Palestinian media said a 70-year-old man was injured in the Birzeit area. The incidents come amid heightened tensions across the West Bank during the olive harvest, which has repeatedly been disrupted by attacks on Palestinian farmers and their property.
The U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack on American photojournalist Heidi Levine and was monitoring the situation. "The Trump administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans," an embassy spokesperson said, adding that the State Department provides appropriate consular assistance to Americans facing difficulties abroad. "We are in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank. We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests and convictions of those responsible." The embassy declined further comment, citing privacy and other considerations.
The Washington Post also condemned the attack and called for a full investigation. "This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank," said Matt Murray, the newspaper's executive editor. "She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist." Murray said the newspaper was relieved that Levine had received medical care and was safe, but was "outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job," urging authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and take appropriate follow-up action.

====================================================================================================

Israel picks between 'secular democracy or theocracy' in election, chess master Garry Kasparov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:27:27 UTC
22:27:27 KST

When Israelis head to vote on October 27, they won't just be picking the next government; they will be deciding whether Israel becomes "a secular Hebrew democracy, or a rigid, rabbinical theocracy," Garry Kasparov, a Russian chess grandmaster, political activist, and writer, wrote in an op-ed for the New York Times published on Thursday.
"Just as Abraham Lincoln observed that the government could not persist 'half slave and half free,' Israel cannot go on half theocratic and half secular," Kasparov, whose father was Jewish, argued.
"Americans resolved that contradiction over four years of brutal civil war. Israel’s election on Oct. 27 offers a bloodless way out of this morass," he wrote.
"Democracies are built on compromise," Kasparov said. "But sometimes a compromise can turn dangerous."
Growing up in the Soviet Union shaped Kasparov's view of Israeli democracy
He explained that his upbringing in the Soviet Union shaped his perception of both the US and Israeli democracies. "I see this dynamic at play in two democracies with which I closely identify: the United States and Israel."
"As a young Soviet with a Jewish father, I grew up to become a staunch supporter of Israel, an outpost of liberalism surrounded by illiberal, Moscow-backed Arab states," Kasparov wrote.
"While I rejected the anti-Americanism and anti-Zionism of the Communist regime under which I was raised, I also sought a textured understanding of the United States and Israel."
Israel faces a breaking point, risk of permanent rupture
"I learned early on that the United States had reached a breaking point just 84 years after independence. America’s founders included men who owned slaves and men who did not. They could not both midwife the union and challenge the 'peculiar institution.' This guaranteed the birth of the United States but cursed the young nation with an affliction that nearly caused a permanent rupture."
Kasparov believes that Israel is also facing this affliction and risk of permanent rupture. Rather than the divisive issue being slavery, the divisive issue that Kasparov says has placed Israel at this crossroad is the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) draft to the IDF. He clarified in the NYT that "There is, of course, no moral equivalence between the haredim, as the ultra-Orthodox are called in Israel, and slave owners."
He cites then-prime minister David Ben-Gurion's original agreement with the haredim as the thing that set in motion the aforementioned split. In 1948 Ben-Gurion approved a temporary agreement with haredi yeshiva students, granting 400 people an exemption from army service to study Torah. Today, upwards of 50,000 people evade IDF draft to study Torah.
"The pact haunted their descendants and today is sustained by a nationalist far right and an unscrupulous prime minister willing to bend the law to stay in power," Kasparov said.
Haredi draft is 'corroding' Israel's social compact
"In Israel today, ultra-Orthodox political power is corroding the social compact that holds the country together."
"Israelis of Ben-Gurion’s generation may not have understood the kind of foundation they were laying," Kasparov argued. "They may have presumed they were simply handing out draft exemptions to a few hundred young men. Many of the American founders similarly expected slavery to peter out over time."
"Instead, slavery expanded significantly after 1776, just as religious influence in Israel exploded in the decades following 1948. The draft exemption became especially infuriating to secular Israeli Jews after Oct. 7 and the war in Gaza."
The haredi draft is not the only way Kasparov thinks that religious influence is corruptive to Israel. He argues that their power over Israeli law, from marriages, divorces, and funerals to transportation and public services on Shabbat, is "toxic" and unfair to the millions of Israelis who do not observe Shabbat.
"The ultra-Orthodox parties in the Knesset are so single-minded that it seems they will support anyone, no matter how clouded by accusations of misdeeds, who preserves their special privileges," Kasparov wrote in the NYT. "This is how the haredim have become indispensable accomplices and supporters to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition."
Netanyahu's relationship with the haredim in Knesset
"Without the ultra-Orthodox, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would not have backing for many of his authoritarian endeavors," he argued, and similarly, "Without Mr. Netanyahu, the ultra-Orthodox would lose their protected status."
Despite his comments that Israel is choosing between secular democracy or rigid theocracy, Kasparov added that he does not want religion and culture to be suppressed. "When I was growing up in the Soviet Union, Communist thugs enforced atheism and suppressed Jewish culture. This is not what I want for Israel."
"I simply believe in equality before the law and an Israel that embodies its founders’ aspirations of being a 'light unto the nations,' rather than an international pariah held back by far-right and religious special interests," Kasparov wrote.
"Israel’s election on Oct. 27 offers a bloodless way out of this morass."
