Russian political scientist and election expert Alexander Kynev is unable to walk after being denied crutches at a Moscow detention center, a journalist who received a letter from him said.
Kynev, who was arrested in late September on drug charges, has been transferred to Moscow’s Pre-Trial Detention Center No. 4, known as “Medved” (“Bear”), journalist Gleb Yarovoy said. His leg was reportedly broken during his arrest.
“He writes that he is still in a cast and has about three more weeks to ‘walk’ around in it. Except he can’t walk,” Yarovoy wrote.
Kynev also said he was being held in quarantine and receiving no information about the outside world, according to Yarovoy.
Moscow’s Perovsky District Court ordered Kynev into pre-trial detention on Sept. 25 on charges of attempting to sell a large quantity of drugs. He denies wrongdoing and faces between 10 and 20 years in prison if convicted.
The legal news Telegram channel Slovo Zashchite reported that Kynev suffered two fractures to his shinbone after being beaten during his arrest and was taken to the hospital at Moscow’s Matrosskaya Tishina detention center. His lawyer, Mikhail Biryukov, previously said he could neither confirm nor deny that account.
The Medved detention center, in Moscow’s Yuzhnoye Medvedkovo district, previously held opposition politician Ilya Yashin while he was under investigation for spreading “false information” about the Russian military, the investigative outlet Agentstvo noted.
Other former inmates include police rights activist Vladimir Vorontsov, former monk Nikolai Romanov and Andrei Bykov, the former head of the Federal Penitentiary Service’s research institute.
Yelena Masyuk, a former member of the presidential human rights council, previously documented allegations of extortion and abuse at the facility, including beatings by fellow inmates and cases in which prisoners were driven to suicide.
Kynev remained in Russia and had regularly commented on the Sept. 18-20 State Duma elections before his arrest.
He estimated that turnout would have been around 40% and the ruling United Russia party would have won no more than 35% of the vote without electoral fraud. He also warned that the party’s record haul of 349 seats could backfire.
A specialist in Russian regional politics and elections, Kynev previously taught at the Higher School of Economics and headed independent election monitor Golos’ analytical department.
The Justice Ministry designated him a “foreign agent” in February 2026, accusing him of spreading false information about government policies and the electoral system, as well as cooperating with an organization designated “undesirable.”

Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:26:47 UTC
22:26:47 KST

Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives and severely beat Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine.
Israeli settlers brutally attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a photojournalist working for The Washington Post in the occupied West Bank on Friday, beating villagers and setting olive groves ablaze.
The attack was among several targeting Palestinians trying to gather their olive harvest, with further assaults and arson reported in nearby communities as well.
These incidents are just the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms on local communities in the West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces.
Veteran journalist Heidi Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault on Friday in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. A Palestinian man was also shot in the thigh by Israeli soldiers, according to a witness who spoke to Al Jazeera and the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Here is what we know.
What happened during the attack?
Dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire.
Levine, an American freelance photojournalist who works for The Washington Post, fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera.
Levine later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”.
Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, the Washington Post reported.
Nathaniel said he and others managed to reach her when the settlers briefly backed away, but she struggled to stand. “She was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground,” he said.
As they helped her towards paramedics, settlers charged again, throwing more stones, he added. Levine was eventually taken to hospital in Ramallah.
Nathaniel said Israeli soldiers arrived after the settler assault and opened fire and used tear gas against Palestinians, shooting a man in the leg. “They do nothing to stop the settlers, and they speed into town and start firing their guns and tear-gassing, and they shoot a Palestinian man in the leg,” he said.
“They’re pointing their guns at the paramedics who are helping him, shoving journalists, including myself,” Nathaniel said, adding that the man was eventually taken away in an ambulance.
“We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities,” Matt Murray, executive editor of The Washington Post, said in a statement.
Wafa also reported that Israeli forces fired live ammunition and tear gas at Palestinians during the attack. After the soldiers left, Palestinians returned to harvesting their olives, Nathaniel added.
Where else have olive pickers been attacked?
There was violence in other parts of the occupied West Bank on Friday, as well. In Burqa, east of Ramallah, four Palestinians were reported to have been injured in a settler attack on olive pickers. In nearby Turmus Aya, settlers assaulted farmers and burned vehicles and olive trees. A civil defence volunteer was also injured, according to Wafa.
The attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians gathering olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters.
Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted. On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues.
How widespread are attacks?
The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks, and have stepped up as the seasonal Palestinian olive harvest gets under way.
The Israeli rights group Yesh Din has recorded at least 170 pogroms since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, Reuters reported.
The violence threatens Palestinian livelihoods and access to their land. Farmers endure assaults, the destruction of trees and the theft of crops, while settlers have also begun stealing olives from Palestinian-owned groves themselves.
Al Jazeera correspondent Tareq Abu Azzoum reported that the intimidation extends beyond agricultural land to Palestinian homes and vehicles, creating pressure on communities to leave.
“People there are still living under threat of attack, not just on their agricultural lands, but also on their properties,” he said.
“Vehicles and houses have been repeatedly hit by settler attacks, which have been used by the Israeli military, apparently, to create a deterrent environment with Palestinians expected to leave these areas so they can later turn them into Israeli settlements.”

Fuel prices rise again in Switzerland
Fuel prices in Switzerland have risen again following a brief lull. Both petrol and diesel have recently gone up by five cents per litre, according to the latest figures from Touring Club Switzerland (TCS).
Accordingly, the average price of a litre of unleaded 95 has risen by 2.4% since last week to CHF2.16. Unleaded 98 now costs CHF2.27 per litre, representing a rise of 2.3%.
More
Why Switzerland’s fuel stockpiles are for Swiss use only
Diesel has also become more expensive again. The average price rose by 2.1% to CHF2.45 per litre. This means it is now just one cent below the annual high of CHF2.46, which was reached in mid-September.
Following the sharp price rises in September, fuel prices had recently eased slightly for a short while. The price fluctuations are attributable, amongst other things, to the tense situation on the international fuel markets.
Added to this are transport problems in Switzerland, as low water levels on the Rhine are making imports more expensive.
+ Switzerland’s fossil fuel dependence explained
Meanwhile, prices on the international oil markets fell slightly on Friday. A barrel of North Sea Brent crude cost around $105 in the morning, which is still significantly higher than before the start of the war in Iran at the end of February, when the price stood at around $72.
However, changes in the oil market usually take some time to be reflected at Swiss petrol pumps.

Bulgaria Asks NATO for Air Defense After Ship Attack

13:24:21 UTC
22:24:21 KST

Bulgaria has asked NATO for aircraft, air defense systems, counter-drone equipment and air patrols, Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 16, as drone strikes on merchant ships creep toward the country’s Black Sea coast.
Stoyanov told reporters that Sofia requested “the entire spectrum of available assets” to show a strong allied presence in the region, according to Bulgarian outlet Novinite.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He said it is still unclear what help Bulgaria will actually receive.
Stoyanov said Romania and the Baltic states have similar needs, and that defense ministers from Turkey and Romania, along with the chiefs of the general staff of all three countries, are expected to meet soon. He also cautioned that absolute security in the Black Sea cannot be guaranteed, even with allied forces deployed.
Earlier this week, Stoyanov said Bulgaria would deploy two additional drone systems and more missile systems to the Black Sea area, Newsweek reported, citing Bulgarian news agency BTA.
The request follows a turbulent fortnight off Bulgaria’s coast. On Oct. 6, drones hit two commercial ships, the Alfa Watan and the Able, in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew went missing, while the Able’s 18 crew members were rescued. It was the first such attack in the economic zone of a NATO member.
A week later, on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian-owned, Malta-flagged cargo ship Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones roughly 18 nautical miles off the coast near Byala. Its crew survived. Prime Minister Rumen Radev said a second vessel was struck and sunk about 17 nautical miles off the village of Krapets, and Reuters said 11 sailors were missing.
Moscow Airports Suspend Flights Again Amid Drone Alerts
Radev said Bulgaria lacks solid evidence to accuse any specific party but suggested that Russia benefits from the attacks. He summoned Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova, who said she had no information on Russian involvement and did not rule out a third-party provocation, according to ARY News. Ukraine claims that Russia is responsible.
The Oct. 6 attack came a day after a drone strike sank the Turkish-owned grain ship Royad Mammadov off Romania, killing two crew members. The Romanian Naval Authority said the incident occurred in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, outside its territorial waters.
President Volodymyr Zelensky blamed Russian drones, though Romanian authorities have not officially confirmed a drone strike.
Bulgaria’s shift
Calls for NATO help are coming from a government that has distanced itself from Kyiv.
Radev, a former president and long-time critic of military aid to Ukraine, won the April 19 parliamentary election in a landslide. On June 9, Stoyanov said Bulgaria would send no more weapons to Ukraine, adding Bulgaria had approved 13 military aid packages since 2022.
On July 14, Radev said Bulgaria would no longer take part in the Coalition of the Willing that seeks to provide postwar security guarantees to Ukraine; he has halted government-supplied military aid since taking office but has not stopped commercial arms sales to Kyiv.
Speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara earlier that month, Radev said Bulgaria had exhausted what it could give from state stockpiles but could still repair Ukrainian military equipment.
Sofia also reportedly vetoed EU sanctions on Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church and a confidant of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and sought the removal of oil billionaire Vagit Alekperov from the lists. Radev argued that religion should stay separate from sanctions policy.
Producer of Soviet-standard ammunitions
Bulgaria is not a military heavyweight, but it matters to Ukraine for what it can produce.
Because of its communist-era industrial base, it is one of the few countries outside Russia that can produce Soviet-standard munitions, and output surged after Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Emilian Gebrev, owner of arms maker Emco and a survivor of two nerve-agent poisonings, said that Russian military intelligence agents repeatedly sabotaged his facilities. Bulgarian prosecutors have charged six officers serving in Russia’s Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU) in connection with the incidents.
Geography matters too.
Bulgaria borders neither Ukraine nor Russia, but it holds a strategic position on the Black Sea. With Russia bombing Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, Kyiv increasingly relies on Danube River ports and shipping routes close to the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
Romania’s foreign ministry says, per Maritime Executive, that between 20% and 30% of globally traded wheat and grain transits the corridor. That makes the waters off Bulgaria both a lifeline for Ukraine’s exports and a growing test of whether NATO can protect shipping in its own backyard.

EU fast-tracks merger of three European firms into one SpaceX rival. It wants to end reliance on US satellites that failed Ukraine this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:23:39 UTC
22:23:39 KST

The EU plans to fast-track antitrust approval for Project Bromo, a satellite venture meant to cut Europe's reliance on American space technology, Bloomberg reports. The news comes days after the White House ordered the Pentagon to slow Starshield, the military-grade Starlink service Ukraine's forces use, according to Reuters.
Project Bromo would merge the satellite businesses of Italy’s Leonardo and France’s Airbus and Thales into one company. Bloomberg calls it the bloc’s answer to SpaceX, and the EU sees it as a regional giant able to compete with US and Chinese rivals.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has backed the project, Eunews reports.
“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” she said at an international space summit in Paris last month, citing Bromo by name.
A year of quiet groundwork before the filing
Over the past year, the partners and EU officials have worked through potential competition concerns so they can be resolved before a formal application, according to Bloomberg. The companies have not yet applied, but Brussels expects them to in the coming weeks.
For large deals, regulators usually hold such preliminary talks to flag obstacles early. If the companies offer concessions, such as selling some assets, the deal could clear after a first-phase review of a little over a month. If competition concerns remain, the Commission could open an in-depth probe lasting several months.
The caveat behind the SpaceX-rival label
A fast review is not a free pass. Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera has warned that the project cannot expect one, and unions and suppliers have raised concerns about jobs and competition, Bloomberg reports. Von der Leyen’s public backing drew criticism from some members of the European Parliament.
Her support “doesn’t mean we are not going to apply and to enforce our own regulation,” Ribera told Bloomberg TV.
Why it matters to Ukraine
The push is part of a wider European scramble for space autonomy. Ukraine wants to build a satellite system of its own that no single company controls.
This week showed why. After the Starshield order, the military-grade terminals stopped working on fast-moving objects, and now work only at speeds of up to 160 kph, a person in Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told Reuters. Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed the interceptor drones that shoot down Shaheds.

Hungary’s veto is no more. Now Ukraine must catch up with Moldova in the race to join the EU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:22:00 EEST
22:22:00 KST

Hungary’s veto is no more. Now Ukraine must catch up with Moldova in the race to join EU
The Hungarian government has finally lifted its veto on Ukraine’s progress towards EU membership after blockading it for several months. At two intergovernmental conferences with Ukraine and Moldova in Luxembourg, ministers from the 27 member states officially gave both countries the green light to proceed in the accession negotiations.
The two clusters opened for both countries form the core of economic integration with the EU, covering, among other things, the rules of competition.
Meanwhile, another priority popped up in Luxembourg.
It’s also about competition – but not in an economic sense.
When the accession negotiations were opened, the EU was willing to keep Ukraine and Moldova in sync and avoid decoupling the two countries in the accession process. But when it comes to closing the negotiations, Ukraine is seriously lagging behind.
European Pravda sources indicate that Moldova is to begin an official progress assessment, also known as an IBAR (Interim Benchmark Assessment Report), this year. Chișinău intends to demonstrate that it has met the initial accession benchmarks set by the EU over the summer. Kyiv is still a long way off this stage, but Vsevolod Chentsov, Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration, has emphasised that this is becoming a priority for Ukraine as well.
EU officials in Brussels have also noted that Ukraine has begun to mention the term IBAR, but they say Kyiv is still limiting itself to talk rather than action.
As a result, the EU is making more ambitious statements about Moldova, suggesting, for example, that accession negotiations with Moldova could be concluded in 2028.
It is already clear that further concessions from Ukraine will be required in order to open the two remaining negotiating clusters, and Hungary will no longer be the source of the problems. Countries with elections just around the corner, including Poland and France, could become centres of resistance. That’s why it’s important that the clusters are opened before these countries enter the final stages of their election campaigns. There were some encouraging, though cautious, signs of progress in Luxembourg.
The foundations of EU accession, but in the economy
On 13 October, on the sidelines of a ministerial meeting in Luxembourg, the European Union greenlit the next steps towards accession for Albania, Moldova and Ukraine. The EU opened two negotiating clusters for Ukraine: Clusters 2 (Internal Market) and 3 (Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth).
"Tomorrow, I will be happy to replace the 17 red tokens on the 'enlargement wall' in my office with yellow ones for Ukraine," said European Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, who is responsible for accession negotiations with candidate countries, commenting on the decision.
As a result, Ukraine now has 24 of the 33 main negotiating chapters open – that is, the majority.
In any discussion of negotiating clusters in the EU accession process, the one most often mentioned is Cluster 1: Fundamentals. It includes issues such as the rule of law, combating corruption, democracy and more. Under the EU’s established rules, a candidate country’s progress on the Fundamentals determines the course of negotiations across all the other chapters.
The recently opened clusters do not have the same status, but they are crucial too.
"Clusters 2 and 3 form the economic core of Ukraine’s accession process and, in many respects, the economic core of our country’s transformation," Deputy Prime Minister Chentsov explained in Luxembourg. "The chapters we have opened now concern virtually every aspect of how the economy functions. This is about bringing our economies closer together, strengthening Europe’s competitiveness and building a more resilient European future. Today, we took another important step towards that goal."
The European Union has now officially committed to the gradual integration of candidate countries. A key element of this approach is granting them access to the tools and mechanisms of the single market even before they formally join the EU.
This will only be possible after economic reforms have been implemented – the reforms covered by Clusters 2 and 3.
A new priority for Ukraine
Ukrainian officials discussing EU accession used to emphasise that the main challenge was to open all the negotiating chapters.
This task was on the Ukrainian government’s agenda last year, but it proved impossible to accomplish back then because Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán had blocked Ukraine’s path to EU membership, rallying his electorate around the idea. With the recent change in the Hungarian government, the process has begun to move forward, but not immediately, and only gradually.
Throughout this period, Ukrainian diplomats were also working to ensure that the European Union did not decouple Ukraine and Moldova. The EU was receptive to this argument, so the two countries proceeded jointly through all the legal stages on the path to accession.
A future EU member must incorporate the provisions of the EU’s acquis communautaire into its national legislation. Within the framework of the negotiations, a candidate country can only demonstrate to the Europeans that certain provisions have been implemented and negotiate transitional periods or specific exemptions.
Each candidate country faces its own challenges along the way and has its own list of benchmarks that are set by the EU when each negotiating cluster is opened. Each country also conducts its negotiations with the EU separately, and progress depends on achievements – on the reforms implemented.
Therefore, once negotiations have begun across all clusters, keeping Ukraine and Moldova in sync will become less important. But until all the clusters are opened, the two countries will continue to be coupled.
Now a new factor has emerged that could put Moldova ahead of Ukraine.
This is the IBAR (Interim Benchmark Assessment Report), a decisive intermediate stage on the path to EU accession.
A special procedure applies to two chapters within the Fundamentals cluster – the rule of law, anti-corruption, human rights and related issues.
Ukraine has been given interim benchmarks for these clusters. Only after these have been met will the EU provide the final criteria for the chapters.
Most importantly, meeting the interim benchmarks gives a candidate country the right to begin closing negotiating chapters – that is, to receive official confirmation that Ukraine or Moldova meets the requirements for EU accession.
The IBAR report serves as that confirmation.
Two European Pravda sources say that Moldova is preparing to initiate its IBAR process, which could begin as early as November. This would automatically put Moldova ahead of Ukraine in their couple, since Ukraine has not yet reached this stage.
"Undoubtedly, the main priority for the government and parliament is to meet the interim benchmarks and secure a positive IBAR outcome. We are also eagerly awaiting the opening of the remaining two negotiating clusters," Chentsov said in Luxembourg.
However, when European Pravda asked a follow-up question about when Ukraine might achieve this, the deputy prime minister declined to make any prediction, saying "As soon as possible."
That makes sense, since the main tasks are largely beyond the government’s control.
The list of criteria Ukraine must meet to secure IBAR approval includes anti-corruption legislation, rule-of-law reforms, reform of the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) and other measures. All of these require decisions by the Ukrainian parliament, the Verkhovna Rada. Bills addressing many of these issues have already been submitted, but have not yet been brought to a vote.
Vsevolod Chentsov has hinted that he sees room to negotiate compromises with Brussels.
It is not yet clear whether the EU is willing to make concessions on these reforms. However, any concessions are unlikely to be radical, as such an approach would not be acceptable to many EU member states.
Nevertheless, the fact that the deputy prime minister has frequently brought up the IBAR has not gone unnoticed in the European Union.
"This is the first time we have heard the Ukrainian government emphasise the IBAR, and that is a good thing. But we also need to see decisions, not just statements," one senior EU official told European Pravda.
During the most recent plenary weeks in parliament, anti-corruption bills have remained off the agenda despite repeated appeals from the EU, including a personal appeal by Ursula von der Leyen during a conversation with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. According to European Pravda sources, she received assurances from the Ukrainian leader that Kyiv does intend to implement these reforms.
It’s not just about Hungary
In discussing the IBAR, we shouldn’t lose sight of Ukraine’s earlier objective: opening the remaining negotiating clusters.
The new government of Péter Magyar blocked Ukraine’s progress for several months. Initially it imposed a veto without making any demands, echoing the bad old days of Viktor Orbán. Later, certain developments persuaded Budapest to change its approach. A constructive dialogue began, leading to a proposed solution: Ukraine would adopt amendments to its Law on Education, while the Hungarian government would present this as its own achievement to the Hungarian public and give the green light to further progress in Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations.
Recent developments suggest that Hungary has indeed changed its approach to relations with Ukraine, at least for now.
The Hungarians were entirely constructive in the negotiations over the education law. And Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who has long avoided meeting the Ukrainian president, suddenly took the initiative himself, proposing talks with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels. They are expected to meet on Friday.
But the next obstacle to Ukraine’s progress towards EU membership could be Romania.
For the last six months or so, Romania has been in political crisis. This made the prolonged absence of an official response particularly concerning, given that the draft education law had been sent to the Romanians as well as the Hungarians. Eventually, President Nicușor Dan publicly expressed his full support for the law, which has now been passed.
Meanwhile, the task of opening the remaining two clusters has not gone anywhere.
These negotiating blocks are considered the most politically sensitive.
Cluster 4 (Green Agenda and Sustainable Connectivity) also covers transport and the single market for services – issues that are sensitive for Poland.
Cluster 5, which deals with agriculture, is even more sensitive – and not just for Poland. The EU’s Common Agricultural Policy is widely considered to be long in need of reform. In particular, the current rules governing the distribution of agricultural subsidies would not be able to accommodate Ukraine’s integration. Brussels is therefore already exploring compromise options that would clear the way for Kyiv’s accession.
There are no concrete solutions yet, but everyone is committed to finding them.
"Ukraine will become part of the European agricultural policy, but under a special model. The EU member states and, of course, Ukraine will have to decide exactly what that model will look like," European Commissioner Marta Kos told European Pravda.
"I see no reason why we should not be able to reach an agreement and open the clusters by the end of this year," Deputy Prime Minister Chentsov added, reiterating Kyiv’s position: exemptions for Ukraine are possible, but they must be temporary rather than permanent.
The political debate on this issue is expected to take place this week at the EU summit, to which President Zelenskyy has also been invited.
Not all of the EU sources who spoke to European Pravda share the optimism that a solution will be found by the end of the year. Marta Kos has also been cautious in her forecasts, speaking of hope, not certainty.
Still, Ukraine’s main problem remains not the opening of the clusters, but the implementation of reforms.
Unless Ukraine meets the benchmarks – above all those covered by the IBAR – there will be no meaningful progress.
And a difference in rhetoric regarding Ukraine and Moldova is already evident.
At the European Commission and in EU capitals, Chișinău is being praised for fulfilling its commitments.
"Everything is going really well at the moment. We support Moldova’s ambition to become an EU member by 2030. And if we look at past experience, we can see that it is technically possible to conclude accession negotiations as early as the first or second quarter of 2028," Kos added.
No similar forecasts were made about Ukraine this time.
Also telling was the way the Irish presidency referred to progress on reforms in its official statement on the opening of the negotiations. "We encourage Ukraine to continue to implement necessary reforms, particularly in the area of Fundamentals," Thomas Byrne, Irish Minister of State for European Affairs, said as he announced the opening of the negotiating clusters for Ukraine.
Unless Ukraine speeds up the pace of reform, the gap could widen further. The IBAR issue clearly illustrates this trend.
Sergiy Sydorenko,
Editor, European Pravda, Luxembourg-Brussels

Russian attacks killed 328 civilian Ukrainians during September: Kyiv, Kherson and Sumy suffered the most – UN
Russian attacks on Ukraine killed 328 and injured 2105 civilian Ukrainians during September 2026.
Source: the report from the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU)
Quote: "The highest for September since the start of the full-scale invasion and 85 per cent higher than in September 2025 (249 killed; 1,068 injured)."
Details: Civilians most often suffered from:
- long-range missiles and drones – 165 killed and 1,119 injured (53% of the total number)
- short-range drones – 87 killed and 475 injured (23%)
In September, civilians were killed and injured in 22 regions of the country, as well as in the capital. Most often, they were residents of:
- Kyiv – 32 killed and 340 injured
- Kherson – 16 killed and 202 injured
- Sumy – 11 killed and 131 injured
- Zaporizhzhia – 7 killed and 127 injured
The Monitoring Mission also confirmed data regarding 18 killed and 44 injured civilians in the temporarily occupied territory of Ukraine.
Overall, from January to September 2026, the number of civilian casualties amounts to 2,570 killed and 15,211 injured. This figure is 59% higher than for the corresponding period in 2025.
Background: In July 2026, at least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 were injured as a result of Russian attacks. This is the highest monthly number of civilian casualties since May 2022.

Ukraine will need at least another EUR 70 billion next year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated, also calling on European leaders to help secure this support.

He said that Ukraine stops most Russian assaults on the front line thanks to drones and cuts Russian supply lines with these technologies.
"And our drones are helping to weaken Russia’s economy. Right now, we could produce two or three times more drones – depending on the type. But we simply don’t have enough money for that," the president said.
He urged leaders to invest in Ukrainian defense, as well as in the joint production of drones and other weapons systems in European countries.

The Ukrainian company SkyFall has developed and submitted for testing a new medical evacuation drone called StarGate.
This was reported by the Associated Press.
The drone was developed over the past year specifically to transport wounded soldiers from hard-to-reach areas of the front lines.
The idea to create a medical evacuation UAV arose at the request of a commander with the call sign Flint from the 475th Assault Regiment, Code 9.2.
В Україні випробовують безпілотник StarGate для евакуації поранених.
Відео: Associated Press https://t.co/WeWt81apDd
— Владислав (@Vladislav110528) October 16, 2026
The hexacopter is equipped with a medical capsule featuring a fixed stretcher and is capable of lifting a payload of up to 150 kg, allowing it to transport a soldier in full gear.
The drone’s maximum speed reaches 105 km/h, and its one-way range is 15 km.
The stated cost of a single StarGate system is approximately $50,000, depending on the configuration.
To ensure resistance to electronic warfare, the drone uses dual communication channels via Starlink and the L-Link system, as well as AI-based navigation.
In the event of a complete loss of control and GPS signal, the system is capable of autonomously plotting a route and returning to a safe zone.
During testing, the drone also demonstrated a system for defending against attacking FPV drones using a net launcher.
The system has now been transferred to one of the combat units to evaluate its effectiveness and reliability in combat conditions.

A rare Apple computer signed by Wozniak sold for a record $1.15 million
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:18:33 EEST
22:18:33 KST

A rare Apple computer signed by Wozniak sold for a record $1.15 million
Kyiv • UNN
The 1976 Apple-1 Hatfield was sold at Bonhams for a record $1.15 million. The computer is operational and bears Steve Wozniak’s signature, along with a letter from Jobs.
One of the rarest computers in Apple’s history went under the hammer at a Bonhams auction in New York. At the end of the auction on October 14, two bidders remained and continued bidding until the price reached $1.15 million — a record for a production Apple-1, reports UNN, citing Bild.
Details
According to the media outlet, the computer, named Hatfield, was released in 1976 — the year Apple was founded. It has remained operational, and the signature of the company’s co-founder, Steve Wozniak, is on its circuit board.
Along with the device, the buyer received a letter from Steve Jobs written in January 1978. At the time, Jobs offered the computer’s original owner, Fred Hatfield, an exchange for the circuit board of the latest Apple II model with 4 kilobytes of memory. Hatfield refused and preserved the historic specimen.
The Apple-1 was the company’s first product. The computer was sold as an assembled circuit board to which the user connected a keyboard and monitor. According to the Apple-1 registry, the existence of 94 units of this model has been confirmed. The Bonhams auction house believes that fewer than 75 computers have survived, with even fewer still operational. Before the auction, the Hatfield was valued at $500,000–800,000, but the final amount significantly exceeded the upper end of the estimate.

Liberman accuses Eisenkot of plotting coalition with Netanyahu as opposition feud deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:18:02 UTC
22:18:02 KST

With just 11 days until Israel's election, polls largely show a deadlock between the rival political blocs, leaving parties seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu struggling to find a viable path to forming a government. Senior opposition figures warn that the stalemate benefits Netanyahu, who could remain in office until another election if his rivals fail to assemble a coalition. The growing divisions erupted Friday as Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman launched a scathing attack on Gadi Eisenkot, accusing him of preparing to form a government with Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox parties.
Liberman, who had already rejected Eisenkot's proposal for a minority government, published a lengthy social media post titled "Gadi Eisenkot: Benny Gantz 2," accusing the former IDF chief of staff of putting personal political ambitions ahead of the opposition's shared goal of replacing Netanyahu. "The 'largest party' campaign Eisenkot is running is not designed to transfer a single vote from the draft-dodging bloc to the serving bloc, but to siphon votes from within the bloc itself," Liberman wrote, referring to the dispute over military service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men. He argued that Eisenkot was seeking to surpass Likud in parliamentary seats to strengthen his negotiating position in potential coalition talks with Netanyahu.
Liberman accused Eisenkot of pursuing a government with Netanyahu and ultra-Orthodox leaders Yitzhak Goldknopf and Aryeh Deri, while keeping the possibility of a minority government on the table as leverage to secure the first term in a rotating premiership. He pointed to remarks by Likud Minister Miki Zohar about possible cooperation with Eisenkot, reports of an initiative by President Isaac Herzog to establish a Netanyahu-Eisenkot government and alleged briefings from the White House. "The pieces begin to fall into place," Liberman wrote, adding that positions taken by Eisenkot's associates on military conscription and constitutional issues reinforced his suspicions.
Liberman also rejected claims that he was trying to prevent Eisenkot from becoming prime minister. "Since the October 7 massacre, I have repeatedly made it clear: We will not join a coalition that depends on Ra'am or the Joint List, whether through direct or indirect support," he wrote, referring to Arab political parties. He said the four parties in the opposition bloc must secure a solid parliamentary majority to establish a "Zionist and liberal government" and prevent Eisenkot from "saving Netanyahu for a second time."
Eisenkot responded Friday without mentioning Liberman by name, urging voters to disregard the political infighting. "We are 11 days away from the most consequential election since the establishment of the state," he wrote. "At such a historic moment for Israel, composure and focus on the objective are essential. I ask Israelis to ignore the spin." He warned that Israelis would not forgive politicians who allowed personal interests to prevent the replacement of the government. "To the people of Israel seeking change, hold your heads high. In 11 days, Israel will be a better country. I promise."
Blue and White chairman Benny Gantz also weighed in, accusing Liberman of leading Israel toward a political dead end. "In 30 years in Israeli politics, Liberman has not done 10% of what Gadi Eisenkot and I have done for the State of Israel," Gantz said. He claimed Liberman was reacting to his exposure of a plan to establish a minority government with Naftali Bennett and Arab parties, and renewed his call for a broad Zionist unity government crossing the existing political blocs.
The confrontation follows tensions over an understanding reached among opposition leaders at a meeting in Yair Lapid's home three weeks ago. A senior opposition figure told ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth that Liberman believed Eisenkot had violated the agreement by campaigning to become the bloc's largest party. "Liberman was furious about Eisenkot's largest-party campaign. He saw it as an act of deception after they had agreed that this would not happen," the official said, adding that Liberman feared the strategy could cost the entire bloc the election.
Eisenkot has argued that he could establish a minority government composed exclusively of Zionist parties without formally seeking support from Arab or ultra-Orthodox factions. The proposal was intended in part to counter Netanyahu's campaign claims that Eisenkot would rely on Arab political leaders Ahmad Tibi and Mansour Abbas. Liberman has ruled out the arrangement, reiterating that he will not participate in a government dependent on Arab parties or one that includes ultra-Orthodox factions. With neither bloc showing a clear majority in the polls, the dispute has exposed the opposition's central challenge: agreeing on a government capable of replacing Netanyahu.

China said it plans to restrict or ban exports of 40 technologies that span artificial intelligence, chips and solar power as its technology race with countries including the United States intensifies.
The draft proposal released by Ministry of Commerce would ban exports of 14 technologies, including AI-driven malicious code generation and mutation technology, as well as AI models trained on Chinese core data.

At summit, EU leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
October 16, 2026
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where leaders from across the bloc pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.
What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?
"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
"One thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops this war."
The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.
After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."
Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine
Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."
"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defense and funding," he added.
During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia.
"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said.
When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.
Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."
Trump denies responsibility for restrictions on Starshield
Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.
However, on Friday, Trump denied that he or Starlink founder Elon Musk were responsible for these restrictions. "I don't think it was me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump told journalists.
He added that any limit to Ukraine's access to the Starshield system was not imposed by the United States.
Musk had said that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company, SpaceX, which operates Starlink.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Europe is working to help Ukraine with satellite and early warning systems.
"We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed," Macron told reporters.
Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM
The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.
"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."
Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.
"I assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.

Foreign Tourist Revenue in Croatia Rises Nearly 5%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:17:00 UTC
22:17:00 KST

Croatia recorded 20.1 million tourist arrivals and 104.9 million overnight stays from January through September 2026, while revenue from foreign visitors rose by nearly 5% in the first half of the year, according to data from the Croatian National Tourist Board and the Croatian National Bank.
Tourist arrivals increased by 2% compared with the first nine months of 2025, while overnight stays grew by 1%, the tourism board's figures showed.
Revenue generated by foreign tourists reached 4.587 billion euros in the first six months of 2026, according to central bank data cited by the Ministry of Tourism and Sport. The amount was 212.4 million euros, or nearly 5%, higher than in the same period a year earlier. The revenue figures cover the first half of the year, not the full nine-month period.
The Adriatic coast accounted for 100.5 million of the 104.9 million overnight stays recorded between January and September, marking a 1% increase year over year. Continental Croatia, including Zagreb, registered 4.4 million overnight stays, also up 1% from the same period in 2025.
The figures highlight the central role of coastal destinations in Croatia's economy. Tourist spending supports hotels and other accommodation providers, as well as restaurants, transportation, retail and services. However, the concentration of visitors also increases pressure on infrastructure and natural resources.
In September, Croatia welcomed 2.6 million tourist arrivals and recorded 14.3 million overnight stays, with both measures rising by 3% compared with the same month in 2025.
The increase after the main summer peak is important for the use of tourism infrastructure and employment beyond the traditional summer season. Assessing the effects of a longer season more precisely would also require figures on tourist spending, average length of stay and regional revenue.
Tourism and Sport Minister Tonči Glavina credited the results to changes in tourism policy designed to reflect shifts in the market.
“The excellent figures seen during the pre-season are the result of robust strategic and promotional initiatives, which we tailored to market changes. This has allowed us to sustain positive trends in Croatian tourism, even during this exceptionally challenging year,” Glavina said in an official press release from the ministry.
According to data cited by the minister, revenue from foreign tourists in the first half of 2026 was 120% higher than in the corresponding period of 2016. This is a nominal comparison and does not by itself establish the increase in real economic benefits, as it does not adjust for inflation or changes in prices.
Despite the growth, Croatia's tourism industry faces competition from other Mediterranean destinations as visitors become more attentive to costs. Glavina said tourist behavior was changing, with some travelers choosing shorter stays and managing their budgets more carefully.
For Croatia, continued growth will therefore depend not only on visitor numbers but also on service quality, transport accessibility and the value offered to tourists.
The results for the first nine months reinforce Croatia's position in the European tourism market. The sector's long-term sustainability will depend on raising the economic value of tourist visits, extending the season and limiting pressure on coastal areas.

In Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, settlers assaulted Palestinians picking olives and torched three Palestinian vehicles in the Al-Nabaat area, local sources said. Warning sirens sounded to alert residents to the attacks.
The Palestinian civil defence said illegal settlers then attacked an emergency crew responding to the blaze, leaving one member with bruises, before setting fire to a civil defence vehicle.
The agency condemned the assault, warning that attacks on emergency crews and their vehicles while carrying out humanitarian duties pose a direct threat to efforts to protect lives and property and respond to emergencies.
The Palestinian rights group Al-Baydar said American journalist and international solidarity activist Heidi Levine was also wounded when illegal Israeli settlers assaulted her in Turmus Ayya in the presence of Israeli forces.

The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its teams treated a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man injured in the attack and were taking both to hospital.
In Burqa, east of Ramallah, the Red Crescent reported four injuries following an Israeli settler attack on Palestinian farmers.

The olive harvest is a vital source of income for thousands of Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank, where farmers face growing attacks and restrictions on access to their land during the season.

The airport on the Greek island of Chios will be closed from November 15, 2026, to March 15, 2027, for runway modernization. Local authorities opposed the decision. The Independent reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the Hellenic Civil Aviation Authority (HCAA), the suspension of airport operations is linked to a large-scale runway reconstruction. The work is expected to ensure uninterrupted air connections throughout the 2027 tourist season and mitigate the effects of winter weather conditions. At the same time, during the repairs, emergency flights, including medical evacuations, search-and-rescue, firefighting, humanitarian, government and other flights of national importance, will be able to operate using helicopters that land and take off directly on and from the parking apron.
After the modernization is completed, the runway will be 1,799 meters long, allowing it to accommodate larger types of aircraft. The publication recalled that Chios, the fifth-largest Greek island, is located in the northern part of the Aegean Sea. The island's authorities called the airport closure an economically unviable measure, as the government had initially planned to close the airport on January 15, for two months.
The early closure will seriously affect the island's economy and society, especially during the holiday season (Christmas, New Year), when people plan trips, family visits and medical checkups. Chios, as a border island located 5 miles from Turkey, depends on air connections with the capital for reasons of health, entertainment and freedom

'Gas deals will follow' — Zelensky warns Trump could ease more sanctions on Russia

'Gas deals will follow' — Zelensky warns Trump could ease more sanctions on Russia
U.S. President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia risks paving the way for further sanctions relief for Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 16.
Zelensky warned that easing sanctions could eventually lead to the normalization of relations with Moscow, despite Russia showing no readiness to agree to even a ceasefire in Ukraine.
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky told reporters in Brussels.
"In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
"It will all come down to the banking system, individual people, and the chemical industry."
Zelensky said his main concern was the fate of frozen Russian assets. European diplomats previously told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow was seeking their release from the United States in exchange for agreeing to an energy ceasefire with Ukraine.
"What I consider to be risks are frozen assets," he said. "If I don't defend them, who will do it?"
The deal has strained Ukraine-U.S. relations after Washington unexpectedly announced an arrangement allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky criticized the decision on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
Tensions had already escalated after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising global fuel prices, a claim disputed by experts. His administration also threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halted the attacks.
The latest rift follows months of failed attempts to negotiate an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. As diplomatic efforts have stalled, Russia has continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of the coming winter.
Russia offered the United States nothing in return for sanctions relief on diesel.

Iran manages to ship some gas, jet fuel despite US blockade, sanctions, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:13:54 UTC
22:13:54 KST

Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements told Reuters.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Approximately 4.1 million barrels of LPG made it through the blockade
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US Military describes blockade as 'ironclad'
The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad." The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
A US military official told Reuters that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade. Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
US Treasury questioned shipping data
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt," the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime."
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers.

Iran's navy reports oil tanker fire in Gulf of Oman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:12:50 UTC
22:12:50 KST

Mohammad Sio
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Iran's navy said Friday that an oil tanker caught fire in the Gulf of Oman while attempting to cross a restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking systems switched off, according to a statement carried by state broadcaster IRIB.
The navy's public relations office said monitoring teams detected the burning tanker during surveillance operations in the eastern part of the strategic waterway.
The vessel had disabled its tracking systems and was attempting to navigate a “prohibited area” in the Gulf of Oman, the statement said.
The navy warned that unauthorized movements through restricted maritime routes and areas pose security risks to other vessels.
The statement did not identify the tanker, its flag or operator, or specify what caused the fire. No information was provided on possible casualties or the condition of the crew.
The incident comes amid a series of maritime security incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has imposed restrictions on commercial shipping.
On Tuesday, the Iranian Navy reported that another tanker caught fire after sustaining damage while attempting to cross a restricted area east of the strait with its tracking systems switched off.
On Wednesday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank after striking a naval mine while attempting to navigate an unauthorized route south of the strait.
The IRGC Navy warned local vessels and fishermen to exercise caution over containers floating on the water's surface following the sinking.
The latest incidents come amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial passage for global oil and gas shipments.
Maritime traffic through the waterway has been severely disrupted since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

The EU wants an AI revolution. But on whose terms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:12:00 UTC
22:12:00 KST

The EU wants an AI revolution. But on whose terms?
October 16, 2026
Step-dancers spun across the circular stage in the middle of a dark hall, entrancing an audience of policymakers and tech bosses. Not simply another bureaucratic conference, the International AI Summit, hosted in Dublin this week, aspired to something more spectacular — a grand announcement that Europe is ready for its artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.
Among the more than 1,500 expected guests were Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis and Microsoft president Brad Smith, in addition to high-ranking European Union and Irish officials. The event was a key part of Ireland's term as president of the EU Council, but a lack of critical voices to counterbalance the AI enthusiasm on display has drawn accusations of tech boosterism.
The summit was "almost like a party political broadcast on behalf of AI," Barry O'Sullivan, an AI professor at University College Cork, told DW.
AI to help Europe's competitiveness
The overarching theme was how to use AI to get Europe's sluggish economy moving, boost innovation and catch up with the US and China.
On panels packed with senior executives, the potential benefits were made clear: detecting early signs of cancer, improving warnings of extreme weather, and optimising power distribution to save energy. Turning those promises into reliable services, however, still requires testing and validation.
Ireland's interest in these issues doesn't come purely from goodwill towards its fellow EU member states. The country hosts the European operations of several of the world's largest technology companies, and relies heavily on the taxation of multinational firms. Foreign-owned multinationals paid €28.8 billion in corporation tax in 2025, accounting for 87% of the total, excluding exceptional Apple tax proceeds. That includes pharmaceuticals and other sectors, not just technology.
This means Dublin has a clear interest in shaping European rules while keeping investors on board. But Europe's financial firepower remains far behind America's: Private AI investment reached $286 billion (about €253 billion) in the US in 2025, compared with $21 billion (€18.6 billion) in Europe, according to Stanford University's AI Index.
But does Europe even need to compete on the same terms? O'Sullivan thinks it should focus on its own strengths, including industrial robotics and specialised applications: "We have a unique kind of AI opportunity in Europe, and that's what we should back."
Using foreign models could help European businesses move faster. But it also leaves them dependent on suppliers elsewhere, which can change prices, restrict access and decide which capabilities to release.
EU rules under pressure
EU representatives at the summit were quick to underline that rules were now in place to reap AI's benefits while mitigating its risks.
Michael McGrath, the Irish commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection, spoke of a balance between AI's potential and the "appropriate guardrails" required to ensure trust.
The AI Act bans certain practices and imposes stronger requirements on sensitive uses. Its Omnibus amendments, in force since July 2026, aim to simplify compliance, though have als delyed some safeguards. Rules covering areas including employment and education now apply from December 2027; those for AI embedded in regulated products from August 2028.
The Commission has said that companies need time to adjust to new standards and guidance. Critics, however, believe protections being delayed under pressure to compete.
For O'Sullivan, regulation and innovation are not contradictory. "The idea that you can't have regulation and innovation is just a nonsense," he said, pointing to pharmaceuticals and medical devices.
Demonstrations outside the venue
For protesters outside, assurances made by politicians and tech firms ring hollow. Paul Murphy, an Irish lawmaker from the socialist People Before Profit party, argued that even though Europe's regulations are strong than those in the US, the bar remains low. With the latest amendments, he sees a move towards deregulation.
"Big tech is setting the pace and everybody's expected to just get on board," he told DW.
Instead, he wants civil society, trade unions and politicians to discuss how the technology should develop and how limited resources like water and electricity should be used.
Inside, union representative Fionnuala Ní Bhrógáin, one of the few critical voices on stage, questioned who would benefit from higher productivity. Optimization, she said, can put higher pressure on workers.
Murphy, too, fears an increased pressure to work faster, with less autonomy and more supervision. Whether an hour saved on emails becomes time to think, or leads to more assignments, depends on employers' decisions and workers' bargaining power.
O'Sullivan, on the other hand, said that AI removing mundane tasks gives employees "more time to think, and to be more creative in their jobs."
A heavy environmental toll
In Ireland, the question of resources is particularly pressing. Data centres used 23% of the country's metered electricity in 2025. That includes cloud storage and other services, not just AI. Murphy argued that their expansion raises household bills and undermines climate goals.
Renewable energy could help meet demand. But additional clean electricity must also replace fossil fuels, while housing and other industries need grid capacity too.
"The sustainability of AI is a huge problem," O'Sullivan agreed, calling for the sector to reduce its overall energy footprint.
The future of AI
Back inside the hall, even industry leaders acknowledged the need for boundaries. Hassabis, the chief scientist of Alphabet, called recent AI hacking incidents "early warning shots" and advocated international oversight. Microsoft president Smith said: "We need law. We need regulation."
Their warnings follow concrete failures. During cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI models bypassed isolation controls, hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, Hugging Face, which hosts AI models and datasets. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, the results could have been much worse. Anthropic separately disclosed unintended actions by its AI on real websites, including a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.
Speakers on and off the stage agreed: The incidents show just how difficult it can be to keep increasingly autonomous systems under control. Developers' assurances alone cannot guarantee safety. Nor can regulation eliminate every risk. But for O'Sullivan and Murphy, it remains essential.
Europe wants to shape AI without compromising on the benefits its promises.This balancing act is a difficult one, involving choices about investment, resources and the distribution of gains. Even a spectacular opening performance cannot dance around those questions.
Edited by: R. Casey

Banks are delaying bail payments to the HACC: how this may be linked to Pyshnyi and NABU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:11:40 EEST
22:11:40 KST

Banks are delaying bail payments to the HACC: how this may be linked to Pyshnyi and NABU
Kyiv • UNN
Lawyers report delays and returns of bail payments for the HACC, while the media suggest a possible connection between the problems and the situation surrounding NBU Governor Andriy Pyshnyi.
Despite statements by National Bank of Ukraine Governor Andrii Pyshnyi about hundreds of successful transactions to the account of the High Anti-Corruption Court to pay bail, lawyers report numerous cases of payments being delayed and returned. According to "Sudovo-Yurydychna Hazeta", banks are delaying and returning payments, as well as demanding additional documents, UNN writes.
The publication "Sudovo-Yurydychna Hazeta" suggests that problems with transferring bail payments may be related to the "personal situation of the head of the National Bank and the possibility of influence on him by NABU".
Earlier, the media reported that Andrii Pyshnyi's surname appears in the materials of criminal proceeding No. 52025000000000150, related to former prosecutor Kostiantyn Kulyk and funds of Oschadbank, which was previously headed by the current head of the National Bank. Pyshnyi has not been served with a notice of suspicion, but on October 1, Member of Parliament Yaroslav Zhelezniak announced the opening of proceedings regarding the possible provision of false testimony by the NBU Governor to the parliamentary Temporary Investigative Commission.
In addition, the NABU and SAPO operation "Forrest Gump" dealt an additional blow to the reputation of banking supervision; according to the investigation, it involved the legalization of UAH 150 million in bail funds through Sense Bank. After public statements by Member of Parliament Danylo Hetmantsev regarding the regulator's approval of the bank's supervisory board members, Pyshnyi explained the situation in the Verkhovna Rada on August 20.
"The NBU Governor found himself in a situation where NABU has leverage over his official position. In such a situation, every hryvnia of bail in the HACC account becomes a personal risk for the NBU Governor: after ‘Forrest Gump,’ it was he who had to answer. It is easier not to approve a single payment than to risk one's position. Therefore, in our opinion, banks were made to understand that it was better not to process such payments, while society is being shown UAH 141 million of ‘success.’
Who benefits from this? First and foremost, the prosecution. The head of the regulator, regarding whom NABU reportedly has materials, is unlikely to argue with the bureau, and pressure on him is, in our opinion, entirely possible. And a person who continues to remain in custody solely because the court-ordered bail cannot be posted for them is much more ‘open’ during interrogations. The defense believes that this is precisely how pressure is created on suspects in order to obtain the testimony that is needed from them," journalists from "Sudovo-Yurydychna Hazeta" stated.
As the publication writes, citing information from the defense, 70 participants made 139 attempts to make payments totaling UAH 117.2 million, but only about 16% of the total amount—UAH 18.9 million—was credited. In 26 cases, bail providers were unable to deposit a single hryvnia. There were also 42 refusals at cash desks or in banking applications, 13 returns of payments already accepted, totaling UAH 13.7 million, and 14 cases in which banks refused to establish or continue banking relationships.
At the same time, NBU Governor Andrii Pyshnyi reported that during August and September 2026, banks carried out 527 transactions to deposit bail into the HACC account, totaling more than UAH 141 million. According to him, this included 178 cash transactions totaling UAH 64 million and 349 non-cash transactions totaling UAH 77 million. Another UAH 4.5 million, he said, was received by October 10.
However, these statistics do not reflect the number of payments that banks refused to accept, delayed, or returned.
"Sudovo-Yurydychna Hazeta" provides specific examples of cases in which bail could not be posted. In particular, on October 14, one of the bail providers transferred UAH 395,000 through Raiffeisen Bank, providing the court ruling, a tax return, and an account statement. However, as of October 16, the funds had not reached the HACC and had been returned to the payer.
In another case, a relative of a suspect transferred UAH 292,100 obtained as a loan secured by a car. PrivatBank returned the payment, citing allegedly incorrect details. Another payment of UAH 151,000 was initially accepted by the bank but later returned. A second attempt to deposit UAH 150,000 in cash also did not result in the funds being credited to the court as of October 16.
Attorney Oleksandr Babikov also confirmed the problems with posting bail in a comment to UNN. According to him, over the past month and a half, attorneys have repeatedly complained about difficulties transferring funds in criminal proceedings related to corruption offenses.
Some banks are refusing to continue cooperating with individuals who have already posted bail
According to the attorney, such situations create risks for the right to a defense, since a delay in posting bail may result in a person remaining in custody even though they could be released on bail.
Attorney Oleksandr Babikov suspects that the systemic problems may be related to requirements or actions by the financial regulator that affect banks’ decisions.
At the same time, I cannot assert what specific role NBU Governor Andriy Pyshny is playing in this. If such events are occurring systematically, one may assume that someone is coordinating these processes. But I do not know for certain who is behind this or from whom the relevant instructions originate. We can only speculate
If the version about instructions from the NBU governor is confirmed, the question will arise as to whether regulatory mechanisms are being used to exert informal influence on banks and, through them, on the possibility of posting bail in cases considered by the HACC. The information on whether banks received relevant instructions or recommendations, and who may have initiated them, also requires separate verification.
If it is established that officials gave instructions to delay or block payments for personal reasons, this could raise questions about the legitimacy of the use of official powers and the independence of banking regulation.
The editorial office will contact the NBU for an explanation regarding the reasons for the delays and returns of payments, the existence of recommendations to banks, and the possible role of the regulator’s leadership. UNN will also contact NABU regarding information about a possible investigation into Andriy Pyshny.
