Nets error causes duplicate charges for customers in three Nordic countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:11:29 UTC
22:11:29 KST

A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh. 
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament. 
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark. 
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed. 
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well. 
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament. 
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview. 
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea. 
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Lidl has Denmark’s cheapest basket of organic groceries, analysis finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:11:20 UTC
22:11:20 KST

A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh. 
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament. 
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark. 
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed. 
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well. 
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament. 
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview. 
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea. 
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russia's diesel fuel production capacity is more than sufficient to supply the domestic market and export deliveries, even taking into account refinery turnarounds, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum.
"Diesel fuel production capacity is twice the demand of the domestic market. It is enough even taking into account maintenance work on individual units; it is enough both to secure the domestic market and to support export supplies in line with the figures we discussed earlier," Novak said.

"Any attacks, if they lead to the shutdown of primary equipment for repairs, adversely impact product output," he added.

This 19th-century Portuguese farmhouse in the Algarve is being transformed into a wellness retreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:10:46 UTC
22:10:46 KST

Shanti-Som Algarve will offer six different programmes focusing on things like detoxing, relaxation, and burnout recovery.
Wellness retreats have been soaring in popularity over the past few years, with resorts making use of increasingly fancy tools to kickstart your health journey (hyperbaric chambers or cryotherapy, anyone?).
But that’s certainly not the only way to do things, as proven by Shanti-Som, the wellness retreat brand that first opened its doors in Marbella in 2011.
Now set to open a second resort in Portugal in February 2027, Shanti-Som Algarve will offer six structured programmes focused on different goals, with the aim that the healthy habits you learn are simple enough to keep up with long after you leave.
The new 22-room retreat, which is just a 20-minute drive away from Faro Airport, is set within a restored 19th-century farmhouse surrounded by four hectares of orange and almond orchards.
“We see Shanti-Som as a hybrid of a holiday, a private wellness club and a gym,” hotel manager Ophélie Acris said.
“You can switch off completely and be looked after, but you also leave with real, practical ways to feel stronger, healthier and happier.
“Whether someone comes for better sleep, more strength, a reset or simply time away from everyday demands, the experience is shaped around what they need.”
What to expect at Shanti-Som Algarve
Guests can choose from six programmes: relaxation, yoga, pilates, detox, strength and fitness, and burnout and nervous system recovery, with the latter two being exclusive to Shanti-Som Algarve.
Strength and fitness is aimed at those who are looking to focus on longevity, bone density and muscle strength as they are getting older, and includes one-on-one training sessions, reformer Pilates, guided hikes and a full health check with a nutritional consultation.
As for burnout and nervous system recovery, guests will instead spend their days doing breathwork, guided meditations, sound healing and hot-cold contrast therapy, alongside life coaching sessions.
Unsurprisingly, the property has an impressive wellness area, complete with an infinity pool, sauna, hammam, ice bath and gym, plus private treatment rooms for massages or facials.
Each of the retreats are full-board, and you can book in for as long, or as little time, as you need.
Outside of the resort, Shanti-Som Algarve is close to beaches like Praia da Falésia and Praia da Marinha, as well as Ria Formosa lagoon.

US military’s shortage of missile defense munitions to persist until at least 2030 — TV

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:09:51 UTC
22:09:51 KST

NEW YORK, October 16. /TASS/. The US military is facing a critical shortage of missile defense munitions, and the shortfall is expected to continue for another five years, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter, CBS News reported.
According to the report, inventories of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles are expected to remain at critically low levels until 2030 due to shipments to Ukraine and the depletion of arsenals in the Middle East. It noted that during the Iran hostilities, the US military had expended up to 61% of its pre-war stockpile of PAC-3 missiles and approximately 82% of its THAAD interceptors, while new contracts take between 3.5 and 4.5 years to fulfill.
According to CBS News, defense contractor Lockheed Martin unveiled a plan to quadruple annual THAAD interceptor production from 96 to 400 units. US officials and industry experts estimate that even if no additional munitions are used, it will take at least five years to replenish stockpiles to December 2025 levels due to limited production capacity.

Centre expands Census enumerator pool to include private school teachers, clerks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:08:48 UTC
22:08:48 KST

Census 2027 to be India’s first fully digital enumeration (AP photo)
NEW DELHI: The Centre has widened the pool of people who can be appointed as Census enumerators, allowing teachers from private educational institutions, government employees and clerical staff to take up the duties under amended rules notified on Friday.The ministry of home affairs (MHA) notified the Census (Amendment) Rules, 2026, under Section 18(1) of the Census Act, 1948. The changes amend the Census Rules, 1990, which lay down the categories of people eligible to carry out enumeration work.Under the amended rules, teachers working in educational institutions run by the government, local authorities, aided or unaided private bodies, societies and trusts can be appointed as enumerators.The eligibility list also covers clerks and other officials working for the Central and state governments, local authorities and various establishments. These include public sector undertakings, statutory bodies, banks, companies, institutions, societies and trusts.
The changes broaden the range of people who can be assigned Census duties beyond the categories specified under the earlier rules.The amended rules also give state governments and Union Territory (UT) administrations the option to appoint any other person they consider suitable for the work.
The amendment replaces the existing entries against serial number 5 in the table under Rule 3 of the Census Rules, 1990, to specify the categories of people eligible for appointment as enumerators. The rules came into force immediately after their publication in the Official Gazette.The notification was issued by Mrityunjay Kumar Narayan, Registrar General of India and Census Commissioner, under the ministry of home affairs.The Census Rules were first published in the Gazette of India on December 31, 1990. They have since been amended through notifications issued in 1994, 2009, 2018 and 2022.

Around one fifth of Western firms left Russia, those remaining operate responsibly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:08:08 UTC
22:08:08 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. About 80% of Western companies that were present on the Russian market before the onset of the special military operation continue their operations in the country, behaving as conscientious and socially responsible business entities, Russian presidential commissioner for the protection of entrepreneurs' rights, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP) Alexander Shokhin said in an interview with TASS.
"We see a lot of pressure both from parent companies and official structures, urging them not to draw too much public attention to their presence in Russia. Indeed, many companies have stayed. Some 15-20% of companies have left, while the rest have remained and are behaving as conscientious employers and socially responsible businesses. <…> Moreover, they realize that they must abide by certain rules of the game, such as demonstrating social responsibility, paying taxes, and complying with other legal requirements, so that they wouldn’t be relegated to the category of entities temporarily managed by Russian executives," Shokhin said.
However, Western businesses understand the threat of retaliation from Russian authorities, he added. "The more sanctions packages the European Union or other countries impose, the more vulnerable they become, because they realize that many of those decisions are based not on economic or other criteria, but rather on geopolitical ones and the principle of reciprocal action. We understand that a complete mirror-like response is hardly possible. They impose sanctions, but it is difficult for us to impose sanctions on those who do not do business with us. Therefore, so to say, those who work conscientiously end up on the front line, forced to answer ‘for the other guy’ sitting in the State Department or the European Commission," the RSPP chief explained.
The Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs is also subject to Western sanctions, he noted. In particular, Shokhin cited the US State Department’s wording that the RSPP is subject to sanctions because it brings together executives and major companies that make a significant contribution to strengthening the country’s budget, its technological development and defense capabilities.
"We don’t dispute this. Moreover, we consider it positive that the US State Department recognizes us as the country’s leading business association. After all, we aren’t being accused of, say, any kind of unscrupulous conduct, but we are being accused precisely of doing what we were created to do. This means we are performing our functions well. Nevertheless, for our partners, caution certainly wouldn’t hurt," he stressed.
Shokhin expressed confidence that Western businesses would be represented at the Russian Industrialist forum in St. Petersburg scheduled for October 22-24. "However, we see that companies sometimes feel uncomfortable joining our platform, partly because the RSPP, as an association of employers, is under sanctions," he concluded.

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu built Israel’s military power, but undermined its security - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:07:42 UTC
22:07:42 KST

Israelis will vote on security on October 27. The Torah portion read 10 days earlier tells them what security is, and who has failed to deliver it.
Ten days before Israelis vote, the Torah portion of Noah tells of two catastrophes: the flood and the Tower of Babel. Twice humanity undoes itself: first by tearing itself apart and then by forcing itself into one mold.
The destruction is not done by an enemy at the gate. It is inflicted from within.
The Torah charges the flood generation with a word no Israeli can hear without flinching: “hamas.” The Malbim explains it as the robbery of justice and fairness: stolen courts and stolen fair dealing, the two things that stand between ordinary people and the strong.
Israel has met “hamas” from outside with courage, at a terrible price. This election asks about the other kind.
Israelis will vote, as always, on security.
A reservist friend of mine, a Mizrachi father of three, told me: “I don’t vote Likud because I admire [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu. I vote because I want my kids to sleep, because I don’t trust the alternatives to keep us safe, and because I’m tired of being spoken about like I’m a problem.”
He is not a problem. He deserves an answer, not a lecture.
What makes a country secure, not merely powerful?
Power is the capacity to strike, and Israel has it in abundance. Security is a society’s capacity to absorb a blow, hold together, and sustain itself. Power did not save Be’eri or Nir Oz.
The prophet Isaiah teaches that peace, quiet, and lasting security are the work of righteousness. Security is not where a nation begins but what it harvests.
Israel’s founders built the state on “the foundations of freedom, justice, and peace.” Three stones. Test any government against them.
The first is freedom, which lives or dies by the rule of law, binding the ruler as tightly as the ruled. Without it, freedom is a favor, withdrawn at will by whoever holds power.
Babel is the Torah’s portrait of its absence: one language, one purpose, and a power from which nothing would be withheld. That is not a strong government, but an unrestrained one. Nobody living under it is free.
The outgoing coalition set about building that tower, changing how judges are chosen and legislating that from January 2027 the attorney-general’s opinions will not bind the government. The tower was visible from Gaza.
In March 2023, Yoav Gallant, then the defense minister, warned that the rift over the judicial overhaul posed “a clear and immediate danger” to the security of the state. The next day Netanyahu announced his dismissal.
In July, the head of the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) warned him of war, judging that our enemies saw weakness. On October 7, our enemies acted on what they saw.
Avi Gil, Netanyahu’s military secretary that morning, broke his silence last week: recommendations for targeted operations in Gaza were not accepted.
He also said the prime minister prioritized his coalition over a deal to bring home living hostages. Netanyahu claimed Gil chose not to wake him.
I cannot tell you whose account is true. Neither can you, because three years on, there is still no state commission of inquiry.
THE SECOND stone is fairness: a society invested in the other is the opposite of “hamas.” When Reuben and Gad asked to settle beyond the Jordan River, Moses asked whether they would sit at home while their brothers went to war. They promised to march at the front.
In July, while reservists served round after round, the coalition passed legislation to protect draft evaders from arrest. In September, the Supreme Court struck the law down as an unconstitutional injury to equality.
Meanwhile, one Israeli in six lives in poverty. Men and women do not fight hardest for a tower built on their backs. They fight hardest for a home where everyone counts.
The third stone is peace, and here the record is starkest: for 15 years, Netanyahu’s governments claimed they could “manage the conflict,” containing Hamas with periodic blows and Qatari cash he allowed into Gaza from 2018, by his own reported account, to keep the Palestinians divided.
Molad’s study, The Failure of Deterrence, concluded that this concept “planted the seeds of the catastrophe.” Quiet bought is not peace built.
Tamir Heyman, former head of Military Intelligence and now head of the Institute for National Security Studies, described an unwritten security doctrine taking hold since October 7: war as a permanent condition; peace no longer a goal but a means; separation from the US as “inevitable and even essential;” and the state’s Jewish identity placed above its democratic one.
The Declaration of Independence David Ben-Gurion read says the opposite: a Jewish state built on freedom, justice, and peace, with equal rights for every citizen.
Ben-Gurion taught that the state is built in the quiet between wars; this doctrine builds it by and for war. It was never put to the people. It is being put to you now.
Washington is already answering: 60% of American adults view Israel unfavorably, and in June, US Vice President JD Vance said that in Israel’s place, he “might not be attacking the only powerful ally” it has left.
Israel used to count on both American parties. Thanks to this government, it cannot count on one.
Three foundation stones, and on every one the record runs the wrong way. That is the opposite of security.
After the flood, God set a rainbow and promised never again to destroy the world. He undertook what He would not do, and nothing about what we should do. The rainbow is no guarantee of our safety. It is a transfer of responsibility.
I have spent enough years close to politics, including as chief executive of Britain’s Conservative Party, to be wary of politicians’ promises, and I cannot promise you the opposition is equal to every task.
But the test is not who sounds toughest.
Ask three questions: Who will restore institutions every citizen can trust? Who will share the burden fairly, so the reservist no longer carries it alone? Who will rebuild the alliances and political horizon that turn power into lasting security?
Noah’s father named him with a prayer: that this child would bring comfort from the toil of their hands. Every Israeli parent prays the same: that the children sleep, the sirens stop, and the uniform can finally be hung up.
My reservist friend deserves that comfort. He will not get it from the man who has promised it since 2009 and delivered the polar opposite.
On October 27, when we vote on security, we must vote for the real thing: the foundation stones that enable us to be a free people in our land.
The writer is co-founder of The London Initiative, a former chief executive of the Conservative Party, and a former chairman of the Jewish Leadership Council.

The Cabinet of Ministers removed the resolution on the reservation of employees from the agenda and will hold consultations with businesses — Zheleznyak
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:06:44 EEST
22:06:44 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers removed the resolution on the reservation of employees from the agenda and will hold consultations with businesses — Zheleznyak
Kyiv • UNN
The government removed from the meeting agenda the resolution on reducing the reservation quotas. The document is planned to be revised after consultations with businesses.
Following a barrage of criticism from representatives of strategic businesses, relevant associations, analysts, and lawmakers, the Cabinet of Ministers removed from its agenda consideration of a resolution limiting reservation quotas. The government plans to hold additional consultations with business representatives. MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported this, citing sources in the government, according to UNN.
"Two sources from the Government confirmed to me that, following the publicity surrounding the issue of the resolution on reservation, it was removed from today's Cabinet meeting. That is, for now, there will be no final approval today, and certainly not in the form that had been planned. Once again, this concerns today (as of this morning, the Government was still planning to submit it for approval at the 3:30 p.m. meeting)," the MP reported .
According to him, consultations and substantial revisions to the government initiative will be carried out, particularly regarding the risks identified by businesses.
Business representatives, MPs from the relevant committee, and industry associations stress that the Government prepared the changes without proper consultations or an assessment of the economic consequences, once again changing the rules for businesses operating under wartime conditions.
The greatest concern was caused by the Government's initiative to reduce reservation quotas. For example, quotas for defense-industrial and energy companies were planned to be reduced from 100% to 85%, and those for the utilities sector from 75% to 60%. Business representatives warn that such restrictions could lead to the loss of qualified personnel, especially highly specialized employees who are virtually impossible to replace quickly; shutdowns of production facilities; the disruption of defense contracts; interruptions in energy supplies and the provision of housing and communal services; and could also create threats to the state's food security. Ultimately, this would negatively affect the army's defense capabilities and the country's economy.
Businesses are also drawing particular attention to the fact that the potential mobilization effect of the proposed restrictions is disproportionate to the possible economic losses. Tens of thousands of employees could lose their "reservation," but this would not mean that these employees would necessarily join the military. At the same time, the outflow of qualified personnel threatens to reduce production, decrease tax revenues, result in lost investment, and lead to the relocation of Ukrainian enterprises abroad.
Representatives of the defense industry stress that the loss of even one highly specialized specialist could halt an entire production cycle, meaning that a 15% reduction in reservations could cause significantly greater losses to the state's defense capabilities.
The creation of a new Coordination Center, which, according to the Government's plan, would review the status of critically important enterprises, was also criticized. Businesses point to the lack of transparency in decision-making criteria, the absence of clear appeal procedures, and the risks of a subjective approach to determining reservation quotas. Additional concern was caused by corruption risks, which the NACP points out, related to the new body's broad discretionary powers.
Businesses demand that efforts to combat abuses in the reservation system not result in the weakening of the economy and the state's defense capabilities. Entrepreneurs and industry associations called on the Government to preserve the current reservation quotas and predictability of the rules, conduct full-fledged consultations, and take into account the specific features of critically important enterprises.
On October 16, 63 members of parliament registered draft resolution No. 16160 in the Verkhovna Rada, which provides for the annulment of the Cabinet's October 13 decision on reservation.

Ethiopia announces interim government in Tigray, aims for polls in six months
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday announced the appointment of an interim administration to prepare elections in the northern Tigray region previously controlled by the Tigray People's Liberation Front that has clashed with government forces since September. The recent conflict revived a war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020 and 2022.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced Friday an interim administration would be established in the northern Tigray region, which has been controlled by rebels who have clashed with federal forces in recent weeks.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched a major offensive against government forces on September 23, before being pushed back and losing control of its strongholds, including the regional capital.

The region had been outside of Addis Ababa's control and did not participate in June federal elections, which were resoundingly won by Abiy's Prosperity Party.
The federal government caretaker administration, which aims to create "a stable political situation so that free and transparent elections can be held", will administer Tigray for the next six months, Abiy's office said on social media following a cabinet decision.
The TPLF leadership "did not desire peace", it said, instead initiating the latest "devastating war".
The region fought a 2020-22 war against federal forces – supported by Eritrean troops – which left an estimated 600,000 dead before a 2022 peace deal ended the fighting but provoked lingering discontent over the terms.

In late September, the TPLF formed an uneasy alliance with several disparate armed groups opposed to the government.
The group has also moved closer to neighbouring Eritrea, long at odds with Ethiopia.

Zelensky explains how Ukraine uses Starlink to intercept Shahed drones
According to him, after Starlink’s performance was reduced, the Ukrainian military lost the ability to intercept some of these targets.
He made this announcement during a press conference in Brussels, according to Ukrinform.
“We sometimes imagine that Starlink is used by the Armed Forces of Ukraine to carry out precision strikes. No. We do not use Starlink to attack or respond within the territory of the Russian Federation. That is precisely why we appealed to SpaceX and the White House to grant us this capability. If we had it, we wouldn’t have had to ask,” Zelensky said.
He explained that Ukraine uses Starlink to operate interceptor drones that destroy “Shahed” rockets attacking the civilian population, and called the speed restrictions on the system an unpleasant and dangerous surprise.
“That’s why they didn’t shut down Starlink, but reduced its speed, and when they reduced the speed, we were unable to shoot down a certain number of ‘Jet-Shaheds.’ This is very unpleasant. We were unable to use it [the tool] to protect the population. This is very painful and unpleasant. The ‘Jet Shahids’ were traveling at speeds of over 400 km, but they reduced our speed to 70…,” the President said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov, a special advisor to the President on technological issues, stated that SpaceX imposed speed limits on Starlink terminals while in motion overnight, and the Ukrainian Defense Forces did not receive any warning.
A source in the Ministry of Defense also reported that the Starlink operational restrictions detected overnight complicated the work of unmanned systems, logistics, and the Defense Forces’ “middle strike” operations.
In addition, the President’s special advisor on technology, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, emphasized that by limiting the operating speed of Starlink terminals, SpaceX is effectively depriving Ukraine of the ability to defend itself against “Shahed” drones.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

UK to Retrofit Donated Weapons for Ukraine With British Sensors, Guidance and EW Systems
Britain plans to retrofit British military technology onto weapons and equipment donated to Ukraine by other countries, while accelerating long-range and air-defense support ahead of winter, UK Defence Journal reported on October 15.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham outlined the plan during talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street. The two also discussed Russia’s continuing attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure following US President Donald Trump’s call for an energy ceasefire, according to the UK government.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to UK Defence Journal, Burnham stated that Britain would continue developing battlefield solutions for Ukraine, including fitting British capabilities onto equipment supplied by other partners.
The approach could involve integrating British sensors, seekers, fuzes, datalinks, or electronic warfare systems with donated hardware. Ukraine has received equipment from more than 50 countries, ranging from Soviet-era systems to modern Western weapons produced to different technical standards.
UK Defence Journal noted that many donated systems lack the communications, guidance, or targeting equipment needed to operate effectively within modern battlefield networks. Retrofitting British components could allow older or incompatible platforms to be integrated more effectively into Ukrainian combat operations.
Burnham and Zelenskyy also discussed accelerating long-range defensive support before winter. Britain intends to continue diplomatic efforts aimed at increasing international supplies of military equipment to Ukraine, the report noted.
The talks also covered a new British package of Lightweight Multirole Missiles designed in part to counter Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones.
UK Defence Journal highlighted the Geran-3, a jet-powered version of the Iranian-designed Shahed-136 design, as one of the threats driving demand for faster interception systems. The drone’s higher speed reduces the time available to detect and engage it compared with propeller-driven Shaheds.
Lightweight Multirole Missiles are built by Thales in Belfast and can be used against aerial targets including drones. Production is now running at four times its 2022 level, with £100 million ($132.6 million) committed to further expansion, according to the UK Defence Journal.
Britain has already pursued a similar integration model through Stone Cloak, a compact electronic warfare system designed to prevent Russian air defenses from tracking drones. UK Defence Journal reported that the system is produced under a British contract, while its intellectual property has been transferred to Ukraine for domestic mass production.
Britain had already announced a £45 million ($59.7 million) surface-to-air missile package for Ukraine and committed £1.6 billion ($2.12 billion) to deliver more than 5,000 Lightweight Multirole Missiles over four years. Of the new package, £10 million ($13.3 million) is being accelerated to meet Ukraine’s winter air-defense needs.

From Samarkand to Paris: Preserving Central Asia's scientific heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:00:40 UTC
22:00:40 KST

From the scholars of the Silk Roads to new research institutions in Tashkent, Uzbekistan is seeking to make its historical legacy more accessible. Experts meeting at UNESCO headquarters in Paris examined its contribution to world civilisation and the value of shared cultural knowledge.
For centuries, Central Asia was a crossroads of scientific discovery, scholarship and cultural exchange. Its historic cities, including Samarkand and Bukhara, developed into important centres of learning, connecting intellectual traditions across the Silk Roads and contributing to advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and religious thought.
Today, Uzbekistan is seeking to make that legacy more accessible internationally through research institutions, museum collections, digital technologies and academic cooperation.
These efforts were explored at an international conference held at UNESCO headquarters in Paris, bringing together more than 300 participants, including scholars, diplomats and representatives of international organisations, according to the organisers.
The event was organised by the Islamic Civilization Center in Uzbekistan, alongside the country's Permanent Delegation and National Commission for UNESCO, its foreign ministry and several scientific and cultural institutions.
The initiative has its roots in a broader effort outlined by Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the UN General Assembly in 2017, when he called for greater international recognition of Central Asia's intellectual heritage and emphasised the importance of education and religious tolerance.
In a further address to the UN in September 2025, he proposed presenting the scientific and spiritual legacy of the region's leading scholars at major international venues. The Paris conference, alongside presentations at UN venues in New York and Geneva, formed part of that programme.
Central Asia's intellectual legacy
Much of the discussion focused on Mawarannahr, historically known as Transoxiana, the region between the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers, encompassing much of present-day Uzbekistan and parts of neighbouring Central Asian countries.
The region produced or attracted scholars whose work influenced intellectual traditions across the Islamic world and beyond.
In an address reported by the Islamic Civilization Center, Mahmud Erol Kılıç, Director General of the Research Centre for Islamic History, Art and Culture (IRCICA), highlighted the contributions of Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Farabi, Ibn Sina and Al-Biruni.
Their work reflected a scholarly tradition in which mathematics, medicine, philosophy and religious studies developed through exchanges of knowledge across different regions.
Farhan Ahmad Nizami, Director of the Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies, also stressed that the region's historical monuments reflect a broader history of creativity and cultural exchange.
"Civilisations are not growing in isolation. We cross-fertilise each other, and it is a message that we need to share to see that we have much more in common than elements that separate us," Salima Dalibey, representing the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, told Euronews.
Mehrdad Shabahang, head of UNESCO's Silk Roads Programme, highlighted the role of research institutions in documenting that shared history.
"These centres like the Uzbekistan Islamic Civilisation Center can help us to identify, to document and also to promote our shared past, our shared history," he said.
Firdavs Abdukhalikov, director of the Islamic Civilization Center, also emphasised the international significance of this legacy.
"Cultural heritage and our great ancestors belong to the whole world," he told Euronews.
Beyond the museum
A central part of this effort is the Islamic Civilization Center in Tashkent, whose museum exhibitions trace more than 3,000 years of history on the territory of present-day Uzbekistan, according to the Center.
Its activities include the study of rare manuscripts and historical artefacts, alongside digital technologies designed to support research and make collections accessible to a broader audience.
Abdukhalikov emphasised that its purpose extends beyond displaying historical objects.
"It is not just a beautiful, large building and museum. It is a major platform for scholarship and education," he told Euronews.
Frédérique Beaupertuis-Bressand, a specialist in the history and art of the Timurids, described the museum as a valuable resource for researchers and visitors.
"Finally, culture is being given the prominence it deserves. We can see these objects, touch them, and study them," she said, adding that access to collections offers further opportunities for historical research.
The Center is also connected to a wider network of specialised institutions, including international research centres dedicated to Imam Bukhari, Imam Termizi and Imam Maturidi.
Sali Shahsivari, managing director of the Al-Furqan Islamic Heritage Foundation, welcomed the expansion of these institutions, saying they were helping to bring greater attention to the region's cultural heritage.
The discussions in Paris also explored opportunities for international research cooperation, including joint studies, the digitisation of historical sources and closer collaboration between academic institutions. The Center also highlighted its use of digital technologies and artificial intelligence in researching and presenting cultural heritage.
The discussions also considered how a better understanding of shared cultural heritage could contribute to dialogue between different societies.
"We live in a time where hate speech spreads very fast, so these opportunities to sit, speak, exchange ideas and dialogue help people understand each other and prepare for a culture of peace," Salima Dalibey of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation told Euronews.

Neet rates higher in England’s smaller cities and towns than in biggest cities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:00:11 UTC
22:00:11 KST

Smaller cities and towns across England have higher rates of young people not in employment, education or training than the nine largest cities, analysis shows.
The Centre for Cities, an independent thinktank dedicated to improving the economies of the UK, used 2021 census data to work out the rates across 41 cities and towns in England.
Of those places, 10 of the smallest cities and towns had higher rates of 16- to 24-year-olds out of employment and education – an average of 15.7% of their youth population, compared with an average of 13.9% across the nine largest cities.
It comes amid a national debate over chronic youth unemployment in the UK, with the latest ONS data showing just under 1 million young people are not in employment, training or education (Neet).
An interim report published by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn in May found that the UK was “at risk of a lost generation”, with young adults facing a “perfect storm” of challenges. His final report is expected soon after the budget on 28 October.
The Centre for Cities analysis shows London (117,095) and Birmingham (44,995) have the highest number of Neets in absolute terms, representing rates of 13.1% and 15.9% respectively. The average Neet rate across England is 12.6%.
In Blackpool, 2,660 of young people are not in education, employment or training, a rate of 21.2%. In Slough, 2,170 young people are Neet (14.1%). The Shropshire town of Telford has 2,780 Neets (15.1%).
Rob Johnson, a senior analyst at the Centre for Cities, said the higher rates of Neets in smaller towns and cities were often a reflection of their general economic performance. In particular, he said such areas could be affected by their proximity to larger cities, but the figures could also be a reflection of the weakness of bigger city economies in the north and Midlands.
“A big root cause of higher rates of Neets in these places is because we know these are cities that have weaker economies,” he said. “The big headline [is] of 1 million Neets across the country but it’s actually more important to understand where those people are. The scale is important, but you just need to know the extent of the variation across the country.”
Johnson said the picture was mixed across smaller cities and towns. “Somewhere like Slough, which is actually quite a productive economy, does have a relatively high rate of Neets. There’s an issue there about connecting those people to the local economy.”
For some in Telford, 30 miles north of Birmingham, the answer to the UK’s chronic crisis of youth unemployment may lie in its local shopping centre.
The Skills Shop, a new youth employment hub opened by Telford College in partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions, aims to connect young people with education, local employers and mentors to tackle the high Neet rates in the region.
Sarah Davies, the executive director of employer engagement and partnerships at Telford College, said there were multiple drivers for the Neets crisis, including the Covid-19 pandemic, mental health disorders and changes in the job market, and there was no “one size fits all” solution.
“It’s a national concern because young people are our future. If you’re out of work, you’re more likely to stay out of work,” she said. “If you ask any young person, they’d rather be working than sat at home. Nobody wants to sit at home on TikTok all day.”
One of those benefiting from courses at the college is George Bate, 21, who is learning to become a HGV driver after graduating from university with a degree in games design. He said he had been unable to pursue a career in gaming due to a lack of opportunities and so embarked on the HGV course after he was signposted by the jobcentre.
“I’d applied to most of the stuff around the area and just didn’t get a response, so that was the disheartening part. I couldn’t find anywhere that was willing to take me,” he said. “A lot of the time, it’s not even a person who reviews any of your [applications].”
When asked about narratives surrounding young people being “lazy”, Bate said there was a lack of employment opportunities as well as an absence of career progression. “It makes it so much more stressful to find a career when you know that some of them don’t have the correct amount of upward mobility,” he said.
Charlie Pryce, 19, is also taking the HGV course and said he had applied for other jobs but faced several barriers to further training and employment.
“People our age, we’ve got a long life ahead of us and we actually want to do work. We might not start off the best but I think we can grow into the role,” he said. “It’s not nice sitting around not doing anything. It’s nice to get out there and do stuff and feel like you’re actually providing something and just working hard.”
George Hounsell, the CEO of 4 All Foundation, a charity working across Shropshire, Telford and Wrekin, said many of the young people he had worked with cited issues such as the lack of opportunities and barriers to transport. “We have lots of families not being able to afford to drive or not being able to afford public transport. That’s a big problem,” he said.

Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Artemis II results show how much science people can do at the moon
The crew’s observations highlight what human eyes can add to lunar exploration
Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.
“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”
NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.
Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.
With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.
“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”
How astronauts learn to observe the moon
Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.
Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.
“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.
That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?
During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.
The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.
“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”
One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.
“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”
Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.
“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”
But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”
“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.
“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”
Astronauts spotted tiny impacts on the moon
Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.
“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”
Before launch, the science team identified and prioritized observations they hoped the crew would be able to make during the flyby. Impact flashes were at the top of the list. Seeing the flashes would give scientists a way to estimate how often the moon is struck by incoming rocks, and how large those rocks are. That’s an important thing to know for protecting future missions where astronauts will walk on the surface or build a long-term moon base.
Scientists didn’t know whether the astronauts would see any flashes at all. They saw five. The flashes were “pinpricks of light lasting less than a second, with no color associated with the flash,” Heldmann said at the meeting.
Comparing the number of flashes per minute to theoretical models of how many impacts the moon might experience, scientists determined that the incoming rocks were tiny, about 8.5 grams and just over 4.5 centimeters across — about the size of a golf ball.
“With these observations, we believe that the Artemis II crew set a record for the smallest meteorites ever optically observed to impact the moon,” Heldmann said.
The resulting craters are probably less than a meter wide, too small for cameras on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to see.
That’s good news for future astronauts. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is supposed to bring astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since Apollo. If successful, it will be a two-week mission using landers from spaceflight companies Blue Origin or SpaceX. The probability of dangerous impact during such a mission is less than 1 in 10 million, Heldmann said. For a larger moon base meant to last a decade, the probability is higher, but still low.
“Now we can start to quantify those impact probabilities, which turns out are very very low,” she says. “Crews will be very safe.”
The moon has more color than it seems
The moon’s muted colors were another high-priority observation for the science team. Lunar hues and brightnesses can change with terrain roughness, surface temperature and mineralogy — and they’re much more discernable with human eyes than with cameras. The crew also saw how colors changed as the viewing angle and light levels changed.
“This is such a cool demonstration of the value of human eyes as scientific sensors,” said planetary scientist Ariel Deutsch, also of NASA Ames.
Combining the crew’s observations with other data going back to the 1970s let scientists connect colors to composition. Blues were associated with titanium-rich volcanic rocks. Browns reflect different iron levels. Greens are from glass formed during volcanic eruptions or asteroid impacts.
Future astronauts could use this information to create terrain maps and to find specific materials on the moon for sample collection or resources.
The crew also was enamored with the terminator, the boundary between light and dark, which revealed lunar topography in a new way.
“Even as rugged as the far side looks … man, when you look at the terminator, it is just, like, impossibly rugged,” Wiseman said during the flight. “And it reminds you that the whole farside is that way. It’s just the terminator is really bringing out the shadows and the hills and the valleys. And it is just — it’s unbelievable.”
The lighting at the terminator is similar to what future astronauts might expect at the moon’s south pole, where the sun will be low on the horizon and may cast dramatic shadows.
“We want to make sure we have a good handle on that for both science and operations and exploration,” Heldmann said.
What Artemis II taught NASA for future moon missions
With the lessons from Artemis II in hand, now it’s the next astronauts’ turn.
Some recommendations coming out of Artemis II focus on improving conditions in the spacecraft and weaving science into mission planning better. For example, due to time constraints, the astronauts’ cameras were not calibrated before flight. The team is now trying to calibrate them back on Earth, but it can’t re-create how the windows affected images because the windows were charred on the way back through Earth’s atmosphere.
Another takeaway from Artemis II is to continue to refine and train astronauts in descriptive notetaking. The audio notes will be even more important for the first landed missions, where astronauts in spacesuits will not be able to write in a notebook.
“We want to train astronauts to be field scientists, regardless of the landing site, regardless of the mission that they’re given,” Young says.
The buddy system of two astronauts at the windows, two talking to the ground, led to better science, the team concluded.
“The crew had scientific discussions and tried to understand what they were viewing,” Heldmann says. For surface missions, where time is limited and choices must be made quickly, that collaboration will be even more important.
The crew also commented on how helpful it was.
“When we actually do go down there to the surface, I know for safety reasons that we would never send someone alone, but I just want to really emphasize how important the discussion time was,” Glover said. “When we started to talk, we not only got better science discussion, we got better human connection.”

Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:00:00 EEST
22:00:00 KST

Zelenskyy confirms Starlink speed restrictions hindered interception of jet-powered Shaheds
Ukraine was unable to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones to protect civilians because Starlink connection speeds had been reduced.
Source: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking after meetings on the sidelines of the EU leaders' summit on 15-16 October, as reported by European Pravda's correspondent in Brussels
Details: Zelenskyy added that the reduction in Starlink speeds had also prevented Ukraine from striking military targets in occupied territories and delivering water and food to Ukrainian troops.
He also stressed that the Armed Forces of Ukraine do not use Starlink to conduct long-range strikes on Russian territory.
"We use [Starlink] to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that strike our civilians and kill our families. We use specialised interceptors that move at high speeds. Interceptor drones that operate specifically with Starlink," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed out that Starlink had not been switched off, but its connection speed had been reduced.
Quote: "When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept some of the jet-powered Shaheds… In other words, we were unable to use a tool to protect civilians. This is very painful and unpleasant."
Details: The president explained that jet-powered Shaheds fly at speeds of more than 400 km/h, while the Starlink restrictions had reduced the equipment speed available to Ukrainian troops intercepting Russian drones to 70 km/h.
Zelenskyy also said Ukraine uses Starlink for mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in temporarily occupied territories, but the reduction in connection speeds had prevented it from carrying out those operations as well.
In addition, Starlink is needed to deliver water and food to Ukrainian troops who spend weeks or months on the front line in areas under the Russians' full drone surveillance.
Zelenskyy noted that the Defence Ministry is in daily contact with the United States and had recently received information that the connection speed had been resumed.
"If that is the case, we are very grateful," the president added.
"We approached SpaceX and the White House to ask them to enable this capability," Zelenskyy said, noting that Ukraine has not received a positive response to its request.
Background:
- Reuters previously reported that the order to restrict the use of the Starshield satellite system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications and drone control, had come from the White House.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation and report back to Congress on the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- Axios previously reported that Trump's administration supposedly had nothing to do with the incident. Washington attempted to shift responsibility to SpaceX, saying the White House does not control the company's actions.
- Zelenskyy publicly described the communications restrictions as a mistake that would lead to casualties and destruction.

Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra Review: The First Real AI PC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

The Surface Laptop Ultra is a true MacBook Pro competitor for Windows—if only it weren't for the lack of battery life.
Courtesy of BH Photo
Save this story
Save this story
Rating:
7/10
Open rating explainer
WIRED
The brightest laptop display ever made. MacBook-like design and build quality. Magnetic USB-C port is clever. Performs well unplugged. Music-ready speakers.
TIRED
Battery life can’t compete with the MacBook Pro. Some very popular games aren’t supported yet. Lower-tier RAM options limit AI capabilities.
A new fleet of Windows laptops has arrived, and the Surface Laptop Ultra is its flagship vessel. Ever since it was announced, it's been one of my anticipated laptops of the year. It not only promises to be a beefed-up evolution of the Surface Laptop (a laptop I already really liked), but also debuts a brand-new piece of silicon: the Nvidia RTX Spark N1X "superchip."
The goal is a single laptop that can handle on-device AI, gaming, content creation, and nearly anything else you might throw at it. If that sounds a bit like a MacBook Pro, you're on the right track. But unlike previous attempts to dethrone Apple, the Surface Laptop Ultra is trading blows with the very best. I just wish it had the battery life to truly keep up with the MacBook Pro.
Killer Looks and Sounds
This isn't Microsoft's first foray into a more powerful laptop. The company first tried that in 2021 with the Surface Laptop Studio. At the time, it was the company's answer to the MacBook Pro: a laptop-tablet hybrid oriented toward the growing class of content creators and media professionals. It even came with a discrete graphics card (though not a particularly good one).
The Surface Laptop Ultra rejects the Studio's form-factor experimentation and opts for a more straightforward but polished approach. It's a powerful clamshell laptop that's designed for people who need the extra performance—whether for gaming, content creation, or on-device AI workflows. The ideal demographic, I suppose, is someone who does some of all of that.
At 4.4 pounds, the Surface Laptop Ultra is lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro but slightly thicker. It's actually the thickest of all the new N1X laptops, with HP's OmniBook Ultra being the thinnest. The Surface Laptop Ultra appears thinner than it actually is, though, thanks to the inventive way it hides its side vents—so discreet that it's hard to photograph them. The design has just enough small touches like that to make it stand out. There's also a soft dip into the keyboard well, with a unique look that matches the curved lip of the underside vents. I appreciate the modern vibe of the rounded screen corners, though some apps don't account for them well and nearly cut off elements of the Title Bar. One other minor annoyance is that there's no lip for your finger when the device is closed. You can slide your fingernail in between, but in most cases, you'll need two hands to open it.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
But once opened, the Surface Laptop Ultra gets mostly compliments from me. The keyboard is fantastic, as is the extra-large touchpad with haptic feedback. I still dislike the power button placement (why not put it in the top right like every other laptop, as an obvious button, instead of between keys?), and the keycaps could be a bit larger. But overall, I was very happy and comfortable typing and swiping on the laptop.
I was also very pleased with the audio. The aforementioned underside vents also hide the four speakers, which sound fabulous. I was really impressed by how loud, rich, and full these sound, perhaps only second to the 16-inch MacBook Pro (and 15-inch MacBook Air). There's even a hint of bass!
Next to those speakers are lots of useful ports. You have the usual for a laptop of this type, including HDMI, USB-A, a headphone jack, an SD card slot, and three USB4 Type-C ports. The system can support up to three 4K external monitors or a single 5K display. Regardless of the resolution, you're maxed out at a 120 Hz refresh rate. This is slightly behind the latest MacBook Pro, which can support two 5K displays at a 120 Hz refresh rate. But overall, I'm really happy with this mix of connectivity—in fact, it just might be the most well-rounded offering I can imagine.
The Surface Laptop Ultra has a trick up its sleeve involving magnets. The Surface Laptop has long used the Surface Connect, a proprietary magnetic power port that can also plug into Microsoft's Surface Dock. The Surface Laptop Ultra now uses USB-C, and how Microsoft engineered it to make it magnetic is impressive. Disappointingly, only the USB-C port on the right side has this magnetic feature, but all USB-C ports deliver power. You've always been able to buy third-party add-ons that do something similar, but it's a really neat bit of innovation.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
Shines Bright
What I appreciate most about all the Surface Laptop designs is the 3:2 aspect ratio display. I often find that more vertical space comes in handy, especially if you frequently work with documents, spreadsheets, and websites. Combined with the smaller 15-inch touchscreen (compared to the typical 16-incher), this makes for a more compact laptop to carry. At a full inch narrower than the 16-inch MacBook Pro, it fits in a laptop bag a bit more easily.
The screen is extremely sharp, with a pixel density of 257 pixels per inch, just barely exceeding the 16-inch MacBook Pro. Like the MacBook Pro, the Surface Laptop Ultra's display uses Mini-LED backlighting. OLED is far more commonly used in Windows laptops, though, which make up for their lack of brightness with extreme contrast and stronger color performance. But here, the Surface Laptop Ultra clearly has its targets on the MacBook Pro. That may change soon with the rumored launch of the OLED MacBook Pro.
With 1,344 dimming zones, it's the brightest laptop screen ever made. Using my colorimeter, I measured 987 nits of brightness in SDR and 1,945 nits in HDR in a 9 percent window. The result is pretty stunning HDR performance. Games and movies look spectacular on this screen, even without the perfect black levels OLED would provide. Add in the 120-Hz refresh rate, and you have a beautiful display for gaming—especially in more visually immersive, single-player games.
But the screen is highly reflective. This was also true of the standard Surface Laptop, but it's noticeably more reflective than a MacBook. Even with the brightness fully maxed, I still found myself staring at my reflection when viewing websites with dark backgrounds—and that's despite this being unquestionably the brightest screen ever put in a laptop. The reflections are really my only complaint. Otherwise, it's one of my favorite displays I've tested.
The 1080p webcam isn't particularly impressive. It struggles in low light, and the image is pretty noisy. The MacBook Pro webcam has better image processing, brightening faces without overexposing.
The Nvidia N1X Arrives
The Nvidia N1X is a first-of-its-kind chip in Windows laptops. Qualcomm broke open the floodgates in 2024 with its Snapdragon X chips, of which the Surface Laptop was an early adopter. These were primarily an answer to the MacBook Air, and later to what would become the MacBook Neo. But Qualcomm's chips never scaled up to the performance needed to match something like the M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. That's where the Nvidia N1X steps in.
Both the Snapdragon X and N1X use a System on a Chip (SoC) design, which packages the CPU, GPU, and memory together. It's the same design Apple Silicon chips use, and—importantly—it lets both the CPU and GPU access local memory. This is crucial for enabling the much faster local AI processing, which needs to feed that GPU as much memory as possible. The N1X comes in two configurations: an 18-core system (5,120 GPU cores) and a 20-core system (6,144 GPU cores). Think of these like Apple's M5 Pro and M5 Max, with the main differences being GPU performance and configuration options. For example, if you want 128 GB of memory to hammer home that AI performance, you have to go with the 20-core N1X. In fact, the 18-core model is limited to just 24 GB or 32 GB of RAM (and from what I've seen so far, the Surface Laptop Ultra is the only N1X laptop to be sold with only 24 GB of memory).
I tested the 32 GB model, paired with the higher-end 20-core CPU. In terms of core count, the graphics card in this configuration of the N1X sits right in between the mobile RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5080. That sounds promising on a laptop this thin, but the core count alone doesn't mean you should expect it to perform at the same level in games. The N1X is capped at 80 watts, which puts a serious limit on in-game frame rates. Gaming as a whole, however, is also handicapped by the nature of this being an Arm-based system. In nearly every game you play, the Surface Laptop Ultra will need to rely on app emulation, which does reduce performance. As Nvidia points out, though, emulation has its biggest impact on the CPU. So, even if applications like games aren't optimized for Arm, they should still run OK. That's exactly what I experienced with the handful of games I tried. You'll need to play most games at medium settings or lower to get decent frame rates, and usually you'll want to play at 1920 x 1200 resolution.
Despite scoring lower than the M5 Max MacBook Pro in 3DMark tests, the Surface Laptop Ultra delivers up to 20 percent faster frame rates in games like Cyberpunk 2077. That's one of the few titles where I could directly compare the two systems. I also tested games like 007: First Light, Marvel Rivals, and Black Myth: Wukong. Seeing so many popular titles run on an Arm system is exciting, and Nvidia is clearly investing heavily in the future of gaming on Arm. However, a list of fairly high-profile multiplayer games aren't compatible yet due to anti-cheat systems, including PUBG, Valorant, and League of Legends. Those are some heavy hitters to be missing at launch, but Nvidia says support is coming. I did run into some glitches, though, such as in 007: First Light, where I couldn't adjust the display resolution in the options menu. That's frustrating as the game otherwise plays well on the system.
Photograph: Luke Larsen
Regardless, these are the most powerful integrated graphics we've seen in a Windows laptop, leaving Intel's Panther Lake X9 in the dust. But if you want the best bang-for-your-buck gaming performance, you're much better off buying a dedicated gaming laptop. The RTX 5060 in a Lenovo LOQ 15, for example, can draw up to 115 watts and deliver up to 22 percent better performance in games like Cyberpunk 2077 and Marvel Rivals. It's also around a thousand dollars cheaper. If gaming were the main point of the Surface Laptop Ultra, that would feel like a disappointment.
But AI performance is the real reason this laptop (and the N1X as a whole) exists, and that's where it shines most. I ran it through Procyon's latest AI benchmarks, which include text generation, image generation, and computer vision. The Surface Laptop Ultra is around 25 percent faster than the Dell XPS 14 at generating text in these lighter models, which only range from 3.5-billion parameters up to 12-billion. Nice to see, but not exactly a dramatic leap ahead. Meanwhile, the Razer Blade 16 with an RTX 5090 (and 32 GB of RAM) posts nearly twice the scores in these tests. That's a more expensive laptop, of course, but it also doesn't go around claiming to be designed for AI.
Clearly, these entry-level configurations of the Surface Laptop Ultra are more for AI dabblers than true enthusiasts. Adding more memory doesn't necessarily solve that problem. I'm also testing a 128-GB version of the HP OmniBook Ultra right now (with the same N1X chip), and I was hoping to see it run some larger models. And while you can certainly load up a 70-billion parameter model in LM Studio, performance on it is very slow. Without more raw GPU compute on hand to speed things up, these more impactful models feel too slow to use daily work. They can, however, still be used in situations that require more complex reasoning, such as for coding, when it's worth waiting for the actual correct answer.
Running local AI models as a computing task that lots of people will want to do is still a question mark for me. As long as free cloud-based models are faster and more useful, I have a hard time seeing people spend extra cash on a computer just to run a model locally. This will undoubtedly change as models improve, but right now, it'll have a limited appeal in that regard. The real benefit might be in agentic AI that gives you access to your local files on your computer and lets you do things that aren't possible in a basic ChatGPT session. I ran a very basic test in LM Studio Bionic, asking it to analyze a folder of local text files and generate a comprehensive summary using Gemma 4 E4B, a 4.5-billion-parameter model. It took 8 minutes to process the request and another 2 minutes to deliver the 853-word response. There's enough performance here to explore and experiment with on-device AI—but the speed may get frustrating. I say all that less to criticize the Surface Laptop Ultra and more just to set expectations on what laptops can do right now.
If the N1X has one serious weakness, it's the CPU. The N1X is 20 to 24 percent slower in CPU benchmarks, in both single-core and multi-core performance tests. Switching from Balanced to Performance Mode in the Windows Settings, however, makes a big difference. It's a 20 percent increase in single-core performance when enabled, a bigger delta than on other laptops. It's fast enough not to be a major bottleneck, but I'd expect to see improvement in future generations of the N1X chip.
At What Cost?
Photograph: Luke Larsen
The Surface Laptop Ultra is not the only RTX Spark laptop launching today. Many of them major Windows laptop manufacturers has one, and they all lean into high-end hardware, including nearly every premium feature possible. I'm still testing some of these models, including the closest competitor, the Lenovo Pro 9n. It has a 15-inch screen, the same N1X chip, and 32 GB of RAM. From what I can tell so far, these laptops perform fairly similarly, within a few percentage points.
But against something like the Razer Blade 16, the Surface Laptop Ultra faces a closer rival. You can buy the RTX 5070 model of the Blade 16 with 32 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage for $2,999—a similar configuration and price to the Surface Laptop Ultra. They are a similar size and are both well-built. The Surface Laptop Ultra has a sharper and brighter screen, but the Blade 16 has a faster refresh rate. Higher-end configurations of the Razer Blade 16 with the Intel Core Ultra 9 386H even match the Surface Laptop Ultra's battery life, which lasted only 12 hours in a local video playback test. Both devices are what I'd call “do-it-all” laptops. I think the Surface Laptop Ultra is the better overall laptop, largely because of its better keyboard and touchpad. It also has the option to configure it with up to 128 GB of memory, whereas the Blade 16 maxes out at 64 GB. But if you'll spend more time gaming than running local models, the Surface Laptop Ultra (and any of the N1X devices) is the wrong choice.
The Surface Laptop Ultra is also priced nearly the same as the 16-inch MacBook Pro. For $2,999, you get 24 GB of RAM and a terabyte of storage. Both offer a lower-tier performance option, either the M5 Pro or the 18-core N1X. The Surface Laptop Ultra lets you configure the system with 128 GB of memory with only a terabyte of storage, whereas the MacBook Pro forces you into 2 TB. The MacBook Pro still has the edge in polish, whether that's better speakers and a webcam, a less reflective screen, or more comprehensive app support. The major disadvantage, however, is battery life. The MacBook Pro offers a full nine or ten more hours of battery life than the Surface Laptop Ultra. No getting around that. The MacBook Pro also tends to stay a bit quieter. That's part of the magic sauce of what makes the MacBook Pro feel special. The problem has never been that we don't have powerful-enough laptops. The difficulty is in not having to make compromises to achieve that performance, and battery life has always been the most challenging to overcome. Unfortunately, the Surface Laptop Ultra (and the other N1X laptops for that matter) still don't quite make the cut.
And yet, I'm drawn to the brighter screen and taller aspect ratio of the Surface Laptop Ultra, as well as its 15-inch size. I've always found the 16-inch MacBook Pro to be a bit unwieldy. We may be just weeks away from seeing what Apple has in store for a lighter MacBook Pro with a touchscreen. But for now, if you want to dabble in gaming, content creation, and AI workflows, it's probably the best laptop you can buy that isn't a MacBook Pro. And even more importantly, I foresee it starting a new era in Windows laptops that will grown into something truly special in the not-so-distant future.
Luke Larsen is a product writer and reviewer at WIRED, covering laptops, PCs, Macs, monitors, and the wider PC peripheral ecosystem. He’s been reporting on tech for over a decade, previously at Digital Trends as the senior editor in computing, where he spent seven years leading the publication’s daily coverage. ... Read More
