Explainer-Will a new leader and a new name boost the rebellion in eastern Congo?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:55:44 UTC
21:55:44 KST

Explainer-Will a new leader and a new name boost the rebellion in eastern Congo?
DAKAR, Oct 16 - The former president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Joseph Kabila, took over leadership of rebel forces occupying eastern regions this week, in the most significant shake-up of the uprising in years.
The move gives the rebels a highly prominent Congolese figurehead and could boost their efforts to present themselves as a national movement rather than a Rwandan proxy, diplomats, rebel sources and analysts said.
The big questions now are whether Kabila can translate his political stature and regional connections into broader support for the rebellion, and whether his leadership will significantly alter the balance of power on the ground in the fractured country.
WHAT DOES KABILA'S LEADERSHIP CHANGE?
The most obvious change is the name.
After Monday's announcement of Kabila's new role, the rebels — an alliance of the Alliance Fleuve Congo coalition and the M23 armed group — said they would now be known as the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN).
The name suggests a greater focus on national Congolese, not regional, affairs.
Even before the leadership change, the rebels said their main aim was to remove Congo's current president, Felix Tshisekedi, from power, accusing his administration of corruption, discriminatory policies and crackdowns on opponents.
But UN experts and analysts said the violence has been primarily driven by long conflicts over power, identity and resources dating back to the 1990s genocide in neighbouring Rwanda and even earlier.
Western countries and UN experts have accused Kigali of backing M23. Rwanda denies the allegations, but has acknowledged coordinating with the rebels on security matters.
Much of the rebel leadership remains in place. Kabila takes over as president, while former Alliance Fleuve Congo coordinator Corneille Nangaa and M23 political leader Bertrand Bisimwa become vice presidents.
Veteran M23 leader Sultani Makenga also takes a vice-presidential role, and remains chief of the rebel armed wing, preserving his central role in the movement.
WHY IS KABILA STILL IMPORTANT YEARS AFTER HE LEFT POWER?
The appointment of Kabila — who led Congo from 2001 to 2019 — puts a high-profile Congolese face on the rebellion.
It could also broaden the rebellion's appeal beyond its eastern stronghold. Kabila is from the southern Katanga region, where there is mounting resentment towards the administration of his successor as president, Tshisekedi. But the rebellion has not yet reached the province.
Kabila also brings greater political weight than Nangaa, as well as influential connections in Congo and beyond, particularly in Namibia, Kenya, South Africa and other parts of the region, which he regularly visits. But it is not yet clear if they would translate into tangible support.
HOW WILL THIS AFFECT THE REBELLION ON THE GROUND?
It remains to be seen how much support Kabila will be able to rally around the rebellion.
After remaining in power for two years beyond his mandate, Kabila left office deeply unpopular in much of Congo, including in Katanga.
His political network has weakened in recent years. Many former allies have switched allegiance to Tshisekedi, gone into exile or been imprisoned.
Since Monday's announcement, several prominent figures from his political camp have publicly broken ranks with him.
A Congolese court sentenced Kabila to death in absentia for treason a year ago after allegations that he had joined the rebels. He was also placed under US sanctions in April for providing material support to the rebels and destabilizing eastern Congo.
A 2021 investigation by international media outlets and anti-corruption groups based on millions of leaked bank documents showed that Kabila and his family amassed significant wealth during his nearly two decades in power. It is not clear where this money is held and how he could mobilise it.
WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR PEACE TALKS?
AFC/M23 had been negotiating with the Congolese government in Qatari-mediated talks and signed a declaration last year committing both sides to a permanent ceasefire and broader peace negotiations.
The FRN said on Wednesday it "assumes all of the rights, obligations, and commitments" of AFC/M23, "including those undertaken in the context of the Doha negotiations."
At a UN Security Council meeting on Tuesday, Congo stressed the need for all parties to make good on promises, while the US called for the pursuit of negotiations.
It remains unclear how much either side is committed to the peace process, with both blaming the other for the continued fighting. REUTERS

Thousands march in Albanian capital as anti-government protests spread
TIRANA, Oct 16 - Thousands of young Albanians marched through Tirana on Friday, breaking some windows and traffic lights on the fourth day of an increasingly violent student-led campaign to force Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
The demonstrations, which are spreading through the country, turned into a riot in the capital on Thursday, with protesters smashing windows, raiding a bank and clashing with police. They follow months of mostly peaceful demonstrations that the students say the government ignored.
"They are pushing us to the limits," said 19-year-old protester Enea, declining to give a second name for fear of arrest. He said his message to Rama was: "To resign as fast as possible before everything burns down."
The students accuse officials of corruption and neglecting education and say they are angry about the sale of pristine parts of Albania's coast to a luxury resort development backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
The unrest is a challenge for Rama, who won a fourth term last year on promises to take Albania into the European Union and is aiming for membership as early as 2028.
"We will not bow to violence," he said on Facebook.
BUSINESSES APPEAL TO PROTESTERS TO LEAVE THEM ALONE
The students, many wearing masks, faced off against lines of riot police in front of the Education Ministry building. Some small businesses had their shutters down and notes on their facades saying: "We are with you. Do not damage our business all over the town."
In the coastal town of Lezha, police clashed with stone-hurling protesters. Protests have also spread to Elbasan, Skhodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to garbage bins, local media reported.
"We've been protesting peacefully for 140 days, and nothing was heard. So this is our only chance to be heard and get our rights that we deserve," a 19-year-old protester who gave her name only as Klea said.
The demonstrations were sparked by the plans to build the resort, which has faced legal challenges.
Villagers told Reuters in July that their land was wrongfully sold for development. Reuters later reported that the man who sold the land was wanted by prosecutors for drug trafficking, charges his lawyer denied.
Reuters found no evidence of wrongdoing by Kushner, who is not directly involved in the villagers' dispute.
Political analyst Afrim Krasniqi said younger generations saw no future in Albania. "They see that all resources in the country, political resources, economic, everything is in the hands of oligarchs," he told Reuters.
Corruption scandals have tarnised Albania's image over the years and analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking, complicating its efforts to join the EU.
Along with Montenegro, Albania is leading the accession process among Balkan countries.
The unrest is part of a wave of student activism in Europe. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education. REUTERS

Turkey and Morocco Lead Fuel Supplies to Russia as Seaborne Imports Fall 44%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:54:13 UTC
21:54:13 KST

Turkey and Morocco became Russia’s largest suppliers of seaborne oil products in September, as total imports fell 44% from August’s record, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Russia imported 234,000 metric tons, down from 416,000 in August. Despite the decline, September remained the second-highest month in the think tank’s data, which extend back to January 2022.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The figures cover seaborne shipments and do not establish that Russia’s domestic refining capacity has recovered.
Turkey becomes Russia’s largest supplier
Turkey supplied 55% of September’s imports. Four cargoes loaded at the southern port of Mersin carried 130,000 tons of fuel worth €94 million ($106 million), according to CREA.
Three cargoes contained gasoline and one contained diesel. The total was about three and a half times the 37,000 tons shipped from Mersin in August.
Russia supplied 89% of Mersin’s seaborne oil-product imports in the first half of 2026. CREA said some of that fuel might now be returning to Russia amid its domestic shortages. The loading port does not, by itself, establish where a cargo was refined.
Gasoline shipments from Morocco increase
Morocco was Russia’s second-largest supplier, shipping 96,000 tons in September, up from 70,000 in August and 39,000 in July.
All three September cargoes contained gasoline, according to Kpler shipping data cited by CREA. They were loaded at the Horizon terminal in Tangier and unloaded at St. Petersburg and Murmansk, with Gazprom and Surgutneftegas among the listed buyers.
How Long Will Russia’s Diesel Supply Last? A Breakdown by Country
Indian shipments pause as South Korean deliveries shrink
Russia received no seaborne oil-product shipments from India in September, compared with 160,000 tons in August. However, a 40,000-ton cargo arrived from India in early October.
South Korean deliveries fell to 8,000 tons in September from 95,000 in August. None had arrived in October as of Oct. 13, CREA said, linking the slowdown to threatened legal action against South Korean exporters.
Kyiv Post previously reported on questions over South Korea’s fuel shipments. Seoul subsequently said the shipments were not prohibited, while investigating the trade.
The latest report’s August figures differ from earlier estimates cited by Kyiv Post. Its September comparison uses an August total of 416,000 tons.
Russian-derived fuel reaches sanctioning countries
CREA also identified seven September shipments to EU ports from refineries processing Russian crude, despite the bloc’s ban on products made from Russian oil, which took effect on Jan. 21, 2026.
Six shipments came from India and one from Turkey. Italy received three, Romania two, and Spain and the Republic of Cyprus one each.
The refinery’s use of Russian crude does not establish that every exported cargo contains Russian-derived fuel. CREA identified the shipments as requiring scrutiny under EU guidance.
Refineries in India, Turkey and Brunei that process Russian crude exported €1 billion ($1.12 billion) of oil products to sanctioning countries in September. CREA estimated that €295 million ($332 million) of those products were refined from Russian crude. Recipients included the EU, Australia, the US and New Zealand.
The findings come after Washington’s Oct. 9 agreement to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, which drew objections from European governments. Kyiv Post has examined the proposed supplies against fuel consumption. September’s lower import total alone does not establish how much additional diesel Russia can produce or export.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to tighten controls on advanced AI chips and servers exported to China, bringing its rules closer to US restrictions, Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said.
In a Monday interview with Bloomberg, Kung said the country would add advanced semiconductors and AI servers to its export control list. Unauthorized shipments of restricted equipment could then lead to criminal charges under the Foreign Trade Act, the minister said.
Kung said the changes are part of the commitments under the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, which covers economic cooperation and security. He said some export controls would follow US rules but did not say when the new measures would take effect.
CNA reported that the country already requires permits for exports of sensitive technologies, particularly those with potential military uses. However, advanced AI chips and servers are not specifically covered by the proposed restrictions, making some unauthorized shipments difficult to prosecute under existing export laws.
The planned changes come as concerns over efforts to smuggle restricted AI equipment into China grow. The US has tightened controls on advanced semiconductor exports since 2022, citing concerns that the technology could strengthen China's military, per Reuters.
In August, prosecutors indicted nine people over an alleged scheme to illegally export AI servers to China. Authorities said the case involved 130 servers, including 74 allegedly shipped to China through other countries using false documents.
Prosecutors filed charges including breach of trust and document forgery, rather than offenses specifically involving unauthorized AI hardware exports. The case highlighted difficulties in enforcing US technology restrictions through Taiwan's existing laws.
A separate US investigation also uncovered attempts to bypass export restrictions. Reuters reported that a contractor linked to Super Micro Computer pleaded guilty in a case involving the diversion of Nvidia-powered AI servers to China.

Chinese visitors and students are welcome in Taiwan, but they have to respect local laws, the agency said. Wang reportedly later apologized and denied any threats of aggression against the president.

Ordered the execution of Ukrainian prisoners of war in Vovchansk — an Russian commander and four subordinates have been served notices of suspicion
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:52:15 EEST
21:52:15 KST

Ordered the execution of Ukrainian prisoners of war in Vovchansk — an Russian commander and four subordinates have been served notices of suspicion
Kyiv • UNN
Five Russian servicemen were notified in absentia of suspicion of having shot three Ukrainian prisoners at the aggregate plant. One accomplice has already been sentenced to life imprisonment.
Law enforcement officers have identified five more Russian servicemen involved in the execution of three Ukrainian defenders on the premises of the Vovchansk Aggregate Plant in the summer of 2024, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
As reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, the suspects include a battalion commander who issued orders to kill prisoners, a senior officer at the position who relayed them to his subordinates, the direct perpetrator of the executions, and two accomplices.
In June 2024, a Ukrainian serviceman, having become disoriented during combat, found himself at the occupiers’ positions and surrendered because of the enemy’s numerical superiority. After interrogating him, Russian servicemen with the call signs "Kot" and "Altai" reported to the senior officer at the position, "Krasavchik," who had received an order from the battalion commander, "Yenot," to kill the prisoner. On his instructions, the defender was taken to the plant’s checkpoint, where "Kot" shot him in the head, while "Altai" guarded the perimeter.
In early July, following a similar scheme, the occupiers executed two more Ukrainian servicemen who had been captured during fighting in Vovchansk. They were interrogated after being tied to poles and, following an order from "Yenot," relayed through "Krasavchik," were taken to a pumping station. There, "Kot" and "Altai" shot each of them in the back of the head. Both defenders died at the scene. Two more servicemen with the call signs "Koba" and "Voodoo" escorted the prisoners and guarded the area.
Prosecutors reported that the roles of the perpetrators were established through testimony, radio intercepts, information from electronic devices, and recordings from unmanned aerial vehicles.
Five Russian servicemen have been notified in absentia that they are suspected of the following:
• "Yenot" and "Krasavchik" — of issuing orders to violate the laws and customs of war, combined with intentional murder;
• "Kot" — of violating the laws and customs of war, combined with intentional murder committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy;
• "Koba" and "Voodoo" — of aiding and abetting the commission of this crime.
The actions of the suspects have been classified under Part 2 of Article 438, Part 5 of Article 27, and Part 2 of Article 28 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, in the version in force before October 24, 2024, according to the role of each individual.
Another participant in the executions — Serhii Tuzhylov, with the call sign "Altai" — was previously sentenced to life imprisonment. His defense attorney is currently appealing the verdict in the appellate court.

A brilliant reflection on the links between craftsmanship and contemporary art, particularly on the Murano glass tradition. This was the lecture delivered at the Indian Museum by Italian master Jean Blanchaert as part of the “Contemporary Art Days” promoted by the Consulate General of Italy in Kolkata.

BRUSSELS — The leaders of Denmark, Italy and Poland are pushing the European Union to significantly harden its stance on irregular migration, according to three EU diplomats and draft language seen by POLITICO.
Migration “represents a concern for many European citizens and poses a challenge for the cohesion of our societies … and [is] negatively affecting crime rates,” reads a draft of summit conclusions circulated ahead of a lunchtime discussion on the topic at a leaders’ summit in Brussels, backed by Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen and Poland’s Donald Tusk.
“The European Council further underlined the importance of ensuring full control of irregular arrivals, including by avoiding measures that could create incentives for illegal migration,” reads the draft seen by POLITICO.
Advertisement
The bloc’s 27 leaders were due to discuss migration during a special session on Thursday requested by Meloni and Frederiksen following a tense back-and-forth with Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez in June.
Tensions have risen further after Spain’s Ceuta exclave was overwhelmed by migrants during the summer and as far-right parties have made gains around the bloc.
The draft also “calls the Commission to explore [a] possible consultation mechanism to encourage coordination on national measures potentially affecting other Member States while respecting national competencies.”
While the last phrase does not name any one country, Sánchez has clashed with Meloni over his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis as well as Spanish measures to regularize around 1 million migrants.
However, language discussing the impact of migration on social housing was removed from the draft over concerns that it could be perceived as provocative toward Spain.
One of the diplomats — who, like the others, was granted anonymity to discuss confidential information — said the updated draft was unlikely to win unanimous support from all the leaders, but had been proposed to bring the language closer in line with political sentiment and spark debate.

Brand, once one of Britain's most high-profile broadcasters and the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial accused of three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old denies the allegations and told police after his arrest that he had never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity.
The second of the complainants told London's Southwark Crown Court that in 2001 Brand had tried to pull her into the male toilets at MTV Europe, in London, where she was working.
Initially she said she had exchanged "banter" with Brand about the T-shirt he was wearing, which she told him she liked, but she said his demeanour had changed after she accompanied him to show him where the bathrooms were located.
She said Brand had been quite affable but then become "a wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet".
BRAND'S LAWYER SAYS INCIDENT 'SHORT-LIVED'
"He grabbed me by the arm and started to pull me and said 'come on, come in with me'," she said. "He started to plead almost, 'go on, go on, come in'."
She said although he had grabbed her arm hard she was able to wrench her arm free.
"I said to him 'what are you doing, are you mad, let me go'," she told the court.
She said when he realised "it wasn't happening" because she was too strong, he went into the toilets. The whole incident lasted about 20 seconds, she said.
The woman did not report what had happened to her employer at the time, saying it would be just her word against his, but went to the police after seeing a 2023 documentary about Brand.
His lawyer Ian Winter put it to her that Brand had pleaded with her to go into the toilet for some sort of sexual activity and had accepted she was not consenting, with her view of what had occurred changing after she had seen the documentary.
It was a "very short-lived, very minor incident where he tried to get you into the lavatory and you refused and he left it there", he suggested.
All six of the complainants, who are legally entitled to lifelong anonymity, came forward after the documentary, Judge Joel Bennathan told the jury on Thursday.
The trial, which is expected to last around six weeks, continues. REUTERS

Experts: Cyberattack on French supermarkets serves as a warning sign for Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:48:05 UTC
21:48:05 KST

Cybersecurity experts believe that the cyberattack on French supermarkets on the night of the 12th of September—which resulted in the destruction of a large quantity of food—serves as a warning sign for Estonia, reports ERR News.
During the cyberattack, the perpetrators gained access to temperature control systems and raised the temperature in refrigerators and freezers to 50 degrees Celsius. As a result, a large amount of food was spoiled, causing significant financial losses. Estonia, too, must be prepared for such threats.
Toomas Lepik, a cybersecurity analyst at Tallinn University of Technology, stated that such incidents are possible and that the threat is very real. Fortunately, Estonia has not yet encountered problems of the kind seen in France; however, this does not mean that such an event could not occur due to a mistake or lax adherence to cybersecurity protocols.
Estonian Minister of Justice Liisa Pakosta, who is currently attending a cybersecurity conference in Singapore, described the incident in France as shocking. She pointed out that society must adapt to a new reality: cyberattacks no longer affect only computers and information systems. At the same time, the Minister emphasized that Estonia adheres to some of the strictest cybersecurity regulations in the world. She noted that companies providing essential services—including those involved in food security—are subject to stringent cybersecurity requirements, which must be met. 
Businesses must ensure that software is updated in a timely manner, systems are properly connected, and access is restricted so that unauthorized individuals cannot gain entry. 
Regarding entities such as grocery stores, the Minister stated that regular audits are conducted at major companies responsible for food security.
However, these requirements do not apply to all grocery stores. Pakosta added that both the government and businesses need to invest more in cybersecurity to ensure the security of their systems. She explained that while Estonia faces financially motivated cyberattacks on one hand, there are also attacks specifically targeting the state and society as a whole. As a digital nation, Estonia must pay greater attention to this issue. The Estonian supermarket chain Selver is closely monitoring events in France to prevent similar situations in its own stores. It is currently unknown who orchestrated the cyberattack on the French stores or whether a ransom will be demanded. Selver’s Communications Manager, Mariann Järvela, confirmed that the chain has not faced such attacks. She emphasized that the supermarket chain is doing everything possible to prevent such an occurrence, noting that every company and retail chain has its own strict protocols and systems in place to manage these matters. Järvela stated that, overall, Selver is well-protected against such threats.
Järvela added that the consequences of the incident in France do not differ significantly from those caused by a power outage—scenarios for which the supermarket chain already conducts training exercises.

'Thanks a lot, Trump': Wyoming conservatives divided ahead of US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:48:00 UTC
21:48:00 KST

'Thanks a lot, Trump': Wyoming conservatives divided ahead of US midterms
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Famous for its cowboy culture, Wyoming is the least populated, the most rural and the most conservative of all the US states. With two weeks to go until the midterm elections, our reporters James André and Sylvain Rousseau travelled across this Republican stronghold and found that the party of US President Donald Trump is deeply divided in the Cowboy State.
Come election season in the United States, news networks tend to flock to the swing states, the battlegrounds that shape the outcome of the vote. Two weeks ahead of the US midterm elections, FRANCE 24 decided to go in the opposite direction and visit the reddest of the red states: Wyoming.
US President Donald Trump carried 70 percent of the vote in Wyoming in his three presidential runs. The state is so overwhelmingly Republican that the decisive vote is not the midterm election there, but rather the Republican primaries that took place on August 18. The results are very clear.
In 2024, Wyoming voters had given an outright majority to the ultra-conservative Freedom Caucus, a hard-right organisation that emerged in the wake of Trump's MAGA movement. Wyoming was the first and only state to offer this national movement a majority. In the 2026 primaries, the Freedom Caucus was aiming for a supermajority in both chambers of the Wyoming Congress. But it got a spectacular rebuke from voters, losing its majority in the state House of Representatives and official posts across the board.
This electoral defeat is significant because the Freedom Caucus is the local incarnation of a form of "ultra-Trumpism". For two years, its lawmakers imported a hardline version of Trump's methods and agenda to Wyoming. They cut budgets and passed bills aligned with their conservative views. They sought to reform education, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. They also constantly attacked the state's rare Democrats, and what they call RINOs (Republicans in Name Only): traditional, old-school Republicans whom they accuse of betraying the party's values.
In the meantime, the more traditional forces within the Republican establishment got organised to take their party back. During the campaign, political action committees spent millions trying to sway Wyoming's 580,000 residents. The state is a perfect target with a very small, already conservative population and two US Senate seats in Washington – just as many as California or Texas.
This report goes inside the battle within the Republican Party between the ultra-conservative bloc and the more moderate traditionalists. It also explores a paradox: Wyomingites are turning on Trump, but will carry on voting Republican – no matter what.

- Scotland already benefits from over £2 billion a year in MoD spending, which supports more than 12,000 jobs.
Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander today welcomed the Scottish Government’s decision to match fund the UK Government’s £10 commitment to create two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges (DTECs) in Scotland, as part of a £50 million Scottish Defence Growth Deal.
The DTECs will help provide young people with new specialist pathways into high-skilled, well-paid careers in defence engineering, advanced manufacturing and maritime technology are coming to Scotland.
The colleges will be located to support Scotland’s defence clusters in the East and West of the country and will benefit from the engineering and innovation centres previously announced as part of the Scottish Defence Growth Deal.

  In March we announced a £10 million commitment to develop two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges in Scotland. I’m pleased that the Scottish Government has now agreed to match fund these colleges to give our young people the skills they need to secure high-skilled, well-paid careers in Scotland’s defence sector in the years to come.
  Scotland is a defence industrial powerhouse and is already benefiting from increased UK Government investment as we deliver a defence dividend for Scotland, creating new skilled jobs, new training places and new opportunities for communities while keeping us and our allies secure. It is crucial that we continue to develop the skilled workforce needed to support this growing sector.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard MP said:
  Finally matching DTEC funding is welcome news for Scottish careers. The colleges will provide routes into high-skilled, well-paid roles in the defence sector which is crucial to the work of keeping the UK safe around the clock.
This is an important part of our £50 million Defence Growth Deal - announced back in March - to boost growth opportunities for Scotland that supports our Armed Forces.
Industry analysis suggests there could be demand for up to 50,000 additional defence jobs across the UK by 2034/35.

The Scottish Secretary launched the UK Government’s Defence Growth Deal on 12 March, committing £10 million towards the creation of two DTECs — one in the East and one in the West of Scotland — as part of a wider £50 million deal.

Limburg named the world’s “most intelligent region”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Limburg named the world’s “most intelligent region”
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Limburg has been named the world’s smartest region by the US-based think tank Intelligent Community Forum (ICF). The southern province, known for its hills and regional dialects, beat finalists from countries like Taiwan and Canada.
The award was presented to Brightlands, a network of four business and research campuses in the province that focus on health, AI, sustainable chemistry and food research. The ICF, a federation of 200 cities and regions, ranks areas around the globe each year on factors like economic and social development.
The jury praised the cooperation between government, business and research institutions at the campuses, as well as the way Limburg rebuilt itself after its coal mines closed half a century ago. After natural gas was discovered in 1959, “the region lost not only jobs but also security and hope,” ICF founder Robert Bell said.
Brightlands was set up in 2014 by the provincial government, education institutions and local businesses, according to L1 Nieuws.
The Maastricht campus focuses on health and is linked to the university hospital, while Heerlen, home to pension fund ABP and the national statistics office CBS, specialises in data and AI.
The materials campus is on the Chemelot chemical site in Sittard-Geleen, and Venlo’s food campus uses infrastructure left over from the 2012 Floriade horticultural expo.
Limburg beat six other finalists, from Brazil, Turkey, the US, Canada, Spain and Taiwan. Last year’s winner was Durham Region in Canada. The Brainport region around Eindhoven won in 2011.

Trump’s Betrayal of Ukraine and the Free World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

When Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky addresses the international community, he speaks for a nation fighting for its sovereign existence on the active front line of European democracy, holding back Russian anti-Western imperial ambitions.
Whatever his domestic shortcomings may be, his leadership and diplomacy during a wartime state of siege are backed by the courage of a people refusing foreign authoritarian subjugation with its genocidal traits.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But what he encounters from US President Donald Trump and his political entourage is not strategic solidarity but transactional disdain – an impulse to treat Ukraine’s survival as a disposable bargaining chip both abroad and in American domestic politics.
While continuing to ingratiate himself with authoritarian Russian war criminal Vladimir Putin, Trump has gone so far as to call for Zelensky’s removal.
This posture is far more dangerous than ordinary campaign rhetoric, or crude lack of diplomacy. It signals a retreat from the post-1945 rules-based international order, an implicit repudiation of NATO, and an open invitation to revanchist powers to redraw sovereign borders by force.
Trump’s antagonism toward Kyiv is neither accidental nor isolated; it is the cornerstone of a transactional worldview that views democratic alliances with contempt, authoritarian leaders with deference, and Zelensky and his country as an insubordinate nuisance.
Ukrainian Composer’s Opera on Abducted Children Premieres in Warsaw
Trump’s recurring threats to halt military assistance and force Kyiv into an immediate, lopsided settlement with Vladimir Putin reflect an instinct to accommodate Moscow while abandoning a democratic partner under fire.
For a political figure who frequently presents himself as a master dealmaker, demanding that the victim of aggression concede territory and sovereignty looks less like shrewd negotiation than preemptive surrender for reasons that are still unclear but suspect.
His isolationist claim that supporting Ukraine is a peripheral distraction from core American interests rests on a profound strategic error. Ukraine is not asking for foreign troops; its forces are actively degrading the conventional military capability of Moscow –historically, and today even more so, the primary security threat to Europe.
Abandoning Ukraine would shatter Western deterrence worldwide. Authoritarian regimes in Beijing, Tehran, and Pyongyang are closely watching Washington’s resolve. If the United States forces Kyiv into capitulation, it will demonstrate to China that Western democratic stamina is fleeting – drastically increasing the risk of an invasion or blockade of Taiwan, a crisis that would inevitably threaten global trade and risk pulling American forces into a Pacific war.
In Europe, a Russian victory would place Moscow’s forces directly along the borders of Poland, Romania, Moldova, and the Baltic states, elevating the risk of a miscalculation that could trigger NATO’s Article 5 and require direct American military intervention.
Moreover, and what is often overlooked, the economic reality of security assistance contradicts populist talking points: most allocated funds remain in the United States, expanding domestic manufacturing capacity and replacing aging military stockpiles with modern systems.
Trump’s record demonstrates that this hostility toward Ukraine is part of an established global pattern: accommodating authoritarian adversaries while antagonizing historic partners.
While autocrats in Pyongyang, Moscow, and Beijing have enjoyed personal deference, democratic allies face continual coercion. Trump has repeatedly subjected Canada, the European Union, and NATO members to punitive tariffs and questioned collective defense arrangements.
This is not hard-nosed negotiation; it is the strategic unraveling of the Western alliance. When foreign policy is reduced to personal leverage and real-estate transactionalism, strategic alliances cease to be treated as enduring commitments.
This transactional approach to statecraft cannot be separated from the continuous political spectacle used to deflect scrutiny from unresolved ethical and legal questions at home.
Let’s be clear. Trump is calling for Zelensky’s replacement while Russia intensifies its drone and missile attacks on Ukraine. After almost five years of all-out war against Ukraine, Russia has failed to break the spirit and resistance of its indomitable people. Now the current US president is colluding with Putin even more brazenly than before in calling for Kyiv’s de facto capitulation.
Could anyone have imagined Washington pursuing such a nefarious policy and siding – as it has been doing under Trump, Rubio, Vance, Hegseth, and co. – with anti-democratic countries in the UN and elsewhere?
But fortunately, this abysmal situation may not continue indefinitely.
Ukraine’s faith in the American project rests not in single political figures but in the institutional resilience and moral clarity of its people – and in the principles of liberty, national sovereignty, and the rule of law deeply woven into the American identity.
As key electoral tests approach, the world looks to the American citizenry to reaffirm that the United States remains a beacon of freedom, rather than an accomplice to autocracy.
The democratic world cannot accept betrayal as the new norm. For the West, the choice is stark: stand firm with those defending democracy today or prepare to pay a vastly higher price tomorrow. The US appears to be signaling that it may have already chosen not to remain with its allies, that it has become something else.
Meanwhile, left with the stark choice, or rather, ultimatum, of “to be, or not to be,” Ukraine will continue to fight for its existence, with or without those who turn their backs.
Fundamental change should begin in Washington, not Kyiv.

USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:46:50 UTC
21:46:50 KST

USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
Scientists have created a potentially renewable source of engineered immune cells that fight cancer, offering a promising path toward longer-lasting, ready-made immunotherapies.
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- Keck School of Medicine of USC
- Summary:
- USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.
- Share:
Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.
The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.
The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.
"The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.
Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors
Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.
Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.
Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.
The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.
"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."
This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.
Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer
Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.
They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.
One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.
Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.
Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.
Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.
To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.
Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells
Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.
The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.
Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.
This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.
To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.
Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."
Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors
The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.
They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.
CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.
The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.
The added signal offered another potentially important advantage. It remained effective even when the immune characteristics of donor cells did not match those of the recipient.
That finding raises the possibility of developing off-the-shelf treatments using cells manufactured in advance from donors. Unlike personalized cell therapies, which must be prepared separately using each patient's own cells, such products could potentially be produced in larger batches and made available to multiple patients.
Engineered Cells Slow Cancer Progression in Mice
After successfully expanding and engineering GMPs from both mice and humans, the researchers investigated their therapeutic potential in mouse experiments.
When administered to mice, the progenitor cells established themselves in the bone marrow and other locations responsible for blood cell production. These environments provided places where the GMPs could generate additional engineered macrophages and related immune cells.
This was an important difference from treatments using mature macrophages. Instead of relying solely on immune cells that may disappear relatively quickly, the progenitors could provide a continuing source of replacement cells from within the body.
The strategy may therefore help overcome the rapid clearance that has limited macrophage therapies, including approaches evaluated in recent clinical trials.
The researchers tested the engineered cells in mice with blood cancers and solid tumors. GMPs carrying CAR receptors slowed disease progression in both types of cancer.
The effects were even stronger when the progenitors carried both CAR receptors and the additional signal designed to activate other immune cells. This combination improved the treatment's ability to stimulate a broader antitumor response.
Although these findings are encouraging, the cancer-treatment results remain preclinical. Further research will be needed to establish whether engineered GMPs can be used safely and effectively in people, particularly if they are intended to persist and produce immune cells over extended periods.
Potential Applications Beyond Cancer Treatment
The scientists also explored whether their approach could help treat conditions involving defective immune defenses.
In a separate mouse experiment, they studied chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder that interferes with the ability of certain immune cells to kill harmful microbes. People with this condition are particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because their immune cells cannot eliminate some pathogens effectively.
When the researchers administered GMPs to mice with the disorder, the cells restored the animals' ability to fight bacterial infection.
This result suggests that renewable, genetically engineered immune cell progenitors might eventually have applications beyond cancer, including treatments for inherited immune deficiencies and potentially infectious diseases.
The broader lesson, according to the researchers, is that the developmental stage of an immune cell may be just as important as the genetic modifications used to turn it into a treatment.
By engineering cells before they fully mature, scientists may be able to create therapies that are easier to manufacture, more adaptable, and capable of maintaining a continuing supply of specialized immune defenders.
"Our study suggests that the future of immunotherapy may depend not only on designing better CAR receptors, but also on choosing the right developmental stage of the cell," said Ying.
About the Research
The study, published in Cell, is titled "Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy."
Along with Ying, Yue, and Majeti, the research team included Zheng Guo, Crystal Pan, Xueyuan A. Jing, Tai Nguyen, Jiaqi Tang, Yanpui Chan, Humberto Contreras-Trujillo, Du Jiang, Xue Yan, Hang Xiang, Xugeng Liu, Xiao Wang, Ziyuan Wang, Natalie Shu, Daniel B. McKim, Rong Lu, and Chao Zhang of USC; Litao Tao and Celia Bloom of Creighton University; Asiri Ediriwickrema and Sebastian Koschade of Stanford University School of Medicine; and Yingxiao Shi of Harvard Medical School and the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute.
Financial support came from the Chen Yong Foundation of the Zhongmei Group, a sponsored research project from Myelogene Inc., the L.K. Whittier Foundation, the Eli and Edythe Broad Innovation Award, the Ming Hsieh Institute for Research on Engineering Medicine for Cancer Award, the USC SBIR/STTR Planning Award, the Xia Research Fund, and the Wu & Jiang Research Fund.
Majeti also reported support from the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research. Guo received funding through the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine Predoctoral Training Fellowship.

Top German court orders Cabinet minister to delete video accusing Left Party of antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:44:36 UTC
21:44:36 KST

Ayhan Simsek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Germany’s top court has ordered Economy Minister Katherina Reiche to remove an Instagram video from her ministry’s official account in which she accused the Left Party of openly embracing antisemitism.
The Federal Constitutional Court said in an interim order published on Thursday that sharing such claims from an official government account may violate the socialist Left Party’s right to equal participation in political competition.
“This is particularly relevant given the ongoing discussions regarding the formation of a government in the city-state of Berlin,” the court said, referring to exploratory talks after the Left Party’s election victory in the German capital on Sept. 20.
“The continued circulation of the statements in question is capable of severely discrediting the applicant in the public eye. This could also make it more difficult for potential coalition partners to enter into a coalition agreement with it,” the court said.
“Consequently, political realities could be created that extend far beyond the negative characterizations directed at the applicant,” it added.
 
Video to remain offline until final decision
The judges ruled 6-2 that the video must remain offline until a final decision on the Left Party’s complaint, for no longer than six months.
The court did not rule on whether Reiche’s remarks were unconstitutional and stressed that she remains free to express her views on the topic as a politician or as a private citizen.
The Left Party took the case to the Karlsruhe-based court after the ministry refused its demand to delete the video by Sept. 29, arguing that a federal ministry must not use state resources and official authority to campaign against a political party.
Reiche, a conservative politician from Chancellor Merz’s center-right CDU, argued through her lawyers that the remarks were constitutionally sound and did not violate the government’s duty of political neutrality.
In the clip, posted on Sept. 24 and taken from a speech she gave a day earlier at a business event, Reiche warned against a possible Berlin government involving the Left Party, criticizing its long-standing plans to expropriate large private housing companies as a response to soaring rents.
She also attacked it as a party “that openly embraces antisemitism, that makes Jews in this city afraid.”

How Probate Timelines Differ Between Countries and What Families Should Know  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:44:29 UTC
21:44:29 KST

Six weeks in one country. Three years in another. Same estate value, same number of heirs, wildly different outcomes. The gap is not luck, and it is not the lawyer.
Probate moves at the speed of the local court system, and court systems are built on very different assumptions. Get a handle on which assumption applies to your situation and the whole process gets easier to plan for. Money stops sitting in limbo. Siblings stop calling you every week asking why nothing has happened.
Most estates clear the system without a fight, but the ones that stall usually stall for predictable reasons. If you are navigating a Florida estate right now, working with an experienced probate lawyer davie residents can count on keeps the local filings on schedule while you sort out anything happening abroad.
What Actually Drives the Clock
Three things decide how long an estate sits open: whether there is a will, whether anyone contests it, and how much the government wants to review before it lets assets move. That last one varies enormously.
In the United States, probate is a state court function, so the timeline you get in one state tells you almost nothing about another. Some states run simplified procedures for smaller estates that take weeks. Others have a mandatory creditor claim window that alone can stretch past six months, and nothing in the system lets you shorten it. The Florida Courts system publishes its own guidance on how estate administration is handled within the state, and it is worth reading before you assume a timeline you heard from a friend in a different state applies to you.
Here is what almost nobody explains up front. The clock rarely starts when your loved one dies. It starts when the executor formally opens the case, and that can be weeks later if the family is still searching for documents or waiting on a death certificate. Everything after that is measured from a date the family controls.
Translation? Get organized early. Not later.
Why Some Countries Take Years
Civil law countries, including Germany, France, and much of Southern Europe, handle succession quite differently from the common law tradition in the US, the UK, and Australia. In several European systems, heirs may need formal notarized acceptance of the estate before assets transfer, and that paperwork can crawl through notary offices with heavy backlogs.
The European Union has worked to simplify cross-border succession through its Succession Regulation, which lets families designate a single applicable law for an estate spanning multiple member states. Streamlined on paper. Slow in practice, because notaries in different countries still coordinate on their own schedules.
I have watched a family wait eighteen months for a notary appointment in one member state while a sibling in another country had already filed taxes on their share. That is not a failure of the system. That is the system working exactly as designed, just slowly. If you have relatives in multiple countries, assume the slowest jurisdiction sets your real timeline, and plan your cash flow around that.
Small Estate Shortcuts Worth Knowing
Many jurisdictions offer a fast lane for smaller estates, and too many families never ask about it. In Florida, for example, an estate may qualify for summary administration when the non-exempt assets fall under a set threshold or when enough time has passed since the death. Do not assume the threshold mentioned in one conversation applies to you. Ask directly and confirm the current number.
Questions to ask an attorney before you assume you are stuck in full formal probate:
- Do the non-exempt assets fall below the local small estate threshold?
- Has enough time passed since the date of death to qualify for a shortened process?
- Are any assets held in a trust or with a named beneficiary, and do those skip probate entirely?
- Are there out-of-state properties that would need a separate ancillary filing?
- What is the mandatory creditor claim window in this jurisdiction, and is it waivable?
That fourth question trips up a lot of people. A vacation cabin or a rental property in another state is not covered by the primary probate case. It needs its own filing, in its own court, under its own rules. Families discover this months in, right when they thought they were almost done.
The Cross-Border Scenario Nobody Plans For
Consider a family in Davie with a parent who owned a condo in Florida and an apartment in São Paulo. Two estates, two legal systems, two sets of heirs who may not share the same assumptions about who gets what. If a will exists but was drafted abroad, a local court may need to determine whether it is valid under the laws of the state where it is being submitted. That determination alone can take months.
The practical move is to treat each jurisdiction separately from day one. Line up a professional in each place rather than asking one attorney to handle everything. Coordinate on the sequence, not on the paperwork, because the forms do not translate. Getting an estate valuation done for the foreign property early saves you from redoing it later when the market has moved.
What This Means for Your Planning
If probate is already open, your job is simple: keep answering the attorney, keep providing documents, and stay ahead of deadlines. The estate does not close any faster because you sent a frustrated email. It closes faster when nothing sits on your desk.
If you are still in the planning stage, this is where a conversation pays for itself. Estate values shift, tax rules change, and a will drafted a decade ago in a different country may not reflect what you want today. According to the World Bank, sound legal and judicial institutions are a foundational part of how economies function, which is a formal way of saying: the courts matter, and they behave differently everywhere.
Here is the part I would push back on if a client insisted otherwise. Everyone wants the cheapest option, and in a single-jurisdiction estate with a straightforward will, the cheap option is often fine. Cross a border, though, and the money you save up front rarely survives the first delay. I have watched a family try to handle two countries with one attorney and spend more on rework than they would have spent on both professionals combined.
What to Do in the First Two Weeks
1. Order at least ten certified copies of the death certificate. You will run out of the first six, guaranteed.
2. Locate every will, and find out whether the original exists or only a copy. Courts care about the difference.
3. List every asset by location, not just by value. The location drives which process you need.
4. Identify the named beneficiaries and confirm whether any accounts have designated beneficiaries, since those skip probate.
5. Confirm the small estate threshold in each relevant jurisdiction and ask whether you qualify.
Skip step three and you will discover a second filing at the worst possible moment. I have seen it happen twice in one year. Neither family was careless. They just assumed everything sat in one state because their parent only ever mentioned one address.
The Bottom Line
Speed in probate is not a measure of how good the estate plan was. It is a measure of how well you understood the rules before you started. A well-prepared family can move through a slow jurisdiction faster than an unprepared family moves through a fast one, and the difference shows up in weeks, not days.
So here is the question worth sitting with: if your estate landed in court tomorrow, would your family know which jurisdictions are involved, which documents matter, and who to call first? If the answer is no, you already know what to do this month.

Why Commercial Buildings Lose Heat on the Coldest Nights  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:44:26 UTC
21:44:26 KST

The building didn't fail in January. It failed in the ten months before January, a fraction of a degree at a time. Nobody filed a work order because nobody felt anything yet. That's the pattern I've watched play out in warehouses, restaurants, and small office parks along Lake Erie's snowbelt. Heat loss in commercial spaces is almost never a single dramatic breakdown. It's slow drift: a heat exchanger sooting up, burners running a little rich, a vent damper stuck half open, and a filter rack that hasn't been touched since the last tenant moved out. You don't notice a 4 percent drop in output. You notice the Monday after Christmas, when the building hasn't held 65 degrees and your whole crew is standing around in coats.
Here's what actually happens in that moment, and this is where owners get taken advantage of. Somebody calls the first number that answers and asks for prompt commercial furnace repair, and a truck shows up with a guy who knows rooftop units but has never touched a 40-year-old boiler. He replaces a $200 part. The heat comes back. Three weeks later it's out again, and now you've paid twice for one diagnosis. If you get a sense the tech on your roof is guessing, ask them to walk you through the combustion readings before they touch the gas valve. Any professional will. A parts-swapper won't. So why does heat choose the worst possible week to quit? Physics and scheduling, mostly. Here's the trifecta.
Load, Pressure, and the Calendar Stack Against You
When the outdoor temperature sits in the teens, your heating unit is running close to 100 percent of its rated capacity for hours. There's no headroom left. Any small deficiency that stayed invisible at 40 degrees, like a partially clogged burner orifice, becomes a real problem at 12 degrees. You can see how outdoor conditions drive building loads in the basics laid out by the Department of Energy. I'd read the load material before I'd read anything a vendor hands me.
The second factor is pressure. Commercial buildings pull air in and out constantly. Kitchens exhaust enormous volumes. Bathroom fans, dock doors, and lobby entrances all fight for make-up air. That imbalance can pull combustion gases back down a flue or starve a unit of the air it needs to burn cleanly. Then the pressure safety switch trips, and your furnace shuts down on its own. That's not a furnace that broke. That's a building that stopped being a closed system. If your unit keeps locking out without a clear reason, ask about building pressure before anybody replaces the control board.
The calendar part is simpler and more painful. Every commercial property manager schedules fall maintenance in the same six-week window, then trusts it for the rest of the winter. New tenants move in during November, a wall gets cut for a new network closet, a dock shelter tears and never gets patched. Your building changed. Your heating load changed with it. Your service contract didn't.
What Healthier Buildings Do Differently
The facilities I've seen go through a serious cold snap without a crisis aren't the ones with the newest equipment. They're the ones with a short, unglamorous inspection habit and a clear escalation path. The U.S. General Services Administration is worth a read if you want an institutional benchmark for how high-performing facilities approach operations and tenant comfort. It's public, and it's free of a sales angle.
Start with a two-part triage. First, decide whether you have a building problem or a unit problem. Cold complaints clustered in one zone with everything else fine means a unit. Complaints spread across zones, or a whole floor that won't hold temperature, means a building problem, and you'll waste money chasing the equipment.
Second, get hard numbers before you authorize anything. Ask for combustion analysis, temperature rise across the heat exchanger, and static pressure. Those three readings tell a competent tech almost everything about whether a unit is underperforming or just undersized.
Two small things you can check today without a ladder: whether last winter's roof unit filters were actually changed on the schedule someone wrote down, and whether every exterior door you own still closes on its own.
A Framework I Actually Use: The Four-Leaf Diagnostic
I built this after watching too many owners pay for the same repair twice. Picture four leaves, and you only get to fall back on a service call when you've checked all four.
Leaf 1, Thermal: Is the unit producing heat at all, and is that heat reaching the spaces that need it? This is where airflow, duct leakage, and zoning get tested.
Leaf 2, Fuel: Is the burn clean, and is the supply pressure right? Soot on a heat exchanger is a symptom, not a problem to wipe off.
Leaf 3, Safety: Is every interlock, roll-out switch, and pressure switch doing what it was built to do, and is the flame proving properly? You never bypass these for a quick fix, no matter what a tenant says.
Leaf 4, Environment: What's the building doing to the equipment? Negative pressure, dirty make-up air, and unbalanced exhaust all belong here.
Most failures I've seen land in Leaf 1 or Leaf 4, and both are cheap to fix once you know where the problem lives. My honest take: if a technician can't tell you which leaf the problem sits on before they start talking about parts, get a different technician.
How to Pick a Vendor Before the Crisis Hits
Do this in October, not at 2 a.m. Nobody answers the phone well when the pipes are already cold.
- Ask for the names of two commercial accounts they service in your building class, and call them without warning.
- Request a written diagnosis before work starts, not a verbal estimate.
- Confirm their techs are trained and certified on the specific brand on your roof, not just heating in general.
- Check whether they carry the parts that fail most on your equipment, or whether you'll wait four days to order them.
- Ask who answers at night, and whether that person can authorize the repair.
I'd add one more that most owners skip: ask whether they test the building or just the box. A vendor who only looks at the furnace will fix it, and you'll call them back next winter. A vendor who reads static pressure and building balance will tell you the furnace was never the whole story.
Diagnostics Should Follow a Standard, Not a Gut Feeling
If you want to know whether the work is being done to a real benchmark, look at what the National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes on building performance and measurement. You don't need to read a technical report to get value from it. You need to know that measurement standards exist, so you can ask whether your vendor is using one or just going by feel.
A vendor who can point to a method is easier to hold accountable than one who says "we just know." That's not a small difference when you're the person signing the invoice.
Before You Sign Anything This Winter
Commercial heat failures trace back to drift, and drift is invisible until the temperature drops. Keep a simple log of what your building's heating load looks like in shoulder seasons, so you know when something changed. Check pressure balance annually, especially after a tenant build-out. And when a unit does go down, get the diagnosis in writing before you approve a repair.
The next cold snap is already on the calendar. What's the one reading you don't have yet on your building, and who would you trust to walk you through it without selling you something you don't need?

TALLINN - Led by Telia Estonia, partners of the 5G-BALTICS project from the three Baltic states convened in Tallinn to review the progress of establishing 5G infrastructure along the Via Baltica transport corridor and to plan the next phases.
Following an extensive planning and preparation phase, the project in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania is now entering the practical implementation stage, with construction work already underway in several regions.
The project aims to provide uninterrupted 5G coverage along the entire 663-kilometer Via Baltica transport corridor, from Tallinn to the Lithuanian-Polish border. The establishment of this unified digital corridor will enhance cross-border digital connectivity and network reliability among the three Baltic states, pave the way for new digital services, and support regional economic development.

In Estonia, construction of the fiber-optic network and 5G masts has commenced in multiple locations. Concurrently, preparations are underway for the deployment of active 5G network equipment.
In Lithuania, work is ongoing to achieve the project's two primary infrastructure objectives: building communication masts with the required electrical connections and rolling out the fiber-optic communication network.
Once construction and setup are complete, the project will move into its next crucial phase: the practical testing of the 5G network, currently scheduled for 2027.
During the testing phase, project partners will evaluate the network's performance, connection stability, and service quality across the entire transport corridor, with a special focus on cross-border areas. The tests will include assessing the network's performance with everyday digital services, such as music and video streaming, participating in online meetings, using navigation apps, and playing online games.
5G-BALTICS (uninterrupted 5G coverage across the entire Via Baltica corridor) is a Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) project aimed at establishing seamless 5G coverage along the Via Baltica transport corridor in Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. The project (No. 101181148) is implemented with the support of the European Union (EU).

Best UK Websites for Finding Local Services  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
