British food and drink exports to EU collapse by more than a third since Brexit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:34:37 UTC
21:34:37 KST

Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit with eggs, chicken and potato producers badly hit, new figures show.
Analysis by the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) of HMRC data shows a sharp fall in exports in the year to July compared with the same period in 2019, with sugar dropping the most, down 70%.
Data for the first seven months also shows poultry exports fell 53%, with eggs and egg products sold for confectionary and baking industries down 65% for the same period.
Full-year data from 2019 to 2025 showed an even deeper impact since Brexit with exports of eggs and egg products down 74%.
The NFU president, Tom Bradshaw, said: “The EU is our largest trading partner for agri-food products, accounting for 68% of agri-food exports last year, but trade volumes have fallen over a third since 2019.”
Boris Johnson’s government signed a deal on the UK’s future trading and security relationship with the EU in late 2020, after the UK’s formal exit earlier that year.
Andy Burnham is reconsidering Labour’s red lines on EU membership under pressure to repair the economic damage of Brexit. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far.
Food exporters have long complained over the added paperwork that Britain’s exit has brought. Since Brexit all food exports are required to have customs paperwork with different codes for every single product. This includes, for example, every variation of an egg product, whether it is fresh, dried, steamed, shelled, or contains added water or sugar. The paper pulp used in egg cartons as well as the eggs also need health certification to show they are free of disease.
Also hit hard by Brexit is the horticultural sector with seed potatoes from Britain, mainly Scotland, banned from the EU after trade negotiators failed to agree on equivalent standards in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement in 2020. Horticultural exports fell more than 50%.
Pre-Brexit, Scotland exported around 20,000 tonnes of seed potatoes, worth almost £11m, to Europe each year.
Speaking in parliament earlier this week Andy Burnham said that Brexit trade barriers meant “entire truckloads of plants or fresh product can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or minor paperwork delay”.
He hoped to “land a positive outcome” in the upcoming UK-EU reset talks with a new agreement removing many of the sanitary and phytosanitary checks on fresh farm produce exports that came in after Brexit.
Burnham told MPs: “Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports.
“British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage.”
A deal to ease sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) checks was largely agreed in May giving food producers time to prepare for changes expected to come in next summer, but key details remain to be finalised.
The NFU is calling for “transition arrangements” for some UK crops that have been grown with fungicides or breeding techniques not yet approved in the EU.
This is to allow those harvesting this autumn and winter to make use of the new export freedoms when they come in next year.
Bradshaw said: “British farmers and growers must retain access to precision breeding technologies that will help to strengthen food resilience to extreme weather and to science-based plant protection products that help protect food being grown for 29m households from pests and diseases.
“Any changes must also provide an appropriate transition period to minimise disruption for farm businesses and we will continue to make this case to government while we await the final agreement.”

5 ways to make Halloween decorations friendlier to wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:33:03 UTC
21:33:03 KST

Recently, a slender, yellow-striped California whipsnake, small enough to fit in a person’s hand, was brought to the California Wildlife Center in Calabasas. Its lower body was so twisted in fine strands of fake spiderwebs that it was essentially a ball, with twigs and leaves stuck in the mess.
“Had that gone on much longer, it could have started severing into its skin,” says Lauren Michaels, director of animal care at the center. Fortunately, the snake recovered and was eventually released. Not every animal is so lucky, though. Cambria Wells, the center’s education and outreach manager, recalls a hummingbird that was similarly wrapped in webbing and didn’t make it.
Every Halloween season, wildlife rehabilitation centers across the country see cases in which birds, bats, snakes, rodents, deer and other wild animals become injured or entangled in seasonal decorations.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The good news is that you can have a spooky spectacle in front of your house and still protect wildlife. Here are five ways to make your Halloween display friendlier to the creatures that fly, slither and scurry through your yard.
Skip stretchy fake spiderwebs
Of all the Halloween decorations people display outdoors, synthetic spiderwebs are the most dangerous, according to many wildlife experts. Made of strong, stretchy plastic, the webbing’s thin, hard-to-see strands can cling to animals and become wrapped around their bodies, posing a serious entanglement hazard. Trapped animals can go hungry, suffer constriction injuries, or even dislocate their limbs as they struggle to free themselves, Wells explains.
To get the spiderweb look without the stretchy strands, the best option is a solid web decoration made from rigid plastic or metal, she advises. Rope-style webs are safer than stretchy spiderwebbing, but they can still pose an entanglement risk.
If you do use stretchy or rope webbing outdoors, Wells recommends pulling it taut against a solid surface, such as your house, rather than across an open space where an animal could fly or travel through it.
Stick with solid decorations
The same principle applies to other decorations. Choose solid objects over anything with netting, strings, ropes, ribbons or other materials in which an animal could become entangled. Think tombstones, solid skeletons, signs or other decorations that hold their shape and don’t have loose or dangling parts.
Popular inflatables can be a safer alternative to netting or webbing, but you should make sure their anchoring cords and power cords are secured and check regularly for damage.
In general, look for durable decorations you can reuse year after year rather than items that are designed to be thrown away after a single season to reduce the broader environmental impact of your Halloween display, Wells notes.
Turn Halloween lights off when you go to bed
“Lighting is an underappreciated form of impact on wildlife,” Wells says. Artificial light can interfere with wildlife behavior and disorient migrating birds, many of which travel during the middle of the night and the early morning at this time of year, she explains.
If you want lights as part of your decor, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommends opting for ones with warmer colors, such as amber, orange or red, rather than blue, white or other cooler-colored lights, whose shorter wavelengths are more disruptive to biological rhythms.
But regardless of the type of lights you use, the simplest and most effective step, Wells says, is to turn them off when you go to bed, giving wildlife darkness during the overnight hours.
Deck your windows
Window decals, creepy figures, glowing jack-o’-lanterns and other decorations displayed on or just inside your windows can still be seen from the street without introducing loose materials into your yard that wildlife could encounter.
Decorate with natural materials
Pumpkins are a Halloween staple, but you should remember that they’re also food. If you want to keep wildlife from chowing down on your carefully carved jack-o’-lantern without harming any creatures, Wells says, try bringing it in in the evening or coating it with a bitter apple spray or cayenne pepper diluted with water.
When spooky season is over, you can then compost your pumpkins or dispose of them according to your local food- or yard-waste guidelines. You can also check whether a local wildlife center or animal sanctuary accepts intact, untreated pumpkins for animal feed.
Other natural materials, such as gourds, hay, and cornstalks make for festive decor, but Wells suggests choosing materials from your local area to reduce the risk of introducing invasive plants or seeds.
If you find an entangled animal, call for help
If you discover an animal caught in or injured by Halloween decorations, resist the urge to untangle and release it. Injuries may not be obvious at first, and the animal may need medical care.
Instead contact a local wildlife rehabilitation center for guidance. You can find nearby resources through Animal Help Now.

The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germany’s nuclear failure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:32:52 UTC
21:32:52 KST

The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germany’s nuclear failure
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- PNAS Nexus
- Summary:
- Scientists investigating Nazi Germany's secret nuclear program have uncovered evidence that its final experimental reactor was nowhere near as close to working as previously claimed. Analysis of surviving uranium cubes and wartime documents reveals that Germany lacked the enormous quantities of uranium and heavy water needed to make its reactor operational.
- Share:
During World War II, the United States raced to develop the atomic bomb partly out of fear that Nazi Germany might build one first. But how close did Germany actually come to achieving that goal? A new scientific investigation suggests the Nazi nuclear program was much further from success than its leading physicist claimed.
By examining surviving uranium cubes and previously documented historical evidence, researchers have uncovered major limitations in Germany's final experimental nuclear reactor. Their findings indicate that the project was not simply missing a few materials. The reactor would have required far more uranium and heavy water than Germany had available during the war.
The Race to Build an Atomic Bomb
The Manhattan Project, the secret American effort to develop nuclear weapons during World War II, was driven partly by the possibility that Nazi Germany might achieve a similar breakthrough first. Scientists knew that whoever succeeded could gain an unprecedented military advantage.
One possible route to an atomic bomb involved building a nuclear reactor capable of producing plutonium, a radioactive element that can be used in nuclear weapons. Inside a reactor, uranium atoms undergo nuclear fission, a process in which their nuclei split apart and release energy along with additional particles called neutrons. Under the right conditions, those neutrons trigger further fission reactions, creating a sustained chain reaction.
Although Nazi Germany pursued nuclear research through a program known as the Uranprojekt, historians have long debated how close its scientists came to developing a functioning reactor.
Germany's final attempt was an experimental reactor known as the B8 pile, constructed in 1945 under the direction of physicist Werner Heisenberg. The device used cubes of natural uranium suspended in heavy water, a specialized substance that played an essential role in controlling the nuclear reaction.
Why Heavy Water Was Essential to Nazi Germany's Reactor
Heavy water looks much like ordinary water, but its hydrogen atoms contain an additional neutron. This subtle difference makes it particularly useful in certain nuclear reactors.
In a reactor, heavy water serves as a neutron moderator, meaning it slows down the neutrons released during fission. Slower neutrons are more likely to trigger additional fission reactions in uranium, helping sustain the chain reaction needed for a working reactor.
For Germany, however, obtaining enough heavy water was a major obstacle.
During the war, the only European facility capable of supplying the heavy water needed by the German program was the Norsk Hydro plant in Vemork, Norway. Germany gained control of the facility after occupying Norway in April 1940.
Recognizing its importance to Germany's nuclear ambitions, Allied forces targeted the plant through sabotage and bombing operations. A major American bombing raid struck Vemork on November 16, 1943, contributing to the eventual end of heavy water production there.
Scientists Reexamine Hitler's Final Nuclear Reactor
When American forces discovered and dismantled the B8 reactor in 1945, it had never achieved criticality. In nuclear physics, criticality refers to the point at which a chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, with each generation of fission reactions producing enough neutrons to maintain the next.
Reaching this threshold is a fundamental requirement for operating a conventional nuclear reactor. Despite its name, criticality does not mean that a reactor is about to explode. It simply means the nuclear chain reaction can continue without relying on an external neutron source.
Heisenberg, who led the German reactor effort, maintained that the B8 experiment had come close to reaching this milestone. He argued that the device needed only a relatively modest increase in its uranium supply to become operational.
But a new study led by Timothy Koeth and his colleagues challenges that assessment.
The researchers examined two surviving cubes of natural uranium that had been used in the German nuclear project. They also studied historical records, technical reports, correspondence, and other archival documents to reconstruct the reactor's capabilities and determine what would have been required for it to work.
Their findings paint a very different picture of Germany's nuclear progress.
A Massive Uranium and Heavy Water Shortage
According to the researchers' calculations, the B8 reactor would have needed approximately twice as much uranium and more than twice as much heavy water as it actually contained to achieve a sustained nuclear chain reaction.
The required quantities exceeded the materials available to Germany during the war. In particular, the heavy water needed for a functioning reactor was far beyond the amount the German program could obtain from its Norwegian supply.
The researchers also examined whether German scientists could have avoided the heavy water shortage by using graphite, a form of carbon that can also slow neutrons in nuclear reactors.
This approach had worked for American scientists, who achieved the world's first controlled, sustained nuclear chain reaction using a graphite-moderated reactor in 1942.
However, the graphite available in German-controlled territory contained impurities that made it unsuitable for the same purpose. In particular, traces of boron could absorb neutrons that would otherwise help sustain the reaction, preventing the reactor from reaching criticality.
That meant Germany could not simply substitute graphite for heavy water to overcome its supply problems.
Why Nazi Germany's Nuclear Program Was Doomed
The findings suggest that Heisenberg significantly underestimated how much additional material his reactor would have required.
Rather than standing on the verge of a functioning nuclear reactor, the German scientists faced shortages they could not overcome with the resources available to them.
The research also provides a clearer explanation for why Germany's nuclear program failed to make the transition from experimental reactor designs to a working reactor capable of producing material for an atomic bomb.
Based on the designs and materials available during World War II, the researchers conclude that Nazi Germany lacked the resources necessary to make either its heavy water reactor or a graphite-based alternative operational.
More than eight decades after the war, the surviving uranium cubes have helped resolve a longstanding historical question, revealing just how far Nazi Germany remained from achieving a critical step toward building an atomic bomb.
Story Source:
Materials provided by PNAS Nexus. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Patrick J Park, Brittany Robertson, Miriam E Hiebert, Jason Zhao, Ciara B Sivels, Timothy W Koeth. Nuclear archaeology reassesses Heisenberg’s last reactor experiment. PNAS Nexus, 2026; 5 (9) DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag282

EU unveils new strategy to step up fight against human trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:31:02 UTC
21:31:02 KST

Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The European Commission unveiled a new strategy to combat human trafficking on Friday, setting out six priorities, including the use of technology, cooperation with the private sector, tackling organized crime, and plans to strengthen partnerships with non-EU countries.
More than 20,000 victims of human trafficking were registered across the European Union in 2023 and 2024, marking a 16.1% increase, according to a Commission statement.
Women and girls accounted for 63% of registered victims, most of whom were trafficked for sexual exploitation, while children represented 15% of the total.
Men made up 74% of victims trafficked for labour exploitation.
The first priority focuses on harnessing modern technology to improve the prevention, detection and investigation of human trafficking.
The second priority aims to strengthen cooperation with the private sector to reduce exploitation risks and improve early detection.
Under the third priority, the EU will step up efforts to disrupt transnational trafficking networks linked to organized crime through cross-border cooperation, intelligence-led policing, financial investigations and asset recovery.
The bloc also called on member states to expand cross-border operational cooperation through joint investigation teams, with support from Europol and Eurojust.
The fourth priority addresses trafficking risks linked to migration by strengthening screening procedures, border processes and safeguards in reception conditions.
The fifth priority focuses on improving preparedness and rapid responses during crises, while the sixth priority aims to strengthen the protection of people vulnerable to trafficking.
The strategy will be discussed by the European Parliament and the European Council.

ASML eyes hybrid bonding, report finds, as Chinese firms adopt chip packaging technique
The company has reportedly filed dozens of patent families related to the technology, which can improve chip performance
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML is expanding into next-generation hybrid bonding, a technique that creates dense electrical connections by directly joining chips or silicon wafers, according to a new report. Major Chinese companies are also adopting the technology to improve chip performance.
ASML submitted 27 patent families related to hybrid bonding tools between December 2022 and November 2024, according to a report published by semiconductor and AI supply chain research firm SemiAnalysis on Thursday. The number could be higher because of publication delays affecting recent filings, it said.
The filings suggest ASML is moving beyond lithography, a market it dominates, into back-end processes as demand for high-performance chips surges amid the global artificial intelligence boom.
The company had also begun developing the architecture for a hybrid bonder with Dutch technology firms Prodrive Technologies and VDL ETG, according to SemiAnalysis, citing industry media reports.

Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:30:07 UTC
21:30:07 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win
With global institutions under attack and Trump’s power politics on the rise, the award is a firm rejection of the ‘might is right’ doctrine
4-MIN READ4-MIN
5
 Listen
Commodore C. Uday Bhaskar is director of the Society for Policy Studies (SPS), an independent think tank based in New Delhi. 
The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself.
The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law.
The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump.
Whatever one’s view of Venezuelan politics, that act made a mockery of an institution founded on Alfred Nobel’s will: that the prize go to the person who has done the most for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and for the promotion of peace congresses. A Nobel Prize cannot be re-gifted like a souvenir. As the organisers made clear, “a medal can change owners, but the title of a Nobel Peace Prize laureate cannot”.

Iran win U23 World Greco-Roman team title
TEHRAN - Iran U23 Greco-Roman team managed to win the team title of the U23 World Championships in Las Vegas, United States.
Iran finished with 119 points, five more than Kazakhstan which finished a surprising second with 114 points. Russia was third with 105 points.
Asian silver medalist Erfan Jarkani held on to a 1-1 criteria lead against Manato Nakamura (JPN) to win the 63kg gold. Nakamura challenged at the end of the bout but there was no foul or fleeing from Jarkani, who won with a final score of 2-1.
At 87kg, Yasin Yazdi, also a Asian Championships silver medalist, won his career first-ever gold medal with a 4-0 victory over Temirlan Turdakyn from Kazakhstan in the final. He got the par terre position in the first period but did not score any points.
However, he began the second period with a takedown and that eliminated any chances of him being put in par terre. Yazdi was awarded the second passivity as well which extended his lead to 4-0.
"I’d been waiting for this gold for about two or three years," Yazdi said. "I was able to win it here, and I hope I can keep winning gold medals in the future."
Yazdi said that before the final, he was aware of the Turdakyn's shortcoming and prepared more for exchanges in standing than par terre.
"Before the final, I knew I could win the match because I felt my opponent wasn’t as well-prepared as I was," he said. "My opponent was tall and I may have trouble taking him down and controlling him on the mat. So, I focused most of my effort on the standing exchanges. I could tell that my opponent was starting to get tired in the last 30 seconds of the first period, so in the second period I put even more pressure on him."

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:26:15 BST
21:26:15 KST

Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
- Published
Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades.
Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too.
So what is happening?
How big and unusual are these protests?
Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë and Vlora in the west, Gjirokastër in the south and Korçë in the east.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.
Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign.
The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead.
The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder.
One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue.
- Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania 
  - Published2 days ago
- Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania 
  - Published4 June
So has the Flamingo movement radicalised?
The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.
The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.
Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."
Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
How is the government handling the unrest?
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.
"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.
"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."
Is Albania safe to visit?
Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being.
The UK government has urged visitors to check media, external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities.
Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path.

MP: Eesti 200 should 'lick its wounds' and sit out 2027 elections

MP: Eesti 200 should 'lick its wounds' and sit out 2027 elections
Eesti 200 MPs Ando Kiviberg and Toomas Uibo say their struggling coalition party should skip next March's Riigikogu elections and instead focus on rebuilding for 2031.
Kiviberg told ERR he has not decided whether to run for reelection in March, but if the party decides to run, he would have to act as a team player.
Still, he sees little sense in the party throwing money away at this point, believing Eesti 200 should sit out the 2027 elections instead.
"The party should lick its wounds, do a little soul-searching and commit to preparing properly for 2031," Kiviberg said. He added that he has already discussed the issue with other party members but expects a final decision to be made at Sunday's party council meeting.
Party whip Toomas Uibo, meanwhile, said voters have already made up their minds about Eesti 200, as their rating hit a historic 1.3 percent low in Norstat polls earlier this month.
"I don't know if miracles like this happen, but right now I don't see any point in wasting taxpayer money on running in the elections," he admitted.
While members may still decide on a different course on Sunday, Uibo likewise believes Eesti 200 should instead regroup and focus on the 2031 elections.
Potential Greens merger raises questions
Eesti 200 and the nonparliamentary Estonian Greens are discussing a possible merger, but Kiviberg said this may not necessarily be the right move. "Several party members I've spoken with share my views," he said.
Uibo noted he was unsure whether the two parties have enough in common to unite.
"Of course, you can't expect two different parties to come together and agree on absolutely everything," he said, adding that the question is whether both parties are willing to set enough aside and compromise. "It's still unclear how much common ground we have."
Kiviberg nonetheless ruled out running on another party's ticket next spring and said he has received no such offers. He said he remains committed to Eesti 200 because he believes its ideas are necessary and sound, and will ultimately benefit the country. The question, he said, is how effectively the party has put those ideas into practice.
While Uibo and Kiviberg argued that Eesti 200 should sit out the upcoming elections, fellow MP Peeter Tali told ERR he currently intends to run.
"A politician has to run," Tali said. "If they're no longer a politician, then they don't have to."

Hungary, Ukraine agree to reset ties, Magyar says
BUDAPEST, Oct 16 - Budapest and Kyiv agreed to put their relations on a new footing, Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Friday after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, as the leaders aim to calm tensions over minority rights.
Magyar has taken a less confrontational stance towards Kyiv than his predecessor Viktor Orban. He had repeatedly said that Hungary would not send arms to Ukraine, however, and demanded progress on the rights of its ethnic Hungarian minority.
"I assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post after what he called his first official bilateral meeting with Zelenskiy in Brussels.
Magyar also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
Zelenskiy called the meeting "very good" and said that the two leaders discussed a lot of topics. He also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
Warmer relations between Hungary and Ukraine are pivotal for the European Union's backing for Kyiv in Russia's war in Ukraine. Former Prime Minister Orban had opposed the flow of billions of euros in aid to Ukraine and its EU membership.
Orban made scepticism towards support for Ukraine in its war with Russia a central plank of his campaign ahead of an April election that ended his premiership after 16 years.
On Tuesday, Ukraine took a step forward in its European Union membership bid, opening talks with the bloc on internal market and competitiveness standards, after Hungary dropped its objections.
Magyar's government backed the move after Ukraine's parliament passed legislation on Monday expanding the rights of Hungarian speakers and other minorities to receive education in their native language.
"I welcomed the political agreement reached between Hungary and Ukraine on strengthening the rights of the Transcarpathian Hungarian minority," Magyar said after his meeting with Zelenskiy.
He also said that he considered the passing of the legislation on minority education "as the first step in restoring mutual trust" between the two countries. REUTERS

Euronews could not independently verify the claims.

On Tuesday, Ukraine carried out one of its largest drone operations against the Russian capital, deploying close to 500 drones.
On 9 October, according to multiple reports, the presidential aircraft carrying Vladimir Putin — returning from a summit in Turkmenistan — was unable to land in Moscow due to a drone attack and was diverted to St Petersburg. Putin's plane was not reported to have been a direct target.
Russian officials have neither confirmed nor denied the reports.
Ukraine has not officially confirmed any organised campaign to shut down Russian airports, in what media outlets have dubbed "Operation M&Ms".
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not yet authorised the military to proceed with an original, more aggressive plan for such a campaign, according to reports.
In September, Zelenskyy said Russian skies "are becoming unsafe" and that "drones will appear in the skies over Russia, and that will have to be taken into account", urging international airlines to stop flying to Russian airports.
Kyiv has targeted Russia's military, energy and commercial facilities in a bid to defund Moscow's war machine, as its all-out war in Ukraine continued well into its fifth year.
Yet US President Donald Trump reiterated criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries in an interview, calling them "a disgrace" after his shock announcement of a deal to purchase diesel from the Kremlin.
"There are many targets that can be hit. But when you shell oil refineries that produce, you know, diesel fuel, and we and the whole world need that, (Zelenskyy) is not doing the world a favour," Trump said.

Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Russian strikes and winter hardship may drive more Ukrainians from homes, UN agency warns
GENEVA, Oct 16 - Millions of Ukrainians face another winter of hardship as attacks on critical infrastructure, damaged housing and rising living costs threaten to force more people from their homes, the United Nations migration agency said on Friday.
With temperatures set to fall in the coming months, many families are struggling to secure reliable heating, electricity and water after years of war, the International Organization for Migration said.
This week, Russian missiles and drones have rained down on Ukrainian cities, amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
"Winter is fast approaching in Ukraine, and for many Ukrainians, the months ahead could be the most difficult since the full-scale war began," Dejan Keserovic, IOM deputy chief of mission in Ukraine, told reporters in Geneva via video link from Kyiv.
Nearly 3.6 million people remain internally displaced across Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, while an estimated 3.8 million have returned after displacement, often to damaged or partially destroyed homes, according to the latest IOM figures.
Ukrainians who returned to their homes within the last three months are the most likely to say they intend to leave again, reflecting growing concerns about deteriorating living conditions, the IOM said.
European countries such as Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic currently host around 6 million Ukrainian refugees.
Keserovic said he expected host countries to be preparing for more Ukrainians to leave if the situation got worse.
Repeated Russian strikes on energy and other critical infrastructure have put increasing pressure on Ukraine's electricity, heating and water systems, while drone and missile attacks continue to kill and injure civilians across the country, the IOM said.
Reliable access to water is emerging as a major concern because water systems depend heavily on electricity, the IOM said. The UN agency has installed 31 solar power stations to support water systems across Ukraine, but warned that needs remain immense.
The IOM also warned that funding shortages could hamper aid efforts, with less than 7% of its 2026 Ukraine response plan funded so far, and said urgent resources were needed to improve insulation as households face freezing conditions. REUTERS

Phoenix Suns owner Mat Ishbia predicts team will win opening round playoff series — and the NBA season hasn't even started
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:24:49 UTC
21:24:49 KST

Mat Ishbia says owning the NBA's Phoenix Suns and the WNBA's Phoenix Mercury isn't enough — winning is what he really wants.
Ishbia has owned the Suns and the Mercury since 2023. He and his brother, Justin, own a minority stake in MLB's Chicago White Sox. Justin will take over as controlling owner of the Sox in the coming years.
But unlike billionaires such as Stan Kroenke, Josh Harris and John Henry, who all own multiple teams, Ishbia says he's not interested in building a sports conglomerate. He's only interested in buying teams if he thinks he can move the needle on winning.
"I have different goals. Those guys are obviously doing great things. But my view is not to be some sports empire," Ishbia told CNBC Sport in an exclusive interview. "I'm not making investments in sports. I'm buying a team that I can impact and help win and help compete and do some cool things with the fans."
That's not a common message among many sports investors these days, who seem to be desperate for ways to put their money into live sports teams even as valuations climb higher and higher.
Ishbia said that as the owner of both the Suns and the Mercury he's extremely hands-on. "I'm very active in the Phoenix Suns and Phoenix Mercury at a high, high level right now, and I get very much in the weeds," he told me. "If I can't impact it in a positive way, I'm not going to do it. So I'm not just making investments here and there."
That puts pressure on Ishbia to deliver. The Mercury made the WNBA Finals in 2025 but fell back to 16-28 this year, making them one of the worst teams in the league.
The Suns shipped All-Star forward Kevin Durant off to the Houston Rockets and still managed to make the playoffs last season (where they were swept in the first round by the Oklahoma City Thunder). But this season the Western Conference is stacked with teams with credible championship ambitions, including the Thunder, the San Antonio Spurs, the Denver Nuggets, and the Minnesota Timberwolves.
That said, Ishbia isn't shying away from making concrete predictions about this season for the Suns.
"You should be thinking that we're going to be better than we were last year," he said. "As in, we're going to make the playoffs. We're going to win the first playoff series."
Ishbia bought the Suns and the Mercury for a combined $4 billion. Less than four years later, CNBC values the two teams together at just shy of $7 billion.
Ishbia told CNBC he recently turned down an offer for a small minority stake in the team ("a couple percent") that would have valued the two teams together at more than $8 billion.
"I think most people will put my basketball teams, the Suns and Mercury, at between an $8-and-$9 billion valuation right now, and I think that that's going to continue to grow," Ishbia said.
UWM share plunge
Mark Walter, CEO of Guggenheim Partners and TWG Global, agreed to sell his majority stake in the Lakers in August, less than a year after acquiring control of the team. Prior to the transaction, there had been a flurry of media reports about federal criminal and civil investigations into the accounting and disclosures involving Walter's insurance businesses. In August, TWG Global issued a statement saying, "despite what has been reported, there has been no fraud."
Ishbia says the Walter sale has put more attention on his outside businesses — primarily United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), the nation's largest mortgage lender. Ishbia and his family control the company, and Ishbia is the CEO.
UWM shares are down about 80% in the past 12 months amid a weak housing market. In 2024, Hunterbrook Media investigated UWM's alleged practice of turning independent mortgage brokers into non-independent funnels for billions of dollars of mortgages. "Litigators and mortgage experts say UWM's conduct could constitute fraud and run afoul of laws passed after 2008 to protect borrowers," Hunterbrook reported.
At least two lawsuits were filed against the company in the wake of Hunterbrook's analysis. Some of the claims are ongoing and some have been dismissed by a judge.
In August, UWM suspended its dividend. Hunterbrook wrote another story questioning the hedging practices of the company.
"Considering Hunterbrook's history of publishing inaccurate allegations that have spawned multiple litigation matters, many of the claims have been resolved in UWM's favor, it is difficult to view this inquiry as a legitimate journalistic exercise," a UWM spokesperson told Hunterbrook in August.
Ishbia said UWM is in excellent health.
"We had a great third quarter," said Ishbia of the upcoming earnings period. Ishbia said he's already seen the numbers.
"We're the best mortgage company in the country, so we are the best," he said. "We're not relying on only rates dropping. We do 60%-plus purchase business. The more purchase business you do is less reliant on rates. People aren't going to refinance when rates are 7% but they're still going to buy houses."
Ishbia said UWM's share performance will have no impact on his ownership of the Suns. He said during the Suns' media day on Sept. 28 that he plans to own the team for the next "40, 50 years."
According to an SEC filing, his holding company, SFS Corp, took out five loans with JPMorgan with principal amounts of $610 million, $605 million, $435 million, $225 million and $460 million which mature in 2028, 2029, 2028, 2029 and 2030, respectively.
A spokesman for Ishbia said the loans are actually credit facilities available to Ishbia and his family members, and the amounts owed on the facilities are nowhere near the amount available to them.
"I don't owe JPMorgan billions of dollars in loans," Ishbia said. "I've got enough money in my bank account, and I have enough money in my business, outside of my mortgage business, outside of my basketball business, that I'm doing great."
Anti-tanking stance
Ishbia promised never to purposefully tank a season while he's owner of the Suns. The NBA has made tanking more difficult by changing the draft rules beginning in 2027 to disincentivize purposeful losing. And that's just fine with Ishbia.
"I don't believe in that whole, 'you win for a couple years and you're gonna tank.' That whole tanking thing is for losers. I don't believe in it. I'm never gonna be part of it. I'm glad the NBA got rid of that nonsense," Ishbia said.
He also said the league is working on a "new contest" for NBA All-Star weekend, though he declined to give details on it. The All-Star Game is in Phoenix in February.
Ishbia wants "more star power" in the game and said he's speaking to NBA Commissioner Adam Silver about new ideas to bring in a higher number of the league's top players.

American journalist, Palestinians injured in clashes with masked Israeli settlers in West Bank
Several Palestinians and an American photojournalist working for the Washington Post were injured after a group of masked Israeli men attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank, according to videos, eyewitnesses and Palestinian authorities.
Video of the incident obtained by CBS News showed a group of around 20 masked men clad in black or gray clothes descending a hill from the area of an Israeli settlement outpost into an olive grove near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah.
Another video from the incident showed two vehicles set on fire and a Palestinian man with a bloodied face being escorted away from the area by a woman and a man.
Among the injured was Heidi Levine, a veteran American photojournalist working with the Washington Post.
Video shared by the Israel-based Foreign Press Association showed Levine was surrounded by masked men, pushed to the ground and beaten, and her camera equipment taken from her.
While Levine was on the ground, the video showed the masked men throwing stones and firing slingshots at Palestinians, who then responded by throwing stones themselves.
Levine was taken to a hospital in Ramallah for medical treatment. Footage of Levine in her hospital bed showed she had a large wound on one of her legs and one of her hands had been bandaged.
"I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me," Levine said from her hospital bed.
In a statement, the Washington Post confirmed the attack, saying Levine "was knocked to the ground, repeatedly kicked and robbed of her cameras and phone despite wearing a protective vest marked 'PRESS' and a helmet."
Israel's police and military said they had opened investigations into the incident.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a statement Friday condemning the violence but added the facts surrounding the incident "remain unclear."
"Footage shows masked individuals on both sides hurling objects, amid reports of fireworks fired at Jewish youths," the statement said. "Other footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual. The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence."
The Israeli military said its forces used riot control measures to disperse the confrontation. The military added that soldiers fired warning shots in the air and also fired toward a suspect who ran toward soldiers holding "a sharp object and posed a threat to them."
"The Israel Defense Forces strongly condemns this incident and views any manifestation of violence with utmost severity. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the Israeli military said.
A U.S. Embassy spokesperson said they are monitoring the situation and talk regularly with partners about improving security in the area.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the U.S. Embassy's statement said.
The Binyamin Regional Council, an Israeli governmental body responsible for settlements in the area of the clashes, said the Palestinian Authority had sent activists to deliberately provoke residents of the Israeli settlement outpost near Abu Falah.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society said it treated three Palestinians for injuries at Abu Falah. The wounded included a man who had been shot in the thigh, according to WAFA, the official media arm of the Palestinian Authority.
Clashes between Israeli settlers and Palestinian olive pickers also took place on Friday near the villages of Burqa and Turmus Ayya, which are located in the central West Bank, WAFA reported. The Palestine Red Crescent treated four people for injuries sustained at the clashes near Burqa, WAFA said.
Attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank have surged in recent years, particularly after the establishment of Israel's current hard-right government in late 2022, according to statistics released by the United Nations humanitarian office.
Netanyahu has condemned the violence and vowed a crackdown against what he says is a small group of several hundred wayward youths responsible for attacks on Palestinians.
Despite those public promises by Netanyahu, the violence has continued in recent weeks.
Human rights groups and critics say the government is complicit in the attacks and that Netanyahu's condemnation appears to be posturing since the Israeli military often intervenes on the settlers' side and the perpetrators are rarely prosecuted.
Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, last month condemned Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, calling the behavior an "act of terror" as he visited with Palestinian American residents shaken by months of attacks.
Over the past 18 days, Yesh Din, an Israeli settlement monitoring group, says it has documented 486 violent incidents against Palestinians across 181 different Palestinian localities, and that 234 of these incidents were related to the olive harvest.
In August, three journalists from NBC and a Palestinian woman they were interviewing were attacked by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

Iranian president warns US-Israeli war damaging ecosystems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:22:28 UTC
21:22:28 KST

Kanyshai Butun
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday that the US-Israeli war against Iran is causing serious damage to the country’s ecosystems and called for international mechanisms to protect biodiversity, according to Armenian news agency Armenpress.
Addressing the COP17 Leaders’ Summit in the Armenian capital Yerevan, Pezeshkian warned of the devastating environmental consequences of war, saying military aggression threatens biodiversity, natural resources and future generations.
He said wars destroy forests, fertile lands, wetlands and water resources, while weapons release hazardous chemicals and heavy metals into the environment.
“The destruction of the natural environment is a direct consequence of war. This issue poses a serious threat to the well-being of future generations in our region, including Iran. The environmental consequences of military aggression require urgent security measures from the international community,” he said.
Meanwhile, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for environmental commitments to be translated into practical results, warning that desertification and water scarcity threaten sustainable development and global stability.
He emphasized that environmental issues must take precedence over political differences and that decisions must lead to practical results.
“For millions of people, water shortages and degraded land have already become a daily reality. The most difficult consequence is that this process extends beyond borders, undermining sustainable development and threatening global stability,” Tokayev said.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov similarly called for addressing global challenges by strengthening international cooperation and the concerted efforts of all states.
He reaffirmed his country’s support for Armenia’s initiative to establish the Yerevan Platform on Mountain and Freshwater Ecosystems, expressing the readiness to actively engage in its work.
Armenia holds the presidency of COP17, which takes place in Yerevan from Oct. 19 to 30, bringing together government delegations, international organizations, and civil society representatives to assess progress in biodiversity conservation and discuss further action.

MEA confirms Jaishankar-Rubio talks in Mumbai after Rahul’s jibe over India visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:21:08 UTC
21:21:08 KST

S Jaishankar will hold talks with US secretary of state Marco Rubio on October 20.
NEW DELHI: The ministry of external affairs (MEA) on Friday confirmed that external affairs minister S Jaishankar will hold talks with US secretary of state Marco Rubio on October 20, while also hosting UAE deputy prime minister and foreign minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Mumbai on October 19 and 20.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal announced the engagements while responding to a question from news agency ANI about whether Jaishankar was expected to hold any meetings in Mumbai next week.“So on October 19 and 20, the external affairs minister will host in Mumbai the deputy prime minister and foreign minister of UAE, Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, for an official visit, on 20th October, external affairs minister will hold talks with the US secretary of state Marco Rubio and attend the celebration of the 250th anniversary of the independence of the United States of America as the guest of honor,” Jaiswal said.ALSO READ: ‘Ensure safety of Indian nationals’: MEA’s strong message to US after alleged Hindu temple attack plotHe also explained that hosting foreign dignitaries outside the national capital was not unusual, pointing to previous engagements held in different Indian cities.“This has been the practice for the last decade or so that we have hosted foreign secretaries outside Delhi. The Prime Minister hosted the Prime Minister of Spain in Baroda. He hosted chancellor Merz in Ahmedabad. Prime Minister of Mauritius was hosted by him in Varanasi, and then the external affairs minister hosted the foreign ministers Meeting in Goa.
He hosted the foreign minister of Botswana in Kevadia in Gujarat, and the external affairs minister also hosted the Heart of Asia Conference in Amritsar,” Jaiswal said.
Rahul's jibe at govt over Rubio’s visit
The clarification comes after Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi over Rubio’s upcoming visit to Mumbai, alleging that officials in the external affairs ministry were unclear about the developments.“Mr Rubio has summoned his employee to Mumbai. Modi ji, your officials in the external affairs ministry are confused about what's going on. You might want to explain. Unless, of course, you want me to,” Rahul posted on X on Friday.His remarks followed criticism from Congress a day earlier, after US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said American officials expected Jaishankar to meet Rubio in Mumbai. The party questioned why the Indian government had not publicly announced the minister’s engagements.
Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh had described the ambassador’s statement as “extraordinary” and questioned why details of Jaishankar’s planned meeting with Rubio were being communicated by a US official rather than India’s foreign ministry.“Why is the MEA silent on the external affairs minister's tryst with Mr Rubio in Mumbai?” Ramesh asked, adding that India was learning about the developments from the US ambassador.The US state department announced on Tuesday that Rubio would visit India from October 17 to 22 to strengthen energy cooperation. His itinerary includes Mumbai and Jamnagar, following a visit to Samarkand in Uzbekistan.

What to know about the Iran war today:

- The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. leaves the Middle East, a spokesman for Iran's army said Friday. "If it does not leave, we will expel it," Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X.
- Ships remain exposed to "indiscriminate attacks" in the Strait of Hormuz, even if they try to hide their movements by switching off tracking systems, a maritime monitor warned Thursday, confirming three strikes on vessels in the waterway this week.
2 missiles strike airport in Yemen's port city of Aden, officials say
Two missiles struck the airport in Yemen's port city of Aden on Friday night, police said, blaming Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the second such attack in less than a week.
Police said no casualties were reported as fighting escalates in the latest front in the Iran war, one in which the rebels have attacked both neighboring Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognized government that's backed by the kingdom.
A security official and a traffic controller told The Associated Press an area of the Aden airport that hosts a military unit aligned with the Saudi-backed government was hit. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks
Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides.
"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh.
Regardless of how involved Iran has been in Houthi attacks, the two groups have long held close ties.
They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its Axis of Resistance — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
"The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next."
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have killed about 20 people in the last several weeks, including 13 in one strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport last weekend.
CBS/AFP
Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions, says country ready for talks
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister.
In his meeting with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for closer ties with Georgia, weeks after Tbilisi cut aviation links between the two countries following U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian airlines.
The two met on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity summit in Armenia's capital, Yerevan.
"Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the malicious propaganda against our country to be lies," Pezeshkian said, according to a statement from his office.
"We have always been ready for dialogue. They think they can force us to surrender, but we will not bow to coercion," he added, calling U.S. sanctions against Tehran "unjustifiable and inhumane."
Georgia's Civil Aviation Agency said in September it would comply with U.S. sanctions, while Kobakhidze insisted Tbilisi was not imposing its own bilateral sanctions on Tehran.
Saudi-hosted Asian Cup soccer tournament remains on schedule despite Houthi attacks
Asian Cup organizers insisted Friday the continental soccer championship set to be held in Saudi Arabia in early 2027 remains on track despite a wave of missile and drone attacks on the host country in recent days.
The Saudi organizing committee issued a statement Friday saying it is continuing to coordinate closely with the Asian Football Confederation. The tournament is scheduled for Jan. 7 to Feb. 5.
"Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services," Saudi organizers said. "The focus remains on delivering a world-class tournament experience for participating teams, fans and media from across Asia, while bringing the continent together through football."
South Korea's Professional Footballers' Association had earlier expressed concerns following a series of attacks on the Asian Cup host country by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"The continued military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that can never be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, head of the South Korean player union, said in a statement. "The safety of our national team, as well as all players participating in the Asian Cup, is a serious concern."
At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom.
Several sporting events have already been canceled or postponed in Saudi Arabia, including Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis tournament; women's tennis' WTA Finals, which were moved to the U.S.; multiple matches for the Saudi soccer club Al-Nassr, which features Cristiano Ronaldo; and an Olympic qualifying event for BMX cycling.
AP/CBS
Attacks on Yemen government palace compound killed 5, officials say
Attacks on the palace compound of Yemen's internationally recognized government Thursday killed at least five people and wounded more than a dozen others, government officials said.
In a Facebook post late Thursday, Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said security guards and other employees at Maashiq palace in Yemen's southern port city of Aden were among the casualties.
Aden has been the seat of Yemen's government since 2015. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they targeted a military operations headquarters associated with Saudi forces backing the government.
Two of the missiles launched by the Houthis on Thursday struck near the headquarters of the Saudi-backed coalition forces in Aden, causing damage, a Yemeni government official said.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak to the media, said Friday the missiles landed near the compound used by the coalition in Buraiqah, a neighborhood west of the palace. No senior officials were there at the time of the attack, he said.
Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles and drones
Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced a series of interceptions in successive X posts on Friday, saying Saudi forces had destroyed a ballistic missile, two cruise missiles and three drones over Saudi Arabia or the Red Sea.
In a first tweet, Al-Maliki said coalition forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Yanbu.
A second post announced the interception and destruction of two cruise missiles over the Red Sea.
He then reported three drones had been intercepted and destroyed in Saudi Arabia's southern region and the Riyadh region.
Iraq says Iran war has deprived it of $60 billion in oil export revenue
Iraq has lost around $60 billion during the U.S.-Iran war, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Thursday, as the fighting has blocked or severely impeded a waterway crucial to its oil exports.
OPEC member Iraq was producing about 4 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) before the conflict, and exporting about 3.5 million bpd – mostly carried by tankers out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's ongoing threat to vessels that fail to seek its permission to transit the strait has forced Iraq, which lacks sufficient storage capacity, to halt most production and fall back on limited exports via Syria and Turkey, by truck and pipeline respectively. Syria is set to provide an overland oil route to bypass the strait, the head of Syrian Petroleum Co. said last week.
"Iraq has suffered losses estimated at around $60 billion during the recent war between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran," Hussein told his Italian counterpart in Rome, according to a statement from the Iraqi foreign ministry.
After a heavy drop in production, Iraqi oil exports, which provide about 90% of the country's revenues, recovered modestly last month, reaching 2.6 million barrels per day between Sept. 1 and 21, according to the oil ministry. But at the same time, Iraq's foreign currency reserves have shrunk by $20 billion and consumer prices have risen sharply, plunging it into economic crisis.
CBS/AFP
Norwegian teen sentenced in U.K. to 20 years in prison for plotting murder for Iran-linked gang
A Norwegian teenager convicted of traveling to Britain to carry out a contract killing on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot someone unknown to him for $28,000 last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, in northern England, with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K.
In bodycam video released by police from the early hours of March 19, 2025, Natland emerges topless from his room and mimes a shooting gesture at a firearms officer before being slammed against a wall.
It remains unknown who his intended target would have been.
Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to London's counterterrorism police unit.
Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to "contribute to murder" and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy.
CBS/AP
Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman
The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area."
The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman."
The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels."
At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week.
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region"
The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday.
"If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X. "If it does not leave, we will expel it."
He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel.
Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels, Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission.
Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turn off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection.
Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide"
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country.
Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions."
"What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News.
"As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"
CBS/AFP
White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say
The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.
A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."
A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.
CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.
Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.
