Russian troops liberate 12 communities in Ukraine operation over week — top brass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:19:44 UTC
21:19:44 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated 12 communities in the Kharkov and Zaporozhye Regions and the Donetsk People’s Republic over the week of October 10-16, including two communities during the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlements of Lukashovo, Lobanovka, Reznikovo, Kupino, Nefyodovka and Chernoye and yesterday they established control of the settlements of Varvarovka and Nikolayevka in the Kharkov Region through active and decisive operations. <…> During the week, Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlements of Novotroitskoye, Petrovskoye and Lidino in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said in a statement.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup East units continued their advance deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Nikolskoye in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry reported.
Russian troops deliver eight precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered one massive and seven combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics and telecommunications centers and ammunition depots over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 10-16, 2026, the Russian Armed Forces delivered one massive and seven combined strikes, hitting military-industrial enterprises, logistics and telecommunications centers, transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, sites producing and storing unmanned aerial vehicles, ammunition and materiel depots, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
Russian troops delivered strikes over the week, degrading some infrastructure facilities of Ukrainian ports used to receive and store military supplies, it said.
"In addition, some infrastructure facilities of Ukraine’s ports used to receive, store and distribute military cargo were degraded," the ministry said.
Russian troops struck 15 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons and military hardware to the Ukrainian army over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the week, 15 dry cargo ships involved in the delivery of Western weapons, military hardware, fuel and equipment for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarts Ukrainian attempts to break out of encirclement in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarted all the Ukrainian army’s attempts during the past week to break out of the encirclement in the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units continued tightening the ring of encirclement of enemy formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. <…> All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement were thwarted," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 1,675 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,675 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed five enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of six mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, two airmobile brigades, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, four territorial defense brigades and a National Guard brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,675 personnel, five armored combat vehicles, 82 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,550 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,550 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 18 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,550 personnel, 18 armored combat vehicles, 94 motor vehicles, 12 field artillery guns and 11 electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,155 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed nine enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, a mountain assault brigade, an airmobile brigade, an unmanned systems brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,155 personnel, nine armored combat vehicles, 198 motor vehicles, 13 field artillery guns and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 2,740 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 2,740 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 37 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an airborne brigade of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and three National Guard brigades," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 2,740 personnel, 37 armored combat vehicles, 76 motor vehicles, 11 field artillery guns and 11 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,695 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,695 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed seven enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an assault brigade, three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and two marine infantry brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,695 personnel, seven armored combat vehicles, 53 motor vehicles, three field artillery guns and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 240 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 240 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Last week, Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade," the ministry said.
"As many as 240 [Ukrainian] military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 116 motor vehicles, five artillery guns and nine electronic warfare stations were destroyed," the ministry reported.
Russian air defenses intercept 5,695 Ukrainian UAVs, four cruise missiles over week
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 5,695 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and four Flamingo cruise missiles over the week, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down seven guided aerial bombs, two rockets of the US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, four Flamingo long-range cruise missiles, a Neptune long-range missile and 5,695 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 263,235 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,251 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,790 multiple rocket launchers, 36,738 field artillery guns and mortars and 74,686 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

Extra levies on financial sector won't kill anyone says Giorgetti
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:19:13 CEST
21:19:13 KST

Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti
said Friday that the additional taxes the government intends to
impose on banks and insurers in the 2027 budget law will not be
too severe.
                                    
"I confirm that a contribution will be requested from the
financial system because we believe it can afford it," Giorgetti
said.
                                    
"We also believe the terms will be sustainable," he added,
stressing that "keeping the (bond) spread under control is in
everyone's interest" and that banks hold billions of euros in
Italian BTP bonds on their balance sheets.
                                    
When asked about possible legal challenges by the banks, the
minister commented: "every Italian could take the government to
court for raising taxes. We'll try to figure out the right
course of action; I don't think anyone will die over it."
The government's Draft Budgetary Plan (DBP) says the financial
sector will make a contribution of five billion euros to the
2027 budget package, and an additional three billion euros in
2028 and two billion in 2029.
                                    
The 2026 budget law included extra levies on banks and insurers
worth around 4.4 billion euros.

Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:18:06 UTC
21:18:06 KST

Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse
Families demand justice for the 35 people killed; relatives say they had warned that the roof was leaking.
Authorities in Pakistan have ordered inspections of regional schools after the collapse of a classroom roof killed at least 34 children and a teacher.
Reports on Friday said that the government has ordered the administration of the northeastern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to launch the checks after the deadly incident at Al-Khair school on Thursday.
At least 34 students aged 13 or younger, as well as a teacher, were killed in the roof collapse.
There are conflicting reports about whether the inspections will cover both public and private schools or only private schools. The province’s education department has been given three days to report its findings, according to The Associated Press news agency.
Schools are to be classified as safe, in need of repairs or improvements, or potentially unsafe. Various structures will be assessed, including roofs, ceilings, walls and staircases.
Police arrested Mohammad Khan, the owner of Al-Khair school, shortly after the roof of mud and bricks collapsed.
The building was structurally weak, according to Peshawar Police Chief Saeed Ahmed, who also said that Khan had told officers that recent rains had weakened the structure.
Bereaved families are demanding justice, with some of the victims’ relatives maintaining that they had warned Khan about rainwater repeatedly seeping into classrooms.
Dozens of mourners gathered outside the school on Friday to remember those who died.
Pakistan’s construction standards are widely reported to be poor and builders commonly use substandard materials.
The roof of a private tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore collapsed in June, killing 14 people.

Italy: Nationwide air traffic control issues disrupt flights at Rome airport

At Rome’s Airport, at least 12 flights had been cancelled by mid-morning, affecting services to Milan Linate, Bari, Riyadh, Tirana, Turin, Trieste, Valencia, Munich, Lyon, Catania, Venice and Trapani. Other departures faced delays of 15 to 60 minutes, leaving travellers gathered around departure boards to check updates. Passengers were advised to contact their airlines for the latest information.
The problems were detected overnight by ENAV, Italy’s air navigation service provider. Contingency systems kept operations running normally until 6am, but as traffic increased, regulators imposed flow-management measures that temporarily cut the country’s air traffic capacity by 50 per cent. ENAV said it was using alternative data-transmission systems to maintain as many departures as possible, including intercontinental flights.
The company said technicians had traced the anomalies to the data network and were working to establish the cause and restore full capacity. It ruled out a cyberattack or sabotage and said flight operations remained safe. Similar delays and cancellations were reported across Italy at airports including Milan, Bergamo, Naples, Venice, Palermo and Cagliari, while passengers were warned that further disruption could follow.

Dubois vs Wardley 2: WBO title fight announced in London
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of October 18, Dubois will face Wardley in a rematch for the WBO heavyweight title. The fight will take place at The O2 arena.
On the night from Saturday, October 17, to Sunday, October 18, a fight for the WBO heavyweight title will take place in London at The O2 arena, with the reigning titleholder Daniel Dubois facing Fabio Wardley in a rematch, UNN writes.
On Saturday at London’s O2 Arena, Daniel Dubois will defend his WBO heavyweight title against his compatriot Fabio Wardley in a rematch of their thrilling first encounter in May.
The first fight
In May, Dubois and then-WBO champion Wardley met for the first time in Manchester. In that bout, Dubois won by technical knockout in the 11th round, although the fight was difficult for Dubois.
The fight took place at the Co-op Live arena. According to the agency, Dubois was late for the bout because of traffic jams on the roads.
In just the 10th second, Wardley knocked Dubois down with a right-hand punch, and later
repeated this in the third round. Despite this, the former IBF champion managed to turn the fight around and gradually took control.
Despite being knocked down twice, Dubois was able to adapt, and starting in the fourth round, he took the initiative, forcing Wardley into exchanges and breaking his opponent’s nose.
At the beginning of the 11th round, referee Howard Foster stopped the fight.
For Wardley, this defeat was the first of his professional career. His record now stands at 20 wins, 1 loss and 1 draw.
After the fight ended, Wardley asked: "Where is my mum? I want to tell Mum that I’m all right".
For Dubois, the victory marked a comeback after his defeat by Ukrainian Oleksandr Usyk, who knocked out the Briton in the fifth round at Wembley Stadium in July last year and took his IBF belt.
The rematch in London
In August, Dubois and Wardley’s promoter Frank Warren, who, despite his promise, never gave Oleksandr Usyk a Bentley, announced the rematch in the ring at The O2.
"On October 17 here at The O2 in London, there will be a rematch. It will be one of the best heavyweight fights we have seen in recent years. It will be a rematch between the reigning champion Daniel Dubois and former champion Fabio Wardley. On October 17, you will see a brilliant fight. Don’t miss it," Warren said.
Standing in the ring opposite Wardley, Dubois said: "Another confident victory and an amazing performance. I can’t wait. Let’s get started. It’s just war. When you go into the water, you inevitably get wet. I enjoy every moment of this. I can’t wait".
Wardley replied: "We went into that fight with boundless confidence, but adjustments need to be made. I proved that I can adapt and that I can change, and that is exactly what we need to do for this fight".
The day before, the boxers held a face-off ahead of the fight.
Where to watch, favorite
The fighters are scheduled to enter the ring at 00:30 on Sunday, October 18, Kyiv time. Boxing fans will be able to watch the fight live on the DAZN video platform. The broadcast will be available with a one-time subscription costing 913 hryvnias. The fight is also included in the service’s monthly subscription plan.
Bookmakers consider Dubois the favorite, offering odds of 1.3 on him. Wardley’s victory is priced at 3.75.

Russia seizes more EU companies’ assets over Ukraine support
- Russia seized assets of four EU companies, including Tarkett, Menshen, Sverige International Holdings and Ontex, in retaliation for Europe’s support for Ukraine.
- The Kremlin said the move was linked to “illegal expropriations of Russian property” and was “reversible”, while Putin warned of “certain downsides” for taking Western assets.
- The companies said they were assessing the impact, as EU leaders backed Zelensky and Russia criticised the EU for freezing about €210 billion of its sovereign assets.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russia has seized local assets of four companies from France, Germany, Sweden and Belgium, according to a decree by President Vladimir Putin, in retaliation for Europe’s wartime support for Ukraine.
The decree on Oct 15 listed assets belonging to French flooring maker Tarkett, German packaging maker Menshen, Swedish packaging maker Sverige International Holdings and Belgian hygiene product company Ontex.
The decree also listed Russian assets of former European metal-packaging business Eviosys acquired by US packaging group Sonoco in December 2024. The decree listed the assets as owned by Sonoco’s Dutch unit.
EU leaders rallied around President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit on Oct 16 at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine amid fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
The Kremlin said that the assets’ takeover continued a trend after a similar move in September against food giant Nestle and retailers Auchan and Metro.
“Their country of origin was one of the factors taken into account in making the decision,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, adding that these countries were involved in “illegal expropriations of Russian property”.
Temporary administration of the European companies’ properties was handed to Russian companies that had been largely unknown.
Putin notes ‘downsides’
Ontex, which employs 350 people in Russia and operates a factory outside Moscow, said it has been informed about the decree and will “consider appropriate actions to safeguard its assets and the continuity of Ontex Russia’s operations”.
Sonoco said in its 2025 report that it had finalised its own exit from Russia in 2022 but acquired more assets, making up 0.5% of the company’s total, as part of the Eviosys deal.
Tarkett said it was “losing effective control over its operations in Russia” and was assessing the situation.
The Kremlin said the measures responded to EU nations’ involvement in “direct battlefield hostilities” but were also “reversible”.
Speaking to Russian businessmen just before the decree was published on Oct 15, Putin acknowledged that taking Western assets had “certain downsides” without giving more details.
He urged the Russian businesses taking over the assets to seek domestic financing sources instead.
Putin cited the 2008 global financial crisis, which had a profound impact on the Russian economy, as an example of the risks of excessive exposure to global markets. He said foreign countries pursued their own interests through investment.
There have been some reports that the US could seek control of some Russian assets frozen in Europe as part of efforts to provide incentives for Russia to negotiate with Ukraine.
Russia criticises the EU for freezing about €210 billion (S$302 billion) of its sovereign assets in response to the war and for targeting assets belonging to Russian companies in Europe and other Western countries. REUTERS

Self-employment declines as freelancers quickly find new jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:14:18 UTC
21:14:18 KST

Self-employment declines as freelancers quickly find new jobs
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
After two decades of mostly uninterrupted growth, self-employment in the Netherlands has declined this year for the first time, with former freelancers quickly finding new jobs, according to the Dutch central bank (DNB).
There are 10% fewer self-employed workers this year than in 2024. Their numbers have fallen by some 131,000 since the end of 2024, when they peaked at almost 1.3 million.
In mid-2026, around 12% of the workforce was primarily self-employed, still a substantial share by international standards.
Little impact on unemployment
But according to the DNB, the decline has had little impact on unemployment, with half of former freelancers finding paid work within three months. About a third move to permanent positions or to jobs with prospects of a permanent contract. Others move into flex work. Only 7% become unemployed, which is comparable to previous years.
“Leaving self-employment therefore mainly results in movement within the labour market rather than a greater flow into unemployment,” the DNB said.
About half of former self-employed workers move to different sectors entirely, especially healthcare and social care, education and government, retail, transport and hospitality.
The DNB says this confirms that the Dutch labour market is dynamic. However, its research does not show how people’s income, productivity or employment conditions change after they leave self-employment for new work.
The DNB says it cannot say definitively why the decrease is happening. It does note that stricter enforcement against so-called false self-employment since 2025 may play a role.
“We observe relatively high levels of movement between self-employment and employment in sectors where false self-employment is frequently debated, including healthcare, construction, facility services and business services,” it said.

Ukraine exports gas for first time since start of full-scale war
Companies sold about 12.75 million cubic metres of natural gas at the first export auction held by the Ukrainian Energy Exchange (UEEX) on 15 October.
Source: the auction results published by the UEEX
Details: The sale prices ranged from €69 to €69.03 per MWh.
The largest volume was sold by Naftogazvydobuvannia PrJSC, at about 7.78 million cubic metres. The remaining gas was sold by Naftohazdiia LLC, Naftohazheorozvidka LLC and Kosul LLC. All four companies belong to the DTEK Group, Ukraine's largest private energy company.
In total, they sold about 12.31 million cubic metres of gas.
All four companies initially offered the gas at €87 per MWh. The final prices were about 21% lower. They were also 19% below the last recorded price at the Dutch TTF hub, which stood at €85.5 per MWh.
The export price was 89% higher than the domestic price.
Deliveries are scheduled to take place at the Polish border between 26 October and 31 December. Full prepayment is required for all lots. Deliveries will proceed subject to the sellers obtaining the relevant export licences from the Ministry of Economy.
For reference: Following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, the government banned gas exports. A government decision on 7 October 2026 reintroduced permission to export gas.
Background:
- In late August, Ukraine accumulated enough gas to meet the basic scenario for getting through the winter.
- The export sales limit stands at 15% of the volume of gas delivered by a producer to the gas transmission system in the previous month. Gas exports are prohibited during winter.

Russia Hospitalizes Five After Suspected Mpox Exposure, Launches Emergency Disease Investigation

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Ukrainian embroidered clothing brand Etnodim has partnered with British content creator of Ukrainian origin Max Klymenko to launch a charity shirt inspired by his popular TikTok series Career Ladder, with profits from sales going toward supporting Ukrainian children affected by Russia’s war.
The collaboration brings together Klymenko’s internationally recognized social media project, which has helped him attract nearly 10 million TikTok followers, and traditional Ukrainian craftsmanship.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In his Career Ladder series, Klymenko interviews people from a wide range of professions, including public figures such as Will Smith, Gordon Ramsay, French President Emmanuel Macron, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The concept of exploring different careers inspired Klymenko and the Etnodim team to highlight traditional Ukrainian occupations, some of which are gradually disappearing.
The resulting shirt features embroidered representations of historic crafts and professions, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting, and milling, reflecting the importance of preserving Ukraine’s cultural heritage.
“We wanted to convey the idea of equal opportunities without stereotypes and remind people that every profession has its own value. The embroidery features traditional Ukrainian crafts that are gradually disappearing, including blacksmithing, pottery, harvesting and milling. The composition on the shirt’s side panel is inspired by Apple Picker, a work by Ukrainian artist Oleksandr Saienko,” the Etnodim team explains.
Beyond its connection to the TikTok series, the design also draws on Klymenko’s personal memories of growing up in Ukraine, particularly his childhood experiences with his grandmother.
According to the press release, conversations about his upbringing, family memories, and current work helped shape the creative direction of the collaboration.
“When I think about my childhood, I immediately think of my grandmother: the time I spent with her, the little forts made of yarn I used to build when visiting her, and all the wonderful things in her house that have stayed in my memory. Decorative plates, a large wooden spoon with classic red and colourful Ukrainian patterns, and a knitted picture of Mykolaiv landscapes hanging on the wall—that picture is probably the most vivid work of art I remember from childhood,” Klymenko said.
The partnership also reflects Klymenko’s continued involvement in charitable initiatives supporting Ukraine and his efforts to introduce Ukrainian culture and experiences to international audiences.
As part of the initiative, profits from sales of the Career Ladder shirt will be donated to Kids of Ukraine to support its SviTY programme, which assists teenagers affected by the war.
The programme focuses on emotional recovery, education, and personal development, helping young people acquire new skills, identify their strengths, and explore future career opportunities.
Through the collaboration, Etnodim and Klymenko aim to combine the promotion of traditional Ukrainian crafts with practical support for children and teenagers navigating their futures amid the ongoing war.
In another recent collaboration, German sportswear brand PUMA joined forces with Ukrainian fashion label CHER’17, marking its first partnership with a local fashion brand in Ukraine.
According to a press release, the CHER’17 x PUMA collection explores the unpredictability of everyday life under the campaign slogan “No plan is a plan.” The collection reinterprets PUMA’s signature designs through details inspired by unexpected mishaps and everyday imperfections.

“Not a Single Minute”: Von der Leyen Slams Russia’s Ceasefire Violations as EU Prepares 22nd Sanctions Package
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union would not lift any sanctions against Russia until Moscow ends its war against Ukraine, accusing the Kremlin of escalating attacks instead of observing the energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump.
Speaking to journalists ahead of the second day of the European Council meeting in Brussels on October 16, von der Leyen said the EU was preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Of course, we supported President Trump's energy ceasefire, but we've seen that Russia did not respect it. Not a single minute. Instead, Russia escalated. And therefore, we have to increase the pressure on Russia. We're working now on the 22nd sanctions package. And one thing is absolutely clear. We will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops the war,” von der Leyen stated.

Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says

- Category

Ukraine Could Get Starlink Deep Inside Russia in Exchange for 100-Day Oil Strike Pause, WSJ Says
Two Republican US senators have proposed expanding Starlink coverage roughly 300 kilometers, or 186 miles, inside Russia in exchange for Ukraine suspending strikes on Russian oil refineries for 100 days, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
Senators Roger Wicker and Kevin Cramer presented the proposal to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during an October 9 visit to Kyiv as part of a bipartisan congressional delegation, according to the report.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zelenskyy indicated that he was prepared to accept such an arrangement, the sources said.
The expanded coverage could give Ukrainian forces reliable satellite connectivity during operations against Russian ballistic missile launchers located deeper behind the border.
That would potentially allow Ukraine to target the systems before they launch missiles rather than relying solely on air defenses to intercept incoming weapons after they are fired.
Zelenskyy has publicly said Ukraine could also consider halting strikes on Russian refineries in return for additional US-made Patriot interceptors. The Starlink proposal would offer a different form of protection by helping Ukrainian forces target the launch platforms themselves.
According to the WSJ, the senators viewed the proposed arrangement as a possible first step toward reviving a stalled diplomatic process.
The discussions come amid growing pressure from Washington for Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure. US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on October 11, after which Ukraine temporarily suspended strikes on Russian energy facilities.
Despite Kyiv observing the pause, Ukrainian forces subsequently stopped receiving US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile launches, according to Ukrainian officials. The military version of Starlink, Starshield, was also restricted, complicating frontline operations and middle-strike missions against Russian military targets.
Reuters separately reported that the instruction to restrict Starshield came from the White House, although its sources did not identify who specifically ordered the measure. A senior US official said Trump personally had not issued the order.
Previously, Ukraine lifted restrictions on strikes against Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure after observing a three-day pause requested by Washington, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated.
“The ban has been lifted. We’ve had enough,” Zelenskyy said.

Portuguese journalist and writer Joaquim Letria dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:10:34 UTC
21:10:34 KST

Joaquim Letria, regarded as one of the leading figures in Portuguese journalism, died this Friday at the age of 82.
Journalist and writer Joaquim Letria died this Friday, at the age of 82. The news was reported by the newspaper Observador, citing a close source.
The journalist had been in a weakened condition for some time, but was not ill, according to the same source. A family source gave this account to the Lusa news agency.
Born in Lisbon in 1943, Joaquim Letria is regarded as one of the leading figures in Portuguese journalism. He founded the weekly newspapers O Jornal and Tal & Qual and also served as deputy news director for Non-Daily Programmes at RTP in the years following the 25 April revolution. He was also elected president of the Journalists' Union.
He began his career as a journalist in 1963 at the newspaper Diário de Lisboa and went on to build an international career, first at the news agency The Associated Press and later as a correspondent for Deutsche-Presse Agentur, until 1970. Letria also worked for the BBC in London.
He was known for the many facets of his professional life, having been the author and presenter of several radio and television programmes. He received the Press Prize in the Television category in 1974.
An author, recognised for his many technical books on journalism and for the title "A Verdade Confiscada", published in 1998, he also taught for more than 20 years at the Higher School of Journalism in Porto, at Universidade Independente and Universidade Autónoma de Lisboa, as well as at the Higher Institute for Information and Administration Sciences (ISCIA) in Aveiro.
He was a member of the Portuguese Communist Party until 1968 and later served as spokesperson for the then president of the republic, Ramalho Eanes, until 1986.
The Minister for Culture, Youth and Sport, Margarida Balseiro Lopes, expressed her sorrow at the journalist's death, describing him as "one of the most prominent figures in post-25 April journalism".

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:10:00 UTC
21:10:00 KST

EU summit: European leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
October 16, 2026
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where leaders from across the bloc pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.
What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?
"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
"One thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops this war."
The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.
After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."
Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine
Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."
"The winter package is not only energy, it's also air defense and funding," he added.
During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia.
"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said.
When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.
Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."
Trump denies responsibility for restrictions on Starshield
Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.
However, on Friday, Trump denied that he or Starlink founder Elon Musk were responsible for these restrictions. "I don't think it was me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump told journalists.
He added that any limit to Ukraine's access to the Starshield system was not imposed by the United States.
Musk had said that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company, SpaceX, which operates Starlink.
Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Europe is working to help Ukraine with satellite and early warning systems.
"We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed," Macron told reporters.
Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM
The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.
"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."
Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.
"I assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.

Europe's far right has a Putin problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:09:43 UTC
21:09:43 KST

Europe's far right has a Putin problem
Rassemblement National (RN) candidate Marine Le Pen in Paris, France, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Anne-Christine Poujoulat / AFP via Getty Images)
Europe's far-right parties grow increasingly divided on something that once united them — sympathies for Vladimir Putin's Russia.
As nationalists and right-wing populists across Western Europe move closer to power, many are seeking to distance themselves from their past admiration for a country waging Europe's largest war since 1945 while conducting hybrid attacks against much of the continent.
Despite finding common ground on dislike of liberalism, NATO, and the EU, Europe's far right is being forced to rethink its relationship with Moscow — much like it had to do with U.S. President Donald Trump.
France's National Rally (RN) and the U.K.'s Nigel Farage now harden rhetoric on Russia while signaling a more conditional, rather than simply hostile, approach to Ukraine, as part of a strategy to cast a wider net of voters.
But the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has emerged as Europe's largest and most extreme nationalist party, is moving in the opposite direction.
The split comes at a critical moment. The National Rally's Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential election next April, the AfD is leading the German polls, and Farage's Reform party was, until very recently, a favorite to win the next elections in Britain.
Experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent explain the reasons behind this divide and what the coming string of European elections could mean for Ukraine.
Farage, Le Pen seek Russia detox
For years, far-right leaders have been ranked among the most Moscow-friendly voices in European politics.
In 2014, Farage, the man who later led a campaign to push the U.K. out of the EU and whose Reform party now polls second at 22%, expressed his admiration for Putin as an "operator."
As recently as 2024, while Russia’s full-scale invasion had already been raging for two years, he suggested that the eastward expansion of the EU and NATO provoked the war.
Comments like these have made it easy for his opponents to blast him as a Putin fan.
Now, Farage seems intent on proving he is no such thing.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?"
Last year, the Reform leader called the Russian dictator a "very bad dude" and said NATO should shoot down Russian jets intruding into its airspace.
On Ukraine, he has cautiously affirmed support for Ukraine — even backing the idea of using frozen Russian assets for Kyiv's benefit.
And while he criticized plans for a post-war "reassurance" force in Ukraine as outlined by the Labor government, Farage backed sending British troops to the country, if on a temporary basis and as part of a U.N. peacekeeping mission.
Reports have emerged that Farage is even considering a trip to Ukraine as part of his quest to brush off his Russia-friendly image.
A similar shift is taking place across the English Channel.
Prior to 2022, Le Pen said that the Russian occupation of Crimea was not illegal, and her party took out a loan from a Russian bank.
But after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, she backpedaled.
Now, the three-time failed presidential candidate sees she has a real chance to win, with a court clearing a path to her candidacy despite last year's embezzlement conviction.
As the vote nears, she is treading cautiously on foreign policy.
Le Pen has condemned Russian aggression and has backed continued military assistance to Ukraine, even as she wants Paris to cut financial aid — citing France's own budget constraints — opposes Kyiv's EU membership, and is skeptical about future EU aid if it burdens France.
She also said she would be happy to visit Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The RN's younger co-leader, Jordan Bardella, has taken a tougher stance on Russia, naming the country a threat — something that Le Pen avoided in a recent interview with the Financial Times.
Both party chiefs also blasted Moscow in September over its seizure of European business assets in the country and denounced Russian interference and destabilization efforts.
Elsewhere in Europe, far-right parties have proved they can tone down their views on Russia and Ukraine in exchange for government seats.
Matteo Salvini, head of Italy's League party, remembered for once sporting a T-shirt with Putin's likeness, has largely fallen in line behind Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's firmly pro-Western, pro-Ukraine course, save for some symbolic resistance.
And the former Dutch government also maintained its support for Kyiv, even though Geert Wilders's far-right Party for Freedom (PVV) was the strongest party in a short-lived coalition.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a right-wing populist, while expressing his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine, echoed Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said on Oct. 16.
Elsewhere, the far right doubles down
This shift is far from uniform, however.
As Meloni, Italy's right-wing, anti-immigration prime minister, prepares for the 2027 elections, she faces a new pro-Kremlin challenger.
Roberto Vannacci, a retired army general, left the League in February to found his own nationalist party, National Future.
Vannacci, a former military attaché in Moscow, has famously said he prefers Putin over Zelensky.
With support reaching as high as 8% in recent polls, National Future has already surpassed Meloni's junior coalition partners.
But the most striking example is the AfD, currently the strongest opposition party in Germany, nearing 30% in polls.
The AfD was seen as so extreme that the far-right European Parliament group expelled it at the RN's urging in 2024, prompting the AfD to form a new ultranationalist coalition, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN).
The party campaigns on a halt to military and financial aid to Ukraine, the lifting of sanctions against Russia, and the resumption of Russian energy purchases.
Given the AfD's particular brand of extremism and Berlin's role as the leading military donor to Ukraine, this is an especially worrying signal for Kyiv and Europe.
Like in the U.K., the next German parliamentary elections are expected no later than 2029.
Why the difference
With Russia's full-scale war nearing its fifth anniversary, many countries have seen the public's support for Ukraine cool — but not collapse.
Politicians vying for victory in upcoming elections have to take this into account, with the U.K. being a prime example.
Farage's party certainly has a reputation to fix, after its former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, was sentenced to prison for taking bribes from pro-Russian Ukrainian politicians.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?" Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, comments on Reform's strategy.
A poll from last fall shows that 59% of Brits support continued assistance to Ukraine, and slightly over half back sanctions even at the cost of paying more for energy and food.
The support is somewhat cooler in France, where 47% favor continued arms deliveries to Ukraine, down from 65% in 2022.
Yet this is not an insignificant number, and the majority of French people — including a little over half of RN voters — see Russia as an enemy, according to polls.
Anton Shekhovtsov, a visiting senior fellow at Central European University in Vienna, notes that Le Pen likely remembers well the "reputational nightmare" her Russian loan has caused.
"Everybody just pointed to that loan and said, 'you're all Russian Trojan horses in France,'" Shekhovtsov said in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
Now, Le Pen likely sees an example in Meloni — a politician who emerged from a similar far-right background but maintained a pro-Western course, the expert notes. Meloni's government has been Italy's longest-serving since World War II.
But the AfD has doubled down on its pro-Russian course, despite the majority of Germans continuing to support Ukraine. It does not seem to be hindering its rise.
Jakub Wondreys, a researcher at the Hannah Arendt Institute for the Research on Totalitarianism in Dresden, offers an explanation.
"The key factor is the party's internal division, which we don't see elsewhere. It is specific to German politics, and to the AfD itself," Wondreys tells the Kyiv Independent.
While all parties have different wings, the AfD is notably decentralized, with the former border between West and East Germany surviving as a key divide.
The AfD's extremist, more Moscow-friendly wing is rooted in East Germany, a former Soviet satellite state. The "moderates" are stronger in the west, the researcher explains.
The AfD is growing nationwide, but the east remains its main stronghold — as evidenced by its recent victories in regional elections there. This means that the more extreme wing of the party is also its loudest and most influential one.
This split was laid bare when the AfD's two leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, disagreed over a trip by a group of their colleagues to Sochi last November.
Weidel, who hails from what was West Germany, criticized the visit, while Chrupalla, himself born in socialist East Germany, downplayed it, adding that he does not consider Russia a threat.
Recent polls show that 54% of Germans from what was East Germany think aid to Ukraine has gone too far, compared to 39% in the west. Eastern Germans are also less likely to see Russia as a threat.
Yet even an RN or Reform victory would not bode well for Ukraine, regardless of their change of rhetoric, experts warn.
As Bale points out, no matter its public posturing, a Reform government "might try to spend less money on defense aid behind everyone's back."
Just on Oct. 12, Farage pledged to take a "keen look" at whether British aid to Ukraine is being swallowed up by corruption there and signaled that London's support cannot be limitless.
The RN's victory might not end military support for Ukraine, but it will likely curtail the financial assistance and weaken the European sanctions push against Moscow.
And Shekhovtsov warns that even if Le Pen does not adopt overtly pro-Russian positions after the elections, her victory could be such an upset for France and Europe that it might shift political attention away from supporting Ukraine.
The coming election season has the potential to shake the European pro-Ukraine coalition to its core.

In 2003, just 21,000 species remained in our country. By the spring of this year, their numbers had reached an estimated 4.7 million,” Tokayev said.

“Around 70 percent of its range in our country are within protected areas. Reliable and sustained protection and systematic scientific monitoring have helped its population grow from critically low levels of 90s last century to nearly 190 animals today. Behind all these recoveries are years of hard and dedicated, determined work by the authorities, scientists and international partners,” he noted.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev expressed his gratitude to the Russian Federation and its President, as well as the United Nations Development Programme, the World Wildlife Fund, and other international partners, including NGOs, for their assistance in restoring the population of the Turan tiger.
He emphasized that in July this year, a tiger was released into the wild for the first time in 70 years, marking a milestone for Kazakhstan.
The Head of State also noted that efforts are underway, in cooperation with Czech, German and Hungarian partners, to reintroduce the Przewalski’s horse to Kazakhstan.
The President also highlighted the need to protect the Caspian Sea and its unique biodiversity.
“At the recent first Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan, I called for urgent, coordinated action to prevent fatal damage to this fragile ecosystem. The future of Caspian seals causes a particular concern. Its population has fallen from one million to 270,000 over the past century. In Kazakhstan, the Caspian seal has been officially listed as a rare and endangered animal. We urge all five littoral states and international community to increase efforts to protect these species. The tragedy of the Aral Sea is a stark reminder of the devastating cost of reckless exploitation of nature and we must not allow the Caspian Sea to suffer the same fate,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized

“Millions of Ukrainians who fled and returned are now at risk of being displaced once again, as conditions deteriorate by the day and people face desperate choices in the struggle to survive.”
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in February 2022, triggering the biggest refugee crisis in Europe since World War II.
- Fragile existence -

The IOM has developed 31 solar power stations across the country to support water systems, as these were “harder to attack and harder to destroy completely”.

UN says Gaza malnutrition gains fragile as commercial supplies halt
GENEVA, Oct 16 - Gains in tackling malnutrition in Gaza remain fragile and could be undermined by disruptions to supplies entering the Palestinian enclave, the UN children's agency UNICEF said on Friday, urging that all crossings remain open.
Israel said on Wednesday commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza because of what it described as a dispute over taxes between local merchants and militant group Hamas.
That has cut off a vital source of food and other goods in a territory where most depend on humanitarian assistance after three years of war, repeated displacement and stringent Israeli restrictions on aid deliveries.
Although the ceasefire has improved aid access and reduced large-scale fighting, humanitarian agencies say ongoing strikes, continued displacement and widespread destruction have left civilians highly vulnerable.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva, UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said the flow of both commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.
“The impact on children obviously will be felt if this situation is not resolved," he said.
"We can't go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods, and services that they require."
A new UNICEF report published on Friday found that while the ceasefire since October has allowed more humanitarian aid and commercial supplies to enter, acute malnutrition remains a risk.
The report said progress in pushing back the threat of famine, confirmed by a global food security monitor in August last year, had been achieved through a scaled-up food and nutrition response, the easing of restrictions on the entry of food and nutrition supplies, and the ceasefire.
However, those gains remain fragile, it said.
“Acute malnutrition rates have fallen, but only one in three children under the age of two is currently achieving minimum dietary diversity,” the report stated. A survey conducted by UNICEF in June also found a significant prevalence of chronic malnutrition, affecting one in eight children under five.
UNICEF also called for improvements in living conditions in the largely devastated enclave, where some 800,000 children are still displaced and most live in tents or unsafe buildings as winter approaches, saying better shelter and basic services are essential to support a lasting recovery. REUTERS

Explainer-Why is the battle for Yemen's Taiz so important?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:05:27 UTC
21:05:27 KST

Explainer-Why is the battle for Yemen's Taiz so important?
Oct 16 - The city of Taiz is rapidly emerging as the most important battlefront in Yemen's reignited civil war, pitting the Iran-allied Houthis against the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition.
Houthi forces have encircled Taiz in recent weeks by cutting its main road south to Aden, causing widespread displacement and worsening a humanitarian crisis.
Here's what you need to know:
WHY IS TAIZ SO IMPORTANT?
Any Houthi victory in Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, would mark one of the biggest turning points in the country's long civil war, which resumed this summer after a four-year truce.
Taiz city has an estimated population of almost 600,000, said Katja Juric, Aden-based head of programmes for the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Government sources said 80,000 had fled in the latest fighting.
Taiz has been on the frontline between the Houthis and the government since the first days of the conflict that started in early 2015 and has long been seen as a bastion of opposition to the Iran-allied group.
It is the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen: the rugged hills above both Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based, and the flat coastal plain around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
A Houthi takeover of Taiz would make it much harder for government forces to maintain their counterattack around Bab el-Mandeb and keep the Houthis at arm's length from Aden.
It would also mean a resounding symbolic defeat for the government and the military coalition of Saudi-backed Yemeni forces fighting the Houthis.
WHAT'S THE MILITARY SITUATION AROUND TAIZ?
For years the city has sat at the tip of a government salient stretching north into Houthi territory.
The Houthis held areas to the north, east and west of Taiz, while government forces had the city and its immediate surroundings including Jebel Sabar, the high mountain rising above it to the south.
As fighting in Yemen resumed in recent weeks, the Houthis began making advances to cut off Taiz by seizing territory to the south of Jebel Sabar along the road to Aden, which snakes about 200 km (125 miles) through rugged hills where fighting is slow and difficult.
Sections of the road are now under Houthi control, including at the towns of al-Turbah and Mudiriyat al-Misrakh, leaving Taiz encircled since early October, with the Houthis sometimes shelling government positions in and around the city.
Government forces, backed by airstrikes from the Saudi-led coalition, are trying to drive the Houthis back from their recent gains and reopen the road, but were still losing ground around Taiz rather than recapturing territory in mid-October.
WHY IS TAIZ A STRONGHOLD OF OPPOSITION TO THE HOUTHIS?
Taiz had a long history of difficult ties with rulers from north Yemen and was a hotbed of the 2011 Arab Spring uprisings that toppled veteran former president Ali Abdullah Saleh.
While the Houthis adhere to the Zaydi school of Shi'ite Islam, Taiz is predominantly Sunni Muslim.
Saleh and the Houthis joined forces to seize the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, derailing a political transition that arose out of the Arab Spring and had led to a proposal for a federal, democratic state.
In early 2015, army units loyal to Saleh seized positions in the city, leading to big protests there followed by armed clashes. Protesters accused Saleh and the Houthis of mounting a coup d'etat.
Months of fierce fighting in and around the city followed, with the Houthis and Saleh's army units battling local fighters and army brigades from Yemen's now fragmented military that backed the government.
Taiz citizens endured shelling, sniper fire and terrible shortages in a long siege before government forces eventually drove the Houthis and their allies from the city and re-established a land route to Aden.
The fighting in the city lasted throughout 2015 and parts of 2016, and the siege ran for long stretches until 2017.
WHAT IS THE HUMANITARIAN SITUATION IN TAIZ?
The latest fighting has displaced at least 121,000 in Taiz province, according to the IOM, though many of these are from rural areas outside the city.
Inside Taiz, residents have told Reuters about the shortages they now face of basic items and the huge increase in prices they see in the city markets since the Houthis cut the road to Aden.
Aid agencies have reported widespread shortages of fuel, food, medicines and clean water. Wheat flour stocks in the city are nearly exhausted, the World Food Programme said in mid-October.
The situation risks worsening existing health problems. The UN children's agency UNICEF recently found that one in three of the children it screened in Yemen was malnourished. Cholera, dengue and malaria are all present in Yemen too.
WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?
Government forces backed by Saudi airstrikes are still trying to take back territory to reopen the road, but there is no guarantee they will succeed.
The Houthis, who have upped their attacks on Saudi targets while showing themselves better armed and organised than in earlier phases of the war, are meanwhile trying to cement their siege of Taiz and move closer towards the city.
That might lead to a prolonged siege of the kind that Taiz experienced in the earlier phase of the war.
It's also possible the Houthis might try to take the city. Local opposition means resistance could be fierce and any such attempt could cause a long, bloody battle. REUTERS

Starvation killed 466 Palestinians since 2024, says Gaza Health Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:05:11 UTC
21:05:11 KST

- More than 1.4M people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through end of 2026.
- More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition recorded among children under 5
At least 466 Palestinians, including 157 children, have died from malnutrition and starvation since 2024, Gaza's Health Ministry said Friday.
The figures were released on World Food Day, observed annually on Oct. 16.
At least 189 elderly people died of starvation, representing 40.5% of the deaths, it said.
In August 2025, the UN declared famine in Gaza.
More than 1.4 million people are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026, the ministry added.
 
Starvation as a weapon
Israeli authorities have used starvation as a weapon during the genocide in Gaza since October 2023, according to Palestinian government bodies and rights organizations.
Israel tightened restrictions on crossings in March 2025, preventing thousands of aid trucks waiting at border crossings from entering the enclave.
The restrictions followed widespread hunger in northern Gaza caused by the blockade and limits on food and relief supplies, forcing some residents to eat animal feed and wild plants.
In late May 2025, Israel allowed 87 aid trucks to enter Gaza for the first time after 81 days, according to Gaza’s government media office.
Aid later continued to enter on a limited and intermittent basis under strict restrictions until February 2026, when Israel allowed a limited increase in the number of trucks entering the enclave under a ceasefire agreement.
Palestinian officials said the shipments still lacked sufficient quantities of essential food items.
According to Gaza’s government media office, Israel has allowed in only about 34% of the humanitarian aid trucks agreed upon.
 
Malnutrition reaches 'catastrophic levels'
“Malnutrition and starvation rates in Gaza have reached catastrophic levels that are killing children, the elderly and vulnerable groups,” the Health Ministry said.
More than 1.4 million Palestinians, around 67% of Gaza’s population, are expected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026.
More than 158,000 cases of acute malnutrition were recorded among children under 5 from 2024 through August 2026, the ministry added.
Of them, 18% of children were suffering from severe acute malnutrition that threatened their lives, while 12.2% of children were affected by stunting, indicating the impact of food shortages on their development.
The mortality rate among children under 5 rose from 13.6 to 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births between 2022 and 2025, the ministry said.
It estimated that 74,200 children will need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027.
 
Pregnant women
Among pregnant women, the ministry said the prevalence of anemia rose to 61% in 2026, compared with 41% before the war.
“Around 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded during the first half of 2026, more than three times the number recorded during the previous six months,” it added.
“One in three pregnancies in Gaza is now classified as high-risk,” the ministry continued.
“The figures show that the health consequences of the food crisis are increasingly affecting mothers and unborn children, in addition to children,” it said.
 
Calls for urgent international action
“The right to food is a fundamental human right that does not cease to exist during war,” the ministry said.
It called on the international community and the UN to take immediate action to ensure the safe, sustained and unrestricted entry of food, therapeutic nutritional supplements and medicines into Gaza.
The ministry urged that children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, and the elderly be given priority as the groups most vulnerable to malnutrition.
It also called for support to revive local food production to help curb the worsening humanitarian crisis.
The figures come amid the humanitarian consequences of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, which has caused widespread destruction to infrastructure, health facilities and food production sources.
The war has also damaged farmland, food production facilities and water networks, undermining residents’ ability to meet their basic needs locally.
Repeated displacement, loss of income and soaring prices have further increased families’ dependence on humanitarian aid, while access remains irregular.

Lai said the government has spent the past decade improving access to water, electricity, land, and workers to support industrial growth. Projects connecting water systems across western Taiwan have also made it easier to move water between regions when needed.

Somalia sets date for delayed presidential election
Somalia has scheduled its presidential election for May 15, 2027, following constitutional changes that extended President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s term by one year, the country’s electoral commission announced on Thursday. The decision comes amid opposition criticism of the amendments adopted earlier this year.
The announcement was made by Abdikarim Ahmed Hassan, chairman of the National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission, during an appearance on state television. Elections for both chambers of parliament will take place on April 15, one month before the presidential vote, he said.
The commission also released a timetable for preparations, with voter and political party registration set to begin on November 1, 2026, according to the Somali National News Agency (SONNA).
Mohamud’s presidential term was originally due to expire in May 2026. However, constitutional amendments approved by parliament in March extended the presidential and parliamentary terms from four to five years, pushing elections back to 2027. Opposition leaders, including former presidents and prime ministers, rejected the changes and called for elections to be held as originally scheduled.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed has challenged the constitutional amendments in the Supreme Court, arguing that they were adopted without proper legal procedures or broad political agreement. He also rejected the new election timetable, warning that it could lead to “parallel elections, political divisions, internal conflict and a threat to Somalia’s statehood,” Somalia Today reported on Thursday.
Somalia last held a presidential election in 2022, when lawmakers elected Hassan Sheikh Mohamud for a second term, defeating Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed. The vote followed months of delays and was conducted through an indirect system in which members of parliament chose the president.
The country also faces continuing security challenges from Al-Shabaab, an armed group affiliated with Al-Qaeda that has fought Somalia’s federal government since 2007. The terrorist group conducts raids, bombings, and targeted assassinations in an effort to destabilize the Somali government and regional security structures, and also establish its own rule based on a hardline interpretation of Sharia law.

World Insights: Shoring up power, eroding public trust: Takaichi takes hit over minister's resignation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:00:12 CST
21:00:12 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday appointed ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) lawmaker Arata Takebe as the new farm minister to succeed Kazuo Yana, who resigned a day earlier in what was effectively a dismissal over a string of scandals.
Yana, who joined the cabinet for the first time when Takaichi reshuffled it on Sept. 17, served less than a month, becoming the first cabinet minister to step down over scandals since Takaichi took office last October.
Analysts said Takaichi had prioritized consolidating her own power in making personnel appointments while disregarding appointees' political integrity. The latest controversy has not only dealt a heavy blow to her political credibility but could also affect the implementation of related policies.
If the Takaichi administration remains fixated on right-wing policies and relies on stoking populist sentiment to maintain its approval ratings while failing to address the public's concerns, its governing prospects will only grow dimmer, analysts warned.
"CUTTING LOSSES" UNDER PRESSURE
Japanese media reported in late September that Yana had told a local LDP meeting in May that fiscal 2026 road budgets had been sharply cut for Nasukarasuyama City and Nakagawa Town, two municipalities in his constituency whose mayors did not support him in the House of Representatives election in February.
He was also quoted as saying it was "only natural" to allocate more funds to places that rely on LDP lawmakers.
The remarks sparked a widespread backlash. Yana initially declined to comment on his activities before taking office, saying the issue was outside his ministerial jurisdiction. However, as the controversy escalated and opposition parties pressed him on the matter in the Diet, Japan's parliament, he retracted the remarks and apologized on Oct. 5.
More trouble soon followed. On Oct. 7, Japanese media reported that Yana had arranged free shuttle bus rides for supporters during the 2024 and 2026 House of Representatives election campaigns, possibly in violation of the Public Offices Election Act, which prohibits the provision of benefits and vote-buying.
Answering questions at a House of Representatives session Tuesday, Yana claimed his camp had confirmed with local electoral authorities in advance that the arrangement was lawful. After opposition lawmakers exposed the claim as false, however, he backtracked the following day.
Takaichi had initially made clear that Yana would stay in his post. But as the scandals snowballed and opposition parties stepped up pressure for his resignation, the prime minister shifted her stance, criticizing Yana's remarks and saying she "will not hesitate" to dismiss him "if illegality is found" in his conduct.
With both Takaichi and Yana already scrambling to contain the fallout, fresh media reports emerged on Wednesday that a woman who had helped with Yana's campaign in the 2024 lower house election was paid to call voters and urge them to vote for him, another possible violation of the Public Offices Election Act.
Following the series of allegations and mounting criticism, Yana submitted his resignation at a meeting with Takaichi on Wednesday night, and the prime minister accepted it.
According to analyses by Japanese media, opposition parties, which hold a majority in the Senate, or the upper house of the Diet, have recently moved toward a consensus on submitting a censure motion against Yana.
Although such a motion is not legally binding, its passage would inevitably disrupt parliamentary deliberations and hinder the Takaichi government's legislative agenda, including a bill to temporarily cut the consumption tax on food. Under this pressure, Takaichi had no choice but to let Yana go.
CRONYISM UNDER FIRE
Although Takaichi has tried to contain the damage by cutting Yana loose, questions over her judgment in personnel appointments persist.
Opposition parties and Japanese media commentators argued that Yana's remarks demonstrate that he is unfit to serve as a cabinet minister, or even as a lawmaker, and that Takaichi has made light of the issue, downplaying its gravity.
Kyodo News quoted an LDP lawmaker as saying that Yana believed he would not be replaced because he enjoyed Takaichi's favor, leading him to treat the scandals dismissively. The lawmaker described this as "a downside of (Takaichi's) cronyism."
In fact, Yana is not the only member of Takaichi's reshuffled cabinet embroiled in scandals.
On Tuesday, education minister Yoshihiro Seki admitted that an LDP branch he heads had held political fundraising events within parliamentary office facilities in 2020 and 2024, in breach of the rules.
Because the revenue from both events far exceeded their expenses, and the format of such events makes it easy to conceal the identities of those who bought tickets, a Japanese law scholar described the practice as an egregious form of fundraising that exploits loopholes in the system.
Moreover, both Seki and Yana had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal that came to light in late 2023.
Separately, Hiroshi Nakatsuka, the minister in charge of regulatory reform from the Japan Innovation Party, the LDP's junior coalition partner, was reportedly arrested and indicted in 2007 over a bid-rigging case involving a public construction project while serving as mayor of Hirakata in Osaka Prefecture. He was subsequently convicted.
The string of controversies has cast serious doubt on Takaichi's personnel decisions.
Toshiko Takeya, former Komeito party leader, criticized the LDP for still failing to get to the bottom of the systemic problems behind the slush fund scandal.
Akira Koike, head of the secretariat of the Japanese Communist Party, said the new cabinet lineup showed no sign that Takaichi had reflected on the scandal.
CONSOLIDATING POWER AT EXPENSE OF LIVELIHOODS
Japanese media reports suggested Takaichi's appointment of "scandal-tainted" politicians was intended to shore up her own power base.
In its coverage of the September cabinet and LDP executives reshuffle, Fuji Television Network noted that Takaichi has long struggled with a weak power base within the party. As a result, it said, she relied on the faction of Taro Aso, whose backing helped her win the party leadership race, in making personnel appointments, while bringing in lawmakers implicated in the slush fund scandal to win over members of the former Abe faction.
So far, however, the strategy appears to have backfired.
A poll released by the Asahi Shimbun in late September found that 68 percent of respondents considered the appointment of lawmakers implicated in the slush fund scandal problematic, a view shared by more than half of cabinet supporters and LDP supporters.
The latest poll by public broadcaster NHK, released on Tuesday, showed the Takaichi cabinet's approval rating falling to its lowest level in NHK polling since the prime minister took office.
The top two reasons respondents gave for not supporting the cabinet were that they "don't expect its policies to work" and "cannot trust the prime minister."
While seeking to consolidate her power base by appointing scandal-tainted politicians, Takaichi has not done much to improve people's livelihoods.
The same Asahi Shimbun poll found that 76 percent of respondents considered it problematic that the government had repeatedly promised a consumption tax cut on food without clearly explaining how the measure would be funded.
Meanwhile, a quarterly survey released by the Bank of Japan on Tuesday showed that nearly 90 percent of households polled expected prices to continue rising over the coming year, underscoring persistent public pessimism about the price outlook.
An editorial in the Shimbun Akahata argued that the root of the Takaichi administration's problems lies in a policy agenda focused more on military buildup and constitutional revision. Unless the administration changes course, the editorial warned, the rift between the government and the public will only deepen. ■
