Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:50 UTC
20:32:50 KST

Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
As the US attacks the ICC, Kuala Lumpur welcomes a leader the court’s prosecutor wants arrested. Middle powers must defend international justice.
On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya with a guard of honour and an official luncheon, in the military chief’s first visit since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea in the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people.
Kuala Lumpur calls this pragmatic diplomacy. In reality, it lends a middle power’s credibility to the Trump administration’s retreat from international accountability, weakening the laws and institutions smaller states rely on most.
Domestic pressures
Since May, a surge of online hate speech and misinformation has targeted the Rohingya, Malaysia’s largest refugee community. By late July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than 100 Rohingya told UNHCR that residents of their Penang village had driven them out.
The hostility ignores the facts: Malaysia’s police chief says Rohingya account for 0.02 percent of crime. Yet research by INITIATE.MY and the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found AI-generated content amplifying anti-Rohingya disinformation across Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, casting refugees as a threat and legitimising vigilante violence.
Electoral politics plays a part. After heavy losses in three state elections, and with a general election due by February 2028, Anwar’s coalition may see a hard line on Rohingya returns as a show of control, though voter disillusionment and right-wing rivals make any electoral gains uncertain.
Impunity goes mainstream
Malaysia is not acting alone. Mongolia hosted Vladimir Putin in 2024 despite an ICC arrest warrant, and Hungary welcomed Benjamin Netanyahu in 2025 despite another. Kuala Lumpur denies this is recognition, yet Anwar says Malaysia will work towards Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN, and Min Aung Hlaing wants a seat at the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Each welcome makes the next easier and tells leaders accused of atrocities, from Netanyahu to Min Aung Hlaing, that diplomatic rehabilitation is possible without accountability.
ASEAN has tried this before. In April 2021, Min Aung Hlaing agreed to the Five-Point Consensus, then ignored it: The violence continued, the ASEAN special envoy never met Aung San Suu Kyi, and inclusive dialogue never began. The bloc’s one real lever was excluding military leaders from its summits. Myanmar Specialist, Arkar Hein, said “Welcoming him back with nothing asked in return rewards that defiance and tells Naypyidaw that time and a staged election can achieve what
compromise would otherwise require. Each handshake abroad also makes the regime less willing to offer its opponents real concessions, and convinces them that only the battlefield will decide Myanmar’s future.”
A question of consistency
Malaysia has spent decades building its credibility as a regional peacemaker, a hard-won reputation it now puts at risk. It has facilitated the Bangsamoro peace process since 2001, helping negotiate a landmark peace agreement in the southern Philippines, and has facilitated talks in southern Thailand since 2013. In November 2024, Anwar welcomed the ICC’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, saying they “should be arrested even if they are visiting other countries”. That same month, the ICC prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity targeting the Rohingya, and an Argentinian court has since issued its own.
The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice centres on the 2016-17 operations Min Aung Hlaing commanded, which killed thousands of Rohingya, included mass rapes and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. UN investigators called for him to face genocide charges. Malaysia is not a party to the Rome Statute and has no legal duty to arrest him. But its credibility as a peacemaker and on Palestine rests on applying one standard to everyone.
Returns without safeguards
The returns rest on assurances no independent body can verify. UNHCR says it was not involved in the returns and had no access to verify that they were voluntary, and that safe conditions do not exist. Those returned reportedly included 27 children. Though not a party to the Refugee Convention, Malaysia is bound by the customary principle of non-refoulement, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar has warned of substantial risks.
Naypyidaw says no Rohingya are involved because it does not recognise them as citizens, but other returnees also risk arbitrary detention, prosecution and forced recruitment. The military does not even control Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army holds more than 90 percent of the territory. On September 28, a day before returns began, a military air attack reportedly killed at least 50 civilians there, following more than a dozen other mass killings by the military earlier this year.
Nor can the military-backed government deliver the peace that safe return requires. Its election saw no voting in 67 of 330 townships, and when Min Aung Hlaing offered peace talks in April, the National Unity Government (NUG) and major ethnic armed groups refused. Without a ceasefire and an inclusive political process, assurances of safe return ring hollow.
Malaysia’s frustration is nonetheless legitimate. It has hosted refugees for decades with little international support, and resettlement has shrunk since the Trump administration suspended United States refugee admissions in January 2025. But failed burden-sharing cannot justify returns without safeguards.
Pressure on the court
The ICC exists so that victims of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity can find justice when their own states fail them. That mission now faces unprecedented pressure. On October 9, hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, the Trump administration sanctioned the court itself. Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Chad and Venezuela have announced their withdrawal.
Yet middle powers can push back. Seventy-nine ICC members, including Canada, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, backed the court after the first US sanctions in February 2025, and in May Hungary’s new government reversed its predecessor’s withdrawal. In Southeast Asia, the Philippines surrendered former President Rodrigo Duterte to The Hague, and on October 8 judges found him fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity, with proceedings due to begin on November 30.
Middle powers should say no
Middle powers like Malaysia, and blocs such as ASEAN and the European Union, cannot stop US sanctions, but they need not follow the Trump administration’s lead. As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told the World Economic Forum in January, middle powers “must act together, because if we’re not at the table, we’re on the menu”.
Malaysia and its neighbours should lead by saying no: No to efforts to weaken the court, no to treating Min Aung Hlaing’s presidency as a clean slate, and no to Rohingya returns into an active conflict. Malaysia should back efforts to hold him accountable if ICC judges issue a warrant, and reconsider acceding to the Rome Statute, a move it abandoned in 2019.
Saying no does not mean disengaging. Kuala Lumpur should tie Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN to real progress on the Five-Point Consensus, starting with an end to violence and inclusive dialogue involving the NUG and ethnic armed organisations. At home, it should pause returns until an independent body confirms they are safe and voluntary, and hold accountable those who evict, threaten or attack refugees.
Malaysia should not carry this burden alone. ASEAN partners, members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and donors should fund refugee registration, education and integration, and resettlement countries should restore their commitments. Governments should also hold tech platforms accountable for amplifying anti-refugee disinformation and require swift action against incitement.
For years, Malaysia has offered refuge to the Rohingya and others fleeing Myanmar when few countries would. That record gives it the standing, and the responsibility, to defend the system of international justice it has long championed.

UN Geneva meeting to coordinate Sudan peace efforts
The United Nations and Switzerland will host a major coordination meeting in Geneva on peace initiatives for Sudan. The parties to the conflict will not be attending.
A total of 27 delegations are expected at the Palais des Nations for this sixth meeting, said Naila Hajjar, a member of the team working with the UN Special Envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto. Previous meetings had taken place in other countries.
On the agenda are efforts to reduce clashes and advance the political process. In particular, it is necessary to assess how the various initiatives can reinforce one another, Hajjar explained.
Among the countries expected to attend are the members of the Quad (the United States, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt and Saudi Arabia), as well as Qatar, Turkey, Germany and Norway, which are also involved.
The permanent members of the UN Security Council and international organisations active in Sudan will also take part.

Nevertheless, information will be relayed to these parties, particularly following the meeting. The aim is to produce a joint statement. The delegations will be led by ministers, deputy ministers or senior officials.

Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:14 UTC
20:32:14 KST

Guterres urges faster action and financing to stop biodiversity loss
The United Nations Secretary-General appealed on Friday for governments, businesses and communities to accelerate efforts to protect biodiversity for future generations and all life on Earth.
Guterres was speaking in Yerevan, Armenia, ahead of the opening of the COP17 UN biodiversity conference next week.
“The food we eat, the water we drink, the very air we breathe – all are the gifts of biodiversity,” he told the Leaders’ Summit. “Yet every day, humankind saws another branch off the tree of life.”
Extinction risk
The UN chief said factors such as climate disruption, overgrazing and excessive use of fertilisers and pesticides “are driving the triple planetary crisis of pollution, biodiversity loss and climate chaos”.
As a result, more than a million species face the risk of extinction, “edging us ever closer towards an uninhabitable world,” he warned, adding that “it doesn’t have to be this way”.
Progress falling short
Mr. Guterres said the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed four years ago, had inspired action worldwide.
Nearly 90 per cent of parties have established national biodiversity targets, while more than half have developed national road maps. Since 2022, an additional 1.3 million square kilometres of land and six million square kilometres of ocean have received formal protection.
However, “progress is uneven, and far too slow”, he said. Even if countries fulfil their current commitments, only 26 per cent of terrestrial ecosystems and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030 – “well short” of the Framework’s goal of conserving 30 per cent of the world’s land and sea by that date.
He also highlighted “major gaps” in national targets linked to economic systems, including commitments to reduce incentives that harm nature. Finance, technical capacity, cooperation and data collection remain inadequate, he said, noting that biodiversity financing is less than half of the $200 billion agreed under the Framework.
He stressed that biodiversity cannot be treated separately from conflict, food insecurity, disease threats or climate change. “Addressing any of these crises requires addressing them all,” he said. “And there is no time to waste.”
Government leadership required
The Secretary-General first called for government leadership, urging countries to meet the “30 by 30” target and “shift from policies that destroy nature, to practices that sustain it”.
Priorities include zero-waste and circular economies, sustainable farming, regenerative agriculture, stronger monitoring and transparency and firmer enforcement of existing laws.
He welcomed the Yerevan Declaration and its commitment to integrate biodiversity into government policies, budgets and regulations.
Redirect finance towards nature
His second appeal focused on finance as “the stark truth is, we are spending money on the wrong things”. He noted that for every dollar invested in protecting nature, $30 is spent on activities that damage it.
“In 2023, $7.3 trillion flowed into nature-negative industries,” he said, including polluting heavy industry, destructive agribusiness and fossil fuels.
“I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
The Secretary-General said that meeting global biodiversity, climate and land-restoration goals would require annual investment in nature-based solutions to reach $571 billion by 2030 – equivalent to about 0.5 per cent of global gross domestic product.
Private sector involvement
“But governments cannot do this alone,” he said, calling for the private sector to step up. He pointed to the UN-backed Cali Fund as a mechanism through which companies benefiting from nature can help finance its protection.
Mr. Guterres also cited the rapid growth of renewable energy. The cost of solar power has fallen by almost 90 per cent since 2010 and investment in clean energy is now nearly double investment in fossil fuels. Moreover, renewable energy prevented emissions last year equivalent to the combined emissions of the United States, the European Union and Japan.
“But these benefits are not shared equally around the globe,” he said, noting that many developing countries have been unable to invest sufficiently in both nature and human development due to debt burdens, limited public budgets and an inequitable international financial system.
Participation from across society
The Secretary-General’s final appeal was for broad participation, particularly from young people, civil society, women, Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
“Environmental decline often falls hardest on the most vulnerable, and those who did the least to cause the problem. But the solutions often arise from these same groups,” he said.
With 76 days remaining until he leaves office, Mr. Guterres said that confronting climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution had been among his highest priorities.
“Let us act with the urgency this moment demands,” he said. “For our children. For our future. And for all life on Earth.”

These are the most underrated travel destinations in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:31:54 UTC
20:31:54 KST

A little known region in Romania – Bucovina – topped the list for 2027 in a new ranking of underrated travel destinations by Time Out.
Major tourist destinations like Venice or Barcelona are popular for a reason, but when our love for certain cities is negatively impacting the locals who made it great in the first place, it’s time for a rethink.
The world is a big ol’ place, and there are plenty of lesser-known spots crying out for more visitors. Plus, you’ll have a far better time without having to constantly battle crowds.
Which is where Time Out’s list of the world’s most underrated travel destinations comes in.
Updated annually, the latest ranking has 41 cities and regions on it – and this year’s number one spot is in Europe.
Romania’s Bucovina topped the list for 2027, with Time Out drawing a comparison to the better known Translyvania, saying the region has “the same wild mountain scenery, age-old traditions and mind-boggling architecture”, but without the crowds.
Bucovina has been growing in popularity in recent years as the gateway to Via Transilvanica, the 1,400 km-long hiking trail that our writer Rebecca Ann Hughes took on earlier this year.
Europe’s most underrated travel destinations
The next highest-rated underrated travel destinations in Europe are Spain’s Asturian cities, which placed third.
Coastal spots here have already proven popular, but Time Out suggests heading to cities like Oviedo, Gijón and Avilés, particularly if you’re a foodie.
If you’re looking for a crowd-free beach escape, look no further than Zambujeira do Mar, which ranked sixth overall.
The cliffside town in Portugal’s Alentejo region is home to a Blue Flag-listed beach, and with the exception of the weekend of the MEO Sudoeste music festival, you won’t find many other tourists here.
Placing ninth overall is Carry-le-Rouet in France. The magazine compared the seaside resort to more popular spots like St. Tropez and Cannes, declaring it to be “just as idyllic with sea-to-cliff landscapes, turquoise waters and fresh seafood at a fraction of the cost”.
Just outside of the top 10, The Azores ranked 12th overall. The remote Portuguese archipelago has been attracting more attention in recent years, having been dubbed the “Hawaii of Europe”, but it has been working to ensure its tourism develops sustainably.
A destination certified by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council, there are numerous policies in place to protect the nine islands’ cultural, historical and natural assets.
The top 10 most underrated spots globally
- Bucovina, Romania
- South Dakota, US
- Asturian cities, Spain
- Osa Peninsula, Costa Rica
- San Martín, Peru
- Zambujeira do Mar, Portugal
- Bisbee, Arizona, US
- Shenzhen, China
- Carry-le-Rouet, France
- Tioga Pass, California, US

‘Subsidising suicide’: UN chief urges governments to stop propping up polluting fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:31:33 UTC
20:31:33 KST

Fossil fuels are 'boiling our planet', says Guterres. Yet COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia are expanding them, a new report shows.
"Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide," UN chief Antonio Guterres told leaders today (16 October) ahead of next week's UN biodiversity summit, COP17.
At an event in Yerevan, Armenia, Guterres said governments were still "spending money on the wrong things" and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.
He urged countries to stop subsidising the production of fossil fuels that are "boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity".
"I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead," he said.
EU finance ministers earlier this month called for a phaseout of fossil fuel subsidies at the COP31 climate negotiations taking place in November.
Slow progress on pulling funding for nature-harming activities
Nations have made little headway since pledging in 2022 to reduce public spending on activities that harm nature such as mining, fossil fuel extraction and intensive farming.
Countries have vowed to reduce harmful subsidies by $500 billion (€447b) a year by 2030 but little progress has been made.
"Nature won't thrive on good intentions," Guterres said.
The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about $30 (€27) still goes into activities that degrade it.
This includes an estimated $2.6 trillion (€2.3t) a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.
Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations in Yerevan starting on 19 October where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.
Guterres launched a report on 15 October showing that the world was off track to achieving the 2030 biodiversity targets enshrined in a landmark pact dubbed the Paris Agreement for Nature.
"The war on nature has not yet ended," he said.
What is the Paris Agreement for Nature?
Signed by nearly 200 countries and territories, the nature pact laid out 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030. These included reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30 per cent of the world's land and oceans, known as 30x30.
"It's not all bad news... There is progress, but not enough," Guterres told reporters in Yerevan. "We are far from what is necessary."
The report showed that government policies were insufficient to meet the centrepiece 30x30 biodiversity goal. Taken together, government pledges would cover only 27 per cent of land and inland waters by the end of this decade if enacted in full. For oceans, the figure would be just 12 per cent.
Other targets were lagging further behind. Guterres said countries must honour their financial pledges to developing countries.
The lack of finance has been identified as a particular barrier to achieving the biodiversity goals.
"Biodiversity is in crisis. Species are disappearing and ecosystems are collapsing," said Sue Lieberman from the Wildlife Conservation Society.
"Governments and all stakeholders must see that investing in nature is not a luxury, it is the very key to our survival."
He also emphasised tackling government spending that harms nature, pointing to the "very strong influence" of some sectors that had "too much power" over government including industrial fishing, fossil fuels and logging operations.
COP31 hosts ramp up fossil fuel production
A Global Witness report released this week reveals the power of that influence.
Using data from independent energy consultancy Rystad, the environmental NGO's investigation found that the two COP31 hosts Türkiye and Australia are ramping up fossil fuel production ahead of the major international climate negotiations taking place next month.
Turkish national oil firm TPAO is set to nearly triple gas production. Two of Australia's biggest fossil fuel firms are also on course to hike oil and gas production: Woodside are set to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032 while Santos is on course to increase crude oil production eight-fold by 2035, according to the report.
Türkiye has come under scrutiny for its centrepiece COP31 electrification target. While it aims to raise the global share of energy demand by electricity to 35 per cent, up from around 20 per cent, by 2035, it stops short of specifying how the electricity should be generated. This, critics say, could allow governments to count expanded gas-fired generation as progress towards electrification targets
Efforts to reach a global consensus on setting concrete targets or pathways for phasing out fossil fuels have stalled and the contentious issue is not an official item in the COP31 negotiations.
Earlier his year, about 60 nations demanding faster action on fossil fuels staged their own breakaway conference outside the United Nations process.
Separately from the COP talks, which operate on a consensus-based decision-making process, some countries – including Germany, France and the Netherlands – have released voluntary roadmaps away from fossil fuels. Brazil is expected to follow suit in November.

IMF suggests UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks, as Healey prepares budget raid – business live

IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks
Heather Stewart
Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economics editor, reporting from Bangkok this week:
We’ve just been in the IMF’s Europe press conference, where the topic of bank taxes in the UK came up [following our report that the chancellor is poised to tax Britain’s banks].
Asked about the possibility at JohnHealey’s upcoming budget, HelgeBerger, the economist who is deputy director in the IMF’s European department, suggested there might be better places to look to balance the books.
Berger pointed out that Healey’s predecessor, RachelReeves, had raised taxes in her budgets, saying:
“The last two budgets involved increasing government revenue, and ultimately there’s a moment where this becomes less productive but there’s still areas where Britain can make additional headroom available: modernising the property taxes or VAT, these are good examples. We wouldn’t recommend labour tax.”
Berger added:
“Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP - historically, for Britain, a high number - then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”
He pointed to cost-cutting measures including removing the pensions triple lock, and “better targeting social benefits,” adding, “so I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”
The International Monetary Fund has urged John Healey to target savings on pensions and welfare, instead of taxing Britain’s banks at the budget later this month.
Berger replied that given the UK’s historically high tax-to-GDP ratio, it might be better to “put the emphasis” on cuts.
He said if additional tax revenue were needed, reforming property taxes or VAT might be a good place to start.
He added:
“Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP – historically, for Britain, a high number – then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal [spending] side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”
Berger’s comments came as shares in some UK banks dropped today, as traders anticipated a tax hit in the budget. LloydsBankingGroup and NatWest both fell by around 1%.
News of Healey’s plans provoked a backlash from some quarters.
The CBI said the chancellor should:
avoiding further sector-specific taxation, including on a banking sector already facing a higher tax rate than competing international financial centres.”
Healey "considers new UK investor visa for wealthy foreigners"
Bloomberg are reporting this afternoon that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is considering introducing a new UK visa route for wealthy foreigners.
The goal would be to attract immigrants who can help spur economic growth.
Proposals under considerion, they say, include a visa program directing immigrants to invest in innovative and high-growth sectors. Applicants might also be able to pay a flat-rate tax in exchange for investing in “qualifying investments”.
Bloomberg’s LucyWhite reports:
One option being considered by Healey’s team is a proposal by the Institute for Public Policy Research, which recommends a visa program directing immigrants to invest £5 million ($6.7 million) over five years in a vehicle overseen by the state-owned British Business Bank. The pooled funds would be directed into innovative and high-growth sectors and pay out a set rate of return “significantly lower than market rates.”
Under another proposal by lobby group Foreign Investors for Britain, applicants would pay £2.5 million minimum into “qualifying investments” such as those run by the BBB. In return, they’d be allowed to pay an annual flat-rate tax of £200,000 for up to 15 years.

Elsewhere in the markets, the US dollar has dipped after Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh resisted hinting that his central bank might raise interest rates later this month.
Warsh declined to give any guidance about the Fed’s next move, during his appearance at the IMF’s Annual Meeting today, saying only:

I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.”
The pound is now up almost a whole cent against the dollar, at $1.336.
Over on Wall Street, shares in AI company CoreWeave have tumbled again at the start of trading, as concerns grow over its borrowing levels.
CoreWeave are leading the fallers on the Nasdaq index, down 7%.
Yesterday, the cost of protecting CoreWeave bonds against default rose to the highest intraday level on record.
CoreWeave runs AI datacentres, funded by issuing high-yield debt.

Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at StoneX, says:
CoreWeave was among the names caught up in the recent sell-off, although the stock recovered yesterday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the company’s financial position was improving and its cost of capital was falling. That is hardly an impartial endorsement, given Nvidia’s sizeable interest in CoreWeave, so the more important question is whether the recovery can be sustained once the immediate reassurance fades.
More broadly, this week’s price action suggests the market debate is beginning to shift. The question is no longer simply how large the AI opportunity can become, but how profitable the enormous investment required to realise it will ultimately be.
The head of the IMF on Friday isued an appeald to global leaders to cooperate in the face of multiple economic risks, such as rapid advances in AI and the Iran war.
Kristalina Georgieva said the sheer speed of technological change added to the long list of challenges, including disruptions to the global trading system, high food and energy prices and lingering wars, all of which threatened to widen the gulf between advanced economies and the world’s poor.
Bond markets, she said, were clearly sensing the risks, with US, German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields reaching their highest levels in decades.
“The need of the hour is for urgent and practical international cooperation,” Georgieva told at a plenary session today.
Audit, tax and business advisory firm, Blick Rothenberg argues that increasing the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% back to 8% might backfire.
Artur Vorobyev, a director at Blick Rothenberg, says:
Although this may sound like a reversal of a tax cut, when the surcharge was reduced in 2023, corporation tax increased from 19% to 25%. The combined rate on bank profits went up from 27% to 28%. Increasing the surcharge to 8% now would bring the combined rate to 33%. This is a significant rise and is counterproductive if the Government wants banks to invest and lend more to aid growth.”
Bloomberg: UK banks warn Healey’s tax plan will curtail economic growth
Bloomberg are reporting that the UK’s banking industry has “ramped up lobbying” against extra taxes planned by Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey.
They are apparently warning that a hike could shrink economic output by £6bn over five years and hit areas outside London the hardest.
Bloomberg add:
Pushing a surcharge banks pay on top of a standard corporation tax to 8% from 3% would also cut lending by about £10 billion by 2029 and reduce investment into the UK, according to a letter sent earlier this week to Healey by David Postings, chief of industry lobby group UK Finance.
Demonstrators have been protesting against the IMF and the World Bank at their meeting in Bangkok today, for the second day running.
According to the Bangkok Post, they encountered a police blockade which prevented them walking to Queen Sirikit National Convention Center, where the annual meetings are being held.
The Assembly of the Poor put the number of local and international protesters at 1,000 but the Metropolitan Police Bureau estimated about 800.
IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks
Heather Stewart
Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economics editor, reporting from Bangkok this week:
We’ve just been in the IMF’s Europe press conference, where the topic of bank taxes in the UK came up [following our report that the chancellor is poised to tax Britain’s banks].
Asked about the possibility at JohnHealey’s upcoming budget, HelgeBerger, the economist who is deputy director in the IMF’s European department, suggested there might be better places to look to balance the books.
Berger pointed out that Healey’s predecessor, RachelReeves, had raised taxes in her budgets, saying:
“The last two budgets involved increasing government revenue, and ultimately there’s a moment where this becomes less productive but there’s still areas where Britain can make additional headroom available: modernising the property taxes or VAT, these are good examples. We wouldn’t recommend labour tax.”
Berger added:
“Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP - historically, for Britain, a high number - then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.”
He pointed to cost-cutting measures including removing the pensions triple lock, and “better targeting social benefits,” adding, “so I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.”
Higher taxes on banks could have an impact on the FTSE100 since the banking sector makes up nearly 20% of the UK blue chip shares index, says Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.
The UK’s banking sector has been extremely resilient this year and has performed positively, for example Lloyds Banking Group is higher by 20% in the past 12 months. The risk is that downward pressure will now build, and this will dim the attractiveness of the entire index.
We will need to wait for the Budget to get the details of this tax, afterall, this is the Labour Party and they are well known for their U-turns. The Chancellor may need to water down plans for a tax if he wants to avoid denting both the economy and the FTSE 100.
Back in Bangkok, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva has warned that the risks of artificial intelligence may exceed its opportunities if no adequate safeguards and ethical framework are put in place.
During a panel discussion that included Anthropic co-founder JackClark, Georgieva said AI was already strengthening the global economy, but could also deliver negative shocks if it failed to deliver major productivity gains as quickly as hoped, Reuters reports.
Georgieva says:
“If there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities. And above all, we do need an ethical foundation, and I’m not sure we are there as a society.”
The pound has touched its highest level against the US dollar in over three weeks.
Sterling has gained half a cent to $1.3335, its highest level since 23 September.
Traders are expecting the Bank of England to raise interest rates in November – higher rates are typically good for a currency’s value.
Investors will also be weighing up the impact of the budget later this month – and wondering whether John Healey will maintain the UK’s fiscal headroom – the buffer for meeting its borrowing rules.
Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at global financial services firm and FX specialists Ebury, says:
“The question that matters most to us is how the budget could affect the pound and the gilt market.
We see the fallout in markets as dependent on whether Healey can keep the economic damage to a minimum, while convincing markets that future spending plans won’t come at the expense of debt sustainability.”
Pensioners could suffer if the government hikes taxes on banks, points out Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell:
“The government might argue that banks are doling out significant amounts of money in dividends to shareholders, implying there is plenty of scope for them to pay a little bit more tax. The flipside is that any hit to dividends to offset higher taxes would penalise the large number of people in retirement who invest in banking shares for income.
In other banking news, the UK government reportedly tried to persuade UBS to shift its headquarters and stock market listing to London in the event of the bank relocating out of Switzerland.
Rachel Reeves pitched London as a potential new home for UBS in discussions with the bank’s chair Colm Kelleher during her time as chancellor, according to people briefed on the talks.
The pair discussed the possibility of UBS moving its legal headquarters and listing to the UK if it were to redomicile, the people added, with the most recent meeting taking place earlier this year.
Will Howlett, financials analyst at QuilterCheviot, points out that the jump in bank profits means tehy can absorb higher taxes.
He also suggests that higher bank taxes are already ‘priced in’ to the company’s share prices, saying:
“With the runup to the Budget and the rumour mongering that comes with it now in full flow, the government seems to be giving the UK’s banking sector some mixed messages. John Healey has called the UK’s banks a ‘jewel in the crown of the economy’, yet briefings suggest they are going to get hit by a fresh increase in the levy on its profits.
“The banks did manage to escape such measures last year, but with higher interest rates now expected for longer, the government may be thinking now is the time they can strike, especially if they want to limit the number of personal taxes they go after at the budget. The government is facing increased fiscal pressure as a result of the Middle East shock, and while economic growth is solid just now, this would appear easier pickings to help bolster the public finances.
“That said, much of this is reflected in valuations, with UK domestic banks already trading at a discount to European peers. That may explain the relatively muted reaction to share prices this morning. More domestically focused banks, like Lloyds and NatWest have seen drops in their share prices of around 2%, although this is far smaller than the approximately 6% hit you would see if the surcharge were raised by 5 percentage points back to the 8% where it stood previously. Much of the bad news is already priced in at a time where the banks are also able to absorb such a hit thanks to the profits they are making at the moment as a result of higher interest rates.

The EU is discussing the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine again — who is for it and who is against it

The EU is discussing the use of frozen Russian assets for Ukraine again — who is for it and who is against it
Kyiv • UNN
EU leaders have resumed discussions on using Russian assets to support Ukraine. Belgium stated that its position remains unchanged.
European leaders on Friday, October 16, resumed discussions on using frozen Russian sovereign assets to support Ukraine, despite Belgium's continued opposition to the scheme, which it successfully blocked last year. Rapporteur reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
"The frozen assets are there: they should be used to support Ukraine. It's that simple," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said ahead of the second day of the EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where Ukraine's financial needs were to be discussed with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also noted that these assets, the vast majority of which are located in Belgium, are the "most obvious place to turn to" in order to support Ukraine, which, according to the publication's estimates, will face a $78 billion funding shortfall next year.
These assets "serve a dual purpose: they will finance Europe's defense, but they will also mean that Russia, which is currently causing so much destruction both in Ukraine and in Europe, will itself pay for everything it is doing," Frederiksen said.
The EU's chief diplomat, Kaja Kallas, also proposed using Russian assets to cover Ukraine's impending budget shortfall. "I am sure that [the leaders] will raise this [issue] today," she said. "Ukraine needs this money right now."
The comments came several weeks after Sweden, Spain, Poland and the Netherlands wrote to the European Commission, urging it to revive last year's heated debate on using these assets to support Ukraine.
Belgium rejected Germany's initiative last year to provide a "reparations loan" backed by the assets, citing legal and financial risks for Euroclear, the Brussels-based securities depository that holds €190 billion in Kremlin funds intended for use in the loan.
Ultimately, EU leaders decided to issue €90 billion in joint debt to finance Ukraine, as well as to freeze the Russian assets indefinitely.
The remarks also came several hours after Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever told reporters that his country's position remained unchanged.
"At the end of a conflict, there is always a peace agreement, and part of that peace agreement is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever said at a press conference that began after midnight on Friday.
"Are there people on this planet who might dream of doing this differently this time and using these assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is: yes, there are. Are they in this building? They are. Are there [some] outside this building? Yes, there are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," he said.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin also hinted that he did not want to resume discussions on the frozen assets on Friday.
"We strongly supported the issue of seizing [these] assets and the possibility of using them, but ultimately it produced no results," said Martin, whose country currently holds the presidency of the Council of the EU.
"I recognize the amount of energy and effort that went into this last time. I would be more supportive of doing something effective, efficient and as quickly as possible on this issue," Martin said.

Nuremberg at 80: How do you put a death machine on trial?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:29:28 UTC
20:29:28 KST

Nuremberg at 80: How do you put a death machine on trial?
On the night of October 16, 1946, 10 individuals were hanged in the Nuremberg prison. These were the main Nazi criminals who had been captured and brought to trial.
Despite the horrifying scale and brutality of the crimes, the Nuremberg Trials remain one of the most controversial proceedings in world history.
Justice instead of revenge
The idea of an international tribunal to address Nazi atrocities had been considered for some time. In 1942, the Soviet Union established a special Extraordinary Commission that gathered information about these crimes. Tragically, it had a lot of work to do. The USSR became the primary battleground for the bloodiest and most brutal war in Europe.
The range and nature of the crimes committed on Soviet soil were staggering: genocide against multiple peoples, mass killings on various grounds, all sorts of war crimes, deliberate attacks on medical facilities and civilian infrastructure, arbitrary executions, economic exploitation, and sexual violence. Essentially, every town liberated from the Nazis had enough evidence to warrant its own tribunal. When the concentration camps were liberated, it became clear that Allied propaganda had not exaggerated but rather understated the extent of Nazi atrocities.
In addition to the Soviet government, the exiled governments of occupied countries – Belgium, Czechoslovakia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Poland, Norway, France, and Yugoslavia – also wanted to hold the Nazis legally accountable for their crimes.
The outlines of the future tribunal began to take shape in the fall of 1943 during a conference in Moscow attended by the foreign ministers of the ‘Big Three’ – the USSR, the UK, and the US. The three powers agreed that Nazi leaders who committed crimes across multiple nations should be tried by an international court.
At that time, even the idea of lynching Nazi leaders seemed valid. Benito Mussolini was executed along with his mistress by Italian partisans on April 28, 1945, without any trial. Their mutilated bodies were publicly displayed. No one mourned Mussolini; similarly, no one would have objected if a Red Army soldier had shot Hitler.
Sporadic acts of vigilante justice also occurred as the war neared its end. A well-known incident involved American soldiers executing the staff of the Dachau concentration camp. Polish troops beat to death Oscar Dirlewanger, the commander of a punitive brigade responsible for countless deaths in Belarus and Poland.
Yet vigilante justice was not what the Allied leaders envisioned.
The men in the dock – and those who escaped it
It became clear that the crimes committed were not only widespread but complex. Determining individual responsibility was not always an easy task. The Nazis had taken measures to conceal their atrocities whenever possible; for example, they buried the remains of over 100,000 people, mostly Jews, after executing them at Babi Yar ravine near Kiev. Furthermore, once the Reich collapsed and arrests began, everyone began shifting blame onto one another, particularly onto those who had already died.
By April and May of 1945, most of the individuals who would eventually be tried at Nuremberg had been apprehended. Of course, many key figures were never tried.
For obvious reasons, Minister of Propaganda Joseph Goebbels and Hitler himself were absent from the trial: both had committed suicide before they could face justice. Heinrich Himmler, the head of the SS, was captured by two freed Soviet prisoners, yet during a medical examination, he swallowed a poison capsule and died. Heinrich Müller, the leader of the Gestapo, likely shot himself in late April or early May 1945. His body was discovered months later in a temporary grave.
The fate of Martin Bormann, Hitler’s private secretary and head of the party chancellery, was unknown for many years. He went missing, which in 1945 could imply that he had fled under an assumed identity. However, today we can say with certainty that Bormann was killed in the final hours of the defense of Berlin, while attempting to break out of the encircled city alongside a column of German troops.
Twenty-four people were tried in Nuremberg. The most prominent among them was Hermann Göring, the commander of the Luftwaffe, who held numerous official and unofficial positions, served as Hitler’s close associate, and was considered the second most powerful man in the Reich.
Other figures included the Minister for Occupied Eastern Territories and the Nazis’ chief ideologist Alfred Rosenberg; Chief of the Armed Forces Command Wilhelm Keitel; Minister of Foreign Affairs Joachim von Ribbentrop; and the head of the security service Ernst Kaltenbrunner.
Nuremberg’s Palace of Justice was chosen for the trials for several practical reasons. It had direct access to the prison, was in relatively good condition, and was well-equipped to accommodate large numbers of people.
Unprecedented crimes, untested law
The decision was made to conduct the trials according to established legal standards, allowing the defendants the right to defend themselves. The Nazis found attorneys to represent them. Admiral Karl Dönitz took an interesting approach: he secured a maritime law specialist as his lawyer, but said that if he were not allowed to work with him, he would choose the admiral of the Allied forces who commanded submarines as his lawyer.
Rosenberg pursued a different strategy by trying to recruit Hans Frank, who was also being tried for war crimes as the governor of occupied Poland, and happened to be a lawyer by training. However, this request was denied. Furthermore, since the court needed to address the criminal status of certain organizations, and Martin Bormann was absent from the trial, the court appointed its own attorneys. The judges were from the USSR, the US, the UK, and France.
A significant challenge arose from the fact that some legal norms were developed during the trial itself. As a result, defense attorneys argued that the court was fundamentally unlawful since it relied on laws that did not exist at the time the defendants committed their crimes. Certain participants stated that Nuremberg represented “victor’s justice.” This sentiment partly fueled Winston Churchill’s earlier wartime suggestion to execute the political leadership of the Reich outright. The problem was that such a trial was unprecedented – nothing similar had ever been attempted before – and required the unveiling of many layers of guilt to find the responsible persons.
For example, one of the most repugnant acts leading to the mass death of people was the so-called Barbarossa Decree issued in May 1941. This document was signed by Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel, chief of the German armed forces. It effectively removed accountability for crimes committed by Wehrmacht soldiers and officers against Soviet civilians. Such actions could only be punished if they harmed German interests. If a soldier looted and killed a peasant, Keitel technically bore no responsibility, as the soldier operated within the legal framework that existed at the time.
Additionally, during the trial, Keitel’s attorney attempted to shift all blame onto the dead Hitler, citing that Keitel “was just following orders.” Moreover, the fact that the USSR did not sign several international agreements designed to protect war participants, especially prisoners of war, compounded the issue. The mortality rate among Soviet POWs during WWII exceeded 50%; in absolute terms, 3.3 million out of 5.7 million documented prisoners died. And this was just a small part of the challenges faced by the judges at Nuremberg.
The prosecution comprised four categories of crimes: crimes against humanity, crimes against peace, war crimes, and general conspiracy crimes. There was a significant challenge in aligning the legal positions of the USSR, the UK, and the US. Soviet law existed as an independent branch but was rooted in continental legal principles; meanwhile, the British and Americans relied on their own legal frameworks; for instance, the concept of ‘conspiracy’ was unique to these countries and was not typical in Soviet or German law.
Additionally, the Allies often favored a compromise stance whenever they could have been held accountable for similar actions themselves. This enabled Admiral Dönitz to mitigate his own sentence: although German submarine forces under his command fought ruthlessly, British and American submarine forces could have been accused of similar conduct.
Witnesses, evidence and Göring’s defiance
In some cases, the Allies had to make real compromises with their conscience. One such case involved Erich von dem Bach-Zelewski, who participated in the proceedings as a witness. This man had directly overseen mass killings during counter-partisan operations in Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Poland.
A horrifying tactic employed by his subordinates involved rounding up villagers in partisan areas into one building, which was then set ablaze. The mass slaughter of Poles during the Warsaw Uprising in 1944 is another example of his policy – about 15 civilians were killed for every lost insurgent.
Zelewski understood that his survival depended on betraying others, so he turned on everyone, revealing their darkest secrets. Hermann Göring shouted from the defendant’s stand, “You disgusting traitor, swine!” but there was nothing he could do. Ultimately, a German court sentenced him to life in prison, not only for his wartime actions but also for murders committed during the power struggles in Germany in the 1930s.
The tribunal had volumes of documents to examine. American judge Robert Jackson later recalled that he had approached stories of Nazi atrocities with skepticism before the trial, but was horrified by the reality that unfolded before him. He was particularly struck by an SS report detailing the destruction of ghettos – Jews leapt from burning buildings, and some attempted to crawl away on broken legs; they were hunted down like game.
While most defendants tried to speak evasively, Hermann Göring stood his ground until the very end. He was informally dubbed ‘Fuhrer of the Defendants’. Göring urged his co-defendants to remain defiant and not to confess. He showcased his skills as an orator, made sarcastic remarks, and effortlessly parried the initial accusations.
According to him, Gestapo actions and concentration camps were just a response to the terrorist actions of the communists; and the extermination of Jews was merely harsh rhetoric, there were no actual plans for their annihilation. He claimed to have had no hand in any acts of aggression, insisting he was always taken by surprise by such acts. He also maintained that the Reich had to strike preemptively against the USSR to defend itself from potential Soviet aggression. As for the humanitarian catastrophe in occupied territories – that was the fault of the Soviet authorities and their scorched-earth tactics; and any crimes committed by German soldiers were merely isolated incidents.
Göring steamrolled over Justice Robert Jackson with his shameless demagoguery. However, the Allies had seized enough documents to bring down the Reichsmarschall. Soviet prosecutor Roman Rudenko and British prosecutor David Maxwell-Fyfe hammered Göring with his own orders that led to mass starvation. Göring knew that he intended to starve millions and openly discussed it in his circles.
In contrast, Albert Speer, the Minister of Armaments, didn’t plead for mercy; he acknowledged his guilt and presented himself as a humble technocrat, successfully avoiding the gallows.
The defense generally argued that the Nuremberg Tribunal established no new legal norms, yet the entire legal framework had been crafted specifically for this trial. Moreover, the conspiracy concept (one of the four main charges) allowed individuals to be condemned for being affiliated with criminal organizations. This was an unprecedented model in continental European law, including German law, and many lawyers deemed it inapplicable.
Even the term ‘genocide’ was used retroactively, having only emerged during the trial itself. Additionally, the defense reduced the discourse to the notion that the defendants were either uninformed or inadequately aware of the crimes being committed, while the actual perpetrators were presumably already in their graves.
The verdicts and the gallows
Out of 24 defendants, only 12, including Göring and Keitel, received death sentences. In reality, there were only 11, as the fate of Bormann remained unknown. Three others received life sentences – including naval commander Erich Raeder and Minister of Economics Walther Funk – but both were released in the 1950s. Rudolf Hess, one of Hitler’s associates, was sentenced to life in prison and committed suicide in 1987 at age 93. Albert Speer and the leader of the Hitler Youth organization Baldur von Schirach both received 20-year sentences. Interestingly, three people were acquitted: propagandist Hans Fritzsche, diplomat Franz von Papen, and financier Hjalmar Schacht.
Two others managed to evade justice altogether. Party official Robert Ley committed suicide before the trial even began, while Göring somehow obtained poison and took it just hours before his execution.
On the evening of October 15th, three gallows were erected in the prison gymnasium. Before midnight, the condemned were roused from their cells and led out. Execution began just after one o’clock, and by 2:45 AM, it was all over. The bodies were transported to Munich for cremation, and their ashes were scattered.
But that wasn’t the end of it. Following the main trial, there were 12 ‘mini-trials’ which focused on Nazi doctors, judges, and the case of the Einsatzgruppen (paramilitary death squads), among others. In total, 142 more individuals were found guilty, with 13 sentenced to execution. Many of these defendants were just as monstrous as those hanged in the primary trial. For instance, doctors were accused of a range of inhumane experiments on human subjects, including frostbite experiments, the deliberate poisoning of victims, and intentional infection with deadly diseases, among other atrocities.
Among those hanged was Waldemar Hoven, the chief physician at the Buchenwald concentration camp, who conducted gas poisoning experiments on inmates. A whole team of SS officers was convicted in connection to the Einsatzgruppen case. For unclear reasons, out of 24 individuals, only a few were actually executed, despite all being directly responsible for the murders. Among those executed was Paul Blobel, who organized the mass killings at Babi Yar. Additionally, separate trials occurred in various countries under their national laws. In Norway, 12 Germans and 25 collaborators were executed. In Poland, Rudolf Höss, the commandant of Auschwitz, was hanged following a separate trial.
***
The Nuremberg Tribunal was an impressive judicial process, and the Allies’ decision to hold it deserves commendation. The trial wasn’t perfect and it’s true that it departed from traditional methods of justice. Many legal norms were established retroactively; moreover, in the subsequent trials, many Nazi criminals managed to escape justice. However, Nuremberg wasn’t merely about ‘victor’s justice’. No one would dare say that those horrific criminals were hanged unjustly. Most importantly, while the principles of justice established in Nuremberg may have been imperfect, they are still effective in situations reminiscent of the horrors perpetrated by the Nazis.

German parliament backs tobacco tax hike for revenue, public health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:28:41 UTC
20:28:41 KST

Ayhan Simsek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Germany’s lower house of parliament late Thursday approved a phased-in increase in the tobacco tax that is expected to raise the average price of a pack of 20 cigarettes from roughly €8 ($9) now to about €9 next year and nearly €12 by 2030.
The Bundestag backed the measure with votes from the governing coalition of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left SPD. Officials project the step will generate roughly €12 billion in extra federal revenue over the four years.
The increases will take effect step by step each January from 2027 through 2030. Brand cigarettes could cost as much as €14 by the end of the period. Fine-cut tobacco used for rolling cigarettes will also become significantly more expensive.
The figures are average projections based on the higher rates the coalition approved; manufacturers will set the actual retail prices, which can vary by brand.
The government has cited both the need to consolidate the federal budget and protecting public health. The additional revenue is not earmarked and will enter the general budget. Past tobacco tax rises have mainly helped close fiscal gaps.
Health experts see higher prices as an effective way to encourage people to quit. The German Cancer Research Center has reported that about 131,000 people died in Germany in 2023 from tobacco-related diseases. A 2025 survey found that 19% of people age 15 and older in the country smoke.

He is suspected of establishing and leading a criminal organization, as well as seizing more than UAH 71 million while setting district heating tariffs in Ivano-Frankivsk. According to the investigation, the man headed a criminal organization of five people, including the founder and executives of private companies that produced and transported thermal energy in the Ivano-Frankivsk municipality. The organizer was the ultimate beneficial owner of the affiliated enterprises.
During the 2021–2023 heating seasons, the participants submitted inaccurate calculations to local government bodies for setting tariffs: they artificially inflated heat production costs and concealed the actual losses incurred during its transportation.
As a result, the budget of Ivano-Frankivsk suffered losses of more than UAH 71 million, while city residents paid for heat they did not actually receive.
In December 2025, the man was notified in absentia that he was suspected of misappropriating property on an especially large scale through abuse of office. In January 2026, he was notified of new charges—establishing and leading a criminal organization, misappropriating property on an especially large scale, and entering knowingly false information into official documents (Part 1 of Article 255, Part 4 of Article 28, Part 5 of Article 191, Part 1 of Article 366 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The investigation established that the suspect had left Ukraine back in June 2025. On January 22, 2026, he was placed on an international wanted list
Prosecutors from the Ivano-Frankivsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office are currently preparing a request to the competent Spanish authorities for his extradition to Ukraine.
In March 2026, prosecutors referred the indictment against the other four members of the organization to court. The trial is ongoing.

US in ‘denuclearisation’ talks with Russia and China: Trump
The US and Russia each have more than 4,000 warheads. China is set to catch up with them within five years, Trump says.
The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced.
Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”.
China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years.
“The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking to Russia about that, and we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.”
China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. Newsmax reported that Trump spoke with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the subject, but no further details regarding the talks with either Russia or China were revealed.
Russia has the world’s largest stockpile of nuclear warheads, and the US is close behind, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI).
The two countries together possess an estimated 86 percent of all nuclear weapons globally.
China has the third largest nuclear arsenal, according to SIPRI, having expanded it to 620 warheads in the past year.
Trump’s claims came shortly after the expiration of the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, an arms control agreement between the US and Russia to limit their nuclear arsenals.
A month after the treaty expired, French President Emmanuel Macron announced the Forward Deterrence Initiative as Russia’s nuclear sabre-rattling during its war on Ukraine has spooked Europe.
Former Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs Gareth Evans told Al Jazeera that the world’s interest in the risk of nuclear weapons has waned.
“[The] world … has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding,” he said

Europe’s best party cities for a Halloween night out, according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:26:02 UTC
20:26:02 KST

From Edinburgh’s fiery Samhuinn festival to Dublin’s Gothic celebrations, Europe has plenty of ways to get into the Halloween spirit.
Halloween falling on a Saturday in 2026 means plenty of us will be keen to make the most of the spooky holiday, even travelling abroad to celebrate it.
Now, a new ranking has revealed the best party places to experience All Hallows' Eve across the globe.
Travel experts at Adventure360 analysed some 113 cities worldwide to uncover where travellers can find the biggest Halloween celebrations this year.
Each individual city was scored on the number of Halloween events happening between 30 October and 1 November, as well as the size of its nightlife offering and late-night restaurant scene.
The safety of the city was examined, too, and the report noted whether or not the destination hosts a signature Halloween or Day of the Dead event. In the end, each city was given a score out of 100.
In first place was New York, with a score of 91.1 out of 100, and it was followed by another US city, Chicago, which got a score of 80.1.
In terms of countries, the US had the most showings in the top 10, with New Orleans coming in at number nine but, continent-wise, Europe was revealed to be far and away the best Halloween destination, with five spots on the list.
Edinburgh is in third place, thanks in part to its legendary Samhuinn Fire festival, while Dublin follows close behind, partially because of its Bram Stoker festival.
Madrid, London and Prague also feature in the top 10, despite none of them actually offering a signature Halloween event; they’re just that spooky!
Within the Halloween top 20, other European cities included Rome, Berlin, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Budapest, and Lisbon
The world's best Halloween party cities 2026
How the cities rank out of a score of 100, according to the Adventure360 study:
- 1. New York, USA – 91.1/100
- 2. Chicago, USA – 80.1/100

Europe’s top five cities for Halloween parties
Following the ranking, these are the five best cities to spend Halloween in Europe this year – and the reasons why.
Edinburgh, United Kingdom
Scotland’s capital Edinburgh may only have a relatively small number of nightlife venues and late-night restaurants, but it boasts plenty of Halloween-themed events, not least the Samhuinn Fire festival.
The event brings a dramatic twist to Halloween, with Calton Hill transformed by fire, drumming, acrobatics and elaborate costumes.
Taking place on 31 October, the event reimagines ancient Celtic traditions marking the end of summer and the arrival of winter, with performers acting out the battle between the Summer King and Winter Queen.
Dublin, Ireland
Dublin has just seven Halloween-themed events – one of the lowest amounts in the top 10 – but it makes up for it with its legendary Bram Stoker festival.
This year, the celebration of the city’s Gothic heritage will take place from 23-26 October, with four days of spooky events inspired by the author of Dracula.
Expect haunted walking tours, horror theatre, candlelit library visits and a spectacular parade. There’s family-friendly fun, too, including Stokerland, a free gothic-themed park at St Patrick’s Park.
Madrid, Spain
Madrid may not have one big signature Halloween celebration, but there’s plenty to get stuck into.
For a dose of horror, head to MADHORROR at IFEMA Madrid, running from 30 October to 2 November, with haunted houses, horror films, gaming and comic-book events.
After dark, join a ghost and legends walking tour through the old town, or head to Malasaña for costume parties and late-night drinks and eats.
London, United Kingdom
Although England’s capital doesn’t have a signature Halloween event, it does have some 22 themed happenings, as well as more than 1,000 nightlife venues and 2,600 late-night restaurants, which is the highest number in the top 10.
Head to Kew Gardens for its illuminated Halloween trail, featuring Dracula’s Lair, live performers and a Headless Horseman, or explore the capital’s darker history on a Jack the Ripper walking tour.
For something quirky, the London Transport Museum is holding a Halloween silent disco among its historic trains and buses.
Prague, Czechia
Prague’s Gothic streets make a fitting backdrop for Halloween, with plenty of ways to get into the spooky spirit.
While the Czech capital doesn’t have a signature event, Wonderland Halloween takes over the historic Lucerna Great Hall on 30 October for a night of elaborate costumes, live performances, DJs and theatrical decorations.
For something more low-key, join a ghost tour through the Old Town’s narrow lanes and medieval underground passages, where guides share tales of murder, alchemy and restless spirits.
On 30 October and on Halloween night itself, the legendary five-floor nightclub Karlovy Lázně will play host to its annual Wicked Weekend event.

Swiss journalist risks court sentence for exposing top banker
ZURICH, Oct 16 - Zurich prosecutors this week charged Swiss journalist Lukas Haessig with violating banking secrecy over reporting that set off a high-profile corporate criminal trial of the former boss of Raiffeisen Bank Switzerland, Haessig said on his financial blog Inside Paradeplatz.
• Zurich-based Inside Paradeplatz published a series of articles in 2016 about Pierin Vincenz, former CEO of Raiffeisen Bank Switzerland, and his business partner Beat Stocker, who were found guilty of fraud in April 2022
• That verdict is currently under review by a higher court expected to rule in January 2027
• Police in June 2025 searched the blog's Zurich office and home of its founder, seizing evidence linked to suspected violation of Swiss banking law
• Prosecutors had dropped the case in December 2025, but Zurich's High Court in April said a court must decide how the banking secrecy provision should be interpreted after a complaint by Stocker
• Article 47 of the Swiss Banking Act criminalises disclosure of confidential information leaked by bank insiders, with penalties of up to three years in prison or a fine
• Press freedom group Reporters Without Borders Switzerland called the charges troubling and said Article 47 of the Swiss banking act must not be used to prosecute journalists
• Inside Paradeplatz's reporting was clearly in the public interest, Reporters Without Borders said, adding the banking secrecy law had a chilling effect and pointing to "legal shortcomings" in Switzerland on press freedom
• Prosecutors said the presumption of innocence applies to Haessig. No court date has yet been set REUTERS

Coercive diplomacy: What does the call between Netanyahu and al-Sharaa really mean?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:24:04 UTC
20:24:04 KST

The phone call between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Syrian interim leader Ahmed al-Sharaa—following months of firing salvos via fighter jets, missiles, and third-party intermediaries, alongside strikes that targeted the courtyard of the Syrian Ministry of Defence and the perimeter of the presidential palace—was no ordinary diplomatic formality. Rather, it was a condensed moment signalling a tectonic shift in the geopolitics and power balance of the Middle East.
When Netanyahu and Sharaa speak directly to discuss sectarian tensions in the Druze-majority province of Sweida, we are not merely witnessing a localised security arrangement dictated by geography and overwhelming force. We are standing before a series of uncomfortable questions shaping the region’s future: Is Syria capitulating entirely to the rhythm of Israeli power, which has established itself as an unyielding arbiter in the new Syrian landscape? Or is this a pragmatic response from Damascus to pressure from an Arab bloc seeking regional normalisation—a bloc that views any effort to rebuild and reintegrate Syria as passing, one way or another, through the neutralisation of active fronts with Tel Aviv?
Furthermore, who granted Israel and Netanyahu the political and international mandate to act as the self-appointed custodian over Syria’s Druze minority?
The most realistic answer lies elsewhere: in a devastated economy, a shattered state apparatus, and a transitional authority that has come to realise that rebuilding Syria requires, above all, zeroing out external hostilities. States emerging from the crucible of war do not enjoy the luxury of managing multiple conflicts at once. Today’s Syria looks far closer to this exhaustion model than to the legacy slogans of traditional “Resistance.”
Yet, the phone call poses far larger strategic dilemmas than it answers: Is this a tactical manoeuvring aimed at preventing escalation and buying time, or the beginning of a structural shift redefining Syria’s place on the regional map? Is Sharaa treating Israel as an unalterable geopolitical reality, or is the entire region entering an era where ideological mantras surrender to the imperatives of economic survival, reconstruction, and stability?
Anticipating an answer requires reading this new Syrian stance not as absolute surrender, but as a tightrope walk driven by a “survival mindset.”
Sharaa lacks the military capacity to engage an adversary that strikes the heart of Damascus with international impunity. Conversely, he understands that total compliance with Israeli terms risks sparking domestic fragmentation and delegitimising his rule regionally.
Hence, the most plausible regional scenario is Damascus moving toward ending the “active state of war” without entering the formal fold of political normalisation—establishing a security framework for borders and minorities that satisfies regional patrons while isolating Syria from radical axes to minimise reconstruction costs.
On the Israeli side, Netanyahu is attempting to engineer an advanced “politico-security belt” reaching deep into Syria’s social fabric.
By asserting proxy guardianship over minority populations like the Druze, Tel Aviv aims not only to secure its northern border, but to institutionalise a model of a “regional patron” holding the keys to stability in broken neighbouring states.
This style of power projection forces any future government in Damascus—whether led by Sharaa or another—to operate within a security architecture drafted in Tel Aviv long before it reaches the halls of the United Nations.
Ultimately, what transpired was not the announcement of a new alliance, but a mutual acknowledgment of a new balance of power. It is an equilibrium in which Netanyahu realizes his security influence remains incomplete without ordering his immediate Syrian backyard, while Sharaa recognizes that reclaiming statehood may require, for the first time in decades, managing relations with Israel through state pragmatism rather than ideological rhetoric.
The significance of the call lies not in its brief duration, but in its role as a barometer for a Middle East where yesterday’s political impossibilities have become today’s negotiating points.
Yet, all these calculations could swiftly evaporate or invert should Netanyahu lose power in the upcoming Israeli elections.
READ: Damascus rejects Israeli politicisation of Syria’s Druze after Netanyahu’s brief call with al-Sharaa
The core dilemma rests not solely within Syria, but in the nature of the Israel that Netanyahu embodies today. Under his tenure, Israel has transformed from a state seeking security-driven compromises into an actor behaving as the region’s absolute power, backed by an unprecedented surplus of self-confidence—perceived by its adversaries as military hubris and by its leadership as earned strategic dominance. Thus, any potential Syrian opening cannot be disentangled from the persona of the man wielding power in Tel Aviv.
Is Damascus reaching out to Israel as a permanent state institution, or is it coercively adapting to an extraordinary “Netanyahu moment” and the hard facts it has established on the ground? This question is no less vital than the issue of normalisation itself. If Netanyahu departs the political stage and Israel reverts to more conventional, less aggressive security calculus, the strategic weight of these contacts may shift overnight. They may well be reinterpreted as fleeting security arrangements dictated by temporary power dynamics rather than enduring strategic realignments.
When the dust settles, we may discover that the true historical event was not the phone conversation between Sharaa and Netanyahu, but the historical epoch that produced the phenomenon of Netanyahu itself—an era that compelled the entire region to redefine power, deterrence, and sovereignty under the weight of a prolonged war that has not yet ended, but will not forever remain governed by the logic of a victor who believes history moves by his will alone.
