Deputy BSW leader Claudia Wittig insisted that Berlin should go further than a one-off fuel agreement and resume regular imports of Russian oil and gas to help rescue German industry.
- 15:56 GMT After all the applause, embraces, and promises of unwavering support, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz confirmed the summit had achieved exactly nothing on Ukraine, and that “there were no decisions, but there was an exchange of views.” He also confessed that the €90 billion loan already agreed for Kiev “will not be enough” and that EU members will need to empty out their pockets once again while the European Commission assesses how much more is needed. Merz also found room to endorse Ukrainian strikes on Russian communications and energy infrastructure, describing them as “right, reasonable, and understandable.” Finding agreement on Europe’s own finances, however, has proved difficult, Merz admitted, stating it was impossible to predict whether leaders would reach a budget deal. Discussions could continue at an additional November meeting and at December’s regular summit, he said.

At the same time, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas pointed out at the summit that while the bloc can bankroll Kiev, it cannot offer an alternative to Starlink.
- 14:46 GMT Zelensky’s updated €70 billion demand has prompted EU leaders to ask the European Commission to find other ways to cover Ukraine’s estimated funding gap next year, according to four of the bloc’s diplomats. The suggested options include tapping frozen Russian assets, using unused SAFE defense loans and issuing more common debt – reportedly the likeliest route, repeating the approach behind the €90 billion loan already being disbursed. The idea of seizing frozen Russian assets still faces Belgium’s resistance and warnings of legal and financial fallout. More joint borrowing would put another bill on Europe’s books, and EU member states are already struggling with energy costs and competing spending demands. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson was even more categorical about increasing spending on the bloc, telling reporters after the summit that “Sweden is not an ATM for the European Union budget.” The Commission is expected to present its options at the informal EU summit in Dublin on November 13. For now, leaders have agreed that someone should work out where the money will come from.
- 13:54 GMT Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker questioned Ukraine’s shifting financial demands ahead of the summit and demanded to see the actual numbers before dishing out any more funds to fill Zelensky’s ever-growing budget hole. “So many numbers are swirling around that you have to put them in order… you have to make it transparent, where this hole comes from,” he said. Ukraine’s proposed budget put next year’s shortfall at roughly $40 billion. The country’s prime minister subsequently cited needs exceeding $52 billion, plus $45 billion in off-budget military requirements. In his Friday address, Zelensky put the number at a staggering €70 billion in additional financial and military support, far exceeding Brussels’ previous estimates; it would come in addition to the €90 billion support loan slated to be rolled out this year and next year. The requests come against a familiar backdrop of corruption investigations, including an alleged $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom linked to Zelensky’s former business partner Timur Mindich, and more recent cases involving inflated defense construction contracts. - 13:50 GMT Zelensky expressed horror and shock at the prospect of Russia getting its frozen foreign assets back, begging the Europeans to hand them over to Kiev before that happens. “Ukraine would like to receive these funds in some kind of format,” he said, insisting that Russia should not have an opportunity to influence future discussions about its own reserves. He also thanked the EU for last year’s €90 billion bailout, before making clear he doesn’t intend to stop dipping into their pockets. The appeal follows reports that US negotiators proposed releasing some of the frozen Russian assets as part of a peace settlement. European officials have rejected the initiative and have revived, yet again, the debate on how to appropriate the funds. “The frozen assets are there: that’s what should be used for supporting Ukraine. Simple,” Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said. Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen called them “the most obvious place to look,” with Kiev estimating a $78 billion funding black hole next year. However, “simple” has yet to convince Belgium, which has repeatedly blocked the previous scheme, warning that appropriation could trigger enormous legal liabilities and undermine confidence in Europe’s financial system. Moscow has condemned confiscation as theft and threatened retaliation.
- 12:41 GMT In the final question of the press briefing, Sky News decided to take part in the Zelensky show and give him a clippable moment. “Are you a scapegoat for Trump’s midterm troubles,” the outlet’s reporter asked. Zelensky said nothing, glanced at his notes, and said “that is my answer,” prompting laughter from the press room.

Moscow has repeatedly denied plans to attack the bloc, dismissing the allegation as a pretext for European rearmament and continued funding for Kiev. A number of EU military officials have also cited a lack of evidence for any such plans.

In the same breath, however, he acknowledged that the restrictions had also disrupted medium-range strikes. He denied using the network for attacks deep inside Russia, but complained that lower speed limits had deprived Kiev of other strike capabilities. EU leaders pledge continued support for Ukraine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:35 CST
20:08:35 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 16, 2026 shows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a European Union (EU) summit in Brussels, Belgium. European Union (EU) leaders vowed Friday to continue financial and military support for Ukraine, and reaffirmed their commitment to advancing its EU accession process, as Zelensky joined the second day of an EU summit here. (Xinhua/Weng Xinyang)
BRUSSELS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- European Union (EU) leaders vowed Friday to continue financial and military support for Ukraine, and reaffirmed their commitment to advancing its EU accession process, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky joined the second day of an EU summit here.
The bloc must increase its support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia to bring Moscow to the negotiating table, said European Council President Antonio Costa.
"This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions," Costa told reporters alongside Zelensky and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Von der Leyen said the EU was working on its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, accusing Moscow of failing to respect an energy ceasefire proposed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The EU leaders also discussed Ukraine's preparations for the coming winter and its financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027.
Zelensky thanked the EU for its continued support and said Ukraine's top priority was securing energy supplies ahead of winter, along with air defense systems and funding.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas also called for stronger support for Ukraine ahead of winter, while acknowledging Europe's dependence on U.S. military technology.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately, in the short term Europe can't replace this capability," Kallas told reporters ahead of the summit.
She also acknowledged difficulties in coordinating with Washington over the conflict, saying the EU was trying to persuade its American partners to increase pressure on Russia.
Costa and von der Leyen reaffirmed their support for Ukraine's EU accession, welcoming the opening of two additional negotiating clusters. Von der Leyen said the goal was to open the final two clusters by the end of the year, while Zelensky pledged to continue implementing necessary reforms. ■

U.S. companies to top CIIE exhibition area for eighth straight year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:19 CST
20:08:19 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on preparations for the 9th China International Import Expo, in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- U.S. companies will top the exhibition area at the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) for the eighth time, with their area up 1,500 square meters from last year, an official said on Friday.
The ninth CIIE will be held in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE was designed to expand China's opening up and turn its vast market into a shared opportunity for the world.
Preparations for the ninth CIIE are basically complete. A total of 162 countries, regions and international organizations will take part, with 4,142 overseas companies exhibiting, China's Vice Minister of Commerce Yan Dong told a press conference.
The overall exhibition area will exceed 440,000 square meters for the first time. In the enterprise exhibition, companies from the United States, Germany, Britain and France will lead the pack in terms of exhibition space.
For the first time, the number of Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders attending the event will surpass 300. Additionally, over 2,000 companies will be exhibiting at the CIIE for the first time.
This year's CIIE will feature over 200 representative global debuts and first-time exhibits. A variety of cutting-edge innovations that empower industries and enhance people's lives will be showcased together, including endoscopic surgical robots and cochlear implants.
Ahead of this year's CIIE, matchmaking sessions themed under "export to China" were held in countries including Egypt, Germany and Britain, bringing procurement talks to the doorstep of trading partners.
The CIIE is a prominent example of China's efforts to expand imports and provide more channels for quality products from around the world to enter the Chinese market. This commitment has remained high on China's agenda, and the results are tangible.
According to the General Administration of Customs, China's imports reached 16.7 trillion yuan (about 2.48 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first nine months of this year, up 22.3 percent, the fastest growth since 2021.
Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao said earlier this year that China's market holds huge potential, adding that the country will bring in more agricultural goods, quality consumer products, advanced technology equipment and key components. Meanwhile, platforms like the CIIE will be fully used to expand import channels, he said.
"Exports and imports are like two wheels of a vehicle. The more balanced they are, the smoother and farther it goes," Wang said. ■

The idea was to allow residents to express their views on whether or not they agreed "that the Lisbon City Council" should cease "to authorise the operation of electric scooter-sharing schemes in the municipal public domain once the current licences have expired."
In an interview with the Now outlet on Thursday, the mayor indicated that he would present the proposal at a council meeting, expressing hope that the Socialist Party, which also voted in favour of a similar suspension in Braga, would support the decision, so that an "immediate suspension of shared scooters" in the city could be implemented.

T-beam installation completed on 2nd China-Mongolia cross-border railway
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:11 CST
20:08:11 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The installation of all T-beams on the Gantsmod-Gashuunsukhait railway, the second cross-border railway link between China and Mongolia, was completed on Friday following the placement of the final prefabricated beam.
Measuring 32.6 meters in length and weighing approximately 134 tonnes, the final T-beam was installed by China Railway Construction Bridge Engineering Bureau Group Co., Ltd. The milestone lays a solid foundation for subsequent construction work.
The Gantsmod-Gashuunsukhait railway is the second cross-border railway link between China and Mongolia, nearly 70 years after the Erenhot-Zamiin-Uud railway opened in 1956. The project is expected to become a new link in infrastructure connectivity between the two countries.
The railway is being jointly developed by China and Mongolia under the principle of "unified design, independent construction and integrated commissioning." The line crosses the border at the Gantsmod port in China and the Gashuunsukhait port in Mongolia before connecting to Gashuunsukhait station in Mongolia's Umnugovi Province.
Construction of the cross-border railway project began in May 2025. The route is 9.91 kilometers long, including a 6.08-kilometer cross-border bridge section that requires the installation of 760 T-beams. The heaviest individual beam weighs 149.5 tonnes.
Handling and installing such heavy structural components requires a high level of technical expertise, rigorous safety management and precise equipment operation. Construction has also been complicated by the route's desert environment. Having overcome numerous challenges, the project team completed all work to high standards and quality.
The Gantsmod-Gashuunsukhait railway marks a significant step forward in strengthening strategic alignment and practical cooperation between China and Mongolia.
Once operational, the railway is expected to transport 30 million tonnes of cargo annually, linking the Gantsmod Railway with Mongolia's southbound railway network. The project is expected to expand bilateral trade, improve transport and logistics connectivity, and stimulate economic activity along the route. It could also support the development of cross-border logistics services, industrial parks and border trade facilities in both countries.
The railway is expected to play an important role in deepening China-Mongolia economic cooperation and advancing high-quality cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative. ■

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Azerbaijan, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
BAKU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met with Israeli President Isaac Herzog at the latter's request on the sidelines of the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia here on Thursday.
Herzog said the Jewish and Chinese peoples have a long history of exchanges. The two peoples helped each other during the World Anti-Fascist War, forging a friendship that has become a memorable chapter in history.
Israel firmly adheres to the one-China policy and is committed to advancing friendly relations with China, he said. Israel is willing to take the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries next year as an opportunity to expand exchanges and cooperation in areas such as science and technology, investment and people-to-people exchanges.
Herzog briefed Wang on Israel's views and position on the situation in the Middle East, saying that Israel seeks peace, not war, but faces threats and challenges to its national security that require a strong response.
China has always been an important constructive force in promoting peace in the world and the region, Herzog said. Israel attaches importance to the relevant initiatives and proposals put forward by China, appreciates China's efforts to promote regional peace and stability, and stands ready to maintain communication with China, he added.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that during World War II, both the Chinese and Israeli peoples suffered greatly from the ravages of war and extended a helping hand to each other in times of hardship, giving rise to many moving stories.
Since the establishment of diplomatic relations more than 30 years ago, bilateral relations have developed steadily and practical cooperation has yielded positive results, Wang said, adding that the key lies in upholding mutual respect, treating each other as equals and pursuing mutually beneficial cooperation.
Next year will mark the 35th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between China and Israel and the 10th anniversary of the establishment of their innovative comprehensive partnership. China stands ready to work with Israel to take the anniversaries as an opportunity to review experience, advance cooperation and consolidate the foundation of public support for bilateral relations, Wang said.
Wang said promoting peace and reconciliation in the region is the cornerstone of China's Middle East policy. China has consistently maintained that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century and that the two-state solution is the right way to resolve the question.
The situation in the region remains tense, while peace and tranquility are still on a long way to go, Wang said, the current top priority is to open full access to the Gaza Strip. The 2 million civilians there must not be left struggling on the brink of survival, nor should the humanitarian catastrophe be allowed to continue spreading; Israel should halt and reverse the forced establishment of settlements in the West Bank, he added.
Wang stressed that since the beginning of this year, President Xi Jinping has put forward a series of initiatives and proposals to promote peace and security in the Middle East, which are public goods that China has provided to the Middle East and the world.
China stands ready to work with the international community to uphold and practice the vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative and sustainable security, encourage all parties to return to the track of dialogue and consultation as soon as possible, and seek political solutions to conflicts, Wang said.
Wang said Herzog's father, former Israeli President Chaim Herzog, promoted the establishment of diplomatic ties between China and Israel during his presidency and was the first Israeli president to visit China.
The elder Herzog wrote in his memoir that compromises and negotiations do not always result in losing something, but often bring about important gains and long-term trust. These words remain relevant and instructive under the current circumstances, Wang said.
The Palestinian question is the root cause of the Middle East issue, Wang noted, adding that both the Jewish and Palestinian peoples have the right to live in peace and establish independent states.
China believes that as long as all parties remain committed to and maintain their resolve to pursue peace, seek a path to peace by moving toward each other, and stay on the right course of the two-state solution, the peace that people have long yearned for will eventually come, Wang said. ■

Explainer: Will Washington pull the trigger on Houthis?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:09 CST
20:08:09 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi group of resuming attacks on Saudi Arabia and deliberately seeking to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
"The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump wrote on Truth Social, warning that he would "never forget" the attacks.
Following a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, speculation is mounting over whether the United States will enter the fray militarily.
ALLY BUT NOT WAR PARTNER
The Trump administration has so far stopped short of joining Saudi Arabia's direct military campaign against the Houthis, despite Riyadh's calls for greater U.S. involvement. Multiple U.S. media outlets reported in September that Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud urged Trump to order U.S. strikes against the Houthis, but Trump declined, opting instead for intelligence sharing and targeting assistance.
The exchanges reflect the limits of the U.S.-Saudi security alignment. Although Washington has a longstanding interest in Saudi security, it does not automatically share Riyadh's military objectives in Yemen. For the United States, protecting its ally and safeguarding regional shipping routes do not necessarily require directly taking part in Saudi offensive operations.
Ali Bin Hadi, an Aden-based military observer, told Xinhua that he saw "little appetite in Washington for another confrontation with the Houthis" after previously seeking to disengage from that front. "Washington may help contain the fire, but it is unlikely to step into it," he said.
Jarrah Mutlaq Al-Qazaa, media adviser at the Kuwait Journalists Association, said that continued escalation could alter Washington's calculation. He said the likelihood of direct U.S. military involvement would depend largely on whether Houthi attacks continue to cause heavy casualties, the extent to which Riyadh seeks U.S. participation, and whether Washington sees scope for limited strikes capable of restoring deterrence without drawing it into a prolonged war.
Trump's remarks on Tuesday offered a further indication of his approach. He told reporters he might ask Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests. "President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask," Trump said. The comment reflects Washington's apparent preference for greater involvement from regional partners rather than committing U.S. forces directly.
DEPLETED MUNITIONS LIMIT OPTIONS
One reason Washington may be reluctant to launch military strikes against the Houthis is its depleted weapons stockpiles after months of operations against Iran, during which it has used substantial numbers of missile interceptors to defend its bases and allies. This depletion has not only left Gulf partners, Saudi Arabia in particular, increasingly vulnerable, but also constrained its options in pondering any direct military intervention against the Houthis.
The Congressional Research Service, in a report updated on Oct. 5, noted concerns over the stockpiles and availability of U.S. munitions, including missiles and interceptors, following the U.S.-Israeli military operations against Iran that began in late February. The report warned that depleted stockpiles could narrow Washington's options for sustaining operations and supporting its allies.
Citing a Congressional Budget Office estimate, the report said the United States had "probably used between one-half and two-thirds" of its inventory of certain missile interceptors. Such weapons are critical to protecting U.S. forces and regional allies against missile attacks, while replenishing stocks could take considerable time.
Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, was quoted by Reuters as saying that Saudi Arabia's air defense capabilities and integrated defense network remained less advanced than those of Israel or Ukraine. He added that Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defense against air attacks harder than defending Israel or any single U.S. base.
The challenge is also compounded by the Houthis' evolving military capabilities. The group has developed greater capacity to assemble and deploy drones and missiles, while years of fighting have given it experience in adapting its tactics.
OIL PRICES RAISE POLITICAL STAKES
The conflict also carries domestic political risks for Trump as the United States approaches its Nov. 3 midterm elections.
On Tuesday, Trump accused the Houthis of "purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections." He warned: "I'll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget!"
His remarks linked the security crisis to a domestic concern that could weigh on voter views of his administration.
The economic pressure is already evident. U.S. Consumer Price Index rose 3.7 percent in September compared with a year ago, while gas prices jumped 9.1 percent from the previous month, according to data released Wednesday by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
And rising fuel costs driven by the conflict in Iran have piled pressure on Americans ahead of the midterm elections.
A Pew Research Center survey released Oct. 8 found that 74 percent of Americans were "very concerned" about gasoline and energy prices, up from 60 percent in July. Separately, 84 percent of registered voters said the economy was "very important" to their vote in the Nov. 3 mid-term elections. The findings suggest that any further rise in fuel prices could add to voters' economic concerns as they assess the administration's performance.
Against this backdrop, energy prices have become an increasingly prominent concern for the Trump administration. ■

Disaster Risk Reduction Week: building resilience starts at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:08:04 UTC
20:08:04 KST

Disaster Risk Reduction Week: building resilience starts at home
TEHRAN – Iran is marking Disaster Risk Reduction Week from October 13 to 19, focusing on the importance of improving the health of individuals, families, and the safety of homes, raising public awareness, and strengthening family economic resilience before the disaster strikes.
The beginning of the week coincided with the International Disaster Risk Reduction Day, IRNA reported.
 
The days of the week highlight the following topics:
 
Tuesday, October 13, ‘healthy individual, the cornerstone of societal resilience’
 
Wednesday, October 14, ‘family mental health, the first step towards resilience’
 
Thursday, October 15, ‘a safe and resilient home for everyone’
 
Friday, October 16, ‘raising social children, a resilient generation’
 
Saturday, October 17, ‘a resilient home, simple steps to take from now on’
 
Sunday, October 18, ‘resilience culture, training everyone’
 
Monday, October 19, ‘family economy, a resilient family’
The International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction was started in 1989, after a call by the United Nations General Assembly for a day to promote a global culture of risk-awareness and disaster reduction. Held every 13 October, the day celebrates how people and communities around the world are reducing their exposure to disasters and raising awareness about the importance of reining in the risks that they face.
Themed ‘Resilience Starts at Home’, this year the day highlights that everyone deserves a home that is safe, affordable and able to withstand the hazards around it. There’s no place like home. It is where we seek comfort, safety and shelter. But when floods rise, extreme heat takes hold or other hazards strike, the place meant to protect us can become the frontline of disaster.
Making that possible takes more than individual preparedness. Governments need safer planning and building standards; businesses must put long-term safety before short-term gains; and communities need information, resources, and a voice in decisions about where and how they live.
Around the world, solutions are already taking shape — from families moving to safer homes in the Philippines to centuries-old earthen building techniques keeping homes cooler across West Africa.
 
Because resilience is not only about rebuilding after disaster. It starts before disaster strikes, and it starts at home.
UNESCO chair inaugurated
In September, Minister of Science, Research, and Technology Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, and the Secretary-General of Iran’s National Commission for UNESCO, Hassan Fartousi, inaugurated the UNESCO Chair in Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience Engineering at Kharazmi University.
The chair is established on a synergistic approach aligned with the Sendai Global Framework for Risk Reduction, the Sustainable Development Goals, and UNESCO’s approaches to expanding education, science, technology, knowledge exchange, climate considerations, and the development of sustainable communities, msrt.ir reported.
According to Kharazmi University, the establishment of the chair represents a scientific and strategic imperative, given the current national and regional conditions in the country, such as climate change, the growing complexity of hazards, the expansion of human settlements, technological and human-induced risks, and the cascading effects of disasters.
This UNESCO Chair develops effective methods to assess and mitigate risks from natural hazards to existing and new school infrastructure, contributing to improved equitable access to safe learning environments for children in vulnerable communities, ensuring continuity of education services, and reducing life losses. The Chair has created a community for resilience engineering exceeding 3,000 members from more than 100 countries, instrumental in sharing knowledge to support disaster risk reduction initiatives.

Japan weather agency apologizes for mistakenly issuing "9.9-magnitude" earthquake warning
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:08:00 CST
20:08:00 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 16, 2026 shows a pop-up alert on a mobile phone, canceling an early warning of a megaquake and strong seismic shaking, in Tokyo, Japan. Japan's weather agency on Friday apologized for mistakenly issuing an early warning of a megaquake and strong seismic shaking around midday. The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said the error was caused by its system misidentifying the epicenter and overestimating the temblor's magnitude as a catastrophic 9.9. (Xinhua/Jia Haocheng)
TOKYO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Japan's weather agency on Friday apologized for mistakenly issuing an early warning of a megaquake and strong seismic shaking around midday. The warning was canceled minutes later but temporarily disrupted train services in parts of the country.
The Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said the error was caused by its system misidentifying the epicenter and overestimating the temblor's magnitude as a catastrophic 9.9.
The agency said it is investigating the cause of the erroneous projection.
At around 12:40 p.m. local time, the JMA issued the alert for a wide area stretching from northern to central Japan, warning that strong shaking could occur in those parts. However, eight minutes later, it issued a follow-up notice canceling the warning.
The agency later confirmed that a 6.9-magnitude earthquake had struck Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula at a depth of about 160 km at around 12:38 p.m.
The early warning had forecast shaking of up to 7, the highest level on Japan's seismic intensity scale, but the strongest shaking actually recorded was an intensity of just 1, in Hakodate City, Hokkaido Prefecture, according to the JMA.
Public broadcaster NHK reported that the JMA's earthquake early warning system detects the faint tremors in the initial moments of an earthquake and automatically estimates its focus, magnitude, and seismic intensity using waveform data observed by seismographs near the epicenter.
When the system forecasts strong shaking of lower 5 or above on Japan's seismic intensity scale, it issues an earthquake early warning. ■

Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:07:38 EEST
20:07:38 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) welcomes the efforts of the government and the Verkhovna Rada to reinvigorate reforms in Ukraine. Resuming these reforms is a key condition for the successful completion of the combined second and third reviews of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program by the end of this year. A second essential condition is the provision of financing assurances from partners, stated Mateusz Szczurek, Director of the IMF’s European Department.
"We plan to conduct the second and third reviews of the program by the end of this year. Naturally, this depends on the resumption of reforms, as well as on the provision of financing assurances by partners," he said during a press conference held on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
Szczurek emphasized the critical importance of adopting legislation and implementing other measures related to revenue mobilization and public administration, as these are vital for securing further donor financing, starting as early as 2026.
Regarding new assumptions and the potential need to revise the EFF program, the IMF European Department Director pointed to the Ukrainian government’s draft state budget for 2027, currently submitted to parliament, which is based on the assumption that the war will continue for a longer period.
"This, of course, increases the financing requirement for 2027 (...) As for the structuring aspects, that is a topic for discussion during the combined second and third reviews of the program, so we will provide details once they are made public," noted Szczurek.
During this year’s IMF Annual Meetings, held from October 12–18, the Ukrainian delegation is discussing with the Fund the implementation of the new four-year Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program, valued at $8.1 billion, which was approved at the end of February this year. This program is part of a broader $136.5 billion external financing package for the 2026–2029 period, based on the baseline scenario.
In July, the IMF completed the first review of the program and disbursed a second tranche of approximately $690 million, bringing the total funding received under the new program to $2.2 billion. At the same time, it was noted that some of the program’s structural benchmarks had not been met by their respective deadlines. Following the first review, the EFF program was updated to include eight additional structural benchmarks, seven of which are fiscal in nature.
Discussions are currently underway to combine the second and third program reviews, with the aim of presenting the matter to the Executive Board before the end of this year. This would coincide with the approval of a combined third and fourth tranche disbursement, totaling approximately $1.65 billion.
"Bringing this to the Board depends on receiving sufficient and credible financing assurances to cover the projected funding gap, on terms that are consistent with maintaining Ukraine’s debt sustainability," IMF spokesperson Julie Kozack stated in early October.
Finance Minister Marchenko noted that, ahead of the expected IMF mission visit in November, it would be desirable to secure confirmation for all sources of the $52.6 billion in external financing required for the 2027 state budget; currently, about $32.6 billion of that total still awaits confirmation.
According to Marchenko, Kyiv expects the European Union to fulfill its commitment to cover two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs for next year as well—a move that would increase confirmed funding by approximately $17.5 billion. As for the remaining balance of roughly $15 billion, the minister explained that there are several potential sources to cover it, including bilateral financing, guarantees, and programs with international financial institutions.

Pezeshkian urges ‘peace diplomacy’ to protect biodiversity, condemns ecocide
TEHRAN – President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for “peace diplomacy” to protect biodiversity, condemning the devastating environmental impact of wars of aggression as ecocide and urging the international community to establish effective, transparent and enforceable mechanisms to safeguard natural heritage during wartime.
Speaking on Friday, October 16, at the summit of heads of state and government held as part of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Pezeshkian said war is not only a threat to people and infrastructure but also a direct driver of environmental destruction. “War burns forests, destroys wetlands, contaminates soil and water, and displaces wildlife,” he said.
Pezeshkian described environmental cooperation as a bridge between nations, stressing that biodiversity conservation could serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
“In a region facing security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations,” he said.
Such cooperation, he added, can pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned and in harmony with the natural world.
“Today, we stand at a pivotal moment in history when biodiversity is no longer merely a scientific or environmental concern. It is also an issue of peace and security, human health, food and water security, and intergenerational justice for all the inhabitants of our planet,” Pezeshkian stressed.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran was among the first countries to recognize the legal and international significance of this issue and become a party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). However, Iran’s relationship with biodiversity goes far beyond its membership in an international convention.
With an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and an extraordinary diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources, Iran is the custodian of an invaluable and irreplaceable natural wealth. This heritage is the result of millions of years of evolution, natural dynamism and adaptation, and is reflected in the culture, customs, livelihoods, indigenous knowledge and historical identity of the people of this land.
Owing to its exceptional geographical location, Iran lies at the intersection of several biogeographical regions. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, and from arid and desert landscapes to the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran is home to thousands of plant and animal species, as well as valuable genetic resources. These natural assets underpin the country’s ecological stability and sustainability, provide a vital foundation for water and food security and human health, strengthen resilience to natural hazards, and serve as a cornerstone of sustainable development.
In Iran, biodiversity, together with climatic and geographical diversity, is deeply intertwined with human history and civilization. Friendship with, respect for and protection of nature are integral to the cultural, religious and ritual identity of Iranians. Nature has long been regarded as an inseparable part of human life and a trust to be preserved for future generations. Many traditional ways of life, agricultural and livestock-raising practices, the use of medicinal plants, and the indigenous knowledge of Iranian communities have evolved over time through an understanding of and adaptation to nature, reflecting thousands of years of interaction between humans and the natural world.
For Iran, therefore, biodiversity conservation means far more than protecting species and their habitats. It means safeguarding a natural, cultural and civilizational heritage.
In my country, drawing on a long-standing culture of respect for nature and in line with national and international goals and commitments, the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plan has been developed and approved. The Department of Environment has been designated as the national coordinating authority, while a mechanism for non-governmental participation, with priority given to local communities, has also received government approval.”
He highlighted that protecting threatened species and restoring vulnerable populations are among the key priorities. These efforts include expanding protected areas and monitoring flagship wildlife species.
“War does not target only human lives and economic infrastructure. It also damages nature: burning forests, destroying wetlands, contaminating soil, threatening water resources, destroying habitats, displacing wildlife, and introducing chemicals and heavy metals into natural cycles. The environmental consequences of war can persist for years after hostilities have ended.
The international community now recognizes that environmental destruction during armed conflicts is not a minor or incidental consequence of war. Such damage is directly linked to the security and well-being of future generations.
In our region, including Iran, the environmental consequences of military conflicts must receive greater attention from the international community. The war of aggression launched by the United States and the Israeli regime in our region has threatened natural ecosystems and damaged environmental protection infrastructure built over years of efforts to conserve biodiversity. Attacks on industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollutant emissions, and soil and water contamination have all contributed to these threats.
This is not merely a domestic issue or one confined within a country's political borders. Nature recognizes no political boundaries, and the spread of water, soil, and air pollution does not stop at national frontiers. The environmental damage caused by war is therefore global in nature and requires international solutions.”
The effects of war on ecosystems can persist for years or even generations, affecting areas hundreds or thousands of kilometers away. One stark example is the scale of destruction in Gaza, where, according to experts, parts of the territory's soil may remain incapable of supporting natural life, vegetation, and ecological cycles for hundreds of years. The destruction caused by wars of aggression in our region amounts to what is known as “ecocide,” or environmental genocide, and must be condemned, Pezeshkian underlined.
“The international community is expected to establish effective, transparent, and enforceable mechanisms to protect natural heritage and biodiversity. No country should be allowed to treat nature as a silent and defenseless victim of war.
The Islamic Republic of Iran is committed to implementing the Convention on Biological Diversity and advancing global goals for nature conservation. In Iran, we pursue the protection of natural areas, wetlands, forests, rangelands, wildlife habitats, and genetic resources alongside sustainable development.
However, we must be realistic and fair. A country facing the mounting pressures of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, and dwindling natural resources, while also grappling with the effects of economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources, needs genuine international cooperation to implement its environmental programs and repair the damage it has sustained. This is particularly true when the country has been targeted in two consecutive years by what it describes as criminal wars involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases allegedly intended to cause environmental damage, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.”
He emphasized that biodiversity conservation will remain confined to negotiations, resolutions, and the setting of targets unless it is backed by adequate financial resources, equitable access to knowledge and technology, and capacity-building.
“If developing countries are expected to protect their forests, wetlands, species, and genetic resources, they must also be provided with the means to fulfill that responsibility. This is the true meaning of environmental justice.
We therefore call on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions, and relevant organizations and bodies working in environmental protection and sustainable development to strengthen mechanisms for mobilizing financial resources, assessing environmental damage, restoring damaged ecosystems, and supporting affected countries in addressing the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.”
In conclusion, Pezeshkian said that the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready to cooperate constructively with the international community in this joint effort by sharing its scientific and academic capacities and experience with other countries. “We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as an important pillar of “peace diplomacy.”
In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the unlawful and expansionist presence of powers, climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations. These bridges can pave the way toward peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future in which human life is aligned with and harmonious with the natural world.
 
It is a future free from war, bloodshed, and destruction, in which biodiversity serves as a shared foundation for the well-being and prosperity of present and future generations.”

‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:05:45 UTC
20:05:45 KST

‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
Forged signatures and thumbprints – even of dead and fictitious people – allegedly used to get land for bauxite mine.
Koraput, India – Raghunath Khara was shocked to look at his thumb impression on a piece of paper that declared he had consented to a government proposal to mine his village’s pristine forest land for bauxite.
He says he never gave that thumb impression.
“I always sign in English. It was someone else’s thumb,” alleged Khara, a shopkeeper in Balda village in the tribal-dominated Koraput district of Odisha state in eastern India.
Khara is among hundreds of people from Indigenous tribes in Balda and neighbouring Bannur village who have lost their lands to the new bauxite mine. It is being developed by Kalinga Alumina Limited, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises Limited, a conglomerate owned by Gautam Adani, India’s second richest businessman and close to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The $24m project will consume a large chunk of the tabletop Balda Hill – home to forests, grasslands and caves that are considered sacred by at least 10 tribal villages surrounding it.
To push the project, the purported signatures and thumb impressions of nearly 600 tribals were allegedly collected during village council meetings in Balda and Bannur held on October 9 last year. Bannur is 5km from Balda.
Khara says he never attended the meeting at Balda and was instead protesting against the proposed mine with his wife, sister and other villagers about 100 metres from the village council office.
“It [thumb impression] was fake. We didn’t attend the village meeting at all. We were all busy protesting outside,” he told Al Jazeera.
India’s constitution recognises the rights of Indigenous communities over their traditional lands. Forest laws and laws granting autonomy to tribal areas dictate that village council resolutions are mandatory for any diversion of such lands for other purposes.
A resolution passed in a village council meeting is valid only if 50 percent of all the adults in the village consent to it in writing. Government documents claim all the 580 adults – 360 in Balda and 227 in Bannur – agreed to give up their land for the Adani mine. But the elected village heads in both villages denied any signatures were collected and called the two meetings “invalid”.
Even photographs taken by villagers at both council meetings show a combined attendance of about 100 people – nearly 40 in Balda and 68 in Bannur – far below the minimum 50 percent quorum required to pass a valid resolution.
Moreover, the villagers allege that most signatures on the resolution documents are fake, forged or impersonated.
They also claim the documents contain signatures of fictitious persons and even the names of people who died years ago. Some even said their signatures from a previous, unrelated village council meeting were fraudulently pasted onto the bauxite mine document.
Al Jazeera emailed the Adani group and its communications chief on August 18 seeking responses to the accusations of forgery and fraud. Then we followed up with a second request for comments on September 25, but did not receive any response. Al Jazeera also sought responses from Manoj Satyawan Mahajan, the district magistrate — the most senior bureaucrat in Koraput – to the concerns raised by villagers but did not receive a response. Rohit Varma, the superintendent of police for Koraput district, also did not respond to Al Jazeera’s queries.
‘They took the paper away from me’
Many of those who attended the meetings said they were opposed to the mining project.
“We were told that if mining was allowed, the village would get roads, jobs, drainage and water connections and a school built,” said Madhav Kuntili, a farmer in Bannur.
Koraput is one of India’s least developed districts and similar promises often have a significant sway. Kuntili said a document was passed around, seeking signatures.
“I said if the forest was being diverted, then I would not sign it. They took the paper away from me,” he told Al Jazeera.
Across Balda and Bannur, Al Jazeera met many villagers who said they were shocked to find their signatures or thumb impressions on the resolution.
Rama Hantal sat motionless by the doorway of his rusted tin-and-wood hut. The 60-year-old has been paralysed for several years and is unable to talk.
“There is no chance he could have attended the meeting or even signed,” said Chandrama Hantal, his daughter-in-law.
While Hantal had apparently signed the consent form in Odia, Odisha’s official language, Chandrama saw a thumb impression against her name. She also denied attending the meeting.
Among the signatories are three Gurubari Kharas – their purported thumb impressions in support of the mining project.
In Balda, villagers could only track two “Gurubaris” – one living 3km away who denied attending the meeting – and another from the village itself, who had died well before the village council meeting was held.
“My mother died in February 2025. How can they forge her presence and signature eight months later?” asked her son, Sahdev. She was nearly 75 when she died of natural causes.
Two other persons from the first Gurubari’s family are also listed as signatories – her bedridden husband, who has been paralysed since falling from a tree three months before the council meeting and her nephew. Both deny attending the October 9 meeting.
The third Gurubari remains untraced.
Al Jazeera interviewed more than 20 people and accessed records from both Balda and Bannur villages, but could not trace at least 67 persons named as signatories in the resolution.
In Bannur, at least three deceased persons were represented through thumbprints. The families of all three – who are also listed in the documents as consenters – confirmed the deaths of their kin.
“My mother died four years ago,” said Nakul Alang, the 35-year-old son of Sanai Alang who is listed at serial number 108 in the Bannur resolution.
Nakul’s signature appears in Odia, but he says he was working at a construction site in Visakhapatnam, a coastal city in Odisha’s neighbouring Andhra Pradesh state 170km (105 miles) from Koraput.
“I don’t know who put our names and signatures,” he told Al Jazeera.
Hurried, ‘fraudulent’ meeting
On page 10 of the 16-page Bannur resolution document, 13 names are written by the same hand, followed by a neat array of thumb impressions next to them.
When Sunadhar Muduli, a 50-year-old farmer, saw the sheet, he immediately recognised that it was his own handwriting.
“But none of us ever attended the Gram Sabha meeting,” he said.
Muduli said Ramnath Pungi, who works for the local revenue office on contract, visited the village in December and handed him a registry. He was asked to fill the names of those residents who wanted to get their traditional lands recognised by the government.
Many tribal communities, who have been historically kept out of land documentation, have been cultivating on “government-owned” lands for generations. There have been frequent promises to transfer such lands to their names, and it is not uncommon practice in the region to send contracted officials to collect information about farmers.
“He said he needed everyone’s signatures. I told him I would gather the residents, but he said that was not necessary. That I could sign on their behalf,” said Muduli, who then called some residents to get their permission.
“I wrote down the names on one side of the page and then he and I placed our thumbs alternatively against the name. It was his idea and I just followed the instructions,” he said.
It was only in June when Al Jazeera visited Bannur that Muduli saw the inclusion of the same sheet as part of the mining resolution draft.
Pungi also confirmed to Al Jazeera that the signatures were taken on another pretext.
“I was paid 3,000 rupees to collect documents and sign land settlement documents from each village. That’s what I did. I only submitted the signed sheet to the [revenue] office,” he said.
“I did not know they would use it for this [Adani project]. I am also against mining in our region.”
Official guidelines state that the announcement of a Gram Sabha meeting should be made two weeks before the scheduled date in order to ensure a quorum.
However, several residents told Al Jazeera that the notices announcing the meeting were pasted outside the village council offices on October 8, only a day before the meeting. The notices, accessed by Al Jazeera, were dated September 22 and September 23, 2025.
‘Abnormally rushed’ mining approval
Meanwhile, the government pushed the Adani mining project in Odisha – hastily, according to the residents and activists.
In February 2023, the Odisha government declared Adani Enterprises as the preferred bidder for the mine at Koraput, triggering immediate protests by the tribal people in Balda and Bannur. They marched to the local government office to protest against the mining of 157 hectares of forest land by destroying the trees around them and displacing residents.
Two years later, on March 6, 2025, the state government held a public hearing – a mandatory process to obtain approvals where villagers are given details of the project and their objections formally recorded. An overwhelming number of villagers expressed their opposition to the mining project.
Despite the objections, an environmental clearance – a key approval given by the government after assessing possible ecological damage of a project – was granted a few months later.
Under Indian laws, forest-dwelling communities who have been historically left out of land -ownership can seek individual or community rights over traditional forest lands. Balda and neighbouring communities applied for rights over 2,500 hectares of forest land in 2025. A majority of those claims overlapped with the mining lease area.
Usually, the settlement of claims involves the collation of claims and documents, approval from local bodies, verification by officials and ample time for appeals if the claims are modified or rejected. The process is usually notoriously slow.
In January, authorities “settled” these community rights claims without informing the village councils in the area. Less than one-fifth of the claimed area was recognised while the entirety of the mining area was excluded from the claims. Villagers are usually given time to appeal.
However, in this case, two appeals committees affirmed the decision in just three days, without even allowing the villagers time to submit their appeals, allege the villagers.
Ajaya Muduli is part of a three-member team authorised by the affected villages to approach any court in India, sign documents, take necessary legal steps and liaise with government committees in their fight to prevent the takeover of their lands.
Muduli told Al Jazeera that the land acquisition process was “abnormally rushed”.
“We have safeguarded this sacred land for centuries and yet were not even consulted,” Muduli told Al Jazeera. “This is a clear tactic forcing the mines on us without our consent while snatching our rights.”
Immediately after the October 9 Gram Sabha meetings, the villagers wrote to the local authorities asking for the deliberations to be held again. They flagged the hurried nature of the meetings and pointed to the fact that the village heads had declared them “invalid”.
Yet, on October 15, the allegedly forged resolutions were added to the official file. It was only on February 11 this year that those documents were made public on the environment ministry’s website.
So far, more than 50 people from several villages in Koraput have issued sworn affidavits declaring that they did not attend the village council meetings and that their signatures or thumb impressions were forged. They have also filed petitions in court and with district authorities, as well as complaints with the police, alleging forgery and demanding an investigation into the land given for the Adani mine.
In March, the 10 affected villages around Balda Hill held meetings where they rejected the previous resolutions passed by their village councils and reiterated their opposition to the proposed bauxite mine.
In May, Muduli approached the court on behalf of the villagers. But it was too late.
On May 7, all required approvals were granted to Kalinga Alumina Limited and the forest land was handed over for the $24m bauxite mining project, with an associated alumina refinery on a lease of 50 years. No compensation has been promised to the villagers.
“What they have done is illegal, but we will not back off,” Balda resident Rajendra Khara told Al Jazeera.
While the approvals have been granted, actual work has not started on the ground. Villagers have vowed to stop construction. “Whatever happens, we are never going to give it to Adani. This is our ancestral land,” Rajendra said.
‘Deeply troubling trend’
Arpitha Kodiveri, assistant professor of political science at Vassar College in the United States who has worked on environmental law and justice related to mining in India, told Al Jazeera that bypassing the consent of landowners sets a trend for illegal practice.
“What you are starting to see across multiple jurisdictions is an administrative approach to bypassing the consent provision. What I fear is that it has become an illegal administrative practice of implementing the consent provision without adhering to procedure and law, and that is something we should be worried about,” she said.
Kodiveri said alleged irregularities in the consent process could also provide grounds for the affected parties to challenge the government clearance granted to such mining projects. She also argued that the rules should make consequences for irregular consent practices clearer and must seek accountability when mandatory provisions are bypassed.
“Guidelines must be established so this process is implemented in spirit and not just in letter, and to signal to administrative actors that there are consequences for practising fraudulent signatures or taking signatures of the deceased. This has happened so many times in Odisha and elsewhere that it is a deeply troubling trend.”
Land Conflict Watch, a New Delhi-based research organisation, has tracked at least 28 instances of consent-related “conflicts” from projects such as mining, plantation, energy and other infrastructure across India since 2003. The organisation also found allegations of forgery, evasion of mandatory public consultations and forceful mining of ancestral land while studying such conflicts.
Even the studies conducted by the government show a similar trend.
A 2024 report by India’s Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), an independent constitutional authority, on land management in tribal-dominated areas revealed 136 consent violations in mining and other projects. In 73 of these violations, no Gram Sabha meetings were held, while in another 29, land acquisition was done while disregarding the views of the village council.
Over the past few years, however, allegations of outright forgeries of Gram Sabha resolutions have emerged.
In 2023 in Sijimali, about 180km from Balda, villagers discovered similar forged consents and meetings for a bauxite mine by Vedanta Resources, India’s largest mining company backed by a London-based conglomerate. At least eight villages denied consent to hand over 708 hectares of forest land, despite official documents claiming otherwise.
Sijimali has seen near-continuous protests since, escalating to violence in April when clashes between the police and protesters injured 70.
“If the Gram Sabha has not given consent, then the forest clearance given is illegal. It has to be quashed. They are making a mockery of the law,” Shomona Khanna, a Supreme Court lawyer specialising in environmental and tribal law, told Al Jazeera.
“These are criminal offences … Any person who dispossesses a forest dweller of their forest right or interferes in the enjoyment of the forest right is committing a crime, which is called an atrocity under Indian law,” she said.
Back in Balda, the villagers fear that if mining starts, the rainwater-fed streams that sustain paddy cultivation will dry up. Forests that provided gourds, fruits, flowers, bark, firewood and medicinal plants will be affected.
Like many Indigenous tribal communities, their animist faith is linked to the surrounding forests – home to small shrines, idols and caves considered to be sacred.
“The forest is everything for us,” said Raghunath Hanthal, a 70-year-old priest in Balda. “Our maa [goddess] is here.”
On the official document, the priest’s name is listed as serial number 171, with his purported signature in Odia.
“I did not even go to the meeting. We were here, protesting that day,” he said. “Taking away our forests will not just destroy our livelihood, but it will incur the wrath of our goddess.”

India-Russia trade jumps in first half of 2026 – envoy
Trade between India and Russia reached $38 billion in the first half of this year and is on track to reach the $100 billion annual target set for 2030, Indian Ambassador to Russia Vinay Kumar has said. 
“We think we are on the right path to achieve the target,” Kumar told The Tribune newspaper on the sidelines of the second Russia-India TIME Business Forum in Kazan on Thursday. He said India was sourcing energy and fertilizers from Russia while exporting pharmaceuticals and expanding opportunities for skilled workers. 
The two countries are making a concerted effort to diversify trade and deepen economic ties, with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin giving personal attention to the relationship. The Kazan forum, in the Russian Republic of Tatarstan, follows the INNOPROM.India trade fair held in New Delhi last month. 
The $100 billion trade target was set during Modi’s visit to Moscow in July 2024.

The strong growth in trade has continued beyond the six-month period cited by the Indian envoy. Bilateral commerce reached $47.7 billion in January-July, up 24.3% year-on-year, according to Indian Commerce Ministry figures cited by Russian lender Sberbank.
India’s imports from Russia totaled $44.9 billion during the seven months, including $36 billion in crude oil purchases. Indian exports reached $2.8 billion as Russia bought more chemicals, electrical goods, medical equipment, seafood, tea, and spices.
Bilateral goods trade grew from around $13 billion in 2021-22 to nearly $60 billion in 2025-26, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said in August. However, the trade imbalance also widened as India bought Russian oil in huge quantities amid disruptions in the Middle East caused by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.
New Delhi is seeking to expand shipments of pharmaceuticals, engineering goods, chemicals, food products, and auto components to Russia to lower the deficit.
Both sides are working on a bilateral investment treaty and strengthening local currency payment mechanisms to facilitate trade. India has also launched free trade negotiations with the Eurasian Economic Union, which includes Russia, to expand market access.

Estonia wants to block Russian gas transit through Baltics for good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Estonia wants to block Russian gas transit through Baltics for good
Energy minister Erkki Keldo (Reform) wants to work with Latvia to permanently stop Russian gas transit through the Baltics, with other options on the table if talks fail.
Speaking to ERR, the Estonian energy and environment minister said he plans to meet his Latvian counterpart as soon as Latvia's new government is in place.
"The valve, so to speak, that we can physically control on the Estonian side is closed, so nothing can flow through there," Keldo explained, referring to a natural gas pipeline that runs through Southeastern Estonia. "But the other physical pipe and valve are on the Latvian side, and we need to discuss this with the Latvians and Lithuanians."
He noted that the section of pipeline belongs to state-owned grid operator Elering and is used solely for transit, stressing that no gas from it can enter Estonia's domestic network.
Keldo declined to speculate before the two ministers met on whether Latvia would agree to shut off the supply, but he made his own position clear.
"We'll look at what intervention options and solutions are available," he said. "Since, unfortunately, [the pipeline] is operated by a Latvian state-owned operator, this is also a matter for negotiations with our neighbors and allies. But I can certainly say that I don't think this is right."
The minister said sanctions or other measures should be considered only after talks with Latvia.
The two countries have both advocated raising the cost of Russia's continued aggression in Ukraine through sanctions and additional tariffs, Keldo noted.
In light of this, while no Russian gas has flowed through the pipeline for more than two years already, he hoped his Latvian counterpart would help find a way to ensure it won't resume in the future either.
"I believe and hope we can reach an agreement with the Latvians," the minister said. "But if we can't, we'll have to look at what other options are available."
Sector politicians unaware
Earlier this week, Eesti Ekspress reported that Estonia is maintaining a natural gas pipeline running through Võru County that Russia can use to supply its exclave of Kaliningrad Oblast.
The paper noted that none of the Estonian politicians responsible for overseeing the sector in recent years were aware of the Russian gas pipeline arrangement.
Kaliningrad relies on Russian gas to fuel its power plants. After Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania disconnected from the Russian-controlled power grid in February 2025, the exclave was left as an isolated energy system.

DPP's Su Chiao-hui pitches family-focused New Taipei campaign

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP New Taipei mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) is campaigning to attract investment, create jobs, and improve housing and public services ahead of the Nov. 28 local elections.
CNA reported that Su pledged to keep businesses, investment, and skilled workers in New Taipei during a campaign visit to Wugu District on Thursday. She also proposed a new exhibition center, faster light rail construction, and more schools, childcare centers, and public facilities.
Su is running against KMT candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), a former Taipei deputy mayor with more than 40 years of government experience. While Lee has built his campaign around public works and administrative experience, Su is emphasizing family support, housing, and economic opportunities.
Born in Taipei, Su studied law at National Taiwan University before earning master's degrees from Boston University and the University of Pennsylvania. She worked as a lawyer and later served as executive director of the Eball Foundation before entering electoral politics, per Legislative Yuan.
Su is the daughter of former Premier Su Tseng-chang (蘇貞昌), who previously served as Taipei County magistrate before the county became New Taipei. She entered the legislature in 2016 after defeating incumbent KMT Legislator Huang Chih-hsiung (黃志雄), per TVBS.
Su has since won two more legislative terms and served as chair of the DPP's New Taipei chapter. Her legislative work has covered education, culture, industrial development, and transport, providing experience she is drawing on in her campaign for mayor.
Housing is one of Su's main campaign priorities, particularly for young people and families facing high living costs. She has proposed creating an urban renewal department and offering eligible families rental housing with leases of up to 20 years, per Newtalk.
Childcare is another focus, with Su calling for more support for childcare workers and families caring for older relatives. She also wants to expand temporary and nighttime childcare services to help parents working irregular hours, per Liberty Times.
Su has challenged Lee's approach to childcare, arguing that expanding services requires more than constructing new facilities. When Lee proposed establishing childcare centers in every school, she said hiring enough qualified workers should take priority.
Transport is another area where the candidates have outlined different priorities. Lee has proposed a 30-minute Greater Taipei travel network, while Su has focused on improving connections between New Taipei's growing residential areas, industrial districts, and existing public transport systems, per CTS News.
The DPP has not governed New Taipei since it became a special municipality in 2010, with the KMT holding the mayoralty under Eric Chu (朱立倫) and Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜). Su hopes to end that run by offering voters a stronger focus on affordable living, family services, and local economic development.

France, Germany strike bargain on Made in Europe, car emissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:04:07 UTC
20:04:07 KST

France's President Emmanuel Macron (L) greets Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz ahead of a round table as part of a European Union summit in Brussels on October 15, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — France and Germany said Friday they had struck a deal to favor European-made cars under a landmark EU industry bill in exchange for weakening a 2035 vehicle emissions target, ending months of wrangling between the bloc’s two biggest economies.
Under the agreement, Germany would accept stricter “Made in Europe” — or local content — requirements for the automotive industry in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act, a longstanding French demand, while France would back Berlin’s push to relax the EU’s plan to phase out new combustion-engine cars.
The EU’s current target is for companies to reduce emissions from new vehicles by 100% from 2021 levels by 2035, with the possibility to “earn” 10% of emissions leeway through initiatives like offsets and investments.
Advertisement
France and Germany now want to soften the 2035 target to 90% but without having to offer investments in alternative fuels to compensate the remaining 10%, as proposed by the European Commission.
“This balanced approach will enable the European Union to pursue its climate objectives while strengthening the technological sovereignty, industrial base and international competitiveness of its automotive industry,” the two countries said in a joint statement.
“We hope that this Franco-German dynamic can swiftly lead to an agreement with our partners, for our jobs and our industry,” French President Emmanuel Macron said in a post on social media.
An Elysée official on Friday made clear that, under the Franco-German deal, the scope of Made in Europe for automotive can be extended to the U.K. and Switzerland under certain conditions. — addressing a key concern of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government ahead of a Nov. 20 U.K.-EU summit in Brussels.
The agreement was reached after the German Social Democratic Party, the junior partner in Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government, dropped its opposition.
Advertisement
“This is a modern realignment of German industrial policy that places significantly greater emphasis on preserving jobs and production sites,” said German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider, who is from the SPD.
“The clear expectation for German companies is that they will use these new opportunities to make investments and guarantee jobs here in Germany,” he added.

“These restrictions must be lifted,” Wadephul said, arguing that Germany finances some of the Starlink equipment used in Ukraine.
“And so, of course, we insist that it works if we are paying for it. Ukraine must continue to receive full support,” he said.

Germany had questions for the US “that we will clarify,” he said.
Sources in Ukraine’s defense ministry told Kyiv Post on Thursday morning, Oct. 15, that Starshield connectivity while in motion had been restored and remained operational, according to reports from military units. However, the sources did not specify the speeds at which the service was functioning or whether any speed restrictions remained.

Le Pen Looms Large as Macron Enters Final Months on EU Stage
That update confirmed the resumption of service but did not establish what caused the disruption or how it was resolved.
On Wednesday, ministry sources told Kyiv Post that SpaceX had introduced speed restrictions overnight without advance warning to Ukraine’s defense forces.
They described a limit of 160 kilometers per hour, or about 100 mph, although units reported losing connectivity at speeds ranging from approximately 72 to 161 km/h (45 to 100 mph).
The restrictions hampered drone missions, including interceptor and medium-range strike operations, and reduced capabilities for logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relay.
Ukraine is seeking to raise the operating speed limit to 450 km/h (280 mph) to allow interceptor drones to pursue faster Russian aerial threats, including jet-powered drones.
Dan Rice, president of American University Kyiv and a former special adviser to Ukraine’s military commander-in-chief, warned that such restrictions could have deadly consequences.
Speaking to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Rice described the scale of the threat facing Ukrainian air defenses.
“When you have 500 inbound Shaheeds, jet-powered Shaheeds, and I was hit within 400 meters [1,312 feet] twice this week,” he said, “you need to have interceptors going out to protect Ukrainian civilians.”
Rice warned that interference with high-speed interceptor operations could allow Russian drones to reach civilian targets, including schools, hospitals, and residential buildings.
Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the restrictions also impaired Ukrainian drone missions against Russian military logistics and command facilities approximately 150-250 kilometers (93 to 155 miles) behind Russian lines.
The consequences extend beyond battlefield efficiency.
In an interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the restrictions had already cost Ukrainian lives.
“People are dying because of his decision,” Zelensky said.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely,” he added.
However, the Ukrainian leader stopped short of identifying who had ordered the restrictions.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to… I don’t know really,” Zelensky said when asked whether he was angry with Elon Musk.
“We are professionals. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he added.
The controversy has also clarified who ultimately controls the military satellite system.
Starshield is a government-focused version of SpaceX’s Starlink network, developed for military and national security operations. Unlike commercial Starlink, the Starshield services at issue operate under US government control.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, confirmed Wednesday that restrictions on the system were a government decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X.

World’s first fielded laser downs drones in Korea test
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
12:02:57 BST
20:02:57 KST

A South Korean laser air defence weapon destroyed all three target drones put up against it during a Republic of Korea Army exercise, at a cost the manufacturer puts at around one dollar fifty a shot, according to the company.
Hanwha Systems said its Cheongwang, the Laser Air Defence Weapon Block-I, and a 30kW class vehicle-mounted high energy laser cannon took part in the Army TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise run by Republic of Korea Army Headquarters on 14 October. Around five hundred people watched, among them the Chief of Staff of the Republic of Korea Army along with military officials, academics and industry figures.
Joohun Shin, head of the Laser Systems Business Centre at Hanwha Systems, said: “Laser weapons are core assets that will fundamentally change the game of air defense. Driven by unmatched technological capability and proven operational performance, we will accelerate our entry into the global market to establish both Cheongwang and the high-mobility, high-power 50kW Laser Armored Vehicle as key next-generation export items for K-Defense.”
Cheongwang, whose name means light of the sky, was developed by Hanwha Systems with the Agency for Defense Development and is the first laser weapon of its kind to be fielded operationally anywhere. The company puts the cost of a single engagement at about a dollar fifty and says the system can keep firing for as long as it has power, with no magazine to run down and no resupply chain behind it.
A Shahed type attack drone costs tens of thousands of dollars and the missiles fired at it cost far more, so an attacker generating cheap airframes in quantity wins on arithmetic even when every shot works. A laser inverts that, provided it can generate the power, hold the beam on target long enough to burn through, and see through the weather.
Hanwha ran a similar demonstration on 16 September at the 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition, where it said Cheongwang neutralised four drones and two uncrewed aircraft in succession in front of domestic and international guests. It also showed a 50kW Laser Armored Vehicle there, a more powerful and more mobile system it is developing in-house for export, and took that vehicle to MSPO in Kielce in September, the largest defence exhibition in eastern Europe.
Britain has been working the same ground through DragonFire, the laser directed energy weapon developed by MBDA, Leonardo and QinetiQ with Dstl, which hit aerial targets in trials in the Hebrides in 2024 and is being accelerated towards installation on a Royal Navy Type 45 destroyer. The Strategic Defence Review committed further money to directed energy, and the Army has been trialling laser systems mounted on Wolfhound vehicles.
