Black Sea Disruptions Leave Bulgarian Steel Plant Without Billets
The crisis in the Black Sea has disrupted raw material supplies to Bulgaria’s ferrous metals industry, forcing a plant in Debelt to operate only two weeks a month
The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions in Bulgaria (CITUB) staged a protest in central Sofia demanding a 10% public-sector wage increase in the 2027 budget, rejecting the proposed minimum monthly wage of 660 euros and calling for guarantees against indiscriminate job cuts, BTA reported.
Trade union representatives gathered near the National Assembly carrying placards calling for decent wages, protection for jobs and incomes, and an end to in-work poverty. Police maintained a heavy presence, while traffic around Knyaz Alexander I Square was halted. The protest was set to continue with a motorcade along major boulevards and streets in the capital, with the Sofia Municipality announcing traffic and parking restrictions.
Earlier in the day, union representatives met with Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Galab Donev to discuss next year’s budget. The talks ended without a concrete agreement, although CITUB and the Confederation of Labour “Podkrepa” were assured that the proposed 660-euro minimum wage was not yet a final decision. The sides also agreed to explore whether the planned 5% wage increase could be raised to 10%.
CITUB President Plamen Dimitrov said the draft budget being sent to Brussels included a 5% increase in wages and a minimum monthly wage of 660 euros. The union is seeking a 10% rise to help workers keep pace with inflation, which Dimitrov estimated would require an additional 300 million to 350 million euros.
“Our goal is to secure a 10% increase in remuneration to keep pace with inflation,” Dimitrov said. He argued that the additional funding would not undermine the budget deficit and rejected the proposed taxation of food vouchers.
Dimitrov also questioned the macroeconomic assumptions underpinning the budget, arguing that projected gross domestic product was too low and that tax revenue and the level of redistribution were therefore also underestimated. He said potential reserves could be found in these calculations.
The union estimates that raising wages in the sectors it represents would require 781.31 million euros. Dimitrov separately put the funding needed for the wage measures under discussion at about 400 million euros, specifying that the actual figure was 380 million euros, which he said was manageable within the available budget framework.
The union is seeking wage increases for teachers and other public-sector employees, including a proposed 7.5% rise for teachers instead of the planned 5%, alongside a higher minimum wage. Dimitrov said the union could not yet be satisfied because no specific commitments had been made, although he remained cautiously optimistic. He expects the full draft budget for next year to be presented by the end of next week.
The planned 5% increase would not apply to the “Security” sector, where job cuts are also expected, according to information shared during the meeting. Trade unions are demanding that the government rule out blanket percentage-based cuts across the public-sector workforce.
Dimitar Manolov, president of the Confederation of Labour “Podkrepa,” said the outcome of the meeting had been predictable and that the unions had not received concessions. He proposed limiting the planned salary increases to the first half of the year, followed by a midyear assessment to determine whether further increases were possible.
Manolov also addressed the proposal to impose a 7% tax on food vouchers worth more than 100 euros. If the measure could not be avoided, he said, the unions had suggested applying it as a social security contribution rather than a tax. Although this would reduce the transfer to the state social security system, it would mean the amount was included in employees’ social security income, which he considered beneficial.
Since the beginning of the week, workers from different sectors have held protests in several Bulgarian cities. Their demands include a 10% increase in public-sector pay in 2027, protection against indiscriminate job cuts and additional funding for preschool and school education, public administration, health care, transport and communications, culture, agriculture, and the environment and water sector.
Speaking from the protest podium, CITUB Vice President Todor Kapitanov called on members of Parliament to heed the unions’ demands. Representatives of several trade federations said current pay levels were insufficient.
Protesters said the minimum wage remained below the level they had been seeking for years, despite previously reaching 50% of the average gross wage. They also argued that Bulgarian prices had reached European levels while wages continued to lag behind.
Other demonstrators called for 9.2 million euros in the budget to raise the salaries of employees of the State Fund “Agriculture.” Some said that while the government repeatedly discussed the state budget deficit, household budgets had also been running short for years.
“Wages run out by the middle of the month,” protesters said.
Labor and Social Policy Minister Natalia Efremova also addressed the rally, outlining planned social spending increases in the 2027 budget despite the European Commission’s insistence on spending cuts because Bulgaria is subject to an excessive deficit procedure.
Efremova said the budget would provide higher one-time birth allowances for first, second and third children, with some seeing particularly significant increases, as well as a larger allowance for the second year of maternity leave.
She said the government was trying to reconcile union demands for the highest possible minimum wage with employers’ concerns about their ability to absorb higher labor costs. The proposed minimum wage for next year had been set at 660 euros, with additional payments for length of service and professional experience on top of that amount.
Efremova said the government wanted workers to improve their qualifications and earn more rather than remain employed at the minimum wage level.

The last thing I did for my mother was illegal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:47 UTC
20:00:47 KST

My mother is in a Ziploc bag on my lap, wedged between a half-eaten bag of trail mix and my purse.
My stomach is queasy from the switchbacks up to Yosemite, where I’ve come to spread her ashes, and I’m having an existential crisis.
I had imagined this day as a beautiful send-off that would feel profound. Instead, it was all improvisation: a plastic bag, a last-minute decision, and ginger chews to stop me from being carsick.
I thought my 20s would be about kissing the wrong people in Los Angeles bars, not reading paperbacks on a hospital cot while my mom underwent her fifth brain surgery. My friends were off at college, debating sororities and semesters abroad; I was learning an entirely different set of skills.
At 21, I learned my mom had glioblastoma, a deadly brain cancer. Soon I was in the Bakersfield law library, Googling how to become my 16-year-old brother’s legal guardian, and learning that the same charm I used to snag me a table at Nobu could also get my mom a better room at Cedars-Sinai hospital. She ended up in the room Elizabeth Taylor had died in a few weeks earlier, a detail she loved to regale her friends with.
I don’t remember much from that last month of her life. I mostly just remember the goop I wiped from her eyes as she settled into her final nap. The home hospice nurse told my brother and me to give our mother “permission” to let go. Her fragile body was still fighting, and the nurse believed she was holding on for us. So through our snot and tears, we told her to go. But secretly, in every paused breath, I hoped she wouldn’t.
She passed away within eight months of her initial diagnosis. She was 44 years old.
When the paramedics arrived, I left the room. A white sheet over her body would finalize things in a way I wasn’t ready for yet. Eventually, in the middle of everything else, I had to figure out what to do with her body.
Then there was the price tag. A typical funeral with a viewing and burial in the US costs $8,300. Even cremation now costs more than $2,200 – an unthinkable sum for me at the time. I was a senior airman in the US air force, making about $2,200 a month.
When you can’t afford to pay, you end up grieving illegally – as I did.
My mom had asked to be cremated. Because my family and I were “sharing” her remains, we needed a way to divide her across multiple people: me, my brother and my aunt.
The cheapest option the funeral home offered was a maroon plastic box. I bought one, brought her home, and we portioned her into plastic bags.
Later, my aunt took me to a boutique and helped me pick out little wooden boxes for each of us. Small carved wooden things, prettier than what the funeral home had offered – and cheaper. It felt like a repair. It also didn’t quite work. The box had seams, and my mother kept slipping out of the cracks, a thin layer of her showing up on shelves and dressers and inside drawers.
When it came time to drive to Yosemite, I put her back in a plastic bag.
One thing I didn’t know was that scattering human remains in a national park requires a special use permit. That seems obvious now, but when you’re grieving, reading any fine print is a big undertaking.
The industry of dying wasn’t always so onerous. Before the civil war, most Americans died at home and were prepared for burial by their own families. Embalming became widespread only after the war, when battlefield deaths created a mass market for preserving bodies long enough to ship them north.
What followed was tradition making way for a business model: the funeral home, the professional embalmer, the licensed director, the sealed casket, the manicured lawn cemetery.
One factor pushing the industry toward higher prices is consolidation. Over the last two decades, large death-care conglomerates have absorbed independent funeral homes, in some markets amassing enough pricing power to draw federal antitrust action. What used to be a family business is, increasingly, a subsidiary.
None of this happened by accident, and it is not, as the industry sometimes claims, a response to what families want. Justin Crowe, the founder of Parting Stone, a Santa Fe company that turns cremated remains into solidified stones, told me that the shift from burial to cremation went from 5% in 1970 to over 63% today.
“When the customer said, actually, we want cremation,” he said, “I think the industry kind of made a mistake at that moment. It didn’t really nurture that change. It didn’t provide the value to the experience of cremation, like it had to the experience of burial.”
What families were asking for, in other words, was a cheaper, less institutional death – one where the body didn’t disappear into a funeral home and come back as an invoice. But what they got was the same process, marked up, only this time with cremated remains.
And a growing number of families, faced with a version of dignity they could not afford, began improvising.
My friend Danielle Directo-Meston, a fellow journalist in Los Angeles, grew up in a family where death doesn’t happen offstage.
“Filipinos, my family in particular, we go to the cemetery to hang out,” she told me. “We just hang out there for most of the morning and afternoon. And then we’ll go get lunch together.”
They go to sit with relatives who have died, to clean the graves, adorn them with flowers, and spend time as a family; it’s a habit with roots in Undas, the Filipino tradition of spending All Saints’ and All Souls’ Day at the family plot.
Unlike many Americans, Danielle was raised to be comfortable around the dead. She has also had a lot of practice. In the last several years, she has lost a cousin in a motorcycle accident, an uncle after a series of strokes, and both of her grandmothers. She was still not prepared for how the American death-care industry actually operates.
The clearest example came at Rose Hills, a large cemetery in Whittier, California. Rose Hills is owned by Service Corporation International, a conglomerate absorbing independent funeral homes across the country. Danielle’s family was there for a gathering, honoring a passed loved one, when a salesperson approached them.
“When you’re at the cemetery having a family gathering,” she said, “they have salespeople try to sell you on more plots.”
She made it clear this wasn’t one bad day, or one bad salesperson. It was the norm. Anyone attending a service there would encounter it.
After watching her family cycle through this multiple times, Danielle made a different choice for herself. She decided to preplan her own funeral with a Washington-based company that offers natural organic reduction, the process of transforming a human body into soil, legal in a growing number of states.
“It’s around $5,000, which is doable,” she said. “I can pay that when I’m alive, and no one has to worry about it. Compared to $20,000 just for the plot alone at the cemetery, and that’s on top of the mortuary and all of that stuff.”
Danielle will be composted. I scattered my mother by hand in a national park without a permit. Neither of us did what the industry wanted us to do.
Somewhere between the seventh and the eighth bend, I pulled over and slid down an escarpment to an opening with shrubbery and trees. There wasn’t anything particularly special about the space, except for how the light passed through the leaves.
The year before she died, my mother told me she was taking me and my brother to Hawaii. It would have been our first family trip; the furthest we had ever vacationed was Kern River, 90 minutes from home. She had spent years trying to piece together where she came from. Her father was Hawaiian and had left when she was a baby. Her mother had never known her own father either. So my mother spent her life learning who she was the way you learn a language, alone and slowly.
She had already booked the flights for October. But by fall, she was too sick to travel. She died on 26 December after a few months in hospice care, exactly one year after she had told me about the trip.
I looked down at the bag in my hands. I wished I had planned her scattering at night under a full moon, where I could dance naked in front of a fire and chant her blessings. Or that I had carried her to the Redwoods, finding a spot at dawn when the rocks are covered in moss and dew, and the air is crisp. Or even better, smuggled her to Hawaii, and released her over the Pacific at sunset - her favorite time of day.
Instead, I settled on a sunny spot by a newborn tree. It was about 3ft high and eager to grow taller. It would usher in her remains with enthusiasm, and its new life would overcome her old one; a suitable symbolism for the cycle of life.
I opened the bag and shook it around, flinging her into the breeze, watching the particles of a woman who loved me travel toward Half Dome.
I walked back to my car and stretched my arm out the window on the drive down, surfing the wind with my hand. Pieces of my mother flew out from under my fingernails. It is the most loving thing I have ever done for her.

Fiery speeches, LED hats and infighting: inside an Alberta separatist conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:46 UTC
20:00:46 KST

The debate began with a simple question in a dark Calgary hotel ballroom: does Alberta need Canada?
By the time the audience was asked to vote at the end, more than three-quarters had answered no – a decisive measure of the convictions of a room packed with some of Alberta’s most ardent independence supporters, some of whom had paid C$900 (£480) for a “visionary” weekend pass.
But outside the comfort of the ballroom, the debate is far from settled. Across the province, the forthcoming 19 October referendum on separatism has divided communities, prompting accusations of treason and grift and, at times, bitter feuds between former allies. One recent poll shows support for independence at only 14%.
You wouldn’t know it from the WeUnify’s Reclaiming Alberta conference though.
“This is a matter of survival,” conservative activist and broadcaster Faytene Grasseschi told the crowd, which erupted into applause after she said Alberta’s oil resources had been “usurped” by the federal government and the Canada she had been born into “doesn’t exist any more”.
In the main halls outside the ballroom, attendees milled around the vendor stalls. A handful donned a $6,500 (£4,925) helmet that resembles white colanders hastily attached to a bike helmet, bathing the user’s head in red LED light supposedly for treatment of “Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, dementia, traumatic brain injury, [and] brain fog”. Others took in sales pitches about the need for gold and silver as paper money “fails”.
But the busiest stall belonged to the group Let’s Talk Alberta. It says it is neither a political party nor a campaign organisation but its five bound pamphlets include a 52-page volume titled Every Argument to Stay is a Reason to Leave. The pamphlets were written by its founder, Chris Scott, a cafe owner who attracted widespread attention during the Covid-19 pandemic after he was arrested for violating public health orders. After a lengthy legal battle, he was acquitted.
On stage, Scott told the crowd the push for independence would be a “wake-up call” for the rest of the country and reflected a fight against what many in the movement see as an entrenched political elite – a fight that needed to happen “come hell or high water”.
After initial efforts to bring a referendum question on independence were derailed by First Nations groups, Albertans will now be voting on the question of whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or whether the provincial government should begin the legal process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation. With just days to go, the foot soldiers and the faithful of the independence movement have begun their final pitches for what they envision will one day be a wealthy, “anti-woke” nation – one unshackled from the control of the federal government, or even a vassal of the United States.
The conference, which was organised by the WeUnify movement, brought together Alberta separatists, veterans of the pandemic-era “freedom movement” and conservatives united by a distrust of established institutions.
Speakers reserved their harshest words for Justin Trudeau, who, despite resigning as prime minister more than a year ago, remains a bugbear for the separatist movement. Sheane Meikle, a volunteer with Let’s Talk Alberta, said the independence movement was gaining support.
“We’re getting far fewer Trudeau salutes when we wave flags on the side of the road,” he said – a reference to the raised middle finger.
Meikle, 58, has spent months travelling the province with Scott, adding more than 32,000 miles to his van as part of a quest to convince sceptical Albertans of the benefits of separation. The referendum had been “longtime coming” for the movement, he said. “Even if the results don’t go our way, it doesn’t mean we’re done. This is a movement now that’s sustained.”
Not everyone agreed the conference was the best idea, though. Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of Alberta’s modern separatist movement, admitted in an interview that he regretted participating. “It’s just an echo chamber in there – I’m not changing any minds that are already made up for separatism. I shouldn’t be here. I should be out campaigning.”
In September Wilson brought together 45 unnamed contributors to publish the Alberta Transition Plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning Alberta from a province into an independent country.
“We have everything. Alberta is an economic powerhouse. But we’re also on the ground with our face in our dirt and our arms tied behind our backs because of Ottawa,” he said, referring to a longstanding belief that the federal government continues to exert unfair influence over the oil-rich province. “That’s how many Albertans feel, and that’s why they want change.”
His blueprint, however, has drawn criticism for leaving major questions about the costs and practicalities of independence unresolved. The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy recently estimated that the costs associated with separation could cost Alberta between C$50bn and C$170bn over its first five years and warned substantial annual deficits were possible.
Nor have the secessionists built the political machinery that could bring it about. The campaign has no official leader, nor an organised movement under the guise of a political party. No elected officials have campaigned for independence. Unlike Quebec, where independence parties have run explicitly on the idea and won, Alberta has only ever elected a separatist candidate once, and he lost his seat months later. In previous elections, separatist parties have won an average popular vote of 1%.
In the absence of coherent leadership, prominent figures have been thrust into the limelight, often with chaotic results. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is embroiled in legal battles over allegations that millions of dollars in disputed First Nations trust funds were mishandled. Mitch Sylvestre, head of the Alberta Prosperity Project and owner of a sporting goods store, told the Toronto Star he fears King Charles will have him assassinated. David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organizer, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.
But for Meikle and others, the movement is “grassroots” and would only be damaged by the presence of elected officials. “We just need our politicians to get out of the way and stop being so biased towards this movement,” he said. “They shouldn’t be using taxpayer money to campaign against us.”
For many here, the coronavirus pandemic remains an animating force. Some of the panellists and speakers were prominent lawyers who challenged and in some cases won cases against the government for overreach in shutdown laws.
It was the pandemic – and the political atmosphere that followed it – that got Betty Field, a retiree who worked in the oil sector, interested in the independence movement. Her husband, Gord Pick, chimed in that even supporters of federalism should vote against unity “to put a little fear of God into Ottawa”.
But the lack of a leader has led to divergence over messaging and strategy. In early October, the Globe and Mail reported on ties between the Alberta separatists movement and Republican operatives, and meetings between those unelected Albertans and White House staff. Among items allegedly discussed were oil revenues that could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country, as well as Alberta’s fresh water resources.
“We wouldn’t want to be part of the US,” said Pick. “Why trade one overlord in Ottawa for another in Washington?”
Outside, fresh off their weekly dinner of liver and onions – “just the best in Calgary, hands down!” – friends Vera Patten and Lisette Bourget stand in the waning sun, smoking a cigarette. When a conference attender offers to hold the door for them, Patten says politely: “Oh we’re not with you.”
“I hope they lose,” she adds after a small crowd, also out for a smoke, returns back inside. “It’s just disgusting. I can’t believe how they’re trying to break up this country.” A veteran of the oil industry, Patten has lived in Calgary for decades and says only damage can come from separation. “This needs to stop, and I’m hopeful that after the vote – that they lose.”
Wilson said the movement had other plans.
“The separatist movement in Alberta started before my parents were born – and they’re dead,” he said. “Because if you’re a separatist, you see a better opportunity for your friends, neighbours and your grandkids. And you never give up on that. Even if the vote goes poorly, it will not end. In the same way that winters won’t end and springs won’t end, this movement won’t end either. It’s here to stay.”

‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:46 UTC
20:00:46 KST

For passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist in London after the first UK services started in September.
Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shocked TfL approved it so soon. I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.”
London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demanding Transport for London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations.
Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’s first autonomous cabs for hire.
The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost.
Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides.
The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses at TfL have expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.
In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.
The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said.
TfL is understood to see little benefit in the addition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets, even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic.
For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road.
Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start of Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat.
As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets.
That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twice rebuffed in licence renewals as not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene.
City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday.
Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.”
Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.”
Faisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT. We thought, we’re not earning as much driving but we’ll be safe for a while, support the family, pay the bills. But robocabs are a massive concern.
“People might be interested but it will decimate the livelihoods of many people including me – I really wanted some authorities to say no.”
Abdurzak Hadi, an Uber driver and theLondon chair of the ADCU, said Saturday’s protests would follow a similar action held at Waymo’s base in Park Royal in August. He said: “For me as a driver, I’m thinking about competing with a machine that’s not going to get tired, and could work 24 hours a day.
“But as a Londoner with family, I’m thinking about safety. As licensed drivers we’re taught by TfL about safeguarding, looking out for a vulnerable child, or for abuse. Or looking after passengers who can only read your lips. We’re a safety net. But losing my job – that’s also losing a safety net for my family.”
A recent report from the Centre for British Progress thinktank said more than 400,000 UK drivers (121,000 in London) would soon find “much of this work obsolete”, and urged the government to tax autonomous vehicles to help pay for the social consequences and economic losses.
The GMB union has demanded a “just transition” to help drivers reskill and find new work. Speaking at the Labour conference last month, the GMB’s Mark Betteridge said the union was not against change but added: “The people who do these jobs will know the reality far better of what change will look like … Drivers tell us they want some sort of transition plan to get through this.”
The roads minister, Justin Madders, told the meeting that autonomous vehicles could bring “opportunities for well-paid and unionised jobs” and the government wanted Britain to be a “world leader” in the technology. But, he added: “Sometimes government hasn’t worked on the impact on workers … We’re absolutely committed to making sure that doesn’t happen that time.”
An Uber spokesperson said: “Drivers and AVs [automated vehicles], which we believe will also offer considerable benefits to cities, are both expected to grow side by side for quite some time. That said, we shouldn’t hide that autonomous mobility will impact workers, riders, and the communities they live in.
“We are in conversations with the government and local stakeholders to ensure we can realise the promise of AVs while not leaving drivers and communities behind.”
Uber said it had not significantly increased its share of fares in London but VAT changes meant drivers were keeping less of the fares customers paid, and it said it was the only private hire operator in the UK recognising its drivers as workers with employment protections.
Wayve said that with Uber it was taking a “deliberately phased approach”, and had engaged extensively with political leaders, community organisations and accessibility advocates. A spokesperson said its robotaxis could “make a positive contribution to London’s transport system, helping to improve road safety, expand connectivity and give people more ways to travel.
“There is clear excitement in the potential for this technology to support safer, more accessible journeys, provided it is introduced responsibly and in partnership with the city. We have a positive, constructive relationship with TfL and we’re working pragmatically together to ensure any future services meet its expectations.”
A spokesperson for Khan said the mayor was committed to ensuring that Londoners benefitted from the opportunities new technologies could bring but shared “concerns about potential impacts on safety, congestion and jobs”, as any changes needed to “work for our world-leading transport system – including taxi and private hire services, and those who drive them”.

Billionaires Are the Symptom, Not the Disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

After nearly a century, America has rediscovered the wealth tax. This November, Californians will vote on Proposition 40, a union-backed initiative levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state's billionaires. Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna have introduced a federal version; a dozen states have advanced millionaire or billionaire taxes this year; and Maine, Washington, Hawaii, and Rhode Island have all enacted one. Not since the Progressive Era has taxing the rich had this much momentum.
The energy is easy to understand. The 25 wealthiest Americans pay a “true tax rate” of just 3.4%—a fraction of what nurses and teachers pay—while holding about 2% of the nation's wealth. That’s nearly as much as the entire bottom half of the country combined.
This spring, Forbes counted a record 3,428 billionaires worth $20.1 trillion, up $4 trillion since last year. Elon Musk topped the list at $839 billion, and this summer he became history's first trillionaire. At the same time, workers' share of economic output fell to 52.8%, the lowest since records began in 1947. Today, billionaire wealth is at an all-time high while labor's share is at an all-time low.
One obvious response is to tax the fortunes at the top and redistribute those funds. But I worry that the wealth-tax movement is aimed at the wrong target. Billionaires create a lot of damage, to be sure. As Alex Gibney’s new documentary Musk lays out, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent nearly $300 million helping elect a president and then slashed federal agencies, including several investigating his own companies. Still, he and his tech-bro pals are not themselves the underlying reason for our economic dysfunction.
In my view, the root cause is corporate power—the way modern corporations are owned, governed, and permitted to organize markets and politics to their own advantage—and how relentlessly that power has concentrated over the past 50 years. The evidence is everywhere. Since the late 1990s, three-quarters of American industries have grown more concentrated. Corporate margins have roughly tripled since 1980, and after-tax profits—below 10% of GDP for virtually all of 1950 to 2010—now exceed 12%, near the record. Economist Thomas Philippon calculates that weakened competition costs the typical household about $300 a month.
Since 1970, when Milton Friedman declared that a corporation's only social responsibility is profit, businesses have been re-engineered around delivering the most value possible to shareholders. Today, the bulk of many senior executives’ pay comes in the form of stock options and share buybacks (when a company spends its earnings to buy up its own stock and lift the price), which now send over a trillion dollars a year to shareholders rather than into wages or investment. Before 1982, this practice was viewed as market manipulation. In the following decades, the forces that once pushed back against inequality were gutted: union membership fell from 20% of American workers to 10%, and antitrust enforcement was consistently muted.
This is where billionaires come in. Nobody earns $839 billion from a paycheck. A fortune of that scale can only be made by accumulating equity. That is, gains from corporate profits. Profit is simply what remains after wages are held down, taxes are minimized, and costs are pushed onto workers, communities, and the environment. It makes little difference whether the claim to those profits comes from founding a company or, as with hedge-fund and private-equity fortunes, from the fruit of corporations other people built. Because the richest tenth of Americans own nearly 90% of household stock-market wealth, every dollar shifted from paychecks to profit flows almost undiluted to the top.
You don't have to look hard for examples. The Walton fortune rests on wages so low that a federal watchdog found Walmart among the biggest employers of workers on Medicaid and food stamps. In other words, taxpayers are subsidizing the payroll beneath a dynastic fortune. Amazon founder and CEO Jeff Bezos's wealth compounded over years during which Amazon paid no federal income tax on billions in profit while fighting its warehouse workers' union drives. In each case, the fortune is substantially extracted from workers and the public, not the market reward it is billed as.
None of this would last without help from Washington. Over the past half century, political spending has become a core business strategy and arguably the highest-return investment a large company can make.
In a 1971 memorandum, future Supreme Court justice Lewis Powell urged the Chamber of Commerce to put business on a political war footing. Today, lobbying has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry and business now outspends labor and public-interest groups 34-to-one. Since Citizens United removed the last meaningful limits on business political spending in 2010, every election has cost more than the last—nearly $16 billion in 2024, mostly corporate money.
Under President Donald Trump, the exchange has become impossible to ignore. Corporations lined up with seven-figure donations to his inaugural fund; oil executives, who were asked point-blank for $1 billion at a Mar-a-Lago dinner, have watched climate rules fall ever since; Paramount paid $16 million to settle a lawsuit legal experts dismissed while its merger awaited federal approval; and the crypto industry, having spent more than $130 million on the 2024 races, saw the enforcement cases against it evaporate, and this fall is spending hundreds of millions on 2026 midterm races.
This is why a politics aimed only at billionaires will miss the mark. I support wealth taxes, and I hope Proposition 40 passes. Yet wealth taxes only claw back winnings after the fact. This year's Forbes’ Billionaires list added 390 newcomers. Taxing Musk, Bezos, and other billionaires does not touch the executives, boards, investment funds, and political machines that keep minting new ones.
What would it mean to take aim at the root cause of inequality instead? First, we must recognize that the shareholder-primacy firm is a policy choice—the product of lobbying and lawmaking since the 1970s—and policy choices can be remade by rebuilding labor power through labor-law reform and sectoral bargaining, reviving antitrust, and getting corporate money out of politics. Early American corporate charters, after all, were granted for limited public purposes and could be revoked when abused.
It also means redesigning ownership itself. In my research on alternative corporate models, I have studied companies that are deliberately structured so that no one can extract a dynastic fortune, because the equity is legally locked to purpose. When Patagonia's founder moved the company into a purpose trust in 2022, such extraction became impossible by design; Bosch has been majority-owned by a foundation for decades and competes ferociously. Steward ownership, employee ownership, and benefit corporations are working alternatives operating in thousands of companies around the world and address wealth concentration at its source.
The wealth-tax debate, in other words, is about how to redistribute the gains that came from corporate power. But we need to redistribute corporate power itself.
None of this argues against Proposition 40 or its state and federal counterparts. Vote for them, pass them, let the revenue fund healthcare and schools. It is an argument about where attention needs to be focused next. History tells us that previous American confrontations with concentrated wealth, from Progressive Era trustbusters to the New Deal, succeeded not merely by taxing the winners but by restructuring corporate power through antitrust enforcement, securities regulation, and protecting labor rights.
The real question facing America is whether corporations exist to serve society, or society exists to serve corporations. A politics that stops at the wealth tax has already conceded the answer.

AWOL Vision Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector Review: A Top Buy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Works well in a dark room or in daylight. Provides a brilliantly colorful video image. The projector itself packs amazing sound quality. Plenty of settings are available to tweak to get the perfect picture.
TIRED
Slight issues with auto-keystoning and height channel audio.
It takes a special home theater projector to get me to stick through a movie like Supergirl. Critics panned it for dark themes, and its visually dark tones make it literally tough to see. But when I used the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max to project it onto a 120-inch screen with Dolby Atmos sound blasting from every corner of my basement, the film looked stunning.
The Aetherion Max, with its precise picture-quality settings and sharp 4K clarity, provides an experience rivaling that of a movie theater. Supergirl might suffer from bad CGI and even worse dialog, but the projector's features, like Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, brought the film to life, making reds and blues pop with amazing vividness.
Priced at $4,499, this ultrashort throw model sits right next to the wall or projector screen. In some ways, it reminds me of the LG Micro RGB Evo television with highly adjustable picture-quality settings. Ultimately, though, I'm a fan of the Aetherion Max because it projects a breathtakingly colorful image.
An Engineering Marvel, Except for the Remote
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
Before taking stock of its powerhouse specs, I noticed the Aetherion Max's design. Shaped a bit like a Tesla Cybertruck, the silver projector has sharp edges that lend a modern look. The front of the machine (the side that faces you) has no buttons except a single white line that animates when you power it on—a detail I found to be distracting and then powered off. The other side (which faces the screen) is where you'll find three HDMI 2.1 ports (including one for eARC passthrough audio), a USB-A port for a local storage device, optical and 3.5mm audio-out ports, and a 1 GBps Ethernet port for wired streaming.
This model runs on Google TV, and that’s a relief because it meant setup only took a few minutes. Auto-keystoning with manual screen-size options worked just fine. There’s also a QR code you can use to automate keystone correction from your phone, but my room was too dark, and it didn't work for me. (AWOL Vision reps told me it should have worked fine even in a dark room like mine.)
The portable projector weighs 19.3 pounds—notably less than its 23-pound competitor Hisense XR10 Smart Projector (8/10, WIRED Recommends)—and I found it both easy to grip and move around between rooms. For wireless streaming, the Aetherion Max supports Wi-Fi 7, offering nice compatibility and speed. It also runs quite fast thanks to 8 GB of internal RAM and offers 128 GB of internal storage for storing content, though I relied mostly on streaming.
Unlike the highly rated Xgimi Titan Noir Max, the Aetherion Max's iris does not adjust dynamically as you watch content. But similar to the Hisense XR10, you can adjust picture-quality settings to match the room. For example, Dolby Vision Bright works best in a bright room, allowing the iris to let in more light.
For color accuracy, the projector hits 110 percent of the Rec. 2020 spec. That means if you watch a movie that meets that color spec, like Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 or Inside Out, you will see the entire color palette. AWOL Vision also lists the contrast ratio as 6,000:1 and lumens at 3,300 ISO, but—as I've learned from personal experience—those specs are not the final arbiter of picture quality. Many other factors come into play, including the darkness level of a room.
Photograph: John Brandon
The weak spot here is the remote, which is functional if not impressive. I like its large Home button that’s centered and easy to find in the dark without looking. There’s also a button for Google Gemini and convenient shortcuts for apps like Netflix. My main issue is with the volume buttons, placed just above the shortcuts, but small and hard to find. Only the upper half of the remote is backlit, which uselessly doesn't extend to all of the buttons, including volume.
Don’t Fear the Bright Sunshine
The Aetherion Max's ability to work in a brightly lit room blew me away throughout testing. I watched the movie Mayday on Apple TV+ from start to finish in broad daylight, projecting the image on a wall that measures nearly 16 feet diagonally. I didn't notice any contrast problems and could see nighttime scenes just fine. The slight warping on my wall distorted the image a bit, but that's to be expected of ultrashort throw models.
In my windowless testing room, with a full surround-sound system that even includes height channel speakers in the ceiling, the Aetherion Max performed even better. To test a projector's contrast ratio and brightness, I typically play dark scenes in the movies Awake and The Creator, and I've never seen the scenes look as great as they did when rendered by the Aetherion Max. I didn’t even have to tweak the picture-quality settings (and generally when I test these specs, such is not the case).
Dark scenes in House of the Dragon, which I streamed using the HBO Max app, did require some user intervention, though. A beach scene in the moonlight involving a mysterious dragon would be hard to render even on high-end home cinema projectors, but once I enabled Dark Detail and Enhanced Black Level, I could suddenly see everything clearly, just as the TV show creators intended.
Indeed, every time I ran into a slight issue with picture quality, I found a matching setting that solved the problem. In a dark hallway scene during the movie The Batman, gun flashes looked bright red and clear, but some amber tones on Batman looked a shade too dark. Once I switched to Dolby Vision Bright, I could easily make out the grimaces and muscle flexes. Some projectors look a bit out of focus on the edges, but that's not true with the Aetherion Max; in Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu on Disney+, a snowy scene showcased the extreme pixel clarity all the way to the ends of the screen.
Photograph: John Brandon
Photograph: John Brandon
For games, I tested NBA 2K27 with the new Nvidia GeForce driver on an Alienware Aurora gaming laptop. The jaw-dropping graphics, which use realistic lighting and details, made a convincing case for Anthony Edwards of the Minnesota Timberwolves being in my testing room. When I tried Onimusha: Way of the Sword on PC, I was equally blown away by the crisp graphics. At this larger size, with ultra-clear pixel depth across the entire screen, every samurai slash seemed more realistic. Great for gaming, the projector uses extremely low latency—just 1 millisecond—for no lag, graphical stuttering, or delays, allowing for quick controller responses.
Sound is strong on the projector itself. When I watched the movies Civil War and Unbroken via an Onkyo TX-RZ50 AV receiver, I felt I was in a movie theater. A slight glitch was that the audio cut out when I used height channel speakers for 7.1.2 sound (AWOL Vision is investigating why).
The Aetherion Max also passed demo-reel benchmarks with flying colors—for the most part. While scenes with flowers, white mist over a snowy mountain, water in the deep blue ocean, and two horses in a field looked mesmerizing and realistic, it was tough to make out dark trees on a dark background. The skin-tone test also yielded unimpressive results. I’m not sure why, but two faces looked way too similar in a group shot, and a few other tests showed a lack of tonal variety. Adjusting settings didn’t help. However, this detail didn’t heavily factor into my overall takeaway of the projector, since it's a subtle color benchmark.
The AWOL Vision Aetherion Max is ultimately an amazing projector: a rock star of color accuracy, with crisp pixel clarity across the entire image and superior contrast. While the price is in line with other high-end models, this is one seriously capable home cinema model.
John Brandon is a contributing writer for WIRED. He reviews televisions, projectors, speakers, and other AV staples. He started writing full-time in 2001 and has been featured in Forbes, Popular Mechanics, The Telegraph, Minnesota Monthly magazine, and many other publications. He lives in Minneapolis–Saint Paul. AI-Generated Hot Girls Are Ripping Off Comedians to Boost Their Horny Content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Last week, the stand-up comedian Julia Jasunas was on Instagram when she got a DM from a fellow comic. Did she know, her friend wrote, that a random Instagram influencer had ripped off a joke from her stand-up act?
Initially, Jasunas was mad but not overly shocked. Plagiarism is not uncommon in the stand-up comedy world, and comics are “really sensitive about it, because there's not a ton of protection against it,” she tells WIRED. “So we all look out for each other.” Then she clicked on the link.
The video was of a purported stand-up comic named Aylen Skye, a buxom blond with leonine cheekbones and 250,000 Instagram followers. In the clip, Skye, wearing a crop top and Daisy Dukes, tells a joke about renting out a room in her two-bedroom apartment to a cute guy. To Jasunas’ shock, it was, verbatim, her joke, down to the “ums” and “ahs.”
Whoever Skye was, she didn’t appear to be a comic; the website she advertised in her video, AylenTV.com, redirected to NSFW content on Fanvue, a subscription-based OnlyFans competitor that markets itself as the “No1 AI monetisation platform for creators.” And not only did she appear to not be a comic, she also didn’t seem to be real. After looking at Skye’s comments section, Jasunas was fairly convinced she was AI.
“You look at any female comic’s comments section and you’ll see all these men berating her, objectifying her body, saying she’s not funny or the joke is bad,” she says. But with Skye, all of the comments were positive. “That’s how I knew she was fake,” she deadpans.
For Jasunas, being ripped off by a sexy AI-generated comedian was “violating on so many different levels.” “It’s one thing to have your jokes stolen,” she says. “It’s another to funnel your work into something so sexualized, for someone else’s profit.” She immediately reported the video to Meta for impersonation, but says Meta told her it did not violate community guidelines because Skye wasn’t pretending to be Jasunas; it was just passing off her joke as its own. “They just didn’t seem to care,” Jasunas says. (The majority of Skye’s posts are now flagged as AI content, though the account itself is not.)
Jasunas is far from the only stand-up comic to have been targeted by Skye. Nor does Skye appear to be the only AI-generated hot girl account targeting comics. WIRED has identified eight comics whose videos have been replicated by scantily clad, AI-generated women, many of whom follow each other on social media. All of the videos are copies of already-successful viral stand-up clips, except the AI-generated counterparts are playing to bigger audiences, with better lighting, better sound, and more skintight outfits—essentially, all the elements required to ensure virality. The accounts also post flirty, clearly AI-generated late-night TV show interviews with hosts like Conan O’Brien and Jimmy Kimmel, as well as the occasional “edgy” racist or transphobic joke catering to the MAGA crowd.
Though Instagram’s community guidelines prohibit impersonation, such policies don’t extend to copying someone else’s content, particularly if that content isn’t copyrighted. The platform also does not have any prohibitions against AI content, so long as it is appropriately labeled as such. Some of the accounts are labeled as AI-generated—but others are not, or their videos are inconsistently labeled. (Skye did not respond to a request for comment, though it has commented on many stand-up comics’ videos calling it out: “if you focused on putting out content instead of making whinny [sic] posts like this, you’d be as successful as me,” it wrote on one comic’s Instagram post.)
Particularly grating to the comics being ripped off is that some of the AI-generated videos perform better than the originals, spawning calls for increased protections for original content on Instagram. “AI is evolving very fast, and we need rules to protect creators before this becomes a bigger issue,” says Mandy Martino, who also had one of her jokes lifted by Skye. “It’s not just about a joke being stolen—it’s about this being a change that we need to get ahead of. And Instagram saying this isn’t a problem is the scariest part.”
Comics have been complaining about AI accounts stealing their content since June, with the stand-up Steph Clark regularly documenting such “weird pick-me AI slop” on her Instagram. In one early video, the AI stand-up in question is a leggy redhead sitting on a stool, awkwardly delivering a nonsensical punch line comparing faking orgasms to being a bad cook, a vacant expression on its face.
In the following months, however, the technology for such clone videos has improved exponentially, to the degree that it’s difficult to tell whether or not the women in the videos are actually real people. One such example is Tiffany Sloane, which identifies itself as an actress in its bio on Instagram, where it has more than 375,000 followers. A pear-shaped 19-year-old bombshell with a septum piercing and a BBL, Sloane does crowd work and jokes about quarter-zips and Jimmy Buffett songs on its Instagram page—which, similar to Skye, also includes a Highlights link to its OnlyFans profile.
Since starting the Instagram account in August, Sloane amassed a robust following and is also on TikTok and Facebook, where it has built out a “super horny AI-generated short-form video content farm,” as the writer Ryan Broderick puts it. On October 3, the comedian George Brett Olson posted a viral video captioned “AI stole my joke!!!” showing a side-by-side comparison of his stand-up bit—a joke about how Republicans ignore the risks of AI in favor of manufacturing panic over illegal immigration—next to Sloane’s near-identical one. In both clips, the comics are standing in front of identical backdrops and wearing similar salmon shirts and khaki shorts. Only the punch line, which features an expletive in Olson’s version, is different.
“I was kind of in shock,” Olson tells WIRED of seeing Sloane’s video for the first time. “I just thought it was so weird to see people openly stealing in real time.” He says his followers told him they reported it to Meta, and according to them, Meta responded by saying Sloane’s video did not violate any community guidelines. “I couldn’t believe it,” he says. “This is my intellectual property. I created it. And not only did this person or whatever steal it, they stole my likeness too.”
After Olson made his video calling out Sloane, he was flooded with comments from fellow stand-ups and fans supporting him and vowing to report Sloane’s account to Instagram. Even Sloane weighed in, leaving a comment on Olson’s page saying, “sorry, won’t happen again” before deleting its video, as well as many other Reels on its page. (Sloane didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
Ultimately, however, Olson was dispirited by the inaction on Meta’s end. After tagging Instagram head Adam Mosseri, Mosseri responded by saying that while he did not think it was “practical for us to try and ban AI content” from Meta, the platform was “very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an AI creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that.”
Responding to WIRED, Francis Brennan, a spokesperson for Meta, declined to comment further, saying, “Our policies are pretty clear around this stuff, and Adam’s comment speaks for itself.” All of the AI-generated accounts flagged by WIRED are still on the platform.
As of now, there’s very little that comedians can do about AI creators “ripping off content wholesale.” Legally, jokes have historically enjoyed very little copyright protection, in part due to the ephemeral nature of stand-up and the fact that many setups and punch lines have been used in the industry, with slightly different variations, for years. There’s also the matter of the financial stakes being relatively low, according to Aaron Perzanowski, now a law professor at the University of Michigan, who told NPR in 2017, “when you're talking about accusations of infringement dealing with fairly low-dollar-value creative work, we don't see a lot of litigation." (Olson says this sentiment was echoed by an intellectual property lawyer he consulted with, who he claims told him that unless Sloane was making millions of dollars on OnlyFans, threatening a lawsuit was probably more trouble than it was worth.)
The negative sentiment against these AI-generated creators does not appear to be shared by some in the tech industry, such as Andreessen Horowitz partner Justine Moore, who publicly praised Sloane in an X post, referring to her online presence as “a genius marketing hack.”
Olson is not overly optimistic that AI evangelists will rush to the defense of the creatives whose labor is being exploited. Nor, for that matter, does he believe that the “lizard-brained” commenters rushing to post horny comments on Sloane’s and Skye’s pages particularly care whether they’re real, or who actually crafted the jokes they’re telling in their viral clips.
“To me, we're asking the essential question, does the artist matter?” he says. “And to those 350,000 people that follow Tiffany Sloane, the answer is clearly no. And that’s really demoralizing.”

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:57:32 UTC
19:57:32 KST

INTERVIEW – Armenian church official sees Türkiye-Armenia normalization as path to ‘stronger friendships’
Vice president of Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation welcomes efforts to improve bilateral ties, expresses hope that land border will soon reopen
Beril Canakci
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
DIYARBAKIR, Türkiye
A senior official of the Armenian church foundation in southeastern Türkiye’s Diyarbakir province has voiced support for the ongoing normalization process between Ankara and Yerevan, saying growing contact between the two sides will deepen friendship.
“We view the ongoing rapprochement between Armenia and Türkiye very positively,” Ohannes Gafur Ohanyan, vice president of the Surp Giragos Armenian Church Foundation, told Anadolu.
Ohanyan spoke during a visit by 7 Turkish and 7 Armenian journalists to Surp Giragos Armenian Church in Diyarbakir’s historic Sur district as part of an EU-funded media tour aimed at supporting normalization between Türkiye and Armenia.
“We believe that as these kinds of visits and events increase, the friendship between the two countries will grow even stronger,” he said. “Hopefully, the borders will open soon too.”
Türkiye and Armenia do not have diplomatic relations, and their land border has been closed since 1993. The two countries launched a normalization initiative in late 2021, appointing retired Turkish Ambassador Serdar Kilic and Armenian parliament Deputy Speaker Ruben Rubinyan as special envoys.
Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry said in May that technical and bureaucratic work to reopen the shared border with Armenia was still ongoing, although preparations for direct trade had been completed.
In early May, Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz visited Armenia, where officials signed a memorandum on the joint restoration of the historic Ani Bridge, a medieval structure spanning the border between the two countries.
During a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last month, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan also discussed advancing normalization, strengthening trade and economic ties, and improving regional transport links.
Center of attraction for Armenians worldwide
The local Armenian community in Diyarbakir comprises roughly 60 to 65 people, according to Ohanyan. Despite its compact size, social and community life surrounding the church remains active, with regular religious services organized around major holidays.
"Because we do not have a permanent resident clergyman here, we hold around 8 to 10 services a year during important religious holidays," Ohanyan said.
Describing Surp Giragos as an 800-year-old church and the largest Armenian church in the Middle East, he said it draws Armenians from Armenia as well as from the diaspora in Europe and the US.
Following decades of disuse, comprehensive restoration initiatives spearheaded by the local foundation and supported in subsequent years by Turkish state institutions including the Culture and Tourism Ministry, allowed the site to formally reopen for worship.
The church was later damaged during 2015 clashes in Sur involving the terrorist group PKK. It was restored with funding from Türkiye’s Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, under the coordination of the General Directorate of Foundations, and reopened for worship after seven years.
The foundation’s second church, the roughly 500-year-old Surp Sarkis in the Alipasa neighborhood, fell into disrepair over time because it had no congregation and was further damaged in the February 2023 earthquakes centered in Kahramanmaras. Restoration work began in 2024 with a grant from the Culture and Tourism Ministry.
"Surp Sarkis has been in ruins for nearly a century," Ohanyan noted. "We have made considerable progress and have largely completed the structural work on the main building."
Ohanyan also called on businesspeople, philanthropists and the wider public for further support.

Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate without repeating their studies: the government explained the mechanism
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:53 EEST
19:56:53 KST

Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate without repeating their studies: the government explained the mechanism
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian children abroad will be able to receive a school-leaving certificate through recognition of their foreign education and a Ukrainian studies component. The program can be completed in person or remotely.
Ukrainian schoolchildren who are abroad because of the full-scale war can obtain a Ukrainian certificate of completion of secondary education without having to repeat the full educational program. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said this during his speech in parliament on October 16, UNN reports.
To this end, the state has provided for the possibility of recognizing the results of education at foreign schools in combination with the study of Ukrainian studies subjects.
Details
The issue of providing education to Ukrainian children abroad was raised by Deputy Speaker of the Verkhovna Rada Olena Kondratiuk. According to her, based on estimates cited in a report by the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine and the Accounting Chamber for September 2026, between 320,000 and 400,000 Ukrainian children are currently studying outside Ukraine. Kondratiuk emphasized that one of the state's key tasks remains preserving these children's connection with the Ukrainian education system, as well as creating conditions for their return after the war ends.
In particular, she asked how effectively the mechanisms for reintegrating schoolchildren, simplifying the recognition of education documents, and providing opportunities to study the Ukrainian language at educational institutions in other countries are working.
Answering the question, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi emphasized that Ukrainian children abroad remain one of the priorities of the state's education policy.
Our children abroad are our children; they are Ukrainian children. And we must do everything so that, once the danger of war has ended, they return to Ukraine and support and develop the Ukrainian economy
According to the head of government, education is one of the most important tools for preserving the younger generation's connection with Ukraine. At the same time, he acknowledged that children who are already studying at schools in their host countries often do not have the opportunity to fully master the Ukrainian educational program in parallel because of the excessive workload.
How Ukrainian schoolchildren abroad can obtain a certificate
To solve this problem, the state proposed a Ukrainian studies component that makes it possible to combine education at a foreign school with the study of subjects necessary to preserve ties with Ukrainian education. According to the head of government, the relevant program can be completed either directly at educational centers abroad or remotely through Ukrainian schools.
It (the program, — ed.) can be completed at verified centers operating in other countries—there are already more than 120 of them that have been verified by the Ministry of Education. It can also be done remotely through Ukrainian schools operating in a remote-learning format
The program provides that, in their free time outside their main studies, Ukrainian children study the Ukrainian language, the history of Ukraine, the geography of Ukraine, cultural studies, as well as individual subjects of their choice. In other words, schoolchildren do not need to repeat the entire program they are already studying at educational institutions in their host countries.
As the head of government explained, under the agreements reached, the Ukrainian side may recognize the results of education obtained abroad. After completing the Ukrainian studies component, the child will also be able to receive a Ukrainian document certifying completion of secondary education. This, in particular, opens the possibility of admission to Ukrainian universities and allows schoolchildren to remain part of the Ukrainian educational and cultural environment.
In addition, the government is cooperating with Ukrainian communities abroad, including religious communities, to support the activities of educational centers and provide them with educational literature.
Ukrainian as a second foreign language in European schools
Particular attention during the discussion was devoted to the possibility of studying Ukrainian as a second foreign language in schools in European countries.
Olena Kondratiuk noted that the relevant practice already exists in a number of countries that have taken in Ukrainian refugees. According to her, approximately 45 Polish schools are already working in this direction. Similar approaches are being applied in certain educational institutions in the United Kingdom and Austria. The lawmaker also noted France's active involvement. In her view, expanding such opportunities will allow Ukrainian children to take relevant exams in their host countries while maintaining their knowledge of their native language.
Kondratiuk also emphasized that introducing Ukrainian as a second foreign language could become an alternative to studying Russian in European schools. She urged the Ukrainian authorities to intensify cooperation with the education ministries of European Union states to expand this practice.
Some Ukrainian children abroad may remain outside the education system
Another problem highlighted by the Deputy Chairperson of the Verkhovna Rada was the absence of some Ukrainian children from education institution registration systems.
Kondratiuk emphasized that meetings with the education ministers of European countries revealed that some Ukrainian children are studying neither in local schools nor remotely at Ukrainian educational institutions. She called this a serious gap requiring the attention of the Ukrainian authorities and the education agencies of the host countries.
In Kondratiuk's view, Ukraine should maintain regular contact with such children, ensure their access to education, and create conditions enabling them to remain part of the Ukrainian educational space even during an extended stay abroad.
Previously
Earlier, UNN reported that due to the war and the search for prospects, female graduates are leaving Ukraine en masse to study abroad.

Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
Countries along NATO’s eastern flank are growing increasingly concerned about the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine.

Poland’s armed forces said on Friday that they had scrambled fighter jets during the attacks and no violation of the country’s airspace was recorded.
It was just the latest such alert as Poland and other countries along NATO’s eastern flank grow increasingly concerned over the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine as Russia appears to be accelerating its tests of regional defences. Later on Friday, Bulgaria’s defence minister said Sofia has requested help from NATO to bolster its defences.
During air attacks across Ukraine overnight, numerous strikes hit the Volyn region, cutting electricity to 370,000 people across the western district, which sits on the border with Poland. Governor Roman Romaniuk reported that two people were injured.
In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number.
Private power company DTEK announced on Friday that it had implemented emergency power cuts across Kyiv due to ongoing strikes.
In Russia, officials said air defences had blocked a Ukrainian drone attack against a heating plant in the Vladimir region.
Ukraine has had significant success in attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure and its oil refineries in particular. However, that strategy has provoked anger from United States President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for pushing up global oil prices.
Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow.
Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said the capital’s four airports and St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport had suspended operations.
Ukrainian attacks killed two people in the Russian-controlled Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed governor said.
Concern over Russian activity near NATO territory has grown since the summer as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported numerous intrusions of drones into their airspace and waters.
That activity appears to be becoming more bellicose. In recent weeks, drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing.
Drones hit two ships off Romania’s coast this week. A hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria’s coast on Tuesday prompted Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Friday that while the evidence pointed to Russia, his government does not have proof.
Shortly afterwards, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters that Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and antidrone systems to bolster its defences.

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:55:27 UTC
19:55:27 KST

Iran ships some LPG, jet fuel despite US blockade, data shows
DAMASCUS/LONDON, Oct 16 - Iran has managed to export some liquefied petroleum gas and jet fuel since July, despite a US naval blockade, shipping intelligence showed and people involved in security said.
Tehran has in recent weeks been concealing such cargoes among a growing volume of ship-to-ship transfers by other Gulf producers off Oman, four people in maritime security who track Gulf oil movements told Reuters.
The Iranian exports and methodology are reported for the first time here. While a fraction of its former energy exports, the cargoes are rare evidence of petroleum products getting through a blockade that has halted Iran's crude exports.
Analysis by US advocacy group United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), which monitors Iran-related tanker traffic using ship and satellite tracking, shows at least eight gas tankers carrying Iranian LPG have left the Gulf of Oman since mid-July.
Another tanker carrying Iranian jet fuel reached Myanmar in September, additional satellite imagery and analysis by maritime intelligence group SynMax show.
The US imposed targeted sanctions in 2023 on Myanmar's jet-fuel industry, citing military airstrikes on civilians that the United Nations says have killed thousands of people. Myanmar's military government has repeatedly denied targeting civilians, saying its operations are directed against armed groups.
Six of the eight gas tankers and the jet fuel tanker are under US sanctions for transporting Iranian petroleum and petrochemical products, a Reuters analysis of the vessels and sanctions imposed on ships by the US Treasury showed.
"What we have seen passing is a handful of tankers carrying Iranian LPG, but the overwhelming majority of tankers laden with Iranian products have been redirected by US forces," said Jemima Shelley, senior research analyst with UANI.
Shelley said some Iranian LPG tankers transferred cargoes near the Omani coastal towns of Shinas and Sohar, while others waited in the Gulf of Oman before heading past the US blockade, which US Central Command has said sits across the Gulf of Oman near the Iran-Pakistan border.
The total amount of these LPG cargoes was estimated at 4.1 million barrels, Shelley said.
Shelley said the shipments were driven "more by opportunism" than showing a new trend of Iran trying to export its oil and petrochemicals by using smaller ships.
Most of the cargoes sailed to Malaysia's Eastern Outer Port Limits to conduct further STS transfers for likely destinations in China, Shelley said, based on UANI's analysis.
The Iranian government did not respond to a request for comment. Myanmar's military-backed government did not respond to a request for comment on whether the country had received Iranian jet fuel.
US MILITARY SAYS BLOCKADE 'IRONCLAD'
The US military's Centcom said its naval blockade, which was first imposed on Iran-related oil exports on April 13, is "ironclad". The blockade was lifted in June after the US reached a draft understanding with Iran, but it was reimposed on July 14 following the collapse of the agreement.
A US military official told Reuters that the passage of a vessel does not necessarily mean it had evaded the blockade. Every ship was assessed individually, including through a review of its papers, and some vessels could be allowed through for humanitarian reasons, the official added.
The official said the appearance of a vessel on US sanctions lists is not the only factor to make it subject to the blockade, adding that US forces are also closely monitoring some ships without taking action against them for operational reasons.
Centcom said in an update on October 13 that during the three months of the latest blockade, four commercial vessels had been disabled and 135 ships had been turned around by US forces.
The US military has turned around ships from Asia and also seized some tankers, previous Centcom statements said.
Washington has coupled its blockade with a sanctions campaign aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial links and depriving it of revenue. Last week, it imposed fresh sanctions on 17 vessels involved in transporting Iranian crude, petrochemicals and petroleum products.
A US Treasury spokesperson questioned shipping data suggesting vessels had evaded the blockade, saying ships could spoof their locations or use false identities when loading.
Such data "should be taken with a grain of salt", the spokesperson said.
The Treasury spokesperson said Operation Economic Outcast, together with the blockade, was "suffocating the Iranian regime".
Torbjorn Soltvedt, principal Middle East analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said although there was no sign of Washington easing its blockade, worsening economic conditions in Iran could push Tehran to take greater risks.
"If Iran can move product tankers through, even in small numbers, jet fuel may be a good option. Iran's aviation industry is under increasing pressure from US sanctions, with a growing number of planes grounded, and a potential surplus of jet fuel at Iranian refineries," Soltvedt added.
Iranian crude exports fell to zero in September, according to Kpler, the first month without a shipment since the analytics firm began tracking the producer in 2013.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the blockade prevented most Chinese purchases of Iranian oil and left Iran unable to deliver crude to customers. REUTERS
