Italy cuts air traffic in half amid data transmission issue
October 16, 2026
Air travelers across Italy faced delays and cancellations on Friday because of a problem with the country's air traffic control systems.
The ENAV air traffic control authority ruled out foul play such as a cyberattack, and said it was forced to introduce temporary restrictions of the volume of flights after identifying a data transmission problem.
Major airports in cities like Rome and Milan warned of likely disruptions and advised passengers to check with their airlines.
What did authorities say about the problem?
ENAV said it first identified the issue overnight. It was forced to restrict the volume of flights at around 6 a.m. (0400 GMT/UTC) as the number of scheduled services increased.
"We would like to inform you that this morning we guaranteed the greatest possible number of departures, including intercontinental flights," ENAV said.
Shorter-distance services were more likely to be interrupted.
"Despite the anomalies encountered on the data transmission network, we are deploying all available resources to minimize disruption and restore full operations as soon as possible," ENAV said. "We confirm an operational capacity of 50% of total air traffic, ensuring maximum safety at all times, which remains the Company's top priority."
ENAV said it had ruled out the possibility of the disturbance being caused by "malicious acts."
Rome airports operator ADR warned passengers that "flight delays and cancellations may occur" and advised passengers to contact their airline if uncertain. Milan airports company SEA issued a similar notice.

Hurricane Trudy weakens but may regain strength off Mexican coast
MEXICO CITY, Oct 16 - Hurricane Trudy weakened on Friday but could regain strength in the coming hours, meteorologists warned, as the storm approached Mexico's western coast, packing winds of up to 140 km per hour (85 mph).
Further strengthening is forecast before Trudy nears Jalisco and Colima states in central-western Mexico late on Saturday as a life-threatening major hurricane, Mexican authorities and the US-based National Hurricane Center said.
The center of Trudy will approach the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico on Saturday and pass near the coast Saturday night into Sunday, the NHC said in its latest advisory.
"Trudy will remain a dangerous hurricane as it moves near Mexico's central-western coast this weekend, bringing strong winds, rough seas, and torrential rain," said private forecaster AccuWeather.
Earlier, Trudy had reached Category 3 and was expected to intensify to a Category 4 hurricane.
Any change in its path closer to shore will increase the severity of its impact, the head of Mexico's weather agency, Fabian Vazquez, said at a press conference.
"Everyone in this region needs to be very careful and stay alert over the weekend," he added.
Mexico's civil protection agency asked residents to prepare by securing doors and windows, and removing objects that could be thrown around by the strong winds.
In the coastal resort city of Acapulco, fishermen pulled their boats ashore after authorities closed some fishing and tourist ports to small vessels.
The storm is expected to produce up to 15 inches (38 cm) of rain in the states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco, increasing the risk of life-threatening flooding and landslides, according to the NHC.
Mexico's Pacific coast has already been battered in recent weeks by storms that left several dead and caused severe flooding.
Tropical Storm Simon continues to weaken farther northwest offshore, after dropping heavy rain along the coast earlier as a hurricane.
Last week, Tropical Storm Rachel hit the Baja California peninsula, damaging some 1,500 homes. REUTERS

American attack helicopters open fire in Korea
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:35:07 BST
19:35:07 KST

American Apache crews carried out aerial gunnery at the Rodriguez Live Fire Complex in South Korea at the end of September, validating weapons employment, target engagement and crew coordination under live-fire conditions, according to the unit.
The crews came from 4th Battalion, 2nd Aviation Regiment, part of 2nd Combat Aviation Brigade in the 2nd Infantry Division and Republic of Korea and United States Combined Division. The division said the training strengthens combat readiness and proficiency, and the imagery released shows AH-64 Apaches engaging simulated targets at low level over wooded ridgelines, with rocket motor flashes beneath the fuselage and impact smoke rising from the hillsides.
Rodriguez Live Fire Complex sits near Pocheon in Gyeonggi Province, around twenty-five kilometres from the Demilitarised Zone, and it is the principal range on the peninsula where American and South Korean units can shoot and manoeuvre together with live ammunition. Its proximity to the border has made it a politically sensitive site, with noise and safety complaints from nearby villages a recurring issue.
2nd Combat Aviation Brigade is the only permanently forward-stationed combat aviation brigade in the United States Army, and the “Fight Tonight” tag the division attaches to its material reflects what the formation exists to do, which is to be ready for combat without a deployment timeline. The brigade operates from Camp Humphreys, the largest American overseas base, and its Apache battalions are among the few American attack aviation units held at that readiness state permanently.
The British Army flies the AH-64E Apache from Wattisham Flying Station under 1 Aviation Brigade Combat Team, having completed the transition from the Westland-built Mk1 fleet, and the American and British fleets now operate the same baseline aircraft. British crews train in similar gunnery cycles at ranges including Castlemartin and Otterburn, and have exercised alongside American attack aviation in Europe and the United States.

'Switzerland plus' deal option for UK as it seeks closer ties with EU, senior MEP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:34:25 UTC
19:34:25 KST

Bernd Lange's comments come as the Brexit debate has once again reignited across the UK after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for the country to readdress its relationship with Brussels.
A "Switzerland plus" deal is an option for the UK if it decides to go further in deepening its ties with the European Union, a senior member of the European Parliament has said.
Speaking in London on Thursday, Bernd Lange, a German politician who heads the Parliament's International Trade Committee, said the EU's "doors are open" to Britain.
"At the moment, my feeling is Switzerland plus," he said during a panel discussion at Europe House, suggesting this could involve "some kind of political cooperation" as well as agreements on areas such as trade, security, raw materials, and digital policy.
"Of course, the last step to come back is not forbidden. But that's in your hands," he added.
Lange, who was involved in Brexit negotiations, made the comments during a trip to London this week, where he is also due to meet with UK Trade Minister Anas Sarwar as well as MPs Stella Creasy and Liam Byrne to discuss options for bringing the UK and the EU "closer together."
The Guardian newspaper reported that Lange said a Switzerland plus deal could be negotiated within months of any decision to strengthen relations with Brussels and that he would "love to see the UK back."
Switzerland is not a member of the EU but has a number of bilateral agreements with the bloc that allows the country access to parts of the single market and ensures what it calls "smooth relations" across areas including trade, security, transport, and education. Switzerland pays a financial contribution to the EU's economic and social cohesion fund in return for its partial integration into the single market. The arrangement also includes free movement of people.
Brexit debate reopens
Lange's comments come as the Brexit debate has once again reignited across the UK after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for the country to readdress its relationship with Brussels.
Burnham told MPs earlier this week that "sticking with the current status quo is not good enough for Britain" and that a conversation over future relations must be had "if we are serious about promoting growth, controlling immigration, upholding our values and security."
Burnham, who recently said Brexit had "done more harm than good," has repeatedly signalled his intention to move the UK closer to the EU and said re-entering the bloc was one of a number of potential options for the country.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused the prime minister of "unpicking" the Brexit withdrawal agreement with the EU and warned he would not get a better deal.
A UK-EU summit is now set for 20 November.

Digested week: No Nobel again for Trump but he looks a cert to retain Fifa peace prize | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:34:15 UTC
19:34:15 KST

Monday
It might have been more, shall we say, diplomatic if Donald Trump had taken some deep breaths after finding out he had been overlooked for the Nobel peace prize for the second year running before virtually declaring war on Norway. But maybe we should just be grateful he refrained from rubbishing the South African human rights activist Navi Pillay, who picked up the award, and shelved his plans to livestream the execution of the Norwegian prize committee. There again, you can understand his frustration. It’s hard to think of someone who has done more to make the world a safer place. Where would we be had not The Donald started a war with Iran which he shows no sign of knowing how to finish and which has forced up the price of global energy? And it was so good to see him intervening so positively in Russia’s war with Ukraine by appearing to side with the aggressor. These are just the things everyone is looking for in a Nobel peace laureate. The president is also put out that no one has noticed he has personally ended eight global conflicts; though it would be helpful if he could let us know which ones. Are they ones he has personally started – Trump appears disappointed that Argentina hasn’t invaded the Falklands again – or ones that only he knows about. During a press conference at Chequers in 2025, he claimed to have brought about a lasting peace between Albania and Azerbaijan. Maybe there are other wars going on we just don’t know about. Perhaps Australia and New Zealand have been bombing each other for years with neither side noticing. And perhaps the border between France and Italy has been a no-go zone ever since the fight between Zinedine Zidane and Marco Materazzi in the 2006 World Cup final. Still, Trump looks a cert to retain Gianni Infantino’s Fifa peace prize – if only because it seems likely to be scrapped, making him the only winner.
Tuesday
We may be facing higher levels of global threat and energy costs, but the political outlook isn’t all bleak. You’d need to have a major sense of humour failure not to be enjoying Reform sliding in the polls and falling out with one another. Things seemed to start going wrong when the Guardian exposed Nigel Farage’s £5m bung from the Thai-based crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne. Nige has still not come up with a convincing explanation of how the money would be spent. Other than maintaining an expensive lifestyle. Then there was the Channel 4 sting when two of Farage’s closest political allies were caught allegedly trying to take an illegal overseas donation. Nige’s excuse? He wasn’t listening to his conversation with the donor. Who hasn’t dozed off when there’s £500,000 at stake? Since then everyone in Reform appears hell-bent on being the worst versions of themselves as the party loses support by tacking ever further to the right. On Monday, Robert Jenrick declared he would personally be happy to give the order for the Royal Navy to blow every small boat crossing the Channel out of the water. This was too much for Zia Yusuf. Zia is widely loathed within the Reform elite but no one has found a way of saying no to his money, so he gets to call himself the bogus title of shadow home secretary. His main objection to Honest Bob’s plan is that he wasn’t the one to think of it first. Meanwhile, Nige just sits back and pockets the money. Seemingly unable to stop his party collapsing around him.
Wednesday
After several years of consultation, the Bank of England has announced the four animals, insects and birds that will appear on the new banknotes. What goes on what denomination has yet to be decided, but the ones chosen are the European hedgehog, the barn owl, the buff-tailed bumblebee and the Atlantic puffin. And while I’d have quite liked to have seen my much-missed dog Herbie, who died last year, on one of the notes, they all seem reasonable choices to me. I guess the last thing the Bank wanted was to start a war between cat and dog lovers. But not everyone is happy. Partly because they are mad but mostly because they don’t apparently understand how the selection process worked. It was the public who got to choose both the theme of the banknotes and the actual creatures. Needless to say, leading the charge against the new notes are Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, who see the hedgehog and the puffin as some kind of woke symbols. A country going to the barn owls and the bumblebees. They have moaned, what was wrong with having Winston Churchill? Are we now ashamed of our past? No, you halfwits. You don’t have to plaster Churchill’s face on everything to prove you are British. Most of us are secure enough in our identity not to need countless flags and symbols as a reminder. It’s just nice to have a change from time to time. And how many people used to see Churchill’s face on a £5 note and feel a well of pride every time you wanted to buy a sandwich? For that matter, how many people even use cash these days? Mind you, once AI has mined all our data from our emails and bank accounts we could be back to a cash and letter-writing society.
Thursday
In one of his last conversations with a close friend, Jeffrey Archer was asked if he had any regrets. While he admitted to having some flaws, Archer went on to say that there was nothing he would change. I find that remarkable. I’m not expecting him to apologise for having invented so much of his life – a fantasist is going to fantasise – and he had every right to be proud of his book sales. But not to feel a tiny bit of regret about having lied on oath and being sent to prison. Or feel guilty for the lives he ruined as a result of his lies. That feels borderline sociopathic. Isn’t it human to wish you had done some things differently? I’ve been thinking about this now I’ve turned 70. There’s a lot about my life that I love – family, friends, job – but I have a lasting sadness and guilt about my 20s that I find hard to forgive. The waste, the self-destruction, the damage I did to myself and others. Many of those who knew me had doubts I would even live to 30. I had those doubts, too. And sometimes didn’t much care either way. So yes, I have a whole decade I would love to have done differently. The repair job has been a lifetime’s work and it’s still ongoing. It will probably always be thus.
Friday
The Celebrity Traitors continues to be addictive television. A class above the civilian version, partly because we all know something about the celebs, but mainly because the game is different. The civilians are playing for money, the celebs are playing for screen time. That’s why Amol Rajan was gutted to be banished inside 24 hours. The one exception was Richard E Grant, who didn’t care one way or the other. Since his wife died he’s become more disinhibited. The worst has already happened to him. Halfway in, Maya Jama and James Acaster are making great traitors. Maya because she’s so hard to read as her face doesn’t move, James because he genuinely believes he’s too nice to be a traitor while stabbing his friends in the back. I’m amazed Jerry Hall is still in. Not because she’s particularly suspicious but more because she’s incredibly annoying. And why has no one asked her what it was like being married to Rupert Murdoch? The faithful who is playing a blinder is Sharon Rooney. So far she has said and done nothing to attract the film crew, which means she’s likely to be around for a while yet. Being boring is not a bad strategy. I’d like to see a version of The Traitors for politicians, and in my forthcoming shows (Birmingham MAC on 31 October, Huntingdon theatre in Worcester on 26 November) I will be inviting the audience to offer suggestions for possible contestants. So please come along and let’s see if we can make it happen.

Putin Hands Control of 5 Western Firms to Ukraine War Veteran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:33:30 UTC
19:33:30 KST

President Vladimir Putin signed a decree Thursday placing the Russian assets of five major Western manufacturing companies under the temporary management of a little-known firm owned by an ex-official who fought in Ukraine.
The targeted European and U.S. assets include French flooring giant Tarkett, Belgian hygiene manufacturer Ontex Ru, German plastic packager Menshen, corrugated producer Kappa Rus and metal packaging producer Eviosys, a subsidiary of the U.S. Sonoco Products Company.
Their combined 2025 revenue exceeds 53 billion rubles ($633.2 million), with Tarkett accounting for 19.3 billion rubles, Kappa Rus 16.5 billion rubles, Ontex Ru 10.3 billion rubles, and Eviosys and Menshen 6.1 billion rubles and 1.4 billion rubles, respectively.
Putin’s decree hands management rights to Tsentr Kapital Management Company, a Moscow entity established in February 2026, according to corporate registry data cited by RBC.
Tsentr Kapital is owned by 47-year-old Marat Mirkhaidarov, the former deputy governor and chief of staff of Far East Russia’s Zabaikalsky region.
Mirkhaidarov volunteered to serve in Ukraine with Chechnya’s Akhmat unit in early 2024, according to exiled media reports.
“I’m a patriot, I served in the special military operation [in Ukraine]. I have combat awards,” Mirkhaidarov told the Agentstvo outlet on Friday, expressing caution about his and his family’s safety over the news.
Mirkhaidarov stepped down from his regional administration post in March 2025, citing the need for medical rehabilitation after sustaining injuries during a delivery mission near the frontline.
Putin signed an order in 2023 granting the state the authority to place foreign assets under its temporary management. The regime strips foreign owners of operational control over their Russian subsidiaries while preserving nominal legal title.
Moscow has described the asset seizures as a response to “hostile actions” taken by “unfriendly” foreign governments.
On Friday, the Kremlin said the latest transfers represent a continued policy “trend” targeting countries that froze more than 210 billion euros in Russian reserves in Europe.
“Their origin was one of the factors taken into account when making the decision,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
“We’re talking about those countries that take part in illegally holding Russian money, Russian assets. These are countries that take part in the illegal expropriation of Russian companies’ property,” Peskov said.

“The security of the Gulf and Saudi Arabia is linked to Egypt’s national security,” Sisi said, describing the relationship as “not merely a gesture of goodwill, but a reality and a shared interest.”
The Egyptian president reaffirmed Cairo’s support for Saudi Arabia’s stability, saying that targeting the Kingdom was contrary to both Arab and Egyptian national security interests.
He described Saudi Arabia as a highly influential regional state and stressed that threats to its security were unacceptable.
While reiterating Egypt’s commitment to de-escalation and diplomatic solutions to regional crises, Sisi warned against any violation of Saudi sovereignty or threats to maritime security in the Red Sea.
“We act with great restraint and strive to find solutions,” he said, “but we will not allow anyone to violate the borders of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, nor will we permit threats to the security of the Red Sea or its shipping lanes.”
Sisi said Egypt was seeking to prevent further escalation across the region while addressing security challenges along its own borders.
Turning to Sudan, he said Cairo had spent years working to resolve differences between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces in an effort to prevent the conflict from escalating.
He added that Egyptian mediation efforts had achieved temporary progress, but the situation had ultimately developed in a direction that Cairo had hoped to avoid.

The new multiannual financial framework (MFF): A future vision for the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:32:30 UTC
19:32:30 KST

The EU's new multiannual financial framework for 2028-2034 should channel funds more efficiently to bolster the bloc's competitiveness and future resilience, argues Markus Töns, the SPD parliamentary group's spokesperson on European affairs, in an opinion piece for Euronews.
Currently, negotiations are under way on the European Union's new Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028 to 2034.
The Commission's proposal one year ago charted a new course. In the wake of the Draghi and Letta reports on boosting the EU's competitiveness and future viability, the MFF has been realigned in order to use funds more efficiently.
Overall, the proposed new structure is welcome, as it opens up future prospects and offers the chance to respond more flexibly to crises and challenges.
But this restructuring brings not only opportunities; it also entails major cuts.
Many social projects in Germany are funded solely by the EU
Social, cohesion and agricultural support programmes such as the European Social Fund Plus (ESF+) and the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) are to be grouped together in the so-called first pillar.
Because funds are no longer firmly earmarked for individual programmes, a battle over distribution is looming.
The detailed allocation will then lie with the member states under their National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP).
Although the Commission has already proposed a quota of 14% for the social field, this is where most is at stake. Many, particularly social, projects in Germany are financed exclusively by the EU.
The German budget cannot plug this gap if EU funding is not continued. Once such structures have been dismantled, they will not easily be rebuilt. That is why we are calling for a minimum quota of 20% for social projects.
If this cannot be agreed at European level, our goal is at least to enshrine it for the German NRPP in a federal-state ordinance.
Fortunately, Germany has already reached agreement that tried-and-tested federal allocation structures will be maintained and that the EU's preference for centralised national allocation will not be followed.
Future industries: Using funding to narrow the global gap
The biggest innovation lies in the second pillar with the Competitiveness Fund.
Its purpose is to support innovation and investment in the single market. It should not be overlooked that the EU, and Germany in particular, remain key industrial locations.
In future industries and artificial intelligence, however, we are currently lagging far behind on the global stage.
Targeted funding now gives us the chance to reduce this deficit. If we want to strengthen our European resilience and drive forward the transformation of the economy, we must now be bold and take a major step forward.
New MFF: Sanctions mechanisms as an additional tool
Europe's responsibility in the world is reflected in the third pillar. This will place a stronger focus on the common foreign and security policy, but also on European development cooperation.
Both within Europe and in our relations with international partners, the new MFF offers the chance to set the course.
Not only through innovation guidelines, but also through sanctions mechanisms when countries turn away from the rule of law.
A clearer distinction from extremist and terrorist organisations when allocating development aid would also be welcome as a supplementary guideline.
The best-known EU programmes are Horizon and Erasmus, in which non-member states can also participate. Joint research and education programmes are a European strength, because they build networks and encourage people to look beyond their own horizons.
By placing them in the second pillar, there is an opportunity to give them even greater weight and to promote their links with the economy in a meaningful way.
This enables Europe's innovative power to unfold across the board through targeted cooperation between young people, new ideas and investment.
That is precisely what we must keep bringing to the fore in times of ever-growing challenges and economic as well as geopolitical pressure: this is about Europe's future.
A Europe in peace and prosperity, offering diverse opportunities and bringing its citizens ever closer together. An EU that also continually reaches out to its neighbours.
If no MFF is adopted by 2028, funding will expire
It is therefore wrong to regard the EU budget from a national perspective as a necessary evil.
Recently, however, Germany has joined the "Frugals" (Editor's note in German: "die Sparsamen" meaning Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark and Finland) in calling for cuts of around €200 billion.
In its proposal, the Irish Council presidency likewise spoke of €141 billion. The single market and European cooperation are our greatest assets. Every euro paid to Brussels returns many times over.
Despite all the tensions surrounding the German budget, paying in less would restrict Germany's options.
Chancellor Merz has already threatened a European shutdown (in German: "Haushaltsperre", that is, a budget freeze) if the member states cannot agree on radical cuts. Unlike a national budget that has not been adopted, the MFF does not move into provisional budget management.
If no new MFF is agreed by 2028, funding simply comes to an end.
Cutting agricultural subsidies is not 'sacrosanct'
If cuts do ultimately prove unavoidable, it is essential that they are applied horizontally, contrary to the proposal from the Irish Council presidency.
That means reductions are made evenly across all areas. Agricultural subsidies under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) are still often treated as sacrosanct, even though that is no longer appropriate.
Twenty-first century funding programmes must adapt to the realities of the time. The CAP cannot be exempt. Modern agricultural support must be targeted, not sprayed everywhere like water from a watering can, simply to avoid slurry being dumped in front of the European Parliament.
Here too a perspective could be created, namely that of sustainable, climate-friendly farming which guarantees Europe's food security. This would again create opportunities for research, innovation and cooperation.
There is no question that rural areas will continue to receive support through the LEADER programme (Editor's note: EU funding instrument for the autonomous and sustainable development of rural areas), but this too must no longer be distributed blindly on the basis of land area; it has to be awarded with a focus on innovation.
Only in this way can we address the real problems on the ground and increase the attractiveness of rural regions.
A digital tax would send a signal to the USA
Another challenge is repaying the Next Generation EU Covid support instrument and the interest arising from the borrowing, which comes on top of the new MFF.
To repay it, the EU wanted to introduce new own resources. That has still not happened.
Yet only own resources can act as an effective lever for stable financing, because there can be no fresh borrowing.
On NextGenerationEU (Editor's note: NGEU is the EU's temporary recovery instrument to tackle the economic and social impact of the COVID-19 pandemic) Germany's Federal Constitutional Court has taken a clear position, stating that it is a one-off.
New own resources would also offer a dual opportunity, as they could serve as instruments of political steering.
For example, a digital tax would send a clear signal to the USA. Without agreement among EU finance ministers on new own resources, or a willingness on the part of the member states to channel more money from their national budgets to Brussels, European funds will remain scarce.

Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:32:03 UTC
19:32:03 KST

Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
- Date:
- October 16, 2026
- Source:
- University of Konstanz
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.
- Share:
Plastic pollution is one of the world's most persistent environmental problems. Vast amounts of discarded plastic accumulate in the oceans, sometimes forming enormous garbage patches that threaten marine life. Most conventional plastics break down extremely slowly because microorganisms struggle to digest the synthetic polymers from which they are made. Instead of disappearing, these materials gradually fragment into increasingly smaller particles, including microplastics and nanoplastics.
Yet plastic waste is not completely beyond the reach of nature. Bacteria and other microorganisms can colonize its surfaces, forming communities known as biofilms. These communities create a distinctive microbial ecosystem that scientists call the "plastisphere."
Researchers at the University of Konstanz have now discovered an unusual enzyme that could reveal how some bacteria are becoming better equipped to break down certain types of plastic. The enzyme can digest particular polyesters and biodegradable plastics, but it has another unexpected ability: it can also break down penicillin, suggesting a possible connection to antibiotic resistance.
Scientists have nicknamed it the "Pac-Man enzyme" because its molecular structure features a remarkably wide opening where chemical reactions take place, known as the active site. The discovery suggests that bacteria may be adapting to digest certain plastic materials more quickly than researchers previously believed.
However, the findings also highlight an important limitation. For microorganisms to make a meaningful difference in reducing plastic pollution, more plastic products would need to be made from biodegradable materials that contain chemical bonds microbes can break apart.
Testing How Bacteria Break Down Bioplastics
To investigate how microorganisms digest biodegradable plastics, University of Konstanz biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied the entire process of microbial decomposition. They wanted to determine not only whether the materials could be completely broken down, but also which microorganisms were responsible and what biological mechanisms allowed them to do it.
The researchers examined the composition of the microbial communities involved and analyzed their collective genetic information (the metagenome). This approach allowed them to search for genes that might produce enzymes capable of breaking apart plastic polymers.
Their experiments focused on long-chain aliphatic polyesters (LCAP), a class of biodegradable plastic materials developed by a research team led by chemist Stefan Mecking. These materials contain chemical bonds that certain microorganisms can potentially break down, unlike the more resistant structures found in many conventional plastics.
The collaborative findings were published in The ISME Journal.
To observe how the bioplastics behaved in a natural environment, the team placed samples beneath the surface of forest soil at the university's botanical garden.
"We buried small pieces of LCAP bioplastic film in the upper humus layer in the forest at the university's botanical garden, about ten centimeters deep," explains Harry Lerner.
"This layer is where the breakdown of cellulose and other natural polymers, such as cutin - a plant-based polyester - takes place."
Humus is the upper layer of soil rich in decomposing organic matter, where microorganisms play a major role in recycling nutrients. Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls, while cutin is a naturally occurring polyester that helps form the protective outer covering of plants.
The researchers selected this environment because its microorganisms already possess the biological machinery needed to break down complex natural materials.
Bioplastics Disappeared Within About a Year
Alongside the outdoor experiment, the scientists carried out laboratory tests using soil collected from the same forest. They mixed powdered bioplastics into the soil and monitored microbial activity over the course of an entire year.
One important measurement was the amount of carbon dioxide, or CO2, released from the samples. As microorganisms consume and metabolize organic materials, they produce carbon dioxide through respiration. Tracking this gas helped the researchers determine how actively the microbes were breaking down the plastics.
The buried plastic films remained in the forest soil for a full year, allowing the team to compare decomposition under natural conditions with the carefully monitored laboratory experiments.
To assess the results, the scientists also tested cellulose, other biodegradable plastics, conventional polyethylene plastic, and soil samples without added materials.
"Cellulose, other types of bioplastics such as PHBV and PCL, as well as high-density plastic (HDPE) and untreated soil were used as controls in the laboratory. We found that all bioplastic materials were completely degraded within roughly 250 to 330 days. Cellulose broke down after about 80 days, whereas virtually no degradation occurred for HDPE," says Lerner.
The difference was striking. While the biodegradable plastics were completely broken down within approximately nine to eleven months, conventional high-density polyethylene showed almost no decomposition.
These results demonstrate why the chemical makeup of plastic matters so much. Some polymers contain bonds that microbial enzymes can attack, allowing bacteria to dismantle them into smaller molecules. Others, including widely used polyethylene, are far more resistant to biological degradation.
Mysterious Holes Reveal How Bacteria Eat Plastic
When the researchers recovered the plastic films from the forest soil, they discovered something unexpected.
Using electron microscopy, which can reveal structures far too small to see with an ordinary light microscope, the team examined the surfaces of the buried materials. They found numerous tiny holes, each approximately matching the dimensions and shape of an individual bacterial cell.
The unusual pattern suggested that bacteria were doing more than simply attaching themselves to the plastic. They appeared to be breaking into the material itself.
"We hypothesized that bacteria are coated with plastic-depolymerases anchored to their cell surfaces. This would enable them to digest their way into the material and become embedded within the film, leaving behind microscopic holes of exactly this type," explains Lerner.
Depolymerases are enzymes that break large molecules called polymers into smaller chemical units. If these enzymes are attached directly to the outside of a bacterium, they could allow the microorganism to digest the surrounding material while remaining in close contact with it.
This would help explain the microscopic cavities observed in the plastic films. Rather than relying entirely on enzymes released into the environment, the bacteria might be able to break down the material directly at their surfaces.
Scientists Identify the Plastic-Eating "Pac-Man Enzyme"
To find the biological machinery behind this unusual behavior, Lerner extracted DNA from the entire community of microorganisms living in the soil samples.
He then sequenced the genetic material and carefully analyzed the extensive data to determine which microbes and genes became especially abundant as the bioplastics decomposed.
One gene stood out. It was strongly enriched specifically in forest soil containing LCAP, suggesting that it could play an important role in breaking down the biodegradable polyester.
Further analysis revealed that the gene produces an esterase, a type of enzyme capable of splitting certain chemical bonds found in esters. These bonds are present in many naturally occurring substances as well as in various biodegradable polyesters.
What made this particular enzyme especially interesting was how it was positioned on bacterial cells.
Its genetic instructions included a secretion signal that directs the enzyme outside the cell, along with a lipid anchor that holds it firmly to the cell membrane.
This arrangement means the enzyme can remain attached to the bacterium's surface while attacking nearby plastic molecules. Its unusually exposed active site also provides space for the enzyme to interact with polymer chains.
The researchers had identified the molecular mechanism they were looking for, along with the enzyme they named "Pac-Man."
A Surprising Connection to Antibiotic Resistance
The discovery became even more intriguing when scientists examined the enzyme's molecular structure.
Although it resembled esterases, which are known for breaking down ester bonds, it also shared structural similarities with another important family of bacterial enzymes: beta-lactamases.
These enzymes are well known for their role in antibiotic resistance. Some bacteria produce beta-lactamases that disable antibiotics such as penicillin by breaking open a critical part of their chemical structure, known as the beta-lactam ring.
"Its structure resembles that of esterases, but also that of beta-lactamases, which are bacterial enzymes that are capable of cleaving the beta-lactam ring of certain antibiotics, such as penicillin, thereby making bacteria resistant to antibiotics," says Lerner.
Laboratory experiments confirmed that the newly discovered enzyme was capable of performing both types of chemical reactions.
It could break polyester chains into their individual building blocks, known as monomers, while also cleaving penicillin.
This dual activity was particularly surprising because plastic degradation and antibiotic breakdown are usually considered separate biological functions.
The finding raises the possibility that some enzymes involved in plastic decomposition could also contribute to antibiotic resistance. However, demonstrating that an enzyme can chemically break down penicillin in the laboratory does not establish that it provides antibiotic resistance to living bacteria.
Could Plastic-Eating Bacteria Help Solve Plastic Pollution?
The discovery also raises a broader question about how rapidly microorganisms can adapt to synthetic materials introduced into their environment.
For most of Earth's history, plastic pollution did not exist. Microorganisms evolved enzymes to digest naturally occurring substances, including plant fibers and other complex organic molecules.
Modern plastics have introduced an enormous new collection of potential carbon sources into the environment, but many of these materials remain chemically inaccessible to microbes.
"The plastisphere is a new habitat in our environment," explains Schleheck.
"Humans have only been introducing plastic into the environment in significant quantities for around 50 to 75 years. Since then, it has theoretically been available to microbial communities - such as bacteria, yeasts and fungi - as an additional source of carbon and energy for their growth. By 'theoretically', I mean that they would certainly like to use the plastic as a growth substrate - but they cannot, because the materials are actually indigestible to microbial metabolism and are therefore hardly degraded."
The Pac-Man enzyme suggests that this barrier may not be absolute for every type of plastic.
Some bacteria appear capable of using specialized enzymes to attack biodegradable polyesters, potentially allowing them to exploit these materials as sources of energy and nutrients.
For scientists studying plastic pollution, the finding offers a promising clue about how biological degradation might be improved. It also suggests that microbial communities could be adapting to certain synthetic polymers more rapidly than previously anticipated.
However, the results do not mean that bacteria are suddenly capable of consuming the enormous amounts of conventional plastic already accumulating in the environment. The experiments showed that polyethylene remained largely unaffected, even as the biodegradable plastics decomposed.
Instead, the researchers emphasize the importance of designing materials that microorganisms can actually digest.
"I find this encouraging, because it seems that bacteria can adapt to breaking down polyester plastics more quickly than we expected. To tackle the environmental problem of plastic pollution, we humans need to work with the capabilities of microbes. Ideally, this would involve using only polymers with biochemical breaking points, such as the hydrolysable ester bonds in polyesters like LCAP or other types of bioplastics," concludes Schleheck.
The discovery offers a glimpse of a potentially more sustainable approach to plastic production. Rather than expecting microorganisms to break down materials that are naturally resistant to decomposition, scientists could develop plastics with chemical structures that make biological recycling possible.
The Pac-Man enzyme illustrates how bacteria can exploit these molecular weak points, offering new insight into the relationship between plastic pollution, microbial adaptation, and the future of biodegradable materials.

Journal Reference:

Türkiye targets stronger laws against capital market crimes by early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:31:31 UTC
19:31:31 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Türkiye plans to complete legal changes to strengthen its fight against capital market crimes by the beginning of 2027, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said Friday.
The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Simsek said in a statement on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, outlining steps to improve market transparency and bolster investor confidence.
Relevant institutions are implementing significant regulations, taking into account assessments by international index providers, he said.
Regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board have strengthened the flow of information and made ultimate share ownership more transparent, Simsek added.
A fund guide announced at the end of August enabled weekly disclosure of hedge fund portfolios, alongside announcements when funds traded on the Turkish Electronic Fund Trading Platform, known as TEFAS, cross specified shareholding thresholds.
The measures also introduced concentration limits for funds and required borrowing transactions to take place on organized markets on a collateralized basis.
Simsek said authorities would closely monitor the results and take any additional steps without delay in consultation with stakeholders.
“Our priority is to complete the liquidation of problematic funds and protect investors' rights,” he said.
Sanctions will be applied resolutely against those who disrupt the fair and competitive functioning of markets, he added.
“Our goal is to establish a transparent, reliable, and efficient capital market where investor rights are protected,” Simsek said.

Ukraine Gets Two-Thirds of Its Allied Intelligence From Europe, France Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:31:30 UTC
19:31:30 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Gets Two-Thirds of Its Allied Intelligence From Europe, France Says
European countries now provide roughly two-thirds of the intelligence Ukraine receives from its international partners, with France among the major contributors, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on France Inter on October 15.
“Two-thirds of the intelligence provided to Ukraine today comes from Europeans, including France,” Barrot said.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
His comments come as Kyiv faces uncertainty over US intelligence support following tensions surrounding Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The figures suggest that Europe has already assumed a much larger role in supplying the battlefield and strategic intelligence Ukraine needs than it had earlier in Russia’s full-scale war.
According to Militarnyi, European assistance covers a broad range of intelligence capabilities, including optical and radar satellite imagery, signals intelligence, information on Russian force movements, and warnings about ballistic missile threats. The latter have become especially important because ballistic weapons leave Ukrainian civilians and air defense units very little time to react after launch.
European countries can detect some ballistic threats using ground-based electronic intelligence systems and long-range radars capable of tracking missiles once they rise beyond the radar horizon. France is also investing heavily in expanding those capabilities.
Paris recently announced a major modernization of its Nostradamus strategic radar in the Eure-et-Loir department. The over-the-horizon system is capable of detecting activity thousands of kilometers away, covering an area stretching from the North Sea toward the Ural Mountains without mechanically rotating its antennas.
Developed by France’s ONERA aerospace research agency in the 1990s, Nostradamus spent years largely mothballed. France is now bringing the system back into a more active role amid growing threats from Russia and Iran, investing more than €50 million in its modernization.
Unlike conventional radar, Nostradamus uses high-frequency radio waves reflected by the ionosphere, allowing it to detect objects far beyond the normal line of sight. Its antennas are arranged across roughly 12 hectares in a star-shaped configuration and can monitor an enormous volume of airspace extending from ground level to an altitude of around 250 kilometers.
Earlier, Russian leader Vladimir Putin stated that Moscow will consider using all available weapons, including its nuclear arsenal, if Kaliningrad or any other Russian territory faces a direct attack or blockade.

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:28:56 BST
19:28:56 KST

Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
- Published
A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) for causing his death.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him, Paphos District Court previously heard.
The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas.
Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier.
He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter."
Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end.
"Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."
Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws.
They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening.
At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard.
The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead.
"The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou.
His failure to establish that the window was not closed led to the tragic result, the judge added.
"It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences," he said.
The judge added there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings.
She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child".
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him".
While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk.
After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court".
He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
"Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said.
He described his client as an "incredible father".
"[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side."

Türkiye targets 4.2% growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:27:45 UTC
19:27:45 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2% in 2027 from a projected 3.3% this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said Friday with next year's proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government's 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yilmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye's trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7% in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2%, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yilmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5% by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation, and innovation, he said.
Employment is expected to increase by 657,000 people next year, with labor force participation reaching 53.4% and unemployment declining to 8%, from a projected 8.1% in 2026.
 
Inflation forecast to decline to 21%
Yilmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30% in September, was expected to reach 28.4% by the end of this year before declining to 21% by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yilmaz said, reiterating the government's medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2% of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6% in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security, and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
Goods exports this January-September rose 5.2% year-on-year to $211 billion, bringing the rolling annual total to a record $283.7 billion, Yilmaz said.
The share of medium-high- and high-technology products in exports reached 44%, compared with around 28% in the early 2000s, he added.
 
Budget spending projected at $551.2B
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.276 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.408 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5% of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8% of GDP.
Yilmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion, personnel spending at $143.7 billion, and current transfers at $206.7 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1% of GDP, below the initial 3.5% projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176% to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.
Türkiye's EU-defined general government debt declined to 22.3% of GDP in the second quarter from 23.1% in the first, Yilmaz added, describing low public indebtedness as an important advantage amid global uncertainty.

NCP parliamentary group proposes tightening Finland's asylum rules
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:27:07 EEST
19:27:07 KST

The National Coalition Party's (NCP) parliamentary group wants Finland to move towards a policy of selective immigration, in an aim to give the country more control over who can enter and remain in Finland.
The group published its new immigration policy guidelines on Friday, with proposals prepared under the leadership of MP Atte Kaleva (NCP), who has led the work since January.
They have proposed moving asylum processing outside the EU and tightening the conditions for family reunification and access to social security.
"This means that Finland must be able to decide under all circumstances who is allowed to enter the country and under what conditions, as well as who is allowed to remain here," Kaleva said.
The proposals include linking immigrants' eligibility for unemployment benefits to their employment history in Finland and tightening the conditions for receiving the national pension and guarantee pension.
Asylum processing outside the EU
The parliamentary group proposes transferring asylum processing entirely to reception and return centres outside the EU.
It also wants to restrict repeated asylum applications deemed unfounded and make returns more efficient.
"Asylum has been misused as a channel for mass migration, which it was never intended to be. We are returning to protecting individual people who are in need of protection. This also removes the market for people smuggling," he said.
The group further proposes that serious or repeated criminal offences could lead to the revocation of a person's residence permit and their deportation.
Regarding quota refugees, the group proposes that authorities also take into account their prospects for integrating into Finnish society and culture.
"We have certain fundamental values in Finland that we cannot compromise on: democracy, individual freedoms, equality, the equality of women and girls, and minority rights," Kaleva said.
"If a person is unable to adapt to these values, then of course they cannot be accepted into Finland," he added.
Unemployment benefits linked to work in Finland
Under the proposals, immigrants' eligibility for unemployment benefits would depend on the work they had done in Finland. The level of support would vary according to the length of their employment.
The group also proposes tightening family reunification rules by requiring the person bringing family members to Finland to be able to support them through employment or business activities.
Kaleva said the party wanted to encourage work-based immigration, but opposed the creation of a low-wage labour market in Finland.
"We cannot create a cheap labour market in Finland, where people come here to work for companies that do not pay a sufficient salary," he said.
Kaleva said responsibility for integration should lie primarily with immigrants themselves, but also with their employers.
The parliamentary group's proposals were outlined in its new immigration policy programme, titled 'Towards Selective Immigration' (Kohti valikoivaa maahanmuuttoa), included in their press release (in Finnish).

Iran Moves Ballistic Missile Production Underground After US and Israeli Strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:26:22 UTC
19:26:22 KST

Iran continues to expand its underground infrastructure, likely for ballistic missile production, despite extensive damage to its main missile facilities from US and Israeli strikes.
This is according to a study by the US Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI), based on an analysis of satellite imagery of three major missile complexes: Parchin, Khojir, and Shahrud.
Solid rocket fuel production facilities at all three sites remain inoperable following Operation Epic Fury. Large amounts of debris from destroyed structures are still scattered across the sites, and the restoration of production equipment has made virtually no progress.
Meanwhile, activity was observed near an underground tunnel complex at the Shahid Boroujerdi site, near Parchin. Despite damage to some of the tunnels, Iran quickly rebuilt an auxiliary building and filled in craters left by strikes involving penetrator munitions.
Satellite imagery of the site also revealed containers approximately 5 to 13 meters long that may be used to store or transport missiles.
Analysts suggest that the underground complex may have been used to manufacture or assemble missile weaponry.
At another major site in Khojir, much of the production infrastructure remains destroyed, while several entrances to the Shahid Movahed underground complex remain blocked.
The lack of visible activity has led researchers to question whether missiles are currently being assembled there.
Meanwhile, in Shahrud, Iran continues construction of a new tunnel complex. Work began in fall 2024 with the construction of two entrances into the mountain range, and following Operation Epic Fury, a third entrance was likely started.
These tunnels could be used to move critical production processes underground.
FPRI analysts note that it is difficult to determine the exact timeline for the resumption of Iran’s missile production. However, if resources are concentrated at a single facility and specialized equipment is available, Iran could potentially resume operation within a year.
Militarnyi previously reported that in May 2026, US and Israeli intelligence agencies said Iran had resumed limited production of ballistic missiles and launchers. Tehran was using stockpiled components, repaired production lines, and undamaged facilities.

Ukraine makes its anti-drone road nets a national standard in a new strategy for defensive lines through 2028. It has already strung over more than 1,000 kilometers of road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:26:04 UTC
19:26:04 KST

Ukraine’s government has approved a Strategy for the Engineering Equipment of Defensive Lines through 2028. It makes strengthening anti-drone protection of logistics routes one of its priorities, the Defense Ministry says.
Russian FPV drones hunt almost anything that moves within 15 to 30 kilometers of the front, which has forced Ukraine to drape its logistics roads in overhead netting, wire-mesh canopies and reinforced barriers that catch an attacking drone before it reaches a vehicle. Ukraine had already built more than 1,066 kilometers of such protection by mid-July and aims for 4,000 kilometers by the end of 2026.
The new strategy turns that scramble into a single national standard, setting deadlines, assigning responsibility, and building control mechanisms, the ministry explained.
“Solutions that have proven effective we will scale. But we will also account for new challenges, threats and changes in Russian tactics. The main goal is the protection of our service members and civilians,” the Defense Ministry says.
One digital map for every trench and net
The plan puts the entire defensive network onto a screen. To track and monitor the state of defensive lines, Ukraine will introduce a single digital geographic information platform, built on and expanding existing systems, including the DELTA situational-awareness system.
The database will hold object passports, photographs, and data on each structure’s location and condition, helping officials verify that work is done, identify repair needs, and distribute resources on evidence rather than guesswork.
From trenches to supply roads, one cycle
The strategy covers the full span of military engineering. Its main lines of work are building and maintaining fortifications, laying engineering obstacles, strengthening anti-drone protection of logistics routes, using modern designs, materials and camouflage, creating a reserve of construction materials, and maintaining digital records of the work.
Developed on the Defense Ministry’s initiative based on combat experience, the document spans the entire cycle from planning and construction to accounting, upkeep, and restoration, the ministry noted. Financing will come from the state and local budgets for the relevant year and from other sources not prohibited by law.

“Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” said the Association for Human Mathematics.
After causing an uproar among mathematicians, ChatGPT maker OpenAI is donating millions of dollars to a maths foundation.
The move comes days after the Association for Human Mathematics (AHM) slammed the artificial intelligence company and alleged plagiarism for solving a decades-old math problem.
In September, OpenAI said an unreleased AI model had cracked a major result on the Navier-Stokes equations, which apply Newton’s second law of motion to fluids, a problem that has stumped mathematicians for almost a century.
But, according to TechCrunch, two human mathematicians say they were close to a similar result, and they question whether OpenAI’s work drew on theirs. OpenAI denies seeing their work. One of the mathematicians, Levent Alpöge, works at Anthropic and was collaborating in a private capacity.
The Sam Altman-led company said on October 6 the model had published more than 700 manuscripts and produced almost 400 other mathematical results, which aimed to tackle some of the most complex questions in maths and computer science, according to OpenAI.
AHM said “Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done,” adding that OpenAI had a “total disregard for the norms of scientific research”.
On Thursday, OpenAI announced on social media site X that it would make a $5 million donation to the maths-focused Simons Foundation, intended to “help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI”.
“We want to support the mathematics community in turning progress in AI into deeper human understanding and new discoveries,” OpenAI said in a post on X.
“To support that goal, we are contributing $5 million (€4.5mn) to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI, including the results we recently published.”
The money will pay for “workshops, conferences, and special programs,” OpenAI said. “We will also provide access to our models and computing resources to Simons Foundation-supported researchers.”
The initiative totals $15 million in combined funding and resources from the Simons Foundation, Anthropic and OpenAI.

Turkish foreign minister to attend Muslim bloc OIC meeting in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:22:43 UTC
19:22:43 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend a meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), scheduled to take place in Baghdad on Saturday and Sunday.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, Türkiye will hand over the OIC chairmanship to Iraq at the meeting, which will be held under the theme, Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development.
Türkiye has held the rotating chairmanship since June 2025.
The meeting is expected to address Israel's ongoing genocidal policies in Gaza, its occupation and annexation activities across Palestine, developments in other conflict zones across the Islamic world, counterterrorism, UN reform, Islamophobia and the situation of Muslim communities in non-OIC member states.
The meeting is expected to conclude with the adoption of the "Baghdad Declaration."
Fidan is scheduled to address the meeting and hold bilateral talks with his counterparts on the sidelines of the visit.
 
Unity on Palestine
In his address, Fidan is expected to stress that Israel's aggression and expansionist policies remain the greatest security threat in the Middle East.
He is also expected to emphasize the need for OIC member states to demonstrate a united stance in response to Israel's actions and coordinate their efforts with responsible international actors.
Fidan is expected to call for decisive measures against countries that relocate their embassies to Jerusalem and efforts to prevent further initiatives of this kind, stressing the importance of preserving the city's status.
He is also expected to reiterate that implementing a Palestinian state based on a two-state solution is the only path to a just and lasting peace, and underline the vital importance of ensuring that humanitarian aid reaches those in need in Gaza fully and without interruption.
 
Regional security and minority rights
He is further expected to highlight the importance of demonstrating strong solidarity with Turkish Cypriots and supporting efforts to end the unjust isolation they face.
Fidan is also expected to stress the importance of OIC-led efforts to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Muslim Turkish minority in Western Thrace and the Muslim Turkish population living in the Dodecanese Islands.
On Syria, he is expected to call for continued joint efforts to preserve the country's territorial integrity and unity, revive its economy and help it achieve a prosperous future.
Regarding Lebanon, he is expected to underline the importance of safeguarding the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity for regional stability and stress that Israel must withdraw completely from southern Lebanon.
Addressing tensions in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, Fidan is expected to highlight their adverse consequences, particularly for Gulf countries, and describe attacks against these states as unacceptable.
He is also expected to emphasize that ensuring freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is essential for regional stability and global trade.
Fidan is further expected to strongly condemn Houthi attacks targeting civilians and critical infrastructure and reaffirm Türkiye's solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
 
Organization of Islamic Cooperation
The OIC, formerly known as the Organization of the Islamic Conference, was established on Sept. 25, 1969, at a summit in Rabat, Morocco, in response to the arson attack on Al-Aqsa Mosque in occupied East Jerusalem.
With 57 member states, the OIC is the world's second-largest intergovernmental political organization after the United Nations and the only official body representing Muslims worldwide.
The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), Russia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Thailand and the Central African Republic hold observer status at the OIC.
Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed of Mauritania was elected the organization's new secretary-general at the 23rd Extraordinary Session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers, held in August this year.
 
Türkiye and the OIC
Türkiye is one of the OIC's 25 founding members. Its Permanent Mission to the organization began operations in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, on July 24, 2015.
Türkiye assumed the OIC chairmanship for its 51st session at the Council of Foreign Ministers meeting held in Istanbul on June 21-22, 2025. It has previously hosted Council of Foreign Ministers meetings three times, in 1976, 1991, and 2004.
Türkiye hosts the second-largest number of OIC-affiliated institutions after Saudi Arabia.
Several OIC-affiliated bodies are based in Türkiye, including the Statistical, Economic and Social Research and Training Centre for Islamic Countries (SESRIC), the Research Centre for Islamic History, Art and Culture (IRCICA), and the Standing Committee for Economic and Commercial Cooperation of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (COMCEC), one of the OIC's four standing committees.
Other affiliated institutions, including the Islamic Cooperation Youth Forum (ICYF), also operate from Türkiye.

The Ministry of Defence is committed to automating at least twenty per cent of its Human Resources, Finance and Commercial functions by July 2028 and to moving Regular personnel out of administrative work and into front-line roles, according to a written answer in the House of Lords.
Lord Sarfraz, the Conservative peer, asked how many military personnel have been released from back-office roles to front-line roles as a result of automation since the publication of the Strategic Defence Review in 2025.
Lord Coaker, Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Department remains committed to maximising the operational effectiveness of the Armed Forces and ensuring that Defence personnel are focused on activity that best supports front-line outcomes. As set out in the Strategic Defence Review, Defence is taking forward work to move Regular personnel from administrative activity into front-line roles and to automate at least 20% of Human Resources, Finance and Commercial functions by July 2028.
“This commitment is being delivered through the Defence Reform and Efficiency Plan, including the Corporate Services Modernisation programme, which is redesigning and modernising Defence’s People, Finance and Commercial services. The programme is simplifying policy and processes, standardising activity, consolidating services where appropriate and introducing modern digital tools to reduce manual work, strengthen access to reliable management information and improve the user experience. This will reduce the back-office burden, improve productivity and release capacity for front-line activity while maintaining effective support to all personnel.”
July 2028 gives the department a little under two years from now to hit the target.

Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:21:12 UTC
19:21:12 KST

Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
It is the first time the president has definitively addressed nuclear weapons, but he did not deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’.
United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition, nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future.
In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax.
The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Here’s what we know:
What did Trump say?
Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite.
He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon.
“I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said.
He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”.
Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not.
“Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.”
Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran.
Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”.
Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop.
When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory.
What is the ‘mother of all bombs’?
The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters.
It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said.
“Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.”
However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access.
What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons?
Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out.
Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran.
In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait.
He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
Experts widely interpreted his statements as a threat of nuclear destruction, but one that still failed to force Iran to the table.
Although Trump largely moved away from his sabre-rattling rhetoric in the following weeks, he reiterated at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month that he could “annihilate” Iran. He also told the assembly that he believed a deal would emerge after the midterms.
What is a ‘tactical’ nuclear weapon?
“Tactical” nuclear weapons (TNW) are smaller nuclear munitions designed for the battlefield as opposed to strategic nuclear munitions designed for mass destruction.
Some perceive TNWs as having a lesser impact than an atomic bomb, but experts warn that their names are misleading and they can nevertheless be devastating. Their explosive yield, between 0.3 and 50 kilotons, can impact areas within a 500-600km radius.
The US dropped a 15-kiloton nuclear bomb on Hiroshima, meaning that weapon would today be considered a TNW. The US, North Korea and Russia have TNWs in their arsenals, although no country has ever used them. TNWs are not subject to any international treaties and are largely unregulated.
What might another US attack on Iran look like?
With Trump failing to rule out dropping the MOAB, analysts speculate that the US might launch another – perhaps final – intensive bombing campaign targeting Iran’s nuclear and defence sites, particularly Pickaxe Mountain.
The US could also continue its naval blockade on Iranian ports, while providing escorts for commercial ships through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has vowed to respond to escalatory strikes by targeting oil and digital infrastructure in neighbouring Gulf states.
Senior defence officials have also warned that Iran will invade its neighbours if the US launches a ground operation, although Trump appears to have ruled that out.
Earlier in the war, he hinted at the possibility of sending ground forces to retrieve some 400kg of highly enriched uranium that Washington and Israel claim Tehran has hidden underground.
Trump’s phone calls in March to Kurdish militia groups fighting Iran provoked speculation that Washington could coordinate with them for an invasion, although that did not happen.
