Expert: Trump does not have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:21:00 UTC
19:21:00 KST

Expert: Trump does not have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate
While Donald Trump's unpredictable behavior and disruptions to Starlink are complicating the situation in Ukraine, the U.S. president does not have the power to force Ukraine to surrender, security expert Ilmar Raag finds.
Security expert Ilmar Raag shared his view on social media that U.S. President Donald Trump is not Estonia's ally. Raag explained on ETV's "Ringvaade" that Trump and the United States should not be equated.
"We have American allied troops here in Estonia and when our military personnel interact with them, they are doing their own jobs. I also hear about what is happening in Washington. Following Trump's latest statements, there are senators in the Republican camp who say they disagree with him. I have to say that if there are Americans anywhere whom I consider my Americans, they are the Republicans who are currently standing up to Trump."
Trump, who has recently been pressuring Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to make peace, signed a diesel fuel deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin last week in an attempt to regain popularity in the United States ahead of the midterm elections. In recent days, he has also threatened to stop sharing U.S. intelligence with Ukraine and has partially restricted the war-torn country's access to the Starlink satellite communications system. During a visit to the United Kingdom, Zelenskyy told journalist Piers Morgan on his show that he felt betrayed by Trump.
"First of all, we can say that no major catastrophe is going to happen immediately, for two reasons. First, although American intelligence is very important, it does not do everything. When we talk about Starlink, it serves many different functions in drone warfare, but not all of them. For example, units can still communicate with one another via Starlink and headquarters can communicate with teams on the front line operating these drones. That accounts for half of what Starlink does. The problem is that the most effective drones the Ukrainians have will naturally be affected if Starlink's more important functions — those provided by Starshield — are not working," Raag said.
According to Raag, it is impossible to say for certain whether the Starlink disruptions were accidental or deliberate, but the coincidences are significant enough to suggest that something else may be behind them.
"It appears to be some kind of unilateral action by a smaller group. You can see that Ukrainians are receiving warnings about incoming missiles too late after Starlink actually stops working for them. The Americans are not speaking with one voice, saying they made a decision and acted accordingly. Some are saying one thing, while Trump is already saying it never happened. This shows that the head does not know what the tail is doing, or vice versa. That brings us to the second argument that describes the current situation: Trump, being as unpredictable as he is, could change his mind yet again," Raag explained, adding that this was a sign that Europe needed to take responsibility for its own affairs.
European leaders have responded to Trump's statements and decisions. While many have condemned the U.S. president's rhetoric, others believe Trump should be approached more calmly to avoid provoking him further.
"It is true that Trump is a very emotional man and in some ways he thrives on conflict — he can always escalate things further. In that respect, European leaders have already realized that if they keep their heads down and wait a little, perhaps the midterm elections will come around and Trump will lose much of the power he currently holds. That is what many are hoping for," the security expert said.
According to Raag, surveys conducted in the United States show that most Americans consider Putin the aggressor and support Ukraine, raising hopes that if Trump suffers a defeat in the midterm elections, Congress may adopt a more supportive position toward Ukraine.
"Ukraine cannot afford a situation in which people are losing their lives while Trump is allowed to play games, shifting back and forth. People are dying in the meantime. In that respect, Trump is influenced most by his approval ratings in the United States, fuel prices and, ultimately, European leaders as well. He has now demonstrated several times that when Europe says a very clear 'no,' Trump returns to his previous positions," Raag said in response to the host's question about whether diplomatic exchanges had become too heated.
There are also concerns that if Trump stops receiving praise from Europe and Ukraine, he may become more interested in holding talks and making deals with Putin.
"But what can he really agree on? Trump can conclude various economic agreements with the Russians and do business with them. But Trump does not actually have the power to force Ukraine to capitulate. That is not going to happen and Trump has realized that as well. Perhaps that is also one of the sources of his frustration — that he simply cannot do it, just as he cannot impose on the Iranians the peace terms he has been announcing for quite some time," Raag said.
According to Raag, the war has escalated since August, but the Ukrainians are holding out and have already learned how to deal with the challenges they face.
"The escalation began in August when it became clear that the Ukrainians currently lack sufficiently effective air defenses against ballistic missiles and therefore face a very difficult winter. However, they have spent several years learning and the Ukrainians themselves say that although they curse Trump and Putin, they will survive this," Raag said.

Putin seizes five more European firms, continuing Russia's hostile asset crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:18:40 UTC
19:18:40 KST

The decree covers a flooring manufacturer, a paper packaging firm, a hygiene products maker, and two metal- and plastic-packaging companies, all of which continued operating in Russia after the all-out invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree ordering the compulsory seizure of Russian assets belonging to French flooring manufacturer Tarkett and four other European companies, whose combined annual revenue exceeds 50 billion roubles (€532 million).
The assets have been placed under the interim control of a management company called Centre Capital, registered in February 2026.
Its chief executive is listed as Marat Mirkhaydarov, former head of the administration of the regional governor of Zabaykalsky, who stood down in 2025 following an injury sustained in Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine.
The decree also covers paper packaging producer Kappa Rus, formerly part of Ireland's Smurfit Kappa, hygiene product maker Ontex RU, part of the Belgian Ontex group, metal packaging manufacturer Eviosys Packaging Kuban, part of US-based Sonoco Products Company, and Menshen Packaging CIS, owned by German plastics producer Menshen.
All five companies continued operating in Russia after the country's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Tarkett, which ranks third globally by floor covering sales and leads the market in vinyl flooring according to its 2024 annual report, kept two plants in Russia out of its 34 production sites worldwide and continued paying taxes to the Russian budget.
The latest seizures follow a series of similar moves in September, when Putin placed the Russian assets of Swiss food giant Nestlé, German hypermarket chain Metro, French retailer Auchan and home improvement chain Leroy Merlin under temporary administration.
Those assets were transferred to a company called LEV Management, established shortly before the decision and reported by Russian media to have links to the country's security services. A manufacturer of plastic dispensing systems owned by French holding Aptar Europe Holding was also placed under temporary administration shortly afterwards.
A presidential decree signed in April 2023 established the mechanism for such seizures, authorising the imposition of temporary administration over certain Russian assets of foreign companies.
Western governments and international legal experts have described the move as unlawful expropriation. Companies whose assets are seized can, in principle, pursue compensation through international arbitration under bilateral investment treaties Russia has signed with EU member states, although enforcing judgments against the Kremlin and its entities is nearly impossible.
The first targets under that decree were Danish brewer Carlsberg and French dairy group Danone.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov directly linked the transfer of Nestlé's and Auchan's assets to the fact that they are companies from what Moscow terms "unfriendly countries".
“Unfriendly countries” is an official Russian government designation applied to all EU member states, the US, the UK and other states that imposed sanctions following the 2022 full-scale invasion, in an attempt to dissuade them from aiding Kyiv.
Russia has framed the asset seizures in part as a response to the EU’s decision to freeze approximately €300 billion in Russian sovereign assets following the all-out invasion.

Türkiye targets 4.2 percent growth in 2027 as government unveils budget proposal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:16:26 UTC
19:16:26 KST

Türkiye expects economic growth to accelerate to 4.2 percent in 2027 from a projected 3.3 percent this year, supported by an improving global outlook and a recovery in external demand, Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said on Oct. 16 with next year’s proposed budget in hand.
Presenting the government’s 2027 budget proposal at the presidential complex in Ankara, Yılmaz said stronger growth among Türkiye’s trading partners would create opportunities for exports and support balanced economic expansion.
The Turkish economy grew 3.7 percent in 2025, he said, adding that investment outpacing private consumption had strengthened production capacity and improved the composition of growth.
“In 2027, we expect our growth to rise to 4.2 percent, supported by the anticipated improvement in the global outlook and the recovery in external demand,” Yılmaz said.
The government aims to gradually accelerate growth to 5 percent by the end of its medium-term program through policies focused on productivity, technological transformation and innovation, he said.
Yılmaz said annual inflation, which fell below 30 percent in September, was expected to reach 28.4 percent by the end of this year before declining to 21 percent by the end of 2027.
“Price stability is the fundamental priority of our program,” he said.
Fiscal discipline and incomes policies will continue to support monetary policy, while supply-side measures, particularly in social housing and food, will reinforce disinflation.
Despite fluctuations stemming from energy and commodity prices, the underlying inflation trend continues to improve, Yılmaz said, reiterating the government’s medium-term goal of achieving lasting single-digit inflation.
He said the current account deficit was expected to fall below 2 percent of gross domestic product next year from a projected 2.6 percent in 2026.
Türkiye will continue policies to boost exports, strengthen energy supply security and reduce dependence on energy imports, he added.
The 2027 budget proposal projects expenditures of 27.28 trillion Turkish liras and revenues of 23.41 trillion liras ($551.2 billion), with national income expected to reach $2.24 trillion.
The figures imply a budget shortfall of $78.1 billion, equivalent to a projected 3.5 percent of GDP. Excluding earthquake-related expenditure, the deficit is forecast at 2.8 percent of GDP.
Yılmaz said the proposal would be submitted to parliament with President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s signature, calling it a budget of “resilience, prosperity and transformation.”
Interest expenditures are projected at $80.2 billion. The budget is expected to maintain a primary surplus next year.
For 2026, the government forecasts a deficit of 3.1 percent of GDP, below the initial 3.5 percent projection, despite spending pressures from higher energy and commodity prices.
Urban transformation funding will rise 176 percent to $5.57 billion in 2027, Yilmaz said, with disaster resilience remaining a priority alongside expanded social and rental housing provision.
Earthquake reconstruction spending over 2023-2026 totaled $109 billion at current prices, equivalent to $104 billion, he said, with 455,357 independent units completed and delivered.

Dinh identified banking restrictions as the main operational concern. He called for flexible settlement frameworks, such as bilateral barter trade or compliant local-currency clearing, to reduce exchange costs and transaction friction. Official Vietnam–Iran trade is around $170 million, but much of the real trade may pass through third countries. To make flows more direct and transparent, businesses need market intelligence, trade expos, and official business-matching platforms.

&quot;We can no longer do this&quot;: Le Pen opposes further financial support for Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

19:15:35 KST

"We can no longer do this": Le Pen opposes further financial support for Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Marine Le Pen said that after winning in 2027, she would end financial aid to Ukraine within six months. She is also opposed to Ukraine joining the EU.
French far-right politician and representative of the National Rally party Marine Le Pen said that Europe, and France in particular, can no longer increase its financial support for Ukraine. UNN reports this, citing Financial Times and French media.
Details
If she wins the 2027 presidential election, she plans to stop direct financial aid to Kyiv six months after taking office. The politician also opposes Ukraine's membership in the European Union and any further increase in European countries' financial commitments.
In an interview with the Financial Times published on October 14, Marine Le Pen said that European states had already undertaken significant financial commitments to support Ukraine and that the possibilities for further increasing aid were limited. According to the French politician, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy needs to be openly told about the financial constraints faced by European partners.
To deal honestly with Mr. Zelenskyy is to tell him, in fact to warn him: listen, we cannot do more. We have already provided loans totaling €90 billion, of which €18 billion falls to France. That is a truly large sum
She emphasized that France could no longer afford to support Ukraine at previous levels because of the difficult situation with its public finances. In addition, Le Pen questioned the rationale for further financing Kyiv through the European Union if this would result in an additional financial burden on the French budget.
The politician also called for a significant reduction in the EU budget and a limitation of the powers of European institutions.
Le Pen promised to stop funding Ukraine six months after winning the election
On October 14, while in Brussels, Marine Le Pen clarified her position in an interview with the Belgian television channel VRT News. She said that if elected president of France, she would not stop financial support for Ukraine immediately after taking power. Instead, she envisages a six-month transition period.
From the moment of my election, for six months we will maintain aid so as not to leave anyone in an impossible situation. But after that, we will stop financial aid to Ukraine, because we no longer have the ability to provide it
At the same time, she did not rule out maintaining certain forms of military cooperation, including operational support and the training of Ukrainian service members.
Le Pen opposed Ukraine joining the EU
The politician separately criticized the prospect of Ukraine's membership in the European Union. According to her, Ukraine's accession to the EU could lead to significant economic losses for France, particularly in the agricultural sector. Le Pen claims that Ukrainian agricultural products would create additional competition for French farmers and that the distribution of European subsidies would change to France's disadvantage.
In her conversation with the Financial Times, she called Ukraine's possible accession to the European Union a "harakiri" for France, linking it to threats to national sovereignty and significant economic losses.
What Volodymyr Zelenskyy replied to Le Pen
On October 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on the French politician's statements in an interview with the Financial Times. The head of state emphasized that Ukraine's cooperation with France and other Western partners is not limited to financial support. According to him, European states are gaining valuable experience from the Ukrainian military that can be used to develop their own defense technologies and improve the combat readiness of their armies.
In particular, the president mentioned the Franco-Italian SAMP/T air defense systems, which were improved based on experience from combat use, as well as SCALP/Storm Shadow cruise missiles. Zelenskyy emphasized that Ukraine's experience of modern warfare has practical value for European defense companies.
We also give something in return
In his view, French industry could benefit from the joint production of weapons, technological cooperation, and the use of Ukrainian military expertise.
The president also expressed the conviction that Le Pen does not fully take into account certain aspects of defense cooperation between the countries.
What is known about financial support for Ukraine from the EU
Despite Le Pen's statements, the European Union continues to provide Ukraine with military, economic, and budgetary assistance. In particular, the EU approved a €90 billion loan program for 2026–2027. It provides funding for Ukraine's defense needs and support for the state budget. However, funds under this program are disbursed gradually, and their allocation depends on the agreed conditions and Ukraine's implementation of the necessary reforms.
In addition, European institutions are considering mechanisms for further financing Ukraine in view of the country's significant needs amid the continuation of the full-scale war with Russia.
Context
Marine Le Pen is one of the leading representatives of France's far-right forces and has consistently advocated reducing France's financial contributions to the European Union budget. She has repeatedly criticized European sanctions against Russia while stating that she condemns Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Against the backdrop of preparations for the 2027 presidential election, Le Pen has stepped up statements regarding the need to review France's foreign policy and budgetary priorities.

Ethiopia's Abiy names new Tigray government, wants polls in six months
NAIROBI, Oct 16 - Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has named a caretaker government to stabilise the northern Tigray region and prepare for an election within six months, after fighting erupted between a rebel alliance and federal troops.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) led an offensive last month against Abiy's government, reigniting a war that killed hundreds of thousands between 2020-22.
Renewed conflict has led to the severing of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of backing the rebels, which Eritrea denies.
The TPLF, Tigray's ruling party, dominated Ethiopian politics for decades until Abiy took office in 2018. Since fighting erupted, Ethiopia's military and a pro-government militia have made significant advances and taken control of large parts of Tigray including the regional capital Mekelle.
The temporary administration will be in office for six months, Abiy's office said, to create a stable political climate for free and transparent elections within six months.
"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle of conflict," Abiy said in a statement posted on X.
The administration will also repair damaged infrastructure and help displaced people return to their homes, he said.
A TPLF spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tigray is yet to recover from the humanitarian toll of the previous war, which pushed hundreds of thousands into famine. Around 750,000 Tigrayans were still internally displaced as of February, according to the UN refugee agency, and the region faces drought linked to El Nino.
There are fears that unrest could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders in the fragile Horn of Africa region where other powers vie for influence.
In addition to Eritrea, Ethiopia's government has accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting the rebel alliance.
They have denied the allegations. REUTERS

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has become a tool of Western influence that selectively targets countries of the Global South while shielding European interests and ignoring crimes in Ukraine, international legal analyst and academic Alexandre Guerreiro has said. He accused the tribunal of applying double standards rather than delivering universal justice.
Criticism of the ICC has intensified in recent months amid growing accusations of political bias and selective justice. Venezuela, Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have moved to withdraw, accusing the court of serving Western interests and engaging in “neocolonial repression.”
In an interview with RT on Thursday, Guerreiro argued that the court had abandoned its original purpose as an independent institution capable of holding perpetrators accountable regardless of nationality, and has become increasingly politicized and dominated by European powers.
“In practice, what we have is a court that serves European interests, colonialist interests,” he said, arguing that the tribunal is used to pressure Global South nations while avoiding similar scrutiny of European countries.
Guerreiro pointed to the court’s handling of cases involving Afghanistan, Iraq and Kenya, arguing that political interference had repeatedly undermined the principles of impartial justice.
He also accused the ICC of ignoring alleged crimes in Ukraine, including the deadly May 2014 Odessa clashes between Ukrainian nationalists and opponents of the Western-backed coup in Kiev, as well as the sniper shootings during the preceding Maidan unrest.
“This is not justice,” he said, arguing that the court only pursues cases that serve the interests of the current Ukrainian authorities and the Western bloc as a whole.
The remarks come days after Washington imposed sweeping new sanctions on the ICC, accusing it of overstepping its jurisdiction in cases involving American and Israeli nationals. The court issued arrest warrants in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Meanwhile, the ICC’s investigation into alleged war crimes by American forces in Afghanistan has produced no criminal charges against US personnel.

Europe Has No Starlink Replacement as Ukraine Faces Satellite Disruptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:14:27 UTC
19:14:27 KST

Europe cannot replace Starlink anytime soon, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned Friday, as disruptions to Elon Musk’s satellite network raised concerns over Ukraine’s battlefield communications.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” Kallas told reporters ahead of an EU summit attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine relies on Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones used to shoot down Russian attack drones.
Starlink’s satellite network is unmatched in scale, while its business model and portable, affordable terminals give it a major advantage over competitors that rely on bulkier, more expensive equipment.
Kyiv reported restrictions on military Starlink connections this week, with Ukrainian officials reporting slower speeds on some terminals on Wednesday. Musk said any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his SpaceX company.
Europe scrambles for alternatives
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had mapped the critical military capabilities Europe lacks and must develop.
“We need to fill these gaps as soon as possible,” she said.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs acknowledged that Europe was not yet equipped to provide a full alternative.
‘We Pay for It’: Germany Demands Starlink Restrictions in Ukraine Be Lifted
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine actually to fight or fight back,” he told reporters on Friday, according to AFP. Europe has some comparable capabilities, but not enough to meet Ukraine’s needs.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told AFP he had discussed the issue with French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday, focusing on how European countries could provide more satellite communications services in the near future.
EU eyes satellite backup
The European Commission is negotiating Ukraine’s participation in GOVSATCOM, an EU program that pools satellite resources to provide secure communications for government users.
“We are currently in talks with Ukraine to fully associate Ukraine to GOVSATCOM,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said on Wednesday.
The system could give Kyiv another way to maintain secure communications during Russian attacks on infrastructure and disruptions to conventional networks. But Brussels has yet to confirm whether it can match Starlink’s capabilities for combat operations.
The EU could add commercial satellite services as early as 2027, potentially helping meet military needs, Regnier said. Its longer-term plan, the IRIS² constellation of more than 300 satellites, is expected to become fully operational in 2029.
Until then, Ukraine remains heavily reliant on Starlink – and Europe has no immediate replacement for a system critical to its war effort.
Why Ukraine needs another option
The European discussions have gained urgency after restrictions detected overnight on Oct. 13-14 disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
Ukrainian defense ministry sources said units received no advance warning and reported connections dropping at different movement speeds, approximately 72 to 161 kilometers per hour (45 to 100 miles per hour).
The ministry contacted the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners while checking backup communications channels.
The disruption affected interceptor and medium-range strike drones, alongside reconnaissance, logistics, and communications relay missions.
The reported speed limits concern how fast a terminal is moving, rather than its internet download speed.
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Wednesday evening that connectivity at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (99 miles per hour) was being restored, while calling for Starshield’s speed restriction to be removed entirely.
That partial restoration does not resolve every operational requirement. Two Ukrainian officials told RFE/RL that connections had improved below the threshold, but restrictions continued to complicate interception of Russia’s jet-powered drones.
One Ukrainian source said operating speeds needed to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour).
President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused those responsible of deliberately restricting the service during Russian attacks, saying the disruption weakened Ukraine’s defenses and endangered civilians. Who authorized the restrictions remains disputed.
Musk said Starshield systems are controlled by the US government and that their operational limits are determined by the US military and ultimately the president. A senior White House official, however, told Axios that the Trump administration was not involved.
Why switching networks will take time
According to Reuters, Europe has no ready-made replacement that Ukrainian troops can immediately attach to their drones.
Eutelsat already provides connectivity in Ukraine through its low Earth orbit and geostationary networks.
But independent satellite consultant Christian Freiherr von der Ropp told Reuters that OneWeb faces capacity and performance constraints, while terminal cost, weight, size, and power consumption limit frontline suitability.
Switching would also require replacing thousands of terminals: Starlink equipment uses proprietary technology and cannot simply connect to OneWeb.
European political pressure to develop alternatives is growing. In a statement on Thursday, Oct. 15, Renew Europe President Valérie Hayer urged EU leaders to strengthen support for Ukraine and address dependence on American satellite services.
“Recent days have also shown the urgent need for a European alternative to Starlink,” she said.
Russia races to build its own Starlink
Russia could deploy an alternative to Starlink across the front line within a year, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Madyar” Brovdi warned in May.
Russia’s main project is Rassvet, developed by Russian company Bureau 1440. The company launched 16 spacecraft in March 2026, while six Rassvet satellites were in orbit at the time, according to Russian media outlet Kommersant.
Despite the limited constellation, Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi reported that the satellites’ regular passes over Ukraine could provide usable coverage for some frontline applications. However, Rassvet remains far behind Starlink in scale and established operational capability.
Russian troops have also relied on alternative equipment, including terminals referred to as “Gazprom.” In an intercepted conversation published by Kyiv Post in February, a Russian serviceman dismissed one such terminal as “f**king shit.”
Starlink operates more than 7,800 satellites, while Russia is still building its network. Moscow’s ability to expand Rassvet and improve its terminals could nevertheless become a growing concern for Ukraine, particularly as both sides depend increasingly on satellite connectivity to control drones and coordinate battlefield operations.

BRICS includes longtime members Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa, plus recent additions Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates.

Turkish exports increased in eight of the 10 BRICS member states, with shipments in Ethiopia surging the most by 79.6 percent.
The chemicals and chemical products sector accounted for most of these exports to the bloc, generating $3.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, the data showed.
Mining exports grew 33.5 percent to $2.1 billion, a net gain of roughly $539 million, followed by the jewelry sector, whose exports fell 45 percent to $1.3 billion.
The textiles and raw material exports climbed 8.7 percent to $1.2 billion at the same time.

Türkiye plans to complete legal changes to strengthen its fight against capital market crimes by the beginning of 2027, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Oct. 16.
The planned measures will also address coordinated transactions by funds, Şimşek said in a statement on Turkish social media platform NSosyal, outlining steps to improve market transparency and bolster investor confidence.
Relevant institutions are implementing significant regulations, taking into account assessments by international index providers, he said.
Regulations introduced by the Capital Markets Board have strengthened the flow of information and made ultimate share ownership more transparent, Şimşek added.
A fund guide announced at the end of August enabled weekly disclosure of hedge fund portfolios, alongside announcements when funds traded on the Turkish Electronic Fund Trading Platform, known as TEFAS, cross specified shareholding thresholds.
The measures also introduced concentration limits for funds and required borrowing transactions to take place on organized markets on a collateralized basis.
Şimşek said authorities would closely monitor the results and take any additional steps without delay in consultation with stakeholders.
“Our priority is to complete the liquidation of problematic funds and protect investors’ rights,” he said.
Sanctions will be applied resolutely against those who disrupt the fair and competitive functioning of markets, he added.
“Our goal is to establish a transparent, reliable and efficient capital market where investor rights are protected,” Şimşek said.

Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:09:14 UTC
19:09:14 KST

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.
The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.
While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.
Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.
What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, filled with false leads.
A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.
The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.
This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll has been visited dozens of times.
In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said severe weather had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.
“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.
Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute, said: “We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience. This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

The 45.7 x 57.5 x 25.4-centimeter vehicle weighs up to 12 kilograms, can continue operations for up to 2 hours at a depth of 300 meters, has an LED-backed high-definition camera to see in deep waters, and can move in any direction with its eight thrusters against ocean currents, per Poseidon.

19:08:30 KST

In the summer of 2019, Yuli Edelstein, then speaker of the Knesset, came to meet with us at The Jerusalem Post.
Israel had held an election in April that failed to produce a government and was forced back to the polls in September. It was the first time in the country’s history that one election had led almost immediately to another, and Edelstein, then a senior figure in Likud, had a clear message: This would not happen again. Whatever the personal differences between the political camps, the country would find a way to form a government.
Sadly, he was wrong, as were many of us who believed that Israel’s politicians would eventually come to their senses. Instead, the country went to the polls five times in three-and-a-half years, until the current government was established following the election at the end of 2022.
When people think about October 7, they understandably focus on the intelligence failures, the IDF’s failure to defend the border, and the questions surrounding the warnings that did or did not reach Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Some go further back to the year before the attack, when the government’s judicial overhaul tore Israeli society apart. Rarely, though, do we go back further than that.
The truth is that Israel arrived at October 7 battered, divided, and polarized in ways we have yet to fully process. The judicial overhaul was devastating, but it did not come out of nowhere. It followed five elections marked by relentless political fighting, personal rivalries, and the growing belief that defeating the other side mattered more than governing the country. The overhaul deepened those divisions, eroded trust in institutions, and made the country weak and vulnerable.
Hamas saw an opening in this division and took it on October 7. The fact that we have yet to establish a commission of inquiry into the events that led to the attack is a gamble with Israel’s future.
This history matters as we approach the October 27 election, because the polls suggest that another stalemate is a real possibility. Neither bloc appears to have the 61 seats needed for a conventional majority government, and neither seems capable of persuading enough politicians from the other side to join it. Much can change before election day, particularly with undecided voters and parties hovering around the electoral threshold. But we need to ask now what outcome is actually in the country’s interest.
The opposition’s criticism of Netanyahu is legitimate. He has been in office for too long, the failures have piled up, and it is time for change. His decision to govern with the far Right has caused Israel immense damage, internally and internationally. But Netanyahu is also right that the opposition’s boycott of him has contributed to the prospect of deadlock. This is what happens when personality politics overwhelms almost everything else.
Three possibilities to avoid another election
ANOTHER ELECTION, in my mind, would be catastrophic. Israel is militarily stronger today because its enemies are weaker, but military superiority does not remove the danger of political paralysis. With so many challenges still unresolved, returning to the cycle of election after election would put us back on the same destructive path that preceded October 7.
If avoiding that outcome is the objective, there are essentially three possibilities.
The first is that one side wins 61 seats, as hard as that is to imagine based on current polling. It could be Netanyahu and it could be the opposition. This would be the clearest outcome – one side would win, and while the other would be angry and disappointed, the voters will have spoken. Even if one side does not get 61 in its current form, we cannot rule out defections – parties switching alliances – something that has happened repeatedly in the past.
The second possibility is that neither side reaches 61 seats and the opposition tries to establish a minority government. The most plausible version would bring together Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, and Yair Golan. They would not need the Arab parties to vote in favor of the government, but they would need enough Arab MKs to not vote against it.
Such a government could remove Netanyahu from office and establish a state commission of inquiry into October 7, a lofty objective that should have been done a long time ago. Beyond that, however, it will not be able to function, and the minority government would be established simply to take the country straight back to another election.
As tempting as this might be, there is a danger in this that the opposition should not underestimate. Firstly, the path leads anyhow to another election, no different than the deadlock option. Second, there is a chance that Netanyahu would return even stronger after the next election, arguing that he had warned voters Eisenkot and Bennett would govern with the support of Arab parties and that they had proved him right.
The third possibility is what is often referred to as a unity government. I know how unrealistic this sounds today, but it deserves consideration if the alternative is yet another election. In many respects, this would not even be unity across an enormous ideological divide. The principal obstacle between Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman, and Golan is not necessarily their view of Israel’s central security challenges but their view of one another.
Set aside judicial reform for a moment and consider the major issues. Is there really such a vast difference between them on confronting Iran, rebuilding support in the United States, the future of the Palestinian conflict, or maintaining far stronger defenses along the borders with Gaza and Lebanon?
There are meaningful disagreements on the rule of law, the West Bank, and responsibility for October 7, and they cannot be wished away. But there is also more than enough common ground to at least explore whether a stable government could be formed.
THE OBVIOUS objection is that Netanyahu cannot be trusted. He has broken political promises in the past, manipulated coalition partners, and brought down governments when it served his interests. All of that is true, and anyone considering joining him would have to enter such an arrangement with eyes wide open and an incredible amount of suspicion.
But politics is not about choosing between a good option and a bad one. Often, it is about deciding which of the bad options will do the least damage. If the alternative to exploring a unity government is another election, followed perhaps by another stalemate, which course would be worse for the country?
Netanyahu has been a central figure in Israeli politics for more than 30 years, since first becoming prime minister in 1996. He is a political chameleon who knows how to move left, shift right, settle in the center, and adapt his alliances based on political survival. If staying in office requires him to govern with different partners, and to accept different constraints, he usually knows how to do so.
None of this means that Netanyahu can suddenly be trusted politically, and we have no way of knowing whether he has changed. Is survival in office the only objective for him today, or is there still something within him that will put the country first even if it means restraints and policies that for the last four years he has avoided, like a commission of inquiry?
It is true that such a government might prove impossible, and that even if formed it will quickly collapse. But surely we owe it to ourselves to test the possibility rather than dismiss it outright.
Edelstein’s warning in 2019 was that Israel could not afford to become a country incapable of forming a government. We ignored that warning and allowed years of political division to become normal. October 7 should have taught us that national security depends not only on military strength but also on social cohesion and leadership capable of putting the country ahead of personal rivalries.
Hopefully, October 27 will produce a clear winner. If it does not, Israel’s political leaders will have to decide whether their refusal to sit together matters more than the country they are supposed to serve. After everything Israel has endured, another round of elections cannot be treated as an acceptable outcome.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at JPPI, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

The battle for Israel: As Netanyahu rallies the Right, Eisenkot makes his move for power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:07:56 UTC
19:07:56 KST

As the election nears, Netanyahu targets right-wing alternatives, while Eisenkot seeks the commanding lead that would make him the opposition’s undisputed PM candidate
Think of Israel as one big cruise liner. Considering the country’s hyper-stressed reality, that may require some imagination, but bear with it for a moment.
On the starboard side of the ship, the right side, are all the voters in the pro-Netanyahu camp, split into different halls and ballrooms.
The Likud occupies the biggest hall, with smaller rooms for Shas, United Torah Judaism, Otzma Yehudit, and the Religious Zionist Party.
On the port side, separated from starboard by a hallway with doors leading to both sides, are the rooms of the anti-Netanyahu camp.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar has the biggest room there, followed by Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad, with smaller rooms for the Democrats and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu.
In the hallway itself stand Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s reservist-economist party. Behind the ship, in a separate tugboat, sail the two Arab parties.
As the cruise liner steams toward its destination, Election Day, just 11 days away, representatives of the two sides shout the expected accusations across the hallway.
From one side: “You are responsible for the worst disaster in Israel’s history and are leading the country toward catastrophe.” From the other: “You will join forces with those in the tugboat and establish a Palestinian state.”
But the more consequential action is taking place on each side of the ship.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu looks down the hallway, trying to persuade Winter’s and Hendel’s voters to abandon them and come to his side of the ship. Over on the port side, Eisenkot is trying to expand his already large ballroom at the expense of the rooms occupied by those sharing his side of the liner.
Netanyahu intensifies campaign to consolidate right-wing voters
Those two maneuvers are dominating the final stretch of the voyage to Election Day. And what is a sure sign the campaign has entered that final stretch? Netanyahu’s sudden ubiquity on the airwaves.
After months when the prime minister’s interviews were largely reserved for foreign media, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and various podcasts, he showed up in Israeli studios this week, and not only on Channel 14.
Granted, on Tuesday he was, again, on Channel 14, where a “home crowd” greeted him rapturously. But the next day he was on Channel 11, and in between he appeared on Army Radio.
His message had two parts: the election is perilously close, and right-wing voters cannot afford to gamble.
The first is familiar. Netanyahu has sounded the same alarm in numerous campaigns, warning his voters that victory is slipping away. On Channel 14, he anticipated the obvious response: people would dismiss this as his traditional gevalt campaign. This time, he insisted, he really is worried. The race is tied, he said.
And where, precisely, did he see right-wing voters gambling?
Once you cut through the familiar warnings about Eisenkot joining forces with Ahmad Tibi and the election determining whether a Palestinian state will be established, a much smaller target comes into view: Winter’s party.
Netanyahu’s relentless attacks on the retired brigadier-general stand out in this final stretch. At a time when he might be expected to concentrate his fire on Eisenkot and Bennett, he is devoting considerable energy to a small party standing in the hallway.
Netanyahu said he had tried to persuade Winter to join the Likud and, when that failed, to team up with another small right-wing party. That, too, failed, so now he is going after him mercilessly.
In one of the anti-Winter messages he put out this week, Netanyahu charged that Winter would take right-wing votes and carry them over to Liberman on the port side of the ship.
“It’s no coincidence that a senior figure on Liberman’s list, Yulia Malinovsky, says that ultimately Winter will join a government with Liberman. That’s what will happen. That’s the plan,” Netanyahu said.
Then came a blistering comparison with Bennett, who formed a government in 2021 with Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid and Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am.
“If he walks like Bennett and talks like Bennett, he’s Bennett. Vote Likud, vote Right. Winter is not right-wing. Winter is Bennett 2. We mustn’t squander the Right’s votes. Don’t vote for Winter.”
Winter's coalition conditions complicate Netanyahu's election strategy
Netanyahu’s concern is twofold.
First, Winter’s party will fail to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, sending votes cast by people on the Right down the drain. Of the 19 major polls taken since October 1, the party crossed the threshold in 11, including four of the seven taken in the last week.
That is enough to keep Winter in the race, but hardly enough to reassure Netanyahu that the votes will count.
The second concern is that Winter will cross the threshold, then peddle his seats elsewhere.
Winter and others in his party say they will recommend Netanyahu to the president as prime minister. But they also say they will not join a government in which the haredi parties hold the balance of power unless those parties agree to a widespread haredi conscription law.
But what if Netanyahu does not accept those conditions? Asked precisely that in a Channel 12 interview on Saturday night, Winter replied, rather inelegantly, that Netanyahu could essentially “go take a hike.”
Nobody owns me, he declared
Winter did not explicitly rule out joining an Eisenkot or Liberman government. He did, however, rule out sitting with Yair Golan, because “he smears Israel abroad.”
For Netanyahu’s campaign, that left an opening wide enough to drive a campaign bus through.
A recommendation is one thing; a commitment to join a government is another. Winter is offering the former, with conditions attached to the latter. Netanyahu wants right-wing voters to hear that distinction and draw the conclusion he is supplying: Winter could be Bennett all over again.
The pressure has extended to billboards and signs in areas where candidates on Winter’s list live. Davidi Ben-Zion, eighth on the list, withdrew, reportedly telling colleagues that pressure on his family, including negative posters strategically placed near the bus stops his children use, had become too much.
Netanyahu’s concerns also extend to the other party in the hallway: Hendel and Zelekha’s.
In the Channel 14 interview, Netanyahu went after Zelekha, whom Netanyahu – as finance minister – appointed accountant-general in 2003. Despite the party’s appeal to right-wing voters, Netanyahu charged that Zelekha had voted for Meretz in the past and participated enthusiastically in anti-government protests on Balfour Street in Jerusalem and Kaplan Street in Tel Aviv.
He also attacked Zelekha on his home turf, the economy, challenging his credentials as a free-market champion.
Hendel and Zelekha’s party crossed the threshold in all seven major polls taken this week. But unlike Winter, they have not pledged to recommend Netanyahu. Hendel says the party will use its leverage to establish a broad Zionist government without the Arab and haredi parties.
Given the coalition arithmetic, how that government would come together remains an enigma. Like Winter, Hendel is clearer about his conditions than about how he would assemble a government that meets them.
But Netanyahu doesn’t need their coalition plans fully worked out to worry about them. He needs the voters attracted to those parties back in his camp.
Eisenkot seeks commanding lead to establish opposition leadership
Across the ship’s hallway, Eisenkot has a different calculation.
His campaign to make Yashar the largest party is aimed, in part, at voters already on his side of the boat. He wants them to leave the other rooms and enter his ballroom.
For Netanyahu, the immediate task is to consolidate the camp. For Eisenkot, it is also to establish who commands it.
That is why the leaders of the other parties in his bloc are less than enthusiastic about his strategy. A voter moving from Bennett, Liberman, or Golan to Eisenkot does not enlarge the bloc. It enlarges Eisenkot.
The bigger Yashar is, and the wider its lead over the Likud, the stronger his claim to form the next government – even if his bloc falls short of 61 seats.
Eisenkot repeated one phrase this week: Netanyahu must not be allowed to win by losing. By that, he means Netanyahu must not remain caretaker prime minister through another cycle of inconclusive elections simply because no one else can form a coalition.
In a Yediot Aharonot interview this week, Eisenkot said, “If you [Netanyahu] think you will do to me what you did to others in the past – meaning, remain in office at the head of a caretaker government – that will not happen.” When Israel held five elections in under four years, from April 2019 to November 2022, Netanyahu served 19 months as caretaker prime minister over two stretches.
Eisenkot considers minority government to prevent Netanyahu remaining in office
One route Eisenkot envisages to prevent a repeat of that scenario is to bring a minority government to the Knesset for approval and secure the support of a majority of those voting.
A government does not need 61 members to win such a vote; it only needs a majority of those in the plenum casting a vote. This scenario would be made possible, for instance, if the Arab parties simply don’t vote.
Once this minority government is approved, Eisenkot can then attract defectors from the other side of the ship. A substantial lead over the Likud would give that effort greater public legitimacy.
There are other considerations, too.
First, in the unlikely event that a rotation agreement with the Likud became a serious possibility, a decisive lead in seats would bolster his claim to go first as prime minister.
More immediately, the larger Yashar becomes, the harder it would be for Bennett or Liberman to argue that someone else should lead the bloc.
The four parties in the “change bloc” have yet to agree on a mechanism to determine their prime ministerial candidate after the election.
Eisenkot has said, logically enough, that the leader of the party that wins the most votes should be the bloc’s candidate. Since Yashar currently leads the bloc by a considerable margin, that formula would obviously favor him.
It remains unclear, however, whether the others are prepared to accept this. But the wider the gap, the harder it would be to explain why the leader of a much smaller party should get the top job.
Eisenkot is campaigning both against Netanyahu and for an outcome within his own bloc that would make his leadership hard to challenge.
Both Netanyahu’s and Eisenkot’s maneuvers make sense.
Netanyahu wants to prevent right-wing votes from being lost or carried into another government. Eisenkot wants to ensure that, if there is an opportunity to replace Netanyahu, he will be the one to seize it.
But both maneuvers have their limits. For Netanyahu, keeping his passengers together does not guarantee enough support to retain command. And for Eisenkot, having the biggest ballroom on one side of the ship does not guarantee enough support to become captain of the whole vessel.

Thousands Protest Corruption as Clashes Escalate in Albania

2026-10-16

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign despite three days of escalating youth-led protests over corruption, education costs and a lack of job prospects, with demonstrators clashing with riot police, setting fires and vandalizing government buildings in Tirana and other cities, Reuters and EFE reported.
Thousands of young people took to the streets of the capital on Thursday, October 15, demanding Rama’s resignation and accusing his Socialist government of corruption and neglecting education. The demonstrations have intensified since Tuesday, when around 20 people were arrested during an attack on the Ministry of Education. A fire broke out at the building on Wednesday, and more than 70 police officers were injured during the unrest. A similar number of protesters were arrested on Thursday.
Police Chief Skënder Hita said few of those detained were students, while EFE found that most demonstrators were teenagers, many of them high school students. By mid-afternoon, Tirana’s Traumatology Hospital had treated 26 people.
Riot police took a tougher approach on Thursday, using tear gas, stun grenades and water cannons against crowds throwing stones, cobblestones and fireworks. Demonstrators failed to reach the Ministry of Education, Parliament, the headquarters of Rama’s Socialist Party and the government headquarters, with police blocking access to the sites late into the night.
The unrest left Tirana’s streets strewn with burned-out trash bins, smashed bus-stop glass and toppled traffic lights. Protesters set fire to a kiosk, broke into a bank and attacked the entrance of the Ministry of Economy, which had already been damaged on Wednesday, before entering the building and vandalizing its furnishings. In one incident, a police commander was critically injured after a rock hit him in the head.
Demonstrations also took place in Elbasan, Korça, Durrës and Shkodër. Some students told EFE that violence was the only way to make a corrupt and arrogant government listen to their demands.
Rama told Reuters on Thursday that he would not step down, arguing that his victory in the May 2025 election gave him greater legitimacy than the protests. His Socialist Party won an absolute majority for the fourth consecutive time, and Rama, who has been in office since 2013, was elected to a fourth term last year.
The prime minister said he was willing to discuss rising education costs but would continue in office, arguing that his responsibility was to listen, find solutions and keep Albania moving forward. Resigning, he said, would betray the voters who had given him a strong mandate to complete negotiations for European Union membership.
The protests reflect anger over corruption, the cost of living, limited employment opportunities and the lack of prospects after graduation. A student who identified herself as Kiara told Reuters that corruption and poor job opportunities were among the main concerns, saying that finding work often depended on personal connections: “knows someone who knows someone else.”
Protester and lawyer Lulzim Tanushi accused Rama of abusing his authority since taking power and damaging people’s lives. He said the public was angry because its concerns had gone unheard until now.
The current unrest follows months of peaceful demonstrations that began in May over plans to sell land in a nature reserve on Albania’s southern coast for a luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump. The movement, known as the Flamingo Revolution after the animals living in the reserve, has broadened into demands for greater democracy and transparency.
In July, residents of a village near the planned resort told Reuters they believed their land had been unfairly sold to developers. Reuters subsequently reported that prosecutors were seeking the person who sold the land in connection with drug smuggling, allegations his lawyers denied.
Several protesters aged between 16 and 18 accused Rama of selling out the country through such real estate projects. The leaderless Flamingo Revolution platform told EFE that the students’ demands reflected the movement’s wider concerns.
“The students’ demands are a natural extension of the main concerns of the protest movement, particularly fighting corruption, addressing the rising cost of living, and holding the prime minister accountable for his arrogance,” the platform said.
Rama’s government denies the corruption allegations. The prime minister has also blamed the violence on the conservative opposition, accusing it of seeking to “bring Albania down every time it tries to move forward.”
Albania has long been affected by corruption scandals, while political analysts have described the country as a hub for criminal gangs laundering proceeds from drug and arms trafficking. These problems complicate its bid to join the European Union, despite progress under Rama’s leadership toward a target of membership by 2030.
Rama said corruption had to be tackled and that the EU had recently recognized Albania’s efforts were stronger than ever. He argued that some people, both inside and outside the country, did not want Albania to lead the EU candidate countries, but said violence would not derail its European ambitions.
Parliament Speaker Niko Peleshi, a member of the Socialist Party, attributed the demonstrations to the efforts of “evil forces” seeking to steer Albania away from Brussels.
The EU mission in Albania said in a post on X that constructive dialogue was the only way forward.

Social media favourites, Pompeii's cats star in new photo book

2026-10-16
10:06:50 UTC
19:06:50 KST

Photographed by thousands of visitors every year, the cats of Pompeii’s Archaeological Park now star in a new book. Around 50 live among the ruins.
After charming thousands of visitors and turning into genuine social media celebrities, the cats that live inside the archaeological area of Pompeii have now become the stars of a photographic book dedicated to them.
The book, entitled Cats of Pompeii, is published by Giunti Editore in collaboration with the Pompeii Archaeological Park. Richly illustrated, it tells the stories of the everyday life of the feline colony that inhabits the UNESCO World Heritage site.
The volume grew out of photographs donated to the Park by archaeologist and photographer Silvia Vacca and offers a journey into the most unusual and captivating side of the ancient city. The shots capture the cats as they roam among domus, gardens and Roman streets, providing an original perspective on a presence that has long since become an integral part of the Pompeian landscape.
The Park’s feline colony numbers between forty and fifty animals, and their presence is constantly monitored through a management and protection system that makes it possible to combine animal welfare with the conservation of the archaeological heritage and the safety of visitors. The Park has also introduced a video surveillance system to prevent animals being abandoned.
Thanks to cooperation with the charity Archeogatti Onlus, chaired by Antonella Carotenuto, the Archaeological Park also ensures sterilisation campaigns, health checks, measures to prevent abandonment, and the management of feeding the colony and arranging adoptions for some of the "archaeologist" cats.
Cats in ancient Pompeii
The presence of cats in Pompeii is a symbolic feature of life at the site. Ongoing archaeological research sheds light on the relationship between humans and felines in the ancient world, while today these animals remain a familiar sight and are much appreciated by visitors from all over the globe.
The camera lens reveals intimate, evocative images taken during the Park’s quietest moments, when the streets of the ancient city fall silent once more. Out of this comes a portrait of a different Pompeii, where safeguarding cultural heritage goes hand in hand with protecting the animals that have inhabited its spaces for years.
"Cats of Pompeii" is available at sales points in the Pompeii Archaeological Park and through Giunti’s distribution channels.

Technical fault disrupts flights across Italy, cyberattack ruled out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:06:14 UTC
19:06:14 KST

Flights across Italy were severely disrupted on Friday after technical issues affected the data transmission network supporting air traffic control nationwide, Italian news agency ANSA reported.
Air navigation service provider ENAV said it had introduced measures to regulate traffic flows as air traffic increased and technical anomalies persisted.
“Given the gradual increase in air traffic and the persistence of the anomalies, measures to regulate traffic flows were introduced to continue ensuring the highest level of operational safety,” ENAV said.
The measures included temporarily reducing the capacity to manage aircraft in Italian airspace.
Cyberattack ruled out
ENAV said the possibility of malicious activity had been ruled out, stressing that neither a hacker attack nor sabotage caused the disruption.
The anomalies were detected overnight in the geographical data transmission network supporting air traffic control services across the country, the company said.
As technical checks continued to identify the source of the fault, ENAV said it was investigating the causes and working to restore the systems.
Several airports across Italy reported flight delays and cancellations as a result of the disruption.

British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:05:54 UTC
19:05:54 KST

A British man has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) after his two-year-old son fell 10 metres (33ft) to his death from the fourth-floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he approached it with the boy to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.
The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
In emotional scenes at the court, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday in Cyprus, as a “tragic event”.
“Jail is not appropriate,” the judge said, telling the courtroom that as there was “clearly no intent to kill” she had decided against a custodial sentence and would instead order Foster to pay the fine.
The Essex-born auditor, who had previously appeared in court visibly distraught, struggled to hold back tears as the sentence was handed down. As it dawned that the case was finally over, he hugged his lawyer before telling reporters: “Thank you for your support. I’m looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter.”
The light sentence – the minimum for the charge – meant Foster could retrieve his passport and other documents he had been forced to surrender. More usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents, the charge carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison.
Speaking outside the district court in Paphos, the defendant’s lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said Foster, who works for one of the UK’s big four accounting firms, would finally be able to grieve.
“He’s been through a lot and it’s been very emotional but he’s relieved it’s over,” he said of his client, who posted €30,000 in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August before being forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus for the proceedings.
“This case should not have gone to court. We asked for the charges to be suspended. Unfortunately this was not accepted.”
Alexandrou had appealed to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds, arguing that prosecution “does not serve the public interest”. The request was denied.
The boy fell to his death from the window of the King Evelthon hotel within hours of the family arriving in Paphos.
In mitigation on 5 October, Alexandrou recounted how Foster was making his way to a lift along the corridor when he stopped at the window and the “inconceivable” occurred. The Briton, he said, had not realised the window was ajar when, lifting the child, who was excitedly pointing to the hotel’s waterpark outside, he “lost control” and he slipped through his hands. The boy was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after suffering severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.
Summing up, Christodoulidou said while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.
“It is no exaggeration to say that for the rest of his life he will have guilt for losing his child in such a tragic way,” she added. Mitigating factors presented by the defence, including the Briton’s lack of criminal record, as well as his guilty plea, had also played a role in her decision, she explained. In a country so dependent on tourism, criticism had mounted as Cypriot human rights defenders, media pundits and foreign diplomats all questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials approached the case.
A former British colony, the eastern Mediterranean island attracts roughly 4 million visitors and is particularly popular with tourists from the UK.
Alexandrou, the lawyer, said he had advised his client to admit the negligence charge to avoid a potentially drawn-out and disturbing trial when he and his family were still processing the grief of their “unimaginable loss”.
Conceding the case had been “emotional” for the entire defence team, the lawyer added: “He can finally grieve. Now that the court proceedings are over, the explosion of his emotions at the loss of his child will be immediate.”
In a statement issued after the sentencing, the Foster family said: “Today marks the end of the legal proceedings in Cyprus, and we are grateful to the court and Judge Christodoulidou for her decision to apply the maximum mitigation afforded to her.
“We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end. Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day.
“Our focus now is on supporting one another and finding a way forward as a family. We ask that our privacy is respected as we do so.”

Hegseth's TV instincts backfire as Trump rejects execution livestream
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:05:49 UTC
19:05:49 KST

Hegseth's TV instincts backfire as Trump rejects execution livestream
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 - As he took to the stage this week at an Army event, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remarked how much it looked like a TV set. The former Fox News host said that put him at ease, even as the first in a series of anti-war protesters shouted at him.
But Hegseth's TV instincts, while perhaps one of the tools he relies on most in his Pentagon role, appear to have failed him on Thursday when President Donald Trump pulled the plug on his plans, announced last week, to livestream the Army's firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan.
Trump had been unaware of Hegseth's unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution, said a White House official who spoke on condition of anonymity. Many fellow Republicans, along with religious leaders and international observers, raised objections to the plan, and defense officials who spoke to Reuters on Thursday expressed relief that the livestreaming would not go forward.
Defense secretaries often cycle out after a couple of years in the job and speculation in Washington has mounted whether Trump might see value in bringing new management to the Pentagon after November's midterm elections.
But Republican strategists said it was too soon to say whether Trump's decision to overrule Hegseth would affect their relationship, which has remained strong despite mounting public opposition to the war in Iran.
"They've been kind of very closely knit and I don't know whether it means anything at all," Republican strategist Douglas Heye said. Charlie Black, a veteran Republican strategist, said it would likely blow over.
"It's a wild thing but nobody will remember it next week," Black said, adding Trump "did the right thing."
The Pentagon sought to downplay the first major public split between Trump and Hegseth, saying the two spoke before the US president posted his decision on Truth Social.
"The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," said Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's chief spokesperson.
CONGRESSIONAL WORRIES
Trump regularly extols Hegseth publicly, and has given the former Army National Guard soldier significant leeway as he seeks to reshape the Pentagon, including by firing its most senior officers.
But after narrowly winning Senate confirmation, Hegseth has failed to win over many Republicans who voiced concerns over his qualifications for the job. Some Republican lawmakers and congressional aides have expressed worries over his expected plans to draw down forces in Europe.
One Republican lawmaker filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth last month, accusing him of abusing his office by executing an order for hostilities against Iran without approval by Congress.
While Representative Thomas Massie's measure is not expected to succeed, Democrats could look to move forward with impeachment proceedings if they win control of the House in the upcoming elections in November.
At times, the conflict between Hegseth and members of Congress has become personal. Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Democratic Senator Mark Kelly after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence community urged US troops to refuse illegal orders.
Kelly on Thursday introduced a bill that would prohibit livestreamed executions.
"Livestreaming an execution is un-American and dangerous. It is the kind of thing we see with regimes like Iran and the Taliban in Afghanistan," Kelly said in a statement.
The event would have been extraordinary, even for a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or livestreamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone by firing squad since 1945.
Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder for shooting dead 13 people and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast Fort Hood base in 2009. Now 56, he requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.
Hegseth had argued that making the event public would help show "there's serious consequences for these types of things."
Trump appeared to accept Hegseth's argument, saying on Thursday livestreaming it "might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan."
But Trump, who is himself a former reality television star, ultimately decided a public show went too far.
"Many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote. REUTERS
