Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress takes aim at judge who jailed Bolsonaro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:05:36 UTC
19:05:36 KST

Brazil's incoming right-wing Congress takes aim at judge who jailed Bolsonaro
BRASILIA, Oct 16 - Brazil's next Congress is spoiling for a fight with the Supreme Court, including plans for an unprecedented impeachment of one of its justices that could dramatically expand the reach of a right-wing agenda, more than a dozen experts and officials at both the Senate and court told Reuters.
Driving the effort are allies of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro who dominated legislative elections this month and plan to take aim at Alexandre de Moraes, the Supreme Court justice responsible for the ex-president's arrest and conviction on coup-plotting charges.
That would represent a major escalation by the legislative branch in a years-long power struggle with an empowered Brazilian judiciary, reasserting the influence of Congress and potentially pushing the court to the right for years to come.
If Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the former president's son, beats leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in an October 25 runoff as polls now suggest, a defanged judiciary would also reduce one of the main checks on his power.
BLOCKING RIGHT-WING POLICIES
Brazil's Supreme Court was the main obstacle to his father's agenda during his 2019-2023 presidency, blocking efforts to weaken environmental protections, ease pandemic restrictions and facilitate gun purchases, for example.
The top court continues to hold back some of the most strident right-wing legislation, effectively defining policy on matters from Indigenous rights to regulating the internet.
This month's election could prove pivotal, as the next president could name at least 4 of the court's 11 justices, including an already vacant seat and replacements for 3 justices who will reach the mandatory retirement age of 75 before the president's term ends.
After former President Bolsonaro named two justices to the court, a victory by his son could spell a majority of the court appointed by the Bolsonaro family by the time he would leave office in 2031.
Impeaching Moraes, 57, would hasten that majority's arrival.
"Should Flavio win, the next administration and the Senate can reshape the majority of the 11-member bench, which means defining, literally, the balance of power in Brazilian democracy for a generation," said Bruna Santos, director of the Brazil Program at the Inter-American Dialogue.
SCORNED BY TRUMP, MUSK
Ex-President Bolsonaro has been in jail since November for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. Moraes, who oversaw the case, became one of Brazil's most polarizing figures, drawing even the ire of US President Donald Trump, who described the case as a "witch hunt" and briefly sanctioned the judge in 2025.
Moraes also drew criticism when he ordered X suspended in Brazil in 2024, after the platform defied court orders. Its owner Elon Musk accused him of censorship and authoritarianism.
Bolsonaro supporters have rallied to remove the judge after a federal police report revealed communications between Moraes and a jailed banker accused of the country's biggest-ever banking fraud. Bolsonaro, who himself is being investigated for ties to the same banker, has also called for Moraes' removal.
"Defending the Judiciary means confronting this problem — opening an impeachment process and giving him the right to a defense, concluding it and turning this page," Senator-elect Domingos Savio, from Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL), told Reuters.
Lula has publicly supported unsealing the investigation, calling for transparency, disclosure, and an impartial investigation into all allegations of corruption.
Neither Moraes nor the Supreme Court responded to questions from Reuters. He and the wider court have defended their actions as necessary to uphold Brazilian law and protect democratic institutions. He has referred to the probes as politically and electorally motivated as revenge for the conviction of former President Bolsonaro, and requested his own investigation into another justice who released the reports.
LEGISLATIVE FIREPOWER
Senator Bolsonaro's running mate, lawmaker Alfredo Gaspar, told Reuters there is "a need to review what is happening today in the relationship between the Supreme Court and the other branches of government, and that involves examining whether justices have committed impeachable offenses."
Brazil's constitution allows the Senate to try Supreme Court justices for infractions that violate the constitution or risk public security. Votes from two-thirds of the 81-member Senate — 54 senators — are needed to convict and remove a justice.
Senator Bolsonaro's allies may already be close when the next Senate takes office in February. His party won a record 28 seats, and the senator has already secured backing from five other parties that together hold another 22 seats.
That would bring the conservative coalition to 50 senators. The remaining four votes could come from the 15 senators with non-aligned parties.
Since 2023, there have been 48 unsuccessful requests to impeach Moraes within the Senate, which never made it to trial because the Senate president must choose to advance a complaint against a justice.
That could change, as Senator Bolsonaro's campaign manager Rogerio Marinho is likely to become the next Senate president.
Marinho has in recent days told several Supreme Court justices that Brazil's upper house will not seek opportunities for revenge, he said to journalists, though adding that the current Senate is "failing to act" to hold justices accountable.
"If impeachable offenses are committed, they must be investigated. No one is above the law," Marinho said. REUTERS

The 41-year-old has separately faced questions about her legal credentials after giving an inconclusive account of whether she had passed the bar exam, a requirement to practise law in the United States.
Zacharia describes herself as a lawyer and lists herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative non-profit. She has also said she previously worked at a law firm in Beijing.
Asked about her legal background on Thursday, she said she had registered to take the bar exam but became “distracted and overwhelmed” by plans to move to China with her husband.
She said she did not retake the exam after returning to the United States because of the birth of her first child.

Former parliamentarian targeted for banned Israeli wine purchase

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Former parliamentarian targeted for banned Israeli wine purchase
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A complaint has been filed against former orthodox Protestant SGP MP Roelof Bisschop, who said publicly that he had bought wine in protest against the Dutch ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements, public broadcaster NOS reported.
Pro-Palestinian group BDS Netherlands (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) filed the criminal complaint with the public prosecution service (OM). Activists had earlier reported Bisschop to the fiscal investigation service FIOD.
Bisschop bought two bottles on September 23, the day after the ban took effect, and posted a photo of them on social media. Two days later he told Christian television channel Family7 that the purchase was a “statement” against the ban.
Since September 22, the Netherlands has banned imports of goods from illegal settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories and the Golan Heights. The rules also ban buying and selling such goods, intermediary trade and any form of circumvention.
In its complaint, BDS Netherlands said Bisschop had deliberately acted against the sanctions policy and promoted this on several platforms.
“Anyone who, as a former MP, publicly announces they are deliberately testing the law can expect the OM to look at whether that is a criminal offence,” the group said in the complaint.
It is not yet clear whether the wine is covered by the ban. The producer, Teperberg Winery, has vineyards in the occupied West Bank and is on a UN list of companies active in settlements. However, it says these wines are made just inside Israel. Bisschop told NOS he did not know exactly where the bottles came from.
The OM said it is aware of the complaint and will assess whether there are grounds to open an investigation.

Türkiye's Fidan to attend OIC foreign ministers' meeting in Baghdad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:01:07 UTC
19:01:07 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will attend the 52nd session of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s (OIC) Council of Foreign Ministers in Baghdad on October 17-18, Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry has said.
Held under the theme “Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development”, the meeting will see Türkiye transfer the organisation’s rotating presidency to Iraq, which it has held since June 2025.
Discussions are expected to cover Israel’s actions in Gaza and across the occupied Palestinian territories, other conflicts in the Muslim world, counterterrorism, United Nations reform, Islamophobia and the situation of Muslim communities in non-member countries.
The meeting is expected to conclude with the adoption of the Baghdad Declaration.
Fidan to call for coordinated action on Palestine
In his address, Fidan is expected to describe Israel’s aggressive and expansionist policies as the biggest security threat to the Middle East and urge OIC members to coordinate their response with responsible international actors.
He is also expected to call for steps to protect Jerusalem’s status, oppose further moves by countries to relocate their embassies there, and reaffirm that a two-state solution leading to an independent Palestinian state is the only path to a just and lasting peace.
Fidan is expected to stress the need to ensure uninterrupted humanitarian aid reaches people in Gaza.
Regional security and freedom of navigation
The Turkish foreign minister is also expected to address rising tensions in the Gulf and around the Strait of Hormuz.
He is expected to emphasise the importance of ensuring safe and free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al Mandab for regional stability and global trade, while condemning Houthi militia attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure and reaffirming Türkiye’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
Fidan is also expected to call for the protection of Syria’s and Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, including a complete Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon.
OIC to discuss rights of Muslim communities
The meeting is also expected to address the rights of Turkish Cypriots, who face what Ankara describes as unjust isolation, as well as the fundamental rights and freedoms of the Muslim Turkish minority in Western Thrace and Muslim Turkish communities in the Dodecanese islands.
The OIC, established in 1969, has 57 member states and is the world’s second-largest intergovernmental organisation after the United Nations.
Türkiye is one of its 25 founding members and took over the rotating presidency at the previous Council of Foreign Ministers meeting in Istanbul in June 2025.
Fidan is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with counterparts on the sidelines of the Baghdad gathering.

Copenhagen establishes support groups for parents of children missing school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:01:06 UTC
19:01:06 KST

A debate in Denmark over a proposed law granting citizenship to 2,055 people has centered on whether the applicants have been checked well enough for anti-democratic opinions.
Liberal Alliance, a political party in Denmark, carried out its own check of the people listed in the citizenship bill. During this review, the party found a woman who had repeatedly praised Hamas and former Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh. 
Following the discovery, Liberal Alliance wants the woman called in for an interview with Indfødsretsudvalget, the Naturalization Committee of the Danish parliament. 
Alex Vanopslagh, the leader of Liberal Alliance, spoke about the matter to the Danish newspaper Politiken.
“As we see it, it just emphasizes the need to wait to grant more citizenships until a proper screening model is in place, so that we can specifically catch some types who, based on what we can see so far, appear strongly anti-democratic,” he told the newspaper.
Every six months, a new bill is introduced in Folketinget, the Danish parliament, to give people Danish citizenship. This happens after an application process that is often long and detailed. This process was also followed under the previous coalition government in Denmark. 
The most recent round of citizenships was scheduled at the same time a parliamentary election was called in the spring. Because of the election, the bill that included citizenship for the 2,055 people was delayed. 
The delay gave momentum to demands from opposition parties. They argued that officials must carry out a more thorough review of the people on the list to find out if any of them hold anti-democratic views. Socialdemokratiet, the Danish Social Democratic Party, supported this demand as well. 
However, the new government decided to present the citizenship bill before a new screening system was ready. This choice led to a larger debate during the opening of the Danish parliament. 
During that debate, Rasmus Stoklund, the political spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, said that if opposition parties found a person on the bill who had anti-democratic views, they could inform the Naturalization Committee. Liberal Alliance has now acted on that suggestion.
Politiken also spoke with the woman identified by the party. She denied that she supports Hamas or any killings.
“I do not support anyone who kills anyone. Because I do not like anyone killing anyone, regardless of whether they are Israeli, Russian or anything else,” the woman told the newspaper.
She stated that she is ready to attend an interview with the committee to explain her position.
Other political parties have reacted differently to the proposal. Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, supports calling the woman in for an interview. 
However, Enhedslisten, the Danish left-wing Red-Green Alliance party, strongly opposes the idea. 
“It is deeply concerning that Liberal Alliance now to such an extent wants to begin exercising thought control,” Peder Hvelplund, the citizenship spokesperson for Enhedslisten, told Politiken.

Some adults’ brains look older than their age, and gut biology may be part of the picture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:55 UTC
19:00:55 KST

Some young and middle-aged adults have brain activity patterns that look “older” than their actual age, and new research suggests these differences are linked to thinking skills, mood, and the gut. Adults with older-looking brain patterns tended to score somewhat lower on tests of working memory and executive function, report more depressive symptoms, and have modestly different gut bacteria and stool chemicals. The findings were published in eBioMedicine.
A central concept in this research is the brain aging index. Researchers train a computer model to estimate a person’s age from brain scans alone, and the index is the gap between that estimate and the person’s actual age. A positive score means the brain looks older than expected, while a negative score means it looks younger. The authors of a 2017 review argued that such estimates could serve as a marker of brain health, pointing to evidence that an older-appearing brain is linked to poorer cognitive and physical aging and a higher risk of death.
Most of this research has focused on older adults who are already at risk for cognitive decline. However, the authors of a 2024 review argued that middle age may mark a turning point, with biological changes during this period shaping a person’s later brain health.
At the same time, evidence has grown linking the digestive system to brain health. A 2025 study comparing people with Alzheimer’s disease, people with mild cognitive impairment, and healthy adults found that gut bacteria and stool chemicals shifted step by step across these groups, and these shifts were tied to brain shrinkage and poorer thinking skills. A study covered by PsyPost in 2024 similarly found that depressed adults tend to have an imbalance of gut bacteria that relates to altered brain connectivity.
This progression of research led Kanhao Zhao, who conducted the study during his postdoctoral training under Arpana Church at the Church Lab at the University of California, Los Angeles, to test whether gut biology relates to early brain aging in young and middle-aged adults. The work was supported by National Institutes of Health grants awarded to Church.
“Most brain-age research has focused on older adults or people who already have neurological disease,” Zhao, who is now a postdoctoral scholar in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University School of Medicine, told PsyPost. “We therefore wanted to ask whether meaningful differences in brain aging could already be detected in young and mid-life adults, and whether these differences were linked not only to cognition and mental health, but also to gut microbial and metabolic features.”
To investigate this, the research team analyzed brain imaging and biological data from healthy adults aged 18 to 65. They divided the data into three separate groups to ensure their results were consistent across different samples: a discovery group of 674 people, a replication group of 444 people, and an independent group of 344 people.
The participants underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. This technique measures changes in blood oxygen levels, which rise and fall with brain activity, while a person lies still and rests. By tracking which regions rise and fall together, a pattern known as functional connectivity, scientists can see how different brain regions communicate.
Participants also completed various tests to measure their cognitive and emotional health. These included assessments of intelligence, working memory, executive function, and self-reported questionnaires for depressive symptoms.
In the independent group of participants, the researchers collected stool samples. They analyzed these samples using metagenomics, which sequences the genetic material of the bacteria living in the gut, and metabolomics, which identifies specific metabolites. Metabolites are the small chemical molecules left over from cellular processes, digestion, and bacterial activity.
Across all three groups, the model’s age estimates tracked participants’ actual ages reasonably well, though imperfectly: its predictions were off by about 6 to 9 years on average. People whose brains looked older than expected showed a consistent pattern. A higher index score was associated with stronger connections involving the default mode network, a set of regions most active during inward-focused thought such as daydreaming and recalling memories, and the frontoparietal network, which helps control goal-directed thinking. The strongest links involved the precuneus and posterior cingulate cortex, regions along the brain’s midline that are involved in internal thought and memory retrieval.
At the same time, people with older-appearing brains showed weaker connections in the ventral attention network, a brain system that helps humans orient themselves to sudden changes in their environment. This network imbalance was linked to worse performance on cognitive tests. Individuals with a higher brain aging index scored lower on performance IQ, working memory, and executive function tasks, while also reporting more symptoms of depression.
These associations were modest. Correlations between brain-age scores and individual test results ranged from about 0.12 to 0.38, meaning brain-age scores accounted for at most about 14 percent of the variation in any single measure, and usually much less. Not every measure lined up: verbal IQ showed no reliable link in either group where it was tested, and several test scores were linked in one group but not another. In the first group, the links held after accounting for participants’ actual ages.
“The effects should be viewed as meaningful population-level associations rather than as a diagnostic test for an individual person,” Zhao noted. “An important strength of the study is that the brain-age pattern was examined across multiple independent cohorts, but the associations with cognition, mood, and gut biology were generally modest. At this stage, the brain aging index is better understood as a research marker of individual variability in brain health than as something that could tell a person how quickly their brain is aging in a clinical setting.”
The gut findings were similarly small. In the 182 participants with complete data, a combined profile of gut bacteria and stool chemicals accounted for only about 2 percent of the differences in brain-age scores, though this was more than would be expected by chance. The bacteria most strongly tied to older-looking brains in this profile included species of Clostridium and Collinsella, and the stool chemicals included ceramides and 24-hydroxycholesterol, fat-related molecules involved in inflammation, cellular stress, and cholesterol processing.
Some of these bacteria have been tied to inflammation in other research, but the authors note that in these healthy adults they appeared alongside bacteria typically associated with a healthy gut. People with younger-looking brains, by contrast, had higher levels of stool chemicals related to neurotransmitter function and amino acid processing. One of the molecules most strongly tied to a younger-looking brain was estetrol, a form of estrogen, which the authors suggest could hint at a protective role for reproductive hormone pathways.
“What I found particularly interesting was that the signal was not confined to the brain,” Zhao said. “We observed coordinated associations involving functional brain networks, cognition and mood, and gut-derived biological features, including microbial and metabolic signatures related to lipid metabolism, immune and vascular processes, synaptic function, and mitochondrial pathways. This convergence across very different biological levels suggests that understanding brain aging may ultimately require looking beyond the brain alone.”
Notably, the cognitive and mood measures were tied to the brain network patterns rather than directly to any specific gut bacteria or stool chemicals.
“One important message is that people of the same chronological age can show meaningful differences in how their brain networks resemble patterns associated with aging,” Zhao explained. “We also found that these brain-age differences were linked to patterns in gut microbes and metabolites, suggesting that brain aging may be related to broader biological processes across the brain-gut system rather than occurring in isolation.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. “The most important caveat is that this was a cross-sectional observational study, so our findings do not establish causality,” Zhao emphasized. “We cannot conclude that particular gut microbes or metabolites cause the brain to age faster, nor that changing the microbiome would necessarily make the brain ‘younger.'”
Because everything was measured at a single point in time, it is also possible that brain changes influence the gut, or that other factors, such as diet, shape both. Zhao also noted that the brain-age measure is a “statistical index derived from functional connectivity, rather than a literal measurement of the biological age of a person’s brain.”
Additionally, the gut microbiome analysis was conducted on 182 participants, mostly women, and the cohorts drew on datasets from the U.S. and Japan. The researchers note that larger, more balanced studies will be necessary to verify the exact bacterial and metabolic signatures identified in this group. The genetic sequencing used in the study also identifies broad bacterial species but cannot pinpoint specific bacterial strains, which might have differing effects on human health.
“The next step is to move from cross-sectional associations toward longitudinal and prospective studies,” Zhao said. “We would like to determine whether these brain-body signatures can predict future cognitive trajectories and whether they change in response to modifiable factors or interventions. More broadly, we are interested in expanding beyond the brain-gut axis toward a more integrated view of brain-body aging. Emerging research suggests that brain function is also closely related to cardiovascular physiology and other organ systems.”
“In future studies, we hope to combine brain imaging with cardiac imaging, physiological signals such as ECG and PPG, and molecular measurements to better understand how aging processes across different organ systems interact,” he added. “Ultimately, our goal is to identify multimodal biomarkers that explain why individuals age differently and may eventually help guide personalized strategies for maintaining brain health.”
An ECG records the heart’s electrical activity, while PPG uses light sensors, like those in many smartwatches, to track pulse and blood flow.
Studying these processes over time could help scientists develop interventions to maintain brain health during middle age. “I think an important broader message is that brain aging is unlikely to be a process that begins suddenly in old age,” Zhao concluded. “Individual differences in brain network organization and their relationships with cognition and peripheral biology can already be observed much earlier in adulthood. Understanding these earlier differences may eventually help us shift the focus from treating late-stage decline toward identifying trajectories of brain health before substantial impairment develops.”
The study, “Brain-gut crosstalk associated with brain ageing in young and mid-life adults: a multicohort cross-sectional study,” was authored by Kanhao Zhao, Gabriel A. Vignolle, Jennifer S. Labus, Emeran A. Mayer, Allison Vaughan, Marika Dy, Priten Vora, Ming W. Hung, Keith Vossel, Chris Gill, Daniele Del Rio, Catherine Stanton, R. Paul Ross, John F. Cryan, Rima Kaddurah-Daouk, Yu Zhang, and Arpana Church.

Leonardo DRS wins place on US counter drone contract
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:00:20 BST
19:00:20 KST

Leonardo DRS has been awarded an indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity contract with a ceiling of 500 million dollars and a three-year period of performance by Joint Interagency Task Force 401, giving it the right to compete for orders to field counter drone sensing equipment to American forces, according to the company.
The arrangement covers the rapid delivery of integrated counter uncrewed aircraft system sensing capabilities supporting force protection and low altitude air defence, with task orders competed over the life of the contract.
John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS, said: “Today’s threat environment is evolving faster than ever, and our customers need proven capabilities delivered at operational speed. This JIATF IDIQ positions DRS to accelerate the delivery of integrated C-UAS sensing technologies through rapid fielding of operationally relevant capabilities that help protect forces and strengthen low-altitude air defense as new threats emerge.”
Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager at the Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit, said: “Our counter UAS and air defense radars have demonstrated proven detection, tracking, and force protection performance in operational environments. We design, manufacture, and deliver combat-proven sensing systems at speed, and we’re ready now to support JIATF with mission-ready expeditionary radar capability that can be fielded rapidly as operational needs for C-UAS evolve.”
The award is one of ten made under an effort the American side calls Domestic Shield, aimed at protecting prioritised military facilities and assets inside the United States from drones. Combined ceilings across the ten run to roughly 4.15 billion dollars. Seven firms, including RADA Technologies, hold awards at the 500 million dollar level, alongside Allen Control Systems, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield, Napatree Technology, SRC and L3Harris WESCAM. Echodyne and PVP Advanced EO Systems hold 250 million dollar awards and SmartShooter 150 million.
The task force is directed by Brigadier General Matt Ross. Brent Ingraham, Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology, said the multi-vendor marketplace enforces strict open architecture standards, which is the mechanism intended to let new sensors and effectors be swapped in as the threat changes.
Orders under the arrangement have already started moving. SRC received a first delivery order worth 10.24 million dollars for one Gryphon R1440 and two R1540 radars with integration, installation, support and training.
RADA came to Leonardo DRS through the merger with the Israeli radar maker RADA Electronic Industries in 2021, and its compact active electronically scanned array radars are widely used for short range air defence and counter rocket, artillery and mortar work, including on American vehicle-mounted systems. Leonardo DRS is the American arm of the Italian group Leonardo and trades on Nasdaq.

Human Judgement Is the Most Powerful Technology in the AI Age
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

In Ukraine, a Russian drone guided by artificial intelligence killed three civilians at a gas station, including a 19-year-old university student. In Gaza, an AI-assisted intelligence tool helped Israeli forces locate a Hamas commander. The subsequent airstrike killed him and, according to independent estimates, at least 125 other people.
Different wars. Different circumstances. But a deeply troubling question: As machines become more involved in decisions of life and death, are we losing sight of the human beings whose lives hang in the balance?
That question brought me back this month to a small white house in Reykjavík, Iceland.
Forty years ago, Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met at Höfði House, representing rival nuclear superpowers divided by decades of distrust. They left without an agreement. Yet their willingness to talk, listen, and imagine what had seemed impossible helped lay the groundwork for historic nuclear arms reductions.
I remember that moment vividly. I was a young Icelandic exchange student living in the United States, watching two world leaders meet in my small home country. I could never have imagined that 40 years later, as President of Iceland, I would return to that same house to ask a new generation of leaders to find the courage to talk.
The enduring lesson of Reykjavík is not simply about nuclear weapons or diplomacy. It is about the extraordinary power of human connection and dialogue. And we urgently need to remember it.
Never have we possessed more sophisticated tools to communicate, yet our ability to understand one another seems increasingly fragile. We are connected across continents in milliseconds, but too often separated by fear, anger, and mistrust.
Our technologies can transform medicine, education, and human prosperity. Yet they can also accelerate conflict, undermine democracy, and challenge human control.
Crucial questions for the AI age
Thanks to new technologies like AI, our power has grown exponentially. But has our wisdom kept pace?
Over the past week, Iceland has explored that question not only through another conventional summit, but through a journey from remembrance to dialogue, and from dialogue to responsibility.
We began with a traveling exhibition from the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the testimony of a survivor of the atomic bombing. More than 80 years later, she still vividly recalls what she describes as the sudden appearance of a thousand suns, followed by unimaginable destruction, decades of devastating illness, and the stigma endured by survivors. No discussion of nuclear deterrence should ever lose sight of the human lives behind those words.
We then confronted the promises and dangers of artificial intelligence with technology experts, including Tristan Harris and Aza Raskin. The central question was not simply what AI can do, but what we should allow it to do—and who gets to decide.
Perhaps the most important conversations, however, happened far from the conference halls.
Across Iceland, young people invited fellow citizens to put down their phones and sit together to discuss the future they want to create. Students, parents, grandparents, teachers, and neighbors talked about education, belonging, technology, nature, and peace.
The young people were not asking adults to arrive with all the answers. They wanted to be heard. To be taken seriously. To have a voice in decisions that will shape their lives long after today's leaders have left office.
They understood something we too often forget: decisions made far from the people they affect are rarely wise ones.
I found that both humbling and hopeful.
Because dialogue is more than exchanging opinions. At its best, it is an act of recognition: I see you. Your experience matters. Your future matters. Even when we disagree, we share responsibility for what comes next.
The demands of dialogue
The purpose of dialogue is not always consensus. It is connection. And connection is where trust begins. Without trust, even the most brilliant solutions struggle to take root.
We carried that spirit back to Höfði House, where leaders from politics, technology, science, business, and civil society gathered to ask what responsible leadership demands of us today.
The result was A Call from Reykjavík, signed by three women presidents and open to others who wish to join. It calls for meaningful human control over powerful technologies, insists that decisions about war and nuclear weapons remain firmly in human hands, and places peace and responsibility to future generations at the heart of leadership.
The following day, in a public conversation moderated by renowned journalist Christiane Amanpour, President Nataša Pirc Musar of Slovenia, former Irish President Mary Robinson and I reflected on the choices before humanity.
Forty years after two powerful men met in Reykjavík, three women—indeed, three world leaders—came together to continue the conversation. Not because women have all the answers. We do not. But because progress requires more voices, more perspectives, and a willingness to listen across differences. And because the future must never belong only to those who currently hold power.
I do not believe dialogue is a soft alternative to leadership. I believe it is one of its most demanding forms.
It takes courage to listen to someone with whom we profoundly disagree. Humility to acknowledge what we do not know. And strength to resist reducing complex human challenges to slogans, enemies, or simple answers.
Dialogue does not mean abandoning our values, excusing aggression, or accepting injustice. Nor is it a substitute for action. It is how we begin to build the trust and understanding that make lasting action possible.
AI-assisted warfare
The wars in Ukraine and Gaza remind us of the devastating human cost of conflict. AI-assisted warfare adds another dimension: the danger of placing ever greater distance between those making decisions and those living with their consequences.
We must not surrender human judgment, accountability, or conscience to machines.
But technology alone is not the problem, and technology alone cannot provide the answer. We also need stronger human infrastructure: relationships, institutions, shared values, and habits of cooperation that allow us to respond collectively to danger.
We must equip the next generation not only with technical skills, but with the deeply human capacities to shape our future: listening, critical thinking, empathy, courage, and collaboration. In an age of intelligent machines, these may be our most essential skills.
Iceland is a small nation. We cannot dictate the course of global affairs. But perhaps our size reminds us of something larger nations sometimes forget: no one can build a peaceful future alone.
Forty years ago, Reykjavík showed that even the deepest divisions need not determine our destiny. Today, we need a new Reykjavík moment. Not one confined to a single house, summit, or handful of world leaders.
We need it in parliaments and boardrooms, classrooms and communities, across generations and between nations in conflict. Wherever fear has replaced curiosity, wherever people have stopped listening, wherever power has outrun wisdom.
The world does not lack intelligence, information, or ambition. What we too often lack is the courage to truly connect.
Of course, dialogue alone will not save us. But without it, I struggle to see how we can save ourselves.
The future will not be shaped only by the power of our technology or our weapons, but by the quality of our conversations—and the courage of the choices that follow.
Fortunately, we still have time. And we still have each other.

India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
The SIR is disenfranchising marginalised communities and advancing the Hindu nationalist project.
Over the weekend, thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, faced mass detentions and a heavy police crackdown in New Delhi. The demonstrations, which have brought together youth activists and opposition parties, centre on the removal of more than 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, raising profound questions about the state of Indian democracy.
The deletions are the result of the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) undertaken by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI periodically revises electoral rolls to add new voters and remove the names of those who have died or permanently moved away. The last intensive revision was completed in 2003-2004. What makes the current SIR unprecedented, however, is its scale, the arbitrariness and overreach of its procedures, and the mass disenfranchisement that has followed. The exercise has disproportionately affected Muslims, women, migrants and other marginalised communities while also raising questions about the legitimacy of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP’s) electoral victories in Bihar and West Bengal.
Both the ECI and the ruling party have defended the exercise by using the language of “purification”. In a caste society, that rhetoric is deeply troubling but also revealing. The bureaucratic procedures and technological infrastructure underpinning the exercise barely mask its intention to create two classes of citizenship in India, one endowed with political voice through the right to vote and the other reduced to what the philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls “bare life”.
The SIR’s intent, procedures and outcomes reveal a sinister design: to maximise voter exclusions rather than enhance voter participation. This subverts the promise of universal adult suffrage, a cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. The ECI initially excluded the government-issued Aadhaar card from the list of documents accepted for voter verification during the SIR, supposedly because it was considered “overinclusive”. If that did not expose the exercise’s exclusionary intent, the ECI’s invention of the category “logical discrepancy” during the West Bengal SIR certainly did. This pseudo-legal innovation accounted for 2.7 million of the nearly 9 million names removed from electoral rolls in Bengal. The demand for educational certificates, land records, legacy documents and family trees as evidence also places a heavy burden on poor and marginalised voters, especially in regions still reeling under mass poverty, landlessness and rampant illiteracy. With the “burden of proof” shifted to ordinary voters, the SIR aims to achieve precisely what it set out to do: mass deletions and consequent disenfranchisement.
Customised apps and online forms, digitised electoral rolls and the requirement to upload scanned documents in prescribed formats are all presented as evidence of the SIR’s efficiency and objectivity. But this approach ignores the digital divide in a deeply unequal society. Technology does not operate outside relations of power. In fact, it often serves as a mechanism of control. The category of “logical discrepancy” relies on an AI-enabled application, ERONET (Electoral Roll Officers’ Network), which compares voters’ details with older electoral rolls and flags discrepancies in names and family relationships. The use of such centralised systems has also raised questions about who controls electoral data and how these discrepancies are assessed. Women are particularly vulnerable to these procedures. Many change their names or addresses after marriage and may lack the documents needed to establish links with older electoral records. The excessive exclusion of women demonstrates how ostensibly neutral technological procedures can reinforce existing inequalities and weaken people’s political voice.
The SIR’s purported neutrality is at odds with its effects, which fall heavily on the weak and the marginalised. Among religious minorities, Muslims across the country bear a particularly heavy burden of deletions. In Bengal, Muslims reportedly accounted for about 65 percent of the 2.7 million people removed from electoral rolls on grounds of “logical discrepancy”. With only 19 specially constituted tribunals to handle more than 3.8 million appeals, the corrective process in effect has remained inaccessible to many excluded voters. In Hyderabad, 1.94 million names were marked for deletion under the “absent, shifted, dead and duplicate” (ASDD) category. An estimated 40.7 percent of those entries appeared to belong to Muslim voters, compared with Muslims’ 30 percent share of the city’s population. In some constituencies in Hyderabad’s Old City, Muslims accounted for as much as 80 percent of the names marked for deletion. The pattern is repeated in the National Capital Region, Delhi, where nearly one-third of the existing electorate was missing from the draft SIR roll. Studies flag especially high rates of exclusion in areas with large minority and migrant populations and among residents of informal and unauthorised settlements. The disproportionate exclusion of Muslims suggests an ideological alignment between the SIR’s ostensibly impersonal bureaucracy and the social and political programme of the Hindu right.
As a political and ideological instrument, the exercise has proved to be doubly potent. Through mass deletion of voters from targeted social categories, such as Muslims, it has contributed to shrinking the electoral base of the BJP’s principal rivals. The elections in Bihar and Bengal after the SIR suggest a discernible pattern. In the 2020 Bihar Assembly elections, the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD)-led alliance lost to the BJP-led alliance by just 0.03 percentage points in vote share. In contrast, in the 2025 elections after the removal of 6.8 million names from the existing rolls and the addition of 2.1 million new voters, the BJP alliance’s lead increased to nearly 9 percentage points. Analysis of the 2026 Bengal Assembly elections also points to the decisive role SIR deletions played in the electoral outcome. The exercise disproportionately affected Muslim, migrant and poorer voters in districts where the BJP had historically struggled to gain support. In many constituencies won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the party’s margin of victory.
Furthermore, the bureaucratic exercise reinforces the larger ideological project of a “pure Hindu” nation. It has also legitimised calls for the expulsion of “Rohingyas”, “infiltrators” and “Bangladeshis”, terms used as dog whistles for Muslims, helping to polarise elections along communal lines. Although Bengali Hindus and others also found their names removed from electoral rolls, the political messaging around the SIR in a communally charged election campaign cast Muslims as a suspect community, imperilling their civil and social rights. Predictably, the newly elected BJP governments in Bihar and Bengal moved to deny Public Distribution System benefits to those who found their names expunged from the electoral rolls.
The SIR is thus fuelled by the imagined spectre of a vile and illicit intruder who must be expelled to preserve the existing order. It follows the Supreme Court-supervised National Register of Citizens (NRC) in Assam, which left 1.9 million of the state’s residents, mostly Bengali speakers, essentially stateless. It also resembles the Citizenship Amendment Act of 2019, which introduced religiously differentiated access to citizenship, an affront to the republic’s secular structure. The recently established High-Level Committee on Demographic Change, mandated to assess demographic changes occurring across India due to “illegal infiltration” and “abnormal” population changes among “religious and social communities”, is cut from the same cloth. Ultimately, the SIR is one of several instruments at play to criminalise, disenfranchise and denationalise social groups and communities considered inimical to the Hindutva vision of an ethnic state.

Cost-of-living demonstrations to grip pre-election France

PARIS – After weeks of student protests, France is set to be swept by broader, nationwide demonstrations on Oct 17 over the cost of living, setting up a potentially fraught period ahead of presidential elections in 2027.
The prospect of the two movements merging, perhaps with outbreaks of violence, poses a big challenge to the government – and an opportunity for far-left and far-right presidential candidates jockeying for power.
The country’s Yellow Vest movement, which eight years ago staged street protests against President Emmanuel Macron and his government, called the Oct 17 “yellow and youth” demonstrations and urged millions to turn out.
It has appealed to teachers, workers, pensioners and farmers, as well as students, in an online call spread through social media.
“I have a feeling that (Oct 17) will be a sort of culmination,” 18-year-old Marie-Lou, a protesting university student in the city of Lille, told AFP.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Oct 15 he feared clashes after what he called “urban violence” during the student protests.
Lecornu is under pressure to get a cost-cutting budget through Parliament. It aims to tackle France’s growing public debt by raising more tax revenue and reducing expenditures.
Yet the Yellow Vest and student movements are demanding the government spend more money.
They want protection from inflation sent surging above 3% by the Middle East war, and boosted public services, particularly education.
Anger at police
There is also public anger at perceived police brutality during the student protests, during which several teenage protesters were maimed and thousands were arrested.
Francois Boulo, a figure within the Yellow Vest movement, told AFP there was no coordination with the various groups expected to take part on Oct 17, “but we all had the same reaction when we saw the police violence against the students”.
The growing unrest on France’s streets and the country’s fragmented political system are weighing on the final months of Macron’s presidency, ahead of elections in April and May to choose his successor.
They are also fertile ground for opposition parties and their candidates.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, has backed the student protests and marched in a demonstration on Oct 13 supporting them.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner according to surveys, has positioned her National Rally party on the side of the police, consistent with its law-and-order messaging.
Macron this week said he believed the “legitimate” demands of the protesting students were being “exploited for political purposes”, according to a government spokeswoman.
Prepared for violence
Organisers of the Oct 17 demonstrations have set up a website showing more than 500 demonstrations planned across France.
The Paris police banned a major march through the tourist and business heart of the capital, saying it could only take place in the east of the city.
But authorities and demonstrators were both preparing for possible violence.
Paris police have launched legal action against an influencer on Twitch who urged his hundreds of thousands of followers to take part in the demonstration “war zone”.
And on Oct 16, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told France 2 television that officers could use stun grenades in case of “extremely serious urban violence”. He had previously suspended their use during the student protests after one stun grenade blew off the hand of a 15-year-old.
Demonstrators have set up a smartphone app giving the real-time location of police, tear gas and helicopters. AFP

Press review: Russian asset grab back on EU agenda and Starlink or no, Ukraine to fight on

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. This week's EU summit returns to the idea of seizing Russian assets; facing threats of being cut off from Starlink, Ukraine makes other plans; and what is the future of the US Green Card Lottery. These stories topped Friday's newspaper headlines in Russia.
Izvestia: EU revisits idea of confiscating Russian assets at summit
The EU opened a two-day summit in Brussels on October 15. For the first time since the special military operation began, the Europeans postponed discussions on Ukraine to the second day of the event as they decided to discuss the European Union’s new budget for 2028-2034 first. Earlier, the European Commission (EC) proposed a bloated budget of €1.76 trillion.
Meanwhile, European auditors are ringing alarm bells about the growing debt, which could climb to €1 trillion by 2027 and cause a "hole" in the current budget. Moreover, all EU economies are struggling amid the energy crisis around the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
The problem is also aggravated by Kiev's growing demands. According to the draft budget, the EC proposed allocations of up to €88.8 billion for 2028-2034.
However, there is no extra money, and the EU is now coming back to the idea of using frozen Russian assets by transferring them to a special European structure to finance Ukraine further down the road. "This idea is being considered and revisited," French member of the European Parliament Thierry Mariani told Izvestia. "Belgium, which holds the bulk of these funds, dissuaded its partners from putting that idea into practice in December, and the EU eventually agreed a €90 billion loan. Today, Kiev insists that this issue be reconsidered," he noted. "As regards Belgium, it considers this idea crazy as Moscow could immobilize European assets in response," Mariani warned.
Today, the likelihood of using these assets for a loan to Ukraine is extremely low. Such a step would require absolute unanimity within the European Union, Mikhail Vedernikov, a senior researcher at the Institute of Europe of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Izvestia. However, some leaders, including Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, have openly opposed this initiative and promised to block it. Nevertheless, Slovakia will hold an early election in 2027, with Fico’s positions assessed as quite weak. If left-liberal politicians who support the policy course pursued by Brussels come to power in Bratislava, a decision on assets may well be made in a year, the expert concluded.
Apart from Russia’s assets, European bureaucrats will discuss additional restrictions on Moscow. According to Politico, the EU is planning to call for more restrictions on Russian oil exports in the summit communique. Earlier, Brussels approved a 22nd sanctions package, blacklisting hundreds of new Russian individuals, lenders and oil tankers. However, the EU’s sanctions policy cannot affect Russia’s policy on Ukraine, Mariani argued. "This shows that this sanctions policy does not work and only leads to impoverishing the population," the politician maintained.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Ukraine ready to push ahead amid potential Starlink cutoff
Tensions between Kiev and Washington will seemingly escalate after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky said that the Ukrainian armed forces will continue to target Russian oil refineries. Earlier, according to media reports, the Americans warned Kiev that the United States would in that case "immediately" cancel intelligence sharing, cut off the Starlink satellite internet system, and halt military aid.
Even as this has not happened yet, the possibility remains, observers say. Therefore, the Zelensky regime is apparently preparing to wage combat against Russia without support from the United States, relying on NATO’s European allies and the EU instead. This slightly increases Russia’s chances of achieving the objectives of its special military operation and defeating the enemy faster. Whether things progress that way - only time will tell.
A recent remark from SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has been making the rounds in the media and with pundits, after the billionaire called on Zelensky to resign, otherwise "the slaughter" would continue. The call came after almost identical statements from US President Donald Trump.
"It is Musk who owns the rights to Starlink, therefore he can de facto influence Ukraine’s defensive capabilities," retired Lieutenant-General Yury Netkachev, a military expert, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. According to him, with the diesel deal and ambitions to ease sanctions on Russia, Trump has provided Moscow with an opportunity not only to improve its economic situation but also buttress its position in negotiations to end the conflict.
However, Netkachev warned, one should not be lulled into a false sense of security by this "friendly" position of the current US administration, for Trump’s foreign policy options could be significantly curtailed following the Congressional election, and the US political elite may return to supporting Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Kiev's intelligence situation isn't all lost without the US. "Two-thirds of the intelligence received by Ukraine come from European countries, primarily France," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told France Inter. According to him, among other things, European countries share satellite images that Kiev uses to detect targets. His remark came amid reports that the US has threatened to limit information sharing because of strikes on Russian oil refineries. Barrot also said the Europeans provide the bulk of support for Ukraine. The EU has recently transferred €6 billion to Kiev, he added.
Vedomosti: Odds US brings back Green Card Lottery
The US State Department was ordered to reopen the Green Card Lottery by October 18 and publicly announce the registration dates on its official platforms. The order came from a US federal judge in California, according to the court’s database updated on Wednesday night. Registration will remain open for 30 days, in line with the court order. In other words, anyone who wants to can enter the 2027 drawing.
The issue reverberated after the Trump administration formally refused to open registration citing delays, even as back in November 2025 the US Department of State shared plans to reopen registration for the 2027 fiscal year running from October 1, 2026 on its website.
It is worth noting that the Green Card Lottery is a mandatory process, as Congress authorizes the allocation of up to 55,000 such documents annually to foreign citizens. However, only a portion of all available Green Cards are distributed through the lottery, not all of them. According to the US Department of State’s website, 20.8 million people applied for the 2026 program, from which 129,516 individuals were selected. Among Africans registered for the DV-2026 Diversity Visa Program, the bulk was from Algeria (5,457 applicants), Afghanistan led all Asian countries with 4,200, the Bahamas - North America with 23, 599 Australians led the way for Oceania, and 1,596 Peruvians from South America. Russia led all European countries with 5,510 registered and selected applicants, followed by Ukraine with 5,283.
Even as the DV-2026 program was mandated by federal law enacted by Congress, the Trump administration effectively delayed the start of the registration process, Marina Chernykh, a research fellow at the Institute for US and Canadian Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences, explained to Vedomosti. According to her, the California court ruled that the US State Department provide an opportunity for applications to be submitted, whereas the federal government insisted that it is no longer possible to carry out the program as originally intended now that the established deadlines have passed. The Trump administration has the right to appeal the ruling at the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Filing an appeal would not automatically nullify the court ruling as a separate court decision will be required for that. The case could eventually be taken to the US Supreme Court, the expert noted.
"And the US Supreme Court is highly likely to rule in Trump’s favor as the majority of judges there are conservative. At the same time, it cannot be assumed that the administration can simply ignore the ruling as it was handed down by a court of first instance," the expert concluded.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Archaic Russia-EU partnership agreement clashes with present-day antagonism
The agreement on partnership and cooperation concluded between Russia and the European Union signed more than three decades ago makes little practical sense after Brussels openly declared Russia its opponent and adversary, said participants in a round table discussion at the Federation Council on Thursday.
The EU has essentially transformed into an anti-Russian military bloc, Rossiyskaya Gazeta quoted Grigory Karasin, chairman of the upper chamber’s Committee on International Affairs, as saying. There have been statements from European politicians, including Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski or European Commissioner for Defense Andrius Kubilius, about preparations for war with Russia in 2029-2030.
The matter is not limited to rhetoric only as Sweden and Finland have joined NATO, EU countries are sharply increasing their defense expenditure, military construction has been expedited, and exercises to simulate scenarios of a blockade of the Kaliningrad Region and Russia’s Baltic seaports are held near national borders.
Karasin also pointed to the EU’s expansion plans at the expense of Moldova, Ukraine and Armenia. At that, the senator emphasized, Russia is not threatening European countries nor is it planning to do so, while the European people seem to agree, as evidenced by the rising popularity of opposition parties in Germany and France.
The EU has undergone a major evolution, Federation Council Deputy Speaker Konstantin Kosachev argued. Originally a purely economic association, the EU is increasingly mulling militarization, including its own army. "Never before has there been a single international organization built on regional economic integration that set establishing an army as its goal. This is a first," Kosachev noted. "The idea of militarization has completely consumed the minds of European politicians, who have also embraced extreme Russophobic rhetoric," he added.
Kosachev commented on the Partnership and Cooperation Agreement, which was signed in 1994 and entered into force in 1997. He singled out Article 55 as the most objectionable part of the document which envisaged the unilateral harmonization of Russian laws with European ones. "Thank God, this article--along with all the other provisions of the agreement--has been frozen," he said. The agreement’s initial ten-year term expired in 2007 and it has been automatically renewed on an annual basis ever since until one of the parties provides written notice to the contrary. "It has lost any practical meaning. The EU has openly declared us its adversary and enemy, while the agreement envisages partnership and cooperation," Kosachev maintained.
Vedomosti: Russia could step in to meet Africa's growing electricity needs
African countries are facing electricity shortages even as they have enough oil and gas and capabilities to generate power from renewables. Key obstacles include a lack of capital and grid weaknesses. Russian technology could be in demand in the fields of nuclear-and natural gas-based power generation, hydropower and energy-related engineering, but prospects here depend on project economics and the specific needs of certain countries. Russian and African experts told Vedomosti which areas of partnership can yield a long-term effect and what has prevented a transformation from individual supplies to complex projects.
Today, African countries need to supply electricity to a growing population, their industries, transport, and digital economy, Alexey Maslov, a professor and director of the Institute of Asian and African Studies at Lomonosov Moscow State University, noted. While many of these countries possess gas, oil, and coal reserves, along with potential for hydropower, solar, and wind energy generation, the mere availability of such resources does not guarantee a stable supply, he argued.
According to Nikita Panin, an expert at the analytical department at the HSE Centre for African Studies, countries with a developed industrial base need large-scale power generation. Meanwhile, the need for localized power generation is already reflected in projects currently under discussion between Russian companies and their African partners. There is no universal solution for the continent as the specifics of each country require an individual approach, he explained.
As African partners view it, technology transfer should be accompanied with the development of local competences, Anna Abaho, a senior lecturer in international relations and security research at Nkumba University in Uganda, told Vedomosti. She linked Russian-Ugandan cooperation to industrial electrification, food production, irrigation and refrigeration of agricultural products. The country needs engineers and technical specialists capable of maintaining the equipment for that, she said.
A transition to purer energy does not mean Africa will abandon traditional sources in the next few years. The continent is expanding access to electricity amid the rising demand from industries, transport, and cities. For this reason, a variety of technologies, ranging from gas and hydropower to solar generation, energy storage, and nuclear projects, will be needed in the energy mix, Maslov argued.

Vincent Thomas Bridge to close for 16 months, raising fears of traffic and pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Vincent Thomas Bridge to close for 16 months, raising fears of traffic and pollution
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
After years of planning, California transportation officials are preparing to shut down the Vincent Thomas Bridge on Nov. 7 to replace its deck.
The bridge will be closed to all traffic for 16 months. Locals aren’t looking forward to increased traffic congestion, noise and air pollution, and disruptions to operations at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach.
Caltrans said the deck replacement is necessary to preserve the structural integrity of the bridge and improve safety for maintenance workers, truck drivers and the traveling public.
As the California Department of Transportation prepares to re-deck a bridge near the Port of Los Angeles, port officials are hoping to increase the height of the bridge as well.
The Vincent Thomas Bridge is a key artery connecting San Pedro to Terminal Island, where the Port of Los Angeles and Port of Long Beach are located. It opened in 1963 and spans just over one mile.
“It’s not only for employees going back and forth through the port complex,” Elise Swanson, president of the San Pedro Chamber of Commerce, said in an interview last year. “The bridge is really a connection to our communities for art, culture, dining.”
The bridge runs along State Route 47 between Interstate 110 and Terminal Island. The island connects on its east end to Long Beach via the Long Beach International Gateway Bridge.
Caltrans said it held more than 100 public and stakeholder meetings to prepare surrounding communities for construction, including developing the traffic detour route.
Veterans Stadium in Long Beach is set for demolition to build a modern sports complex. See what’s coming next and how the site’s history is being honored.
Officials have completed road improvements along the detour route and will deploy traffic control officers at 18 key intersections during the bridge’s full closure.
The detour route will take traffic to and from Terminal Island along Front Street and John S. Gibson Boulevard in San Pedro and along Harry Bridges Boulevard and Henry Ford Avenue in Wilmington. The route also utilizes the state highway system, including Interstate 110 and Interstate 710.
Community members are concerned the closure will increase traffic in residential areas not along the designated detour routes. Although vehicles will be encouraged to use the official route, Caltrans acknowledged that drivers will take the path of least resistance to their destination.
The Port of Los Angeles announced it moved more cargo in September than in any other single month in its history.
“What is being done to address increased traffic that will flow on unofficial detour routes,?” asked one community member during a virtual open house on Wednesday.
Caltrans said it has notified Google Maps and Apple Maps about the closure and the designated detour route.
“We are engaging with navigation providers with the goal of trying to direct people away from neighborhood streets to use the designated detour routes and also the state highway system,” said Siew Mei Tan, chief of Caltrans’ District 7 Office of Mobility Programs. “We understand that there are a lot of concerns about traffic cutting through streets in the neighborhood.”
With distinct Gothic-style design details and appearances in many movies and TV shows, Los Feliz’s Shakespeare Bridge has become a prized neighborhood emblem.
Caltrans is also working with the Los Angeles Unified School District to distribute air filters to schools in the area. Qualifying residents will also receive air filters to mitigate pollution from diesel and heavy construction equipment.
“Traffic will be idling more frequently, and there may be increased air pollution and impacts in the community because of traffic related to this project,” Nathan Bass, a Caltrans public information officer, said at the open house.
Other residents voiced concerns at the open house about the bridge’s structural integrity.
“I’m very concerned about the possible corrosion, specifically rust, of all the hardware that holds the bridge together and that attaches the cables,” one participant said.
The Port of Los Angeles had hoped to raise the height of the Vincent Thomas Bridge to allow larger cargo ships to pass underneath.
Caltrans said several investigations concluded the bridge is safe for travelers. The deck replacement is necessary because traffic loads on the span have become increasingly heavy, and salt air has eroded bridge materials.
Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, previously asked Caltrans to consider raising the bridge’s height as part of its existing construction plans. Seroka said raising the bridge would allow larger, more efficient cargo ships to access capacity at the port.
Officials rejected that request last December, saying the deck replacement had to begin as soon as possible and it could not accommodate additional planning to raise the bridge.
The bridge will probably reopen to traffic in early 2028, Caltrans said, and construction work will continue after it reopens until early 2029.

Jabra Enhance Select M3 Review (2026): A Big Price for Small Wins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Outstanding quality. Great noise control at lower volumes. Autofocus improvements are noticeable, if short of life-changing.
TIRED
The massive case desperately needs a redesign. Still very expensive. Poor streaming quality.
This fall, hearing-aid manufacturers have been busily rolling out new and improved devices en masse, including Jabra, a leading maker of direct-to-consumer, over-the-counter devices. The brand has replaced its entire product lineup with all-new gear, swiftly retiring the Jabra Enhance Select 700, 500, 300, and 50R, all of which were only a year or two old. Three new models replace them: Enhance Select M3, M2, and M1. Each of the M-series hearing aids looks and works about the same as the models from last year and the year before that. Most of the updates here happen under the hood—but even those changes are hardly extreme, as I learned with the M3 pair I tested.
Historically, a more expensive device has meant a slightly smaller chassis—not so with Jabra's new hearing aids. Each of the three new models weighs the same: 2.12 grams, give or take a few hundredths of a gram, depending on the ear tip you choose. While the M2 and M1 share an identical form factor, the M3 is a bit squatter in design, measuring a few millimeters shorter than its siblings. Even so, all three are virtually indistinguishable unless you look at the fine print. That is, unless you select the red model; it's an M3 giveaway, as the M1 and M2 aren't available in that color.
Jabra M1 on left, M3 on right
Photograph: Christopher Null
Taking the traditional form of behind-the-ear teardrops, the M3 aids feature a single button on the back. Various presses and holds let you use these buttons for power, volume adjustments, and environmental mode changes that work to varying degrees of usefulness. Even so, the device is among the best available right now.
Within Earshot
Photograph: Christopher Null
Jabra calls its audio enhancement system SoundScape, which launched last year and claims to reduce noise and improve overall speech clarity. SoundScape features are variably available across the three devices in the M line, and two new capabilities are exclusive to the M3. These include a revamped autofocus tool that “locks onto” speech in complex, noisy environments, like restaurants, which I found to be moderately effective. I experienced clean dialog, even when a conversation partner walked fully around me in a circle.
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
ScreenshotSoundScape app via Christopher Null
The other new SoundScape feature for the M3 is an advanced adaptive listening mode that's responsive to a given environment (whether a restaurant, outdoors, or several other options) in real time to optimize noise reduction. The environmental modes weren’t very useful; keeping the hearing aids in “all around” mode, then tweaking levels manually (especially noise reduction) was the best way to improve the hearing experience.
I tested the M3 hearing aids in a variety of settings and am pleased to report that they work just as well as previous Jabra generations. Clarity in quiet environments (like having a one-on-one conversation or watching television) was just about perfect. Keeping the volume at 30 percent maximized hearing improvement while minimizing hiss, which grows geometrically louder with each upward tick of volume level.
Bluetooth streaming quality has never been Jabra’s strong suit, and while these new devices support Auracast—which lets various audio sources broadcast directly to the hearing aid—I don't expect I’d use any of the streaming modes much. Overall streaming audio quality on the M3 offers a slight improvement from previous generations, but music and movie audio are both too washed out at any level below the highest volume. And any amount of ambient noise still kills the experience completely.
Programming on Demand
Photograph: Christopher Null
The app and other features in the new lineup remain remarkably similar to previous Jabra models. Jabra has a history of offering great customer service: All purchases include three years of access to on-staff audiologists who can make tuning adjustments live over video chat and train new users on their hearing aids. Jabra’s built-in self-test system also remains top-notch, allowing you to create an audiogram from scratch in just a few minutes.
Its massive case unfortunately hasn’t changed, providing three recharges of your spent hearing aids before it also needs to be plugged in. A fully charged pair of hearing aids still lasts for 24 hours, as specified. In fact, I got closer to 26 hours in my testing before I needed to power up.
Notably, pricing also remains consistent, with the M3 starting at $1,995—the same launch price as the Jabra 700 last year. If history is any guide, a few months of patience are likely to reward you with a $200 price cut, and Jabra coupons are available fairly regularly. It's still a big ask for a nonprescription product. But to be fair, you’d likely pay twice as much for a prescription aid that can match the quality of these latest M3s.
My bottom-line recommendation? If you can afford the two grand for the Jabra M3 hearing aids, you'll get the most advanced over-the-counter devices available. That said, those with more modest means will do nearly as well with the $1,695 M2 or $1,195 M1 hearing aids—or one of the even more affordable options featured in my Best Hearing Aids buying guide.
