The New Fan’s Guide to the Unreal World of Nathan Fielder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

There has been no shortage of coverage on Elizabeth Holmes, the Silicon Valley fraudster whose biotech startup Theranos reached a peak valuation of $9 billion in 2014 before its supposedly groundbreaking blood test machine was revealed to be vaporware. Books, magazine articles, documentaries, TV dramatizations—the exposés have piled up high.
So, you might ask yourself, why the hype for the forthcoming You Can See Everything, yet another documentary about Holmes, and one that spans three hours?
The excitement is thanks to Nathan Fielder, one of the film’s directors. (Fielder codirected the documentary with Lance Oppenheim). Fielder is a cult-favorite television auteur whose devotees have awaited his showdown with Holmes ever since rumors about him visiting her in prison surfaced last year.
Now that Fielder appears poised to break the containment of an obsessed fan base and conquer the cineplex, it behooves you to get caught up. This will not be a typical documentary: Fielder has made a career of heightened unreality, sowing confusion wherever he goes. To give you some notion of what to expect from his analysis of Holmes, here’s a rundown of his unusual and captivating style.
Business Bona Fides
One reason Fielder makes sense as an interlocutor for big tech’s most notorious con woman is his own history of corporate chicanery. In his breakout TV series Nathan for You (2013–2017), he contrived and implemented bizarre publicity stunts for struggling small businesses. (While he jokes that he “graduated from one of Canada's top business schools with really good grades,” the fact remains he did graduate, unlike Holmes, a Stanford University dropout.)
Andrew Bricker, an associate professor of English at the University of Ghent and academic coordinator for the research project Democratic Literacy and Humour, writes in an email that it’s important to recognize that, throughout his career, Fielder has always played the same altered version of himself, leaving us unsure just who he really is.
Fielder “has made the borderlands of persona and person so ambiguous, so indeterminable, so indefinable, that none of us is entirely in on the joke,” Bricker says.
Nathan for You and Fielder’s subsequent HBO series The Rehearsal, Bricker explains, cast him as “a kind of outlandish problem-solver, someone possessed of what I sometimes call the engineer’s brain, which sees the world strictly through the radically simplified framework of problems and solutions, even if the solutions themselves, ouroboros-style, always lead to new problems.”
Indeed, in his fixer role on Nathan for You, Fielder seeks out overcomplicated loopholes and goes to great lengths to carry out any particular scheme once he sets his mind to it. To help an international exporter avoid high shipping costs on smoke alarms, for example, he comes up with a plan to market them as musical instruments. Then he creates an instructional DVD on how to play one, forms a band that records an original track that includes the device’s shrill beeping, and gets the song featured on the local news, all to legitimize the tariff dodge.
Fielder’s Nathan for You promotions involved careful readings of pertinent laws in order to skirt liability—he went viral by opening a coffee shop called Dumb Starbucks—as well as clever hoaxes and media manipulation. He staged a video of a pig saving a goat from drowning in a pond at a petting zoo, successfully tricking social media users and news stations into thinking it was real, and founded Summit Ice, a nonprofit winter apparel brand that stands against Holocaust denial, which earned it mainstream exposure.
Holmes, of course, played investors and the press for years with savvy PR, styling herself as the next coming of Steve Jobs in order to hype a bogus advance in medical science. If there’s anyone who can grasp the scope and scale of duplicity it took to make the world believe in a nonexistent product, it’s Fielder.
Awkward, Maybe Neurodivergent … and Mean?
Early in his career, Fielder tackled the business world with a recurring spot on the satirical CBC Television news show This Hour Has 22 Minutes. His segment, “Nathan on Your Side,” was a send-up of local consumer advocacy investigations and an early showcase for Fielder’s deadpan humor, as seen in a 2008 report where he role-plays as a customer at an electronics store and invites a salesman to pitch him on an MP3 player but continually dismisses these efforts because he is “just browsing.”
Throughout Nathan for You and The Rehearsal, Fielder has relied on this discomfiting affect to maximize the awkwardness of his conversations with everyone he encounters. Although polite and unassuming—many of his fellow Canadians relate—he lets heavy silences linger, maintains uncomfortable eye contact, and never quite breaks, no matter how funny a situation may be. Fielder also has a knack for flatly echoing what someone else has told him in a way that underscores its absurdity.
With these tics, Bricker says, Fielder often catches his interview subjects off guard, spurring them to blurt out surprising confessions.
Holmes is an ideal target for this poker-faced approach. Kate Rennebohm, a professor of film at Lawrence University, has written about the ethics and artifice of HBO’s The Rehearsal, which follows Fielder as he constructs elaborate simulations of pivotal life events in order to better understand human behavior. Rennebohm writes in an email that Holmes the fraudster represents something like an ultimate test of Fielder’s methods.
Holmes is, according to Rennebohm, “a woman whose infamy rests solely on her apparent ability to totally disregard reality.” For this reason, Rennebohm expects Fielder’s skills as a performer and instigator “will get perhaps their most strenuous exercise yet in this match.”
Bricker says that “we are about to witness a bizarro-land Frost/Nixon, where both interviewer and subject have almost exclusively inhabited semi-fictional personae in public”—Fielder as a mad social scientist, Holmes as an inventor ahead of her time.
But while Holmes may be deserving of invasive scrutiny, some critics are unable to stomach how Fielder incorporates unwitting, ordinary people into his satirical plots, occasionally allowing them to look somewhat foolish or flustered while he remains unflappable. Just as your appetite for “cringe” comedy will determine whether you laugh at the scenarios Fielder orchestrates, the shows have turned into litmus tests on questions of conscience and empathy. Does he take advantage of the working-class folks and background performers drawn into his elaborate web of control, or is he merely reflecting a dysfunctional society back to us?
This tension, along with Fielder’s preoccupations and overall demeanor, have occasioned plenty of speculation around whether he has ever been diagnosed with a mental condition. The Rehearsal has led to viewers theorizing that Fielder is on the autism spectrum or otherwise neurodivergent. Fielder acknowledged this discourse in the second season of the show and underwent an fMRI brain scan that could have pointed toward such a diagnosis, though he did not divulge the results.
Others have thrown the word “sociopath” around when discussing Fielder’s work, but not always in a negative sense. As one X user recently noted in a post anticipating You Can See Everything: “Nathan Fielder doing a movie about how Elizabeth Holmes is a deceptive sociopath feels exactly like when Dexter takes down a worse serial killer.”
Unpredictable Anthropology
Even starting from the simplest premise, Fielder ventures into strange territory. In a Nathan for You episode in which he counsels a realtor to employ a psychic medium to ensure that the homes she’s selling aren’t haunted, she drops the bombshell that she was once choked by a ghost in Switzerland. In another, Fielder has a gas station owner advertise impossibly cheap prices, attainable only through a hilariously inconvenient rebate process. Yet the memorable part of the segment is when the business owner reveals that he drinks his grandson’s urine when he feels scared.
Fielder often follows up on peculiar discoveries, allowing people’s eccentricities and the unintended consequences of his own meddling to dictate where he goes next. As such, there’s an investigative element to his process that is certainly appropriate when dealing with an enigma like Holmes, a convicted criminal who continues to proclaim her innocence with a cheery warmth that comes off like utter self-delusion.
In 2023, Fielder and Oppenheim, the codirectors of You Can See Everything, moved into the Del Mar, California, house shared by Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans. The group lived together in the house for over a month, right up until the day Holmes reported to prison for her 11-year sentence. They weren’t sure if what they were shooting could be turned into a movie, but as Fielder said at the New York Film Festival last month, a sense of deepening mystery compelled them to move forward.
“Lance and I would talk about what we thought happened there, and we’d completely disagree on … what we thought was happening,” he explained. “And we were like, ‘Oh, this is really interesting, if we can’t agree on what’s happening, there’s something here.’”
Fielder has “a remarkable talent” for using those frictions to twist and expand his narrative, Rennebohm says. She cites The Rehearsal's second season, which is inspired by Fielder’s theory about how the breakdown in communication between airline pilots and copilots can lead to deadly accidents. In order to act out his model of cockpit cooperation, he spends two years earning a commercial license for himself, ultimately flying a Boeing 737 full of actors (all of whom have scripted roles to perform while aboard) from San Bernardino, California, to the Nevada border and back.
When it comes to Fielder following a thread as far as he can, Rennebohm says, “I expect this document of his time with Holmes to be no different.”
The Search for Reality
What has emerged in Fielder’s most recent output might be described as anxiety over the nature of truth.
The Rehearsal (2022–present) is, on its face, a setup to explore the way we conduct ourselves under destabilizing circumstances. In the first season, Fielder concocts a scene where a man can practice confessing to his bar trivia team that he lied about having a master’s degree. For the rest of the season, Fielder is consumed by an elaborate, multi-episode experiment in which a woman evaluates what life would be like as a mother, aided by child actors (and Fielder serving as her platonic coparent).
Yet there are countless moments when Fielder is more concerned with the authenticity of these staged interactions—and their ongoing failure to fully match reality—than their potential outcomes. The actual subject of the show, we learn, is his fanatical mode of observation.
Fielder is often shown walking around with a laptop attached to his torso with a harness so he can take notes on the move. He catches the smallest inaccuracies and oversights, and he tweaks the next reproduction accordingly. He intuits the psychological dissonance of pretending to do something instead of really doing it, and he has frank interviews with his cast and consultants in hopes of closing those gaps.
The Rehearsal, according to Rennebohm, “offers the fictionalized Nathan the chance to substitute manufactured, seemingly controllable realities for the reality of his actual life, though often even these fabricated scenarios ultimately resist Nathan's totalitarian drives.”
Bricker points out that the fundamental “paradox” of Fielder’s “supposed revelations of truth” is that he only arrives at his conclusions through his constructed persona and meticulous simulations. “Even if these are true moments of authentic self-disclosure, how would we even know, given the artificial framework of their disclosure?” he asks.
But that, too, makes You Can See Everything a fascinating proposition. Bricker notes that Fielder and Oppenheim are in a position to play with the “mushy boundaries between reality and fiction” through dramatic reconstruction, stylization, and careful editing.
Rennebohm says that Holmes also serves as an avatar of a tech industry with ambitions of exceeding or dispensing human reality itself. In this and so many other ways, a face-off between Fielder and the disgraced startup founder is the collision of an unstoppable force and an immovable object. All you can do is brace for impact.

Why is France Burning?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The French like to take to the streets, and they do it often.
On Sept. 17, students at Lycée Saint-Exupéry, a rather underprivileged high school in the Paris suburb of Créteil, erupted in protest over the abysmal conditions of their institution: chronic shortfall of teachers, poor facilities, long declining quality of education. Two weeks later, a wave of protests had swept cities across France. Students from hundreds of schools and scores of universities joined the protests, backed by their parents, teachers, and trade unions. More than 160,000 students and trade unionists protested across France on Tuesday in the third week of demonstrations.
France has never seen so many violent incidents in a movement made up largely of high school students. So far, over 200 students, 85 school staff, and 700 police officers have been injured in clashes across the country. Protesters have broken into schools and, in some cases, set fire to occupied or blockaded buildings. On Oct. 5, a 15-year-old boy had his hand blown off by a police grenade during a protest in Lens in northern France, an incident that crystallized the heavy-handed response authorities had adopted from the earliest days of the protest. More than 6,000 protesters have been arrested, most of them minors, and later released without charge.
The protests erupted after nearly a decade of Macronisme, the right-of-center, top-down governing style that President Emmanuel Macron of France incarnates. And they express a broader discontent: anger over disparities in school quality, university admissions decisions, and latent racial discrimination, and a sense among young people that those in power were not listening to them, that the country offered them little hope for the future.
The protests are also occurring amid a wider crisis of political confidence in the country. France is holding its presidential elections in April 2027, and the far-right and far-left are leading the opinion polls. The frontrunner is Marine Le Pen, who has worked for years to make her far-right party, the National Rally, more electable while campaigning on immigration, crime, and denunciation of an out-of-touch political class. Her party is already the largest opposition party in parliament, and a snap legislative election following the presidential vote could entrench it further.
On the other side is Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of France Unbowed, a far-left party, who is promising a sweeping redistribution of power and resources toward the working class. Both have built much of their appeal on opposition to the political establishment, the promise to wish away budget constraints, and deep hostility toward the European Union.
If France today feels like it is at a crossroads, it is because it is. The postwar model of a large welfare and regulatory state, run by a class of civil servants charged with modernizing the economy, tempering market forces and defining the common good, has run its course.
The collapse of postwar France
France now runs one of Europe’s largest budget deficits: its public debt stands at 119.3 % of GDP and is expected to rise next year. Fears of a crippling financial crisis are growing. Borrowing costs have risen so high that France is drawing comparisons with Greece, whose debt crisis in 2010 threatened the survival of the Eurozone. And with economic growth stagnating, there is no easy way out.
If anything, France would need to spend more: on defense, as Russia grows more threatening, the war in Ukraine continues, and the United States retreats from its traditional role as Europe’s security guarantor; on new technologies, as the country that once produced Concorde and high-speed trains now trails in high-tech innovation and AI; on strained public services, from schools to hospitals to neglected neighborhoods; and on infrastructure capable of withstanding the growing effects of climate change.
Successive French governments have promised to turn things around and allow for these badly needed investments in the country’s future, but none has succeeded.
The French malaise goes deeper. Inequality has been one of the students’ central grievances. They are not wrong. As in many countries, economic inequalities in France have widened over the past two decades under the combined effects of globalization, industrial decline, and the growing concentration of inherited wealth.
In Capital in the Twenty-First Century, the French economist Thomas Piketty showed how wealth perpetuates across generations and widens the divide between those who own capital and everyone else. This concentration of wealth and power remains deeply resented: for many, President Macron’s original sin is still his brief stint at the Rothschild investment bank before entering politics.
But the most injurious form of inequality lies elsewhere: in the power of France’s national meritocratic myth, which holds that people broadly owe their social position largely to their academic performance. At the top of that system sit the highly competitive grandes écoles, the elite institutions of higher education that have produced leaders in politics, culture, and business.
What makes the myth so corrosive is not that academic achievement goes unrewarded but that it remains a pretty reliable path to better jobs, higher status, and positions of power. In such a system, students from underfunded public schools face a profound disadvantage compared with peers who attend better-resourced schools and whose better-educated parents know how to navigate the system.
Private schools offer another route, but are still frowned upon as a way to buy an advantage. It is no surprise that the protests broke out in Créteil, a working-class suburb just outside Paris, where schools are chronically under-resourced.
We shall always have Paris
Racial and geographic discrimination also contribute to the crisis of France. The collection of ethno-racial statistics is prohibited by French law; it is a laudable restriction in principle but problematic in practice. Visible minorities remain vastly underrepresented among France’s political and business elites.
Families with immigrant backgrounds, many with roots in African and Asian countries once colonized by France, are disproportionately concentrated on urban peripheries, where jobs are scarce and residents often face discrimination from employers elsewhere.
Islamophobia has also grown over the last decade amid conflicts in the Middle East and a string of Islamist-inspired terrorist attacks. Rhetoric once largely confined to the far right has seeped into the mainstream right, where calls for “order” and “security” often carry an anti-immigrant charge. Macron’s references to the “decivilization” of some young people and former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau’s description of immigrants’ participation in the protests that followed the police killing of a teenager in 2023 as a “regression towards ethnic origins” are emblematic of that shift.
There is another problem with France’s meritocratic ideal: Paris. Political power, economic opportunity, cultural prestige, and elite education remain extraordinarily concentrated in the capital. The result is a deep economic divide between Paris and the rest of the country and an elite that lives largely among its own, surrounded by people with similar educations, careers, and assumptions, and cut off from much of the country.
The Yellow Vest revolt of 2018 to 2019 was an earlier social explosion of precisely that resentment. It is hardly surprising that students are denouncing the unequal distribution of resources between Paris and the rest of the country, or that the protests began in Créteil, close enough to the capital for the contrast to be impossible to miss.
When students from my own former school, the elite Lycée Henri-IV, where I was a rather poor student, joined the movement in its third week, I noticed how carefully they described themselves as protesting “in solidarity” with less privileged schools. They knew which side of the divide they were on. So much for meritocracy.
Racing to the Elysée
Where does this leave France? With the presidential elections approaching next April, political parties are scrambling to position themselves in relation to a protest movement that has shown no sign of abating. On Oct. 6, more than a quarter-million people took to the streets as high school students were joined by university students, teachers, parents and trade unions. An even wider “national day of protest” is planned for Oct. 17.
Both familiar and new dynamics will shape the election. The familiar one is the runoff dilemma: voters may once again be asked to support a candidate from the opposite political camp simply to prevent Le Pen from reaching the Élysée. Le Pen made the runoff in both 2017 and 2022 and is leading the polls by a large margin. This time, however, the field trailing her is unusually fragmented. Two former prime ministers under Macron, Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, are in the race; Philippe is competing with Mélenchon for second place, while Attal trails both.
Whatever the outcome, the presidential vote may resolve little. A president from the far-right National Rally could find herself governing without a stable parliamentary majority or broad support among the public or within the civil service. A compromise candidate from the center or left could face the same fractured parliament that has bedeviled the final years of Macron’s presidency, during which France has had five prime ministers in two years.
What is new is the extent to which France is being reshaped by forces now familiar across the globe: a crisis of confidence in democracy, conservative billionaires building media empires and financing ideological movements, polarizing social media, foreign interference in elections, and growing voter distrust of supranational institutions, including the European Union.
France, unlike the United States, places strict limits on campaign spending, but money still shapes the broader political ecosystem. Pierre-Édouard Stérin, a self-described “conservative libertarian,” has committed substantial resources to organizations seeking to advance right-wing and far-right agendas. The industrialist Vincent Bolloré has assembled a vast media empire that includes CNews, a Fox News-style channel that has become an important platform for the nationalist right.
Europe on the line
Whatever the result of the Presidential elections, the outlook is troubling for Europe. A Le Pen or Mélenchon presidency would test European cohesion on everything from Ukraine and relations with Russia to migration, budgets, and the authority of the European Union. But even a more centrist president would likely lack a strong enough coalition to govern effectively, mirroring the current situation in Germany, where Chancellor Friedrich Merz is hobbled by unpopularity and a surge in support for the far-right Alternative for Deutschland.
With France and Germany together accounting for roughly 40% of the E.U. economy, political weakness in both capitals would deprive Europe of its traditional engine at a particularly dangerous moment. Europe faces mounting pressure on three fronts: China’s industrial onslaught, reflected in an annual trade deficit of roughly €360 billion; Russia’s war against Ukraine and escalating “gray warfare” operations; and the American turn against the postwar international order on which Europe has long depended. All this comes as Europe must also prepare for the profound disruptions of climate change and AI.
The remedy laid out by Mario Draghi, famed for rescuing the euro during his tenure as president of the European Central Bank, calls for greater integration of the single market, more investment and industrial consolidation, and a greater capacity to act collectively. France is indispensable to any such reforms. A politically paralyzed France would leave Europe weaker at precisely the moment when it can least afford it.
The revolution still to come
At the heart of the French Revolution of 1789 was the abolition of the privileges of the aristocracy and clergy. Close to two and a half centuries later, privilege remains deeply embedded in French society, dispersed across an array of almost caste-like social and professional groups, from journalists, lawyers, and intellectuals to civil servants and unionized workers, each with its own advantages, protections, pension arrangements, and claims on state resources. The result is a politics in which almost everyone agrees that reform is urgently needed, provided someone else pays, and their own group’s advantages remain untouched.
If this sounds like an overreading of 1789, consider Macron’s own choice of title for the book that launched his presidential bid: Révolution. His presidency may not have proved entirely revolutionary, yet many of his larger prescriptions have aged well: governments around the world have embraced state-led industrial policy, greater strategic autonomy, and reduced dependence on fossil fuels, while distrust of American hegemony and calls for deeper European integration have gained traction as the postwar order fragments.
Macron can also claim some credit for preserving, and in places renewing, France’s traditional strengths: an electricity system powered largely by nuclear energy, global leadership in luxury goods, tourism and hospitality, and a deep reservoir of scientific talent, now exemplified by Mistral, Europe’s closest thing to a world-class AI contender.
A skilled diplomat and relentless advocate for the multilateral system, Macron has also taken principled stands on Ukraine, Gaza, Lebanon, debt relief for the world’s poorest countries, and climate change, while carefully navigating France’s relationships with America and China. France’s permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council gives it diplomatic weight far beyond the country’s economic size, a status French diplomats ironically describe as “flying first class on an economy ticket.”
Yet neither these prescriptions nor these assets have been enough to reverse France’s decline over the past two decades. Perhaps what has been missing is a revolution not so much in policy as in political culture: a new social compact in which the sacrifices required to adjust to France’s reduced means and diminished relative power are accepted because the burdens are seen to be shared fairly. If such a revolution is to come, it is less likely to start in the Élysée or the ministries than among the students in the streets demanding to be heard.

Dinosaur fossil hidden in London’s Natural History Museum for 100 years identified as new species
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:58:55 UTC
18:58:55 KST

The 120-million-year-old skull fragment belongs to Europe’s first known megaraptoran, a predator featuring powerful arms and sharp claws.
A dinosaur fossil that spent almost a century in the collections of London’s Natural History Museum has been identified as a new species.
The skull fragment belonged to Invictibellatrix amberina, a previously unknown carnivorous dinosaur that lived around 120 million years ago. It’s also the first confirmed evidence of a megaraptoran dinosaur in Europe.
The fossil was originally discovered at the foot of a cliff on the southwest coast of the Isle of Wight by amateur fossil hunter Reginald Walter Tooley. After his death in 1924, the Natural History Museum acquired more than 1,000 specimens from his collection, including the fragment.
Although scientists knew it belonged to a dinosaur, exactly which one remained a mystery for decades.
Now, researchers have taken another look at the fossil using CT scanning technology, allowing them to examine its internal structure and create a 3D model. Their full findings were published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.
"More dangerous than a T.rex"
Professor Paul Barrett, the study’s senior author from the Natural History Museum, says, "Despite over 200 years of collecting, the Isle of Wight continues to surprise us with new dinosaur species, and finds of carnivorous dinosaurs, such as Invictibellatrix, have been particularly elusive."
"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," he added.
Despite their name, megaraptorans were not the small, bird-like dinosaurs we commonly associate with the word "raptor". They were larger predators, more closely related to tyrannosaurs, with "slender heads", "large arms" and "giant curved claws", according to the Natural History Museum.
Invictibellatrix amberina is estimated to have measured between 3 and 4 metres (10 and 13 feet) in length and stood around 1.5 metres (5 feet) tall. It lived during the Early Cretaceous period, when dinosaurs dominated terrestrial ecosystems.
Researchers have also suggested that it may have had feathers, although its exact appearance still remains uncertain.
According to Dr Cassius Morrison, a researcher at the University College London's (UCL) Earth Sciences department, the species would have eaten small dinosaurs, lizards and mammals - similar to the role in the food chain a hyena holds today.
"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex. We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small," explains Dr Cassius Morrison, who led the study.
The discovery is particularly exciting because megaraptorans have previously been identified in Asia, Australia and South America, but never conclusively in Europe.

Pickleball Mania Hits Copenhagen: New Arena Debuts October 17

On Saturday, 17 October, Danske Pickleballers will unveil a new indoor facility, transforming the industrial expanse of Nordhavn’s Tunnelfabrikken into a dedicated winter arena for the sport.
The facility, located at Tunnel Arena, is a notable architectural pivot for the building, which in the 1990s served as the site where tunnel elements for the Øresund link were cast. Now, the raw industrial hall is set to become the city’s primary hub for pickleball enthusiasts, offering six new professional-grade courts.
A transatlantic inspiration
The journey to this new facility began across the Atlantic. In April 2024, Joachim Litman, co-founder of Danske Pickleballers, visited his father in New York. While he had originally hoped to play padel, the high cost of courts in the city led him to a local schoolyard in East Harlem instead.
Pickleball is a very sociable game where both kids and seniors can have fun. Photo: Danske Pickleballers
There, he discovered the distinct culture of pickleball—a game defined by its low barrier to entry and social nature. Litman recalls being hooked from the “first dink,” struck by the ease of joining a game: you simply place your paddle in the queue and wait for four players.
It was a space where he could play alongside a five-year-old and a 95-year-old on the same day, a level of inclusivity that left a lasting impression.
Upon returning to Copenhagen, Litman founded Danske Pickleballers alongside friends Mathias and Lucas. The club, which began with chalk lines in city parks, has grown to over 100 members, with its activities conducted in both Danish and English.
The grand opening
The opening event at Tunnel Arena is designed not just for seasoned players, but as a social meetup for those looking to try the sport. The event runs from 11:00 to 20:00 on Saturday, 17 October, at Oceanvej 1, Nordhavn.
The programme for the day includes:
- 13:00: Official opening and ribbon-cutting ceremony.
- 13:45: Opportunities to play with coaches, with no prior experience necessary.
- 14:00–16:00: First sushi service.
- 16:30: Exhibition match featuring some of Denmark’s top players.
- 17:15: A social tournament with rotating partners and a DJ, aimed at helping attendees meet new people.
- 18:00–20:00: Final sushi service.
Entry is 25 DKK, which includes the use of paddles and balls. Whether arriving solo or with friends, the club encourages newcomers to join in, aiming to make the venue a social hub throughout the winter months.

‘True character of protests exposed’: Dharmendra Pradhan attacks Rahul Gandhi over regime change remark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:56:35 UTC
18:56:35 KST

Dharmendra Pradhan criticized Rahul Gandhi for allegedly exploiting student protests to undermine India's democratic structure.
Dharmendra Pradhan, who had resigned from the post of Union education minister after Cockroach Janta Party protests over paper leaks in July, accused Rahul Gandhi of using students as cover to destabilise India's political system.Citing Bangladesh's Gen Z uprising and calls for “regime change”, Pradhan alleged that the protests were part of a deliberate attempt to spread anarchy and challenge the country's democratic order.In his post on X, Pradhan said the “true character” of protests launched in the name of national interest, fixing the system and students’ welfare was no longer hidden.“However, these anti-national elements dreaming of power on the strength of foreign forces should understand that in India, change of power is determined only through democratic processes,” he said, adding that the people would never accept what he described as an undemocratic mindset.Targeting Rahul Gandhi, Pradhan accused the Leader of Opposition of repeatedly disrespecting the people's mandate and undermining democratic institutions when electoral outcomes did not favour the Congress.He alleged that the party sought to create distrust in constitutional institutions for political gains, adding that its approach reflected a mentality in which the rights of citizens had been trampled.
“Rahul Gandhi, the anti-Constitution figure who roams around holding the Constitution, has been repeatedly rejected by the people,” Pradhan said, accusing him of insulting the electoral mandate and questioning constitutional institutions out of a desire for power.He described Rahul Gandhi's alleged attitude towards democracy as “extremely shameful”.The Congress, meanwhile, defended its call for “regime change”, saying it referred to defeating the BJP through democratic elections rather than destabilising the country.Addressing a press conference titled “Albert Pinto Ko Gussa Kyoon Aata Hai”, party leader Pawan Khera questioned defence minister Rajnath Singh’s allegations linking youth-led protests against the Election Commission to a Bangladesh-style political upheaval.“Changing the regime through elections is precisely the Opposition’s goal, what else would our purpose be?” Khera said, accusing the BJP of having “lost the habit of practising democracy”.The “regime change” remark emerged amid the ongoing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of irregularities in the electoral process.Student activist Neha Bora invoked Bangladesh’s Gen Z uprising, while senior advocate Prashant Bhushan described the agitation as a “fight for regime change”.
The remarks drew criticism from BJP leaders, including Dharmendra Pradhan, who accused the protesters and opposition leaders of attempting to destabilise India’s political system.The controversy also brings renewed attention to the Cockroach Janta Party’s (CJP) protests against Pradhan over the NEET-UG examination controversy, when protesters demanded accountability over alleged examination irregularities and questioned the government’s handling of the issue.

Russian drone attack injures 7 in Ukraine’s Rivne
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:56:19 UTC
18:56:19 KST

Russian drones struck Rivne, a city in western Ukraine, overnight on October 16.
The strikes hit civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings, said Oleksandr Koval, head of the Rivne region administration.
Seven people sought medical attention after the strikes.
Drones continued attacking Rivne the morning of October 16.
Ukrainian media reported that drones hit the “Ekvator” shopping center and the “Demaks” home improvement hypermarket. Footage posted online shows the buildings destroyed.
Russian drones last attacked Rivne on October 13, when a strike hit an academic building at Rivne State University of the Humanities and injured 30 people.

New laser factory opens in Lithuania with ambition to become one of world's largest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:52:00 UTC
18:52:00 KST

A new laser factory, Litilit, has opened in Vilnius, with its founders aiming to make it one of the largest in the world.
“The factory being established in Lithuania will be one of the world's largest in terms of femtosecond laser production capacity and will serve as a model that we plan to replicate in other regions in the future, together with international partners,” said the company's chief executive, Nikolajus Gavrilias.
The factory aims to produce up to 1,000 lasers a year in its first year of operation, with capacity set to increase to 3,000 within a few years, he said.
The factory on Plungės Street, near Gariūnai in Vilnius, covers about 4,000 sq m. It will house a metalworking workshop and automated laser assembly and testing facilities.
“Lithuania has more than 40 years of experience in developing ultrashort-pulse lasers. We undoubtedly have one of the world's strongest photonics communities. By this measure, we are as much as 100 times ahead of any other country in the world,” Gavrilias said.
Economy and Innovation Minister Edvinas Grikšas said Lithuania had all the necessary conditions to become not only a developer of advanced technologies but also a global manufacturer.
“The opening of Litilit's new factory is an excellent example of how Lithuanian science, engineering expertise and business ambition are being turned into products for the global market. The €6m investment and planned capacity of up to 3,000 lasers a year show that Lithuania's laser industry has significant growth potential,” he said.
“Our goal is to create the conditions for companies like this to expand in Lithuania, create high-value jobs and strengthen the country's position as a global technology leader,” Grikšas added.
Gintarė Verbickaitė, head of the largest startup organisation in the country, Unicorns Lithuania, who attended the factory's opening, said: “This is a truly exciting moment. We sincerely hope that Litilit will become Lithuania's first high-tech unicorn and inspire a new generation of high-tech innovators.”
In April, Lithuania's national development bank ILTE lent €8m to support the development of laser technology by the start-up Litilit. The technology uses next-generation femtosecond laser systems that generate ultrashort pulses.
Litilit's chief executive previously told the BNS news agency that the funds were intended for a research and development (R&D) project.
The laser technology sector is one of Lithuania's strongest industrial sectors. It has grown from fundamental research, which began more than 50 years ago, into a self-sustaining ecosystem.
According to the Lithuanian Laser Association, more than 60 companies currently operate in the sector, employing at least 2,250 specialists. Together, they generate annual revenue of €345m.

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

Israeli ad firm under fire over harvesting data to deploy spyware
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:50:41 UTC
18:50:41 KST

Israeli digital advertising firm Discover-Tech exploited a vast commercial ad network to collect personal data and deliver mercenary spyware to targeted devices worldwide, according to an investigation published Thursday by Canadian cybersecurity watchdog Citizen Lab and New York-based ad security firm Confiant.
The operation used advertising infrastructure for covert surveillance, allowing operators to identify potential targets, track their online activity and deliver spyware while evading detection. Confiant described the campaign as highly sophisticated, citing its anti-interception measures and precise targeting capabilities.
The investigation linked the operation to Israeli spyware company Candiru, which has been blacklisted by the United States and rebranded as Integrity Labs, and surveillance vendor Intelos. The companies allegedly exploited commercial advertising inventory across major platforms, including Google, Beeswax and Russia's Yandex, to track targets and compromise consumer devices.
"The core finding is the weaponization of ad infrastructure for advanced staging, preliminary targeting, and payload delivery, characterized by exceptional technical sophistication, robust anti-interception measures, and surgical micro-targeting," Confiant said in its findings.
Citizen Lab described the campaign as the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through online advertising, a method researchers called "AdFection."
Devices belonging to staff members at international news network Al Jazeera were among those infected through weaponized ad placements, which operated silently without visible pop-ups or suspicious links.
Discover-Tech operated a specialized system called Controlium that turned routine commercial advertising auctions into a surveillance system.
After analyzing 4 billion bidding records, researchers found that the company distributed ads across nearly 200,000 unique websites and mobile apps on Android and iOS devices in dozens of countries over a four-month period.
"Discover-Tech serves roughly 10 million ad impressions a day, and each one feeds an identity graph built from device fingerprints, IP addresses, advertising IDs, and often the publisher’s own first-party cookies," Confiant said.
Investigators found that the ads routinely collected user session cookies, authenticated login tokens and personal identifiers directly from publisher websites, exfiltrating the data even when European Union privacy regulations prohibited processing without consent.
Citizen Lab also identified an affiliated threat actor, dubbed Dark Cartographer, that used Discover-Tech's infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across mobile telecommunications providers. The group matched digital advertising identities with phone numbers to identify mobile subscribers on a large scale.
Geographic data revealed sharp spikes in traffic that researchers said pointed to deliberate intelligence operations rather than ordinary commercial advertising campaigns.
Palestine emerged as the most heavily targeted territory, where Discover-Tech served nearly 2% of all digital advertisements, peaking at roughly 10% on April 7. One in every 36 Android ads in the territory originated from the firm.
Surveillance traffic also reached sensitive administrative and institutional networks, including the Armenian Prime Minister's Office, international organizations, judicial agencies, universities and defense organizations.
Investigators detected targeted connections to Candiru servers in nine countries, with Belgium accounting for 56% of observed activity, followed by the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Mexico, Spain and other countries.
Following disclosure of the joint investigation, Google, the European advertising association IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi cut off Discover-Tech's access to their digital advertising systems.

NAZA premieres in UK as filmmakers condemn silence over Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:50:12 UTC
18:50:12 KST

Breadcrumb
NAZA premieres in UK as filmmakers condemn silence over Gaza and Israeli threats
Israeli documentary NAZA premiered in UK cinemas on Thursday evening, with its filmmakers denouncing the silence surrounding Israel’s genocide in Gaza as they face threats of prosecution and loss of citizenship from Israeli authorities. The nationwide screenings preceded its general release on Friday.
Speaking at a London Q&A, co-director Yuval Abraham said the soldiers and intelligence officers who testified in the film had "different motivations to speak", with some describing their disillusionment after joining the military following the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.
"There are soldiers who describe going to the army after the massacre of October 7th, feeling like that’s what they should be doing–and then after a moment or after some time having disillusionment or a sense that they are themselves involved in crimes," he told a packed London audience.
Others, he said, spoke because they felt there was no space for their accounts in Israel’s media.
"Much of the Israeli mainstream media has been either justifying or completely ignoring the crimes in Gaza, and so sometimes all it took was asking a question," Abraham said.
"These questions that you saw tonight … are still unfortunately not asked enough."
Directed by Abraham and Rachel Szor, two of the four filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning documentary "No Other Land", NAZA draws on anonymous testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel about the systems underpinning the mass killing of Palestinians. Its title is a Hebrew military acronym for "collateral damage", used to describe the anticipated killing of civilian in an airstrike.
But Abraham said the interviews were not straightforward accounts of remorse. Some participants moved between regret and justifications for their actions, revealing the human mechanisms that allow the military’s machinery to function.
"In the same human being … on the one hand there was maybe regret over what they’ve done, or even an intuitive sense that they should be speaking out," he said. "But on the other hand, it was just as easy for them to justify and to put on the hat of the intelligence operative or soldier, and to speak from that place."
The filmmakers were interested in those contradictions, he added, because alongside examining systems operating at scale, "we are also looking at the mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings".
The film’s rooftop interviews from Tel Aviv are interspersed with views into Israeli homes, including people watching television news. Szor said those images examined an everyday Israeli ritual–sitting down for the evening bulletin–and what was absent from it.
The intention was "to see the absence of what is there, or justification or the dehumanisation, the words that [are] being used in the media", she said.
Abraham also challenged the idea that intelligence officers necessarily remained detached from the Palestinians whose deaths they helped authorise and were responsible for. While military terminology stripped people of their humanity, surveillance could also simultaneously give officers intimate access to their lives.
"As one person says in the film, we don’t say 15 people will be killed–men, women, children. We say 15 naza," he said.
Yet officers could sometimes access a microphone or phone inside a home being targeted, he added.
"They can listen in and they hear the family or they hear children … that’s [a] very intimate kind of knowledge about the people you are about to kill."
Szor placed that surveillance within the wider infrastructure of Israel’s occupation, linking physical control over Palestinians to control over their telecommunications. "Palestinians have been under Israeli military occupation for a very long time," she said. "The control is not only physical control … but it’s also control over telecommunication infrastructure, and this leads to mass surveillance."
The film, she added, examines "the relationship between the surveillance of that controlled population and the killing of that population"–a relationship with roots not only in Gaza but also in the occupied West Bank.
Israeli threats against filmmakers and sources
Thursday’s premiere came days after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu demanded an investigation into the anonymous military sources featured in the documentary.
His office said on Sunday that he had asked the military chief of staff, the head of the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service and the state attorney to investigate the participants and prosecute them. Netanyahu also described the film as "false, misleading and biased".
The move followed his September pledge to advance legislation stripping citizenship from people who "defame" Israeli soldiers and increasing the statutory damages available in defamation cases twentyfold. Culture Minister Miki Zohar has accused the directors of "treason against the state", while far-right activists have demonstrated outside their families’ homes.
At the Q&A, Executive Producer Jonathan Glazer described the authorities’ reaction as "the rage of cognitive dissonance" when a society is confronted with violence that challenges its understanding of itself.
"You only have two choices, which is to kind of move into some place of truth and honesty, or to sort of explode like a volcano," he said. "I think that reaction … the film describes it."
Paul Lewis, Head of Investigations at The Guardian, said the filmmakers’ relative privilege compared with Palestinian journalists documenting Israel’s assault did not diminish the personal risks they faced.
"There is a cost to them both. The response from the Israeli government is absolutely appalling," he said. "No one who works as a filmmaker or a journalist should be punished for an exercise in telling the truth."
The panellists pointed to the tension between official efforts to discredit the testimony and threats against those who provided it.
"One of the things they say is … this film is false, misrepresentative, tells lies. Simultaneously, Bibi Netanyahu [is] saying that people in the film should be prosecuted for revealing state secrets," Lewis said. "Those two things don’t really make sense."
Despite the backlash, NAZA has secured theatrical distribution in more than 50 countries. Following its Venice premiere, where it won the Special Jury Prize, the film screened at the New York Film Festival and began its US cinema release in late September. Its international rollout includes France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Canada and Australia.
Israeli cinemas, however, had not agreed to show the documentary as of Thursday, despite an offer to screen it without charge. Abraham has said the filmmakers approached cinemas in Israel in the hope that audiences there could watch it alongside its international release.
The film will also be available worldwide for free on The Guardian’s website from late November, providing an online route for Israeli viewers to see the testimonies. Abraham has said access will have no time limit, citing the film’s "interest and public importance".
For Szor, however, reaching audiences does not guarantee that the violence documented will end.
Reflecting on "No Other Land", which she and Abraham previously made with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, she questioned what international recognition had changed for the communities whose destruction it recorded. The documentary won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.
"We won the Oscar with that film, and still … the communities there are still destroyed," she said, referring to Israel’s continued displacement and annexation of communities in the South Hebron Hills, where much of the film takes place. "A lot of the world has seen it. It’s all known, and those things are still going on."
"We still made another film, so of course we still either believe in it, or that’s what we chose to do," she added. "I don’t know if it has an impact or it doesn’t."

Population of rare Hainan gibbons gradually increasing — newspaper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:49:52 UTC
18:49:52 KST

HAIKOU /China/, October 16. /TASS/. The small population of rare gibbons in the southern Chinese province of Hainan is gradually increasing, Hainan Ribao reported.
According to the newspaper, there are now 44 gibbons on the island, comprising seven groups, compared to 35 five years ago. The local ecosystem continues to recover and thrive. Since the establishment of the Hainan Rainforest National Park on October 12, 2021, scientists have discovered 91 new species of wild flora and fauna within its boundaries.
The article pointed out that the International Union for Conservation of Nature has recognized Hainan’s gibbon conservation model as an exemplary model for protecting rare species. Thus, the global community has adopted the experience of China’s southernmost province to restore biodiversity in other regions of the world.
Hainan Ribao noted that the abovementioned forest park effectively protects more than 95% of the territory where trees have virtually remained untouched by human activity, which comprises 55% of the island’s natural forest. The Chinese authorities provide round-the-clock monitoring and control of this area, including through the use of satellite data. According to official statistics, the Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP) of this region increased by nearly 4.4 billion yuan, or about $655 million, from 2019 to 2024.
The newspaper emphasized that a 466-kilometer tourist route encircles the forest park. It connects nine provincial administrative units and boosts revenue for local companies operating in the culture and tourism sectors.
Hainan gibbons inhabit the central and southern parts of the island. They prefer to live in the tree canopy about ten meters high, making it difficult to monitor these primates that do not reproduce well in captivity. These mammals feed on both plant matter and small animals. In China, they are under the vigilant protection of the state.

Cyber attackers hit Zurich and Swiss Post pension funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:49:29 UTC
18:49:29 KST

Cyber attackers hit Zurich and Swiss Post pension funds
Following a cyberattack on an external software provider, personal data at the Zurich pension fund – and possibly also that of Swiss Post – was also stolen.
The Swiss city of Zurich said that the pension funds and payments are still functional. Other Swiss pension funds have already been victims of cyberattacks in recent days.
The attack took place at the end of September, Zurich said. Ahead of a switch to a new management system, the pension fund’s data had previously been transferred. The pension fund has filed a criminal complaint.
The fund is trying to determine exactly what information has been stolen and how many people are affected. In the worst-case scenario, the data breach includes personal contact details (name, address, email, telephone number), social security number, marital status, information on partners, the IBAN number and pension-related data such as insured income and assets.
The administrative system used by the funds to manage assets and pay out pensions is not believed to have been affected by the attack.
The Swiss Post pension fund also stated this evening in a press release that it had been the victim of the attack on the software provider. It is not yet clear whether policyholders’ data has been compromised.
In any case, pension assets and pension benefits are not at risk, according to the statement from Swiss Post. However, personal data such as name, address, date of birth, social security number, contact details, email address and pension details may have been affected by the cyberattack.
The cyberattack has also affected other pension funds. Last week, it emerged that data had also been stolen from the Bern Pension Fund and the Bern Teachers’ Insurance Fund.

The world’s best countries to live in for 2026 – and six of the top 10 are in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:49:23 UTC
18:49:23 KST

Monaco topped the ranking thanks to its high quality of life and infrastructure, with Andorra hot on its heels in second place.
Been dreaming of a life abroad, but haven’t decided on where to go yet? Then you might just want to take a look at this new ranking.
Produced by Nomad Capitalist, the Nomad Lifestyle Index evaluated 63 destinations against five pillars: Nature and climate; tax; residence and access; safety and freedom; and quality of life and infrastructure.
Within these pillars, the ranking looked at things like air quality, extreme weather risk, routes to legal residence and citizenship, the Global Peace Index, life expectancy, cost of living and broadband speed, among others.
After crunching the numbers, the top 10 is filled with European countries, including the number one spot: Monaco.
Every destination was given a score out of 100 for each of the five pillars, which were then used to calculate an overall score.
The three top destinations – Monaco, Andorra and the United Arab Emirates – were separated by just 0.74 points.
The best places to live in Europe
Monaco claimed the top spot as it was the only country to receive a perfect 100 score under the quality of life and infrastructure pillar, but it also ranked highly for its safety and freedom score.
In second place, Andorra leads in the safety and freedom pillar while also having the fourth-best nature score, with the cleanest air of any European country included in the Nomad Lifestyle Index. It was pipped to the top spot because of its route to citizenship, which takes 20 years of residence and requires a language and history test.
Malta took fourth place, with praise for its strong passport and route to naturalisation within five years. It also ranked highly in the nature pillar, but was held back by its tax score and quality of life and infrastructure rating.
Portugal, a long-time favourite of digital nomads, came fifth, ranking highly for its safety and freedom, residence and access, and tax scores, but was let down by its nature score as it is exposed to extreme weather conditions as a result of climate change.
Cyprus placed sixth, coming second in the residence and access pillar, with a strong passport and seven years to naturalisation. Its quality of life and infrastructure score held it back, as well as the air quality.
Rounding out the top 10 is Switzerland, which performed well in the safety and freedom pillar.
The top 10 destinations to live around the globe
- Monaco – 73.89
- Andorra – 73.68
- United Arab Emirates –73.15
- Malta – 72.11
- Portugal – 70.09
- Cyprus – 68.42
- Singapore – 67.12
- Cayman Islands – 66.50
- New Zealand – 66.43
- Switzerland – 65.44

Shield AI software lets Taiwan drone boats shadow intruder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:47 UTC
18:48:47 KST

- Shield AI’s Hivemind fused radar and AIS data to let two Thunder Tiger SeaShark drone boats jointly patrol and escort a target in Dapeng Bay.
- In Shield AI’s simulation, five Hivemind-run boats covered 50 nautical miles versus 6 for fixed patrols, with the same 95% identification rate.
Shield AI has released new details on how its Hivemind autonomy software steered two Taiwanese uncrewed boats through a joint patrol off southern Taiwan, fusing radar and ship-tracking data into a single picture and switching the pair from patrol to escort duty without an operator directing each move.
The U.S. company described the July demonstration with Taiwan-based Thunder Tiger Corp. in a case study published this month. Hivemind ran aboard Thunder Tiger’s SeaShark 600 and SeaShark 800, six- and eight-meter uncrewed surface vessels, during a patrol in Dapeng Bay in Pingtung County. Shield AI said the teams went from first software integration to the live demonstration in six weeks, starting with digital models of both boats before testing the software on their actual hardware.
“We sought out the world’s strongest technology: Shield AI’s Hivemind. We chose them because we know they have already integrated and tested on 30+ platforms,” said Bryan L., who leads Thunder Tiger’s USV division.
At the start of the mission, planners split the patrol area into two sectors and assigned one SeaShark to each. Both boats used maritime radar and the Automatic Identification System, the transponder network that ships use to broadcast their identity and position, to watch the water around them. When a third boat playing a vessel of interest entered the area, Hivemind matched the radar contacts with the AIS reports, which update at different rates and often place the same boat in slightly different spots, and merged them into one continuously updated track shared by both SeaSharks.
The SeaShark 600 then fed live electro-optical and infrared video of the target to operators ashore. Hivemind paused the patrol and ordered the two boats into an escort, placing one off the target’s port side and the other off its starboard side to give operators two angles on the vessel and put the boats in position to support an interdiction if ordered. Once the target left the area, the software ended the escort and sent both SeaSharks back to their original sectors.
Shield AI also ran a simulation of a larger fleet. Five uncrewed boats using Hivemind’s adaptive patrols covered a 50-nautical-mile (93 km) stretch, compared with 6 nautical miles (11 km) for five boats on fixed patrol patterns, while both groups kept a 95% vessel identification rate. The company said that works out to roughly 8.3 times the coverage with the same number of boats, with real-world results depending on sensors, speed and sea conditions.
“We are very optimistic about Hivemind, which brings autonomy to USVs for area search, target tracking, and the execution of these missions,” said William Chen, chairman of Thunder Tiger.
The demonstration took place on July 29 and was attended by personnel from Taiwan’s state-run weapons developer, the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, and the Coast Guard Administration, Focus Taiwan reported. The two companies signed a partnership in May to bring Hivemind to Thunder Tiger’s uncrewed systems, starting with the SeaShark line, and The Defence Blog covered the public showing of the boats. Shield AI also signed a contract with the National Chung-Shan Institute in February 2026 covering Hivemind tools for Taiwanese-built platforms.
Hivemind, which Shield AI says has been integrated on more than 30 platforms including F-16 fighters and drone boats, is entering a market Taiwan is building quickly. The island’s coastline runs more than 1,500 km (930 miles) across the main island and outlying islands, and Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense has requested funding for 1,320 uncrewed surface vessels along with thousands of coastal reconnaissance and attack drones, according to the Taipei Times.
Shield AI said the six-week effort with Thunder Tiger established a repeatable path for installing Hivemind on other uncrewed boats.

Italy and Spain move to end border dispute after Meloni-Sánchez talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:10 UTC
18:48:10 KST

Italy's Giorgia Meloni, who met with Spain's Pedro Sánchez, agreed a short extension to align the expiry of Italy’s border controls with Spain’s reciprocal measures. Rome and Madrid say they will seek alternatives but remain at odds over migration.
Italy extended its temporary border checks on arrivals from Spain by just seven days on Friday, in a sign of thawing relations between Rome and Madrid after weeks of tensions over migration.
The decision followed a one-on-one meeting between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her Spanish counterpart, Pedro Sánchez, on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels, a diplomat told Euronews.
The border checks were initially introduced on 1 August for one month, following the arrival of almost 90,000 irregular migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. The Italian government subsequently extended them by 15 days on three separate occasions, de facto suspending free-circulation rules with Spain.
Spain introduced a reciprocal measure, also renewed each time, in retaliation for the checks, which it considered unjustified. The latest Spanish extension was due to expire on 22 October. As a result, the two countries’ measures are now aligned and will expire on the same day.
The interior ministers of the two countries are expected to work out alternative measures next week, according to Italian and Spanish diplomatic sources.
The random controls are currently happening at airports and ports, as the two countries have no land borders.
Almost 500,000 people were checked in the first month of border controls, according to the Italian Interior Minister. Thirty-one of them, including eight Moroccan citizens, were refused entry, while the Minister did not indicate whether they had entered Spain with the massive influx to Ceuta.
According to the Spanish government, no irregular migrants have moved to mainland Spain from Ceuta.
Meloni, who leads a far-right government, and Sánchez, a centre-left leader, have repeatedly clashed over migration policy.
They are also set to find themselves on opposite sides at Friday’s European summit, where migration is once again on EU leaders’ agenda, with a strategic discussion scheduled over lunch.
Among other topics, Spain’s plan to regularize around 600,000 undocumented migrants will be discussed. Several countries are concerned about a possible domino effect across the EU and the risk that the measure could act as a “pull factor”, attracting more irregular migrants.

UK government signals possible intervention in Sky’s $2.1B ITV broadcasting deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:48:04 UTC
18:48:04 KST

Rabia Ali
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
The UK government has signaled it could intervene in Sky’s proposed £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion) takeover of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming business over concerns about media ownership, the diversity of news coverage and viewers’ access to quality programming.
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said in a written statement to Parliament Thursday that she was “minded to” issue a public interest intervention notice, a formal step that would trigger reviews by media regulator Ofcom and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).
The deal would give Sky, owned by US media giant Comcast, control of ITV’s Media and Entertainment business, including its television channels and streaming platform ITVX. ITV Studios, its television production business, is excluded.
Nandy raised concerns about freedom of expression and the diversity of views in the news media as well as the concentration of media ownership.
She also questioned how the deal could affect the availability of varied, high-quality programming on streaming and other on-demand services used by UK audiences.
Existing legislation does not explicitly cover the impact of mergers on programming availability through on-demand services, Nandy said, adding that the government could extend the relevant public-interest rules.
Sky announced the deal on July 6, saying the combined business would account for around 20% of all in-home viewing in the UK.
The company said the takeover would strengthen British broadcasting’s ability to compete with global streaming platforms.
“We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's Media & Entertainment business together will create a stronger British media business, better able to compete with global streaming platforms, support great British programming and trusted news and deliver more for audiences,” a Sky spokesperson said.
Sky has also pledged to preserve ITV’s identity, free-to-air services and public-service broadcasting obligations, and maintain separate editorial voices for ITV News and Sky News.
Nandy said no final decision had been made. Sky and ITV have until next Tuesday to submit written responses.
If she issues the notice, Ofcom would examine the deal’s public-interest implications, while the CMA would assess its potential impact on competition. Nandy would then decide whether a more detailed investigation was needed.

UK Sends Ukraine More Storm Shadow Missiles as US Presses Kyiv to Halt Strikes

Britain is supplying Ukraine with additional Storm Shadow cruise missiles to counter Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure before winter, as London backs Kyiv’s ability to strike targets inside Russia despite US pressure to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed replenishing the missile stocks during their meeting in London on Wednesday, Oct. 14.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
London considers strikes on Russian facilities used to launch attacks against Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure a defensive measure, the sources said.
They pointed to Russia’s increased production of jet-powered drones and missiles, saying Ukraine needed the means to counter the growing threat.
The British position contrasts with that of US President Donald Trump’s administration, which has demanded that Ukraine stop drone attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine resumed those attacks on Thursday, Oct. 15, in response to continuing Russian strikes on its energy infrastructure.
Trump called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace” and accused Kyiv of driving up global energy prices, even as Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
“Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” Trump told Newsmax in an interview published on Thursday, when asked about Ukraine’s decision to resume attacks on Russian refineries.
Europe Has No Starlink Replacement as Ukraine Faces Satellite Disruptions
However, energy analysts say Trump’s deal to resume Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly lower fuel prices, as the main driver of the global price surge has been the US-Israel war with Iran, which has disrupted oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Bloomberg’s sources, London does not believe Kyiv should stop striking Russia while Moscow continues attacking Ukraine.
The distinction concerns both the targets and the broader question of Ukraine’s right to respond: the reported British position supports attacks on facilities enabling Russian strikes, while Washington has specifically pressed Kyiv to spare refineries.
Britain began supplying Storm Shadow missiles to Ukraine in 2023. Their use was initially restricted to targets within Ukraine, including Russian-occupied territory. Ukrainian forces first used them against military targets inside Russia in late 2024.
Manufactured by MBDA, Storm Shadow is an air-launched cruise missile designed to strike high-value targets. It flies at low altitude to reduce detection, and the manufacturer lists its range as more than 250 kilometers, or about 155 miles.
Bloomberg also reported that Burnham announced plans in August to share technical information and designs for long-range missiles to support assembly in Ukraine, as establishing that production capability would take time.

Danish PM says Ukraine needs frozen Russian assets as it is running out of money
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has said Ukraine needs funding to continue fighting Russia and that frozen Russian assets are the most obvious source of additional EU support.
Source: Frederiksen speaking ahead of the second day of the European Council meeting in Brussels on 16 October, as reported by European Pravda
Quote: "Waging war is expensive… And Ukraine is now running out of money. This has already happened. They cannot buy what they need. They cannot produce what they need."
Details: Frederiksen noted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainians have become even more intense than they were "until quite recently".
"So we have an urgent problem in finding funding for 2026 at the European level. We must ensure there will be enough funds at the European level for the war effort in 2027. This is what I will raise at the meeting," the Danish prime minister stressed.
She pledged that Denmark "will continue to provide whatever assistance we can".
Asked where additional funding for Ukraine could come from, Frederiksen stressed that "frozen assets are the most obvious source to turn to".
Quote: "Not only would this help finance Europe's defence, but it would also mean that Russia, which is currently causing so much damage to Ukraine and Europe, would have to pay for everything it is doing… I still believe this is one of the best solutions we have right in front of us."
Background:
- The EU's support for Ukraine is to be discussed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in attendance at the EU leaders' summit in Brussels. EU leaders have publicly assured Zelenskyy that sanctions against Russia will under no circumstances be eased.
- Meanwhile, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has firmly opposed discussing the idea of using frozen Russian Central Bank assets to benefit Ukraine.
- European Pravda previously reported that the EU leaders' summit on 15-16 October would not produce decisions on funding for Ukraine or Russian assets because no agreement has been reached on the issue.

Norwegian Multimillionaire Accused of Fraud in NATO Ship Servicing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:45:53 UTC
18:45:53 KST

Norwegian authorities have arrested four people, including a multimillionaire, on suspicion of systematic fraud against NATO.
The Norwegian national broadcaster NRK reported the arrests, citing Økokrim, Norway’s National Authority for Investigation and Prosecution of Economic and Environmental Crime.
The main suspect is a man over the age of 50 whose wealth is estimated at more than 100 million Norwegian kroner (€8.5 million). He owns a company that provided maintenance services for NATO warships in Norwegian ports.
According to investigators, the businessman and his employees systematically overcharged for work performed and submitted fraudulent invoices to NATO between 2021 and 2025. The total damages are estimated at at least €1 million.
NATO investigators uncovered the alleged misconduct in 2023, prompting a joint investigation with law enforcement authorities in Norway, Germany, and Romania.
The Norwegian millionaire, who is the main suspect, denies any wrongdoing, stating that he does not understand the basis for the charges. However, a court has already ordered him to be held in custody for two weeks.
As previously reported, Norwegian authorities are also investigating an unexplained case of military assistance to Ukraine involving respiratory masks supplied by the company Watchbird. The Parliament’s Standing Committee on Scrutiny and Constitutional Affairs has opened a so-called scrutiny case against the government.

Daily Update: Russia Loses 1,790 Troops, 6 Aircraft in One Day
Russia lost an estimated 1,790 troops and six aircraft over the past 24 hours, while fighting across the front surged to 304 combat engagements, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on October 16.
The latest Ukrainian estimate puts Russia’s cumulative personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, at approximately 1,561,020. The six additional aircraft raised Russia’s estimated aviation losses to 449, while helicopter losses remained unchanged at 356.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian forces also lost 15 armored combat vehicles, bringing the cumulative figure to 25,552, while tank losses remained at 12,414. How a Ukrainian Developer Built an FPV Simulator to Hunt Russian Shaheds
Ukrainian FPV combat drone simulator Remote Reaper officially launched out of Steam Early Access with version 1.0, marking the software’s largest update since development began.
The full release introduces airborne targets—specifically Shahed drones—alongside a time trial racing mode, new missions, and various technical enhancements, according to dev.ua.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Developer Vladyslav Fomenko built the project independently in direct collaboration with active military drone operators. To recreate flight mechanics with high accuracy, Fomenko personally tested uncrewed aerial vehicles at training grounds.
The software recreates real operational conditions, simulating the impact of electronic warfare systems, adverse weather, armored vehicle protection, and terrain topography.
"Shooting down Shaheds is more fun with friends," Fomenko noted, highlighting the simulator's online cooperative multiplayer feature, as reported by dev.ua.
The addition of aerial targets stands out as the core upgrade in version 1.0. Intercepting Iranian-designed attack drones requires operators to apply distinct handling techniques and approach vectors compared to ground strikes, alongside detonating the payload while airborne.
The update also incorporates a time trial mode featuring three dedicated tracks for flight skill practice, as well as new combat scenarios covering multiple rocket launcher hunting, infantry engagements in foggy conditions, and expanded tutorial courses.
Visual damage displays appear on struck targets, while opposing infantry can now deploy smoke screens to break line of sight.
Control options expanded to include gamepad support within a simplified control scheme, improved navigation on Steam Deck devices, and an updated flight compass with target tracking markers.
The program retains a detailed drone builder that factors component weight into flight duration, alongside a custom mission editor supported by Steam Workshop integration.
Previously, it was reported that Ukrainian defense company TENETA developed a new lightweight, single-use anti-drone device designed to counter enemy FPV drones and reconnaissance quadcopters.
