Nearly 400 Foreign Companies Request Access to Ukraine’s Russian Weapon Intelligence
The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine has received more than 650 registration applications for its unified research portal for captured adversary hardware, known as TrophyLab.
Among these requests, 389 applications have come from foreign manufacturers of military equipment and weaponry. Registration on the portal is also accessible to Ukrainian manufacturers, military units, and government institutions, according to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
TrophyLab gathers unique information regarding captured Russian military hardware to support engineers, scientists, and defense technology producers from Ukraine and partner nations.
The database is actively populated by units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine, the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense, the Security Service of Ukraine, and specialized scientific institutions.
Every registered researcher has the opportunity to submit a request to receive a sample or its physical fragment for independent evaluation.
According to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, access to TrophyLab enables faster and secure information sharing regarding Russian hardware to accelerate the creation of effective countermeasures for the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
The development comes as Russia continues introducing new weapons into its arsenal. Ukrainian military technology expert and defense adviser Serhii Flash said on July 14 that Russia has begun deploying the low-cost, highly maneuverable Banderol cruise missile, although production has yet to reach the planned rate of 120 missiles per month.
According to Flash, achieving that production target would allow Russia to launch an average of four Banderol missiles per day. However, he said the manufacturing facility has not yet reached the required output. The missile is launched from airborne platforms, primarily the Orion medium-altitude, long-endurance unmanned aerial vehicle.

US Senators Seek Probe Into Ukraine Starshield Disruptions As Zelenskyy Attends EU Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:42:58 UTC
18:42:58 KST

BRUSSELS -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, has no interest in peace talks and criticized a US deal with Moscow on diesel exports, saying it will hand more money to the Kremlin to fund its war against his country.
Speaking during a European Union summit in Brussels on October 16, Zelenskyy also said that speeds of US company SpaceX's satellite communications, crucial for Ukraine's defense, had not returned to previous levels but were "being restored" after having slowed in recent days.
EU leaders signaled support for Zelenskyy and Ukraine at the summit, which came amid a new flare-up of tensions between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump, who has stepped up pressure on Kyiv to reach an agreement to end the full-scale war Putin launched in February 2022.
"Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form," Zelenskyy said at a press conference. "He’s playing with words.... Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war."
Russia has rejected repeated calls for a full cease-fire and has appeared to ignore what Trump said on October 11 was a limited truce barring attacks on energy infrastructure, as its forces hammer Ukrainian cities, power plants, and other facilities with winter on the way.
Disruptions to the Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, left Ukraine particularly vulnerable earlier in the week. Starshield is overseen by the US government, and Ukraine uses it for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes, and interceptor drones.
For a few nights, speed limits in the system “were lower and when that happened, we were unable [to shoot] down jet-powered Shahed drones” Zelenskyy said, describing the situation as “very painful and very unpleasant." There were numerous casualties ion Kyiv and elsewhere as intensified attacks.
"Has the speed been fully restored to what it was before? No. Is the speed being restored now? Yes," Zelenskyy said.
The satellite problem added to concerns in Ukraine after Trump announced on October 9 that he and Putin had agreed by phone to a deal that would send Russian diesel to world markets including the US, where high fuel prices are adding to challenges facing Trump's Republican Party ahead of midterm Congressional elections on November 3.
At the press conference, Zelenskyy said that "cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal." He said it would "never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war."
Trump has repeatedly called on Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian refineries, blaming those attacks -- and not the decreased energy flows from the Mideast resulting from the US-Israeli war with Iran that began in February -- for high diesel fuel prices.
On October 10, Trump said that Kyiv "better damn well" stop hitting Russian refineries and that Ukraine should "get a new president," blaming Zelenskyy for the lack of a peace agreement.
Trump, who made ending Russia's war on Ukraine a priority when he started his current term in January 2025, told US media outlet Newsmax on October 15 that peace between Russia and Ukraine would only be possible if Zelenskyy left office.
"Zelenskyy is not a good guy for us to deal with," he said in an interview. "He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. No, I'm not a big fan of Zelenskyy," Trump said, adding that he believes both leaders wanted peace but found Zelenskyy more difficult to negotiate with than Putin.
Russia, among other demands, has said Ukraine must hand over the portion of the eastern Donetsk region that Moscow's forces have been unable to capture in years of very deadly fighting. Ukraine says that is unacceptable, signaling it could agree to a cease-fire that would leave the front lines in place as talks commenced.
Speaking at what Russian media said was a command post on October 16, Putin said he had instructed Russian forces not only to drive Ukrainian troops out of regions Moscow baselessly claims as Russian territory, but also to establish a "security zone" beyond those regions. He said Russian control of that zone would not be subject to negotiation.
Separately, Putin ordered Russian forces to continue their "massive and coordinated strikes against enemy targets."
In an interview published on October 15 by the Financial Times, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian energy facilities because Moscow had not halted its own strikes. "We're done," he said after stating that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian refining operations for three days.
Zelenskyy also told the British newspaper that the satellite communication slowdown was described to Kyiv as a technical glitch even though it remains unclear who authorized the restrictions, whether they affected commercial Starlink or Starshield, and whether Washington also reduced intelligence support to Kyiv.
US news outlet Axios, citing unnamed sources, reported that the White House told Ukraine it does not control SpaceX. Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS" -- meaning the US president.
Asked about the matter on October 16, Trump told reporters, "It wasn't me. And I don't think it was Elon." According to Reuters, he also said he has a good relatonship with Zelenskyy.
At the press conference a few hours earlier, Zelenskyy seemed careful to avoid criticizing Trump directly, saying he had had “a couple of meetings with the American President and we are always finding topics for discussions and for making decisions.”
He also said Kyiv still was talking with the US negotiation team and that they would meet “at a certain level in the coming days.”
European leaders pledged support for Kyiv, even if few concrete measures appeared to be forthcoming.
Speaking ahead of the summit, European Council President Antonio Costa reaffirmed that the EU's support for Ukraine was stronger than ever, stressing that this was no time to withdraw assistance or ease sanctions on Russia.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added that the EU had supported Trump's proposed energy cease-fire, but Russia had failed to respect it "for a single minute." She added that EU sanctions would remain in place until Russia stopped the war and that Brussels was preparing another round of sanctions on Moscow.
Zelenskyy used his meeting with the European leaders to seek air-defense support ahead of the winter. Speaking about the US-made Patriot missiles, the Ukrainian leader said “Most of PAC-2- and PAC-3 are now being sent to the Middle East. It’s an open secret we are not a priority destination for these systems.”
He added that his EU counterparts received “a bare minimum” of what Kyiv’s needs this winter adding that there are enough PACs in Europe for Ukraine to go tough this winter.”
Asked in Brussels whether Ukraine had resumed targeting Russian refineries, Zelenskyy said only that he “usually doesn’t comment details about our operations.”
Meanwhile, overnight Russian attacks injured five people in Ukraine's central Cherkasy region, where a drone strike set fire to an apartment building in Uman, regional officials reported on October 16.
Lutsk, in Ukraine's Volyn region, was left without electricity following a Russian drone attack, according to city authorities.
Earlier in the day, Russian authorities said their defense forces had repelled a Ukrainian drone attack targeting heating infrastructure in the Vladimir region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin also reported that 94 Ukrainian drones had been shot down near the capital over period of eight hours, while four were downed over the Leningrad region, according to the regional governor.
All four Moscow airports were temporarily closed amid the drone attacks, with flights diverted to other cities, Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency reported. An air raid alert was also declared in the Leningrad region.
In Washington on October 15, a bipartisan group of nine US senators called for an investigation into the disruptions to Starshield.
"We write with grave concern regarding reported disruptions to critical US-supported communications and intelligence-sharing capabilities in Ukraine that have endangered American personnel and potentially compromised Ukraine’s ability to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks," they said in a letter to the Defense Department's inspector general.
The senators urged an immediate probe to determine whether any US officials "directed, authorized, approved, or had advance knowledge of changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements, warning capabilities, or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine."
Separately, Pope Leo spoke by phone with Putin on October 16, expressing "deep concern" over the humanitarian situation in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, where residents remain trapped amid landmines and face starvation in the largely destroyed urban area.
The Vatican said that during the call, the pontiff called for a truce to allow the delivery of first aid and food supplies and to facilitate the voluntary evacuation of the civilian population. The Kremlin said Putin supported the initiative to deliver supplies and was ready to "cooperate on this matter."
Ukrainian volunteers who spoke with RFE/RL earlier this year said Oleshky is an important staging ground for Russian attacks on parts of southern Ukraine. They said local residents had effectively been turned into "human shields" by Russian forces operating in the area.
According to Ukrainian authorities, Kyiv has sought to establish a humanitarian corridor linking Oleshky with government-held territory since the spring, but Moscow has not agreed to the proposal.

Platform workers' grueling hours raising health and safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:39:00 UTC
18:39:00 KST

Platform workers' grueling hours raising health and safety concerns
Many food couriers and ride-hailing drivers in Estonia work exhausting hours that put their health and road safety at risk, but the government has no plans to intervene.
A recent study by the Foresight Center and the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM) found that a quarter of food couriers and ride-hailing drivers work more than 50 hours a week, well above Estonia's standard 40-hour workweek.
"The study also found that many couriers and drivers were working more than 100 hours a week," said Olavi Miller, an expert at the Foresight Center.
Such workloads can harm workers' health and raise concerns about road safety. But while the MKM doesn't condone excessive workloads, Hedi Arukase, the ministry's deputy secretary general for labor and equality, says platform workers are independent contractors, not traditional employees, and thus are free to set their own hours.
"Unfortunately, there isn't much we can do about it," she said.
Money is a major reason workers put in such long hours. About 90 percent earn additional income elsewhere, while platform work is the sole source of income for roughly 2,000 people. Two-thirds earn less than €1,200 a month.
Social protections are another concern. Not all platform workers contribute to pensions, and most rely on other jobs or educational institutions to qualify for Estonian Health Insurance Fund (EHIF) coverage. Fourteen percent have no health insurance at all.
Ex-minister: They chose this job
MP Signe Riisalo (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu's Social Affairs Committee and former minister of social protection, said platform workers are all independent, capable adults who have chosen this form of employment, but did also acknowledge a broader problem.
"Is this a broader problem for society? Yes, it is," Riisalo said. "And do we need to look for solutions? Yes, we do."
One option would be for platform workers to unionize, she said, "because social protections can be provided by an employer, which in their case is the platform."
A new EU directive aims to make platform work more transparent, and legislation to implement it in Estonia is currently pending in the Riigikogu. Arukase said the bill should help workers better understand their employment conditions and figure out how to earn more in less time.
--
Editor: Merilin Leetna, Aili Vahtla

The man, whose identity has not been disclosed, told officials that he was bringing the animals as a gift for a Brazilian colleague. The Mexican national was denied entry into Germany and sent back to Istanbul. The surviving animals, meanwhile, have been placed in the care of a snake farm in Germany.

Tesla unveils new Roadster sports car
Tesla has unveiled its redesigned Roadster electric sports car, featuring SpaceX cold-gas thrusters and a suction system designed to enable extraordinary driving maneuvers, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing Tesla’s official website.
The company presented the vehicle yesterday, showcasing technology that combines active aerodynamics, powered fans and rocket-inspired components.
“We already put Roadster in a rocket. Now we put a rocket in Roadster,” Tesla said.
Real life, baby https://t.co/3QEqn18wig
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026
According to the manufacturer, the car’s fan and ground-sealing system pulls air from beneath the vehicle, generating enough suction to hold it upside down even while stationary. Active wings and powered fans are designed to improve traction and cornering performance.
Tesla says the vehicle’s cold-gas thrusters use electric actuators to make rapid adjustments, helping stabilize it in flight. The company specifies that flight-related features are available only with the Rocket configuration, which will not be offered in all regions.
Tesla has outlined three configurations: Performance, Thrust and Rocket. In its announcement, the company described Performance as a two-seat version intended for road use, while the two-seat Thrust adds rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters for claimed acceleration from zero to 60 mph, approximately 97 km/h, in under one second.
The manufacturer notes that the specifications displayed on its Roadster webpage primarily reflect the optional Thrust upgrade.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Tesla had planned to unveil its long-delayed second-generation Roadster on October 1, nearly nine years after first presenting the high-performance electric sports car.

Parashat Noah: The main thing is the intention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:32:29 UTC
18:32:29 KST

One of the most dramatic events to shape the world and humanity was the Flood, which swept across the earth and destroyed everything on it, leaving only Noah and his family, the animals he had brought into the Ark, and the fish in the waters.
At the beginning of Creation, the world was created in perfection and goodness, destined to exist without death or disease.
However, following Adam’s sin and his expulsion from the Garden of Eden, evil entered the human experience.
Humanity eventually reached a state in which, in the words of the Torah, “the earth was filled with violence.”
Violence, corruption, and the absence of moral boundaries undermined the very foundations of human existence, until the world reached a breaking point.
The Flood was therefore a turning point in the history of Creation, an attempt to halt the downward spiral and open a new chapter in the history of the world.
When Noah and his family emerge from the Ark, they encounter a world entirely different from the one they had known: ruined, desolate, and silent, no longer filled with the human activity that had been inseparable from their lives.
Try to imagine that moment. A small family stands before an immense, empty world, with no cities, no communities, no other human beings, and nothing of the familiar world they once knew.
No one is there to welcome them. There is no one with whom to share their feelings, and no certainty about what life will look like from that point onward.
What would be the first thing you would choose to do in such a moment? How does one respond to destruction on a scale that is almost impossible to comprehend?
The Torah describes Noah’s first act:
“Noah went out, together with his sons, his wife, and his sons’ wives.
“Noah built an altar to the Lord, and taking from every clean animal and every clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar” (Gen. 8:18-20).
Noah does not begin his new life by trying to rebuild the world, constructing a home for himself, or first attending to his family’s practical needs. The first act described in the Torah is building an altar and offering a sacrifice to God.
This act acknowledges the Creator’s sovereignty, gives thanks, and submits oneself before the One who governs the world. Noah recognizes that even when reality appears harsh and incomprehensible, the world does not operate by chance. In the very midst of devastation and destruction, he expresses his connection with the One who spoke the world into existence.
Then an unexpected turn takes place. The Torah describes how Noah’s act leads to a divine promise concerning the future of all humanity:
“The Lord smelled the pleasing aroma, and the Lord said to Himself: I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth; nor will I ever again destroy every living thing as I have done” (Gen. 8:21).
World continues to exist with evil in it
God promises that He will never again bring a Flood to destroy all life on earth, and that the world will continue to exist even though evil remains within it.
Yet this very promise raises a question. For many years, Noah stood alone against an entire generation, admonishing its members, trying to influence them and change their ways. Nevertheless, the Flood was not averted. Yet now, after the destruction, a single act of his elicits such a profound response. What was it about this act that gave it such extraordinary power?
The Mishna in Tractate Makkot states:
“Rabbi Hananya ben Akashya says: The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel; therefore, He gave them an abundance of Torah and commandments, as it is stated: ‘The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious’” (Makkot 3:16).
The Rambam, Maimonides, explains this teaching of the Mishna, establishing an important principle for understanding the significance of the commandments:
“One of the fundamental principles of faith in the Torah is that if a person fulfills one of the 613 commandments properly and correctly, without involving any worldly objective whatsoever, but performs it purely for its own sake, out of love, that person merits the World to Come through it.
“Rabbi Hananya therefore said that because of the great number of commandments, it is impossible for a person not to perform at least one of them perfectly at some point during his lifetime, thereby meriting the eternal survival of the soul through that act” (Commentary on the Mishna, Tractate Makkot).
These words express a central principle of serving the Creator. The commandments are not merely a list of actions a person must perform; they express the relationship between the individual and God.
A person may perform a good deed to earn honor or gain status. He may also act out of habit or loyalty to the tradition in which he was raised. In the language of our Sages, all these may be considered commandments performed shelo lishma – not purely for their own sake.
Maimonides points to the central goal of fulfilling the commandments: performing them lishma, for their own sake, out of love for the Creator and a desire to fulfill His will, without any personal interest mixed in.
We can now understand that Noah’s efforts before the Flood do not diminish his righteousness. However, when a person acts before an entire community, additional motives may accompany his actions.
After the Flood, the situation is entirely different. Noah builds an altar and offers a sacrifice without seeking to prove his righteousness to anyone, compete with anyone, or gain status. After all, the world is empty of other people. He acts solely because he wishes to serve his Creator and acknowledge His goodness. This is a pure act performed lishma, for its own sake.
Such a clean and genuine act, performed entirely for the sake of Heaven, has the power to ensure the world’s continued existence forever. For this is the very purpose of Creation, and now that this purpose has been fulfilled, humanity can endure.
This idea is relevant to our everyday lives as well. The deeper test often comes precisely when no one is watching.
Imagine someone driving alone late at night who finishes drinking a cup of coffee. He could throw the empty cup out the window, thinking that no one will notice.
Yet in that moment, he discovers whether keeping the environment clean and acting responsibly toward it are values he truly believes in, or whether he observes them only because he fears the reaction of others.
In a generation in which sharing our experiences and actions has become central to social life, this aspect of serving God deserves our attention as well.
People share acts of kindness, charitable donations, volunteer initiatives, and other good deeds on social media.
This has a positive side: publicizing a good deed can inspire others, encourage them to act, and create additional circles of generosity.
However, alongside the benefits of sharing, we must not lose the ability to do good without telling anyone about it.
When every action becomes an opportunity to share, a person may grow accustomed to measuring a deed’s value by the degree of exposure and recognition it receives. Instead of asking whether he has done the right thing, he may find himself wondering whether he will receive positive responses and whether others will think more highly of him as a result.
It is therefore important to preserve an inner space where our good deeds remain between ourselves and our Creator, without needing applause or expecting recognition.
The writer is rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.

World Bread Day: Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries up to USD 1.6B
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:32:11 UTC
18:32:11 KST

World Bread Day: Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries up to USD 1.6B
Kazakhstan exports wheat to 29 countries, with shipments worth 1.6 billion US dollars, according to data released by the Kazakh Agriculture Ministry ahead of World Bread Day, celebrated annually on October 16, Qazinform News Agency reports.
More than half of Kazakhstan’s wheat exports go to Uzbekistan, which accounts for 51% of total exports, or 4.2 million tonnes. Other major destinations include Tajikistan with 16% (1.3 million tonnes), Azerbaijan with 8% (652,000 tonnes), Afghanistan with 6% (496,300 tonnes), and Italy with 5% (418,700 tonnes). Other importers include Algeria and Kyrgyzstan.
The country’s export capacity is supported by strong grain production. Kazakhstan harvests an average of 18 million tonnes of grain annually, while domestic consumption and processing amount to nearly 9.5 million tonnes. This allows the country to fully meet domestic demand while maintaining substantial export volumes.
Flour production is twice the level of domestic consumption, ensuring that the baking industry operates primarily on locally sourced raw materials. Between January and August 2026, Kazakhstan produced 325,500 tonnes of bread.
The annual production capacity of the country’s bakeries stands at 502,000 tonnes, with current utilization at 35.5%. Producers continue to expand their product range in response to consumer demand, manufacturing both bakery and flour-based confectionery products with short and extended shelf lives.
To support the sector, the Government has introduced several support measuers. Under the 2021-2030 Agro-Industrial Complex Development Concept, enterprises expanding production of bakery or confectionery products with annual capacities exceeding 2,000 tonnes are eligible for reimbursement of 25% of investment costs. Flour producers also benefit from a tax incentive, with value-added tax reduced by 80% under Article 490 of the Tax Code.
World Bread Day was established in 2006 at the initiative of the International Union of Bakers and Confectioners. The date coincides with the anniversary of the founding of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) on October 16, 1945.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan’s grain harvest reached 23 million tonnes.
Reports highlighted Kazakhstan’s grain rail shipments hit record 1.45 mln tons in September.

Belgian PM explains why EU summit did not move on frozen Russian assets
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has firmly opposed discussions on the idea of using frozen assets belonging to Russia's Central Bank.
Source: De Wever at a press conference following the first day of the EU summit, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Belgian prime minister, who has consistently opposed the transfer of frozen Russian funds held in the EU to Ukraine, told journalists that his position remains unchanged.
He believes dialogue can begin only after the war ends, meaning the funds cannot be used now.
"In every war, even in World War II, they [immobilised assets] were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there is always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilised assets," he said.
De Wever said he is opposed to developments taking a different course now, despite some EU leaders seeking to put the issue back on the agenda.
"Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalising those assets earlier for certain purposes? The answer to that question is yes, there are. Are they in this building [the European Council – ed.]? They are. Are they outside this building? Yes, they are. Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't. It's the best answer I can give you," he said.
The Belgian prime minister also noted that the current rules require unanimity for any action to be taken regarding the funds.
Background: No decisions on financing for Ukraine or on frozen Russian assets are expected at the summit due to a lack of agreement on these issues.

Parashat Noah: How prayer becomes an ark that carries us through turbulent times - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:31:55 UTC
18:31:55 KST

‘And God said to Noah, ‘Come into the teiva, you and all your household’” (Gen. 7:1).
The teiva – the ark – is one of the defining images of the parasha: a vessel of refuge carrying Noah, his family, and the living creatures through the waters of the Flood toward a renewed world.
Yet the Hebrew word “teiva” has another meaning. It can also mean “a word.” The Baal Shem Tov, the 18th-century founder of the Hassidic movement, takes “Bo el hateiva” (“Come into the ark”) as an instruction to enter the words of prayer.
Fittingly, this teaching opens “Amud Hatefila” – “The Pillar of Prayer” – an extensive compilation of his teachings on prayer found in Baal Shem Tov al HaTorah, parashat Noah.
Here the ark becomes the starting point for an entire approach to prayer – one of deep concentration, attachment to the sacred letters, and awareness of the Divine within them.
In prayer, he teaches, you should immerse yourself in each word “with your whole body and all your powers.” Rather than allowing the words simply to pass through our lips, we are invited to experience them fully.
'Worlds, souls, and Divinity'
The Baal Shem Tov takes the teaching further. Within every letter, he says, are “worlds, souls, and Divinity.” As letters join together to form words, prayer becomes more than a sequence of words to be recited. The teiva itself becomes a spiritual space that can hold and carry us.
Yoram Raanan’s painting gives striking visual expression to this understanding of “teiva.” He created the work spontaneously, allowing paint to drip and flow across the canvas. From this spontaneous process, a ship emerged. Its great curved form fills the lower half of the painting, while long vertical lines rise like masts above it.
Within the form of the ship, a stringed instrument, perhaps a lute, came into being. The curved hull becomes the body of the instrument, while the vertical lines perform both functions visually – at once masts and strings. Ship and instrument inhabit the same form – one carrying us across, the other giving voice to sound.
Above them, small forms move through the expansive blue-green field. Some appear as golden birds, others as drifting clouds, while still others remain more elusive. “They intermingle,” Raanan says, “like the words of prayer.”
The transformation seems particularly fitting for the Baal Shem Tov’s understanding of “teiva.” The ship carries us; the instrument gives voice to prayer. The word becomes both vessel and sound.
Throughout the painting, forms seem to shift and flow into one another. Water becomes sky. Ship becomes lute. Birds and other forms seem to pass between different realms.
The painting gives visual form to something difficult to describe: to enter the teiva is not merely to pronounce a word of prayer, but to enter its sound, its movement, and the world it contains. Just as the ark carries its passengers through the waters of the Flood, the words of prayer can become a vessel that carries us.
But the ark does more than carry. It is also a place of protection. When the world outside becomes stormy, the teiva offers refuge.
The Baal Shem Tov’s teaching gives this ancient image an inner dimension. In difficult or turbulent times, we, too, can find a protective space within sacred words and prayer.
And Raanan’s lute adds another possibility: music, too, can become a place of refuge. Sound moves through us and changes how we feel, carrying us when words alone are not enough.
This image has particular resonance just after the cycle of the Jewish holidays. We have emerged from weeks of prayer, reflection, celebration, and sacred time, and suddenly we are back in the ordinary rhythm of the year.
The Baal Shem Tov’s teaching offers us a way to take something of that experience with us: the words of prayer can carry and sustain us as we move into the year ahead.
Noah could not remain in the ark forever. Eventually, the waters receded, the door opened, and he stepped onto dry land to begin again. The ark had carried him through the Flood; now he had to build life anew.
Raanan’s teiva, at once ark and lute, seems to hold both possibilities. The ark offers refuge; the lute gives us a song for the journey. We enter the teiva, and it carries us into the year ahead.
The writer is the author of Art of Revelation: A Visual Encounter with the Jewish Bible, a commentary on the paintings of her husband, artist Yoram Raanan. She teaches Jewish meditation and is currently writing ‘Art of Transformation,’ a book exploring the relationship between art, Jewish spirituality, and inner transformation, from which this article is adapted.

Heads of Polish and Ukrainian national remembrance institutes hold first meeting since 2018
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:30:54 UTC
18:30:54 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Senior delegations from Poland and Ukraine’s state institutes of national remembrance have held talks in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, marking the first time the heads of the two organisations have met in eight years.
The meeting, at which the two sides discussed issues including exhumations of World War Two victims and possible joint research projects, comes as Poland and Ukraine seek reconciliation over historical issues that have regularly caused tensions between two otherwise close allies.
📢 14 października 2026 r. we Lwowie delegacja Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej spotkała się z przedstawicielami ukraińskiego Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej. Było to pierwsze bezpośrednie, robocze spotkanie szefów tych instytucji od 2018 r.
➡️ Stronie polskiej przewodniczył kierujący… pic.twitter.com/qHpZwLeCEa
— Instytut Pamięci Narodowej (@ipngovpl) October 14, 2026
News of the meeting was announced on social media by Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), which noted that it was “the first direct, working meeting between the heads of these institutions since 2018”.
The IPN is currently headed by its deputy president, Karol Polejowski, because Poland’s parliament has been unable to agree on a permanent new president. The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) is led by Oleksandr Alfyorov.
“The first topic of discussion,” according to the IPN, was the planned reburial of 115 Polish soldiers recently exhumed in Lviv, where they died in 1939 defending the city (then part of Poland and known as Lwów) during the Nazi-German and Soviet invasions.
Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026
Their exhumation resulted from a diplomatic breakthrough last year between Warsaw and Kyiv that saw Ukraine lift a moratorium on exhumations that had been in place since 2017 in protest at the dismantling in Poland of a monument to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
Ukraine has also allowed the exhumation on its territory of Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, which were led by the UPA. Poland likewise recently granted permission for Ukraine to search for Ukrainian victims of a massacre led by the Polish Home Army in the village of Łasków (Laskiv in Ukrainian).
At this week’s meeting, the UINR gave an update on its work in Łasków, where it has uncovered the remains of 30 people.
The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance has found 30 human remains in a village in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians in WW2
It thanked Poland for permission to search the site, calling it a step towards "true reconciliation" https://t.co/BeeEtl6gCa
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026
The IPN and UINR also discussed planned exhumation work in the now-depopulated village of Huta Pieniacka (Huta Peniatska in Ukrainian), where the local Polish population was massacred in 1944 by a Nazi SS regiment mainly made up of Ukrainians.
There was also “willingness on both sides to restore cooperation in the field of historical scientific research”, said the IPN. “The possibility of undertaking joint educational initiatives was also discussed.” The two sides also agreed to hold another meeting in Warsaw, though no date has been set.
This week’s meeting comes after a period of tension over historical issues between not only Poland and Ukraine more broadly, but also the two countries’ remembrance institutes.
In February this year, the IPN criticised Alfyorov over an interview in which he initially called the Volhynia massacres “one of Poland’s state myths”, before later appearing to correct himself and saying it was “not a myth, but one of the key elements of the Polish grand narrative”.
By contrast, “for most Ukrainians, this is just a local episode of history”, added Alfyorov. Referring to Poland’s recognition of the massacres as a genocide – a term Ukraine rejects – he asked if Polish massacres of around 28,000 Ukrainians during the war should also be called a genocide.
In response, the IPN called Alfyorov’s remarks “outrageous” and declared that the Volhynia massacres were “not an ‘episode’, but rather one of the largest genocides against civilians in 20th-century Europe”. It also condemned Ukraine for honouring figures associated with the massacres.
The UINR, for its part, criticised a law proposed by Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki (a former head of the IPN), that would criminalise the promotion of ideologies associated with World War Two Ukrainian nationalist groups.
Ukraine has criticised a law proposed by Poland's president that would criminalise promotion of historical Ukrainian nationalist ideologies, equating them with Nazism and communism
It warns of "retaliatory measures" if the bill is passed https://t.co/TaX2Vj5z8v
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2025
In another sign of reconciliation, in May the UINR and Poland’s Mieroszewski Centre held a historical congress in Warsaw, bringing together more than 100 historians “to discuss complex issues of the shared past and explore common approaches to their interpretation”, in the words of the Ukrainian foreign ministry.
However, that same month, President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted a diplomatic crisis by approving the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the UPA”. That prompted Nawrocki to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle.
Since then, both sides have made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”.

Feature: Where trees take root, friendship grows
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:30:44 CST
18:30:44 KST

ROME, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- When Chinese sand-control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was named one of the 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) on Thursday evening, retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky was there to share the moment.
Sitting in the audience, Sakolsky grew teary-eyed as he applauded Yin's achievement. Later, he was invited to join Yin on stage. The two friends embraced once again and held up an award together. "Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," he told Xinhua.
For him, the recognition was about more than Yin's achievements in combating desertification. It was also a celebration of a friendship that had spanned more than two decades, crossing continents, languages and cultures.
Their story began in 1999, when Sakolsky, who came from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, was teaching English at a school in central China's Henan Province under a teacher exchange program between the two countries.
One evening, a television program caught his attention. It showed Yin planting trees to hold back the encroaching sands of the Maowusu sandy land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.
Maowusu spans parts of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Ningxia in northern China and has long been a major front in the country's desertification control. It lies within the Three-North Shelterbelt Program, launched in 1978 and scheduled to run through 2050.
Watching Yin's efforts, Sakolsky was deeply moved. "I was so touched that I started to cry," he recalled. "I honestly cannot tell you why. Something just happened to me. I just felt like I needed to help."
Inspired by Yin's determination, he raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her and her husband in planting trees. Today, the saplings purchased with the donation have grown into more than 50,000 trees.
More than two decades later, their connection was rekindled. In May this year, Yin turned to social media in search of the American teacher who had helped her years earlier. In late August, Sakolsky returned to Inner Mongolia at her invitation.
The reunion brought back memories of the landscape he had first seen in 2000, when sand dominated the scene. This time, the transformation was striking.
"When I went back this year, it was like a mother and father seeing their children," Sakolsky said. "When I was there in 2000, there was all sand, just sand; now it was all green. Everywhere was green. It was beautiful."
Their reunion in China was not the end of the story. Less than two months later, the two met again, this time in Rome, where they attended the World Food Forum, hosted by FAO.
On Tuesday night, after a busy day, Sakolsky returned to his hotel carrying gifts for Yin and her family. Dressed in a red Tang-style jacket, he proudly showed off the cloth shoes Yin had given him earlier.
"They are perfect. She did not know what size my feet are, but she made the perfect fit," he said, giving two thumbs up.
Yin had also prepared a dark gray suit specially tailored for him, two bilingual magazines documenting their story, and a delicate porcelain tea set from Jingdezhen, a city in east China's Jiangxi Province renowned for its porcelain.
"Sakolsky, whom I regard as an elder brother, and I had not seen each other for 26 years. I never thought that just over two months later, we would meet again here," said Yin.
Sakolsky, in turn, had brought gifts for Yin's family: a miniature set of footballs for her grandson, Halloween-themed mugs for her granddaughter, and a T-shirt bearing the University of Pittsburgh logo for her son.
He also gave Yin a sweatshirt bearing the logo of his hometown football team in Pittsburgh.
The gifts were thoughtful tokens of a bond that had grown far beyond their initial encounter. Though they came from different countries and spoke different languages, they had found a way to understand and care for each other.
"We do not speak the same language; we do not look the same, but we are brother and sister, and we understand each other," Sakolsky said.
Their friendship has also resonated far beyond the two individuals. Yin sees their friendship as a reflection of the need for international cooperation in environmental protection.
"It is like the vision of a community with a shared future for humanity proposed by China. Although we come from different countries, we live on the same planet," she said. "We must unite to cherish nature and protect our planet."
In remarks at a state dinner hosted by U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House in September, Chinese President Xi Jinping mentioned their story, saying it "touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between our two peoples."
For Sakolsky, hearing his name mentioned by the Chinese president was almost beyond belief.
"When I heard President Xi mention my name, I thought I went crazy. I'm just a simple social studies teacher who did something nice. And he knows me. I could not believe it," he said.
But the recognition, he said, carried a message far greater than his own story.
"That tells you that the message has been heard: America and China must build a bridge for the world to get better," he added. ■

China to adjust train numbering system, add X-series for higher-speed trains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:30:31 CST
18:30:31 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- China will adjust its national train numbering system and introduce a new "X" series for future trains with maximum operating speeds above 350 km/h, China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway) announced on Friday.
The change will be implemented in two batches in late November and late December. China Railway said train services will continue to operate according to the current timetable after the adjustment.
China's newest high-speed train, the Fuxing CR450 electric multiple unit (EMU), which has a maximum test speed of 450 km/h and an operating speed of 400 km/h, has passed all type tests by March 2026, said Zhao Hongwei, chief researcher at the China Academy of Railway Sciences Corporation Limited (CARS). It is currently the world's fastest high-speed train by operating speed.
The CR450 achieves this speed while consuming about as much electricity as existing high-speed trains. Zhao noted that at 400 km/h, the CR450 uses less than 22 kWh per kilometer, while data from CARS show that 350 km/h high-speed trains use 19.5 to 23.5 kWh per kilometer.
Under China Railway's numbering system, prefix letters indicate a train's speed category or service type. After the adjustment, the new X-series will be used for trains with maximum operating speeds above 350 km/h, while the G, T and K series will denote trains with maximum operating speeds of 350 km/h, 300 km/h and 200-250 km/h, respectively.
In recent years, China's railway network has continued to expand, and the number of train services has grown significantly. From 2014 to 2025, the number of 300-350 km/h high-speed train sets increased by 209 percent, from 1,018 to 3,149 standard sets. Against this backdrop, some train number series are approaching the limits of available number ranges, a key issue the adjustment aims to address.
According to a railway science and technology innovation plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) issued on Monday, China will plan no fewer than 20 typical application scenarios or demonstration projects in areas such as the 400 km/h high-speed train operating system. ■

EU will probably have to give new loan to Ukraine, Estonian PM Michal says

China's R&D spending up 8.2 pct in 2025
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:30:12 CST
18:30:12 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- China's research and development (R&D) expenditure rose 8.2 percent year on year to 3.93 trillion yuan (about 584.5 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) said on Friday.
Over the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-2025), the country's R&D spending rose at an average annual rate of 10 percent, and China now ranks as the world's second-largest R&D investor, said Luo Qiushi, an NBS statistician.
China's R&D intensity, which measures spending as a share of GDP, rose 0.11 percentage points to 2.8 percent last year, exceeding the OECD average of 2.72 percent for the first time and ranking 12th in the world.
By type of R&D activity, spending on basic research, applied research and experimental development grew 13.3 percent, 3.2 percent and 8.4 percent year on year to 283.46 billion yuan, 444.16 billion yuan and 3.2 trillion yuan, respectively.
In 2025, the growth rate of funding for basic research exceeded that of R&D expenditure by 5.1 percentage points, maintaining double-digit growth momentum.
Currently, China ranks second globally in total funding for basic research.
Enterprise R&D spending exceeded 3 trillion yuan for the first time, accounting for 77.4 percent of the total.
Enterprises have accounted for more than 77 percent of the country's total R&D spending for four consecutive years, and their contribution to the overall increase reached 73.7 percent, cementing their role as the main engine of China's R&D spending expansion, according to the NBS.
In 2025, government-affiliated research institutions and higher education institutions accounted for 11.6 percent and 8.7 percent, respectively, of the total R&D spending, with proportions roughly unchanged from the previous year.
Regional innovation hubs played a prominent role. In 2025, R&D expenditure in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Yangtze River Delta, and Guangdong reached 536.82 billion yuan, 1.22 trillion yuan, and 551.04 billion yuan, respectively, representing year-on-year increases of 10.3 percent, 8.7 percent, and 8.1 percent.
The combined R&D spending of these three major innovation hubs accounted for 58.8 percent of the national total, up 0.4 percentage points from the previous year.
In 2025, the national fiscal expenditure on science and technology reached 1.32 trillion yuan, an increase of 55.53 billion yuan, or 4.4 percent, year on year.
Of this total, central and local fiscal spending on science and technology amounted to 447.32 billion yuan and 871.12 billion yuan respectively, accounting for 33.9 percent and 66.1 percent of the total national fiscal science and technology expenditure.
Overall, in 2025, the scale of R&D funding continued to expand, with a rapid increase in the proportion allocated to basic research, according to Luo.
Looking ahead, efforts will be intensified to increase total R&D expenditure, consolidate inclusive policies in the field of scientific and technological innovation, and establish a science and technology finance system that aligns with innovation needs, Luo said.
It is essential to effectively leverage fiscal funding as a guiding force in science and technology investment, improve the diversified investment structure, and provide a solid guarantee for accelerating the advancement of high-level self-reliance and strength in science and technology, Luo added. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's economy grew 5.3 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, slowing from 6 percent in the preceding quarter, according to advance estimates released on Friday.
Growth was supported by positive performances across all economic sectors except mining and quarrying, which contracted during the quarter, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said in a statement.
For the first nine months of 2026, the economy expanded 5.5 percent, accelerating from 4.8 percent in the corresponding period a year earlier.
The services sector remained the main driver of growth, expanding 5.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with 5.9 percent in the preceding quarter.

The agriculture sector rebounded, growing 1.3 percent after contracting 3.7 percent in the preceding quarter.
In contrast, the mining and quarrying sector contracted 4.9 percent, reversing 9.2 percent growth in the preceding quarter. ■

Study finds enriching life experiences may ease impacts of trauma on aging brain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:29:59 CST
18:29:59 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- An Australian study has found that developing cognitive reserve via enriching life experiences could reduce overall cognitive and psychological impacts of traumatic experiences in later life.
The study, involving 745 adults aged 50 to 86, explored the effect of traumatic events on cognitive function. Participants completed several assessments to measure their traumatic event exposure, post-traumatic stress symptoms and cognitive performance, according to a statement released recently by Australia's Adelaide University.
About 87 percent of participants reported at least one direct traumatic experience, said Sabrina Sghirripa, a researcher at Adelaide University and lead author of the study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders.
"However, not everyone who experiences trauma develops cognitive deficits in later life, suggesting protective factors, including cognitive reserve, may promote resilience," Sghirripa said.
Researchers found that people with higher cognitive reserve were less likely to be affected by post-traumatic stress symptoms and maintained better cognition in the face of exposure to traumatic events.
Cognitive reserve refers to the brain's adaptability in maintaining cognitive abilities as it ages. It can be built throughout life by enriching experiences such as education and leisure activities, the study showed.
The findings suggest that developing cognitive reserve may help reduce the cognitive and psychological impacts of trauma, Sghirripa said, adding that interventions like leisure activities and social engagement could benefit older members of the community in building cognitive reserve.
"Staying socially connected and engaged in meaningful activities may help protect cognitive and mental health in later life," even among people who have had many adverse life experiences, she said. ■

EU leaders demand joint action to tackle soaring energy prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:28:19 UTC
18:28:19 KST

EU leaders are pressing Brussels for coordinated measures to ease soaring energy costs, bolster fuel supplies and support struggling industries, as the crisis strains national budgets and tests the bloc's climate ambitions.
EU leaders have called for a coordinated European response to the energy crisis, urging the European Commission to introduce targeted, temporary measures to ease the burden on households and businesses, including extending financial support to industries hardest hit by soaring energy prices.
After European Council summit negotiations that went into the night on Thursday, the leaders also raised concerns about the security of energy supplies, asking the Commission to improve the capacity and efficiency of European oil refineries, which have been in decline since 2009.
They also expressed interest in exploring voluntary joint energy purchasing, similar to the platform launched by the Commission to help replace Russian gas supplies following Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
The calls came amid a severe energy crisis threatening European industry and leaving millions of households at risk of energy poverty this winter.
Rising energy prices and inflation rates have prompted several EU capitals to ask the European Commission for more support.
Italy and Greece recently urged Brussels to allow for extra spending without incurring infringements due to the extraordinary circumstances posed by the energy shock.
Diesel markets are expected to remain tight well into 2027, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on 14 October, and wholesale diesel prices in Europe could rise again in the coming weeks.
Diesel prices have retreated from September’s records above $200 a barrel, but benchmarks "remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their pre-crisis levels", the IEA stated.
EU countries received in May the green light from the Commission to offer direct financial support to the hardest-hit, energy-intensive sectors, including farmers, heavy manufacturing, and haulers. But as the energy crisis lingers, public funds shrink.
Greece’s PM Kyriakos Mitsotais called for a coordinated EU response rather than relying solely on national measures.
“Energy costs have fueled a new surge in European inflation,” he said on Thursday, arguing that Brussels must consider “additional measures and further flexibility” to help the most vulnerable households and businesses.
The Greek leader cautioned that negotiations would take time, saying he did not expect a deal “today or tomorrow”.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo has also called for immediate action from the EU to address soaring energy prices.
"We need short-term measures because we have to guarantee cheap prices for people and companies," he said.
Energy crisis squeezing finances
The measures are intended to cushion the immediate economic impact of the crisis, but they also expose the limits of EU governments’ ability to insulate their economies from geopolitical shocks.
Desmond Lawrence, senior investment strategist at the US asset manager State Street Investment Management, warned on 14 October that France and Belgium are slowly heading towards an unsustainable debt burden.
The shockwaves from the escalation in the Middle East have renewed concerns about disruptions to energy supplies and strategic shipping routes, particularly the Strait of Hormuz. Ukraine's military strikes on Russian refineries are also aggravating the fuel crisis.
EU leaders warned that the Middle East crisis risks causing lasting disruption to global supply chains, especially for energy, fertilisers and food — a predicament that may stretch the Commission's "targeted and temporary" measures indefinitely.
Such a scenario adds another headache to ongoing political talks on the bloc's next multi-annual budget, which was recently met with backlash from net contributors Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden for being overly ambitious.
The outcome of the talks will influence the EU's energy transition goals, which the Commission stands by as the most effective way to strengthen strategic autonomy and lower energy prices in the long term.
However, EU leaders also welcomed the Commission's proposal to delay one-year monitoring and reporting methane rules for oil and gas importers.
The decision was criticised by environmentalists who argued its revenues could range from roughly €5.3 billion to €13.6 billion under standard market pricing, spiking even higher during supply crises.
The proposal follows pressure from French President Emmanuel Macron, industry and the United States, the EU's biggest supplier of liquefied natural gas (LNG). It still requires approval by the European Parliament.

Fed’s Warsh sees AI boosting productivity but gives no signal on next rate hike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:27:55 UTC
18:27:55 KST

US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said in Bangkok on Friday that the global economy has proved surprisingly resilient and called AI the most consequential change of his lifetime, but gave no hint on interest rates ahead of the Fed’s meeting this month.
The global economy has held up better than Kevin Warsh would have predicted earlier this year, the US central bank chief said on Friday, calling AI the biggest economic shift he had seen.
Speaking in Bangkok at the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, Warsh offered no clue on the Federal Reserve’s next rate decision, due on 28 October.
Almost everywhere, the economy is showing a resilience "I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago," Warsh said in a discussion on stage with IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva.
The Fed chair was most upbeat about the US, stating during the event that a broadening investment surge that "isn’t just AI" had given the economy "plenty of tailwinds", momentum "certainly not found everywhere in the world".
Energy prices have soared since the US and Israel went to war with Iran in late February. This, along with an AI investment boom, has fuelled inflation in many economies, forcing central banks to raise rates.
The Fed, which has seen inflation run above its 2% target for over five years, raised rates by a quarter point to 3.75-4% in September, its first hike since July 2023.
"At the Federal Reserve, we made very clear that we would deliver price stability," argued Warsh, who took over as chair in May.
He said he had heard the same "resolve" from central bankers in Bangkok, calling the wave of rate hikes, including two by the European Central Bank, a "synchronous tightening" that leaves "no free riders".
The IMF on Tuesday nudged up its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1% but said risks were tilted to the downside. Rich countries also face soaring borrowing costs, with the 10-year US bond yield above 5% and the French bond yield trading around 4.8% at the time of writing.
A 'bumpy' road for AI
Much of Friday's discussion focused on AI, which Warsh said was "probably the most consequential change" for the US and global economies in his lifetime.
Before taking office, he had argued that an AI-driven productivity boom could curb inflation and make room for lower interest rates. On Friday, he acknowledged that for now, the investment frenzy was pushing prices up by fuelling demand.
Minutes of the Fed's September meeting noted that data centre construction had driven up the cost of chips, computer equipment and electrical components.
However, over time, Warsh expects AI to boost the economy’s capacity to produce, bringing a "huge benefit" at home and abroad.
He also expects it to change central banking as "we torture data with old-fashioned models," he said. "Not so long from now, it won’t be torture."
Despite the optimism, the Fed chair also warned that the road ahead was "likely to be a very bumpy one", both in understanding the technology and because "we really don’t know what the market structure is going to be".
Eyes on the next Federal Reserve meeting
Warsh, who has promised fewer hints about where policy is heading, kept to that pledge.
"I don’t prejudge meetings," he said, though he noted the world had "broadly conformed" to the Fed’s expectations since September.
US consumer price inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% as petrol prices surged, though core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was 2.6%.
Wholesale prices rose 6.3% year on year, the most since 2022, while the economy added just 29,000 jobs last month.
Bets on an October hike have swung this week, jumping from about 22% to around 50% after Wednesday’s inflation figures before falling back to about 30%, according to CME FedWatch, a tool that tracks market pricing.
Markets currently put the chance of a December hike at around 90%, while the September minutes showed that most Fed officials expect another hike this year.
New York Fed President John Williams, vice chair of the Fed’s committee, told Bloomberg on Tuesday that "it may be appropriate to have one more rate hike", but saw no need for more in 2027.
On the other hand, Fed Governor Michelle Bowman said at the Bangkok meetings on Wednesday that she felt no urgency to act.
The decision comes days before the 3 November US midterm elections.
September’s hike defied US President Donald Trump’s demands for lower rates, though he still backs Warsh, his pick for the job.
Friday’s remarks were among Warsh’s last before the Fed’s quiet period, which starts on Saturday and bars officials from discussing policy until after the meeting. Investors will next hear from him at his press conference after the decision.

Will Mathis, commanding officer of Theodore Roosevelt. “Port visits like this are vital for crew morale and mission readiness, allowing our Sailors to rest, recharge, and prepare to operate seamlessly alongside our allies during exercise Keen Sword.”
While in port, staff from Carrier Strike Group 9 will hold professional exchanges with officers from the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force to align tactical procedures ahead of the exercise, which the U.S. Navy refers to as Keen Sword 2027. Keen Sword is held every two years and is designed to improve how Japanese and U.S. forces train, plan and fight together. The U.S. Navy did not give dates for this year’s exercise or say how many ships and aircraft will take part.
“The U.S.-Japan Alliance serves as the cornerstone of peace and security across the region,” said Rear Adm. Marcos Jasso, commander of Carrier Strike Group 9. “Every engagement with our JMSDF allies and the Japan community deepens the mutual trust vital to keeping this region free and open, especially as we transition to complex bilateral operations during Keen Sword.”
Before the visit, commanders reminded crews that they are expected to keep good order and discipline, follow the liberty policy and treat their Japanese hosts with respect. U.S. forces in Japan have tightened liberty rules in recent years after incidents involving service members, particularly on Okinawa, drew criticism from Japanese officials.
Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class carrier, carries an air wing of fighter jets, early warning aircraft, electronic attack jets and helicopters. Chosin is a Ticonderoga-class guided-missile cruiser and Decatur an Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, both armed with the Aegis air defense system and vertical launch cells for air defense and strike missiles.
The strike group is conducting routine operations in the U.S. 7th Fleet area, which covers the western Pacific and Indian Ocean, and will move from the Yokosuka port visit into bilateral operations with Japanese forces during Keen Sword.

Clashes erupt at Argentine student protests
October 16, 2026
Protesters took to the streets in Argentina's capital, Buenos Aires, to demonstrate against libertarian President Javier Milei's cost-cutting measures for education.
Thousands of students, university staff, trade unionists and opposition supporters crowded outside the parliament, demanding the implementation of a law to finance universities.
While the rally was largely peaceful, clashes also erupted, with reports of masked individuals throwing stones at police, injuring at least eight officers. Some 25 people were arrested, according to the country's National Security Ministry.
Reports said other protesters had tried to push those throwing stones back. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva said the protesters wanted to "sow chaos," posting on her X account that the right to protest is not "a right to exercise violence."
Milei vetoes law, refuses to release funding
This was the fifth protest over the Milei government's education spending to take place since Milei entered office in 2023.Such a demonstration also took place in May, in which organizers say some 1.5 million people took part.
Milei vetoed a law, passed by Congress in 2025, requiring the government to invest more money in public universities.
The University Funding Law says the state should increase employees' salaries in line with inflation dated to December 2023. It also calls for the restoration of student scholarships and more funding for universities' operations.
Congress subsequently overrode Milei's veto, and several court rulings have instructed the government to release the funds, but it has so far refused to do so.
According to Milei, who was elected after promising wide-ranging cost-cutting measures, justified his veto by saying "there is no money" for inflation-linked spending increases.
A government spokesperson said the law had been "suspended" due to the government's legal action against it.
The first half of 2026 saw public spending on universities fall by 41% in real terms, according to the Center for National Economic Research of the University of Buenos Aires.
Argentina's education system is considered to be among the best in South America. Study at public universities is free, drawing students from across the region.

Romania resumes search for seven missing sailors from drone-hit ship
BUCHAREST, Oct 16 - Romania resumed a search on Friday for seven sailors missing from a chemical tanker hit by a drone near its Black Sea coast, the latest in a series of attacks highlighting risks to commercial shipping near NATO's eastern flank.
The missing crew were among 12 sailors aboard the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader, which was struck early on Thursday about a mile outside Romanian territorial waters. Five crew members were rescued, but efforts to find the others have been hampered by strong winds and rough seas.
"Our colleagues returned today to search the ship and continue the mission to identify the rest of the crew," an interior ministry spokesperson told Reuters.
Officials said a Black Hawk helicopter would place four rescuers aboard the vessel while a ship continued searching nearby waters.
The Wine Trader was one of two tankers hit by drones within about 12 hours near Romania's Black Sea coast.
The second vessel, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, was struck inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday. Its crew were unharmed and the ship was towed to the port of Constanta.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones, while a NATO military source said the drones came from Russia.
The attacks have intensified concerns about the spillover of the Russia-Ukraine war into Black Sea shipping lanes. Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is a key export route for Ukraine.
At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria in the past 10 days, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents occurred outside NATO territorial waters.
Bulgaria has asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its sea capacities, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday. Romania's president said the country had also asked for additional equipment. REUTERS

Israeli settlers burn olive trees, injure journalist in West Bank attack

- Witnesses said about 80 settlers used gas canisters and slings, while Israeli military jeeps arrived and soldiers fired tear gas. Reuters also saw at least one armed settler fire a gun.
- The attack adds to a surge in settler violence, with Yesh Din reporting at least 170 attacks since Sept 27. The violence has drawn international condemnation and pressure on Netanyahu’s government.
AI generated
ABU FALAH, West Bank – Clad in black and their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on Oct 16 on a West Bank village’s annual harvest that injured at least two people including a journalist.
Some 80 settlers, some of them carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill above a terraced olive grove where villagers from Abu Falah had gathered to pick ripe fruit, a cherished annual tradition in Palestinian life, Reuters witnesses said.
The settlers took positions in front of the terraced lanes of olive trees. Some of them used slings to launch rocks towards Palestinian villagers, who descended towards the bottom of the hill before picking up and throwing stones to defend themselves.
“The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the attack in Abu Falah.
Partway through the attack, at least two Israeli military jeeps sped through the area, kicking up dust as villagers ran out of their way.
The attack continued after the military’s arrival, with Israeli soldiers firing tear gas in the direction of the Palestinians who had dodged the jeeps. The sound of live gunfire could be heard in the area, and a Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a gun.
In a statement, the Israeli military said soldiers and border police fired what it described as warning shots after deploying to the area and at one point fired towards a person who the troops believed had posed a threat.
“Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area,” the military said. “Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable,” it added.
Washington Post journalist injured
Palestinian medics said two people were injured and taken to hospitals in the area of Ramallah. One of them was Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post. Videos of the attack showed Levine lying on her side on a dirt path with her hands over her face as at least three settlers surrounded her.
Speaking from a hospital bed later, Levine, who is in stable condition, said: “I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me.”
Levine said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened, after which medics rushed her in an ambulance to a clinic in Abu Falah and then to hospital in Ramallah.
Her voice shook as she spoke and she had bandages over her left hand. The Washington Post later reported she suffered lacerations across her body and a broken rib, and would need surgery on one hand after a finger was ripped open, exposing bone.
In a statement, Matt Murray, the Washington Post’s executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident.
“This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said.
“She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities.”
The US State Department said it condemned criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and supported holding the perpetrators accountable.
“The Department of State is aware of these reports. We are greatly concerned when any American is harmed overseas and stand ready to provide all appropriate consular assistance,” a department spokesperson said.
The department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance, he added.
Settler violence has surged in West Bank
Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has surged, with at least 170 attacks since Sept 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.
The settlers have been emboldened by the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has overseen a rapid expansion of settlements and smaller outposts across the West Bank.
Netanyahu has criticised the violence but has taken few steps to crack down on incidents that have drawn international condemnation and sanction plans by longtime Israeli allies, including Britain.
In a statement, Netanyahu’s office said the incident was under investigation.
The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians. UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
The Abu Falah attack followed a similar attack on the morning of Oct 16 in the area of Turmus Ayya village, where settlers burned three cars after attacking a group of farmers harvesting olives. The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack in Turmus Ayya, said the settlers “snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him”. REUTERS

German MPs clash over colonial genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:22:55 UTC
18:22:55 KST

German MPs clash over colonial genocide
German lawmakers have clashed over demands for reparations for the killing of tens of thousands of Africans in colonial-era Namibia in what is widely regarded as the first genocide of the 20th century.
The Bundestag debated opposition motions on Wednesday seeking recognition, an apology and redress for the Ovaherero and Nama communities. Both proposals were referred to the German Foreign Affairs Committee for further consideration.
Germany ruled present-day Namibia from 1884 to 1915. Between 1904 and 1908, its forces waged an extermination campaign against the Ovaherero and Nama, driving families into the desert and imprisoning survivors in concentration camps. Estimates suggest that up to 80% of the Ovaherero and about half the Nama died.
Berlin recognized the atrocities as genocide in 2021 and pledged €1.1 billion ($1.23 billion) over 30 years for reconstruction and development. It, however, explicitly ruled out legal compensation claims arising from the arrangement.
Christian Democratic Union lawmaker Thomas Rachel criticized the German government’s prolonged failure to confront the atrocities.
“I am still ashamed today in the face of the indescribable suffering inflicted on people at that time… One might note that it took a long time before the German federal government recognized the horrific atrocities in Namibia as genocide,” Rachel told the legislature.
Green MP Jamila Schafer urged parliament to “explicitly recognize the genocide against the Ovaherero and Nama, as well as colonial crimes committed against the Damara and San, and ask their descendants for forgiveness.”
Alternative for Germany MP Ronald Glaser opposed the €1.1 billion commitment, arguing that Berlin had no legal obligation to pay. He called for a commission of historians to investigate the events.
The Left’s motion sought recognition of legal liability and comprehensive reparations paid directly to descendants, alongside measures to return land, looted cultural property and human remains.
Ovaherero and Nama representatives have rejected development funding as a substitute for reparations and say they were excluded from negotiations. Germany maintains that community representatives were involved on the Namibian side.
The dispute comes amid growing African and Caribbean demands for redress for slavery and colonial crimes. The African Union has designated 2026–2035 a reparations decade and established expert bodies to develop a common continental position and legal strategies. The Caribbean Community has revised its ten-point reparations plan, seeking measures including monetary compensation, debt cancellation and investment in health and education.
On March 25, the UN General Assembly adopted a Ghana-led resolution declaring the trafficking and racialized enslavement of Africans “the gravest crime against humanity” and calling for reparations. The measure secured support from 123 countries, including Russia and China, while the US, Israel, and Argentina voted against the resolution, and the UK and all the EU states abstained.
