‘A direct cultural threat’: your questions on the rise of the right across Europe answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

Support for far-right parties has been growing across Europe, with radical right, populist parties in coalition governments in Croatia, Czechia, Italy and Finland, and leading in the polls in Austria, Belgium, France and Germany.
The Guardian reported this year that nearly a quarter of voters in Europe voted for far-right parties in their most recent national elections, a fivefold increase since 1995.
In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland recently booked a historic state election victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Elsewhere, though – in the Netherlands, in Hungary and in Sweden, where the Sweden Democrats lost vote share – far-right parties have suffered defeats. But their ideas – and their influence on mainstream politics – are today clearly visible across the continent, notably on policies around immigration and law-and-order.
The coming months will see further crucial elections, beginning in Spain in November and continuing in France, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Slovakia, Poland and Italy next year.
How might these elections shape the political future of Europe? What is the impact of their policies – and what might prevent their continuing rise?
The Guardian’s Europe correspondent Jon Henley has reported for the Guardian from 23 of the EU’s 27 member states, while Europe community affairs correspondent Ashifa Kassam was on the ground in Sweden and Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state to speak with people ahead of the elections.
Jon and Ashifa answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below.
One user asked: It’s no secret in Europe that Donald Trump and his allies are funding far-right parties all over the continent. Trump is unpopular enough in Europe that even the majority of people planning to vote for the AfD et al despise him. So how can so many Europeans who hate Trump still vote for the far right?
Jon Henley: You’re absolutely right about the Trump administration’s efforts to promote far right parties in Europe. That was made very plain in the US National Security Strategy policy document last year – I wrote about that here.
But while there may be an ideological affinity between European far right and nationalist voters on issues like anti-immigration, hostility toward the EU, and softer stances on Russia, Trump’s “America First” policies (demands re Greenland, tariff threats, etc.) and constant unpredictability pose major problems for far-right leaders trying to look credible in Europe, because they scare all European voters – including far-right voters.
Leaders including Giorgia Meloni in Italy and Marine Le Pen in France have openly criticised Trump and distanced themselves from his more erratic pronouncements, conspiracy claims and hostility toward European security.
European far-right voters’ support for Trump varies from country to country but is broadly low – clearly peace and security in Europe matter more than anti-immigration sentiment. Ultimately, nation-first means putting your nation first, and Trump has made clear that the US’s interests are not Europe’s interests.
The evidence would seem to suggest that many of Europe’s far-right voters think their own far-right parties will be more responsible as regards (many of) those issues – though whether they actually will be or not is moot, of course.
00000000000000000000 asked: How do you measure when a grassroots movement represents a genuine structural shift versus an isolated vocal minority?
Ashifa Kassam: Our jobs involve covering a wide range of community actions, whether it’s people fighting back against datacentres, protests against tourism, or the vandalisation of mobile phone masts by people who seemingly linked them to the coronavirus pandemic.
Oftentimes the reporting starts small and local. For example, perhaps it’s focused tightly on a protest against tourists in Barcelona or a push to restrict cruise ship dockings in Dubrovnik. From there, myself and the editors often continue to watch these movements and their reach; are politicians responding in any way? Are others joining in? Will the movements lead to policy changes? These are the kinds of questions that I tend to consider when deciding how much to make of the grassroots movements and how much coverage to give them.
At times it’s been incredible to see just where these movements will go, whether it’s the housing protests in Spain that led to snap general elections or the opposition movement that coalesced around Péter Magyar in Hungary in 2024 and which, more than a year later, saw him oust Viktor Orbán from power.
Gramoun-kal asked: Can the EU survive the rise of the extreme right? What if AfD and RN get into power at the same time?
Jon Henley: One of the very few upsides of Brexit is that hardly any European far right parties now want their countries to leave the EU. Instead, they want to “transform it from within”, turning it more into a looser “Europe of nations”.
But that’s not to say the EU would not be considerably weakened by, say, a President Le Pen, who could paralyse decision-making, challenge the supremacy of EU law and push a “France First” agenda undermining the single market and Schengen free-travel zone and opposing EU expansion, climate action, etc.
I’m not sure there’s any imminent risk of the AfD coming to national power in Germany (and if Le Pen wins France’s presidential election, which isn’t certain but looks highly plausible, she is also unlikely to have a parliamentary majority, which will limit her room for manoeuvre).
Plus, the AfD is too extreme even for the RN – Le Pen’s outfit (which kicked the AfD out of its European parliament grouping a while ago over various issues including comments to the effect that not all Nazis were bad), has repeatedly made it clear it is not an ally of the German party and does not share its views on eg. “remigration” – the mass deportation of immigrants.
But for sure – if Spain, Italy, France and Poland all see far-right parties in government after elections due over the next 12 months or so, the EU will face some major challenges. I don’t think it will collapse, but it will certainly find it even harder to reach agreement on many major issues than it already does, and so move (even) more slowly. Natalie Tocci wrote a great comment piece about this.
OrangeSpaceMan5 asked: Do you see Nato and the EU disintegrating if we see Far-Right victories across Britain, Germany and France?
Jon Henley: No, I don’t see the EU and Nato disintegrating, just becoming a lot more complicated/difficult to run … The EU could be “eroded from within” above all by far right-led governments using their veto (as Orbán did with Hungary) in major decisions like the EU budget, EU enlargement, the green deal, etc. They may well also simply ignore EU law, as Orbán also did. And for Nato, see previous answer – it would survive but become more paralysed in terms of longer term decision making.
Ashifa Kassam: I think we saw a glimpse of how complicated things can become in the European parliament after an EU vote earlier this year aimed at increasing deportations. The immediate aftermath laid bare just how deeply polarised the EU has already become, as right-wing MEPs chanted “send them back” and centre-left and left-wing MEPs shot back with “Shame on you.”
ElendX asked: Why and how have the left and centre parties failed to respond to the concerns of the electorate? How do they now need to respond?
Ashifa Kassam: What comes to mind immediately is the housing crisis in Spain and beyond. It’s been just over two weeks now since the Spanish protests and encampments over the housing crisis burst into public view, laying bare the long-simmering anger over soaring housing costs.
I think it’s an issue that has long been overlooked by many left and centre parties across Europe, even as vulnerable people and minorities have been disproportionately affected, and analysts warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. Last year I spoke to Jaume Collboni, the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, who (along with 21 mayors across Europe) are urging the EU to treat the surging housing costs as a “new pandemic” by unleashing billions in funding to boost affordable housing and give mayors a seat at the table to ensure measures capable of tackling housing speculation. Speaking to me, Collboni warned: “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse.”
I also think left and centre parties have done little to address the precariousness of the labour market, ie. the rise of gig jobs and, in many cases, the deterioration of public services. If you keep an eye on the Eurobarometer, the cost of living constantly ranks among the top concerns for people across Europe, hinting at the idea that this could be fertile territory for politicians to focus on. Immigration, in contrast, was in 7th place in the most recent survey.
Jon Henley: I think broadly speaking mainstream parties have failed to adequately address people’s concerns about the cost of living, declining public services (healthcare, education, transport), economic/job security, etc. – as I said above, fear of/anger at some kind of “loss of status” is one of the key drivers of the far right vote. (I’m not suggesting that’s easy – it clearly isn’t, economies are struggling.)
I’d also add that far-right parties are clearly extremely effective at exploiting voters’ concerns politically, including by pointing the finger at the group they think are most to blame and promising to fix things by getting rid of them.
And I’d also note that mainstream parties really have not helped themselves by adopting far-right parties’ framing on several issues in hopes of hanging on to disillusioned voters – electoral evidence shows that almost never works, mainly because, as Marine Le Pen’s father Jean-Marie put it, people tend to prefer the original to the copy.
Dc740 asked: Did you measure any change in online activity for extremist parties like Vox in Spain after the Yandex datacentre was targeted by Ukraine?
Ashifa Kassam: Funny you should ask – earlier this week, I sent out queries on this to several research groups, so it’s something we’re looking into. It’s a really interesting question. Last week, in an interview with news site Eldiario.es, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez was asked whether he was worried about foreign interference in the elections given his high profile opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and the US-Israeli attack on Iran. His answer: “Yes, and not only by nations, but also by non-state actors.”
Capitao_barbosa asked: How much foreign funding, especially from Russia and America, is being funnelled to these parties? And can we value how much indirect support (bots, disinformation by state actors, algorithm meddling on X, etc.) they are receiving?
Jon Henley: Our data team looked at this question a couple of years ago, before the last European parliament elections. They concluded a quarter of all private money donated to political parties in the EU was going to far-right, far-left and populist movements – aided by the fact that only a quarter of EU countries require parties to identify private donors – with €97m (about one in every seven private donation euros across the EU) going to far-right parties.
A European parliament report from 2023 estimated that about $1.18bn in funding towards organisations targeting LGBTQ+ rights and promoting traditional family policies flowed into Europe from 2019 to 2023, and a 2022 declassified US intelligence assessment found the Russian government had covertly funnelled at least $300m to foreign political parties, often in Europe, from 2014.
Ashifa Kassam: We’ve also had some recent reporting on the flow of funds from the US. In July, the Guardian reported that Donald Trump’s state department intended to allocate $12m to organisations in the UK founded by prominent conservatives. Of these funds, $7m was to go to 878, a thinktank that describes itself as being devoted to “the rediscovery of our ancient culture” and “ending mass migration.”
In July, the state department issued a notice of funding, offering grants for organisations and institutions interested in promoting what it described as “civilisational self-confidence in Europe”.
While research out of Europe, such as the Munich-based Ifo Institute, has found “no correlation” between migration and higher crime rates, the US state department notice suggested it was hoping the grants would lead to outcomes including reports on the impact of mass migration on local safety and tools to analyse impact of mass migration on democratic institutions.
One user asked: How serious would you describe the threat these far-right parties pose to democracy? And to what extent do you think there is a collaboration between them and powerful social media personalities or state sponsored online social media propaganda?
Jon Henley: Some far right parties definitely pose more of a threat to democracy than others. Political scientists divide far-right parties into those that essentially operate within basic democratic norms (“radical right” parties), and those that seek to overturn the system, to the extent even of condoning violence (“extreme right” parties).
If we take one example, AfD in Germany could be described as extreme right in some respects (and some local branches are indeed classified as such by German domestic intelligence). Some of its positions are in clear contradiction with liberal democracy: it is openly racist, homophobic, misogynistic. It believes citizens should be ranked by its own warped criteria, including ethnicity, gender and religious belief. It flirts continually with Nazi rhetoric, imagery and symbolism.
On this question I recommend this column by Cas Mudde, a top scholar of populism and the far right, after AfD won in the recent state elections in Saxony-Anhalt. He argues that mainstream parties have to wake up to the fact that they are not in a battle that’s about vote share and elections, it’s about democracy itself.
Ashifa Kassam: I would add that we’ve seen some fairly high-profile examples of collaboration, from Elon Musk’s repeated endorsements of the AfD on X to his 2025 X talk with the party’s co-leader, Alice Weidel. The Guardian has also regularly explored the interplay between the far right and social media, such as a 2025 investigation that looked at how a network of far-right Facebook groups had become an “engine of radicalisation” by exposing hundreds of thousands of people in Britain to racist and extremist disinformation.
KilmaSelth asked: Do you think the hard right parties tend to moderate as they approach power, or do they maintain their radicalism?
Jon Henley: Based on Meloni and Le Pen, I would for a long time have said yes – Meloni basically struck a bargain to get elected in which she promised to be responsible on the economy, in the EU and as regards foreign policy, as long as she could do her culture-wars stuff domestically. Le Pen has spent years “detoxifying” the National Rally and kicking out over-radical undesirables. But if you look at AfD, they haven’t moderated their language at all – if anything, they’ve hardened it – and it manifestly is not doing them any harm. And as Meloni and Le Pen have moderated their positions, we’ve started to see them being outflanked on their right, by the likes of Roberto Vannacci and his National Future in Italy and Eric Zemmour’s Reconquête in France. So I think we may be heading into a period where the former far right is effectively now part of the political landscape, like “regular” parties that will sometimes win and sometimes lose elections, and will be increasingly challenged on their right by more extreme elements.
Ashifa Kassam: Vox offers another way to look at this question, as the party was founded in 2013 by disgruntled members of the conservative People’s party (PP). Its leader, Santiago Abascal, is a career politician who was among those who saw an opportunity to push further on the right flank of Spanish politics when it came to Catalan separatism, immigration, abortion and LGBTQ+ rights. It was a hardline stance that was often (but not always) diluted when Abascal was part of the PP; now as a separate party, they’ve seized on their electoral momentum in some regions to push the party to heed their agenda.

Jon Ossoff’s rise to US Senate was meteoric – how high can he go?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:56 UTC
18:00:56 KST

Jon Ossoff has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, he declared during a debate this week. Jon Ossoff has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, he told a local TV station last month. Jon Ossoff has “zero interest” in running for president in 2028, he told MS Now – twice – in August.
The Democratic US senator for Georgia said as much to CNN. And the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. And MS Now, again. And in his second Senate debate on Tuesday night.
Are you getting the message?
Plenty aren’t. It doesn’t matter how many times the media-savvy senator delivers his well-rehearsed line: in Washington, and beyond, there is markedly more than “zero interest” in the prospect of Ossoff running for the White House.
His political rise in a Republican-leaning swing state, his viral speeches on conspicuously national issues, and Democratic demand for a new figure to lead the party forward are conspiring to fan the flames of speculation.
But when Ossoff, 39, lands on a message, he sticks to it like gum under a desk. His discipline and doggedness show up in Senate hearings, in campaign rallies and debates – railing against “the Epstein class” and mocking Trump in blunt snippets that spread far and wide online.
After Donald Trump won Georgia by two points in the 2024 presidential election, Ossoff had been expected to face one of the most bruising contests of any incumbent US senator this November. The race, however, does not appear close. Ossoff – whose team declined repeated requests for an interview for this story – has consistently led between four and eight points in most polls against his challenger, the Republican congressman Mike Collins – a lead no Democrat has posted in Georgia since the late 1990s.
On the debate stage in October, Ossoff hammered away at Collins, dubbing the encounter the “trial of Mike Collins”, and demanding Collins explain his votes in support of the Iran war and the president’s tariffs, as well as ties to white nationalists in his office and his family.
“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff declared. “His office has been in cahoots with some of the most notorious white supremacists in the country. He himself has amplified neo-Nazi propaganda. He’s never apologized for it. And he should tonight.”
Ossoff’s ability to deliver such lines – as memorable as they are clippable in this social media age – is part of his broader approach to winning support, vote by vote, in a state where it cannot be taken for granted.
“A campaign is just a bigger, longer jury trial,” said Charlie Bailey, director of the Georgia Democratic party, and a trial lawyer by trade. “The best trial lawyers, they are themselves. They talk plainly to the jury. They say straightforward things, and the jury can tell that they’re being themselves, and they just believe what they are saying.”
When Ossoff talks to voters, “it not only matches up with their experience, their anger, and their frustration; they know he’s telling the truth”, Bailey said. “That’s leadership.”
Ossoff has not always been a winner. His meteoric political rise dates back almost a decade, to a defeat.
When Republican Tom Price resigned his congressional seat in February 2017, after Trump appointed him to serve as health and human services secretary, Ossoff stepped into a special election with a “jungle” primary for Georgia’s sixth congressional district: the candidates of all parties run on a single ballot, with a runoff between the top two if no one wins more than 50% of the vote.
It looked like a stretch. “You have to remember, everyone on the local level was a Republican,” said John Ernst, former mayor of Brookhaven, a city in Atlanta’s northern suburbs; at the time, Ernst was the only Democratic mayor in the district.
The district was, in short, “the bastion of the proto-Maga movement”, said Ernst, “but without the craziness. It’s the business wing of the movement.”
But Atlanta’s streets had filled that year with women in pink hats in the largest such demonstration since the civil rights movement, and they were looking for a way to strike back.
This special congressional election provided stunned Democratic voters their first chance to register their outrage at Trump’s provocations, at least by proxy.
“There’s all this momentum, and there’s all these people excited, and things are going pretty crappy at the national level, and I probably then started to think, ‘Huh, this is interesting,’” Lynn Deutsch, mayor of Dunwoody, Georgia, said. Ossoff raised an eye-watering $23m in small donations from around the country.
While Ossoff took the former Georgia secretary of state Karen Handel to a runoff, Handel – a notably moderate Republican – beat Ossoff 52-48. But Ossoff walked away with the largest Democratic donor database in the US.
After his 2017 defeat, “everyone” was asking Ossoff the same thing, according to Ernst. It is a question he is likely to get just as much, if not more, should he meet expectations and win next month: what is he going to do next?
“Think about it. He was a guy who came out of the blue,” Ernst said. “He wasn’t a known entity outside of a few congressional offices in Washington DC.”
He didn’t completely come out of the blue, of course. Ossoff grew up in Northlake, then a middle-class unincorporated part of DeKalb county near Atlanta. His mother, Heather Fenton, is a prominent political figure in her own right, who co-founded New Power Pac, which worked to elect women to local offices in Georgia. His father, Richard Ossoff, was an attorney.
In his youth, Jon Ossoff took his parents’ political capital and an education at Atlanta’s elite Paideia school to an internship with Representative John Lewis before undergraduate study at Georgetown.
He later worked for Hank Johnson, a Democratic congressman who represents part of Atlanta and DeKalb county. Ossoff left to earn a master’s degree from the London School of Economics in 2013.
Using $250,000 of an inheritance to buy a stake in a documentary film company, Ossoff spent the next four years in London, producing investigations as the CEO of Insight TWI, covering corruption and human rights abuses, looking at Fifa, Beijing’s investments in Africa, and working on a documentary on female Yazidi soldiers, which aired on the BBC.
He returned home to run for Congress. And one defeat was not enough to kill his political aspirations. Following his 2017 loss, however, Ossoff decided against challenging Handel to a rematch in 2018. Instead, he started building political relationships across the state of Georgia, using his war chest and new national standing to help Democrats in local elections.
Ossoff campaign in 2017 sowed seeds that he subsequently spent years watering.
“When I ran in 2011 for the first time on council, I did it by myself. I had no idea what I was doing,” Deutsch said. “I ran for mayor [in 2019] but I wasn’t going to do it by myself. So I convened all these women … and they had all helped on the Jon campaign. And they had all knocked on doors for Ossoff.”
One by one, local offices began to flip. Dissent against the Trump administration from Atlanta’s professional class had crystallized into sustained, organized political action.
Three years after Ossoff’s loss, Democrats had taken control of local offices in most of Atlanta’s affluent, politically powerful northern suburbs. Many had been involved with Ossoff’s congressional campaign.
“There was just an energy about him,” Deutsch said of Ossoff, in the shadow of Trump’s first presidency. “And remember, everybody was operating kind of from a space of panic, right? What the heck just happened? And when you talk about the areas that flipped, they’re generally highly educated. We didn’t just flip because there were Democrats who weren’t voting. We flipped because there were people who were independents, mostly, that said, ‘I can’t vote for Republicans any more.’”
When Ossoff announced his campaign for US Senate in November 2019, no one knew what was on the horizon. The Covid-19 pandemic turned the race on its head, as he accused his opponent – the incumbent Republican senator David Perdue, one of the wealthiest lawmakers in US history – of corruption.
Perdue was the most active stock trader in the Senate, and made some opportune trades during the pandemic. Ossoff pounced, characterizing his opponent as a caricature of Gilded Age wealth.
“It’s not just that you’re a crook, senator. It’s that you’re attacking the health of the people that you represent,” Ossoff told Perdue during one debate. “You did say Covid-19 was no deadlier than the flu. You did say there would be no significant uptick in cases. All the while, you were looking after your own assets and your own portfolio. And you did vote four times to end protections for pre-existing conditions. Four times.”
Perdue pulled out of the final debate, as money poured into the race. Ossoff debated an empty podium to make his message heard.
Perdue raised about $100m to defend his seat. Ossoff raised more than $150m to challenge him.
But Georgia voters had heard enough. Ossoff beat Perdue by about 56,000 votes, 50.6% to 49.4%.
“Everybody who cast your ballot, everybody who put your faith and confidence in democracy’s capacity to deliver the representation we deserve, whether you were for me or against me, I’ll be for you,” he said in his victory speech.
Donald Chase is a peanut farmer from south Georgia. He lives 30 miles (48.2km) away from Plains, where Jimmy Carter rose from obscurity to the White House 50 years ago. There are few Carter Democrats left in south Georgia. But there are some Republicans voting for Ossoff; Chase is among them.
“He’s not afraid to stand up, and I appreciate that,” said Chase. “The second thing is he’s demonstrated really clearly that he’ll come to south Georgia, that he’ll listen to the issues, and he’ll try to do something where he can.”
“Republican leadership in Georgia has done a lot of good things,” added Chase. But tariffs and diesel fuel prices have damaged the peanut business.
“The tariff situation, I saw it coming, and I just was – this is going to hurt peanut farmers,” he said. “Our two primary export countries are Canada and Mexico. And with this latest spat, I will call it, the tariffs on peanut products went up 295%.”
Ossoff still faces the same challenge Democrats up and down the ballot face, two years after the party’s crushing defeat to Trump: motivating the base.
A young Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) worker, who requested anonymity for fear of political retribution, described life under the leadership of the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr – a key Trump appointee – while watching Atlanta’s Pride parade this month.
“We’re personally very, very burnt out, and very overstretched,” she said. “We’re just nervous that we’re going to get fired every single day.”
She has knocked on doors for Ossoff in the past, and plans to vote for him. But that’s about it.
“I feel like I’ve done that a lot over the past few years, especially for Stacey Abrams and Kamala [Harris],” she said. “I think I’m just burnt out. I’m going to vote and I’m going to encourage people to vote, but I’m not doing what I’ve done in the past because it’s just been too much.”
At the same event Rockwell McKay said: “Even if his heart is in the right place and he’s trying to do these things, he can’t do it in two or four years.
“They churn up in the House with the Democrats and the Republicans. In the next three or four years, we’ll have somebody else in wanting to redirect their movement. I don’t see it.
“I’m past the Obama shit, with the hope,” he added. “Fuck all that.”
Ossoff is, in many ways, unique. Should he ever find himself drawn away from Georgia, Democrats in the state fear his successes would be hard to replicate – in part because he has a gift for being the right person, in the right place, at the right time.
Contributors have given him more than $98m for November’s election, with about 90% of donations under $100. Ossoff had about $43m as cash on hand at the end of July: the largest war chest of any US Senate candidate in this election cycle, and 20 times as much as Collins, his opponent.
“Eventually, Jon Ossoff maybe should run for president, but not anytime soon,” said Deutsch, the Dunwoody mayor, who took solace in the fact he had “not indicated that it’s on his short-term, or even medium-term, plan”.
As senator, he has pushed hard to end stock and cryptocurrency trading by members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children; campaigned for a constitutional amendment to eliminate corporate spending in elections; and investigated abuses and corruption in federal prisons.
His departure from the role “would be a terrible loss” for Georgia in the Senate, she added. “But one of my young adult children, who lives in Texas, wants him to run. He thinks he’s the only choice. And I’m like, I don’t think so.”
Ernst, the former Brookhaven mayor, can see the appeal of an Ossoff presidential bid. “I mean, in this day and age, being a Democrat, white, male – young, white male – it’s kind of rare,” he said, as the Senate generally skews older. “And no one says he’s a raging liberal. No one says he’s conservative. No one says he’s moderate. He’s just Jon Ossoff.”
Johnson, the congressman for whom he used to work, said: “I think Jon’s cultivation of support from small-dollar donors from across the country strengthens his ability to pursue policy goals that favor the common good, as opposed to policies that favor the wealthy and the well connected.”
Twice, in 2017 and 2020, Ossoff found himself at the center of America’s political attention. Both times, he capitalized on that attention – to the political benefit of Democrats, and the financial benefit of his future campaigns.
Might he do it a third time? The chances are greater than zero.

Bulgaria seeks NATO anti-drone systems, says defence minister
SOFIA, Oct 16 - Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defences after a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday.
Drones hit two ships which caught fire off Romania's Black Sea coast this week. On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast following a drone attack, prompting Sofia to summon Russia's ambassador.
The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict poses to commercial shipping near NATO's southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defences in the Black Sea.
"We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision," Stoyanov said.
NATO did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Stoyanov said he planned to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October. REUTERS

Why a new US–Israeli war against Iran could carry enormous risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

In recent days, three developments have emerged as key preliminary indicators that the US may be preparing to step up its military campaign against Iran. First, the dispatch of a third aircraft carrier strike group alongside additional American forces toward the waters surrounding Iran; second, the directive from the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) to achieve full operational readiness; and third, the continuation of economic pressure, sanctions, and blockades, alongside disputes over the Strait of Hormuz and diplomatic friction surrounding negotiations.
While these developments clearly signal an expansion of military options and an intensification of coercive pressure, they do not, on their own, constitute definitive proof of an executive decision to launch a broad war. This new force posture serves at least three strategic functions: deterrence, diplomatic leverage in negotiations, and operational preparation of a military option. Consequently, while a war posture increases the statistical probability of conflict, it does not in itself demonstrate a definitive decision to enter a major war.
Military power is not measured solely by the quantity of aircraft carriers, planes, or missile launchers. Rather, sustained combat power is a function of the equilibrium between consumption capacity, stockpiles, production, replenishment, human resources, logistics, and the ability to absorb the total costs of warfare.
Consequently, transforming a military posture into a major war requires the simultaneous presence of at least four structural capacities.
First, a sufficient reserve of munitions and weaponry must exist to execute initial operations and sustain subsequent engagements against Iran—a country that possesses the largest and most diverse missile arsenal in the region.
Second, robust equipment replenishment capacity is required, ensuring that if missiles, ammunition, aircraft, defence systems, or command assets are consumed or destroyed during hostilities, military industries can replace them at a commensurate rate—an outcome that appears practical implausible for the US regime.
These two requirements would appear to be unachievable at the moment. An April 21 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies shows that in four out of the seven key categories of munitions analysed, expenditure during the 40-day conflict likely exceeded half of pre-war inventories, and replenishing some of these stockpiles could require between one to four years.
Alongside the depletion of ammunition stockpiles, the Ramadan War has imposed tangible costs upon the air fleet of the hostile United States administration. According to an official report by the US Congressional Research Service on 5 October, at least 81 US military aircraft, including fixed-wing planes, helicopters, and unmanned systems, have been destroyed or damaged.
Third, sufficient human resource and logistical capacity must exist to sustain long-term operations at a vast distance while simultaneously maintaining the US regime’s existing military commitments and global readiness across other regions.
Fourth, the capacity to absorb the economic and geopolitical fallout must be present, including the ability to withstand spikes in energy prices, supply chain disruptions and diminished oil transits through the Strait of Hormuz, fiscal strain, the depletion of strategic reserves, vulnerable military bases, and domestic political pressure ahead of the November elections.
Iran’s ability to disrupt confidence at the world’s primary energy chokepoint has become a strategic lever that substantially raises the cost of any military adventure for the global economy and decision-makers in Washington.
The cumulative weight of munitions constraints and the economic variables examined places enemy decision-makers before three plausible strategic trajectories:
In the first scenario, the American and Zionist regimes rely on the continuation of a heavy military posture, economic sanctions, maritime pressure, intelligence operations, and cognitive warfare without initiating a major new conflict. Operationally, this option is entirely feasible. Its primary appeal for Washington lies in avoiding further depletion of its vulnerable stockpiles of Patriot, THAAD, and Tomahawk missiles, as well as preventing additional aircraft losses. Nevertheless, evidence suggests that this path is not without cost or hazard: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace entails persistent insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz, oil flows remaining below normal capacity, recessionary pressure on global energy demand, continuous attrition of forces deployed to the region, and increasing difficulty in managing unintended maritime incidents.
In the second scenario, the US/Zionist axis considers executing limited, phased air and missile strikes against specific targets—including Iranian military, missile, nuclear, or energy infrastructure—rather than entering directly into an all-out war; an option cited by Axios sources as one of the plans under active consideration. Although the presence of three aircraft carrier strike groups and current stockpiles render such strikes operationally viable in the short term, the central dilemma of this scenario remains escalation control. When an actor initiates a limited attack under the assumption that the opponent’s response will remain bounded, it exposes itself to inadvertent escalation due to asymmetrical perceptions of thresholds and the absence of unilateral control over the defender’s decisions.
The third scenario—direct entry or a gradual slide into a full-scale regional war—represents the most costly and perilous trajectory facing the US regime and the genocidal Zionist entity. Should such a scenario materialise, the conflict is unlikely to remain unidimensional. Operationally, it could encompass, simultaneously or sequentially, high-intensity air combat, mass missile exchanges, severe disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, cyber operations, and strikes against enemy regional bases and energy infrastructure across the broader region. In such a context, a punitive operation could rapidly degrade into a multi-front war of attrition.
Alongside military variables, the autumn political and electoral calendar constitutes another factor influencing calculations regarding the timing and ceiling of escalation. The deployment of a third aircraft carrier and 10,000 additional troops toward the waters surrounding Iran coupled with the Pentagon’s directive to US Central Command to complete operational preparations explicitly demonstrates that the timing of potential operations within Washington and Tel Aviv’s decision-making circles is being weighed against the November congressional mid-terms, as well as the Zionist parliamentary elections scheduled just one week prior.
A further dimension concerns apprehension over Iran’s potential capacity to sever subsea internet cables, thereby completely severing connectivity across the Arabian Peninsula as well as the aggressor Zionist state, and disabling all exchange and financial markets dependent on this network infrastructure. Crucially, through the establishment of its National Information Network and its relative independence from western-dominated internet financial transactions, Iran has shifted the balance in this domain to its own strategic advantage.
From the standpoint of deterrence theory, inflicting costs that outweigh the scale of the initial strike often serves as a rational mechanism to fundamentally reshape the adversary’s cost-benefit calculus regarding subsequent actions. Given Iran’s documented capabilities, should such a miscalculation be committed by the US or the Zionist regime, a plausible strategic posture for Tehran would involve launching a multi-domain, asymmetrical, and extensive response designed to defy containment or mitigation. Consequently, even a limited military strike would impel Iran to formulate a response that far exceeds the initial scale of aggression. This underlying logic of an escalatory response to limited warfare significantly raises the calculative risks of any new military venture.
The principal danger in the current security environment is not necessarily a pre-planned decision to wage an all-out war, but rather the escalation—whether intended or unintended—of a small war into a major war through crisis instability.
If the deployment of military force as a pressure tactic leads to a miscalculation and a limited strike, and that limited strike is met with an asymmetric, multi-domain response, a cycle of reciprocal retaliation will take hold. This chain reaction could impose a war whose full consequences its initiators lack the capacity to absorb.

U.S. Army wants autonomous missile launchers ready by August 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:57:49 UTC
17:57:49 KST

- The U.S. Army is seeking proposals for CAML-Lite, a light autonomous missile launcher, with prototypes to fire live munitions at Talisman Sabre 2027 in Australia.
- The Army expects to award prototype agreements around Dec. 18, 2026, and wants companies to share demonstration costs.
The U.S. Army has asked industry for a lighter version of its planned autonomous missile launcher and wants working prototypes ready to fire live munitions in Australia during the Talisman Sabre 2027 exercise in August 2027.
The service released a request for solutions briefs for the Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher-Lite, or CAML-Lite, on Oct. 15. Companies have until Oct. 23 to respond. The Army plans to invite selected firms to submit full prototype proposals on Nov. 6 and expects to award prototype agreements around Dec. 18, 2026, according to the notice, issued by the Program Executive Office for Missiles and Space at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama.
CAML is the Army’s effort to field a missile launcher that can drive itself or carry an optional crew, fire both offensive and defensive missiles, and reload with as little human involvement as possible. In the notice, the Army says current launcher units depend on large crewed resupply teams that put soldiers at risk and slow how quickly batteries can set up and move. It wants a common launcher design that can deploy worldwide and accept new munitions without being locked into one vendor’s proprietary systems.
The light variant is meant to be fielded quickly and tested early to shape later buying decisions. Each prototype must be a complete system with its own mobility, launcher and reload capability, and must be able to operate in convoy, follow waypoints on its own, be driven remotely or be driven by a crew. Bidders must show their system can fire live munitions at the August 2027 demonstration, and company personnel, not soldiers, will operate and maintain the vehicles there.
The Army wants a range of approaches, from complete prototypes to mature vehicle concepts and modular designs, and says some companies may already have suitable vehicles or subsystems. Only U.S.-based companies cleared to handle SECRET information and hardware are eligible.
Companies will also be expected to share the cost. The Army says it has limited money for the demonstration and does not plan to cover all of it, and a larger company investment, measured as a share of the demonstration cost, will count in a bidder’s favor.
Each agreement will include a priced option for one to six additional prototypes, along with training and contractor support, for testing and experimentation with soldiers, including the 25th Infantry Division in Hawaii. The Army may also use that option to buy launchers for international partners, naming Australia. After Talisman Sabre, the service expects to select one or more vendors and exercise the option, then move into a second phase aimed at production-representative prototypes.
Australia’s role ties into a recent change to the program. Army acquisition official Frank Lozano said this week that the service is adding a third, light CAML variant in partnership with the Australian military, alongside the medium and heavy versions already planned, Breaking Defense reported. He said more than one vendor will work on the light launcher.
The wider CAML program is intended to give the Army a replacement for the Typhon long-range launcher, which the service found too large to operate easily on the battlefield, and to cut the number of launcher types it fields. The Army has said future CAML versions could fire missiles including the Tomahawk and the PAC-3 MSE interceptor. In August, it awarded the Georgia Tech Research Institute an agreement worth up to $33.4 million to serve as weapon systems integrator for CAML prototypes.
The CAML-Lite notice does not specify which munitions the light launcher must carry, leaving bidders to propose munition types and whether they will supply them or request them from the government. The Army plans a system checkout and readiness review in March 2027 ahead of the Talisman Sabre live-fire demonstration that August.

Swiss luxury group ‘interested in buying’ diamond giant De Beers
Swiss luxury goods group Richemont is reportedly part of a consortium that aims to buy South African diamond giant De Beers.
According to Bloomberg, the Richemont is in talks with the major United States jewellery retailer Signet Jewelers to join a consortium that intends to acquire the South African company.
The entity in question, the Global Diamond Consortium (GDC), is reportedly in a very strong position in the acquisition negotiations, according to Bloomberg, which cites several sources close to the sale process.
The GDC is led by former De Beers CEO Gareth Penny and is said to have been designated as the preferred bidder in July by De Beers’ owner, the British firm Anglo American, which holds an 85% stake in De Beers and has stated its intention to divest as early as 2024.
The consortium also includes the governments of Namibia and Angola, as well as major diamond producers.
The sale of De Beers comes at a time when demand for precious stones is recovering from one of the deepest crises the sector has ever seen, said Bloomberg.
When contacted by the agency, neither GDC, Signet Jewelers nor Richemont confirmed any interest in acquiring De Beers.

airBaltic asks US court to approve 250,000-euro monthly advisory fee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:56:53 UTC
17:56:53 KST

Latvia’s national airline airBaltic has asked a US court to approve the appointment of financial advisory group Seabury, with a monthly fee of 250,000 euros and additional success-based payments for securing financing and carrying out restructuring transactions, according to documents filed by the airline.
The court has not yet approved the application, which is scheduled to be considered on Monday, the 19th of October.
According to the documents, Seabury has been providing investment banking and financial advisory services to airBaltic since March 2026 as part of the airline’s restructuring process.
In addition to the monthly fee of 250,000 euros, Seabury would be entitled to success fees for securing financing, restructuring debt, renegotiating fleet and contractual arrangements, attracting new equity and completing other transactions. After crediting the monthly fees against the success fees, the total success-based compensation must not exceed 18 million euros.
The documents outline several potential payments.
 For example, Seabury would receive a fee equivalent to 2.25% of any new debtor-in-possession (DIP) financing secured. If airBaltic uses the full 350 million euros in available DIP financing, the corresponding fee would amount to approximately 7.9 million euros, according to calculations by news agency LETA.
Seabury would also receive 1.15% of financed and trade debt converted into airBaltic equity or otherwise extinguished during the restructuring. A separate fee of 3% would apply to newly raised equity capital, although this would not apply to funds provided by the Latvian government.
A further one-million-euro fee is envisaged for structuring and negotiating a commercial agreement, such as a joint venture or expanded codeshare arrangement, with a strategic partner providing new equity or debt financing.
Seabury would also receive hourly payments ranging from 350 to 1,490 US dollars for liquidity management services.
 The fees for these services would be capped at 325,000 dollars for September, 225,000 dollars for October and 75,000 dollars for each subsequent month.
AirBaltic disclosed that during the 90 days preceding its Chapter 11 filing, it paid Seabury 872,715 dollars in professional fees and reimbursed 144,531 dollars in expenses.
The airline has also submitted an application seeking court approval for the appointment of legal adviser Milbank, which has been working on the potential restructuring since April 2026.
According to the filing, Milbank received 6.64 million dollars during the year preceding the Chapter 11 application, as well as an additional advance payment of 100,000 dollars. The documents also disclose the law firm’s billing rates, with associate lawyers charging between 745 and 1,820 dollars per hour.
Meanwhile, on the 2nd of October, airBaltic engaged US business advisory firm Riveron RTS to assist with preparing its restructuring plan, administering creditor claims and producing financial reports for the court.
According to the documents, 
Riveron RTS will help prepare schedules of assets and liabilities, establish a database of creditor claims,
 submit monthly reports to the court, develop the restructuring plan, prepare financial forecasts and assess which contracts should be retained or terminated.
As previously reported by LETA, airBaltic has initiated a restructuring of its financial obligations under Chapter 11 of the US Bankruptcy Code.
The airline has secured binding commitments from lenders to provide up to 350 million euros in new DIP financing to maintain liquidity and operations throughout the Chapter 11 proceedings.
AirBaltic has already received the first 140-million-euro tranche, of which 78.925 million euros will be used to purchase eight aircraft and seven engines.
The financing was arranged by Strategic Value Partners (SVP), with commitments from Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management and Strategic Value Partners.
The interest rate is SOFR plus 8%, currently equivalent to approximately 12%. 
However, the financing arrangement also includes additional fees of up to 52.5 million euros.
Consequently, the airline will abandon its previous plan to raise up to 257 million euros from bondholders at an annual interest rate of 25%.
At the same time, a bondholder group known as the Ad Hoc Group has filed objections with the court concerning the terms of the DIP financing and its potential impact on the collateral securing bondholders’ claims.
Chapter 11 protection shields airBaltic from creditor enforcement actions while it restructures its financial obligations.
The airline has emphasised that flights and customer services will continue as normal.
 All flights will operate according to the planned schedule, existing tickets and reservations remain valid, and passengers can continue purchasing tickets and travelling with airBaltic as usual.
The restructuring process is expected to result in a reorganisation plan requiring court approval. AirBaltic anticipates completing the proceedings by mid-2027.
In 2025, airBaltic Group’s revenue increased by 4.2% compared with 2024, reaching 779.344 million euros. The group recorded a loss of 44.337 million euros, approximately 2.7 times smaller than in 2024.
The airline carried 5.2 million passengers in 2025, representing a 1% increase compared with the previous year.
German national airline Lufthansa became an airBaltic shareholder in summer 2025.
Currently, the Latvian state owns 88.37% of airBaltic, Lufthansa holds 10%, and Aircraft Leasing 1, a company belonging to Danish businessman and financial investor Lars Thuesen, owns 1.62%. The remaining 0.01% belongs to other shareholders.
AirBaltic’s share capital amounts to 41.819 million euros.
Summary: airBaltic is seeking US court approval to pay financial adviser Seabury 250,000 euros per month and additional success fees of up to 18 million euros as the airline restructures its debts under Chapter 11.

Egypt's army is intensifying strikes on Sudan's 'illicit mines'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:54:52 UTC
17:54:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt's army is intensifying strikes on Sudan's 'illicit mining activities'
Tensions are rising between Egypt and Sudan—at the pubic level at least for now—after the Egyptian army bombed sites mined by hundreds of Sudanese for gold on 11 October, killing dozens of miners and wounding others.
Over 70 Sudanese artisanal miners were killed in the strikes, according to eyewitnesses who were present at the site at the time of the Egyptian strikes.
Videos filmed during and after the Egyptian aerial attacks showed the bodies of the dead victims spread out in the area as smoke billowed in the background.
Having affirmed that the strikes were carried out on the Egyptian side of the border, the Egyptian army said they were part of its campaign against "illicit mining" activities in the area.
It added in a statement on 12 October that warning leaflets were dropped to people in the area to caution against illicit mining for gold.
The strikes were the second by the Egyptian army on the Egyptian side of the border with Sudan in less than five months.
In mid-June, army fighter aircraft bombed mining sites in the border area, killing around 23 Sudanese artisanal miners. Law-enforcement personnel and army troops also rounded up hundreds of miners.
Increasing mining activities, particularly gold, Egyptian military analysts said, are part of fallout from the civil war in Sudan which has caused chaos on the shared border with Egypt.
"Criminal gangs are stepping up their activities in the border area, using the Sudanese army's preoccupation with fighting inside Sudan," Gen. Nasr Salem, the former Egyptian reconnaissance commander, told The New Arab.
"This adds more pressure on the Egyptian Armed Forces which have to solely bear the responsibility of securing the border," he added.
In its 12 October statement about the strikes, the Egyptian army said law-enforcement personnel would continue to impose full sovereignty within Egypt's boundaries to protect its capabilities and national wealth.
Public outrage
The strike triggered a wave of anger inside Sudan, raising questions about its possible effects on relations between Cairo and Khartoum in the near future.
Reaction from the Sudanese in the immediate aftermath of the attacks was mainly confined to social media, but it then seeped into the streets.
On 12 October, a Sudanese gunman opened fire on Egyptian truck drivers south of Khartoum, killing two and leaving a third injured.
A day later, protests were reported in a number of Sudanese cities, especially in Nyala, the capital of the state of Southern Darfur in south-western Sudan.
Photos circulating on social media showed the demonstrators carrying the Sudanese flag and placards criticising alleged silence by Sudan's ruling Transitional Sovereignty Council (TSC).
Most of the anger on the Sudanese side was driven by belief that the strikes were carried out on the Sudanese, not the Egyptian, side of the border.
This was why some people called on the STC to issue an official condemnation of the attacks and launch an enquiry into them.
Cairo moves to contain crisis
The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said it closely followed the killing of the two Egyptian truck drivers, describing the event as "sorrowful".
The Egyptian ambassador in Khartoum, who had just submitted his credentials to TSC Head Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan only a day earlier, had also checked on the condition of the wounded victim who was hospitalized at a hospital in the Sudanese capital.
The statement of the Egyptian Foreign Ministry on the shootout came only a day after the Egyptian and Sudanese foreign ministers talked on the phone.
During the call, each of the two top diplomats expressed respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the other's country, according to a statement by the Egyptian Foreign Ministry.
Concern over rising anti-Egypt sentiments in Sudan reverberated, meanwhile, quickly across Egyptian social media sites where users expressed support for actions taken by the Egyptian army to defend national borders against intrusions by Sudanese artisanal miners.
Egypt, analysts argue, has been solely bearing the brunt of securing its shared border with Sudan since the outbreak of the Sudanese civil war in April 2023.
Gen. Salem said illicit mining was only a small detail in the larger picture of a long list of other border infringements from the Sudanese side, including the smuggling of subsidized Egyptian goods into Sudan and the trafficking of Sudanese persons into Egypt.
The war has also caused around 1.5 million Sudanese to cross the border into Egypt for refuge, adding to the economically-struggling northern neighbouring country's economic strains.
RSF financial engine
The Transitional Sovereignty Council has mourned the death of the artisanal miners and ordered the formation of a panel to investigate the incident, in an apparent attempt to appease an angry Sudanese public.
However, most condemnation for the strikes came from the backers of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary militia battling the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) for control over Sudan.
This probably highlights links between the militia and rampant illicit mining activities and gold smuggling in the border area between Egypt and Sudan, Sudanese analysts said.
Sudanese political analyst Salah Khalil described gold mining and smuggling as major "financial lifelines" for the RSF.
"The militia uses revenues from mining and smuggling operations to bankroll its military activities and war against the SAF," Kalil told TNA.
He added that the paramilitary group also uses the same revenues in the purchase of arms from other countries.
Nyala is known to be a stronghold of the RSF. On the same day of the Egyptian airstrikes against Sudanese artisanal miners, the Sudan Founding Alliance, an organization established by the RSF in February 2025, claimed that the Egyptian strikes were staged in North Al-Wadi, a mountainous gold-mining region in the far northeast of Sudan's Red Sea State.
It slammed Egypt for allegedly violating Sudanese sovereignty and accused it of wanting to wrest Sudan's resources.
According to international investigative organization Global Witness in 2019, RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo (Hemedti) has used front companies and banks based in Sudan and the United Arab Emirates to capture a large part of Sudan's gold industry.
Beyond gold
Several Egyptian and Sudanese analysts link the war in Sudan to a larger struggle redrawing the regional map and control over vital maritime chokepoints and ports.
The crackdown on gold mining and smuggling would deal a painful blow to the RSF and consequently attempts by the militia's regional backers to defeat the SAF and control Sudan, Sudanese analysts said.
Nevertheless, the same measure would be far from enough to defeat the militia once and for all, they added.
Khalil called for parallel measures to gradually weaken the militia, including cutting off support from Sudan's neighbouring countries, especially Libya, Chad and Ethiopia.
"Severing these lifelines will leave the militia high and dry and contribute to its defeat over time," he said.

From the sell-off of the Soviet defense industry to domestic ballistic missiles: what Ukraine lost and is restoring
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:54:31 EEST
17:54:31 KST

From the sell-off of the Soviet defense industry to domestic ballistic missiles: what Ukraine lost and is restoring
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine has a powerful missile legacy; however, after the collapse of the USSR, a significant portion of the industry's production capabilities and technological potential was lost. Modern developments are paving the way for the restoration of Ukraine's own ballistic missile capabilities.
For decades, Ukraine lost defense enterprises, technologies, and engineers, even though after the collapse of the Soviet Union it inherited a powerful missile industry. Now, amid a full-scale war, the country is trying to restore these capabilities. UNN, together with experts, examined why Ukraine lost part of its industrial potential and how difficult it is now to rebuild its own missile school.
Two years to develop a ballistic missile
After decades of decline in Ukraine’s defense industry, the country developed its own FP-7 ballistic missile in a short period of time. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced its first combat use on October 1, 2026.
According to its CEO, Iryna Terekh, Fire Point created the missile in just two years.
When it comes to the development timeline for what one might call a conventional ballistic missile, it generally takes around 15 years on average, although it can range from 7 to 30. Before the FP-7, the shortest recorded development time for a ballistic missile was 7 years, whereas we reduced it to two
She said that the team worked intensively, sought to optimize the development process, and move to testing as quickly as possible. Some solutions had to be invented anew.
The CEO of Fire Point also noted that the company financed the development with its own funds.
The development of the FP-7 in two years shows that Ukrainian companies are capable of rapidly creating complex missile technologies even amid a full-scale war. It is now important to build on this result: establish serial production and continue developing the technologies.
But why does Ukraine have to restore its missile industry amid a war at all, if it once had a powerful industrial base and participated in the creation of strategic missile systems?
What Ukraine inherited after the collapse of the USSR
After the collapse of the USSR, Ukraine inherited part of the Soviet defense industry. The country had design schools, production facilities, engineers, and experience working on complex technological projects.
At the same time, military experts note that the inherited industry was not fully autonomous. According to defense industry expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi, Ukraine received "fragments of broken production chains without a closed cycle and a specific pool of customers"—mostly authoritarian countries in the Third World, while no one even attempted to integrate into the U.S. or European markets.
After gaining independence, Ukraine needed to restructure this system to meet its own needs, determine priorities for developing the army, and create conditions for modernizing enterprises. However, for decades the defense industry did not receive sufficiently consistent support, while a significant part of state policy focused on using resources that were already available.
Military expert Ivan Stupak believes that Soviet stockpiles largely created a false sense of adequacy.
Until 2013, there was a department for surplus property, which was simply sold off. I knew people who worked at "Ukrspetsexport," and they told me: "We sold a tank to Pakistan, sold a plane somewhere else—everything is fine, we are making money." And these huge stockpiles created the illusion that we did not need to do anything
According to him, the country had technical developments that it could have used to advance its own missile programs, but it failed to do so in time.
How selling off assets turned into the loss of technologies
The problem was not only that Ukraine failed to create enough new weapons. The production capabilities themselves gradually weakened: enterprises lost orders, equipment became outdated, cooperative ties collapsed, and skilled workers left the industry.
Defense industry expert Anatolii Khrapchynskyi attributes this to the lack of a long-term defense strategy and the state’s inability to restructure the inherited industry for new conditions.
In his assessment, some enterprises found themselves in a situation where they had to maintain production without stable orders or clear development prospects. This led to bankruptcies, the loss of equipment, and a reduction in technological capabilities.
The main problem of those twenty years was the absolute absence of a state defense doctrine. Instead of modernization and a transition to domestic production cycles, the country lived in an infantile illusion of security under the umbrella of the Budapest Memorandum, selling off Soviet arsenals for pennies and sincerely believing that it would never again need an army or defense industry
One of the most difficult consequences was the loss of specialists. Engineering expertise is developed through years of practical work, and without stable production, young specialists have no opportunity to gain experience and learn from their senior colleagues.
Money can buy any five-axis machine tool or build a clean hangar, but it is impossible to instantly restore the culture of chemistry, materials science, and solid-state physics. Over these two decades, we completely destroyed specialty chemicals and propellant production: the Shostka giants ("Zirka" and "Svema") deteriorated to such an extent that the country lost the complete production cycle for creating nitrocellulose, artillery propellants, and solid rocket fuel—something that cannot be restored without decades of chemical schools. We completely buried our own military microelectronics and microwave technology (ultra-high frequencies): plants such as Lviv's "Polaron," Kyiv's "Saturn," and Zaporizhzhia's "Gamma" no longer grew crystals or produced componentry for radars and active radar homing heads, which left us dependent on imports even for basic sensors. This was compounded by the degradation of specialty metallurgy: the loss of technologies for precision casting of monolithic blades for aircraft and gas-turbine engines, as well as special armor-grade and heat-resistant titanium alloys
According to him, another consequence was the loss of schools of large-scale engineering design.
Mykolaiv's heavy shipbuilding disappeared forever: along with the bankruptcy of the Black Sea Shipyard and the Shipyard named after the 61st Communist, the school of calculating and welding ocean-class hulls, aligning shaft lines, and coordinating thousands of suppliers for cruisers and aircraft carriers also died. Aircraft manufacturing at Kharkiv's KhAZ and Kyiv's "Aviant" lost the culture of serial assembly: one may have the brilliant Antonov design bureau, but if a plant produces one aircraft in ten years, engineers forget how to organize a serial takt-time assembly line
He emphasized that this concerns not only equipment and infrastructure, but also the experience passed from one generation of engineers to the next.
The main irreparable loss is "shop-floor memory." If the chief metallurgist or optical-mechanical alignment technologist at the Arsenal plant retires without passing the nuances on to an apprentice, the technology dies forever. And it is impossible to train a chief designer of a missile system or a developer of a thermal-imaging array with money—you need 15–20 years of continuous practical work on actual serial products for that
How to develop Ukrainian missile manufacturing
Restoring lost production capabilities is very difficult. Experts note that this requires not only engineering solutions, but also stable funding, long-term state orders, specialist training, and a clear strategy for developing the defense industry.
Military expert Ivan Stupak emphasizes that the full-scale war has forced Ukraine to accelerate weapons development. However, speed must not replace a systematic approach: defense technologies require long-term investment, and the result cannot always be achieved within a single budget year.
The defense industry does not work in such a way that you provide money today and go to a store tomorrow to buy a missile. You can invest in 2026 and see the result only in 2032
In his opinion, Ukraine needs a mechanism to support promising military developments modeled on the American DARPA agency, which funds research and development in defense technologies.
We have a great many talented people who can create extraordinarily interesting things. The main thing is to provide them with funding and ensure its stability
At the same time, Anatoliy Khrapchynskyi believes that restoring Ukraine's defense industry depends not only on financing individual enterprises but also on changing state policy. In his opinion, Ukraine needs to move from situational decisions to a long-term strategy that would provide for the development of private defense companies, the localization of critical components, and cooperation with European and American manufacturers.
True independence is not only a final break with moscow, but also a rejection of the role of an eternal supplicant with an outstretched hand before Western partners. We need our own agency: an aggressive focus on private defense tech, a rigorous review of the ineffective state sector, rapid localization of critical components, and parity-based integration into European and American production chains as an equal partner hardened by a major war
Fire Point could become one example of such development. Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, suggests that the company could become the foundation for further development of Ukraine's missile program and the creation of an entire family of ballistic missiles. He noted that the company is gradually expanding its areas of work—from drones and cruise missiles to ballistic weapons.
International cooperation could play a special role. Anton Zemlyanyi notes that Fire Point's plans to establish joint ventures with European manufacturers could help scale up production, attract partners, and reduce the risks of Russian strikes on production facilities. In the future, this could also open up new opportunities for integrating Ukrainian developments into European defense programs.
However, in the analyst's opinion, Ukraine should not build its missile program around a single manufacturer alone.
I would also not rule out other manufacturers, including state-owned ones. It is in Ukraine's interests to have several capable producers of missile weapons rather than depend exclusively on a single private company. This would create a broader production base, strengthen competition, and reduce risks for the missile program as a whole
Ivan Stupak emphasizes that the main lesson of previous decades is the need to invest continuously in one's own defense industry rather than remember it only when the country finds itself facing a large-scale military threat.
If you do not finance your own army, you will then have to stand for a year asking other countries for help. And there may not be another opportunity to do so

Israel halts commercial shipments into Gaza as winter shortages loom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:53:56 UTC
17:53:56 KST

Israel has halted commercial shipments into Gaza for a second consecutive day, cutting off a vital source of food and other essential supplies as Palestinians face worsening hardship and prepare for winter.
Israeli authorities blamed the suspension on Palestinian merchants protesting taxes imposed by Hamas, but Gaza's private truckers union disputed that account, accusing Israel of imposing the restrictions itself.
The suspension threatens to disrupt supplies of fresh food, meat and winter clothing in the war-ravaged territory, where nearly 2 million people depend on goods entering through Israeli-controlled crossings.
With access to Gaza tightly restricted, any interruption to commercial deliveries risks driving up prices and leaving families struggling to afford basic necessities.
Humanitarian organizations warn that aid deliveries alone cannot meet the population's needs.
While aid agencies generally supply staples such as flour, private merchants play a crucial role in bringing in perishable foods, including fruit and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body responsible for coordinating humanitarian affairs in Gaza.
A functioning commercial market is also essential to keeping prices within reach for families who have already endured years of war, displacement and severe shortages.
"The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people," said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council. "The markets need to be functioning."
COGAT announced the suspension Wednesday, saying it had followed a decision by Palestinian merchants a day earlier to stop coordinating shipments because of Hamas-imposed charges and alleged threats against importers.
"We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas's taxation mechanism and threats against them," said Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, COGAT's deputy spokesperson. "The merchants don't want to bring goods into Gaza."
The agency said no private-sector vendors had attempted to bring goods into the territory since merchants notified Israeli authorities Tuesday.
But Nahed Sheheiber, head of Gaza's private truckers union, rejected Israel's explanation, saying Israeli restrictions, rather than a voluntary decision by merchants, were responsible for the suspension.
"The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments," Sheheiber said. "The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza's merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions."
Following COGAT's announcement, the union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to raise concerns that Israel was using fees charged by the ministry as a pretext to restrict commercial supplies.
Sheheiber said the ministry had asked merchants to pay 10,000 Israeli shekels, or about $3,226, for each truck entering Gaza. During the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab said the payment was not a tax but a donation intended to help pay civil servants in the territory.
The competing accounts leave uncertainty over the immediate cause of the halt, while the consequences for Gaza's already fragile supply network could be severe.
Israel has long accused Hamas of imposing fees on imported goods to finance its operations. However, the suspension places the immediate burden on Gaza's residents, who rely on shipments approved by Israeli authorities for much of their food and other essential supplies.
It also remains unclear whether aid agencies will be permitted to increase deliveries to offset the loss of commercial goods.
COGAT estimates that Gaza's population of roughly 2 million requires about 250 truckloads of goods each day. That figure is substantially below the minimum of 600 trucks per day stipulated under a ceasefire agreement brokered by the United States a year ago.
The suspension comes despite signs of improvement in Gaza's food security earlier this year. The world's leading authority on food insecurity reported that conditions had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but remained at crisis levels, with most families still unable to obtain enough food.
The assessment warned that "even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains," underscoring the risks posed by the interruption of commercial deliveries.
For families already struggling to secure food, the loss of another supply channel could mean higher prices, fewer choices and greater difficulty obtaining essential goods as temperatures fall.
The restrictions also highlight Gaza's dependence on access controlled by Israel. Merchants coordinate with suppliers outside the territory, but their shipments must undergo Israeli military inspections before entering. That system leaves the enclave particularly vulnerable to decisions that interrupt the movement of goods.
The broader humanitarian crisis stems from the war that began Oct. 7, 2023, following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel that killed about 1,200 people in Israel and took 251 hostages.
Israel responded with an extensive bombardment and ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
The ministry says more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the cease-fire took effect.
Women and children account for about half of those killed, according to the ministry.
