Experts: French grocery store cyberattack a warning sign for Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:52:00 UTC
17:52:00 KST

Experts: French grocery store cyberattack a warning sign for Estonia
A cyberattack on French grocery stores Sunday that resulted in large quantities of food being destroyed is also a warning sign for Estonia, cybersecurity experts say.
Hundreds of grocery stores in France were hit by a cyberattack on Sunday when hackers raised the temperature of refrigerators to as high as 50 degrees Celsius. As a result, large quantities of food were spoiled, causing financial losses for the stores. Estonia must also be prepared for a similar threat.
"Things like this can happen and the threat is very real. Fortunately, Estonia has not experienced a problem like the one in France, at least to my knowledge. But that does not mean something similar could not happen at some point because of mistakes or poor cyber hygiene," said Toomas Lepik, a cybersecurity analyst at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech).
Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta, who is attending a cybersecurity conference in Singapore, described the incident in France as shocking. She said society must adapt to the reality that cyberattacks are no longer limited to computers and information systems. At the same time, Pakosta said Estonia has some of the strictest cybersecurity requirements in the world.
"We have particularly strict cybersecurity requirements for companies providing vital services, including those responsible for food security, and these requirements must be met. Companies need to ensure their software is up to date, that systems are properly connected and that they are not accessible to just anyone passing by. As for how much companies in Estonia, such as grocery stores, have done to mitigate this risk, all I can say is that larger companies responsible for food security are required to undergo audits," Pakosta said.
However, these requirements do not apply to all grocery stores. Pakosta added that both the government and businesses need to invest more in cybersecurity to ensure their systems are secure.
"On the one hand, we face financially motivated cyberattacks, but we also face attacks directed against our country or society as a whole. As a digital nation, we all need to pay much more attention to this," she said.
Estonian supermarket chain Selver is also closely monitoring the incident in France to prevent a similar situation at its stores. It remains unclear who was behind the cyberattack in France and whether a ransom demand will follow.
"I can confirm that Selver has not experienced any incidents of this kind. We are doing everything we can to ensure that it never happens. I believe every company and every retail chain has its own strict rules and systems governing how these things work. Overall, I believe we are well protected against this kind of threat," said Selver communications manager Mariann Järvela.
Järvela added that the consequences of the incident in France are not significantly different from those of a power outage, a scenario for which the supermarket chain already conducts emergency preparedness exercises.

Diplomats to MEMO: Colombia’s ICJ withdrawal reflects alignment with US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:51:51 UTC
17:51:51 KST

Colombia’s decision to withdraw from South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), followed by the opening of its embassy in occupied Jerusalem on Wednesday, has drawn criticism from former Latin American ambassadors, who see the moves as a significant shift in Bogotá’s foreign policy, particularly its stance on Palestine.
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that it had informed the Court of its decision to withdraw the declaration of intervention filed on 5th April 2024 under Article 63 of the ICJ Statute.
The move marks a reversal of the position taken by former President Gustavo Petro, whose government cut diplomatic ties with Israel in May 2024 over its military offensive in Gaza and backed South Africa’s case at the ICJ.
The ministry explained that the decision was made under the president’s constitutional authority to manage foreign relations, while emphasising that Colombia remains committed to its obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Speaking to MEMO, Roberto Mayorga Lorca, professor of Economic Law and former Chilean ambassador to the Philippines, criticised the Colombian government’s change of position. “The shift by Colombia’s current government regarding the genocide in Gaza has been regrettable,” Mayorga said.
He argued that since President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August, Bogotá had moved away from condemning Israel’s actions in Gaza, to adopting what he described as a position of “complicity or concealment”.
Mayorga identified four major developments behind the policy shift: the restoration of diplomatic relations with Israel, the relocation of Colombia’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, the lifting of restrictions on exports to Israel, and the withdrawal of Colombia’s intervention in the ICJ proceedings.
READ: Flavio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in Brazil alarms Palestine supporters
Mayorga said the change reflected Bogotá’s increasing alignment with US foreign policy. “The explanation for this shift appears to have been provided by the Foreign Ministry itself, which indicated that Colombia was aligning its position on this matter with Trump’s policy,” he said.
Colombia opened its embassy in occupied Jerusalem today, marking a major shift in its traditionally pro-Palestinian foreign policy under newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella. pic.twitter.com/F8xGscfv0J
— WAFA News Agency – English (@WAFANewsEnglish) October 14, 2026
Former Chilean Ambassador Nelson Hadad also linked the decision to Colombia’s change of government, arguing that the new administration had fundamentally altered the country’s foreign policy. Hadad described the withdrawal as part of a broader realignment with Washington under US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“The new government is a right-wing, perhaps even far-right administration, highly submissive to US policies defined by President Trump and his Secretary of State, Marco Rubio”, Hadad told MEMO.
“This represents a complete and profound change from Colombia’s position under President Petro, resulting from the influence and pressure exerted by President Trump”.

Israel welcomed the withdrawal, with Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar thanking President de la Espriella following diplomatic discussions aimed at restoring bilateral ties. The rapprochement has extended beyond diplomatic relations. Colombia opened its embassy in Jerusalem and restored its previously suspended free trade agreement with Israel, further reversing policies introduced under Petro’s administration.
Mayorga said the change reflected Bogotá’s increasing alignment with US foreign policy. “The explanation for this shift appears to have been provided by the Foreign Ministry itself, which indicated that Colombia was aligning its position on this matter with Trump’s policy,” he said.
Mayorga, meanwhile, warned of the broader political and ethical implications of Colombia’s decision. “Politically, it has provoked opposition across the political spectrum at a time when global public opinion, including sections of the Jewish community, condemns what is happening in Gaza,” he said.
He argued that governments remaining silent in the face of alleged atrocities risk undermining international efforts to uphold accountability. “Ethically, it demonstrates the lack of morality of some governments in the face of situations of evident dehumanisation, such as the attempted extermination of an entire nation,” Mayorga added.
“Colombia está con nosotros”. Las palabras de nuestro primer ministro @netanyahu en la recepción organizada por el @IsraelMFA por la inauguración de la Embajada de Colombia en Jerusalén 🇮🇱🇨🇴 pic.twitter.com/9znJgegzu5
— Israel en Colombia (@IsraelinCol) October 14, 2026
Addressing the legal implications of Colombia’s withdrawal from South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ, the Professor of International Relations at the Central University of Chile (UCEN) Nelson Hadad argued that the decision would have little impact on the proceedings or the court’s eventual judgment.
“I believe Colombia’s withdrawal will have no significant legal consequences. It is simply the withdrawal of one country and does not affect in any way the outcome we expect from the court,” he said.
He also rejected the suggestion that the move constituted a diplomatic victory for Israel, stressing that it would have “no influence whatsoever on the court’s eventual ruling.” Hadad expressed confidence that the ICJ would ultimately find that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, while pointing to the deliberate deprivation of food, water and medicine as conduct relevant to the legal definition of genocide.
READ: Chile’s envoy to Israel at center of political storm over remarks about Palestinians
He further warned that Colombia’s decision formed part of broader political efforts to undermine international judicial institutions and weaken accountability for alleged violations of international law. “The objective is to destroy and dismantle the authority of international courts,” he said, accusing the United States of targeting both the ICJ and the International Criminal Court (ICC) to shield Israel from legal scrutiny.
Hadad argued that such withdrawals could weaken international efforts to combat impunity, “This action also undermines humanity’s aspiration to end impunity and pursue the prosecution and punishment of individuals and countries that violate international law and commit the most inhumane, degrading and abominable crimes.”
He added that other countries could follow Colombia’s example, potentially reducing the diplomatic pressure on Israel without necessarily affecting the legal proceedings. “The objective is to prevent further pressure from being placed on Israel and to limit the number of countries seeking sanctions against a state that fails to fulfil its obligations as a member of the United Nations.”

Cabinet expands small grants program for social service providers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:51:50 EEST
17:51:50 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers has decided to extend the small grants program for social service providers and has increased the maximum grant amount to $65,000, the Ministry of Social Policy reported.
According to the message, the list of services eligible for grant funding has been expanded to include: the reintegration of children and families returning from deportation, forced displacement, or temporarily occupied territories; emergency (crisis) intervention; respite care services for foster parents and parents in family-type children's homes who care for children with disabilities; and day care for children with disabilities (regardless of the specific disability subgroup).
It is noted that the small grants program is currently active in 10 regions and the city of Kyiv, with 130 territorial communities participating in the project.
"Since the project began, nearly 57,000 people have received social services. Small grants have helped communities introduce new services and expand existing ones. Now, it is important to scale this experience so that support becomes accessible to even more families," the Ministry stated.
The project is implemented with the support of the UK Government under the SPIRIT programme, in cooperation with the Ministry of Social Policy, the Social Protection Fund for Persons with Disabilities, and UNICEF in Ukraine. The project is administered by the NGO Yednannia (Unity).

Flash floods destroy villages in central Nepal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:51:27 UTC
17:51:27 KST

Flash floods have swept through Nepal’s central Gorkha district after a pre-dawn landslide on 11 October blocked the Budhi Gandaki River, triggering severe downstream flooding. Two villages in the worst-affected Chumanubri rural municipality were reportedly destroyed, with homes, roads and bridges washed away. Part of a hydropower station was also damaged.
After river levels surged from 2 metres to nearly 8.5 metres within hours, the national disaster risk reduction and management authority reported that 204 homes were damaged, and more than 650 people had been affected. More than 100 foreign trekkers were stranded in the popular hiking region. The floods come just two months after catastrophic flooding and landslides devastated parts of the country on the border with Tibet, leaving thousands dead or missing.
An exceptionally deep area of low pressure barrelled towards Iceland this week. The central pressure was measured at 931mb on 14 October. The pressure plummeted by 49mb in 24 hours, meeting the thresholds for explosive cyclogenesis, or a weather bomb. The system brought sustained winds of 55–60mph to the southern shores of the island before moving north-east through the North Atlantic towards Norway.
However, Iceland was spared the strongest winds as the track of the storm meant they remained out at sea. The system also affected areas beyond Iceland: a 108mph gust was recorded at Bealach Na Bà, in the Scottish Highlands, in association with a trailing 1,000-mile cold front that stretched from Norway to the mid-Atlantic.
Summer-like conditions have extended even further into meteorological autumn in Portugal. After temperatures of 40C at the end of September, on 14 October a maximum of 35.6C was recorded in the southern town of Mora, representing a climatological anomaly of more than 10C.
The heat was not localised, with numerous stations recording temperatures well into the mid-30s celsius. The latest forecasts show that the high pressure and unseasonably warm upper air temperatures will remain in place for the next few days. Looking further ahead, however, temperatures are expected to slowly return towards the average around the middle of next week.

Romania Proposes Joint NATO Command in Black Sea to Counter Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:50:13 UTC
17:50:13 KST

Romania has proposed establishing a joint military command for NATO’s Black Sea countries to counterdrones following a series of attacks on civilian vessels.
Romania’s acting Defence Minister, Radu Miruță, announced the proposal following a phone call withhis Bulgarian counterpart.
The two sides agreed to jointly present the initiative to NATO leadership. The proposed structure would be led by participating countries on a rotating basis.
Bucharest has expressed its readiness to lead the command first, starting in 2028.
Miruță stressed that recent drone attacks on vessels and the discovery of naval mines require a coordinated response from allies. In addition, Russia’s repeated strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure pose security threats to the entire Black Sea region.
The initiative was proposed following a series of drone attacks on civilian shipping off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania.
According to The Insider, six merchant vessels came under attack over a period of a week and a half.
On October 14, an unidentified drone attacked the Comoros-flagged tanker YARA J in Romanian territorial waters.
The following day, a fire broke out aboard the San Marino-flagged vessel Wine Trader. Earlier, on October 6 and 13, drones attacked four merchant vessels near Bulgaria.
Militarnyi previously reported that Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey had called on NATO to strengthen security in the Black Sea region and provide additional counter-drone capabilities.
On October 15, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte discussed maritime security and the recent attacks on merchant vessels with the leaders of the countries involved. Following the meeting, he said the Alliance was already expanding its counter-drone capabilities on the eastern flank and would continue adapting its defences to address emerging threats.
Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey already have experience operating a joint military command in the Black Sea. In particular, in 2024, they established a mine countermeasures group to neutralise naval mines, with leadership rotating among the participating countries.

New home sales rise 4 percent in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:49:54 UTC
17:49:54 KST

New house sales in Türkiye rose 3.9 percent year-on-year to 51,519 in September, according to official data released on Oct. 16.
New homes accounted for 36.2% of total housing transactions during the month, data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) showed.
Overall house sales fell 9.3 percent from a year earlier to 142,390, as existing home sales dropped 15.3 percent to 90,871.
Adjusted for calendar effects, new house sales increased 3.8 percent annually. On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, they rose 5.5 percent from August, while existing home sales remained unchanged.
Mortgaged house sales climbed 5.1 percent year-on-year to 23,397, accounting for 16.4 percent of total transactions.
Sales to foreign buyers increased 9.9 percent to 2,167, representing 1.5 percent of the total. Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 388, followed by Iraqis with 166 and Germans with 162.
In January-September, new house sales edged down 0.6 percent from the same period last year to 359,913, while total housing transactions declined 7.2 percent to 1.09 million.
In the first nine months of 2026, home sales to foreigners declined by 4.3 percent year-on-year to 15,308 units, according to TÜİK data.

Drone strikes in Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:48:48 UTC
17:48:48 KST

Romanian warships sail during a Romanian Navy led exercise outside Constanta, Romania, on April 16, 2024. (AP Photo/Andreea Alexandru, File)
A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
The attacks in the two countries’ exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine.
Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube River ports, leaving Kiev increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine’s Danube ports.
In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones on Oct. 14 and 15, one in Romania’s territorial waters.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan said on Oct. 15 in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned.
Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia, and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament.
“The problem is that we cannot prove it.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Oct. 15 that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.”
“NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said.
“NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.”
A source in Romania’s defense sector, who was not authorized to speak publicly about the incidents, told The Associated Press that the attacks are designed to hurt Ukraine economically and that “Romania is not the target right now.”
“All summer we’ve been hunting all kinds of [drone] debris, water drones, sea drones, air drones, debris in the water, on the beaches,” they said. “If this continues, someone should do something about that.”
The source added they have heard Türkiye “would like to summon all the riparian [Black Sea] states to plan a mission to escort these convoys” through a militarized safe corridor.
“I’m not sure about Turkish, but our Romanian vessels don’t have anti-air defense systems to protect against drones,” they said. “That would be a high risk for the Navy, for military vessels to escort this.”
In July, Romania, Bulgaria and Türkiye expanded the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Force naval pact to “expand the missions to the protection of critical submarine infrastructure,” according to Romania’s Defense Ministry. It would include, it said, a permanent naval presence in Romania’s exclusive economic zone.
Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Oct. 14 that the country plans to join NATO’s Drone Edge project by the end of October. Launched in July, the initiative, which Romania also joined, aims to invest over $40 billion in “counter-drone capabilities” over the next five years.

Protecting property rights during wartime: is it possible to inherit property located in temporarily occupied territories?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:47:39 EEST
17:47:39 KST

Protecting property rights during wartime: is it possible to inherit property located in temporarily occupied territories?
Kyiv • UNN
Occupation does not terminate property rights or inheritance rights. Heirs are advised not to delay submitting an application, to collect evidence, and, if necessary, to apply to court.
The full-scale armed aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine has presented the domestic legal system with a number of challenges that law-enforcement practice had not previously encountered systematically. One such challenge has been the formalization of inheritance rights to property located in temporarily occupied territories. This concerns tens of thousands of real estate properties, including residential buildings, apartments, and land plots, whose owners have died, while their heirs are forced to exercise their rights in the absence of physical access to the property, the loss of title documents, and the objective impossibility of carrying out some legally significant actions. Attorney Anastasiia Tsykalo, head of the administrative law practice at the "LOGIC Law Company," told UNN in a comment how property remaining in the TOTs is inherited.
The attorney explains that the starting point for any legal analysis of this category of cases is that the fact of a territory’s temporary occupation does not, in itself, terminate a citizen’s ownership rights to property and, accordingly, does not deprive their heirs of the right to inherit.
"This is consistent both with the constitutional guarantees of the right to private property and with the provisions of the Law of Ukraine "On Ensuring the Rights and Freedoms of Citizens and the Legal Regime in the Temporarily Occupied Territory of Ukraine," which expressly defines the occupied territories as an integral part of the territory of Ukraine. Thus, the legal problem faced in practice lies not in the very existence of the right, but in the difficulty of exercising, confirming, and formalizing it under conditions in which the usual mechanisms for interacting with government authorities and accessing documents have become significantly more complicated," Tsykalo states.
Do not put off inheritance until later
According to the attorney, one of the most common problems in cases involving the inheritance of property left in temporarily occupied territories is the passive position of heirs.
"In practice, situations are often encountered in which people postpone contacting a notary, waiting for the territory to be de-occupied, access to the real estate to be restored, or the possibility of obtaining documents that remain at its location. At the same time, such a position may create additional legal risks," says Anastasiia Tsykalo, head of the administrative law practice at the "LOGIC Law Company."
The attorney emphasizes that the Civil Code of Ukraine provides a six-month period for accepting an inheritance by submitting the relevant application. Missing this period does not in itself mean the loss of the right to inherit; however, it may subsequently require applying to court and proving the validity of the reasons why the heir was unable to exercise their right in a timely manner.
"When considering such cases, courts assess the specific circumstances of each situation, including the person’s ability to contact a notary, the existence of objective obstacles related to military actions or the occupation of the territory, as well as the heir’s conduct and actions aimed at accepting the inheritance. That is why, in cases of this category, it is important not only to formally comply with the established deadlines, but also to promptly record the person’s intention to accept the inheritance and take the necessary legal measures to protect their rights," the lawyer explains.
According to Tsykalo, in such cases the attorney’s primary task is to timely prevent risks arising for the heir and ensure that an application to accept the inheritance is submitted even in the absence of a complete set of documents for the property. It is important here that Ukrainian legislation provides special mechanisms for formalizing inheritance rights for internally displaced persons and citizens residing in areas of active hostilities or temporarily occupied territories, including the possibility of contacting a notary regardless of the place where the inheritance was opened in cases established by law.
The loss of the original property documents does not mean the loss of ownership rights
Another significant problem in cases in this category is proving the deceased’s ownership of the real estate in the absence of the original documents, which physically remained in the occupied territory, were lost, or were issued decades ago under procedures that do not correspond to modern registration systems.
"In such a situation, the absence of the original document is not tantamount to losing the ability to formalize an inheritance. The subject of an attorney’s professional legal work is a systematic search for alternative sources confirming ownership: information from the State Register of Real Rights to Real Estate and archival registers that existed before its introduction; sale and purchase, gift, and exchange agreements; privatization certificates; state acts confirming ownership of land; decisions of local self-government bodies on the allocation or assignment of land plots; technical documentation from the Bureau of Technical Inventory; and other written evidence that indirectly confirms the fact of possessing and disposing of the property," the lawyer lists possible ways to resolve the problem.
If the evidence is insufficient, go to court
If the totality of the available evidence is insufficient for the notarization of the inheritance, it becomes necessary to apply to the court to establish the relevant legal fact, in particular, the fact that a title document belongs to the deceased or the fact of the deceased’s ownership, which constitutes an independent category of cases in separate proceedings.
Established case law demonstrates that there is no universal algorithm, the attorney says.
The scope of legal support, the lawyer explains, depends on a combination of factors: whether documents are available, the circle of heirs and potential disputes between them, the nature of the real estate, and the date on which the inheritance was opened in relation to the beginning of the occupation of the particular territory. In some cases, standard notarial proceedings based on registry information are sufficient; in others, a full-fledged court process is necessary.
According to Tsykalo, the attorney’s task in this category of cases is a preliminary legal assessment: establishing the fact that the inheritance was accepted in a timely manner, evaluating the sufficiency of the evidentiary basis, determining whether legal facts need to be established through court proceedings, and forecasting the risk of future disputes between the heirs.
"Formalizing an inheritance involving property left in temporarily occupied territories is one of the most challenging areas of modern civil-law practice. The war has created significant obstacles to the exercise of inheritance rights, but it has not terminated citizens’ rights to the property belonging to them. The decisive principle in such cases should be the timeliness of action by the heir and their legal representative: contacting a notary, properly recording acceptance of the inheritance, and collecting and preserving evidence of ownership must be carried out regardless of the actual possibility of accessing the property itself. Protecting ownership rights in wartime consists not only in restoring violated rights, but also in taking measures in advance to prevent possible legal risks," the attorney concludes.

Bulgaria Wants Real-Time Data From Business. Gambling Is the Test Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:45:24 UTC
17:45:24 KST

Bulgaria Posts One of EU's Sharpest Annual Industrial Declines
Industrial production in the eurozone fell by 0.5% in August 2026, while Bulgaria recorded a monthly increase of 0.8% after a sharp decline in July
Bulgaria's government is moving away from trusting what companies report and towards watching what they do. In the space of two weeks, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has announced plans for a central registry of food prices and published draft rules that would require gambling operators to feed betting data directly to the National Revenue Agency (NRA). Together, the two initiatives point to a broader shift in how the state intends to supervise business.
The idea is not new. Retailers in Bulgaria have long been required to register sales through fiscal devices connected to the NRA, which gives the tax authority a near-live view of cash turnover. What is changing is the scope.
On 3 October, Radev told parliament that work on an electronic food price registry was "actively progressing". The registry would give the consumer protection and competition regulators actual pricing data instead of relying on voluntary pledges from supermarket chains. Bulgaria has never had such a system, although similar registries already operate in several European countries.
The draft amendments to the Gambling Act go further. The Ministry of Finance published the bill for public consultation on 23 September, and comments are open until 23 October. Under the bill, slot machines and casino equipment would have to connect to NRA systems and automatically report deposits, wagers and winnings. That would extend to land-based venues a monitoring model already used for online betting.
The scale of the market explains the urgency. As Novinite reported when the measures were unveiled, NRA figures show online betting volume rising from BGN 44 billion in 2023 to roughly BGN 66 billion in 2025. Over the same period, the number of companies licensed for online betting grew from seven in 2019 to 26.
The draft would also set a minimum monthly fee of €100,000 for each online operator. It would introduce a unified 23% rate on the difference between wagers and winnings for slot and casino games. And it would require every licence holder to be a Bulgarian company or to operate through a registered place of business in the country. Existing operators would have until 31 March 2027 to comply.
Direct reporting sounds like a simple data connection, but it reaches deep into an operator's systems. Every bet and payout has to be traceable from the player's wallet through the game server back to the studio that supplied the game. Online operators rarely build their games themselves. Most source titles from dozens of studios through a casino games aggregator, a single integration point that passes content, transaction records and reporting data between the studios and the operator's platform. When regulators demand live data, those intermediary layers become part of the compliance chain.
Bulgaria knows this industry from the supply side as well. The country is home to established slot manufacturers and game developers, including Sofia-based EGT and Amusnet, whose content is distributed internationally. The draft also introduces separate one-time state fees of €25,000 to €100,000 for licences covering the manufacture, import, distribution and servicing of gaming equipment. Domestic suppliers, not only operators, will therefore feel the reform.
The government's explanatory memorandum, available with the draft on the Ministry of Finance consultation page, states openly that one goal is to consolidate the sector. A €100,000 monthly floor amounts to €1.2 million a year in fees before an operator has earned anything. That is manageable for a market leader but heavy for a small licensee.
Operators will also have to pay for system integrations with the NRA, establish a local legal presence and work under a near-total ban on advertising. The draft additionally terminates affiliate licences from 1 January 2027. For many operators the likely response is to cut costs elsewhere: fewer in-house systems, more outsourced technology and a sharper focus on the markets that justify the expense.
Gambling is an easy place to start. Its revenues are digital, its regulator already receives online betting data, and the industry has few public defenders. The harder question is whether the model spreads.
A food price registry would bring the same logic to retail, where margins are thin and data systems are far less standardised. If parliament passes the gambling bill largely intact, it will be the clearest signal yet that Bulgaria intends to supervise business through data flows rather than paperwork. Companies in other sectors would be wise to treat it as a preview of what they may soon face.
Casino gaming is one of the most closely supervised leisure industries around, yet there is no single rulebook that governs it.

Taiwan buys three years of support for MQ-9B drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:45:13 UTC
17:45:13 KST

- Taiwan is paying General Atomics $38.8 million for MQ-9B contractor logistics support through August 2029 under a sole-source Foreign Military Sales contract.
- Taiwan has ordered four MQ-9Bs, with the first two handed over in March 2026 and the remaining two due in 2027.
Taiwan is paying General Atomics Aeronautical Systems $38.8 million to keep its new MQ-9B SkyGuardian drones flying, under a contractor logistics support deal that runs through August 2029, the U.S. Department of War said.
The award, announced on Oct. 15 in the Pentagon’s daily contract list and signed on Oct. 1, covers sustainment services and contractor logistics support for Taiwan’s MQ-9B fleet. Contractor logistics support means the manufacturer handles much of the maintenance, spare parts supply and technical support for the aircraft instead of relying entirely on the operator’s own maintenance system.
Taiwan is covering the full cost through the Foreign Military Sales program, and all of the money was obligated at signing. The U.S. Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, which manages the sale for Taipei, awarded the contract to General Atomics on a sole-source basis, with the work to be performed at the company’s facility in Poway, California.
Taiwan has ordered four MQ-9Bs, a medium-altitude, long-endurance drone developed from the Reaper that can stay airborne for more than 40 hours. The State Department approved the sale in 2020. The U.S. government then signed a $217.6 million contract for the first two aircraft in May 2023 and a $250 million contract for the final two in March 2024, with two ground control stations included across the deals, Defense News reported.
The first two drones were handed over to the Republic of China Air Force at a ceremony in the United States on March 17, 2026, attended by Taiwanese Vice Defense Minister Hsu Szu-chien. The aircraft were to stay in the U.S. for several months of testing, and Taiwan’s air force chief of staff said they were scheduled to arrive on the island in the third quarter of 2026. The remaining two are due in 2027.
Taipei plans to use the drones for long-range surveillance and reconnaissance around the island, where Chinese military aircraft and ships operate almost daily. Analysts have said the MQ-9Bs could take over some patrol missions now flown by Taiwan’s fighter jets and its aging P-3 maritime patrol aircraft, and help locate targets for Taiwan’s anti-ship missiles.
The drones will join a fast-growing Taiwanese unmanned fleet. The Ministry of National Defense announced plans in July 2025 to buy nearly 49,000 drones of five types for about NT$50 billion ($1.56 billion), alongside locally developed systems from the state-run National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology.
Under the new contract, General Atomics will support Taiwan’s MQ-9B operations through Aug. 31, 2029.

Ukrainian Composer’s Opera on Abducted Children Premieres in Warsaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:44:22 UTC
17:44:22 KST

Warsaw, Oct. 16 – The Polish National Opera at Teatr Wielki presents the fully staged world premiere of “The Mothers of Kherson,” an opera by Ukrainian composer Maxim Kolomiiets with a libretto by acclaimed American playwright George Brant. Commissioned by New York’s Metropolitan Opera, the work brings Russia’s abduction of Ukrainian children to the international stage.
Conducted by Canadian-American maestro Keri-Lynn Wilson and directed by Barbara Wysocka, the production combines artistic achievement with a call for international attention to the fate of Ukraine’s children.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“One of history’s most sinister war crimes”
Ahead of the premiere, Wilson dedicated her message to Ukrainian families still waiting for their children to return.
“As we have our final dress rehearsal this evening in Warsaw for ‘The Mothers of Kherson,’ my heart is with my beloved sisters and brothers in Ukraine who are waiting and hoping for the more than 20,000 children who are still missing – innocent victims of Russia’s brutal child kidnapping program,” Wilson said.
“Our world premiere Friday night is the true story of the mothers who embark on the heroic journey to rescue their children,” adding that “we hope the world will join us in bearing witness to one of history’s most sinister war crimes.”
Wilson conducted the opera’s concert premiere in Kyiv in early June at the National Opera of Ukraine. The Warsaw production marks its first fully staged performance.
22 US Lawmakers Press Trump to Enforce Russia Sanctions Ahead of Oct. 18 Deadline
                                                                                                                                                                         Photo via Kinga Karpati & Daniel Zarewicz                             
According to Ukraine’s “Children of War” platform, 20,651 children had been registered as deported or forcibly displaced since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Of these, 2,689 had been returned, according to the figures provided for this article.
Three women, one mission
The opera follows three women from southern Ukraine: Kateryna (Izabela Matuła), Dasha (Kamila Dutkowska), and grandmother Olha (Małgorzata Walewska). They undertake an exhausting journey to recover children taken to Russian-controlled territory.
                                                                                                                                                                         The final dress rehearsal. Photo via Krzysztof Bielinski.                             
Based on real events, the work explores maternal love, solidarity, and the trauma of families torn apart by war. It opens with a lullaby combining an authentic Ukrainian folk melody with a newly composed section by Kolomiiets – a musical reminder of the protection every child deserves.
Ukrainian baritone Andrii Bondarenko plays Vitaly, a Ukrainian Armed Forces serviceman and Kateryna’s husband, whose story connects the opera to the liberation of Kherson from Russian occupation on Nov. 11, 2022.
An international commission for Ukrainian music
The production marks a significant milestone for Ukrainian contemporary opera, bringing Kolomiiets’s work to two leading international institutions and ensuring that the stories of Ukrainian families reach audiences beyond the country.
In an interview with Kyiv Post, Kolomiiets discussed creating the opera and bringing Ukraine’s wartime experience to the international stage.
Metropolitan Opera General Manager Peter Gelb has also spoken about the institution’s commitment to Ukraine and the role of culture in bearing witness to the war. “This war is now longer than World War II, I think… It’s good for Ukrainian citizens to understand that there are efforts being made. I mean, even if the US government has stopped helping Ukraine, the fact that its premier arts institution has never given up in supporting Ukraine, and that we’re bringing this story to the world… I think by doing it here, first [it] shows the Ukrainian people that the world has not forgotten them” Gelb said.
Since 2022, Gelb and Wilson have become the prominent international advocates for Ukrainian music. Wilson conducted concerts in Ukraine and abroad, while also supporting Ukrainian musicians through the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra.
The opera’s US premiere at the Metropolitan Opera in New York is scheduled for the 2027-28 season.

At least 12 dead after migrant boat sinks off Gambia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:43:01 UTC
17:43:01 KST

The IOM says increased controls in traditional departure spots in Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal have pushed some migrants seeking to reach Europe further south, towards countries such as The Gambia.
At least 12 people died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Gambia, the Red Cross said.
The incident occurred off of Jinack Kajata in the country's North Bank region, the Gambia Red Cross Society (GRCS) said on Thursday. The migrants were reportedly heading towards Europe via the West African Atlantic Route.
"The number of people missing remains uncertain, and further updates are expected as response efforts continue," the GRCS said in a statement, adding that it was "working closely with relevant authorities and response partners as the situation unfolds."
According to Gambian media, the village of Jinack Kajata on Jinack Island has become an increasingly popular launch site for migrants looking to make the journey to Spain's Canary Islands in the Atlantic Ocean.
The United Nations' International Organization for Migration (IOM) says the West African Atlantic Route is a key pathway for West African migrants travelling to Europe, despite it becoming increasingly dangerous.
"Data from the West African Atlantic Route show that while arrivals to the Canary Islands fell considerably since the 2024 peak (62 per cent decrease from 2024 to 2025), recorded deaths and disappearances remained broadly unchanged, falling 4 per cent from 2024 to 2025 (1,215 to 1,172), highlighting how the route has become much more dangerous for migrants," the IOM said earlier this week.
It added that increased controls in traditional departure spots in Morocco, Mauritania, and Senegal have pushed some migrants seeking to reach Europe further south, towards countries such as The Gambia.
"These alternative departure points can add up to 750 kilometres to the crossing, extending some journeys to approximately 2,200 kilometres and exposing people to longer periods at sea, more remote and less monitored coastlines, and greater risks of shipwreck, dehydration and disappearance," the IOM said.
In July, dozens of migrants were reportedly dead or missing after a vessel travelling from The Gambia was shipwrecked off the coast of Mauritania.

By this summer, European leaders had managed to persuade Trump to show a degree of sympathy for Ukraine’s long fight against the Russian invasion.
At the Group of Seven (G-7) summit in France, President Emmanuel Macron engineered a brief meeting with Trump at which Zelensky showed him pictures of a cathedral in Kyiv decimated by Russian missiles.
“The western alliance is in a weaker position now than it was a few days ago,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told reporters as she arrived for talks in the Belgian capital on Oct 15.
“If you do not support Ukraine, then you put Europe as a whole, and in my view therefore also NATO as a whole, in a much, much more dangerous situation.”
Their latest falling-out is happening at a particularly inopportune moment.
Winter is setting in and Ukraine has a shortage of the US-made Patriot interceptors needed to shoot down Russian missiles.
Kyiv’s military costs are also blowing a hole in its budget that Europe is struggling to fill.
Meanwhile, Russia is striking more civilian targets, leaving Kyiv experiencing intermittent power and water supply cuts.
In November, Russian President Vladimir Putin will have a chance to meet with Trump at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China – where neither Zelensky nor the Europeans will be present.
Trump, for his part, is weeks away from a midterm election where his Republican party is expected to suffer heavy losses – sending him searching for quick ways to lower gas prices.
That fixation is informing Trump’s push to buy Russian diesel despite sanctions, and his calls for Ukraine to halt attacks on oil refineries, even if experts say the US war on Iran is the largest culprit behind high fuel costs.
“The most important thing that we’re going to discuss today is what he needs for this winter. It’s all about this winter,” Kulberg told Bloomberg.
“We also have to understand that the United States is now running into the midterms. It’s election time,” Kulbergs said. “That’s a different vibe.”
For now, most Europeans are recommending that Zelensky temper his criticism of Trump, given there is no alternative to working with the US, the people said.
The country continues to sell Ukraine weapons and share intelligence vital to Kyiv’s defence.
If that intelligence disappeared, Europe would not have a good solution, one official said.
That’s likely why EU leaders were careful not to be too publicly critical of Trump as they arrived on Oct 15 for their summit in Brussels.
Behind closed doors, however, several still expressed shock at the US president’s recent behaviour, the people said.
An Elysee official said France’s priority is for Europe to continue supporting Ukraine.
A German chancellery spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
Europe is sticking to its guns by upholding sanctions and insisting that Ukraine shouldn’t cede territory in a peace settlement, especially after Kyiv’s forces regained some lost ground in the eastern region of Donbas Putin wants to control.
US leverage over Ukraine has also diminished over the last few months.
While intelligence remains an important factor, the money to support Kyiv and buy US weapons comes primarily from Europe.
Ukraine is also finally receiving ammunition for F-16 fighter jets to shoot down Russia’s menacing jet-powered drones.
Meanwhile, Washington’s efforts to deliver peace, which Trump promised to bring shortly after taking officein 2025, haven’t made much headway.
The latest meetings in Florida over the weekend, which the Ukrainian delegation cut short following Trump’s Russia diesel deal, largely focused on going over the same set of points that the president’s envoys – Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner – drew up months ago, according to people familiar with the matter.
During a meeting on Oct 12, EU foreign ministers privately agreed that Europe’s policy on Ukraine must remain constant, regardless of the gyrations in Washington, according to people briefed on the discussions.
They resolved to engage the US when it’s possible, and maintain their support for Kyiv when it’s not.
“We definitely have a different approach to this war,” EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas told reporters in Brussels on Oct 15. “We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender. Squeezing Ukraine is not the right approach.” BLOOMBERG

Cambodia fully restores centuries-old West Mebon Temple in famed Angkor park
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:39:41 CST
17:39:41 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 15, 2026 shows part of the restored West Mebon Temple in Siem Reap province, Cambodia. Archaeologists have successfully restored the centuries-old West Mebon Temple within Cambodia's UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park, according to an APSARA National Authority (ANA) news release on Friday. (ANA/Handout via Xinhua)
PHNOM PENH, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Archaeologists have successfully restored the centuries-old West Mebon Temple within Cambodia's UNESCO-listed Angkor Archaeological Park, according to an APSARA National Authority (ANA) news release on Friday.
Situated on an island in the middle of the West Baray -- the Angkor area's largest reservoir -- the temple is surrounded by vast expanses of water, creating a distinctive and captivating landscape.
While the ANA prepares the site for its official opening in November by cleaning the area, organizing the surroundings, and enhancing the environment, eager tourists have already begun visiting the temple to take photographs and admire its remarkable architecture.
Through a joint effort between the ANA and the French government, the temple underwent extensive restoration to recover its former appearance after suffering significant structural damage and stone loss over the centuries.
"The completion of this work marks an important achievement in the ongoing efforts to preserve and restore Angkor's cultural heritage," the news release said.
Built in the middle of the 11th century as a Hindu sanctuary, the West Mebon Temple was constructed using laterite and sandstone. A short boat trip takes visitors to the monument, which marks the exact center of the massive 8 km by 2.2 km reservoir, the ANA said, adding that the site offers a uniquely serene atmosphere, especially at sunset.
The West Mebon Temple stands as one of the major cultural monuments within the Angkor Archaeological Park, Cambodia's most popular tourist destination, located in northwestern Siem Reap province. ■

S. Korea's interbank forex trading volume grows in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
16:39:38 CST
17:39:38 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's interbank foreign exchange trading volume grew in the third quarter due to a substantial rise in foreign exchange (FX) swap transactions, central bank data showed Friday.
The daily average transaction of foreign currencies and derivatives in the domestic interbank market increased 2.25 billion U.S. dollars from three months earlier to 55.65 billion dollars in the July-September quarter, according to the Bank of Korea.
FX swaps served as the main driver of growth, mounting 1.80 billion dollars from the previous quarter to hit a daily average trading of 25.92 billion dollars in the third quarter.
Spot exchange volume ticked up 0.07 billion dollars to 23.48 billion dollars, and forward contracts trading added 0.20 billion dollars to 2.60 billion dollars.
The transaction of other derivatives, including currency swaps and options, was up 0.18 billion dollars to 3.66 billion dollars.
The daily average volatility in the South Korean won versus U.S. dollar exchange rate advanced to 0.52 percent in September from 0.31 percent in August.
The won versus dollar exchange rate slightly dipped to 1,352.8 won per dollar at the end of September from 1,368.6 won tallied a month earlier.
Premium on credit default swap, which gauges credit risk for five-year government bonds, averaged 22 basis points in September, unchanged from the previous month. ■

Hezbollah acknowledged on Thursday that a shipment of explosives seized by Lebanese authorities last week belonged to the group, saying it was intended for use against Israel.

On Monday, Salam confirmed the seizure of “hundreds of kilogrammes of explosives” and pledged to pursue the investigation thoroughly and expand its scope to identify everyone involved in what he described as a criminal operation, as well as those behind it, and uncover their plans and objectives.
He said his government would take firm action against any weapons held, transported or used outside the framework of state authority.
Since the beginning of October, Lebanese authorities have seized three shipments of explosives being transported from eastern Lebanon.

No, this oil tanker didn’t carry Russian diesel to the United States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:36:46 UTC
17:36:46 KST

No, this oil tanker didn’t carry Russian diesel to the United States
Following US President Donald Trump's October 9 announcement of an agreement signed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel into the United States, a number of pro-Russian social media accounts began claiming that a Russian oil tanker was already carrying thousands of barrels of diesel to the United States. The ship was actually carrying fertiliser.
US President Donald Trump announced on Friday, October 9, that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import millions of tons of Russian diesel.
“Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel,” Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
The next day, the pro-Russian X account Russian Market (which uses the handle @runews) posted that Russian diesel was already being delivered to the United States, scarcely a day after the deal.
The account claimed that the Minerva Zen, an oil and chemical tanker, was carrying close to 280,000 barrels of diesel from Russia… and was bound for the United States. The post even featured a map of the route it was taking, starting with when the cargo was supposedly loaded on September 22 in Saint Petersburg, Russia.
The fake news spread quickly, appearing in different posts and garnering more than 570,000 views on X. It was also picked up by media outlets in Nigeria.
A ship carrying fertiliser, according to Tanker Trackers
This claim, however, is wrong. The Minerva Zen was not carrying diesel from Russia.
It is true that the Minerva Zen, an oil and chemical tanker (which means it is equipped to carry chemical products as well as petrol products), did leave the port in Saint Petersburg on September 23. You can see this on the site Global Fishing Watch, a site that makes it possible to follow marine traffic.
MarineTraffic, another site that tracks ships across the globe, shows that the Minerva Zen docked in Wilmington, North Carolina on the night of October 11 to 12.
The FRANCE 24 Observers team spoke to Tankertrackers.com, a company specialised in tracking oil tankers in particular, who said that the Minerva Zen wasn’t carrying diesel but fertiliser, specifically urea ammonium nitrate (UAN). This information was confirmed by the economic intelligence company Vortexa.
“When the US imposed sanctions on Russia back in February/March 2022, they banned the import of hydrocarbons such as crude oil, fuel oil, LNG, etc., but they allowed fertiliser,” Tanker Trackers said.
As you can see on a site that records imports, Russian fertiliser was also imported into Wilmington back in June. The June cargo was delivered to a company called Eurochem North America, which specialises in fertiliser production. According to Tankertrackers, the October 12 delivery was also bound for Eurochem North America.
Cargo not unloaded in the port’s petrol terminal
Another supporting the information that the Minerva Zen was not carrying diesel is that the tanker was not unloaded in the port’s "Apex Oil Co Wilmington" petrol terminal, which is located to the south of Wilmington port.
According to the data gathered by MarineTraffic, the tanker was unloaded in the “NSCPA” Terminal located to the north of the port. This terminal is where agricultural and chemical products as well as containers are unloaded.
Finally, Minerva Marine, the company that owns the Minerva Zen, told US local TV station Wwaytv3 that the tanker was carrying urea ammonium nitrate, not diesel.

The naval detachment departed from Vladivostok on September 10 for the Asia-Pacific deployment. Earlier, the ships made a business port call to Jakarta, Indonesia.

Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:36:13 UTC
17:36:13 KST

Norway wealth fund urged to ease nuclear arms ban after Gaza investment row
Review prompted by Gaza action calls for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift ethical risk limitations on its investments.
A government-appointed committee has called for Norway’s sovereign wealth fund to lift limitations on its investments based on ethical risks, including those regarding nuclear weapons and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
In a report released on Thursday, the committee said the world’s largest sovereign wealth fund, which controls assets totalling nearly $2.3 trillion, should be allowed to invest in companies that produce nuclear weapons. With reference to Gaza, it also called for the fund to refrain from involvement in “diplomatic” issues.
Led by former Central Bank Governor Svein Gjedrem, the committee recommended easing the fund’s investment conditions as part of a broader overhaul that would give its manager, the Central Bank, greater discretion over how it addresses ethical risks.
The review was prompted in part by controversy over the fund’s disinvestment last year from United States construction giant Caterpillar. The fund said the move was prompted by Caterpillar’s purported involvement in rights violations perpetrated by Israel amid its genocidal war on Gaza and in the occupied West Bank. Washington has since pressured Oslo over the move.
“Parts of the rationale for the appointment of the Committee was the Fund’s management related to the war in Gaza,” the committee commissioned by the government said. In the report, it argued that decisions regarding “another state’s conduct” should not be made by the fund but “reserved for the ordinary diplomatic channels of the Norwegian authorities”.
The unanimous recommendations of the committee in the report, which was submitted to the Ministry of Finance, also called for a review of the fund’s exclusion of investment in companies involved in the production of nuclear weapons.
Citing Norway’s reliance on NATO’s nuclear deterrent and a worsening security environment, the report suggested that investments in companies based in the US, United Kingdom and France that are involved in the production of nuclear weapons should be allowed.
The proposals also extended to reshaping the role of the fund’s independent ethics watchdog, allowing a number of assessments of potential investments to remain confidential.
‘Pandora’s box’
The report has already provoked a backlash in Norway, with opposition politicians slamming the potential changes. Meanwhile, analysts suggested that weakening ethics considerations could have a wide impact.
“If the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund – often considered a global gold standard – changes its posture towards nuclear weapons, it will open Pandora’s box for many global investors to follow suit,” Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School, told Al Jazeera.
The committee framed the proposed change as an obligation to protect Norway’s national security, citing the country’s dependence on its allies’ nuclear umbrella.
“The global security situation has changed. Norway is building up its defence capabilities, and the protection provided by NATO’s nuclear umbrella has become increasingly important. The companies that would be reincluded produce weapons that Norway needs for its own defence”, the report argued.
Gareth Evans, former Australian foreign minister, told Al Jazeera the report was “an encouraging initiative in a world that has become alarmingly complacent about the risks of nuclear war, with every major nuclear arms control agreement dead, dying or on life support, and the longstanding taboo against threat or use eroding”.
Amid US President Donald Trump’s shake-up of NATO, European countries are increasingly looking to join France’s nuclear deterrent umbrella.
Trump said on Thursday that Washington is holding talks with Russia and China aimed at denuclearising the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
However, Loh warned that shifting the Norwegian fund’s investment conditions could encourage investment by others in nuclear companies “in scenarios different from the Norwegians’ condition of the invested companies being based in allied, nuclear-armed NATO countries”.

Economists warn Lithuania’s 2027 budget risks rising debt and deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Lithuania’s proposed 2027 budget will further widen the government deficit and increase public debt, while ambitious revenue targets could prove difficult to meet, economists warned Friday after the government approved the draft budget.
The spending plan reflects continued fiscal expansion, with expenditure growing faster than nominal gross domestic product, even when the impact of European Union structural funding is excluded, said Indrė Genytė-Pikčienė, an economist at Artea Bank.
“Next year will be another year of generous fiscal expansion,” she told BNS, adding that declining EU structural support and fewer one-off economic tailwinds would make the outlook more challenging.
Tadas Povilauskas, an economist at SEB Bank, said fiscal policy would again stimulate the economy through borrowing. But rising deficits and public acceptance of persistent overspending could make it more difficult to consolidate public finances in the future without slowing economic growth.
The budget deficit is set to grow mainly because of higher social benefits and public-sector wages, much of which is linked to automatic indexation of pensions, benefits and salaries, Povilauskas said.
He questioned the need for an additional 150 million euros earmarked for a proposed family support package, arguing that some spending increases went beyond what indexation required. He also criticised the lack of emphasis on improving public administration efficiency.
However, he said higher social spending could support domestic businesses by boosting consumption among lower-income households.
Revenue targets under scrutiny
Genytė-Pikčienė questioned whether the government would collect all the revenue projected in the budget. Lithuania’s economy benefited this year from increased consumption following a reform of the second-pillar pension system, but that boost is expected to fade next year.
Povilauskas also described several revenue forecasts as ambitious.
Excise tax revenue is projected to rise by 11%, while value-added tax revenue is expected to increase by about 7.2%. He questioned whether the VAT target was realistic, particularly because 158 million euros of the expected increase is attributed to improved tax administration.
Household consumption is expected to grow more slowly next year as the effect of withdrawals from second-pillar pension funds fades, he said.
He also urged caution over the plan to collect 2.1 billion euros in corporate income tax, noting that the target for this year is expected to be missed.
Debt costs and EU deficit rules
Genytė-Pikčienė said the projected deficit was significant enough to raise the possibility of an infringement procedure by the European Commission because it would exceed the EU’s Maastricht deficit limit of 3% of GDP. She noted, however, that Lithuania was not the only country exceeding the threshold.
She warned that relying on borrowing to finance public spending could create serious long-term problems as debt servicing costs rise and leave less room for future policy decisions.
Povilauskas said interest payments would increase by 370 million euros next year, adding the equivalent of 0.3 percentage points of GDP to budget expenditure.
Public debt is expected to rise by another 6.5 billion euros in 2027, following an increase of 6.8 billion euros this year, reaching 48.2% of GDP by the end of next year.
The government is financing much of the increase in defence spending – from 2% to 5% of GDP over several years – through borrowing, while also increasing other expenditure, Povilauskas said. The Finance Ministry has acknowledged the risk that public debt could approach 60% of GDP by the end of the medium-term planning period.
Genytė-Pikčienė said lawmakers should carefully scrutinise any additional spending proposals during the budget process to prevent the deficit from growing further. She stressed that national defence and security must remain priorities because they are essential to economic prosperity, attracting foreign investment and supporting business stability.
Social spending and inflation
The draft budget maintains a strong focus on social spending and raising incomes, Genytė-Pikčienė said.
The average old-age pension is set to increase at a double-digit rate, while pensions for people with the required length of service are expected to rise by 11%. Salaries for teachers, statutory officers and cultural workers are planned to increase by 7.5%, with pay for judicial assistants rising by nearly 6%.
The government is seeking to offset pressure on household purchasing power from imported inflation, including higher fuel prices and heating costs, by increasing incomes, she said.
Lithuania has refrained from introducing broad measures to counter energy price increases, unlike some neighbouring countries, instead relying more heavily on income growth to cushion the impact on households.
Economist Romas Lazutka criticised the proposed 150 million-euro family package, saying its measures were universal rather than specifically targeted at people in the greatest need.
He said much of the budget deficit was effectively predetermined by legislation and existing commitments, including social benefits, education spending and public-sector collective agreements.
Reducing the deficit would likely require cuts to social spending, a politically unpopular step that would be difficult to implement, he said.
Lazutka also pointed to what he described as a structural imbalance between the state budget and the Sodra social insurance fund. Sodra regularly records a surplus and builds up reserves, while the central government runs a large deficit and borrows at interest rates higher than the returns earned on those reserves.
The arrangement means the government is paying more to borrow than it earns by investing money accumulated in the social insurance system, he said.

Türkiye and 18 other countries condemn Colombia's West Jerusalem embassy opening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:34:34 UTC
17:34:34 KST

Foreign ministers from Türkiye and 18 other countries have strongly condemned Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem, describing the move as contrary to relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and an obstacle to international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.
In a joint statement dated October 16 2026, the ministers from Türkiye, Algeria, Djibouti, Indonesia, Palestine, Qatar, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Malaysia, Egypt, Pakistan, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Jordan and Yemen said they firmly rejected the opening of the Colombian embassy in the city.
The ministers reiterated that any measures or decisions intended to alter the legal or historical status of occupied Jerusalem, or to recognise the city as Israel’s capital, were null and void and had no legal effect.
They cited relevant UN Security Council and General Assembly resolutions, particularly Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980. These resolutions reject attempts to change Jerusalem’s character or status and call on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions to Israel from the city, which forms part of the Palestinian territories occupied in 1967.
The statement called on the Colombian government to reconsider and reverse its decision, comply with its obligations under international law and refrain from measures that undermine the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.
These rights, the ministers stressed, include the right to an independent and sovereign Palestinian state, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

KMT's Ko Chih-en makes second bid for Kaohsiung mayor

17:33:18 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) is seeking to lead the southern city with a campaign focused on jobs, affordable housing, and infrastructure.
Speaking at a youth forum at National Sun Yat-sen University on Wednesday, Ko said Kaohsiung needs better job opportunities to keep young people from leaving. The former professor said her 26 years of teaching had made her particularly concerned about graduates struggling to find work outside science and engineering, CNA reported.
Ko is making her second bid for mayor after losing to incumbent DPP Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) in 2022. She is running against DPP Legislator Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) in the Nov. 28 local elections, hoping to regain the city for the KMT, per UDN.
Born in Pingtung, Ko studied education at National Chengchi University before earning a master's degree from Michigan State University. She later received a doctorate in educational psychology from the University of Southern California, per Legislative Yuan.
Before entering politics, Ko taught at Tamkang University for more than two decades and served as dean of student affairs. Her academic career helped establish her reputation as an education specialist.
Ko was first elected to the Legislative Yuan in 2016, representing a district in New Taipei. She lost her re-election bid in 2020 but returned in 2024 as a KMT legislator elected through the party-list system, per Yahoo News.
Ko has also held senior KMT positions, including deputy secretary-general and head of the party's women's department. She previously led the National Policy Foundation, a KMT-affiliated think tank that develops policy proposals.
In 2022, Ko challenged Chen in Kaohsiung, a longtime DPP stronghold. She received 529,607 votes, or 40.16%, against Chen's 766,147 votes, or 58.1%, per Business Today.
Ko has remained active in Kaohsiung politics since her defeat while serving in the legislature. Her latest campaign emphasizes economic development, better public services, and more investment in areas outside the city center, per UDN.
At Wednesday's forum, Ko said Kaohsiung's young workforce had declined by about 100,000 in recent years. She called for higher wages, stronger local industries, and more job opportunities beyond the technology sector.
Ko has also proposed affordable housing for working families who cannot afford homes at market prices. She wants the city's growing concert and tourism industries to create more lasting jobs for local businesses and workers.

Strong winds fuel fires near Los Angeles as the region recovers from last year's deadly blazes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:33:00 UTC
17:33:00 KST

California wildfires force evacuations near Malibu
October 16, 2026
Several brush fires burned across southern California on Friday, forcing evacuations near Malibu as hot, dry winds fueled the flames.
The rapidly spreading Bryson Fire grew to about 81 hectares (200 acres) and threatened a Los Angeles County juvenile detention and rehabilitation facility, which was evacuated Thursday night.
What is happening near Malibu?
Authorities ordered residents to leave the Encinal Canyon area near Malibu, a coastal town west of Los Angeles. Surrounding parts of the Santa Monica Mountains were placed under evacuation warnings.
The National Weather Service forecast stronger gusts overnight that could intensify the fires.
The Bryson Fire was first reported around 5 p.m. local time Thursday (0000 GMT Friday), north of Malibu. A large plume of dark smoke rose above the hills and could be seen from miles away.
Los Angeles County officials urged residents to follow emergency instructions and check on neighbors who might need help, if safe to do so.
"If you feel unsafe due to a fire nearby ... do not wait for an official alert to leave," officials said.
The blaze was burning about 32 kilometers (20 miles) west of the area devastated by the Palisades Fire in January 2025.
Where else are firefighters battling blazes?
In Azusa, north of Los Angeles, about 200 firefighters tackled a wind-driven fire that burned more than 16 hectares (40 acres).
Crews stopped its forward spread by mid-afternoon, and evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel Mountains were downgraded to warnings.
Further south, a fire at Camp Pendleton, a military base near San Diego, burned more than 3.8 square kilometers (1.5 square miles), threatening buildings and infrastructure.
Power companies cut supplies to about 127,000 customers across California to reduce the risk of electrical equipment sparking further fires.
The Palisades and Eaton fires killed 31 people in the Los Angeles area in January 2025. Forecasters said the current winds were not expected to reach the strength recorded during those disasters.
Edited by: Natalie Muller
