Prices have risen again: which products became more expensive in Ukraine in just three days
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:32:45 EEST
17:32:45 KST

Prices have risen again: which products became more expensive in Ukraine in just three days
Kyiv • UNN
From October 12 to 15, 2026, prices increased for tomatoes, chicken, bananas, grains, and oil. A basket of seven items became 1.94% more expensive.
In Ukrainian supermarkets, average prices for a number of popular food products increased between October 12 and 15, 2026. Pink tomatoes, chicken and bananas became notably more expensive. The price increase also affected grains and sunflower oil. Although in most cases the difference amounts to just a few hryvnias, even such short-term fluctuations gradually increase Ukrainian families’ expenses on everyday shopping.
Which products Ukrainians already have to pay more for, how much the cost of a typical grocery basket has changed, and what factors may affect price tags in supermarkets were examined by UNN.
Tomatoes lead in price growth: how much they cost in October 2026
Pink tomatoes saw the largest price increase since the beginning of the current week. If a kilogram cost an average of UAH 112.33 on October 12, by October 15 its price had risen to UAH 115.67. In just three days, tomatoes became UAH 3.34, or 2.97%, more expensive. A similar trend can be observed in the plum tomato segment. Their average price increased from UAH 99.33 to UAH 100.79 per kilogram. Thus, the increase amounted to UAH 1.46, or 1.47%.
Both varieties of tomatoes have now exceeded the mark of UAH 100 per kilogram. At the same time, pink tomatoes remain almost UAH 15 more expensive than plum tomatoes. Experts analyzing the fruit and vegetable market explain that one possible reason for the increase in tomato prices is the seasonal decline in supply. In autumn, the amount of vegetables grown in open fields on the Ukrainian market gradually decreases. Meanwhile, greenhouse produce accounts for an increasingly larger share, and its cost depends on expenses for heating, electricity and maintaining the necessary growing conditions.
In addition, at the beginning of October, EastFruit analysts reported a reduction in tomato supply at trading platforms and an increase in wholesale prices. This may have created conditions for a further increase in vegetable prices in retail chains.
At the same time, it is important to take into account that the retail price depends on a number of components that may not be immediately obvious: logistics costs, the trade markup and the promotional policy of a particular supermarket. Therefore, an increase in the average price over three days does not mean that tomatoes became more expensive by the same amount in all stores across Ukraine.
Chicken and bananas increased in price by almost 3%
Among meat products, chicken carcasses showed a noticeable price increase. The average cost of one kilogram rose from UAH 114.25 on October 12 to UAH 117.50 on October 15. The price difference was UAH 3.25, or 2.84%. In terms of the absolute price increase, chicken almost matched pink tomatoes.
It should be noted that for buyers purchasing a whole carcass weighing more than one kilogram, the actual increase in the cost of the purchase will be higher. For example, a two-kilogram carcass at the average price on October 15 would cost UAH 235. Just three days earlier, on October 12, the same purchase would have cost UAH 228.50.
Chicken prices may be affected by producers’ expenses on feed, electricity, veterinary services, transportation and product storage.
Bananas ranked third in terms of the rate of price growth. Over three days, the average price per kilogram increased from UAH 76.33 to UAH 78.13. The tropical fruit became UAH 1.80, or 2.36%, more expensive. This happened because, unlike local seasonal vegetables, bananas come to Ukraine mainly from abroad. Accordingly, their price depends on the terms of import purchases, international logistics, transportation within the country and the exchange rate. In particular, changes in the value of foreign currencies may affect the purchase prices of imported products, since settlements with suppliers are made primarily in currencies other than the hryvnia.
Groceries are also becoming more expensive: how much buckwheat, rice and oil cost now
The price increase also affected long-shelf-life products that Ukrainians traditionally buy in reserve.
In the grains segment, buckwheat rose in price the most. The average cost of one kilogram increased from UAH 82.57 to UAH 84.10. The difference was UAH 1.53, or 1.85%. At first glance, this is an insignificant increase. However, for families that regularly consume buckwheat, the price increase will result in additional expenses. Thus, five kilograms of the grain would cost UAH 420.50 at prices on October 15, compared with UAH 412.85 three days earlier. According to experts, the increase in buckwheat prices may be related to the volume of the harvest, offers from processing enterprises, and the cost of storage and delivery to retail chains.
The price of long-grain parboiled rice changed somewhat less. While a kilogram cost an average of UAH 61.37 on October 12, by October 15 it already cost UAH 62.20.
Among the popular products that Ukrainians buy daily for their tables, the price of refined sunflower oil "Oliyna" increased the least. A bottle with a volume of 850 ml cost an average of UAH 107.20 on October 12, while on October 15 its price was UAH 107.67. In other words, the price increased by 47 kopecks, or 0.44%. For now, such a fluctuation does not provide grounds to speak of a significant increase in the price of sunflower oil overall. To assess the market situation, it is necessary to take into account price dynamics over a longer period, as well as the cost of products from other manufacturers.
In addition, supermarket promotional policies affect the prices of grocery products. The end of temporary discounts or changes in the product range may affect the average cost of goods even without a corresponding increase in manufacturers' selling prices.
How much the Ukrainian consumer's grocery basket rose in price over three days
To assess the impact of the price increase on daily expenses, one can compare the cost of a hypothetical grocery basket made up of all seven analyzed items.
It includes one kilogram each of pink tomatoes, plum tomatoes, a chicken carcass, bananas, buckwheat, and rice, as well as one 850 ml bottle of sunflower oil. As of October 12, the total cost of such a set was UAH 653.38. By October 15, the same list of products would have cost UAH 666.06. In three days, the hypothetical grocery basket had increased in price by UAH 12.68, or approximately 1.94%.
The largest contribution to the increase in total expenses came from the higher prices of pink tomatoes and chicken. Together, these two items added UAH 6.59 to the cost of the basket, accounting for more than half of the total increase.
Should we expect food prices to continue rising
The price increases recorded between October 12 and 15 indicate a short-term rise in the cost of certain everyday products. However, economists emphasize that it is incorrect to draw conclusions about an overall acceleration of food inflation based solely on seven product items. They explain that a comprehensive assessment of the price situation requires taking into account a much broader range of products, changes in prices over several weeks or months, as well as official state statistics.
According to forecasts from fruit and vegetable market analysts, the prices of vegetables may soon be affected by a seasonal reduction in the supply of open-field produce. For imported fruit, purchase prices and logistics will remain important, while for meat and grains, production costs and the balance of supply and demand will be key.
Possible disruptions to energy supplies remain an additional risk factor for the food market, as refrigeration equipment, warehouses, processing enterprises, and retail chains depend on stable access to electricity.
Recall
Earlier, UNN reported that young potatoes had tripled in price in a week. The price rose from UAH 20 to UAH 60 per kilogram. Meanwhile, old potatoes cost several times less.

Mapping sanctions against Israel: 121 measures across 61 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:32:44 UTC
17:32:44 KST

The Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) has launched a new database mapping sanctions and restrictive measures imposed on Israel by countries around the world. The database identifies 121 measures across 62 countries, including 93 currently in effect, 19 classified as historical and nine proposed or planned measures.
The Foreign Ministry said the figures presented in the report do not accurately reflect the sanctions situation. Diplomatic officials added: "Ultimately, there are no substantial sanctions against Israel. Will that continue? There's no guarantee it will last forever. It's possible that, at some point, the outcome will be different."
The database allows users to examine measures by country, category and status, and to view their geographic distribution on a world map. The findings indicate that pressure on Israel is not confined to a single sector. Financial measures account for the largest category, with 40 measures, about one-third of the total. Defense and security and trade follow, with 24 measures each. The database also records 14 diplomatic measures and 12 legal measures.
According to JPPI Director General Dr. Shuki Friedman, the findings should be assessed not only by the number of sanctions but, more importantly, by their potential cumulative impact on Israel's economy and its ability to maintain international trade relationships, investment flows and supply chains.
"Anyone who thinks sanctions against ministers, individuals in the West Bank or products from the area will stop at the Green Line is mistaken," Friedman said. "Sanctions have a ripple effect. When they accumulate, they can affect banks, companies, investors and trading partners that have no connection whatsoever to the person or entity being sanctioned. The real danger is the transition from targeted sanctions to damage to the systems on which Israel's economy and security depend."
The database also identifies the countries where the highest number of measures have been recorded. Spain leads with 10 measures, followed by the United States with eight, all currently limited to the academic sphere, along with two "historical measures" and five proposals to prevent supplies of various types of weapons. Britain follows with seven measures, while Belgium and Turkey have five each.
However, the number of measures does not necessarily indicate their severity or potential impact. A single measure may be far more consequential than several others. The map is therefore intended primarily to illustrate the scope of the phenomenon and its geographic spread. Alongside European countries, where a substantial share of the measures is concentrated, the database includes measures from North America, Latin America, Asia, Africa and Oceania.
"The figure of 121 is only the starting point," Friedman said. "The important question is what will happen if this trend continues. A single sanction may be limited in scope. But 121 measures across 62 countries already warrant a systemic assessment. Israel needs to examine this risk as it would any other strategic threat: map it, prepare for it and act to prevent further deterioration.
"A national mechanism is needed to address the risk, one that examines the implications of these measures for the financial system, trade, investment, supply chains and the defense industry. The response cannot be limited to dealing with each sanction separately. It requires a comprehensive approach."
Diplomatic officials said the map contains distortions, noting, for example, that European Union sanctions are also counted at the individual country level. They also argued that entry bans imposed on certain individuals should not be equated with sanctions against Israel itself.
"Ultimately, there are no substantial sanctions against the State of Israel, and that was not a foregone conclusion," the officials said. "There was a realistic possibility of a different outcome, in which we would have ended 2026 facing EU sanctions against Israel. A great deal of the Foreign Ministry's energy was devoted to thwarting those measures."
They added: "There were sanctions that were prevented. The major threat was thwarted. If the EU had decided to undermine the trade agreement, every Israeli citizen would have felt the impact. The economic consequences would have been dramatic, but that was prevented. That diplomatic Iron Dome continued to hold.
"When you're inside an Iron Dome and a lot of missiles are fired at you, some get through. But the warhead carrying a ton of diplomatic and economic explosives did not penetrate. Ultimately, we succeed because we have friendly countries we can mobilize, such as Germany, Italy and the Czech Republic. It's not just Hungary. Hungary has changed, and the diplomatic Iron Dome remains intact."
The officials continued: "It's true that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir cannot enter the EU and that there are sanctions against settlers. But ultimately, people shopping at supermarkets in Ramat Gan and Tel Aviv are not feeling the impact of the biggest weapon, which is the trade agreement. The Horizon agreements and the Open Skies agreement have also been preserved."
However, they warned that the situation could change. "Will this continue? There's no guarantee it will last forever. It's possible that, if the trends continue in the same direction, the outcome will be different in the future."
According to the officials, "The Netherlands, Spain and Ireland are frustrated that they cannot achieve the outcome they want in Brussels. At the last meeting of European foreign ministers, there was frustration that it wasn't working. So, with no other choice, they are pursuing other channels, such as the Dutch sanctions.
"We are managing to preserve the core interests, and we have also reversed negative measures in countries such as Slovenia and Colombia. It's painstaking, thankless work because nobody sees what we have managed to prevent."
The officials nevertheless acknowledged that measures introduced by Spain, Ireland and Britain concerning trade with Israeli settlements "are not positive," adding that a concerning consequence is the shift toward action by individual countries.
The Foreign Ministry said in response: "The figures presented in the report do not accurately reflect the sanctions situation, whether political or economic. The Foreign Ministry is continuously engaged in this effort and is investing enormous resources in the fight against sanctions targeting Israel.
"For example, through a sustained effort lasting a year and a half, we prevented sanctions against Israel in the European Union and numerous other countries. We are also investing considerable efforts in reversing sanctions imposed by hostile governments following changes in leadership. We have done so with considerable success in Colombia, Slovenia and elsewhere.
"Countries that promote or impose sanctions against Israel undermine their own standing and influence in the region. As we have demonstrated in our dealings with various countries, most recently the Netherlands and Britain, Israel will respond firmly and forcefully to any country that takes such measures against it."

Cameroon’s rising femicide toll fuels protests, calls for justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:32:23 UTC
17:32:23 KST

Geraldine Achiah had been married for barely two months when she died in September, leaving behind an 18-year-old son who is struggling to come to terms with her death and demanding justice for what relatives allege was a fatal beating by her husband.
Achiah, an elementary school teacher in her 30s, had encouraged her only child, Courage Abombi, to pursue his dream of becoming a mechanical engineer. He sat for a university entrance exam just one day after her burial.
“My mom died an unexpected and painful death,” Abombi said.
Her death has become part of a growing crisis of femicide in Cameroon, where nearly 70 women have been killed this year in gender-related killings, according to the Ministry of Women's Affairs. The figure exceeds government estimates of at least 50 cases in 2023 and 67 in 2024.
The rising toll has prompted protests in major cities, including Douala and Yaounde, with demonstrators demanding stronger legal protections, more effective investigations and accountability for perpetrators. Many cases remain unresolved, while others go unreported.
Manfred Amambua, Achiah's husband, has denied killing her, police said. He has been charged with murder and is being held in jail awaiting trial. His lawyer was unavailable for comment.
Hospital records obtained by The Associated Press (AP) documented “several bruises on her face and lips” before her death. Ndzana Bienvenu, an officer involved in the investigation, said police had also collected phone footage showing Achiah and her husband after the alleged beating, along with a blood-stained bedsheet.
Her relatives say they want justice not only for Achiah but also for other women who have died in similar circumstances.
“We want justice for our daughter who died a violent death. This was a teacher who imparted knowledge on thousands of young Cameroonians,” said Regina Ngukum, Achiah's cousin.
Activists say femicide in Cameroon is fueled by economic dependence, unequal control over family property and inadequate legal protections in a society where men traditionally hold greater authority within households.
Financial hardship can make it difficult for women to leave abusive relationships, particularly when they have children to support. Some endure violence in the hope that their partners will change, activists say, while stigma and limited resources can make seeking help even harder.
“The current economic situation in the country is not helping matters. With limited resources, many women tend to endure violence in their marriages, hoping that their men will change, which is not usually the case,” Women's Affairs Minister Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa recently told the state broadcaster.
Ondoa described femicide cases in Cameroon as having reached a “cruel” and “alarming” proportion and pledged further government action.
The crisis mirrors a wider global pattern. About 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or other family members in 2024, according to United Nations data.
Activists argue that Cameroon needs stronger laws and a more effective judicial system to prevent gender-related killings and ensure perpetrators face meaningful punishment.
The country's Penal Code criminalizes offenses including rape but does not explicitly define femicide as a separate crime. Cases are therefore handled under broader provisions governing homicide and other violent acts.
Similar approaches are used in many African countries, where killings motivated by gender are generally prosecuted under existing homicide laws, although some governments have taken legal or policy steps specifically addressing femicide.
Cameroon's government is preparing a bill that would establish femicide as a standalone criminal offense while strengthening broader protections against gender-based violence. The proposed legislation is expected to be submitted to parliament for consideration in November.
Activists caution, however, that changing the law alone will not resolve the problems that allow cases to stall or perpetrators to escape accountability.
Carole Grace Mbarga, a Cameroonian activist based in the United States, said investigations and court proceedings can be undermined by intimidation, corruption and procedural errors that may lead to reduced charges or acquittals.
“When investigations drag on, evidence deteriorates, witnesses lose confidence, and families become discouraged,” she said.
Even when convictions are secured, the penalties can fall short of victims' families' expectations. In 2025, a man who pleaded guilty to killing his wife received a suspended five-year sentence and a fine of 52,000 CFA francs, equivalent to about $90.
For activists, such outcomes reinforce concerns that the justice system does not adequately deter violence against women.
Family members and friends gathered in Yaounde for Achiah's burial following her death just two months after her wedding in July.
Her relatives are now waiting for the legal process to take its course while joining a broader movement demanding action against femicide. Thousands of people have taken part in protests in Douala and Yaounde, calling on authorities to strengthen protections for women and ensure that cases are properly investigated and prosecuted.
Laura Sen, one of the protest organizers, said the proposed legislation must be accompanied by efforts to address systemic barriers and improve support for victims of domestic violence.
For women facing abuse, leaving a relationship can be especially difficult when they depend financially on their partners or fear social stigma. Those raising children may face additional obstacles.
Achiah's death has left her son grieving the woman who supported his ambitions and helped him imagine a future beyond their loss.
Abombi said he continues to pray that the legal process will deliver justice for his mother.
“I pray that justice will follow its due course and that her killer will face the law,” he said.
He also described dreams in which his mother returns to comfort him.
“She keeps appearing to me in a dream, consoling me not to despair and that she is still with me,” he said.

Estonia gets €32m EU funding for 'free world's first line of defense' surveillance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:31:00 UTC
17:31:00 KST

Estonia gets €32m EU funding for 'free world's first line of defense' surveillance
The European Commission has given preliminary approval for nearly €32 million toward Estonia's eastern border drone surveillance system, a project already partly built.
The funding is the latest installment in a program announced in March, with the first fixed systems installed on the south-eastern border in May and the full system due by the end of 2029.
The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) will continue building the multi-layered integrated drone detection and air surveillance system on the EU's external border in cooperation with the Estonian Defense Forces (EDF).
"In cooperation with the Defense Forces, we can buy and install radars and cameras, equipment needed for drone detection, and the IT system supporting them, for a shared situational picture," said Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200).
"This will improve our ability to detect and assess potential threats so we can respond quickly. Our aim is to prevent threats before they reach the point of affecting the security of Estonian people," the minister went on.
Taro said Estonia's eastern border is currently the free world's first line of defense. "The European Union's support for strengthening drone surveillance here says that we have done good work so far, have been on the right path, and shows trust in our skills and capability to protect the EU's external border."
Veiko Kommusaar, deputy director general of the PPA for border management, said the Commission's decision was a clear sign of trust in Estonia and confirmed that the EU sees strengthening the external border as a shared security question.
"With this support, we can, over the next three years together with the Defense Forces, take air and land surveillance on the eastern border to the next level, create a more complete situational picture and improve our ability to detect and assess potential threats on land, on the Narva River and in the airspace," Kommusaar said.
He added that the investment's greatest value is not its individual radars or drones, but the ability to see what is happening on the eastern border as a whole, and to be able to respond to potential threats faster and more precisely than ever before.
The funding comes through the EU's border management and visa policy fund, with 10 percent national co-financing.
The system was announced by Prime Minister Kristen Michal in March, with over €200 million earmarked for drone defense and around €214 million for drone surveillance and countermeasures over four years. The first fixed counter-drone systems were installed on three sections of the south-eastern land border in May, and the PPA says full coverage of the Russian border should follow. The first phase — the external border and Estonia's four largest cities — is due by the end of 2027, with the full system complete by the end of 2029.

From Hormuz to Bab el-Mandeb: Saudi Arabia’s difficult choices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:29:20 UTC
17:29:20 KST

Developments in Yemen today cannot be separated from the repercussions of the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran. The prolonged nature of this war, and the fact that it remains unresolved, arguably compel the countries of the region to reassess their strategic realities from a perspective different from the traditional approach that has shaped their thinking for decades. The US-Israeli war against Iran has brought about significant shifts in the region’s military, economic and political calculations, confronting Tehran with serious challenges and looming threats to its security, economy and future regional standing. For its part, Iran has drawn on a range of strategic assets at its disposal across the region to mitigate these threats by raising the costs borne by its Gulf neighbours. This Iranian strategy has exposed serious challenges facing the Gulf states, particularly Saudi Arabia, the most influential among them, with direct implications for their security and economies. Examining the escalating confrontation between Yemen and Saudi Arabia offers a means of analysing the challenges confronting the Kingdom today within a broader, emerging strategic perspective on the region and its future.
Saudi Arabia is facing a renewed wave of Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting its airports and oil facilities, alongside threats to Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. These targets are not new. The Kingdom faced similar attacks during the earlier years of the war in Yemen, before the de-escalation that followed the 2022 truce. That period of relative calm began to unravel on 13 July 2026, when the coalition targeted the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing. The Yemeni government claimed responsibility for the operation, while the Houthis attributed it to Saudi Arabia. Following this, the Houthis announced that they had targeted Abha airport, before declaring a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia on 20 July. Within Yemen, the escalation has shifted from exchanges of strikes to battles aimed at changing territorial control, particularly along the western coast. Last month, Houthi forces advanced towards Mokha and areas bordering the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi-backed government forces then launched a counter-offensive at the beginning of this month, announcing that they had recaptured Mokha, Dhubab and positions overlooking the strait. Fighting between the warring parties continues.
Since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, Saudi Arabia has faced mounting pressure on the routes through which it exports oil, the mainstay of its economy. Its eastern oil export route through the Strait of Hormuz has been hit by the turmoil in shipping arising from US-Iranian confrontations in the strait. As the Kingdom became increasingly reliant on transporting oil overland through the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, this alternative route was also interrupted, having assumed greater importance following the damage to its eastern maritime outlet. The East-West Pipeline was targeted in a drone attack last month, for which Riyadh held Iraqi groups close to Iran responsible, before operations resumed. The blockade declared by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia’s western maritime outlet and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait added a further, compounding burden, particularly on the passage of Saudi oil tankers through the strait. Houthi attacks on Saudi oil tankers were not confined to the waters around the strait, but extended as far as the waters off Yanbu.
These developments explain the shift in Saudi Arabia’s stance towards the Houthis. After years of seeking to consolidate the de-escalation and negotiate a political settlement, Riyadh has once again turned towards military confrontation.
Recapturing coastal positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become an objective linked to protecting its economic interests and exports, particularly amid the disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. In 2023, Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman affirmed Saudi Arabia’s support for dialogue aimed at reaching a comprehensive political settlement under United Nations auspices. By contrast, Reuters reported at the beginning of this month, citing informed sources, that Riyadh was preparing a ground offensive to be carried out by Yemeni forces with Saudi air support. The agency also quoted Western diplomats and Gulf officials as saying that Riyadh could not enter into new peace negotiations while the Houthis remained in control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. This shift has been reflected in Saudi air support for the latest offensive launched by Yemeni government forces against the Houthis.
Nevertheless, a return to war offers Saudi Arabia no guarantee of a decisive outcome. The previous war, which began in 2015 and involved a Saudi-led coalition with the participation of the United Arab Emirates, failed to achieve its objective of defeating the Houthis. Nor did it restore the government that the Houthis had driven out of Sanaa, leaving the capital and most of northern Yemen under their control. Similarly, the US air campaign against the Houthis in 2025 failed to eliminate their power in Yemen, despite costing more than $1 billion, destroying weapons and facilities, and killing Houthi field commanders. The campaign ended with an agreement to halt reciprocal attacks between the United States and the Houthis, an arrangement that did not extend to Israel.
Nor will the recent Mecca Alliance between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey help the Kingdom in its fight in Yemen beyond defensive and technical support, particularly while the alliance remains in its early stages.
It is also difficult to rely on the United States, given Washington’s refusal to meet a Saudi request to participate in air strikes, limiting its involvement to providing advice, intelligence and targeting data. US strategy in the region is based on expanding the role of regional partners in defending themselves, the region and US interests within it. This explains Trump’s request to Turkey a few days ago to intervene in support of Saudi Arabia.
These developments compel the countries of the region to reassess their security calculus and strategic balances, recognising that Iran and its allies are part of the regional reality and that lasting stability cannot be built by disregarding them. Relations based on cooperation and mutual interests remain an essential foundation for such stability, alongside the need to establish a balance between the instruments of power available to the Gulf states and those possessed by Iran. Throughout the current war against it, Iran has demonstrated that it possesses significant strategic assets that have inflicted heavy costs on the countries of the region, exposing an imbalance in their ability to impose comparable costs in return. If the Gulf states possessed instruments of power that made harming their security and interests costly for Iran, the costs of escalation would become mutual, potentially encouraging the parties to seek balanced political solutions that support cooperation and future stability.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Ukrainian defense company December1 and Lithuanian company Pekkla have signed a memorandum to establish a joint venture in Lithuania.

Production is scheduled to begin in 2027.
The parties have agreed to jointly manufacture the Damba electronic warfare (EW) system, developed by specialists atDecember1.
The partners will cooperate under the Build with Ukraine programme, with support from the Lithuanian government. The finished products will be supplied to meet the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Pekkla designs and develops unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). The company will serve as December1’s local partner in Lithuania, responsible for infrastructure, regulatory support, and recruiting local engineers. December1 will provide the technical expertise.
December1 says that Damba is one of the most widely used electronic warfare (EW) systems in Ukraine.
According to the company, thousands of Damba systems have been deployed along the front line and at critical infrastructure facilities across Ukraine. The system can counter various types of drones, including FPV drones, reconnaissance UAVs, and Shahed drones, at ranges of up to 50 km.
December1’s Director of International Development, Illia Kabachynskyi, noted that this is the company’s first experience establishing a joint venture.
In addition to the Damba system, December1 manufactures the Drone Sensor Providence drone detection system and othercounter-drone solutions.

2026-10-16

17:26:35 KST

Burhan Sansarlioglu and Emir Yildirim
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
Global markets traded on a positive trend on Thursday with declining government bond yields and a recovery in tech stocks that had plummeted the previous day.
US macroeconomic data continue to set the direction of global markets.
The monthly Producer Price Index (PPI) in the US rose 1.3% in September, while surging 6.3% annually, faster than expected.
US producer inflation reached its highest level since March 2022 on a monthly basis and since December 2022 year-on-year.
Hotter-than-expected consumer inflation combined with the acceleration in producer inflation, fueling growing concerns that the US Federal Reserve may hike rates.
US retail sales rose above expectations by 0.8% on a monthly basis in September, reinforcing expectations that the Fed will continue its tight monetary policy.
The negative trend in tech stocks due to concerns over artificial intelligence investment profitability reversed following statements by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
Lingering concerns over the broader technology sector fueling worries about economic growth prompted investors to turn to bonds, dropping bond yields.
The US 10-Year Treasury yield fell 11 basis points on Thursday to 5.08%, while it is trading flat on Friday.
The US dollar fell 0.2% to 101.9, while gold is trading just above its previous close at $4,171 per ounce on Friday.
December-delivery Brent crude is down 0.5% at $105.4 a barrel on Friday after the International Energy Agency (IEA) reached an agreement to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel into the market, in addition to the remaining oil that was released at a record level from the emergency reserve.
 
Major chipmaker stocks down
The US Treasury Department added some 16 people and 10 entities allegedly linked to Iran to its sanctions list to further block Tehran’s access to the global financial system.
Meanwhile, the New York Stock Exchange traded positively on Thursday, led by gains in healthcare sectors, which also helped offset declines in tech stocks.
Shares of chipmakers Nvidia, AMD, and Intel declined 2%, 1.5%, and 3%, respectively.
Pharmaceutical giant Eli Lily’s shares gained 3.5%, health insurer UnitedHealth shares rose 2.8%, and retail titan Walmart’s shares grew 1.5%.
At the same time, top executives at SpaceX and Tesla are reportedly considering a merger, according to a Barclays analysis, driving SpaceX shares down 2.3% and Tesla shares to drop 1.3%.
Additionally, the US initial jobless claims rose to 199,000 in the week ending Oct. 10, coming in within estimates.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 1.08%, the S&P 500 rose 0.33%, and the Nasdaq Composite was up 0.08% on Thursday. American indexes started Friday on a positive trend.
Meanwhile, European stock markets traded mostly positively with strong corporate earnings and gains in healthcare companies.
The UK’s economy grew above estimates by 0.1% month-on-month and 2.1% year-on-year, driving up the British pound/US dollar exchange rate to 1.33 on Friday, its highest since Sept. 30.
The eurozone’s industrial production fell 0.5% on a monthly basis and 1.1% year-on-year in August, above estimates.
Germany's DAX 40 gained 0.33%, the UK's FTSE 100 rose 1.08%, and France's CAC 40 was up 0.78% on Thursday, while Italy's FTSE MIB 30 fell 0.72%. European indexes started Friday on a positive note.
Near Friday’s close, Asian equity markets traded higher amid a recovery in tech stocks.
SK Hynix shares surged 3.8%, Samsung Electronics rose 4.6%, Kioxia grew 3.2%, and Sony’s shares were up 2.4%.
South Korea’s Kospi rose 3.9%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 gained 2%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng climbed 1.1%, and China's Shanghai Composite was up 1%.

Editor's note: The story has been expanded with additional comments made by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis expressed his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine in its next seven-year budget, in comments made to journalists at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
The EU operates on a seven-year budget cycle that needs to be unanimously agreed upon, and leaders hope to reach consensus on the 2028-2034 budget before the end of the year, as 2027 will be a bumper year for elections across the bloc.
While consensus on the budget as a whole remains out of reach, support for Ukraine seemed like a consensus issue until Babis' latest comments.
"I don't like that there are 100 billion euros ($112 billion) from the European budget for Ukraine, that this money should be borrowed," Babis said.
"It should not be in the multi-year financial framework, where member states don't have enough money," he added.
The 100 billion euros figure is already outdated, reflecting the amount initially proposed for the budget by the European Commission earlier in the year.
That figure was reduced to 89 billion euros ($100 billion) in June as part of a first compromise proposal, and it remained unchanged in the second and latest compromise, published Oct. 10.
"In any case, Czechia will not guarantee for it," Babis added.
Surprising in the other direction was Babis' criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump, after portraying himself as aligned with Trump for several years.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said, echoing President Volodymyr Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S. against Ukraine.
Babis said the day before that Europe needs to agree on how to proceed with issues such as peace talks, given that at the moment, "we are completely out."
His turn on Trump brings Babis closer to the European mainstream, with many EU leaders not holding back in condemning the U.S. president for his latest overtures towards Moscow.

Government agrees 60 million euro fuel-price relief package, rejects Finns Party proposal
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:24:02 EEST
17:24:02 KST

The government has reached an agreement on a 60 million euro package aimed at easing the impact of rising fuel prices.
Environment and Climate Minister Sari Multala (NCP) confirmed to reporters in Parliament on Thursday that a deal had been agreed, noting that all governing parties support the package as a whole.
The measures include a reduction in vehicle tax, an increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, and fuel subsidies for the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors.
The government has also agreed to introduce flexibilities in the fuel distribution obligation, which sets requirements for the share of renewable fuels blended into transport fuels. The limits on cross-fulfilment and over-compliance will both rise from 30 percent to 100 percent, allowing companies to meet their obligations more cost-effectively, the government said.
However, the government has not adopted the broader reduction in the distribution obligation advocated by the Finns Party.
The package consists of: 30 million euros for fuel subsidies for businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors, 20 million euros to reduce vehicle tax, up from the previously agreed 10 million euros, and 10 million euros to raise the maximum commuting expense deduction from 7,000 euros to 7,800 euros in 2027.
Multala acknowledged that the measures would have only a limited impact on consumers’ fuel costs.
"We cannot afford to make tax cuts worth hundreds of millions, for example," she said.
According to a press release, published by the ministry on Friday, the 60 million euro package will be funded from within the government's spending limits.
Of the total, 40 million euros will be redirected from funding for biogenic carbon capture capacity that will go unused this year, with the remaining 20 million euros coming from the cutting of funding for basic transport infrastructure management.
Finns Party says measures are insufficient
The Finns Party has criticised the agreement, arguing that the package should have gone further in easing the fuel distribution obligation to bring down prices at the pump.
Jani Mäkelä, chair of the Finns Party parliamentary group, said his party had accepted the agreement because "some solution had to be found".
"The government seemed to be quite incapable of acting in this matter, and the prime minister also had to save face," Mäkelä said.
Mäkelä further argued that easing the distribution obligation, as proposed by his party, could have reduced fuel prices at the pump by a significant amount.
He said the fact that the government had agreed on the package was not sufficient reason to rule out that option.
"If the distribution obligation cannot be compromised in a situation where the price of fuel is so high, it reflects a certain mindset," Mäkelä said.
Multala was asked whether the Finns Party could have been persuaded to accept the agreement if the funding had come from money allocated to climate action. She replied that the question should be put to the party itself.
Orpo defends government’s decision
Speaking in Brussels on the sidelines of an EU meeting, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) said that easing the distribution obligation would not have brought down fuel prices quickly.
"Being in the government means that when we are making decisions together, sometimes it is difficult to defend them, even if we have made the decision ourselves," Orpo said.
He stressed that the government had little room for manoeuvre during the negotiations, but noted he was pleased that the money had been directed towards commuters and professional transport.
Fuel prices are also on the agenda at the EU summit. Orpo said high prices at the pump were linked to the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine.
Relief measures will not lower pump prices directly
Hanna Kalenoja, a leading transport expert at the Central Chamber of Commerce, said the measures would not directly affect petrol and diesel prices.
Instead, they would ease costs for some motorists and businesses, but not all, she noted.
The vehicle tax reduction will be reflected in the tax bills of eligible car and van owners, rather than at the petrol station.
For example, a household whose vehicle tax period began in July would not see the reduction until its next tax period in July next year, Kalenoja said.
She estimated that the vehicle tax cut would save eligible motorists around 12 euros per year. The reduction applies to older cars and vans.
The increase in the maximum commuting expense deduction, meanwhile, could benefit people with high travel costs.
The government also plans to raise the maximum deduction, with Kalenoja estimating that the change would benefit people who commute more than 60 kilometres.
The deduction can be adjusted through a revised tax card, although eligibility depends on the circumstances of the commute. In some cases, expenses can be deducted based on the use of a private car if public transport is not reasonably accessible.
The fuel subsidies are aimed at businesses in the transport, agriculture and forestry sectors. A similar subsidy was made available retrospectively through the State Treasury in 2022.
Experts welcome decision to retain distribution obligation
Kalenoja said she was largely relieved by the government's decision, particularly because it did not ease the distribution obligation.
The requirement sets the minimum share of renewable fuels that must be included in transport fuels. Reducing it would lower the share of low-emission biofuels.
According to experts, easing the obligation would not necessarily have an immediate impact on pump prices. Kalenoja also warned that it could undermine planned investments in the biogas sector.
"It is a big relief that the decision not to lower the distribution obligation was made now," she said.
The Confederation of Finnish Industries (EK) also welcomed the decision in a statement on Thursday.
However, Kalenoja said it was disappointing that the government had not included a reduction in diesel excise duty in the package.

Russia’s Digital Development Ministry has proposed using artificial intelligence to analyze VPN services’ characteristics, aiming to detect and block them more effectively.
The proposal appears in one draft version of a national plan for implementing AI technologies through 2030, the Russian business daily Kommersant reported.
The plan’s drafters said AI could achieve 95% effectiveness in blocking VPN services.
The Digital Development Ministry told Kommersant that “the current version of the draft national plan for implementing AI technologies contains no such information.”
A source who spoke to the outlet, familiar with discussions around the initiative, said algorithms for intelligent traffic analysis are already in use, though these do not constitute AI.
“AI tools make it possible to find VPN servers relatively quickly based on indirect signs: how a node behaves, what hosting it uses, what neighboring addresses look like. And most importantly, this makes it possible to respond more quickly to changes in network activity,” a source in the industry told Kommersant.
However, several sources told the outlet that the use of AI, “especially during the initial stages of training,” would likely result in the erroneous blocking of “legitimate traffic.”
Demand for VPNs has surged in Russia amid blocks on popular social networks, services, and messaging apps. Russian authorities have responded by stepping up efforts to combat circumvention of these blocks. Russia’s budget for the next three years earmarked a record 60 billion rubles for traffic filtering. Reports have repeatedly said the Digital Development Ministry wants to charge higher rates for international traffic (operators treat VPN traffic as international).

"After about 10 minutes, they tried to make me get up; they pushed me back to the ground and continued kicking me," she said. "I tried to hold on to my cameras and my side bag, but in the end they just ripped everything from me and kept kicking me."
According to the IDF, soldiers initially fired warning shots into the air in an effort to disperse the crowd upon arriving on scene, eventually targeting an individual who approached them with a sharp object.

The Prime Minister's Office (PMO) condemned the attack in an X/Twitter post later on Friday, noting that the facts "remain unclear and are under investigation."
"Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone - Jews, Arabs, Christians, or journalists," the statement read. "Those responsible will be held accountable."
The statement indicated that "serious questions remain" regarding who specifically was responsible for the attack on Levine, emphasizing the presence of "200 Arabs and far-left activists... (and) approximately 40 Israeli youths" at the site of the attack.
"The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," the statement continued. "We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria. The facts must determine the conclusions. Not the headlines."

"We are appalled by this unjustified attack on a journalist who was doing her job," he said. "We call on the authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and act on its findings."
In addition, the US Embassy in Jerusalem told N12 that it is aware of the incident and is "monitoring the situation."
"We condemn criminal violence and call for the investigation and prosecution of those responsible," it said.
Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot also responded to the incident in a post on X/Twitter, calling it "unacceptable" and referring to the perpetrators as "violent lawbreakers."
"This handful of rioters does not represent the public in Israel. The actions of this handful stain an entire nation and severely harm the security of all Israeli citizens and IDF fighters," he said. "I back the IDF in its sharp and clear condemnation of the incident. It is incumbent upon the Israel Police to take harsh measures against this criminal violence."
Mateh Binyamin Regional Council accuses PA of bringing terrorists to attack Israelis
The Mateh Binyamin Regional Council provided a different course of events.
According to the council, the Palestinian Authority "led hundreds of anarchists and terrorists into a direct confrontation with Israelis near Abu Falah, all under the cover of the olive harvest."
"Footage from the scene shows terrorists launching fireworks directly at people and hurling stones at Israelis, while journalists stand behind them, documenting this deliberate provocation," the council said.
"The event was orchestrated by the PA; its patrol vehicles were present and highly visible at the scene, even though it is in Area B, where Israel holds responsibility for security," it added.

The council did not explicitly comment on Levine's reported wounds.

The incidents reportedly involved vehicles being set on fire, attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters, and attacks on Palestinian homes.
In the village of Burin, a confrontation broke out during the olive harvest. Additional incidents were reported in the village of Burqa, east of Ramallah, and in Turmus Ayya. The incidents reportedly included at least four vehicles being set on fire, one of which was a civil defense vehicle, and attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters.
In a separate incident, shortly before midnight, settlers reportedly attacked Palestinian homes in the Wadi al-Sheikh area of the town of Beit Ummar, north of Hebron.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said that two wounded Palestinians, a 63-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man, had been treated and taken to the hospital. Another Palestinian was reportedly shot in the knee.

Israeli security forces arrested a suspect after he fled an olive grove near Kafr Kara, Israel Police announced later on Friday.
The police and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) conducted a manhunt for the suspect lasting several hours prior to his arrest.
An M-16 rifle was also found in the vicinity.

The authority stressed that truck drivers must comply with regulations governing transport within Sudan, exercise the utmost caution and avoid entering designated areas under any circumstances.
The instructions are based on directives issued by Egypt’s Ministry of Transport on 11th May 2025, requiring drivers to avoid conflict zones and unload goods only in safe areas of Sudan’s Northern State.

Ofgem could force energy suppliers to pay rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:14:53 UTC
17:14:53 KST

Energy suppliers could be forced to pay a charge to rivals if they lure customers with cheaper deals, as the industry regulator for Great Britain attempts to prevent suppliers going bust this winter.
Ofgem has published a consultation on a proposal to reintroduce the market stabilisation charge (MSC), which aims to prevent suppliers failing if there is customer exodus, as it frets over the impact of sharp swings in energy prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The charge was last activated between April 2022 and March 2024, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sparked soaring wholesale prices that caused more than 30 energy companies to go bust.
“We’re preparing for what is likely to be a difficult winter for many households,” said Neil Kenward, the interim director general of markets at Ofgem. “While the energy market is stronger than it was during the energy crisis, volatility remains and the market stabilisation charge helps to protect consumers from that volatility.
“In volatile market conditions, it’s important that suppliers can continue to secure the energy their customers need without taking unsustainable risks.”
Under the mechanism, the MSC would be triggered if wholesale prices fall more than 10%. At that point, suppliers who win customers by being able to then offer cheap deals would have to compensate rivals 85% of the drop in wholesale rates.
“When wholesale prices fall sharply, suppliers that have bought energy in advance for customers on default tariffs can face losses if large numbers of customers switch to cheaper fixed deals,” Ofgem said.
When Ofgem last activated the MSC in 2022 Martin Lewis, the founder of the consumer advice site MoneySavingExpert, swore at the regulator on a press call and said the mechanism sold consumers “down the river” because it would deter competition. He later posted an apology for his “emotional rant” on the social media platform X.
Reacting to Ofgem’s consultation, Lewis said on Friday that consumers’ will not get as good deals if wholesale prices drop because the mechanism acts as a “switching penalty”.
He added: “The new supplier can’t pass a chunk of the saving from lower wholesale rates on to you, because it has to hand much of it to your old supplier. The cheap fixes and switcher deals offered will be a lot more expensive, in order to protect energy firms’ profits. It ain’t good for consumers.”
He questioned the need to reintroduce the mechanism, pointing out that many energy companies have made significant profits since last time it was triggered.
“The supplier market is pretty stable, and I doubt we are at the domino risk of suppliers going bust in the way they did in the early 20s,” he said. “Protecting them over winter by effectively dampening competition … feels raw. I don’t like it.”
Ofgem said that reactivating the MSC would not “automatically create charges or increase customer bills”.
The consultation is seeking views on how the mechanism should operate, including trigger levels, notice periods and deactivation arrangements.
“The MSC supports responsible energy purchasing and helps reduce the risk of instability in the market during periods of significant price volatility,” Kenward said. “By acting now, we can help maintain a stable and resilient energy market and protect consumers from the costs and disruption that can arise when markets become unstable.”
Households are facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter after rising market wholesale prices pushed up the government’s price cap from this month.
 
About 22m homes are paying the equivalent of £1,723 a year for typical gas and electricity usage between October and December, up from £1,663 for the July to September period.
 
Ofgem’s quarterly energy price cap is forecast to climb by the equivalent of a further £149 a year in January, according to energy consultants at Cornwall Insight, which would put the average annual bill at £1,872.
The chancellor, John Healey, is planning a major intervention to cut energy bills for poorer households in this month’s budget.

Indonesian stocks plunge 11% as MSCI proposes emerging market downgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:13:31 UTC
17:13:31 KST

The index provider is weighing reclassifying the country from emerging market to standalone status, potentially forcing funds tracking MSCI's emerging market indexes to sell their Indonesian holdings.
Indonesian shares lost about 11% on Friday. This was the largest single-day fall in 28 years, as the country's stock market status came under scrutiny from one of the world's largest stock market index providers, threatening outflows from global investment funds.
MSCI said that following investors' concerns, Indonesia's continued emerging-market status was "no longer appropriate". The index provider is launching a consultation on a proposal to classify Indonesia as a "Standalone Market", which would leave the country outside MSCI’s main global market groupings.
MSCI classifies markets as developed, emerging, frontier or standalone.
The proposed reclassification would move Southeast Asia's biggest economy out of the emerging market category, bypassing frontier market status, and put it in the same category as Jamaica, Panama and Palestine.
This could result in global funds tracking MSCI's emerging market index having to sell their Indonesian holdings.
The index provider said in a statement that "market participants had raised significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market". These include a lack of clarity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading.
The index provider had already raised the possibility of downgrading the country's status in January. Following that, authorities in Jakarta said in April they had completed reforms, hoping to avoid the downgrade.
MSCI noted that although Indonesian authorities have announced reforms, sufficient progress has not been made and "significant concerns remain around market dysfunction".
"MSCI expects to proceed with the proposed reclassification unless the consultation identifies clear evidence of material improvements in market governance and functioning to warrant reconsideration."
MSCI will announce its final decision by the end of June 2027.
According to Bloomberg, this comes as a hit to investors' confidence at a time when global funds have already pulled a net $4.9bn from the country's stock market so far this year – leaving the country on track for the worst year ever. Jakarta's benchmark index has fallen approximately 39% since January, dragging down the local currency; the rupiah has lost about 8%. That’s even as Bank Indonesia reiterated its commitment to maintaining rupiah stability.

Cabinet resolution on changing reservation procedure still being coordinated, Rada committee opposes lowering defense industry quotas – MP Friz
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:12:15 EEST
17:12:15 KST

The Verkhovna Rada Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence at its meeting on Thursday reviewed the issue of changing the reservation system announced by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine and adopted a decision pointing out the groundlessness and risks of lowering employee reservation quotas for military-industrial complex (MIC) enterprises, said Committee member Iryna Friz (European Solidarity faction).
"The Committee's decision points out the groundlessness and risks of lowering quotas for the MIC. I must emphasize that the government's proposed reduction of reservation quotas to 85% for defense and energy enterprises, and to 60% for heat and water supply enterprises and other public utilities, creates risks for the stable operation of both the defense industry and critical infrastructure," Friz wrote on Facebook on Thursday evening.
She also noted that, based on the reports from representatives of the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Defense, the final text of the Cabinet resolution does not yet exist: "it is still undergoing coordination, revision, and waiting for a political decision."
"Given the presented arguments of government officials, it is worth noting that the percentage reductions for individual sectors voiced in the media lack methodological calculations and consequence modeling. This was pointed out by Committee members to the CM representatives," the MP reported.
Friz also reported that during the review of the resolution on reservation changes, the Ministry of Defense provided its remarks regarding the unacceptability of reducing 100% reservation at MIC enterprises to 85%.
She believes that the government's proposed reduction of reservation quotas to 85% for defense and energy enterprises and to 60% for heat and water supply enterprises and other public utilities creates risks for the stable operation of both the defense industry and critical infrastructure.
In addition, according to the MP, members of the parliamentary national security committee did not receive exhaustive arguments from government officials regarding the expediency of creating a Coordination Center, its functionality, and powers.
As reported, a group of MPs from all parliamentary factions appealed to Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky demanding the cancellation of plans to create a Coordination Center for organizing reservations. Head of the Sub-committee on Cybersecurity Issues MP Oleksandr Fedienko emphasized that the appearance of a new body creates risks of delays in reservation procedures for MIC, energy, and critical infrastructure enterprises, which threatens the non-fulfillment of state contracts.
According to available information, the draft government resolution On Certain Issues of Organizing the Reservation of Conscripts for the Period of Mobilization and in Wartime stipulated that without a positive recommendation from the Coordination Center, enterprises would not be able to obtain the status of critically important or a reservation quota exceeding 50%. Parliament already appealed to the government for a similar reason in July 2026, after which a similar initiative was canceled.
The Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs (SUP) opposed another tightening of restrictions on the reservation of conscripts without prior impact assessment and discussion with business.

Wildfire kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

Blaze kills 4 firefighters in Indonesia's Mount Bromo national park
October 16, 2026
At least four people have died and two others suffered severe burns while battling wildfires in a national park on Indonesia's main island, officials said on Friday.
They were trapped by thick smoke and fast-spreading flames in the Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park in East Java, a Forestry Ministry statement said, as the country's worst wildfires in a decade swept through the area.
The southeast Asian country has been battling a months-long crisis of blazes and toxic smoke, forcing schools to shut down and causing a surge in respiratory complaints in the region.
The victims were part of a 12-member firefighting team consisting of national park personnel, members of the community fire brigade, and local volunteers, said East Java police spokesperson Jules Abraham Abast.
"This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation," the ministry statement said, adding there had been a jump in hotspots detected by satellites as areas of unusually high temperatures. Not all hotspots necessarily translate into individual fires.
By Thursday evening, the number of hotspots in Indonesia stood at 799 , up from 372 a day earlier. The forest and land fires have worsened this year as weather phenomenon El Nino prolonged the dry season.
Toxic haze spreads across southeast Asia
The smoke from Indonesia's wildfires are causing a health crisis in neighboring southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
Malaysia on Friday ordered hundreds of schools to close down due to deteriorating air quality.
Singapore, meanwhile, topped IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta sixth.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan rejected calls from some lawmakers to seek compensation from Indonesia, saying the crisis should be addressed through diplomatic engagement and established mechanisms.
He said Malaysia was coordinating assistance for Indonesia and would push for stronger regional cooperation on haze management.
Singapore probing companies linked to fires
Singapore also called for closer cooperation. Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said authorities were investigating companies allegedly linked to Indonesian forest and land fires that have worsened the haze.
"Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries," he said.
Singapore enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014 after a bout of severe pollution.
The law allows authorities to target companies whose activities overseas cause or contribute to unhealthy haze levels in Singapore. That said, legal experts cautioned that pursuing companies under the law will be challenging.

Radicals seek to spread threats to Central Asia, Russia via Afghanistan — Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:09:17 UTC
17:09:17 KST

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Radicals seek to use Afghanistan as a springboard for spreading threats to Central Asia and Russia, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
"We take note of the fact that, according to available data, terrorist and extremist groups maintain a significant presence in Afghanistan’s areas bordering Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, where they have training camps and strongholds. Members of these groups seek to infiltrate Central Asian countries, particularly disguised as refugees and even tourists," he pointed out, addressing a conference on security issues in Central Asia and Afghanistan involving the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).
"According to our assessments based on intelligence data, the main threat comes from militants of the Islamic State-Khorasan Province group, a regional branch of the international terrorist organization Islamic State, which is outlawed in Russia. It openly pursues the goal of undermining the Kabul government’s ability to maintain stability in the country," Lavrov went on to say.
"Besides, radicals also seek to use Afghanistan as a kind of springboard for spreading terrorist activities to both Central Asia and Russia. The Terrorist International (I can think of no other way to describe it), which is based on the other bank of the Panj River unites militants of Central Asian, North Caucasian and Uyghur origin who gained combat experience in armed raids in the Middle East and Africa, as well as preachers of radical Islamic ideas, clandestine madrasas and propaganda resources in the information field, especially on social media," the top Russian diplomat added.
In his view, developments in Afghanistan could still negatively affect regional security, "particularly if unscrupulous external players use those processes to achieve their short-term goals, which certainly do not serve the interests of Central Asia and Russia."
"We try to remain realistic and thus realize that it will take a long time to overcome the unfortunate legacy left by the United States and other NATO countries following two decades of their inglorious occupation of Afghanistan," Lavrov concluded.

Trump Rejects Zelensky and Criticizes Ukraine’s Attacks on Russian Refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
08:09:00 UTC
17:09:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Newsmax that he did not want to deal with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whom he accused of refusing to pursue a peace agreement with Russia, while calling Ukraine’s renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries a disgrace.
Trump said he believed any eventual agreement with Moscow could be reached without Zelensky, arguing that the Ukrainian leader claimed to want peace but was not prepared to compromise.
“He doesn't want to settle. He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. No, I'm not a big fan of Zelensky,” Trump said.
The U.S. president also blamed former President Barack Obama’s administration for the origins of the war, claiming that Ukraine had been made to “give up Crimea” during his presidency. Trump described the peninsula, which is temporarily occupied by Russia, as particularly valuable because of its location and landscape.
“Crimea is the most valuable part, by far, of Ukraine. You know what I'm talking about. Four sides of ocean. Most beautiful piece of land. I'm a real estate developer. I know good land,” Trump said.
Asked about Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries, Trump called them disgraceful and said they were pushing up global energy prices.
“I want Zelensky to stop, and I want Putin… Now, if you tell me that Zelensky is again shooting at refineries, all he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace,” he told Newsmax.
Trump also attributed Russia’s failure to capture Kyiv quickly at the start of its full-scale invasion in 2022 to weather conditions and a military commander’s decision to turn tanks into muddy farmland. He suggested that Ukraine’s ability to repel the advance was partly a matter of luck.
“Then it was supposed to be a very quick war. And if you remember the tanks going up the highway right into Kyiv, had the general, who was obviously not a very good general, not made a right turn into farmland, which was soaked and soaking wet from the heaviest rain in 10 years, they say. He went right up into the mud, and it was like quicksand, and those tanks, so they [the Ukrainians] got… I don't know if you call it lucky or not lucky, frankly,” Trump said.
He argued that Ukraine should make concessions to Russian President Vladimir Putin because Russia has a much larger population from which to draw soldiers in a prolonged war.
“But Russia is a massive country. Russia has millions of people,” Trump said.
The comments came as tensions between Washington and Kyiv intensified over Russian oil, a proposed diesel supply agreement between Trump and Putin, and restrictions affecting Ukraine’s Starshield satellite communications system.
According to Reuters, citing two U.S. officials and a senior Western official, the order to restrict Starshield came from within the White House. Pentagon officials had been instructed to slow the system for the Ukrainian military, although the sources did not identify who made the decision or who was responsible for implementing it.
The restrictions followed Trump’s demands that Zelensky stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. A senior U.S. official denied that Trump had ordered the measure, saying, “No such request was ever made by the president.” The White House declined to say whether another administration official might have issued the request.
After Starshield operations were unexpectedly restricted on October 13 and 14, senior Ukrainian officials contacted the White House, State Department and Pentagon. One Ukrainian official said Washington told Kyiv that the decision had been made by the White House.
Ukrainian officials and military personnel said the restrictions significantly disrupted strike missions against Russian forces and logistics operations in temporarily occupied territories. They also limited the use of interceptor drones against Russian Shahed drones.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX using its Starlink satellite network for government clients and national security agencies, including the Pentagon. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that the system belongs to and is controlled by the U.S. government, meaning restrictions on its speed or use are determined by the Pentagon or Trump.
The disruption began overnight on October 12-13, when Ukrainian military personnel detected sudden speed limits affecting Starlink and Starshield terminals. The systems reportedly shut down when a drone exceeded 160 kilometers per hour and, in some cases, 80 kilometers per hour, making it extremely difficult to intercept Russian drones.
Zelensky described the restrictions as a mistake that would lead to casualties and destruction. On October 15, he rejected suggestions that technical problems had caused the disruption. Ukrainian sources later said the system’s full functionality had been restored and the speed limits lifted.
The dispute has added to concerns about the reliability of U.S. support for Ukraine as the war continues. Trump’s administration has threatened to suspend intelligence-sharing and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts its long-range attacks on Russian refineries, while Washington has also announced a deal allowing Russia to export diesel to the United States and other markets despite sanctions imposed following the full-scale invasion.
Trump has blamed Ukraine’s refinery strikes for higher global fuel prices, while Zelensky has argued that the U.S. war against Iran is responsible for the energy market disruption. Zelensky announced that Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian energy facilities after Moscow continued striking Ukrainian infrastructure despite the energy truce Trump had announced.
The Ukrainian president has also sought backing from European leaders during the EU summit in Brussels. European officials are expected to rally behind Kyiv, as many consider Ukraine’s long-range strikes to be a key source of leverage against Moscow.
Ihor Zhovkva, deputy head of Zelensky’s office, told Euronews’ Europe Today program that Ukraine was working on European alternatives to U.S.-made air defense systems and Starlink communications. He said the European FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program had advanced to direct engagement between defense companies.
“We need a European equivalent of an air defence system,” Zhovkva said, adding that Ukraine wanted to play a leading role in its development. He declined to provide further details about the planned European alternative to Starlink but said progress would be faster than skeptics expected.
“We have a clear timetable and deadlines,” he said. “It will be much faster than ten or fifteen years, and even faster than five.”
Zhovkva also said Europe must participate in any negotiations to end the war, arguing that Ukraine’s future security was inseparable from that of the wider continent.

Polish aid helped Ukraine defend Kyiv during recent attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels where he met with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Oct. 15.
Zelensky said Poland had provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns. Zelensky also hinted at other, more sensitive Polish support which would have to remain confidential; "sometimes it should remain between the two of us," he said.
Tusk gave Ukraine message of solidarity - "you are not alone."
"I would like to assure you, as I have already stated publicly here: Ukraine, your people and you personally – you are not alone… you can count on me personally, on Poland, and also on the EU. After my talks here in Brussels with all the leaders, it is absolutely clear that anything that could help Putin and Russia in this war is unacceptable for Europe and Poland," the Polish Prime Minister said.
In response, Zelensky thanked Tusk for Poland's help for Ukraine as it faces an upsurge in Russian attacks.
"We are very grateful to the Prime Minister, his team, the government, and the entire Polish people for standing with us in this absolutely barbaric war waged by Russia against Ukraine. Thank you for your support and for maintaining close contact throughout these extremely difficult months. These are very hard times. It is no longer just about days and nights – they are attacking us 24/7,” Zelensky said.
The meeting comes as tensions between Kyiv and Washington D.C. show no sign of easing, amid an American push to strong-arm Ukraine into ceasing drone attacks on Russian oil refineries. President Donald Trump has recently falsely blamed Ukraine for record high diesel prices sparked by America's faltering war with Iran.
Polish and Ukrainian relations have also been strained in recent months. In May, a decision by Ukraine to name a military unit in honor of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army led to Polish President Karol Nawrotski stripping Zelensky of Poland's "Order of the White Eagle".
Yet, Poland remains an important strategic partner for Ukraine, as well as a critical source of military materiel.
The same day, in Warsaw, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced that Ukraine expects to purchase an additional 125 million euros (about $1.484 million) worth of Polish weaponry by the end of 2026, financed by a loan from the Polish government.
"We are currently discussing how to finalize this agreement. I hope this will happen in the near future—by the end of the year—since there is political will for it, and funds have been allocated in Poland’s budget,” Sybiha said.
Ukraine is Poland's biggest arms-export customer, taking two thirds of Polish armaments production in 2025, spending 1.68 billion euros (about $1.90 billion) on Polish arms. Besides supplying armaments on a commercial basisPoland has also donated significant amounts of military materiel to Ukraine, including tanks, fighter jets, and artillery systems.
