Russian drones violated Moldovan airspace five times overnight
Several Russian UAVs violated Moldovan airspace on the night of 15-16 October and on the morning of 16 October.
Source: European Pravda, citing TV8
Details: The drones crossed the border amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. The incidents were recorded in northern and south-eastern Moldova. No crashes or explosions were reported.
The first violation was recorded at 23:02. An object crossed the border from the direction of Tymkove in Ukraine's Odesa Oblast and headed towards the village of Ivanovca. Eighteen minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace and headed towards the Ukrainian settlement of Bronit.
The second incident was recorded at 03:37. A drone flew from the direction of the Ukrainian village of Starokozache in Odesa Oblast towards the village of Tudora in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it returned to Ukrainian territory along the same route.
At 03:46, another drone crossed the border in the north from the direction of Mohyliv-Podilskyi, heading towards the town of Otaci. Two minutes later, it left Moldovan airspace near the village of Hădărăuți in Ocnița District.
The fourth violation was recorded at 05:59. A drone entered the country's airspace from the direction of Starokozache and headed towards the village of Căplani in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, the drone left Moldovan territory near the village of Olănești.
At 06:09, the same drone crossed the border again near the village of Purcari in Ștefan Vodă District. One minute later, it left the country's airspace via the Dnestrovsc area in the Transnistrian region, heading towards the Ukrainian settlement of Hradenytsi.
In less than seven hours, Moldova's Defence Ministry recorded five unauthorised incursions by aircraft into the country's airspace.
Background:
- On the night of 14-15 October, a drone once again violated Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Ukraine. Moldova's defence minister said the drone was "definitely" Russian.
- On the morning of 30 September, a drone flew through Moldovan airspace before crashing outside the village of Hîrbovăț in Anenii Noi District and exploding.

UN chief says ‘subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide’

- He said nations are still “spending money on the wrong things”, with about US$2.6 trillion a year in public subsidies that damage nature and the climate.
- Ahead of UN biodiversity talks in Yerevan, he warned the world is off track for 2030 nature targets and called for savings to be used for people and planet.
AI generated
PARIS – UN chief Antonio Guterres on Oct 16 urged governments to stop subsidising the production of fossil fuels that are “boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity”.
Addressing leaders in Armenia ahead of next week’s UN biodiversity summit, Guterres said governments were still “spending money on the wrong things” and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.
“Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said at an event in Yerevan.
“They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”
Nations have made little headway since pledging in 2022 to reduce public spending on activities that harm nature such as mining, fossil fuel extraction and intensive farming.
The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about US$30 (S$38) still goes into activities that degrade it.
This includes an estimated US$2.6 trillion a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.
Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations in Yerevan starting on Oct 19, where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.
Guterres launched a report on Oct 16 showing that the world was off track to achieving the 2030 biodiversity targets enshrined in a landmark pact for nature. AFP

Asparuh Nikodimov, who coached CSKA at the time, later recalled why the Bulgarian team rejected the walkover. “There was no way we could take advantage of people's tragedy,” he said.
CSKA agreed to play in Nice and traveled there by bus. Traffic jams nearly caused the team to arrive late, and the players took to the field with virtually no warm-up.
A famous photograph showing the two captains, Jean-Luc Ettori and Georgi Dimitrov, exchanging club pennants before the match is preserved in Monaco’s museum. The French club continues to hold the Bulgarian side in high regard because of that gesture.
The choreography on Thursday depicted the hands of Ettori and the late Gosho Dimitrov. During the match, Monaco’s social media account shared a photograph of Sector G alongside an emoji expressing gratitude.
In 1982, CSKA went on to eliminate Monaco after drawing 0-0 away and securing a 2-0 victory in Sofia.

Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch uncrewed underwater vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Saab, FMV and the Swedish Armed Forces launch uncrewed underwater vehicle
Less than one year after contract award, Saab, the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Armed Forces have successfully developed, built and launched a demonstrator for a Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (LUUV).
Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle. Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed. The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities. The results will support the continued development of software, sensors and autonomous functions, while also contributing to future product development.
The vehicle illustrates how close collaboration between industry and government authorities can significantly reduce the time from identifying an operational need to testing a new capability.
“This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value. The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities. The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” says Mats Wicksell, head of Saab’s business area Naval.
The demonstrator has been developed to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and to enable operations alongside existing naval platforms, such as submarines.
The rapid development has been enabled by Saab’s software-centric approach and the integration of Autonomous Ocean Core, Saab’s autonomous control system that provides surface and subsurface vehicles with autonomous capabilities. Combined with Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration, this has made it possible to take the project swiftly from concept to sea trials.
The LUUV project builds on Saab’s earlier investments and work in autonomous underwater systems and is now led by FMV in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab. The project provides a basis for Swedish authorities’ decisions regarding the future acquisition and operational use of autonomous underwater systems.

“And this documentary failed to besmirch his character, which presumably was the ultimate objective.”
Farage has made repeated promises over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.

“He must do it and move on … Tell him that from me,” Farage said, to which Sumner said: “You’re protecting him.”
To laughter, Farage replied: “It’s showing a bit of … bit of sorrow. Look, ‘I’m sorry’ is probably a good thing to hear. Just take the fucking deal. Trouble is he’s a rear admiral. That’s the problem.”
Jenrick defended Reform’s vetting policy. “In my experience, all political parties have bad apples. I mean, you can see that’s plain to see from the conduct of other political parties. In fact, Councillor Feeney, the one that you presented before I came online, was for a short time a Reform councillor, but for a much greater time a Conservative councillor.”
He added: “We actually have very strong vetting, and we invest a huge amount in it, and it’s improving all the time. I don’t know what the vetting is like in every other political party. I can say in the Conservative party, because it was my former party, there is absolutely no vetting whatsoever by the central party for local councillors.”

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks

UK and Germany strengthen defence ties in London talks
UK and Germany deepen defence-industrial cooperation at Lancaster House talks, building on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty.
- UK and Germany strengthened defence-industrial cooperation at the latest talks at Lancaster House.
- The talks build on the Trinity House Agreement and Kensington Treaty, reinforcing cooperation between the two nations across air, land, sea and space.
- Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard and German counterpart State Secretary Jens Plötner joined industry leaders to discuss industrial priorities for collaboration.
UK-German work on key industrial collaboration and new technology was advanced yesterday as Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard hosted his German counterpart, State Secretary for Armament and Innovation Jens Plötner, at Lancaster House in London.
The latest UK-Germany Ministerial Group on Equipment and Capability Cooperation (MECC) meeting brought together senior officials and military leaders from both nations to review progress on joint defence capability programmes and to deepen the industrial partnership between the UK and Germany, two of NATO’s leading defence powers.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard MP said:
  Germany is one of our closest and most valued defence partners, and today’s talks demonstrate our determination to turn that ambition into real capability for our armed forces and real opportunity for our defence industries.
As threats to our shared security evolve, the UK and Germany are standing together, strengthening our forces, our industrial bases and our resilience in lockstep.
Discussions built on the Trinity House Agreement, signed in October 2024, which set out an ambitious programme of bilateral cooperation across air, land, maritime, cyber and space domains. The agreement sits under the wider Kensington Treaty, signed in July 2025, which provides the strategic framework for the UK-Germany relationship.
Among the flagship programmes on the agenda was Deep Precision Strike, a joint UK-Germany initiative to develop long-range strike capability, reflecting the shared ambition of both nations to address critical capability gaps and strengthen NATO’s deterrence.
The talks follow the Prime Minister’s visit to Berlin on 8 October, during which the UK and Germany agreed to deepen cooperation on space and to establish a new UK-Germany Counter-Hybrid Partnership, strengthening joint resilience against grey-zone threats.
Following the MECC meeting, Minister Pollard joined State Secretary Plötner at the German Embassy in London for a panel discussion which saw senior policymakers and industry leaders take stock of defence-industrial progress and identify practical priorities for deepening cooperation.
Minister Pollard was joined on the panel by State Secretary Plötner, Dr Philipp Kerth, co-founder and chief executive of German defence technology company Hypersonica, and Alex Zino, Director Business Development & Future Programmes at Rolls-Royce.
The MECC forms part of a wider programme of UK-German engagement in the lead-up to the EU-UK summit. The UK-Germany defence relationship continues to grow as both nations work towards a more resilient Euro-Atlantic security architecture, underpinned by a modern, innovative and competitive defence industrial base at the heart of NATO’s deterrence and readiness.

Zelenskiy blasts Trump's diesel deal and calls Russian peace moves a 'parody'
BRUSSELS/KYIV, Oct 16 - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took aim on Friday at US President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia and welcomed the prospect of European allies stepping up their role in talks, calling Moscow's stance a "parody" of peace negotiations.
At a European Union summit in Brussels, Zelenskiy said Russia did not want peace. He added that Ukraine was still experiencing disruptions to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system used for battlefield operations and to down Russian drones attacking cities far from the frontline.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskiy after Trump again criticised Ukraine, calling its strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace". On arriving at the summit, Zelenskiy pointedly referred to his counterparts there as "real leaders".
The EU was hosting Zelenskiy at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities and fears that the US could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.
Nevertheless, Zelenskiy's tone suggests he has little intention of softening his stance towards the US. Asked at a press conference whether he felt he was being used as a scapegoat by Trump for high energy prices and the trajectory of the Iran war, Zelenskiy paused for a long time, smiled, and said "this is my answer", to laughter in the room.
'MONEY IN PUTIN'S POCKET'
Trump blindsided Zelenskiy last weekend by announcing that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities. Facing US midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that could cost him at the ballot box.
His diesel deal with Russia angered Ukraine and European allies.
"And now we can see how cash will start flowing back into Russia through the diesel deal," Zelenskiy told the press conference on the sidelines of the summit.
"This diesel deal will never be enough to offset the impact of the Strait of Hormuz on global markets. But it will put more money straight into Putin’s pocket to fund this war."
Zelenskiy also accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of not being interested in peace talks in any form.
"Putin does not want peace talks at the moment, in any form," he said. "He's playing with words, claiming they respond... Quite simply, it looks like a parody of a genuine desire to end the war."
The Kremlin said last week that Ukraine had undermined the possibility of an immediate resumption of peace talks after it had hit Moscow with drones during last month's election.
Meanwhile in the latest attacks in Ukraine, Russian drone strikes on the city of Kharkiv killed three people, while strikes elsewhere left hundreds of thousands of people without power.
In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
“Last winter was already hell, this one will be once again like hell,” Michal said.
"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you – for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience," Zelenskiy said in his address to the EU leaders, which he later posted on X.
"This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back."
EU LEADERS GRAPPLING WITH BUDGET
Ukraine's leadership has been alarmed by disruptions to the Starshield satellite system.
A US official has denied that Trump ordered a deliberate slowdown of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service run by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and Trump said this week intelligence sharing with Ukraine continued.
Zelenskiy said the operation had improved but not yet been fully restored, adding the disruption placed civilians at risk.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can't replace this capability," said the EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelenskiy declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ceasefire that Trump had announced.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said in an interview with the Newsmax news outlet.
Russia has also publicly acknowledged the drone attack on a refinery and broadcast images on state media, breaking with its usual practice in order to play up the incident.
While EU leaders hit out at the US deal to buy Russian diesel, they are also grappling with how to tackle energy prices that have soared since the Iran war, exposing divisions between member states on day one of the summit on Thursday.
Splits continued on Friday, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson saying member states were "incredibly far apart" from each other when it came to finalising the EU's own budget. "There isn't even a glimpse, as they say, a shred of agreement on this," he said. REUTERS

Zelensky thanks EU's 'real leaders' for their continued support as bloc confirms new sanctions package on the way
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived for the second day of an EU leaders' summit on Oct. 16, ready to discuss support for Ukraine's energy grid, 2027 budget, and EU membership bid.
Zelensky's visit comes as the U.S. government pivots in a decidedly pro-Russian direction, leading Kyiv and Brussels to condemn Washington's betrayal of Ukraine and emphasize their close ties.
"Our message to President Zelensky is very simple. The support of the EU to Ukraine remains as strong as ever. This is no time to withdraw support... no time to relieve Russia sanctions. It is time to increase our support, increase our pressure," European Council President Antonio Costa said.
"I cannot count the many times you were here, and it shows the closeness that we have," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added.
"I'm so thankful that we have such huge support from EU leaders, real leaders," Zelensky said ahead of the EU leaders meeting, accompanied by Costa and von der Leyen.
"I am thankful the EU stands with us," Zelensky said.
"We supported Trump's energy ceasefire, but we see Russia did not respect it, and so we have to increase the pressure," von der Leyen told journalists, before announcing that the EU is working on a new 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
"Dear Volodymyr, you can count on us not only to support you in war but most importantly for your future as a member of the EU," Costa said.
Costa and von der Leyen both congratulated Zelensky and Ukraine's parliament for passing key reforms that allowed Kyiv's EU membership bid to proceed earlier in the week.
"The goal is toward the end of the year to open the final two clusters," von der Leyen said, in reference to the to-do lists of reforms Ukraine is partway through unlocking.
Zelensky then headed to a meeting with Costa and von der Leyen, after which they are expected to announce a new dedicated EU task force to help Ukraine advance the rule of law, which is essential for the country to unlock EU support funds and become a member of the bloc.

Ensuring security of transport corridors benefits all regional countries: Iranian minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:57:06 UTC
16:57:06 KST

Ensuring security of transport corridors benefits all regional countries: Iranian minister
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Transport and Urban Development, emphasizing the necessity of protecting civilian infrastructure and guaranteeing the continuity of transport and transit flows in the region, presented proposals and called for the formulation of operational and time-bound plans to remove border obstacles, develop rail cooperation, and strengthen the resilience of regional corridors.
According to an IRNA report from the Ministry of Transport and Urban Development, Farzaneh Sadegh, at the 14th Meeting of Ministers of Transport of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) member states in Kazakhstan, expressed appreciation for that country’s hosting and stated: Due to its privileged geographical location, the ECO region has the capacity to become an integrated network of road, rail, and sea routes—a network that can strengthen connectivity among Central Asia, West Asia, the Caucasus, and open waters.
Referring to the approvals of the 13th ECO Meeting of Ministers of Transport in Tehran, she emphasized the necessity of assessing the extent of implementation of past agreements, identifying obstacles, and determining operational priorities, and said: This meeting must lead to specific, time-bound, and measurable decisions for developing regional cooperation.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the damage inflicted on Iran’s transport infrastructure during the attacks by the United States and the Israeli regime, said: Disruption in any part of the region’s transport network, regardless of where it occurs, can increase the time and cost of moving goods and also affect the security of supply chains of other countries.
Sadegh emphasized: Protecting civilian infrastructure, ensuring the security of communication routes, and continuing the flow of transport and transit are common interests for all ECO member states.
She asked the organization’s secretariat to examine the effects of security disruptions on regional corridors and present practical solutions for increasing the resilience of the transport network.
Sadegh further considered facilitating the movement of the road fleet and border crossings among the priorities of regional cooperation and emphasized reducing truck dwell time, simplifying customs procedures, harmonizing transport documents, and exchanging information among border authorities.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, referring to the revival of the ECO train and its successful operation on the Turkey, Iran, and Turkmenistan route, considered this experience a basis for expanding rail cooperation among member states.
Noting that the damaged bridges on the aforementioned rail route were repaired by Iranian engineers within 72 hours and the route was reopened, she emphasized the importance of technical readiness and maintaining the continuity of regional rail connections.
Sadegh also considered the Almaty–Tehran–Istanbul rail connection an opportunity for developing regional trade and proposed that tariff, customs, technical, and operational obstacles on rail routes be examined and a clear mechanism be created for coordinating train movements and developing regular and competitive services.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development listed access of landlocked countries to open waters as one of the priorities of cooperation in ECO and said: Achieving this goal requires the integrated linking of ports, rail lines, roads, and logistics services.
Referring to the capacity of Chabahar Port and other southern ports of Iran, she considered the connection of Chabahar to the country’s rail network an effective factor in strengthening the link between land and sea transport, diversifying trade routes, and reducing transport costs.
The Minister of Transport and Urban Development, further emphasizing the necessity of determining the responsibilities of countries and the secretariat in following up on approvals and presenting a progress report at the next meeting, noted: Developing transport and transit in the ECO region, in addition to increasing trade and economic growth, helps strengthen regional ties and enhance the economic resilience of member states.
Sadegh proposed that the ECO secretariat, in cooperation with member states, prepare a comprehensive report on the extent of implementation of previous approvals and remaining obstacles, formulate a time-bound plan for facilitating road transport, border and customs coordination, and developing rail and multimodal services, and place on its agenda solutions for protecting civilian infrastructure and increasing the resilience of corridors.

At least 4 killed while fighting wildfire in East Java, Indonesia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:55:32 UTC
16:55:32 KST

Saadet Gokce
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
At least four people were killed while battling a wildfire in Mount Bromo in Indonesia's East Java province.
The death toll rose to four on Thursday after another person died while being transferred to a hospital, the state-run news agency Antara reported.
The victims included two officers from Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park and two hotel staffers.
Two other people suffered serious burns while fighting the fire and were hospitalized for treatment.
Probolinggo District Head Muhammad Haris said wildfires had occurred in the national park almost every year, but had not previously caused fatalities.
Twelve people initially joined efforts to contain the current fire under standard operating procedures, but the blaze spread and the team split up, leaving six people trapped as winds shifted rapidly, Haris said.
Indonesia faces an unusually prolonged dry season, with El Nino contributing to conditions favorable for wildfires.

Ukrainian Tencore signs memo with Canadian Dominion Dynamics for joint production of TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles in Canada
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:55:18 EEST
16:55:18 KST

Ukrainian defense company Tencore and Canadian defense-technology firm Dominion Dynamics have announced the signing of a memorandum of understanding, which provides for the production of TerMIT unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) in Canada, as well as the integration of the AuraNet technology suite into these systems.
According to a press release from Dominion Dynamics, the agreement was signed during the AUSA 2026 defense conference in Washington.
Dominion Dynamics reportedly plans to establish production of the TerMIT system at its Canadian facilities, with manufacturing slated to begin in 2027.
Meanwhile, experts from Tencore will oversee the technology transfer process and train Canadian personnel in the assembly of these unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs).
Furthermore, Dominion Dynamics will integrate the AuraNet system—designed for autonomous control and coordination across diverse operational environments—into the TerMIT platform. The company also intends to develop a version of the TerMIT platform specifically adapted for Arctic conditions.
“Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale. Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles," Tencore co-founder Roman Tkachenko is quoted in the press release as saying.
It is noted that the signing of this agreement follows a joint declaration on defense cooperation, which was concluded in September between Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
At that time, the parties committed to producing thousands of combat-tested drones and unmanned systems over the next two years, with one-third of these to be allocated for Ukraine’s defense needs, the company stated.
“This agreement is how two companies start turning that commitment into vehicles, and we intend to move fast,” said Eliot Pence, founder and CEO of Dominion Dynamics.
Dominion Dynamics is an Ottawa, Canada-based defense technology company specializing in the development of autonomy, sensor monitoring, and control systems.
Tencore is a Ukrainian defense technology company that specializes in the development, serial production, and integration of unmanned ground robotic systems (UGRS) for the Defense Forces of Ukraine.

New house sales in Türkiye rise 3.9% in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:54:31 UTC
16:54:31 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
New house sales in Türkiye rose 3.9% year-on-year to 51,519 in September, according to official data released Friday.
New homes accounted for 36.2% of total housing transactions during the month, data from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TurkStat) showed.
Overall house sales fell 9.3% from a year earlier to 142,390, as existing home sales dropped 15.3% to 90,871.
Adjusted for calendar effects, new house sales increased 3.8% annually. On a seasonally and calendar-adjusted basis, they rose 5.5% from August, while existing home sales remained unchanged.
Mortgaged house sales climbed 5.1% year-on-year to 23,397, accounting for 16.4% of total transactions.
Sales to foreign buyers increased 9.9% to 2,167, representing 1.5% of the total. Russian citizens purchased the most homes with 388, followed by Iraqis with 166 and Germans with 162.
In January-September, new house sales edged down 0.6% from the same period last year to 359,913, while total housing transactions declined 7.2% to 1.09 million.

‘CBI’s response to sanctions is to curb inflation acceleration, strengthen economic resilience’
TEHRAN- The Governor of the Central Bank of Iran (CBI) said: Our policy response to sanctions is curbing inflation acceleration and strengthening economic resilience, and taking into account available foreign currency reserves.
According to IRNA from the Central Bank, Abdolnaser Hemmati, Governor of the Central Bank, at a gathering of central bank governors of Middle East, North Africa, and Central Asia (MCI) countries in Bangkok, explained the Central Bank’s monetary policy under conditions of war, sanctions, and restrictions on transferring financial resources.
He added: Our policy response often consists of quantitative restrictions on banks’ balance sheet growth, measures to strengthen asset quality and the financial health of banks, and allocation of reserves through open market operations, credit lines, and financing supply chain instruments aimed at boosting production.
Hemmati noted: In the foreign currency sector, our priority is supplying the people’s basic and essential goods.

The meeting is being held from October 12 to 18, 2026, with the participation of economic and financial officials of member countries.
Examining solutions for developing economic and financial cooperation, following up on issues of interest to the Islamic Republic of Iran in interaction with international financial institutions, and exchanging views on solutions to strengthen sustainable economic growth and increase the resilience of the global economy are among the areas of focus during this trip.
During this trip, while participating in meetings related to the summit, our Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance has on his agenda plans for dialogue and consultations with officials of international financial institutions and economic officials of other countries.

Russia attacked energy infrastructure in Kyiv and four regions, leaving some residents without electricity - Ministry of Energy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:50:36 EEST
16:50:36 KST

Russia attacked energy infrastructure in Kyiv and four regions, leaving some residents without electricity - Ministry of Energy
Kyiv • UNN
Russian drones attacked energy facilities in Kyiv and the regions, causing new power outages. Schedules for power cuts are in effect in some regions.
Russia attacked energy infrastructure in four regions and Kyiv overnight and in the morning of October 16, leaving some residents without electricity. Overall, new power outages have been reported in at least eight regions and the capital. UNN reports this, citing data from the Ministry of Energy and NPC Ukrenergo.
Enemy attack on energy infrastructure
"Overnight and in the morning, Russia attacked a number of energy facilities in Kyiv, as well as the Kyiv, Volyn, Odesa and Rivne regions. As a result, some consumers were left without electricity," the Ministry of Energy reported.
According to the Ministry of Energy, "due to shelling and hostilities, there are new power outages in the Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Kharkiv, Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv regions as of this morning."
Ukrenergo confirmed that "overnight and in the morning, the enemy launched a massive drone attack on energy facilities in several regions." "As a result, as of this morning there are new power outages in the city of Kyiv, as well as the Kyiv, Volyn, Odesa, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Chernihiv regions," Ukrenergo's data show.
Energy workers are working to restore the damaged equipment and return electricity to consumers. Repair work is continuing wherever the security situation allows; however, due to continuous air-raid alerts, crews are forced to interrupt their work, the Ministry of Energy said.
Severe weather
As a result of the severe weather, 12 settlements in the Poltava and Sumy regions remain without electricity.
Repair crews are working to restore the power supply.
Schedules
"Due to grid restrictions caused by Russian attacks, hourly outage schedules and capacity restriction schedules for industry and business are in effect in some regions today. These are necessary measures to stabilize the operation of the power system and prevent larger-scale accidents," the Ministry of Energy reported.
"To avoid overloading equipment damaged by previous Russian shelling, capacity restriction schedules for industry and hourly outage schedules (up to two queues) for all categories of consumers will necessarily be applied in some regions today until the end of the day," Ukrenergo clarified.
Consumers were urged to use electricity sparingly while the restriction measures are in effect.
Consumption
According to Ukrenergo, electricity consumption is in line with seasonal levels. Today, October 16, as of 09:30, it was at the same level as the previous day—Thursday.
Yesterday, October 15, the daily consumption peak was recorded in the evening. It was 3.9% higher than the peak of the previous day—Wednesday, October 14. This was caused by a drop in air temperatures in most regions of Ukraine, prompting consumers to use electric heaters during the evening hours.
"Given the consequences of Russian shelling and the weather conditions, please limit the use of high-powered electrical appliances from 16:00 to 22:00," Ukrenergo emphasized.
It also noted that due to Russian attacks on energy infrastructure, the situation in the power system may change.

====================================================================================================

AI threatens democracy. But we are not powerless: here’s how to fight back | Carine Fouteau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:49:45 UTC
16:49:45 KST

Big tech companies pose an immeasurable threat: socially, politically, militarily and ecologically. They are also causing a profound crisis of information. The tools they design now serve as weapons of mass destruction against democracy. There is so much at stake that an urgent and broad mobilisation is required.
From the harvesting of personal data and the weaponisation of public opinion, to the destruction of jobs, the infringement of civil liberties and environmental damage, ordinary citizens are the main victims of this predatory economy – an economy with an agenda that aligns with the interests of the planet’s most authoritarian and reactionary states.
The threats facing the information landscape affect us all. Journalists of my generation have witnessed four major digital revolutions: the internet, social media, smartphones, and now, artificial intelligence. What fundamentally changes with AI is our relationship with the truth. For big tech companies, the boundary between truth and falsehood has vanished. This makes it essential to reaffirm the role of public-interest journalism. Our mission is to publish information that is in the public interest by seeking the factual truth, standing against “fake news” and propaganda. Our mission is to help create a democratic public sphere that serves citizens.
Yet AI companies are completely reshaping this space to their own advantage; their mission is not the public interest, but generating profits. Their methods include plundering news outlets without authorisation or compensation. By disseminating so-called summaries of our reporting, they siphon off our audiences and revenue, serving the private interests of a select few at the expense of the common good.
The difference between AI-generated content and a real news article is journalism. AI-generated responses are not information. They are merely a logical assembly of words that all too often produces falsehoods, distorts facts and misinterprets information. A real news article is something else entirely. Quality journalism is the product of expertise guided by ethical standards: persuading sources to speak, painstakingly gathering eye-witness testimonies, cross-referencing, verifying and establishing facts. This process relies on reporting or investigative work – in other words, human effort in the field.
Good journalism organises and prioritises information, providing context and nuance; AI, by contrast, levels everything down to the lowest common denominator and breeds confusion. Journalism uncovers facts that certain parties – particularly economic and political powers – would prefer to see hidden, ignored, or suppressed. Generative AI uncovers nothing, it merely regurgitates and condenses existing material.
Quality journalism comes at a high price. Some of the costs can’t even be quantified. Journalists who report from war zones for example, risk their lives. Mediapart’s recent investigation into Jordan Bardella, the head of Marine Le Pen’s far-right party, has resulted in anonymous cyber-harassment and death threats against our editorial team.
Ultimately, media outlets are accountable for the information they publish. They answer to the courts and to their readers. AI companies appear answerable only to their shareholders. They refuse to vouch for the reliability of their conversational agents to evade legal liability. If nothing is done to stop it, this pillaging will result in the destruction of journalism. This is dangerous not just for news publishers, but for all of us, because it signifies the demise of a public sphere defined by free, pluralistic and democratic discourse.
Do we want a public sphere that guarantees access to reliable, independent information, or one governed by algorithms that amplify fake news, deepfakes and propaganda – fuelling fear, anger and division?
Fortunately, the tech companies have sown the seeds of their own downfall. Since they are bleeding dry the very sources of information from which they derive their profits, they are courting their own failure; without quality information, they will produce nothing but AI slop.
This is precisely where we find leverage. OpenAI has admitted that it would be impossible to train today’s leading AI models without using copyrighted material. A Microsoft vice-president acknowledged that training models on quality content significantly improves the quality of output.
The priority is to act collectively, pressuring these platforms by every available means – including legal action – to uphold the rights of the press and the public. Some newspapers, such as the New York Times, have taken legal action. Its publisher, AG Sulzberger, recently cited a figure of $20m spent on litigation. Legal proceedings are also under way in France – notably through the organisation responsible for collecting press-related neighbouring rights.
Beyond pressuring lawmakers at national and European level, we must broaden our fightback to include the entire research and knowledge community – stakeholders who, like us, are committed to the public interest and factual truth.
It falls to us, as journalists, to convince the public that our work is an essential part of democracy. We have to demonstrate that our reporting – aimed at holding power to account – has real impact and drives change; that it makes sense of a rapidly shifting world and serves as a powerful catalyst for civic action.
- Carine Fouteau is president and publishing director of the French investigative news outlet Mediapart
- Mediapart is hosting Hacking Big Tech, a public event about technology, AI and democracy in partnership with the Guardian, in Paris on Saturday 17 October 2026. The conference will be live-streamed free on Mediapart’s website, app and YouTube channel and can be accessed here from 1pm CEST on 17 October

Co-op memorandum signed: Iran, Eurasia take new step for free trade, integration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:49:23 UTC
16:49:23 KST

Co-op memorandum signed: Iran, Eurasia take new step for free trade, integration
TEHRAN- The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade stressed, at the signing of a cooperation memorandum with the member states of Eurasia, the full implementation of the free trade agreement, the removal of trade barriers, and the expansion of transit cooperation.
According to IRNA from the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, on Wednesday evening, at the signing of the memorandum with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union during the second meeting of the Joint Committee for the Implementation of the Free Trade Agreement between Iran and this union, called for operational follow-up of the agreements, the removal of trade barriers, and maximum use of the capacities of this agreement to develop economic exchanges.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade described transparency in import regulations, timely exchange of statistical information, and the removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers as requirements for fully benefiting from free trade.
He emphasized the necessity of following up on issues related to vehicle recycling fees, access of Iranian cement products to the markets of the union’s member states, and requirements for importing food products, and declared Iran’s readiness to cooperate in examining and removing these barriers.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade further called for turning agreements into specific executive plans with a clear timetable and determining the responsibilities of each party.
He proposed that the secretariats of both sides, by creating a mechanism for continuous monitoring of the implementation of the approvals, present a progress report on measures at the next meeting of the Joint Committee.
The Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade stated: The negotiations held will be constructive and result-oriented, and the summary of the negotiations and approvals in specialized committees should be the basis for regular follow-up of commitments.
He expressed hope that the implementation of the agreements, while facilitating the activity of traders and increasing trade exchanges, would lead to strengthening economic cooperation between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union and enhancing the position of the parties in regional and international relations.
The second meeting of the Joint Committee for the Implementation of the Free Trade Agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union was held, hosted by the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, with the presentation of solutions for trade facilitation, the development of economic cooperation, and the removal of existing barriers.
In this committee, the minister responsible for trade of the Eurasian Economic Union, officials of the Economic Commission, ambassadors, deputy ministers of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, representatives of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, the Customs of the Islamic Republic of Iran, the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, the Ministries Transport and Urban Development and Agriculture, and the National Standards Organization of Iran and the Iran Veterinary Organization were present.
Accelerating the establishment of the electronic system for verification of origin, developing transit cooperation within the framework of the International North–South Corridor, and strengthening technical and health cooperation related to trade were among the most important axes of this meeting.
Also, the signing of the cooperation memorandum of understanding between the Business Council of the Eurasian Economic Union and the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture was assessed as a step toward strengthening communication among private sector actors and expanding trade cooperation between the two sides.
Awarding highest honorary badge of Eurasian Economic Union to industry, mining and trade minister
The highest honorary badge of the Eurasian Economic Union was awarded to Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade of the Islamic Republic of Iran, in appreciation of his effective efforts in developing and deepening Iran’s economic relations with this union, by Andrey Slepnev, Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission.
According to an IRNA from the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade, this honorary badge was awarded in appreciation of the measures and efforts of the Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade to expand economic cooperation, strengthen trade interactions, and develop the relations of the Islamic Republic of Iran with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union; cooperation that is pursued with the aim of utilizing mutual capacities, facilitating trade, and expanding economic ties between the parties.
Andrey Slepnev, Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Union, arrived in Tehran on Wednesday to participate in the second meeting of the Joint Committee for the Implementation of the Free Trade Agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union, and in a meeting attended by Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, and other ambassadors of member states, they addressed the presentation of solutions for trade facilitation, the development of economic cooperation, and the removal of existing barriers.
On October 1, the Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), in a meeting with the Trade Minister of the Eurasian Economic Union, referring to the upward trend of trade between Iran and the member states of the union, emphasized the Islamic Republic of Iran’s determination to expand and deepen trade relations and strengthen ties between the private sectors of the two sides.
According to a report by the Public Relations of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, in a meeting with Slepnev, referring to the course of trade between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, said: “Despite all challenges and problems, trade statistics between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union have taken an upward trend, and this promises bright prospects for the development of trade relations in the future.”
The Deputy Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, emphasizing the will and determination of the Islamic Republic of Iran to expand trade relations with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, added: “Iran has regular cooperation and trade relations with Russia and other member states of the union, and we are striving to make these ties deeper than before.”
Dehghan Dehnavi also expressed hope that the second meeting of the joint committee of Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union will be held in Tehran soon, and continued: “Holding this meeting in Tehran can be a suitable opportunity to strengthen communication between the private sectors of Iran and the member states of the union and to form new economic and trade cooperation.”
The Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization also stressed the continuation of consultations and the use of existing capacities to develop economic and trade cooperation between Iran and the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union.
It is worth noting that Dehghan Dehnavi traveled to Minsk to participate in the 19th meeting of the Joint Economic Cooperation Commission of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Belarus.
Also, in mid-September, Iran’s Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, offering a positive assessment of the results of his Tuesday meetings with officials of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), announced the proposal of initiatives such as setting a base currency to accelerate transactions and appointing special representatives to resolve obstacles facing bilateral trade.
According to IRNA, Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, speaking to reporters after separate meetings and talks with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission at the union's headquarters in Moscow, added: "We held very good sessions."
He stated: "On Iran's behalf, we expressed our interest and readiness to expand relations and fully implement the free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union, and that we are prepared to cooperate with this union in various fields; the union's officials, in turn, expressed their willingness and interest in expanding ties with our country."
The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, referring to the efforts of the enemies of the Iranian nation to fuel economic warfare and block trade and financial channels, said: "What is evident is that, thanks to God, these countries support Iran and our economy, and that Iran has managed to maintain production and trade relations with countries under the toughest conditions." He added: "The member states of the Eurasian Economic Union are equally committed and eager to develop these relations."
Continuing his Moscow visit agenda for multilateral consultations, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance attended the Eurasian Economic Union's headquarters and met with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade to discuss accelerating bilateral trade.
Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, and Bakytzhan Sagintayev, Chairman of the Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission, emphasized their shared determination to expand cooperation during this meeting.
Prior to this meeting, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance held a separate session with Andrey Slepnev, Minister in charge of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission, and a group of union officials to review the progress of cooperation following the implementation of the free trade agreement. Slepnev, noting that the second meeting of the Iran-EAEU working group would be hosted by Tehran in the coming months, expressed hope that the upward trend in bilateral trade would continue.
Iran's Ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, and Mehdi Heydari, Deputy Minister of Economy and head of Iran's Organization for Investment, Economic and Technical Assistance, accompanied Madanizadeh during these meetings.
The free trade agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union came into force in May 2025 after completing legal procedures in the signatory countries, subsequently eliminating customs duties on 87% of goods in bilateral trade.
Within this cooperation framework, the path has been smoothed for Iranian goods to enter the market of over 180 million people in the union's member states, and reciprocally, this opportunity is available for traders from the five signatory countries in commerce with Iran.
Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia are members of the Eurasian Economic Union, and Iran holds observer status in the union.
The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a regional economic integration bloc in the post-Soviet space, established by a treaty signed in 2014 and launched on January 1, 2015. Its five member states are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia, with Iran, Cuba, Moldova, and Uzbekistan holding observer status.
Modelled in part on the European Union, the EAEU aims to create a single internal market with the free movement of goods, services, capital, and labour. Its core objectives include improving living standards, ensuring sustainable economic development, and boosting the global competitiveness of member economies.
The bloc is driven by institutions such as the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council and the Eurasian Economic Commission. While the EAEU has expanded external ties—notably through a free trade agreement with Iran—internal integration remains uneven, with Russia dominating trade flows in a "hub and spoke" model. The bloc has set a long-term vision to become a self-sufficient and attractive macro-region by 2045.

University's satellite collects data on space radiation at various heights above Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:46:24 UTC
16:46:24 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 16. /TASS/. The ArcticSat-1 spacecraft of the Northern Arctic Federal University (NArFU) collected data on space radiation at different heights above the Arctic. Researchers obtained data from 500 to 200 km, and there is practically no information about radiation at low levels in the circumpolar regions, leader of the university's Space Monitoring Center Roman Alyoshko told TASS.
"The main data that we were collecting is data on space radiation," he said. "This is an urgent task exactly for the polar regions. During the spacecraft's mission, we collected data on space radiation, starting from altitudes of about 500 km when it was launched into orbit, and then it was gradually decreasing over about a year and a half, to 200 km when it already began burning up. And it is even more relevant data when it was in low orbits of about 200 kilometers. There are practically no spacecraft in such orbits, and therefore data on space radiation at these heights is very valuable."
ArcticSat-1 belongs to a group of satellites that fly in low orbits, at an altitude of 400-600 km. Strictly speaking, there is no space vacuum there, and therefore the satellite constantly touches the atmosphere molecules and gradually loses speed. It does not have an engine to compensate for this, so the satellite is slowly descending. The lower is the satellite, the denser is the air and the faster is the deceleration. The Sun also affects the descent rate: with high solar activity, the atmosphere heats up and "swells", increasing the braking effect at the orbit altitude.
ArcticSat-1's orbit is polar, with an inclination of about 97 degrees. In such an orbit, the spacecraft passes over high latitudes, where the geomagnetic field does not protect well from space particles. This coincides with the project's main topic: the impact of space weather on small spacecraft in the polar regions.
"We have focused on how this affects satellites. We were receiving data on space radiation and at the same time we were receiving information about the satellite. Our goal is to make recommendations for operators of such satellites on what to do in a certain situation. In case of a very strong surge of space radiation, it may be reasonable to put the satellite into the sleep mode, that is, not to interact with it - not to cause breakdowns," the scientist said, adding it was important to find how to "prolong the life" of such satellites.
An octopus in space
On board the satellite was an art object, an octopus, - Octo-Pax by artist Nastya Miro. This is a figurine of about ten by ten centimeters, made of a domestic metal powder composition. It was in a separate cube chamber inside the satellite. Inside the chamber was also a camera facing the art object.
The octopus, according to calculations, burned down along with the satellite. The art object ended the journey the way the artist had intended it to happen: it did not stay in orbit. Entering the atmosphere, the figure traveled the same path as the spacecraft. "This fate fits deeply the project's idea. Octo-Pax was holding in its tentacles debris that is common for the orbit, and symbolized the space's cleanup from debris. The art object did not become part of this debris, as it dissolved into the atmosphere, without leaving anything behind over there - outside the Earth," the university said.
The ArcticSat-1 satellite burned down in dense layers of the atmosphere. It had worked in orbit for about a year and a half. Scientists will be processing the data obtained by it for about a year.

S. Korea's job growth stays in 100,000 range for 3rd month in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
15:43:48 CST
16:43:48 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's job growth stayed in the 100,000 range for a third straight month, driven by a turnaround in the manufacturing industry in over two years, statistical ministry data showed Friday.
The number of employed people aged 15 and older gained 113,000, or 0.4 percent, from a year earlier to 29,266,000 in September, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
After hitting a decrease of 40,000 jobs in May, employment rebounded in June with an increase of 63,000 before surpassing the 100,000 threshold in July, August and September.
The overall employment rate for those aged 15 and older slipped 0.2 percentage points year on year to 63.5 percent in September, but the OECD-standard hiring rate for those aged 15-64 rose 0.2 percentage points to 70.6 percent.
Employment among manufacturers mounted 16,000 in September on a yearly basis, marking the first rebound since June 2024.
Jobs lost in the construction industry reached 48,000 last month, extending the losing streak to 29 months.
The accommodation and food services sector, a key indicator of domestic consumption, saw a drop of 97,000 jobs, keeping a downward trajectory for two consecutive months.
The losses were offset by strong hiring in the health and social welfare service, the transport and warehousing, and the finance and insurance industries, which recorded job increases of 207,000, 54,000 and 32,000 each.
The cold spell for youth labor was prolonged. The number of employed people aged 15-29 plummeted 147,000 in September from a year earlier, continuing to go down for 47 straight months.
The youth employment rate tumbled 1.1 percentage points to 44 percent, falling for 29 months in a row.
The elderly population compensated for the slack in youth hiring. The number of jobs for those aged 60 and older surged 172,000, while the figures for those in their 30s and 50s swelled 81,000 and 48,000 each.
The number of unemployed people totaled 600,000 in September, down 34,000 from a year earlier. The unemployment rate dipped 0.1 percentage points to 2 percent.
The expanded jobless rate, called the labor underutilization indicator, shrank 0.6 percentage points to 7.3 percent, while the corresponding rate for those aged 15-29 added 0.5 percentage points to 15.6 percent.
The economically inactive population, who had no willingness to seek a job and remained unemployed, rose 179,000 from a year earlier to 16,188,000 in September.
The reading for discouraged jobseekers dwindled 1,000 to 368,000 last month.
The number of the "take-a-rest" group, who replied that they took a rest during a job survey period, reduced 25,000 to 2,497,000 in the cited month. ■

Minister for Aged Care and Seniors Sam Rae said in a statement on Friday that Australia will establish its first Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner from July 2027, after legislation passed the federal parliament with bipartisan support on Thursday.
Rae said the new commissioner will work directly with regulatory systems that oversee the aged care sector to communicate feedback and priorities from Indigenous elders and inform government decisions.
"Every older Australian deserves care that sees them, knows them and treats them with respect," he said.
"The establishment of Australia's first permanent Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Aged Care Commissioner will give an independent voice to First Nations peoples and deliver better outcomes for them and their communities."
The federal government's landmark Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety, which handed down its final report in 2021, found that the system failed to provide culturally safe care for Indigenous Australians and made several recommendations for reform, including a dedicated commissioner.
Rae said that the commissioner will be appointed following consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organizations and advocates. ■

Police Raid Sofia and Burgas Neighborhoods Ahead of Bulgaria’s Elections
Bulgaria’s Interior Ministry launched coordinated police operations in Sofia, Burgas and Aytos on Friday to combat vote-buying ahead of the October 25 elections, with officers also uncovering a laboratory producing synthetic drugs at a private residence in Burgas.
The operations began early in the morning in Sofia’s Hristo Botev neighborhood, Burgas’ Pobeda district and the town of Aytos. Police are checking locations where they have received information about people suspected of involvement in election-related offenses.
“The goal is singular: to ensure a fair vote and allow citizens to cast their ballots freely and without interference on election day,” Chief Inspector Ivaylo Indzhov, head of the Security Police unit at the First District Police Department in Burgas, said.
In Sofia’s Hristo Botev neighborhood, which is predominantly inhabited by Roma people, police teams have been deployed at the entrances and exits of the area. An operation was also conducted near School No. 94 on Friday morning.
Police reported that approximately 50 addresses had been inspected, warning protocols were being issued and citations had been handed out under the Civil Registration Act. Officers also located one person wanted by the authorities.
The operations are being carried out jointly with teams from the General Directorate of Gendarmerie and Counter-Terrorism. Authorities are also taking measures to ensure voting machines, ballots and election documents can be transported to polling stations without disruption.
In Burgas, no vote-buying-related arrests had been made at the time of the report. However, three people were detained for possessing narcotics, Indzhov said.
Police patrols and gendarmerie units have been positioned at the entrances and exits of the Pobeda district, while officers are checking residential addresses and commercial premises. A search of one private home uncovered a laboratory for manufacturing synthetic drugs.
Indzhov said the police operations would continue through the end of election day on October 25, with a larger law enforcement presence planned on the day of the vote, particularly in neighborhoods with predominantly Roma populations.

Syria's 2013 Baniyas massacres: What happened and who was Ali Kayali?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:42:31 UTC
16:42:31 KST

The arrest on Thursday of Ali Kayali, better known as Mihrac Ural, has renewed attention to the 2013 massacres in the village of al-Bayda and the Ras al-Nabaa neighbourhood of Baniyas, both in Syria’s western Tartus Governorate.
They involved mass killings and summary executions of hundreds of civilians, including women and children, during the tenure of ousted Syrian regime leader Bashar al Assad, who led the country from 2000 until late 2024.
The Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) said the General Intelligence Directorate had arrested Kayali while he was attempting to flee across the border, describing him as the “main suspect” in the Baniyas massacres.
Videos circulated online showed mosques in Al-Bayda broadcasting chants of “Allahu Akbar,” with those sharing the footage saying residents were celebrating news of his arrest.
The massacres took place on May 2 and 3 2013, when Assad regime forces and allied armed groups carried out military operations in Al-Bayda and the Ras al-Nabaa neighbourhood of Baniyas that included summary executions and mass killings of civilians.
The massacres
According to an August 2013 report by the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Syria, regime forces surrounded Al-Bayda on May 2, closed access routes and shelled the town before entering alongside members of the National Defence Forces.
The commission documented arrests and summary executions of civilians as well as dozens of bodies found inside homes and in the streets. Some had been burned, while others bore signs of having been beaten with blunt objects.
The following day, the operation extended to Ras al-Nabaa, where attacking forces surrounded the area, prevented residents from leaving through the main roads, shelled the neighbourhood and then entered it. Families, including children, were among those executed.
The UN commission found that the two operations were linked and said there was no indication of armed opposition activity in either area during the killings.
It estimated that between 150 and 250 civilians were killed in Al-Bayda and between 150 and 200 in Ras al-Nabaa.
The UN investigation concluded that Assad regime forces and allied armed groups, including the National Defence Forces, were responsible for killings amounting to war crimes.
Kayali’s role
During the Syrian uprising, Kayali led an armed group known as the Syrian Resistance, which fought alongside Assad regime forces and took part in military operations in several parts of the country.
Syrian authorities linked Kayali and his group to the Al-Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa massacres and announced his arrest more than 13 years after the killings.
On October 4, Syria’s Interior Ministry announced the arrest of Jamal Trabelsi, Kayali’s deputy.
The ministry said Trabelsi had participated in combat operations in support of the former regime, including the Al-Bayda and Ras al-Nabaa massacres, as well as fighting in the countryside of Hama, Idlib and Aleppo.
Kayali’s arrest came 11 days after his deputy was detained, marking a new development in efforts to pursue those accused of violations committed during the former regime’s rule.
In May, residents of Baniyas and its countryside marked the anniversary of the massacres, demanding accountability for those responsible and answers about the fate of missing people.

Suspected arson in Amsterdam evacuates 55 homes, man arrested
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
A 26-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of arson after a fire broke out in an underground parking garage overnight Friday.
The parking garage is located on Theodoor van Hoytemastraat in Amsterdam Nieuw-West, where some 55 homes above it had to be evacuated.
The local safety authority, which coordinates emergency services, said the building sustained significant damage and that the apartments are currently uninhabitable. Power to the area has also temporarily been shut off.
Police are looking into the possibility that the incident stemmed from a personal conflict. The suspect was arrested early Friday morning.
One person at the scene went to hospital of their own accord, but no other injuries were reported. Five cars caught fire in the blaze, and the car park sustained heavy smoke and structural damage.
Residents were put up in a nearby hotel. As of Friday morning, they were still unable to return home pending a damage assessment. Authorities say the building’s electrical and sewage systems were also damaged.
Some surrounding homes and businesses have also been left without electricity.
Police are asking anyone who may have witnessed the incident between 2-3am to contact the investigation tip line at 0800-6070.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Major electrical equipment makers are benefiting from rising electricity demand driven by AI development, CTEE reported Friday.

Institutional investors expect Fortune Electric, Shihlin Electric & Engineering Corp., Chung-Hsin Electric and Machinery Manufacturing Corp., and Allis Electric Co. to post higher fourth-quarter revenue than a year earlier. Full-year revenue and profit are also forecast to reach record highs.
The companies are benefiting from semiconductor factory construction, capacity expansions, and AI data center development. They are also receiving orders related to Taiwan Power Co.’s grid resilience program, which aims to shift Taiwan from a centralized power grid to a more distributed system to reduce the risk of widespread outages, according to Stockfeel.
Order backlogs extend at least through 2029. The companies are already securing orders for delivery in 2030.
Shihlin, Chung-Hsin, and Allis reported record revenue for September and the first three quarters. Fortune Electric’s revenue recovered in August and September as a US shortage of railcars that had disrupted its transformer exports gradually eased, pushing its first-three-quarter revenue to a record high.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taipei residents rate public transport in the capital as the best in the world, according to Time Out Worldwide.
The London-based media group said it quizzed 24,000 residents across the world to rate their hometown’s public transportation network on a scale of one to five. Taipei received the accolades of “good” and “amazing” from 95% of locals, Time Out said.
Singapore ranked second with 93.5%, followed by Hong Kong, Edinburgh, and Seoul. Taipei’s Mass Rapid Transit network won praise for its spotlessly clean stations, the way lines are painted on the platform to show where passengers should line up, and the punctuality of trains.
Time Out also pointed out the scale of the system, with more than 767 million passengers last year, or an average of 2.1 million per day. The network’s EasyCard also gives access to buses and to the use of YouBikes, while allowing travelers to purchase items at convenience stores, Time Out noted.

US, Israel aggression severely damaged regional ecosystems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:39:32 UTC
16:39:32 KST

Addressing the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17), held in the Armenian capital of Yerevan on Friday, Pezeshkian emphasized that US and Israel waged an unprovoked war of aggression against the Iranian nation which produced adverse effects on the ecosystem of the regional countries.
Condemning the destructive impact of wars of aggression on nature, Iranian President Pezeshkian termed it "ecocide," or environmental genocide, stating that preserving biodiversity can be important arenas for peace diplomacy.
Iranian president called for stronger international mechanisms to assess and repair environmental damage caused by armed conflict, warning that war threatens biodiversity far beyond national borders.
Turning to the Israeli massacre of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, he stressed, “Gaza stands as a stark testament to ecocide, with devastation whose horrific impacts will endure for generations.”
President Pezeshkian warned that war caused lasting environmental devastation, citing that Gaza's contaminated soil as proof that ecological damage crosses borders and requires international intervention.
Nations subjected to illegal sanctions and foreign-imposed wars must not be forced to pay the heavy toll of these crises, Pezeshkian warned.
Protecting biodiversity can be an important arena for peace diplomacy, he said, stressing, “Not only war is merely a threat to humans and infrastructure, but also as a direct cause of the destruction of nature.”
War burns forests, destroys wetlands, pollutes soil and water, and displaces animal species, he underlined.
“We believe that biodiversity conservation can serve as a significant arena for "peace diplomacy." In a region grappling with security crises stemming from the illegal and expansionist presence of powers, as well as climate change, water scarcity, and ecosystem degradation, environmental cooperation can build bridges between nations, the bridges that pave the way for peace and security for all, peace with nature, and a future lived in harmony with the natural world.”
Pezeshkian described the environmental devastation caused by the wars in the region, including in Gaza, as “ecocide” that must be condemned, adding that pollution and ecological damage transcend national borders.
He then called on the international community to ensure that nature is not treated as a “silent and defenseless victim” of war. He said international agencies and relevant institutions should strengthen mechanisms for assessing environmental damage, mobilizing financial resources, restoring damaged ecosystems and supporting countries affected by the environmental consequences of armed conflicts.
Highlighting Iran’s biodiversity, which spans the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests, the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Sea of Oman and Caspian Sea, Pezeshkian said nature conservation is part of the country’s cultural and civilizational heritage. He noted that Iran has adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan, designated its Department of Environment as the national coordinating body, and prioritized the protection of endangered species and the expansion of protected areas.
The president also stressed that developing countries need fair access to financial resources, modern technologies, scientific knowledge and capacity-building opportunities to meet their environmental commitments.
He said countries facing economic sanctions or military aggression should not be left to bear alone the environmental costs of sanctions or wars they did not initiate. Without adequate funding and equitable technology transfer, he warned, global biodiversity targets would remain little more than declarations and negotiations.
“What has happened in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ‘ecocide or environmental genocide,’ which must be condemned,” he said.
Pezeshkian also pointed to the combined effects of climate change, drought, water scarcity, desertification, economic sanctions and restricted access to technology and financial resources on Iran’s environmental protection efforts.
He said Iran has been targeted by criminal wars for two consecutive years, involving the extensive use of destructive and prohibited weapons, with attacks in many cases deliberately aimed at damaging the environment, including strikes on fuel storage facilities in the capital.
The president called for genuine international cooperation to help Iran implement environmental programs and compensate for the damage inflicted.
He said Iran’s diverse ecosystems, species and genetic resources formed a natural and cultural heritage shaped by millions of years of evolution over time. From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman and Caspian Sea, these resources underpin the country’s resilience and sustainable development, he said.
President Pezeshkian said Iran had adopted a national biodiversity strategy and action plan and designated the Department of Environment as its national coordinator. Priorities include expanding protected areas to 28 percent, monitoring key species, developing wildlife rehabilitation centers and implementing action plans for 25 vertebrate species. National task forces have been established for species including the Asiatic cheetah and Persian fallow deer, he said.
Turning to armed conflict, President Pezeshkian said war burns forests, damages wetlands, contaminates soil and water, destroys habitats and introduces pollutants and heavy metals into natural systems. Such harm can persist for years after fighting ends and affect the security and well-being of future generations.
He said the United States and the Israeli regime are causing environmental damage through military operations in the region, citing damage to industrial and energy facilities, fires, pollution and harm to protective infrastructure. He said environmental impacts crossed political borders and required solutions.
Referring to Gaza, he warned that damage to soil and ecological systems could endure for generations and described the destruction as ecocide, which he emphasized should be condemned.
President Pezeshkian also highlighted the challenges facing countries dealing with climate change, drought, water scarcity and desertification while facing economic sanctions and limited access to finance and technology. Biodiversity commitments, he said, would remain on paper without adequate funding, fair access to technology and capacity-building.
He called on United Nations agencies, international financial institutions and environmental and sustainable-development bodies to strengthen funding mechanisms, assess environmental damage, restore affected ecosystems and support countries dealing with the consequences of armed conflict. Countries under sanctions or subjected to military aggression should not be left to bear these costs alone, he said.
Pezeshkian said Iran’s commitment to biodiversity protection is rooted not only in its international obligations but also in its longstanding cultural and civilizational heritage.
He noted that Iran is a country with an ancient tradition of living in harmony with nature and has a remarkable diversity of ecosystems, species and genetic resources.
From the Hyrcanian and Arasbaran forests to the Zagros Mountains, deserts and the coasts of the Persian Gulf, the Sea of Oman and the Caspian Sea, Iran’s natural wealth provides a foundation for water and food security, public health, resilience to natural hazards and sustainable development, he said.
Respect for nature, Pezeshkian added, has long been part of Iranian cultural, religious and ritual identity. Traditional agriculture, animal husbandry, the use of medicinal plants and indigenous knowledge have also developed through centuries of interaction with the natural environment.
Protecting biodiversity, he added, could become an important arena for peace diplomacy, with environmental cooperation serving as a bridge between nations and helping advance peace with nature and a safer future for coming generations.
Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to share its scientific expertise, academic capabilities and experience with other countries, describing biodiversity conservation as an important avenue for “peace diplomacy.”
Cooperation could help bridge divides between nations and contribute to peace and security, coexistence with nature, and the well-being of present and future generations, he concluded.

Chicken satay brings the flavors of Malaysian street food to the buffet. The grilled skewers are served with cucumber, red onion, and peanut sauce, pairing lightly smoky chicken with a creamy dip.
For a different take on coconut-rich flavors, Malaysian curry noodles are served in a fragrant, coconut milk-based broth with a rich blend of spices and a hint of heat from sambal. Topped with chicken breast, fish balls, and fried potatoes, the dish is finished with calamansi juice for a refreshing citrus kick.
The dessert station offers a distinctly Malaysian treat with colorful layers of shaved ice, red beans, attap seeds, grass jelly, and creamed corn. Malaysian brand D Masking’s Musang King durian ice cream adds a rich, fragrant finish to the refreshing combination.
Iced Milo brings another familiar taste of Malaysia. Diners can also add Milo powder and ice cream at the dessert station to create local-style variations.
