TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Health and Welfare Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) warned Friday that the TPP’s proposed healthcare premium exemptions for people ages 65 and older would shift costs to younger generations.
The TPP legislative caucus proposal would exempt individuals from paying health care premiums if they are exempt from individual income tax or have an individual income tax rate below 20% in the previous year, per UP Media. The party said disparities in healthcare subsidies for older adults prompted it to take action.
During a livestream Thursday night, the TPP caucus said the proposal would benefit both people ages 65 and older and their adult children, who are responsible for caring for their aging parents and raising their young. The party estimated that about 90% of people ages 65 and older fall below the 20% individual income tax bracket.
Shih said the proposal would shift costs to people ages 15 to 64, per Liberty Times. Depending on whether the additional costs are passed on to individuals or households, he estimated that annual health care premiums could increase by NT$3,000 (US$92.47) per person or NT$8,000 per household,.
Shih called for a return to the healthcare system’s founding principle: “From each according to their ability, to each according to their needs.”
KMT legislative caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) backed the TPP’s proposal, arguing that if only older residents in special municipalities received healthcare premium exemptions as a benefit, residents elsewhere would be unfairly disadvantaged, per UDN. He called for equal treatment across the country.
The DPP opposed a similar proposal in 2024. At the time, then DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Wu Szu-yao (吳思瑤) said the measure could increase the financial burden on younger generations and questioned its legitimacy, per Rti.
However, the party’s position appeared to soften. DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) welcomed proposals to improve care for older adults but cautioned against making promises without identifying funding sources, per CNA.
He urged opposition parties to consult with the executive branch before introducing policy proposals, citing potential separation-of-powers concerns.

Beaten to Death? Police Investigate Murder of 83-Year-Old Man at Sofia Metro Station
An 83-year-old man has died in hospital after being found in a coma with multiple injuries inside an elevator at Sofia’s Joliot-Curie metro station, bTV reported, citing the Interior Ministry.
Emergency services received a report of a person in distress at around 1:30 PM on October 15. Medical teams found the elderly man in critical condition, suffering from multiple injuries and severe craniocerebral trauma.
He was stabilized and taken to St. Anna Hospital in Sofia, where he later died despite medical staff's efforts. The possibility that he had been beaten has not been ruled out, according to unofficial information.
A day after the incident, no arrests had been reported and no official information about suspects had been released. Pretrial proceedings have been launched on suspicion of murder, but the circumstances of the attack and the identity of the perpetrator remain unknown. Authorities have not publicly disclosed a possible motive.
Nikolay Naydenov, executive director of Sofia Metro operator Metropolitan, told bTV that the incident did not involve the operational safety of the metro system, but instead reflected conditions in the surrounding infrastructure and society.
“The metro is safe - there are no incidents related to operational safety. Incidents linked to the surrounding infrastructure reflect the current state of our society. We are grateful that citizens raised the alarm and called our staff,” Naydenov said.
He explained that metro employees cannot be expected to detect a crime in real time when it takes place in areas surrounding the metro system. Naydenov confirmed that video surveillance cameras cover the area and expressed confidence that the Interior Ministry would identify those responsible.
He also stressed the importance of witnesses reporting suspicious incidents, noting that members of the public alerted authorities to the man’s condition, prompting metro staff and medical teams to respond.
“I urge anyone who notices something amiss, and has a phone in hand, to call 112,” Naydenov said.

Carnival Cruises axes half of Australian fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:38:12 UTC
16:38:12 KST

In short:
Carnival Cruises will drop two of the four cruise ships in its Australian fleet.
All other major cruise lines have pulled their full-time Australian ships.
Australia is a hard market for cruises to stay profitable, according to an industry expert.
Carnival Cruises has announced it will remove two of its four Australian cruise ships from March 2028, despite more than 1.4 million Australians going on a cruise last year.
Carnival, which is the only major cruise company operating full-time in Australia, announced it was pulling the Carnival Adventure and the Carnival Luminosa.
Other major cruise operators such as Disney and Royal Caribbean no longer operate full-time in Australia.
Carnival said ship schedules were considered years in advance and it was considering "long-term certainty and globally competitive operating conditions to support itinerary planning and investment".
The decision was an economic one, according to Chris Frame, a maritime historian.
"Australia is an end-of-the-line destination, and it's a huge investment."
Mr Frame said higher levels of regulation, such as tough biosecurity rules, and little cruise infrastructure made it hard for cruises to stay profitable in Australia.
"Berthing fees are higher than other markets, refuelling is higher and provisioning the ship with food is higher, as you just don't have the economies of scale."
He said that for the company, the ships were assets and "they can always be redeployed somewhere else more profitable".
New changes to cruise laws
The moves comes after a decades-old temporary exemption, allowing cruise ships to circumvent Australian labour laws, was extended earlier this month, but with new protections added for workers for the first time.
Earlier this year, an ABC News investigation revealed that workers had accused the company of 12-hour work days for seven days a week, medical neglect, not providing safe drinking water and wages less than $3 an hour. Carnival denied the allegations.
Carnival's country manager Peter Little said in a statement the company had "greater exposure to changes in local market and operating conditions" than other cruise lines. Carnival did not respond to requests for comment.
However, Jake Field of the Maritime Union of Australia claimed this was the third time Carnival had threatened to withdraw from Australia, and that it was a negotiating tactic.
"There are 80 cruise vessels that are scheduled to come to Australia, only four of them don't have collective agreements with their crews, and those are the four Carnival ships," he said.
"We'll still be surrounded by water, and be an international cruise destination. Those 80 other cruise ships will still be coming here."

South Korea reviewing plan to expand Gulf operations, deploy additional maritime patrol aircraft: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:37:50 UTC
16:37:50 KST

Saadet Gokce
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
South Korea is reviewing plans to expand the operational area of one of its naval units operating around Somalia to the Gulf of Oman and deploy an additional maritime patrol aircraft amid increased shipping concerns, JoongAng daily reported Friday.
The Cheonghae Unit has operated in the Gulf of Aden off Somalia since 2009, escorting South Korean vessels and protecting them from piracy.
The proposed expansion would require adding a clause to the unit's deployment consent motion to cover other waters during emergencies involving South Korean nationals.
The government is also considering deploying a long-range maritime surveillance aircraft, potentially a P-8A Poseidon.
The Cheonghae Unit currently consists of one 4,400-ton-class destroyer, one maritime operations helicopter, up to three rigid-hull inflatable boats, and up to 320 service members.
South Korea’s Defense Ministry denied that the review to expand the unit's operational range was a response to a US request for troop deployment, saying it was considering submitting an extension motion before the current deployment authorization expires. It added that no details had been finalized.
There was no immediate official confirmation from Seoul on the issue.
The Gulf of Oman links the Strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea.
The discussions come as Seoul weighs possible contributions to efforts to ensure safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz amid pressure from Washington.
The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial energy corridor for South Korea, while the conflict involving Iran and increased activity by Yemen’s Houthi group around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait have raised concerns over shipping and crude supplies.

In the Dnipropetrovsk region, three police officers are suspected of a robbery attack on a resident of Nikopol, during which they seized his cryptocurrency and cash worth more than $68,000. Under the procedural guidance of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor's Office, three police officers were notified of suspicion of a robbery attack on a resident of Nikopol. According to the investigation, they seized his cryptocurrency and cash worth a total of more than $68,000
The suspects include the deputy head of one of the police departments, the deputy head of the Department for Combating Drug-Related Crime of the regional Main Directorate of the National Police, and an operative of that department.

On the night of June 18, 2026, two of the suspects attacked him in the middle of the street, while the third coordinated their actions. They knocked the victim to the ground, used tear gas, fired several shots at him with a traumatic weapon, handcuffed him, and beat him.
Threatening him with a pistol, the attackers forced the man to transfer cryptocurrency worth $51,000 to a prepared wallet. After that, he was supposed to call his mother and demand that she hand over all the family's savings. Fearing for her son's life, the woman gave them more than $17,000.
After taking the money, the suspects threatened to kill the man if he contacted the police or a hospital. According to the investigation, they divided the money among themselves
The police officers' actions were classified under Part 4 of Article 187 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine — robbery committed by a group of persons acting pursuant to a prior conspiracy during martial law. On October 14, the court ordered pretrial detention for all three, with the right to post bail — UAH 3 million for each.
The pretrial investigation is ongoing. Other individuals who may have been involved in the crime are being identified.

US missile defence shortages could last until 2030, ousted general warned: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:36:45 UTC
16:36:45 KST

Ousted US Army Chief of Staff General Randy George warned months before the US-Israeli war against Iran that American missile defence stockpiles were critically low and could take until 2030 to recover, CBS News reported on Thursday, citing US officials familiar with his assessment.
George raised the warning in late December, two months before the conflict began. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed him from his post in April as the war was under way.
The assessment, included in the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 force allocation planning, identified shortages of Terminal High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) interceptors and Patriot missiles, with supplies expected to remain at strategically low levels until 2030.
Officials attributed the shortfall to weapons transfers to Ukraine, US military support for Israel and limited defence industry production capacity, according to the report.
War further strains supplies
The conflict with Iran has added pressure on US stockpiles. A Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimate found that US forces entered 2026 with about 2,300 Patriot interceptors and used between 1,050 and 1,430 of them during the conflict.
The US had about 355 THAAD interceptors before the war, of which an estimated 190 to 290 were expended, according to the estimates.
Mark Cancian, a retired Marine colonel and senior adviser at CSIS, told CBS News that the systems would be crucial in a potential conflict with China.
“Air defence, missile defence, that will be huge,” he said, explaining that a major confrontation with Beijing would require substantial interceptor supplies.
Replenishing the stockpiles could take years. CSIS estimates that new THAAD interceptor contracts take more than four years to fulfil, while Patriot PAC-3 orders take an average of three and a half years.
Pentagon denies shortage
The Pentagon rejected claims that US forces face a shortage of munitions.
“Claims of US munitions shortages are false,” chief spokesperson Sean Parnell told CBS News.
He added that Washington retained “everything required to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing”.

MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Air defenses shot down 644 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry said in a statement.
A civilian was injured in the Rostov Region, where falling drone debris also damaged production and storage facilities.
TASS has gathered the key information about the consequences of the attacks.
Scale of attacks
- On-duty air defenses intercepted and destroyed 644 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions from 8:00 p.m. Moscow time on October 15 to 8:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 16 (5:00 p.m. - 5:00 a.m. GMT), the Defense Ministry said.
- According to the ministry, the drones were shot down over the Bryansk, Vologda, Volgograd, Voronezh, Vladimir, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Nizhny Novgorod, Novgorod, Orenburg, Oryol, Pskov, Rostov, Ryazan, Samara, Saratov, Smolensk, Tambov, Tver, Tula, Ulyanovsk, Moscow, Leningrad, Krasnodar and Tatarstan regions, as well as Crimea and the Black Sea.
- Air defenses downed another 15 drones heading for Moscow, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on the Max social media platform.
- Earlier, Sobyanin said that 37 drones had been shot down shortly before midnight.
- A total of 57 drones flying toward Moscow have been shot down since midnight, according to TASS calculations based on data from Sobyanin.
- About 50 UAVs and projectiles were destroyed in Russia’s southern Rostov Region overnight, Governor Yury Slyusar said.
- According to him the city of Bataisk and nine districts came under attack.
- Air defenses shot down 27 Ukrainian drones over the central Kaluga Region, Governor Vladislav Shapsha wrote on Max.
- Another 15 Ukrainian drones were downed over the central Tula Region, Governor Dmitry Milyayev said.
- Earlier, he said that ten UAVs had been destroyed.
- Air defenses downed 12 Ukrainian drones over the western Smolensk Region last night, Governor Vasily Anokhin said.
- Ten Ukrainian UAVs were destroyed over the Voronezh Region in southwestern Russia, Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max.
- Eight drones were shot down over the central Yaroslavl Region, Governor Mikhail Yevrayev said on Max.
- An attack involving three drones was repelled in the northwestern Novgorod Region, Governor Alexander Dronov said.
Consequences
- A man was injured in a drone strike in the Aksaisky District of the Rostov Region, Governor Slyusar said.
- The man has been taken to the hospital.
- Falling drone debris damaged production and storage facilities in the Aksaisky District.
- A fire broke out but it has now been extinguished.
- The windows of two private houses were damaged in the Kuibyshevsky District.
- There were no casualties.
- Falling drone fragments damaged several windows and balconies in an apartment building, as well as a car, in a municipality in the Voronezh Region, Governor Gusev said.
- The windows of three private houses were damaged in another municipality.
- Emergency response teams are working at the sites where drone debris fell.
- The central Vladimir Region came under attack overnight, including an attempted strike on heating infrastructure in the regional capital, Governor Alexander Avdeyev said.
- According to him, minor damage was reported but there were no casualties.

Deutsch-Französische Einigung zu „Made in Europe“ und Autoabgasen verzögert sich – SPD erhebt Einwände
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:35:00 UTC
16:35:00 KST

Deutsch-Französische Einigung zu „Made in Europe“ und Autoabgasen verzögert sich – SPD erhebt Einwände
Der Vertragsentwurf sieht strengere Zulassungsbedingungen für Nicht-EU-Länder hinsichtlich der Teilnahme an öffentlichen Ausschreibungen und der Inanspruchnahme öffentlicher Fördermittel vor und mildert das Verbot von Verbrennungsmotoren ab dem Jahr 2035 ab.
Der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron auf dem internationalen Pariser Autosalon an der Porte de Versailles in Paris am 12. Oktober 2026. | Poolfoto von Thibault Camus/AFP via Getty Images
BRÜSSEL — Frankreich und Deutschland konnten sich am Donnerstag nicht auf einen gemeinsamen Standpunkt zum Geltungsbereich der künftigen „Made in Europe“-Vorschriften der Union sowie zu größerer Flexibilität bei der Reduzierung der CO2-Emissionen und zum Verbot von Verbrennungsmotoren ab 2035 einigen.
Der Entwurf des Gegenseitigkeitsabkommens, über den POLITICO erstmals im Juli berichtet hatte, stellt eine bedeutende Annäherung zwischen den beiden Ländern dar und sollte eigentlich in Kürze unterzeichnet werden. Am Donnerstagabend geriet das Abkommen jedoch ins Stocken, da der Koalitionspartner SPD Einwände erhob. Befürchtet wurde, dass wichtige Umweltziele gestrichen worden seien.
„Eine endgültige Einigung steht noch aus“, erklärte ein Sprecher der deutschen Bundesregierung.
Advertisement
Anfang dieser Woche hatte der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron angedeutet, dass nun Deutschland am Zug sei. „Auf der anderen Seite des Rheins gibt es politische Zwänge, und ich respektiere die Koalitionsgespräche voll und ganz“, sagte Macron am Montag am Rande des Pariser Autosalons.
Gemäß den Bedingungen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens würde Deutschland strengere „Made in Europe“-Kriterien für den Automobilsektor im „Industrial Accelerator Act“ akzeptieren, auf die Frankreich gedrängt hat, im Gegenzug für eine Abschwächung des Verbots von Verbrennungsmotoren, einer der langfristigen Forderungen Berlins.
„Angesichts der erheblichen technologischen, wirtschaftlichen und geopolitischen Veränderungen seit der Einführung des bestehenden Rechtsrahmens sollte das Automobilpaket ein besseres Gleichgewicht zwischen Klimazielen, industrieller Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, technologischer Entwicklung und der Stärkung der europäischen Wertschöpfung herstellen“, schrieben die beiden Länder in einem POLITICO vorliegenden Vertragsentwurf.
„Auf der Grundlage der deutsch-französischen Ministerräte in den Jahren 2025 und 2026 schlagen Deutschland und Frankreich daher ein ausgewogenes Verhandlungspaket vor, das ehrgeizige CO2-Reduktionsziele mit zusätzlicher Flexibilität und gezielten Anreizen für die europäische Wertschöpfung verbindet“, heißt es in der Vereinbarung weiter.
Derzeit sieht das Ziel der EU vor, dass Unternehmen die Emissionen von Verbrennungsmotoren bis 2035 um 100 Prozent gegenüber dem Niveau von 2021 senken, wobei sie die Möglichkeit haben, sich durch Initiativen wie Ausgleichsmaßnahmen und Investitionen einen Spielraum von 10 Prozent bei den Emissionen zu „erwerben“.
Im Rahmen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens wollen Frankreich und Deutschland das Ziel für 2035 auf 90 Prozent absenken und im Gegenzug für Investitionen in alternative Kraftstoffe einen zusätzlichen Spielraum von 10 Prozent einräumen (was insgesamt 80 Prozent ergibt).
Advertisement
Entscheidend für die Stahlhersteller und die linke SPD in Deutschland wäre, dass das deutsch-französische Abkommen die Investitionspflicht für „grünen Stahl“ abschaffen und damit einen wichtigen Anreiz beseitigen würde.
„Das zerstört den Leitmarkt für die Stahlindustrie“, erklärte ein Lobbyist der Branche gegenüber POLITICO unter der Bedingung der Anonymität, um über dieses heikle Thema sprechen zu können. Da der Vertragsentwurf keinen Druck auf die Automobilhersteller ausübe, „grünen Stahl“ zu beziehen, werde dieser dadurch zu einem „nice-to-have“-Extra, erklärte die Person.
Als Zugeständnis an Berlin wird im Vertragsentwurf betont, dass der sogenannte „Utility-Faktor“ – mit dem die Emissionen von Plug-in-Hybridfahrzeugen anhand des Verhältnisses zwischen der Nutzungshäufigkeit des Elektromotors und des Verbrennungsmotors berechnet wird – auf der Grundlage von Laborergebnissen und nicht, wie von der Kommission gefordert, anhand von Daten aus dem realen Fahrbetrieb ermittelt werden sollte. Diese Änderung wird den Automobilherstellern helfen, mehr Plug-in-Hybride zu verkaufen und gleichzeitig die übergeordneten Emissionsziele zu erreichen.
Als Gegenleistung für diese Emissionszugeständnisse schloss sich Deutschland der Forderung Frankreichs an, den Geltungsbereich der „Made in Europe“-Regelungen im Rahmen des „Industrial Accelerator Act“ der EU in Bezug auf den Automobilsektor einzuschränken.
Der Text gilt nur für die 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten und wird unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen auf das Vereinigte Königreich ausgeweitet.
Der EU-Industriekommissar Stéphane Séjourné erklärte am Dienstag gegenüber POLITICO, er unterstütze das Abkommen als Weg aus der Sackgasse, und fügte hinzu, dass das Vereinigte Königreich derzeit die Voraussetzungen für das Label „Made in Europe“ erfülle.
Advertisement
Die Vereinbarung könnte den Stillstand sowohl bei der CO₂-Verordnung als auch beim IAA beenden, bei denen Frankreich und Deutschland bisher auf gegensätzlichen Seiten standen. „Die Bestandteile dieses Gesamtpakets sollten so schnell wie möglich und gleichzeitig verabschiedet werden“, schrieben die beiden Länder.
Die britische Regierung begrüßte die mögliche Einbeziehung des Vereinigten Königreichs in die „Made in Europe“-Vorschriften für Kraftfahrzeuge.
„Dies ist ein deutsch-französischer Vorschlag, und es muss noch ein europäischer Prozess durchlaufen werden, aber sollte er bestätigt werden, begrüßen wir das Ziel, das Vereinigte Königreich in den ‚Industrial Accelerator Act‘ einzubeziehen – das wäre eine gute Nachricht für die britische Automobilindustrie sowie für die Arbeitsplätze und Investitionen, die sie im gesamten Vereinigten Königreich sichert“, erklärte ein Sprecher von Downing Street Nr. 10 in einer Stellungnahme.
Sollte der deutsch-französische Deal unterschrieben werden, muss es noch von den anderen EU-Mitgliedstaaten und vom Europäischen Parlament gebilligt werden, die derzeit über das „Industrial Accelerator Act“ und das Automobilpaket, einschließlich der Emissionsziele für Automobilhersteller, beraten.
Carlo Martuscelli, Francesca Micheletti und Graham Lanktree haben zu diesem Bericht beigetragen.

Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The order was communicated to senior Pentagon officials, although the sources did not identify who authorised it.
Starshield, a military-grade satellite network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX, supports Ukrainian battlefield communications and drone operations. Ukrainian officials reported this week that satellite receivers installed on fast-moving equipment had stopped functioning, disrupting drone strikes against Russian positions and operations to intercept incoming Russian drones.
A Ukrainian Defence Ministry source told Reuters on Thursday that the receivers had resumed working while moving, but only at speeds below 160 kilometres per hour.

The disruption comes amid mounting tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
In an interview with Newsmax aired Thursday, Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of contributing to rising global fuel prices by targeting Russian refineries.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said, arguing that attacks on diesel production facilities threatened supplies needed by the United States and other countries.
Trump also renewed his criticism of Zelenskyy, saying he considered the Ukrainian leader more difficult to negotiate with than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine resumed refinery strikes on Thursday following a three-day pause intended to accommodate Trump's calls for an energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy ended the suspension after Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite a ceasefire announcement made unilaterally by the US president.
The breakdown followed Washington's controversial agreement with Moscow to ease sanctions in exchange for additional Russian diesel supplies. Under the arrangement, Russia is expected to release more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel onto US and international markets.
Zelenskyy has criticised the deal, warning that renewed energy revenues could help finance Russia's continuing invasion. Some US lawmakers have raised similar concerns.
According to sources cited by the The Financial Times, Washington had threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and weapons procurement arrangements unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries.
European leaders have meanwhile reaffirmed their support for Ukraine. Following talks with Zelenskyy, French President Emmanuel Macron said France remained committed to helping Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks and protecting its civilian population and infrastructure.

Live: Jillaroos begin home World Cup against Fetu Samoa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:33:23 UTC
16:33:23 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Australia defeats Fetu Samoa 40-0 in Rugby League World Cup
Australia's quest for a fourth consecutive Women's Rugby League World Cup has started with a bang courtesy of a 40-0 victory over Fetu Samoa.
Unbackable favourites leading into the tournament opener, the Jillaroos overcame an ill-disciplined opening 10 minutes to shut out Samoa in the seven-try rout.
Things were far from easy for Australia in the second half, but the damage was already done by half-time, with five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and reigning Dally M medallist Tamika Upton leading the way with two try assists apiece.
Kelleher, making her Jillaroos debut, was named player of the match, where she was dangerous in attack and her kicking game troubled Samoa.
Speaking to ABC Sport, Kelleher said she had been waiting a long time for her chance to play for the Jillaroos.
"It's a dream come true," she said.
"Was in the squad last year, but got my debut jersey this year. So excited and so happy to be here."
Despite the 40-point win, it was far from a perfect performance from the reigning world champions.
"We still have a lot of things to fix from today. It wasn't perfect out there," Kelleher said.
Samoa, in their first World Cup since 2008, had several chances early but lacked the class to capitalise against their much-fancied opponents.
Gold Coast Titans star Jaime Chapman ended her three-year Jillaroos exodus by scoring Australia's first try in the 11th minute, beating opposite winger Freedom Crichton Ropati out wide.
Australia's greatest ever try-scorer, Julia Robinson, lived up to her reputation seven minutes later when she beat three would-be defenders for her 23rd Jillaroos try in 14 appearances.
Tries to back-rower Shaylee Bent and hooker Keeley Nizza followed in quick succession before lock Olivia Kernick crossed moments before halftime to seal a 28-0 lead at the break.
Kernick turned playmaker in the opening five minutes of the second period when she handed the ball off for Keilee Joseph to extend the Jillaroos' lead.
Brave defence might have turned the tide for Samoa, who ground their way to more opportunities at the Jillaroos end over the final 25 minutes.
Prop Laikha Clarke went the closest to securing some consolation points for Samoa, but was ruled to have dropped the ball over the line.
Of further concern for Samoa was a suspected knee injury in the dying stages to centre Sarina Masaga.
A try in the final two minutes from Australian centre Jessica Sergis capped the Jillaroos' victory and extended their almost three-year unbeaten run.
Samoa's men thrashed France in the opening match of the day, putting on a record score to win 78-4.

Samoa have opened their World Cup campaign by crushing France in a 78-4 win that gives an early boost to the Pacific nation's hopes of reaching the knockout stages.
In a 14-try-to-one victory in which centre Stephen Crichton kicked 11 goals and Melbourne flyer Sua Fa'alogo crossed four times, the Samoans barely worked up a sweat at Western Sydney Stadium in Sydney on Friday.
Taking on a French side mostly made up of Super League players, the star-studded Samoan team raced out to a 28-0 lead inside 20 minutes.
The only blemish for coach Ben Gardiner was the sight of Brisbane winger Deine Mariner going off in the first half with a suspected injury.
And while they had lapses of discipline and concentration with the result sewn up — France scored their sole try through winger Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet — the heavy win will increase Samoa's points differential and their hopes of making it to the semi-finals.
One of Samoa, England or Tonga will miss the knockout stages as a result of the new tournament format, in which the top two teams from across group B and group C make it to the last four.
Samoa face Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby next week before concluding their pool games in an all-Pacific match-up for the ages against the Tongans.
The Kumuls on home soil and Tonga in Sydney will provide a much sterner test than the French, who were left for dead in a blistering opening quarter.
Mariner scored the opening try for the Toa in the third minute soon after his father Lapi had sung the country's national anthem that brought stars including Jarome Luai and Spencer Leniu to tears.
Benaiah Ioelu, Jermaine McEwen, Fa'alogo, and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow all crossed in the next 15 minutes as the French defence was cut to shreds.
Aispuro-Bichet briefly stemmed the bleeding before Fa'alogo went in again just before halftime to make it 34-4 at the break.
The French had little resistance in the second period, with Fa'alogo adding two more while Crichton, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Shawn Blore, Izack Tago, Francis Molo and Ioelu all went over.

1-MIN READ1-MIN
 Listen
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said on Friday he accepts the deployment of US military MV-22 Osprey transport aircraft at the Futenma air station, reversing the southern Japan prefecture’s long-standing opposition to their presence.
Previous prefectural governments, under governors critical of US bases, had opposed the deployment of the tilt-rotor aircraft since before they were first stationed at the base in 2012, citing safety concerns. Koja assumed the post of Okinawa governor late last month.
“More than 10 years have passed since the deployment. Considering that the Self-Defence Forces operate the aircraft, it is not realistic to call for a reversal of their deployment or use,” Koja told reporters at the prefectural government office.
In a break from his predecessors, Koja, who won the gubernatorial election backed by Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s ruling Liberal Democratic Party, supports the plan to relocate US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in densely populated Ginowan to the coastal Henoko area in Nago within Okinawa.

Transfer of Tarkett assets
Putin has signed a decree placing the assets of flooring manufacturer Tarkett under the temporary management of Management Company Center Capital LLC.
According to the document, 100% of shares in the authorized capital of Tarkett Sommer LLC held by Tarkett JSC were placed under temporary management.

The decree by the head of state also placed the Russian assets of Ontex, the company that owns the diaper brand Helen Harper, under the temporary management of Management Company Center Capital LLC.

Helen Harper is one of the brands under which the company sells its products.

Moreover, the presidential decree placed the assets of three foreign packaging companies under the temporary management of Management Company Center Capital LLC.

G7 nations to provide EUR 260 mln for urgent repairs to Chornobyl NPP containment structure following Russian drone attack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:28:25 EEST
16:28:25 KST

The G7 nations will provide EUR 260 million to fund urgent repairs to the New Safe Confinement structure at the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) in Ukraine, which sustained significant damage following a Russian drone strike in February 2025, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Thursday.
“The EBRD is grateful to the G7 nations for their continued leadership and commitment to nuclear safety at Chornobyl. We join the G7 in calling on the wider international community to contribute to these efforts at a donor conference we are convening in Paris on 9 November 2026, co-chaired by France, Ukraine and the EBRD,” EBRD President Odile Renaud-Basso said.
According to a press release, the decision was announced following a meeting of G7 finance ministers held during the autumn meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank in Bangkok. The G7 nations expressed deep concern regarding risks to nuclear safety resulting from the Russian attack, pledged to mobilize funds for the restoration of the containment structure, and called on other international partners to help cover the remaining financial requirements.
Preliminary assessments indicate that at least EUR 500 million will be needed to repair the damage and restore the structure to full functionality. The work needs to be completed by 2030 to limit the risk of corrosion of the steel arch and safeguard the structure’s 100-year design life.
Chornobyl’s New Safe Confinement was severely damaged by a Russian drone strike on 14 February 2025. The attack breached the structure’s inner and outer cladding, damaged critical systems and severely compromised its two primary functions: containing radioactive material and enabling the safe dismantling of the unstable original sarcophagus over Reactor Four.
The EBRD has led global efforts to stabilise and manage risks at Chornobyl since 1995, mobilising over EUR 2.5 billion in international contributions – much of it from the G7 nations – and providing more than EUR 700 million of its own resources to fund nuclear safety and decommissioning projects linked to the site. The Bank is now leading international efforts to restore the full functionality of the New Safe Confinement and to mobilise the remaining funding needed for urgent repairs.

Moscow, St. Petersburg airports halt flights overnight amid drone attacks. Almost 200 flights delayed or canceled.
Rosaviatsiya restricted flights arriving at and departing from Moscow’s Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports starting the evening of October 15.
The restrictions remained in place until early morning on October 16. Almost 160 flights were delayed or canceled, most of them at Vnukovo and Sheremetyevo: 66 and 79, respectively, the Moskva news agency reported.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said air defense forces shot down 94 Ukrainian drones heading toward the Russian capital since the evening.
St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport was also closed, with restrictions lasting until 9 a.m. The St. Petersburg-based news outlet Fontanka reported that 37 departing flights and nine arriving flights were canceled or delayed. Four drones were shot down over the region, according to Leningrad region Governor Alexander Drozdenko.
The Atlantic journalist Simon Shuster wrote the day before, citing sources, that Ukraine’s campaign to paralyze operations at Russian airports is ”just getting started.” On September 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russian skies are “becoming unsafe,” because “drones will start appearing in Russia’s skies in a way that will have to be reckoned with.” According to Shuster, Ukraine has used long-range drones in recent weeks to make the airspace around Russian airports harder to use. Zelensky, however, has not yet approved implementation of the original plan, which called for much more aggressive tactics.
Moscow’s airports suspended operations increasingly often in October. The independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo calculated that the four airports were closed for a combined 101 hours during the first 14 days of the month, compared with just 46 hours for all of September.

"Among the suspects are a deputy head of a police department, a deputy head of the drug-related crime combating department of the Main Directorate of the National Police in the region, and an operative of this department," the report on the Telegram channel states.
According to the investigation, the police officers learned that a local resident possessed a significant amount of cryptocurrency and decided to seize his funds. The victim was knocked to the ground, tear gas was used against him, he was shot several times with a traumatic weapon, handcuffed, and beaten.
Threatening him with a pistol, the attackers forced the man to transfer cryptocurrency worth $51,000 to a prepared wallet. Afterward, he was instructed to call his mother and demand all family savings. Fearing for her son's life, the woman handed over more than $17,000.
Having seized the funds, the suspects threatened to kill the man if he contacted the police or a hospital. According to the investigation, they split the money among themselves.
The actions of the police officers have been qualified under Part 4 of Article 187 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – robbery committed by a prior conspiracy of a group of persons under martial law. On October 14, the court chose pre-trial restraint measures for all three in the form of detention with the right to post bail of UAH 3 million each.
The pre-trial investigation is ongoing to establish other individuals who may be involved in the crime.

'Hope better sense prevails': SC flags traders' livelihood concerns as Delhi braces for CJP's Tiranga march
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:23:19 UTC
16:23:19 KST

SC declines urgent plea against Central Park closure ahead of ’s Tiranga march
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday declined an urgent hearing on a plea challenging the New Delhi Municipal Council's decision to shut Central Park in Connaught Place ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) proposed ‘Lehra do Tiranga’ protest, saying it hoped “better sense will prevail” among all concerned.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi said it was conscious of the difficulties that a closure could cause to small shopkeepers and their families, while observing that the right to protest, the need to maintain law and order and the livelihood of traders were interconnected issues.
“We hope better sense will prevail on everyone. Small shopkeepers earn their livelihood during these days. We know the hardship and difficulty entire families will face,” the bench said.Justice Bagchi said the court could intervene if the restrictions resulted in business losses, adding that it would consider exercising its constitutional jurisdiction if required."If there's loss of business, we will exercise our powers under Constitutional jurisdiction. Let's cross that bridge when it comes," Justice Bagchi said.
During the hearing, the petitioner's lawyer submitted that the NDMC had issued directions late Thursday night to close Central Park, effectively preventing businesses from operating in the area. The civic body had announced that the park would remain closed to the public on October 16 and 17 for administrative reasons.The bench indicated that the plea could be listed on October 26 or 27.
CJP says protest will go ahead
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has called on citizens to gather at Central Park with the national flag at 5 pm on Friday, alleging that party members Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were jailed for unfurling the Tricolour. The party has said it will proceed with the march despite the closure of the park and security restrictions.In a post on X, Dipke defended the party's protests, rejected allegations that it was promoting anarchy and accused the government of restricting democratic rights.
"Businesses do not suffer because of peaceful protests. They suffer when the govt decides to shut down an entire city, suspend internet services and restrict the movement of its own citizens and turn the city into a war-zone.""Since its inception, the Cockroach Janta Party has maintained that we will always follow Mahatma Gandhi’s path of peace and non-violence, and we have stood by that commitment. We have organised protests in Mumbai, Pune, Jaipur, Lucknow, Bengaluru and Nagpur, and every single one of them has been peaceful. I was personally assaulted in Jaipur, but even then, I chose not to retaliate because responding to violence with violence goes against everything we believe in. We would rather exercise the rights guaranteed to us by the Constitution, drafted under the leadership of Dr. BR Ambedkar, than resort to physical force. Our strength comes from our commitment to constitutional values, and no amount of provocation will make us abandon them.""Despite this, there are constant attempts to portray us as anarchists simply because we refuse to remain silent. But demanding answers from the govt is not anarchy, protesting against injustice on the streets is not anarchy, and questioning those who hold public office is certainly not anarchy. These are the most fundamental expressions of democracy. The very party that is in power today spent decades organising protests, taking to the streets and questioning the governments of the day when it was in opposition. Had the same restrictions, intimidation and police crackdowns been used against them, many of those who occupy positions of power today might never have reached where they are. It is deeply hypocritical to celebrate protests as a democratic right when you are in opposition and treat the same act as a threat to public order when you come to power."ALSO READ: ‘No one called Mahatma Gandhi African’: Sanjay Raut slams order against actor Imran Khan"We are not asking for privileges or special treatment. We are simply asking to exercise the rights that belong to every citizen of this Republic, irrespective of which party is in power. So let us fulfil our duty as citizens of this country by questioning those we elect, demanding accountability and speaking up whenever we witness injustice.""A govt that has been elected by the people is bound to listen to the people, not silence them. Democracy does not end once the votes have been counted."
Security tightened ahead of ‘Lehra do Tiranga’ march
The proposed demonstration comes amid a standoff between the CJP and Delhi Police over protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The CJP had announced the march after Das and Ranka were arrested for allegedly entering Jantar Mantar, which had been denotified as a designated protest site, and raising slogans demanding Kumar's resignation. They were subsequently remanded to five days of judicial custody and lodged in Tihar Jail.Dipke has urged political parties and civil society organisations to set aside ideological differences and join the demonstration."I request all political parties and civil society groups to rise above ideology and come together. If the right to vote is not saved, democracy will not be saved," Dipke said at a press conference on Thursday.He also questioned the scale of voter deletions during the SIR exercise and alleged that the revisions could affect electoral outcomes."The margin of victory in 2024 was just 2 per cent. Over 13 crore voters deleted -- around 14 percent," he said."Where 2 per cent is deciding the election, you are deleting 13 crore votes. What is this if not a setting?" he added.The CJP has alleged that the government is shielding Kumar from scrutiny. These allegations have not been established by the court.
Police cite law and order concerns
Delhi Police has said Connaught Place is not a designated site for protests and that demonstrations can be held at Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground after obtaining the requisite permissions."Jantar Mantar has been denotified as a designated protest site. Protesters can hold demonstrations at Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground or CBD Ground after obtaining the requisite permission," a senior police officer said.Security has been tightened around Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar, with several companies of paramilitary personnel stationed in the national capital. Police are deploying personnel at strategic locations, erecting barricades and regulating the movement of protesters and commuters to prevent any untoward incident.The NDMC issued its closure notice on Thursday, stating that Central Park would remain shut on October 16 and 17 for administrative reasons. The decision came a day after the CJP announced its proposed march at the park, located in the centre of Connaught Place's inner circle.The party's agitation began in Mumbai on October 2 and subsequently moved to Delhi. On October 10, a planned demonstration at Jantar Mantar was met with a police crackdown, with Dipke, Das and Ranka detained at the airport after arriving from Mumbai. Opposition leaders, activists and students were also detained during protests in the capital.
On October 13, CJP members entered the barricaded Jantar Mantar site carrying the national flag and were detained.Opposition parties and student organisations have separately held demonstrations against the SIR exercise and demanded accountability from the Election Commission. INDIA bloc MPs marched towards the Election Commission headquarters on October 6 and were stopped by police barricades. Opposition leaders later met President Droupadi Murmu on October 9 to raise their concerns.The CJP has since framed its proposed Connaught Place march as a campaign for voting rights and the constitutional right to protest, setting up another confrontation over the restrictions imposed on demonstrations in central Delhi.

Southern California wildfire prompts evacuations as Bryson Fire grows to 200 acres
Los Angeles County issues evacuation warnings across wide area; officials warn of heightened fire danger due to strong winds
Berk Kutay Gokmen
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
ISTANBUL
A wildfire burning in the hills of Malibu in Southern California grew to about 200 acres (809 decares) by nightfall, prompting evacuation warnings and orders across a wide area as officials warned of heightened fire danger due to strong winds.
The Bryson Fire broke out in the state’s Encinal Canyon area, near the Camp Kilpatrick juvenile detention facility, according to CBS News on Thursday.
Los Angeles County issued evacuation warnings and orders covering areas stretching toward Leo Carrillo State Park, Pepperdine University, and the Pacific coast.
Pepperdine said the blaze was burning about eight miles northwest of its Malibu campus, adding that winds were blowing southwest, away from the university.
“The fire does not currently pose a threat to Pepperdine’s Malibu campus,” the university said on US social media company X.
Camp Kilpatrick evacuated 38 young people from its detention facility, transferring them to Barry J. Nidorf Juvenile Hall in Sylmar.
“We understand that an evacuation can be stressful for youth and their families,” the Los Angeles County Probation Department said, adding that staff were providing support and parents and legal guardians were being notified.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said city officials were closely monitoring developments, although the fire remained outside city limits.
The Los Angeles Fire Department “is prepared to respond to any fire threat that could emerge,” Bass said.
She added that resources had been positioned across several areas, including the San Fernando Valley, Santa Monica Mountains, and West Los Angeles.
Meanwhile, Southern California Edison initiated a public safety power shutoff affecting more than 60,000 residents.
The National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning, citing an expected moderate-to-strong Santa Ana wind event that could increase critical fire danger through Saturday.

Europe's answer to Starlink: Who is building IRIS² and what is Germany's role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:18:59 UTC
16:18:59 KST

Who controls the satellites on which armies rely? Reports of Starlink limits in Ukraine highlight the question. The EU is building IRIS², a 348-satellite network with a Bremen manufacturer.
This week, the Ukrainian army reported restrictions to the Starlink satellite service. The connection drops as soon as the receivers are travelling at more than 160 kilometres per hour, as is the case with drones.
The service was initially partially restored, but an upper limit remained in place. It is unclear who ordered the restriction.
SpaceX boss Elon Musk rejected responsibility that the company ordered the shutdown. Starshield is under the direct control of the US government, he wrote on X.
It is important to distinguish between the two systems: Starlink and Starshield are both developed by SpaceX but aimed at different customers. Starlink is the service for private and business users, Starshield is designed for governments and the military.
Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski reacted sharply on X, writing: "Hey, Elon Musk, you big man, are you once again playing politics with your products? As your European customers we are keeping a close eye on you."
Poland has paid for a large share of the Ukrainian terminals. This has once again raised the question of how dependent armed forces are on satellite links. Europe has therefore been working for some time on its own solution.
The European answer: IRIS²
The EU has been developing IRIS², its own satellite network, for around six years. The acronym stands for "Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite".
In German this roughly means infrastructure for resilience, connectivity and security via satellites. The system is intended to provide secure connections for governments, companies and citizens and to close mobile coverage gaps in Europe and Africa.
For encryption it will rely on quantum technology via the European quantum communication infrastructure EuroQCI.
In early August, the European Commission and the SpaceRISE consortium agree on the implementation. The network will grow to 348 satellites, 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit.
A further 66 additional satellites are intended specifically to strengthen defence, security and emergency services. According to the Commission’s calculations, this will increase secured capacity for public-sector users by 60 percent in the EU and by 54 percent worldwide.
The focus is on states, the military and critical services; later on, private individuals are also to be able to use the network. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029. Initial services are to be introduced gradually from 2029 or 2030.
Germany's role
Germany is represented by the Bremen-based space company Orbitale Hochtechnologie Bremen (OHB).
On 31 August it signed a contract worth just under €1 billion with satellite operator SES for 18 satellites in medium Earth orbit for IRIS².
A single satellite weighs around 2.6 tonnes at launch. OHB chief executive Marco Fuchs sees the programme as an important step towards greater European independence.
Germany’s share of the project sparked disputes early on.
In December 2023, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs sent a strongly worded letter to the companies involved demanding urgent clarification of the German industry’s participation and its share in value creation, as reported by the Frankfurter Rundschau daily.
Bundeswehr: Its own satellite network?
Independently of IRIS², the Bundeswehr is planning its own satellite network. It is a national project financed by the federal government.
Major General Armin Fleischmann, the Bundeswehr’s space commissioner in the Cyber and Information Domain, told regional public broadcaster MDR that the plan is for a constellation similar to Starlink, only smaller.
He told the Handelsblatt business newspaper they wanted to have "flying Fritzboxes" in space. The network is initially to cover NATO’s eastern flank, under national control. Individual components will come from Western partners, including the United States.
As early as September 2025, defence minister Boris Pistorius announced at the space congress of the Federation of German Industries in Berlin that a total of €35 billion would be invested in military space projects by 2030. In July he visited OHB in Bremen to inspect satellite programmes and ongoing production.
The project is called SATCOMBw 4, short for satellite communication of the Bundeswehr. In its final expansion stage, according to the Bundeswehr, it is to comprise a three-digit number of satellites in low Earth orbit and cost between eight and ten billion euros. An initial partial constellation with up to 40 satellites is scheduled to be operational as early as 2029, with full operations planned from 2030.
The joint venture "OHB Rheinmetall Space Networks", based in Bremen, is bidding for the contract According to company information, OHB would be responsible for the satellites, Rheinmetall for the ground stations and end devices. No decision has yet been taken.
Industry reports suggest that the contract award could come around the turn of the year, though insiders consider early 2027 possible as well. OHB would then be involved in both major projects: in IRIS² as satellite manufacturer and in the Bundeswehr network as part of the joint venture.
Up to now, the Bundeswehr has been using two of its own satellites in geostationary orbit at around 36,000 kilometres altitude, COMSATBw-1 and COMSATBw-2, launched in 2009 and 2010.
Their successors are being built by Airbus and are scheduled to be handed over in orbit in 2029. The first of the three German radar satellites SARah was launched in 2022 on a Falcon 9 rocket from SpaceX.
Young Belgian company helping to build Europe’s satellite network
The satellites for IRIS² are being built by several companies. The largest share will not be supplied by an established group but by a young company:
Aerospacelab, founded in 2018 and based in Charleroi in Belgium, is building 264 satellites for low Earth orbit.
The order volume amounts to €2.4 billion, according to the company. The satellites are to be delivered by 2030. They will be produced in a new factory in Charleroi, where up to 500 satellites per year are to be built from 2027.
Airbus is building at least 66 satellites in the first layer for military communication, which are due to be ready in 2029. This means the entire low-orbit segment with 330 satellites has been allocated.
Together with the 18 OHB satellites for medium orbit, the network will comprise 348 satellites.
How realistic is 2029?
Whether the timetable can be met remains an open question. The first satellites are scheduled to launch in 2029; according to media reports, the original plan was for them to go up two years earlier.
Experts view rocket launches as the bottleneck. Even the best satellites cannot reach space without rockets and those unable to launch them themselves remain dependent on others.
Europe is relying on the Ariane 6 launch vehicle, which has been lifting off into space since 2024. Andreas Knopp of the Bundeswehr University Munich points out in the weekly paper Das Parlament that the number of launches is limited, while political scientist Antje Nötzold of TU Chemnitz speaks in MDR of a "launcher problem."
So far this year, Ariane 6 has launched four times, three of those flights carrying satellites for Amazon Leo into orbit, the US company’s satellite internet service that is also intended to compete with Starlink.
Amazon has booked at least 18 Ariane 6 launches. In early August, the Commission named the procurement of launch services for IRIS² as one of the next steps.

Are schools ready to operate during blackouts? The Office of the President's response

Up to 96% of schools are prepared for prolonged power outages. More than 60% have autonomous heating, water, and power for up to 8 hours.
96% of schools across Ukraine are ready to operate autonomously during blackouts amid Russian attacks. This was stated by Deputy Head of the Office of the President Viktor Mykyta on social media, reports UNN.
Are schools ready for blackouts, and what are the plans?
As of today, up to 96% of schools across the country are ready to operate autonomously during prolonged power outages and have the necessary infrastructure and supplies
At the same time, according to him, "we have set ourselves the task of ensuring that educational institutions are ready to operate autonomously for more than 8 hours using alternative power sources." "These locations will serve as centers of resilience in the districts," he said.
Do schools have heating?

Italy data network glitch hits airports: Flights delayed and cancellations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:16:43 UTC
16:16:43 KST

A problem affecting Italy's airport data network caused delays and flight cancellations on Friday morning. Enav says it was not a cyber attack or sabotage.
Disruptions and cancelled flights were reported on Friday morning at many Italian airports due to faults in the data transmission network that supports air traffic control services, the national air navigation service provider Enav has announced.
"From 6:00, in view of the steady increase in air traffic and the persistence of the faults, in order to continue guaranteeing the highest level of operational safety, flow management measures have been introduced, which mean a temporary reduction in the capacity to handle aircraft in Italian airspace", reads the statement issued in the morning, which also rules out any link between the faults and hacker attacks or sabotage.
Enav also said that, although the faults were detected during the night between Thursday and Friday, "normal management of air traffic, without any reduction in operating capacity" was ensured until 6:00 on Friday morning.
The authority explained that the source of the faults has been identified in the data transmission network and that it is working to determine the causes and restore full system operations.
Delays and cancellations in Rome, Milan and Naples
Italian airports are nevertheless experiencing disruption because of the network problem. At least four flights have been cancelled at Rome Fiumicino airport, to Milan Linate, Riyadh, Tirana and Trieste, while other services are reporting delays of up to 60 minutes. There are also delays and cancellations at Milan Linate, Milan Malpensa and Naples Capodichino airports.
Airport operators are urging passengers to check the status of their flight with their airline.

Group of forensic experts served suspicion notice for falsifying evidence in interests of SBU official – NABU
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:15:02 EEST
16:15:02 KST

The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office have served notices of suspicion to forensic experts of the Kyiv Research Institute of Forensic Expertise (KRIFE) of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine who drew up deliberately false conclusions regarding the value of elite real estate belonging to the wife of a high-ranking Security Service of Ukraine official.
"In December 2023, the wife of the high-ranking official purchased an apartment for UAH 21.6 million. At the same time, according to the contract, its value was intentionally understated to UAH 12.8 million. In April 2024, a lawyer acting in the interests of the couple initiated a forensic construction and technical examination at KRIFE. Already in May, a commission of experts issued a conclusion stating that the market value of this apartment is UAH 12.3 million, which is UAH 9.3 million lower than the actual price. To achieve this result, the experts intentionally used non-relevant real estate objects for comparison. Subsequently, this document was used by the defense as evidence in the NACP, NABU, and court," the NABU press service reported on its Telegram channel.
In the same month, NABU detectives, investigating criminal proceedings into the apartment's purchase, ordered a commission examination, which was recalled on November 11, 2024, with a request to return the materials without execution.
"However, the experts ignored the investigative demand and continued their research. They agreed on limiting the value of comparison objects to no higher than $2,500–2,600 per square meter (instead of the market $3,000) and consciously chose the cheapest offers starting from $1,550, while ignoring other available analogues. In early December 2024, the experts signed the conclusion but backdated it to November 8, 2024 (i.e., prior to the recall by the NABU detective). Significantly, detectives received a copy of the conclusion not from KRIFE, but from the lawyer of the suspected high-ranking official," the report notes.
NABU emphasizes that such manipulations of evidence would be impossible if an independent expert institution operated under the Bureau.
"The Bureau's leadership has for several years emphasized the critical need to create an independent expert institution. This would eliminate corruption risks, prevent external pressure on experts, and significantly increase the efficiency of pre-trial investigations in top corruption cases," NABU summarized.

Europe Provides Two-Thirds of Intelligence to Ukraine, Says French Foreign Minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:08:40 UTC
16:08:40 KST

Europe now provides two-thirds of the intelligence Ukraine receives from its partners.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot made the statement in an interview with France Inter.
“Two-thirds of the intelligence provided to Ukraine now comes from European countries, including France,” Barrot said.
His remarks come amid US threats to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine following Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
European countries provide Ukraine with several types of intelligence, including optical and radar satellite imagery, intercepted radio communications, information on troop movements, and warnings about ballistic missile threats.
For example, to help detect ballistic threats, European countries provide Ukraine with information collected by ground-based electronic intelligence systems and long-range ground-based radars. These systems can track missiles after they rise above the radar horizon.
France previously announced a major upgrade of its strategic Nostradamus radar, located in the Eure-et-Loir department.
Unique in Europe, the radar can detect threats thousands of kilometres away, from the North Sea to the Ural Mountains,without mechanically rotating its antennas.
Developed in the 1990s by France’s aerospace research agency ONERA, the system had remained mothballed for an extended period.
Amid growing threats from Russia and Iran, France’s Ministry of the Armed Forces has decided to bring the radar back into operation, investing more than €50 million in its modernization.
The radar works by bouncing high-frequency radiowaves off the ionosphere, allowing it to detect objects beyond the horizon. Its antennas, spread across a 12-hectare star-shaped array, can monitor a volume of several million cubic kilometres, from the ground to an altitude of 250 kilometres.
Meanwhile, Germany also plans to deploy a constellation of more than 100 military satellites in low Earth orbit in the coming years to provide secure communications and track missiles.

Source: Ukraine's Air Force on social media
Details: Russia used Shahed loitering munitions, 108 of which were jet-powered, Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoy drones. They were launched from Oryol in Russia, the temporarily occupied part of Donetsk Oblast and Hvardiiske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
Early reports as of 09:30 indicate that Ukrainian air defences had shot down or jammed 114 Russian Shahed-type UAVs, 77 of which were jet-powered, and drones of other types.
Twenty-seven offensive Russian aerial assets struck 24 locations, and downed drones or their debris fell at 14 locations.

A Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Yemen’s interim capital Aden killed five people and wounded 16 on Oct. 15, Health Minister Qasim Buhaibeh said.
The casualties included guards and civilian employees. Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani was at the Al-Maashiq compound but was unharmed, a government minister speaking on condition of anonymity said.
The unnamed minister said five missiles hit command centers used by Yemeni government forces and the Saudi-led coalition. He reported Yemeni and Saudi casualties but gave no breakdown.
Houthi-affiliated media said the group had targeted a military operations headquarters led by Saudi officers and weapons depots at the palace.

The Iran-backed Houthis have seized territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast in recent weeks despite a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015.
Rayed Krimly, the Saudi Foreign Ministry’s deputy minister for public diplomacy, accused Iran of continuing to arm and train the Houthis.
“We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” he said.
Krimly said Riyadh remained in contact with Tehran. He also said the Houthis had refused an invitation to meet in Muscat, which the ministry later clarified was made in July.
The coalition said it intercepted Houthi drones directed at Saudi Arabia’s south, including Khamis Mushait. Yemeni government forces also reported ballistic missile attacks on Marib.
Riyadh’s international airport has been targeted 20 times this month, according to the coalition.

Fonds publics détournés : pourquoi la Cour des comptes européenne pourrait avoir plus de mal à les repérer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:07:57 UTC
16:07:57 KST

La volonté de la Commission européenne de rendre les milliards de l'UE plus réactifs aux crises à venir pourrait aussi les rendre plus exposés aux risques d'abus, avertit la Cour des comptes européenne.
Son président Tony Murphy alerte que les principaux piliers de la réforme du budget à long terme de l'UE, élaborée par la Commission, risquent de brouiller la vision des agents chargés de veiller à ce que les fonds publics soient dépensés comme prévu.
"Il nous est plus difficile de suivre l'argent", a-t-il souligné. "On dit à l'Etat membre : 'Voici une somme considérable, et vous faites en sorte que tout est en ordre.' C'est en quelque sorte d'autocontrôle."
Advertisement
Cet avertissement intervient alors que l'épineux débat du montant du budget 2028-2034 de l'UE est au menu du sommet des dirigeants européens à Bruxelles cette semaine, et que la Cour a constaté une augmentation des irrégularités dans l'utilisation des fonds publics.
Outre le montant total des moyens, se pose la question de leur répartition. Après un cycle budgétaire marqué par la pandémie, les guerres et les conséquences du changement climatique, la Commission souhaite rendre le prochain budget plus agile. Pour ce faire, elle prévoit d'en affecter environ la moitié — soit près de 1 000 milliards d’euros sur sept ans — à une enveloppe unique dans laquelle les pays pourront puiser pour remplir leurs objectifs dans des domaines comme l'immigration, l’agriculture ou le développement régional.
Ces fonds destinés à l'agriculture et au développement régional — souvent octroyés sous forme de subventions aux exploitations agricoles et aux projets locaux — sont depuis longtemps exposés à la fraude et aux détournements.
Selon Tony Murphy, accorder aux gouvernements nationaux une plus grande marge de manœuvre pour réorienter leurs dépenses rendrait le suivi de ces dernières encore plus difficile.
"Il y aura une certaine flexibilité, mais à quel prix ?", a-t-il soulevé lors d'une interview. Une grande partie du contrôle dépendra des mesures de surveillance que chaque pays a déjà mises en place.
D'autant que les irrégularités dans l'utilisation des fonds du budget de l'UE sont en hausse. Les erreurs de versement se sont élevées à 5 milliards d'euros l'année dernière, selon le dernier rapport de la Cour des comptes européenne.
Advertisement
Dans le prochain budget de l'UE, il pourrait même s'avérer impossible d'estimer ce chiffre, a prévenu Tony Murphy, car les auditeurs de chaque pays ont des rôles et des méthodes de travail différents. "Année après année, nous avons constaté que le travail de ces autorités d'audit n'est pas entièrement fiable", a renchéri son chef de cabinet, Wolfgang Stolz, lors de l'entretien.
Dans un communiqué, la Commission a défendu sa proposition, soulignant que les "principes fondamentaux" du système de contrôle actuel resteraient en vigueur. Les autorités nationales "fonctionnent bien", a-t-elle affirmé, tout en précisant qu'elle se réservait le droit de demander aux Etats membres de "modifier le plan ou de mettre en place des mécanismes de correction si nécessaire".
Des fonds mélangés aux budgets nationaux
L'une des innovations proposées par la Commission consiste à intégrer la politique agricole commune (PAC) — qui constituait jusqu'à présent une ligne budgétaire à part entière — dans un fonds gigantesque appelé plan de partenariat national et régional.
Tony Murphy a souligné qu'il ne prônait pas un modèle plutôt qu'un autre. Mais à mesure que les fonds européens s'intègrent de plus en plus aux budgets nationaux, il sera plus difficile pour Bruxelles de contrôler où va réellement son argent. La PAC est plus facile à contrôler lorsqu’“elle n'est pas mélangée à ce méli-mélo”, a estimé le président de la Cour des comptes européenne.
Les articles de presse sur des subventions agricoles versées pour de faux pâturages en Grèce ou sur des fonds destinés à soutenir le tourisme rural en Slovaquie qui financent de luxueuses villas pour les riches illustrent de manière frappante la difficulté de contrôler ces versements dans le cadre du système actuel.
Et le modèle sur lequel repose le nouveau système de dépenses — le fonds de relance post-Covid de l'UE — n'est pas de bon augure, a pointé Tony Murphy. Si les pays ont désormais plus de facilité à affecter les fonds là où ils sont nécessaires, les dépenses sont également devenues plus opaques. Les nouveaux plans nationaux ont été élaborés selon le même modèle.
Advertisement
Dans le cadre du système budgétaire actuel, la Cour des comptes européenne peut se rendre physiquement sur place dans une exploitation agricole bénéficiant de fonds européens. En revanche, dans le cadre du fonds de relance post-Covid, l'UE ne publie chaque année que la liste des 100 principaux bénéficiaires.
"Ce n’est pas très transparent. Je veux dire, où va réellement l'argent de l’UE ? C’est ça qui compte", a insisté Tony Murphy. "On a un fonds qui regroupe différentes politiques publiques, avec des objectifs et des échéances complètement différents, des mécanismes de mise en œuvre différents et moins de prévisibilité."
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Museums fear research funding shuffle threatens key projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:06:00 UTC
16:06:00 KST

Museums fear research funding shuffle threatens key projects
Museums are concerned that the loss of research funding will jeopardize their projects and hope the decision will be reversed.
Under a government decision, the Ministry of Culture's research and development funding, totaling approximately €900,000, will be transferred to the Ministry of Education and Research's budget starting in 2028.
The transfer means that, starting in 2028, the Ministry of Culture will no longer hold funding rounds for creative research, nor will it have research and development funding in its budget to support museum research projects.
The decision stems from a proposal by Minister of Education and Research Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) to channel ministries' research and development funding through the Ministry of Education and Research's strategic research program.
The explanatory memorandum accompanying the regulation indicates that although the funding will formally pass through the Ministry of Education and Research's budget, the Ministry of Culture will retain its own "quota" and decision-making authority to support strategic objectives and research projects within its area of responsibility, including museums. Nevertheless, the transfer of research funding to the Ministry of Education and Research has sparked discontent, particularly among Estonian museums, which have been among the main beneficiaries of these funds.
"This is incredibly bad news and the wording is utterly hopeless. This research funding has been absolutely vital to the Art Museum of Estonia in recent years, supporting virtually all the more substantial parts of our exhibition and publication programs. Now we're supposed to maneuver our way back under the umbrella of universities and convince them that exhibitions and creative research also count as research," Kumu Director Kadi Polli wrote on social media.
Mariann Raisma, director of the University of Tartu Museum, is also unhappy with the plan but remains hopeful that an exception will be made for the Ministry of Culture's area of responsibility when research funding is allocated.
"I still very much hope that this decision is not final. We have a regular meeting of the Museum Council coming up at the end of the month where we will meet with the minister of culture and I sincerely hope that there is still some way to reverse this decision," Raisma told ERR.
According to Raisma, the regulation's entry into force would be very bad news for Estonian museums, which fear that this much-needed funding will effectively disappear for them in the future. One major concern is that the new funding scheme sets a relatively high minimum grant of €150,000 per year for projects lasting two to four years, while museums need grants roughly one-tenth that size.
"Another thing I would highlight about this funding, which was particularly good, is that the amounts awarded were not very large. We weren't distributing hundreds of thousands of euros; instead, the grants made it possible to carry out smaller projects. That suits museums particularly well. Of course, the total amount of funding wasn't very large either, but it has certainly been extremely important for museums," Raisma told ERR.
"We carried out several very important research projects that enabled museums and research institutions to work together on topics for which funding would otherwise not have been available," Raisma said.
Ministry adviser: We'll lose flexibility and some projects will be discontinued
Viivian Jõemets, research adviser at the Ministry of Culture, is also concerned about several aspects of the new funding allocation system. She likewise noted that the program requires projects that are too large for the cultural sector's current capacity.
"The annual budget of €150,000 per project required under the new rules — amounting to at least €300,000 over two years — is unreasonably large for a museum. Current projects at our museums with nationwide responsibilities and research obligations, as well as the National Library, range from €40,000 to €70,000, depending on whether it is a large or small museum," Jõemets said.
According to Jõemets, building research capacity on this scale takes time and cannot be accomplished in a single year. "In the cultural sector, it is simply not possible to immediately develop projects with budgets this large in several important research areas," she added.
"Another concern is that the Ministry of Culture's total sector-specific research funding amounts to approximately €800,000. If we distribute it among smaller groups, each museum can develop something — activities take place and progress is made. But if we allocate very large sums to just three projects across our entire area of responsibility, what happens to all the other important areas of research?" Jõemets asked.
"What will happen to the research areas we have developed so far, such as efforts to advance research at the Art Museum of Estonia and the study of musical heritage? Under the strategic research regulation, it is unclear how we can continue developing our fields in these circumstances," she added.
Jõemets noted that other questions also remain unanswered. For example, if no applications are submitted for a particular research area simply because there are no potential applicants, it is unclear what will happen to that funding within the Ministry of Education and Research's budget.
"But if those funds remained in the Ministry of Culture's budget, we could flexibly reallocate them to other important activities," she added.
Jõemets emphasized that the government's decision to channel sector-specific research funding through the strategic research program affects all ministries and that the Ministry of Culture was granted a one-year extension compared with the others.
"I hope that in the near future there will be an assessment of the successes and shortcomings of the reform of sector-specific research funding, weighing its advantages and disadvantages. Perhaps a new government will want to revisit this decision. For now, however, transferring sector-specific research funding from the Ministry of Culture's budget to that of the Ministry of Education and Research remains the current government's decision," Jõemets said.
Jõemets does not have to worry about losing her position.
"My position at the Ministry of Culture will not be eliminated as part of this reform. Even now, funding rounds for the Ministry of Culture's research programs are administered by the Estonian Research Council under regulations issued by the minister of culture and there will be no significant change in that regard. The only change concerns where and how flexibly we can allocate sector-specific research funding and we will have to operate under a regulation issued by the minister of education and research," she said.
"Not all of the Ministry of Culture's current research activities will be able to continue under this regulation," Jõemets concluded.
