WA Greens kept crisis comms document about Jordon Steele-John
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:05:58 UTC
16:05:58 KST

WA Greens kept crisis communications document about Jordon Steele-John
In short:
The WA Greens maintained a crisis communications document for years in the event that complaints against Jordon Steele-John were made public.
Senator Steele-John has rejected concerns raised against him in a letter by Greens members to leader David Shoebridge. The letter did not contain any specific allegations.
What's next?
Senator Shoebridge says an independent investigation will be conducted.
Members of the WA Greens maintained a crisis communications document on how to respond if concerns about senator Jordon Steele-John were made public.
The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that since 2016 WA Greens staff kept a 47-page document with methods to manage media coverage of any allegations made about Senator Steele-John, and instructed staff to monitor social media discussions by party members.
Greens leader David Shoebridge denied any previous knowledge of the document, saying he understood it be "from some seven years ago".
"I was not aware of the document and I was not aware of the allegations," he told the ABC.
Yesterday the same outlet reported that a number of current and former Greens members had written to Senator Shoebridge asking him to investigate concerns regarding Senator Steele-John's behaviour towards women.
The letter said women had been warned "not to be alone" with the senator and alleged there were "multiple" concerns about his behaviour "in the presence of women" spanning his career in parliament.
No specific allegation has been made against Senator Steele-John, who has said "utterly" rejects "this characterisation of me".
Senator Shoebridge said none of the authors of the letter "asserted to any direct knowledge of the matters involved".
"And of course that creates some additional complexity in dealing with it, but the matters concerned are taken seriously," he told ABC News Breakfast.
"The best way of dealing with this is a fair, an independent and a timely process commissioned by the WA Greens."
In a statement, the co-convenors of the WA Greens said it "responded to allegations about Jordon Steele-John in 2016".
"The allegations were not substantiated and the named persons have never lodged a formal complaint."
"Reference has been made to an internal document that has been provided to the media. The document outlines the management of communications about this matter."
Leader's office denies knowledge
The ABC has confirmed the existence of the crisis communications document, which names several federal Greens members, including senior staff in the leader's office.
The Greens leader's office has denied previously seeing the document and says it has no record of ever receiving it.
"This is not a document made by, used by or seen by the leader's office," a spokesperson for the office said.
"The office is committed to having the matters comprehensively investigated with a fair, independent and timely process.
"Everyone deserves a safe workplace, and all complaints should be considered in a fair and robust process."
A senior staffer named in the document confirmed they had searched their record and found no record of the document ever being sent, shared or accessed by them.
Party members say it is not unusual for a document to identify individuals in the federal party as points of contact.
It is also standard for Greens senators to receive media training from the leader's office, as Senator Steele-John did when he entered parliament.
Senator Steele-John has taken a leave of absence and will not attend parliament while the investigation is underway.
"I utterly reject this characterisation of me, which tries to assert I am someone I am not," he said in a statement on Thursday.
"These claims are made without specifics, any allegation of this nature is extremely serious and must be treated accordingly. If someone has made an allegation, I am prepared to address it."
Senator Shoebridge said he did not know of the complaints until two weeks ago.
"I knew absolutely nothing until assuming this position as leader, and then when I received the correspondence I acted with what I think is timely and appropriate urgency," he said.

Hackers steal data from Swiss magazine Republik
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:04:11 UTC
16:04:11 KST

Hackers steal data from Swiss magazine Republik
Swiss online magazine Republik has fallen victim to a cyberattack. The magazine says user data was compromised, but no credit card details were leaked.
Unknown individuals exploited a security vulnerability in an analytics tool.
On Wednesday morning, one of the analysis tools had stopped working, according to a statement on the Republik website. It marked the end of an unauthorised access incident that had been ongoing since August.
“The security vulnerability had been known since August 6, but we failed to take the necessary countermeasures in good time,” the statement reads.
Republik does not know who was behind the attack. There is much to suggest it was a broad, automated wave of attacks. The attackers are said to have first searched for what was contained in every Metabase installation – the tool with the security vulnerability – such as login details and keys for AI services that could be resold.
So far, there is no indication that anyone specifically targeted Republik. However, the data has been leaked. The attackers certainly accessed the details of active publishers, subscribers, newsletter recipients and all former users.
The data records included email addresses, names and, where provided, telephone numbers, year of birth and gender. This means that people who never had a subscription but merely subscribed to a newsletter were also affected.
When the Metabase was taken offline, the attackers also lost their access, Republik added. On Thursday, following the completion of the initial damage assessment, the magazine reported the incident to the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner.

Five yachts from Guangdong entered Hong Kong waters on Friday as a new scheme to ease cross-border yacht visits took effect.
Nearby vessels sounded their horns as the visiting boats docked one by one at the Lantau Yacht Club in Discovery Bay around noon.
The vessels range from about 13 to 38 metres, with three from Shenzhen, one from Nansha and one from Zhuhai.
Officiating a welcoming ceremony, Acting Financial Secretary Michael Wong said Hong Kong is actively building itself into Asia’s yacht hub, noting that the worldwide yacht market continues to grow – especially the luxury segment – and that the city can capture a share of that growth.
He said the government is rolling out measures to boost the yacht economy, including steps to make visits by such vessels easier, and will host the Festival of Connoisseurs from November 4 to 6.
Wong added that four new marina projects – at the airport, Lamma Island, Aberdeen and Hung Hom – are moving ahead. 
Together they will provide more than 1,100 berths, a 30 percent increase from the existing total, he said. 
Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said there are adequate facilities for mainland yachts to moor and dock in the SAR.
"At the present moment, we have allowed these mainland yachts to dock or moor at five designated mooring anchorage areas, in addition to the existing mooring facilities in yacht clubs. We consider that this could meet the demand," she said.
"Coupled with the real-time dynamic monitoring system, the Marine Department can communicate with the mainland yacht captains so as to facilitate their travel in Hong Kong waters."
Wong thanked the central government and relevant units in Guangdong and Hong Kong for their support in implementing the travel scheme.
"Whether it's Hong Kong yachts heading north or Guangdong yachts heading south, the essence is mutual benefit – a win-win-win," he said. 
"We believe the travel scheme can open up a brand-new maritime channel for residents and visitors on both sides, jointly driving economic development in both places."

Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:56 UTC
16:00:56 KST

Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.
Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.
Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.
Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.
“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”
Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.
Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.
In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.
Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.
The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.
The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.
Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.
The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.
Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.
Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.
SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.
The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.
Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.
Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.
Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”
Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”
Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”
Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”
Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”
General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”
Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”
Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”
CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.

UK could quickly re-enter EU with ‘Switzerland plus’ deal, senior MEP says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:55 UTC
16:00:55 KST

The UK could re-enter the EU in a “Switzerland plus” package that could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties with the bloc, the head of a European parliament committee has said.
Bernd Lange, who was heavily involved in Brexit negotiations, said: “I would love to see the UK back.” He said the EU missed the UK in decision-making because of its strong history of promoting open markets and democracy.
A Swiss style arrangement is often considered a halfway house to full membership of the bloc but involves free movement and regulatory alignment.
Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market across more than 100 agreements with a new framework deal.
This gives it access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
In exchange, Switzerland agreed to the free movement of people and to pay €375m (£326m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds.
Lange, a German MEP who has an important role in the European legislative process as chair of the European parliament’s trade committee, said the Switzerland framework could be a model for the UK, but it was a “passive” agreement that would not involve the country in EU decision-making.
“As a step by step [process], of course, there are a lot of possibilities, but I would love to have the UK come back also in the political decision-making process and politically be engaged. So we have the model of Switzerland … Switzerland plus, I would say, as that has some kinds of engagement but not the full membership.”
He said the decision about what relationship the UK wanted with the EU was entirely “in the hands of the UK”, but if it opted for something like Switzerland plus, an agreement could be achieved quickly, notwithstanding political hiccups.
He was speaking in London, where his schedule includes a meeting with the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, who is part of a team working on the UK’s new position on EU relations.
Lange also threw his weight behind Andy Burnham’s call for the EU not to lock the UK out of Made in Europe legislation that would restrict UK suppliers from inclusion in public procurement tenders as well as some corporate contracts such as car fleets.
French and German leaders were reportedly close on Thursday to agreeing a proposal that the UK could be included, provided it aligned with the EU’s 2024 tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
This week the boss of Mercedes said the EU would be making a “deliberate choice” to harm the EU car industry if it did not allow the UK into the Made in Europe package.
Burnham has backing from the Netherlands, Germany and Italy. France, which came up with the legislative proposals, was opposed, saying it needed to get the legislation on the books urgently to guard against cheap competition from China, and that allowing the UK and other allied countries in could hold up the lawmaking.
Lange said the UK should “of course” be included because it was already aligned with the EU on environmental standards and employment laws.
He said France’s position was “not rational” and “also so emotional” but could be born from the desire to be seen as putting France first before next April’s presidential elections, in which Marine Le Pen, who is opposed to globalism, could take power.
Locking the UK out of Made in Europe could also cause a legal dispute over the trade and cooperation agreement that allows UK goods to be sold in the single market without barriers as long as they the meet the bloc’s standards.
The Made in Europe package, or the Industrial Accelerator Act, is expected to get political approval by the end of the year or early 2027, meaning Burnham does not have much time to get clauses inserted designating the UK as European for the purposes of the legislation.
But Lange said there could be time after that, given the processes of the European parliament, where three committees have scrutinising powers.
“There are 5,100 amendments,” he said, referring to the protracted process ahead, including one on UK inclusion.

Britain is addicted to prisons. Our crumbling probation service proves they don’t work | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:54 UTC
16:00:54 KST

Public services need more investment across the board. Every day, another wretched story. Look at the Institute for Government’s (IFG) Public Services Performance Tracker for a plain assessment of A&E corridor care, councils struggling to meet the demands of social care and the Send system, the courts backlog, GP caseloads or families lost in temporary accommodation. A chancellor approaching a budget is besieged by need. It’s easy for us journalists to pick out shock stories and claim each one is an absolute priority, but how should a chancellor choose?
Today it’s the probation officers, whose conference in Newcastle is launching a ballot for industrial action. Their caseloads overflowed long ago, but now thousands of prisoners released early – 2,000 this month – have been thrust upon them. The responsibility is overwhelming, with officers blamed for crimes their clients commit.
The probation story is told in scores of reports: the National Audit Office found the service running on half the staff needed to cover released prisoners. It also reported failures in electronic tagging, echoed by the IFG reporting only 55% of tags were fitted in time. Napo, the probation officers’ union, blames the problems on awarding contracts to the lowest bidders at prices that mean the job isn’t done properly.
The number of offenders charged with serious further offences while on probation has increased, with the public accounts committee blaming staff shortages. Vacancies leave probation services 25%-30% below target levels. The government is training another 1,300, but that’s not enough, says Napo, considering the high dropout rate once recruits discover the abuse, threats and stress of the work, alongside the fact that the most common cause of staff sickness is mental ill health.
The sheer impossibility of their caseloads caused the government to abandon any attempt to say what their caseload should be, so the “workload measurement tool” was abruptly ditched in September just before the October raft of new prisoner releases. There is no point in stating an official workload standard that can’t be met.
Eleven hostels and seven halfway houses, places that help probation officers supervise released prisoners, have just closed for repairs and because of a lack of staff. Drug addiction and mental health problems untreated in prisons, coupled with cuts to education, training and rehabilitation, make prisoners even less prepared for release.
The probation system was broken by a disastrous privatisation when Chris Grayling (who banned the sending of books to prisoners) split it apart into 21 private companies, with the workforce organisationally divided in two. Private companies only handled offenders judged low to medium risk, while the most serious offenders remained under the control of the state. Companies under-invested, experienced staff left, and none of the innovation promised was delivered. After this ideological privatisation was abandoned in 2021, the probation service never recovered.
The lord chancellor is set to address the probation officer’s conference. “But please,” says Napo chair Ben Cockburn, “no bullshit. Don’t tell us how well we do an exceptionally difficult job. We know that.”. Napo rejected a 5% pay offer on the grounds it falls far behind equivalent offers to workers in local government, police and social work. Under planned industrial action, Cockburn says probation officers will work to contract and refuse unpaid overtime. That, he says, will cause collapse.
What probation officers need immediately is reduced workloads, pruned to the riskiest cases, leaving less serious cases unallocated. “Put the service into special measures,” Cockburn says. He also wants the courts to stop piling on more cases until there are enough staff to cope. “We are firefighting from one emergency to another,” he says – or called away to someone in a police cell, or to a paedophile found dating a woman with a child, or a domestic violence case.
Cutting workloads for probation officers is only a short-term solution, one that avoids the real question. Why is there an ever-rising prison population, despite the sustained, multi-decade fall in crime rates?
“We are addicted to prison,” Cockburn says. In his view, probation works when officers have time for long-term working relationships with offenders. “It’s the best job in the world,” he says, recalling the journey of one prisoner who had committed a terrible crime as a young man. “I saw him in prison, knew him for 15 years, with time for therapeutic work.” But, these days, that’s so rare. “Someone now might see eight different officers, retelling their story over and over, creating no trust.”
Why build more prison cells? An inspection of a brand new private prison, HMP Millsike in East Yorkshire, found it unsafe due to a lack of experienced staff, as well as chronic staff shortages. Even at its opening, it was “chaotic”, lacking basic processes for important things like locking doors and counting prisoners. Hundreds of cells are still empty because of a lack of officers.
Public pressure to lock up more prisoners and supervise them when released will never be matched by a willingness to pay the taxes needed to cover the cost of attracting people to work in this sector. That’s the truth Cockburn wants politicians to be brave enough to tell. This country is not alone in wrongly believing crime is ever-rising when all across Europe it has fallen for decades. But no one believes it. A news and drama fixation on horrific crime stirs primal fears that belie these facts. Politicians everywhere score points with a frightened public by clamouring for more punishment.
When I last visited a hard-pressed prison, I asked the governor what she most needed, and was astonished when she said she wouldn’t invest here, but “right at the start, before the damage is done, in early years”.
Asking where every pound spent does most good is the kind of mega-question budgets don’t answer. But a brave chancellor would cut prison funding down to housing only the most dangerous, and spending better on what works, such as well-funded probation officers.
Keep telling this fact: all crime is horrible – sex crime is at last reported more often – but the overall drop in neighbourhood-level crime in England and Wales has been about 80% since its peak in 1995. Meanwhile, prison numbers have risen significantly. In his upcoming speech at the probation officer’s conference, it would take unprecedented political bravery for the lord chancellor to dare end the pretence that prison works.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

UK law could deny Fayed accusers recognition as victims of human trafficking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:53 UTC
16:00:53 KST

Survivors of sexual violence could wrongly be denied recognition as victims of human trafficking under credibility tests in a new UK law, the independent anti-slavery commissioner has warned.
Eleanor Lyons said the measures in the immigration and asylum bill were fundamentally unfair and could lead to many more victims of slavery and trafficking, including those allegedly abused by Mohamed Al Fayed, being denied support.
Under the legislation, Home Office officials must regard any delay to making a claim of modern day slavery or human trafficking as damaging to their credibility.
Any inaccuracy, inconsistency or omission in a person’s account, as well as any striking similarity to a claim made by someone else, must also be viewed as reasons for disbelief.
Lyons said the credibility tests would harm survivors of sexual violence who often suffered memory loss as a result of their trauma. Many were also reluctant to come forward to disclose their exploitation due to fear of reprisals by their abusers, she added.
“They are basically saying to victims, if you don’t come forward in a timely fashion not yet defined, if there are inconsistencies in your account, and if there are similarities between exploitation and [those of] others, the Home Office decision-maker must question your credibility,” Lyons said.
“For the Al Fayed victims [that] would be particularly concerning because a lot of time has passed [since the alleged abuse], a lot of them were sadly exploited in similar ways to each other, and some of the things that happened to them were completely horrific and they may not be able to recall exactly what time, which place they happened in [due to the impact of trauma].”
Several women who were allegedly sexually abused by Fayed, said they feared the measures would undermine investigations into what they described as the late billionaire’s international trafficking network.
Holly Johnson, who says she was trafficked and sexually abused when she worked at Harrods and Fayed’s Park Lane offices, said the credibility tests would re-victimise survivors.
She added: “Fayed had a specific strategy for trafficking and assaulting women, and many of our stories are really similar. To say someone shouldn’t be believed because their situation is too similar to another victim of that same abuser is absurd.”
No One Above, a collective of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse, said many women delayed reporting their exploitation until after his death in 2023 and Harrods’ declaration in 2024 that those who signed non-disclosure agreements would not have them enforced.
Elizabeth, an NOA member who has been recognised as a trafficking victim by the Home Office, said: “It took that for me to finally believe that I couldn’t have somebody take my house away for speaking out.”
Pelham Spong, who says she was trafficked in Paris on Fayed’s orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him, said she did not go to the Met police until 2017 because she feared her life “was going to be ruined”.
“The thought of speaking out as a 23-year-old with no money, no resources behind me against a billionaire was unfathomable,” said Spong, whose case is being investigated by the French police. “He was so powerful.”
The government has introduced the credibility tests to close what it characterises as opportunities to misuse the National Referral Mechanism (NRM), the system for identifying potential victims of modern slavery and human trafficking in the UK, and to speed up the removal and deportation of illegal migrants.
Eleanora Fais, the anti-trafficking monitoring group coordinator at Anti-Slavery International, said: “If your primary aim is to introduce legislation that is focused on immigration enforcement, safeguarding will come in second place.
“The NRM was always meant to help survivors to disclose and be referred to support needed for the recovery. Alongside that, if they wished to, they could cooperate with police to ensure that perpetrators were brought to justice. If you introduce these criteria to weaken the system, that’s not going to happen.”
Hilary Agg, the head of policy and research at the anti-slavery charity Unseen, said the measures would allow human trafficking to thrive in the UK because fewer victims would be identified and be able to help police to pursue perpetrators.
She added that the tests would harm immigrants and the majority of trafficking and slavery victims, who are British nationals.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “Modern slavery is a barbaric crime, and the government is committed to identifying victims and ensuring they get the support they need. The immigration and asylum bill will strengthen protections and crack down on exploitation, while reducing opportunities for improper use of the system.
“The credibility considerations in the bill are well-balanced and contain appropriate safeguards, which will enhance the robustness of modern slavery decision-making.”
A Harrods spokesperson said it supported all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continued to work closely with the Met police on its investigation.
A Ritz Paris spokesperson said it was “deeply concerned by the allegations that have been reported and takes them with the utmost seriousness. We would like to express our deepest sympathy to the women who have come forward.”
The Fayed estate has been approached for comment.

Why is Switzerland voting again on the ‘marriage tax penalty’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Why is Switzerland voting again on the ‘marriage tax penalty’?
On November 29, the Swiss will vote for the second time this year on how to end the tax disadvantage faced by married couples. After saying yes to individual taxation in March, voters must now decide on the Fair Taxation Initiative submitted by the Centre Party, which wants to keep joint taxation.
It is not the first time that the Swiss have voted more than once on the same issue. The Covid-19 Act was put to the electorate three times in as many years. This time, the Swiss will vote on November 29 on an alternative way of ending the marriage tax penalty – although they accepted the principle of individual taxation just a few months ago.
Why hold another vote on the taxation of married couples?
At present, married couples are taxed jointly. Their incomes are added together to calculate their tax due. For some spouses, this results in a higher tax bill than if they were unmarried. This is particularly the case when both spouses have a high income. It is known as the “marriage tax penalty”.
To put an end to this disparity, on March 8 Swiss voters approved the Individual Taxation Act. This was an indirect counter-proposal by the government to a popular initiative launched by the women’s wing of the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party. The reform is supposed to take effect in 2032. From then on, each taxpayer will be taxed based on their own tax return, at federal, cantonal and municipal levels alike.
The Centre Party, however, is not in favour of this principle. It decided to press ahead with its own popular initiativeExternal link, which proposes a different way of ending the tax discrimination faced by some married couples. The text, entitled “Yes to fair federal taxes for married couples – to finally put an end to marriage-based discrimination!”, was submitted to the Federal Chancellery on March 27, 2024, accompanied by 102,051 valid signatures.
What does the Centre Party’s initiative entail?
The initiative calls for the joint taxation of married couples to be maintained, but only for direct federal tax. This means that the spouses’ incomes would be added together and the couple would file a joint tax return. The text also stipulates that married couples should not pay more tax than unmarried people in a comparable financial situation. This principle would be enshrined in the Constitution.
The initiative does not set out the exact calculation method, but tasks the legislature with finding a solution. It does, however, provide for a fallback mechanism if no implementing legislation comes into force within three years of its adoption. In that case, the tax authorities would have to carry out two calculations: one based on joint taxation and the other using the tax scales and deductions applicable to unmarried individuals. The lower of the two amounts would then be taken into account.
Who is for and who against?
A cross-party committee supports the initiative. It comprises the Centre Party, the right-wing Swiss People’s Party, the Evangelical Party, the ultra-conservative Federal Democratic Union, as well as the Swiss Farmers’ Union and the “Famille 3plus” interest group. The federal government and parliament recommend rejecting the proposal. The left-wing Social Democratic Party, the Green Party, the Radical-Liberals and the Liberal Greens are also against.
What are the arguments in favour of the initiative?
The proponents regard it as the fairest solution to end the tax penalty on marriage. They argue that individual taxation disadvantages families in which one parent provides the bulk of the income, while the other earns little or nothing at all. Their model, they say, allows couples to decide for themselves how to divide paid work and family responsibilities, without being penalised fiscally for this choice.
They also stress that the initiative does not require a complete overhaul of the tax system, as it builds on the existing joint taxation model. This, they argue, would preclude the additional administrative burden linked to individual taxation, which would generate some 1.7 million extra tax returns, according to government estimates.
Lastly, the initiative’s proponents highlight the situation of retired couples who have organised their lives for decades on the basis of joint taxation. A change in system could put them at a disadvantage, as they can no longer adapt the division of labour and income that prevailed during their working lives.
And the arguments against?
The opponents argue that the goal of ending the tax penalty on marriage was already achieved with the approval of individual taxation last March. They therefore call for this democratic decision to be respected.
The critics also point out that, in certain situations, the initiative could create a new form of inequality, this time to the detriment of unmarried people. They could end up paying more tax than married couples in a comparable financial situation.
Furthermore, the adoption of the proposal would create a situation at odds with the principle of taxing each taxpayer individually. As the Centre’s initiative concerns only direct federal tax, it could give rise to a dual system: married couples would be taxed jointly at federal level, but individually at cantonal and municipal levels.
Lastly, according to the opponents, joint taxation provides less of an incentive to engage in gainful employment than individual taxation, particularly for the person bringing in the household’s second income. They therefore believe that the initiative does less to promote equality between women and men.
What about the fiscal cost of this reform?
The financial implications of the initiative would depend on how it is implemented. If the proposed alternative method of calculation were applied, it would result in an estimated reduction in direct federal tax revenue of between CHF700 million ($842 million) and CHF1.4 billion per year, according to the federal government’s dispatch to parliamentExternal link. By way of comparison, the individual taxation system approved in March is expected to result in a shortfall of around CHF630 million per year in direct federal tax revenue.
Will individual taxation be scrapped if the initiative is accepted?
Not necessarily. Even if the Centre’s initiative is accepted on November 29, the law on individual taxation, approved by the electorate in March, will remain in force. The federal government has set its implementation for 2032.
However, acceptance of the initiative would give rise to a contradictory situation. The Constitution would enshrine the joint taxation of married couples for direct federal tax, whereas the law would require a shift to individual taxation. It would then be up to parliament to resolve this contradiction.

During the night of October 16, Russia launched 149 drones at Ukraine, most of them—108—jet-powered. A total of 114 of them were shot down or suppressed, including 77 jet-powered drones (51.7%). UNN reports this, citing data from the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
What Russia attacked with and from where
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of October 16 (since 18:00 on October 15), the enemy attacked with 149 Shahed-type attack UAVs (108 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Russia; the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk; and the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea—Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
How the air defense performed
According to preliminary data, as of 09:30, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 114 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (77 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types
Hits by 27 enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 24 locations, as well as the سقوط of downed targets (debris) at 14 locations.
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — MediaTek is reportedly in final talks with TikTok parent company ByteDance to develop custom-designed chips for data centers, potentially adding another major cloud service provider to its customer base after Google.
Citing people familiar with the matter, Bloomberg reported Thursday that the two companies are nearing an agreement. The size of the potential order has not been disclosed, according to Reuters and CTEE.
ByteDance, based in China, is investing more heavily in hardware to expand its AI computing capacity. US export controls have limited its access to the most advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, according to CTEE.
Like Alibaba and Tencent, ByteDance faces difficulties obtaining these chips, while domestic suppliers such as Huawei may not fully meet its needs. The company has therefore been exploring alternatives through partnerships with chip designers.
A deal would expand MediaTek’s data center business and strengthen its position in the market for custom AI chips. MediaTek declined to comment on the reports.
The custom-designed chips the company is reportedly developing for ByteDance are intended for AI inference, the process by which trained AI models generate answers or predictions. The chips could reach design completion in the first half of 2028.
Mass production could potentially begin as early as 2029. If annual orders reach 1 million units, the project could generate NT$649 billion (US$20 billion) to NT$811 billion in revenue, Bank of America said.
However, working with a Chinese customer would require MediaTek to balance commercial opportunities against US export control requirements. Chinese media reports suggested that any agreement would have to comply with applicable regulations.

TOKYO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Genta Koja, governor of Japan's southern prefecture of Okinawa, said Friday he accepts the deployment of U.S. military MV-22 Osprey transport aircraft at the Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in the prefecture, local media reported.
Kyodo News said the move marks a reversal of the prefecture government's longstanding opposition to the aircraft's presence.
Speaking to reporters at the Okinawa prefectural government office, Koja said the Osprey transport aircraft have been deployed locally for more than 10 years, and that since the Japan Self-Defense Forces also operate the aircraft, demanding their withdrawal or a halt to their use is "not realistic."
Previous prefectural governments, under governors critical of U.S. bases, had opposed the deployment since before the aircraft were first stationed at the base in 2012, according to Kyodo News. Koja assumed the post of Okinawa governor last month.
The tilt-rotor transport aircraft have been involved in a series of major accidents, and because of concerns over flight safety and noise, residents in Okinawa have long opposed their deployment. ■

Taiwan-US Mighty Hornet IV attack drone tests completed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:51:12 UTC
15:51:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Tests with the Taiwan-US-developed Mighty Hornet IV high-speed attack drone were successful, reports said Friday.
The drone was developed by the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology in cooperation with Kratos Defense and Security Solutions of the US. Kratos Unmanned Systems Division President Steve Fendley told M News Thursday he is visiting Taiwan to witness flight tests in the south.
Despite strong winds and gusts, the projectile maintained control and hit all targets, he said. The Mighty Hornet IV has a reported range of 1,000 kilometers, a top speed of more than Mach 0.7 to Mach 0.85, and can be used to intercept similar enemy drones, per Liberty Times.
The Hornet’s price tag of less than NT$16 million (US$500,000), its speed, and its ability to change directions take it close to the capabilities of a traditional fighter jet, according to Fendley.
A potential enemy might have to spend NT$32 million to NT$65 million on each anti-air missile to try and take down a hornet, making the cost of such a campaign unsustainable, he said. As a result, the enemy would have to find a balance between the cost of interception and the cost of the damage inflicted by the drone.
Fendley identified coastal defense against approaching ships as the main use for the attack drone. In addition, the projectile does not need an airport runway to take off, and preparations only require 30 minutes, Liberty Times reported.

Across China: International visitors explore four decades of greening in Xinjiang's Kekeya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
14:50:52 CST
15:50:52 KST

American actor and television presenter Steven Weathers observes an exhibit at the Kekeya Memorial Hall in Aksu City, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Oct. 14, 2026. Kekeya's afforestation project, launched in 1986, marks its 40th anniversary this year. The project aimed to combat desertification and reduce the impact of shifting sands and dust storms on nearby residents. The visit to Kekeya was part of the third installment of the 2026 "Xinjiang in Four Seasons" tour, which brought international social media influencers to cultural sites, agricultural facilities and other destinations across Aksu Prefecture. (Xinhua)
AKSU, Xinjiang, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- After viewing photographs of the area's earlier landscape at the Kekeya Memorial Hall in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, American actor and television presenter Steven Weathers was impressed by the transformation of Kekeya, not only for its greenery, but also for what the trees produced.
"It's not just green, but it's practical. It's orchards of apples and other fruits," Weathers said during a visit with international guests.
Kekeya's afforestation project, launched in 1986, marks its 40th anniversary this year. The project aimed to combat desertification and reduce the impact of shifting sands and dust storms on nearby residents.
Through the sustained efforts of volunteers and forest rangers, about 80,000 hectares of forests were planted from 1986 to 2020. The number of dusty days in nearby Aksu City fell from about 100 in 1980 to around 30 in 2022.
For Weathers, who has lived in China for more than two decades, an encounter at the memorial hall brought that history closer.
He recalled meeting 81-year-old Imam Memet, the first head of the Kekeya forestry station, which was established in 1986. Meeting a man whose earlier life was documented in the museum's photographs gave the story a human dimension.
"His son was with him. And his grandson even helped out as a 12-year-old at the time, just carrying branches and moving things around," Weathers said.
Reflecting on the planning behind China's greening efforts, he added that coordination was something he believed the United States could learn from China.
Local governments also encouraged residents to help preserve the hard-earned forests while supporting their incomes through the cultivation of cash crops, including apples, walnuts and jujubes. The juicy Aksu apple has become Xinjiang's signature agricultural product.
For Ugandan journalist Jenipher Asimwe, the connection between ecological protection and economic activity was a key lesson of the visit. An apple orchard the group visited near the memorial hall left a particularly strong impression on her.
She told Xinhua that the orchards demonstrated how restoration could support both environmental protection and local development.
The visit reminded her of semi-arid areas in Uganda, where, she said, livestock keepers face water shortages during dry periods. She expressed hope for more cooperation between Uganda and China to explore locally suitable approaches to land restoration and agricultural development.
"If you came here, as I did, you cannot even know that it was once a desert," she said.
The greening effort has also shaped wider ecological work in Aksu. At a July press conference marking the anniversary, local authorities described how the region had combined ecological restoration with fruit cultivation, processing and other industries.
The visit to Kekeya was part of the third installment of the 2026 "Xinjiang in Four Seasons" tour, which brought international social media influencers to cultural sites, agricultural facilities and other destinations across Aksu Prefecture.
For Asimwe, the transformation also underscored the importance of sustained effort.
"You cannot say that it was a one-day thing," she said. "It was done step by step." ■

Education ministry under scrutiny over Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:50:25 UTC
15:50:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The education ministry has been criticized after canceled overseas internships left participants facing financial losses, raising concerns over its Taiwan Global Pathfinders Initiative, CNA reported Friday.
Student advocacy group EdYouth, the Taiwan Youth Association for Democracy, and other youth organizations held a press conference Friday to demand stronger protections for participants. They raised concerns about unclear spending, selection procedures, and overseas activities that differed from what had been promised.
Launched in 2025, the initiative provides young Taiwanese with opportunities to study, train, and gain work experience abroad. The government has set a budget of NT$10 billion (US$308 million) for the program from 2025 to 2028.
PTS reported that a participant who had quit his job for an internship in Canada learned in August that the program had been canceled just one month before departure. The cancellation left him unemployed and facing financial losses.
The ministry later confirmed that two Canadian internships had been canceled, affecting four participants. Officials attributed the cancellations to changes in Ontario's internship rules and the withdrawal of overseas partners, per Taisounds.
The incident raised concerns about whether the ministry had secured reliable agreements with overseas partners before accepting applicants. DPP Legislator Chang Ya-lin (張雅琳) called for clearer responsibilities and stronger safeguards when partners withdraw.
UDN reported that a student who had joined the initiative said actual activities sometimes differed from those advertised. One participant expecting to attend a competition instead visited the venue and nearby attractions.
EdYouth Chair Tsai Chi-yeh (蔡其曄) urged the ministry to improve screening and disclose more information before participants depart. He also called for closer supervision of partner organizations and reasonable compensation when promised activities cannot proceed, per Knews.
The groups questioned the involvement of travel agencies in organizing overseas programs. They said outside contractors should handle logistics without compromising the quality of activities.
In response, Youth Development Administration Deputy Director-General Chen Yi-tsung (諶亦聰) said overseas projects are proposed about a year in advance, making some changes “difficult to avoid.” Chen claimed that the ministry has “strengthened” its agreements this year by requiring written confirmation from universities and overseas partners, per CTS News.
Chen said organizers must first arrange alternative activities when original plans fall through. If no suitable replacement is available, participants may receive compensation equal to 10% of their approved grant, under a new mechanism being planned.
The ministry said travel agencies may only handle administrative tasks, including flights, accommodation, and transportation. Officials also plan to strengthen screening and record selection proceedings to improve transparency and fairness.

Poverty rises in Lithuania, including among people with jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:50:00 UTC
15:50:00 KST

Poverty has increased in Lithuania over the past five years, even among people who have jobs, the head of a national anti-poverty network said Friday.
“The situation has definitely worsened over the past five years, particularly for certain groups. These include pensioners, people with disabilities, single people and the unemployed,” Aistė Adomavičienė, director of the National Network of Poverty Reduction Organisations, told LRT RADIO.
“What also concerns us is that the share of working people living in poverty has increased by a full percentage point. That means having a job does not automatically protect you from poverty,” she added.
Adomavičienė said other indicators also pointed to growing financial pressure. The poverty risk gap, which measures how far the incomes of people at risk of poverty fall below the poverty threshold, is widening. The current threshold is 699 euros, she said.
“Against the backdrop of inflation, we can see that the financial squeeze on people is increasing and the situation is not getting any easier,” she added.
The latest review of poverty and social exclusion found that 7% of Lithuania’s population lives in absolute poverty, meaning they cannot afford even basic necessities.
Poverty is more widespread in rural areas, Adomavičienė said, although child poverty has declined.
“Where Lithuania is doing relatively well is child poverty. Over the past decade, we have made a breakthrough, which means we have experience and know how to address the problem,” she said. “The question is how much of that progress we can extend to other groups.”
People with disabilities remain particularly vulnerable. According to data from nongovernmental organisations, 50.5% of people with disabilities in Lithuania were at risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, the highest share in the European Union where the average was 28.8%.

Air defense is the top priority, first and foremost anti-ballistic defense and everything that helps intercept jet-powered shaheds. We also discussed how Denmark can help provide financial support for our resilience. We agreed that our teams will continue working at their level. We appreciate that we can always count on Denmark. Thank you, Mette!” the message reads.
Earlier on Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever; the two leaders discussed the supply of F-16 fighter jets and the ammunition for them. In addition, Zelenskyy held a series of meetings with the NATO Secretary General, the Prime Minister of Poland, the President of France, and the King of Belgium.

Four killed battling Indonesia fires as Singapore vows action over toxic haze

Four people died on Indonesia's Java island fighting the blazes that have been sending toxic smoke across southeast Asia, closing schools and fuelling a surge of respiratory complaints in the region, authorities said on Friday.
The impact of the months-long fires has prompted Singapore's leader to vow legal action against any companies responsible for the blazes that have made regional air quality among the world's worst.
Singapore again topped IQAir's live ranking of the world's most polluted major cities on Friday, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta sixth.
"Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries," said Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, without giving further details.
Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state.
Legal experts have cautioned that pursuing companies linked to the smoke is challenging, with investigations reliant on cooperation from foreign authorities.
Singapore enacted the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act in 2014, after a severe pollution episode in 2013. Another spell occurred in 2015.
The law allows authorities to target companies whose activities overseas cause or contribute to unhealthy haze levels in Singapore.
Establishing responsibility is challenging because it requires authorities to share maps pinpointing fire hotspots, with overlapping land claims further complicating matters.
Singapore's investigations into four Indonesian companies over their alleged role in the 2015 haze crisis remain open, a case that strained relations with Jakarta at the time.
Other chances for legal action, including a possible case at The Hague-based International Court of Justice, were also low as it needed Indonesia's consent for jurisdiction in the case.
'Do everything we can'
Singapore's air pollution surged to 251 on IQAir's Air Quality Index level into very unhealthy levels at around 0400 GMT on Friday.
Under the Swiss-based company's system, readings of 151-200 are considered unhealthy, 201-300 very unhealthy and above 300 hazardous.
"We cannot control the weather or the winds, nor can we directly control what happens beyond our borders," said Wong.
"But we will do everything we can to protect Singaporeans, while working with our neighbours to address the underlying causes of the haze."
The smoke is a direct consequence of the fires, which four people lost their lives battling in East Java's Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park on Thursday, Indonesia's forestry ministry said in a statement.
Two others suffered serious burns and are receiving further medical treatment.
"This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation," it said, adding personnel safety remained a primary concern.
The forestry department in the same statement said there was a significant jump in hotspots in several areas in six "priority provinces" where 615 so-called hotspots were detected.
A hotspot is a location where a satellite detects an unusually high temperature, indicating a potential fire or other strong heat source.

Senior Brethren had 'brief' meeting with far-right figures during election

Brethren Church member admits to 'brief' meeting with far-right figures during 2025 federal election campaign
In short:
The spiritual leader of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church has denied allegations he coordinated church members to volunteer in the 2025 federal election campaign.
His son Gareth Hales says he encouraged members of the church, but did not instruct them to participate.
What's next?
A final report into the 2025 election is due by the end of the year.
The spiritual leader of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church (PBCC) has denied coordinating a pro-Liberal campaign in the 2025 federal election, as his son acknowledged meeting far-right figures accused of targeting MPs.
Several politicians have alleged Brethren members intimidated rival candidates and campaigners, while Nine newspapers reported church members paid far-right influencers, including Neo-Nazi associates, to follow and heckle the prime minister.
Giving evidence before the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters, senior elder Bruce Hales denied any knowledge of a coordinated campaign by the church.
"I did not coordinate such activities. I did not direct such activities. I did not fund such activities," he said.
"If anti-social acts were committed by any individual of any faith … I cannot answer for them".
Gareth Hales, Mr Hales's son, said he met with Chris De Bruyne and Morgan C Jonas, figures described by independent MP Andrew Gee as "far right", during the campaign.
But he described the encounters as "brief" business meetings, and said he was unaware of their political affiliations at the time.
Mr Hales Jnr also revealed he met then-opposition leader Peter Dutton at a petrol station media event, which he had heard about through "word of mouth".
"I don't recall, but I dare say it was probably a friend of a friend," he said.
He denied allegations that a company he formerly associated with, Sante Global, paid Neo-Nazi associates to disrupt Anthony Albanese's campaign.
Mr Hales Jnr said his own involvement in the election was limited to volunteering at four polling booths and maintained he had only a "very, very light-touch" role.
He admitted to encouraging some church members, but did not specify how many people he counselled, or the nature of his encouragement.
"I didn't direct or coordinate, but yes, if I was on a call, a leader is expected to encourage, inspire, if at all possible," he said.
It was also revealed members of the PBCC, which has a global congregation of 56,000, had met with US President Donald Trump in New York, although Mr Hale was not present.
The line of questioning of both senior PBCC men was likened to a "witch hunt" by Coalition members, with Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie going as far as accusing the committee of religious discrimination.
Where did 'Make Australia Smile Again' come from?
The committee spent considerable time litigating the origin of signs reported in several electorates that read "Make Australia Smile Again".
Mr Hales was questioned about the similarity to a sermon he gave the month before the election, in which he urged parishioners to pray for "good government" because Australia "needed to be happy again, smiling again".
He agreed that it was rare for his message, sent online to church members around the world, to be misinterpreted.
"Very, very rarely do I have to go back and explain what I meant," he said.
Asked whether his four sons, one of whom was later photographed campaigning, interpreted that as an endorsement for the Liberal Party, Mr Hales said he did not know.
"I think if they had asked me about them and asked permission [to campaign], I would have denied it," he said.
"The first indication I had that my eldest son was out on the polling booths was a photograph in the paper, and I was a bit surprised."
Mr Hales Jnr gave evidence he never saw the "Make Australia Smile Again" signs and was surprised when the Liberal Party's internal review described Brethren members involved in the campaign as a support group.
"I was not aware that was how the Liberals regarded us," he said.
When pressed on who he meant by "us", Mr Hales said he was referring simply to members of the Australian public.
Fiery Coalition members label questioning a 'witch hunt'
Chair Jerome Laxale said there had been "thousands and thousands" of church members who "flooded" polling booths during the campaign.
Mr Hales Jnr pushed back, asking how Mr Laxale knew those people at the polling booths were Brethren members.
"It was well documented," Mr Laxale said.
The inquiry was littered with interjections from Coalition members, who described the line of questioning as a "witch hunt".
Liberal senator Richard Colbeck repeatedly interrupted questioning and labelled the hearing "ridiculous".
"This is not the Spanish Inquisition," Senator Colbeck said.
Bruce Hales's role in the church
Mr Hales told the committee he succeeded his father, John Hales, as the senior elder and was not elected but assumed the position "spontaneously".
He said members followed his teachings, which they believed came from God.
"I would think that they would say that what I get, I get from the Lord," he said.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese previously described the Brethren as a cult, which Mr Hales rejected.
"We are not a cult. We are Christians,"
Mr Hales said.
Mr Hales said although he was the spiritual Brethren leader, he did not have authority over individual members, who were "entitled to make their own decisions".
Mr Hales Jnr said he did take part in the campaign as a volunteer for the Liberal Party in his capacity as a "private citizen".
He said campaigning alongside someone — in this case, fellow Brethren members — did not mean "adopting every opinion they have ever expressed".
"The committee chair is now taking a dangerous step, using a group of volunteers' religious identity to associate them publicly with ideologies apparently held by others," he said.

'I want children to know what it felt like to be held hostage': Keith Siegel speaks out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:41:55 UTC
15:41:55 KST

Since returning from captivity in Gaza, I have been trying to relearn how to live. To be a husband, a father, a grandfather and a member of my family again. To return to the small things that once seemed obvious. Sitting with my family, leaving the house, making plans for tomorrow.
But coming home does not erase what happened, nor does it bring us back to the lives we had before October 7.
For 484 days, I was held hostage in Gaza. Days during which my freedom, my sense of security and even my ability to make the most basic decisions about my own life were taken from me.
During that time, my family was forced to confront an unimaginable reality. My wife, Aviva, who was abducted alongside me and released before I was, returned home but continued to live with the reality of my captivity every passing day.
I came home to a family that had been waiting for me, but also to a family that had endured an incredibly difficult period of its own. We have all changed. There is a deep desire to return to life, to enjoy simple moments and to be together again. But there are also memories, pain and struggles that do not end on the day you come home. Recovery is a long process, and even the smallest things can be challenging.
I share this because I want people to understand that the story of October 7 did not end when I was released from captivity. It continues to affect me and my family every day, just as it does thousands of others who experienced that terrible day and the difficult period that followed.
Each of them has a different story. Some lost the people they loved most. Others hid for hours as terrorists moved around their homes. Some survived the massacre at the Nova music festival. Others fought to defend their families and communities. There were also members of the security and emergency services who, during those terrible hours, risked their lives and struggled to save others.
Each carries a part of that day's story, a part that no one else can tell in their place.
There is no single story of October 7
Twenty years from now, when children in Israel learn about October 7, what will they know about what happened to us? They will certainly learn about the attack, those who were murdered, the abductions and the war. They will see photographs and videos and hear about decisions that were made and failures that occurred.
But I also want them to know what a mother felt as she sat with her children in a safe room, hearing terrorists outside the door. What a family went through when they did not know whether they would ever see their loved ones again. What it means to be held hostage, cut off from the world and the people you love, without knowing whether you will ever return.
Our national memory cannot be built solely on headlines, ceremonies and memorials. It must also be built on the voices of the people who were there, because there is no single story of October 7. There are thousands of stories, and each one is part of the truth.
In the coming years, books will be written, films will be made and memorial ceremonies will be held. All of these are important, but I believe that we, the people who experienced these events, must play a central role in shaping how they are remembered.
Not everyone who was affected is able or willing to speak, and the decision not to share or talk about what happened must also be respected. But those who choose to tell their stories must be given the space to do so in their own way and in their own words.
In captivity, I was stripped of control over my life. Today, as a free man once again, I can choose when to speak, what to share and how to tell the story of what I went through. That choice has enormous meaning for me.
More than just a date in the history books
This is one of the reasons I chose to take part in the "Salon Otef" initiative, led by the organization "255," of which I am a member. The organization brings together returned hostages and their families, supports them through the complex challenges that continue long after they return home, and works to ensure that our stories are heard in our own voices and told in the ways we choose.
Through Salon Otef, hundreds of survivors, returned hostages, family members and members of the security and emergency services meet with tens of thousands of people. Not through a television screen, but face to face. People sit together, listen and ask questions. It is precisely through these personal encounters that people can understand things that are difficult to convey in a newspaper headline.
This week, I will travel to Ethiopia, where I will hold a Salon Otef gathering with the Jewish and Israeli community in Addis Ababa. Alongside members of the public, diplomats, government representatives and civil society leaders will also attend. There, too, thousands of miles from Israel, I will speak about the abduction, captivity, coming home and life afterward.
October 7 is part of the history of the State of Israel, but it is also part of the collective memory of the entire Jewish people. It is important to me that our stories reach Jewish and Israeli communities around the world, and that they hear them directly from those who lived through them.
Three years have passed since October 7. For many of us, the struggle continues and will probably continue for many years to come. I do not know whether it is possible to become exactly the person I was before that day. But I do know that I want to keep living, to be with my family and to keep telling my story.
I do not want October 7 to become just another date in the history books 20 years from now. I want future generations to know the people behind the numbers, the lives they led, what they endured and the journeys they have been on ever since.
We cannot change what happened to us. But we have both a responsibility and a right to determine how our story is told and how it will be remembered.
Keith Siegel was abducted from his home in Kfar Aza on October 7 and returned from captivity in Gaza after 484 days. This week, he will hold a special Salon Otef gathering for the Jewish and Israeli community in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

In Israel, Netanyahu’s ultimate legacy is the opposition he has forged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:41:15 UTC
15:41:15 KST

In Israel, Netanyahu’s ultimate legacy is the opposition he has forged
As Israel heads to the polls on October 27, Benjamin Netanyahu’s most enduring domestic legacy may be the right-wing opposition he faces, analysts say.
Benjamin Netanyahu had barely reached the United Nations podium when a sea of delegates jumped from their seats and began walking out in protest at the Israeli prime minister’s speech at the UN General Assembly in late September.
Undeterred, a grinning Netanyahu, who is seeking re-election later this month while being wanted by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes in Gaza, shot back: “If there are any other moral cowards who haven’t left the hall, please do so now.”
For his supporters watching in Israel, it was precisely what they wanted to hear.
“When they see Netanyahu at the United Nations,” his former aide, Mitchell Barak, told Al Jazeera, “that’s what they want – and it’s hard for them to imagine anyone else doing that.”
He added: “For many in Israel, but not all, he’s the only man that can truly lead Israel. He makes them proud to be Jewish.”
On October 27, Israel must choose between Netanyahu and an assorted number of rivals who are unified by little other than their absolute opposition to Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
In the eyes of both his supporters and his opponents, as well as much of the world, Netanyahu has become the face of modern Israel.
Born in Tel Aviv in 1949 to Benzion Netanyahu and Tzila Segal, he spent his early years between Israel and the United States, the few constants in his life being the profoundly pessimistic views of his father – a right-wing historian who saw a world fundamentally opposed to the existence of Jews – and the military legacy of his brother, Yonatan, who was killed in 1976 while leading a raid to rescue hijacked Israeli hostages in Entebbe, Uganda.
Since then, Netanyahu has gone through numerous iterations.
In 1982, he was named deputy chief of mission at the Israeli embassy in Washington, DC. Two years later, he was appointed Israel’s ambassador to the UN, before returning to Israel to join the cabinet of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir as deputy foreign minister in 1988.
In 1996, Netanyahu became Israel’s youngest prime minister, leading the first in a series of coalitions that also saw him serving a record 12-year tenure from 2009 to 2021. He returned to power for a sixth term the next year, leading the most far-right government in Israel’s history.
From the outset of his political career, he faced growing accusations of having deliberately engineered division to further his own political and personal ends.
“Netanyahu is the perfect encapsulation of Israel’s political polarisation,” said political analyst Nimrod Flaschenberg. Describing Netanyahu as “always” being “in campaigning mode”, he said the Israeli leader “is very good at building coalitions that reflect public opinion, as well as steering that opinion in his own direction”.
Hardwired division
Under Netanyahu’s leadership, Israel has continued to lurch to the right, rejecting the path towards a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict set in motion by his predecessor, the assassinated Yitzhak Rabin. At the same time, vast swaths of the Israeli electorate have also grown accustomed to the violent expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and reconciled themselves to the genocide in Gaza following the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023 – for which many still blame Netanyahu for alleged security failures – as well as the multiple wars waged at his direction since.
In July 2018, Netanyahu’s coalition passed the Nation-State Law, declaring the right to national self-determination “unique to the Jewish people”, stripping Arabic of its status as an official language and making the development of Jewish settlements a national value. In the law’s wake, settler violence in the occupied West Bank has surged, with the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recording 1,291 attacks in 2023 and 1,835 in 2025. At least 1,071 Palestinians, including 233 children, have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces or settlers since October 7, 2023, according to OCHA, amid what a senior UN official called “virtually no accountability”.
More immediately, Netanyahu’s current coalition has seen some of Israel’s most controversial figures – such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, convicted of incitement to racism and support for a “terrorist” group, and the explicitly pro-settlement Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich – placed at the heart of power.
“Netanyahu didn’t create the racism and fascism in Israel, but he’s helped it,” said outgoing parliamentarian Aida Touma-Sliman, of the left-wing Hadash party. “He’s smart. He knows exactly what he’s doing when he includes people like Smotrich and Ben-Gvir in his government, and he knows the outcome of those appointments.”
“He thrives in chaos,” said Barak, Netanyahu’s former aide from the 1990s. “He’s all about the big picture, of ends justifying means.”
Running through the prime minister’s recent military campaigns have been his long-standing battles against any kind of domestic judicial restraint. Dogged by corruption cases dating back to 2019, which could see him serve time in prison if convicted, he has been locked in a confrontation with the same legal establishment attempting to hold him to account.
In January 2023, he and his right-wing allies sought to overhaul the judiciary, shaking off much of the oversight of the courts over government action. The proposals led to demonstrations on an unprecedented scale, with hundreds of thousands taking to the streets to protest against the contentious move. In June 2024, Netanyahu went so far as to appear to suggest that the division created by his reforms was somehow responsible for his own heavily criticised response to the October 7 attack.
The ‘devil’ you know
Still, while opinion polls show Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies tied with the broad anti-Netanyahu bloc of similarly right-wing and militaristic parties, the prime minister’s support has weakened. Likud won 32 seats in the 2022 election, but most recent polls project a gain of about 20 to 22, with former supporters appearing to shift either to the opposition or to harder-line right-wing parties.
The alliance opposing Netanyahu has yet to nominate an official leader, but former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is widely seen as its most likely candidate for prime minister.
“We need to be clear about this,” said Barak. “He’s essentially running unopposed. It’s Netanyahu versus a coalition of opponents.”
“Think about it,” said Touma-Sliman, pointing out the double standards after the prominent leader of a party representing Palestinian citizens of Israel was forced to withdraw from the election over his remarks about the Gaza war. “He’s helped create a system where Arab MK Sami Abu Shehadeh is barred from running, and he, a war criminal who has led his country through a genocide, is not”.
For his supporters, noted Flaschenberg, Netanyahu “remains Israel’s only possible leader”. But for his opponents, “He’s the devil. He’s corruption personified, responsible for everything leading up to October 7 and everything afterwards.”
However, his ultimate legacy may still lie ahead, the analyst suggested, recalling the words of former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who once cited the rightward tilt of the opposition as her greatest legacy.
“Netanyahu’s legacy lies with the opposition. All of the main contenders are right-wing, militaristic and ultimately racist,” said Flaschenberg. “That’s Netanyahu’s legacy.”
