UK ‘an outlier in Europe’ for letting Farage and other politicians present TV shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:54 UTC
15:00:54 KST

The UK has been confirmed as an outlier in Europe for allowing Nigel Farage and other serving politicians to present TV shows covering current affairs, according to an unprecedented analysis of broadcasting rules.
Farage is one of a series of Reform UK figures who are permitted to present shows on the rightwing network GB News. The Reform MP Lee Anderson and former candidate Matt Goodwin also have regular slots on the channel.
Their status as presenters has led to repeated concerns about the enforcement of Britain’s rules on impartial broadcasting.
Last month, Farage used his first GB News show for six months to defend his party’s decision to accept two record £36m donations from the crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo.
However, an international study has confirmed that the UK’s decision to allow politicians to present such shows is highly unusual across Europe. In 35 of the 37 European nations studied, regulators found no recent examples of serving politicians presenting news or current affairs programmes. Only Iceland, which has a population of about 400,000 people, and Malta bucked the trend.
In Malta, political parties are even permitted to own television channels. There have been instances where MPs have presented interview programmes, although according to its regulator these are not the norm.
Eight countries – including France, Georgia and Norway – expressly ban politicians from presenting news or current affairs programmes, either through broadcasting legislation or other restrictions.
The practice is constrained indirectly in 26 countries via rules covering impartiality, transparency or independence from government.
Three countries – Armenia, Finland and Malta – had no specific legislation or regulation covering the issue. However, regulators in Armenia and Finland reported no examples of it occurring.
The study, by an academic from the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism for the Demos thinktank, will be used as evidence by critics who believe that Ofcom, Britain’s media regulator, has failed to protect impartiality by allowing the politician-led shows.
Ofcom has said that such shows are within broadcasting rules because they are classed as “current affairs” shows by the watchdog, rather than news programmes – a distinction that has been challenged by critics, given the politicians regularly discuss some of the biggest news stories of the day.
The analysis, by the research associate Dr James Painter, found the issue had only caused a serious debate in the UK. “This demonstrates the extent to which the UK is an outlier in Europe with regards to the practice of political presenting news and/or current affairs programmes and the regulatory framework that surrounds it,” the analysis concluded.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, has previously raised concerns about allowing serving politicians to present TV shows and has said she was “exploring action in this space”. However, it remains unclear whether she is considering a change in the law.
GB News has always said Reform politicians are allowed to present current affairs programmes under Ofcom’s rules – a point it has proved in court. Angelos Frangopoulos, its chief executive, has also said its coverage includes a range of political perspectives.
An Ofcom spokesperson said: “Ofcom’s broadcasting code … is clear that no politician may be used as a newsreader, interviewer or reporter in any news programmes unless, exceptionally, it is editorially justified.
“While politicians are permitted to present non-news programmes – provided they are not standing in an election taking place – such programmes must still comply with the other due impartiality rules in the code.
“The code contains rules which Ofcom considers best secure the standards objectives set by parliament – including the special protection afforded to news over non-news content. Changes to the standards objectives are rightly a matter for government and parliament.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:54 UTC
15:00:54 KST

The director Jonathan Glazer has called Israel’s retaliation against NAZA’s film-makers and the military figures interviewed in the award-winning documentary “much more venal” than anticipated.
Since the film’s release, the Israeli government has denounced it and pursued those involved, announcing plans aimed at stripping citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers; accused NAZA’s co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, of treason; and ordered top legal and security officials to find and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the documentary for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
Speaking to the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.
He noted that it was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.
“Both films deal with dehumanisation,” Glazer said. “And how we get to where we do as a species by othering and dehumanising, and what that then leads to.”
The Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA in an attempt to counter the film’s findings. When asked whether he was surprised by the intense reaction of the Israeli government to NAZA, Glazer said some of it was expected but that, “in my point of view, it was much more venal” than anticipated.
Abraham said the film allows viewers to look at the “mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings”, and Szor said the idea to shoot footage looking inside Tel Aviv citizens’ apartments was to focus on the “ritual” of people gathering around the TV to watch the “news and to see the absence or justification” of the devastation happening in Gaza.
NAZA is in UK cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. When the film opened in Italy last month, it surpassed the Marvel movie Avengers Endgame: Encore to open at No 1.
The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.
Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize.
Israeli government officials have attempted to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.
The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while the military has issued a 10-page response to NAZA, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
Demonstrators have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.
Szor and Abraham addressed the backlash to their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”
The Zone of Interest won the Oscar for best international film in 2024. Accepting the award, Glazer said he refuted his “Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people” in Gaza and Israel, comments that led to backlash and an outpouring of support.
He went on to say: “All our choices were made to reflect and confront us in the present, not to say look what they did then, but rather look what we do now. Our film shows where dehumanisation leads at its worst. It’s shaped all of our past and present.”

Four years after the promises of Cop15, our biodiversity targets are slipping away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:53 UTC
15:00:53 KST

The world has lost its way on nature once again. Next week, biodiversity Cop17 begins in Yerevan, Armenia, and expectations are low. Very low.
Almost four years ago, governments reached an historic agreement at the biodiversity Cop15 to halt the destruction of Earth’s ecosystems – to rapturous applause in Montreal, Canada. I still remember the excitement in the hall in the early hours of that freezing December morning.
Governments had never met a self-mandated target on biodiversity loss, but there was a sense after the Covid-19 pandemic that this time really would be different. The 23-point deal included targets to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore 30% of the planet’s degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems, and tackle $500bn of environmentally damaging subsidies. Almost every country in the world, apart from the US and the Vatican, backed it.
Yes, the agreement was flawed, and barely matched what the science tells us we need to do to stop biodiversity loss. But it was a serious, considered plan to tackle the underlying causes of the largest loss of life since the dinosaurs (this time, humans are the asteroid).
Since then, though, action has fallen short. More on why that is, what it means and what is at stake at Cop17, after this week’s climate headlines.
Essential reads
- A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry
- ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
- ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war
In focus
The summit in Yerevan is about assessing progress towards the targets, and the scorecard does not look good. In preparatory meetings governments have acknowledged (pdf) that they are way off track from meeting any of the targets. The traffic-light system used to rate actions towards the targets from countries is awash with yellow, orange and red.
“Unless collective implementation accelerates rapidly, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved,” the pre-Cop17 report reads. “Parties and other actors have taken action to address all 23 targets; however, no target presents a fully positive picture. The available evidence indicates that there are gaps in the collective progress. Without urgently addressing these gaps and barriers, it will not be possible to meet the 2030 targets and mission, in turn placing achievement of the 2050 goals and vision [to live in harmony with nature] in jeopardy.”
This time, it is hard to be too angry with some governments. Countries including Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort, bringing back the caspian tiger. The EU did attempt to enact the targets with the nature restoration law – but it quickly became a culture-wars issue. Swathes of the world, though, have turned against action on the environment.
Donald Trump’s return to the White House has been catastrophic for the conservation sector, caught in his administration clampdown on the climate and “woke” policies. Through USAID and partner organisations, the US government provided, on average, 12.1% of the world’s biodiversity funding between 2015 and 2022, according to the OECD. Almost all of that has gone, hitting everything from anti-rhino poaching initiatives in east Africa, to efforts to combat illegal fishing in the Galápagos.
Power has also drained out of multilateral organisations such as the UN. Tech billionaires and the architects of AI are more powerful than many countries. Trump’s second term has seen a return to might-is-right politics that is dismissive of the international cooperation needed to make an agreement like this a reality.
So what next? Cop17 in Armenia is likely to be a moment where the calamity of the last four years crystallises – and governments must try to pick up the pieces.
“There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, who was UK environment minister when that landmark Cop15 deal was reached in 2022. “That’s where we are today.”

The paper recommends freezing the “national living wage” at £12.71 for five years and abolishing the Low Pay Commission (LPC), the independent body that recommends the yearly increase.
It also recommends returning employer national insurance contributions to pre-April 2025 levels and reinstating the two-year qualifying period for unfair dismissal, which was abolished under Labour’s Employment Rights Act.
The paper says a five-year freeze could result in an increase of about 270,000 young people in work, by suggesting that for every 1 percentage point increase in the minimum wage there is a a 0.37 percentage point decrease in the youth employment rate.
The report’s authors said they “do not present these findings as costless to workers” and that minimum wage workers’ purchasing power would be eroded by 9% to 12% over the five years due to projected inflation of 2% to 2.5%, a cumulative loss over five years of about £8,900.
The Labour business minister Kate Dearden said the recommendations were “tin-eared” and showed a pattern from the Conservatives of disparaging the minimum wage.
“It’s clear that Kemi Badenoch’s top team are determined that the lowest paid workers should be worse off,” she said. “The Conservatives opposed the minimum wage when the last Labour government introduced it, and now they’re showing again how little they understand the pressures facing people on the lowest pay. It’s the same old Tories, they haven’t changed.
“This Labour government believes that if you work hard, you should be able to get on in life. That’s why we’ve boosted work for the lowest paid, introduced more rights at work, and are giving people breathing space they deserve on the cost of living.”
Labour has previously said it intends to equalise the different rates of minimum wage – promising to give 18- to 20-year-olds the full rate. But rising youth unemployment has led to a debate at the top of government over how fast it should meet its promise.
The LPC last year recommended a 4.1% increase in the main rate of the minimum wage, and an 8.5% rise in the youth rate. The rates now stand at £12.71 and £10.85 respectively.
The commission will tell the government in October what it is recommending for the financial year starting on 1 April 2027, though ministers are not bound to accept the commission’s recommendations.
Earlier this year, ministers changed their guidance to the LPC to reflect the concerns in government over unemployment among young people, in the hope that it might recommend a lower level this year to make it easier for employers to take on younger staff.
The LPC has said it does not believe wage rises are contributing to higher youth unemployment rates. “While the commission recognises that labour market outcomes for young people have deteriorated over the past two years, we are not aware of any robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to these falls,” it said.

‘A haven of soft light, warm sunshine and sandy beaches’: readers’ favourite autumn escapes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

Collioure is a Mediterranean dream
Last October, while I was cycling around south-west France, near the Spanish border, a tip from a local waiter led me to Collioure, near Perpignan. The town was like a Mediterranean dream, where the summer crowds had faded, leaving behind a peaceful, artistic haven of soft light, warm sunshine, cobbled streets, sandy beaches – and the Pyrenees as a backdrop. In the early evening, the still balmy autumn air was perfect for wandering through the quiet, pastel-coloured alleyways of the Le Mouré district to enjoy €5 off-season happy hour wine with fish tapas. I had planned to stay a weekend but ended up staying a week, seduced by Collioure’s perfect autumn cocktail of chilled Catalan culture and sunkissed seaside sensuality.
 
April
Peaceful Portuguese sunsets
Sitting outside in T-shirt and shorts on the deck of a boat gliding along the Tagus River in Lisbon, sipping a glass of crisp Portuguese wine as the setting autumn sun illuminated the pastel-coloured hills, is a lasting travel memory for me. October temperatures were still in the mid-20s, perfect for exploring fascinating areas on foot, or hanging out of trams as they rattled up and down the cobbled streets. In the evenings, I joined local people basking in the remaining warmth of the year at outdoor cafes or waterside tavernas like Ponto Final, enjoying coffee and pastries, or anchovies and beer, while watching magnificent sunsets without the summer masses.
 
Nicoletta
Wild times in St Davids, Pembrokeshire
My autumn escape is St Davids on the Pembrokeshire coast. Once the summer crowds disappear, it feels wonderfully wild and tranquil. We walk the coast path towards Whitesands, stopping to watch for seals below the cliffs, before heading back into tiny St Davids for something warm to eat. The beaches are often almost empty and, even when the weather turns, the dramatic sea and windswept coastline are part of the charm. My tip is to visit in early autumn; pack proper walking boots and layers, and embrace the weather – you get one of Britain’s loveliest coastlines almost to yourself.
 
Tess
Baroque beauty in eastern Germany
Görlitz makes for a fascinating autumnal base, with its location on the German-Polish border to the east of Dresden. The highlights were day excursions to Bad Muskau, where there is a wonderful baroque palace, and the Rakotzbrücke (Devil’s Bridge), reached by a narrow-gauge forest railway (waldeisenbahn.de). It’s a part of Germany rarely visited, but those who go there will be rewarded with amazing photographs.
 
Martin
Bliss on a lesser-visited Canary island
The Canary Islands are well-trodden choices for autumn sun, but the island of El Hierro remains a wilder alternative to Tenerife or Lanzarote. The scenery is beautiful and bizarrely varied: from pine forests to black volcanic lava flows – most of which you’ll have to yourself. You can pass hours exploring the rugged coastlines, where volcanic swimming holes such as Charco Azul can be found. We spent a blissful few hours there, relaxing on the rocks and looking out at the Atlantic. There are no big resorts but plenty of guest houses and smaller hotels, and sunshine is almost guaranteed into November.
 
Leo Mark
Dramatic Devon walks
We stayed in Woolacombe, north Devon, with our three-year-old in October 2023 and the off-season suited us well. The three-mile beach gave us room for proper sandcastle engineering, and the Atlantic offered drama rather than deckchair weather. We watched the sunset turn the sea orange and purple from the hill above the bay. We could walk into the village, then use Woolacombe as a base for Mortehoe and the South West Coast Path. Pack waterproofs as well as sunglasses: north Devon makes no promises. But on a bright autumn day, those enormous sands feel almost privately hired.
 
Katharina Parsons
Coast, culture and cable cars on Madeira
Funchal on Madeira is my pick for an autumn escape because it still feels properly alive after summer. The seafront is made for slow walks in the sunshine, with cafes and gardens open year-round. You can browse the colourful Mercado dos Lavradores, ride the cable car for views over the terracotta rooftops and Atlantic, then cool off at one of the city’s lidos. The weather is pleasantly warm rather than overpowering, while the mountains and levada (aqueduct) walks are within easy reach. It combines coast, culture and dramatic scenery without feeling like a resort that closes down for winter.
 
Bernice
Clifftops and crab rolls in the Scottish Borders
If you’re looking for a cracking wee coastal escape, head straight to St Abbs in the Scottish Borders. My wife and I absolutely fell in love with its rugged charm and bonny views. First off, Marvel fans will know it as New Asgard from Avengers: Endgame, and taking a selfie by the official sign set the right tone. Beyond the film fame, the dramatic clifftop walk up to St Abb’s Head is brilliant, packed with seabirds and proper fresh sea air. Afterwards, grab a fresh crab roll down at the harbour cafe – nae hassle, just proper good cheer.
 
Craig
Nonstop sun in a Cretan haven
Autumn came brutal and early to Crete this month. But the ferocious northerly that drenched the northern coast got stuck on the White Mountains. And on just one tiny south-west speck of the island, the sun shone all and every day. Palaiochora is a year-round magic place anyway. No big hotels. Still proudly Greek. A place where the town’s rhythms are set by the comings and goings of the Loutro ferry. But this past week, while thunder stalked the mountains, we swam and walked every day. “We’re unique,” said the man at the cafe. “Please don’t tell anyone.” What have I done?
 
Kay Jones
Winning tip: Fiestas and feasts in Zaragoza, Spain
For an autumn city break, Zaragoza comes alive during the Fiestas del Pilar in October. We spent a week there, wandering bustling streets lined with people, many in traditional dress, queueing to lay flowers at the vast floral tribute to the Virgin Mary in Plaza del Pilar. Along the river, food stalls served Aragonese specialities, from chistorra (sausage) and stews to roast chestnuts and sweet wine. Between festivities, we explored the stunning Aljafería Palace and discovered tiny tapas bars tucked down side streets. The city felt wonderfully local, lively and full of surprises.
 
Carrie

Ministers have been asked to extend Service Pupil Premium funding and wraparound childcare to the children of Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel, and have replied that existing arrangements are kept under review, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Rachel Gilmour, the Liberal Democrat member for Tiverton and Minehead, asked what assessment had been made of the adequacy of welfare and family support for Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel and their families, and whether eligibility for schemes open to armed forces families would be extended to them.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “The Ministry of Defence recognises the importance of supporting Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA) personnel and their families. RFA personnel and their families have access to a range of welfare and family support services, and we continue to keep these arrangements under review to ensure they remain appropriate to the needs of the workforce.
“Support available for RFA personnel and their families includes enhanced leave entitlements and tailored assistance through mechanisms such as Occupational Health, keep-in-touch days, and reasonable workplace adjustments. Further support is delivered through the Employee Assistance Programme, the Defence Health and Wellbeing Portfolio, and Family and People Services, with the RFA workforce also benefitting from an extended welfare network under the umbrella of expert services, including the Navy Families Federation, ensuring holistic support for employees and their families.”
Royal Fleet Auxiliary personnel are civilians employed by the Ministry of Defence who crew the ships that fuel, supply and support the Royal Navy at sea, and their conditions sit outside the arrangements that cover service families.
The Royal Fleet Auxiliary employs around 1,800 people and crews the tankers and stores ships that keep the Royal Navy at sea, along with the Bay class landing ships and the aviation training ship Argus. Its sailors are civil servants and not service personnel, which is the distinction the question was aimed at. Pay and conditions have been a running problem, with members of the RMT and Nautilus International taking strike action in 2024 over a long period of below-inflation awards, and the service has struggled to hold on to qualified officers.

Chen Rung-rou (陳容柔), a coordinator at the Taiwan International Workers Association, said Taiwan should establish a direct hire system for foreign contract workers, which would allow them to voice grievances to the authorities.
Shih Yi-hsiang (施逸翔), a coordinator at the Taiwan Association for Human Rights, called on the Ministry of Labor to launch a full investigation into the alleged abuse and to review the contract performance system.
In response, the Ministry of Labor vowed to step up inspections and rein in companies that use the contract system to evade labor regulations. The ministry said in a statement Thursday that foreign workers dispatched to Taiwan under such contracts must receive the employment protections and occupational injury compensation guaranteed under law.

No breakthrough: EU budget talks have stalled
Kyiv • UNN
EU leaders failed to reach an agreement on the long-term budget at the summit in Brussels. The countries are arguing over cutting spending and increasing the budget.
European leaders failed to agree on the EU's long-term budget on the first day of the summit. UNN reports this with reference to DW.
Details
Talks among European leaders on the EU budget for the next seven years failed to produce a breakthrough and will continue in December, according to information received from sources in the German government overnight into Friday, October 16, by AFP. According to the publication's sources, several positions clashed during the summit of heads of state and government of EU member states in Brussels, leading to "controversial debates." As the agency notes, these positions were known even before the talks began. Some countries, including Germany, Austria, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands and Finland, are calling for spending cuts, while others, including France, Spain and Poland, are advocating an increase in the EU budget.
Last summer, the European Commission presented a draft long-term budget worth almost two trillion euros. Ireland, which holds the presidency of the Council of the EU, proposed cutting the budget by €140 billion (approximately 8%).
Ireland's proposal envisages cuts to EU budget spending in the areas of competitiveness, scientific research, defense and foreign policy.
The EU wants to agree on the budget by the end of the year
At the summit, France focused on introducing new pan-European levies that would make it possible to increase the budget without raising member states' contributions. In particular, the proposal concerns levies on digital services, crypto-assets and online gambling.
EU wants to impose a tax on U.S. big tech - media07.10.26, 13:08 • 5328 views
The next EU summit will take place in December. Many of the EU's 27 member states want to approve the long-term budget by the end of the year, since in 2027 euroskeptic and populist forces may come to power in several countries as a result of elections.
Thus, far-right politician Marine Le Pen may win the presidential election in France. As AFP reports, the country's current head, Emmanuel Macron, has already warned that in such a case reaching an agreement on the EU budget would be "difficult."
Before the talks began, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called for the draft budget proposed by the European Commission to be "substantially" reduced and categorically rejected the idea of allocating additional funds to the traditional major spending areas—agriculture and cohesion policy.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker did not rule out the possibility that the talks could drag on and continue next year.

Ukraine pushes for European alternatives to US air defences and Starlink amid tensions with Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:59:59 UTC
14:59:59 KST

As tensions between Kyiv and Washington deepen Ukraine is looking to Europe to help secure its long-term defence and technological independence. A senior Ukrainian presidential official told Euronews that concrete plans are already taking shape.
Ukraine is pushing ahead with plans to develop European alternatives to US-made air defence systems and Starlink satellite communications, with concrete discussions already under way and Kyiv expecting progress considerably sooner than sceptics anticipate, a senior Ukrainian presidential official has told Euronews.
In an exclusive interview with the Europe Today programme ahead of Friday's EU summit in Brussels, Ihor Zhovkva, deputy head of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office, said Ukraine was seeking to reduce its reliance on American capabilities as uncertainty over Washington's support places growing pressure on Europe to strengthen its own defences.
"We are, of course, relying on the unique capabilities provided by the United States, whether air defence systems or Starlink," Zhovkva said.
"But Ukraine has already begun substantive discussions with European countries about a European air defence system."
He pointed to FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile programme launched in Paris in July, saying discussions had progressed to direct engagement between defence companies.
"We need a European equivalent of an air defence system," he said, adding that Ukraine intended to take a leading role in its development.
Kyiv is also pursuing talks on a European alternative to Starlink, with Zhovkva confirming that negotiations were under way but declining to disclose further details.
"European countries must have their own corresponding system," he said.
Zhovkva argued that both projects were essential not only to Ukraine's defence but also to Europe's wider security.
Asked whether developing these systems would take too long, Zhovkva dismissed such concerns.
"We have a clear timetable and deadlines," he said. "It will be much faster than ten or fifteen years, and even faster than five."
He declined to give a specific date.
Europe faces growing pressure to sustain Ukraine's defence
The plans come amid mounting tensions between Kyiv and Washington, including over US President Donald Trump's pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes against Russian oil infrastructure, and growing concerns about the reliability of American military support.
Russia has meanwhile intensified its aerial campaign against Ukraine, with fresh attacks on energy infrastructure raising fears of another difficult winter.
Zhovkva said securing additional air defence systems and interceptor missiles, alongside measures to protect Ukraine's energy infrastructure, would be among Zelenskyy's main priorities at the EU summit.
"Every country that can provide such assistance, whether systems or missiles, should do so," he said, adding that those unable to supply equipment should contribute financially.
Whether Europe can make up for any reduction in American military assistance, however, remains uncertain.
Zhovkva acknowledged that despite substantial contributions from countries such as Germany, European support was still falling short of Ukraine's needs.
With Kyiv facing a further funding shortfall next year, he stressed the importance of maintaining existing military commitments while securing additional European financial support.
Europe must have a seat at negotiating table
Zhovkva argued that European security guarantees should form the foundation of Ukraine's long-term security arrangements, identifying sustained support for its armed forces, joint defence production and EU membership as essential elements.
"The foundation of security guarantees for Ukraine is a strong, powerful army," he said, stressing the importance of reliable long-term financing.
"Without a clear understanding that Ukraine will become a member of the EU, we cannot speak about full-fledged security guarantees."
Yet despite growing tensions with Washington, Zhovkva acknowledged that European guarantees could not work alone.
"They cannot exist without support from the United States of America," he said.
With Washington seeking to revive diplomatic efforts to end the war, Zhovkva reaffirmed Kyiv's readiness to negotiate, while insisting that European partners must be involved at every stage, including any eventual talks between leaders.
"Ukraine is ready for negotiations now," he said.
"Europe, in the broader sense of the word, must be present at the table," he added, arguing that Ukraine's future security was inseparable from that of the wider continent.

Türkiye adds 12,000 hectares to forest conservation network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:57:27 UTC
14:57:27 KST

Steep forested slopes with green and yellow foliage rise above a lake, where trees along the shoreline are reflected in the water. (AA Photo)
Türkiye has expanded its strict conservation forest network to 60 locations by shielding nearly 12,000 additional hectares from human intervention, aiming to secure water resources and combat climate threats.
The General Directorate of Forestry, operating under the Agriculture and Forestry Ministry, increased the number of designated forests from 55 to 60, according to data compiled by the state-run Anadolu Agency.
The five additions raised the network’s total area from 246,446 hectares to 258,387 hectares, marking an increase of 11,941 hectares across the country.
The expansion forms part of broader efforts to protect the ecological value and resilience of existing forests alongside increasing woodland cover. It supports Türkiye’s 2053 net-zero emissions and green development goals, aligning with national climate policies.
These forests help regulate water flows, reduce regional flood risks, support vulnerable wildlife and ma-intain carbon storage, extending their protective role beyond conserving tree populations.
Protecting ecosystems is becoming as critical as planting new forests as climate change, drought, deser-tification and biodiversity loss pose growing global threats. Authorities aim to preserve Türkiye’s natural heritage for future generations.
Operating as strictly safeguarded ecological zones, these forests serve vital protective functions across the country. The category includes areas shielding land against landslides, protecting transportation networks from sandstorms and preventing sediment from filling riverbeds. Burned state forests also receive this designation while recovering.

Lab preserves crater lake microbes in central Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:57:18 UTC
14:57:18 KST

Lake Meke’s volcanic cone rises from a dry, exposed lake bed in the Karapınar district of Türkiye’s central province of Konya. (AA Photo)
Researchers in Türkiye’s central province of Konya are preserving microbes from drought-hit Lake Meke at minus 80 degrees Celsius, for use in restoring its ecosystem and developing biological fertilizers to help agriculture adapt to climate change.
Selçuk University Agricultural and Climate Change Application and Research Center collected soil samples from the lake bed and surrounding land in Karapınar district.
Center Director Professor Dr. Kubilay Kurtuluş Baştaş said the research team isolated new bacteria species not previously held in its collection. The samples will provide a resource to revive the ecosystem if the lake’s microbial structure deteriorates.
“When the lake is revived, we aim to return it to its original state by reintroducing the biodiversity we have preserved,” he said.
The research began with a search for useful bacteria to support farming under changing climate conditions before scientists expanded the process to include the lake’s microbial heritage.
The team identified salt-tolerant bacteria associated with phosphate, phosphorus, nitrogen and sulfur, Baştaş said. Some could be used to tackle rising salinity in farmland and improve soils, while helping plants adapt to harsh environments.
Further molecular biology and genetic research will expand to produce biological fertilizers, offering both economic and scientific benefits for Türkiye, he said.
Lake Meke, a geological heritage site, formed through a volcanic eruption 5 million years ago. Prolonged drought dried its surface water, making the preservation of its microscopic life critical for future ecological restoration.

LAS VEGAS, United States, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Beyond pandas and the Great Wall, high-tech innovation is emerging as a new draw for international visitors eager to experience China, tourism professionals told Xinhua at IMEX America 2026, which wrapped up Thursday.
Industry insiders said that while China continues to attract visitors with its rich history, vibrant culture and diverse landscapes, its rapid advances in science and technology are offering new ways to experience the country.
As a major global trade show for the meetings, events and incentive travel industry, the three-day event drew around 3,700 exhibitors from event planning, hotels and other sectors worldwide.
Visitors stopped by the China exhibition booth for discussions and business meetings on the country's technological capabilities and innovative strength.
They told Xinhua that foreign tourists are drawn to experiences ranging from climbing the Mutianyu Great Wall with robotic exoskeletons to having coffee delivered by drones and charging phones wirelessly at bus stops.
Lutti Colautto, CEO of Brazilian company Lampada.ag, a pioneer in the live marketing market, said he had returned from China about a month earlier after visiting Guangzhou, Liuzhou and Shanghai.
Marveling at China's achievements in electric vehicles, artificial intelligence (AI), robotics and new retail models, he shared his experiences on social media. "Twenty days in China changed the way I think about innovation, technology and business," he wrote.
"My feeling was that I was in the future," he said, noting that China's advances in AI and the development of future cities make the country particularly appealing.
China is not just a travel destination, but also an important place to learn about technological innovation, broaden business perspectives and explore future growth opportunities, he said.
Varun Doshi, founder of Canada's Yatriseva travel agency, said China's strong manufacturing sector and numerous high-tech industries had left a deep impression on his clients.
Many of his clients from Canada and India, who work in industries such as furniture and machinery, visit China annually.
"Recently, the trend is that they also want to take their families to China because they also want the families to learn how China is advancing with the world, and how beautiful the country is, how beautiful the people are, how hardworking the people are," he added.
Antoine Herblot, a French travel agent at China's tour operator Jade Dragon DMC, said social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and Rednote showcase not only China's tourist attractions but also its modern lifestyle and technological advances.
"I can feel the new generation is more and more interested in China, and so many efforts have been made by the Chinese government to open to the world," he noted. ■

This photo taken on Oct. 15, 2026 shows a scene of the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku, Azerbaijan. The 7th CICA summit was held here on Thursday. Participants exchanged views on security and development in the CICA region, the implementation of confidence-building measures and ways to strengthen practical cooperation. The summit adopted and issued the Baku Declaration of the Seventh CICA Summit. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
BAKU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) was held in Baku, the Azerbaijani capital, on Thursday.
Participants exchanged views on security and development in the CICA region, the implementation of confidence-building measures and ways to strengthen practical cooperation.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev chaired the summit and delivered a speech.
Azerbaijan's two-year CICA chairmanship has helped advance cooperation in areas such as transport, connectivity, digitalization, environment, tourism, education, science and technology, while strengthen CICA's capacity to promote dialogue, economic development and mutual understanding among member states, he said.
The summit adopted and issued the Baku Declaration of the Seventh CICA Summit.
The declaration reaffirmed member states' commitments to the UN Charter and the universally recognized norms and principles of international law, as well as their resolve to implement confidence-building measures in five dimensions -- military-political, new challenges and threats, economic, environmental and human -- as set out in the CICA Catalogue of Confidence Building Measures.
The declaration underscored the need for multilateralism and enhanced cooperation amid an increasingly complex international environment.
It also commended the progress made under Azerbaijan's CICA chairmanship in CICA's institutional development, including establishing the CICA Women Council, institutionalizing the CICA Finance Summit, and operationalizing the Partnership Network of Leading Universities.
The summit also admitted Laos as CICA's 29th full member. It extended Azerbaijan's CICA chairmanship for the 2026-2028 period and appointed Sultan Hajiyev as CICA secretary general for 2026-2030.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, as Special Representative of Chinese President Xi Jinping, attended the Summit.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, put forward four proposals to advance cooperation among CICA member states, urging efforts to jointly safeguard peace and stability, promote prosperity and revitalization, promote exchanges and mutual learning among civilization, and improve global governance.
The creation of CICA was proposed by Kazakhstan in 1992 at the 47th session of the United Nations General Assembly.
The multinational forum aims to promote peace, security and stability in Asia by developing and implementing multilateral confidence-building measures and strengthening cooperation in related areas. China is a founding member of CICA. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: Sowing hope in tropical paddies -- Chinese hybrid rice tech delivers bountiful harvests in Philippines
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
13:56:45 CST
14:56:45 KST

Chinese hybrid rice promoter Zhang Zhaodong observes rice in an experimental field in Laguna province, the Philippines, on May 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Rouelle Umali)
MANILA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- At a hybrid rice experimental field in Nueva Ecija, the Philippines, ripe rice plants spread like a golden carpet, their panicles heavy with tightly packed grains. John Davidson pressed down a sturdy rice stem, and it quickly sprang back upright.
"The Philippines endured persistent heavy rains in August, yet most of our Chinese hybrid rice plants withstood the harsh weather and grew well," said Davidson, 35, a technician at the Longping High-tech Philippine R&D Center, a Chinese agricultural company named after Yuan Longping, affectionately known as the "father of hybrid rice."
Friday marks World Food Day. Rice is a staple in Southeast Asian countries. For decades, Chinese technicians have traveled to farmlands across Southeast Asia to breed hybrid rice varieties adapted to local conditions.
Twelve years ago, Davidson received six months of technical training from Chinese experts, learning hybrid rice techniques including artificial pollination, seed selection and cultivation. "Thanks to China's expertise, we could breed more productive seeds and help more farmers achieve stable harvests," he said.
The Philippines has high temperatures and humidity, and is frequently struck by typhoons and dry-season water shortages. As one of the world's largest rice importers, the country has long grappled with food insecurity, with its rice inflation rising over 20 percent yearly in September.
"To support local people to secure their food supply, we uphold the idea that giving grain feeds hunger for a moment, but supplying seeds and passing on skills brings lasting harvests," said Guo Xiaobo, head of the Longping High-tech Philippine R&D Center.
The center, founded in 2007, operates over 10 hectares of experimental fields in Nueva Ecija. It has tested and bred more than 300 hybrid rice varieties annually in recent years, with nearly 30 varieties having obtained certification from the Philippine authorities cumulatively. Last year, it sold over 6,000 tonnes of seeds locally.
"We are deeply rooted in our tropical farmlands. Luckily, our high-yield and stress-resistant rice varieties earn local recognition," said Guo.
Data from the Philippine Rice Research Institute shows hybrid rice seeds have accounted for 14 percent of total rice seed usage in recent years. Industry estimates put hybrid rice output at 30 to 40 percent of the country's total rice production.
Another Chinese hybrid rice promoter working in the Philippines is 74-year-old Zhang Zhaodong, who received the Award for Promoting Philippines-China Understanding in June. He was also honored with the Philippine Secretary of Agriculture Award in 2021, hailing him as "a pioneer in the development, production, and commercialization of the hybrid rice technology" in the Philippines.
At the breeding base in Laguna province, Zhang walks through the paddies day after day, his trouser cuffs stained with mud and his feet caked in dirt. To cultivate rice, he often erects bamboo poles at the four corners of each one-square-meter test plot, with white woven fabric strung around the perimeter to ensure breeding purity.
In 1999, Zhang was dispatched to the Philippines by Yuan Longping and joined the local firm SL Agritech Corporation. The team later developed SL-8, a high-yield hybrid rice variety suitable for tropical cultivation.
Farmer Ronald de Lima recalled that when he planted local inbred rice about 30 years ago, the yield was just over four tonnes per hectare, while when he later planted SL-8, the output generally reached 10 tonnes per hectare.
"We were amazed by the Chinese technology, and started to plant hybrid rice one after another," said de Lima. "Thanks to hybrid rice, many fellow farmers bought vehicles and built new houses as harvests and lives have been getting better."
Zhang's team has recruited and trained hundreds of local technicians across the Philippines. After farmers purchase SL-8, these technicians deliver germinated seeds to households and provide guidance on cultivation management and pest and disease control.
"Promoting hybrid rice is far more than distributing seeds. It means visiting rural communities to demonstrate cultivation techniques day to day under scorching sun, and earning trust bit by bit," Zhang said.
Along with the hybrid rice's promotion, Zhang's team has also extended the industrial chain to rice processing and sales. Dona Maria, a rice product of SL Agritech, is frequently seen in local supermarkets at a price above the market average, and is exported to 14 countries and regions including the United States and the United Arab Emirates.
Furthermore, Zhang's team has shared breeding expertise to countries and regions including Malaysia, Bangladesh and Nigeria. In December 2025, Zhang signed a cooperation agreement on hybrid rice with the University of Mpumalanga in South Africa. The university stated that the "landmark partnership aims to revolutionize rice farming in South Africa, boost food security and create jobs."
According to the 2026 edition of The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World released by the United Nations in July, 7.8 percent of the world's population, or about 645 million people, faced hunger in 2025. Geopolitical tensions and climate-related shocks, among other factors, could jeopardize recent progress.
Against this backdrop, Chinese hybrid rice technology has been trialed or promoted in over 70 countries and regions. China has trained more than 14,000 professional hybrid rice technicians worldwide, steadily lifting food supply capacity and taking concrete action to help address food shortages in the Global South.
"My goal is to bring hybrid rice to suitable lands across the tropics, steadily raise grain yields and contribute to easing global food shortages," said Zhang. ■

JAKARTA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia's benchmark stock index tumbled over 11 percent on Friday and the rupiah weakened sharply after global index provider MSCI announced a proposal to reclassify the market from "emerging" to "standalone" status.
The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 8 percent at Friday's opening, triggering a 30-minute trading halt. As trading resumed, selling pressure intensified, pushing the index down as much as 11 percent, heading for its steepest single-day slump since January 1998.
The severe market sell-off followed MSCI's statement that maintaining Indonesia's emerging market status might be "no longer appropriate." A reclassification to "standalone" status would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by billions of dollars in passive investment, forcing funds that follow or are ranked against the indexes to sell.
However, MSCI has not made a final decision on Indonesia's status.
In the foreign exchange market, the Indonesian rupiah dropped to 18,070 per U.S. dollar, hovering near its lowest levels since early August and approaching a historical low of 18,190. ■

New support measures to boost tourism beyond Tallinn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:56:00 UTC
14:56:00 KST

New support measures to boost tourism beyond Tallinn
The Ministry of Economic Affairs plans to provide grants to regional tourism organizations to encourage tourists to visit parts of Estonia outside Tallinn.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs wants tourism to play a greater role in the economies of rural areas. To that end, it has drafted a regulation providing grants to tourism development organizations, primarily in regions outside Tallinn.
The grants are intended for organizations officially known as destination management organizations (DMOs). For example, DMOs in southern Estonia include the Tartu County Tourism Foundation and The Onion Route (Sibulatee), while those in Pärnu County include the Tõstamaa Manor Foundation and the nonprofit Soomaa Tourism. On the islands, DMOs include the Hiiumaa Development Center and the municipal governments of Saaremaa, Ruhnu and Muhu.
Organizations receiving grants will be expected to develop rural tourism in cooperation with local governments, businesses and other partners to increase tourism's contribution to local economies.
"The main aim of the new grant regulation planned for 2027-2029 is to make funding for regional tourism development more stable and long-term," Kristina Jerjomina, head of tourism at the Ministry of Economic Affairs, told ERR.
She added that grants have so far been awarded for shorter periods, but under the proposed changes, funding would be provided for three years. However, recipients' required co-financing would increase from 50 percent to 55 percent by the third year to reduce dependence on government funding.
According to Jerjomina, greater emphasis will be placed on reducing tourism seasonality to encourage travel beyond major centers outside the peak summer season, as well as on the impact of tourism on regional economies and ensuring positive visitor experiences.
"At the same time, the use of grants and reporting requirements will be simplified, the range of eligible expenses will be expanded and the total annual funding available will increase by approximately €200,000," Jerjomina explained.
Under the tourism action plan for the coming years, the share of overnight stays outside Tallinn should reach at least 53 percent by 2029. The share of overnight stays during the spring, fall and winter months should rise to 65 percent by the same year.
To achieve these goals, the grants are intended to support the continued development of cultural, heritage, culinary and other tourism offerings to meet the expectations of international visitors. The draft regulation places particular emphasis on improving quality and making these experiences available during the low season, with the aim of increasing tourism revenue.
Plans also call for continued digitalization and automation in the tourism sector, including making more services available for online booking.
Rural tourism bottleneck getting from the bus station to the forest or manor
Transportation is also a challenge. According to the explanatory memorandum accompanying the draft regulation, one of the biggest bottlenecks in regional tourism is how visitors can get from a bus or train station to a forest trail, manor or museum or find parking information they can easily understand.
Organizations receiving grants to develop rural tourism will not be expected to buy buses or operate routes themselves. Instead, they will be required to discuss ways to improve the situation with regional public transportation centers, local governments, technology companies and tourism businesses.
Tourism development organizations will also be tasked with identifying which tourist attractions most urgently need better access, analyzing visitor travel patterns and determining which solutions could be tested.
The grants will total €1.97 million annually, with funding allocations taking into account how far a destination is from Tallinn and how well it is connected to other areas.
Under the draft regulation, regional impact calculations will be based on the assessment that access to services, jobs and infrastructure is best in Tallinn and neighboring counties, while more remote regions need additional incentives and support to retain residents and services.
"Using a regional impact indicator makes it possible to direct more funding to destinations where tourism development can make the greatest contribution to regional balance, increased business activity and job creation outside Tallinn and Harju County," the explanatory memorandum states.
Grant recipients will also be required to ensure that their region's tourism services and destinations are accurately listed in the visitestonia.com database.
The regulation is still in draft form and the ministry is accepting feedback until October 26. The final wording will be determined after the consultation period.
--
Editor: Karin Koppel, Marcus Turovski

Alone in Gaza: Genocide leaves Palestinian man without family or a home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:55:23 UTC
14:55:23 KST

Alone in Gaza: Genocide leaves Palestinian man without family or a home
One man wanders Gaza in search of somewhere to sleep, having lost his family in an Israeli bombing.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Every morning, Mahmoud Khalla goes to the nearby cemetery to visit the graves of the family members he lost during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
He has held on to this morning routine in the months since he buried them, imagining his family is still around.
For Mahmoud, 40, the cemetery is the resting place of some of the people he has loved the most in his life.
His wife, his three children, his parents, his two brothers and their families, his sister and her children, and other relatives had all gathered in their family home in Jabalia, northern Gaza, on December 21, 2023.
An Israeli strike then targeted the five-storey family home, destroying the building and killing all 39 people inside. Mahmoud left his home shortly before it hit and is the only one left in his family.
The siege
Mahmoud remembers that day with heartache. Israeli tanks had surrounded the area near the house in Jabalia, northern Gaza, making it dangerous for people to move around. Food was already scarce due to the ongoing Israeli siege. In the evening, Mahmoud left the house in search of provisions to feed his family.
“I told them I would go and see what was available,” he told Al Jazeera. “As soon as I had been out for about 15 minutes, I heard a huge explosion.”
“I ran back and discovered that the targeted house was ours. I was in complete shock. But I pulled myself together. With the help of a few neighbours who were still in the area, we tried to rescue anyone who might be under the rubble.”
Israeli air attacks, quadcopters and surveillance aircraft continued to target the area. It made it impossible for Mahmoud and his neighbours to search for survivors.
“A surveillance aircraft dropped a bomb on us, so we immediately ran away,” he says. “We came back the next morning.”
Ambulances and civil defence teams were also unable to reach the site that night.
With this sense of helplessness, he imagined that some of his family might still be alive under the rubble, waiting to be rescued. He felt as though he had died a thousand times that night.
The following morning, he returned to the site and called out to his family members who might be beneath the ruined home. Nobody answered, and it was at this moment he realised he had lost nearly every person he loved.
“There were five floors of rubble. It was impossible for us to pull anyone out,” he said.
Alone
That attack marked the beginning of a long period of emptiness for Mahmoud. With his home destroyed and almost all of his relatives killed or displaced to the south, he had nowhere to go.
“Even my uncles had been killed,” he says. “Their house, opposite ours, was targeted nine days before our family home. Eighteen people were killed in that attack. The rest of the family had gone south.”
Mahmoud spent the following months displaced and alone. He moved between the streets in search of somewhere to sleep for the night. It was difficult to find shelter among displaced families when he had no relation to them.
“I was sleeping in the streets, or in cars or vehicles whenever I found one that was open,” he says. “I was totally lonely and homeless.”
With no shelter at all, Mahmoud was vulnerable to Israeli attacks. The struggle for food became as urgent as the need to find somewhere safe to sleep.
“You don’t know whether a bullet will hit you, whether a rocket will come, whether you will find food or where you will sleep,” he said.
Recovering his family
After a “ceasefire” was announced for Gaza in October 2025, families began the difficult search for their missing loved ones. Nearly a year later, an estimated 8,000 people remain missing, their bodies likely under the rubble of their homes or in other locations.
Months after the “ceasefire” began and bombing decreased, Mahmoud started recovering the remains of his family members himself. They had been entombed among the remains of their home for the last 29 months.
“The feeling that my family was still under the rubble, without being buried, was very difficult,” he says. “It never left me.”
He approached the civil defence, the Red Cross and other authorities for help. But he says a severe shortage of equipment and a huge number of other families requesting assistance meant they could be of little help.
Eventually, with the help of friends and neighbours who volunteered to work alongside him, he began the heartbreaking task of recovering his loved ones himself by hand.
He began recovering the remains around May this year, in a process that took three months.
“Sometimes, we managed to recover one person in a day. Sometimes, it took two days,” he said.
The first people he found were two relatives who had been sheltering with the family. The last were his sister and her children, who had been buried together.
He buried his family members at a cemetery near Jabalia an-Nazla, in northern Gaza.
“I felt a great sense of relief when I finally buried them,” he said. “It took me three months to recover all of their remains, working day by day.”

====================================================================================================

Macron’s final stretch marred by student protests, police scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:54:38 UTC
14:54:38 KST

France is facing a growing wave of unrest as high school students protest for better-resourced schools, clashing with police forces accused of using excessive force to suppress demonstrations.
The protests, which have spread across the country in recent weeks, have led to mass arrests, hundreds of injuries and mounting criticism of the government’s handling of public dissent.
The confrontations have also exposed tensions within the police, with some officers and their unions accusing the state of putting them in dangerous situations without adequate equipment or clear instructions.
For President Emmanuel Macron, who is due to leave office in May, the unrest is an unwelcome end to nearly a decade in power marked by repeated protest movements and disputes over the use of force against demonstrators.
The latest demonstrations have drawn particular scrutiny because so many of those arrested are teenagers, some of whom have suffered life-changing injuries from weapons used by riot police.
The protests have also attracted public sympathy as France grapples with record poverty and mounting public debt, with students demanding better-funded schools, particularly in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris and other cities.
Yet the demonstrations have also provided cover for violent groups that police say are exploiting the crowds to attack officers, set fires and damage property.
According to government figures, more than 900 police officers and nearly 150 teachers and other school employees have been injured during the unrest. Police say demonstrators have thrown rocks, fireworks and other projectiles at officers, turning some gatherings into violent confrontations.
The competing accounts have intensified a national debate over how France should balance the right to protest with public safety, and whether its security forces are equipped and trained to manage increasingly volatile demonstrations.
Walid Hrar, a police officer and union representative in Paris’ northern suburbs, said France’s long tradition of revolution and civil disobedience helps explain why protests can escalate so quickly.
"This is the country of the French Revolution. Everyone boasts about it, in fact. Some political parties don’t hesitate to say that we need to disobey the law. That’s what Robespierre and other revolutionaries taught us in 1789,” he said.
"France always tends to react rather than anticipate,” he added. "In other words, we’re always going to extremes.”
The response by security forces has become a central point of contention, particularly their use of so-called less-lethal weapons, including grenades, projectile launchers, tear gas and water cannons. Some officers also use riot shields fitted with powerful strobe lights to control crowds.
Critics argue that the deployment of these weapons, combined with inadequate training and poor equipment, increases the risk of serious injuries for both protesters and police.
Jean-Marie Godard, an author who specializes in French policing, said officers were being sent into volatile demonstrations without sufficient preparation.
"We’re sending poorly equipped, untrained public security police officers to violent demonstrations who are likely to become agitated very quickly out of anger and fear,” he said.
Hrar said some officers assigned to crowd-control duties lacked specialized training and protective equipment. He cited uniforms that were not flame-resistant, worn-out helmets and shields unsuitable for the conditions.
"We send them in because we need the manpower,” he said.
He also said officers who lack authorization to use certain riot-control projectiles and grenades can struggle to keep attackers at a safe distance, forcing them into direct physical confrontations.
"So unfortunately we make do,” Hrar said. "You’ll inevitably end up in direct physical confrontation. When that happens, there are injuries on both sides.”
The police union Alliance announced this week that it would file a legal complaint against the state, accusing authorities of endangering officers through unclear and contradictory instructions.
The union said officers had been left "isolated, betrayed, abandoned, exposed to violence."
The complaint adds to mounting pressure on the government over its management of the unrest, with officers arguing that authorities have failed to provide the resources and operational guidance needed to keep demonstrations under control.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said security forces had used crowd-control weapons at least 18,000 times during the protests, primarily smoke and tear gas, but also projectiles and grenades.
One of the weapons was a launcher-fired grenade that produces a deafening blast. Nunez said it had been used about 40 times before he suspended its deployment against high school students after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
The minister defended the use of crowd-control equipment, saying officers deployed it when necessary and in proportion to the threat.
"All this equipment, all these forces, all these intermediate weapons, are used whenever necessary, with proportionality, to mark an escalation of the response, to keep people at a distance or sometimes to put them out of action,” he said.
Nunez maintained that the rules governing the use of projectiles were strict and clearly defined.
"We avoid everything above the neck,” he said.
But investigations into alleged police misconduct have raised questions about whether those safeguards are being followed in practice.
An officer suspected of firing a projectile that partially blinded a 16-year-old was charged this week with aggravated violence.
The case was among 36 investigations into alleged police misconduct reported by Nunez as of Tuesday. Four concerned injuries described as mutilating, while six involved significant injuries. Other investigations involved alleged beatings, insults and suspected sexual assaults, including a case in which an officer was accused of attempting to drown a protester.
France has more than 250,000 police officers and gendarmes, but the scale of its security apparatus has not prevented recurring confrontations between law enforcement and protesters.
Sebastian Roche, a policing specialist at France’s National Center for Scientific Research, said the government’s political assessment of a protest movement often determines how security forces respond.
He pointed to differences in the treatment of high school students and farmers, who have used road blockades, fires and manure dumped on government buildings to press their demands. Farmers wield considerable political influence in France, Roche said, and have sometimes faced a more accommodating response from authorities.
"It’s the political definition of the movement that defines the police response,” he said.
That distinction has fueled criticism that the state applies different standards of force depending on who is protesting and how politically influential the demonstrators are.
Public attitudes toward the police have also shifted, partly because of the constant circulation of videos showing officers confronting demonstrators, Hrar said.
He recalled how police officers were widely praised for their bravery during the terrorist attacks in France in 2015, a period when their role in protecting the public drew broad recognition.
"When you bombard people every single day with images of police intervening with batons, shields and tear gas, you’re inevitably going to create a negative impression,” he said.

Caught up with Taylor Swift: BTS set a new record on Spotify
Kyiv • UNN
BTS became the first group to reach 10 billion Spotify streams in a year. The album Arirang garnered more than 5 billion streams.
K-pop supergroup BTS has become the first group in the world to reach 10 billion streams on Spotify in a single year. The group’s label announced this on October 16, UNN reports, citing Yonhap.
Details
Although solo artists such as Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande and Bad Bunny have reached this milestone, this is the first time a group has reached 10 billion streams on Spotify, according to BigHit Music.
Streams of BTS songs on Spotify more than doubled compared with last year’s 4.5 billion, following the release of their fifth studio album, "Arirang," which came out in March.
The album alone has amassed more than 5 billion streams since its release, becoming the most-streamed album on Spotify among albums released this year.
"Arirang" attracted significant attention as the global K-pop sensation’s first full-length project in nearly four years, released after all of its members completed their mandatory military service and reunited. On the day of its release, March 20, the number of streams exceeded 110 million.
It also became the group’s first album to top the Billboard 200, the leading U.S. albums chart, for three consecutive weeks since the release of Mumford & Sons’ album "Babel" in 2012.

Rajnath Singh targets Rahul Gandhi

Istanbul faces more rain as flood searches continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:53:44 UTC
14:53:44 KST

Istanbul remains gripped by the aftermath of its heaviest rainfall in eight decades on Oct. 16, with municipal crews working to clear flood debris and repair damage as meteorologists warn of further downpours and renewed flooding.
Heavy rain began lashing Türkiye’s largest city on the morning of Oct. 14, intensifying throughout the day and triggering widespread disruption and flash floods. Footage showed cars being swept away by fast-flowing floodwaters.
Four people have been reported dead in the flooding. A 14-year-old was electrocuted after stepping into a puddle in a park in the Fatih district, while a 34-year-old slipped on a sidewalk in Sarıyer and suffered a fatal head injury.
Search operations later uncovered another body along a stream in Istanbul’s Kağıthane district, bringing the death toll to three.
On Oct. 16, rescue teams found the body of a person reported missing in Ayazağa, a neighborhood in Sarıyer. 
Among the hardest-hit locations was Sarıyer’s Ayazağa neighborhood, where power and natural gas outages persisted until noon on Oct. 15, leaving local bakeries and markets unable to operate.
On Oct. 16, Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi and Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum visited Ayazağa.
“We are experiencing the worst flood disaster since 1942,” Çiftçi told reporters during the visit.
Çiftçi said the number of people reported missing fell from five to four, adding that one of the missing individuals had lost contact with authorities after their phone battery ran out during the flooding.
Following the discovery of the body of a missing person, shortly after Çiftçi’s visit, search efforts were continuing for three other people.
“We experienced this problem because of inadequate infrastructure and haphazard urbanization. We will address the needs here. We will provide shelter for those who need accommodation and food for those who need food,” Kurum said.
Although the intensity of the downpour eased on Oct. 15, meteorological authorities warned that another spell of heavy rain was expected to reach Istanbul on Oct. 16 and 17, raising concerns about renewed flooding.
Rainfall recorded across Istanbul over the 48-hour period from Oct. 13 to 15 exceeded the long-term average for September and October. Precipitation reached 272 kilograms per square meter in some parts of the city, equivalent to approximately one-seventh of the area’s annual rainfall.
As the rain temporarily subsided on the morning of Oct. 16, Istanbul’s municipal crews began clearing the damage left behind by the floods.
Cleanup and repair operations were underway across the city, particularly in the districts of Beykoz, Şile, Sarıyer and Kağıthane, where torrential rain had caused flooding.
Response teams were active across the area, pumping water out of affected properties and removing ruined belongings. Crews also cleared streets of mud and debris before deploying washer trucks to clean the roadways.
Heavy rain caused a section of road outside Eyüpsultan to collapse. Crews cordoned off the area while heavy machinery worked to stabilize and clear the site.

G-7 to launch exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:53:00 KST

G-7 to launch exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks
BANGKOK – Finance leaders of the Group of Seven (G-7) grouping agreed to hold tabletop exercises to guard against AI cyberattacks, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, as policymakers increasingly seek to coordinate responses to growing cyber security risks.
The agreement comes after the International Monetary Fund warned this week that confidence could be undermined by an AI-enabled cyberattack on a critical service of a financial institution.
“The G7 finance deputies had been discussing the idea of doing tabletop exercises on frontier AI, which was signed off at the ministerial level,” Katayama told reporters on Oct 15.
She made the remarks after attending a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors of the G-7 advanced economies held on the sidelines of the IMF’s annual gathering in Bangkok, the Thai capital.
The plan will feature simulations evolved by G-7 finance authorities to test how they can respond to AI-driven cyberattacks, said a Japanese finance ministry official who attended the finance leaders’ meeting.
The results will test effectiveness of existing protocols and be used to revise manuals to better tackle such incidents, the official told reporters.
The exercises by G-7 finance ministries and central banks could include private financial institutions depending on the nature of simulations, the official added.
Banking regulators globally are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, Reuters reported, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability.
Among them is the Bank of England, which is working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, its deputy governor said on Oct 15, adding that they can no longer assume their defences are immune to AI-enabled cyberattacks. REUTERS

Lihtsad uudised 16. oktoobril
"Lihtsad uudised," meaning easy or simple news, is for anyone who wants to improve their Estonian language skills. Read a selection of this week's news stories below.
Ülle Madise astus Eesti presidendi ametisse
Ülle Madise astus esmaspäeval Eesti presidendi ametisse, andes riigikogus ametivande.
Madise saabus koos abikaasa Lauriga Kadriorus asuvasse presidendi kantseleisse, kus neid võtsid vastu president Alar Karis ja Sirje Karis. Seejärel suunduti Toompeale, kus Karis pidas oma viimase kõne presidendina ning Madise andis ametivande ja pidas oma esimese kõne riigipeana.

Ülle Madise on 51-aastane ja pärit Tartust. Aastatel 2015–2026 töötas Madise õiguskantslerina. Esimesed ametlikud visiidid presidendina tegi Madise Lätti ja Soome.
Ukraina rünnakute järel vähenes Yandexi liiklus Eesti veebilehtedele ligi 100 protsenti
Venemaa Yandexi võrgust Eesti veebilehtedele tulev liiklus vähenes pärast Ukraina rünnakuid ettevõtte andmekeskustele peaaegu nullini.
Riigi infosüsteemi ameti (RIA) teatel langes 13. oktoobriks Yandexi päringute arv septembri keskmisega võrreldes 420 korda. Kokku vähenes päringute arv 99,8 protsenti.
Ukraina ründas eelmisel nädalal kolme Yandexi andmekeskust, mis asuvad Moskva lähedal, Sasovos ja Kalugas.
RIA sõnul on veel vara öelda, kas see mõjutab Venemaa küberrünnakuid Eesti vastu. Rünnakuteks kasutatakse Yandexist sõltumatuid süsteeme.
Politsei pidas Tallinnas Nõmmel kinni kümme ebaseaduslikult riigis viibinud inimest
Politsei pidas pühapäeva õhtul Tallinnas Nõmme linnaosas kinni kümme ebaseaduslikult Eestis viibinud inimest. Neist üheksa viidi kinnipidamiskeskusesse ja üks haiglasse.
Kella 19.30 paiku sai politsei teate kahest mehest, kes seisid Valdeku tänaval ühe maja juures ja paistsid olevat eksinud. Politsei pidas mõlemad mehed kinni. Tegemist oli Sudaani kodanikega, kes viibisid Eestis ebaseaduslikult.
Mehed rääkisid politseile, et läheduses varjavad end veel teisedki. Politsei asus piirkonda läbi otsima, kasutades droone, maastikusõidukeid ja koeri. Otsingutel aitas ka päästeamet.
Droon märkas metsas liikuvaid inimesi ning politsei leidis sealt veel kaheksa meest. Üks meestest kukkus põgenedes ja vigastas kätt.
Kõik kümme meest viibisid Eestis ebaseaduslikult ning isikut tõendav dokument oli neist vaid ühel.
Hiiumaal ei saa naised enam sünnitada
Alates juulist ei saa Hiiumaa naised enam kodusaarel sünnitada. Endiselt pole selge, kuidas korraldada sünnitajate transport mandrile ja tagasi ning kes selle eest maksab.
Kärdlas elav Kärolyn Kivistik ootab oma viiendat last, kelle sünnitähtaeg on 8. novembril. Haiglakott on tal juba pakitud. Kuna ta ei soovi sünnituse ajal reisida, läheb ta tõenäoliselt nädal varem Tallinna. Pere hinnangul kaasneb sellega ligi 1000 eurot lisakulusid.
Hiiumaa haiglas on sünnitusabi osutamiseks vajalikud ruumid ja seadmed, kuid puuduvad töötajad. Lastearst läks juulist pensionile ning septembris puudus neljal päeval ka naistearst.
Haigla juhi Riina Tamme sõnul esitati esmaspäeval haigla nõukogule tegevuskava, kuid sünnitajate mandrile ja sealt tagasi toomise küsimus on endiselt lahendamata.
Tamme hinnangul on tegemist regionaalpoliitilise probleemiga, mis ei puuduta ainult Hiiumaad.
Eesti esimene selge keele standard aitab tekste arusaadavamaks muuta
Oktoobri alguses jõustus Eesti esimene selge keele standard, mis annab soovitusi avaliku teabe arusaadavamaks kirjutamiseks.
Standardi koostanud komisjoni juhtinud Kristel Ressi sõnul tuleb teksti kirjutades kõigepealt mõelda sellele, kes seda lugema hakkab. Näiteks külmas paadis telefonist juhiste lugemine erineb kodus teksti lugemisest.
Ressi sõnul on standard abivahend, mitte rangete reeglite kogum. Ta sedastas, et esimest korda on kõik need soovitused koondatud ühte lühikesse juhendisse.
ERR-i keeletoimetaja Ester Põldma sõnul on soovitustest kasu kõigile, kes kirjutavad veebitekste. "Lugeja peaks juba esimesel lugemisel aru saama, mida lausega öelda tahetakse," ütles Põldma.
