Investigation: How scammers exploit Ukraine’s occupation to deceive foreign men
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

Investigation: The romance scam tricking men into ‘rescuing’ Ukrainian women from Russian occupation
The Kyiv Independent uncovers how scammers on dating sites pose as women trapped in Russian-occupied Ukraine, using fake identities to talk foreign men into sending them money. (Daria Filippova / The Kyiv Independent)
Stefan, a 48-year-old Austrian national whose name has been changed at his request, had been looking for a Ukrainian partner. Having previously dated a Ukrainian woman, he said he was drawn to what he viewed as the importance of family in Ukrainian culture.
He met "Alona Panchenko," who claimed to be from the Russian-occupied city of Enerhodar in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, on the international dating website Christian Cupid. Soon after they matched, she suggested moving their conversation to email.
As their relationship continued, however, he began noticing that something was off.
Over the next three months, they exchanged lengthy emails but never spoke by phone or video. "Alona" said she had no mobile phone and could only communicate via an old tablet connected to public Wi-Fi due to conditions in occupied Enerhodar.
Her story grew increasingly desperate. She said she was unemployed, had run out of money, and had even been hospitalized with "severe exhaustion" after going two days without food. Eventually, she told Stefan the only way they could meet was if he helped her escape the occupied territory.
To support her story, "Alona" regularly sent photos that supposedly showed herself and life in Enerhodar.
The evidence she provided was fabricated. The Kyiv Independent traced her portraits to another person, found that photos she claimed she had taken in Enerhodar came from a local media outlet, and identified signs of AI manipulation in some images and videos. The ID she shared also contained an invalid number and an AI-edited portrait.
The request for money revealed another inconsistency. "Alona" instructed Stefan to list Ukraine as the recipient's country of residence when making the transfer through Western Union. That contradicted her claim that she was living in Russia-occupied Enerhodar, where Western Union does not operate.
Stefan says he never sent the money. But other men interviewed by the Kyiv Independent did.
Since 2022, the non-profit Helping to Leave has received thousands of requests to rescue people from Russian-occupied territories. Some of those requests were to rescue women who may have never existed at all.
The charity has helped thousands of people flee occupied areas, and its team was used to urgent pleas for evacuation. But over time, a different kind of request began arriving.
Foreign men started writing to Helping to Leave asking to rescue Ukrainian women they had met online, women they believed were trapped in Russian-occupied territories.
Some asked the charity to arrange an evacuation. Others had already sent money, believing they were paying for the woman's escape and that they would finally meet once she reached safety. They never did.
Over the past four years, the non-profit says it has received around 200 such requests, which now arrive up to four times a week, according to Nataliia, the project's communications specialist, who asked to be identified only by her first name due to the sensitive nature of her work with people in Russian-occupied territories.
Ukrainian and international media have long documented romance scams in which foreign men send money or travel to Ukraine to meet women who turn out to be fake. But the war has given scammers a new way to exploit the sympathy of unsuspecting foreigners.
An investigation by the Kyiv Independent into 58 cases referred by Helping to Leave found evidence that many of the women were not under Russian occupation at all.
Instead, scammers appeared to be using stolen photos, fake identities, forged documents, and, in some cases, AI-manipulated images and videos to convince men to send money.
The women who 'needed to escape'
The Kyiv Independent spoke to two foreign men who had online relationships with women claiming to be trapped in Russian-occupied territories. Their stories followed a pattern: no video calls, escalating crises, and urgent requests for money.
Karsten R., a German citizen, described a similar experience to that of Stefan with a woman calling herself "Viktoriia Kremenchutska." She claimed to be trapped in Russian-occupied territory, avoided video calls, and asked for money to escape.
After Karsten agreed to send money, she said she had begun her journey. But as she supposedly made her way out, she repeatedly asked for more funds — first to cross the checkpoint between occupied and Ukrainian-controlled territories, then to pay off an alleged debt she said was preventing her from leaving.
The documents and images she sent were also fake. Her passport copy was forged — the photo was photoshopped, the surname had a typo, and the font was inconsistent with a Ukrainian passport, the Kyiv Independent found. The photos, supposedly of her, turned out to be images of another woman — a woman from Russia. Other photos showed signs of AI manipulation.
"I told her, 'I want to see your suitcases. I want to see you holding a piece of paper with my name and the date on it," Karsten told the Kyiv Independent. He received the photo he demanded — but the Kyiv Independent confirmed it was AI-edited.
Even after discovering the fake documents and images, Karsten struggled to let go. At one point, he considered driving to a Ukrainian border crossing when "Viktoria" said she was trapped there trying to leave. Eventually, he became convinced he was talking to scammers.
Following the faces used in the scams
The Kyiv Independent examined 58 cases referred by Helping to Leave, using available photos and contact details to trace the identities behind the profiles.
The relationships mostly started on dating websites, including UkraineDate, Christian Cupid, and International Cupid. In several instances, the women contacted men directly through Instagram or X. Some cases could not be verified because the available information, such as photos or contact details, was insufficient.
Using facial recognition tools and open-source research, the Kyiv Independent matched 22 profile photos to real women. Two more profiles appeared to rely on AI-generated identities. The remaining cases could not be verified, as they did not include any photos of the women they believed to be communicating with.
Out of the 22 profiles that used real photos, only seven used names that matched the women pictured. In some cases, the women even joined video calls to confirm their identity. But they lied about their whereabouts: the women identified were either living in Ukrainian-controlled territory or had moved abroad. None were in the Russian-occupied territories.
Not all accounts that used real women's photos actually belonged to them. In the remaining 15 cases, the names and surnames did not match the women whose photos appeared on the profiles. Ten of the 15 women were popular Instagram bloggers from Russia, Moldova, Ukraine, Germany, Denmark, and Latvia.
Dozens of women's photos were repeatedly reused across several dating profiles under different identities, often with the accounts presenting themselves as Russian women, the Kyiv Independent found.
This was the case with the images used by "Alona" and "Viktoriia," which were found across multiple profiles. The Kyiv Independent traced the photos used by "Alona" to Natalia Cernisova, a woman from Chisinau, Moldova, and those used by "Viktoriia" to Anna Kolesnyak from Russia. Both women run popular Instagram blogs.
In addition to stolen photos, the accounts used by both "Alona" and "Viktoriia" also sent images and videos that appeared to be AI-manipulated.
The profiles used by "Alona" and "Viktoriia," along with several others reviewed by the Kyiv Independent, are listed in the Ukrainian Dating Scammer Blacklist maintained by Ukrainian Passport, a platform that helps foreigners verify women from Ukraine and Russia.
An investigator with Ukrainian Passport, who asked to not be identified for safety reasons, said some scammers use content from popular Instagram influencers to create fake profiles, and in some cases may even be working with the influencers.
"If necessary, the influencer will even record a video to make the profile seem authentic, while being careful not to reveal too much. Later, she can always say it was for an audition or so. We've seen that happen before," he told the Kyiv Independent.
Anna Bauer, founder of the Kyiv-based Grace Family dating agency, described another way real women's identities can unintentionally enter the online dating ecosystem.
She said scouts sometimes recruit women for professional photo shoots, after which their photographs may be sold between dating agencies. This creates a risk that legitimate images can later be misused by fraudulent operators.
The Kyiv Independent received a response from one Ukrainian Instagram blogger, Anastasiia Mazur-Palamarchuk, whose photos were used in one of the scam profiles. She said her images were used without her consent.
"I'm not registered on any online dating website," she said.
Fact sheet: Top lies scammers use about occupied territories
The Kyiv Independent is listing several common lies used by scammers, based on the conversation with Nataliia from Helping to Leave and its own expertise.
- Claiming it is possible to escape directly across the front line
Scammers often invent stories about crossing directly from occupied territories into Ukrainian-controlled areas through the front line, sometimes fabricating tales of "special drivers" or secret humanitarian corridors.
Civilians cannot cross active front lines because of ongoing fighting and the constant air attacks in front-line areas.
There is currently only one existing humanitarian corridor, located in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast. The crossing point, which is located on the Ukraine-Belarus border, is used almost exclusively by people fleeing the occupied territories.
People leaving occupied territories have to first go to Russia, then to Belarus, before reaching Ukraine or neighboring EU countries. The journey is usually made by bus or train, while specialized transportation is needed only in specific cases, such as for people with disabilities. Some also leave Russia by air, for example by flying to Georgia, though this route is less common.
- Dramatizing their own situation
While living under Russian occupation is indeed dangerous and harrowing, scammers often exaggerate the severity of their own living conditions to explain why they cannot communicate frequently, and to build sympathy with the men.
Helping to Leave gave an example of a woman who said she lived in Donetsk. She claimed she was living in her basement because of constant shelling, had almost no internet connection, and thus couldn't do a video call.
But the city of Donetsk isn't being shelled. Although Ukraine conducts drone strikes on occupied territories, it says they target military facilities. While this can't be independently verified, the reported death toll from such strikes is typically much lower than that of Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian areas. There is no evidence that Donetsk is under such threat that residents would live in basements.
- Claiming bribes are mandatory at checkpoints and filtration points
Scammers use these claims to extort more money from victims, saying the women cannot pass security checks unless bribes are paid to border guards and officials.
While before the full-scale war, bribes might have been an option for some to travel between the occupied parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts and Ukraine-held territories, this practice doesn't exist anymore as there are no checkpoints between these territories.
People who fled occupation with the help from Helping to Leave have not reported being asked to pay bribes along the way, the organization told the Kyiv Independent.
- All messaging apps are blocked under occupation
Some scammers claim they can't use phones or messaging apps or make video calls because everything is blocked under occupation.
Many popular messaging apps continue to work in occupied territories, often with the help of VPN services. Limiting communication to email allows scammers to hide their identity and manage multiple victims simultaneously without having to do voice or video calls.
- Absence of a Russian passport as an excuse and proof of loyalty
Scammers claim they can't travel through Russia because they only hold Ukrainian documents. They also use this to appeal to the victim's political sympathies.
In reality, taking a Russian passport in the occupied territories is not a political choice but a matter of survival: It is nearly impossible to access healthcare without Russian documents. This is part of Russia’s policy of forced passportization in occupied Ukraine, which means many people living under occupation have likely been forced to obtain Russian documents.
- Demanding highly inflated evacuation costs
Scammers also request exorbitant travel expenses, far exceeding the actual cost of public or private transportation.
According to Helping to Leave, women in these cases typically ask for around 800 euros or $800 — roughly twice the actual cost of the journey from the Russia-occupied territories to the government-controlled part of Ukraine through Belarus.
Compiled by Yuliia Taradiuk.
A recurring playbook across 58 cases
A review of emails and messages shared with Helping to Leave and the Kyiv Independent revealed recurring elements in how women claiming to be trapped in Russian-occupied territories describe their situations.
The women presented themselves as trapped and abandoned, with no help available from Ukrainian authorities or humanitarian organizations. In some cases, they suggested that evacuation assistance did not exist, leaving the men to believe they were the only ones who could help.
"Natalia (from Helping to Leave) won't help me get out of here. How can you not understand that?" "Alona" wrote to Stefan.
In reality, when women from the cases reviewed by the Kyiv Independent were referred to the non-profit, they either never contacted it or did not cooperate when coordinators tried to understand what assistance they needed.
When it came to appearing live on a video call with the men, the women similarly said it was impossible, claiming unstable internet in occupied territories, outdated devices, or blocked messaging services.
None of them shared personal social media accounts, either. But in many cases, the Kyiv Independent found that the women whose photos were used in the dating profiles were active on Instagram, where their lives looked nothing like the stories the men were being told. It is unclear whether the real women knew their images were being used.
After matching on dating websites, conversations usually moved to email, Telegram, or WhatsApp. Telegram accounts often hid phone numbers, while WhatsApp accounts were typically registered with Ukrainian numbers.
Some women also sent WhatsApp live locations that appeared to show them in occupied territories. But such data can be manipulated using GPS spoofing tools, making it unreliable as proof of someone's whereabouts. This can be done using specialized apps. The Kyiv Independent was able to share a live location in Paris while physically in Ukraine in just 10 minutes.
When the Kyiv Independent contacted the phone numbers and Telegram accounts provided by the women to the men who believed they were dating, none answered. Most phone numbers were invalid or no longer active, suggesting they may have been temporary numbers used only as burner numbers for the scam and later discarded.
When text messages and excuses failed to persuade men to send money, the people behind the profiles turned to documents to try and back up their claims.
Many women sent what they claimed were Ukrainian passports, but all except one contained signs of digital manipulation, including altered personal details, edited photographs, or invalid passport numbers, the Kyiv Independent found.
Some also sent fake travel tickets or documents that appeared to show fines or penalties allegedly preventing them from crossing the border. They claimed these payments were necessary before they could continue their journey.
Once trust had been established, requests for money followed.
Most of the women suggested cash pickup services such as Western Union, RIA, or MoneyGram. Some also requested PayPal transfers. These methods allowed money to be collected without directly revealing bank account details.
Karsten, who believed he was helping "Viktoriia" escape the city of Donetsk, received a copy of what she said was her ticket for a direct taxi ride from Russian-occupied Donetsk to Kyiv. But the route itself should have been a warning sign: That journey is impossible as it would require crossing an active front line.
He covered the 280-euro "ride." The document he was sent was a crudely photoshopped Ukrainian railway ticket.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion, civilians leaving occupied Donetsk for Ukrainian-controlled territory have generally had to travel through Russia before entering Ukraine through a third country.
Who benefits from the scheme?
Determining who was behind the scheme was one of the most difficult parts of the investigation.
In some cases, the women whose images were used in the profiles took part in the conversations themselves. The Kyiv Independent found four cases in which the women agreed to video calls with the men, confirming that the person in the photos matched the person on the call.
Many profiles never moved beyond text messages. It was much harder to determine who was actually operating the account when the photos had been taken from unrelated women and there was no live contact.
But money transfers provided some clues.
Some women asking for cash pickup through Western Union, RIA, or MoneyGram instructed the men to use the names listed on their dating profiles and to select Ukraine as the recipient's country of residence. Because cash-pickup services require recipients to show identification matching the transfer details, whoever collected the money was likely using the same identity the victim had been shown.
The instructions also contradicted their stories: Despite claiming to live under Russian occupation, the women asked men to list Ukraine as their place of residence when sending money.
While Ukraine and most of the international community recognize the occupied territories as part of Ukraine, in practice they are controlled by Russian authorities and cut off from Ukraine's financial system.
Western Union does not operate in Russian-occupied areas, a customer service representative told the Kyiv Independent. This means any money sent to Ukraine could only have been collected in Ukrainian-controlled territory, not in the occupied areas where the women claimed to live.
The Kyiv Independent also identified at least two cases with apparent links to Russia. In one, the "woman" asked the victim to pay a travel agency she said was helping her leave the country. The bank details she sent named the recipient as Vladislav Gafarov, a Russian national, with an account at a Russian bank.
The phone number the "woman" used to message the victim belongs to Gafarov, according to a leaked 2023 database of clients of Russian microfinance organizations. The same database lists him as an employee of the S.M. Budyonny Military Academy of Communications in St. Petersburg.
Another possibility is that some accounts may be managed by multiple people.
Karsten, who believed he was in a relationship with "Viktoriia," also came to suspect he had not been talking to just one person. Looking back, he noticed that the writing style would sometimes change dramatically — with some messages feeling as though they had been written by a woman, while others seemed to come from a man.
By the time he stopped sending money, Karsten had transferred 2,500 euros. Some victims sent even more: One man who contacted Helping to Leave had transferred around 9,000 euros.
From dating agencies to fake profiles: How the scam works
The use of Ukrainian women's identities in online romance scams is nothing new.
Over the years, Ukrainian and international media have documented cases in which foreign men were persuaded to send money or travel to Ukraine to meet women they believed they had formed relationships with, only to discover the relationships were not genuine.
Some traveled across the world only to be stood up, while others realized the dates were part of a business model designed to keep them paying for restaurants, messages, translators, and other services.
Similar scams have also been reported in Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Ghana, and Nigeria, among other countries.
While there are legitimate matchmaking services, past investigations have found cases in which agencies relied on fictitious profiles or paid chat operators to prolong conversations and keep foreign clients spending money.
In 2023, Ukraine's largest job-search platform Work.ua listed matchmaking agencies among common fraud operations that it blocks from its platform.
A video call should be one of the first steps when building a relationship with someone met online, according to Anna Bauer-Zuieva, owner of Grace Family, a long-running Ukrainian dating agency.
"It’s not about sending videos back and forth — it's about a real face-to-face (call)," Bauer-Zuieva told the Kyiv Independent. She said asking a person to show their surroundings during a live call can verify their story.
Scammers often rely on emotional pressure, presenting themselves as vulnerable and in urgent need of help. People looking for a genuine relationship, she said, usually do not begin by presenting themselves as someone who needs to be rescued.
For those who have already fallen victim, recovering money can be much harder. Once money has been collected by a scammer, it is generally not possible to recover it through services such as Western Union and Ria. The companies encourage customers to report suspected fraud, while PayPal advises users to contact customer support if they believe they have been targeted.
Victims can also report suspected fraud to Ukrainian police. According to Ukrainian Passport, people who are outside Ukraine can submit an application, appoint a lawyer in Ukraine to represent their interests, and provide testimony via video call.
For those who want to help people living in occupied territories, Nataliia from Helping to Leave said the safest way is to support verified humanitarian organizations rather than send money directly to someone they have only met online.
Yuliia Taradiuk and Natálie Zehnalová have contributed to this piece.

The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:52 UTC
14:00:52 KST

Back in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”.
The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”.
This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate.
Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net: the Timms review on personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and the Milburn review into young people who are out of work.
It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system.
An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months?
That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “welfare inquiry” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances.
Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch to radically means-test Pip. But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one is becoming “cool”, as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills.
The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for the launch of Reform TV on YouTube, with the party’s proposed £50bn benefits cuts presumably being lined up as viral content.
Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric as energy and housing costs are set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old.
A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, but Whitehall sources say there are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work.
Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising. For decades, the right has set the boundaries for what Britain’s safety net can be, resulting in little more than subsistence-level benefit rates, an ever crueller culture of testing and a sicker population.
The conventional wisdom has always been that change can only go one way: the benefits system can repeatedly become more punitive and error-strewn, but never more compassionate or accurate. For a leader who has defined himself as someone unafraid of large-scale change, Burnham is well placed to challenge that orthodoxy – if he wants. The opportunity to transform the benefits system does not come up often, and it is rarer still for a Conservative prime minister not to be at the helm.
It’s unfashionable to say it out loud but the truth is that Labour has the power to radically improve the disability benefits system: introduce more evidence-based assessments and reduce the need for mass appeals against incorrect decisions; stop using public money to line the pockets of private companies; and end unnecessary reassessments for lifelong disabilities. Similarly, ministers can address why more people need disability benefits in the first place: by investing in threadbare mental health support; addressing NHS waiting times and poor preventive health services; fixing Access to Work; and tackling employer attitudes to disabled candidates.
The right has long believed it has a monopoly on Britain’s benefits system, as if it were still paternalistic Victorians punishing and pitying the lower orders. But check the calendar and it is 2026. There is a Labour government in office and two big wads of research coming that can at last lay the groundwork for remaking our safety net. The millions who rely on it must hold their breath to see whether that chance will be grabbed or thrown away.
- Frances Ryan is a Guardian columnist

Helen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almond | The sweet spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:52 UTC
14:00:52 KST

I’ve been making versions of these baked oats ever since discovering Heidi Swanson’s recipe in Super Natural Every Day. This is my favourite store-cupboard version, for when stone fruit and berries have slipped out of season. Morello cherries are a dark, tart variety of sour cherry, with an intensity of flavour and bright acidity that stand up particularly well to baking. I love them here paired with almonds and coconut drinking milk (the light kind sold in cartons, not the rich tinned variety). The cherries I use are whole fruit in syrup, which I drain and dot over the oats – they remain distinct while becoming deliciously jammy as they bake. Almost any fruit compote or jam will work here, though, so choose your favourite.
Baked oats with morello cherries and almond
Jarred cherries come in many forms, so if yours is more like a compote or jam, simply add it in small teaspoonfuls instead.
Prep 10 min
 
Cook 45 min, plus cooling
 
Serves 4-6
30g unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly, plus extra for greasing
 
210g jumbo rolled oats
  
1 tsp baking powder
  
1 tsp ground cinnamon
  
½ tsp fine sea salt
  
1 large egg
  
60ml maple syrup, plus extra to serve
 
500ml coconut drinking milk
  
1 tsp vanilla extract
 
100-120g morello cherries in syrup, drained, or cherry compote or jam
 
30g flaked almonds
  
Icing sugar, for dusting (optional)
  
Yoghurt or cream,
  to serve
 
Heat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½ and lightly grease a 26cm ovenproof dish that’s about 5-6cm deep – the oat mixture will form a fairly shallow layer.
Put the oats, baking powder, cinnamon and salt in a medium bowl, mix well, then tip into the greased dish. In a large jug, whisk the egg, maple syrup and melted butter, then add the coconut drinking milk and vanilla, and whisk again to combine. Pour this evenly over the oats, then gently press down any oats that remain dry.
Dot the drained cherries evenly over the oats. If using a thicker compote or jam, drop small teaspoonfuls over the surface, then use the tip of the spoon to drag each one out slightly, creating ripples rather than deep pools. Scatter over the flaked almonds.
Bake for about 30 minutes, until golden on top and just set in the centre. Leave to stand for five to 10 minutes before serving, dusted with icing sugar if you like, and with yoghurt or cream and a little extra maple syrup alongside.

Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said.
Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business.
“We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said.
Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit, Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them.
“We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said.
Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far, with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product.
At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty”.
In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit.
She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU.
“We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now.
“We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.”
Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’”
Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East.
Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market.
“This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said.
“You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?”
Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said.
“The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”

Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.
Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.
Manasif’s death sentence has now reportedly been upheld by the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.
His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.
Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a “horrifying” surge in executions under the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record 356 people put to death in the country. Most of those executed are foreigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes.
At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.
Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing the death penalty for children in 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.
However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, it executed Ali al-Subaiti, along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti, for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.
The UN’s independent human rights experts have previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18.
 
“They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”
Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.

Commercial kitchen staff exposed to high levels of air pollution, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

Each time we enjoy a meal out or order a takeaway, someone cooks for us in a commercial kitchen. In the UK, 3.6 million people work in catering and hospitality. In the US it is estimated at close to 16 million. A first-of-its-kind study in the US has found catering staff can experience high air pollution at work – and that this can affect diners too.
Dr Drew Michanowicz, senior author of the study at non-profit research institute PSE Healthy Energy, said: “I was motivated by what we have learned over the years about what just 30 minutes of gas cooking can do to air quality in homes with the realisation that millions of people cook for a living for hours on end.”
The researchers measured air pollution in 27 kitchens including fine-dining and casual full-service restaurants, those serving pizza and Chinese cuisine, catering facilities and kitchens in senior-living communities, universities and schools.
Although the kitchens met US legal limits for air pollution in workplaces, nitrogen dioxide in 17 kitchens was greater than the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for indoor air. All of these kitchens cooked with fossil-gas or propane.
Nitrogen dioxide is a pollutant in diesel exhaust, which has led to many UK and European cities introducing clean air and low-emission zones.
Three all-electric kitchens, a full-service restaurant, a school cafeteria, and a conference centre kitchen were part of the study. These had the lowest air pollution, indicating benefits from decarbonisation in catering and ending fossil-gas combustion.
The electric kitchens also had the lowest temperatures, an obvious benefit for staff welfare.
This summer’s European heatwave forced some restaurants in the UK to cut hours or close due sweltering conditions. Christopher Galarza, a chef who worked with the researchers, said: “I’ve worked in kitchens where the heat was so intense that you would finish a shift drenched in sweat, dehydrated and physically spent.”
The study also found air pollution did not stay in the kitchen. Median concentrations in dining areas were greater than WHO guidelines for outdoor air pollution.
Dr Yannai Kashtan, first author of the study from PSE Heathy Energy, said: “It is difficult to contextualise the relative risk to diners, but as a diner in a restaurant with gas-fired appliances you may be exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide.”
One result surprised the research team. Kashtan said: “In two-thirds of the gas kitchens, we measured higher levels of pollution overnight and in the early morning, when all the appliances were off. The culprit? Pilot lights that burn 24/7, whether or not ventilation is on.”
In the UK many commercial kitchens have automatic systems that cut off gas when ventilation is not operating.
Michanowicz said commercial-grade cooking appliances were not included in US energy efficiency regulations that led to pilot lights being phased out in the residential sector. “In most full-service kitchens with multiple appliances like ranges, griddles, fryers, ovens, steamers, and broilers, upwards of 20-30 small flames may be constantly burning,” said Michanowicz.
In the study, air pollution from pilot lights spread into dining areas, increasing exposure for cleaners and other workers and the health risk for other people in multi-use buildings.

These are the world’s best destinations for ‘golden hour’, according to a meteorologist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

Greece dominated the golden hour list, with four destinations making the top 10, including the Lindos Acropolis in Rhodes.
Even amateur photographers know that the best time to get snapping is during “golden hour” – but not all are created equal.
Some are far longer than an hour, others shorter; clouds can get in the way of the effect, as can rainfall; and light pollution can have an impact, too.
Luckily for us, travel company Kuoni has teamed up with meteorologist Jim Dale from British Weather Services to create a ranking for the world's best spots for golden hour.
Having analysed 165 destinations against metrics including cloud cover, light pollution, rainfall, artificial brightness, wind speed and average sunset duration, 20 places made the final list.
Greece dominated the rankings, with four places making the cut – ahead of Namibia with three, and two each for the US, Australia and Botswana.
“There’s something about that soft, warm light of golden hour that makes a destination feel truly unforgettable, whether you're watching the sun dip below the Acropolis in Lindos or over the dunes of the Namib Desert,” Marco Rocha, the product, commercial and operations director at Kuoni, said.
“What's interesting is that the best golden hour locations aren't always the most obvious ones – clear skies, low light pollution and a bit of local knowledge often matter more than a destination's reputation.”
Golden hour destinations you need to know about
Jordan’s Wadi Rum came out on top overall, with little cloud cover and almost no rain, followed by Sossusvlei in Namibia, the desert landscape with no light pollution and sunsets that last an average of 27.9 minutes.
Namibia has three locations in the top six. As well as Sossusvlei, Damaraland placed third, with Etosha National Park in sixth.
Chile’s Atacama Desert came fourth, with Kuoni noting that wildlife like flamingos, alpacas and Andean foxes make a visit here even more special, while Wahiba Sands in Oman rounded out the top five.
As for Europe, Lindos Acropolis in Rhodes narrowly made it into the top 10, with Kuoni noting that its perch 116 metres above the sea gives you uninterrupted golden hour views most evenings.
Next up was Paphos in Cyprus, coming in 16th, followed by Rhodes Town (17th), Cape Sounion in Athens (19th), and Zante’s Navagio Shipwreck Beach (20th).

Germany pressures Croatia to resolve bilateral disputes with Montenegro over EU accession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

The German government is pressuring Croatia to swiftly resolve its bilateral disputes with Montenegro, which would otherwise risk derailing Podgorica's accession process.
Berlin has stepped in, asking Croatia to constructively resolve the bilateral disputes that threaten to derail the accession of the EU’s most advanced candidate, four officials with direct knowledge of the matter told Euronews.
Earlier this week, Zagreb circulated an eight-point list of grievances that it wants resolved before Podgorica can finalise its accession bid. Behind the scenes, Berlin has been manoeuvring to ensure that enlargement does not lose momentum.
Berlin also recently offered to mediate, but the offer has not been put into practice. The government of Chancellor Friedrich Merz is positioning itself as an honest broker, fearing that unresolved bilateral problems could jeopardise the enlargement process.
“There are issues which we have signalled to our Montenegrin neighbours for years,” Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković told reporters ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Thursday.
“In the last two years, there has been no progress whatsoever,” Plenković said, arguing that his country has been “extremely constructive” in the accession talks with Montenegro.
In recent weeks, the European Commission has been participating in the talks between the two countries, and several member states have worked to keep enlargement from stalling over bilateral issues.
In particular, France wants to avoid trouble with enlargement for domestic reasons, while Luxembourg has taken aim at using the accession process to resolve bilateral issues.
All three European governments have been actively talking with Croatia to pressure it into resolving the bilateral issues. But the strongest push comes from Germany, which is seeking to get the enlargement process going.
The disputes mostly stem from the legacy of the Yugoslav wars of the early 1990s, including property claims and contested borders. They threaten Montenegro’s ambition to become the EU’s 28th member state by 2028.
Croatia’s stance has also drawn public criticism, including from EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who said on the margins of the European Council that the accession process should not be hijacked by bilateral issues.
Zagreb has been accused of raising the disputes at the last minute to exert maximum pressure on Montenegro. Croatia counters that the issues are long-standing and that it has made only a handful of symbolic requests.
Zagreb points out that the investigation of war crimes and reparation of victims are targets Podgorica needs to fulfil to close its accession work. Still, EU officials fear the tide could quickly turn against enlargement if Montenegro’s accession is not finalised soon.
A string of elections is scheduled in key member states next year, including in France, where far-right leader Marine Le Pen, traditionally a sceptic of EU expansion, is the favourite to win the presidential race.
Germany has been pushing for new ways to enlarge the EU, including a special “associate candidate” status for Ukraine, the notion of “gradual integration” of candidate countries and stronger democratic safeguards for newcomers.
Montenegro would also be the first country to join the bloc under the current enlargement methodology.
The Berlin Process, an intergovernmental initiative launched in 2014 to promote regional cooperation among Western Balkan countries, is chaired this year by Podgorica, which has worked closely with the German government through the forum in recent months.
EU officials read Germany’s move on the bilateral matter as Berlin taking ownership of the process.
Montenegro’s accession also comes against a broader geopolitical backdrop, in which Brussels is increasingly using enlargement to anchor its immediate neighbours to the West amid growing tensions with Russia.
As Podgorica is first in line, a disruption caused by what some regard as futile bilateral issues could have a devastating effect on the other “frontrunners”, namely Albania, Moldova and, most notably, Ukraine, whose accession bid will likely be closely linked to the eventual peace negotiations with Moscow.
In other words, Germany believes it is time to move ahead with Montenegro’s accession, given the effort Podgorica has put in, and a geopolitical picture that demands enlargement keep its momentum.

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:57:28 BST
13:57:28 KST

They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
- Published
Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.
"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.
Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.
US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.
In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.
The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.
"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."
Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.
"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"
Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.
Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.
One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.
"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.
And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.
Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.
"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.
Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.
Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.
Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.
Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.
Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.
"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."
He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.
"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".
Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.
"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."
The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."
The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.
The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.
Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.
Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".
Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.
The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.
"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"
"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."
Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.
The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.
For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.
There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.
Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

Children bear brunt as Ethiopia fighting fuels fears of wider war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:55:00 UTC
13:55:00 KST

Ten-year-old Iyerusalem lies in a hospital bed in northern Ethiopia, her amputated legs propped up by rolled blankets as she struggles with pain and the loss of her older brother, who was killed alongside their horse when fighting struck their home.
“I was in our compound with my older brother and our horse when we were hit. My brother and the horse died,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP) from Ayder Comprehensive Specialised Hospital in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region.
Iyerusalem is among dozens of civilians wounded since fighting erupted between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and Ethiopian federal forces on Sept. 23, reviving a conflict in a region still scarred by the devastating 2020-22 war.
Federal forces repelled the TPLF offensive and took control of Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 after rebel leaders and fighters abandoned the city.
The fighting has nevertheless left civilians, including children, with severe injuries and families mourning relatives killed in bombardments.
Many wounded people come from remote villages in southern Tigray, hours from medical care along difficult roads affected by fighting and shelling.
Iyerusalem, from Qarsole village in Alamata district, said her amputated legs were causing severe pain.
“If I get medical treatment and can walk again, I want to go back to school,” she said, as her father, Hiluf, watched anxiously.
Nearby, 12-year-old Hana was recovering from severe facial injuries and a broken leg. The explosion that wounded her killed her mother and brother.
“First I heard a loud explosion, and the whole house shook. I was scared and did not even know what had happened. I could not open my eyes or my mouth,” she said.
“The sound of the explosion keeps coming back in my head.”
In another room, Betelhem, 10, was being treated for a broken leg, while her 6-year-old sister, Melet, had suffered a neck injury. Their pregnant mother was killed when heavy artillery struck their home.
“The bomb hit our house directly, all these people have died, but no one is being held responsible. There is no government,” said their father, Haftom, a 39-year-old shopkeeper.
Birhanu Hailemariam, the emergency coordinator at Ayder hospital, said 34 people wounded by heavy artillery, drones, gunfire and explosives had arrived in recent days. Twenty-three were children, and one patient had died.
Medical staff lacked basic equipment and medicines, including anesthesia, he said.
“But we are doing our best to treat everyone,” he said.
Although the latest fighting had not reached the scale of the previous Tigray war, which the African Union (AU) estimates killed about 600,000 people, fear remained pervasive among patients and medical workers.
“Both are hurting people,” another doctor said of the TPLF and federal forces, asking not to be identified.
Families were reluctant to assign blame for attacks. Hiluf said he did not know who had bombarded his village and feared reprisals if he accused either side.
“I do not want to fight with anyone,” he said. “Let there be peace for us.”
Farther north, residents of the border town of Zalambessa say they are caught between Ethiopian and Eritrean troops as the risk of a broader conflict grows.
Eritrea has deployed thousands of troops to northern Tigray to support forces opposing Ethiopia's central government, according to a security source.
“Ethiopian troops are on one side, and Eritrean troops are on the other,” said Selam, 33, whose first name was changed for security reasons.
Eritrean soldiers initially advanced south before drone strikes forced them to retreat into the surrounding mountains, she said. Although the area was no longer seeing active fighting, her home and small shop had been without electricity or water for a week.
“We are caught in the middle and living in deep anxiety,” she said.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported that Ethiopian federal forces had moved heavy weapons toward Zalambessa in recent days. Eyewitnesses reported seeing a substantial convoy of tanks and other heavy weaponry advancing from the south, though AFP could not independently verify the reports.
Residents described deserted streets, closed businesses and growing shortages as blocked roads disrupted supplies.
“Most people only go out to attend church and pray,” said Hadush, 45, who also requested anonymity.
“Now there is no bread,” he said, describing the worsening hardship.
Selam said federal soldiers were preventing residents from traveling to Adigrat, about 30 kilometers (18 miles) south, making it difficult to visit relatives or obtain essential supplies.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel did not respond to AFP questions about the reported presence of Eritrean troops.
The military buildup has raised international concern that the fighting in Tigray could draw the neighboring countries into another war.
On Wednesday, the United States urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to pursue “de-escalation,” calling on all countries to respect their neighbors' sovereignty and territorial integrity and avoid cross-border incursions.
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993. The countries fought a deadly border war from 1998 to 2000 before relations improved in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office and pursued closer ties with Asmara.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the two countries severing ties this month amid the renewed Tigray conflict.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which launched its offensive on Sept. 23. Eritrea alleges that Ethiopia intends to exploit the fighting to invade its territory and seize Assab port on the Red Sea.
The TPLF initially made gains in the Afar region but has since retreated ahead of advancing federal forces, abandoning towns for the surrounding hills.
Federal troops took Mekelle without resistance on Oct. 3 and subsequently seized several other towns without encountering opposition. The latest reported advance brought government forces to Rama, about 7 kilometers (4 miles) from the Eritrean border, according to two residents.

Reserve Bank governor paid $1.2 million as RBA workers fight real wage cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:50:02 UTC
13:50:02 KST

Reserve Bank governor paid $1.2 million as RBA workers fight real wage cuts
In short:
RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26.
RBA workers are demanding an 11 per cent pay increase over three years, but the RBA is offering 9.5 per cent.
What's next?
The latest data show Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, but economists say the RBA may not have finished lifting rates.
The Reserve Bank's senior officials are among the highest paid people in Australia.
RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26, with a base salary of $1.01 million.
Deputy governor Andrew Hauser received total remuneration of $955,033, with a base salary of $903,217.
The RBA's four assistant governors received total remuneration between $743,000 and $868,000 each, and its chief operating officer received total remuneration of $905,543.
The figures can be found in the RBA's 2026 annual report, which was released on Thursday afternoon.
The median annual earnings for all employees in Australia is $74,672.
In March this year, Ms Bullock received unwanted media attention when she and her husband bought a $2 million home in Yamba, in northern NSW, on the same day that the RBA lifted interest rates on February 3.
It was her third investment property.
Her property purchase was recorded in her declaration of material personal interests on the RBA's website.
The RBA governor's pay is slightly above most federal departmental or agency heads, which are mostly clustered around $900,000-$1,000,000.
However, the chief executives of some publicly owned corporations are paid far more.
Ellie Sweeney, the NBN Co chief executive, received $3.4 million in total remuneration in 2025-26, up from $1.9 million a year earlier, making her Australia's highest-paid public servant.
Paul Graham, the chief executive of Australia Post, received $3.3 million in 2024-25. Dennis Barns, the chief executive of Snowy Hydro Limited, received $2.1 million in 2024-25.
RBA workers don't want a real wage cut
The RBA is currently arguing with junior RBA staff about pay and conditions.
Lower-ranked RBA staff have been asking for a pay increase of 11 per cent over three years and an inflation-protection mechanism that triggers additional pay rises if inflation outpaces wages, to avoid real wage cuts in coming years.
But last month, hours after the RBA lifted rates for the fourth time this year, Ms Bullock emailed RBA staff and asked them to vote for a pay offer of 9.5 per cent over three years.
A majority of RBA staff had rejected a similar proposal in July.
The Finance Sector Union says enterprise agreement negotiations have been dragging on since late last year and the RBA has refused to move on its original pay offer.
The latest round of voting for the RBA's proposed enterprise agreement will close on Monday at 5pm.
After lifting interest rates last month, Ms Bullock said she sympathised with the plight of Australian workers.
But she said the only way workers could keep receiving sustainable increases in real wages was from productivity growth, and Australia's economy was struggling to deliver it.
"People are feeling, quite rightly, very annoyed and very upset about the fact that the costs of everything are rising, that their wages are not keeping pace with that, they’re seeing real wage cuts," she said.
"If we don't get productivity growth, there's not going to be real wage rises coming down the pipeline."
According to the RBA's annual report, the bank has 2,201 employees, equating to 2,082 full-time equivalent employees.
It has 76 senior executives, and another 222 highly paid staff.
The RBA's workforce has increased by 8 per cent over the past 12 months. The RBA says that reflects the additional resources it needs to implement its transformation and change agendas.
The additional staff are concentrated in technology and corporate support functions.
Higher unemployment will help to control inflation
Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.
It is higher than the RBA forecast for this point in its rate-hiking cycle.
At a fireside chat last month, Ms Bullock said Australia may need an unemployment rate of 5 per cent to get inflation completely under control.
"[W]hat level of unemployment eases the pressure on the supply side of the economy?" she asked.
"I think between 4.5 and 5 will probably take enough heat out of the labour market that it'll ease pressure on inflation,"
she said.
On Thursday, Bureau of Statistics data showed that Australia's unemployment rate has risen 0.6 percentage points (from 4.1 per cent to 4.7 per cent) since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February this year.
Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan said outside of the COVID-19-related volatility, it was the largest nine-month increase in unemployment in more than a decade.
"The deterioration is also more pronounced than the RBA had forecast back in August," he said.
"Importantly, it's too early to see any effect from the RBA's September rate hike, which we think will weigh on both GDP growth and labour demand in coming quarters."
RBA records $11.3 billion negative equity position
The RBA's annual report shows the bank had a "negative equity" position of $11.3 billion at the end of June (compared with a negative equity position of $5.3 billion in June 2025).
The deterioration in its net equity position reflected a large "accounting loss" in 2025/26, which was partially offset by valuation gains on its gold holdings.
The RBA's Governance Board says negative equity does not affect the RBA's ability to operate effectively or perform its functions, but it is important that the equity position is restored over time.
"This can be achieved by retaining future year profits," the RBA says in its annual report.
"Based on market expectations for the cash rate as at 30 June 2026 and market prices and exchange rates at this time, negative equity is expected to diminish over the next few years.
"However, a return to target for the Reserve Bank Reserve Fund probably remains more than a decade away."

Risk of electric battery fire: VW recalls thousands of cars again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:47:55 UTC
13:47:55 KST

Car maker Volkswagen is recalling more vehicles in Germany, this time electric models. Faulty batteries could, in the worst case, trigger fires.
A few weeks ago it was a faulty screw; now a suspected battery defect means VW has to recall thousands of cars once again. In the worst case, there is a risk of fire.
Recall campaigns are already reported to be under way in the United States and the United Kingdom, and models in Germany are now also being recalled. According to the authorities, around 22,000 ID.4 electric cars are affected in the US.
VW prepares recall in Germany
With recalls already under way in the US and the UK, VW is planning and rolling out recall campaigns in Germany and other markets.
Some battery cells in Volkswagen electric cars are defective. Internal quality checks have revealed the problem, according to Handelsblatt. A Volkswagen spokesperson told the outlet that several thousand vehicles are affected.
VW cited production faults at suppliers as the cause of the faulty battery cells. The issue is limited to a specific production period.
Because of the defect, the batteries may be exposed to increased thermal stress, according to the information available. In extreme cases, a fire in these electric vehicles cannot be ruled out, VW said.
According to Handelsblatt, the VW ID.3, ID.4, ID.7, ID Buzz and Cupra Born models produced between 2023 and 2025 are among those affected. The company has not yet confirmed this list of models.
The recall is being prepared in close coordination with the relevant authorities, the spokesperson said. It has not yet appeared in the databases of Germany’s Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA).
VW sets out immediate measures
To prevent possible damage and incidents, the group is now recommending that potentially affected cars be charged only to a maximum of 80%. The manufacturer plans to recall some of the vehicles to service centres to check the batteries. Once the batteries have been inspected, the charging limit will be lifted for cars in which no fault is found.
If a defective battery is identified, the high-voltage battery module would not necessarily have to be replaced and could potentially be brought up to date with a software upgrade.
Customers whose vehicles are affected will be contacted by the company, according to the report. Owners will receive a letter informing them of the next steps.
A damaged screw led to a recall of around 2.86 million VW and Audi vehicles worldwide in September. The component could have caused the steering to fail, the KBA warned.
20% of VW deliveries are electric
VW’s electric-car business is strongest in Europe compared with the rest of the world.
The share of battery electric vehicles in Volkswagen Group’s European deliveries rose to 20% in the first three quarters of 2026, meaning one in five vehicles delivered was fully electric.
Overall, the group is grappling with falling demand worldwide, with business in China in particular slumping. In Germany, VW continues to dominate both the market for new electric car registrations and the used EV market.

ICMR picks 7 centres to develop priority medical devices, diagnostics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
04:35:27 UTC
13:35:27 KST

NEW DELHI: Seven research centres across leading Indian institutions have been selected by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) to develop priority medical devices and diagnostic technologies, with projects spanning portable screening for primary healthcare, biomaterials and technologies for eye and vascular diseases.The selected institutions are the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs) at Kharagpur, Delhi, Bombay, Kanpur and Madras, the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), Bengaluru, and Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore.
Among the selected projects, IIT Bombay's centre, led by Dr Abhijit Majumder, will focus on portable screening, monitoring and point-of-care medical technologies for primary healthcare. Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham's centre, led by Prof Gopal S Pillai, will work on developing, validating and translating healthcare technologies for ophthalmic and vascular diseases, while IISc Bengaluru will focus on biomaterials and translational medical devices.IIT Kharagpur's PRAGATICAR, led by Prof Suman Chakraborty, will focus on frugal diagnostics, regenerative and personalised healthcare, artificial intelligence, digital health and advanced therapeutics. IIT Delhi's CAR-PATH, led by Prof Vivekanandan Perumal, will work on priority applied technologies for healthcare.At IIT Kanpur, Prof Amitabha Bandyopadhyay will lead a multidisciplinary proposal to develop 10 priority healthcare products.
IIT Madras will host TARaNGaM, a translational hub for next-generation medical technology, devices and diagnostics, led by Prof Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam.The initiative aims to accelerate the development of affordable, accessible and indigenous healthcare technologies addressing unmet clinical needs. To identify these needs, ICMR undertook an exercise involving clinicians from different healthcare settings, including tier-1, tier-2 and tier-3 cities, and drew up a curated list of around 100 priority medical device and diagnostic technologies.Under the original call for proposals, applicants were required to propose the development of at least eight to 10 technologies from this list, covering a mix of low-risk and high-risk products. The scheme provides for funding of up to Rs 15 crore per centre over five years, with an emphasis on regulatory-compliant product development and eventual commercialisation.
The call prioritised institutions with a track record in research, prototyping, technology transfer and commercialisation. It also required centres to leverage existing infrastructure, build a trained medical technology research workforce and continue functioning beyond the funding period, with host institutions expected to sustain them as permanent activities.The key challenge will be translating research into validated products that can address clinical needs and reach patients. The results list does not specify the individual devices to be developed by most of the selected centres, their development timelines or when the technologies could become available for clinical use.
