Twenty-two US lawmakers demand Trump immediately impose Russia sanctions under Graham Act
Twenty-two Democrat and Republican members of the US House of Representatives have written to President Donald Trump demanding the full and immediate implementation of the sanctions against Russia provided for under the Graham Act.
Source: Congressman Jim Costa's website; Ukrainian journalist in Washington Ostap Yarysh on Facebook
Details: The letter was authored by House Foreign Affairs Committee member Jim Costa, together with the co-chairs of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus in the House of Representatives: Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Brian Fitzpatrick and Joe Wilson. The lawmakers stressed that the first mandatory deadline for the key sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to take effect expires on 18 October.
They emphasised the need to step up economic pressure on Moscow ahead of winter.
Quote: "As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war. Utilising the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously."
Details: In the letter, the lawmakers also expressed deep concern over the US Department of the Treasury's decision on 9 October to issue General Licence No. 135, which permits transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading and import of Russian diesel fuel into the US.
They called on the administration to immediately revoke this permit and prevent any new exemptions that restore the flow of petrodollars into the Kremlin's war chest.
Furthermore, the House members have asked the administration five questions and demanded written answers by 18 October. They want to know what steps will be taken to ensure the full implementation of all mandatory sanctions, tariffs and bans, and whether the White House intends to delay any provisions or grant exemptions to them.
The lawmakers are also calling for the administration to publish a list of Russian officials, oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies targeted by the restrictions and to clarify whether foreign banks and Russia's shadow fleet operators will also be affected. They are further demanding details of which countries will face secondary tariffs for purchasing Russian energy, what safeguards will be in place for allies, how pressure on Putin will be measured, and why sanctions are being eased despite the existing legislative ban on Russian energy imports.
Among the 22 signatories to the letter are leading representatives of both parties, including Republicans Michael McCaul, Joe Wilson, Brian Fitzpatrick and Don Bacon, as well as Democrats Steny Hoyer, Jim Costa, Marcy Kaptur, Josh Gottheimer and Dina Titus.
Background:
- On 17 September, the US Congress passed bill H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The legislation authorises 500% tariffs on Russian goods, secondary tariffs of up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, and mandatory sanctions against key sectors of the Russian economy.
- On 19 September, US President Donald Trump signed the Graham Act into law, setting the first 30-day deadline for the implementation of its provisions for 18 October.
- On 9 October, the US Department of the Treasury, through the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), issued General Licence No. 135, allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel fuel.
- On 14 October, a bipartisan group of 12 US senators sent a strongly worded letter to Donald Trump, calling the diesel deal with Moscow a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and urging him to immediately revoke the licence and move to full implementation of the Graham Act.

"There is a lot of internal disquiet about this."
'Opposed … subject to proper process'
Multiple senior Liberals told the ABC the matter had not been considered by shadow cabinet or discussed in the Coalition party room, and that could only happen after scrutiny by the parliament's joint standing committee on trade.
"You can't short-circuit that by [writing] an op-ed," one said, framing Senator Canavan's intervention as a clear attempt to strongarm Liberals, reigniting tensions between the parties that plagued the leadership of Angus Taylor's predecessor, Sussan Ley.
The joint standing committee process is still some time away. While the deal's text was agreed between leaders this year, it will not be signed until Australia and each EU member country complete the requisite legal checks, most likely early next year.
Some Liberals believe this leaves time to renegotiate aspects of the deal. Two Liberals seeking to downplay any disagreement said the agreed position was "opposed to the deal as it stands, subject to the proper parliamentary and Coalition process".
Senator Canavan used more cautious language in a press conference today, saying the opposition was "opposed to the deal in its current form".
Farrell says veto would be 'vandalism'
The government has rubbished the idea that renegotiation would be possible.
"There is no room … the deal is done," Senator Farrell said today.
The minister has projected confidence that the Senate, where the government does not have the numbers in its own right, will not stand in the way of the deal, telling the ABC on Wednesday he believed "enough senators … understand how important this is".
One interpretation of that comment is that Senator Farrell believes enough Liberals might cross the floor to vote for the deal, although none of those who spoke to the ABC suggested they would.
Another is that Senator Farrell is confident that the Coalition – or at least the Liberals – will eventually land in favour of the deal, a view shared among some European diplomats, who have directly lobbied Mr Taylor and other Liberals in recent weeks.
One diplomat from an EU nation told the ABC it would be "very damaging" if Australia did not ratify the deal and echoed Senator Farrell's comments: "There is no appetite [in Europe] to revisit this … the deal is done."
The deal broadens access to the European market for Australian beef and sheep meat exporters, although not by as much as those industries had hoped. It also secures access for Australian fruit, vegetable and seafood.
Senator Farrell told the ABC it was clear that the Nationals would vote against the deal.
"At a time when Australians are facing cost-of-living pressures, the National Party have chosen to block our farmers from 27 new export markets, lock in high tariffs on Aussie businesses, and kill local jobs," he said.
"Once a long-standing party of government, the Nationals have reduced themselves to desperate populism, dressed in fake fluoro."
The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry supports the deal. Chief executive Andrew McKellar told the Insiders: On Background podcast it was not "perfect" but was in the national interest.
"From a business point of view, we are strongly supporting the fact that it should be ratified and passed into legislation in the Australian parliament," he said.
"If we lose that opportunity now, it's gone forever and, honestly, that would be very short-sighted."

UN needs reform like never before — would-be secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:42:00 UTC
12:42:00 KST

WASHINGTON, October 16. /TASS/. The United Nations needs reform like never before in order to correspond to modern challenges, Guyana's UN envoy Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, who has been nominated to the post of the next UN secretary-general, said.
"Attention is <…> rightfully placed on reforms of the United Nations. It has never been louder to call for reform, in my view," she said at the Washington-based Stimson Center in Washington.
In her words, the question should be raised whether "the structures of 1945 are relevant to 2026 realities."
"And that brings in the issue or the matter of Security Council reform. Of course, the Secretary General doesn't have a role in that as such, that's for member states. But then you have the reform of the agencies, funds, and programs, and we have over 35 of them. Are they fit for today, and what do we need to do? Can we reduce the overlaps, or eradicate the overlaps, the duplication, so that we can deliver better on the ground," the diplomat continued.
In her view, there is also the need for a "reform of the UN Secretariat - that comes under the Secretary General as well - to be more effective, more efficient, and in lockstep with member states, and not the other way around."
She added that "the organization, as it currently is, must change."
"We are 19 years away from the centenary of the UN, and so now is the time to reform and to remake that UN," Rodrigues-Birkett concluded.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has called for reforming the UN Secretariat as it has been taken over by one group of states pursuing their own interests. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the organization has been under pressure for a reform. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi believes that changes within the organization should start from a reform of the UN Security Council.
Currently, seven candidates are vying for the post of the UN secretary-general: Rafael Grossi (Argentina), head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA); Rebeca Grynspan (Costa Rica), Secretary-General of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD); Macky Sall, former President of Senegal; Maria Fernanda Espinosa Garces, former Foreign Minister and Defense Minister of Ecuador; Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana’s Permanent Representative to the UN; Ivonne Baki, former Ecuadorian Ambassador to the US and France; and Olara Otunnu, Uganda’s former Permanent Representative to the UN.
Antonio Guterres, who has headed the UN since 2017, will complete his term on December 31, 2026. Members of the Security Council select a candidate to recommend for the post of UN chief. The General Assembly then votes to formally appoint the new UN secretary-general.

Bank of America’s $1.21 billion fine highlights US banks’ anti-money laundering failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:34:47 UTC
12:34:47 KST

Bank of America’s $1.21 billion fine highlights US banks’ anti-money laundering failures
Bank of America has been ordered to pay more than $1.21 billion in U.S. penalties after regulators found that it failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions and violated sanctions rules, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
According to the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the enforcement actions announced on October 13 include the third-largest penalty in the department's history and the largest ever imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). More than $1 billion of the suspicious transactions involved national security and other priority financial crime risks, including activity indicative of Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money laundering linked to the southwestern U.S. border.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that failures at major financial institutions could threaten the broader financial system. He said the consequences of inadequate compliance extend beyond individual banks, "exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks."
The Treasury said Bank of America had prioritized revenue over compliance requirements and relied heavily on inquiries from law enforcement agencies and other financial institutions rather than its own monitoring systems. In its settlement with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the bank admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required due diligence on certain foreign bank accounts and file suspicious activity reports.
The penalties involve three regulatory actions. FinCEN assessed a $1.2 billion penalty, which includes credit for a $750 million civil penalty imposed by the OCC. Separately, Bank of America agreed to pay approximately $11.6 million to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle 475 apparent sanctions violations. These involved transactions subject to sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Myanmar, Somalia, narcotics trafficking and global terrorism.
The OCC had previously identified significant weaknesses in the bank's compliance systems and issued a cease-and-desist order in December 2024 requiring corrective measures. However, regulators found that the bank's anti-money laundering program remained deficient and ineffective, with weaknesses in transaction monitoring resulting in delayed reporting of suspicious transactions worth billions of dollars.
More than a year after the 2024 order, Bank of America continued to fail to escalate potentially suspicious transactions for investigation. The OCC also identified a systemic gap in the bank's monitoring program that allowed potential trade-based money laundering transactions to be processed without adequate scrutiny.
Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould described the violations as egregious and persistent, saying the bank's failure to address longstanding compliance weaknesses justified the OCC's largest financial penalty to date. He warned that financial institutions failing to maintain effective anti-money laundering programs could face significant regulatory action.
Under the settlement terms, Bank of America must engage an independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that escaped detection and report the findings to FinCEN. The bank must also undergo independent assessments of its transaction monitoring, customer due diligence and foreign correspondent banking controls.
"Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," Bank of America said in a statement. The lender added that it had invested billions of dollars in technology and assigned thousands of employees to combat financial crime.
The financial penalties have also affected the bank's earnings. On October 14, Bank of America reported third-quarter net income of $6.9 billion, or $0.91 per diluted share. Its results included a non-tax-deductible regulatory settlement charge of $1.2 billion, reducing earnings by approximately $0.17 per share.
Several major U.S. financial institutions have faced substantial penalties for similar compliance failures in recent years.
In November 2023, cryptocurrency exchange Binance agreed to a $3.4 billion FinCEN penalty and a separate $968 million OFAC settlement for violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws. The agreement also required five years of independent monitoring. The FinCEN penalty remains the largest in U.S. Treasury history.
In October 2024, TD Bank's U.S. subsidiaries received a record $1.3 billion FinCEN penalty as part of a broader settlement exceeding $3 billion. The bank pleaded guilty to violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, while the OCC imposed an asset growth restriction limiting its U.S. banking subsidiaries to $434 billion in assets.
Earlier, in 2018, U.S. Bank was assessed a $185 million civil penalty for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. Regulators found that the institution had configured its monitoring software to limit the number of suspicious activity alerts rather than expanding its capacity to investigate potentially illicit transactions.
The Bank of America settlement came just five days after American Express National Bank received a $350 million civil penalty from the OCC on October 8. Regulators cited systemic failures in the bank's anti-money laundering controls that resulted in approximately $13 billion in suspected trade-based money laundering activity not being properly identified, evaluated and reported over the preceding decade.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that the U.S. Secretary of State is set to travel to Uzbekistan and India from October 17 to 22.

White House Ordered Restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield, Disrupting Drone Defense – Reuters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:34:19 UTC
12:34:19 KST

The order to restrict Ukraine’s military-grade Starshield satellite communications system came directly from inside the White House, according to a Reuters investigation published Thursday, Oct. 15, revealing that Washington moved to limit technology essential to Ukraine’s battlefield operations and defense against Russian drones.
The restrictions disrupted Ukrainian strike missions and slowed interceptor drones used to protect cities from Russian Shahed attacks – at a time when Moscow was launching hundreds of drones and missiles against Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter told Reuters that Pentagon leaders received instructions from within the White House to slow the SpaceX-operated Starshield service used by Ukraine’s military.
The officials did not identify who issued the directive or who implemented it. A senior US official denied that President Donald Trump personally requested the restrictions.
“No such request was ever made by the president,” the official told Reuters.
The White House did not answer questions about whether other administration officials had issued the order.
The revelation comes amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump demanding that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries even as Moscow continues attacking Ukrainian power plants and residential areas.
Trump Calls Ukraine’s Strikes on Russian Oil Refineries a ‘Disgrace,’ Says Zelensky Harder to Deal With Than Putin
US restrictions undermine Ukraine’s drone defenses
Ukrainian military officials reported that Starshield terminals stopped functioning when mounted on fast-moving platforms, disrupting drone guidance systems operating over Ukrainian territory.
The restrictions affected attacks on Russian military positions and logistics facilities in occupied Ukraine, while also limiting high-speed interceptor drones designed to destroy incoming Shaheds before they reach Ukrainian cities.
As Kyiv Post first reported Wednesday, Ukrainian forces experienced sudden Starshield restrictions without advance warning, with military units reporting lost connections at speeds ranging from 72 to 161 kilometers per hour (45-100 mph).
The disruptions affected interceptor drones, medium-range strike missions, reconnaissance, frontline logistics and communications relays.
By Thursday morning, Ukrainian Defense Ministry sources confirmed to Kyiv Post that connectivity while moving had been restored, although it remained unclear whether all speed restrictions had been lifted.
Ukraine is seeking to raise the operating speed limit to 450 km/h (280 mph) to allow interceptor drones to pursue faster Russian aerial threats, including jet-powered drones.
Dan Rice, president of American University Kyiv and a former special adviser to Ukraine’s military commander-in-chief, warned that such restrictions could have deadly consequences.
Speaking to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, Rice described the scale of the threat facing Ukrainian air defenses.
“When you have 500 inbound Shaheeds, jet-powered Shaheeds, and I was hit within 400 meters twice this week,” he said, “you need to have interceptors going out to protect Ukrainian civilians.”
Rice warned that interference with high-speed interceptor operations could allow Russian drones to reach civilian targets, including schools, hospitals and residential buildings.
Retired Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said the restrictions also impaired Ukrainian drone missions against Russian military logistics and command facilities approximately 150-250 kilometers (93 to 155 miles) behind Russian lines.
The consequences extend beyond battlefield efficiency.
In an interview with Piers Morgan on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the restrictions had already cost Ukrainian lives.
“People are dying because of his decision,” Zelensky said.
“I’m sure that they knew what they did. Absolutely,” he added.
However, the Ukrainian leader stopped short of identifying who had ordered the restrictions.
“I don’t know, him or somebody pushed him to… I don’t know really,” Zelensky said when asked whether he was angry with Elon Musk.
“We are professionals. If you are losing the speed of Starlink, we understand what’s going on. So they switched off. That’s their decision,” he added.
Musk confirms US government controls Starshield
The controversy has also clarified who ultimately controls the military satellite system.
Starshield is a government-focused version of SpaceX’s Starlink network, developed for military and national security operations. Unlike commercial Starlink, the Starshield services at issue operate under US government control.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, confirmed Wednesday that restrictions on the system were a government decision.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk wrote on X.
Starshield restrictions follow US pressure to stop Russian refinery attacks
The White House directive emerged amid an increasingly bitter confrontation over Ukraine’s campaign against Russian oil infrastructure.
During eight hours of talks in Miami on Oct. 9, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner took a tough position toward Ukrainian officials, Axios reported, citing a person familiar with the discussions.
The US delegation expressed frustration that Kyiv had continued targeting Russian refineries despite repeated American requests to stop.
Washington also defended Trump’s agreement to allow more than 2.25 million barrels of Russian diesel onto US and international markets, arguing that the arrangement could encourage Moscow to soften its position in peace negotiations.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened to cut off US intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued the attacks. A US official denied that such a threat was made.
Zelensky had offered to suspend refinery strikes if Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s power plants, but Trump wanted Kyiv to halt its attacks unilaterally, according to the US official.
Bipartisan backlash in Congress over Trump’s Russian diesel deal
A bipartisan group of 12 US senators urged Trump to reverse the diesel agreement, warning that it would provide Moscow with additional revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
On Thursday, 22 US lawmakers called for full enforcement of Russia sanctions ahead of an Oct. 18 deadline, targeting Moscow’s energy revenues, foreign banks and sanctions evasion networks. They also demanded that Washington revoke the authorization allowing Russian diesel transactions.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian refinery strikes for soaring energy prices, although energy analysts point primarily to the US-Israeli war with Iran and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
In an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post, former US Ambassador to Ukraine Steven Pifer warned that the diesel deal would do little to lower US fuel prices while helping finance Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“American dollars will be going to purchase Russian fuel, and that’s going to help the Russian military machine buy more missiles and bombs to use against Ukraine,” Pifer said.

U.S. retail sales up in September amid surging gas prices

WASHINGTON, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- U.S. retail sales rose 0.8 percent in September to 745 billion U.S. dollars, largely driven by higher gasoline prices that boosted consumer spending at gas stations, according to data released Thursday by the Commerce Department.
Excluding sales at gas stations, retail sales increased just 0.2 percent during the month, suggesting underlying consumer demand remained subdued.
While rising retail sales are generally seen as a sign of economic resilience, analysts said the September increase offered a less encouraging picture of consumer spending, as higher fuel costs accounted for much of the growth.
"Retail sales definitely looked weak in September," Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua.
Experts also noted that high gas prices are harming many Americans, forcing them to cut back or reduce their savings.
Gary Hufbauer, a nonresident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said: "About 50 percent of households are living paycheck to paycheck, and if they are squeezed by gasoline prices, they have to cut back elsewhere. But the other 50 percent just reduce their savings to pay for higher gasoline prices."
High energy prices could create a new wave of inflation, he added.
"The longer energy stays elevated, the more likely it generates a new wave of inflation. Another six months would run this risk," Hufbauer said.
The data were released just weeks before November's midterm elections, at a time when underlying prices are already high and gasoline prices threaten to make matters even worse. Republicans could take a beating at the polls over voters' displeasure with high prices that show no sign of coming down.
However, even if Democrats take control of Congress, the party will have its work cut out after the dust settles, as pushing down gas prices means finding a solution to the war in Iran, which seems improbable at the moment.
At the same time, underlying inflation continues unabated. Experts said getting back to pre-COVID price levels requires the Fed to step in and raise interest rates. However, the central bank has shown no desire to hike rates to the 5 percent level, or higher, that economists say is needed to tame inflation.
Some experts noted that the GOP is caught between a rock and a hard place.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West said, "Republicans are caught between fighting inflation and a slowing economy, which is a big problem for them in November."
"Gas prices should drop when the Iran War ends, but it is not clear how (Donald) Trump brings that conflict to a reasonable conclusion," West said. ■

SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's export volume kept double-digit growth in September amid an explosive global demand for semiconductors and computer storage devices, central bank data showed Friday.
The export volume index surged 32.1 percent in September from a year earlier, after soaring 25.9 percent in August, according to the Bank of Korea.
It marked the fastest pace in over 16 years since January 2010, maintaining an upward trajectory for 11 consecutive months since November 2025.
In terms of volume, exports for computers, electronic and optical devices skyrocketed 46.6 percent due to a massive demand for memory chips and solid state drives used for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Backed by high chip prices, the export value index shot up 89.2 percent in September compared to the same month last year.
The import volume index gained 11.1 percent year-on-year in September, while the import value index spiked 26.9 percent.
The higher inbound shipment was led by semiconductors, computers and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The net terms-of-trade index for goods, or a ratio of export prices to import prices, soared 25.4 percent in September on a yearly basis due to a faster increase in export prices than import prices. ■

Macao exhibition traces 3,000 years of Chinese glassmaking
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
11:31:21 CST
12:31:21 KST

MACAO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- A fleeting flower bloom finds lasting form in glass at an exhibition in China's Macao Special Administrative Region (SAR), tracing more than 3,000 years of Chinese glassmaking.
"Luminous Brilliance: The Artistry of Zibo Liuli" at the Poly MGM Museum brings together nearly 180 ancient and contemporary examples of liuli, or Chinese art glass. Its opening ceremony was held on Thursday.
The sculpture "Eternity," by Liu Yuan and Wang Tongqiang, captures a short-lived cereus blossom in violet and blue glass. The artists heated the material over a flame, pulling and bending it into petals before it cooled and hardened, according to the museum's exhibition guide.
Other exhibits include eye-patterned beads from the Warring States period and Qing dynasty imperial glassware.
The exhibition draws on the traditions of Zibo, a glassmaking center in east China's Shandong Province. Vice Mayor Guo Qing said the city's industry now spans materials research, design, production and cultural tourism, with artisans practicing techniques including glassblowing and carving.
Organizers include the National Museum of China, China Poly Group and the Zibo Ceramics and Glass Museum. The exhibition is free and runs through March 31, 2027. ■

China's storage deployment helping change economics of renewable electricity: IRENA official
China

2026-10-16

A man tries on an interactive device during the 2026 World Energy Storage Conference in Ningde City, southeast China's Fujian Province, Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Guo Qi)
FUZHOU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 World Energy Storage Conference runs from Wednesday to Friday in Ningde City, east China's Fujian Province, bringing together participants to discuss cutting-edge technologies, prospects for the energy storage industry, and China's position in the global energy storage market.
In 2025, global annual battery storage additions hit roughly 307 GWh, with China accounting for 56 percent.
The scale of deployment in China has become central to the global storage market and is "helping to change the economics of renewable electricity," said Ilina Stefanova, head of the Coalition for Action at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), at the opening ceremony.
China's experience in technology, manufacturing, deployment and grid integration will matter not only domestically, but also for the global energy transition, she added.
As renewables become a major energy source worldwide, storage is evolving from a supporting facility into essential new infrastructure for power systems. It must meet diverse grid demands while continuously improving reliability and stability, said Zeng Yuqun, founder and chairman of China's leading battery manufacturer CATL, which is based in Ningde City.
Industry figures show China is responding to these demands.
China's new-type storage industry has achieved notable results, said Xiong Jijun, vice minister of industry and information technology, in the opening speech. China's storage battery output exceeded 420 GWh in the first half of 2026, up about 110 percent year on year. The industry is advancing along multiple technological routes, with lithium batteries playing a leading role alongside sodium-ion and flow batteries.
The government will balance development and safety, strengthen technological innovation, adhere to demand-driven principles and foster a global industrial ecosystem, while firmly guarding against rat race competition and guiding the industry from scale expansion toward innovation-led growth, Xiong added.
Ningde City has hosted the conference three times previously, an event that has attracted representatives from governments, industries and academia in over 50 countries and regions. ■
This photo taken on Oct. 15, 2026 shows a scene of the 2026 World Energy Storage Conference in Ningde City, southeast China's Fujian Province. (Xinhua/Guo Qi)

Three children and one teacher were shot dead at an elementary school in the northwestern US state of Oregon on Thursday, police said, adding that the assailant was a 16-year-old who was killed by an armed bystander.
Another child and a teacher were being treated for critical injuries after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary school in Bend, a city of about 100,000 people.
Mike Krantz, police chief of Bend, told journalists that the department first learned of an active shooter after a call from a person who reported being shot at multiple times by a person carrying a long gun.
Dozens of emergency calls then reported that a shooter had entered the school and all law enforcement in the area were called to the scene, Krantz said.
Officers arrived at 1:02 pm local time (2202 CET) within minutes of the calls, said the police chief.
"Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him," Krantz continued.
"Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead."
Officers performed emergency aid on the victims. The three children who died on the scene were aged five, eight and 11, the police chief said.
One teacher was also pronounced dead.
Krantz said one seven-year-old and one 54-year-old teacher with critical injuries were transported by medics to a local hospital.
He added that the shooter was a resident of Bend.
Krantz stressed that the investigation was in its early stages, but told a press conference it appeared "the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting at locked doors."
'Unthinkable tragedy'
Between 400 and 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary, where more than 40 staff work, a police spokesperson had said earlier.
After a lockdown, Bend-La Pine School District said law enforcement was escorting students in buses to a separate location, where families could reunite with their children.
The district's superintendent, Steve Cook, tearfully called the day's events "an unthinkable tragedy."
"We are heartbroken. We are horrified. This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places, and pray that it never happens here," he told reporters.
Parents were anxiously waiting at the site near a church, where parent Drew Sharp told CBS News: "I have faith that he's okay and that he'll be alright."
Sharp said his son was a fifth grader, the highest grade in the school, and that children were disembarking from the bus youngest to oldest.
"Which makes sense," Sharp said, but "it's just more time waiting."
Friday classes at schools across the district along with activities and athletic events were canceled, Bend-La Pine said in a statement.
The elementary school is approximately 270 kilometres southeast of the city Portland. It serves primary-age students in kindergarten through fifth grade.
'Cannot keep accepting this'
The United States, where firearms are readily available, is a frequent scene of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations.
The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on 16 April 2007, when South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.
There have been more than 360 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot.
"Our hearts are with the terrified children and the families anxiously waiting to hear that their loved ones are safe," GIFFORDS, a gun safety organisation, said on X.
"We cannot keep accepting this as a fact of life."
Thursday's shooting was followed by a painfully familiar chorus of calls for action on gun control, pleas that have resulted in little meaningful change.
In the face of decades of massacres akin to Thursday's, the powerful US pro-gun lobby has given millions of dollars to primarily conservative politicians in a successful bid to keep gun laws loose.
"They're killing our babies. Shredding our kids with lead. Forcing us to live in fear," said Janelle Bynum, an Oregon congresswoman, in a statement.
"This continues to happen," she said later, speaking on CNN.
"And it seems as if the adults don't care."

- The launch boosts Tesla’s image, but investors still care more about third-quarter results, sales, and the company’s shift to self-driving tech and robots.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered by rocket-style thrusters on Oct 15 and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.
The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with chief executive Elon Musk’s rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters.
Later in the event, it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the manoeuvre.
Some observers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two tech giants he controls, an idea he has explored by discussing their overlap.
The reveal gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors.
“It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional carmakers,” Gene Munster, managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on social media platform X.
“The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can’t wait to bring (Tesla) and (SpaceX) together,” Munster said.
Musk has played down the car’s importance to Tesla’s finances, describing it in 2023 as a “small potato situation” that would not “move the needle in a major way financially”.
But the car still carries symbolic weight.
“Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker’s best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla’s new halo car,” Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note in September.
Viewers gushed over the spectacle of the launch.
“That was the most insane product demo I’ve ever seen,” Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. “I just saw this in person, and I’m still asking how this wasn’t AI.”
Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at the Oct 15 event, although Tesla quoted a base price of US$200,000 (S$256,000) for the vehicle nearly a decade ago.
Tesla’s reservation page for the Roadster after the event showed a Performance version requiring a US$50,000 deposit and a Thrust variant with “acceleration thrusters” requiring a US$250,000 deposit.
A Rocket variant, which Tesla says is “invite-only”, is a single-seat model with a “full flight system”.
‘Halfway to the speed of sound’
The event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, had all the elements of a classic Musk product reveal: dramatic music, smoke, mechanical hissing sounds and a launch countdown.
“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven’t seen in any movie,” Musk, wearing a silver Western-style belt buckle emblazoned with the Tesla logo, told a cheering crowd of enthusiasts and investors.
The Roadster can accelerate from zero to 97kmh in less than one second and can hit a top speed of more than 370kmh, said Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy.
“Definitely much faster than that,” an excited Musk said. “I think you’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound.”
The Roadster can travel more than 480km on a single charge, which is less than half the distance Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla first revealed a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said deliveries would begin in 2020.
The original Roadster, released in 2008 and sold until 2012, was Tesla’s first electric vehicle and used a Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world’s view of what an EV could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.
The reveal of the second-generation Roadster comes amid a sharp shift in Tesla’s focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and robotics, away from manufacturing cars for human drivers.
In 2026, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab – a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.
Tesla is set to report third-quarter results on Oct 21.
Sales of Tesla’s ageing line-up of EVs have declined over the past two years, although high petrol prices helped boost deliveries in the third quarter.
“The margin and cash flow numbers will carry far more weight with investors than anything they saw at the reveal,” said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at trading platform eToro. REUTERS

The IDF released previously unseen documents written by Hamas's leader, Yahya Sinwar, on Friday, two years after his assassination.
Additionally, the IDF published footage of the military carrying out the assassination, including firing tank shells on the structure Sinwar fled to, and drone footage carrying out searches within the structure the following morning.
In one document, the October 7 massacre's architect demanded that Hamas's Nukhba Force terrorists broadcast their acts to as many media outlets as possible in order to terrorize the entirety of Israel.
Sinwar wrote that "it must be emphasized to those responsible for the [terror cells] that they must undertake their [terror] actions intentionally, document and broadcast the images as quickly as possible."
These "images" should include "stepping on IDF soldiers' heads, shooting at point-blank range, slaughtering people with knives, exploding IDF tanks, prisoners kneeling with their hands on their heads," and more, Sinwar wrote.
"We need to plan in advance for the events that will produce horrific images," he wrote in another document. "Several burning car bombs that exploded inside a post or building and caused terrible destruction. Heartbreaking sights. Enormous fire. Five or ten such pictures will make their [Israel's] heart sink.
"Allah came upon them without them expecting it and cast fear into their hearts. Two or three operations should be organized with the aim of burning down entire neighborhoods, a kibbutz, and the like. They [the terrorists] will spray gasoline or diesel fuel from a special tanker, then burn the place, and broadcast the pictures," the terror leader wrote.
The documents also show how Sinwar tricked Israel's political, defense, and intelligence establishments, and tricked them into believing he was leaning towards a political settlement with Israel.
Sinwar also wrote what could happen in the event that other terrorist organizations from the West Bank and the Iran-led "Axis of Resistance" would join in the massacre.
"There may be indications of the enemy's collapse from the very beginning, and it is possible that the movements of our people in the 'interior,' in Jerusalem and the West Bank, as well as Hezbollah's intervention, will encourage this," he wrote.
"Therefore, we must be prepared to expand the attack to its maximum. The core of the plan should include control of the centers of power and command and control of our central forces. Forces of the Palestinian factions can be sent to population centers, but our forces must be concentrated on important defined objectives and key positions," he added.
What happened during Sinwar's assassination?
Combat teams from the Nahal and 828th Brigades, respectively, were conducting operations in the Tel Sultan neighborhood of Rafah based on intelligence indicating potential high-value Hamas targets in the area, when they spotted terrorists leaving a building.
A firefight ensued; the terrorists scattered, and unbeknownst to the soldiers at the time, Sinwar remained alone, abandoned in a building.
He was killed in a firefight shortly thereafter.
Detailing the combat encounter
Several weeks before Sinwar was killed, the IDF's Gaza Division assumed responsibility for the Rafah sector of the Gaza Strip.
On the day of the engagement in which Sinwar was killed, lookouts spotted three armed terrorists moving through a damaged, IDF-controlled area roughly 300 meters from an ongoing engineering operation, the military said on Friday.
Two of the terror operatives carried a blanket, and the third wore a tactical vest, the military added.
A battalion commander spotted them, opened fire, and wounded one in the arm. This wounded operative was later confirmed to be Sinwar.
Soldiers encircled the area using tanks and drones. One soldier was severely wounded and evacuated during a firefight.
Sinwar, wounded from the aforementioned shooting, fled, entering a separate building from the other two terror operatives.
An IDF Paratrooper Brigade company entered to search the building that Sinwar had entered. A platoon commander noticed a pool of blood, indicating a wounded terrorist nearby. Moments afterward, two grenades were thrown at the soldiers, one of which detonated, the military said.
Soldiers applied heavy fire on the structure, including tank shells, machine gun fire, and small arms fire. That evening, an IDF drone entered the structure and located the remains of a body. Soldiers waited until the next morning to complete searches due to operational risks, the military noted.
When search teams entered the structure, they were able to positively identify Sinwar and confirm his death.

Editor's Notes: A break with Israel would hurt American Jews, too - comment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:18:44 UTC
12:18:44 KST

During a visit to the US a few months ago, I met a woman born in postwar Europe to Holocaust survivors. She told me she felt another Holocaust was coming. Zohran Mamdani had been elected mayor of New York, and she was frightened.
She usually voted Democratic. She and others I spoke with were frustrated and unsure whom to support. Trump offended much of what they believed in. They were trying to work out how to vote without ignoring either their fears or their values.
I listened. I live in Israel, where a Jewish vote for a politician hostile to Israel can be hard to understand. An American Jew may feel just as strongly about Israelis voting for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Reconsidering a political allegiance is reasonable. So is taking the consequences of a change seriously. American Jews have to live with the government they elect, including its decisions about their safety and their economic future.
What if frustration with politics leads some Jews to withdraw from Israel altogether?
My greater concern is that frustration with politics will lead some Jews to withdraw from Israel altogether. That would hurt Israel, and it could also leave American Jewish life poorer. For many families, Israel helps give being Jewish a place in everyday life. Losing that connection would affect what they pass on to their children.
This week, CNN’s Harry Enten presented Siena polling averages showing that Democrats’ lead among Jewish voters in New York on the congressional ballot had fallen from 49 percentage points in 2022 to 13 this year.
A national Mellman Group survey of 800 Jewish registered voters for the Jewish Electorate Institute, conducted in late August and early September, found Democrats ahead by 71% to 23%, essentially unchanged since March. Thirty-five percent of Jewish Democrats said the rise of anti-Israel candidates made it harder to identify with their party. Many still intended to vote Democratic.
British Jews have already been through several such reassessments. JPR, the Institute for Jewish Policy Research, put Labour’s share of the reported Jewish vote at 12% in 2019 under Jeremy Corbyn, when concerns about antisemitism drove many traditional supporters away. Labour recovered to 44% under Keir Starmer in the 2024 election. By mid-2025, its share of Jewish voting intention was down to 30%. Both major parties were losing support to the Greens and Reform UK.
Israel has to keep working with people, despite political changes
Those figures show how much a party’s standing can change. Voters are entitled to ask whether a familiar party still represents them. Its response to antisemitism and its treatment of Israel belong in that assessment, along with personal safety, livelihoods, and other deeply held beliefs. Conduct that would be unacceptable in a rival party deserves scrutiny at home.
Israel has to keep working with people through these changes. Waiting for frustrated Jewish Democrats to become Republicans assumes they will resolve their disagreements in the way most convenient to us. Some will, and others will reach a different conclusion.
The same JEI survey found that 86% of Jewish voters described themselves as pro-Israel, including 65% who criticized some or many Israeli government policies. There is considerable attachment to Israel among people who object to the way it is governed. That distinction should be familiar to anyone who follows Israeli politics.
Natan Sharansky has argued for years that a connection to Israel helps Jews remain Jewish. In The Jerusalem Post in 2022, he identified “only two factors that can slow down the assimilation: tradition and Zionism.” He warned that the grandchildren of Jews connected to neither would probably no longer be Jewish.
I take Sharansky seriously because, for families with little religious practice, Israel can account for much of their involvement in Jewish life. It might be the place where relatives live, where someone studied or volunteered, or where a family’s history becomes easier to understand. A relationship like that takes years to develop. Children learn its importance partly from the attention their parents give it.
The link between religion and Israel also appears in the wider American polling. Gallup has long found that people who attend religious services frequently are more likely to sympathize with Israelis. Its historical research found that association within both major parties.
Pew’s April 2026 survey found favorable views of Israel among 65% of white evangelical Protestants, 64% of Jewish Americans and 35% of Catholics, compared with 22% of the religiously unaffiliated. The pattern varies by religion: Only 4% of Muslim Americans viewed Israel favorably.
For Christian Zionists, support for Israel can be a religious obligation. Christians United for Israel grounds its mission in God’s promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:3: “I will bless those who bless you.” Its supporters understand that commitment as part of their own faith.
Religion has become less important in many Americans’ lives. Gallup’s March 2026 report found that 47% considered it very important in 2025, down from 58% in 2012, although the figure had stabilized in recent years. Gallup’s Frank Newport argued in a 2024 analysis that declining religious involvement was weakening a longstanding source of support for Israel.
We should account for that when deciding where Israel puts its effort. The religious and family connections that made Israel important to many Americans will carry different weight for their children. A sympathetic older generation gives us an opportunity to reach younger people; it provides little assurance that they will share their parents’ views.
Israel’s own politics matter as well. We need a broad unity government to help repair the country internally and improve our standing abroad. I would want Likud, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party, to build it with Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar, former prime minister Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Liberman, Yoaz Hendel, and Ofer Winter. Ben-Gvir, left-wing leader Yair Golan – and the haredi, or ultra-Orthodox, parties would remain outside.
Its ministers should hear Jewish Democrats explain why Trump troubles them with the seriousness they expect when explaining Israel’s security concerns. Work inside the Democratic Party should be a priority. Our diplomats and political leaders need regular contact with Democrats who care about Israel, including when those Democrats have difficult questions.
American supporters of Israel should stand behind leaders prepared to defend the relationship within their own party. Israel has an interest in their success, whatever happens to the Jewish vote in November.
Israel should help families afford Jewish education and give young Jews more opportunities to study, volunteer, and spend time here. They need time outside an organized itinerary to meet Israelis, hear the arguments we have among ourselves, and form their own opinions.
When the parties negotiate Israel’s next government, I want this work to have ministers responsible for it and money assigned in the budget. Ministers should be able to explain which Democratic relationships they are working to repair, which Jewish education programs they are supporting, and how they are helping more young Jews spend time here. We will soon be electing the Israelis responsible for those decisions. Their plans deserve at least some of the scrutiny we devote to the voting intentions of Jews in America.

Taiwan’s former Army chief of staff punished over M1A2T procurement irregularities

03:18:24 UTC
12:18:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army Command Headquarters confirmed Thursday that seven military officials involved in the M1A2T main battle tank procurement project had been disciplined for what it described as “administrative oversight.”
KMT Legislator Ma Wen-chun (馬文君) pointed out in May that the budget for the M1A2T procurement project, which runs from 2019 through 2027, had unexpectedly increased by NT$4.8 billion (US$148 million) to NT$45.3 billion in the 2026 budget, per Storm Media. Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) acknowledged the error at the time and said the officials responsible would be disciplined.
DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) stressed that whether the Army had overlooked the issue or failed to inform the legislature, spending unauthorized funds was illegal. He called on the Ministry of National Defense to take responsibility for the violation.
Department of Strategic Planning Director-General Lieutenant General Huang Wen-chi (黃文啟) explained how the discrepancy arose. During the budgeting process, the Army removed certain items from its proposed procurement package to keep the project within the NT$40.5 billion budget.
However, Huang said the Army ultimately signed the A3 version of the letter of offer and acceptance which reinstated previously cut items, including six M1070 heavy equipment transporters and 14 M88A2 recovery vehicles.
Huang said the Army initially expected exchange rate fluctuations between 2019 and 2023 to help offset the additional costs. However, the strengthening of the US dollar since 2024 undermined the plan.
Ma criticized the Army’s handling, saying it should have requested additional funding if the existing budget was insufficient, per UDN. She argued that raising the cost issue after the US had delivered all the equipment effectively put the legislature under pressure to approve the additional funding.
Asked about the disciplinary action, Army Deputy Chief of Staff Major General Wu Sung-ling (吳松齡) said Thursday that the officials involved, including then-Army Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Chang Yuan-hsun (章元勳), had been disciplined in accordance with Army regulations, per Tai Sounds.
Retired Colonel Chou Yu-ping (周宇平), former head of the Air Force Surveillance Warning Center, said the case reflected the military’s long-standing failure to maintain a sufficient pool of qualified administrative specialists, compounded by overly restrictive procurement rules, per CMedia. He said the military’s practice of rotating personnel among service branches and positions prevented procurement officials from passing on expertise in negotiations, finance and project management.
Regarding procurement regulations, Chou proposed relaxing restrictions to give officials greater flexibility to negotiate time-sensitive deals while providing legal backing for them to seek better terms from the US. He also warned against relying on exchange rate fluctuations to cover budget shortfalls, calling for a more comprehensive exchange rate monitoring and hedging mechanism given that such projects often involve billions of Taiwan dollars.

Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said firefighters extinguished the blazes in Sviatoshynskyi and received no reports of casualties from those incidents.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko also reported reduced water pressure on the capital’s right bank following damage to energy infrastructure in Kyiv region, illustrating how Russian attacks on the power network continue to disrupt other essential services.
Russia strikes Chortkiv twice in western Ukraine
Russian forces also carried out two attacks on Chortkiv, a city in Ternopil region, regional military administration chief Taras Pastukh reported Friday morning.
Emergency crews were dispatched to the strike site, where damage assessments were underway.
There were no immediate reports of casualties, Pastukh said.
Air Force tracks jet-powered drones across Ukraine
Ukraine’s Air Force issued repeated warnings throughout the early hours of Friday as Russian jet-powered drones crossed central and western regions.
The military tracked drones over Cherkasy, Kyiv, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Vinnytsia, Khmelnytsky, Mykolaiv and Dnipropetrovsk regions, with some heading toward Rivne, Lutsk and Khmelnytsky.
The warnings indicated a wide-ranging aerial assault involving fast-moving drones, forcing air defenses to respond across multiple regions.

Ursula von der Leyen suggests creating EU strategic gas reserves — Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
03:12:01 UTC
12:12:01 KST

BRUSSELS, October 16. /TASS/. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has invited European leaders to consider creating the bloc-wide strategic gas reserves, three diplomats and two EU officials have told Politico.
The initiative was put forward amid concerns that the EU may face fuel shortages this winter.
The report says that the existing European gas storage facilities, normally refilled throughout the year by commercial actors, are running at record lows amid high summer prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The report says that the bloc was left "unprepared for winter."
It wasn't immediately clear to diplomatic officials what form the reserve idea would take, Politico wrote.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks starting the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may fill their storage facilities to only 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU nations must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% margin of flexibility is permitted in the event of challenging filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bcm by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the filling target. However, anticipating a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

US lifts some sanctions restrictions on overseas assets of Russia's Lukoil
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
06:03:00 EEST
12:03:00 KST

US lifts some sanctions restrictions on overseas assets of Russia's Lukoil
The US Department of the Treasury has extended until 24 April 2027 the validity of general licences authorising transactions involving some of the overseas assets of sanctioned Russian oil company Lukoil.
Source: a notice from the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
Details: According to the department, the licences cover Lukoil's petrol stations outside Russia and four Bulgarian entities, including an oil refinery in the city of Burgas.
The first licence governs the activities of Lukoil International GmbH, which holds the Russian oil giant's overseas assets. The authorisation also covers entities in which it holds a direct or indirect stake of 50% or more, including its US subsidiaries Lukoil North America and Lukoil Americas Corporation.
The licence allows customers to buy fuel and related goods at Lukoil petrol stations outside Russia. It also permits the provision of maintenance, measures to keep the stations operating or their gradual closure. OFAC said this move is intended to protect retail consumers from the adverse effects of sanctions. Permitted transactions include payments to suppliers, rent, insurance premiums and staff wages.
However, Washington has strictly prohibited the transfer of any funds to individuals or organisations in Russia or to accounts held with Russian banks. The licence also excludes any transactions involving the Central Bank of Russia, the Russian Finance Ministry or the National Wealth Fund.
The second general licence allows transactions involving four of the company's Bulgarian subsidiaries: the Lukoil Neftohim Burgas oil refinery as well as Lukoil Bulgaria, Lukoil Aviation Bulgaria and Lukoil Bulgaria Bunker. The exemptions also cover subsidiaries in which these entities hold a stake of at least 50%, but do not extend to other sanctioned assets belonging to the group.
According to Reuters estimates, the easing of restrictions covers a network of around 2,000 petrol stations across Europe, Central Asia, the Middle East and North America. These include around 200 stations in the US states of New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, 600 in Türkiye and more than 300 in Romania. Lukoil also holds leading positions in the retail fuel markets of Moldova and Bulgaria.
Background:
- On 22 October 2025, the US Department of the Treasury added Rosneft, Lukoil and 34 of their subsidiaries to its sanctions list. Washington said the decision reflected Moscow's unwillingness to take meaningful steps towards ending the war in Ukraine.
- In late October 2025, the Russian oil group announced plans to sell its foreign assets and agreed to sell Lukoil International to commodities trader Gunvor. However, the deal fell through after the US regulator refused to approve the transaction.
- On 10 December 2025, OFAC introduced a special licence allowing Lukoil's overseas assets to be sold to companies not subject to sanctions.
- On 14 April 2026, the US extended the licences allowing the company's foreign petrol station network and Bulgarian businesses to operate until 29 October 2026.
- In early October 2026, The New York Times posted a report saying that negotiations between Donald Trump's administration and the Kremlin had expanded to include discussions about a multi-billion-dollar deal involving Lukoil's international assets. According to sources, a group of investors with links to White House special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner is seeking to acquire the portfolio of oil fields, refineries and petrol stations.

“The Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century,” China’s foreign minister said.
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israeli President Isaac Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan that Israel should stop and reverse its “forced establishment” of West Bank settlements, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement.
Wang told Herzog that China has consistently viewed the Palestinian question as the greatest historical injustice of this century, the ministry said in the statement on Friday.
Wang emphasised that the “two-state solution” is the right path to a resolution and said the immediate priority is to fully open access to the Gaza Strip so a humanitarian “catastrophe” is not allowed to spread.
Wang added that China is willing to work with the international community to push all parties to return to dialogue as soon as possible and seek a political settlement.
Wang is attending the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia, held in Baku, Azerbaijan, as the special representative of President Xi Jinping, China’s state news agency Xinhua reported.
China urges new Middle East framework
In September, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Cairo for the first time in a decade and called on Middle East countries to oppose external influence and consider reshaping the region’s security order.
Xi’s rare visit arrived as Beijing seeks to expand its influence in the region amid the US-Israel war on Iran.
The talks covered the US-Israel war on Iran, with both presidents urging “diplomatic solutions” to reach a “comprehensive agreement to end the war”, according to a statement from Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s spokesperson.
In March, China criticised the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with Beijing demanding an immediate halt to the joint attacks. Wang told his Israeli counterpart, Gideon Saar, that the attack on Iran came as negotiations between Washington and Tehran had “made significant progress, including addressing Israel’s security concerns”, China’s foreign ministry said in a statement following the start of the war.
China was Iran’s largest trading partner, buying up to 90 percent of its oil, according to the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission. In 2021, Beijing signed a 25-year “comprehensive strategic partnership agreement” with Tehran.
At the same time, Beijing has spent the past decade cultivating closer ties with Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, and remains a top trade partner of both the US and Israel.

11:40:17 KST

A bipartisan group of 22 US lawmakers urged President Donald Trump on Thursday, Oct. 15, to fully enforce sweeping sanctions against Russia ahead of an Oct. 18 deadline, warning that continued Russian energy revenues are financing President Vladimir Putin’s war against Ukraine.
In a letter to the White House, Republicans and Democrats called for the full implementation of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, including penalties against Russian officials, financial institutions and foreign companies helping Moscow circumvent Western restrictions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The appeal comes amid growing bipartisan opposition to Trump’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, which lawmakers fear could provide the Kremlin with additional revenue while Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.
“As Russia prepares to wage a fifth winter campaign against Ukraine, the United States has an opportunity to reinvigorate peace efforts by placing maximum pressure on Vladimir Putin and the governments and networks that finance his war,” the lawmakers wrote.
They argued that sanctions enforcement was essential to compelling Moscow to engage seriously in negotiations.
“Utilizing the tools for economic pressure in this law will be decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously.”
The letter was led by Democratic Rep. Jim Costa and senior members of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, including Mike Quigley, Marcy Kaptur, Republican Brian Fitzpatrick and Republican Joe Wilson. Republican Michael McCaul, a former House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman, also signed the appeal.
Russia Strikes Kyiv, Hits Apartment Building in Uman, Injures Five in Overnight Drone Attacks
Lawmakers demand sanctions against Russia’s energy network
The lawmakers urged the administration to target not only Russian officials and state enterprises but also the international financial and commercial networks sustaining Moscow’s war economy.
Their demands include mandatory sanctions on Russian oligarchs, banks and state-owned companies, alongside penalties targeting foreign financial institutions and intermediaries facilitating Russian transactions.
They also called for secondary tariffs on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, measures against vessels operating in Moscow’s shadow fleet, and restrictions on companies helping Russia evade existing sanctions.
The letter emphasizes that foreign governments and financial institutions facilitating Russian energy trade should not be allowed to shield Moscow from the economic consequences of its invasion.
At the same time, lawmakers urged the White House to protect US allies that are actively reducing their dependence on Russian energy, using exemptions and tariff adjustments permitted under the legislation.
The group requested detailed information on which sanctions and tariffs the administration intends to implement by Oct. 18, whether any provisions will be delayed or waived, and how their effectiveness will be measured.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal draws fresh criticism
The letter specifically challenges the Treasury Department’s Oct. 9 decision to issue General License 135, authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel.
Lawmakers warned that relaxing energy restrictions risks restoring revenues to the Kremlin at a time when Washington should be increasing economic pressure on Moscow.
They asked Trump to reverse the authorization and explain how the license complies with existing US restrictions on Russian energy imports.
The controversy follows a separate bipartisan appeal from 12 US senators earlier this week, who criticized the diesel agreement as financially beneficial to Moscow and unlikely to deliver meaningful relief to American consumers.
The senators argued that the volume of Russian diesel expected to enter global markets would have little effect on prices, which have risen sharply amid disruptions linked to the war with Iran.
Trump has defended the agreement as a measure to lower fuel costs, while also blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising energy prices.
Congress demands answers by Oct. 18
The lawmakers outlined five questions requiring clarification ahead of the sanctions law’s first implementation deadline, including which Russian officials, banks and companies would face restrictions and which countries would be subject to secondary tariffs.
They also demanded measurable benchmarks showing whether the measures are reducing Russian energy revenues and discouraging third countries from purchasing Moscow’s oil and gas.
Any presidential waiver, they argued, should be narrowly defined, temporary and linked to verifiable reductions in support for Russia’s war.
The letter further requested congressional briefings and regular updates on enforcement, including reviews of sanctions effectiveness every 180 days.
“Putin has repeatedly shown that he responds to pressure, not goodwill,” the lawmakers wrote.
They concluded that fully enforcing the legislation would demonstrate bipartisan American resolve and increase the economic costs of continuing Russia’s invasion until Moscow agrees to meaningful peace negotiations.
“We remain committed to Ukraine’s defense and to a just and lasting peace,” the letter said.

Economic Watch: Chinese firms bring homegrown expertise, innovation to fuel Dubai's growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
10:37:36 CST
11:37:36 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- A growing number of Chinese companies are expanding their business activities in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), translating their experience in China into more localized business practices that benefit the host community.
From trade to investment, China's economic ties with the UAE are gaining momentum, with Dubai emerging as a magnet for Chinese businesses looking to expand overseas.
In 2025, bilateral trade between the UAE and China reached 108 billion U.S. dollars, making the UAE China's largest export market and second-largest trading partner in the Middle East. Chinese exports totaled 72.88 billion dollars, while imports from the UAE amounted to 35.12 billion dollars. China's direct investment in the UAE reached 2.6 billion dollars last year, official statistics show.
The growing business presence of Chinese firms is increasingly visible in Dubai. The number of active Chinese member companies registered with Dubai Chambers has more than doubled since 2016, reaching 6,650 by the end of September.
CHINESE EXPERIENCE, LOCAL BENEFITS
In Dubai, hot meals now arrive faster and at lower prices.
Since Keeta, the international brand of Chinese food delivery giant Meituan, entered the market in September 2025, the company has brought its homegrown delivery model to the UAE, reshaping the experience for both customers and riders.
At the heart of its service is an "on-time promise" that has made punctual delivery a selling point. For local consumers, the appeal means more competitive prices and meals that arrive hot and on schedule.
Behind each delivery is a logistics algorithm designed to make better use of riders' time. By helping them complete more orders per hour, the system can boost their earning potential, creating an incentive for more people to join the industry.
The ripple effects are reaching beyond the food delivery sector, extending even to driving schools as more job seekers look to obtain the licenses needed to work as riders.
"The entry of new platforms like Keeta is fueling strong competition for riders. This has led to improved pay scales and structured benefits, encouraging more job seekers to invest in a license," explained Suzanne Accetta, CEO of Dubai's First Driving Centre.
Chinese companies are not only improving local consumer services, but also actively aligning their operations with the emirate's long-term development vision.
In 2023, Dubai launched the ambitious Dubai Economic Agenda (D33), a comprehensive 10-year strategy aimed at building the emirate into one of the world's top five logistics hubs.
The plan has opened up opportunities for firms such as Chinese express delivery company J&T Express, which views Dubai as a strategic gateway connecting the company's operations across the Middle East. J&T has now invested in a large automated warehouse and sorting center in Dubai Industrial City, adding capacity to the emirate's logistics infrastructure while advancing its own regional expansion.
EMPOWERING LOCAL INNOVATION, DEVELOPMENT
On Dubai's roads, the arrival of driverless taxis is offering a glimpse of how Chinese technology is helping shape the emirate's next phase of development.
In April 2026, Chinese internet company Baidu, in partnership with Dubai Taxi Company (DTC), launched Apollo Go, a commercial driverless ride-hailing service in the emirate, bringing autonomous driving technology into everyday urban mobility.
"Baidu Apollo reflects the integration of autonomous mobility systems into an emerging global framework for applied AI deployment," Yang Nan, vice president of Baidu and general manager of the overseas business unit, intelligent driving group, said at the Dubai Business Forum China held by Dubai Chambers in south China's Shenzhen on Wednesday.
This launch has highlighted the importance of local regulatory support. In March 2025, Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority signed a memorandum of understanding with Apollo Go to test 100 autonomous taxis. In November 2025, Dubai introduced a comprehensive regulatory framework for autonomous vehicles, setting out safety standards and operational guidelines to support their deployment.
The arrival of driverless taxis in Dubai is setting off changes that extend well beyond the roads, prompting advances in regulation, financial services and the wider innovation ecosystem.
In September, the UAE approved new federal rules covering the inspection, registration, licensing and testing of self-driving vehicles, establishing a common national framework for regulating the technology.
In May, Dubai Insurance launched a specialized coverage framework tailored to DTC's self-driving fleet. By encouraging regulatory and financial services to innovate, the Chinese company is contributing to the broader foundation for Dubai's smart city development.
Building such an innovation-driven economy, however, requires more than advanced technology. It also depends on a steady supply of skilled local talent. Chinese technology company Huawei, for instance, has integrated its ICT Academy into the core curriculum at the College of Technological Innovation at Zayed University in Dubai, bringing courses in cutting-edge artificial intelligence and cloud computing into official degree courses.
Speaking at the forum in Shenzhen on Wednesday, Sultan bin Saeed Al Mansoori, chairman of Dubai Chambers, said China-Dubai ties were entering a new phase, marked by a shift toward the "co-creation of industries, capital flows and innovation platforms." ■

Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
05:16:00 EEST
11:16:00 KST

Ukraine has run out of missiles for Patriot air defence systems – WP
Ukraine has completely exhausted its stock of interceptor missiles for the US-made Patriot air defence systems.
Source: The Washington Post, citing two Ukrainian officials and a NATO representative
Details: According to one source, Ukraine had only 10 Patriot missiles left as of 7 October.
"These were used up during the attacks. Currently, there are only a couple remaining," a Ukrainian official said.
Quote: "A second person familiar with Ukraine's deteriorating air defence situation said the country is out of the sophisticated weapons, which are critical to shooting down incoming Russian ballistic missiles."
Details: A Ukrainian official stressed that "the situation is extremely tense".
CNN reported earlier that Ukraine had run out of Patriot missiles. According to its source, the shortage of ammunition was the reason Ukrainian air defences had been unable to intercept Russian ballistic targets during the latest large-scale attack.
Global missile stocks have been rapidly depleted by the war in the Middle East, launched by US President Donald Trump. In the first month of the war with Iran alone, the US used more than 1,000 Patriot and THAAD interceptors.
Washington has made accelerating production a priority, but manufacturing a single missile can take up to 36 months.
Until now, missiles for Ukraine have been supplied through the PURL programme The Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) programme allows NATO allies to finance purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine , under which European countries pay for US-made weapons.
A senior NATO official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the programme remained operational and that "air defence munitions like Patriot interceptors continue to flow".
However, a Ukrainian official raised concerns about the nature of the deliveries.
"Since May, supplies have been irregular, and right now no one can say with any certainty or guarantee that a delivery will actually arrive," the official said.
Background:
- Throughout the summer and autumn of 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly urged Ukraine's partners to urgently increase supplies of missiles for Patriot air defence systems. In August, he stressed that Ukraine needed between 300 and 360 Patriot missiles to get through the winter safely. Meanwhile, Western deliveries had fallen sharply, from 675 missiles in 2023 to 364 in 2025, with only 264 planned for 2026.
- Meanwhile, according to reports in the media, the governments of Greece and Spain would rather keep Patriot missiles nearing the end of their service lives in storage than transfer them to Ukraine.
