Google boosts news and link visibility in AI mode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
23:47:00 UTC
08:47:00 KST

Google boosts news and link visibility in AI mode
- Google will show website and article links more prominently in AI search results. It will push links higher, expand its carousel, and use preferred sources, social posts and forums.
- The change follows concern from brands and publishers about falling traffic. AI Overviews now has more than two billion monthly users, but studies say summaries cut link clicks.
- Chartbeat reported a 40% drop in Google traffic for news sites between July 2025 and July 2026. In France, Apig told the Competition Authority AI summaries broke 2022 agreements with publishers.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Google announced on Oct 15 it will start displaying links to websites and articles more prominently and higher up in search results powered by artificial intelligence (AI), as brands and news publishers warn of a sharp decline in their traffic.
The Alphabet subsidiary began integrating more AI features in its search results over two years ago.
In May 2024 it launched AI Overviews, where Google generates summarised answers to search queries, rather than only showing links as it historically did.
Then in March 2025 Google added AI Mode which opens in a separate window and provides a more comprehensive answer and more links than AI Overviews.
Now, contextual links will be featured more “more frequently” and higher up in AI-generated search content.
Google will also expand worldwide its link “carousel”, which are cards displayed directly below AI Overviews that show headlines with images for relevant articles.
The algorithm will prioritise articles from sites a user has previously identified as “preferred sources”, and it will also be able to pull in content from relevant social media posts and other forums.
Google will also make links displayed at the end of AI-generated summaries “more engaging and prominent” for users who want to “dig deeper”.
During its second quarter 2025 results, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai said that AI Overviews had more than two billion monthly users in over 200 countries.
Several studies have shown that replacing traditional search with AI summaries significantly reduces the rate at which users open the suggested links.
According to a report by consultancy Chartbeat, news website publishers saw a 40% drop in traffic coming from Google between July 2025 and July 2026.
In August, Apig, a group representing daily newspapers in France, alerted the Competition Authority that AI summaries were in breach of agreements reached with news publishers in 2022. AFP

What is celebrated on October 16 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:38:01 EEST
08:38:01 KST

What is celebrated on October 16 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 16 marks World Food Day, Anesthesiologists' Day, World Bread Day, and Healthy Eating Day. The faithful honor Saint Longinus.
On October 16, the world, under the auspices of the UN, marks World Food Day and World Anaesthesia Day. According to the new-style church calendar, Saint Longinus the Centurion, who stood at the Lord’s Cross, is commemorated, while according to the old style, Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens, is remembered, UNN writes.
World Food Day
An official UN date proclaimed in 1979 at a conference of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization. The date was chosen to commemorate the founding of the FAO on October 16, 1945. The main goal of the day is to draw the global community’s attention to the problems of hunger and malnutrition, ensuring food security, developing sustainable agrifood systems, and overcoming poverty in developing countries.
World Anaesthesia Day
A professional observance for anesthesiologists, resuscitation specialists, and intensive-care physicians around the world. The date commemorates a historic event: on October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital, American dentist William Thomas Green Morton publicly performed the first successful operation under ether anesthesia in history, ushering in modern anesthesiology and painless surgery.
World Bread Day
Established in 2006 at the initiative of the International Union of Bakers and Confectioners. The event is dedicated to one of the most popular and important foods in human history; it highlights the importance of the work of farmers and bakers, promotes breadmaking traditions, and draws attention to the rational use of food resources.
World Healthy Eating Day
A global observance that echoes World Food Day and calls on humanity to reconsider its daily diet. The event emphasizes the importance of consuming high-quality, natural, and balanced foods, and reducing the intake of sugar, salt, and ultra-processed foods to prevent obesity, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.
World Restart a Heart Day
Established by the European Resuscitation Council with the support of the WHO and the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation. The event aims to teach as many people as possible first-aid skills, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and the use of automated external defibrillators to save people experiencing sudden cardiac arrest.
World Spine Day
A global medical initiative under the auspices of the World Federation of Chiropractic, aimed at promoting an active lifestyle, maintaining musculoskeletal health, preventing osteochondrosis and posture disorders, and reducing the risk of chronic back pain through ergonomics and physical exercise.
International Boss’s Day
Established in the United States in 1958 by Patricia Haroski, who worked as a secretary and registered the observance in honor of her manager father’s birthday. The observance is intended to strengthen positive relations between managers and subordinates and express gratitude to top managers for honest leadership, fairness, the organization of work processes, and support for the team.
World Raw Foodists’ Day
An unofficial observance dedicated to promoting raw foodism as a dietary approach involving the consumption of uncooked plant-based foods in order to preserve the maximum amount of vitamins and enzymes.
Memorial Day of Saint Martyr Longinus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Saint Longinus the Centurion, who stood at the Lord’s Cross. According to the Gospel and church tradition, the Roman centurion Longinus commanded the soldiers at the crucifixion of Jesus Christ and, having witnessed the miraculous signs and the Savior’s death, recognized Him as the Son of God. After Christ’s Resurrection, Longinus refused a bribe from the Jewish elders, left military service, was baptized, and set out to preach in Cappadocia, where he later suffered martyrdom by beheading on the orders of Pontius Pilate.
According to the old calendar, the faithful commemorate Saint Hieromartyr Dionysius the Areopagite, Bishop of Athens—a disciple of the Apostle Paul, who was a member of the highest Athenian court, embraced Christianity after the apostle's sermon, and became the first Bishop of Athens, later suffering a martyr's death in Lutetia.

====================================================================================================

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
00:25:06 BST
08:25:06 KST

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
- Published
The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.
Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's Prime Minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?
Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.
"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."
"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.
They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
- France's school protests: What lies behind the anger 
  - Published8 October
They are part of a defiant French tradition.
Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.
This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.
Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."
Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the biggest general strike in French history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.
Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.
"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.
Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.
France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Gulf.
Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.
Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.
The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.
"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".
"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."
I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."
"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters the explosives seized in a car last week were intended to be used in explosive drones targeting Israeli troops.
Aoun told Rubio the Lebanese army and security forces were fully carrying out decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and combat smuggling, the presidency said, adding that Aoun asked Rubio to pressure Israel to halt attacks on southern Lebanese towns and villages.
On March 2, the Lebanese government specifically banned Hezbollah’s military activities after the movement launched rockets at Israel to back up Tehran, pulling Lebanon into the broader US-Israeli war on Iran that began on Feb 28.
Tehran subsequently launched its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon during the war have killed thousands and displaced millions.
Under a deal reached through US-brokered Israel-Lebanon talks, Beirut vowed to disarm Hezbollah, which would in turn lead to Israeli troops gradually withdrawing from Lebanon. But Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain on Lebanese land and Israel has continued striking southern Lebanon. REUTERS

A Neanderthal was killed with a spear 75,000 years ago: scientists found traces of ancient violence

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
02:21:06 EEST
08:21:06 KST

A Neanderthal was killed with a spear 75,000 years ago: scientists found traces of ancient violence
Kyiv • UNN
Traces of a fatal injury to a Neanderthal caused by a sharp weapon were found in Shanidar Cave. A year before his death, he had also suffered a facial injury.
Scientists from the University of Cambridge examined the remains of a Neanderthal who lived about 75,000 years ago. Analysis of the bones showed that he likely died from a blow from a sharp weapon to the chest. Haaretz reports this, citing a study in Scientific Reports, UNN writes.
Details
The remains of the man, known as Shanidar A, were found in Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. He was approximately 45 years old at the time of his death.
Researchers led by Emma Pomeroy discovered a hole in his left shoulder blade. A sharpened stick likely penetrated his chest, passed through his lung, and damaged the bone. Similar marks have previously been found on animal remains.
What else the scientists discovered
Approximately one year before his death, the Neanderthal also sustained facial injuries and lost a front tooth.
Earlier, researchers examined the remains of another Neanderthal in the cave, Shanidar 3, who lived about 50,000 years ago. He had a rib injury and a foot disease that required long-term care.
According to Pomeroy, these findings demonstrate the complexity of ancient human behavior.
I think we should see the same complexity in Neanderthals that we see in people today. Some are violent, some are caring

Airspace closed across much of European Russia amid large-scale drone attack
A large-scale drone attack has effectively created a no-fly zone for civilian aircraft over central and western Russia. All four Moscow airports have completely suspended operations.
Source: Russian media outlet Astra; flight-tracking service Flightradar24
Details: According to Flightradar24, the airspace over most of European Russia remains completely empty. Civilian aircraft are widely avoiding the area.
Temporary restrictions on arrivals and departures have been introduced at Moscow's four airports: Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo.
Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsia) said that many aircraft are being diverted to alternative airports in other cities, supposedly to ensure the safety of civil aviation.
Since 23:00, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin has reported several times that drones heading towards the Russian capital have been destroyed. According to his figures, Russian air defences have shot down 59 drones.
As usual, the Russian official has not reported any consequences of the attacks. However, local residents have been posting photographs and videos on social media showing large fires.
The attack has also affected other oblasts. Rostov Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar reported drone attacks on the Aksay and Chertkovo districts and the city of Bataysk.
"Industrial and warehouse buildings were damaged when UAVs came down. A fire has broken out," Slyusar said.
In Yaroslavl Oblast, the local authorities issued a red-level alert due to attack drones. The press service for Russia's Ministry of Emergency Situations in Yaroslavl Oblast reported an emergency suspension of traffic on the road leading out of Yaroslavl towards Moscow.
In addition, Russian Telegram channels and local residents have reported a series of explosions and intense air defence response in Smolensk and Ryazan.

Cuba expands renewable energy use amid U.S. fuel blockade: FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
07:11:32 CST
08:11:32 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said Thursday that renewable energy now accounts for more than one-fifth of the country's electricity generation as it seeks to reduce the impact of U.S. fuel restrictions.
In a post on X, Rodriguez said the Cuban government and Communist Party were responding to the U.S. energy blockade, which "aims to punish all Cubans," with "greater sovereignty and measures" to ease the impact of U.S. sanctions.
Cuba now has 144 solar parks with a combined installed capacity of 1,418 megawatts, while renewable sources account for 21.4 percent of national electricity generation, he said.
The country also has 44 solar-powered electric vehicle charging stations and 64 public charging stations, he said, adding that all polyclinics, nursing homes, maternity homes and funeral homes have been equipped with renewable energy facilities.
In January, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order imposing sanctions and tariffs on countries and entities supplying fuel to Cuba, a move Havana has condemned as an "energy blockade."
Over the past nine months, Cuba has received only one shipment of crude oil from Russia, totaling about 100,000 tonnes, only enough to meet the country's demand for two weeks.
Cuba is scheduled to submit a resolution to the UN General Assembly on Oct. 29 for the 34th time, calling for an end to the U.S. economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed on the island for more than six decades.
According to Cuban government figures, the blockade has caused nearly 179 billion U.S. dollars in economic losses. ■

U.S. stocks recover as sliding Treasury yields offset hot inflation data

NEW YORK, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks recovered on Thursday as falling Treasury yields provided relief to equity markets, helping technology and semiconductor shares stabilize amid debt-financing worries.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 556.21 points, or 1.08 percent, to 52,177.69. The S&P 500 added 25.12 points, or 0.33 percent, to 7,744.06. The Nasdaq Composite Index increased by 20.16 points, or 0.08 percent, to 26,713.03.
Eight of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the green, with health and materials leading the gainers by going up 1.84 percent and 1.71 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, energy and technology led the laggards by losing 1.55 percent and 0.54 percent, respectively.
Market sentiment found footing as benchmark borrowing costs retreated, allowing heavily pressured tech equities to pare steep losses.
In the AI infrastructure sector, cloud compute provider CoreWeave gained nearly 6 percent, reversing a portion of Wednesday's more than 15 percent drop triggered by concerns over excessive debt accumulation to finance its hardware expansion. Memory manufacturer Micron Technology also recovered most of its intraday decline, closing 1.87 percent higher.
Concerns across the AI ecosystem were compounded by a CNBC report that Anthropic's quarterly revenue reached 16.8 billion U.S. dollars in the third quarter. While representing massive growth, the pace raised questions among some market participants about whether revenue expansion remains swift enough to sustain lofty valuations across underlying chipmakers.
Despite the broader equity recovery, inflation pressures remained pronounced. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that the producer price index (PPI) for final demand jumped 1.3 percent in September, lifting the annualized wholesale rate to 6.3 percent, its fastest pace since 2022.
The sharp acceleration followed Wednesday's hotter-than-expected consumer price index (CPI) reading, further complicating the Federal Reserve's policy trajectory as officials weigh persistent price spikes ahead of their upcoming interest rate decision.
"Today's PPI report, after Wednesday's CPI, confirms inflation is getting worse as energy prices stay high," said David Russell, global head of market strategy at TradeStation. "Election or no election, prices are rising and the Fed might be forced to act."
According to CME FedWatch, traders now see a 29 percent likelihood the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its meeting in two weeks, and an 88 percent likelihood the central bank will lift rates at least a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting.
Broader market gains were underpinned by defensive and consumer-oriented sectors outside of technology. Walmart advanced 1.47 percent, after Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to "buy" from "hold," citing a positive outlook for 2027. The bank expects incremental margins to improve and noted current inflation levels could help the company attract consumers.
Nike jumped more than 5 percent, leading consumer discretionary gainers. Apple, which on Wednesday joined Nvidia as the only companies ever to close with a market capitalization above 5 trillion dollars, ended 0.28 percent lower. ■

Reform councillor resigns after being filmed making racist remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:30:53 UTC
07:30:53 KST

Alan Feeney has resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after backlash over racist comments that were captured in an undercover investigation.
In a Facebook post on Friday, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”
Earlier this week, an ITV investigation revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.
Feeney has apologised for his comments. “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said,” he wrote in a Facebook post.
“The comments do not reflect my true beliefs or opinions, particularly of the communities mentioned in the report. These are communities I have supported countless times in my personal and professional life over many years, many of whom I have been lucky enough to call friends.”
Earlier this year, Feeney won seats in the Shard End ward of Birmingham city council and the Castle Bromwich ward of Solihull metropolitan borough council, and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull.
Following the ITV investigation, which is part of a longer series on Reform UK, Feeney announced on Facebook that he was leaving Reform for “personal reasons”, but kept his seats as an independent councillor before resigning.
In a Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “Byelections will be held on a timescale laid out by those councils in the due course. I hope that in time these councils, and the communities they serve can heal and move on.”
Secretly filmed footage showed Feeney making racist remarks alongside two other Reform candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, while canvassing during May’s local elections. Both Campbell and Whelan have also resigned after the fallout from the investigation.
Nigel Farage has repeatedly pledged to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots”. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.
The clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Feeney calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.
In a Facebook post Feeney wrote: “I understand that my words have caused hurt and anger, particularly among those from the communities I serve. For that, I am deeply sorry. I will be undertaking intensive personal analysis to understand how these sentiments could have taken root, and ensure they can never do so again.”
Alan Feeney and Reform UK have been approached for comment.
